Photograph: Reuters Iran Iran in talks with Oman over shipping but US negotiations on hold, says Tehran Iran discussing creation of temporary route through strait of Hormuz with its neighbour, says spokesperson Middle East crisis live – latest updates Patrick Wintour Diplomatic editor Mon 3 Aug 2026 07.52 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Iran has been in discussion with Oman about the creation of a new temporary route through the strait of Hormuz that would allow commercial shipping to resume, but is not yet reviving talks with the US, Tehran’s foreign ministry spokesperson said on Monday. Esmail Baghaei was responding to claims by Donald Trump that talks between the two sides covering all the major disputes between them could restart as early as Monday. Trump claimed he had held off from launching the biggest strike on any country “since world war two” over the weekend after Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, rang him to urge diplomacy. Trump said the cancellation was conditional on Iran reaching a deal quickly. Trump says Iran talks set for Monday as Tehran and Oman discuss strait of Hormuz deal Read more It is thought to be the 12th time in the war between the US and Iran that Trump has called off threatened strikes. Baghaei’s discussion of a new middle route through the strait of Homuz would represent progress. Iran is claiming full sovereignty over the strait and has been making demands over the routes and future management of the strait, including the possibility of charging fees in return for providing ships with maritime services. One proposal is to create an Omani-Iranian joint company that would provide all the services that insurance companies used to provide at high costs, but at lower prices, and with preferential tariffs for some countries. Unlocking a mutually acceptable route through the strait is the precondition to unlocking all the other agreements laid out in the memorandum of understanding, the ceasefire document both sides signed on 18 June. Disagreements about the memorandum’s obligations has led to a resumption of the war, which has spread to the Red Sea and to Iraq. Last week, Iran’s deputy foreign minister, Kazem Gharibabadi, said Iran was demanding that ships entering the strait take a route to the north close to Iran, but that some ships could take a southern route. Iran rejected the traffic being divided evenly between the two routes, and also that a third country could start de-mining the routes. Baghaei told a press conference in Tehran: “We are now talking about a corridor that will have a round trip route, not two or three separate routes. This intermediate route is to be used temporarily until a decision is made on a fixed route”. He framed the route as an alternative to the transport separation scheme, the previous longstanding prewar route overseen by the UN’s International Maritime Office. He said maps had been exchanged by the two sides. Baghaei stressed that the talks with Oman were bilateral and did not involve the US, adding that the negotiations with Oman had lasted seven to eight days. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, was not due to hold any talks with the US on Monday, he said. He said: “We are focused on reaching an understanding on a route that will ensure safe shipping traffic through the strait of Hormuz. Our effort is to determine a route at the earliest opportunity, with Oman’s consultation and cooperation; a route that will usually be temporary and based on which we can provide shipping in the strait of Hormuz.” He said an agreement on a route would not solve all the problems, pointing to the continuing US naval blockade of Iran’s ports, and that unless the US approach changed, there would be no significant improvement in the situation in the strait. Baghaei implied the talks with Oman would extend beyond a safe route to include future management of the strait. He said: “As a rule, in any understanding regarding shipping traffic between two coastal states, all issues related to the sovereignty and sovereign rights of the two countries, as well as issues of national security, national interests, and issues related to maritime services, are definitely considered and examined.” Recently there had been gloom in Omani circles about reaching an agreement with Iran on routes, leading to a revival of preparations for Oman’s European allies to start to clear the southern route of mines, a step that might have provoked direct conflict between Iran and European powers. Baghaei blamed the US for disregarding the memorandum of understanding by attempting to open up a southern route through Omani waters, arguing that article 5 of the memorandum specified that Iran alone within 30 days was required to return the level of shipping traffic to prewar conditions. He said ships that passed through this Oman route “were moving under pressure from Centcom [US Central Command], and due to intimidation from the American side. Some of these ships were even carrying military equipment, and in the shelter of these large ships sometimes frigates also travelled. “On 21 and 22 June, the US carried out widespread attacks against Iran and suddenly announced that everything was over under the pretext of the incident of seeing several ships in the strait of Hormuz,” he said. In a sign of the pressure Tehran diplomats face, a statement from the Assembly of Experts, the body of clerics that elects the supreme leader, warned against investing any trust in the US, saying: “Hope for understanding and agreement with this bullying regime will lead nowhere.” A section of the statement read: “It is incumbent upon all the free people in every corner of the world to keep aloft the banner of revenge and retribution for the martyred imam.” But the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, said he believed the “memorandum of understanding would prove to be the centre of gravity of our foreign relations in the future”. Saudi intervention came in a week in which Riyadh attacked Iranian-backed forces inside Iraq and raised the temperature in its dispute with the Iranian-backed Houthis in northern Yemen, underlining the extent to which Saudi Arabia fears the consequence of an all-out US war against Iran spiralling out of control across the Middle East. Photograph: Myanmar's Presidential Press and Information Bureau/AFP/Getty Images Myanmar Red Cross visits Aung San Suu Kyi after Myanmar military pushed to prove she is alive Meeting follows years of questions over wellbeing of detained former leader, who was ousted by coup in 2021 Natasha May in Bangkok Mon 3 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT First published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.36 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Myanmar’s detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi has met a representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), the aid organisation has confirmed. The meeting on Monday ⁠followed years of questions over the wellbeing of the 81-year-old , whose whereabouts and health condition have been largely unknown since the elected civilian government she led was ousted by a military coup in February 2021. Little has been seen or heard of Aung San Suu Kyi since late 2022 . Myanmar’s military-backed administrations have repeatedly claimed she is in “good health”, even as international pressure has grown on the country’s ​government to allow independent verification. Aung San Suu Kyi’s son, Kim Aris, who had recently demanded the ruling junta provide proof of life , welcomed news of the meeting. He described it as “the first positive development concerning her in more than five years”, adding: “This is an important first step, but it must not be the last,.” In a social media post, Aris said he hoped the meeting would lead to “greater humanitarian access, direct contact with my mother, credible and independently verified information about her wellbeing, and ultimately her immediate and unconditional release, together with all political prisoners”. Leaked footage and prison logs reveal Aung San Suu Kyi’s life in detention Read more On Monday, Arnaud de Baecque, the resident representative of the ICRC ​to Myanmar, visited Aung San Suu Kyi in the capital, Naypyidaw, the government spokesperson Khine Khine Soe said in a post on Telegram. View image in fullscreen Photo released by Myanmar’s government shows Aung San Suu Kyi cutting a birthday cake during her meeting with Arnaud de Baecque. Photograph: Myanmar President Office/AP In two of the four photographs provided by Khine Khine Soe, Aung San Suu Kyi – dressed in traditional ​Burmese attire – is seen with Baecque in a sparsely furnished, wood-panelled room containing only two chairs and a desk. In another photo, Myanmar’s former leader is seen cutting a birthday cake inscribed with her name. A clothes rack and storage boxes are visible in the background. A fourth image is a closeup of the cake, inscribed with “Happy Birthday Aunty Suu 19.6.2026”. In a statement released afterwards, the ICRC confirmed the visit had occurred and was carried out in accordance with its standards and procedures for visiting people deprived of liberty, including the opportunity to speak with Aung San Suu Kyi in private. “In line with the ICRC’s working methods, detention visits provide people deprived of liberty with the opportunity to exchange news with their families,” the statement said. “As is customary in the ICRC’s detention work, observations and recommendations related to the visit are shared exclusively and confidentially with the detaining authorities.” In late April, after a military-engineered election that allowed the former junta leader Min Aung ​Hlaing to become Myanmar’s ⁠president, authorities said Aung San Suu Kyi had been moved to house arrest. A photograph of the detained former leader was shown on military-controlled TV, however Aris told the BBC the image was taken years ago. While the election was largely criticised as a sham , it has led to diplomatic re-engagement with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean). ‘We feel like we are failing’: Myanmar doctor speaks out as health system teeters on ‘brink of collapse’ Read more Following a meeting between Myanmar’s foreign minister and counterparts from the regional Asean bloc in Bangkok in July, Thailand’s foreign minister, Sihasak Phuangketkeow, called for access to Aung San Suu Kyi “so that we can be able to verify the claims” of her good health. But the new military-backed administration had so far been reluctant to provide access ⁠to Aung San Suu ​Kyi, including a May request by the Philippines to allow an Asean special envoy to visit her. Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPA Nigel Farage Farage admits he discussed returning as Reform leader months earlier than previously stated Admission may undermine Farage’s account of circumstances surrounding £5m gift from crypto billionaire UK politics live – latest updates Ben Quinn Political correspondent Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.19 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nigel Farage has admitted he held talks about the possibility of returning as Reform UK’s leader months before the 2024 general election, potentially undermining his own account of the circumstances in which he received a £5m gift from a crypto billionaire. It was reported at the weekend that Farage had struck a deal with the party’s then leader, Richard Tice, and the convicted fraudster George Cottrell to return to frontline politics. Farage has previously said he did not need to declare the £5m from Christopher Harborne or benefits in kind from Cottrell because he was not in politics at the time they were received. He has said he had no intention of returning to politics until June 2024, just before the election. The tangled financial web at the heart of Reform UK Read more The House of Commons code of conduct states that new MPs must register all “registrable benefits” received in the 12 months before their election. At a press conference on Monday, Farage said: “I had no intention about returning to politics, or as leader of Reform, but in the spring of that year I did talk to Richard Tice about what the liabilities would be if … I was to come back to that position.” The Sunday Times reported Farage had negotiated the deal in March and April 2024, which was said to have involved Reform agreeing to repay or write off more than £1m in loans to Tice’s company. “You would be a bit of a mug if you were to walk into a job and not find out what the potential liabilities were, and they were substantial,” Farage said. A inquiry by parliament’s standards watchdog into whether Farage broke the rules by accepting the £5m and not declaring has been paused after he triggered a byelection by standing down as the MP for Clacton. Bridget Phillipson, the Labour party chair, said: “Nigel Farage has blown a gaping hole in his excuse for why his secret £5m ‘gift’ from a crypto billionaire did not need to be declared. “Farage has desperately tried to distract from his catalogue of scandals. But the embattled Reform leader has run out of road and must come clean with the public. Photograph: South Wales police/PA Crime Man jailed for keeping dead mother’s body in freezer and pocketing her benefits Christopher Phillips, who had been his mother Sylvia’s primary carer since 2008, given two years and four months in prison Steven Morris Mon 3 Aug 2026 08.38 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man has been jailed for keeping his dead mother’s body in a freezer at their shared home for almost three years, during which time he received more than £70,000 of her benefits and other funds. Christopher Phillips, 60, stored the body of Sylvia Phillips, a retired company secretary, in the chest freezer in the living room of their house in the south Wales seaside town of Porthcawl. He regularly placed flowers on top of the freezer, which he bought two days after her death, and carried on talking to her about soap operas and horse racing. When police arrived to check on his mother, who was 89 when she died, he told them she was away in London, but they found her body after spotting flowers on the freezer. Phillips, a former company director, accessed his mother’s bank account, made withdrawals from her savings and pocketed benefits, Merthyr crown court heard. Judge Tracey Lloyd-Clarke, the recorder of Cardiff, sentenced Phillips to two years and four months’ imprisonment. She told him: “You continued to collect her prescriptions and misled medical professionals about her whereabouts, lying when inquiries were made about your mother, repeatedly telling medical staff that she did not wish to attend appointments or undergo tests. “Your mother’s pension and benefits continued to be paid into her bank accounts, which you were able to access.” Ruth Smith, defending, said Phillips had been “exceptionally close” to his mother. The pair had lived together for 50 years of his life and Phillips had been the primary carer for his mother since 2008. Smith said the defendant had told police: “I basically didn’t want to let her go.” She added: “He described talking to her as if she was still alive … sitting next to her, talking to her about television programmes, Coronation Street, the horse racing, just as they always did. “Mr Phillips was a vulnerable individual with a vulnerable mental health situation at the time of his mother’s death.” The court heard Phillips had left work to become a full-time carer in the months leading up to her death in March 2023. He was caught after police carried a welfare check because doctors had raised concerns they had not heard from his mother. When officers attended the house in February this year, Phillips said his mother was in London with cousins. Officers pressed further but Phillips would not give the details of which cousins or where they lived. His mother’s body was found covered with a leopard print throw and alongside it were roses and a birthday card reading “To Mum, from Christopher and Tina” – the latter being the family dog. Phillips pleaded guilty to preventing a decent and lawful burial and two counts of fraud. He received a total of £78,190.92 in state pension, pensions credit, attendance allowance, winter fuel payments, cost of living payments and housing benefit payments that would have ceased had his mother’s death been reported. The senior investigating officer, DCI Claire Lamerton, said: “This is an extremely sad case where Phillips concealed his own mother’s death and financially profited for a significant period. “My thoughts are with Sylvia’s loved ones during such a difficult time, and I hope they have found some peace having been able to properly lay her to rest.” Explore more on these topics Crime Wales news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Richard Tice is under investigation by parliament’s standards watchdog over a possible failure to declare an interest. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA View image in fullscreen Richard Tice is under investigation by parliament’s standards watchdog over a possible failure to declare an interest. Photograph: Neil Hall/EPA Richard Tice Standards watchdog investigating Reform UK’s Richard Tice Party’s deputy leader says on social media the case is related to a complaint by an anti-Israel lobby group UK politics live – latest updates Aletha Adu Political correspondent Mon 3 Aug 2026 08.25 EDT First published on Mon 3 Aug 2026 05.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice , is under investigation by parliament’s standards watchdog over a possible failure to declare an interest. The watchdog did not provide details of the allegation aside from ⁠saying the case was opened on 28 July and would be conducted by the parliamentary commissioner for standards, Daniel ⁠Greenberg. As a matter of procedure, the watchdog never publicly releases details of an allegation being investigated until it has published its conclusion. Tice, the MP for Boston and Skegness, swiftly claimed on X that the inquiry related to a complaint over “whether I should have referenced my register of interests at the start of a debate on UK democracy and Israeli influence”. Without naming the group he was referring to, he wrote on X: “Contrary to garbage in media: Standards Commissioner is considering complaint by anti semitic anti Israel lobby group over whether I should have referenced my register of interests at start of a debate on UK democracy and Israeli influence.” A Labour party spokesperson said: “The Reform sleaze scandals continue to pile up. Richard Tice is now under investigation by the standards commissioner, on top of his firm avoiding paying £600,000 in tax. This means that both Reform’s leader and deputy leader now have standards investigations hanging over them. “With police probes, Nigel Farage’s secret £5m gift, and reports of funding from a convicted fraudster, it’s clear Reform think the rules just don’t apply to them.” Greenberg had also been investigating Farage, Reform UK’s leader, over a £5m gift he received in April 2024 from the Thailand-based crypto billionaire Christopher Harborne, first revealed by the Guardian. That investigation was paused after Farage resigned as an MP last month and triggered a byelection for his Clacton seat in which he will stand again. The contest, in which all the other major political parties have refused to participate,, leaves Farage taking on 33 other candidates including Count Binface and Howling Laud Hope of the Official Monster Raving Looney party The Metropolitan police are also investigating payments to Reform UK, assessing payments made to the party via a company controlled by Tice. The police investigation came after the Guardian revealed last month that Fiona Cottrell made a £1m transfer to Britain Means Business, shortly before donations were made and about half of the funds were passed to Reform UK . Cottrell’s son George has close links to Farage. Last week, parliament’s standards watchdog declined to investigate a complaint made against Tice over an undeclared loan of £78,100 he received in December 2024, months after he was elected as the MP for Boston and Skegness. The commissioner told the Liberal Democrat MP Lisa Smart that he would not take further action on the basis that her complaint had not provided “sufficient evidence” to justify an investigation into a potential breach of conduct. Tice had said the loan was a corporate one, to one of his companies, which he said was not declarable. “I have a number of corporate loans in my companies. None of them are declarable. They are to do with my property business activities, not to do with politics,” Tice said, adding that his shareholdings and directorships were fully declared. In January last year, Tice gave £613,000 to Reform via Tisun Investments in an unusual case of an MP donating to their own party. A month later, a sum of £655,000 was paid into Tisun’s account in what was described by Tice as an overpayment for a property purchase. Photograph: KIVI via Reuters View image in fullscreen An emergency responder at the site of a fatal shooting in Twin Falls, Idaho on 1 August 2026. Photograph: KIVI via Reuters Idaho Man who returned fire at In-N-Out gunman had done firearm training after 2021 mass shooting Police credited Jordan Salinas with limiting number of victims in attack on restaurant in Twin Falls, Idaho Edward Helmore Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.16 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.17 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A healthcare worker returning fire on a 24-year-old gunman who killed three people and wounded several others an In-N-Out Burger in Twin Falls, Idaho, has said his impulse to confront the attacker was “automatic” and “mechanical”. Shooting at In-N-Out Burger restaurant in Idaho leaves three people dead Read more That description from 35-year-old Jordan Salinas came in an interview with the Idaho Statesman that was published on Sunday, providing a detailed account of actions that police credited with limiting the number of victims in the attack a day earlier. Salinas said he was headed out for a horseback riding date with his girlfriend when they stopped at the burger restaurant for lunch at about 2.30pm on Saturday. Salinas saw people fleeing and heard the “pop-pop-pop” of gunfire, according to what he told the Statesman. He said he ran toward the sound in an “automatic” and “mechanical” response, drawing from a shoulder holster a semi-automatic pistol with a suppressor fixed to its barrel. Salinas said he had been training with firearms seriously since a deadly shooting at a mall in Boise, Idaho – about a two-hour drive from Twin Falls – left two dead and four wounded. And he said he watched on Saturday as an attacker later identified as Chad Williams, standing by the drive-through window, lifted a rifle to his shoulder and fired toward cars. Salinas countered by raising his pistol with both hands and firing. “He did not like it when bullets started firing both ways,” Salinas told the outlet. Police later said the attacker died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, crediting Salinas and an off-duty officer for diverting the shooter with return fire. “We believe their actions helped drive the suspect away from the scene, preventing further casualties,” said Matthew Hicks, the Twin Falls police chief, at a news conference. “We want to take a moment and commend the actions of the off-duty officer and the citizen – and their heroic action to stop this incident.” Jack Johnson, the Twin Falls county sheriff, said: “These people are true heroes in our community. They diverted the shooter and without a doubt saved many lives.” Williams, 24, killed three victims before dying by his own hand, police said. Police added that he wounded seven others at the recently opened restaurant in the southern Idaho city of about 56,000 people. Two of the wounded were treated at a hospital and discharged; three were listed as stable; and two were in critical condition. Salinas – a full-time caregiver of his brother, who gets around in a wheelchair – said he felt “no fear” during the confrontation with Williams after following four steps he had learned in firearm training. Those steps, he said, were “observe, orient, decide [and] act”. “There’s a task that needs to be done, and we’re the ones who need to do it,” he told the outlet. The decision to take up firearms training, he said, came after he reasoned that gunmen go after “soft targets”. And a person in a wheelchair, and the aide at his side, would be exactly that, he said. “Everyone says, ‘It’s not going to happen here,’” Salinas said. “But what if it does?” Salinas’ interview and the police’s praise of him came amid a debate over the correct response of bystanders to mass shootings. Some witnesses to Saturday’s attack in Twin Falls were reported to have slowed their cars and shouted at Williams. As of Monday morning, there had been at least 280 mass shootings reported across the US so far this year, according to the Gun Violence Archive . The archive, a nonpartisan resource, defines mass shootings as cases in which four or more victims are shot or wounded. The high numbers of mass shootings annually reported in the US have driven calls for more substantial federal firearms restrictions. But Congress has not implemented such gun control over the years. Photograph: Dario Lopez-Mills/AP Arizona Arizona clergy who learn of child abuse in confessions aren’t required to report it, court rules State supreme court rules in case of two bishops who were silent about three children abused by Mormon parents Richard Luscombe Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.53 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.54 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Clergy members in Arizona who learn of child abuse in the context of religious confession are not required to report it, the state’s supreme court has said in a ruling that protects what church leaders call the “seal of the confessional”. The panel’s ruling ends a long-running case in which three children who were sexually abused by their parents sued the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS), also known as the Mormon church, and two bishops who became aware of the crimes but remained silent. The case has parallels in a short-lived 2025 law in Washington state that would have compelled clergy members there to report sexual abuse. That proposal was permanently withdrawn in October after legal action by the Catholic church. In a statement, the LDS welcomed the unanimous ruling by the state supreme court on Thursday that exempts clergy members as “mandated reporters” if they learned of the abuse of minors in the confession booth or through other “confidential” methods. “The abuse of a child or any person is a tragic betrayal of trust,” it said. “The abuse at the center of this case was reprehensible, and the church has always condemned it. The church is deeply concerned for these children and for all who have suffered abuse. “The church devotes significant resources to preventing abuse, helping victims, and encouraging reporting through safeguarding efforts around the world. The church has always been willing to help the victims in this case and that continues to be true. “Arizona law also recognizes the confidential nature of religious confession. [The] decision affirms that these religious protections are to be respected alongside society’s shared commitment to protect the vulnerable.” The case centered on a 2020 lawsuit filed by the children of Paul and Leizza Adams, who reported being abused by the Cochise county couple over a number of years. Court filings said Paul Adams, who took his own life in jail while awaiting trial, admitted his crimes to a bishop while in confession in 2011. And, court filings said, they were discussed at a formal disciplinary hearing led by a separate bishop the following year. A 2022 investigation by the Associated Press, however, recounted how the church followed its own policy of keeping the information to itself. The second bishop called an internal church helpline for advice, the AP reported, but was advised not to call police or child welfare officials. The abuse continued, and it was not until 2017 that Adams and his wife were arrested after a video they made of some of the abuse turned up in New Zealand. Adams died awaiting trial, and Leizza Adams received a 30-month sentence in 2018 after pleading no contest to two felony charges of child abuse. The Arizona supreme court’s ruling overturned a state appeals court ruling for the children on the grounds that the confession and disciplinary hearing discussions might not have been truly confidential. In the 23-page ruling, John Lopez, the supreme court vice-chief justice, said the US constitution’s first amendment – which addresses religious freedom – prevented courts and juries from assessing religious doctrine when considering a clergy member’s reasons for choosing not to report abuse. “Our decision ‘does not mean that religious institutions enjoy a general immunity from secular laws’,” he wrote, citing a 2020 US supreme court ruling about the church’s right to determine matters of government, faith and doctrine “free of government interference”. “If a court finds a religious institution submitted evidence procured through ‘fraud’ or ‘collusion’ for secular purposes, it will lose the religion clauses’ protection” in the constitution. There was no evidence the LDS church had done so, Lopez wrote. In the US, call or text the Childhelp abuse hotline on 800-422-4453 or visit their website for more resources and to report child abuse or DM for help. For adult survivors of child abuse, help is available at ascasupport.org . In the UK, the NSPCC offers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood ( Napac ) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact the Kids Helpline on 1800 55 1800, or Bravehearts on 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contact Blue Knot Foundation on 1300 657 380. Photograph: Reuters First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: Trump promises new Iran talks as Tehran touts Hormuz shipping deal with Oman US president says he called off another US attack on Iran as part of a push for an agreement. Plus why Pokémon Go is still bring global joy 10 years on Martin Belam Mon 3 Aug 2026 07.36 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 07.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Donald Trump said talks with Iran would happen on Monday but declined to set a deadline for an agreement, after earlier saying he had called ⁠off an imminent attack. For its part, Iran said it was nearing a deal with Oman over a new route through the strait of Hormuz, and it had no plans to receive a delegation or send an Iranian one to any talks. On Saturday night, Trump claimed on social media that Iran and other Middle Eastern countries had asked for time to complete a deal ⁠that would lead to “the immediate, complete and total” reopening of the strait and “an end to Iran’s nuclear threat”. He added that Tehran must “rapidly make a deal”. What has Iran said about the strait? The Iranian foreign ministry spokesperson, Esmaeil Baqaei, told state television on Sunday that a deal was close with Oman over a new route through the waterway. “We are now going to reach an understanding on a route acceptable to both sides – neither the northern route nor the southern route – but one that respects the sovereign rights of both sides and safeguards our national interests and security,” he said in an interview. RFK Jr tells US families to vaccinate children against measles amid outbreak View image in fullscreen Robert F Kennedy Jr has for years amplified misinformation about vaccines. Photograph: Daniel Heuer/Reuters Robert F Kennedy Jr, the US health secretary, on Sunday told American parents that they should get their children vaccinated against measles , as the surge in infections has reached numbers not seen in the past 35 years. Kennedy, a leading vaccination skeptic who has spent years amplifying misinformation about vaccines, including the shot that protects against measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), made his call in the course of a contentious interview with CNN’s State of the Union on Sunday morning. How many measles cases has the US seen? His remark came as the incidence of measles crossed a milestone – the US has officially recorded 2,371 confirmed infections so far this year, surpassing the total tally in 2025 of 2,289. Taken together, in the past two years there have been more measles infections in the US than in the rest of the 21st century combined. The last time a greater number of measles cases was recorded in a single year was in 1991. Republican calls for Max Miller to resign from Congress after abuse allegations View image in fullscreen Max Miller has denied the allegations against him. Photograph: Jonathan Ernst/Reuters The Republican senator Bernie Moreno on Sunday publicly called for Representative Max Miller, his former son-in-law, to step down from Congress amid allegations of domestic and child abuse. As recently as Friday, the Ohio senator had avoided giving his opinion directly on accusations made by his daughter Emily Moreno against the congressman. The senator’s statement came hours after Miller gave a live stream Sunday morning denying allegations of domestic and child abuse and insisting he would remain in the race for re-election. The public appearance came before Wednesday’s deadline to replace him on the ballot. “Just want to be clear: no court, no agency has ever substantiated any allegation of abuse against me. No criminal charge has ever been filed against me,” Miller said on the live stream. Family to sue after woman released from ICE custody froze to death View image in fullscreen Daphy Michel was found dead at a bus stop. Photograph: Michel family/AP The family of a Haitian immigrant who froze to death in early March at a bus shelter in Pittsburgh after she was dropped off in the city by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is poised to file a lawsuit this month against the US and “multiple other governmental and non-governmental entities”, the Guardian has learned. Daphy Michel, 31, had been in county jail for six months after a reported mental health crisis and street incident, and then was arrested by ICE before being released with an ankle monitor. In other news … View image in fullscreen More than 900 people are battling the Spokane Complex fires. Photograph: Tyler Vanwert via Reuters Eastern Washington fires have destroyed 600 structures and forced 60,000 people to evacuate , stretching the ability of federal and local agencies to fight the blazes. The chaos of a mass border crossing has given way to limbo for Moroccans on the streets of Ceuta , the Spanish colonial enclave in northern Africa. Marcy Kaptur is being treated ⁠for non-life-threatening injuries after a car crash in Toledo, ⁠Ohio, on Sunday, ⁠the ​Democratic US representative’s office said. The suspect in an Idaho restaurant shooting that killed three people died of a self-inflicted gunshot wound , police said. Pressure on the Fifa president, Gianni Infantino, to step down has increased as members of Europe’s footballing authority Uefa prepare to oppose his re-election. Stat of the day: Spider-Man: Brand New Day makes debut to $927m box office View image in fullscreen Tom Holland and Marisa Tomei pose before the Spider-Man: Brand New Day premiere in London. Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/AP The Marvel Studios president, Kevin Feige, has hailed the movie’s “phenomenal” opening – the second biggest opening weekend in history – which followed a box office already buoyed up by The Odyssey and Toy Story 5. Building Power: How free childcare started winning US elections View image in fullscreen The Democratic gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong. Photograph: Nam Y Huh/AP Sunny Patel reports for the Guardian’s Building Power series on Francesca Hong, a candidate for Wisconsin governor, who is part of a wave of democratic socialists finding traction with an old idea. Don’t miss this: ‘The language of Pokémon is universal’: why fans are still catching ‘em all View image in fullscreen The Pokémon Go character Quaxly in London. Photograph: Niantic/The Pokémon Company/Martin Belam I originally started playing Pokémon Go as a going out activity with my children. Ten years later, they have (mostly) put away childish things, but I still play it every day without fail. In this lovely piece , Sammy Gecsoyler speaks to devoted players who explain how the game has created a vibrant intergenerational community spanning the globe. … or this: Hide the Pain Harold and Rubik’s Cube creator among social media’s picks for Hungarian president View image in fullscreen Péter Magyar, the Hungarian prime minister. Photograph: Robert Hegedus/MTI/AP Péter Magyar and his newly elected Tisza party asked the public to put forward names for the next president of Hungary, which is resetting its politics after years of being dominated by the rightwing populist Viktor Orbán. The suggestions have ranged from the sensible to the downright bizarre . Climate check: ‘Stop all outdoor activities’ – South Korea records its highest ever temperature View image in fullscreen Children play at a fountain to cool down during a heatwave warning in Seoul. Photograph: Kim Hong-Ji/Reuters South Korea has registered its highest temperature since records began more than a century ago, at 42.5C, as authorities warned people to immediately stop all outdoor activities in affected areas. London’s Kew Gardens has gone without rain for a whole month for the first time in history, as Europe continues to battle a heatwave. Two firefighting helicopters have collided west of Athens , killing the two-person crew of one of the aircraft, as efforts to control a massive wildfire barrelling towards the outskirts of the Greek capital intensified. Canadian Devyn Dalton was the Hollywood star’s stunt double in a pivotal scene. Olivia Bowden spoke to her . https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Spanish army infantry members speak with migrants near Ceuta’s border post, 2 August 2026. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Spanish army infantry members speak with migrants near Ceuta’s border post, 2 August 2026. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Opinion Spain The right’s exploitation of the Ceuta migrant ‘crisis’ almost guarantees that it will happen again Ruben Andersson The EU’s panic and the lack of solidarity emboldens smugglers and the far right – and makes Spain even more vulnerable Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.33 EDT Last modified on Mon 3 Aug 2026 09.54 EDT Share For the European hard right and the White House, it seemed almost too good to be true: left-liberal Spain punished with a migration crisis of its own making. The histrionics came right on cue. As thousands of mainly Moroccan citizens streamed into the tiny Spanish enclave of Ceuta at the tip of north Africa, Spain’s far-right party Vox decried a migrant “invasion”, blaming Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez’s regularisation and leftist politics. The Trump administration did the same. A senior Israeli diplomat goaded Madrid over its “colonial” territories while Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen area. Denmark and Finland backed Italy’s move and, by the weekend, 22 EU leaders had penned a letter pointing an implicit finger at Madrid over its presumed failure to “relentlessly combat illegal migration”. But what these self-ascribed doyens of border control don’t want to understand is that it’s their panic and politicking over migration that has brought us here. Ceuta is hardly a poster-child for Spain’s otherwise liberal migration policy. Rather, since the 1990s it has been the prototype for Europe’s relentless border security battle. Drones, heat detectors, motion sensors, digital watchtowers, Moroccan Auxiliary Forces: Ceuta’s border is so thoroughly militarised that it puts even Trump’s barrier-building – let alone that of Greece, Poland or Finland – to shame. The paradox, as civil guards told me when I last visited in 2023, was that this militarisation had involved ceding control. “Rabat knows it can destabilise Spain with migration,” one chief said, as he reflected on the mass entry of Moroccans in 2021 , after Madrid had angered its partner by taking in Brahim Ghali, the leader of Western Sahara’s Polisario movement, for urgent healthcare. The heavily guarded fences have become a perfect foil for staging a migration crisis. While Morocco is usually tight-lipped about its intentions, at times its ministers have bluntly said it won’t play the “ gendarme ” of Europe unless its partners support its economic and political aims. The quiet at the border since 2021 had little to do with the aggressive security hardware, and everything to do with Madrid’s 2022 endorsement of Rabat’s plan for occupied Western Sahara. So why the latest crisis? While the facts and motives are still being established, it’s unlikely to be a coincidence that, only recently, Sánchez announced a “ new phase ” in relations with Algeria – Rabat’s arch-rival and supporter of Polisario. View image in fullscreen A man attempting to escape the police, Ceuta, 2 August 2026. Photograph: Pedro Nunes/Reuters Sánchez blames the mass entry on people smugglers and misinformation about a recent Spanish supreme court ruling that prevents authorities from summarily expelling migrants who attempt to swim by sea to Spain’s territories in Africa. Yet blaming criminal organisations makes little sense: most of those who made it across were quietly returned within the day – unthinkable, if they had lost their life savings to pay smugglers. The official line from Morocco’s government is that the surge was due to “criminal organisations” and that cooperation with Spain is still “exemplary”. The social media rumour mill did mobilise people to cross; but crucially – according to Spanish intelligence – Moroccan law enforcement stopped controlling the border while its intelligence services failed to notify Spain about the online campaigns. Video clips and accounts from border crossers in numerous media outlets further suggest that law enforcement actively encouraged people to cross. It’s clear to anyone who knows the Ceuta border that nothing dramatic happens there without the Moroccan authorities letting it happen. Yet Spain is unable to call out Morocco as it desperately depends on it. Instead, both Madrid and Brussels showered Rabat with praise this past week. This is the corner the EU has painted itself into: dependent on repressive and undemocratic regimes that use migration threats for their own purposes. This has been a favoured tactic for years across the external EU borders, from Muammar Gaddafi’s threats to Ankara’s antics . And it’s all the more attractive to them thanks to the European obsession about unwanted migration – the higher the stakes, the bigger the rewards. The geopolitics are looking unfavourable to the EU. Since the Abraham accords were signed in 2020, Morocco has strengthened its hand internationally through close alliances with the Trump and Netanyahu administrations. And those two governments see Spain as their arch-foe in Europe. This January, Rabat deepened its military cooperation with Israel. In April, a US House of Representatives committee stated that Ceuta and another Spanish enclave of Melilla were “in Moroccan territory”. Israeli and Republican figures have made increasingly frequent noises of this kind. Recently, Morocco named a highway through Western Sahara after Trump. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more Preview latest after newsletter promotion Why is Ceuta a migration flashpoint and how were so many people able to cross from Morocco? Read more What all this points to is not necessarily some grand conspiracy. Rabat may well have sought to benefit opportunistically and then lost control of events. But it does suggest that what occurred in Ceuta was a geopolitical game with people as its pawns, leaving more than 70 dead . European leaders have become so obsessed with “security” that they can’t see their own best interests clearly. Notably, one of the governments waving the threat of Schengen suspension was Denmark, which should know something about geopolitical blackmail against Europe. Coercive migration pressure, evidence shows , works best when destination regions are politically divided and prone to slanging matches. This is exactly what the far right and government leaders are now indulging as they nervously blame Spain and raise the spectre of another 2015 migration crisis. Having shown their hand to “partner” states and unfriendly regimes alike, these leaders will know exactly which button to push for maximum impact. Through their reaction, EU politicians are not only undermining European solidarity – they are actively encouraging more crisis-generation, while abetting the anti-European forces in the White House and further afield. We need a different kind of migration politics that de-escalates panic instead of inviting it, that prioritises frank diplomacy over one-eyed “combat”, and that weakens the hand of hardmen and smugglers. European leaders could make a start on shifting this dynamic by not turning themselves into useful idiots at the first opportunity. Ruben Andersson is professor of social anthropology at the University of Oxford and author of Age of Security: The Rise of a Global Obsession (William Collins) out 13th August Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: Guardian environment writers Jonathan Watts (left) and Ajit Niranjan Illustration: Guardian Design View image in fullscreen Guardian environment writers Jonathan Watts (left) and Ajit Niranjan Illustration: Guardian Design Conversations Environment ‘The obsession with endless growth can only end in tears’: your questions on extreme weather this summer answered From Europe’s deadly heat to floods in Asia, it’s been a terrifying summer. Environment writers Jonathan Watts and Ajit Niranjan answered Reddit users’ questions about their work – and their sources of hope Jonathan Watts and Ajit Niranjan Mon 3 Aug 2026 10.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Extreme weather supercharged by the climate crisis is fuelling an explosive wildfire season in Europe and extreme rainfall across Asia this summer. Global heating made hot, dry and windy weather stoking wildfires at least 20 times more likely in Spain and twice as likely in France . EU officials have said wildfires could still be burning until early November in what threatens to be a record-breaking year for the area of land burned. Meanwhile, unprecedented rains continue across Asia . As South Korea swings between heatwave and downpour, in Japan and Vietnam torrential rain has led to landslides. Extreme rainfall across the world is more common and more intense because of human-caused climate breakdown. The Guardian’s Europe environment correspondent Ajit Niranjan has been covering the extreme heat and wildfires across Europe this summer, while global environment writer Jonathan Watts reported on the floods in Asia. Ajit and Jonathan answered questions about their reporting and experiences. Read the Q&A below. View image in fullscreen Haze and smoke from the 2023 the Canadian wildfires shrouds the Manhattan skyline in June 2023. Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/Reuters Desenrasco asked: How scared should I be about wildfires? To consider it in the bluntest of terms, wildfires kill surprisingly few people: perhaps hundreds around the world each year, compared to thousands from floods and hundreds of thousands from heatwaves. That is, of course, of little comfort to the people across Spain and France returning to burned-out homes, or to the families of firefighters, locals and tourists who have died in the past few weeks. But what scares me far more is the smoke. Recent studies peg the global death toll from wildfire smoke at 1.5 million people per year. The wildfire season in Canada three years ago was so bad, one study found, that more than 80,000 people died from smoke inhalation – and 20,000 of them were in Europe, as winds carried the pollution over the Atlantic. Sg_plumber asked: How come pretty much everybody (at least on TV) always forgets to mention that yes, the climate crisis is fuelling these extreme weather events ? Jonathan Watts: I agree. This is not just exasperating, it is frightening. The climate and nature crises are the greatest threats humanity has faced, yet many media organisations downplay or ignore it. Social media is even worse, propagating misinformation and distracting people from the root cause of the problem (petrochemical companies, big agriculture and every rising emissions of greenhouse gases). The Guardian is able to devote much of its resources to covering these topics because it does not have an owner and because our readers make very clear that they want a big share of their contributions to go to this topic. Economy-Fee5830 asked: You’ve written about oil majors profiting as the world heats. But European wildfire deaths and flood deaths are overwhelmingly determined by local building codes, evacuation planning and firefighting budgets. Does the Big Oil accountability framing crowd out the more boring domestic policy failures that actually determine the body count? Ajit: I broadly agree with your question but slightly disagree with the premise. Rapid analysis studies in recent years have attributed 40-70% of the death toll from big European heatwaves to the increase in temperatures from carbon pollution. With wildfires and floods it’s much harder for scientists to say how much climate breakdown contributed to the death toll. I’ve covered European floods where they’ve shown the rainfall that triggered the floods to have been made stronger or more likely by up to 20% but, as one scientist put it to me after floods in central Europe last year, it’s a binary problem: the dam will either fail or not. In cases like the floods in Germany’s Ahrtal in 2021, or in Valencia, Spain, in 2024, we saw both jaw-dropping evacuation failures and climate-exacerbated rain. Cutting fossil fuel pollution is indeed a fundamental solution, and it must be accompanied by a never-ending list of other adaptation measures. I would argue our coverage is pretty good at including both bits. Every article I’ve written on wildfires this summer has included rising temperatures and land abandonment. Our flood coverage had the failures of authorities at the forefront. View image in fullscreen Floods in Valencia in 2024 killed 229 people following evacuation failures and climate-exacerbated rain. Photograph: Pablo Garcia/The Guardian Owl1917 asked: With climate anxiety on the rise, particularly amongst younger generations, what advice would you give to those who see the future as hopeless? Ajit: More than anything else, I would challenge anyone who feels hopeless to be specific about what’s troubling them. This is obviously easier said than done, but if you take a couple of hours to write down what it is that scares you about climate breakdown, what makes you angry, and what leaves you feeling hopeless, the fears become (hopefully) easier to confront. In my case, reporting on the climate has made me way less worried about some problems and way more worried about others. In terms of hope, I am, perhaps unpopularly, a firm believer in the idea that we have far more agency than anyone around me seems to realise (with the exception of a handful of scientists). Too many people my age claim a powerlessness that is not backed up by data. Sure, your ability to replace a coal plant with a wind turbine may be limited (it’s still not nothing, if you live in a democracy) but you have power over what you eat, how you get around, how much you buy. Consider diets: our collective choice to eat meat and dairy is responsible for 12-20% of planet-heating emissions, and doctors recommend people in rich countries eat far less of it for their own health, let alone the climate. Does this sound like our actions are pointless? Gold-Loan3142 asked: How do we challenge the mainstream ‘“perpetual growth” economics that infuses almost all discussion of the economy? Jonathan: You have touched on one of the core issues. The obsession with endless GDP growth on a finite planet can only end in tears. The only question is when. There have been numerous academic challenges to this and alternatives, such as Kate Raworth’s Doughnut Economics and Bill McKibben’s Economics as if the World Mattered. There are also some very interesting studies and books on degrowth by the likes of Jason Hickell and many others. If I can stray outside my journalist role, I have long believed that what the world needs is not just economic degrowth but ecological regrowth. We need a system of trade, currency, taxation, incentives that rewards countries and companies for restoring the world’s battered ecosystems. SurinamPam asked: A lot of carbon is emitted for road transportation, building heating/cooling, and electricity generation. And, the world is quickly switching to EVs, heat pumps, and building out solar, wind, and batteries. If all those carbon sources go to zero, how much of an effect will it have on future climate change? Jonathan: That is a fascinating point. I haven’t done or seen the calculations on this. But, speaking far more broadly, the energy transition is one of four great causes for hope that I have right now. Wind, solar and electric vehicles have taken off far more quickly than almost anyone expected even a decade go. This has the potential to change the global balance of power and, I believe, may also be behind rising US aggression in terms of military conflict, tariffs and attacks on democracy. View image in fullscreen Nissan Leaf EVs being made in Sunderland. The rapid switch to electric cars is a cause for hope. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian Distracted-Nomad asked: In terms of advocacy, what are the most powerful things you can say to convince individuals that their efforts (ie lifestyle change) are important? Most people I know say whatever they do won’t make a difference and governments and corporations need to change before we do. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential Preview latest after newsletter promotion Jonathan: This is one of the most common and important questions that climate journalists get. I agree the priority must be political action because the required changes – higher taxes on fossil fuels, a wealth tax on billionaires, more investment in renewables, more incentives for plant-based diets, etc – need to come at a national and international level. That said, I disagree that individual action is meaningless. It can set an example to others. And it can show that change can be beneficial to health and wallet. Imagine, for example, how much money electric car owners have saved during the recent oil price spikes. The key is to do this while never letting the petro-companies off the hook . They have tried in the past to convince people that the responsibility for the climate crisis lies with individual consumers. That was why they pushed the idea of carbon calculators. But the real blame lies with them. Most of the big oil companies are expanding production and making record profits . Karenadona asked: How much longer do we have until we run out of time to save the planet? Ajit: In one sense, it is never too late, and in another sense, it already is too late. The planet will survive, and even apocalyptic scenarios do not really consider an end to life on Earth as a result of climate breakdown. But while there is technically no time limit to action – climate scientists stress that each extra ton of carbon dioxide heats the planet a bit more – the likelihood of triggering catastrophic tipping points rises the hotter it gets. The 1.5C global heating target, which world leaders agreed to in Paris in 2015, looks extremely likely to be missed. (I am not saying definitely, as it is physically still possible, even if emissions have risen to a level where it is perhaps societally implausible.) Keeping below 2C of warming is, however, very much still possible. Current projections put us on track for somewhere between 2C and 3C by the end of the century. Szabolcs85 asked: Is there anything to be hopeful about? The future looks very bleak. Jonathan: I am also pessimistic, but there are still many things to fight for. Every fraction of a degree of warming that we can prevent will help millions of people and billions of other forms of life. UN-led action have already helped in this way, but not enough. But international cooperation is worthwhile. My four other causes for hope: The energy transition , particularly in China. The rise of the rights for nature movement , which - although imperfect – is confronting the core of our problems, which is a broken relationship with the non-human part of the planet. Alternative ways of thinking and being found in the global south, particularly among indigenous communities . The prospect of the global population peaking before 2050 , which should reduce pressure on the environment. Set against this, unfortunately, are the huge military and financial forces of petrostates, such as the US, Russia and Saudi Arabia, often aligned with big corporations. View image in fullscreen Brazilian Indigenous Peoples minister Sonia Guajajara speaks to members at Cop30. Indigenous communities are offering alternative ways of thinking about how we protect the planet. Photograph: André Penner/AP Fraggin601 asked: How do you think our economic systems must change to cope with climate change? Jonathan: Great subject. The first step should be a realistic appraisal of the economic risks posed by the climate and nature crises. Currently, most economists are absurdly complacent. The Nobel prize winner William Nordhaus assumes a very low hit to GDP but he omits – as the commentator Genevieve Guenther notes – the full costs of labour productivity, buildings, infrastructure, transportation, non-coastal real estate, insurance, communication, government services and other sectors. Most worrying to me is that most economic model assume smooth linear warming, even though many climate scientists warn of tipping points that are likely to bring jolts, acceleration and catastrophe. It is as though a doctor treats everything as a chronic, manageable ailment while ignoring the very real risks of acute, life-threatening diseases. Nature also needs to be much more highly valued – and not just in economic terms. Then there is the question of inequality – between nations, communities and species. There is no GDP without a healthy environment. And there is no greater theft from the poor than the loss of clean air, fresh water, fertile soil and a stable climate. On a positive note, I have been very impressed by the recent work done by the World Inequality Lab to try to incorporate more planetary boundaries into their projections of what a cleaner and fairer world could look like. Lightning7Bolt asked: What can a 17-year-old like me do to fight for change? Jonathan Watts: Find out all you can from news articles, books and films. Then spread the word. The great climate science communicator Katherine Hayhoe says the most important thing you can do to fight climate change is to talk about it. Age can be to your advantage. Your generation is the future. Older people are threatening that. Greta Thunberg was 15 when she started fighting for change, sitting outside the Swedish parliament with a sign saying “School Strike for Climate”. By the time she was 17, the movement had gone global. Millions took to the streets and the head of Opec, the world’s biggest oil cartel, declared the youth protest “perhaps the greatest threat to our industry.” View image in fullscreen Greta Thunberg was 15 when she started campaigning. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-bridge-buil.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IAWj A satellite image of bridge construction between Russia and North Korea from late June. Clearly visible at the top right: the large processing facilities on the Russian side. Image: Planet Labs Advertisement For years, Khasan was little more than a very remote place on the edge of Russia . Less than 500 people live in the village in the country's far east, more than 5,600 miles (9,012 kilometers) from Moscow. But it's here that Russia shares a mere 10.5-mile border with North Korea — and Khasan is the only Russian settlement along that short stretch. Since 1959, the so-called Korean-Russian Friendship Railway Bridge has crossed the Tumen River here, serving as the only land connection between the two countries. But in recent years, Russia and North Korea have been building a parallel road bridge just a few hundred yards away. The bridge is now nearing completion ahead of schedule, raising concerns in Kyiv that Russia could use it to secretly bring North Korean troops to the front lines in Ukraine . Since the start of Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Moscow and Pyongyang have improved their ties . Both countries face Western sanctions and are diplomatically largely isolated. In June 2024, Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un signed a strategic partnership deal which in part focused on expanding military cooperation. That meant large-scale weapons shipments as well as the deployment of North Korean soldiers to support Russia's war in Ukraine. At the same time, both governments agreed to build the new road bridge. "The opening of the new bridge will boost bilateral trade, optimize logistics, strengthen cultural ties and transform border regions into dynamically growing economic centers," Russian Transport Minister Andrey Nikitin said at the time. Not particularly attractive to tourists: until now, the only crossing over the border river was an old, single-lane "Railway Bridge of Friendship." Image: Yuri Smityuk/TASS/picture alliance The Washington-based Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) has also pointed to the bridge's economic significance, noting that "the pace at which construction of the road bridge is progressing, and the continued high level of rail traffic at previously dormant rail yards, are clear indicators of the importance and expansion of trade between the two countries during Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine." A project for trade and tourism? But according to British newspaper The Guardian , there are major doubts that civilian economic goals are the project's true primary purpose. Official data shows that trade between Russia and North Korea amounted to just $34 million in 2024. The bridge and its immediate infrastructure are thought to cost roughly $100 million. Satellite pictures of the site show warehouses, customs facilities, truck areas and a helicopter pad being built. Cultivating a "strategic partnership": North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Image: Sergey Bobylev/Sputnik/REUTERS Ukrainian human rights organization Truth Hounds, which has been monitoring the project , also doubts the bridge is for tourism. It is about 125 hours by car from Moscow and about four hours from Vladivostok. "Tourism in North Korea is heavily restricted and, given the country's isolation, cannot expand rapidly," the organization said. If anyone from Russia would visit North Korea, they probably would go to the capital, Pyongyang, rather than the country's remote northeastern region. But Pyongyang is hundreds of miles from the border, and "few people would want to make that journey by car," the group argued. Russia has spent years trying to get tourists to take heavily subsidized flights to visit Pyongyang. However, not many have taken up the opportunity. In 2025, fewer than 10,000 Russian citizens are thought to have traveled to North Korea. Here, the boss makes the beds himself: Kim Jong Un inspects a tourist hotel. But demand from Russians for holidays in North Korea is rather low. Image: YONHAP NEWS AGENCY/picture alliance Or a cover for military transport? Truth Hounds instead concludes that the bridge's real purpose is to deepen military cooperation, particularly by facilitating the transfer of North Korean troops and weapons for the war in Ukraine. According to unofficial information reported by South Korean, Ukrainian and US sources in the middle of last year, North Korea sent between 14,000 and 15,000 personnel to support Russia's war, with many reportedly deployed in Russia's Kursk region while parts of it were under Ukrainian control. North Korea has also supplied Russia with weapons. Road transport, Truth Hounds suggests, is harder to monitor by satellite than rail transport. Trains are confined to fixed tracks, and loading and unloading can take place only at designated rail hubs. Trucks however, can load and unload almost anywhere and satellite surveillance is virtually impossible. Ukrainian sources published this image in October 2024. It reportedly shows North Korean soldiers being issued Russian uniforms at a Siberian military training ground. Image: Ukraine Photo/Newscom/picture alliance Just days ago, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned on X that Russia could deploy as many as 30,000 additional North Korean troops in the war against Ukraine. Military know-how for North Korea Zelenskyy also argued that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un from the improved military partnership. The new bridge could enable Russia to secretly move resources into North Korea. "Russia," Zelenskyy wrote, "is helping North Korea learn how to wage modern war, improve its weapons and gain real combat experience in using them." Observers also believe that North Korea might be receiving some Russian nuclear technology in exchange for helping Moscow in its war efforts. Taken together, Zelenskyy warned in his X post, these developments pose "a threat to everyone in Asia who lives within range of North Korean missiles." This article has been translated from German.
