Jonny Walker This is a press release from Triumph… (July 22, 2026) — Triumph Factory Racing’s Jonny Walker will be joined by Triumph Motorcycles Brand Ambassadors Sam Sunderland and Ivan Cervantes at the 2026 Red Bull Romaniacs. The trio will tackle the iconic hard enduro event aboard near-stock Triumph Tiger 900 Rally Pro motorcycles. Taking place in Sibiu, Romania, from July 28 to August 1, the 23rd edition of the legendary race will once again push riders and machines to their limits across five days of demanding competition. Following the successful introduction of the Adventure categories in 2025, the Tiger 900 Rally Pro returns to the Carpathian Mountains with minimal modifications. All three riders will compete on near-standard motorcycles, with adjusted stock suspension and a select few upgraded parts being the only enhancements made ahead of the event starting. Ivan Cervantes The race begins with the famous city Prologue before four challenging off-road days featuring steep climbs, rocky riverbeds, technical forest singletrack, and mountain traverses. Walker will contest the premier Adventure Ultimate class, while Sunderland and Cervantes will take on the Adventure Core category. As a Red Bull Romaniacs winner on two previous occasions, Jonny Walker returns looking to build on an impressive debut in the Adventure Ultimate class last year. Riding the Tiger 900 Rally Pro, Walker overcame an early setback before claiming three consecutive off-road stage victories to finish second overall, narrowly missing out on the win and proving the capability of Triumph’s adventure platform in one of the world’s toughest races. Now in his second season with Triumph Factory Racing, the British hard enduro specialist heads back to familiar terrain aiming to challenge for the top step of the podium. Sam Sunderland Ivan Cervantes Two-time Dakar Rally winner and two-time FIM World Rally-Raid Champion Sam Sunderland also returns after a hugely successful first appearance at the event in 2025. Racing in the Adventure Lite class, Sunderland dominated the category by winning the Prologue and every off-road day to secure victory by more than four hours. This year, the Triumph Motorcycles Brand Ambassador steps up into the more competitive Adventure Core class, where he’ll face a significantly tougher challenge as he continues to showcase the versatility of the Tiger 900 Rally Pro. Sam Sunderland Jonny Walker Joining Sunderland in Adventure Core is five-time FIM Enduro World Champion Ivan Cervantes. One of the most decorated enduro riders of all time and no stranger to adventure competition aboard Triumph machinery, Cervantes boasts victories at events including 1000 Dunas, Baja Aragón, and the Bassella Race on the Tiger 900 Rally Pro. Returning to Red Bull Romaniacs for the first time in over a decade, the Spaniard brings a wealth of off-road experience and will be aiming to fight for class honours on his first appearance in the Adventure Core category. Red Bull Romaniacs kicks off with the Prologue on Tuesday 28 July, followed by four gruelling off-road days. Jonny Walker Jonny Walker : “I’m really looking forward to getting back to Romaniacs on the Tiger 900 Rally Pro. I had a lot of fun racing the adventure bike there last year and we came incredibly close to taking the win, so the goal is definitely to challenge for the top step again. I haven’t ridden the bike since last year’s event, so we’ll arrive, make the most of our setup, and get straight into racing, but I do have complete confidence in both the bike and the team. It’s a race I know well and really enjoy, with a tough Prologue and four demanding off-road days, and I can’t wait to get back into the mountains.” Sam Sunderland Sam Sunderland: “I’m really excited to be heading back to Red Bull Romaniacs with Triumph. Last year’s event was a great experience and I was genuinely impressed by what the near-standard Tiger 900 Rally Pro could do in such demanding terrain. Stepping up into the Adventure Core class adds another level of difficulty, and I’m looking forward to seeing what we can achieve against even stronger competition.” Ivan Cervantes Ivan Cervantes: “It’s fantastic to be returning to Red Bull Romaniacs after so many years and to be racing in the Adventure Core class with the Tiger 900 Rally Pro. My first experience of Romaniacs was over a decade ago, so I’m excited to come back with much more experience and a bike that I know extremely well. I’ve enjoyed a lot of success with the Tiger 900 Rally Pro at events like 1000 Dunas, Baja Aragón, and the Bassella Race, so I know what it’s capable of. Adventure Core is a very competitive class, but my goal is simply to give my best and fight for the win.” Ian Kimber – Head of Global Racing Programs, Triumph Motorcycles: “We’re really excited to return to Red Bull Romaniacs again this year. With very little preparation last year with the Tiger 900 Rally Pro machines, Jonny and Sam both had great races, and we enjoyed being part of such a world-renowned, and notoriously difficult event. This year we again race with the same bikes, and we know that Ivan and Sam will want to have positive results in the new class, while Jonny will be aiming for a top result in the Adventure Ultimate category. The Adventure classes had so much interest last year and it was great to see, so we’re looking forward to a great race. We’ve done very little to the bikes in terms of modifications, and this is the best test to show their capability. https://www.pocketgamer.com/sofie-scout-.text: Features I happily paid to support Sofie Scout despite my terrible endless running skills Scout's honour By Catherine Dellosa | Jul 23 iOS + Android | Sofie Scout - Road to Poland Prefer Pocket Gamer on Google I've never really experienced what it's like to miss the bus, as I'm usually a pretty prompt pupil, but I can imagine how stressful it must be - especially if you're heading to a once-in-a-lifetime event. That's exactly what the World Scout Jamboree is for poor lil Sofie, and given how I too was once a scout myself, I know that the struggle is very, very real. Now, while I personally wouldn't sprint on foot across Europe just to get to the said jamboree, I admire Sofie's unstoppable determination in Sofie Scout , which is why I have sworn to do everything I can to help her reach Gdansk, Poland in one piece - even if that means leaping across dangerous ravines that seem to appear out of nowhere and vaulting over wayward chickens just randomly clucking away in the middle of the road. Because that is, essentially, what this side-scrolling endless runner is all about. You have one button to jump and another to slide across the floor, as Sofie automatically dashes across the screen filled with all sorts of randomised obstacles. Memorisation will get you nowhere here, as while one run might have you hopping over a cow and then landing on your face, another run might throw an ancient totem at you to cut your trip short. This is where things can get incredibly challenging, because while the premise sounds absolutely charming, you shouldn't make the mistake of thinking it's all easy-peasy from here. The difficulty level is totally S-tier, because you'll need to contend with everything from fiddly jumps that need to be perfectly timed, to tripping just because the tip of your foot grazed a platform you're supposed to jump over by a mere millimetre. I do wish there was some kind of checkpoint that'll keep me from starting over from scratch every time I fall, but thankfully, the absolutely gorgeous pixel art in the background keeps the frustrations at bay. That said, sometimes, it's also a challenge to figure out which items are just background fodder and which ones are actual bushes I need to leap over in the foreground, but hey - nobody said running cross-country on foot would be easy. In any case, I did purchase this endless runner out of pocket simply because I wanted to help support IRL scouts Juno and Ellie make enough money to attend the World Scout Jamboree. Their £3,600 goal, I would assume, is no easy feat, so if my $2.99 can help even just a tiny bit, I'm happy to do my part. If Juno and Ellie's quest sounds at all interesting to you, might I suggest giving Sofie Scout - Road to Poland a go? If nothing else, you'll get to test your own resilience, patience, and quick reflexes across a cute pixel-art runner - and who knows? You might even make it to Poland yourself. Do let me know how it goes, though, as I've never made it past 100 kilometres at this point. This is what happens when I don't keep up with my cardio… Download now! Sofie Scout - Road to Poland Catherine Dellosa Catherine plays video games for a living and writes because she’s in love with words. Her Young Adult contemporary novel, For The Win: The Not-So-Epic Quest Of A Non-Playable Character, is her third book published by Penguin Random House SEA - a poignant love letter to gamer geeks, mythological creatures, teenage heartbreak, and everything in between. She one day hopes to soar the skies as a superhero, but for now, she strongly believes in saving lives through her works in fiction. Check out her books at bit.ly/catherinedellosabooks, or follow her on FB/IG/Twitter at @thenoobwife. https://www.lancashiretelegraph.co.uk/ne.text: People Lancaster-born woman died after spinal injury from fall, inquest hears By James Richings News and Sports Reporter Share 0 Comments (Image: NQ) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A Lancaster -born woman who "loved books, animals and people" died after suffering a spinal injury following a fall at her home, an inquest heard. Beaconsfield Coroner's Court heard how Wanda Jadwiga Van-Der-Zyden, known to family and friends as Lou, was found dead at her home in High Wycombe on April 18 this year, at the age of 72. Assistant Coroner Gemma Brannigan, who conducted the inquest on July 22, recorded a conclusion of accidental death. The hearing was attended by Ms Van-Der-Zyden's sister Barbra, daughter Zara, and Zara’s partner, David. A pen portrait written by Zara was read out by the coroner, describing her mother as a caring and compassionate woman. Born in Lancaster, she was of Polish heritage and grew up with three siblings. The court heard how the 72-year-old had fond memories of family life and was particularly proud of returning to education as a mature student in her 40s. She later worked as a librarian at Buckinghamshire New University, where she enjoyed helping students and supporting them in their studies. However, several serious health conditions, including brain surgery, a stroke and breast cancer, meant she retired on ill-health grounds. Zara described her mother as a devoted animal lover who cared deeply about the natural world. A pescatarian, she supported charitable causes and adored her pets, including an energetic kitten which now lives with her daughter. "She loved books, animals, people, was always caring and had a good heart," Zara said. The inquest heard the family became concerned after messages sent to Ms Van-Der-Zyden went unanswered, with the last known contact taking place on April 16, two days before she was found. After emergency services were called, South Central Ambulance Service and Thames Valley Police attended the property and discovered the 72-year-old near the bottom of the staircase. Her death was formally confirmed at 9.39pm on April 18. Evidence heard during the inquest suggested she may have been heading upstairs when she fell, although the precise circumstances could not be determined. Consultant pathologist Dr Sukhvinder Ghataura, who gave evidence remotely, said Ms Van-Der-Zyden had suffered a fracture-dislocation at the top of her spine, close to the brain stem. He also found evidence of significant heart disease, including an enlarged heart and narrowed coronary arteries. Dr Ghataura said it was not possible to determine whether a cardiac event had caused the fall or whether the fall occurred first and led to fatal complications. It was concluded that both factors likely contributed to her death. Recording her conclusion, the coroner accepted the medical evidence and found that Ms Van-Der-Zyden died from traumatic spine fracture dislocation with heart disease. She said it was unclear exactly how the fall occurred and that she could not determine whether a cardiac event had preceded it, but was satisfied that Ms Van-Der-Zyden had suffered a fall at home. The inquest, which lasted roughly an hour, ended with the coroner offering her condolences to the family and reminding them to "remember the fond memories" they shared with Ms Van-Der-Zyden. Associated Press Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate , whose social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny has made them among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities, were arrested Saturday in Miami as British authorities sought their extradition on rape and sex trafficking charges. The brothers were taken into custody by the U.S. Marshals Service on a sealed warrant, agency spokesperson Brady McCarron said, placing the United States at the center of an international legal saga that has stretched from Romania to Britain. British prosecutors announced Saturday that they were seeking the brothers’ extradition on charges alleging they raped and trafficked women between 2010 and 2017. The dual U.S. and British citizens moved to Romania in 2016. They were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. Last year, they were allowed to leave Romania and flew to Florida on a private jet. The brothers are expected to appear in Miami’s federal court early this week, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke to on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive law enforcement operations. The pending charges in the United Kingdom accused the brothers of abusing women in an area north of London, where they grew up. Their lawyers had said they denied the allegations. Joseph McBride, an attorney representing the Tate brothers, said in a phone interview Saturday evening that he has not been able to speak with his clients but called the new charges out of the U.K. “filth and slander” intended to derail defamation lawsuits filed by the brothers in the U.S. “They’re pulling out all the stops to make sure these guys never get their day in court,” McBride said. “We are confident that once a competent judge sees the facts, and once the Department of Justice confronts this egregious abuse of its own authority, Andrew and Tristan Tate will walk free. America does not do Britain’s political dirty work.” Andrew Tate, 39, first reached a mainstream audience as a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother” in 2016. He was removed from the show when a video surfaced that appeared to show Tate assaulting a woman. He and his brother Tristan Tate, 38, are vocal supporters of U.S. President Donald Trump. Andrew Tate has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from platforms like YouTube, TikTok and Instagram for violating hate speech guidelines. His most widely condemned rhetoric includes comments that women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for their attacks, graphic descriptions of how he might attack women and criticisms of people who seek treatment for mental illness. The Tate brothers have consistently denied allegations of abuse and human trafficking, claiming that violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. In a statement Saturday, the U.K.’s Crown Prosecution Services said that in addition to the charges publicly announced against the brothers in 2025, involving alleged crimes against three women, it was bringing a total of 38 new charges related to “four further victims.” Both brothers are accused of rape and human trafficking. Andrew Tate faces an additional charge of profiting from prostitution, and 19 charges “for offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography,” according to U.K. authorities. “There is no place for male violence against women and girls, and we will continue to work tirelessly to support victims and investigate all reports made to us,” said Karena Thomas, an assistant chief constable of the Bedfordshire Police, which investigated the case. Philippe Van Cauteren appointed curator of Art Encounters Biennial 2027 Art Encounters Biennial 2027: May 21–July 4 Add to Calendar Art Encounters Foundation Timișoara 46C Take Ionescu Blvd. Timișoara Timis 300 124 Romania Hours: Tuesday –Saturday 12–6pm artencounters.ro Facebook / Instagram The Art Encounters Foundation in Timișoara announces its collaboration with Philippe Van Cauteren, Artistic Director of the S.M.A.K. Museum in Ghent (Belgium), as appointed curator of the 7th edition of the Art Encounters Biennial, to be held in Timișoara (Romania). The Biennial will run from May 21 to July 4 2027, opening with a three-day program from May 21–23. The appointment also marks the beginning of a long-term strategic partnership between Art Encounters and S.M.A.K., opening a new chapter in the Biennial's development. Bringing together one of Europe's leading institutions dedicated to contemporary art and one of the region's most important biennials, the collaboration is structured around artistic co-production and professional exchange, with the aim of developing a sustainable model for conceiving and delivering a contemporary art biennial today. Philippe Van Cauteren’s involvement brings to the center of the 2027 edition a curatorial vision built around dialogue with artists and critical reflection on the role of the museum and the biennial in contemporary society. "The invitation to curate the Art Encounters Biennial 2027 is a great honor. I am delighted to contribute to this vital and unique project which promotes the visibility of art and artists through dialogue and collaboration. The opportunity to contribute to the legacy of the Biennial is a chance to learn, to discover, and to share both the local identity of Timișoara, and the constellation of relations that the working process brings. I am convinced that the Art Encounters Biennial 2027 will be more than an exhibition; it will also be a platform for national and international exchanges, including with S.M.A.K., among others." – Philippe Van Cauteren Van Cauteren has led S.M.A.K. (the Museum of Contemporary Art in Ghent) for over 15 years, making it one of the European institutions that have played an active role in supporting contemporary art in recent decades. Under his direction, the museum has developed an internationally relevant collection and initiated numerous collaborations with artists, biennials, and major institutions, including participation in the Venice Biennale. His curatorial practice is recognized for its closeness to artists and its ability to connect local scenes with international cultural networks. Philippe Van Cauteren has published, among others, the book "Letters to Artists," a compilation of letters he has written to artists over the past 15 years. "For us, working with Philippe Van Cauteren and S.M.A.K. represents a partnership grounded in genuine exchange, co-production, and professional development. At the same time, his appointment highlights a curatorial approach we strongly believe in—one that allows the central importance of art in our lives to be recognized by everyone, as a vital force in both personal and collective growth." – Diana Marincu, Artistic Director of the Art Encounters Foundation The Art Encounters Biennial is the flagship project of the Art Encounters Foundation and stands at the intersection between an experimental art festival and a contemporary art biennial. It is based on extensive curatorial research, engaging in a real dialogue with the historical and socio-cultural context of Timișoara. The Biennial’s mission is to become a creative meeting point for artists, communities, institutions, and ideas. Philippe Van Cauteren is trained as an art historian and sociologist. He is the artistic director of S.M.A.K. (Museum for Contemporary Art, Ghent, Belgium). In the past decades he has made exhibitions in Brazil, Chile, Iraq, Turkey, Nepal, Belgium. He was a.o. curator of the Belgian Pavilion (2013) and Iraq Pavilion (2015) in the Venice Biennial, and curator of the first Kathmandu Triennial (2017) in Nepal. In 2027 he will be curator of the Art Encounters Biennial in Timișoara, Romania. Art Encounters Biennial 2027 is funded by the City of Timișoara through the Centre for Projects, and it's organized in partnership with S.M.A.K Ghent. http://www.bozemandailychronicle.com/new.text: INSTAGRAM FACEBOOK On July 6, the Sanders County Sheriff’s Office in western Montana put up a rather odd post on Facebook. It was a picture of a deputy standing with a smiling woman outside the sheriff’s office. “Good afternoon, Sanders County residents,” the post read. “We have met and spoken with Sinija Loze. She works with Families for Education. She is a college student from Latvia doing her summer job selling educational products by Southwestern Advantage. We have verified her information, she does have a accent but is a very nice lady. Her vehicle is a Grey jeep. No need to be alarmed if you see her.” The post got hundreds of reactions on Facebook, and many commenters were either confused or angry. In a since-deleted post on Facebook, the Sanders County Sheriff's Office wrote what a door-to-door salesperson asked them to write. Facebook “I’m genuinely confused about the purpose of this post?” one of the top comments read. “Are people in Montana ‘alarmed’ by someone with an ‘accent’? Literally everybody has an accent.” Someone else wondered if it was the “accent” part or the “selling educational products” that had everyone “on edge.” Many comments were either xenophobic or assailing the sheriff’s office for implying that people with accents were to be feared unless told otherwise. The odd part, however, is that the woman had presented the Sanders County Sheriff’s Office with a script, basically, of what to write. And she’s given it to other sheriff’s offices in Montana, who have also obliged her. By July 11, the original post from Sanders County had been deleted. The Sanders County Sheriff’s Office then posted a response. The post from Sweet Grass County. Facebook “Earlier this week, a young woman who is working in Sanders County as a door-to-door salesperson came in to the Sanders County Sheriff’s Office voluntarily to introduce herself, present her credentials and help prevent any confusion or unnecessary concern while she was working in the area,” the post read. The post went on to say that deputies had “determined that she is legitimately conducting business in our country.” “The intent of the post was never to stereotype, demean or judge her based on her nationality, ethnicity or accent,” the second statement read. “It was intended to support her request ... and reassure residents who had contacted our office with concerns. Unfortunately, the attention surrounding the post has had a very real effect on the young woman involved. She returned to our office today in tears after experiencing hostile interactions while working, including people yelling at her and aggressively telling her to leave.” The post went on to say “disagreement with door-to-door sales does not justify treating another person with hostility or cruelty.” “We recognize that the wording of the original post was interpreted differently than intended,” the statement continued. “For that reason, the original post has been removed. We hope this clarification provides the full context and reminds everyone that there is a real person at the center of this situation who deserves to be treated with basic courtesy and respect.” In an email to the Missoulian, Sanders County Sheriff Shawn Fielders said that the woman presented the phrasing. “The post we put up per her request was the exact same post that Sweet Grass County posted for her,” he explained. “She actually supplied a copy of their post for us to use. That included the part about the accent, she does have a very strong accent and is at times hard to understand so she requested we leave that in the post.” The post from the Laurel Police Department. Facebook Also, the Carbon County Sheriff’s Office posted the exact same wording on June 15, including the part about the accent. The Gallatin County Sheriff’s Office made a similar post, noting the color and model of the students’ cars, but didn’t mention the accent. The Laurel Police Department also posted a similar statement about a different woman from Latvia, using nearly the same language. The woman was also selling educational materials, like study guides for the ACT. “Lilija is driving a white Dodge and has an accent, please do not be intimidated by that,” the Laurel post reads. “If you are not in interested, she will thank you for your time and leave you in a good mood.” Of course, there were plenty of comments on that one too. Some questioned why the post was necessary. The post from Gallatin County. Apparently, young Latvian students have been coming to Montana in the summer for many years to sell books, working for a company called Southwestern Advantage. The Belgrade News profiled a young student in 2023, writing that the company recruits workers in Latvia .{/div}{/div}{/div}{/div}{/div}{/div}{/div} Valley Neighbors of the Flathead, a nonprofit that works to support immigrants in the Kalispell area, chimed in about the Sanders County post. “When Valley Neighbors works to make the Flathead or our region a more welcoming place for immigrants, we sometimes get pushback from folks who take issue with the idea that our communities actively grapple with xenophobia and racism,” the organization wrote on social media. “Earlier this week, the Sanders County Sheriff’s Office made a pre-emptive post about a young Latvian woman who would be going door-to-door as a salesperson. While we certainly can defer to the Sheriff’s Office about their intent, the language they used likely fell short in tone and intention. In (the post) you’ll likely see a lot of cringe xenophobic comments expressed in the comments thread. This incident, in a variety of ways, shows how far Montana has to go.” David Erickson is the business reporter for the Missoulian. Documentary about rock scene in Romanian city where 1989 Revolution started explores the question 23 July 2026 Simona Fodor Like this article? Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn The Vinyl Revolution , a recent documentary by Eric Fretz, a two-time Fulbright Program scholar who taught at West University of Timișoara, delves into a less documented chapter in the history of Timișoara’s rock scene and asks whether music played a role in the lead-up to the 1989 Revolution. From Deep Purple, Led Zeppelin, and Jimi Hendrix to The Rolling Stones or The Beatles, the soundtrack for rock fans in Communist-era Timișoara was much the same as anywhere else in the world. But while audiences elsewhere could simply enjoy the music, in Romania an interest in Western rock could attract unwanted attention from the authorities. Eric Fretz , a professor of Peace and Justice Studies at Regis University in Denver, Colorado, describes the context as “incredibly challenging and dangerous,” referencing stories of young people who were part of the rock and roll scene being taken by the Communist-era police Miliţie or threatened by the political police Securitate. “I grew up outside of Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. I was listening to the same music, but there were no threats against me for listening to rock and roll. I just went to the record store and bought the latest Pink Floyd album and listened to it on my turntable. I really didn't think about the political dimensions of it or worry about what I was doing,” Fretz recalls. Meanwhile, in Romania, rock music could be associated with values seen as incompatible with the communist regime. Access to albums was limited, so fans relied on records brought from abroad, cassette copies, or broadcasts by stations such as Radio Free Europe, which aired the famed pop, rock, and jazz music show Metronom of journalist Cornel Chiriac after it was banned in Romania. These aspects of the local music scene enrich a historical account that records major events, like Bruce Springsteen’s 1988 concert in East Berlin, but not always finds a place for the many local experiences that shaped everyday cultural resistance. “If you look at the historical record around Western rock and roll and Eastern Europe and the Soviet bloc countries in the 1980s, you get this 30,000-foot view of how these Western rockers like Springsteen came in here and did their thing. What's not part of the historical record is, for the most part, these underground bands, the ordinary people who were doing kind of extraordinary things politically with Western-style rock and roll music,” Fretz explains. While he had read about the period in history books, he learned firsthand about Timișoara’s rock scene during his time as a Fulbright scholar at the West University, teaching in the American Studies program in 2016. Throughout the year he spent in the city, he became friends with Emil Biebel, the owner of the record store and pub Viniloteca, located very close to Timișoara’s Maria Square. The square is the place where the protests that sparked the December 1989 Revolution started. “Emil and I just became friends because we both love rock and roll a lot. We just talked about music a lot at the pub there. One day, he and I were talking, and I asked him how the vinyl shop, Viniloteca, started. He told me that in the 1970s and the 1980s, and then after the revolution too, he was smuggling rock and roll records into the country, rock and roll T-shirts, and things like that. I kind of knew that stuff was happening through the Cold War, but I had just read about it in history books, which are abstract,” he recalls. As his Fulbright grant ended, he returned to his teaching position at Regis University, but he left Timișoara looking to come back and learn more about the role rock and roll had played in the city's cultural life during the Cold War. That opportunity came when he received a second Fulbright award and returned to teach at West University last year. “When I arrived here in January of 2025, I didn't really know what I was going to do or what I wanted to do. Emil and I started talking, and he introduced me to all kinds of people. I thought I was going to write another novel about it. But what happened was that about six weeks into my time in the project I realized that it wasn't a novel, it was a film.” He deemed the format of a film more appropriate because “there was just so much going on here in the 1980s in regards to rock and roll and soft-anti regime things.” The Vinyl Revolution is Fretz’s first documentary project. Besides his academic work, he published Groundswell , a surf-themed murder mystery. With his iPhone and some lavalier microphones, he recorded the interviews for the film. Once he was back in the U.S., he worked with Neville Harson, the film’s editor, to comb through archival footage, interviews, and copious notes to put everything together. The through line of the film is the question of whether rock and roll played any kind of role in the inception of the 1989 Romanian Revolution. “That's what the film's really about . It doesn't answer that question. I don't think it's an answerable question. It just raises the question, and it allows the audience to figure it out on their own, to either reject it or accept it,” he explains. The film, which screened last week at the festival Ceau, Cinema! in Timişoara, is geared mainly at American audiences as he wanted “to tell the story about these crazy, brave, young people in the 1980s who were performing rock and roll that was anti-regime.” "I wanted to tell the story about these crazy, brave, young people in the 1980s who were performing rock and roll that was anti-regime" It zooms in on the PM6 (Post Meridian 6) club established in the 1960s by Petru Umanschi and housed at the time inside Casa Tineretului in Timişoara, one of the many Youth Houses that the Union of Communist Youth (U.T.C.) administered throughout the country. While the purpose of such venues was to promote state-approved cultural activities, PM6 became a gateway to Western music and ideas. The organizers played classic FM rock for the attendees to dance to and began inviting local bands to perform on Thursdays. “My sense is that the local rock and roll culture, local music really blossomed from that space at Casa Tineretului. That's where a lot of the local bands that became a big part of TimRock got their start.” Launched in the early 1980s, the festival TimRock grew into one of the defining events of Timișoara's rock scene. Were people at the time aware that what they were doing was subversive? “Yes and no,” Fretz says. “The young people who were playing and listening to rock and roll in the 80s, in Timişoara and throughout Romania, were just trying to make sense of the situation that they were thrown into. Especially when we're younger, that's hard to do. My sense is that over time, these people who were involved in this culture came to understand it in a better way. […] In the 80s, when all this was happening, they were just doing what they loved, and they were trying to live their lives, be young people, have fun, and just learn how to be in this world.” The concert that felt like freedom Another thread of the film follows a concert that took place at the Hungarian State Theatre in Timișoara in the autumn of 1985. The performance was by Metamorf, a band that didn’t release any official recordings. “People I talked to just kept coming back to this concert that they gave in the autumn of 1985, and talking about how anti-regime it was, and how they were there, but they didn't feel like they were in Romania because it was like it was happening in America at the time. So, the other part of the film is trying to figure out what happened at this strange, anti-regime concert at the Hungarian State Theater in the autumn of 1985.” The documentary is built around interviews with people who were directly involved in Timișoara's rock scene during the communist period, among them Emil Biebel, journalist and writer Mimo Obradov, Mirela Iacob, Lili Molnar-Popa, and Metamorf members Tibor Gajdo, Adrian Popescu, and Tavi Iepan. The film also features archival footage provided by the members of Metamorf, including recordings from the band's 1985 concert at the Hungarian State Theatre. Music from that performance forms part of the documentary's soundtrack, alongside music by Phoenix, the prominent Romanian rock band founded in Timișoara in 1962. “I was trying to find some of these recordings and put them on the website so people could listen to them because, basically, they live in boxes, under people's beds. There are other bands like Pro Musica, for instance, that everybody knows about. They're well known, and there's been a really good documentary about them. But there were other, smaller, underground bands that were a part of the culture that I was trying to look at.” The documentary is not intended to be a comprehensive history of Timișoara's rock scene, but rather a focused exploration of two stories that shed light on the city's music culture in the years before the 1989 Revolution. “The film is not comprehensive at all. It just kind of takes a deep dive into two very small things that I thought were important. I know a little bit about what was going on here, but I didn't live here; I just got my knowledge from talking to people, and this isn't a part of the recorded Romanian history at all. So, there really wasn't too much to read. I just did the best that I could to find a way to tell a small part of the story of what was happening here in the 1980s. It's a very limited and narrowly focused view of the rock and roll scene here in Timisoara leading up to the revolution, and so it's imperfect in a lot of ways.” Among many Romanian musicians making music under difficult circumstances, Metamorf stood out to Fretz for their nuanced music. “I just didn't know that there was an underground culture of people who were influenced by Western rock and roll and making their own. That's why Metamorf is so important to me: because their songs are anti-regime, but they're very nuanced. They're really nuanced because they had to be careful what they were saying, because the Securitate and the informers were all over the place. This is not an easy thing to do under any circumstances, but especially those circumstances.” Fretz, who plays in a "little rock and roll band" in Denver, brought Metamorf’s music to the stage during a recent New Year's Eve party. “That was just really fun for us to do, and it's just a way to honor them and all the stories they told me.” How rock reached Timișoara and Romania Another thread in the story of Timișoara's music scene during the communist period is that of records and cassette tapes being smuggled into the country. Fretz has heard many stories about the clandestine trade, including one about flight attendants and pilots in the 1960s and 1970s who returned from international flights with rock albums tucked into their luggage. The records would then make their way to Romanian DJs, who copied them onto reel-to-reel tapes and played the music at discotheques and private parties in Timișoara and across the country. “It came across land and sea, too. It’s just the thing: you can't stop ideas from traveling across borders, no matter how many border guards you have across any given nation state. It's just impossible to do. The whole thing is really about communication and technology, and how, if people want to hear something or listen to something or read something, they're going to get it.” "You can't stop ideas from traveling across borders, no matter how many border guards you have across any given nation state." This continued after the fall of communism, with an informal, music-related economy, he found. As borders opened, people traveled to Budapest, Poland and the former Yugoslavia, returning with pirated CDs and cassette tapes, as well as rock T-shirts and posters that were difficult to find in Romania. Timișoara's location near the Hungarian and Yugoslav borders helped, and, according to the accounts he heard, some border guards accepted bribes and looked the other way. “It was just a very porous kind of community here when it came to borders, immigration, travel, and goods crossing international borders at that time.” The kids are alright In April, the documentary screened at Regis University, in front of an audience of approximately 100 people. “People really enjoyed the film; they were laughing and engaged. The film is kind of funny because the people who are telling the stories are really magnetic, charismatic, and interesting people, and they have a lot of really funny stories to tell. The American audience responded to that, and they responded to the personalities in the film, too.” It was the unknown aspects of the underground scene and of what ordinary people were doing that people resonated with. “Traditional history is fun and great and important to read, but people enjoy this social cultural history because it's human beings who are telling stories about the lives that they've lived.” At a screening in Bucharest, young viewers said the film helped remind them of stories they had heard from their parents about life during communism, and left them wanting to ask them more about that period. “I didn't really need to hear anything else. If you can do something that creates an intergenerational dialogue like that, you can't ask for anything else. That just gave me great hope for young people in the future, and it just made me feel really good about what we did.” "I think there is an argument to be made that Western rock and roll had something to do with inciting some kind of passion within Romanians to say ‘I don't like this world I'm living in, I want to do something about it.’ " Western commercial music is two-pronged, Fretz explains. It has a revolutionary part in that it can make people think about the situation that they're living and give them a sense of how to change that. “But popular music can also be an anodyne and just make people think that what they have is okay and ‘I don't want to push or I just want to party.’ […] That’s what made this story so interesting for me because I think there is an argument to be made that Western rock and roll had something to do with inciting some kind of passion within ordinary Romanians to say: ‘I don't like this world I'm living in, I want to do something about it.’ I don't think it was everything. That would be too much, too broad of a brush stroke to paint. But I think there's enough evidence to make the claim that it had something to do with the political changes that happened here.” The website of the project, with more audio content and a photo archive, can be found here . https://www.romania-insider.com/tarom-ce.text: Transport Romanian government replaces Tarom CEO on alleged unrealistic budget 23 July 2026 Iulian Ernst Like this article? Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn The interim minister of transport, Radu Miruta, announced that the Board of Directors at flag carrier Tarom replaced interim CEO Bogdan Costas with Cristian Anghel, accusing the company’s management of failure to amend the 2026 budget plan that both sides agree is no longer realistic and revise the restructuring plan in line with market developments. The Transport Ministry, as the sole owner of Tarom, has not approved the company’s budget of revenues and expenditures for the current year. “They came up with a ridiculously unrealistic budget. We asked and demanded that it be restored to real figures. They didn't restore it. Maybe because there was no room left for fancy plans using public money,” minister Miruta explained. Tarom needs to break even by the end of the year, under the restructuring plan linked to the state aid extended by the government. Radu Miruta claimed that the dismissed CEO did not take any steps to restore the budget based on real data and delayed the steps to modify the restructuring plan. “The board of directors found today that the director did not take any steps to restore the budget based on real data and unreasonably delayed the steps to the European Commission to modify the restructuring plan, in accordance with market reality. [...]For months, the company's executive management, appointed by PSD, has been asking me to approve, as a shareholder, a budget built on figures that it itself knows are unrealistic,” minister Miruta said. The outgoing CEO claimed that the company took formal steps to amend the restructuring plan. "In May 2026: I officially opened technical discussions with representatives of the European Commission. In May 2026: I submitted to the Board of Directors a formal proposal containing the 4 strategic coordinates on which action was needed to adjust the plan. We know that a more mobile, agile force would have a greater effect against Russia than traditional armour,â the British defence minister at the time, Dan Jarvis, said in Tallinn last week. As part of the move, Britain is increasing the number of troops stationed in Estonia from 800 to 1,200. It will also transform its Armoured Battlegroup in the country into a Mobile Anti-Armour Force equipped with high-tech drones, the UK Ministry of Defence said, adding that the country would also pre-position long-range drones in the Baltics. The lessons of Ukraine show that tanks are becoming less important, according to Tony Lawrence, head of the defence policy and strategy programme at the International Centre for Defence and Security (ICDS) in Tallinn. âTheyâre not, of course, redundant. They are vulnerable and have to sit back a bit more in todayâs warfare,â Lawrence said. However, the move does not mean the UK is turning its back entirely on traditional armoured vehicles, and some of its decisions are already in line with changes previously implemented in Lithuania. The UK is beginning a large-scale procurement of Boxer infantry fighting vehicles, which Lithuania already operates, Lawrence said. âThis is the mobile element that they are talking about in various press releases.â The UKâs move in Estonia also reflects changes in London itself, as well as debates within the NATO alliance. âItâs about the commitment that the UK wants to show to this burden-shifting agenda inside NATO. The UK does not have a good story to tell about defence spending â itâs quite tight. It looks like it will be tight for some years to come,â Lawrence said. British troops (associative) | AP Lithuania and Germanyâs heavy brigade Lithuania has previously announced plans to buy tanks, while Germany is also deploying an armoured brigade equipped with tanks to the Baltic country, even as it highlights the brigadeâs drone capabilities in its public messaging. âThere has been a certain amount of discussion in Estonia, particularly by drone manufacturers who want to make the case that this is the only way to go and that Estonia is far behind,â he said. âBut I think itâs been stronger in Vilnius than here.â According to Lawrence, the type of weapons sent to the Baltic states is also influenced by debates within individual NATO countries, while it is important to maintain different capabilities across NATOâs eastern flank âso that different tasks can be carried outâ. âYou will always have inconsistencies â with Germany heavily emphasising armour and the UK putting more emphasis on drones, you would want to have a more consistent posture across the whole eastern flank. âThe fact is that we, the states that provide land forces, are constrained by domestic interests and policies, so you have to rely on NATO as the planning level above that to smooth out force posture,â Lawrence said. Writing in The Daily Telegraph, retired British colonel Hamish de Bretton-Gordon said the changes in Estonia showed that the role of tanks on the battlefield had changed â they must now operate alongside a range of technological solutions, including drones. âUkraine has fundamentally changed warfare,â Bretton-Gordon wrote. https://finance.yahoo.com/markets/crypto.text: Oops, something went wrong U.S. markets closed Jack Mallers Questioned MicroStrategy’s Bitcoin Strategy, Now He’s Stepping Down From Twenty One Lockridge Okoth July 21, 2026 5 min read XXI 9984.T BTC-USD Jack Mallers has stepped down as CEO of Twenty One (XXI), the Tether-backed Bitcoin treasury firm. His exit lands months after he publicly pressed Michael Saylor over mNAV math and digital credit yields. The Strike founder says he quit after clashing with the board over the company's direction. Critics now tie his exit to the doubts he raised on stage earlier this year. Board Disagreements End Jack Mallers' Twenty One Tenure Mallers announced the decision this week. XXI began trading on December 9, 2025, so his run lasted just seven months. The firm went public with roughly 43,500 BTC, worth about $4 billion at the time. Tether, Bitfinex, and SoftBank backed it. Tether took full control in May 2026 by buying SoftBank's entire stake. He shared more detail in follow-up posts. He walked away, he said, because "the board and I couldn't agree on the future of the company." He also denied a claim by X's Grok chatbot that he collected $140.8 million in pay. His forfeited options, he noted, now expire worthless. The exit leaves the second-largest corporate Bitcoin treasury fully in Tether's hands. XXI is already rethinking its model. Incoming CEO Raphael Zagury wants cash flow, not just more Bitcoin buying. The Saylor Questions That Resurfaced After His Exit The backstory makes the exit sting more. At BTC Prague earlier this year, Mallers challenged Saylor from the audience over mNAV. The metric shows how much the market pays for each dollar of Bitcoin a treasury firm holds. His concern was simple. Some firms count securities as equity even when they are far from turning into shares. That inflates the metric. In an interview at the event, he explained the question he put to Saylor. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kS65L_Lqrg0 "...do you agree with classifying out of the money securities as equity, which obviously that would inflate the equity value, which would make an MNAV metric more attractive," Mallers said. He used XXI's own convertible bond as the example. The bond turns into stock at $13 per share. However, the stock traded near $5 at the time, so that switch was nowhere close. On a panel the same day, Mallers took aim at digital credit. These products pay investors a big yearly dividend that never stops. Stretch, sold by Strategy, paid 11.5% when Mallers spoke. SEC filings show the rate rose to 12% in July. His question was simple. Who pays that bill without real revenue? "You're not doing anything productive in the economy to produce cash flow that can afford the money that you want to give to your grandmother. So, who's coming up with the money?" he said during the panel. Story Continues Saylor responded at length at the time. He framed mNAV as one metric among several and defended the model's math. Those clips are now everywhere again. Many read them as proof that Mallers doubted the sector's core math long before he left it. Rug Pull Claims Meet a Firm Denial The market's verdict was quick. XXI closed near $4.60 on Tuesday, down 13.5% in a day. Early backers paid $10 per share, so they have lost more than half their money. Twenty One Capital (XXI) Stock Performance. Source: Google Finance Critics on X claim losses of up to 85% from the stock's peak, and some accused Mallers of abandoning shareholders. He pushed back hard. "Rug pull? Who pulled what rug? I resigned voluntarily, took no severance, forfeited my options, and walked away because it was the right thing to do. Twenty One also never sold shares via an ATM while I was CEO," Mallers replied on X. Reactions split into three camps. Investor Mike Alfred praised the move as a sign of clarity and alignment. BnkToTheFuture founder Simon Dixon went further. He framed it as Mallers walking away from wrapped securities entirely. A third camp sees a warning for the digital asset treasury (DAT) sector. The model looks strong while premiums grow, they argue. The real test starts when mNAV compresses and capital dries up. The rankings could shift too. Metaplanet crossed 43,000 BTC in July. That nearly matches XXI's stash of roughly 43,500 BTC, putting the second spot in play. Top 100 Public Bitcoin Treasury Companies. Source: Bitcoin Treasuries The debate lands with Bitcoin (BTC) near $66,600 on Tuesday, a five-week high. Mallers, meanwhile, returns his full attention to Strike. There, he wants cash flow, not dilution, to fund Bitcoin buying. Whether his warnings prove right now depends on XXI's next chapter under Tether. If the restructured company delivers without the metrics he questioned, his critique may fade with the drawdown that fueled it. https://www.cei.int/ansa/178173.text: Hungary's Orban-era top prosecutor resigns (ANSA-AFP) - BUDAPEST, 22 LUG - Hungary's prosecutor general said Wednesday he would step down following pressure from Prime Minister Peter Magyar, who called him a "puppet" of nationalist ex-leader Viktor Orban. Gabor Balint Nagy, who was appointed last year under Orban, said in a statement he was resigning "solely to safeguard the interests of the prosecutorial service". He added: "The functioning and independence of the prosecutor's office must not, under any circumstances, be compromised by the disgraceful, politically motivated struggles surrounding the prosecutor general." He also said that the "attacks" on him had "gone far beyond the bounds of acceptable professional and public debate". Since ousting Orban from power in April elections, Magyar has pushed to get rid of a host of top officials including ex-president Tamas Sulyok, who was removed by a constitutional amendment on Sunday. Orban's Fidesz party has denounced Magyar's moves as "autocratic", a charge that was often levelled against the former premier himself during his tenure. The top prosecutor's announcement comes the day after a data centre hosting Fidesz servers was raided over corruption allegations. The prime minister welcomed Nagy's resignation, which will take effect late August. "With this, the country has rid itself of yet another of Orban's puppets who was obstructing the transition to democracy," Magyar said on Facebook. "Gentlemen, who will be next?" he added. https://voiceofvienna.org/austria-sees-m.text: Austria has recorded more deportations than new asylum applications for the first time in over 20 years, marking a significant shift in the country’s migration landscape. The latest figures from the Interior Ministry show a sharp decline in asylum requests, reflecting a trend that officials say has been developing since 2023. Between January and June, 4,903 people applied for asylum in Austria, down 44 percent from around 8,800 applications during the same period last year. According to the ministry, the number is the lowest recorded in nearly 23 years. Family reunification also remained limited, with only 48 people entering the country through the program by the end of June. Interior Minister Gerhard Karner said the figures point to what he described as a “turning point” in Austria’s migration policy. More than 7,000 people either left the country through deportation or other forms of removal during the first half of the year. Among them were 2,200 people with asylum-related status, exceeding the roughly 2,000 first-time asylum applications submitted by newly arrived migrants. Karner called the development “negative migration,” arguing that the trend should be preserved through continued border controls and immigration measures. Of the total asylum applications, only 2,016 came from people newly arriving in Austria. The remainder included applications from children born in the country, family reunification cases, and repeat applicants. Nearly half of all applicants were minors. Syria and Afghanistan remained the largest countries of origin, each accounting for about one-quarter of all applications. However, among newly arrived asylum seekers, Afghans formed the largest group, followed by Syrians and Iranians. Austria currently has 15,278 asylum cases awaiting decisions, with nearly half involving Syrian nationals. While applicants from Iran had the highest approval rate at 76 percent, the recognition rate for Syrians fell sharply to 32 percent, compared with 67 percent last year. Officials also noted that Austria, alongside Poland, has recorded the steepest decline in asylum applications across the European Union. Meanwhile, more than 45,000 people remain in Austria’s basic support system, the majority of them Ukrainians displaced by war. https://www.asahi.com/ajw/articles/16748.text: Skip to content Twitter Facebook 日本語 English HOME What’s New National Report Politics Business Asia & World China Korean Peninsula Around Asia World Sci & Tech Culture Style Food Movies Manga & Anime People Travel Sports Opinion Editorial Vox Populi Views Special The Asahi Shimbun Opinion Vox Populi article VOX POPULI: Hungarian state TV’s apology also a reminder for global media Vox Populi, Vox Dei is a daily column that runs on Page 1 of The Asahi Shimbun. July 23, 2026 at 12:56 JST Share Tweet list Print A TV turned to Hungary’s state news channel in Budapest on July 7 shows a message that begins with, “Public service media cannot lie. We apologize for doing this for many years nonetheless.” (Reuters) In what could have been right out of near-future science fiction, the screen of Hungary’s state-run TV news channel went black and kept displaying the following message for about four hours: “Public service media cannot lie. We apologize for doing this for many years nonetheless.” This happened earlier this month in Hungary, where the general election in April had resulted in the first change of government in 16 years. The winning opposition party, the Respect and Freedom Party (TISZA), had campaigned for the “restoration of freedom of the press.” Defeated Prime Minister Viktor Orban, who had been in power for 16 years and whose political ideology made him an ally of Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump, was known as “Europe’s maverick.” And he complained to the effect that the Hungarian media worked on behalf of the opposition parties. Under the Orban administration, the council that oversaw Hungary’s public news broadcasting was restructured to boost the administration’s dominance. A businessman close to Orban was entrusted with the management of a conservative, pro-administration TV station. And a foundation for “enhancing national awareness” was created to acquire and control financially troubled media. Thus, many media outlets formed the administration’s propaganda machine. According to Yusuke Ishikawa, a co-author of “A Dangerous Confluence: The Intertwined Crisis of Disinformation and Democracies,” Hungary’s public broadcaster has undergone a management overhaul in keeping with the new administration’s policy. The oversight committee’s membership makeup has also been rectified, so that both the government and opposition interests are represented equally. It would be meaningless if these changes only result in creating a new propaganda machine for the new administration. However, Ishikawa said, “So far, the parties involved are proceeding with care.” We in Japan would be wrong to think that what has happened in Hungary is none of our concern. Media outlets must always do “the opposition’s work,” so that the TV screen will never go black. I firmly remind myself anew of this constantly repeated warning: “Journalism is printing something that someone does not want printed. Everything else is public relations.” — The Asahi Shimbun, July 23 * * * Vox Populi, Vox Dei is a popular daily column that takes up a wide range of topics, including culture, arts and social trends and developments. Written by veteran Asahi Shimbun writers, the column provides useful perspectives on and insights into contemporary Japan and its culture. Romanian Business News - ACTMedia :: Services | About us | Contact | RSS Home Daily Financial & banking Economic Companies Energy & Environment Council of Europe calls for strengthening of elderly care system in Romania and investigation of Dumbrava case The Council of Europe Commissioner for Human Rights, Michael O'Flaherty, published on Tuesday a letter addressed to Romanian Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan, following his visit to Romania from May 26 to 29, 2026, in which he makes a series of recommendations regarding the long-term care system for the elderly, the Strasbourg-based organization announced. The Commissioner welcomes progress in the reform of social services and the dedication of staff working in care centers for the elderly. At the same time, he expresses concern about several challenges, including the insufficient recognition of residents as full holders of rights, the shortage of services and the difficulties faced by vulnerable people in accessing care services. Michael O'Flaherty recommends further developing the care system to meet complex needs and ensure better integration of health and social services. As regards monitoring, the Commissioner recommends that inspections of care facilities should pay greater attention to the well-being and rights of residents, in addition to checking formal compliance with standards. He also stresses the need for adequate and sustainable funding so that service providers can provide care according to needs and to the appropriate standards. The Commissioner's visit to Romania focused on the human rights situation of older people living in long-term care facilities and is part of a wider effort on this issue in Council of Europe member states. During his visit, Michael O'Flaherty met with the Minister of Investments and European Projects and Acting Minister of Labour, Dragos Pislaru, representatives of the Ministries of Labour and Health, the Prosecutor General's Office, the Ombudswoman Renate Weber, representatives of the Romanian Institute for Human Rights and civil society. He also visited three long-term care centres in Bucharest and Voluntari, where he spoke with residents, employees and representatives of local authorities. In a letter to Prime Minister Bolojan after this visit, copied to the Acting Minister of Labour, Dragos Pislaru, the Commissioner warns that the lack of care services makes access to them more difficult, in the context of an ageing population and increasing care needs. According to the Commissioner, some of the most vulnerable people, including those living in poverty, with disabilities or mental health problems, often end up not receiving the necessary support due to the fragmentation of care systems. In this context, he recommends developing a system capable of responding to the complex needs of beneficiaries, instead of relying on rigid classifications. The official points out that inspections often focus on compliance with formal standards, without giving sufficient priority to the people at the heart of these requirements. He considers it useful to review inspection methods so that, alongside technical criteria, the actual respect for the rights and well-being of residents is also assessed. Concerns were also expressed during the visit about the adequacy and sustainability of financing long-term care services. The Commissioner recommends that national and European funds be allocated through clear and accessible procedures, so that service providers - mostly non-profit organisations - can continue to provide the necessary care, according to needs and to the required standards. The Commissioner draws attention to care centres operating without a license and calls for a thorough and independent investigation into the Dumbrava case. According to the letter, dated 10 July, this concerns the unlicensed care centre in the village of Dumbrava, Bihor county, which allegedly housed thousands of vulnerable people in abusive conditions and where over a thousand deaths were recorded. The authorities should apply licensing conditions more strictly, adopt the necessary legislative amendments and strengthen monitoring mechanisms, including by increasing support to the Ombudsman. The Commissioner also recommends the establishment of accessible channels through which residents can report problems and seek remedies, as well as support for non-governmental organizations that promote human rights and dignity. In the letter, Michael O'Flaherty welcomes the recent intervention of Directorate for Investigating Organised Crime and Terrorism (DIICOT) and the transfer of residents to hospitals and licensed care facilities. He also expresses concern that the situation in Dumbrava has persisted for so long, despite repeated warnings from civil society organisations and journalists, as well as the recommendations of the Ombudswoman. The Commissioner also notes that the public debate on DIICOT's intervention has become polarised and that individuals who have exposed these abuses have been targeted with hate messages online. He stresses that the proceedings in the Dumbrava case must be conducted with integrity and independence, and the circumstances, including those relating to the registered deaths, must be investigated in detail. At the same time, the Commissioner recommends the analysis and adoption of additional legal provisions, including in the criminal field, if necessary, to combat the operation of illegal centers. In conclusion, he encourages the Romanian authorities to establish clear procedures for reporting and investigating deaths in residential centers for the elderly, following the model of existing mechanisms for people with disabilities. State and territory regulators took action against 589 services and cancelled their approval to operate – meaning they lost access to childcare subsidy funding and cannot legally run. Though, not all of those services were currently operating. The government says state and territory regulators also took 1,538 compliance actions in the March quarter – which puts providers on notice if they are not meeting standards. It was double the number of notices compared with the same time last year. Governments have been under significant pressure to lift safety and standards across the childcare sector following allegations of child sexual abuse and safety breaches. Photograph: Darren England/AAP Queensland Man and pregnant woman found dead in outback Queensland home in apparent murder-suicide after long siege A 45-year-old man and 23-year-old woman were found dead in the Charleville home after a near eight-hour police siege Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Ben Smee and Australian Associated Press Wed 5 Aug 2026 19.41 EDT First published on Wed 5 Aug 2026 18.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A pregnant woman and a man have been found dead at a home in the outback Queensland town of Charleville, in an apparent murder-suicide after a protracted overnight standoff with police. Several streets in the remote town, 600km west of Toowoomba, were locked down by police on Wednesday evening after officers arrived at the property on King Street after reports of “a serious assault”. An emergency declaration, under the state’s Public Safety Preservation Act, was in place for about eight hours. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email When specialist officers entered the home, just before 1.45am, they found that a 45-year-old man and a 23-year-old woman were dead. The incident will be investigated by Queensland police’s ethical standards command because it occurred during a police operation. Police would not confirm whether the incident was being treated as a domestic violence situation. Shaun Radnedge, the mayor of the Murweh shire council, said that based on the information he had been given “there is no ongoing risk to the public”. “The situation has been brought to an end,” Radnedge said. “This tragedy will be felt deeply across our small community. Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Robert Thomson, the CEO of News Corp, has reported robust international results but attacked AI companies for ‘pilfering’ their work. Photograph: Patrick T Fallon/AFP/Getty Images News Corporation News Corp subscriptions fall in Australia as company takes aim at ‘slimy’ AI slop Chief executive Robert Thomson says ‘crass kleptomaniac’ AI companies are ‘in possession of stolen goods’ Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Jonathan Barrett Business editor Wed 5 Aug 2026 19.24 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 19.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google News Corp has reported a slight slide in digital subscriptions at its Australian mastheads, erasing recent gains, among otherwise robust financials at the Rupert Murdoch-backed global conglomerate. Digital subscribers at News Corp Australia – a division that includes the Australian, the Daily Telegraph and the Herald Sun, among others – fell from 1,166,000 to 1,162,000 during the financial year, according to the company’s internal data published in its full year results on Thursday morning. The figures represent a reversal in momentum. The Australian division has grown digital subscriptions in recent years, as it transitions away from its traditional newspaper base. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email News Corp’s broader news media unit, which includes the Sun and the Times in London and the New York Post, recorded mixed results, with advertising revenue still under pressure, falling 2% during the year to 30 June. The news media division also recorded costs linked to the launch of News Corp’s latest newspaper, the California Post, which is the Los Angeles outpost of the New York Post and edited by Australian News Corp veteran Nick Papps. The News Corp chief executive, Robert Thomson, used the release of the company’s financial results to hit out at AI models that “pilfer and profit from our work”, as media companies around the world seek compensation for the use of their content. “Without our journalists, our authors, our data, our brands and our professional expertise, users would be drowning in a slimy sea of AI slop,” Thomson said. “We will pursue those pilferers and companies that are clients of these crass kleptomaniacs should know they are patently in possession of stolen goods.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion News Corp has commercial agreements in place with OpenAI and Meta. The comments come amid contested plans by the Albanese government to expand its news bargaining incentive, which would require tech giants to compensate media outlets for the news on their platforms, either through making commercial deals or paying a higher levy. Photograph: Thames Valley Police/PA View image in fullscreen Andrew Harper, 28, died when he was dragged down a country road in Berkshire by three men fleeing the scene of a quad bike theft. Photograph: Thames Valley Police/PA UK criminal justice Chief constable considers joining legal action if PC’s killers are released early Thames Valley’s top officer says he may join Police Federation in court if convicted pair are freed from jail Geraldine McKelvie Senior correspondent Wed 5 Aug 2026 15.51 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The chief constable of Thames Valley police has said he will consider joining legal action against the government if it fails to block the early release of two of PC Andrew Harper’s killers. The Police Federation is contemplating going to court in its attempts to keep Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers in prison. In August 2019, Harper, 28, died when he was dragged down a country road in Berkshire by a car as Cole, Bowers and their accomplice Henry Long fled the scene of a quad bike theft. All three were convicted of manslaughter in 2020. Cole and Bowers were sentenced to 13 years in prison and could be released early as part of the government’s drive to free up prison places. Long, who was driving the car, was given a 16-year jail sentence and does not qualify for early release. View image in fullscreen Jessie Cole (left) and Albert Bowers are each serving a 13-year sentence for manslaughter. Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA On Wednesday morning, Jason Hogg, who was on duty the night Harper died, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that he would “certainly” consider joining the Police Federation in court action if the government refused to reverse its position, pending legal advice. “I was contacted by the Police Federation yesterday who informed me they are seeking legal advice, exploring opportunities for a judicial review against the government,” he told the Guardian on Wednesday afternoon. “So I’m watching with interest and I will be speaking to the Police Federation again. “But my hope is that we will never get there and that there is no need for the Police Federation to go down the line of a judicial review because the government will listen. ” ‘We fought for a tougher sentence’: victims’ families’ fury over early release scheme Read more Prison capacity in England and Wales is at critical levels. From October, the government plans to release about 5,000 prisoners who have served a third of their sentence. Harper’s widow, Lissie, successfully campaigned for a change in the law after his death. Legislation introduced four years ago – the Police, Crime, Sentencing and Courts Act 2022 – means those convicted of the manslaughter of emergency workers on duty now face mandatory life sentences. However, the law cannot be applied retrospectively. Hogg said he wrote to the prime minister, Andy Burnham , 12 days ago to express concerns that Cole and Bowers might be included in the scheme, but had not received a reply. He added that he planned to write again to Burnham, the home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, and the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to convey “the impact of the decision on the morale of my officers, but also on the 2,000 people who work in policing across the country”. Hogg would not be drawn on whether all prisoners convicted of manslaughter should be exempt from the scheme. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Thames Valley police chief constable Jason Hogg was on duty the night Harper died. Photograph: Jaimi Joy/Reuters The government has already said those serving sentences for rape, serious child sexual offences and grooming will not be released early, after a campaign by victims. “It isn’t my role to set government policy or set the law,” Hogg said. “But I think if you ask most people in the streets, they would probably say people who take the life of another person in our country should remain behind bars as long as possible, and I don’t think that’s particularly controversial.” However, he added that the fact Harper was an emergency services worker is a “significantly aggravating factor”. Hogg said the criminal justice system also needed “greater investment around rehabilitation”. He said the National Police Chiefs’ Council estimated it would cost about £480m to manage the freed offenders in the community. “I think there needs to be a balance between the risk caused [by] prisons being full, but also the risk of releasing people early who still pose a risk to the public,” he said. “One of the challenges around the sentencing act [is that it] releases people on the basis of the crime committed, not on the basis of how reformed they are, have they been rehabilitated, and not on the basis of the risk they pose back in the community. “So if you have somebody who still poses the risk … has felt no remorse, and they are back on the streets early, of course that risk has to be managed by the probation service and policing.” Explore more on these topics UK criminal justice Police Police Federation Prisons and probation Andy Burnham Berkshire news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Photograph: Yves Herman/Reuters Meta Meta says its AI model hacked into another company during testing Company is the third to report such an incident after Anthropic and OpenAI reported breaches during training Reuters Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.27 EDT Last modified on Wed 5 Aug 2026 21.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Meta said on Wednesday that one of its AI models hacked ⁠another company during cybersecurity testing, after an error by its testing partner gave the model unintended internet access. The incident adds to a ⁠growing list of ⁠cases in ​which AI agents from major developers breached systems at other companies during testing, after Anthropic said last week that some of its models ⁠hacked three companies, and OpenAI disclosed that an AI agent breached the startup Hugging Face. AI models have been going rogue in tests – how worried should we be? Read more Meta said a misconfiguration by the independent testing company Irregular inadvertently allowed one ⁠of its models internet access during an evaluation, adding that it was investigating the incident. The model “exploited ​a security vulnerability in a third-party service, ‌in a manner similar ‌to previously reported instances with other companies”, Meta said in a statement. Earlier in the day, ‌The Information, citing sources, reported that Meta’s Muse Spark 1.1 model, which it has touted as its most capable model for real-world coding and agentic tasks, breached an unidentified company and altered its internal systems. A spokesperson for Irregular told Reuters the incident was the “exact same evaluation-environment issue that was already disclosed by Anthropic last week” and that it did ‌not involve a “sandbox escape or a sophisticated cyber action”. “There are no current open issues. Irregular is developing a white paper to share best ​practices for containment and securely running cyber evaluations,” Irregular said. The incidents revealed by Meta and Anthropic were due to mistakes that inadvertently gave their models access to the open internet. That contrasts with OpenAI, whose AI agent independently exploited a novel vulnerability to reach the internet during cyber testing. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Preview latest after newsletter promotion Even ⁠so, the breaches highlight how AI has increased threats to cybersecurity and ​how developers can struggle ​to keep the capabilities of their ​models contained. The disclosures are likely to intensify a US government push to ​better manage AI security ‌risks at a ​time when Anthropic and ​OpenAI are racing to release more capable systems ahead of their planned public listings. Prominent leaders at these labs have called for a slowdown to address risks first.
