Photograph: Posed by models; Solskin/Getty Images AI (artificial intelligence) Danish pupils will have to orally defend essays in attempt to combat AI cheating Government introduces several measures, including monitoring of computers, for pupils aged 16 to 19 Europe live – latest updates Miranda Bryant Nordic correspondent Thu 6 Aug 2026 07.58 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 09.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Danish teenagers will have to make an oral defence of their written essays to combat AI cheating, the government has announced. Pupils aged 16 to 19 at upper secondary school (known in Denmark as gymnasiet ) will also be encouraged to do written assignments at school under controlled conditions, including monitoring of their computer screens, rather than at home. The measures, announced on Thursday as pupils prepare to go back to school next week after the summer break, will come into immediate effect after Magnus Heunicke, the country’s education minister, demanded urgent action. “Unfortunately, we have a problem with AI cheating in upper secondary schools,” he said. “Action is needed now.” AI had posed a growing challenge to teaching and exams, the education ministry said. It is hoped the new measures will help to establish clearer guidelines for when pupils are not permitted to use it. The government is also preparing a comprehensive national strategy for AI use in all schools and the wider education sector. Heunicke said he would speak to schools, teachers and students to “ensure that AI does not undermine students’ competencies, professionalism and, not least, the ability to think for themselves”. The first measure to be introduced is the oral defence of exam assignments written at home. About 9,000 upper secondary school students each year write a big assignment (known as større skriftlige opgave or SSO), which they will now have to defend orally. The ministry said it would speak to schools about the best way to do this. Upper secondary schools will also be required to use monitoring tools to oversee how computers are being used for written exams. They are required to install firewalls to filter what is available on the school network during exams and teaching. The third measure is a plea to schools to encourage pupils to do more of their written assignments at school under controlled conditions, to “follow the students’ work process, provide relevant feedback and create a more accurate basis for assessment”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day Preview latest after newsletter promotion The ready availability of AI tools is upending education around the world for teachers and pupils, leaving governments scrambling to assess if and how they should intervene. In neighbouring Sweden, a study found that the number of students suspended or warned for unauthorised AI use rose by 688% between 2023 and 2025. The government has commissioned a review into how schools are tackling AI cheating, which will report back in April. Announcing the review, Lotta Edholm, the Swedish minister for upper secondary school, said in January: “There is no reason to turn a blind eye to cheating students. Cheating is completely unacceptable regardless of what form. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Gaza Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace issues first building contract – for a military base Exclusive: Louisiana firm awarded tender to build rudimentary outpost to house Moroccan troops Aram Roston in Washington Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump’s Board of Peace, which was set up in January to oversee the reconstruction of Gaza , has finally issued its first construction contract in the devastated territory: a project to build a rudimentary 150-person military outpost to house Moroccan troops, a source familiar with the matter told the Guardian. The contract, which has not yet been finalised, was awarded to Arkel International, a Louisiana-based firm that has previously carried out work with the US government in countries such as Iraq. The Board of Peace is chaired by the US president and led by a team that includes his son-in-law Jared Kushner and friend Steve Witkoff. In an email, a Board of Peace official said the board and a group of Palestinian technocrats installed to oversee Gaza “are in the final stages of preparing several contract awards. None have been finalised.” The Palestinian group is known as the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza . The official said “one prospective contract concerns facilities to support the international stabilisation force (ISF), which will assist in implementing the roadmap’s security and governance arrangements”. They added: “This contract will be one of many that are essential for the future of Gaza .” Trump’s Board of Peace plans to grant itself sweeping immunity, documents show Read more The award comes just days after Trump announced that Hamas had agreed to disarm, though there are considerable questions about how the group would give up its guns. Israel has opposed the plan, and increased airstrikes in Gaza after Trump’s announcement . The Guardian reported in July that the board’s original Gaza reconstruction had shrunk dramatically from an ambitious blueprint to rebuild the whole territory to a small pilot project in the south of the strip. The base now being planned is just 100 metres by 120 metres and is intended to house a contingent of Moroccan troops, who would rotate from a base in Israel, the source said. It would lie in the 60% of Gaza’s territory that the Israeli army directly controls. Israeli forces have also created a buffer zone beyond that area. The source said the base was about a mile from the Israeli border and would have a “quick extraction route” in case the small force came under attack. View image in fullscreen Donald Trump’s original grandiose vision of a reconstructed Gaza is displayed by the president at the World Economic Forum meeting at Davos on 22 January. The UN resolution authorising the Board of Peace had approved establishing an “international stabilisation force” for Gaza, and there have been varying reports on which country would provide these troops. Morocco has promised a small contingent, but the legal framework for the ISF has yet to be finalised, and it is not clear when the deployment would begin. In earlier contract plans seen by the Guardian, the 150-person base was the first phase of a plan to build a 5,000-person military base in Gaza for the ISF . This base would have included “vehicle fighting positions” and a perimeter berm – or raised defensive bank – and would have rudimentary facilities suitable for short-term deployments. The earlier contract said the first phase would consist of “tents and cots for forces to sleep, as well as chemical toilets and handwashing stations. At this phase, this is what we would consider habitable.” Trump announced in February 2025 that the US would “take over” and “own” Gaza, although the agreement that set up the Board of Peace fell short of that. At the board’s first meeting in January, Kushner unveiled a “master plan” to build “New Gaza” with an expansive waterfront city with gleaming mixed-use towers. “It could be a hope, it could be a destination. A lot of industry,” he said. At least 80% of Gaza’s buildings were damaged or destroyed in the war. Ten months after the ceasefire, most of the territory’s 2 million people are still living in makeshift and unsanitary camps. Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A burned car and building after a reported attack by Israeli settlers on the outskirts of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank. Photograph: Zain Jaafar/AFP/Getty Images US foreign policy Top Democrats accuse Trump officials over Israeli settlers’ ‘unbridled violence’ Letter says lifting of sanctions sent ‘clear message’ settlers can use deadly force in West Bank without consequences David Smith Washington bureau chief Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Senior Democrats have accused Donald Trump’s administration of giving a green light to violent Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank, warning that its policies created “a climate of impunity and unbridled violence” that endangers both Palestinians and US citizens. In a letter seen by the Guardian, a group of 19 Democratic senators and representatives call for the restoration of sanctions against extremist settlers and demand independent US investigations into the deaths of nine US citizens killed in the West Bank since 2022. The letter, signed by Massachusetts senator Elizabeth Warren among others, is addressed to Todd Blanche, the acting attorney general, Marco Rubio, the secretary of state, and Scott Bessent, the treasury secretary. It argues that Trump’s promise last year that “I will not allow Israel to annex the West Bank” has been undermined by events on the ground. “In practice,” the Democrats write, “violent settlers and the [Benjamin] Netanyahu government have proceeded to rapidly extend Israeli control over civilian populations in the region.” They urge the administration to use “all the diplomatic and economic tools at its disposal, including restoring sanctions, to end this violence and expansion of settlements”. The Democrats argue that Trump’s decision on his first day back in office to rescind sanctions imposed on more than 30 settlers and organisations linked to violence has had profound consequences. “Ending sanctions against those individuals and entities associated with West Bank extremism sent a clear message,” they write. “Settlers can use violent and deadly force with impunity against Palestinians and Americans while seizing land … and no one will face consequences.” The letter cites UN figures showing 1,835 attacks on Palestinian communities and property during 2025, the highest number since records began, and says the UN has reported that the current pace of settler attacks this year is higher than in any year on record. It highlights repeated attacks on Turmus Ayya , a Palestinian town where the majority of residents are US citizens, including the burning of a family home belonging to Americans from Massachusetts and Washington state. The elected officials also focus on what they say has become an increasingly dangerous environment for Americans. Since Trump returned to office, they write, four US citizens have been killed by Israeli settlers or security forces in the West Bank, bringing the total since 2022 to nine. The victims include the Palestinian American journalist Shireen Abu Akleh , 14-year-old Amer Mohammed Rabea , 17-year-olds Tawfic Abdel Jabbar and Mohammad Ahmed Mohammad Khdour and 20-year-old Sayfollah Musallet, as well as Omar Assad, a 78-year-old Palestinian American, and the Turkish American activist Aysenur Ezgi Eygi. The letter says the justice department “has the authority to independently investigate the killing of Americans abroad” but “has reportedly not opened investigations into any of the killings since 2025. Israel has yet to indict a single person involved in these incidents.” The Democrats also express concern over the detention of US citizens by the Israeli military including 20-year-old Sama Safi , whose access to vital medication was allegedly interrupted after her arrest, and Mohammed Ibrahim , who they say was detained for nine months while aged 15. They urge the administration to secure Safi’s immediate release and “push for the end of unjust and arbitrary detentions in the territory”. The senators and representatives argue that the violence extends beyond Palestinian communities, pointing to repeated attacks on Taybeh, described in the letter as “the last entirely Christian village in the West Bank”. Although the US ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee , described an earlier attack there as “an act of terror” and pledged that those responsible would be prosecuted, the senators and representatives note that “no one has been arrested in connection with these crimes”. Huckabee is an evangelical Christian who has supported Jewish claims on the occupied land that settlers call Judea and Samaria. The letter is signed by Warren, Ed Markey, Jeff Merkley, Patty Murray, Jack Reed, Bernie Sanders , Brian Schatz, Adam Schiff, Chris Van Hollen, Peter Welch and Ron Wyden. The House of Representatives signatories are Katherine Clark, Richard Neal, Jim McGovern, Seth Moulton, Ayanna Pressley, Jake Auchincloss, Stephen Lynch and Lori Trahan. It concludes that Israeli security forces and settlers have attacked and displaced Palestinians in the West Bank “at an unprecedented rate” since the Trump administration took office and argues that Washington’s “deference to the Netanyahu government has contributed to a climate of impunity and unbridled violence towards civilian populations and religious minorities”. It demands answers by 17 August on investigations into attacks on Americans, the lifting of sanctions and the treatment of US citizens detained by the Israeli military. Photograph: Frédéric Soltan/Corbis/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Tarun Tejpal’s acquittal in 2021 was challenged by the Goa government. Photograph: Frédéric Soltan/Corbis/Getty Images India High-profile Indian journalist jailed for 10 years for raping colleague Tarun Tejpal, ex-editor of Tehelka magazine, was initially acquitted in 2021 in case that drew nationwide attention Agence France-Press in Mumbai Thu 6 Aug 2026 07.47 EDT First published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 04.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Indian court has sentenced a high-profile former editor of an investigative news magazine to 10 years in prison after convicting him of raping a junior colleague, overturning his acquittal in a case that drew nationwide attention. Tarun Tejpal, 63, the founder and former editor of Tehelka magazine, was accused of raping a journalist in the lift of a five-star hotel in the western coastal state of Goa during an event in November 2013. He was arrested and spent seven months in jail until the supreme court granted him bail. A court in Goa acquitted Tejpal of charges including rape, sexual harassment and wrongful restraint in 2021. The government of Goa challenged the acquittal before the Bombay high court, which set aside the trial court’s verdict and sentenced him to 10 years in jail on Thursday. “He has been convicted to 10 years of rigorous imprisonment. He has been given two weeks’ time to surrender,” the police investigator Sunita Sawant, who led the case against Tejpal, told reporters. The court also ordered him to pay a £3,900 fine, he said. Tejpal, 63, said he would challenge the conviction in the supreme court. He had initially blamed the assault on “a lapse of judgement” but later alleged the case against him was part of a vendetta by the Bharatiya Janata party (BJP) government in Goa. “For the past 13 years, they have been pursuing me as a part of a political vendetta,” he said after conviction. Sawant told reporters: “This is a sentence where a girl has stood up for her rights … so this judgment is very important for women who are working in any sector.” The case emerged at a time when India’s handling of sexual assault cases was under intense scrutiny after the gang-rape and murder of a 23-year-old student on a Delhi bus in December 2012. That attack triggered nationwide protests and international outrage, and prompted the government to strengthen the country’s rape laws. Tejpal’s case severely damaged the authority and credibility of Tehelka, which had historically championed women’s rights and social justice. The magazine continues to operate under new leadership, but it has failed to regain the influence it had before the 2013 case. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Figures show 2,103 of the Prevent referrals (20%) were because of concerns over extreme rightwing ideology. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Figures show 2,103 of the Prevent referrals (20%) were because of concerns over extreme rightwing ideology. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Prevent strategy Extreme rightwing referrals to Prevent rise 20% amid record anti-terror reporting Scheme aiming to stop people turning to terrorism has 39% overall rise in referrals in year to September 2025 Rajeev Syal Thu 6 Aug 2026 07.53 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 08.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A record number of people have been referred to the government’s anti-terror programme in England and Wales, with a 39% rise over the last year, including a 20% rise in referrals for extreme rightwing ideology, according to official data released on Thursday. A total of 10,293 referrals – up from 7,408 – were made to the Prevent programme in the year to September 2025, which is the highest number since records began 11 years ago. Those referrals to the scheme, which aims to stop people turning to terrorism, involved 9,957 people suspected of extremist or violent tendencies. The rise comes after officials noted a sustained and significant increase in referrals since the Southport attack in July 2024. Axel Rudakubana, who killed three girls at a dance class and tried to murder eight others, as well as two adults, was referred to Prevent three times but his case was closed over a lack of clear ideology. The figures show 2,103 Prevent referrals were because of concerns over extreme rightwing ideology – 20% of the total – up from 1,480 in the previous 12 months. There were 860 referrals (8%) about Islamist extremism, down from 945 over the previous year. Where age was known, 11- to 15-year-olds made up the largest proportion of Prevent referrals (3,655 or 36%), followed by 16- to 17-year-olds (1,379 or 13%), the Home Office said. A total of 818 referrals (8%) related to fascination with extreme violence or mass casualty attacks, 95 (1%) were for “incel” extremism – meaning “involuntary celibate”, the term given to a strand of misogynist ideology – and 32 (0.3%) for leftwing extremism, while 353 (3%) were for multiple ideologies with no dominant ideology identified. More than half (56%) of referrals were for individuals with no identified ideology. The Home Office has also published data showing the ethnicity of referrals to the Prevent programme, although the data is incomplete because it is not mandatory on the referral form. Of 5,315 referrals, 3,600 (68%) were white, 949 (18%) were Asian, 401 (8%) were black and 365 (7%) were listed as “other”. After initial screening and assessment, Prevent referrals who are deemed at risk of radicalisation may be passed to a multi-agency “channel panel”. Chaired by local authorities, these panels determine the extent of a person’s susceptibility to radicalisation, and whether a tailored package of support is necessary to address the risk. Of the 1,100 referrals taken on as a channel case in the year to September 2025 where ethnicity was known, 835 (76%) were white, 159 (14%) were Asian, 59 (5%) were black and 47 (4%) were “other”. Nearly one in five of those referred to the programme – 18% – were autistic, while 36% had at least one mental health or neurodiversity condition listed on their Prevent record. Jacob Smith, the team leader on freedom of expression and belief at Rights & Security International (RSI), said this was a shocking number of autistic people who now have long-lasting police records under a secretive programme. “There is no excuse for unleashing this much suspicion against autistic people,” he said. The security minister, Dan Jarvis, said the record number of referrals underlined the scale of the challenge faced in protecting the public from terrorism. “The statistics also show the crucial role the programme plays in keeping the public safe, with more than 6,000 people moved away from violent ideologies that could have resulted in harm to themselves or others. “We will continue to improve Prevent to ensure it has the tools it needs to do its job of stopping people from becoming terrorists or supporting terrorism. We all have a role to play in keeping each other safe and spotting the signs of radicalisation.” Explore more on these topics Prevent strategy Counter-terrorism policy Far right UK security and counter-terrorism England Wales news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: ‘I would argue that most families are not staying up at night worried about the congressional lines across the state,’ Pia Dandiya says. Photograph: Pia Dandiya for Congress View image in fullscreen ‘I would argue that most families are not staying up at night worried about the congressional lines across the state,’ Pia Dandiya says. Photograph: Pia Dandiya for Congress Florida Florida Democrat switches districts after DeSantis redistricting shake-up Pia Dandiya, a first-time candidate, says voters care more about costs than district lines as she seeks a key open seat Richard Luscombe in Miami Thu 6 Aug 2026 09.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google What is a sanguine new congressional candidate to do when the district they thought they were running in gets torn apart by a governor’s best efforts to gerrymander his state at the president’s behest? For Pia Dandiya, a first-time candidate for the Democratic party in Florida , the answer was simple: pick up some maps, hit the road, and embrace the challenge of conquering a different part of the state. Dandiya, a professional educator dipping her toe for the first time into the often tenebrous world of electoral politics, originally declared her candidacy for Florida’s 21st congressional district, where she was mounting a long-shot campaign to unseat the Republican congressman Brian Mast, an army veteran who bills himself as “Florida’s America first fighter”. But then Ron DeSantis, the Republican governor of Florida and Donald Trump loyalist, intervened. In the consequent Democratic shuffle of candidates , she switched to Florida’s newly configured 22nd – an open seat that Democrats see as one of their best opportunities to reclaim the House majority in November. “Redistricting, to me, represents what people just hate about politics, that it seems like a solution in search of a problem instead of actually solving the problems that are keeping people up at night,” Dandiya said during a meeting over coffee in south Florida last month. “I would argue that most families are not staying up at night worried about the congressional lines across the state, but they are staying up at night wondering how they’re going to make ends meet, about whether we are handing our children a country, that we are leaving them in good hands.” Animated map showing the shifting Florida congressional district boundaries Florida’s new congressional map was one front in an extraordinary national redistricting campaign, encouraged by Trump to shore up Republicans’ narrow House majority. In Florida, DeSantis’s unprecedented mid-decade “gerrymander” was expected to put as many as four additional House seats within Republicans’ reach, giving them the edge in 24 of the state’s 28 congressional districts. With time ticking quickly towards the 18 August primary against attorney Kaysia Earley , the only other Democrat in the race, Dandiya has amassed a string of prominent endorsements. This month, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added her to its coveted Red to Blue program , signaling that national Democrats view her as a top recruit for the district. Formerly enclosed almost entirely in Palm Beach county, district 22 was expanded by DeSantis’s tinkering into a so-called Frankenstein district, stitching together an expansive, diverse swath of south Florida from populated areas on the east and west coasts with sizable rural, agricultural areas in between. The redrawn 22nd district, once a solid blue urban stronghold, now “leans Republican”, according to Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics, but in reality few are certain what to expect given its untested, divergent demographic. For Dandiya, who was born in Palm Beach county, and was a White House fellow at the education department during the Biden administration, the sudden and unexpected switch could have been overwhelming, and at the very least presented a steep learning curve. But the first-generation American, whose parents immigrated from India, and mother of a three-year-old son, said she was never going to back down from the challenge. “I’m a teacher, so I love learning, and I love diving in head first,” she said. “And all the places that are in my district are places that I have visited growing up and as an adult. I think of this the way that I think of having run a high school, it’s similar to running for office, same mission, potentially different environment. And we’re gonna give it our all.” Giving it her all has resulted in long days and higher than expected mileage crisscrossing the state, and speaking to groups of voters and at community events in cities and counties ranging from heavily Democratic to fervently Republican. There is no mystery to it, she said. Only a desire to meet people where they are, and listen to their grievances, anxieties and priorities, which she said are common to all, wherever she has traveled. View image in fullscreen Pia Dandiya speaking with voters. Photograph: Pia Dandiya for Congress Dandiya transferred over from her original district with a substantial war chest, fundraising that has now risen to more than $2m , and carries the endorsement of a significant number of Florida Democratic heavyweights, including the state chair, Nikki Fried, US congresswoman Lois Frankel and a host of state representatives and senators. She has also won the backing of Florida AFL-CIO, the state’s largest public labor union, and Emily’s List , the influential advocacy group supporting Democratic pro-choice women for elected office. “With her background in education, policy, and innovation, she is ready to bring a new kind of leadership to Washington,” Emily’s List said in its endorsement. “One focused on progress, opportunity and putting people over politics.” Dandiya said she was heartened by the reception she has received in places that only two months ago she never envisaged visiting, at least not as a congressional candidate. “The way folks have come out of the woodwork to get excited about being involved in the campaign, figuring out how they can help using their organizing brains and their connecting brains, has just been truly encouraging,” she said. “I’ve become very convinced on the campaign trail that most families want the same things for their lives, they want stability for my generation, they want safety and dignity for my parents’ generation, and they want a world of opportunity for my three-year-old son’s generation. “That rings true in district 22 as much as it does in district 21. What is on south Florida families’ minds, and across the state of Florida, I should say, is very similar. What we are experiencing is universal, it’s not Democratic, it’s not independent, it’s not Republican, it’s what all of us are experiencing, and I think that we need leaders who are willing to fight on the frontlines to put these issues front and center. “We’re on this big adventure together, and we’re going to make it happen.” Explore more on these topics Florida US midterm elections 2026 Democrats US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘We need a wartime mindset and political and policy agenda to tackle the climate emergency.’ Photograph: Alexandros Beltes/EPA View image in fullscreen ‘We need a wartime mindset and political and policy agenda to tackle the climate emergency.’ Photograph: Alexandros Beltes/EPA Opinion Climate crisis We need a wartime mindset to fight the threat of wildfires Seth Klein While many leaders compare the wildfire crisis to the second world war, governments fail to adopt the real lessons of pre-emptive wartime action Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 06.09 EDT Share A s France and Spain battle historic wildfires , comparisons to the second world war abound. “One of the continent’s biggest evacuation efforts since World War II,” reports the Associated Press . The French president, Emmanuel Macron, has called the wildfires his country’s “ most difficult situation since the second world war ”. The images crossing all our screens certainly feel war-like – emergency aircraft and black smoke fill the skies, frantic civilians seeking shelter, historic towns lying in ruins, charred forests and burned-out vehicles, exhausted and sweat-soaked emergency responders. Of course, brutal fires such as these are not restricted to France and Spain. They are hitting much of Europe. Australia has wrestled with escalating heat and devastating wildfires for years; during the fires of early 2020, the Australian government was forced to deploy the most military assets since the second world war. The US has lost entire towns to these climate-induced infernos. Brazil, Greece, Portugal, Chile, Russia, Turkey, Indonesia … all know the terror and loss of the fiery new world in which we reside. Murderous heat, an endangered food supply, decimated landscapes: embrace the Mediterranean life | George Monbiot Read more And in my own country, nearly a thousand wildfires are currently burning across Canada . In Europe , many leaders, including Macron and the Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, have made a point of linking these fires to the climate emergency; in Canada and the US, decidedly less so. Less common still are leaders and media who connect these events to their primary source – our continued combustion of oil, gas and coal (with the Guardian and a few others being notably exceptions). Yet these extreme events leave no doubt: the climate emergency is upon us. The impacts of burning fossil fuels that climate scientists have warned of for years are now here. The province of British Columbia, where I live, seems to go through this every summer now. A few years ago, I recall arriving at a holiday spot my family has visited for many summers, and coming upon a scene unlike any we had ever experienced. Residents in the area had been put on evacuation alert. All afternoon, a fleet of four water-bomber float planes scooped up water from the lake directly in front of our rental house, flying in low over the homes in formation, collecting water in their pontoons and then doubling back to the fire on the mountain ridge behind us to dump their loads. Right up until sundown, four helicopters likewise circled back to the lake in five-minute rotations, dropping enormous buckets on long cords to collect water, and then racing back to the mountain to release their cargo. This continued all week. The noise was deafening. Our peaceful family time suddenly felt more like a scene from Apocalypse Now, as we huddled together and shouted to communicate. As darkness fell, the hills behind us were dotted with flames, and the sky glowed ominously red. This is what people now nervously call “the new normal”, although it is, in truth, not normal and but a taste of things to come. These extreme weather events we are increasingly experiencing – and the warlike mood they create – represent attacks on our soil. They are a call to mobilize. Sadly, however, the emergency-level responses we have seen to date are purely defensive, rearguard actions. Our governments have not yet seen fit to adopt a wartime-scale response that pre-emptively tackles the climate crisis. Beneath the urgency of the present lies a confounding paradox: we mobilize to put fires out, but not yet to prevent them. Sure, every time events like this occur, opinions flow freely about how we need to better prepare for fires, to make our communities and forests more resilient, and to adapt to this new reality. All true. But far too absent from the public debate is a more foundational truth: until we actually mobilize to dramatically expedite the transition off fossil fuels, we will never get ahead of the curve. No amount of fire preparation and planning will save us from an escalation in the horrors we are now experiencing. If the crisis before us is indeed akin to a war – and it is; an existential peril to the people and places we love – then we must genuinely adopt a wartime-scale approach, a new mindset to mobilize all of society, galvanize our politics, fundamentally remake our economy and end our dependence on fossil fuels. The good news: the second world war experience shared by many countries can be embraced as an instructive story, a helpful – and indeed hopeful – reminder that we have done this before. We have mobilized in common cause across society to confront a civilizational threat. And in doing so, we have retooled our entire economy in the space of a few short years. We launched a war on nature. Now we are in a climate warzone | Rebecca Solnit Read more How does one know when a government is in actual emergency mode? From my studies of past mobilizations, real emergency action has certain distinct markers. Governments in genuine emergency mode: Tell the truth about the severity of the crisis and communicate a sense of urgency about the measures necessary to combat it. Spend what it takes to win. Create new economic institutions (state enterprises and public programs) to get the job done. Shift from voluntary and incentive-based policies to mandatory measures. Commit to leave no one behind. None of our governments are yet confronting the climate emergency in this manner. That time, however, will come. All emergencies start were a period of denial, or with a “phoney war” phase of half-hearted engagement (sound familiar?). But then, some sort of alchemy occurs. A combination of events (that’s what these extreme weather emergencies are) and leadership comes together to shift the zeitgeist and move us into genuine emergency mode. We need a “wartime” mindset and political and policy agenda to tackle the climate emergency. Seth Klein is a Canadian climate writer and activist, author of the book A Good War: Mobilizing Canada for the Climate Emergency , and former team lead of the Climate Emergency Unit . its military stance in the Pacific."Our military detected a short-range ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea at around 5:00 pm," South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS) has strengthened surveillance and maintained readiness for possible additional launches while sharing information with its security allies, the United States and Japan, the JCS said.North Korea has repeatedly declared itself an "irreversible" nuclear state since leader Kim Jong- un's 2019 summit with US President Donald Trump collapsed over the scope of denuclearisation and sanctions relief.Tokyo's Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi said earlier this week that Japan's military needs to be boosted with a "sense of urgency and crisis," as a new government assessment warned of growing threats from China, Russia and North Korea.In a statement carried by North Korean state media on Wednesday, Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of leader Kim Jong-un, said Pyongyang's "leadership will "most hostile" enemy.Japan's defence ministry declined to comment directly on Kim Yo-jong's Wednesday diatribe but said the country's defence capabilities "remain bare minimum" and "are not meant to https://www.dw.com/en/marine-one-helicop.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5INLL The White House said President Trump was never in harm's way Image: Eric Lee/REUTERS Advertisement The United States Federal Aviation Administration on Wednesday said it is investigating why a passenger jet was allowed to take off from Reagan Washington National Airport just as President Donald Trump's helicopter, Marine One, was approaching on Tuesday afternoon, in an apparent breach of safety rules adopted after last year's deadly midair collision near the airport. In January 2025, a collision between an American Airlines jet and an Army helicopter near Reagan National killed 67 people and led to tighter separation rules and radar-based tracking requirements. What do we know? Marine One lifted off from near the White House around 2:33 p.m. local time, headed to Joint Base Andrews ahead of a trip to Los Angeles. Reuters cited a source saying the jet involved was Envoy Air Flight 3742, an American Airlines regional jet bound for Pensacola, Florida, which departed a minute later. A second flight, Republic 4700, was rerouted as a precaution after coming within three miles (about 4.8 kilometers) of the airport. The jet was climbing above Marine One, so the two were never on a collision course. "Based on our preliminary safety review, there was momentary loss of separation after which the ​aircraft continued to move away from one another," the FAA said on Wednesday. FAA rules require aircraft near airports to stay at least 1.5 miles apart horizontally and 500 feet apart vertically. Both aircraft landed safely. White House says president was not in danger "Marine One flights are piloted by some of the best aviators in the world, and at no point was the President in harm's way," White House spokesperson Kush Desai said in a statement. The Marine Corps defended the helicopter pilots' actions. "There were no 'close calls' with the routine Marine One movement," Marine Corps spokesperson Capt. Jacob Sugg said in an email to the Associated Press. Under rules adopted after last year's crash, Reagan National is supposed to pause takeoffs and landings whenever a helicopter is on a conflicting route. But sources told Reuters controllers did not halt commercial flights on Tuesday as required. The National Transportation Safety Board said it would investigate, and the FAA said it plans to convene its own safety review. A 37-year-old mother and her two-year-old child were killed in the February 2025 attack, while more than 40 people were injured. What did the court decide about the Munich attack The Higher Regional Court in the Bavarian capital also found that the 25-year-old Afghan national bore a particularly serious degree of guilt, making an early release less likely. The court found that N. deliberately drove into the demonstration from behind. Presiding judge Michael Höhne described the scene as "a scene of devastation" stretching 12 meters (about 40 feet) across and 23 meters long. The court convicted N. of two counts of murder and 23 counts of attempted murder, one more attempted murder count than federal prosecutors had sought. He was also convicted of 19 counts of dangerous bodily harm and three counts of intentional bodily harm. The sentence matched the demand from federal prosecutors. The defense had called for a 15-year prison term and for N. to be placed in psychiatric care. Prosecutors said the attack appeared to have been driven by a complex mix of motives, including religious and political factors, loneliness and diffuse fears. N. did not explain his motive during the trial. https://www.dw.com/en/germany-arrests-uk.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5INZK The investigation was being carried out under the auspices of a new national centre to coordinate defences against "hybrid attacks" Image: Hendrik Schmidt/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement German authorities have arrested a Ukrainian man suspected of spying on a defense company in Bavaria to prepare possible acts of sabotage. Investigators suspect he took photographs of the premises of a Bavarian defense company in June and passed them to handlers working for a foreign intelligence service. What do we know about the case so far? The 33-year-old was detained in the eastern state of Thuringia on Sunday and is now in pretrial detention, Munich prosecutors and Bavaria's State Criminal Police Office said on Thursday . A Munich court issued an arrest warrant on Monday and the suspect is now being held in pre-trial detention in Bavaria. Authorities described the man as a so-called "low-level agent," a term used for people recruited by foreign intelligence services to carry out relatively simple tasks. Prosecutors said he was suspected of acting as an agent for sabotage purposes. The arrest followed cooperation between security and intelligence agencies coordinated through Germany's recently established Joint Center for Countering Hybrid Threats , known as GAZ-Hybrid. Authorities did not identify the foreign intelligence service allegedly involved and said no further details could be released while the investigation continues. German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt had also described the incident as a "new quality of threat" and a possible "hybrid attack scenario," an assessment with which Fricke agreed. Unlike previous drone incidents, the danger is no longer limited to a possible collision with an aircraft or damage caused by the drone itself, the Dresden University of Technology professor told Germany's DPA news agency. An explosive device significantly raises the potential risk, Fricke said. Fricke said investigators now needed to establish where the drone came from, how it entered the airport's restricted airspace undetected and why it was only discovered on the runway. They should also examine how reliably existing security systems can detect small multicopter drones, he said. If investigators confirm a deliberate attempted attack, the incident would show that Germany is still not good enough at detecting such small objects around critical infrastructure , Fricke said. Radar, laser, camera and infrared systems can already be combined to detect drones at an early stage, while algorithms can help predict their flight paths. "The developments are progressing well at prototype level, but implementation on the market and at facilities needs to happen faster," Fricke said. https://www.politico.eu/article/strait-o.text: Negotiations between Iran and Oman on delineating a shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz have reached the final stage, the Iranian Foreign Ministry confirmed on Wednesday. The shipping lane would primarily lie within Iranian territorial waters, with parts extending into Omani waters. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei told journalists that “the geographical coordinates of the proposed maritime route have been agreed upon by both sides,” adding that the bilateral process was “professional” and “forward-moving.” Advertisement Advertisement U.S. President Donald Trump announced last weekend that Tehran had asked Washington to hold off any attack on Iran due to the pending agreement on the strait. “This would include the Immediate, Complete, and Total OPENING OF THE HORMUZ STRAIT, and an end to Iran’s nuclear threat,” Trump wrote on Truth Social . The U.S. reimposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports on July 14 after hostilities between the two countries resumed. The blockade has since become one of the main sticking points in ceasefire negotiations, with Tehran insisting it must be lifted as part of any broader agreement. The strait remains closed as a result of the military strikes launched by the U.S. and Israel, Baqaei maintained in his remarks.

https://www.politico.eu/article/gabriel-.text: PARIS — Former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal is the latest in a string of French presidential candidates allegedly targeted by a Russian disinformation campaign. Attal, the candidate of President Emmanuel Macron's Renaissance party, said on Thursday he had been "a victim" of an electoral "interference" attempt originating from Russia, and that he expected such "destabilization efforts" to increase ahead of France's April 2027 election. Viginum, the country's agency for fighting online disinformation, confirmed it had detected the operation against Attal and attributed it "with a high level of confidence" to "pro-Russian" disinformation tactics. Advertisement Advertisement Former Prime Minister Édouard Philippe, who is also running for president, was the first to be reportedly targeted last week, before center-left parliamentarian Raphaël Glucksmann, who is expected to run, shared that he had been targeted by a "Russian operation" on Monday. Attal said on RTL radio on Thursday the smear campaign against him consisted of falsified news reports about his health and policy proposals, which copied the branding of French news outlets. "Russia wants to steal the election from the French," he said. A 2024 report from Viginum identified a similar "pro-Russian campaign" known as "Matriochka," which involved news and media reports impersonating well-known French outlets. "Combating foreign interference and protecting our democratic framework are a priority," current Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu posted online on Wednesday. "Several instances of foreign interference targeting candidates have already been detected, and in each case, the individuals were immediately notified."

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwym.text: Image source, Telegram/Crimeanwind Image caption, Huge plumes of smoke seen rising in the skies from the site where the Slavneft-Yanos oil refinery in Russia is located By Jaroslav Lukiv Published 6 August 2026, 12:35 BST Updated 1 hour ago Ukraine said it has hit two oil refineries in multiple strikes deep inside Russia with patrol boats and other vessels in the Black Sea also hit. President Volodymyr Zelensky said the Bashneft-Novoil and Slavneft-Yanos refineries were struck in the attacks aimed at limiting oil revenues Moscow "uses to finance" its war. Yaroslavl regional governor Mikhail Evraev said Slavneft-Yanos was on fire after what he called the "largest enemy drone attack". He said four people were injured. Meanwhile, Ukraine said at least 11 people were killed in Russian attacks, and the southern city of Kherson reported a total blackout. Russia said it targeted fuel, energy and transport facilities. In Odesa, no-one is safe from Russia's new Black Sea strikes Published 8 hours ago After deadly Kyiv strike, Ukraine warns interceptor shortage is costing lives Published 19 hours ago Both Russia and Ukraine have in recent weeks intensified attacks on major cities, energy facilities and warehouses, as the vast front line remains virtually static and all mediation efforts to end the war have brought no breakthrough. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Zelensky said on Thursday that the struck Bashneft-Novoil refinery in Russia's Bashkortostan republic was about 1,300km (808 miles) from the Ukrainian border, whereas Slavneft-Yanos was almost 700km (435 miles) away. The Ukrainian president also said that "two military patrol boats and shadow fleet vessels were hit" in the Black Sea, referring to tankers used by Russia to illegally export sanctioned oil. "Russia must choose peace," Zelensky said, adding that Ukrainian attacks were "strengthening chances for diplomacy". Evraev said 93 drones were shot down over Yaroslavl region overnight. "Falling debris hit the oil refinery's storage tanks. Emergency services are working to extinguish the fire," he said. BBC Verify confirmed multiple videos and images shared on social media showing huge smoke plumes rising from the refinery. In one of the verified images there appear to be at least four fires at the site. Energy-generating infrastructure in Yaroslavl has been targeted a number of times by Ukraine. The authorities in Bashkortostan have not publicly commented on the reported Ukrainian attack on the Bashneft-Novoil refinery on 5 August. Image source, DSNS Ukraine Image caption, Private residential houses were hit in Russia's overnight drone attack on Ukraine's north-eastern town of Balakliya, local officials said In Ukraine, three people were killed in the town of Balakliya, Kharkiv region, in an overnight Russian drone attack, the country's state emergencies service DSNS said. It said private residential houses were targeted, with fires reported in two buildings. Kharkiv regional head Oleh Synehubov later said that another two people were killed when drones attacked the train station in Lozova. Another eight people were injured. Later on Thursday, five people were killed in Russian strikes on the central Dnipropetrovsk region, local officials said. In the south, the entire city of Kherson is now without electricity after a "critical infrastructure facility" was hit overnight, regional head Oleksandr Prokudin said. In Ukraine's Black Sea port of Odesa, one person was killed when Russia hit two dry cargo ships. Meanwhile, the Russian military said its forces intercepted or shot down 605 Ukrainian drones overnight over a number of regions. In its latest operational update, the military said it struck Ukraine's fuel, energy and transport facilities, as well as drone storage sites. Beállítom Bruttó 322 800 forint volt Lázár János júliusi fizetése. A Fidesz országgyűlési képviselője továbbra is kerüli a parlamentet, a júliusi szavazások több mint kilencven százalékát kihagyta. Forsthoffer Ágnes májusban még nem büntette a hiányzásokat , júniustól azonban bekeményített . Ha egy képviselő a szavazások több mint negyedéről igazolatlanul hiányzik, akkor a házelnök az igazolatlan távolmaradás mértékével megegyező módon csökkentheti az érintett tiszteletdíját. Ezt Lázár most a saját bőrén is megtapasztalhatta. A fideszes képviselőnek azonban még így szerencséje van, mert az országgyűlési törvény alapján nem vonták le a fizetése kilencven százalékát, hanem a minimálbért megkapta. Mondhatnánk, hogy így legalább első kézből megtapasztalja, hogyan lehet ma Magyarországon minimálbérből megélni, de ez nem igaz. A júniusi vagyonnyilatkozata szerint a képviselői tiszteletdíja mellett havonta több millió forint bevétele van a földjei bérbeadásából, és milliókat kapott az azóta állami kézbe került Jövő Nemzedék Földje Alapítvány kuratóriumi elnökeként is. Lázárnál is kevesebb fizetést utaltak ki Szijjártó Péternek, aki a hónap közepén lemondott a mandátumáról, és a kínai BYD-hoz igazolt. A volt külügyminiszter a hónap első felében egyetlen szavazásra sem ment be, de azért bruttó 256 554 forint így is járt neki. A júliusi nagy hiányzók között volt a fideszes Kovács Sándor és a tiszás Balatincz Péter, ám az ő igazolásukat elfogadta az Országgyűlés elnöke. Utóbbi egészségügyi okokból, kórházi kezelés miatt hagyott ki több ülésnapot, tudtuk meg a Tisza-frakciótól. Nem csökkentette Forsthoffer a szavazások 55 százalékáról hiányzó fideszes Kocsis Máté és KDNP-s Máthé Zsuzsa tiszteletdíját, mint ahogy Orbán Anitáét sem, aki a szavazások 52 százalékát hagyta ki a miniszteri teendői miatt. Lázár és Szijjártó mellett három képviselő lehetett csalódott a fizetésnapon. A júliusi szavazások 62 százalékáról távol maradó Orbán Balázs bruttó 848 ezer forinttal kapott kevesebbet, mint ami a törvény szerint járt volna neki. A Fidesz korábbi kampányfőnökének bruttó 1,5 millió forint volt a júliusi fizetése, ám az vigasztalhatja, hogy hamarosan EP-képviselő lesz, és Brüsszelben ennek a többszörösét keresi majd. Pócs János és Hankó Balázs a júliusi szavazások körülbelül 30 százalékát hagyta ki, de ennél jóval nagyobb mértékben csökkentette az ő fizetésüket a házelnök. A beépített kamerás Ray-Ban szemüveggel villogó Pócs bruttó 2,34 millió forint helyett csak 1 milliót, az NKA-ügyben magyarázkodó Hankó pedig bruttó 2,88 millió helyett csak 1,64 millió forintot kapott a parlamenti adatbázis szerint. Megkérdeztük az Országgyűlés Hivatalát és a két érintett képviselőt, hogy mi az oka az eltérésnek, de cikkünk megjelenéséig nem kaptunk választ. A sok parlamenti hiányzás az alakuló ülés óta visszatérő kérdés. „A munkahelyünket tisztelni kell, ahol a választók bizalmából, őket képviselve dolgozunk” – fogalmazott egy Facebook-posztjában Forsthoffer, és az átláthatóság érdekében elrendelte, hogy a parlament oldalán kereshető módon tegyék közzé, hogy ki mennyit hiányzik a szavazásokról. Májusban még nem alkalmazott retorziót a hiányzókkal szemben, de júniusban már nem fogadta el az indoklás nélküli hiányzásokat, és csökkentette több képviselő fizetését. „Nem szeretném minősíteni a megjelölt okokat, vagy megkérdőjelezni azok valódiságát. Egy bizonyosan látszik: az elmúlt időszakban elromlott az erkölcsi iránytű” – írta a házelnök azokról az indoklásokról, amiket a hiányzóktól kapott az első hónapban. Júliusban Forsthoffer és az összes képviselő fizetése csökkent, miután az Országgyűlés megszavazta a Tisza Párt javaslatát a parlamenti költségek megvágásáról. Van olyan képviselő, aki csak 10 százalékkal kapott kevesebbet, de például Magyar Péter és több képviselő tiszteletdíja 40 százalékkal, bruttó 873 ezer forinttal lett kevesebb. A képviselő tiszteletdíj júliusban már csak bruttó 1,3 millió forint volt, de ennél több fizetés jár a különböző parlamenti tisztségekért és bizottsági feladatokért. Táblázatunkban összeszedtük, hogy miként csökkent a képviselők fizetése a júniusban elfogadott törvénymódosítás után: tisztség 2026. június 2026. július csökkenés mértéke Országgyűlés elnöke 5 892 718 Ft 3 810 625 Ft 35% Országgyűlés alelnöke 4 364 976 Ft 3 142 783 Ft 28% jegyző 3 710 230 Ft 2 880 885 Ft 22% frakcióvezető 4 364 976 Ft 3 470 156 Ft 20% frakcióvezető-helyettes 3 710 230 Ft 3 142 783 Ft 15% bizottsági elnök 3 710 230 Ft 3 142 783 Ft 15% bizottsági alelnök 3 273 732 Ft 2 880 885 Ft 12% törvényalkotási bizottság tagja 3 055 483 Ft 2 618 986 Ft 14% két állandó bizottság tagja 3 055 483 Ft 2 618 986 Ft 14% egy állandó bizottság tagja 2 618 986 Ft 2 357 087 Ft 10% képviselő 2 182 488 Ft 1 309 493 Ft 40% A képviselők ezen felül rengeteg egyéb juttatásra is jogosultak, ezek mértékét ugyancsak jelentősen szűkítették a törvénymódosítással. A lakás- vagy szállodahasználat költsége 31 százalékkal, az irodabérletre fordítható költségek 52 százalékkal, a képviselők munkáját segítő alkalmazottakra fordítható keret pedig 30 százalékkal csökkent. http://global.chinadaily.com.cn/a/202607.text: Search HOME CHINA WORLD BUSINESS LIFESTYLE CULTURE TRAVEL WATCHTHIS SPORTS OPINION REGIONAL FORUM NEWSPAPER MOBILE Home World Europe UK's attitude toward Brexit changing Ten years on, Britons increasingly see the decision to leave the EU as a mistake Ten years after Britons voted to leave the European Union, a broad consensus has emerged that Brexit has weakened the United Kingdom's economy and international influence, even as the prospect of reversing it remains politically remote. The reevaluation of the nation's decision to leave the bloc has set up the tantalizing prospect of the UK eventually rejoining the EU, a possibility that gained a foothold when Andy Burnham took over as the UK's new prime minister on July 20. Burnham, a believer in the importance of the UK being part of the bloc, has ruled out an immediate rerunning of the 2016 referendum that precipitated the country's exit. But it seems highly likely he will take the country closer to the bloc than it has been at any time in the past decade. And the relations between Brussels and London took a step forward this week when European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen messaged Burnham to say she looked forward to working with him for the "prosperity of people on both sides of the (English) Channel". She added in a post on X: "Congratulations, dear Andy Burnham … I look forward to working with you to strengthen the EU-UK partnership." Antonio Costa, president of the European Council, added: "I look forward to continuing to further deepen our cooperation for the benefit of our citizens and businesses. The United Kingdom and the European Union are stronger together." While few people expect the UK and the EU to remarry in the short-term after such an acrimonious divorce, experts say many of the warnings raised by the Remain campaign back in 2016 have largely materialized, while several key promises made by anti-EU Brexit supporters — including stronger economic growth and tighter control over immigration — have failed to deliver in the way that was expected. "There is now a broad consensus that Brexit has inflicted serious economic damage, though not as catastrophic as the more alarmist Remainers predicted," said Vince Cable, who served as the UK's business secretary from 2010 to 2015. Cable attributed the losses primarily to weaker goods exports caused by new regulatory barriers, lower levels of business investment, and reduced exports of financial and professional services to the EU. Colin Ellis, head of economic research at Moody's Analytics, echoed Cable's assessment, saying the UK economy is "around 6 percent permanently smaller" as a result of leaving the bloc, and that it would not fully recover, even if the country were to rejoin. "The fundamental lesson here is that it is a bad idea to deliberately create barriers and frictions between yourself and your biggest trading partners," Ellis said. At the same time, analysts stressed that Brexit has not produced either the economic collapse predicted by opponents or the sweeping benefits promised by supporters. Iain Begg, a professorial research fellow at the European Institute of the London School of Economics and Political Science, said: "Brexit has been neither the 'liberation' that Leave supporters thought they were voting for, nor the disaster that some on the Remain side claimed it would be. There is, nevertheless, a broad consensus that it has been damaging for the UK economy and that few of the promised benefits have been realized." Mike Hawes, chief executive officer of the UK's Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders, said Brexit has brought additional costs, complexity, and regulatory difficulties, on top of customs checks. Despite slowed economic growth for the UK and increased complexity for traders, some gains have emerged from greater regulatory autonomy, including in biotech and data-driven industries, experts noted. "If there has been a benefit, we think about what the UK has done in terms of trade deals. It's been able to sign trade deals relatively quickly," said Hawes. Cable echoed that point, saying some trade agreements have been signed, including the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership. However, Cable said the failure to secure a comprehensive trade agreement with the United States has been one of the biggest disappointments for Brexit supporters, with disagreements over food standards and technological sovereignty. Changing face of immigration Immigration has also remained a politically contentious issue. In the past decade, while migration to the UK from Europe has declined, net migration from other regions has increased sharply. "The most striking consequence was the total failure to rein in immigration after Brexit," Ellis said, arguing that the failure has reinforced perceptions among some voters that key promises of the Leave campaign were not fulfilled. Ellis described the current state of politics in the UK as more ideological and fractious than before, making it harder than it previously was to address challenges, ranging from geopolitical uncertainty to growing fiscal pressures. Before and immediately after the 2016 referendum, most forecasts suggested Brexit would reduce overall immigration. The Home Office, for example, estimated that the post-Brexit system would reduce work-related migration by around 40,000 people per year. What happened instead was more complex. Following the introduction of a new UK immigration system in January 2021, net migration rose sharply, reaching record levels in 2023, when net migration peaked at a historical high of 944,000. Data from the UK's Office for National Statistics suggest that total net migration fell after 2023, and it was 171,000 in 2025. Jonathan Portes, a professor of economics and public policy at King's College London, said that leaving the EU changed the composition of migration flows dramatically, but did not materially alter the balance between labor demand, demographic pressures, and political constraints. "Governments need targets," he said in his article The Impact of Brexit on Immigration to the UK. "But the emotional center of the debate has moved. The increasingly explicit concern is not just how many people come, but who comes, who leaves, and who counts as part of the nation." He added: "This is also why falling net migration has not depoliticized immigration … Public concern is being driven less by statistics than by a broader sense of disorder, asylum politics, visible demographic change and distrust of government." According to the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, the sharp rise in net migration after Brexit was driven by an increase in non-EU citizens coming to the UK, following policy liberalizations made by the Conservative Party government of the day. Indian nationals were, by far, the largest nationality coming to the UK, accounting for 17 percent of overall immigration, said the institute. Parallel future ahead Public opinion has also shifted since 2016 and a majority of Britons now regard Brexit as a mistake, although support for formally rejoining the EU has yet to translate into a major political movement. According to a report by the think tank UK in a Changing Europe, there has been a clear and consistent majority of voters in favor of rejoining the EU since 2022. On average, across polling this year, 60 percent are in favor of rejoining while 40 percent would choose to stay out, it said. Compared with previous governments, former UK prime minister Keir Starmer pursued a more pragmatic approach toward Brussels, while ruling out a return to the single market, which left limited room for substantial economic gains. "The tone has changed since the hostility when Boris Johnson was prime minister, and a closer relationship, though falling short of membership, is being developed," said Begg. The most realistic areas for deeper cooperation include around food standards, youth mobility, security and defense, said to Cable. But the EU increasingly views British efforts as "cherry-picking", rather than a comprehensive reset, he added. "There is a broad acceptance that this approach is too piecemeal, too slow, and too modest," he said. Ellis said recent agreements on sanitary standards and defense cooperation were helpful but unlikely to generate significant benefits. Greater integration in services trade could produce larger gains, he added, although such reforms remain politically difficult. "Given the challenges the EU itself still faces in establishing a genuinely single market for services among its member states, this prospect (of integration with UK in services trade) is highly unlikely," Ellis added. "With British politics so fractious — there is a significant likelihood of a hung parliament after the next election — the EU is likely to be cautious in agreeing to any new relationship with the UK." Looking further ahead, Begg argued that historians are likely to regard Brexit as "a strategic blunder by the UK, motivated by short-term political tactics aimed at curbing populists". Csaba Moldicz, head of the Center for International Economy at Mathias Corvinus Collegium, Budapest, said Brexit altered the legal and institutional framework in which UK businesses operated, and that a new strategy was needed. "The UK did not exploit the newly acquired freedom to pursue an independent trade policy, nor was it able to take full advantage of the growth of Asia's emerging economies, particularly China. I believe that this represents a strategic miscalculation," Moldicz said. For now, despite growing recognition of its economic costs, Brexit appears set to remain a settled — if contested — feature of the UK's political landscape. Some options, such as applying to rejoin the EU by opening accession negotiations, or applying to join its single market and customs union, are on the table for UK politicians, experts said, but there is no guarantee the EU would accept a UK request. Otherwise, the UK could "just muddle along and accept that Brexit is a mistake, but irreversible, and try to maximize the new areas of regulatory freedom", Cable added. Contact the writers at xingyi@chinadaily.com.cn. Wang Mingjie contributed to the story. (Photo: Steven Ferdman / Getty Images) Dive Deeper Speed Read Summary Listen Dive Deeper In the weeks following the unprecedented and illegal June 30 deadline imposed by reportedly foreign-funded hate groups like March and March, the afrophobia that South Africa has become a global pariah for has simmered on. It was the urgent topic of this yearâs Winter Seminar, organised by former president Kgalema Motlantheâs foundation, titled âDialogue Among Equalsâ. The event on Thursday, 23 July 2026 in Sandton, Johannesburg, was massively oversubscribed, indicating the level of interest in what SAâs leaders â Department of International Relations and Cooperation Minister Ronald Lamola, former deputy finance minister and presidentâs special envoy Mcebisi Jonas, Justice Minister Mmamoloko Kubayi and Motlanthe among them â had to say in response. âThat the whole country, the whole state machinery, even the whole fiscal structure of government was redirected because a couple of populist non-state actors demanded that 30 June should be the deadline for foreigners [to leave the country], says something about the state of the state,â Jonas said. On 22 June, Acting Police Minister Firoz Cachalia announced that his department would redirect R600-million in state resources to countering anti-immigrant unrest in and around the false flag operation carried out nationally by the hate group, March and March. Violent incidents By that time, several migrants had been killed and injured in afrophobic attacks, and many so-called foreign-owned businesses had been targeted. Over the following weeks, hundreds more violent incidents were reported, as mobs marched in townships and peri-urban areas across the country, in some cases moving door to door, harassing and displacing families. âCitizens of a sovereign nation are entitled to expect that borders will be managed competently and fairly,â said Jonas. â[But] the deterioration of parts of our cities, the collapse of public services, persistent unemployment and an economy that has failed to generate enough opportunities are the result of policy failures accumulated over many years. They were not created by migrants. SAâs economic crisis is the product of weak growth, poor governance, inadequate education outcomes, infrastructure failures and structural inequality. If every foreign national left the country tomorrow, those problems would remain. In many respects they would become worse.â He quoted the Hungarian academic Frank Furedi, who popularised the phrase the âpolitics of fearâ, and its purpose of weakening social trust. âWhen people see others primarily as threats â whether criminals, extremists, foreigners, disease carriers or sources of offence â social solidarity declines. The result has been a profound turn toward identity politics, in which tribe, religion, race, language and birthplace have become the boundaries of belonging. It is a politics that sorts people into competing camps of insiders and outsiders, and in so doing redefines the nation and challenges democratic ideals of diversity, inclusiveness and egalitarian societies,â said Jonas. We must reinvent not only an economics of inclusion, but a politics of inclusion and a democracy strong enough to defeat those who traffic in anger and fragmentation. That is the SA our children deserve. That is the Africa we all deserve, and that is the future we must have the courage to build. âWithout courage, we will go down,â he said. The Kgalema Motlanthe Foundation Winter Seminar has become a popular forum for dialogue about SA and Africaâs most pressing issues. Speakers railed against the notion that belonging should be determined by tribe or birthplace. âIn SA we need to be alert to the dangers of a politics of ethnic and group division, when political identity is bound up with economic aspirations,â said Jonas. Malign outside networks of funders âWe are witnessing the operation of malign outside networks of funders, organisers and social media operators of bot farms. They bus protesters across provinces. They amplify outrage online. They manufacture narratives designed to pit neighbours against neighbours, communities against communities, and countries against countries.â It was an indication that foreign intelligence agencies were becoming the most important authors of national histories, Jonas said. âWe do not know whether their agenda is to boost the prospects of local political groups, or just to destabilise SA and isolate us from our neighbours. âWhat we can say is that these attempts to direct the blame for SAâs problems at foreign nationals are fundamentally mistaken.â DM Maverick News xenophobia Afrophobia March and March anti-immigrant unrest non-state actors impact Comments Loading your accountâ¦ Scroll down to load comments...
