Europe Romanian health workers in national walkout over government health cuts Doctors, nurses and other healthcare workers across Romania staged a two-hour warning strike July 20. The action affected hundreds of hospitals and healthcare facilities between 9 and 11a.m., with only emergency services and around one-third of normal medical activity maintained. The SANITAS Federation members protest the government’s proposed salary legislation, which they say entrenches pay inequalities across the health sector. They also oppose a freeze on recruitment that has intensified already chronic understaffing. The health workers warn that the government’s austerity measures threaten both their livelihood and patient care. It is reported that an indefinite nationwide general strike will follow on July 28 if the government refuses to meet their demands. Ancillary staff at London hospital walk out over parity claims and union recognition Dozens of ancillary staff working in catering, cleaning and security for outsourcing firm ISS at Chase Farm Hospital in Enfield, north London began a three-day walkout on Wednesday. This follows a stoppage July 15-17. The GMB union members voted by a 95 percent majority for the action. They are seeking parity of terms and conditions with directly employed National Health Service (NHS) staff. They ae also seeking union recognition. Further stoppages are planned if there is no resolution. Strikes planned at UK rail company over safety fears Rail staff working for East Midlands Railway (EMR) are set to walk out on August 1 and the following two Saturdays. EMR runs express services from the East Midlands area of England to London. It also covers Yorkshire and the North West region of England. The Rail Maritime and Transport (RMT) union members plan the stoppages over safety fears following the introduction in April of a fleet of 810 passenger trains. Announcing the stoppages, the RMT said, “EMR has been sending trains into service that are likely to fail and require a full reset which leaves the train with no active safety systems including loss of communication between train drivers, dispatchers and trackside which has occurred at least three times in the last week alone.” EMR driver Shaun Burton was killed June 19 when his Corby to London St Pancras train ran into the back of a stationary train. The International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees has called for an independent worker-led inquiry to prevent another disastrous incident. Strike of housing association workers in London over pension attacks Staff working for the East End Homes (EEH) housing association in London’s Tower Hamlets borough were on strike Monday through Wednesday. They work as administrators, caretakers and housing officers responsible for around 4,000 homes. The Unison union members voted by a 100 percent majority for the action in June. They are opposed to plans by the housing association to move the workers from their current Defined Benefit pension scheme to an inferior Defined Contributions scheme. It would mean workers losing thousands of pounds a year pension income. Staff were assured their pension scheme would be protected when they were transferred from Tower Hamlets Council to EEH back in 2002. The staff, who held six days of stoppages in early July, are set to walk out July 27-31. Belgian firefighters in Brussels strike over staff shortages and poor working conditions Firefighters in Brussels, Belgium held a 24-hour strike from July 21, the country’s National Day, to July 22, protesting staff shortages, worsening working conditions and planned restructuring. The General Union of Public Services members oppose proposed staffing cuts, the removal of emergency vehicles, compulsory personnel transfers, changes to staff benefits and the introduction of an annual evaluation system, which they say will intensify pressure on already overstretched crews. The firefighters’ action follows strikes on December 31, 2025 and February 12 this year over chronic staff shortages. There are a shortfall of 200 full-time equivalent firefighters, while the number of call-outs is increasing. Firefighters insist that adequate staffing and resources are essential to guarantee public safety. Engineers for the Republic of Ireland Electricity Supply Board strike for overtime pay Around 20 engineers employed in the Engineering and Major Projects division of the Irish state-owned Electricity Supply Board (ESB) began industrial action July 15, imposing a ban on non-emergency out-of-hours work. The engineers are responsible for designing, upgrading and maintaining key electricity infrastructure across the Republic of Ireland. The Unite union members demand overtime pay commensurate with fellow workers on premium overtime rates. The engineers receive an “excess hours” allowance which was frozen from 2001 to 2025 and has conditions attached, which they say does not pay them for hours actually worked. The industrial action will remain in place until the ESB management addresses the disputed pay arrangements and the engineers' concerns. Middle East West Bank protest over planned school demolition Palestinian teachers supported by students held a protest outside their primary school in the Israeli-occupied West Bank on July 15. They were protesting plans by Israeli defence forces to demolish the school, which was built in 2016 and serves 190 students. Israel has carried out a series of such demolitions of Palestinian homes and infrastructure over recent years, often citing lack of building permits. Protests in Yemen over deteriorating living conditions Last week saw protests in several southern Yemeni governorates. The protests were in response to deteriorating service and economic conditions. In particular, they are protesting the costs and provision of basic services, electricity, fuel and water. Yemen has suffered years of conflict, leaving it one of the poorest countries in the Middle East. Protests in Iraq over power shortages Residents of the central Iraq city of Najaf protested Sunday against ongoing cuts to the electricity supply. They blocked the Najaf-Kufa road and marched to the governorate and provincial council headquarters. Iraq depends on Iran for around a third of the natural gas used in its production of electricity. The ongoing attacks on Iran by the US have impacted the supply of natural gas. The Ministry of Electricity apologised in parliament for the disruption to electrify supplies citing the regional conflict as well as aging infrastructure, lack of funding and rising summer demands. Africa Health workers in Mozambique extend nationwide strike Health workers across Mozambique have extended their nationwide strike for a further 30 days. They came out against the government’s failure to address longstanding demands over wages, working conditions and the chronic lack of medicines and medical supplies in public health facilities. The action called by the United Association of Mozambican Health Workers (APSUSM) continues as a total stoppage of work in health units across the country. Workers insist the crisis in the public health system is worsening. APSUSM said hospitals and clinics remain plagued by shortages of essential medicines, equipment and basic supplies, undermining patient care and placing impossible burdens on health workers. Union leaders say the government has failed to respond adequately to repeated complaints over deteriorating conditions, prompting workers to prolong the strike despite its impact on already overstretched health services. The extension of the strike underscores the deepening crisis confronting healthcare workers in Mozambique, where low pay, poor working conditions and chronic underfunding have fuelled repeated industrial disputes. The continuing stoppage shows the workers’ determination to fight for improved conditions despite mounting pressure from the authorities. Kenyan doctors in Kisii County begin indefinite strike Doctors at Kisii County Referral and Teaching Hospital have begun an indefinite strike after repeated delays in the payment of their salaries. This follows a warning issued by the Kenya Medical Practitioners, Pharmacists and Dentists Union (KMPDU). The industrial action has severely disrupted services, affecting outpatient clinics, specialist care and other non-emergency services. Doctors withdrew their labour over what they say is the county government’s persistent failure to pay them on time. The strike follows mounting tensions between the union and Kisii County authorities. In June, KMPDU warned that doctors would progressively scale back services if salaries were not paid by agreed deadlines, arguing that chronic delays had caused severe financial hardship for health workers. The union said repeated appeals to county officials had failed to resolve the dispute, leaving doctors no alternative but to strike. The Kisii dispute is the latest involving Kenyan health workers over delayed wages, staffing shortages and the failure of national and county governments to honour agreements. Healthcare workers have increasingly turned to strikes and protests as they confront deteriorating working conditions, while patients bear the consequences of repeated disruptions to already overstretched public health services. Congolese health workers fighting Ebola come under attack, continue their dispute over pay arrears More than a dozen attacks on health facilities and medical personnel have severely disrupted efforts to contain the rapidly expanding Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo’s Ituri province. Treatment centres, burial teams and healthcare workers have come under attack from hostile groups, forcing some humanitarian organisations to withdraw staff from high-risk areas and limiting access to infected communities as the outbreak continues to spread. The deteriorating security situation has compounded an already deepening crisis for health workers. Medical staff have staged strikes over months of unpaid wages while working under hazardous conditions, with more than 100 healthcare workers infected during the outbreak. The violence, combined with staff shortages, insecurity and the absence of an approved vaccine or treatment for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, has undermined contact tracing and delayed urgently needed care. The attacks reflect the broader social and political crisis confronting workers in eastern Congo, where decades of conflict, poverty and mistrust of the authorities have fuelled hostility towards the official Ebola response. International health agencies have warned that unless the safety of healthcare workers can be guaranteed and the necessary resources provided to combat the epidemic, efforts to contain one of the country’s worst Ebola outbreaks will remain dangerously compromised. Miners’ strike in Eswatini declared illegal Workers at Maloma Colliery in Eswatini (formerly Swaziland) began strike action July 13, after rejecting the company’s proposed two-year wage offer of a cumulative 9 percent increase—5 percent in 2026 and 4 percent in 2027. The miners, members of the Amalgamated Trade Union of Swaziland, blocked access to the mine as negotiations over pay broke down. The Industrial Court declared the strike unlawful after the company filed an urgent application, ordering workers to end the stoppage and cease obstructing access to the mine. Management demanded that workers get back to work before they would consider changing their offer. The court ruling underscores the growing together of the employers and the state in Eswatini and throughout Africa. The dispute reflects growing anger among miners over their declining pay relative to rising living costs. Egyptian paper workers hold sit-down strike over unpaid wages Workers at EMAK Paper in Egypt have continued their sit-in for more than a week, demanding payment of overdue wages and improvements to working conditions. Workers say management has failed to resolve their grievances despite repeated appeals, leaving them determined to maintain their protest until their demands are met. The dispute escalated as workers accused management of attempting to wear them down rather than negotiate a settlement. The action follows other labour struggles across Egypt, including strikes and sit-ins by textile, agricultural and other industrial workers over unpaid wages, low pay and worsening conditions, reflecting growing opposition to the impact of the country’s deepening economic crisis. Despite legal restrictions and intimidation, workers in a number of sectors have continued to organise strikes and sit-ins in defence of wages, jobs and basic working conditions. Union calls off strike by Phokwane municipal workers, South Africa A strike at Phokwane Municipality, South Africa has been called off by the South African Municipal Workers’ Union (Samwu). The municipal workers issued a memorandum of demands to the municipality June 19, accusing management of failing to address salary disparities, implement upgrade of the municipality from Grade 2 to 3, appoint interns, absorb contract workers and improve skills development. Concerns were also raised about the unsafe condition of the municipal building, which could collapse at any time. Workers said they had been forced to work in hazardous conditions without adequate safety equipment. They called for provision of personal protective equipment and appropriate tools. The strike disrupted refuse collection, with residents dumping uncollected rubbish outside municipal offices and spreading litter around the streets of Hartswater last week. On July 15, the Labour Court issued an interdict ordering an end to the strike. The court ordered removal of any locks or obstructions preventing access to the municipal building, closed since July 10. The court also barred Samwu members from further strike action, including picketing, but workers continued their action, saying they would strike until their demands were met. Samwu stepped in, calling off the strike after a meeting with management on July 20. The union agreed with management that “service delivery must continue,” ordering a return to work the following day. Management have issued timelines for the issues in the memorandum and committed to implementation of agreed actions, while deferring “some matters” to “a council resolution.” Subscribe to the IWA-RFC Newsletter Get email updates on workers’ struggles and a global perspective from the International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees. http://www.sydneysun.com/news/279203599/.text: Hungary's ex-PM raises banner of revolt against Prime Minister Magyar Mohan Sinha 24 Jul 2026, 05:56 GMT+10 Hungary’s former nationalist prime minister Viktor Orbán, who lost power after 16 years in an election in April, has called on his supporters to restore democracy. Orbán said that Hungary is no longer a democratic state after the new center-right government led by Prime Minister Peter Magyar passed a constitutional amendment. Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s Tisza party has denied accusations that it is acting in an authoritarian way toward political opponents. BUDAPEST, Hungary: Hungary's former nationalist prime minister Viktor Orbán, who lost power after 16 years in an election in April, has called on his supporters to restore democracy. He said that the new government has destroyed democracy in the country. Orbán made his first strong political comments since his heavy election defeat late on July 21 through a Facebook post. He issued what he called a "Statement of Resistance" shortly after his Fidesz party said that prosecutors had searched offices where its internet servers are located. Prosecutors told Reuters in an email that the action was connected to an investigation into suspected misuse of funds and other crimes at the National Culture Fund (NKA) during Orbán's time in government. Orbán said that Hungary is no longer a democratic state after the new center-right government led by Prime Minister Peter Magyar passed a constitutional amendment. According to Orbán, this amendment ended the terms of both the president and the head of the constitutional court. Magyar's Tisza party has denied accusations that it is acting in an authoritarian way toward political opponents. The party has promised to reduce corruption, which it says was widespread under Orbán's government, as part of its effort to bring Hungary back in line with the European Union. Orbán himself faced strong criticism during his time in power over democratic standards in Hungary. His government often clashed with the European Union on issues such as the rule of law and the rights of minorities. Orbán has denied all corruption allegations. He said that a period of tyranny had begun again in Hungary. He also said that the new political system created in this way is not legitimate, and that Fidesz will use all peaceful means, both inside and outside parliament, to oppose what he described as abuse of power. Magyar's Tisza party holds a large majority in parliament, which allows it to reverse changes introduced during Orbán's time in office that Magyar says weakened democracy. The constitutional amendment ended the term of President Tamás Sulyok, stating that there had been a serious loss of public trust in him. Sulyok had been elected in 2024 by lawmakers from Orbán's Fidesz party. Parliament is expected to elect a new president soon. Magyar's Tisza party currently enjoys strong public support. A poll by the polling company Median earlier in the month showed that 60 percent of voters support Tisza, compared to 18 percent for Fidesz. Since the election, Fidesz has faced internal problems, including the resignation of its parliamentary group leader last week. http://www.europesun.com/news/279205966/.text: EU caves in on new Russia sanctions media RT.com 23 Jul 2026, 17:30 GMT+10 The bloc has been forced to approve a watered-down package, including a Greek-backed exemption that allows EU companies to transport Russian LNG The EU has relented on objections from member states, granting what one diplomat has described as an "outrageous exemption," to issue a watered-down sanctions package targeting Russia. Greece successfully lobbied to allow EU companies to continue transporting Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG) to third countries, media reports claimed on Thursday. The package, the EU's 21st since the escalation of the Ukraine conflict in February 2022, was presented by the European Commission in June. It was designed to target Russia's energy, financial, crypto, trade, and fisheries sectors, bar entry to former Russian servicemen, and phase out Russian LNG transportation by EU companies. The bloc held several failed rounds of talks on the package, which requires unanimous approval from all 27 EU member states, with a number of nations arguing that some of the proposals would harm their economic interests. Greece, which has the world's largest independent cross-trade LNG fleet by capacity, warned that banning EU shipping companies from transporting Russian LNG would harm Greek shipping interests, including Dynagas. Dynagas, one of the few European companies that operate ice-class LNG carriers capable of reaching Russia's Yamal LNG project in the Arctic, says its vessels are tied to contracts running until 2065 that predate the Ukraine conflict. It argued that the sanctions could force it to sell its fleet, weakening Europe's shipping industry while benefiting foreign competitors. Greece also reportedly warned that the measure could trigger widespread reflagging to jurisdictions where EU rules would be harder to enforce, and pushed for an indefinite exemption. According to Euractiv and Euronews, citing diplomats, under a compromise brokered by the EU's rotating presidency which is held by Ireland, ambassadorssigned offon the package on Thursday after agreeing to a renewable 12-month waiver allowing the Greek company and other EU companies to continue transporting Russian LNG, subject to annual reviews. They also approved a 12-month freeze on adjustments to the G7's $44.10-per-barrel price cap on Russian oil. Without the move, the cap would have automatically increased on Thursday under a mechanism linked to global oil prices, which Brussels reportedly opposed as it would have raised the ceiling to $58 per barrel, benefiting Russia. Watered-down deal Apart from the Greek concession, the final package is reportedly significantly diluted. A Baltic-backed proposal to ban Russians who served in the military after the escalation of the Ukraine conflict from entering the bloc was scaled back after France,Italy, and Greece pushed back. The measure now only applies to short-stay visas and narrows the criteria from general military service to direct participation in military operations. EU envoys also reportedly dropped plans to phase out Russian fish imports following resistance from Germany, Poland, and Portugal, which sought to protect domestic processors. Efforts to sanction Patriarch Kirill, the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, were also reportedly blocked after opposition from Bulgaria and Italy, ensuring his removal from the blacklist. The package, however, reportedly blacklists around 250 individuals and entities accused of supporting Russia's military operation against Ukraine, "spreading propaganda," or helping circumvent sanctions, as well as more than 600 vessels linked to the supposed 'shadow fleet', which allegedly helps Russia bypass sanctions on oil exports. It also targets Russian banks, crypto platforms, and oil traders. The final version of the package must still undergo technical revisions before being adopted by all 27 member states. Behind Brussels' 'united front' Analysts and diplomats say the long-debated package highlights growing divisions within the bloc as the sanctions increasingly clash with member states' economic interests. "There's no more low-hanging fruit, with 20 packages done," one EU diplomat told Politico. Some say the standoff exposes the fact that there was never actual unanimity on sanctions, and that former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban's departure has deprived other EU capitals of a convenient shield. For years, the scapegoating of Orban allowed other governments to hide behind Budapest while defending their own economic interests. With Peter Magyar now in office and Hungary no longer blocking the sanctions, the objections have openly surfaced. "It has been a surprise and a disappointment how many member states have stalled in their actions," Finnish MEP Ville Niinisto told Politico. Another diplomat said: "Orban was difficult, but he never actually blocked whole packages." READ MORE: Orbans exit through global eyes: Who really gains and who doesnt The package comes as the EU continues to face soaring energy costs after slashing most Russian energy imports following the escalation of the Ukraine conflict, and according to consultancy Wood Mackenzie,risksentering the upcoming heating season with its lowest gas reserves in 15 years. The bloc still imports Russian LNG, which accounts for around 14% of its supplies, even as Brussels prepares to ban purchases from January 1. The EU imported a record 9.89 million tons of LNG from Russia's Yamal project in the first half of 2026, the Financial Times reported earlier this week. Moscow has long maintained that the sanctions will not alter its political course or have a decisiveimpacton its economy, while analysts have warned that the sanctions largely backfire on those that impose them. This expansion is coupled with the company’s recent purchase of approximately 2,500 acres from the provincial land bank, which sextupled the company’s footprint to about 3,000 acres. “Securing this initial $120 million in new contracts and investment is a turning point for HFI,” said Rhiannon Iles, president of HFI Pyrotechnics. “The Township of Edwardsburgh Cardinal’s land bank, completed this past April, made the land available for us to grow, and we are investing to develop it with new buildings, equipment, and utilities. Photo by John Lawless / The Brockville Recorder and Times HFI celebrated this milestone with a groundbreaking event Thursday morning, attended by local dignitaries such as MP Michael Barrett, MPP Steve Clark and Edwardsburgh Cardinal Mayor Tory Deschamps. The groundbreaking signified the beginning of the construction of a new laboratory for quality assurance, which aims to help with innovation and research and development. “This expansion is incredibly important to our council, not only because it brings high-quality, good-paying jobs to our community, but because it transforms lands that sat unproductive for far too long into a hub of opportunity,” said Deschamps. “We are proud to support HFI’s continued success and look forward to the long-term benefits this and other future projects will bring to Edwardsburgh Cardinal.” Read More Prescott-area company helped Artemis II return to Earth HFI Pyrotechnics buys large parcel from provincial land bank HFI said the $120-million investment is the first phase of a five-year growth plan, with more expansion news to follow. Article content Over the next one to two years, HFI will invest in new buildings, civil work, and heavy equipment across the site. That work includes the land bank acquisition; a major project on the production floor to increase capacity for marine location markers with new industrial equipment to raise output; hydro and bandwidth upgrades; and, construction across the site that will include new buildings, access roads, and supporting infrastructure. The investment will bring new contracts, new infrastructure, and new research programs to the site, which will equate to work that is already creating jobs at one of the largest employers in Leeds and Grenville. The company has added 50 positions since November and expects to add more through the rest of this year as production grows. “When I started in 2020 there were 57 employees, and now including the expansion in November, we’re over 150,” said Iles. “In that time, we’ve built some great relationships with the U.S. and some of our other NATO partners. We have shipments going out to Germany, the Netherlands, and Poland all in the next month or so. “But Canada is our No.-1 customer and our most important customer.” HFI designs, manufactures, and supplies specialty pyrotechnic products for military, defence, and commercial customers worldwide. Its products help train and protect armed forces and support search-and-rescue and safety operations. ( AP: Vadim Ghirda ) In short: Andrew and Tristan Tate are facing extradition to the United Kingdom on rape and sex trafficking charges after their arrest in Miami last weekend. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt says the Trump administration is not planning to intervene in the extradition process. The Tate brothers are avid supporters of US President Donald Trump and were part of the hyper-masculine "manosphere" that contributed to his 2024 election victory. abc.net.au/news/white-house-will-not-fight-tate-brothers-extradition-to-uk/106952928 Link copied Share Share article US President Donald Trump will not stop the extradition of influencer Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan to Britain on sex crime charges, the White House says. Self-professed misogynist Andrew Tate and his younger sibling were detained by US authorities in Miami on Saturday, local time, in a move their lawyer called "politically motivated". The Tates are challenging their extradition. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt was asked at a news briefing if Mr Trump or the administration planned to intervene in the extradition process, and told reporters "no". Tate brothers fight extradition to UK Andrew and Tristan Tate's attorney says an attempt to extradite the brothers is politically motivated. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also distanced the administration from the case. "There's no role for us to play at this moment or maybe ever in that regard," he told reporters in the Philippines earlier this week. The Tate brothers are avid supporters of Mr Trump and were part of the hyper-masculine "manosphere" that contributed to his 2024 election victory. Andrew Tate also tried to cultivate relationships in the past with Mr Trump's sons Don Jr and Barron, US media reported. The Tates were arrested after British prosecutors announced new charges of rape, sex trafficking and assault . They now face 59 charges in total — 42 against Andrew and 17 against Tristan. Their lawyer said on Monday that they were innocent and would fight extradition. Loading... "It's politically motivated. There's no question about it," Joseph McBride told reporters outside a Miami court after a hearing on the case . In Romania, where they have been based in recent years, the brothers face allegations of trafficking minors, sexual intercourse with a minor and money laundering. In March 2025, the US state of Florida launched a criminal investigation into the pair. The status of that investigation is unclear. Congresswoman Yassamin Ansari, a Democrat from Arizona, called for a probe into whether Trump administration officials, congressional offices or people close to Mr Trump improperly intervened to protect the Tates. "No individual — regardless of wealth, political party, or access to the first family and the president — is above the law or beyond the reach of justice," she wrote in a letter to House Oversight Chairman James Comer. Log in here » Another person has pleaded guilty in a human smuggling case that involved the drowning of nine people in the St. Lawrence River as they tried crossing into the United States. Two families from Romania and India, along with the man allegedly piloting their vessel, died in March 2023 after they capsized while trying to enter the United States via Akwesasne Mohawk Territory. The U.S. Department of Justice said Thursday that Stephanie Square, 53, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit alien smuggling, four counts of alien smuggling for financial gain and four counts of alien smuggling resulting in death. Searchers look for victims Friday, March 31, 2023 after a boat capsized in Akwesasne, Que. THE CANADIAN PRESS/Ryan Remiorz Officials describe Square as a dual citizen from the Canadian side of Akwesasne. They also say she was the U.S.-based leader of a group that regularly smuggled people across the border via the Mohawk territory, which straddles Quebec, Ontario and New York state. “Aliens attempting to enter the United States illegally across the U.S.-Canada border are exposed to a range of dangers at the hands of human smugglers trying to capitalize on the misfortunes and misplaced hopes of others,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division in a statement. “Here, in the face of known dangers, the defendant directed her co-conspirators to smuggle a family with young children across the St. Lawrence River on a cold, windy night with limited visibility. The dangers materialized into a preventable and tragic loss of life.” Square’s charges only involved the deaths of the Romanian family, which included two children under the age of three. She is set to be sentenced on Nov. 25 and faces between five years and life in prison. Five other people previously pleaded guilty in the case. They are Dakota Montour, 32, and Kawisiiostha Celecia Sharrow, 45, from the U.S. side of Akwesasne; Janet Terrance, 46, of Hogansburg, N.Y.; and Timothy Oakes, 35, and Rahsontanohstha Delormier, 31, of Akwesasne on the Canadian side. The U.S. Justice Department said that during the week of March 27, 2023, a “prolific” Canadian smuggler contacted Square to smuggle the Romanian family across the St. Lawrence. Officials say she recruited multiple people to help, though one refused due to the high winds on the river that night. They say Square enlisted one of her regular drivers, Montour, to take the family to the residence of Timothy Oakes on Cornwall Island, described as a “notorious staging area for cross-border smuggling operations.” Officials say Oakes later took the family to a public boat launch on the island where his brother Casey picked them up and embarked on their ill-fated journey. The bodies of the migrants were pulled from the river in Akwesasne, about 130 kilometres southwest of Montreal, on March 30 and 31, 2023. The body of 30-year-old Casey was found in July 2023. The Romanian family was made up of Florin Iordache, 28; his wife, Cristina (Monalisa) Zenaida Iordache, 28; their two-year-old daughter, Evelin; and one-year-old son, Elyen. Both children were Canadian citizens and the family had been living in the Toronto area. The four other people who died were members of the Chaudhari family from the western Indian state of Gujarat. They included the father, Praveenbhai Chaudhari, 50; mother, Dakshaben, 45; son, Meet, 20; and daughter, Vidhi, 23. This report by The Canadian Press was first published July 23, 2026. [Jiwan Kim, Edaily Reporter] Investor sentiment across South Korea's pharmaceutical and life sciences sectors remained weak on July 22 following the Phase 3 setback for Kolon TissueGene's osteoarthritis candidate TG-C. Kolon TissueGene hit the daily lower limit for a second consecutive session, while affiliate Kolon Life Science plunged 17%. The life sciences sector fell 3.48%, the steepest decline among all industry groups. The pharmaceutical sector closed 0.56% lower. Of its 160 listed companies, only 44 advanced, while 98 declined and 18 finished unchanged. In the life sciences sector, 36 of 91 stocks rose, 47 fell and eight ended flat. NanoEnTek Hits Upper Limit on Additional FDA Clearance NanoEnTek surged to the daily upper limit after securing additional clearance from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration for its hematopoietic stem cell counter. According to KG Zeroin's MP Doctor, NanoEnTek closed at 4,540 won, up 1,045 won, or 29.90%, from the previous session. The company said its ADAM II-CD34 system received FDA clearance for use with cryopreserved hematopoietic progenitor cell-apheresis products, known as cryopreserved HPC-A. NanoEnTek website. (Screenshot by Jiwan Kim) The device had already been cleared for peripheral blood and cord blood testing. The additional indication allows major specimens used in hematopoietic stem cell transplantation to be analyzed with a single instrument. The latest approval brings NanoEnTek's total number of FDA 510(k)-cleared in-vitro diagnostic products to 13, which the company says is the highest among South Korean immunodiagnostic companies. Cryopreserved HPC-A is used in autologous stem cell transplantation for blood cancer patients. Stem cells are collected and frozen before high-dose chemotherapy, then tested for cell count and viability before being reinfused into the patient. The company said the expanded indication enables ADAM II-CD34 to be used in a critical quality-control stage of the autologous transplantation process. NanoEnTek also expects its recurring consumables business to benefit from a larger installed equipment base. Consumables for its in-vitro diagnostics and life sciences businesses accounted for 77.8% of total sales last year. Its high-throughput cell analysis platform, the EVE-HT series, is currently used by more than 30 global pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies. NanoEnTek estimates that cumulative consumables revenue can reach a level similar to the equipment sales price within about three years of installation. A company official said, "The FDA clearance has expanded the clinical application of ADAM II-CD34 and positioned it as a core quality-control instrument in the autologous hematopoietic stem cell transplantation process for blood cancer patients." The official added, "We will expand the presence of the ADAM series not only at blood cancer transplant centers in North America and Europe, but also in the Middle East, where demand for treatment of hereditary blood disorders is high." NGeneBio Jumps on Expansion of Blood Cancer Diagnostic Network NGeneBio also hit the daily upper limit as investors welcomed the expansion of its blood cancer precision diagnostic panel business. The shares closed at 2,370 won, up 545 won, or 29.86%, from the previous session. The rally followed news that NGeneBio had begun supplying its HEMAccuTest blood cancer panel to Seoul National University Bundang Hospital. The company currently supplies the panel to about 20 major tertiary hospitals in South Korea, including Seoul St. Mary's Hospital and Seoul National University Hospital. Overseas, it has expanded into Singapore, Vietnam, Colombia, Germany and Romania. NGeneBio's blood cancer panel business has posted a compound annual growth rate of 36% over the past five years. In the first quarter, domestic sales rose 38% from a year earlier, while overseas sales increased 102%. NGeneBio logo. (Courtesy of NGeneBio) HEMAccuTest analyzes major genetic mutations at the initial diagnosis stage. After treatment, the company's MRDaccuPanel AML FLT3 is used to monitor measurable residual disease and detect possible recurrence. The panel is designed to identify FLT3 mutations, a major biomarker in acute myeloid leukemia, at levels as low as 0.001%. The company said this sensitivity meets the ultra-high-sensitivity assessment requirements recommended by the European LeukemiaNet. NGeneBio is also seeking to use its blood cancer panels as companion diagnostic and biomarker platforms in drug development. Potential applications include selecting patients for FLT3-targeted therapies, evaluating treatment response and monitoring recurrence. Song Myung-jun, head of NGeneBio's diagnostics business, said, "The supply agreement with Seoul National University Bundang Hospital will further strengthen the clinical credibility and practical applicability of NGeneBio's blood cancer panels." He added, "We will expand our position in the precision blood cancer diagnostics market by increasing supplies to major domestic hospitals and securing additional global references." Kangstem, Extends Rally on Big Pharma Organoid Deal Kangstem Biotech continued to rise after signing a material transfer and evaluation agreement, or MTEA, with a global top-five pharmaceutical company. Kang Kyung-sun, founder of Kangstem Biotech and professor at Seoul National University. (Photo courtesy of Kangstem Biotech) The shares gained 145 won, or 6.89%, to close at 2,250 won. Under the agreement, the partner will apply its drug candidates to Kangstem Biotech's hair follicle organoid platform to evaluate efficacy. The goal is to obtain data that may predict clinical outcomes more accurately than conventional animal testing. The company described the contract as the first stage of a strategic partnership that could potentially expand into joint research, research service agreements or licensing deals. Kangstem Biotech's organoid platform uses human-derived tissue to mimic the structure and function of actual organs. It is designed to assess complex cellular responses that are difficult to reproduce using conventional artificial skin models. The company also sees potential applications in transplantable products for hair loss and skin disease treatments. Kangstem Biotech founder Kang Kyung-sun, a professor at Seoul National University. (Courtesy of Kangstem Biotech) Leading Investment & Securities said the agreement demonstrated the global commercial potential of Kangstem Biotech's Real Skin Organoid technology. The brokerage noted that the pharmaceutical partner will test drug candidates using the hair follicle organoid platform, potentially generating data with stronger clinical predictability than animal studies. It added that positive evaluation results could lead to shorter development timelines, improved clinical success rates and follow-on collaboration, including licensing or joint development. Kang Kyung-sun, founder of Kangstem Biotech and a professor at Seoul National University, said six research and business development executives from the multinational pharmaceutical company visited Kangstem Biotech's research facility in May. "It was highly unusual for them to review not only our core organoid technology but also our production capabilities at a level comparable to technical due diligence," Kang said. https://www.cp24.com/news/canada/2026/07.text: A fifth suspect has pleaded guilty in a human smuggling case that resulted in the death of a family, including two young kids under three years old, in the St. Lawrence River in March 2023. Stephanie Square, 53, a dual Canadian-American citizen from the Akwesasne Mohawk Territory, pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit alien smuggling, four counts of alien smuggling for financial gain and four counts of alien smuggling resulting in death, the U.S. Department of Justice said Thursday. According to court documents, Square was a U.S. leader of a human smuggling organization that regularly trafficked migrants across the U.S.-Canada border in Akwesasne, the First Nations territory on the Quebec-Ontario border that also straddles the New York state border. During the week of March 27, 2023, a Canadian smuggler contacted Square to bring a Romanian couple and their two children across the St. Lawrence River into the United States. She also recruited co-conspirators to facilitate the operation, which went ahead despite dangerous weather conditions “so that she would be paid,” the documents stated. READ MORE: According to the DOJ, Square enlisted a driver, Dakota Montour, to drive the family on March 29, 2023, to the home of Timothy Oakes, whose home on Cornwall Island was a “notorious” staging area for human smuggling. After the family arrived, the family of four was transported in Oakes’ car to the tip of Cornwall Island, where Casey Oakes was waiting for them to bring them over the river. “While in transit, the boat capsized due to severe weather. As a result, the Romanian family and [Casey] Oakes died,” the DOJ said. A few days later, police searched the water and found the bodies of the four family members. Casey Oakes’ body was also found eight months later. After pleading guilty on Thursday, Square is set to be sentenced on Nov. 25. She faces a minimum penalty of five years in prison and a maximum of life in prison. Her co-conspirators, Dakota Montour, 32, Kawisiiostha Celecia Sharrow, 45, both of the Akwesasne Mohawk Indian reserve, New York, Janet Terrance, 46, of Hogansburg, N.Y., and Timothy Oakes, 35, from the Akwesasne Mohawk Indian reserve, already pleaded guilty on Jan. 23, 2025, Oct. 8, 2024, March 6, 2025, and May 11, 2026, respectively. Another co-conspirator, Rahsontanohstha Delormier, 31, pleaded guilty on June 26. Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva called the deaths “a preventable and tragic loss of life.” “Human smuggling organizations show a reckless disregard for the safety and well-being of those they transport, often resulting in devastating consequences,” added Acting Special Agent in Charge Anthony Patrone of U.S. Immigrations and Customs Enforcement Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Buffalo. The DOJ said several partners assisted in the yearslong investigation, including the Canada Border Services Agency, the Akwesasne Mohawk Police Service, the Ontario Provincial Police, the Sûreté du Québec, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and the Cornwall Police Service, among others.

http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27920.text: Big News Network.com Hungary's ex-PM demands restoration of democracy BUDAPEST, Hungary: Hungary's former nationalist prime minister Viktor Orbán, who lost power after 16 years in an election in April, has called on his supporters to restore democracy. He said that the new government has destroyed democracy in the country. Orbán made his first strong political comments since his heavy election defeat late on July 21 through a Facebook post. He issued what he called a "Statement of Resistance" shortly after his Fidesz party said that prosecutors had searched offices where its internet servers are located. Prosecutors told Reuters in an email that the action was connected to an investigation into suspected misuse of funds and other crimes at the National Culture Fund (NKA) during Orbán's time in government. Orbán said that Hungary is no longer a democratic state after the new center-right government led by Prime Minister Peter Magyar passed a constitutional amendment. According to Orbán, this amendment ended the terms of both the president and the head of the constitutional court. Magyar's Tisza party has denied accusations that it is acting in an authoritarian way toward political opponents. The party has promised to reduce corruption, which it says was widespread under Orbán's government, as part of its effort to bring Hungary back in line with the European Union. Orbán himself faced strong criticism during his time in power over democratic standards in Hungary. His government often clashed with the European Union on issues such as the rule of law and the rights of minorities. Orbán has denied all corruption allegations. He said that a period of tyranny had begun again in Hungary. He also said that the new political system created in this way is not legitimate, and that Fidesz will use all peaceful means, both inside and outside parliament, to oppose what he described as abuse of power. Magyar's Tisza party holds a large majority in parliament, which allows it to reverse changes introduced during Orbán's time in office that Magyar says weakened democracy. The constitutional amendment ended the term of President Tamás Sulyok, stating that there had been a serious loss of public trust in him. Sulyok had been elected in 2024 by lawmakers from Orbán's Fidesz party. Parliament is expected to elect a new president soon. Magyar's Tisza party currently enjoys strong public support. A poll by the polling company Median earlier in the month showed that 60 percent of voters support Tisza, compared to 18 percent for Fidesz. Since the election, Fidesz has faced internal problems, including the resignation of its parliamentary group leader last week. https://www.mynbc5.com/article/canadian-.text: A sixth and final person has pleaded guilty to their role in a human smuggling job turned deadly that led to the deaths of a five people. The United States District Attorney's Office for the Northern District of New York announced on Thursday that Stephanie Square, 53, pleaded guilty to charges including conspiracy to commit alien smuggling, four counts of alien smuggling for financial gain and four counts of alien smuggling resulting in death. Square, who is from the Akwesasne Mohawk Territory in Canada, was one of six people charged after a Romanian family of four died in March 2023 while being smuggled across the United States border into Canada. One of the smugglers, Casey Oakes, also died when the boat the family was in capsized. Co-conspirators Dakota Montour, 32, and Kawisiiostha Celecia Sharrow, 45, both of the Akwesasne Mohawk Indian reserve, New York, as well as Janet Terrance, 46, of Hogansburg, New York and Timothy Oakes, 35, from the Akwesasne Mohawk Indian reserve, have already entered guilty pleas. Rahsontanohstha Delormier pleaded guilty in June and is due to be sentenced in October. Square, who has dual U.S. and Canadian citizenship, will be sentenced in November.

Photograph: Veronica Miller Australian climate and environmental reporting Bird flu ‘We expected it, but now it’s here’: on the frontline of Australia’s bird flu outbreak, people are distressed As Australia prepares for the H5 bird flu to potentially rip through hundreds of species, residents of the Limestone Coast are already seeing the impacts Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Supported by About this content Petra Stock Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 17.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google It has only been three weeks since H5 bird flu was detected on South Australia’s Limestone Coast and already encounters with sick or dead birds are becoming commonplace. Maureen Christie, who lives in the seaside town of Carpenter Rocks, has been observing and protecting birds in the region for decades. She is now witnessing many stricken and suffering. “It’s just awful,” Christie said, who helped establish the Friends of Shorebirds SE more than 20 years ago. “We expected it but, now it’s here, it’s just traumatic.” The state’s south-east is renowned for its bird life, she said, which includes resident hooded plovers and oyster catchers, along with fly-ins from other countries, such as double-banded plovers, red-necked stints, sanderlings and ruddy turnstones. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Locals have been following state government advice to “avoid, record and report”, she said. Christie said many people have been getting in touch by email and phone to relay their own sightings and reports. “Everybody’s feeling distressed, but everybody’s trying to be supportive of one another.” Since the first case in a local Australian seabird – a greater crested tern – was detected in early July, the region has seen dozens more suspected and confirmed cases, including the first confirmed mass mortality event at Baudin Rocks , a group of islets about 8km from the coastal town of Robe. “Robe has a very special and unique environment that the local community knows, uses, celebrates and cares for,” the president of Friends of Little Dip Conservation Park and Robe Coast Care, Roland Wells, said. There’s everything from migratory, coastal and inland birds, wombats, wallabies and echidnas, as well as marine mammals such as sea lions, seals and dolphins. He said people have undertaken conservation work over many decades to support shorebirds, which makes the recent arrival of bird flu “very upsetting”. The situation has escalated considerably over the past week. Council officers from Robe district council have been identifying and reporting sick and deceased birds almost daily, mainly greater crested terns and some silver gulls. Penguins and dolphins among nearly 400 Australian species under threat from bird flu as ‘true extent of disaster’ revealed Read more A spokesperson for South Australia’s primary industries department said crested terns – which make up many of the bird flu cases – “commonly commingle” with other species like cormorants, gulls, grebes, ducks and other tern species. This increases the potential for transmission. “From a conservation perspective, several threatened and priority species have been identified as high risk, including fairy terns ,” the spokesperson said. “Marine mammals are also being closely monitored, with Australian sea lions and long-nosed fur seals among the species considered most vulnerable to potential impacts from the virus.” Wildlife carers and clinics – now required to don personal protective equipment and undertake strict cleaning and quarantine measures when dealing with other wild birds injured by cars, in dog and cat attacks or entanglement – have been calling on the state government for support. Mish Simpson, from SKER wildlife veterinary centre, said the clinic was already at capacity before bird flu. But now, more wild birds are being brought in because other vets have stopped accepting them, partly due to the additional requirements and the risk of exposure for other animals. Simpson is concerned there is not enough emphasis on slowing the spread, which would give vets, carers and the community more time to prepare. For example, she said, the dead bodies of infected birds are often being left in the environment, where they pose an infection risk to other wildlife, particularly scavengers. As the federal environment minister, Murray Watt, observed on Monday , the events rapidly unfolding in the south-east, and around Australia, are “the beginning of what is likely to be a long, difficult journey in terms of the impacts on wildlife”. In Victoria , the chief veterinary officer, Dr Graeme Cooke, said recent aerial and ground surveillance near Portland and Nelson has already shown “a clear increase in the number of dead terns along that part of the coast”, consistent with deaths in South Australia. “Last week we talked about individual detections; the first cases of the H5 bird flu in Victoria. We are now seeing a change.” What that means for hundreds of native species and the people who care for them remains uncertain. Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/AP View image in fullscreen A bomb disposal robot and forensic technician at Leipzig airport on Wednesday. Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/AP Germany Leipzig drone bomb was found near Ukrainian plane carrying ammunition, say police Germany investigating whether foreign state involved as minister says ‘ripped’ detonator stopped device going off Europe live – latest updates Deborah Cole in Berlin Thu 6 Aug 2026 11.06 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 16.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A catastrophe with multiple casualties was possibly narrowly averted by the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig airport, German officials said, as they examined whether a foreign state could be behind the plot. One of the Ukrainian aircraft next to where the bomb drone was found was loaded with military ammunition, according to a classified police report quoted by the public broadcasters WDR and NDR and the Süddeutsche newspaper. The interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, who said on Wednesday Germany faced a “new level of danger” , said only an apparently “ripped” detonator had prevented the device going off near Ukrainian cargo planes on the tarmac at the shipping and military hub. View image in fullscreen Police officers search an area at Leipzig airport after the discovery of the drone. Photograph: Hendrik Schmidt/DPA/AP The highly explosive Ukrainian cargo, with a tank filled with jet fuel, had apparently been transported from France to Leipzig shortly beforehand and was presumably intended for onward transport, the report said. The airport is about 12.5 miles (20km) from the centre of Leipzig, a city of more than 600,000 people. The facility hosts a major cargo processing centre that employs hundreds of people round the clock and is adjacent to two busy autobahn routes. The Leipzig drone bomb marks a dangerous escalation for Europe Read more The Bild newspaper reported that the drone found near the Ukrainian plane had a handmade remote detonator that did not work, and investigators hoped it could offer clues as to its origin and the culprits. Leipzig airport’s status as a Nato and German military logistics hub, as well as the the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines in Europe, has directed suspicion toward Russia, which German and European authorities say has carried out repeated sabotage attacks. The German government and authorities have stopped short of pointing the finger at Moscow for what marked a clear escalation of the threat level in Europe . But Dobrindt said investigators were treating the incident as part of a “professional hybrid threat scenario” with a focus on “foreign powers” as likely perpetrators. View image in fullscreen The airport is a Nato and German military logistics hub and the base for Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines in Europe. Photograph: Axel Schmidt/Reuters Roderich Kiesewetter, a member of the German parliament’s intelligence committee, blamed Russia directly. “I consider the threat to Germany posed by hybrid attacks orchestrated by Russia to be serious,” said Kiesewetter, a member of the co-ruling Christian Democrats. “I also believe that the attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport was a targeted hybrid attack – in other words, an attempted act of terrorism – orchestrated by Russia .” An airport staff member discovered the drone shortly before midnight on Tuesday, “hovering” near the ground between two Antonov Airlines An-124 cargo airplanes, among ​the world’s biggest freighters. Police said a drone defence sensor system at the airport, considered “critical infrastructure” by Germany, had not picked up the drone. They now believe based on security footage it had been on site for several hours before it was found. Dobrindt told reporters that the drone seemed to have been modified to circumvent electronic detection. It was attached to a package of explosives roughly the size of a fist, according to the WDR-NDR-Süddeutsche report, and investigators said the substance inside was believed to be semtex, a powerful plastic explosive. The discovery of the drone led the airport to suspend air traffic, forcing a DHL cargo plane from Marseille on its approach to take off again. It then collided with what is believed to have been a second drone. The media report said that plane had also been carrying unspecified “dangerous goods” before it made an emergency landing in Hanover, about 155 miles north-west, with minor damage. Bild said the drone that hit the DHL plane had a camera used to film the attack. Air traffic had been diverted on Wednesday from the airport’s southern runway but was back to normal on Thursday with no additional security measures reported. Ukraine has been using Leipzig airport as an alternate location for the transport of military goods since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, according to official records. German defence ministry officials said its armed forces were not conducting military transport operations at the airport at the time of the incident. The airport has previously been targeted. A firebomb, posted via DHL, exploded at the facility in July 2024 while a second was sent to the UK and caught fire at a warehouse in Birmingham . Two similar packages were also found in Poland. A subsequent pan-European investigation identified 22 suspects in Lithuania and Poland who were suspected of having been employed by Russian intelligence. Testimony this week at a trial in Lithuania of five people suspected of mailing the incendiary devices showed how narrowly the plane from Leipzig avoided being set on fire in mid-flight . A DHL company representative told the court the parcel ignited on the ground at its logistics centre at Leipzig airport shortly before loading, rather than during the flight, because the plane was delayed. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Protests have been held over plans to house asylum seekers on the RAF Barnham site near Thetford. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Protests have been held over plans to house asylum seekers on the RAF Barnham site near Thetford. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images UK news Norfolk police arrest two men after officers injured during unrest over asylum plans Homes of people believed to be asylum seekers attacked during two nights of violence in Thetford Matthew Weaver Thu 6 Aug 2026 14.06 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two men have been arrested after police were injured as they intervened to protect men believed to be asylum seekers from angry mobs trying to break into their homes. The arrests followed two nights of unrest in Thetford, Norfolk, involving more than 100 people protesting against plans to house asylum seekers in former military barracks near the market town. The unrest followed the circulation online of a list of properties whose landlords have contracts with a government contractor to provide homes for asylum seekers. Policing powers in Norfolk were boosted in Thetford on Thursday evening and public safety measures have been imposed. Norfolk police said on Wednesday one of its officers was struck by a rock, another officer was bitten and a third was spat at while responding to reports of protesters trying to break into a home in the north of the town. The injured officers were taken to hospital. One man in his 40s, who was arrested on suspected public order offences, remains in custody. A second man, Brian Thompson, 68, has been charged with possession of an offensive weapon, a wooden bat. He is due to appear at Norwich magistrates court on 25 August. View image in fullscreen Damage caused to a house in Thetford where protesters allegedly tried to break into the homes of people believed to be asylum seekers. Photograph: Joe Giddens/PA On Tuesday night, officers intervened to protect five men who were being threatened by dozens of protesters, some of whom tried to break into a property, smashed a window, and damaged a fence and letterbox. Police were responding to a report that between 30 and 50 people were trying to enter a house in the west of Thetford. Video footage of the incident showed the men being escorted to safety by officers as dozens of protesters jeered and shouted abuse at police and the men. Shouts of “refugees not welcome”, “get out” and “bye” could be heard. In another video of the unrest, a man could be heard shouting: “They don’t want the white man any more, they want to swap us.” Later on Tuesday, officers responded to reports of residents being threatened at two homes in the south of the town. Police believed some of those involved had been present at the earlier attempted break-in. At one of the homes, windows were smashed. At another, a resident was forced out and had their mobile phone stolen when a small group forced entry. A man in his 30s who was arrested over Tuesday’s night’s unrest on suspicion of a public order offence had since been released and issued with a conditional caution, police said. The local Labour MP, Terry Jermy, who has previously criticised plans to use the former barracks at nearby RAF Barnham to house up to 1,000 asylum seekers, condemned the violence and what he called “mob rule”. View image in fullscreen The arrests followed two nights of unrest in Thetford involving more than 100 people protesting against plans to house asylum seekers at the RAF Barnham site (pictured). Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images Jermy said protesters were targeting a list of houses of multiple occupation used by Serco to house asylum seekers. “There doesn’t seem to be protests at all of the properties known about thus far, so the potential for increase and escalation is clearly there,” he said. “I’ve had constituents contact me of mixed ethnicity who are terrified that they will be misidentified as asylum seekers and what that might mean for their families.” Jermy said he recognised many of the protesters as local people in the videos of the unrest, but that he believed tensions were being “whipped up by outside forces”. In a statement, Jermy said: “The ugly scenes in Thetford over the past few days have been difficult to watch and are deeply concerning. “People have been pulled from their homes – a place of safety – and forcibly removed, with reports of members of the public breaking into homes, taking property and smashing windows. “I do not know the immigration status of the people placed in these properties or their legal status, but I know they are human beings that must be afforded the same rights that we all expect in this country. “Whatever our own individual views on immigration – mob rule and vigilantism is not acceptable.” View image in fullscreen Under the proposals, the RAF Barnham site could house 1,000 asylum seekers. Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty Images Norfolk police also condemned the violence. The assistant chief constable Julie Dean, who is overseeing the response to the unrest, said: “We will always facilitate and support the right to peaceful protest. However, no matter how strongly those views are held, there is no place for violence, intimidation or criminal behaviour. “We will not stand by and allow violence to take place, whether that is directed towards members of the public, local residents or police officers carrying out their duties.” Policing powers in Norfolk were increased in Thetford on Thursday evening. Public safety measures have been imposed, including people being required to remove a face covering if asked to do so by officers. Police will also be permitted to direct anyone committing, or whom they suspect may commit, antisocial behaviour to leave the area. The measures are in place from 6pm on Thursday until 7am on Friday. Anyone who refuses to remove a face covering when asked to do so may be arrested, the force said. Mick Ferris was killed when a 130kg window fell from the Corniche, a luxury block of flats on the Albert Embankment, central London, in October 2018. Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PA View image in fullscreen Mick Ferris was killed when a 130kg window fell from the Corniche, a luxury block of flats on the Albert Embankment, central London, in October 2018. Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PA London Foster + Partners cleared over man’s death when window fell from London penthouse Court rules architecture firm not responsible for fatal incident but project managers and engineers found guilty of safety breaches Matthew Weaver Thu 6 Aug 2026 14.06 EDT First published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 09.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The architecture firm founded by Norman Foster has been cleared over the death of a man killed by a window that fell 90 metres from a newly constructed London penthouse. Foster + Partners (F+P), the practice behind some of the world’s most recognisable buildings such as the Gherkin and revamps of the British Museum and Germany’s Reichstag, were not held to be responsible for the death of Mick Ferris , a 53-year-old coach driver, in 2018. However, St James, the project managers of the building where the incident took place, and the project’s engineers, Lindner Prater, were found guilty of safety breaches over the death by a jury at Inner London crown court. Ferris was killed instantly when the 130kg (287lbs) window fell from the penthouse of the Corniche, a luxury tower block development on Albert Embankment, on to the street below. View image in fullscreen The jury was told the designers should have considered the risk of the outward-opening, side-hung windows. Photograph: Nick Ansell/PA The court heard that just over a year earlier a window panel had also fallen from the same development. “Miraculously” no one was hurt but no changes were made to the designs as a result of that incident, the court heard. The prosecution, which was brought by the Health and Safety Executive, said Ferris’s death was foreseeable and the designers had ignored concerns about the proven danger of outward-opening windows. After more than 11 hours of deliberation the jury cleared F+P and the building’s design engineer, Wintech. But it found St James and Lindner Prater had failed in their duty to keep the public safe under the Health and Safety at Work Act 1974. The prosecutor Gordon Menzies told the jury it “wasn’t an accident waiting to happen … it was an accident that had already happened in August 2017. The prosecution say it was an accident waiting to happen again.” Ferris was killed by the falling window which had been blown off its hinges when the building was almost complete, the court heard. A woman coming towards him, who was pushing a wheelchair, narrowly missed being hit, jurors were told. A restrictor put in place to prevent the window being blown off had been removed, they heard. The designers had failed to consider the “catastrophic” consequences if something went wrong with this restrictor, the prosecution said. They also failed to take into account the fulcrum effect of an 85cm (33in) window being prised off its hinges, the prosecution said. Jurors were told that after the first window panel fell from the building the designers failed to use the incident as a reason to “go back to the drawing board”. The jury was told of 12 “missed opportunities” where the designers should have considered the risk of the outward-opening, side-hung windows. View image in fullscreen Billboards outside the new development in March 2017. Photograph: Martin Godwin/The Guardian All four defendants denied the charges and claimed they did all that was reasonably practicable to ensure safety. Menzies told the court: “The wind was sufficiently strong to blow the window open further than 8 and a half inches and the oversailing glass clashed with the frame and, as a result, the hinges were prised off.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion Originally the windows had been designed to open inwards, but the design was changed to avoid them clashing with an internal ceiling coffer containing wires and pipes that they would have cleared, the court was told. It was only after Ferris’s death that the window design was changed back to inward-opening, the court heard. The prosecution said F+P should have known such risks due to its specialist knowledge of glass-covered buildings including the Gherkin. Lawyers for F+P said the firm’s role was limited and it was not involved in technical issues. They said it was there to focus on the visual aspects of the design. A spokesperson for F+P said: “Our thoughts remain with Mr Ferris’s family, as they have since October 2018. We note the court’s decision and are grateful to the jury for the time and care they have taken in considering this matter.” A spokesperson for Wintech said: “While the court has reached its conclusion, the tragedy of what happened remains. It is vital that we continue to reflect and learn, and as an industry, remain committed to strengthening standards and practices to help prevent such incidents in the future.” A spokesperson for St James said: “The death of Mick Ferris in 2018 was tragic. Our thoughts remain with his family and friends. We acknowledge today’s verdict and will carefully consider its implications.” Lindner Prater has been approached for comment. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Donald Trump with Jeanine Pirro at the White House in May 2025. Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty Images Donald Trump Trump again rebukes Jeanine Pirro over reflecting pool ‘vandalism’ case President attacks ‘terrible mistake’ of US attorney, who said in court filing damage stemmed from botched renovation Maya Yang Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.51 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 18.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump has doubled down on his criticism of Jeanine Pirro after the US attorney for the District of Columbia publicly challenged his claims that vandals had damaged the recently renovated Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool. “She said there was no vandalism. There was tremendous vandalism,” Trump told NBC News on Thursday. “So, she made a terrible mistake. I don’t understand why she did such a stupid thing.” On Friday, Pirro – a former Fox News host and longtime Trump ally who he handpicked to serve as the top prosecutor for the nation’s capital – moved to dismiss vandalism charges against a former Olympian and three others in connection with incidents at the reflecting pool. In a 20-page court filing, Pirro’s office wrote that the damage to the concrete-bottomed tourist attraction was the result of a “botched” renovation – “not vandalism”. View image in fullscreen The Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool in Washington on Wednesday. Photograph: Eric Lee/Reuters Asked on Thursday whether he would consider replacing Pirro, Trump told NBC: “I think she made a terrible decision. That doesn’t mean change.” The comments came after a reportedly heated Oval Office meeting on Monday with Trump, Pirro, and interior secretary Doug Burgum. According to the New York Times, Pirro accused Burgum of misleading the president about the rushed renovation by a vendor awarded a no-bid contract from the interior department. Later that evening, Trump told reporters he had not “made a determination” yet as to whether Pirro would be ousted. The White House did not immediately reply to a request for comment. Earlier this week, Trump accused Pirro of having “folded like an umbrella” after the justice department dismissed the case against David Hearn, a former Olympic canoeist who faced a felony property destruction charge that carried a potential sentence of up to 10 years in prison and a $1,000 fine for the act of having touched a chunk of the pool’s newly peeled coating. Hearn, 67, pleaded not guilty. In a statement after the charges were dropped, Hearn’s lawyers said the case should never have been brought, and argued that its dismissal “does not erase the abuse of government power in arresting and charging a patriotic American who did nothing wrong”. “The administration owes Mr Hearn an apology,” they said. Hearn is one of seven people who was charged in connection with what Trump claimed were attempts to vandalize the $15m renovation of the reflecting pool that has been plagued by problems the justice department said was “the result of flawed installation by the contractor”. “Frankly, I think she choked,” Trump said from the Oval Office on Monday. An attorney for Hearn has since said that “ all options are on table ” for legal action. Those include “civil suits, bar referrals for the prosecutors involved, request for sanctions, and reimbursement of attorneys’ fees and expenses,” Hearn’s attorney Steven Levin said on Tuesday. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Roberto Vannacci at a National Future news conference in Rome on 5 August. ‘The rest of Europe should sit up and take notice of Mr Vannacci’s rise.’ Photograph: Roberto Monaldo/LaPresse/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Roberto Vannacci at a National Future news conference in Rome on 5 August. ‘The rest of Europe should sit up and take notice of Mr Vannacci’s rise.’ Photograph: Roberto Monaldo/LaPresse/Shutterstock Opinion Europe The Guardian view on Italy’s new far-right party: the rise of a rogue general Editorial The early success of Roberto Vannacci’s National Future sends an ominous signal as extreme politics become normalised Thu 6 Aug 2026 13.29 EDT Last modified on Thu 6 Aug 2026 13.49 EDT Share W hen a serving Italian general published a far-right tract in 2023 entitled The World Turned Upside Down, a disciplinary inquiry swiftly followed. Roberto Vannacci’s text was a sustained exercise in bile and bigotry, attacking among other things the “normalisation” of homosexuality, and questioning whether a high-profile black volleyball star could really be considered Italian. The controversy sent the book into the bestseller charts, and its author was suspended for bringing the army into disrepute. A year out from Italy’s next general election, Mr Vannacci is a problem not for the military but for the country’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni. Now a member of the European parliament, in February he exploited his notoriety to found National Future, a political party which argues that Ms Meloni’s coalition government has sold out its far-right supporters through not being extreme enough. The “true right”, according to the former paratrooper – who once served as a military attache in Moscow – should be pro-Putin and anti-Ukraine, anti-EU, and committed to restoring the “cultural homogeneity” of Italy through the expulsion of immigrants and their descendants. Shockingly, polls are now placing National Future just behind Forza Italia, the second-biggest party in Ms Meloni’s hard-right coalition, and ahead of its third main component, Matteo Salvini’s League. For Ms Meloni, Mr Vannacci’s rapid rise now threatens to become a major dilemma. To beat the combined forces of the left next year she may require the support of a party that does not disguise its sympathy with Italy’s fascist past. But to seek it would give the lie to efforts to present her own Brothers of Italy party (which retains a neo-fascist political symbol in its logo) as part of the mainstream conservative tradition. The rest of Europe should sit up and take notice of Mr Vannacci’s rise. At a time when Russian influence on the far right is already a cause for concern, he has declared himself open to the idea of funding from Moscow and also Beijing. More broadly, the emergence of National Future confirms that as well as dragging mainstream politics towards more extreme positions on immigration, the continent’s far right is itself radicalising. Here, the equivalent can be found in Rupert Lowe’s Restore Britain party, which has been exerting a rightwards gravitational pull on Reform UK. Poland’s nationalist and Eurosceptic Law and Justice party has embarked on a similar trajectory, in order to compete with two newish and growing far-right parties. In Germany, Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) stands on the brink of a historic breakthrough in state elections in eastern Germany, and leads in national polls. The ominous political consequences were on display last week in the panicked overreaction of leaders to the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta. With one eye over her right shoulder, Ms Meloni was at the forefront of divisive early calls for action to be taken against Spain following an incursion by irregular migrants. For his part, Mr Vannacci used the incident to amplify his calls for a Europe-wide “remigration” strategy. Mr Vannacci’s repugnant politics are beyond the pale. In Germany, the chancellor, Friedrich Merz, continues to rule out any form of national alliance with the AfD. Were Ms Meloni to countenance any form of accommodation with Italy’s rogue general, it would demolish her fragile claims to mainstream respectability.
