Share A A A This year’s Melbourne International Film Festival has kicked off. Here we take a closer look at some of what’s on offer. See all stories . With more than 300 films on this year’s program, it’s easy to feel overwhelmed by what’s on offer at Melbourne’s annual cinematic banquet. Our reviewers have done some of the heavy lifting, watching features, animations and documentaries from home and abroad. Among their list of recommendations is the film that was favoured to win at Cannes … The Dreamed Adventure Photo: MIFF Veska is an archaeologist, returned to the remote country where she grew up to dig into Bulgaria’s history, but her sharp dealings with local gangsters suggest that her own buried past is murkier than she might want to admit. German filmmaker Valeska Grisebach (whose previous film, Western , was also set in Bulgaria) enjoys pulling at the threads of male-coded genres; Veska, portrayed by amateur actor Yana Radeva, has something of Clint Eastwood about her, in a narrative that is signposted as a crime thriller. Those crimes remain largely unexplained, however; what counts here are the characters, their drinking banter, ambiguous alliances and the wildness of this country, which feels like the far edge of the world. SB We Are The Shaggs Photo: MIFF Everyone in Ken Kwapis’ documentary has a hot take on The Shaggs, the outsider-art pop group formed by three teenage sisters in Fremont, New Hampshire, in 1969 under the supervision of their tyrannical father. Gradually a cult formed around them, despite their total lack of conventional musical skill. But how far was this simply ironic appreciation, and how far were fans drawn to their unique musical world? A Hollywood veteran well known for his work on sitcoms such as The Offic e, Kwapis might seem like a surprising figure to be telling this story. But the film gains from his light, sympathetic touch, as well as his willingness to keep an open mind on the question of what makes art good or bad. JW Advertisement Elephants in the Fog Photo: MIFF Related Article Australian film Writer, director and actor times two: Harvey Zielinski’s debut double act In a small Nepalese village, a household of kinnar – transgender women traditionally supposed to bring good fortune to weddings and births – use their spiritual gifts to help local farmers keep wild elephants at bay. Director Abinash Bikram Shah provides an insight into the kinnars’ cult, now widely threatened with suppression, within what is loosely a detective story. Kinnar matriarch Pirati (the engaging real-life trans activist Pushpa Thing Lama) is about to formally adopt her favourite trans daughter when the young woman disappears. Pirati suspects murder, but the police are not interested in these outsiders; she must run the culprit to ground. Exotic and inspiring, this is also a dark look at a very specific misogyny. SB The Fence Photo: MIFF Set on a construction site in West Africa, Claire Denis’ adaptation of a play by the late French writer Bernard-Marie Koltes remains wilfully theatrical, yet depends on making us feel the unglamorous starkness of the desert setting, where there’s little to distract from the core realities of work, desire and death. The symbolic fence of the title separates the site’s American foreman, Horn (Matt Dillon) from a visitor (Isaach de Bankole) who comes to claim the body of a dead worker. Much of the film is built on the contrast between Dillon’s mannered gestures and de Bankole’s stillness, but Mia McKenna-Bruce ( How To Have Sex ) is more intriguing than either as Horn’s younger wife, the least predictable element in the design. JW Advertisement Fatherland Photo: MIFF Pipped at the post for the Cannes Palme D’Or, Pawel Pawlikowski’s diamond-sharp sliver of history was nevertheless the festival’s winner for me. Nobel Prize-winning German author Thomas Mann (Hanns Zischler, oozing exhaustion with life) tours the two Germanys in the aftermath of World War II, accompanied by his stolidly self-sufficient daughter Erika (Sandra Huller), to give lectures on the 200th anniversary of Goethe’s death. Both sides of the internal border want to claim Goethe and Mann as their own, despite Mann’s insistence on a tolerant, liberal European humanism that no longer pleases the powerful. Pawlikowski ( Ida, Cold War ) focuses on the Manns’ intimate exchanges, but always with an eye for details that conjure their crucial cultural context. SB Blue Heron Photo: MIFF The Hungarian immigrant family in this first feature by Canadian director Sophy Romvari is unhappy in a way uniquely its own. The life of each family member revolves around the troubled oldest son, Jeremy (Edik Beddoes), who spends much of his time alone in his room drawing maps, and when he does go outside is regularly in trouble with the police. This is an innately painful subject, especially as Romvari has confirmed the story is based loosely on memories of her own childhood. But the tone is equal parts sad, tranquil and perplexing: the tricky structure moves between the 1990s and the present, underlining that reality isn’t identical with our vision of it, either in the moment or long after. JW Rose Advertisement Photo: MIFF Related Article Australian film Writer, director and actor times two: Harvey Zielinski’s debut double act Sandra Huller shows once again what a great screen actor she is in this austere historic fable, set after the Thirty Years War in an anonymous German village. Nobody there recognises the soldier who comes back to claim his father’s old farm, but he is soon accepted as the community sees how hard he works. He has a secret, however, which isn’t rumbled because it is so unthinkable: the village’s new success story is a woman. Austrian director Markus Schleinzer, shooting within a narrow palette of greys, maintains a constant tension as Rose’s inevitable unmasking looms ever closer; while his style certainly isn’t naturalistic, the story – for which there are many real-life precedents – has the ring of truth. SB Chronovisor Photo: MIFF Shot on 16-milimetre film by the US team of Kevin Walker and Jack Auen, this eccentric micro-budget fantasy combines elements of conspiracy thriller, gallery installation, and homage to the written word (Jorge Luis Borges and Roberto Bolano are among the writers name-checked in the credits). At the centre of it all is the (loosely) real-life story of a Benedictine monk who claimed in the 1970s to have invented a machine that could photograph the past, inspiring the wild-goose chase which the academic heroine (Anne Laure Sellier) undertakes decades on. Literally speaking, almost nothing happens on screen, yet the intangible nature of the whole story still inspires fascination and even dread. JW Advertisement Hen Photo: MIFF Eight real hens play one plucky, clucky fictional fowl whose adventures provide a bird’s-eye view of human wickedness: an oddity, certainly, but a thoroughly good egg. Hungarian surrealist Gyorgy Palfi is remembered fondly for the fabulously grotesque Taxidermist ; this film, constrained by the limits of avian actors, is more conventional and thoroughly heartwarming. Hen ’s heroine escapes the battery farm where she was laid, has a couple of scrapes where she is almost eaten, then fetches up as the favoured pet of an old man whose disreputable son-in-law is using his former diner as a holding station for his people-smuggling business. Palfi’s persuasive genius is to tell this story without CGI tricks and without anthropomorphising the star: from beak to tail feathers, she’s always just a bird. SB MIFF runs August 6-23, miff.com.au

(Xinhua/Yao Dawei) BEIJING, July 23 (Xinhua) -- Wang Huning, chairman of the National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), met with Tomio Okamura, speaker of the Chamber of Deputies of the Czech Republic, in Beijing on Thursday. Noting that the friendly communication between the people of China and the Czech Republic has a long history, Wang said that the two countries share huge potential and broad prospects for bilateral cooperation. China is willing to join hands with the Czech side to strengthen practical cooperation and promote the traditional friendship to regain vitality, while respecting each other's core interests and major concerns, he said. Wang introduced China's positions on issues related to Taiwan and Xizang, saying that the CPPCC National Committee stands ready to contribute to promoting the healthy and stable development of China-Czech relations. Okamura said that the Czech Republic adheres to the one-China policy, and the Czech side is willing to take the 10th anniversary of the establishment of the strategic partnership between the two countries as an opportunity to strengthen dialogue and cooperation with China, and promote the development of bilateral relations. The Chamber of Deputies is willing to play an active role in promoting collaboration in various areas between the two countries and enhancing friendship between the two peoples, said Okamura. In other economic news, shipping volumes at the KlaipÄda port have been increasing , while Lithuaniaâs GDP deficit was among the lowest in the EU. Following last weekâs announcement of potential provocations, Lithuaniaâs armed forces have increased protection of the LNG terminal and other critical infrastructure. The military also launched drills focused on protecting infrastructure sites, with Defence Minister Robertas Kaunas repeating earlier warnings that Moscow could be eyeing the Baltics or Poland as the next target. WAR IS CHANGING Britain announced last week it would replace its tanks in Estonia with drones, with officials saying the move reflects lessons from Ukraine and the changing nature of war. Mind you, this doesnât mean the Brits are completely abandoning standard doctrine â they are adopting platforms already in use in countries like Lithuania, including the Boxer IFVs, but the shift still does signal the change of times. StaceviÄius / LRT Lithuanian Prime Minister Mindaugas SinkeviÄius said the new government has no plans to raise taxes on businesses or households, despite removing a previous commitment from its program not to introduce new taxes during its term. Speaking after his first meeting with representatives of the Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists following the approval of the new cabinet, SinkeviÄius said the governmentâs intentions had not changed. âI cannot carve such a promise in stone, but there are no hidden intentions or plans to increase taxes,â the prime minister said. Instead, SinkeviÄius said the government intends to finance its social policy commitments through economic growth, moving funds and reallocating spending rather than by introducing new taxes. Vilnius central business district | V. Raupelis / LRT âWe will look for internal reserves to meet our social goals. That means some sectors will have to operate with less funding than before because priorities will be reviewed,â he said, without specifying which areas could face spending cuts. The new governmentâs program includes a range of social commitments, including financial incentives aimed at boosting the birth rate, changes to child benefits to help families maintain their income after the birth of a child, free meals for primary school pupils, higher funding for extracurricular education, increased pensions and measures to reduce poverty. Business leaders welcomed the prime ministerâs assurances but said they remained cautious about the policies of the centre-left government. âOf course, a left-wing government is a left-wing government, so those concerns exist,â said Vidmantas JanuleviÄius, president of the Lithuanian Confederation of Industrialists. He said the business community had been reassured that social policy would not come at the expense of businesses. Vidmantas JanuleviÄius | P. Peleckis / BNS JanuleviÄius said the confederationâs long-term goal is for Lithuania to surpass Finland in gross domestic product per capita by 2035, arguing that achieving this would require greater investment in manufacturing and a stable tax environment. Opposition lawmaker Raimondas Kuodis of the conservative Homeland Union-Lithuanian Christian Democrats questioned how the government would finance its promises, saying ministers had yet to provide clear answers. âThey donât appear to know themselves, [â¦] neither the finance minister nor the other social democratic luminaries,â he told LRT TV. âA triumph of the hope.â Economist EglÄ StonkutÄ of Vytautas Magnus University said Lithuania already faces pressure to keep its budget deficit within European Union limits, despite temporary flexibility for higher defence spending. She warned that the government would eventually need to address a growing fiscal gap, particularly after current defence-related exemptions expire, and said higher corporate taxes could become one option if policymakers seek additional revenue without alienating their voter base. âThe main two taxes generating most revenue are the value-added tax and the income tax,â she said. âThe social democrats will probably be reluctant to touch them.â Lithuania recently fell 13 places in a global competitiveness ranking, adding to concerns among businesses over the countryâs investment climate. Balandis / BNS Russian businessman Sergei Shnaider, the owner of the Mere discount retail chain operating in Lithuania and Latvia, has been added to the European Unionâs 21st sanctions package. The measures is forcing the chain to close all its supermarkets operating in Lithuania, 15min.lt reported on Friday. According to 15min.lt, several of the Mere shops in Vilnius appeared to be already closed on Friday afternoon. Contacted by BNS, a representative of Mere declined to comment on whether the closures were temporary or if they were linked to the sanctions. âDue to technical issues, we are not operating anywhere in Lithuania,â the representative, who declined to give her name, told BNS. The Ministry of Economy and Innovation confirmed on Friday that the owners of the Svetofor Group â which also owns the Mere stores in Lithuania â are under EU sanctions. As of Thursday, all funds and assets belonging to these individuals within the EU must be frozen, and they are prohibited from receiving funds or other economic resources. Latviaâs Financial Intelligence Unit also reported that the chainâs operators in Latvia will have halt their activities. The Latvian authority said sanctions apply to Latprodukti, which operates the Mere chain in Latvia, and the Latvian branch of Lithuanian company Valiente. Both companies are required to immediately cease operations in compliance with EU sanctions. According to the Financial Intelligence Unit, Shnaider was sanctioned for materially or financially supporting actions that undermine or threaten Ukraineâs territorial integrity, sovereignty and independence. The agency said Shnaider indirectly owns more than 50% of both Latprodukti and Valienteâs Latvian operations. LRT reported last year that Valienteâs shares had been acquired by Spanish company Vigalight, which is owned by three Russian citizens who previously controlled the Mere retail chain. According to Spainâs corporate register, Shnaider owns 79% of Vigalight, while Andrei Veikulainen holds 15% and Valeriy Yakovlev owns the remaining 6%. Last October, Lithuaniaâs then Economy Minister Edvinas GrikÅ¡as said that Mere could be added to the sanctions list despite changes in its ownership structure. Latprodukti, established in 2020, reported revenue of 31.57 million euros in 2024, up 53% from the previous year, according to company filings. It posted a net loss of 71,800 euros after recording a profit in 2023. Its 2025 financial results have not yet been published. The company is directly owned by Serbia-based SKTrade DOO Beograd, while Shnaider is listed as its ultimate beneficial owner. Mere operates 12 stores in Latvia and around 20 in Lithuania. https://www.surinametimes.com/artikel/on.text: Engels One dead, several injured in Czech army helicopter crash PRAGUE – “One person died and several were injured on Thursday when a military helicopter crashed in the Czech Republic with five soldiers on board”, the army and emergency services said. "A Venom helicopter has crashed at the 22nd helicopter base in Namest nad Oslavou. Five soldiers were on board. Emergency services are currently deployed at the scene," the army wrote on X . Petr Janacek, a spokesman for the Vysocina regional rescue services, told AFP that one of the passengers was found dead and three were taken to hospitals in the region, two of them with "moderately serious injuries". A rescue operation was still under way, he said. No information was immediately available regarding the fifth soldier. The Namest and Oslavou airbase is located around 200 kilometers (125 miles) southeast of Prague. Police were informed of the accident at 12:11 pm (1011 GMT), regional police spokeswoman Dana Cirtkova told the CTK news agency. The Czech army bought eight UH-1Y Venom multi-purpose helicopters and four combat AH-1Z Viper helicopters from the United States in 2019, with the final two aircraft delivered in June 2024. American instructors provided training for Czech personnel on the new aircraft until last year. Defense Minister Jaromir Zuna said the incident was "an immense tragedy that affects us all deeply", adding that an inquiry was under way to determine the cause of the crash. Ukraine Culture Security Forum 2.0 highlights culture as a pillar of European security Courtesy of the Ukraine Culture Security Forum 2.0 Participants of the Ukraine Culture Security Forum 2.0 gather in Warsaw on May 7-8. The forum brought together museum professionals, diplomats and cultural experts from seven countries for discussions on protecting Ukrainian cultural heritage during wartime. Thessaloniki, Greece – Ukrainian museum officials, diplomats, cultural leaders and Kyiv’s European partners gathered in Warsaw on May 7-8 for the Ukraine Culture Security Forum 2.0, a major international event focused on protecting national cultural heritage during wartime and strengthening what organizers increasingly describe as Europe’s cultural security. Hosted by the OBMIN Foundation with the participation of the embassies of Germany and Ukraine in Poland, the forum brought together some 160 experts and officials from seven countries. Participants discussed the preservation of Ukraine’s cultural heritage amid Russia’s ongoing attacks, the role of museums in fighting disinformation, and how culture has become intertwined with questions of national security, democratic resilience and postwar recovery. The event was a continuation of a series of conferences launched by the OBMIN network after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Organizers framed the forum as both a response to the destruction caused by the war and a platform for building long-term international partnerships around culture and identity. “Culture is not a luxury – it is a front line,” OBMIN said in a statement opening the forum. Organizers stressed that Russia launched its full-scale war on Ukraine for territorial conquest but also to systematically destroy Ukrainian culture, history and national identity. The first day of the conference took place at the German Embassy in Warsaw and focused on discussions about “weaponized culture,” disinformation campaigns, and the role of museums as “guardians of identity.” The second day moved to PANOPTIKUM, a newly built museum resource center near Warsaw developed by Poland’s National Institute for Museums. Participants examined technical approaches to preserving collections during wartime, including secure storage systems, emergency logistics and restoration tools and techniques. Delegates also visited the Warsaw Gas Museum as part of discussions about industrial heritage and museum resilience. Ukraine’s First Deputy Minister of Culture Ivan Verbytskyi participated in the forum and emphasized the importance of international partnerships for Ukraine’s cultural sector during wartime. “Establishing partnerships and exchanging experience for Ukraine is an opportunity to attract assistance in conditions of limited resources,” Mr. Verbytskyi said. “For international partners, it is an opportunity to study experience in responding and adapting to the challenges of war.” One of the forum’s central topics was international support for the Ukrainian Cultural Heritage Fund, a multi-donor platform created to finance the restoration of Ukrainian cultural heritage damaged or threatened during the war. According to Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture, the fund was established last year and registered in Brussels under European legislation. Its co-founders include Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture, represented by the Ukrainian Center for Cultural Research, and the ALIPH Foundation, an international organization specializing in the protection of endangered cultural heritage. Mr. Verbytskyi also participated in a panel titled “Guardians of Identity: How Museums Define Resistance and Resilien­ce.” Discussions focused on countering disinformation, strengthening sovereignty through culture, and expanding international cultural diplomacy during wartime. Several speakers argued that Russia’s attacks on Ukraine’s museums, archives and monuments should not be viewed as accidents, but rather as part of a broader Kremlin strategy aimed at erasing Ukrainian identity. “Genocide is not just the physical extermination of a people; it is the systematic destruction of their culture, history and identity,” organizers said in one of the forum’s opening statements. Mykyta Poturaiev, chair of the humanitarian and information policy committee in Ukraine’s parliament, addressed the forum via a video message. “Russia is attempting to kill the very essence of what makes us human,” Mr. Poturaiev said. Ukraine’s Deputy Foreign Affairs Minister Olexandr Mischenko participated in a panel titled “False Past, Stolen Future? Disinformation, Culture as a Weapon and the Struggle for Truth,” where he argued that Russian propaganda has become one of Moscow’s primary instruments of war. “Disinformation has long become a component of Russian state policy and one of the key instruments of war against Ukraine and the democratic world,” Mr. Mischenko wrote after the forum. He warned that Russia systematically uses information campaigns to undermine trust in democratic institutions, polarize societies and weaken international support for Ukraine. Mr. Mischenko also drew historical parallels between contemporary Russian rhetoric and propaganda used by Nazi Germa­ny before World War II. “Denial of a people’s right to their own history, culture and statehood has always been a characteristic feature of dictatorial regimes,” he said. According to Mr. Mischenko, Russia continues to portray Ukraine as an “artificial state” without a distinct national identity while simultaneously targeting Ukrainian museums, archives and cultural institutions. He also highlighted Russian information operations aimed at creating tension between Ukrainians and Poles by manipulating historical issues, migration debates and isolated social conflicts. At the same time, the deputy foreign affairs minister thanked Poland and the Polish citizenry for its continued support despite what he described as large-scale Russian disinformation attacks. Participants repeatedly emphasized that Ukraine’s experience in resisting disinformation has become increasingly relevant for the rest of Europe. “Protection of the information space has become an integral component of the security of democratic societies,” Mr. Mischenko said, adding that propaganda and disinformation should be treated “as a full-fledged instrument of aggression alongside military means.” The forum also highlighted the growing role of museums in documenting war, preserving memory and strengthening social resilience. The OBMIN Foundation itself was established shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 as a platform for connecting Ukrainian museums with European partners. The organization currently represents 156 museums across Ukraine, ranging from major national institutions in Kyiv to regional museums focused on local history and culture. According to OBMIN, the network initially focused on emergency assistance and survival support for museums and museum employees during wartime. It later expanded into professional exchanges, digitization initiatives and international cultural projects aimed at promoting knowledge about Ukrainian culture abroad. Representatives of Ukrainian cultural institutions called the forum an important international platform for dialogue and cooperation. Officials from the Andrey Sheptytsky National Museum in Lviv said the gathering united experts and cultural representatives “to discuss the role of culture and the formation of a security system during an existential war.” Franko House in Lviv described the forum as a space for discussing “the role of culture during war and challenges related to preserving cultural heritage, historical memory and national identity.” International museum organizations also participated in the event. The Network of European Museum Organizations (NEMO) contributed to discussions about museum security standards and emergency preparedness. According to NEMO, Poland’s museum sector has significantly expanded its work since Russia’s full-scale invasion, providing humanitarian assistance, training and crisis-preparedness guidance for museums operating under wartime conditions. The Ukraine Culture Security Forum was also presented as a precursor to broader international discussions about reconstruction and recovery. Organizers linked the event to discussions held at the Ukraine Recovery Conference and argued that cultural preservation must become part of Europe’s long-term rebuilding strategy. For many participants, the discussions in Warsaw reflected a broader shift in how European institutions are increasingly understanding culture – not as a secondary issue during wartime, but as a central element of sovereignty, democratic resilience and collective security. “In response to Russia’s attempts to falsify history and manipulate the past,” Mr. Mischenko said, “democratic societies must respond with unity, resilience and systematic protection of truth.” Premium Previous Article Ukraine seeks European role in proposed ‘airport ceasefire’ with Russia Next Article Ukrainian drone strikes deep in Russia grow public alarm Related Posts Britain’s new prime minister reaffirms support for Ukraine in first meeting with Zelenskyy July 31, 2026 1:38 am By Roman Tymotsko Breaking News Deadly strike on defense technology event forces Ukraine to rethink industry gatherings July 31, 2026 1:33 am By Roman Tymotsko Ukraine Olena Teliha remembered as Ukraine marks 120th anniversary of her birth July 31, 2026 1:27 am By Roman Tymotsko Ukraine Comments are closed. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: A Ukrainian interceptor drone on display. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said interceptor missile development must show ‘concrete results’ by the end of this year. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters View image in fullscreen A Ukrainian interceptor drone on display. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said interceptor missile development must show ‘concrete results’ by the end of this year. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: We will build missiles the way we built drones – Zelenskyy ‘Concrete results’ needed by end of the year in developing alternative to Patriot, says Ukrainian president. What we know on day 1,626 Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Thu 6 Aug 2026 21.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Volodymr Zelenskyy has said he wants “concrete results” by the end of this year on producing an anti-ballistic missile defence system for Ukraine. Zelenskyy referred to Ukraine’s role in the Freyja programme to jointly develop a European anti-ballistic system as an alternative to Patriot. “ Ukraine is capable of producing its missile and launcher , while our partners will provide the necessary components and critical elements – radars, sensors, and everything else required … Others spent decades developing their systems. Ukraine must do this as quickly as possible, with concrete results already in place by the turn of 2026–2027.” Zelenskyy said on Thursday night that he had met with senior officials on how to accelerate development “so that Ukrainian weapons manufacturers and developers can deliver real results … We are creating all the necessary conditions to make that happen.” On the offensive side, “ Ukraine is also working to develop ballistic missiles of its own . The tests have shown strong potential. We need to turn this into a real weapon.” The Kyiv region observed an official day of mourning on Thursday after a Russian missile and drone blitz killed 17 people the previous day . In the first six months of this year, 1,396 civilians were killed and 7,978 injured in Ukraine, the UN office in Kyiv said on Wednesday. That was a 37% increase from the same period last year and a 114% jump over 2024, it said, attributing the rise to more long-range aerial attacks by Russia. On the day that Kyiv mourned its dead, the head of the UN appeared to put the blame for civilian casualties on both sides . “These latest series of attacks follow an alarming pattern of escalating strikes against populated areas,” said Farhan Haq, a spokesperson for António Guterres, the UN secretary general. “The secretary general strongly condemns the latest large-scale missile and drone attacks by the armed forces of the Russian Federation on Kyiv and other cities in Ukraine … [Guterres] also condemns the recent Ukrainian drone attacks on several regions of the Russian Federation.” Russia has adjusted its rhetoric lately to claim that its evident strikes killing Ukrainian civilians are targeting military facilities, or militarised civilian sites such as warehouses, ports and logistics depots, while portraying Ukrainian strikes on military and economic targets in Russia as being aimed at civilians. Russian forces have continually bombarded civilians with anti-personnel explosive FPV drones in Ukrainian centres including Kherson , Zaporizhzhia and Kharkiv. Leipzig drone bomb was found near Ukrainian plane carrying ammunition, say police Read more A drone carrying explosives that was found at Leipzig airport had come down near a Ukrainian aircraft loaded with military ammunition , according to a classified police report quoted by the German public broadcasters WDR and NDR and the Süddeutsche newspaper. Deborah Cole reports from Berlin that the German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said only an apparently “ripped” detonator had prevented the device going off near Ukrainian cargo planes on the tarmac at the shipping and military hub. Ukraine hit more oil facilities deep inside Russia , Zelenskyy said on Thursday. Targets included a refinery in Russia’s Bashkortostan region, more than 1,300km (800 miles) from the frontline, as well as a refinery in the Yaroslavl region, almost 700km into Russia. The Yaroslavl governor, Mikhail Yevrayev, confirmed an attack on a refinery, saying oil reservoirs were set on fire. Ukrainian forces hit two Russian military patrol boats in the Black Sea, Zelenskyy said, along with vessels belonging to Moscow’s so-called shadow fleet, which Russia uses to evade western restrictions on its oil exports. He did not give any details. The Russian defence ministry said its air defences shot down 605 Ukrainian drones over its territory. Ukraine will provide assistance to farmers hit by Russian attacks on ⁠shipping and port facilities , Zelenskyy said. Subsidised credits and other assistance with financing would “begin to be implemented in the coming days”. The governor ‌of Ukraine’s Odesa Region, ‌Oleh Kiper, said on Thursday that a Russian attack had damaged a foreign-flagged ship loaded with ‌wheat in Ukraine’s Black Sea area, killing one crew member and causing a fire. Ukraine’s seaports authority identified the ship as sailing under the flag of Guinea-Bissau. Ukraine had established a Black Sea corridor for safe passage of shipping along the coast towards Romania, but ships have recently come under attack in the area. Zelenskyy will on Saturday make his first visit to Serbia since Russia’s invasion. “We need to pull the Serbs away from Russia’s side,” a senior Ukrainian official told Agence France-Presse, calling Zelenskyy’s visit to Belgrade a “slap in the face for the Russians”. Serbia’s president, Aleksandar Vučić, has held talks with Vladimir Putin and maintained friendly relations with Moscow while also trying to join the European Union. Vučić’s office confirmed what it described as an “official visit” by Zelenskyy. While Zelenskyy would state his position, Serbia’s policy “will remain the case until further notice”, it added. Sweden will hand over to Kyiv a seized Russian “shadow fleet” cargo ship which Ukraine says transported grain stolen from its occupied territory , Swedish court documents obtained by AFP on Thursday showed. The supreme court on 4 August dismissed an appeal by Caffa Shipping Ltd, which owns the 96-metre (315-foot) Caffa, to block the transfer requested by Ukraine and approved by two lower courts in Sweden. The Caffa, sailing under a false Guinean flag, was headed for St Petersburg, Russia when armed Swedish police boarded it on 6 March off Trelleborg on its southern coast. Ten of the 11 crew on board were Russian nationals. https://www.politico.eu/article/friedric.text: BERLIN — German Chancellor Friedrich Merz doesn’t seem to think his job will be in danger when he gets back from his summer holiday. “I’m assuming that things will have calmed down a bit by September,” he said last week, after internal dissent over his handling of a cabinet reshuffle boiled over. He may be underestimating the pressure building within his own party. Advertisement Advertisement Ahead of crucial regional elections in September — in which the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has a realistic chance of taking power in a German state for the first time — there is increasingly open discussion of a Kanzlertausch , or chancellor swap, in the fall. Public criticism has mainly come from those ousted from government in the reshuffle. But behind the scenes, a growing number of politicians from Merz’s center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU) are discussing what would, by German standards, be a remarkable scenario: replacing the leader after little more than a year in the job. Europe’s biggest economy has long been one of its most stable democracies, with no history of rattling through leaders like postwar Italy or post-Brexit Britain. But the expected success of the AfD, in elections in which the CDU is expected to lose ground, is upending the country’s conventional political dynamics. The theory behind a Kanzlertausch is that the conservatives will need to stem the fallout from the eastern elections and give themselves a boost by replacing a leader unable to shake his rock-bottom ratings. But the stakes are high. The AfD — now the most popular party in national polls — would seek to capitalize on further coalition unrest. Replacing a chancellor years before the end of his term would mean venturing into largely uncharted political territory. Advertisement Advertisement Only three sitting chancellors have been succeeded by a politician from the same political camp in postwar Germany: in 1963, when the 87-year-old Konrad Adenauer resigned to make way for Ludwig Erhard; in 1966, after Erhard’s coalition collapsed ; and in 1974, when Social Democrat Willy Brandt stood down over an espionage scandal. The current Kanzlertausch scenario — in which Hendrik Wüst, the premier of the western state of North Rhine-Westphalia, has emerged as Merz’s most likely successor — has been widely discussed in German media, including in the latest Der Spiegel cover story headlined “ Palace Revolt .” Conservative politicians confirmed the internal debate to POLITICO, speaking on condition of anonymity given the sensitivity of the discussions. The AfD — now the most popular party in national polls — would seek to capitalize on further coalition unrest. | John MacDougall/AFP via Getty Images The growing discontent, they said, reflected declining trust in the chancellor’s statesmanship and his expected inability to keep the party together if the AfD takes power in September. Polls show that the AfD could win an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt on Sept. 6, while it is poised to win in Mecklenburg–Western Pomerania and do well in Berlin on Sept. 20. A further fear is that individual CDU politicians in eastern Germany might lend their support to an AfD-led state government after the elections — breaking Merz’s long-standing pledge never to allow the far right into government. Advertisement Advertisement One called the debate “speculative” for now and said that the aftermath of the elections in eastern Germany would be “decisive” for the chancellor’s future. They also stressed that, for now, no senior figure has publicly spoken out against Merz. Yet the mounting unease is conspicuous in a party usually known for its discipline. Keeping a cool head If Merz were forced to go, that would seriously disrupt Germany’s consensus-based political system. The move would come less than two years after the previous center-left coalition fell apart and could trigger a snap election. Kai Arzheimer, a political science professor at the University of Mainz, said the fragmentation of Germany’s party system — where centrist parties must forge sometimes awkward coalitions to keep increasingly popular fringe parties from power — has triggered a shift. “Compared with the 1970s and 1980s, Germany has experienced relatively little political stability for quite some time now,” he said. “However, by the standards of what has become the norm in many other European countries, one could also say that Germany has simply arrived where others have been for a long time.” Advertisement Advertisement Appeals for restraint have meanwhile begun to emerge from across the political spectrum. “A Union that is tearing itself apart is of no use to anyone in the democratic center,” said Christiane Hoffmann, a former spokesperson for center-left Chancellor Olaf Scholz, in a lengthy post on X about the current debate. “I am firmly convinced that Friedrich Merz will remain chancellor,” Markus Söder said. | Sean Gallup/Getty Images “A little stability, please,” she demanded. “There’s just headless grumbling and bleating, with no one knowing where it’s all headed. Europe is on fire. Could a few people please keep a cool head?” How a swap could unfold The least disruptive route would be for Merz to step aside voluntarily, allowing his successor to be elected by majority vote. If Merz refuses to go, his opponents would have to oust him through a constructive vote of no confidence, simultaneously electing his successor. Such an extraordinary parliamentary maneuver would risk ripping apart the governing coalition of Merz’s CDU, its Bavarian sister party, the Christian Social Union (CSU), and the Social Democrats. For now, Merz continues to enjoy the backing of leading conservative figures. Advertisement Advertisement “I am firmly convinced that Friedrich Merz will remain chancellor,” Markus Söder, the powerful state premier of Bavaria and CSU leader, said in an interview with public broadcaster ARD over the weekend. “It would throw the conservatives into complete disarray,” Söder said of a potential swap. “Moreover, it could even lead to new elections. And anyone who wants new elections now — in a situation like this, after such a lead-up — is only promoting one thing: bringing radicals to power. That is why my urgent advice is to focus on the work at hand and spend less time speculating behind the scenes.” At national level, POLITICO’s Poll of Polls puts the AfD as the single most popular party with 28 percent support, with Merz’s conservatives on 21 percent. At the same time, only 13 percent of Germans are satisfied with Merz’s performance, according to the latest benchmark ARD-DeutschlandTrend poll released last month . That is the lowest rating for a sitting chancellor in the survey’s nearly 30-year history. Merz’s rock-bottom ratings reflect disappointment over his efforts to revive Germany’s ailing economy and public skepticism over far-reaching pension and health care reforms that will be difficult to implement and are expected to cost the average voter money. For now, Merz’s most viable political strategy appears to be appealing to politicians’ risk aversion in an effort to preserve what remains of Germany’s reputation for political stability. “I can’t imagine many people within the conservative camp saying: ‘This is the solution, and we’re willing to take any risk in the hope that we might then do better in the polls,’” said Arzheimer, the political science professor. “That would be a completely crazy idea.” Advertisement

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c89n.text: Image source, Supplied: Skytraders Image caption, The Skytraders plane landed in Antarctica in total darkness and a temperature of -43Â°C By Helen Livingstone Sydney Published 11 minutes ago An Australian aviation crew has carried out a daring midwinter mission to rescue a US expedition member from a station in Antarctica in freezing temperatures and total darkness. Skytraders said the "extraordinary" mission took place last Friday after a request for urgent help with a medical evacuation from McMurdo Station. After an initial delay due to the weather, the aviation company said it was able to land its Airbus A319 in "extremely challenging conditions" including temperatures of -43C (-45.4F). The patient was then safely transferred onto the plane, known as Snowbird 1, which carried on to Christchurch in New Zealand, where the patient was treated. He is now recovering well. Skytraders deputy chief executive Duncan Mackay told the Australian newspaper the plane had undergone a complete refit into a specialised medevac configuration within 24 hours of the call. However takeoff was then delayed for 12 hours while the crew waited for a suitable window in the weather. The plane eventually took off from the Tasmanian city of Hobart in the early hours of Friday morning, before landing at the US research station on Ross Island. No details were given about the patient or his condition, other than that he was now recovering well. Image source, Supplied: Skytraders Image caption, Pilot Al Wallach said conditions were 'right on the edge of even the most specialised aircraft capability' Mackay said his company believed it was the closest a civilian airliner had operated so close to winter solstice, which was on 21 June. "Skytraders has conducted winter medevacs previously, but never this close to the winter solstice," he told the paper. He said "an enormous amount of experience and familiarity with the conditions" was needed to safely land an airliner on an ice runway in total darkness at -43Â°C. The pilot, Captain Al Wallach said the successful mission reflected the specialist expertise of the team's people, which included the flight crews, meteorologists, operational planers, runway teams and medical personnel. "Every Antarctic mission demands absolute precision, but winter operations raise the complexity significantly," he said "The conditions we encountered were right on the edge of even the most specialised aircraft capability." Skytraders carried out a similar mission in March 2020, when the US requested help evacuating a member of the US Antarctic Program also based in McMurdo, although temperatures were slightly warmer at -30Â°C. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/06/korr.text: Menü Kereső Magasra ívelt a politikai karrierje, most korrupciógyanúba keveredett Ukrajna volt kormányfőhelyettese Külföld Olha Sztefanyisina ukrán miniszterelnök-helyettes és Magyar Levente, a Külgazdasági és Külügyminisztérium parlamenti államtitkára a tárgyalásuk után tartott sajtótájékoztatón, 2025. április 29-én – Fotó: Huszti István / Telex Nyilas Gergely Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Két éve még Ukrajnát képviselte a történelmi napon, amikor az Európai Unió először tárgyalt az ország lehetséges csatlakozásáról, most viszont hatmillió hrivnya (kb. 42 millió forint) óvadék ellenében, a hatóságok folyamatos értesítésével hagyhatja el lakhelyét Olha Sztefanyisina – döntött csütörtökön egy kijevi bíróság. A politikus nagy ívű politikai pályát járva be jutott el a korrupciós vádakig. A 40 éves politikus már 2020-ban Ukrajna kormányfőhelyettese lett, emellé megkapta azt a területet is, amely az Oroszország által két évvel később elindított háború árnyékában még fontosabb lett, mint korábban: ő felelt az ország euroatlanti integrációjáért. Ebben a pozícióban volt akkor is, amikor az ország megkapta a tagjelölti státuszt, ekkoriban a Telexnek is adott interjút . 2024-ben ő képviselte az országot a csatlakozási tárgyalások megkezdéséről szóló döntéskor. Még abban az évben az igazságügyi miniszteri tárcát is átvette, ekkor Magyarországon is tárgyalt Magyar Levente külügyminiszter-helyettessel. Ez is kiemelt feladat volt, hiszen a Fidesz-kormány alatt a magyar–ukrán kapcsolatok a mélyponton voltak, ami akadálya volt Ukrajna érdemi csatlakozási folyamatának. Sztefanyisina politikai pályája ígéretesen alakult még tavaly is, amikor az Ukrajna és az Egyesült Államok közötti kapcsolatokért felelős megbízott, majd az ország washingtoni nagykövete lett . A posztját a hét elején veszítette el, amikor Volodimir Zelenszkij hivatalosan is közölte visszahívását. Valójában ez is hosszú politikai túlélést jelentett, Sztefanyisina ugyanis már 2023-ban gyanúsított volt , akkor egy eredetileg még 2014-hez kötődő ügyben . Eszerint a már akkoriban is az euroatlanti integráció területén dolgozó Sztefanyisina az igazságügyi minisztérium munkatársaként részese volt egy 2,5 millió hrivnyás (akkori árfolyamon kb. 25 millió forint) kifizetésnek. Ez az ügy sem zárult le, de ez nem törte meg a karrierjét, ellentétben a mostani vádakkal, amelyek több ingatlanról szólnak. Miből? Sztefanyisinának a gyanú szerint olyan ingatlanai vannak, amelyek nincsenek arányban az igazolt bevételeivel. Annyira, hogy ezek egy része hivatalosan nem is az ő, hanem egy barátnője nevén volt. Az összegek nem csillagászatiak ugyan – két, egyenként 11 millió hrivnyás (kb. 77 millió forint) lakásról van szó –, de a háborúban ötödik éve védekező Ukrajnában, ahol százezrek járják meg a frontot, sérülnek és halnak meg, a társadalom sokkal tudatosabbá és érzékenyebbé vált a korrupciót illetően. Zelenszkij elnök és Sztefanyisina egyeztet Kijevben, 2025. július 17-én – Fotó: UKRAINIAN PRESIDENTIAL PRESS SERVICE / AFP Ezt mutatta az Ukrajna Nemzeti Korrupcióellenes Ügynöksége (NABU) és a Különleges Korrupcióellenes Ügyészség (SZAP) létrejötte, majd különösen az a társadalmi felháborodás, amelybe az ukrán elnök ütközött , amikor tavaly megpróbálta visszanyesni a két intézmény függetlenségét. Zelenszkij gyorsan visszavonulót fújt, ezután a NABU nyomozása egészen magasra ért, elsodorta az elnöki hivatal rendkívül befolyásos vezetőjét, Andrij Jermakot, aki az idén már hivatalosan is gyanúsított lett egy 100 millió dolláros pénzmosási ügyben. Ebben nemcsak a Zelenszkij egykor bizalmasának tartott Jermak, de az elnök színészi-komikusi pályafutásának beindítója, személyes jóbarátja is érintett . Timur Mindics még elszámoltatása előtt Izraelbe távozott, amelynek állampolgára is. Az elnök ukrán szankciós listára tette egykori barátját. A kiterjedt korrupciós ügyben lemondott az energetikai miniszter, elődje pedig gyanúsított lett . Ma már nem fér bele az igazolatlan vagyon A politikai körökben jelen lévő korrupció Ukrajna függetlenségének első 25 évében sokszor bocsánatos bűnnek számított, de az elcsalt választások utáni 2004-es narancsos forradalom, majd az oroszpárti Viktor Janukovics elmeneküléséhez vezető Euromajdan 2014-es tüntetései után ez fokozatosan változott. A társadalomban megjelenő igény a megtisztulásra a Krím orosz annexiója, majd a kelet-ukrajnai háború kezdetével tovább erősödött, és érezhetően új szintre lépett a sokkal nagyobb társadalmi áldozatot követelő 2022-es orosz invázió után. A korrupció felszámolása ekkor külpolitikailag is létfontosságú volt: az ország alapvető megítélése múlt azon, hogy mennyire számíthat pénzügyi, katonai segítségre Oroszországgal szemben, és hatással volt Ukrajna euroatlanti integrációs esélyeire is – vagyis épp arra a területre, amelyért Sztefanyisina felelt. Így az ő nehezen igazolható forrásokból származó ingatlanjai ebben a társadalmi hangulatban egészen más üzenetet hordoznak, mint tíz évvel korábban lett volna egy hasonló ügyben. A politikusnak egyébként nemcsak a két fenti kijevi ingatlan miatt kell magyarázkodnia, de az anyja nevén lévő másik fővárosi lakásért és az apja nevén lévő parkolóért és raktárhelyiségért is ugyanabban az épületben. Ezek egyikét sem jelölte vagyonbevallásában, ahogyan az egyik beosztottja nevén lévő, a piacon 25 millió forintosra taksált Mercedest sem, amelyet valójában sajátjaként használt – sorolta az Nv.ua. A NABU szerint tavaly egy 550 ezer dolláros (kb. 175 millió forint) házat akart venni, amelynek felét készpénzben, másik felét két lakással fizette volna ki. Ettől elállt, a nyomozás szerint azért, mert épp megkapta washingtoni nagyköveti kinevezését. Sztefanyisina szerint nincs is ennyi pénze „Minden nyomozati eljárás a hatóságok működésének törvényes menete, nem a bűnösség bizonyítéka – kommentálta a helyzetet Sztefanyisina. – Mindezt nyugalommal fogadom, felesleges érzelmek nélkül. Az egész kavarodás csupán vihar egy pohár vízben”. Olha Sztefanyisina az Ukrajnai Korrupcióellenes Főbíróság (HACC) előtt, Kijevben, 2026. augusztus 5-én – Fotó: Ivan Antypenko / Suspilne Ukraine / Global Images Ukraine / Getty Images A NABU azonban másként látja: a nyomozati hatóság szerint Sztefanyisina vagyoni helyzete nem áll arányban hivatalosan ismert jövedelmével: 2024 elejétől másfél éven át összesen 3,7 millió hrivnyát keresett, ehhez képest csak a számlájáról 4,2 milliót költött és ezek felett vannak még az említett ingatlanok. A NABU úgy véli, Sztefanyisina legalább 13 millió hrivnyával nem tud elszámolni. Nem könnyíti meg a volt miniszter és volt nagykövet helyzetét, hogy volt férje miatt is magyarázkodnia kell. Bár Mihajlo Sztefanyisintől már 2017-ben elvált, mégis árnyékot vetett rá, hogy a férfi – egy rendőrből lett vállalkozó – több nagy ingatlanra tette rá a kezét a Kamparitet nevű cégen keresztül, egyebek között a Kijev szívében, a Majdan sarkán lévő egykori szakszervezeti székházra. Sztefanyisina tavaly azt nyilatkozta , hogy érdemi kapcsolatban csak két közös gyerekük révén áll egykori férjével, de a férfit ért korrupciós vádak óta egyáltalán nem beszélnek egymással. Sztefanyisinának csak október elején kell megjelennie a bíróság előtt, addig azonban lakhelye elhagyása esetén tájékoztatnia kell a hatóságot a hollétéről. Legutóbb úgy nyilatkozott, hogy már látja új munkahelyét, amely nem állami szolgálatban, hanem a magánszférában lesz. Elmondása szerint erre szüksége is van, mert sem az állítólagos 13 millió hrivnyás igazolatlan vagyonnal nem rendelkezik, sem a bíróság által meghatározott hatmilliós óvadékra nincs pénze, ezért ennek csökkentését is kérte. https://telex.hu/techtud/2026/08/06/magy.text: Menü Kereső Kipróbáltuk Magyarország legolcsóbb új autóját Techtud Fotó: Macsuga János Macsuga János Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Négy év után ismét eljött az idő, hogy Magyarország legolcsóbb autóját teszteljük. Az arany szín miatt felsejlett bennem a 2022-es legolcsóbb Mitsubishi Space Star kellemetlen emléke, de mostani tesztalanyunk, a Dacia Sandero nemcsak méretben, hanem minőségérzetben is magasabb kategóriát képvisel. Ez már a platformtárs Jogger kipróbálásakor is kiderült, hiszen 2020 óta a Daciák zöme az aktuális Renault-alkatrészek olcsóbb változatát kapja. A cégcsoport már nem azzal akar pénzt keresni, hogy elavult legókockákból építenek autókat. Persze a CMF-B platform sem mai már, az ötödik generációs Renault Clióval mutatkozott be 2019-ben, viszont azóta ennek a modellnek az utódján kívül közel húsz olyan típus jelent meg, ami ugyanezt az architektúrát használja. A harmadik generációs Dacia Sandero 2020-ban jelent meg, de a formája még most is egészen frissnek hat. Az első fényszórói a manapság divatos csíkszemeffektusra építenek, viszont a Daciának csak a tompított fényszórója és a nappali menetfénye LED-rendszerű . Az évek során két ráncfelvarrással is javítottak a Sanderón, a 2022-ben megjelent új Dacia-egyenarc is fiatalítja az autót, 2025-től pedig ismét módosították a lámpákat és a lökhárítókat, valamint új, nagyobb méretű infotainment került a kis Daciába. Fotó: Macsuga János Ami meglepően jól működik, pillanatok alatt párosítható a telefonnal, és ezen felül igazából nem is kéne tudnia semmit, hiszen a klímának vannak hagyományos tekerőgombjai, ezért az érintőkijelző gyári kezelőfelületét csak akkor kell használni, ha ki akarjuk kapcsolni a kötelező vezetéstámogató rendszereket. Erre szükség is lesz, mert a Dacia elég agresszívan pittyeg, ha egy pillanatra azt érzékeli, hogy átléptük a megengedett sebességet, vagy lenézünk az útról. Vészfékezésre viszont egy téves riasztás sem volt a hét alatt, ami akár jót is jelenthetne – de persze azt nem próbáltuk ki, hogy éles, balesetveszélyes helyzetben hogy reagálna a rendszer. Például valóban képes lenne-e megállítani az autót ütközés előtt. A vasban van az árelőny? A Dacia az elérhető ötből mindössze két csillagot kapott az EuroNCAP töréstesztjén, és ez csak részben vezethető vissza arra, hogy bár akkortájt még megengedőbb volt a pontozás, a Dacia viszont a versenytársainál szerényebb menetbiztonsági elektronikákat épített az autóba. A Sandero azért is lett kategóriájának legrosszabb biztonsági besorolású típusa, mert az összes fontos területen 10–30 százalékkal rosszabb értékeket kapott a jobbak közé tartozó Volkswagen Polónál. Valószínű, hogy az ütközésbiztonság szempontjából fontos anyagokban lesz a különbség a két autó közt, hiszen annak ellenére, hogy a Sandero a legnagyobbak közé tartozik kategóriájában, a többieknél körülbelül 100 kilóval könnyebb. A kisautók kategóriájában csak a Suzuki Swift utasai járnak rosszabbul egy balesetben, de a japánok a jobb gyalogosvédelemmel és elektronikával három csillagot értek el. A videófelvételek alapján a Dacia is egy a sok modern autó közül, amelynek utascellája lényegében ép marad egy városi frontális ütközésnél, de érdemes számításba venni a teljes teszt elért eredményét is vásárláskor. Mindebből az autó hétköznapi használata közben semmi nem tűnik fel. Az ajtók súlyosak és vaskosak, mint minden modern autóban, és egészen jónak érződik az összeszerelési minőség, valamint az anyaghasználat is. Mindezt persze a kategória többi tagjához kell viszonyítani. Menet közben nem zörög semmi az utastérben, és még a műszerfal közepére is jutott egy szövetsáv, ami kellemesebbé teszi a mindennapokat a Sanderóban. Nagy kár, hogy az ülések még mindig elég kényelmetlenek és a kárpit is izzasztó. A helykínálat viszont a kategória legjobbjai közé tartozik, még hátul is jól el lehet férni, a 2,6 méteres tengelytáv miatt. A csomagtartó kicsit kisebb a vártnál (328 literes), viszont 70 ezer forint felárért elfért benne egy pótkerék is. Szériafelszerelés az osztottan dönthető hátsó üléssor, ami például a Trend kivitelű VW Polóhoz nem járt, de előredöntött hátsó üléstámlákkal nem lesz sík a raktér, sőt, középen egy vasmerevítés is rontja a pakolhatóságot. A kormányzás vállalható, de a puhára hangolt futóművel együtt egyáltalán nem harapós a Sandero. Lassan reagál az irányváltásokra és kanyarokban dülöngél. Cserébe kicsi-közepes kátyúkon egész jól átlibben, a nagyobbakba viszont már csúnyán beledörren. A legolcsóbb Dacia nagy előnye az egyliteres, 100 lóerős, háromhengeres turbómotor, amivel 10 másodpercen belül gyorsíthatunk álló helyzetből 100 km/óra sebességre. Régen még viccesebb volt ekkora teljesítmény egy kisautóban, húsz éve egyenesen élményszámba ment egy Fiat Panda 100HP, vagyis az olcsó Fiat sportváltozata. Fotó: Macsuga János A Dacia is szedi a lábait, a hatsebességes, viszonylag kellemesen kapcsolható váltóval gond nélkül elnavigálunk a forgalomban. Alacsony fordulaton van némi alapjárati rezonancia és turbólyuk, de semmi extra, szinte az összes modern, kicsi háromhengeres motor ilyen. A gyártó száz kilométerenként 5,4 literes vegyes átlagfogyasztást ad meg, amit meglepő módon nagyjából hozott is az autó a gyakorlatban, csak városban voltak jellemzőbbek a hat liter fölötti értékek. Ezzel az autó körülbelül a Stellantis-csoport 1,2-es turbójának értékeit hozza, a Volkswagen konszern egyliteres motorjához képest pedig jó fél literrel fogyaszt többet. A H5Dt kódjelű, TCe fantázianevű motor tehát jó, de ehhez az összes modern trükkre: a közvetlen befecskendezésre, turbóra, részecskeszűrőre és kettőstömegű lendkerékre is szüksége van, ami később megdrágíthatja a fenntartását. Városi környezetben a Sandero kifejezetten csendes, de autópályán 120 km/óra fölött már elkezd zajongani. A fordulatszám ilyenkor is alacsony marad, így csak egy kis dörmögést hallunk a háttérből, inkább a szél- és a gördülési zaj erősödik fel. A hosszú utazásokban viszont jó partner lesz a manapság már meglepően nagynak számító, 50 literes üzemanyagtank. Öldöklő harc a kisautós szegmensben A harmadik generációhoz érve abszolút vállalható, a versenytársakhoz képest alig, vagy egyáltalán nem rosszabb minőségérzetű autó lett a Dacia Sandero, egyedül a biztonság területén van továbbra is lemaradása. Mindez az európai vásárlókat láthatóan nem izgatja, hiszen 2024-ben és 2025-ben is ez a típus volt a legnagyobb példányszámban eladott új személyautó az Európai Unióban . Fotó: Macsuga János Cikkünk megjelenésekor a Dacia Sandero kedvezményes ára 1 literes, 100 lóerős TCe turbómotorral, manuális klímával, telefontükrözéses infotainmenttel 5,7 millió forint volt. Jelenleg ez a legolcsóbb új autó Magyarországon. Korábban ez a közel 6 millióért kínált, kicsit igényesebb, de gyengébb, szívómotorral árult fapados Volkswagen Polo Trend volt, amelynek teljes magyar kontingensét eladták már a Porsche Hungária tájékoztatása szerint. Az olcsóbb Stellantis-autók, mint az Opel Corsa, a Citroën C3, a Fiat Grande Panda vagy a Peugeot 208, vagy a Suzuki Swift is részt vesznek a hatmillió forint körüli olcsó autók versenyében, de figyelni kell a felszereltségükre. Aki nem fél a kínaiaktól, hatmillió forint alatt az MG3 -ast is választhatja, de az importőr itt is készletakciót jelez. A garanciális feltételeket is érdemes böngészni, elég nagy eltérések lehetnek. A Daciánál 3 évre korlátlan, 5 évre viszont már csak 100 ezer kilométerig kiterjedő garanciát adnak, míg például az Opelnél azonos futásteljesítmény mellett 8 évet vállalnak. Fotó: Macsuga János A fenti kisautókban közös, hogy szinte mindegyik elég idős konstrukció, és a jövőjük erősen kérdéses. Ezek a négyméteres, már éppen használható méretű benzines autók a haláltusájukat vívják, mert a szigorodó károsanyag-kibocsátási és biztonsági normák miatt elszálló fejlesztési és gyártási költségek a legtöbb márka számára gazdaságtalanná teszik a fenntartásukat. A teljes képhez az is hozzátartozik, hogy a gyártók a manapság népszerűbb, terepjárósabb fazonú társaikat kisebb elánnal nyírják ki. Így Opel Mokkát, Ford Pumát , Citroën C3 Aircrosst , Peugeot 2008-at és társait valószínűleg később is vásárolhatunk majd, de drágábban, és a fenntartási költségük is magasabb a sima személyautókénál. https://telex.hu/after/2026/08/06/heaven.text: Menü Kereső Heaven Street Seven: A krézi srácot az Emergency House-nak köszönhetjük After Sajó Dávid „Időnként ezek a dalok megérdemlik, hogy elhangozzanak” – indokolta adásunkban Szűcs Krisztián, hogy miért állt össze pár koncertre idén a 2015-ben feloszlott Heaven Street Seven (HS7). A Budapest Parkban tartott koncertjére készülő zenekar frontembere és dalszövegírója mellett a HS7 billentyűse és producere, Takács-Brouwer Zoltán Jappán volt a vendégünk. Szerinte a júliusi orfűi fellépésük a becsúszó hibák ellenére nem öregfiúk koncert volt, a dalok ugyanúgy működtek. Az eleinte angol nyelvű számokat megjelentető Heaven Street Seven a kilencvenes években az indie- és britpop zenék kedvelőit érte el, Szűcs szerint ez akkor kb. háromszáz embert jelentett Magyarországon. A már kizárólag magyar nyelvű dalokat tartalmazó, a 100 legfontosabb magyar lemez közé is beszavazott Cukor című lemezükkel azonban kitörtek ebből a buborékból. Arról a 2000-ben megjelent lemezről több dal, például a Mozdulj (ennek a klipjében szerepelt Marsi Anikó) és a Sajnálom is népszerű lett szélesebb körben, a Hol van az a krézi srác? -ot pedig döbbenetes módon még a Danubius rádió is játszotta, igaz, a szerkesztők ki akarták szedetni a tudja a halál sort a dalszövegből, amihez a zenekar nem járult hozzá. Szűcs arról is beszélt az adásban, hogyan inspirálta a szintén újra aktív Emergency House a legnagyobb slágerük szövegét. A HS7 tagjai sokáig hittek abban, hogy egy rendszeresen Nyugat-Európában turnézó, külföldön is elismert produkcióvá nőhetik ki magukat, ehhez egy ponton elég közel is álltak, de ahogy Szűcs fogalmazott, a magyar rock ‘n’ roll ugarnak azért vicces és nyomorult dolgai is voltak, így ez az álom elúszott. 2006-ban nagyjából 600 jelentkező együttesből ők kapták az European Breakthrough Awardot, ami azt jelentette, hogy az EU-hoz akkoriban csatlakozó országok zenekarai közül leginkább bennük látta az európai szakma a nemzetközi áttörés lehetőségét. Később a kultzenekarnak számító Churchcsel volt közös turnéjuk, így több száz ember előtt játszottak például Londonban. Utólag a zenekar úgy látja, ez az időszak elszalasztott lehetőség volt, a magyar szakmai szereplők ugyanis nem tettek igazán semmit azért, hogy a HS7-nek tényleg összejöjjön a nemzetközi siker. Cannes-ban már a MIDEM zenei konferencián is látszott, hogy a zenekar ügyét nem veszik komolyan a hazai szereplők, így esély sem volt arra, hogy Yonderboihoz hasonló karriert fussanak be külföldön. Szűcs szerint ebben az sem segített, hogy a HS7 – Robert Musil regényét idézve – úgynevezett tulajdonságok nélküli zenekar volt, nem volt könnyen megjegyezhető háttérsztorijuk, imidzsük, amivel könnyebben el lehetett volna adni a zenéjüket. „Ha én vagyok a világ legjobb biciklise, és kapok egy biciklit, akkor sem fogom utolérni a Trabantot” – mondta Szűcs, utalva ezzel arra, hogy Magyarországról sokkal több pénz, szakértelem és energia kellett volna ahhoz, hogy versenybe tudjanak szállni egy hasonló kvalitású nyugat-európai zenekarral. A zenekar két tagja szerint a Cukor után a Tudom, hogy szeretsz titokban volt a másik esszenciális HS7-lemez, az azt követő, befejezetlennek ható Jazz az útkeresésről szólt, az életművet lezáró, 2012-ben kiadott Felkeltem a reggelt pedig már inkább Szűcs és Jappán közös munkájának tekinthető. A zenekar az utolsó lemez idejére megrekedt, elfáradt, Jappán szerint végül egy megalázó, halászléfesztiválos fellépés után érezte azt, hogy ennek a történetnek vége, nincs értelme tovább csinálni. A HS7 végül 2015-ben jelentette be a feloszlását. A nemrég novelláskötettel ( Utazás a kegyetlenbe ) jelentkező Szűcs a műsorban arról is beszélt, hogy a HS7 nem lesz üzemszerűen működő zenekar, nem írnak új dalokat, ez egy pár koncertre szóló összeállás. Jappán pedig elárulta, hogy felmerült egyszer komolyabban, hogy összeálljon a másik zenekara, a Soerii & Poolek, de jelenleg kevés esélyt lát arra, hogy a Beton.Hofi zenekarában játszó Kovács Gergellyel közös produkciójukat megint színpadra vigyék. https://telex.hu/g7/penz/2026/08/06/paks.text: Menü Kereső Paks még kevésbé fenyegeti a GDP-t, mint az ipari áramfogyasztás korlátozása Pénz A Lágymányosi-öböl a rendkívül alacsony vízállású Dunánál 2026. augusztus 5-én – Fotó: Szigetváry Zsolt / MTI Torontáli Zoltán Sorra jelennek meg a becslések arról, hogy a paksi atomerőmű részleges vagy akár teljes átmeneti leállása mennyibe kerülhet a költségvetésnek, makrogazdasági szempontból azonban ennél is fontosabbnak tűnik, hogy szükség lesz-e a mostani válságban az ipari fogyasztók energiafelhasználásának korlátozására. Számokban: a kormány egyelőre arra számít, hogy 50 milliárd forintot emészt fel Paks – egyelőre részleges – átmeneti leállása. Naponta 1,5-2 milliárd forint plusz költséget jelenthet az, hogy a Pakson meg nem termelt áramot jelentős részben importból kell fedezni. Alulnézet: a kieső mennyiséget nem azért nem tudja az ország döntő részben hazai termelésből fedezni, mert ne lenne erre kapacitás, hanem azért, mert az drágább, mint az import, és így a nemzetközileg összekötött európai hálózatok működési logikája is az import beszerzést erősíti. Tágabb kontextus: bár az import miatti többletköltség magas, a magyar gazdaságot a mostani energiakrízis sokkal inkább a potenciális tovagyűrűző hatásokon keresztül sújthatja. Az MBH becslése szerint ha a jelenlegi helyzet fennmarad, az hetente 0,1 százalékos negatív hatással van az éves GDP-re. A közvetett hatások sokrétűek: a dunai teherhajózást vissza kellett fogni, de energetikai okokból a vasúti fuvarozást is korlátozni kellett, emiatt közutakra terelődik a forgalom, nő az üzemanyag-kereslet, ez pedig könnyen felhajtja az üzemanyagok árát, írta a Portfolio az Akcenta elemzését bemutatva . A dráguló logisztika és energia plusz költségét a cégek a vásárlókra hárítják, azaz nő az inflációs nyomás. Az energiaimport megugrása miatt romlik a külkereskedelmi mérleg, gyengülhet a forint, ami az importáló cégek helyzetét rontja (az exportálókét javítja). Reakció: az Oeconomus Gazdaságkutató Alapítvány friss elemzése szerint az a kérdés, hogy az energiadrágulás miatti veszteségeket ki és milyen mértékben viseli majd. „A háztartások magasabb árakon és alacsonyabb fogyasztáson keresztül, a vállalatok alacsonyabb profiton vagy termelésen keresztül, az állam támogatások és nagyobb költségvetési hiány formájában vagy a gazdaság alacsonyabb beruházással és importkereslettel alkalmazkodik” – írták a negatív hatásokról. Tágabb kontextus: az energiaimport pluszköltsége nem egyenlő a GDP-csökkenéssel, ahogy az Oeconomus is írja, a GDP-t a paksi atomerőmű működésének kieső hozzáadott értéke olvasztja, a komolyabb veszélyt a potenciális tovagyűrűző termelési veszteségek jelenthetik. Bár a lakosság mellett számos ipari szereplő is önkéntes korlátozásokat vezetett be, ezek elsősorban azért fontosak, hogy az ellátás biztonsága fennmaradjon, a fogyasztási csúcsok simuljanak. Ha azonban komolyabb mértékben általánosan korlátozni kell az ipari fogyasztást – ami a kormány közlése alapján szükség esetén előbb történik meg, mint a lakossági korlátozás – akkor az ipar termelése is csökkenhet. Az emiatt le nem gyártott termékek hozzáadott értéke eshet ki a GDP-ből, ami sokkal komolyabb hatás, mint amit a megdráguló import energia okozhat. Felülnézet: ennek alapján makrogazdasági megközelítésben a jelenlegi kényszerhelyzetben még drágán külföldről vett árammal is lehetőség szerint érdemes elkerülni az ipari szereplők fogyasztáskorlátozását. https://telex.hu/english/2026/08/06/we-n.text: Menü Kereső We need to start conserving water or we'll be forced to make drastic adjustments in the not-too-distant future English Márk Szijártó and Balázs Lukács – Photo: Marcell Almási / Telex Mizsur András Andrea Horváth Kávai (translation) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Hungary is currently experiencing a historic drought. Many of our waters look apocalyptic, and due to the Danube’s record-low water levels, the Paks Nuclear Power Plant nearly had to be completely shut down, posing a serious challenge to the country’s energy supply. Telex interviewed Balázs Lukács, the Acting Director at the Centre for Ecological Research, Institute of Aquatic Ecology, and Márk Szijártó, researcher at ELTE’s Department of Geophysics and Space Sciences and research fellow at the József and Erzsébet Tóth Endowed Hydrogeology Chair and Foundation. In this article, we’ve compiled the most important points discussed during the broadcast. 1. Droughts Are Getting Worse Six years ago, Balázs Lukács made a statement which caused quite a stir. He said that if we didn’t take action, the Great Plain would turn into a desert. Since then, the situation has only worsened: six years ago, only 10 percent of our surface waters were considered seasonal, meaning they dry up for shorter or longer periods. Today, this ratio exceeds 30 percent, which is very high, especially given that this change occurred within such a short time. The situation is even worse for bodies of standing water, 50 percent of which tend to periodically disappear. Over the past six years, the impact of drought has dramatically increased in Hungary, with one harsh, drought-stricken year after another, each worse than the last, but thanks to closer monitoring, experts now have more accurate data on the state of our waters, the research biologist said. The problem is that we are unable to retain sudden heavy rainfall because it simply trickles away, and precipitation in winter, which would normally seep into the soil slowly, has been scarce. According to Balázs Lukács, there are some good grassroots initiatives for retaining water, but these are not sufficient on their own. If we are to be effective nationwide in capturing precipitation, we need top-down state programmes and subsidies. 2. János Lázár was right Both experts agreed with János Lázár, who, at his parliamentary hearing last year, said that the Orbán government had made a mistake by not building large reservoirs ten years ago. According to Márk Szijártó, if these reservoirs had been built back then, the water shortage most likely wouldn’t be as severe as it is right now. Experts are divided on whether we should build hydro-electric dams or large reservoirs on the Danube. In the current weather conditions, however, these would only provide a temporary solution, and we would need comprehensive ones instead. We need to prepare for the extreme weather events we’ve seen this year occurring at an accelerated rate. 3. We don't want to invest in the environment According to Balázs Lukács, experts have been signalling for decades that there was a need for water reservoirs; there were even specific plans drawn up, for example, for flooding the low-lying areas of the Tisza Valley, but for some reason this never caught the attention of political decision-makers. Although flood control reservoirs have been built on the Tisza, these are used for reducing peak flood levels, although a few of them were opened last year. We are not addressing environmental issues systematically and are unwilling to spend much on them, even though forward planning could prevent disasters – this problem has persisted through successive government cycles according to the experts. Another factor that made managing the drought more difficult was that water-related sectors (such as wastewater treatment and flood protection) used to be scattered across different ministries. 4. Solutions exist, the only thing missing is political will Hungary isn’t the only country struggling with water shortages nowadays; several other European countries have already taken the lead in addressing the problem. Belgium and the Netherlands have also experienced severe droughts in the past, and Denmark has launched forward-looking initiatives as well. The Danish government is spending a great deal of money on restoring wetlands and previously plowed-over lakes, said Balázs Lukács. One solution could be to widen river habitats and to re-meander rivers, as this would slow the flow of water and allow it to spread out more effectively during floods. Many similar projects have already been implemented in the Netherlands, and these could easily be applied in Hungary as well—it’s simply a matter of political will. “The cost of a single fireworks display on August 20 would be enough to fund the restoration of several habitats—these are not exorbitant sums we're talking about.” There have only been a few habitat restoration programs of this kind in Hungary. Ideally, these should be scaled up nationwide, but currently, the Hungarian government is only funding one such program. 5. Lake Velence is fine According to Balázs Lukács, we don't need to save Lake Velence because it is a sodic lake. Having as little water as it does now is part of its natural cycle. If there were no reservoirs, similarly low water levels would probably occur more often, but the lake would never have dried up completely. Lake Velence is bigger than most sodic lakes, which is why it dries up less often. Its water shortage is actually causing economic and social problems due to the service facilities developed around it. “Lake Velence is doing just fine, thank you very much; its ecosystem actually needs lower water levels from time to time.” 6. Water shortage could become a nationwide issue Balázs Lukács thinks that if we do not take steps towards water conservation, then in the future, during a drought as severe as this one, water restrictions will be necessary across the country. At the time we recorded our interview, there were water restrictions in effect in 600 Hungarian towns and villages. He also noted that tap water is cheap in Hungary compared to other countries, so the public is not compelled to conserve water. Márk Szijártó noted that a significant portion of our drinking water is sourced from the ground—specifically, from shore-filtered wells—, basically, from the very rivers whose water levels are currently low . If we were to draw less water, there would, of course, be more left in the rivers. “The question is whether we’ll start adapting to the future that researchers and experts are predicting—where situations like the current one will become increasingly common—now, gradually, or whether we’ll have to make drastic adjustments in the not-too-distant future, which would be much more painful. If we don’t start encouraging people to cut back now, we’ll have to do it abruptly later, and that will be painful,” said Balázs Lukács. Mindez azzal magyarázható, hogy a két térségben ugyanaz az összeg egészen más ingatlant jelent. Budapesten a 100 millió forint feletti vásárlások jellemzően 85-90 négyzetméteres lakásokra irányulnak, átlagosan 1,6 millió forint körüli négyzetméteráron. Az agglomeráció felé forduló kereslet nem új, de a drágább ingatlanok piacán most még feltűnőbb a trend. A jelenség egy hosszabb ideje tartó népességmozgást követ. A Központi Statisztikai Hivatal adatai szerint Pest megye 2025-ben is a belföldi vándorlás egyik legnagyobb nyertese volt, miközben Budapest vándorlási mérlege továbbra is negatív. A drágább ingatlanok iránti kereslet elsősorban néhány agglomerációs településen koncentrálódik. Pest megyében Érden történt a legtöbb 100 millió forint feletti adásvétel, ezt Szentendre, Budakeszi, Vác, Diósd és Vecsés követi. https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/black-c.text: A drunk tenant who threatened his housemate with two kitchen knives at a HMO in Smethwick has escaped jail. Maciej Pelczar, aged 48, became 'drunk and aggressive' in the kitchen of the Rutland Road address in October 2024, a court heard. Shane Kenny, prosecutor for the Crown, said both Pelczar and the victim resided at the HMO where tenants had their own bedrooms but shared the kitchen and bathroom. READ MORE: Birmingham ANPR cameras issue 65 penalty charges for right turn ban in 10 days Get breaking news on BirminghamLive WhatsApp , click the link to join Outlining the case, Mr Kenny said: "On October 3, 2024, Mr Pelczar was drunk and aggressive and had two kitchen knives in his hand which he was threatening the victim with." Wolverhampton Crown Court was told the matter wasn't immediately reported to West Midlands Police . Instead, referencing court documents, His Honour Judge Perry said there was a "repeat incident" on November 25. The victim then complained to his landlord, who contacted West Midlands Police, and officers later visited the address to arrest the defendant. A statement from the victim which was read out to court said: "I have tried to reason with Maciej about his behaviour and demeanour when he is drunk - but he does not listen. "I'm really scared that one day, when he is drunk, he will actually stab me whether that's his intention or not. "It is like walking on egg shells when he is at home and drunk. "I have not done anything wrong to Maciej and don't deserve to feel this way in my own home." James Kumar, defence counsel for Pelczar, said his client was self-medicating with alcohol at the time for paranoia. Mr Kumar said the defendant, who'd previously lost his job, believed people were "spying on him and after him". Explaining why Pelczar had knives in his hand during the incident, Mr Kumar said: "He said he was in the kitchen making food. He is remorseful." The court heard that nine days after the HMO incident, Pelczar was seen with a knife at Tesco . As a result, he was handed an 18-month prison sentence which was suspended for two years in January this year. Discussing the timeline of events with Mr Kumar, Judge Perry said: "The January matters relate to him being on Tesco car park waving a knife around." Mr Kumar replied: "That was on October 12. The one that's being sentenced today is October 3." The defendant previously appeared at magistrates court on June 12 this year, where he pleaded guilty to threatening a person with a bladed article in a private place. The court heard he changed his plea on the day his trial was due to take place, and he was subsequently awarded 10 per cent credit. Pelczar appeared in the dock on Friday, July 10, wearing a blue shirt and pale green shorts, and he was accompanied by a Polish interpreter. The court was told he'd since been moved to alternative accommodation. Addressing the defendant, Judge Perry said: "I'm sentencing you for October 3. "The complainant didn't make a complaint about that at the time. "It was a later incident that he complained about, nearly two months later. "He didn't complain directly to the police, but complained to his landlord and they referred the matter to police. "In between these two incidents, you were convicted of a further offence in January (this year), that fell between these two incidents, and that's what you are serving a suspended sentence for." Judge Perry noted there were "aggravating factors" in the case, namely Pelczar's "alcohol addiction if you can call it an addiction," he said. Judge Perry said the offence was "too serious" to consider a community order, while a custodial sentence wasn't "disproportionate". The judge also said that Pelczar had a history of "good compliance" with his existing suspended sentence order. As a result, Pelczar, of Eastfield Road, Bordesley Green , was handed an 18-month prison sentence, suspended for two years. In addition, he was handed 30 days of Rehabilitation Activity Requirement, 150 hours of unpaid work and a victim surcharge.
