https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/fia-stewa.text: Archie Griggs Updated Fri, 24 July 2026 at 12:05 pm UTC 0 Charles Leclerc escaped a penalty in Belgium after colliding with Oscar Piastri (Image: Getty) The FIA stewards have decided that Charles Leclerc should have been given a penalty at last weekend's Belgian Grand Prix . His clash with Oscar Piastri became a major talking point after the Ferrari driver escaped punishment, despite Lewis Hamilton being penalised for a similar incident earlier in the race . On the opening lap, Hamilton took out George Russell as the pair battled for position, resulting in the Mercedes driver being forced to retire. It looked nothing more than a racing incident, which Russell agreed with, but Hamilton was hit with a five-second penalty by the stewards. A handful of laps later, Leclerc tangled with Piastri by moving under braking, despite the Australian making no genuine attempt to overtake. However, on that occasion, the stewards decided not to hand down any penalties. That inconsistently was discussed at a meeting between drivers and the FIA ahead of this weekend's Hungarian Grand Prix, according to The Race . It's claimed the stewards have now accepted that Leclerc should have been punished after a "lengthy debate" among those in attendance. The meeting was the first of two annual gatherings to discuss how incidents are dealt with and potential changes to F1's driving guidelines. The stewards have decided that Leclerc should have received a penalty (Image: Getty) The report adds that Leclerc argued the situation in Belgium was not entirely black-and-white, although he previously conceded that he may have overstepped the mark. Reflecting on his battle with Piastri, he said: "At the end of the day my view in the car is that I try to push the things to the limit. "I think with Oscar it was a bit on the other side, so that's probably not the way I want to race all the time. It's also risky for me at the end of the day. You're always trying to leave the smallest place available. That was maybe a bit too sketchy." Leclerc will be hoping to avoid any similar incidents in Hungary this weekend as Ferrari look to head into the summer break on a positive note. EXPRESS SPORT ON FB! http://www.jpost.com/international/artic.text: Britain said its armed forces were ready to protect the country from any attack after Iran's Revolutionary Guards (IRGC) issued a warning not to allow US bombers to fly from UK bases.In a statement on Thursday, the IRGC said the US had flown bombing missions against Iran from Fairford in southwest England, adding that any base used to launch such attacks would be a legitimate target.The new British prime minister, Andy Burnham, was notified last week that London had re-committed to an existing agreement allowing the United States to use British bases for what it described as the collective self-defense of the region."Our armed forces are ready to keep the United Kingdom safe from any kind of attacks, whether it's on our soil or from abroad," a government spokesperson said."This includes through operating a layered approach to air and missile defense, provided by Royal Navy, British Army and Royal Air Force assets equipped with a range of advanced capabilities, working closely with our NATO allies." Britain agrees to support US defensive operationsThe government said on Wednesday that the existing arrangement covered US defensive operations to degrade missile sites and capabilities used to attack ships in the Strait of Hormuz.In response to Iran's warning, the spokesperson said Britain's approach remained unchanged and that it was committed to defending its people, interests and allies in accordance with international law while avoiding being drawn into a wider conflict.The United States carried out a 13th consecutive night of attacks on Iran following the effective collapse of an interim truce, and Tehran fired at US bases in neighboring Arab countries.In March, Iran was reported to have fired two ballistic missiles ​at the US-UK ‌military base on Diego Garcia in the ​Indian Ocean, neither hitting the target.An Iranian-type Shahed drone caused slight damage on March 2 when it hit facilities at Britain's Akrotiri airbase in southern Cyprus. Britain later said the site would not be included in the defensive agreement with the US.Could Iran strike London?Experts say Iran might possess a missile able to strike London, but it was likely to be inaccurate and the risk was low.Britain has long accused Iran of carrying out cyberattacks and using criminal gangs and proxies to target opponents and dissidents in the UK. The security services said there had been 20 potentially ‌lethal ⁠Iranian-backed plots in the last year.Britain this month banned support for the IRGC by using new powers brought in to address what it said was a growing use of state-sponsored proxies.It also followed a spate of attacks on Jewish sites in London. The government said the IRGC had "almost ​certainly" directed a group believed to be responsible for a number of these.Two Romanian nationals, who prosecutors said had been acting for Iran, were jailed this month for stabbing a journalist working for a Farsi-language media group in London.Tehran has always denied involvement in such attacks, calling allegations to the contrary unfounded and politically motivated.

https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/britains-.text: Ciaran McGrath Updated Fri, 24 July 2026 at 12:11 pm UTC 1 Foreign Blue Badge fraud is on the increase (Image: Getty) Criminals are exploiting an informal agreement between the UK and European countries that permits disabled parking badges issued abroad to be used here. However, British authorities have warned that counterfeit documents from overseas are becoming harder to detect due to variations in design. Enforcers say fraud involving foreign Blue Badges is increasing, with fake permits purporting to come from Eastern European countries posing a particular problem. Last month, Enfield Council revealed it had prosecuted 12 people for misusing Blue Badges . One case involved a counterfeit Bulgarian badge. Rumen Aleksandrov, 45, from Palmers Green in north London, was caught displaying a fake Bulgarian Blue Badge featuring a counterfeit hologram and no validity date in his BMW. He ignored a letter from the council questioning his paperwork before pleading guilty in court. The judge imposed a £250 fine, a £100 victim surcharge and £250 in costs. Penalties for those caught abusing the system remain relatively modest, even as inspectors report a rise in fakes. Speaking to The Telegraph , Paul Slowey, chief executive of the National Agency for Blue Badge Fraud Investigations, said mass-produced counterfeit permits are being manufactured to take advantage of the scheme's benefits, which include priority parking, the ability to park temporarily on double yellow lines, and exemptions from congestion charges and tolls. Mr Slowey said: "The level of detected fraud involving fake badges is on the rise. They tend to be English first, then Polish, then other European badges. There seems to be a mass-produced manufactured fake badge as we are finding fakes with common fraud indicators." Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander (Image: Getty) In 2018, Enfield caught another motorist using a fake Polish badge. Adrian Siwak, then 23 and from Tottenham, was stopped after council staff contacted Polish authorities, who confirmed the style of badge he displayed was no longer valid. Siwak drove off without providing his details but was later traced. He pleaded guilty and was fined £150, with £550 costs and a £30 victim surcharge. The growing abuse is making it harder for genuinely disabled people to find suitable parking spaces. Councils have also faced criticism for issuing Blue Badges for certain "hidden disabilities", including anxiety, prompting intervention from Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander in May, who said: "An ADHD diagnosis alone should not get you a Blue Badge." The Blue Badge scheme is overseen by the Department for Transport (DfT), but managed by councils. The department has issued guidance to local authorities on foreign Blue Badges, instructing them to "refuse to recognise an overseas badge if they have reasonable grounds to believe that it is fake or forged". The guidance notes that the DfT is aware of cases where people may be attempting to use fake badges claimed to have been issued by another member state. It highlights that disabled parking badges from some countries "vary in design", making it "hard for local enforcement officers to verify their authenticity". A DfT spokesman said: "Abuse of the scheme, including using fraudulent badges of any kind, is a criminal offence and undermines support for the people this scheme is there to help. "Local councils are responsible for fairly and rigorously enforcing the scheme in their area and have robust powers to act against abuse, including refusing to recognise an overseas badge where there are reasonable grounds to believe it is fake or forged." http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27920.text: Big News Network.com The purge of Orban's Hungary has begun Peter Magyar is dismantling Fidesz's legal, media and financial machinery while building a new order under Western backing On Monday, July 20, Hungary officially entered a new political reality. For the first time in 16 years, the Fidesz party lost control of the country's most important institution - its presidency. Viktor Orban's last remaining pillar of power collapsed. The situation, initially perceived by Fidesz supporters as a temporary political crisis, had become catastrophic by mid-summer, leading to a restructuring of the country's entire legal and political order. Several components can be roughly identified in the purge initiated by the team of new Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar. The main ones include a thorough search for evidence of corruption within Fidesz, blocking any attempts by the new opposition to challenge the ruling party at the legislative and executive levels, and dismantling the symbols of power that had made the party's rule unique on the domestic and international stage. Anti-corruption committees and judicial prosecutions Currently, five parliamentary committees are working with extraordinary powers to investigate corruption; a dedicated anti-corruption ministry is planned for later . These bodies, acting as a 'criminal case factory,' have been given the authority to open archives and refer materials to the courts and the European Public Prosecutor's Office. Key investigations cover strategic contracts, the activities of intelligence agencies, the business sector, and municipal finances. For example, the Strategic Contracts Audit Committee is initiating an audit of contracts for the construction of the Russian Paks II nuclear power plant project and automotive agreements with China. The economic structure of the old regime is being reviewed through the Committee on Large Business and the Reform of State Media. The Committee on Fiscal Decentralization aims to reform the existing budget system. The work has several goals: transitioning from a media 'wolf hunt' to a conveyor belt of show trials against Fidesz elites, and unlocking 18 billion in European funds. The main defendants in the future criminal cases are Orban's inner circle and Orban himself. His son-in-law, businessman Istvan Tiborcz, and his company Elios, which provided street lighting through EU-funded public procurement, are under attack. A second major target is Fidesz's main sponsor, Lorinc Meszaros, and his work on the construction of the Budapest-Belgrade railway (worth approximately $3 billion). Former Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto, who left politics for a position at the Chinese automotive giant BYD, is also being investigated for covert contacts with Moscow and the transfer of classified information. Szijjarto himself has gone on the defensive, stating: "Accusations of treason are excessive; I have never passed classified information to Russia ." The logical conclusion of this legal conveyor belt will inevitably be an attempt to institutionally and personally erase Viktor Orban himself. Although the former prime minister is currently clinging to his parliamentary mandate, his legislative immunity is relatively easy to terminate under the current circumstances: with a two-thirds constitutional majority, Magyar's party could remove this shield in fifteen minutes on live television. An analysis of the legal framework being developed by five commissions jointly with the European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) indicates that legal prosecution of Orban will be based on several articles of the Hungarian Criminal Code (BTK): embezzlement of state property on an especially large scale; abuse of power; budget fraud as part of an organized group; and, finally, high treason. The prospect of this trial being a showpiece leaves Orban with virtually no room for maneuver, forcing him to choose between a public trial or, as Magyar hopes, forced political exile. It's important to understand that what's happening is based on a consensus within Hungarian society: recent sociological research has recorded that 66% of Hungarian citizens demand the prosecution and accountability of senior officials from the previous administration. Magyar's TISZA party itself and its leader are at the peak of their popularity - polls show that the recently divided country is consolidating around the new leader and that approximately 62% of the country's population trusts him. Removing barriers The legal framework that supported the old government's monopoly is also undergoing deep revision and purge. The country has abolished the notorious Office for the Protection of Sovereignty, whose purpose was to identify and block "agents of foreign influence," and nationalized the "Public Interest Trust Funds" created by Orban, which owned and managed colossal state assets, including 21 state universities and large stakes in the country's main strategic corporations (the energy group MOL, the country's largest commercial bank OTP Bank), castles, clinics, and resorts. Magyar introduced a strict term limit for the prime minister and members of parliament - no more than eight years in total. This reform is aimed against Orban specifically - after 18 years at the helm of the country, the former prime minister is now legally barred from any possibility of returning to power. Against the backdrop of these changes, the removal of former President Tamas Sujok took place. He did not wait for impeachment in parliament; he was forced to resign as a result of the 17th Amendment to the Constitution. Furthermore, this amendment effectively purges the judiciary, limiting the age of judges to 70 and shortening their mandates to six years. These measures are aimed at removing those appointed by Fidesz and stripping the president of the Constitutional Court of her administrative monopoly. Finally, Hungary's accession to the European Public Prosecutor's Office has eroded the influence of Attorney General Peter Polt, allowing for the direct enforcement of Brussels' orders to audit public contracts. Furthermore, the lifting of the ban on municipal lawsuits against the center is being used to bankrupt Fidesz-controlled entities through lawsuits for embezzlement. A crucial judicial precedent was the Hungarian Constitutional Court's overturning of Orban's 'solidarity tax' decree, which for years had forced the center to collect additional taxes from opposition cities such as Pecs and Szeged, with the goal of redistributing the money to Fidesz-voting villages in the east of the country. This verdict not only cleared the way for lawsuits filed by wealthy municipalities claiming their regions had been artificially driven into bankruptcy, but also demonstrated the institutional collapse of the previous government. Senior judges who for years had been considered completely loyal to the old regime instantly changed their minds and declared the actions of Orban's cabinet illegal. This served as an official signal to the elites that Orban had finally lost control of the country. Debunking uniqueness On July 7, Hungary's main state television channel, M1, and Radio Kossuth suddenly went offline, with the TV stations rolling out an unprecedented statement: "Public media cannot lie. We apologize for doing so for many years ." This move was initiated by the Commission for the Reform of Public Media. Magyar's message to voters was that behind the facade of a 'struggle for sovereignty,' unique in the EU, lay a usurpation of the media landscape. This paradoxically brought the history of leadership full circle: in all his campaign outings, Orban's image was built on the demonization of former Prime Minister Ferenc Gyurcsany, whose reign from 2004 to 2009 was remembered for a leaked audio recording in which he was heard saying that "we lied morning and evening." Now, in the eyes of the public, Orban himself has been transformed into Gyurcsany. The investigation surrounding the Ludovika University of Public Service has become a painful one. New commissions have opened secret archives and discovered that, under the guise of "climate conferences," a recruitment hub for the Israeli intelligence agency Mossad had operated at the university for years. The university's leadership has already admitted that orders to provide institutional cover came from the very top - from Orban's government apparatus. Following this, the country has taken a fresh look at the uniqueness of Hungary's "sovereign" foreign policy, not to mention the abrogation of his cabinet's anti-Semitic attacks. Magyar: The West's enforcer with an agenda The demonstrative destruction of Fidesz should not be viewed as a local initiative by Peter Magyar. It enjoys significant, coordinated support among Euro-Atlantic elites, who have accumulated a critical amount of anger at Orban. The main beneficiary of this process is European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, for whom the destruction of Orban's legacy is a matter of personal revenge for years of blackmail, vetoes, and caricatured billboards on Hungarian streets. Secondly, there is the head of the European Public Prosecutor's Office, Laura Kovesi: Budapest's official accession to her office provides a historic opportunity to launch a show trial against top Central European politicians. Finally, there are Atlanticist forces in the United States who also stand to gain from a show trial in a country that was previously the main regional stronghold of the conservative MAGA movement. The upcoming criminal trials must be as public and high-profile as possible in order to address the fundamental objective of Brussels and Washington: to mentally nullify the very idea of right-wing sovereignty in the eyes of European voters by demonstrating that slogans about protecting traditional values conceal corrupt schemes. Peter Magyar is currently operating within the Euro-Atlantic mainstream, but it would be a mistake to dismiss him as a run-of-the-mill enforcer. We see before us a confident leader whose primary objective is to secure the field, establish himself, and maintain power. He will emerge as an independent actor only later, once he has settled his tactical "debts" to European institutions and established direct contacts with Washington. Paradoxically, when it comes to the lives of ordinary people in large Hungarian cities, the problems caused by this same fiscal tax haven't changed. Today, the old "illiberal" dictate from the center remains unchanged, demonstrating that political purges from above can be combined with tax collection from below. A typical example here is how, on July 15, the authorities of the traditionally opposition city of Pecs were forced to pay another 600 million forints (almost $1.9 million) into the budget under the old 'solidarity tax' (which itself has not been abolished). In other words, the ordinary Hungarian from Pecs, who voted for change in April 2026, in reality faced the same everyday devastation: due to empty coffers, people wait 40 minutes at bus stops, schools and hospitals remain without repairs, and street lights are turned off after 11 PM to save money. As for Russia, its interests in the region inevitably face a period of protracted uncertainty. Magyar's agenda vis--vis Moscow will boil down to two variables: a decidedly tough public discourse, transparent to the West, and a hidden, pragmatic, and non-public dialogue track. This pragmatism is critically important for Hungary's large business community (including the banking, pharmaceutical, and IT sectors), which largely supported Magyar in the April 2026 elections. The era of Budapest's sovereign maneuvering is over, but the contours of a new Magyar balancing act are only just beginning to emerge. For the first time in 16 years, the Fidesz party lost control of the country's most important institution - its presidency. Viktor Orban's last remaining pillar of power collapsed. The situation, initially perceived by Fidesz supporters as a temporary political crisis, had become catastrophic by mid-summer, leading to a restructuring of the country's entire legal and political order. Several components can be roughly identified in the purge initiated by the team of new Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar. The main ones include a thorough search for evidence of corruption within Fidesz, blocking any attempts by the new opposition to challenge the ruling party at the legislative and executive levels, and dismantling the symbols of power that had made the party's rule unique on the domestic and international stage. Anti-corruption committees and judicial prosecutions Currently, five parliamentary committees are working with extraordinary powers to investigate corruption; a dedicated anti-corruption ministry is planned for later . These bodies, acting as a 'criminal case factory,' have been given the authority to open archives and refer materials to the courts and the European Public Prosecutor's Office. Key investigations cover strategic contracts, the activities of intelligence agencies, the business sector, and municipal finances. For example, the Strategic Contracts Audit Committee is initiating an audit of contracts for the construction of the Russian Paks II nuclear power plant project and automotive agreements with China. The economic structure of the old regime is being reviewed through the Committee on Large Business and the Reform of State Media. The Committee on Fiscal Decentralization aims to reform the existing budget system. The work has several goals: transitioning from a media 'wolf hunt' to a conveyor belt of show trials against Fidesz elites, and unlocking 18 billion in European funds. The main defendants in the future criminal cases are Orban's inner circle and Orban himself. His son-in-law, businessman Istvan Tiborcz, and his company Elios, which provided street lighting through EU-funded public procurement, are under attack. A second major target is Fidesz's main sponsor, Lorinc Meszaros, and his work on the construction of the Budapest-Belgrade railway (worth approximately $3 billion). Former Foreign Minister Peter Szijjarto, who left politics for a position at the Chinese automotive giant BYD, is also being investigated for covert contacts with Moscow and the transfer of classified information. Szijjarto himself has gone on the defensive, stating: "Accusations of treason are excessive; I have never passed classified information to Russia ." The logical conclusion of this legal conveyor belt will inevitably be an attempt to institutionally and personally erase Viktor Orban himself. Although the former prime minister is currently clinging to his parliamentary mandate, his legislative immunity is relatively easy to terminate under the current circumstances: with a two-thirds constitutional majority, Magyar's party could remove this shield in fifteen minutes on live television. An analysis of the legal framework being developed by five commissions jointly with the European Public Prosecutor's Office (EPPO) indicates that legal prosecution of Orban will be based on several articles of the Hungarian Criminal Code (BTK): embezzlement of state property on an especially large scale; abuse of power; budget fraud as part of an organized group; and, finally, high treason. The prospect of this trial being a showpiece leaves Orban with virtually no room for maneuver, forcing him to choose between a public trial or, as Magyar hopes, forced political exile. https://bnn-news.com/bnn-in-focus-those-.text: Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Home BNN in Focus BNN in Focus Latvia Politics BNN IN FOCUS | “Those who fail to deliver on their promises go home” – political analyst gives blunt assessment of parties’ election prospects BNN July 24, 2026 Facebook Twitter Photo: Zane Bitere/LETA As Latvia moves closer to the next parliamentary election, the race for voters’ support is becoming increasingly competitive. Could the popularity of the United List (Apvienotais saraksts) continue to grow, and does Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs have a realistic chance of remaining in office after the election? BNN put these questions to political analyst Filips Rajevskis, co-owner of media company Mediju tilts. “We have seen several cases where a prime minister has remained in office both before and after an election. That happened with Aigars Kalvītis, Laimdota Straujuma, and Krišjānis Kariņš. In Latvia, it is nothing unusual for a prime minister to retain the position after securing a successful election result,” Rajevskis said. The political analyst noted that while there are some similarities with New Unity’s position before the previous election, the current situation is not identical. Unlike New Unity, the United List has not been the smallest parliamentary faction, spent most of the current parliamentary term in opposition, and only recently entered government after receiving a mandate of confidence. He also drew comparisons with Laimdota Straujuma, who became prime minister roughly eight months before an election. “If a government performs successfully during those months, it can earn a much stronger mandate from voters for the next four years. That possibility certainly cannot be ruled out. This time, however, the situation is more unstable because Latvia is facing not only domestic political and economic challenges but also external factors. Those external factors worked in favour of Kariņš and New Unity before the last election. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, and at that moment New Unity appeared to be a stable and credible choice compared with other political forces. But it is far too early to celebrate. Two and a half months is a long time in today’s domestic and international political environment,” Rajevskis said. Asked whether voters could become disappointed if Kulbergs’ government fails to deliver the sweeping changes many hope for—including dismantling the Society Integration Foundation (SIF), improving the efficiency of public spending and implementing the government’s reform agenda—Rajevskis argued that expectations must remain realistic. “The pace of modern life and social media has changed everything. It is impossible to complete all of these major tasks when the government was only approved on the 28th of May and by the 28th of July it will have been in office for just two months. You cannot expect a system that has been built over many years—including the SIF and what critics describe as the pseudo-NGO system—to be dismantled in less than two months. That simply isn’t possible. However, the direction the government chooses could prove decisive in the election. If society believes the course is the right one, the United List could receive significant electoral support and become the dominant political force. At that point, expectations will be much higher and the government will no longer have time to ease into the job. Normally, governments are judged after their first 100 days. This government has not even been given 60 days before people ask: ‘Where are the results?’ We need to remain realistic. Anyone who has ever managed even a small business understands that meaningful change takes time—let alone in government.” Asked whether there are already signs that genuine change is underway, Rajevskis replied that there are reasons for cautious optimism. “I believe there is such a trend. At the very least, those expectations are being actively encouraged. As a result, people now expect to see tangible changes, and the government will have to demonstrate progress. For example, Kulbergs has spoken about 163 million euros allocated to what he calls pseudo-NGOs. That is an enormous amount of money. It could be used to build new hospitals, treat cancer patients, or fund many other priorities. This is not a minor issue—it is a huge amount of taxpayers’ money that is now part of the political debate. People expect sensible, fair and responsible policies, with the right priorities.” Rajevskis pointed to a recent example highlighted on social media platform X by Katrīna Iļjinska. “She noted that a Swedbank folk dance group with just 17 members received 89% of its funding from the state budget last year, while in 2024 taxpayers accounted for 97% of the association’s income. Swedbank earned 152 million euros in profit last year and 218 million euros the year before. Why should my tax money be used to finance a folk dance group belonging to one of the country’s largest banks?” Finally, BNN asked whether political parties that fail to meet voters’ expectations risk being wiped off the political map at the next election. Rajevskis’ answer was unequivocal. “That is the normal political pendulum. Those who fail to deliver on their promises and fail to meet people’s expectations go home.” Read also: BNN IN FOCUS | “We can’t afford to waste public money”: Political scientist calls for sweeping NGO funding reform Follow us on Facebook and X ! http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27920.text: Big News Network.com Romanian jet shoots down drone The UAV was tracked from the Black Sea and destroyed over an "unpopulated area," according to the Romanian Defense Ministry A Romanian F-16 fighter jet has shot down a drone that entered the country's airspace, President Nicusor Dan has said. The drone incursion has not yet been blamed on any foreign military. In a post on X, Dan said that the drone was intercepted around 11 am on Friday, and that an investigation has been launched. The Romanian Defense Ministry said that the drone was picked up by radar over the Black Sea earlier on Friday morning, and was tracked as it moved westward towards the port of Sulina. It was intercepted over an "unpopulated area" around Padina, 90 km northeast of Bucharest, and destroyed with an air-to-air missile, the ministry added. The incident is the third of its kind in Romania over the last two months. On June 5, a Ukrainian naval drone exploded near an oil terminal in Constanta, Romania's largest Black Sea port, while three more detonated offshore. The drones were operated by the Ukrainian navy, which claimed that it lost control of the devices. On May 29, a UAV carrying explosives crashed into an apartment building in Galati, 20km from the Ukrainian border. Authorities in Bucharest identified the drone as a Russian 'Geran-2' kamikaze drone, claiming that it could have been hit by Ukrainian air defenses and veered off course. Dan's response was dramatically different in the two cases. The Romanian president made no formal complaint when the Ukrainian naval drone entered the country's main port while others exploded off Constanta, describing the incident as an unfortunate consequence of the "military operation led by Ukraine against Russian aggression." After the drone crash in Galati, Dan ordered the closure of the Russian consulate in Constanta and attempted to trigger NATO's Article 4, which is invoked when a member state determines that their "territorial integrity...or security" is threatened. Dan also announced that he would "accelerate Romania-Ukraine cooperation on the co-production of drones" and increase military aid to Kiev. Russia argued that its Geran drones carry higher payloads of explosives than the UAV that struck the apartment building, and that a stricken Geran would not have been able to cover the distance from Ukrainian air defense positions to Galati. Moscow suggested that the incident was used by Bucharest to justify plans made in advance - such as closing the consulate and stepping up aid to Kiev. https://english.news.cn/europe/20260724/.text: Romania shoots down drone breaching airspace BUCHAREST, July 24 (Xinhua) -- Romanian President Nicusor Dan said Friday that Romania shot down a drone breaching its airspace in the Buzau County. He said that the authorities are conducting investigations at the scene of the incident to establish all the circumstances in which the drone entered Romania's airspace and to identify it. "It is important to note that the area was uninhabited, which is why the pilot was able to fire from above," Dan added. Romania's Ministry of National Defense said in a press release that its radar surveillance system detected an aerial target approximately 20 km east of Sulina. The track subsequently penetrated the national airspace. An F-16 fighter aircraft of the Romanian Air Force engaged the target with an air-to-air missile and neutralized it over an unpopulated area in the vicinity of Padina, Buzau County. ■ News In-depth Sports Business Culture World China Regions Asia & Pacific Europe Middle East North America South America Africa Organizations Services Weather Live & Work in China Doing Business Investment Visit China Study in China More Special Reports Photos Video Corrections About Us Contact Us Media Qiushi Journal Taiwan.cn Youth.cn GMW.cn CE.cn Ecns.cn China Daily CRI.cn China.org.cn People's Daily

https://www.upi.com/Top_News/World-News/.text: France wildfires force mass evacuations from southwestern Gironde region July 24 (UPI) -- Authorities in France's southwestern Gironde region ordered tens of thousands of people to evacuate from the popular Cap Ferret peninsula vacation spot Friday in the face of an "XXL" wildfire threatening to cut off the promontory. As many as 2,000 escaped by boat. French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 40,000 residents and tourists had been evacuated or were currently being moved from the cape, which is bordered by the Atlantic Ocean to the west and the Arcachon Bay to the east. The fire has burned through at least 25,000 hectares after breaking out Wednesday in Saumos, a small town about 25 miles away to the northeast. Authorities began evacuating of the town of Ares, south of Lege-Cap-Ferret on the Bay of Arcachon side of the peninsula after the fire picked up pace and intensity overnight, said fire and rescue chief Marc Vermeulen. A local council member said 2,000 people had already made the 7.5-mile boat crossing to Arcachon on the southern side of the bay. More than 800 firefighters from across France were battling the flames in an operation run out of a command center set up in a stadium in Le Porge, six miles northeast of Lege-Cap-Ferret. Gironda Prefect Sophie Brocas said 53 homes and a campsite had been razed but that firefighters had managed to save 2,000 houses. More than 23,000 people were also evacuated from homes, campsites, a nursing home and a summer camp due to another wildfire around Biscarrosse, about 15 miles south of Arcachon in the Landes department. Landes prefect Gilles Clavreul said the fire was being fueled by a combination of winds of more than 30 mph and searing temperatures in the high 30s degrees Celsius. Calling the situation very serious, President Emmanuel Macron said France had requested the European Union's civil protection mechanism be activated, which would allow the deployment of firefighting aircraft from other members of the bloc. "We will soon be able to count on reinforcements from two Croatian Canadair aircraft, two Portuguese Air Tractor planes, as well as two heavy Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia," he wrote in a post on X late Thursday night. In Spain, authorities declared a national emergency Friday as they continued to battle three major wildfires west of Madrid in the areas of Villa del Prado and San Martín de Valdeiglesias, as well as Burgohondo in Avila province Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez said Friday that many communities across Spain and beyond were being impacted by fires "ravaging thousands of hectares." "The government has deployed all available resources to halt the terrible fires that are currently affecting numerous areas: Avila, Leon, Toledo, Madrid, and other parts of Spain. We are living through a dramatic situation, not only in various Spanish provinces but also in regions of neighboring countries. Forest fires are ravaging thousands of hectares and affecting numerous communities," he wrote on X . "The government will stand by your side during the emergency and in the recovery," added Sanchez. https://visegradinsight.eu/peter-magyar-.text: Commentary Democratic Security Magyar’s Rule of Law Chainsaw Risks Cutting Down the Roots Prime minister's gambit to bring back democracy in Hungary is a perilous adventure 24 July 2026 Is Péter Magyar about to break the rule of law while restoring it in Hungary? Hungary’s Prime Minister Péter Magyar has done the seemingly impossible – his upstart centre-right party TISZA dealt a stunning electoral blow to the former PM Viktor Orbán and his right-wing nationalist party Fidesz, ending 16 years of their rule in Hungary. With a constitutional supermajority in the parliament, Magyar has set his sights on unlocking frozen EU funds and undoing the governance system established by Orbán. The clock is ticking on getting the EU funds home, as Orbán’s stubborn refusal to fully meet the European Commission’s requirements for releasing the funds has left a chunk of the money with a close, looming expiration date, risking a permanent loss of significant funds for a country whose economy, in particular its public spending and health care, is in dire straits . Recent developments, such as the visit to Orbán’s party’s data centre in an embezzlement probe, raise the crucial question even more: can Magyar fix the rule of law without breaking it, or is he going too fast and too furious in his attempts to dismantle the entrenched remnants of Orbán’s era? https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/worl.text: Archaeologists in Slovakia have uncovered the remains of a large Roman military camp that may have been used by the army of Emperor Marcus Aurelius during wars against Germanic tribes nearly 1,850 years ago. The discovery is unusual not only because of the size of the camp but also because of the way Roman soldiers were buried there.Researchers found skeletons and parts of skeletons in shallow graves, defensive ditches and even inside wells. Alongside the human remains, they also uncovered Roman weapons, armour, coins and the remains of military sandals, giving fresh evidence about a military campaign that took place in the late second century AD.The excavation took place near the town of Surany in southwestern Slovakia. Archaeologists say the findings could help them better understand the Marcomannic Wars, a series of conflicts fought by the Roman Empire under Marcus Aurelius against Germanic tribes living north of the Danube River.Rare camp uncoveredThe remains of the Roman military camp were uncovered over an area of around 7.4 hectares, or about 18.2 acres. The excavation was carried out by MH Invest together with the Institute of Archaeology at the Slovak Academy of Sciences (SAS).According to researchers, the camp had all the features expected in a Roman military installation. It included five entrance gates, strong defensive structures and a curved ditch-and-rampart system that was commonly used to protect Roman marching or legionary camps.The discovery surprised archaeologists because such camps are rarely found almost completely preserved."We have a unique opportunity to explore practically an entire Roman marching camp, which is extremely rare in the European context," Matej Ruttkay, director of the SAS Institute of Archaeology, said in a statement, Live Science reported."We are clearly investigating a place that disappeared immediately after the military conflict between the Romans and the Germans," he added.Links to Marcus AureliusThe newly discovered camp is believed to date to the Marcomannic Wars, which were fought between AD 166 and 180. During this period, Roman forces battled the Marcomanni, a Germanic people who lived north of the Danube in areas that are now part of Slovakia and the Czech Republic.Marcus Aurelius, who ruled the Roman Empire from AD 161 to 180, personally led military campaigns during these wars. His aim was to defend Rome's northern frontier from repeated invasions by Germanic tribes.The conflicts came to an end after Marcus Aurelius died in AD 180. His son, Commodus, later reached a peace agreement with the Marcomanni, according to the ancient Roman historian Cassius Dio.The Surany camp is only the second Roman military site ever discovered in western Slovakia. The first one, found by SAS archaeologists in 2024, is believed to be the place where Marcus Aurelius wrote part of his famous philosophical work Meditations.Skeletons in unusual placesOne of the most striking discoveries at the site was the large number of human remains. Instead of finding organised cemeteries, archaeologists uncovered skeletons and parts of skeletons buried in shallow pits, defensive ditches and even inside wells.The unusual burials suggest that the dead may have been buried quickly after a major event, although researchers do not yet know exactly what happened."Our preliminary findings indicate that in most cases these are Roman soldiers," archaeologist Marek Vojtecek of the SAS Institute of Archaeology said in the statement.The skeletal remains were found together with several pieces of Roman military equipment."Numerous components of Roman military equipment and weaponry were also found with the skeletal remains, such as spears, arrowheads, parts of helmets, segmented and scale armour, legionary brooches, coins, and the characteristic 'caligae' military sandals, from which iron nails on the soles have been preserved," Vojtecek said.These discoveries strengthen the view that the people buried at the site were members of the Roman army.Sandals reveal remarkable detailAmong the discoveries, researchers were particularly excited by the remains of Roman military footwear.Although the leather parts of the sandals had disappeared over time, the iron nails fixed into their soles survived because they became enclosed inside blocks of clay.Scientists used X-ray analysis to examine the clay blocks and identify the original pattern of the sandal nails without damaging them. The preserved remains have now been moved to the specialised laboratory of the SAS Institute of Archaeology for further study."It is literally a miracle to see the original footwear of a Roman soldier and even to be able to determine its size," archaeologist Michal Cheben said.The sandals, known as caligae, were standard footwear worn by Roman soldiers during long military campaigns. Their distinctive iron-studded soles made them easier to identify during excavation.Mysteries remainAlthough the excavation has uncovered important evidence, researchers say the site has also raised several new questions. One major mystery is why the soldiers were buried in such unusual places instead of receiving formal burials.Scientists also want to know whether the soldiers died in battle, from disease or because of some other event. Another unanswered question is why valuable military equipment remained with many of the bodies. Normally, weapons and armour were collected and reused after battles, making such discoveries uncommon."Laboratory analyses and further genetic and anthropological research may provide answers," Cheben said.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/Reuters View image in fullscreen A person worships at the St Jerome Catholic church in the Little Haiti neighborhood of Brooklyn. Photograph: Shannon Stapleton/Reuters US immigration Haitians face arrest and deportation after US removes TPS protections DHS secretary Markwayne Mullin says ‘We’re going after them right now’ despite threat of violence in home country Alexandra Villarreal in New York Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hundreds of thousands of Haitians are faced with the prospect of imminent risk of arrest and deportation – to a home country racked with crime, violence and political unrest – after the Trump administration officially stripped them of humanitarian protections that had allowed them to live and work legally in the United States for years. US district judge Ana Reyes confirmed on Wednesday that her order blocking the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from ending temporary protected status (TPS) for Haiti was no longer in effect. This followed the controversial supreme court ruling in June that upended judicial review of the program and opened the door for immigration enforcement to track down and detain Haitians en masse. Supreme court conservatives accused of advancing ‘white-supremacist agenda’ Read more “We’re going after them right now,” the DHS secretary, Markwayne Mullin, said earlier this week. “These individuals can either self-deport or we’ll arrest you and send you back. It’s that simple.” Enacted by Congress in 1990, TPS protects people who are already in the US when a natural disaster, epidemic, armed conflict or other extraordinary and temporary circumstance affects their country of origin, making it unsafe for them to return home. ‘Devastating’: lives of nurses and patients upended by Trump migrant crackdown Read more TPS holders are eligible for work permits and have added an estimated $262bn to the US economy since 2001, according to the FWD.us advocacy organization, often pursuing careers in essential industries such as construction and health and elder care . But since returning to office last year, the Trump administration has almost categorically terminated existing TPS designations for some of the most dangerous countries in the world – a policy change that eventually led the highest court to authorize ending the program for Haiti and Syria , despite both countries being on the state department’s “ do not travel ” advisory list. “In a stunning contradiction, the administration advises Americans against all travel to Haiti – and instructs those who go anyway to draft a will and submit DNA samples so their remains can be identified,” said Krish O’Mara Vignarajah, president and CEO of the immigrant-serving non-profit Global Refuge. He continued: “That is the government’s own assessment of the danger. To then compel hundreds of thousands of Haitians into such dire circumstances is an unconscionable abdication of our moral responsibility.” More than 300,000 Haitians have lost TPS permission overnight and could endure deportation if they have not applied for another form of immigration relief, such as asylum in the US or a green card. For a wide swathe of people, no such pathway to citizenship exists, even if they have lived in the US for decades. Even so, the thought of returning to Haiti’s life-threatening conditions is “unimaginable” for many Haitians in the US, PBS News reported. “It’s not that we don’t want to go back to Haiti,” said Harriett Cecilia Joseph, a former TPS holder. “It’s just the situation [there] doesn’t allow us to.” Already, removal orders for Haitians in the immigration courts have soared by 96% between March and June, according to the Transactional Records Access Clearinghouse (Trac). And immigration officials have started outfitting Haitians with ankle monitors to track their movements, making them easy to find and detain. “They now face an impossible choice: remain without status and risk arrest and deportation, or return to a Haiti marred by gang violence, kidnapping and the collapse of basic services,” said Vignarajah. Thousands of Syrians , although a much smaller group in the US than Haitians, may be at similar risk of repatriation after losing TPS and their affiliated work permits. At the same time, a US district court on Wednesday also allowed the federal government to end employment authorization for active TPS holders from El Salvador, Ukraine and Sudan, jeopardizing their livelihoods despite their ongoing protections against deportation. With so many immigrants suddenly barred from the workforce, business owners are being forced to let go of employees in industries already hampered by significant labor shortages. Meanwhile, Haitians and their champions are calling on the US Senate to extend TPS legislatively, through a proposal that already passed the House of Representatives in April. “We work hard, we pay our taxes, we give back to our communities and we are a big part of the engine that keeps the United States workforce in many essential industries moving,” Josiane Valsaint, a Haitian who had TPS, wrote for the Guardian. “We deserve to stay here, with our families and loved ones.” Explore more on these topics US immigration Trump administration US foreign policy Haiti US politics Caribbean Americas news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen ELN members at a camp in southern Chocó, Colombia. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian Colombia Colombia on the brink: ELN guerrilla group prepares for return to war As Abelardo de la Espriella takes office as president vowing a new military offensive, the country’s last leftwing rebels are getting ready to fight back Thomas Graham in Chocó; Photography by Santiago Mesa Fri 7 Aug 2026 03.00 EDT Share As the boat approached the riverbank, camouflaged figures watched from the tree line. Behind them, in the dim understory of the jungle, a commander of the National Liberation Army (ELN) sat with his rifle on his lap, amid the buzz and whine of insects and the thwacks of machetes on bamboo as his troops set up camp, hidden from enemy drones. Colombia’s 62-year old armed conflict is on the brink of a new chapter, with the country’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who takes office on Friday, vowing an end to peace talks and launch a new military offensive . Colombia’s last guerrilla group says it is ready for whatever might come. “Where we can go on the offensive, we will,” said the commander of the group’s Western War Front, who goes by the moniker Yerson. “And if the ELN leadership says we have to carry out a military offensive at the national level, we will. Attacks in cities, in the countryside, wherever.” View image in fullscreen Members of the ELN’s Western War Front take part in military exercises in southern Chocó, Colombia. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen A member of the ELN’s Western War Front walks across a wooden raft on the San Juan River in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen A member of the ELN’s Western War Front rests inside a shelter in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian Yerson and his troops were deep in the Pacific department of Chocó, in an ELN stronghold accessible only after hours of river travel, where humid heat soaks through the cloud cover. Occasional communities, each a line of wooden shacks on stilts, broke the dense forest on the banks. Giant mining barges were moored on the river, with diggers clawing up the riverbed to extract the particles of gold it contains. The ELN and rival armed groups fight to control the San Juan River, its resources and its population. At one point in the journey, armed men from the Gulf Clan, a violent paramilitary group, stopped the Guardian’s boat to question the passengers, before promising to liberate the area from the ELN. Yerson was unfazed. “All of the ELN territories are being invaded by bands of mercenaries,” he said. “They are very violent, but they are not disputing political power.” View image in fullscreen Commander Yerson stands in front of an ELN flag at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen ELN members listen as Commander Yerson reads the group’s regulations at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen An ELN member poses for a photograph at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian Colombia’s conflict began in the 1960s, rooted in extreme land inequality and exclusionary politics. Leftwing guerrillas emerged to challenge the state, battling government forces later allied with rightwing paramilitaries, forerunners of the Gulf Clan. Money from cocaine trafficking fuelled all sides. The conflict has killed hundreds of thousands of people and displaced millions. Along with the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc), the ELN was the most important of the guerrilla groups. Founded in 1964, it fused Marxism-Leninism with Che Guevara’s foco theory — the idea that a small armed band in a remote rural area can eventually topple the state — and Liberation theology, which framed the struggle against poverty and oppression as an expression of Christian faith. National Liberation Army (ELN) train in the Colombian Jungle In their pursuit of revolution, the two groups have carried out killings and kidnappings, and forced the confinement and displacement of civilian populations. The Farc demobilised in 2016 after striking a peace deal with the Colombian state, but the ELN says its members will only lay down arms after the country’s political and economic system has been transformed. “The Farc surrendered in exchange for nothing,” said Yerson, adding that subsequent presidents have failed to fully implement the peace deal, while former Farc combatants have been killed. View image in fullscreen A female member of the ELN’s Western War Front at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen An ELN member at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The hands of a member of an ELN member who lost a finger after being bitten by a snake while living in the jungle. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian Gustavo Petro, a leftist who was a guerrilla with the defunct M-19 in the 1980s, was elected president in 2022 on a promise of “total peace”, vowing to make good on the Farcdeal and negotiate with all of Colombia’s remaining armed groups on the left and right. But after a few years, almost all the talks – including those with the largest groups — the ELN, the Gulf Clan and Farc dissidents who refused to demobilise in 2016 — either stalled or collapsed. Yerson rejected the idea that the election of Colombia’s first leftist president meant that the ELN’s goals could be achieved through the current political system. “They handed out lands [to the poor]. They did a kind of pension reform. They were looking for ways to improve healthcare,” he said. “But in the end these are small things. They don’t help with the popular awakening.” View image in fullscreen Colombia’s president-elect, Abelardo de la Espriella, speaks at a security summit in Barranquilla. Photograph: Charlie Cordero/Reuters In Yerson’s telling, Petro was allowed to take power by the “Colombian oligarchy”, which needed to pacify the people after an explosion of inequality protests in 2019 and 2021 , but knew he “was never going to undertake fundamental reforms, that he could be controlled”. Colombia’s political system “is not the democracy it claims to be”, he said. “That is where the trap is.” Now the ELN faces a very different proposition in the form of De la Espriella, a Trump-admiring millionaire who rose to prominence as a criminal lawyer representing accused leaders of the AUC , a rightwing paramilitary group that fought the guerrillas and killed civilians accused of collaborating with them.. De la Espriella has given Colombia’s armed groups a month to submit to him or face the consequences, while promising to deepen security cooperation with the US and build mega-prisons inspired by the Salvadoran president, Nayib Bukele. Security analysts, however, say armed groups have gathered strength and resources in recent years. The ELN has about 6,300 members between armed fighters and unarmed support, spread across Colombia and Venezuela. View image in fullscreen Commander Yerson reads out the ELN’s regulations to at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen An ELN member operates a drone during exercises at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen An ELN member wearing camouflage used by the group’s snipers with a precision rifle at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian The 60 or so fighters in the camp were evenly split between men and women, indigenous and Afro-Colombian members. “The majority [of the ELN] has always been the poor, the lowest down,” said Yerson. “Here, as Chocó is more Afro-Indigenous, that’s what we are.” Each of them had a modern assault rifle, either an AK-47 or an AR-15, some with “Made in USA” stamped on the body. One also had a .50 calibre sniper rifle, the bullets of which can punch through vehicles, while another flew a drone. The camp was deep in ELN territory, and they were relaxed. When someone took out a portable speaker and began to play vallenatos – popular Colombian folksongs – they left their rifles resting against trees or slung them over their backs and paired up to dance, suddenly looking like the young Colombians they are. National Liberation Army (ELN) dance during a break from training Various groups, including the UN and Human Rights Watch, have accused the ELN of recruiting minors — but Yerson said their rules only allow people over 16 to join. It was impossible to verify details of his troops’ backgrounds, as they had been told not to talk. Yerson presented two women to be interviewed in his presence, but they struggled to speak, apparently afraid of saying the wrong thing. Yerson himself described the ELN as “a life choice” for Colombia’s poor, who have few options. “Maybe that’s why they join, but once they are here they come to understand why we are fighting,” he said. The ELN functions by taxing “every commercial entity” in the territory it controls, and in Chocó that means illegal gold mining and logging are their key sources of income, said Yerson. It also carries out kidnappings for ransom. View image in fullscreen Two ELN members rest on the forest floor at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen A female ELN member combs her hair at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen An ELN member adjusts another’s beret before military exercises in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian “We are an embryonic state, and every state takes taxes,” he said. “If they can strangle us economically, we will cease to exist as a rebel organisation.” Yerson claimed coca cultivation has disappeared in ELN territory in Chocó. He denied the group was involved in the drug trafficking, but acknowledged it taxes the business like any other. The US, which has given its military a new role to take on “narcoterrorism” across the Americas , might not think much of that distinction. “The question of guilt doesn’t matter to the US. What matters to them are interests,” said Yerson. “We are the only guerrilla group with political principles left standing in Colombia and the world. We will always be something they want to destroy.” He says the ELN will not simply be on the defensive, but will strike back where it can. A car bomb attributed to the group exploded outside a police station near the border with Venezuela last week, injuring 12 police officers and three civilians, and drone attacks have become common. View image in fullscreen ELN members listen as Commander Yerson reads the group’s regulations at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen A fire burns at night at a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian View image in fullscreen ELN members in thick vegetation near a camp in southern Chocó. Photograph: Santiago Mesa/The Guardian “They have to be legitimate objectives. We don’t put car bombs where the civil population will die,” said Yerson, who pointed to the 2019 suicide car bombing of a police academy in Bogotá that killed 22 as a model. “The comrades could go and make kamikaze attacks of that impact.” Despite the election of De la Espriella and other rightwing leaders across the continent, Yerson was adamant that the ELN was not losing the ideological battle. Voters are being deceived, he said, before quoting the South American revolutionary leader Simón Bolívar: “An ignorant people is the blind instrument of its own destruction. “The ideological battle is not being lost,” he repeated, as if irritated by the phrase. “We are on the right side of history.” Asked whether Colombia was any closer to the ELN’s goals after decades of conflict, Yerson was unsure: “I don’t know. But I can tell you that the only way to win things for the people is through the struggle,” he said. “We’ve been in the struggle for 62 years, and there will be many more.” Explore more on these topics Colombia Americas Share Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Wason Wanichakorn/AP View image in fullscreen Schoolgirls being carried away from the scene of the shooting in Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province. Photograph: Wason Wanichakorn/AP Thailand Thailand school shooting: eight killed including suspected attacker, police say Teenager killed his grandparents ⁠before opening fire at school near Bangkok, where 22 others were wounded Thailand school shooting – latest updates Natasha May in Bangkok Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.33 EDT First published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 00.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Thai teenager killed his grandparents before opening fire at his school, where he shot five people dead and took his own life, police have said, in an attack that has shaken a country struggling to deal with gun violence. Police said the 14-year-old had wounded another 22 people in the school ⁠shooting on the outskirts of Bangkok on Friday morning. Nine people were in a critical condition, the Thai health department said. The suspected attacker fired at least 26 bullets with a gun belonging to his grandfather, and was found with 34 additional ammunition rounds. Police also said the teenager had killed his grandparents before the attack at the prestigious Debsirin Nonthaburi school in the Bang Kruai district of Nonthaburi province. 1:06 Students seek safety during Thai school shooting – video The suspected shooter remained inside the school after reports of the attack emerged, Arsit Sampantharat, the permanent secretary of the interior ministry, told PPTV. Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, an emergency worker, described arriving as the shooting was ongoing. He said his team had treated students with injuries in the back, chest and arms. They found a male teacher lying dead on an upper floor of the school, and in another room they found a female teacher with wounds to her chest and arm, Verapongpradith said. View image in fullscreen An injured teacher receiving medical attention at the scene on the outskirts of Bangkok. Photograph: Chalinee Thirasupa/Reuters Images from the scene about an hour after the shooting showed people standing outside the school comforting one another while police and first responders were inside the building. It appeared to have been secured, although officials had not publicly confirmed the shooter’s status. A witness told reporters that students had hidden in a classroom after hearing gunshots from another building before police officers knocked on the door and escorted them safely from the building. Locator map In the 2025 academic year, the school had about 3,100 students and 147 teachers, according to district authorities. The school is part of the Debsirin network, founded by the Thai royal family. Its alumni include prime ministers, scholars and writers. Thailand is known to have the highest rate of civilian gun ownership in south-east Asia . The Switzerland-based Small Arms Survey in 2017 placed the country 13th globally for small gun possession. View image in fullscreen Police at the scene in Bang Kruai district. Photograph: Lillian Suwanrumpha/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Police outside the property where the teenage suspect is suspected to have killed his grandparents. Photograph: Chanakarn Laosarakham/AFP/Getty Images Thailand has had a series of deadly shootings in the past six years, with children among the victims. Photograph: Martin Meissner/AP Extreme weather Analysis Weather tracker: central and western Europe brace for more sweltering heat Ed Walton High 30s celsius forecast for France, Spain and Italy next week, before affecting Germany, Poland and Czechia Fri 7 Aug 2026 07.59 EDT Last modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 08.15 EDT Share Another pulse of heat is expected to affect central and western Europe next week. The latest forecast models show daily maximum temperatures well into the high 30s celsius widely across France, Spain and Italy during the first half of the week, while Germany, Poland and Czechia will experience the highest temperatures towards the end of the week. The shift in the focus of the heat as the week progresses can be attributed to the movement of high pressure. At the start of the week, low pressure centred in the Atlantic and high pressure centred over the low countries will draw warm air from southern Europe northwards into parts of France. During the working week, the high pressure will slip a little farther south and east, enabling the warm air once situated over western Europe to make inroads into parts of Germany and central Europe. The heat in central and western Europe this summer has been unrelenting. Last week’s weather tracker highlighted record-breaking temperatures for the month of July in Austria. However, only a few days later, on 4 August, the all-time record was shattered with 41.0C achieved in Stammersdorf, north-east of the capital, Vienna. This comfortably broke the previous all-time record set in August 2003 by 0.7C. Unbelievably, that record was broken again the following day when 41.2C was recorded in Deutsch-Altenburg. Slovakia also set an all-time record on the same day, of 41.4C. The continuing European heatwave, associated with a vertically extensive anticyclone, raised the freezing level above 4,000 metres across much of the Alpine region. This represents a level in the atmosphere well above many Alpine glaciers, accelerating the seasonal melting process. On the opposite side of the Atlantic, 51.8C was recorded in Badwater, California, the highest temperature in the US for 2026 so far. Although south-eastern parts of Europe have eluded the worst of the summer heat, wildfires have ignited in recent days. Extremely strong northerly wind gusts in excess of 70mph ripped through the Greek Islands on 29 July, causing medium-voltage power lines to sway and produce sparks that set fire to vegetation below. Part of the palm forest at Preveli beach, Crete, was damaged by a wildfire but the centre of the forest was spared from the worst of the destruction. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/blo.text: Morning and welcome to our UK politics blog. The government said more arrests are being made for illegal working, with Home Office figures showing more than 17,000 people have been arrested since the July 2024 general election – more than double the number recorded in the previous two-year period. Of those arrested, 2,357 people have been deported, according to the Home Office, a 50% increase compared with the number returned between July 2022 and June 2024. Commenting on those numbers on the media round this morning, the border security and asylum minister Anna Turley said it was “the highest levels in British history”. “We’re sending a message that if you think you can come to this country and work illegally and disappear off the books, then our immigration enforcement service will find you [and] will arrest you,” she told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme. Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/AP US Senate Murkowski won’t vote for Trump’s nomination of Blanche as attorney general Alaska Republican is concerned that proposed fund to compensate January 6 rioters will proceed even though Blanche confirmed it was dead US politics live – latest updates Guardian staff and agency Fri 7 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 08.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Lisa Murkowski, Alaska’s moderate Republican senator, announced early on Friday that she will not vote for Donald Trump’s nomination of Todd Blanche as US attorney general, leaving his elevation from “acting” to official confirmation in the post even narrower. Murkowski issued a statement expressing her concerns that the Trump administration could proceed with its proposed fund to compensate rioters who invaded the US Capitol on January 6 in a failed attempt to overturn Joe Biden’s defeat of Trump in the 2020 presidential election. She took her stance even though Blanche confirmed in writing the controversial fund was dead. Experts say Trump could easily reverse it. Murkowski said the Senate only currently has leverage over the fund because Blanche’s nomination to head the Department of Justice is pending necessary confirmation by the upper congressional chamber. Blanche had persuaded the Senate judiciary committee in a 12-10 vote in his favor earlier this week only because he promised Republican holdouts that he would not pursue the payout fund. Blanche issued a formal order late on Sunday terminating Trump’s $1.8bn “anti-weaponization” slush fund designed to compensate political allies who had been “targeted” by the justice department, including prosecutions of January 6 insurrectionists. That move followed weeks of negotiations with two Republican senators who were blocking his nomination to become attorney general – Thom Tillis and John Cornyn, who were eventually swayed by Blanche. Murkowski posted on X on Friday, praising Blanche but then saying “ultimately” she would oppose his nomination, a position she took on Tuesday and is now sticking with. “The country needs an Attorney General who will check the worst impulses of this administration. I hope Mr Blanche is able to achieve that, if confirmed, but I simply do not have confidence that will be the case,” she wrote, as part of a much longer post on the topic. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority, but Mitch McConnell of Kentucky is not currently attending sessions because of his health, giving the GOP little room to lose senators and still confirm the president’s pick. The Associated Press contributed reporting. https://www.dw.com/en/testosterone-and-f.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IBlH More men than ever are taking testosterone-boosting medication Image: BREUEL-BILD/IMAGO Advertisement Making sperm is, in large part, what testosterone is for. Which is why it is ironic when a man who doesn't need it starts taking it anyway: His brain registers an unusually high level of the hormone in his blood, concludes his body has made too much, and sends the order to stop. The testes go silent and sperm production declines. Testosterone is having a moment. It is all over social media, gym culture and wellness forums, sold by online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services. The information surrounding it ranges from oversimplified to outright dangerous. Men are taking more of it than ever, in pursuit of feeling more like men . In doing so, they may be telling their bodies to stop producing it themselves. Here is what the science says — what testosterone does, who genuinely needs treatment, and what it can cost the men who take it without needing it. How does taking testosterone stop sperm production? Your body regulates testosterone the way a thermostat regulates heat. When the brain detects abnormally high levels of the hormone in the bloodstream, it sends a signal to the testes to stop producing it naturally. The testes effectively go offline, and because sperm production depends on what happens inside them, that shuts down too. Some men who self-medicate with testosterone push their levels to more than four times the clinical lower threshold. The consequences include blood clotting disorders, cardiovascular stress, mood instability and, in some cases, irreversible fertility damage. What's sold as a shortcut to strength and libido can, unsupervised, cost a man his fertility. What are normal testosterone levels by age? Testosterone peaks during puberty, typically between 13 and 15. After that, it declines slowly for the rest of a man's life. A lower level at 40 than at 15 isn't a disorder — its aging. What counts as low testosterone? The threshold that doctors use is 300 nanograms per deciliter of blood. But this threshold comes with a condition: It must be confirmed by at least two blood tests taken at different times of the day, because levels fluctuate. Below that number, a doctor may begin to consider treatment. Above 300, there is no clinical basis for intervention. How can you increase testosterone naturally? Before any medical treatment is considered, four key lifestyle factors should be examined: sleep, alcohol consumption, smoking and drug use, and chronic stress. Each of these has a measurable impact on testosterone levels. Addressing them may be all that's needed and carries none of the risks of hormonal therapy. What is testosterone replacement therapy (TRT) and who actually needs it? Testosterone replacement therapy, or TRT, treats a diagnosed hormonal deficiency. It's a legitimate medical procedure — involving injections, pills, creams — that works for men who need it. But plenty of men taking it don't have that deficiency. Men with normal testosterone levels are increasingly seeking TRT out anyway, not as a treatment but as a performance enhancer. They're getting it from unregulated online labs, gym contacts and telehealth services that write prescriptions without adequate medical assessment. Can testosterone therapy cause permanent infertility? In some cases, yes. Men who stop taking testosterone are likely to recover their own production within months. But not all of them. Depending on the dose and how long a man has been using, research puts the share who never recover at somewhere between one in ten and one in five. Low testosterone: What it does to men's health To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Does testosterone therapy actually work – or is it a placebo? Many men who self-administer testosterone report feeling stronger, sharper and more energetic. Some of that may reflect genuine physiological change. A significant portion is likely the placebo effect — a well-documented human tendency to feel better when we believe we are being treated. That does not make the feeling less real. It does mean that unsupervised hormonal intervention is a high-risk gamble for a benefit that may exist entirely in one's mind. The bottom line Doctors' advice is unambiguous: Get tested, know the number, and treat everything else — the websites, the influencers, the gym contacts — as anecdote, not medicine. A lot of men aren't waiting. Chasing peak masculinity online, they're reaching for the one substance that could tell their own bodies to stop making it.
