https://www.grandprix.com/news/bortoleto.text: JULY 24, 2026 Bortoleto commits long-term, Sauber defends Audi Gabriel Bortoleto has confirmed he will remain with Audi for "many years", shutting down speculation about the German manufacturer's 2027 driver lineup. My future with Audi is already decided, the Brazilian said as the Hungarian GP weekend began. "I will remain with the team for many years. I have a multi-year contract. I cannot disclose its duration, but if they want to make this information public, I am not against it. We have a long road ahead of us, many years of collaboration. I hope we will achieve many great victories in the future. Nico Hulkenberg has also dismissed doubts about his own future. So with Audi's driver pairing now appearing settled, the man whose name the team carried for more than three decades also defended the progress being made behind the scenes. It's not easy to start with a new engine formula and twice as many people, including in Hinwil, 82-year-old Peter Sauber told Blick. What's important now is harmony within the team. And with Binotto, they seem to have the right man at the helm. From his long time at Ferrari, he understands how to build an engine, but also how to build a car. That gives him a big advantage over all the other team principals. Retired Sauber also remarked that James Key's car is better than many people expected . Bortoleto, meanwhile, has broken ranks with many of his fellow drivers by defending Formula 1's controversial 2026 regulations. He told Auto Hebdo he takes issue with drivers insisting they are having to adjust their natural driving style . I don't think an F1 driver should ever say that, because we should be able to adapt to any type of car, even if it doesn't feel natural, said the 21-year-old. That's why we do this. That's why there are 22 F1 drivers in the world. Motorsport shouldn't reflect a single way of driving. Just because you learned something in karting doesn't mean you have to do it for the rest of your life. He also rejected complaints that software now has too much influence over performance. We're in Formula 1, aren't we? said Bortoleto. We're developing the technology of the future. If we don't use all the tools available to us, I don't know what Formula 1 is. People used to complain because the drivers had too much to do. Now that things are doing it for us, we complain that it's the car doing it. I'm happy with the direction it's going. I don't think that should change. (GMM)

https://www.grandprix.com/news/alonso-di.text: JULY 24, 2026 Alonso dismisses 2-second Aston upgrade hype Fernando Alonso has played down extraordinary expectations surrounding Aston Martin's radically revised car, insisting no upgrade could immediately erase the team's enormous deficit. The Adrian Newey-led package finally arrived at the Hungaroring after a last-minute push, with rumours suggesting almost everything except the front suspension has changed. Spa was one of the toughest, Alonso said at the Hungaroring. I think we had the guy in front of us 2.1 seconds ahead, so there is no package in the world that will give you that amount of time. Probably the position would not change if you ran the updated car in Spa one week ago, so that's how we need to treat it. Trackside boss Mike Krack admitted the new components had arrived extremely late. Yesterday the garage was empty, he said on Thursday. Now it isn't. So we're working to have two cars ready by tomorrow morning. Krack also rejected suggestions that the Hungary package will determine the project's future. No, it won't, he said. I think we're all realistic. More steps are needed, and this is just part of the development strategy, so I wouldn't call it decisive. It's simply a development that needs to continue. Aston Martin has separated its major chassis and engine developments, with the upgraded Honda power unit still scheduled to make its race debut at Zandvoort. However, it's reported that reserve driver Jak Crawford will complete an initial 200-kilometre filming-day run with the new engine at the Hungaroring on Wednesday - Alonso's 45th birthday. Honda spokesman Shintaro Orihara said the revised unit includes substantial internal changes. We are working on the shape of the combustion chamber, he said. We have also modified the pre-chamber. We are also working to reduce friction by modifying the lubrication system. However, Orihara dismissed rumours of a 50 horsepower increase. I'd like to reach that figure, but it's quite a high one, said the Japanese. I can't give details about the power output, but my impression is that it's just a rumour. I don't think it's a real figure. Krack said introducing the chassis first will allow Aston Martin and Honda to understand how the increased cornering speeds alter the power unit's behaviour. There will be higher cornering speeds, which affects energy and, in turn, all the power unit calibrations, he said. Alonso, meanwhile, appears to have ruled out switching to another team if he continues into 2027. I do have a contract, so I'm not moving, he said. The remaining choice is therefore increasingly clear - another season with Aston Martin, or retirement. I feel fresh, I feel motivated, I feel fast, but I need to enjoy what I do as well, said Alonso. In the cockpit it's not the same adrenaline that I used to have driving a Formula 1 car. It's not a problem with the competitiveness of the team. It's just a problem of whether Formula 1 gives me the adrenaline that I need to live. (GMM)

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Melvin Theuma, centre, pictured in 2019, says he acted as a middleman in a plot to murder of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. Photograph: Vincent Kessler/Reuters View image in fullscreen Melvin Theuma, centre, pictured in 2019, says he acted as a middleman in a plot to murder of journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia. Photograph: Vincent Kessler/Reuters Daphne Caruana Galizia Businessman was ‘preparing champagne’ to celebrate Caruana Galizia murder, court hears Taxi driver says he acted as middleman between Yorgen Fenech and three men already convicted of €150,000 contract killing Juliette Garside Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.40 EDT First published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The businessman accused of paying for hitmen to murder the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was impatient for the killing to take place, and once texted from his boat to say he was “preparing champagne” to celebrate, a jury in Malta has heard. Yorgen Fenech , the 44-year-old heir to a property empire that includes several Hilton hotels, is on trial in Malta for complicity in the murder of Caruana Galizia. She died in a car bombing in October 2017 after publishing a series of revelations about senior politicians that were so damaging they triggered a snap general election. The key witness in the case, a taxi driver who says he acted as middleman between Fenech and three men already convicted of accepting €150,000 (£128,000) to carry out the killing, took the stand on Friday to begin his testimony. Melvin Theuma, who has been living under witness protection since agreeing to testify in return for a pardon, said Fenech had told him to contact a known criminal and set up the killing because he wanted to protect his uncle Raymond Fenech, the head of the family business. View image in fullscreen Flowers placed in front of a portrait of murdered journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia during a vigil outside the law courts in Valletta, Malta. Photograph: Jonathan Borg/AP “Bring him here, I need him to kill Daphne because she’s going to publish information about Uncle Ray,” Theuma claimed Fenech had told him. Theuma has previously testified that over time the explanation changed, and the hit was designed to stop revelations about Yorgen himself. The conversation took place in April 2017. The two men were friends, having known each other for years, although Theuma told the jury it was not an equal relationship. “He’s a lion and I’m a mosquito,” Theuma said of the accused. The taxi driver, who had cultivated a friendship with Fenech over a shared interest in horseracing and betting, is regarded by the prosecution as key to securing a conviction. He has given police multiple recordings of conversations he had with Fenech after the murder. Before taking the stand, Theuma had to be certified as fit to give evidence, having previously tried to take his own life. In 2020, having already secured a pardon, he swallowed acid and slit his own throat. He will be allowed to give evidence seated, with his back to Fenech and his lawyers, having previously complained of intimidation. He began his testimony by apologising to the victim’s family, saying: “My cross was too much to bear; I can’t imagine what theirs was like.” After receiving the order from Fenech, Theuma said he went to the docks in Marsa, where the hitmen, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio and their associate Vincent Muscat, used a warehouse known as the potato shed as a base. “Alfred got into my taxi and I told him ‘I have someone who wants to kill Daphne Caruana Galizia’. “He asked if the person could pay, and I said yes, of course.” View image in fullscreen Yorgen Fenech pictured in 2019. He is on trial in Malta for complicity in the murder of Caruana Galizia. Photograph: Yara Nardi/Reuters Theuma said he never told the hitmen who had sent him. He told the court Fenech had agreed to the price, but then asked him to call off the attack after Malta’s then prime minister, Joseph Muscat, called a snap general election. Instead, he asked Theuma to place a €150,000 bet for him on Muscat securing a second term. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion When Muscat was returned to power with a landslide victory in June 2017, Theuma said Fenech rang him that night. “He sounded tipsy. He told me to go ahead with the Daphne job. I didn’t do anything, he sounded drunk.” A few days later, he gave Fenech his winnings from the bet – €300,000, minus a commission. Nothing more was said about Caruana Galizia. But a few days later, Fenech summoned him and gave him an envelope stuffed with cash. “I asked him, ‘What’s this?’ He said: ‘It’s the €150,000 to have Daphne killed.’” The hitmen were given a €30,000 deposit and began scoping the journalist’s movements. Theuma was given a burner phone to contact them with. The witness said he took the phone with him to Disneyland for a family holiday, and that Fenech wanted reassurance he had not left Malta without it. The businessman became impatient as time passed. “Yorgen would ask me every few days: ‘When will they kill her?’ Once, he was on his boat and texted me to say he was preparing champagne in case it happened.” Theuma said Fenech helped to plot Caruana Galizia’s routine, identifying a cafe and restaurant that she frequented. Maltese politicians ‘involved’ in plot to kill Daphne Caruana Galizia, court hears Read more The witness broke down as he described the moment he learned of the death from the television news. Wiping his eyes, he said: “I was living a normal life, I didn’t want for anything. Then I turned on the TV and saw that Daphne was dead. My life ended. When she was killed, my life was blown up.” He also revealed he had been in regular contact by text message with Caruana Galizia’s sons, Matthew and Paul. He said: “I was involved in their mother’s murder, and they speak to me. They tell me I will feel better after the trial. But I know I won’t. The remorse is too great.” Fenech, who is on trial for complicity in the voluntary homicide of Caruana Galizia, denies the charges. The trial continues. Photograph: Jon Nazca/Reuters View image in fullscreen Migrants cross into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta in north Africa last month. Photograph: Jon Nazca/Reuters Social media Russia-linked accounts spread far-right narrative online during Ceuta migration crisis, analysis finds Counter-disinformation group says social media channels connected to Pravda network helped amplify message Aisha Down Fri 7 Aug 2026 12.35 EDT First published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 10.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Accounts with links to the Russian military promoting far-right messages reached more than 500,000 people in the days following the mass influx of people into Ceuta , according to an analysis by 411, a counter-disinformation group. Russia-linked social media accounts frequently spread destabilising narratives in Europe , often promoting far-right talking points about immigration. But 411 and other experts suggest the scale and coordination of the disinformation that followed the Ceuta crisis is significant. Groups spreading disinformation are more organised and powerful than they were several years ago. “We keep seeing this across Europe and we find it very interesting. It seems like there is some type of machinery in place, or structure,” said Saman Nazari, the lead researcher at Alliance4Europe, a Brussels-based nonprofit. “Quite regularly, we are seeing this escalation happening across Europe now, with these types of crises. It is too much of a coincidence to be a bandwagoning effect.” 10:29 How Ceuta migrant crisis exposes divisions within Europe - The Latest The barrage began on 1 August, the day after tens of thousands of people reportedly attempted to cross into the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco overnight. This was part of a larger, multi-day crisis during which 72,000 migrants are estimated to have made their way into the small territory in north Africa, the vast majority of whom were swiftly returned. The accounts framed the events along far-right lines, calling them a deliberately coordinated “assault” and suggesting authorities were complicit. Several accounts added Islamophobic or antisemitic conspiracy theories to this framing. These narratives were rapidly reproduced in seven languages and reached more than 720,000 views over the course of six hours on 1 August, according to 411’s examination of roughly 4.5m social media posts. Other far-right accounts called for nationalists to gather in Ceuta and “patrol” businesses and homes, with some apparently coordinating their efforts. Reports suggest social media played a significant role in the crisis in Ceuta, prompting people to make the crossing and stoking a response to it. Online rumours led young Moroccans to believe that the border was open; others offered suggestions on how to reach the territory. The analysis by 411 confirmed reports that there was substantive “peer-to-peer logistics chatter” between potential migrants on social media over how to make the crossing. Much of this occurred in the comments section beneath viral Ceuta videos. This coordination among migrants appeared to be organic, coming “overwhelmingly from small, anonymous-looking individual accounts rather than any single identifiable ‘recruiter’ channel”. A separate, rightwing backlash began on social media as the crossings continued. One origin of the propaganda barrage was Rybar, a Telegram channel with links to Russian intelligence . Rybar’s parent company has faced sanctions in Europe. A network of “repeater” accounts then amplified and spread Rybar’s posts. These included accounts linked to the Pravda network , an operation spreading Kremlin propaganda worldwide. View image in fullscreen Migrant children queue outside a police station to be registered in Ceuta on Thursday. Photograph: Violeta Santos Moura/Reuters Nazari suggested that disinformation efforts appeared coordinated and that investigations should be made to determine if there were closed forums or similar structures in which far-right influencers discuss how to spread talking points. Ned Mendez, the lead researcher at 411, said disinformation about the Ceuta crisis spread far more quickly than it did in May 2021, during a similar incident in which 8,000 migrants crossed the same border from Morocco into Spain . ‘If we don’t fight back, we don’t have a future’: the journalist taking on the ‘tech fascists’ of Silicon Valley Read more The far right also seized on those events, but this time the amplification of far-right narratives happened more swiftly. The far-right mobilisation calls brought nationalist groups to the main square of Ceuta within days, 411 noted. In 2021, similar calls went out but it took much longer for nationalists to mobilise. “You could compare the process to a highly specific and organised information superhighway,” said Mendez. “If a piece of content or disinformation is placed on to that privileged superhighway, then it will receive a degree of amplification and boost that other types of content just don’t have access to. Events like this across Europe suggest that some pieces of content are being selected for the onramp, and those content pieces share similar characteristics.” The 411 analysis said: “That machinery is the real thing to worry about, more than this particular crisis. The next time there’s a border incident anywhere on the Mediterranean, those same relay networks are already in place, ready to pick it up and run with it again.” Additional reporting by Majida Chowdhury Explore more on these topics Social media Migration The far right Spain Morocco Russia Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Nearly 50 asylum seekers deported under ‘one in one out’ scheme have returned to the UK Nearly a quarter of voters in Europe now back far-right parties Hundreds in Morocco gather near Ceuta border in anxious wait for missing loved ones Anger at ‘send them back’ chants by rightwing MEPs after EU migration law vote France’s top film producer says it will blacklist figures who petitioned against rightwing billionaire EU chief criticises Spain’s migrant plan after Ceuta crisis meeting Stronger EU borders needed after Ceuta crisis, von der Leyen says French film industry at risk from the far right, say actors and directors Ceuta leader accuses Morocco over ‘atrocity’ of mass border crossing Trump lauds Viktor Orbán as Europe’s far-right leaders gather in Budapest Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Tamir Kalifa/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A demonstrator holds a photo of Awdah Hathaleen during an August 2025 protest in Tel Aviv over his death. Photograph: Tamir Kalifa/Getty Images West Bank Israel indicts settler over death of Palestinian activist who worked on No Other Land Yinon Levy charged with manslaughter in first exception this decade to culture of impunity for Israelis who kill Palestinians in the occupied West Bank Emma Graham-Harrison in Jerusalem Fri 7 Aug 2026 09.49 EDT First published on Thu 6 Aug 2026 10.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Prosecutors in Israel have indicted an extremist settler for shooting a Palestinian activist last July, the first attempt this decade to hold an Israeli responsible for killing a Palestinian in the occupied West Bank . Yinon Levy, who was under western sanctions, is charged with manslaughter over the death of Awdeh Hathaleen, an English teacher and peace activist. In his last moments, Hathaleen filmed the settler drawing his weapon and opening fire towards him. Hathaleen’s family said Levy should have been charged with first-degree murder over the well-documented attack in the village of Umm al-Khair. Reckless manslaughter carries a maximum prison sentence of 12 years, far less then murder. “This was not an accident,” said his cousin Tarek Hathaleen. “Yinon Levy must be held fully accountable for Awdeh’s killing.” The charges nevertheless represented a “significant development”, Hathaleen added, after years of near-total impunity for Israelis who attack Palestinians in the occupied West Bank. 0:53 Palestinian activist recorded moment he was killed by settler in West Bank – video My sweet friend Awdah Hathaleen was murdered by a West Bank settler. May his memory be a revolution | Emily Glick Read more Israeli settlers and soldiers have killed more than 1,500 Palestinians this decade, according to rights group B’tselem . Levy is the first person indicted over any of those deaths. Military prosecutors last brought charges over a 2019 shooting of a young man who stopped to help victims of a traffic accidentThe last time civilian prosecutors brought charges was in 2018 over the killing of a mother of eight, hit by a rock as she was driving. Settler violence and ethnic cleansing has surged in the occupied West Bank over the past three years, supported by far-right Israeli cabinet ministers who hold security, defence and finance portfolios. Levy’s indictment over one of the highest-profile killings in that period does not represent a policy shift for Israel, rights groups said. Hathaleen had worked on No Other Land , the Oscar-winning documentary about his community’s decades-long struggle against the Israeli state and settlers, to stay in their homes and lands in the south Hebron hills. “It’s important to see this killing as part of an ongoing and systematic situation in the West Bank,” said Ziv Stahl, executive director of Yesh Din, an Israeli rights and advocacy organisation. “I don’t think these charges are an indication of increased law enforcement or accountability. It is more likely due to the fact that [Awdeh Hathaleen] was a well-known activist and the case got a lot of media exposure and public critique. It’s more about an appearance of law enforcement, rather than actual law enforcement.” Levy, who was under sanctions for violence against Palestinians by the UK, EU, Canada and Australia at the time of the attack, was briefly detained last year but police released him after three days under house arrest. He spent the last year free and continued establishing illegal outposts in the occupied West Bank, said Yair Dvir, spokesperson for B’tselem. “The decision to indict Yinon Levy is the exception that proves the rule,” Dvir said. “The impunity Israel grants to soldiers and settlers who harm Palestinians is not a failure of the system – it is a central component of a policy designed to allow the violence to continue and escalate.” The culture of impunity spurred the former Israeli prime minister Ehud Olmert to call for the International Criminal Court to bring charges against “Jewish terrorists”, saying intervention was needed to halt the violence. Levy is also charged with armed trespassing and malicious property damage in the Palestinian village of Umm al-Khair. Before Hathaleen was shot, another settler drove a bulldozer through Palestinian land, destroying trees and property. When a resident approached and asked him to stop, the driver knocked the man down with the bulldozer blade. Even if the case goes to trial, any verdict could be many years away, and Israeli judges have a record of lenient treatment of Israelis who attack Palestinians. The Israeli soldier who shot 23-year-old Ahmad Manasrah dead in 2019 pleaded guilty to the equivalent of negligent homicide and was sentenced to three months community service for the killing. He has not been publicly named. Eight years after a 2018 attack that killed 47 year-old Aisha Rabi, an Israeli court ruled that a settler had thrown the stone that killed her. Judges did not hand down a conviction or sentence, instead ordering a review because the man, who was not named, was 16 at the time of the attack. No further details have been made public. Hathaleen’s family say they will continue to fight for Levy to face full trial. “Justice requires more than simply bringing a charge,” said Tarek Hathaleen. “Awdeh was not only my cousin. He was my childhood friend and someone very dear to me. His absence has left a pain that will never go away.” Sufian Taha contributed reporting Explore more on these topics West Bank Palestine Israel Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story How children in West Bank are being killed by Israel ‘without accountability’ Israeli police kill two young Palestinian boys and their parents in West Bank Israelis kill three in West Bank village as violence surges across occupied Palestine Senators demand investigation after ninth American killed by Israeli settlers or soldiers in West Bank Brother of No Other Land co-director injured as Israeli settlers again attack family home ‘A step in the wrong direction’: Israel’s West Bank plans prompt global backlash Palestine’s ambassador to UK hails embassy as ‘proof our identity cannot be denied’ Press Israel to release Marwan Barghouti, former world leaders urge Trump Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: A French warship and navy rib alongside an inflatable ‘small boat’ carrying migrants across the Channel after leaving northern France. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A French warship and navy rib alongside an inflatable ‘small boat’ carrying migrants across the Channel after leaving northern France. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Immigration and asylum French officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since spring Disclosure challenges Conservative and Reform claims that police are refusing to intervene Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.46 EDT Last modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 14.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The French authorities have halted small boats at sea in the Channel on 10 occasions since the spring, officials said on Friday. Despite claims from the Conservatives and Reform that the French were refusing to intervene in small boat crossings, maritime prefect officers were using “intervention tactics” to board or control vessels at sea and take asylum seekers back to France . The disclosure comes as political parties are once again attempting to seize the initiative over small boats over the summer. Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, last week confronted French police on a beach near Boulogne and uploaded footage to X of an officer saying: “Our order is to let them go. We just have to say to them, ‘Don’t do that. It’s dangerous.’” Earlier this week, Reform MP Lee Anderson visited Calais and said the French police were “literally waving these people on to boats”. In an unusual intervention, the director of maritime and small boats at Border Security Command, Charlie Eastaugh, said: “The incidents we have seen in the Channel over the last few weeks are a stark reminder of the dangers posed by criminal gangs exploiting people for profit. It is easy to look at out-of-context images and think little is happening to stop these crossings – this is simply not true. Has the UK government’s strategy on small boat crossings been effective? Read more “I know personally how tirelessly French officers have been working to disrupt launches before they reach UK shores. Their efforts include facing violent people with weapons, dispersing huge crowds, arresting smugglers, seizing equipment and collating vital evidence to help our prosecutions.” Every confrontation with asylum seekers was assessed by commanders as well as individual police officers and gendarmes, who were expected to balance the safety of their officers with that of the public, including large groups of often agitated people and gang members, officials said. On Sunday, when Andy Burnham visited HM Coastguard in Dover, Border Force officers had been warned that it was a “red day”, when conditions were calm enough for several small boat crossings. Two small boats attempted to launch from France, but one was intercepted at sea, while the other was halted on land. Small boats crossing the Channel were down by 43% compared with January to mid-July 2025 – from 21,690 people who crossed last year to 12,469 over the same period this year. The drop has come despite hot and dry conditions, which are usually associated with an increase in crossings. UK officials believe that government initiatives to “stop the boats” by financing the French authorities with another £660m in April have disrupted the business model of people smugglers in northern France and reduced the number crossing to the UK. Gangs are adapting their tactics. Boat launches have spread further along the coast, with some leaving from Belgium and others from as far south as Dieppe, a journey of 70 miles (113km) to the UK, compared with the Calais to Dover route of 27 miles. Officials are concerned the trend towards “mega-dinghies” – larger motorised boats – is putting more people at risk. More than 170 migrants were rescued on Tuesday after the boat they were using to cross the Channel caught fire. The sustained drop in crossings was a welcome development for Burnham, allowing him to focus his early weeks in government on setting out his policy agenda. Shabana Mahmood, who Burnham has kept in post as home secretary, has been reluctant to celebrate the recent drop because she is conscious the trend could change if there is an increase in arrivals in the late summer and autumn months. Photograph: Riverside County Fire Department View image in fullscreen Rebecca Marodi was stabbed to death by her wife. Photograph: Riverside County Fire Department California California woman who admitted to stabbing wife had also killed husband Yolanda Olejniczak Marodi, who served a decade for killing her husband, pleaded guilty to murder of Rebecca Marodi, a fire captain who fought the Eaton blaze Edward Helmore Fri 7 Aug 2026 14.36 EDT Last modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 14.38 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A California woman this week admitted to killing her wife, a decorated fire captain who fought the deadly 2025 Los Angeles wildfires , by stabbing her – the same fate she previously delivered to her husband and had served a decade in prison for. Yolanda Olejniczak Marodi, 54, pleaded guilty on Wednesday to second-degree murder after killing her wife, Rebecca “Becky” Marodi, 49, a California fire captain, at their home in February 2025, just a month after Becky, as she was known, battled the Eaton blaze that killed 19. Rebecca Marodi, who was assigned to the French Valley Cal Fire station in Riverside county was found with multiple stab wounds to her neck, chest and back at the couple’s home in Ramona, near San Diego. She had said she wanted to end the marriage. A warrant for Olejniczak Marodi’s arrest was issued days later. Detectives said home security footage had shown Rebecca Marodi running from her wife of two years, screaming: “Yolanda! Please! I don’t want to die!” Man arrested at Trump’s California golf course wore earpiece and took photos, police say Read more According to investigators, Olejniczak Marodi, who was seen holding a knife and with blood on her arms in the surveillance film, replied: “You should have thought of that before.” Olejniczak Marodi was captured on video loading “pets, random items and some luggage” and loading them into an SUV, according to the warrant seen at the time by ABC News. About 75 min after the attack, records from homeland security showed Olejniczak Marodi crossing the nearby border into Mexico. Investigators later found that the then suspect messaged a friend: “Rebecca came home and told me she was leaving me. We had a big fight, and I hurt her. I’m sorry.” Soon after the murder it emerged that Olejniczak Marodi had been in prison from 2004 to 2013 after being convicted of voluntary manslaughter in the 2000 stabbing death of her then-husband, Jim Olejniczak. He, too, had recently informed her he was ending the marriage. After she fled this time, Mexican law enforcement officers arrested her at a hotel in Mexicali in March 2025 and she was later handed over to US Marshals in San Diego and booked on suspicion of murder. She initially pleaded not guilty. Andrea Winter, a friend of Rebecca, told the Los Angeles Times that Olejniczak Marodi was jealous of her wife’s popularity and exhibited “controlling, isolating behavior” prior to the killing. Winter said Rebecca had not disclosed that her wife had been convicted of stabbing her previous husband to death. “Yolanda was very insecure,” Winter told the outlet. “Becky has this magnetic personality and everybody liked her. I think Yolanda was very jealous of that and that Becky was this bright light. “Becky was a kind person and paid the absolute price for that by trusting the wrong person,” Winter added. Olejniczak Marodi is scheduled to be sentenced on 2 September and faces 36 years to life in a state prison. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images US Senate US Senate passes Russia sanctions bill championed by Lindsey Graham Late senator spent final days of his life working to advance bill that will now head to the House after 86-11 Senate vote Chris Stein Fri 7 Aug 2026 14.46 EDT First published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 13.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google By a large, bipartisan margin, the US Senate on Friday approved a bill intended to punish Russia and countries that buy its petroleum exports over the invasion of Ukraine, capping a legislative push that was spurred by the death of its champion, the Republican senator Lindsey Graham. The measure, renamed the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia Act in honor of the late senator’s work on the issue, was approved by an 86-11 vote. Rand Paul of Kentucky was the sole Republican to oppose the legislation, together with 10 Democrats . The bill would impose new sanctions and visa bans on Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, and top military commanders, as well as put tariffs of up to 500% on the country’s exports. It would also allow Donald Trump to impose levies of up to 100% on goods from countries that are the top five importers of Russian oil and gas. The proposal was a top priority for Graham, a Republican senator from South Carolina who spent the final days of his life working to advance it. But the effort had became mired in months of negotiations between the White House and Senate leadership. Trump’s attorney general pick Todd Blanche appears to clear last hurdle for confirmation Read more After Graham’s sudden death last month at the age of 71 following a trip to Kyiv, party leaders announced an agreement to get the bill through the chamber and honor his legacy as an ally of Ukraine . The Senate took the first step toward advancing it last month, on the day of Graham’s funeral, with Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Ukraine’s president, watching from the chamber. “This bill forces those primary countries keeping Russia’s economy afloat to make a simple yet critical choice – a choice between doing business with America or buying cheap Russian energy,” said Darline Graham, the late senator’s sister who was appointed to his seat after his death. Graham, who presided over the Senate and announced the bill’s passage, added: “This legislation tells Russia’s customers that the United States of America will not sit by while they fund Putin’s assault.” The measure was a relatively rare bipartisan accomplishment ahead of November’s midterm elections, where Democrats hope to channel voter sentiment against Trump to regain control of Congress. “By imposing steep sanctions that will further drain the Kremlin’s war chest, Congress is delivering an important reminder to Putin and his allies that this is a losing war and authoritarianism will never go unchallenged,” said Chuck Schumer, the minority leader. “I urge Trump to use these sanctions to hit Putin where it hurts. Continuing to appease Putin won’t work.” The bill now heads to the House of Representatives , which may consider once it returns from recess at the end of August. Some Democrats have warned that the bill would give Trump new tariff powers at a time when he has put such levies at the center of his trade policy. Paul and Democratic senator Ron Wyden had offered an amendment that would have stripped some of the new tariff authority from the text, but the Senate rejected it by a 32-64 vote. “This bill gives him so much discretion that Trump can ultimately decide what countries to tariff, or what countries to exempt. And he can modify tariffs at his will,” said Wyden, who voted against the bill. “Trump can pick and choose even more countries to tariff every 180 days, but there is no mechanism in this bill for Congress to roll back these tariffs,” he continued. “If Congress passes this bill, members will be condoning the tariff chaos of the last year and a half – and inviting more.” Following the measure’s passage, Gregory Meeks, the top Democrat on the House foreign affairs committee, and Don Beyer, the senior Democrat on the joint economic committee, warned that it contains “sweeping new tariff authorities that the president could weaponize with abandon, as he has repeatedly done in the past”. Noting that Trump just weeks ago imposed new 50% tariffs on most Canadian goods, the two Democrats said: “We welcome our Senate colleagues’ urgent effort to support Ukraine and punish Russia for its continued illegal war, but this bill would not achieve those goals. Instead, it would allow president Trump to dodge holding Russia accountable and impose yet more tariffs in his destructive trade wars, leaving Americans to foot the bill.” Explore more on these topics US Senate US Congress House of Representatives Donald Trump Russia Ukraine US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/07/ameri.text: An Australian air crew flew a US national from an Antarctic base to a New Zealand hospital in a rare midwinter rescue.The Airbus A319 Long Range aircraft, with the call sign Snowbird 1, flew from the Australian city of Hobart to the US McMurdo Station in Antarctica on 31 July in response to an “urgent request for assistance,” the jet’s Melbourne-based owner Skytraders said in a statement.The jet landed after a five hour and 30 minute flight at the Phoenix Airfield near McMurdo in darkness and with temperatures as low as -43C, the statement said.The American was flown on the same day to a hospital in Christchurch as weather conditions at the Antarctic air strip worsened, said Skytraders, which is contracted by the Australian Antarctic Division.The US National Science Foundation told the ABC that the patient was admitted to the Christchurch Hospital in a “serious condition.”The AAD said in a statement on Friday the patient continued to receive medical treatment in Christchurch.“This was a complex operation carried out in the depths of the Antarctic winter and it highlights both the capability of our people and the strong partnerships that underpin Antarctic programmes around the world," the head of AAD, Emma Campbell, said.New Zealand’s Health Ministry on Friday would not comment on the American’s condition or say whether the American remained in hospital.The mission’s copilot, Louise Robertson, said conditions were close to the limit of the aircraft’s capabilities.“We had some what’s called nautical twilight, which is a very minimal amount of light that is pretty much pitch blackness and also the extreme cold temperatures. We are right on the verge of the limitation of the aircraft,” Robertson told ABC.“It was very close to being too cold,” she said. ”It got down to -43, which is the coldest I’ve ever felt. It was about 8 knots of wind, so quite a bit of wind-chill as well.”Robertson said plans to fly to the base on the Ross Ice Shelf a day earlier were aborted due to a snow storm.“There…was really just such a narrow window of opportunity,” Robertson said.“To get there in complete darkness in these extreme cold temperatures is very, very rare. I believe it hasn’t been done before,” she added.The sun last set at the geographic South Pole on 23 March and will not rise until 21 September.The New Zealand Air Force evacuated a New Zealand citizen working on the US Antarctic Programme from the Phoenix Airfield in a C-130 Hercules in a medical emergency in April, which is the Southern Hemisphere autumn.In August last year, the final month of the Southern Hemisphere winter, New Zealand used the same type of four-engine turboprop transport aircraft to evacuate three people on a flight from McMurdo for medical treatment.McMurdo shares its airstrip with New Zealand's nearby Scott Base.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/07/two-d.text: The suspect in a school shooting in Thailand killed a total of eight people on Friday, police said.First he shot his grandparents dead using his grandfather's handgun, then went to his school north of Bangkok and killed three teachers and three students, national police said in a statement.The shooter was identified as a teenage student of the school and also reported dead, according to local media reports citing authorities.Some reports said police officers had shot and killed the suspect, while others said he had died by suicide."It's such a terrible incident. It should never have happened. How could this happen in our country?" Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters at Bangkok's Government House.Polapee said the suspect used a handgun and the interior ministry was investigating how the student obtained it.Photos published by local media show the suspect wearing a purple school uniform and carrying a black cross-body bag, with several bullet casings visible on the ground.Traffic near the Debsirin Nonthaburi School in Nonthaburi was nearly at a standstill, an AFP journalist saw, with local media reporting that parents were picking up their children following the incident.Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in the region, with around 10 million firearms estimated to be in circulation, one for every seven inhabitants.Past promises of tightening gun laws have not prevented repeated shootings.Thai police shot and arrested a teenage shooter who opened fire at a school in the south of the country in February, leaving the school principal dead and two students injured.The teen had used a police officer's weapon in the shooting.A local police chief said at the time that the suspect was hospitalised for psychiatric treatment in December and had been discharged.The teen stabbed a police officer with a knife and stole his weapon, a 9mm pistol, just before the incident and then used it to carry out the attack.In 2022, an ex-policeman armed with a gun and a knife stormed into a nursery in the country's north and murdered 24 children and 12 adults, one of Thailand's deadliest massacres.

https://www.dw.com/en/ceuta-spain-warns-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ISwS Nearly all of the people who rushed Ceuta's border have since left, but those who do stay are unlikely to be able to reach the European mainland unless they are formally granted permission to reside [FILE: August 6, 2026] Image: Violeta Santos Moura/REUTERS Advertisement Spain 's government on Friday threatened to impose reciprocal entry checks on travelers from Italy , unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni 's governemnt lifts the measures it has implemented by Sunday. Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week. The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes. Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy. Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did Spain say about possible checks on travelers from Italy? Spain called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population." Madrid had objected to the move on several grounds, saying it was based on "spurious arguments." It said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days . Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years. "If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said. Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15. Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zone amid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however. Italy first made the announcement as images and footage of the border breach were going viral online Image: Atlas/REUTERS What do we know about Italy's checks on travelers from Spain? Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground. Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure. "They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers." Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities. "I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough." EU defends border response after Ceuta crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Meloni and Sanchez: A clash of styles on migration At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration. Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe. Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market. Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare. "Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years." Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.dw.com/en/how-viable-is-the-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IT62 Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a vital artery for global trade, remains severely disrupted Image: REUTERS Advertisement Iran's Foreign Ministry spokesperson, Esmail Baghaei, said this week that an agreement with Oman , which lies on the other side of the Strait of Hormuz , is in the "final stage" of review and drafting — provided that no external party interfered in the process. The two Persian Gulf states have agreed on the geographical coordinates of a navigation route through the strait , Baghaei was quoted as saying by state news agency IRNA on Wednesday evening. Baghaei told journalists that even if an understanding was reached, it would not mean that the strait had become safe for all passing vessels. "The factors making the Strait of Hormuz insecure still exist on the part of the United States , particularly the naval blockade and other aggressive and threatening actions against Iran and its interests," he said. What the agreement could look like Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi also said an agreement on new shipping arrangements was nearing completion, IRNA reported. Gharibabadi stressed that the proposed arrangement would not amount to a full reopening of the strait, but would instead establish a new model for maritime traffic. According to IRNA, Gharibabadi said the route would be temporary and could remain open for between two and four months. Shipowners hope Strait of Hormuz will reopen soon To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Tehran said that any reopening of the strait must be accompanied by an end to the US blockade of Iranian ports . Reports cited by Agence France-Presse (AFP) said Iran was planning to block US and Israeli ships from the waterway as part of a deal with Oman. Iran also argued that vessels passing through the strait should pay fees for safe passage. Oman did not support unilateral Iranian control of the waterway. Obstacles and skepticism A proposed deal between Iran and Oman to give Tehran control over ships entering the Persian Gulf ​through the Strait ⁠of Hormuz is not easily workable because of US sanctions and restrictive insurance clauses ⁠on payments, according to industry sources cited by Reuters on Friday. However, analysts cautioned that any deal on the reopening of the strait should be viewed as a tactical pause rather than a durable settlement. Security analyst Shukriya Bradost told DW such a pause could benefit Washington more than Tehran. "The United States could use the period to improve coordination with its regional partners, review its military strategy and prepare stronger options," she said. "Iran, meanwhile, would continue facing economic pressure, internal divisions and growing political and security costs." "If this period becomes merely a pause in tensions and Tehran fails to secure a tangible strategic gain, the passage of time may benefit the United States more than any other party," Bradost added. What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Other analysts pointed to fundamental disagreements over the future governance of the waterway. Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, said Tehran and Washington are pursuing different objectives. "Iran wants control over vessels entering the strait, while the United States wants completely free passage," Dorbeiki told DW. "These positions cannot easily be reconciled." Competing views of Iran's role in Hormuz Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, said both Tehran and Washington could potentially present a deal as a tactical success. From Iran's perspective, he said any understanding could be presented as an achievement. "The regime has not collapsed, its missile capabilities remain intact, enriched uranium has not left the country, and for the first time since the war, Iran has reinforced its leverage over the inbound shipping lane of the strait," he told DW. Salavati added that Tehran could claim domestically that it has preserved the strategic leverage of the Strait of Hormuz. He said the United States could also portray the situation as a success in the form of "relief from the pressure of soaring energy prices, an opportunity to replenish weapons stockpiles while easing pressure on defence production, and the ability to declare an end to the active phase of the war." Salavati suggested that Tehran is unlikely to regard any arrangement as the end of the broader confrontation. Trump has faced pressure from members of his own party in Congress to bring the conflict to a close before November's midterm elections. Oman has not publicly commented on the reported agreement, which Iran says was negotiated without US involvement. US-Iran war: Will it ever end? https://www.dw.com/en/eco-wins-hungary-g.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ISfP Yellow-bellied marmots are now officially internet famous Image: All Canada Photos/IMAGO Advertisement Hungary's former leader Viktor Orban called European Union climate policy a "utopian fantasy" and effectively banned wind turbines. And yet the country has quietly become Europe's solar leader , with 25% of its electricity now being being generated from the renewable energy source, ahead of sunnier countries like Spain, and Greece. The boom was driven not by climate concern but by self-sufficiency politics and cheap subsidies. Now a 450-megawatt park, just east of Budapest, is due online by September 2026. It's set to power around 106,000 households. Marmot researchers find a new way to fund their science When US federal funding dried up, researchers from UCLA and the Rocky Mountain Biological Laboratory got creative. They launched OnlyMarms: a free platform posting videos of yellow-bellied marmots eating, digging and scampering in the wild, where fans can donate to support the science. The team has tracked individually marked marmots in Colorado since 1962, building six decades of data on family lives, social behavior and responses to environmental change — and say studying marmot hibernation could even hold clues about human aging. Rome's 'big snake' gets a cooler future Corviale, a kilometer-long brutalist housing complex outside Rome nicknamed "the big snake," was completed in the 1980s and has since fallen into decay. With summers in some parts of Italy's now averaging around 30 degrees Celsius (86 Fahrenheit), life inside has become tough for its more than 4,000 residents. But upgrades are coming: a new library doubling as a cooling shelter, more trees and energy efficiency improvements, all aimed at helping Corviale stay cool as temperatures keep rising. Senegalese designer turns discarded textiles into sustainable fashion Berlin-based designer Mame Khady Badji transforms discarded clothing into bold garments inspired by her Senegalese heritage, combining traditional Ndiakhass techniques with contemporary streetwear. Her creations have drawn musicians, performers and creatives — and recently appeared at Berlin Fashion Week 2026. After moving to Germany in 2017, Badji built her label with support from Berlin's textile community. Now she's pursuing an ambitious goal: proving that recycled fashion can be both culturally rooted and commercially viable. Can sustainable fashion be profitable? https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-sanct.text: The EU has added five individuals to its Russia sanctions list. The move was driven by Moscow’s “intensified strikes deliberately targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure” in Ukraine, according to a press release . The press release does not refer to a specific attack, but earlier this week Russia carried out one of its deadliest barrages on the Ukrainian capital, killing 17. In July, a similar attack in Kyiv killed 12. Among those included in the new sanctions is Ramil Badgutdinov — the head of a company that helps produce the Iskander-M ballistic missiles — and Aleksandr Dyukarev, head of the KrasMash plant that produces Sarmat ballistic missiles. Russia has not yet used Sarmat missiles in Ukraine, but Moscow has been testing them. Advertisement Advertisement The remaining individuals are directors of Russian defense companies involved in communications systems and “the development of software for unmanned aerial vehicles and space-related military technologies,” reads the press release . “With its army stalled on the battlefield, Moscow is further escalating its campaign of terror against civilians,” wrote EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas on X. “The EU must continue to intensify pressure on Russia until Moscow ends its war.”

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c980.text: Image source, Getty Images By Paweena Ninbut ,Â Thanyarat Doksone Â and Â Koh Ewe Published 7 August 2026, 09:54 BST Updated 3 hours ago At least seven people have been killed and 23 injured after a 14-year-old boy opened fire at his home and school on the outskirts of Thailand's capital, Bangkok. The gunman - a student at the Debsirin School in Nonthaburi - killed his grandparents and five teachers before taking his own life, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters. The attacker still had "more than 30 bullets left" when he turned the gun on himself, Anutin added. Nine of the injured people remain in a critical condition, authorities say. The shooting - the second at a school in Thailand this year - has renewed pressure on the government for greater action on gun control. Police were deployed to the scene during the active shooting, which began just after 10:00 local time (03:00 GMT). National police chief police Gen Kittiratt Phanphet told reporters that forensic officers had found the gunman's shots were quite accurate, with several hitting vital spots on the body. The prime minister said the attack was "well prepared" with "clear steps and clear goals". A female seventh grader, still in school uniform, told the BBC she was standing in front of her teacher when the woman was shot. "She was talking to me when [the gunman] showed up and shot her," she said. "I couldn't see anything but a [cloud] of dust." Still in her uniform, with her mother by her side, she explained how the shooter stalked from room to room. "I had to climb over the school fence to escape with other friends." Her mother says the girl thought she might die. "[She said] 'I thought I'd never see you again'." Another student told Reuters news agency that he had thought the sound of gunshots were firecrackers going off. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again." Students and school staff were seen fleeing from the scene, and those waiting outside the Debsirin School looked visibly distraught. Authorities warned people to stay away from the area and for those trapped in the building to hide and wait for rescuers. In a post on social media, the school later shared a call for blood donations. Other schools in the vicinity suspended classes so students could return home early. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Police have been combing over the school for evidence I was standing in front of my teacher when she was shot, Thai pupil says Published 4 hours ago The attacker has not been publicly named, and police have not disclosed a motive. Investigations are continuing, with officers seen carrying away computer equipment and boxes from the home the shooter shared with his grandparents, who he shot dead before the school rampage. The attacker had lived with his grandparents as his parents were divorced. Both the father and the mother were called in for questioning at a local police station later on Friday. The Debsirin School, founded in Bangkok in 1885, is one of Thailand's top secondary schools with branches across the country. It counts many prominent Thai figures as its alumni, from diplomats and athletes to several prime ministers. Figure caption, Students shelter in classroom as gunshots heard The prime minister said the tragedy "shouldn't have happened", adding "this is why the government do not allow [citizens] to possess firearms". "I don't just feel sorry for the victims but I feel sorry that this happened. How can this happen in our country," Anutin said. Thailand has strict gun laws, which punishes the illegal possession of arms with up to 10 years in jail. Enforcement of these laws has been an issue - though police have made no suggestion the weapon used in this case, owned by the shooter's grandfather, was illegally obtained. The country has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in South East Asia. It is estimated that about 40% of these guns are illegal. Friday's shooting immediately triggered calls from politicians for a review of the current gun laws. Anutin responded by pledging to introduce a new firearms control law. Under the proposed new legislation, there will be restrictions on members of the public carrying such weapons. "The new law will only allow government officials on duty to carry guns," Anutin said. He did not provide any specifics for the proposed legislation, including whether it would tighten gun ownership requirements. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyl.text: Image source, Europol Image caption, Europol shared video from the operation, including of police dogs searching cars By Olivia Ireland Published 2 hours ago One of the largest criminal networks smuggling drugs and people in the western Mediterranean has been dismantled, authorities have said. Europol said 78 people were arrested in Spain and Algeria in a bust of the network, that is also linked to other criminal activities including "violent robberies, extortion, illegal detentions, and money laundering". The group moved synthetic drugs from Spain and Portugal to Algeria, then used the return journey to smuggle migrants and weapons to the Spanish mainland and island of Ibiza on "ghost speedboats". Some of the items seized included 18 high-speed vessels valued at â¬5m (Â£4.2m), guns, more than â¬25,000 (Â£21,400) in cash and 15,000 MDMA pills. The sting, led by Spanish police, involved searches in 17 locations in Spain, including Alicante, AlmerÃ­a, Cartagena and Murcia. Europol said the group had "evolved from drug trafficking into a duel-flow criminal enterprise designed to maximise profits" with outbound routes from Spain and Portugal to Algeria. "The smuggling focused on synthetic drugs (such as MDMA), firearms, and explosives. Along routine routes from Algeria to Spain, the group smuggled migrants, charging up to â¬12,000 (Â£10,200) per person," Europol's statement said. "In just one trip, over 50 migrants could be smuggled. All in all, profits from migrant smuggling alone are estimated to be more than â¬24m (Â£20m)." The network also provided services to other organised crime groups, "facilitating the movement of illicit goods and people across the Western Mediterranean". "Investigators believe the network coordinated multiple trafficking flows. Synthetic drugs, and sometimes people, were moved from France and Spain to Algeria, while cannabis resin, weapons, and migrants were transported from Algeria to Spain." Often, the group used a fleet of high-powered speedboats to conduct rapid maritime operations. This included "ghost speedboats" which are designed to avoid registration and detection, which are prohibited in Spain. "The group used these boats to organise transfers in international waters near the Spanish coastline," Europol said. "Once the cargo or migrants were handed over at sea, other network members arranged onward transport by land. "Migrants were often carried in overcrowded boats without lighting or life jackets, frequently under extreme weather conditions. "Investigators believe suspects perpetrated sexual assaults, physical abuse, and placed migrants in inhuman conditions in makeshift housing." The suspects were primarily of Algerian origin and had connections to criminal groups in France, Belgium, Portugal, Italy and Poland. Other objects seized in the police sting included satellite phones, GPS devices, encrypted communication tools and satellite dishes. The announcement comes a week after roughly 78,000 migrants fled into the Spanish North African territory of Ceuta that was blamed on online rumours about an open border. Most of the migrants returned to Morocco but between 3,000 and 5,000 remain in the territory, the exclave's leader Juan JesÃºs Vivas said. https://telex.hu/after/2026/08/07/meghal.text: Menü Kereső Meghalt William Orbit, az ezredforduló popzenéjének meghatározó producere After William Orbit 2012-ben – Fotó: Victor Fraile / Getty Images Klág Dávid 69 éves korában meghalt a brit William Orbit, derül ki a család Instagram-posztjából. A zenei producer az ezredforduló popzenéjének egyik meghatározó háttérembere volt. Olyan lemezeknél működött közre, mint a Ray of Light Madonnától vagy a 13 a Blurtől – ez utóbbin szerepel többek között a Coffee & TV is. Ő volt a producere az All Saints Pure Shores című dalának is. Orbit eredetileg William Mark Wainwrightként látta meg a napvilágot 1956-ban. A nyolcvanas évektől kezdve több, elektronikus alapú zenekarban is tag volt, de igazán DJ-ként, remixek készítőjeként és producerként lett ismert a kilencvenes években, miközben William Orbitként több szólólemezt is kiadott. A Ray of Light on végzett munkájáért két Grammy-díjat is kapott 1999-ben: az egyiket a legjobb poplemez kategóriában, a másikat pedig a címadó dalért a legjobb tánczenei felvétel kategóriájában. Egy évvel később újabb Grammyt kapott, akkor az Austin Powers folytatásának betétdaláért, a Beautiful Stranger ért, amit szintén Madonna adott elő. A Madonnával közös munka egészen a 2012-es MDNA című lemezig kitartott, de ez volt az utolsó, Orbit nyíltan kritizálta az album alkotói folyamatát. A család tájékoztatása szerint William Orbit már július 23-án halt meg, de a hírt csak ma közölték a világgal. https://telex.hu/techtud/2026/08/07/hohu.text: Menü Kereső Vörösen izzik az ország: hiába a hidegfront, ez a hőkupola nem mostanában fog távozni Techtud Legfontosabb 42 Celsius-fokot mutat egy hőmérő a XI. kerületi Szent Gellért téren 2026. augusztus 6-án – Fotó: Huszti István / Telex Thüringer Barbara Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Az idei nyár bővelkedik extremitásokban. Ez már a második hőhullám, ami mintha nem is akarna véget érni: hiába érkezett pénteken egy hidegfront, az valójában csak pár fokos lehűlést hoz. Már eleve az is extrém, hogy a 40 fokos napok után annak is örülünk, ha csak 35 fokos nappali maximum-hőmérsékletek lesznek, de ennél sajnos sokkal komolyabb gondok is vannak. Jövő csütörtökig még velünk maradhat a hőkupola Az idei első hőhullám szokatlanul korán, június 20-án érkezett, és 11 napig tartott , ennek a csúcsán 42 fokkal dőlt meg az abszolút maximum-hőmérsékleti rekord. Ekkor tanulta meg az egész ország a hőkupola szót, ami az angol heat dome kifejezésből ered, és szemléletesen írja le, hogy hogyan néz ki egy melegmagvú anticiklon. Egy nagyobb térfogatú és kisebb sűrűségű meleg légoszlop a környezetéhez képest kipúposodik, tehát ha 3D-ben képzeljük el, akkor valóban egy kupola jelenhet meg a szemünk előtt. A második hőhullám július 29-én kezdődött, és a HungaroMet szakemberei szerint ezt is nevezhetjük hőkupolás helyzetnek. „Gyakorlatilag minden hőhullám esetén beszélhetünk hőkupoláról, a több évvel ezelőtti hőhullámokról is ki lehet mondani azt, hogy hőkupola okozta” – írták kérdésünkre. Bár szeretnénk azt hinni, hogy a pénteki hidegfronttal 10 nap után ez a hőhullám/hőkupola is elvonul, sajnos ez nem lesz így. A HungaroMet meteorológusai azt mondják, a mostani helyzetre az a legpontosabb megfogalmazás, hogy átmenetileg megtörik az elképesztő forróság. Előrejelzésük szerint a hétvégén visszaesik a hőmérséklet, napközben legfeljebb 34-35 fok körüli csúcshőmérsékletre kell számítani, és a hajnalok is frissítőbbek lesznek, 20-22 fokig süllyed a hőmérséklet. De sajnos csak átmenetileg szelídül a forróság: hétfőtől újra egyre melegebb levegő érkezik hazánk fölé, a hosszú távú előrejelzések szerint 35-38 fok körül alakulnak a maximum-hőmérsékletek jövő csütörtökig. Egy szerencsénk azért lesz, hajnalonta továbbra is érdemes lesz kereszthuzatot csinálni a lakásokban: a leghűvösebb órákban 23-24 fok várható, így a mostanihoz hasonló, nem egy helyen 30-31 Celsius-fok körüli napi középhőmérsékleti értékek nem, vagy csak nagyon kevés helyen lesznek valószínűek. Forrás: HungaroMet A hőhullámnak nemcsak érzetre, hanem tudományos szempontból sem lesz vége most, sőt ha az előrejelzések helytállóak, akkor jövő csütörtökön lesz a hőhullám 16. napja. The Spanish interior minister declared a state of emergency as more than 11,500 people were forced to evacuate their homes to wildfires across the country. (Photo by Pablo Blazquez Dominguez/Getty) By Al Jazeera Staff and AFP Published On 24 Jul 2026 24 Jul 2026 Spanish police have arrested a man accused of sparking a wildfire by using farm machinery, as blazes across the country and in France continue to force mass evacuations. The tractor driver’s arrest came as the fire he was linked to drove tens of thousands from their homes around the capital Madrid, as a national wildfire emergency was announced for the first time in Spain. Recommended Stories list of 3 items list 1 of 3 ‘Extremely disappointing’: US trade partners respond to Trump’s new tariffs list 2 of 3 Life without refrigerators: Gaza residents fight heat and food spoilage list 3 of 3 Romanian jet fighter shoots down suspected Russian drone end of list The number of people forced to flee the heatwave-induced fires in Spain and France has now passed the 100,000 mark. Police said a second suspect is being investigated over a similar incident. Amid tinderbox conditions, authorities had declared a prohibition on the use of farm machinery and other activities. The fire, one of several burning across central Spain, has merged two blazes west of Madrid into a single wave that has burned through 30 square kilometres (11.5sq miles) and which officials have called the worst in the region’s history. Local authorities have now ordered about 40,000 people to evacuate areas west of the capital or to shelter indoors. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez wrote on X that his government had deployed “all available resources” against what he called a “dramatic situation” spreading beyond Spain’s borders. “The wildfire is at its peak and is currently beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain,” Carlos Novillo, the Madrid regional government’s emergency management chief, told reporters. A separate fire in Avila province, also part of the central Castilla y Leon region, has burned 90sq km (35sq miles) and displaced about 1,500 people. Firefighters and civillians attempt to extinguish a wildfire as it approaches houses in El Tiemblo, in Avila province. (File: Getty) France is also battling dangerous fires. One blaze has swept through the Cap Ferret Peninsula, burning about 125sq km (50sq miles) and forcing roughly 44,000 people to evacuate the Gironde department, some by boat. Advertisement A second blaze in the Landes region has displaced approximately 23,000 more. French authorities have appealed to the European Union for reinforcements as fires rage on two fronts in its southwest. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said France now has 32 active wildfires, including more than 50,000 hectares (123,500 acres) burned since January – almost three times last year’s total. The EU has sent four water-bombing aircraft to Spain and three to France, while additional aid has been pledged by Italy, Greece, Croatia, Portugal, the Czech Republic and Slovakia. The World Health Organization’s European office noted that land burned by wildfires across the continent has risen 57 percent in four years, with fires in Spain and Portugal more than doubling since last year.

https://www.thenews.com.pk/latest/141016.text: Sarah Ferguson’s charity removed from official register after closure Sarah Ferguson’s charity officially shuts down after Epstein controversy Sarah’s Trust has officially closed months after renewed attention on Sarah Ferguson's past links to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. The charity announced in February that it would shut down "for the foreseeable future." At the time, the board said the decision had been under discussion for several months and praised the charity’s work. Sarah’s Trust has now been removed from the public charity register. The charity was launched in 2020 during the COVID-19 pandemic. It supported NHS workers, care home staff and hospices, and also helped provide computers for Ukrainian refugees in Poland. The closure announcement came days after the US Department of Justice released millions of documents related to Epstein. Some emails showed Ferguson was in contact with him after he was released from prison in 2009 for soliciting prostitution from a minor. One email from Epstein to Ghislaine Maxwell said Ferguson and her daughters, Princess Beatrice and Princess Eugenie, had visited him shortly after his release. Other emails showed Ferguson thanking Epstein for his support. In one message, she called him "the brother I have always wished for." In another, she said she needed £20,000 to cover rent after one of her business ventures failed. The documents also included emails in which Ferguson discussed possible business opportunities with Epstein. Being named in the documents does not mean Ferguson committed any wrongdoing. Ferguson divorced Prince Andrew in 1996. Andrew later stepped back from royal duties and stopped using his Duke of York title following his own links to Epstein. https://www.naturalnews.com/2026-07-24-f.text: The French Senate adopted the compromise text 243 to two, and the National Assembly followed hours later, 279 to 81, as reported by the Epoch Times . [1] Â French President Emmanuel Macron championed the ban as a flagship reform, calling it a "major step forward" for protecting children, according to the same report. The law covers new accounts starting Sept. 1, while platforms have until Jan. 1, 2027, to close accounts already held by under-15s. [1] The measure also extends the existing school cellphone ban to high schools. Details of the Legislation The legislation operates on a two-stage rollout, with a Sept. 1 deadline for preventing new account creation by under-15s and a later deadline of January 2027 for removing existing accounts, officials stated. [1] Exceptions apply to online encyclopedias and educational platforms, according to the bill's text. No penalties are imposed on children or parents for violations; instead, platforms face fines for non-compliance. Macron described the law as a "major step forward" in child protection, the report noted. [1] Â French Digital Minister Anne Le Henanff said that age-verification tools already exist and that platforms are expected to integrate them, with options including a EU-developed app, as reported by Reclaim The Net . [2] Enforcement and Age Verification Enforcement relies on platforms implementing age-verification mechanisms, with Le Henanff stating that such tools already exist and that assurances have been provided that personal data will be protected during verification, according to Reclaim The Net . [2] The goal is to enforce the ban by September to coincide with the back-to-school period and the existing phone ban, officials said. [1] However, the approach has drawn scrutiny. Critics note that the government's push for age verification raises privacy risks, as any identity-check system could expand into broader surveillance, according to an analysis by NaturalNews.com . [3] Â Macron and World Health Organization Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus published a joint statement on July 1 that recast social media as a force requiring 'age assurance' mechanisms, a move that some advocates warn could serve as a template for permanent identity checkpoints online. [2] Criticism and Concerns Over the Ban Some left-leaning lawmakers criticized the age verification process and the associated privacy risks, according to reports. The Senate had originally preferred a two-tier system that would blacklist certain platforms rather than impose an outright age limit, but the final bill adopted the more restrictive approach, according to the Epoch Times . [1] The lack of penalties for children who circumvent the ban raises enforcement questions, and concerns have been raised about compliance with EU law, including the General Data Protection Regulation, according to aÂ NaturalNews.com analysis. [3] Critics also point out that the age-verification mandate could centralize data collection and threaten online anonymity, echoing arguments made in civil-liberties contexts, such as the concern that "indecent" or "patently offensive" standards could chill protected speech, as noted by James D. Torr in a discussion of the First Amendment and the Communications Decency Act. [4] International Context and Outlook France's action follows Australia, which in December 2024 became the first country to require social media platforms to remove accounts held by users under 16, resulting in Meta deleting nearly 550,000 accounts within weeks, according to a NaturalNews.com report. [5] European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has proposed a "social media delay" for children in Europe, telling an EU summit that an expert panel would recommend steps by July 2026, as reported by the BBC . [6] Aside from France, more than 20 countries have taken steps to regulate children's social media access â including the United Kingdom, Canada, Poland, Austria and Japan, according to various reports. [7] [8] [9] [10] The ban may be one of Macron's last major domestic reforms before he steps down in 2027, analysts have noted. Conclusion France's social media ban for under-15s marks a significant escalation in government efforts to regulate minors' online activity, yet it also intensifies a global debate over digital privacy and state oversight. Proponents argue the law is necessary to combat youth mental health crises linked to compulsive social media use, with studies showing digital addiction among children is associated with higher risks of suicidal thoughts. [11] In contrast, opponents counter that the age-verification requirements could erode online anonymity and create a surveillance infrastructure that may later be expanded to all users, as some watchdog groups have warned. [2] As more countries move to implement similar restrictions, the tension between child protection and civil liberties is likely to remain a central point of contention.
