Photograph: U.S. Forest Service/Fishlake National Fores/AP US news Helicopter fighting Utah wildfire crashes with two people onboard, officials say Rescuers not yet able to reach scene of crash near Richfield in central Utah, prompting fears for two missing people Uwa Ede-Osifo Fri 7 Aug 2026 20.12 EDT Last modified on Fri 7 Aug 2026 20.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A firefighting Sikorsky S64 helicopter with two individuals onboard crashed on Friday morning in central Utah , according to federal aviation authorities. The US Forest Service initially declined to comment on the condition of the helicopter’s passengers, asking the public for “patience while we focus on response efforts” in a statement . Emergency personnel are responding near Richfield, a city about 160 miles south of Salt Lake City, an agency spokesperson told the Guardian by email. The exact circumstances surrounding the crash are unknown. At a media briefing on Friday evening, Tyler Hecht, deputy incident commander with Great Basin incident management team, described the terrain as “very difficult”, and said rescuers “have not reached the scene of the accident” in part because the helicopter crash had started a new fire. Asked about the morale of the firefighters battling to control the blaze, Hecht said it was “very somber with what’s going on. You know, they did take a tactical pause, regrouped, and they’re back fighting fire.” The aircraft was in the vicinity of the Widemouth 2 fire , a blaze sparked by lightning that has raced through 105,000 acres since it began on 27 July. It is one of eight large fires burning across Utah, which cumulatively have swept through more than 331,000 acres, according to state data . “Wildland firefighting is among the most dangerous jobs in the world,” Utah governor Spencer Cox wrote in a social media post . “Today is a painful reminder of the extraordinary risks these brave men and women accept to protect us.” The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) are investigating the crash. Photograph: Andrew Eakin/AP View image in fullscreen A woman at a candelight vigil for the victims of the Twin Falls shooting. Photograph: Andrew Eakin/AP Idaho Idaho police release video of In-N-Out Burger mass shooting that killed three Officials praise unarmed employee from nearby store for engaging 24-year-old gunman who later killed himself Guardian staff and agencies Fri 7 Aug 2026 17.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police released video on Friday of a mass shooting that killed three people at an Idaho In-N-Out Burger restaurant last weekend, and praised an unarmed employee from a nearby store who engaged the gunman outdoors, slowing him down and possibly preventing more deaths as authorities were catching up. The video released by the police also showed at least three people confronted the gunman with their own weapons during the incident. “What happened here was violent, frightening and deeply traumatic,” the Twin Falls police chief, Matthew Hicks, said during a news conference before screening an eight-and-a-half minute compilation of surveillance camera and bodycam video of the incident. The distressing video, which was edited by the police to blur faces and omit graphic images, revealed more details of the chaotic scene last weekend. It shows that the gunman walked up to the drive-thru window four times and opened fire, killing an In-N-Out employee, police said. Ten people were shot – inside the restaurant, directly outside, on an adjacent busy road and at a car charging station in a Twin Falls visitor center lot, Hicks said. Hicks said investigators still do noty have a motive for the shooting. The gunman, identified as Chad Williams, 24, killed himself when police officers caught up to him on a nearby walking trail. It should have been a “normal Saturday afternoon”, Hicks said at the televised news conference . “Employees showing up for work. Visitors coming to see our beautiful city. Instead they were confronted with chaos, fear and now loss.” As the shooting unfolded, employees from nearby stores fled to a walking trail. When the gunman headed to the trail, he came across two people, including one with his hands in the air who spoke to him, the video shows. That man distracted the gunman from possibly pursuing others on the trail. Williams subsequently killed himself as police closed in. His body was found near a canyon. “To that young man, you are a hero,” Hicks said of the bystander who slowed the gunman down. “Your courage, your composure, your selflessness in that moment likely gave others the time they needed to escape harm. This community is grateful for you, and we will never forget what you did that day.” Hicks also praised the work of an off-duty state trooper, who shot at Williams from inside the restaurant, and a former police officer, AJ James, who was wounded while confronting him. Authorities had previously credited an armed civilian who fired back and diverted Williams from the restaurant. James ran toward the sound of gunfire from the drive-thru window, while the off-duty officer inside the In-N-Out exchanged gunfire with Williams through the window and directed workers out of the building, Hicks said. He acted “heroically and unbelievably” to try to slow down the shooter, the police chief said, declining to release the off-duty officer’s name. Braxton Steube said he was the person who encountered Williams on the trail after fleeing a Dick’s Sporting Good store. “I said, ‘I have a family.’ I said, ‘You don’t have to do this. I’ll tell you whatever you want. I’ll do anything,’” Steube told KMVT-TV in Twin Falls. “He started to like tear up a bit, it seemed. And he said to me, ‘Just get away from me, man.’” Steube said the gunman shot at him and missed. Police identified those killed as Ashley Garibay, 23, of Stockton, California; Dale Schultz, 66, of Salt Lake City; and Christopher Claunch, 59, of Hagerman, Idaho. Williams had briefly attended the College of Southern Idaho and previously lived in Arizona. https://www.dw.com/en/migrant-tunnels-in.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ISMy Lithuanian authorities have discovered 12 border tunnels so far this year Image: Lithuania's State Border Guard Service Advertisement Migrants are taking a new route to enter the Baltic country Lithuania : underground tunnels. These could be yet another attempt by Belarus to foster political instability, experts say. The country's border guards say they have found 12 such tunnels since the beginning of the year near the Belarusian border, with a length of up to 25 meters on the Lithuanian side. They are expecting more to emerge. Lithuania's border with Belarus is about 700 kilometers long, around 550 kilometers of which are fenced. "We have a ground seismic system, which can detect easily when there's a high level of vibrations over a long period of time," General Rustamas Liubajevas, the commander of Lithuania's State Border Guard Service, explained to DW. "We then wait [outside a tunnel] for the final stage of the digging and when the migrants come out, we apprehend them," he said, adding that up to 40 migrants exiting such tunnels had been arrested. Last year Lithuania registered 1652 irregular border crossings Image: Lithuania's State Border Guard Service Lithuania's prosecutor's office confirmed to DW that a pre-trial investigation was under way concerning approximately 20 people suspected of illegally digging a tunnel. Possible charges also include people smuggling. Due to the investigation, no media visits are currently authorized at the sites. Liubajevas is surprised migrants would attempt a subterranean crossing. "It takes a lot of effort to dig a tunnel and the migrants are arrested almost immediately — at most, one small group gets through," he said. Is Minsk lending a hand? The elaborate nature of the tunnels has led him to believe the migrants aren't working alone. "They wouldn't be able to go through with this without logistical support from the Belarusian authorities, as they need a lot of material like wood to strengthen the tunnels' walls," he stressed, adding that Belarus seemingly wanted to "keep the level of tension at the border high." Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenkohas denied facilitating migration flows to neighboring states. Similar migrant tunnels were discovered in the past in neighboring Poland. Margarita Seselgyte, Director of the Institute of International Relations and Political Science at Vilnius University, seconded Liubajevas' view. "Belarus is watching its border very closely, and the country doesn't fit in the natural migration route of migrants from Afghanistan, Iran or Sri Lanka," she told DW, adding that Minsk had to at least have turned a blind eye to any digging activity taking place near the border. Some experts believe the Belarusian state is envouraging the building of tunnels across the border Image: Lithuania's State Border Guard Service Seselgyte thus sees the tunnels as "a hybrid attack to cause anxiety in our society." "There is no vacuum in the world of security. As Lithuania has been closing vulnerabilities and reinforcing its border fence, Belarus is now helping migrants pass beneath it," she said. A long-running issue at the eastern flank of Europe For her, Minsk is assisting its close ally Moscow . Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 partly from Belarus, where it amassed troops under the pretext of military drills. "Lithuania has been very vocal in terms of defense against Russia, both conventional and hybrid, on an EU and Nato level, and they want to silence that voice by causing chaos in our country," the political scientist said. "The main goal is probably to weaken support for Ukraine and disrupt European unity," she added. Linas Kojala, CEO of Vilnius-based think tank Geopolitics and Security Studies Center, noted that the tunnels were keeping the border force busy – even if only a few migrants got through. He described the tunnels as "just another phase of the attack of weaponized migration we've been facing since 2021." Most of the Lithuania-Belarus border is lined with fencing Image: Arnaud Dumontier/MAXPPP/IMAGO That's when tens of thousands of migrants crossed into Lithuania, Poland and Latvia from Belarus. The European Union called the events a "state-sponsored instrumentalization of migrants at the EU external border," organized by Lukashenko. "Latvia, Poland, Lithuania and other countries have since set up external borders and we've managed to bring down illegal migration to a minimum," Kojala told DW. Lithuania's border guards registered 1652 attempts to enter the country irregularly in 2025. But this number won't go down to zero unless Minsk deals with the problem on its side, according to Kojala. "And that's unlikely: Belarus is clearly trying to pose as many problems as possible." 'Migration has long been used as a strategic tool' Belarus would be far from the first country to use migration as a strategic tool, underlined Robert Gonzci, an analyst at the Migration Research Institute in the Hungarian capital of Budapest. "It's a relatively low-cost, low-risk way of exerting pressure on other countries, and since the 1950s, there've been numerous documented cases of governments creating or manipulating migration flows," he said to DW. He added that even the Assyrian empire – which collapsed in the seventh century BC – used migration to consolidate imperial control. Gonzci didn't rule out that autonomous smuggling networks might be behind the recently discovered tunnels, which Belarusian authorities don't fully control. He added that Belarus and Russia have used weaponized migration to "divert Western attention from Russia's broader strategic agenda and create instability along NATO's eastern flank by fueling political and social tensions within European countries." Poland's EU border: A threat to nature and people To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The states organizing such operations – often authoritarian regimes – enjoyed an inherent strategic advantage, Gonzci stressed. "The target is usually a democratic state facing a fundamental dilemma: They must protect their sovereignty by securing their borders while simultaneously upholding their legal obligations and humanitarian commitments," he said. Eastern countries 'showing resilience' But experts seem to agree that countries on the EU's eastern flank have been doing rather well in that respect. "There's increasing cooperation and coordination between the Nordic and Baltic States and Poland, as these countries are facing similar challenges. And the EU Frontex mission has been sending additional equipment," Seselgyte said. Lithuania is currently receiving technical support from neighboring countries. "We are testing Polish scanning equipment, through which we can identify empty spaces underground. If these tools work well, we'll buy and deploy them," explained Liubajevas. https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-s-zelensky.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ITaA Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic (left) and his Ukrainian counterpart Volodymyr Zelenskyy (right) met in Odesa in June 2025 Image: Goll/Betaphoto/SIPA/picture alliance Advertisement Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic have met several times in the past, often on the sidelines of multilateral conferences, and most recently on July 15, 2026, in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv. On Friday, Zelenskyy arrived in Serbia for his first official state visit to the country. The talks, however, are likely to require careful political balancing. Despite Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine, Serbia remains widely regarded as Europe's most pro-Russian country. There have recently been several signs of closer ties between Belgrade and Kyiv. Ukraine's First Lady, Olena Zelenska, visited Belgrade two years ago. But a trip by the Ukrainian president has been postponed several times. For Vucic, who has ruled Serbia with an iron fist for the past 14 years, the visit is a balancing act ahead of crucial parliamentary elections. A student-led protest movement plans to field its own electoral list, with a realistic chance of seriously challenging Vucic for the first time. The president has been accused of corruption and of exerting control over the media and judiciary. According to opinion polls, the majority of Vucic's loyal supporters side with Russia and oppose Serbia joining the European Union. Pro-government media outlets, such as the tabloid Informer, have openly backed Moscow in the war. Nevertheless, Vucic has portrayed Zelenskyy's trip as an ordinary state visit, saying: "We have several important issues to discuss. One is Ukraine's and Serbia's path toward Europe; the second is our bilateral and energy cooperation." Observers expect the meeting to prove mutually beneficial. "Zelenskyy welcomes anything that comes across as a kind of slap in the face for [Russian President] Putin ," political analyst and pollster Djordje Vukadinovic told DW. "That also applies to the European Union, which certainly played a role in making this meeting happen." Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic (left) and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (right) met at the Ukraine–Southeast Europe Summit in Kyiv in July 2026, weeks before Zelenskyy's first official visit to Belgrade Image: Alina Smutko/REUTERS At the same time, Vucic wants to "present himself as being as open to cooperation as possible with the EU," especially after seeing what happened to Hungary's Viktor Orban. "Brussels still has enough carrots and sticks at its disposal in this part of the Balkans, and Vucic cannot afford to draw criticism from Brussels ahead of the next election," Vukadinovic said. Serbian-made artillery shells Zelenskyy may also be looking to secure Serbian munitions. Large quantities of Serbian artillery shells have already been delivered to Ukraine through intermediaries, despite Serbia's pro-Russian stance and opposition to anti-Russian sanctions. The Financial Times newspaper estimated that the value of military goods delivered to Ukraine totaled €1 billion ($1.15 billion) in 2024. Christopher Hill, a seasoned US diplomat, who recently ended his career as ambassador to Serbia, spoke candidly about how he had brought the Ukrainian military and Serbian defense industry together. "The US began supporting the purchase of significant quantities of Serbian ammunition, which we knew Ukraine urgently needed," Hill told German daily Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung . Countries such as the Czech Republic and Poland officially bought the weapons before transferring them to Ukraine. According to the newspaper, discussions are also taking place behind the scenes about building a joint drone factory using Ukrainian expertise, Serbian workers, and investment from the United Arab Emirates. Zelenskyy's team has reportedly already inspected potential locations in secret. "Ukraine is trying to expand its circle of European partners, including those countries that have not imposed sanctions on Russia," Srdjan Majstorovic of the Belgrade-based think tank European Policy Centre told DW. "At the same time, Serbia has a defense industry whose products matter to Ukraine's war effort." Flip-flopping between Russia, EU Although Serbia continues to promote the narrative of an "Orthodox brotherhood" with Russia, the Kremlin has increasingly signaled its dissatisfaction with Vucic. This is particularly evident in the context of Russian gas deliveries, one of Russia's most powerful sources of leverage. Recently, Serbia has only been offered short-term gas contracts, which has increased economic uncertainty and undermined Vucic's economic model, which aims to attract foreign investors through cheap labor and low energy costs. Zelenskyy's visit comes as Vucic (pictured) tries to balance Serbia’s traditional ties with Moscow against pressure to align its foreign policy with the European Union Image: Djordje Kojadinovic/REUTERS That is why some observers say Serbia is forced to flip-flop between Moscow and the EU — by far Serbia's most important trading partner. Yet political analyst Vukadinovic disagrees. "Superficial observers categorize Vucic's moves as either 'pro-EU' or 'pro-Russia,' but both approaches are equally dishonest — Vucic is looking to spot the greatest threat and how best to benefit, with the goal of holding on to power forever." Vucic finds himself in a precarious situation. The student protests — which began in late 2024 following the collapse of the Novi Sad train station canopy which killed 16 people — have made the outcome of the upcoming parliamentary election, expected to take place this fall, completely unpredictable. The protesters accuse the government of corruption and incompetence. Some opinion polls even place the movement in the lead. Vucic's critics therefore fear large-scale efforts to manipulate the election, for instance, through gifts to voters, exerting pressure on public-sector employees, or "importing" voters from Republika Srpska, the Serb entity of neighboring Bosnia and Herzegovina. EU accession talks EU criticism of Vucic has so far been both restrained and at times contradictory. While the European Commission has recommended moving ahead with Serbian accession negotiations, some EU member states oppose this due to concerns about democratic deficits in the Balkan country. "It is quite possible that Zelenskyy's state visit and Serbia's cooperation with Ukraine will be used by some EU member states and the European Commission to push ahead with Serbia's accession talks, especially now that geopolitical considerations risk overshadowing rule-of-law criteria," Majstorovic said. Yet Vucic also holds a trump card that he regularly plays to his domestic audience whenever he meets Zelenskyy on the sidelines of international summits. Ukraine, like Russia, has never recognized the independence of the former Serbian province of Kosovo . This fact plays well with Vucic's voters. This article was translated from German. https://www.dw.com/en/ceuta-spain-sets-u.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5ISwS Nearly all of the people who rushed Ceuta's border have since left, but those who do stay are unlikely to be able to reach the European mainland unless they are formally granted permission to reside [FILE: August 6, 2026] Image: Violeta Santos Moura/REUTERS Advertisement Spain 's government on Friday moved to impose reciprocal entry checks on people traveling from Italy . The Spanish government had warned that it would do so unless Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni 's governemnt lifted the border measures it has implemented against Spain. Italy's right-wing government announced the checks at the height of the social media panic as tens of thousands of people gained entry to the Spanish exclave of Ceuta bordering Morocco last week. The checks are essentially symbolic, given that Ceuta is not on the European mainland and Italy and Spain do not share a land border, meaning that the vast majority of people potentially affected are tourists on planes. Nevertheless, the issue has turned into a point of dispute between two governments of different ideological persuasions with contrasting messaging priorities on migration policy. Did Morocco instigate the Ceuta migrant incident? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What did Spain say about checks on travelers from Italy? The border controls on Italy will go into effect from midnight ‌on ⁠Saturday ⁠until September 7, the Spanish government said. Border agents will check passport, nationality and visas for Italian passengers and visitors from other ​countries arriving from Italy. Spain had called Italy's decision to impose checks on people arriving from Spain "unjustified, contrary to the interests of the European Union and discriminatory against ​the Spanish population." Madrid said there was no real risk of people who overwhelmed Ceuta's border controls reaching the European mainland, let alone Italy. It pointed to the vast majority of the estimated 72,000 people returning to Morocco within days . Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez also drew attention to the higher numbers of irregular migrants reaching Italian than Spanish territory in recent years. "If [Italy] fails to [remove the entry checks] before Sunday, August 9, Spain will be forced to adopt proportionate measures to protect the interests and dignity of its citizens," the government said. Italy replied later Friday that it would not accept "ultimatums ⁠or ⁠impositions" from Madrid, and that it would maintain the suspension of Schengen rules for non-EU nationals arriving from Spain until at least August 15. Despite Spain's objections, an array of European countries, including Germany, and the European Commission all made comments about the importance of border security to the open-border Schengen Zone amid the public uproar. Italy was among comparatively few to go so far as to frame the issue as "suspending" Spain's Schengen status, however. Italy first made the announcement as images and footage of the border breach were going viral online Image: Atlas/REUTERS What do we know about Italy's checks on travelers from Spain? Details on precisely what checks, if any, Italy has actually implemented over the past week have been thin on the ground. Migration analyst Gerald Knaus told DW earlier this week that the move was "pure populism" and a "completely bizarre" measure. "They don't have a border, so it's only for a few flights," Knaus said. "It makes no sense in the high tourist season. And as Giorgia Meloni indicated, it shouldn't inconvenience travelers." Knaus said the decision could only be understood in the context of domestic political appearances, not foreign policy realities. "I think to understand it, you must understand that on [Meloni's] right, there is a radical right party in Italy that puts pressure on her. And so politicians everywhere in Europe, when they see these images which create fear, are looking for something to say — something to do that makes them look tough." EU defends border response after Ceuta crossing To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Meloni and Sanchez: A clash of styles on migration At least in terms of their stated positions and approaches, Italy and Spain have quite different stances on the issue of migration. Meloni came to power in 2022 in Italy, after several years of much higher irregular migration rates and asylum applications caused in large part by the wars in Syria and Ukraine. She promised a tougher line on migration into one of the most common landing points in southern Europe. Sanchez, meanwhile, has championed a more pro-migration stance during his two terms in office. He argues that Spain's economy needs migration and offered an amnesty and temporary residency permit process earlier this year to irregular migrants already in the country. Sanchez said it was better to grant residency and start collecting taxes than to keep people out of the formal labor market. Migration expert Knaus, however, warned against overstating the practical differences between the two countries, saying Meloni faced similar economic requirements and was actually pursuing comparable policies — only with much less public fanfare. "Italy is doing something very similar. Hundreds of thousands of people are brought in or are already in the country and are regularized for the Italian labour market under Giorgia Meloni," Knaus said. "And 1.6 million people were regularized under various Italian governments in the last 20 years." Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cdew.text: Image source, EPA Image caption, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul has pledged to introduce stricter gun laws Published 3 hours ago Thailand's prime minister has vowed to introduce new gun control laws in the wake of a shooting by a teenager on the outskirts of Bangkok that left eight people dead and 22 injured. The 14-year-old killed his grandparents at the home they shared, before travelling to Debsirin School in Nonthaburi, where he was a student. There, he killed five teachers before taking his own life. Later, Thai media reported that a student had also died from their injuries. Speaking after the attack, Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said he plans to introduce laws that restrict the carrying of firearms in public, with the new legislation only allowing government officials on duty to carry guns. I was standing in front of my teacher when she was shot, Thai pupil says Published 10 hours ago Police Colonel Thadsakorn Konthong said that the gun and bullets used in the attack belonged to the teen's grandfather, with an initial inspection finding signs that the firearm had been searched for inside the grandfather's bedroom. International and local media have reported that the gun was legally registered and had a permit. Thailand has one of the highest rates of civilian gun ownership in South East Asia, with around 10.3 million firearms in civilian possession, around four million of which are believed to be owned illegally. The country has strict gun laws, which punish the illegal possession of arms with up to 10 years in jail, but enforcement of these laws has been an issue. During his time as interior minister, Anutin introduced a number of gun control laws, including a short-term ban on new gun licenses and import restrictions. Speaking on Friday, the prime minister said the tragedy "shouldn't have happened". "I don't just feel sorry for the victims but I feel sorry that this happened. How can this happen in our country," Anutin added. Image source, Getty Images The teenager is believed to have shot his 73-year-old grandfather and 74-year-old grandmother at their two-storey flat at around 05:00 local time on Friday (22:00 GMT on Thursday). Each was killed by a single shot to the head, a Thai police official said. After killing his grandparents, the teenager boarded a school bus carrying the firearm and dozens of bullets, Reuters news agency reported. He then attended his first class at 08:30 and his second at 09:20. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Police have been combing over the school for evidence Around half an hour into his second class of the day, he drew the gun and began shooting. The teenager is believed to have first shot teachers on the school's sixth floor, killing three of them. "He then walked down the stairs and encountered the school's deputy director and the director's secretary, who were going up the stairs to check on the situation," Police Major General Dejrapee Kongdee told Reuters. "The attacker shot and killed both of them on the staircase." Police were deployed to the scene while the shooting was ongoing. They found the attacker, who by then had shot himself, around 10:40, Dejrapee said. Five people were immediately killed and at least 23 were wounded. Later, Thailand's public broadcaster and the Bangkok Post reported that an eighth victim had died. Figure caption, Students shelter in classroom as gunshots heard National police chief Gen Kittiratt Phanphet told reporters that forensic officers had found the attacker's shots were quite accurate, with several hitting vital spots on the body. The prime minister said the attack was "well prepared" with "clear steps and clear goals". According to local media, police have searched devices belonging to the teenager and found several videos relating to school shootings in the US. The teenager has been described as quiet and well behaved by family members in local media. His uncle told Thai media the teen spent much of his time indoors playing violent video games and rarely went outside. He added there was no indication the teenager was planning the attack. The attacker had lived with his grandparents, as his parents were divorced. The Debsirin School, founded in Bangkok in 1885, is one of Thailand's top secondary schools with branches across the country. It counts many prominent Thai figures among its alumni, from diplomats and athletes to several prime ministers. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c07r.text: Figure caption, Students shelter in classroom as gunshots heard By Jonathan Head and Thanyarat Doksone ,Â Reporting from Debsirin School, Nonthaburi Â and Â Tiffanie Turnbull Published 7 August 2026 On Friday morning, as the final classes of the week were under way, panicked students began streaming out of a prestigious school just outside Bangkok. Inside, police say, a 14-year-old boy had opened fire. "I was standing in front of the teacher when she was shot," a shaken seventh grader tells the BBC, near the gates of Debsirin School in Nonthaburi. "She was talking to me when [the gunman] showed up." Still in her uniform, with her mother by her side, she explains how the shooter stalked from room to room. Authorities say he killed five teachers and injured 23 people - including fellow pupils - before turning the weapon on himself. Earlier, he had gunned down his grandparents. "I had to climb over the school fence to escape with other friends," the girl, who the BBC is not naming, continues. Her mother says the girl thought she might die. "[She said] 'I thought I'd never see you again'." Follow live: Thai teenager kills at least seven and injures more than 30 as PM calls shooting 'well prepared' Image source, Reuters Image caption, One student recounts having to climb over a fence to escape One 18-year-old student told Reuters he initially thought firecrackers were going off. "I didn't think it was a gun at first," he said. "There were many shots: bang bang bang. Then it went quiet. Then it started again." Metres from the school gates, paramedics loaded the wounded into ambulances and rushed them to hospital, as milling crowds hugged and cried. Rescue worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith rushed to the scene after hearing children as young as 12 had been hurt. "I saw students who had been shot, some in the arm, some in the back, some in the chest. So I rushed to help get them to the hospital first," the 47-year-old rescue worker told Reuters news agency. One grieving teacher told the BBC his friend was among the dead. "She was my age. We went to this school together as students. Then we both became teachers at this school," the 31-year-old, who declined to give his name, said. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Authorities say the 14-year-old shot five teachers dead, and more than 30 injuries have been reported It is early days in the investigation and police haven't said anything about a motive. They believe the 9mm handgun the shooter used belonged to his grandfather. Forensic officers found the gunman's shots to be "quite accurate", with several hitting "vital spots" on victims' bodies. Others are filling some of the gaps. A teacher at the school has said the shooter was a good student - not aggressive and with good grades - and education authorities have described him as an avid gamer. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said study pressures may have played a role. "We learned that his grandmother was a teacher and she might have been strict with him. From what the police gathered from his close friend, they knew he was quite stressed about it." It is clear authorities will have many questions to answer in the coming days - many of them about what change this crime must trigger. Renewed calls for gun control reform This is Thailand's deadliest mass shooting in years - and the second at a school this year. In February, a head teacher and a female student were shot by an 18-year-old gunman during a school siege in southern Thailand. Four years ago, a 34-year-old in the eastern Nong Bua Lamphu province killed 37 people , most of them preschoolers, in a shooting and stabbing at a nursery. These crimes have resurfaced questions about gun control in the country. "This shouldn't have happened," the boyfriend of one of the killed teachers told reporters, clearly distressed and trying to hold back tears. More than seven million people are believed to own guns in the country, one of the highest rates of ownership in the world. Of those, more than one million are unlicensed owners. Image source, EPA Image caption, The shooting at Debsirin Nonthaburi School is the second in Thailand this year While there are restrictions on gun licences in Thailand, people can still acquire the weapons - legally or illegally - with relative ease. There is a thriving black market, aided by Thailand's porous land borders with four other nations. Problems with corruption and loose regulation in the police and military have seen weapons end up in the wrong hands. Prime Minister Anutin said he had tightened regulations when he was interior minister three years ago - suspending new gun permits. But gun crime remains rife, with deaths from gunshots among the highest in the region. And some in the community are calling for greater action. "An act of violence in an educational institution, which should be one of the safest places in our society, serves as a stark reminder for Thai society to seriously and systematically review gun control measures," Natthaphong Ruengpanyawut, leader of the People's Party - an opposition party - wrote in a Facebook post. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/07/magy.text: Menü Kereső Egészségügy, oktatás, közlekedés – Magyar Péter hosszan sorolta, mire költjük a hazahozott uniós pénzeket Belföld Nádor András Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „Túlzás nélkül mondhatom: ezek a források át fogják alakítani Magyarországot” – jelentette be pénteki Facebook-videójában Magyar Péter. Azt mondta, a kormány intézkedési terve 60 tételben sorolja fel, mire fordítják majd a hazahozott uniós pénzeket. A miniszterelnök szerint a fejlesztések megvalósulásával mindenki érezni fogja, hogy az ország fejlődik. A lakhatás terén most először indul olyan nagy, uniós program Magyarországon, amely kifejezetten megfizethető bérlakások és diákotthonok létrehozását szolgálja, erre 600 millió eurót, vagyis több mint 230 milliárd forintot fordítanak. 54 milliárd forintnyi, korábban magyar költségvetési forrásból megvalósított iskolai beruházást most uniós forrásból fognak elszámolni. Több mint 151 milliárd forintot fordítanak arra, hogy a tanulók és a pedagógusok egyenlőbben férjenek hozzá a digitális oktatáshoz. Az egészségügyre uniós forrásból közel 170 milliárd forintot fordítanak, ebből 24 milliárd megy a háziorvosi ellátás fejlesztésére. Több mint 125 milliárd forintnyi, korábban magyar költségvetésből megvalósuló egészségügyi beruházást és digitalizációs fejlesztést uniós forrásból fognak elszámolni. A miniszterelnök szerint az Orbán-kormány késlekedésének súlyos ára volt, az eredeti helyreállítási terv szerint több mint 500 milliárd forintot is kaphatott volna Magyarország egészségügyre. A közlekedésben évtizedek óta várt járműcserék lesznek, lecserélik a szentendrei, ráckevei és csepeli HÉV elöregedett, 40-50 éves szerelvényeit, helyettük 42 új, korszerű, alacsonypadlós szerelvény jön. Megújulnak a vidéki InterCityk is, 35 új, emeletes motorvonat érkezik. Több százmilliárd jut majd a magyar energiarendszer korszerűsítésére. Új korszak jön a magyar kkv-knak, 645 milliárddal erősítik meg a Magyar Fejlesztési Bankot, hogy az ilyen vállalkozásoknak több finanszírozás juthasson. „Ezek azok a lehetőségek, amelyektől az Orbán-kormány éveken keresztül megfosztotta Magyarországot.” Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Menü Kereső Magyar Péter szerint nem lesznek meglepetések a köztársasági elnökjelöltek nevei között Belföld frissítve Klág Dávid Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Nem lesz meglepetés a köztársaságielnök-jelöltek neveiben, mondta Magyar Péter miniszterelnök a pénteki miniszterelnöki tájékoztatóján. Magyar pénteken elmondta, hogy három jelöltből választja meg majd kedden a parlament Magyarország köztársasági elnökét. A miniszterelnök elmondta, hogy nagyjából tíz név merült fel érdemben a pozícióra. Ezeket a neveket megtárgyalta a Tisza elnöksége, az elnökség pedig pénteken azt a döntést hozta, hogy szombaton három nevet fog ajánlani a pártfrakciónak megfontolásra. Ebből a három névből fog kikerülni az, akit a parlament megválaszt köztársasági elnöknek majd kedden. Magyar szerint aki figyelte az utóbbi napok eseményeit, annak nem lesznek meglepetések a nevek. A miniszterelnök elmondta, hogy olyan emberre van szükség a pozícióra, aki nem töltött be korábban, és sem most nem tölt be semmilyen pártpolitikai tisztséget. Magyar egy későbbi kérdésre elmondta, hogy van olyan jelölt, akiről posztolt a Facebook-oldalán, amikor találkozott vele. Fülöp Botondról, Romsics Ignácról és Baka Andrásról a miniszterelnök elmondta, hogy mindhárommal beszélt, mindhárom munkáját ismeri, és mindegyikből jobb köztársasági elnök lenne, mint az utóbbi tizenhat évben bármelyik. Hozzátette, hogy olyanokkal is tárgyalt, akikről nem rakott ki fotót, mert „az algoritmus nem engedte”. A Tisza Párt parlamenti frakciója szombaton szavaz arról, hogy kit jelöl köztársasági elnöknek. A hivatalos jelölés határideje jövő hétfő tíz óra, a folyamatot ehhez igazítják. Az Alaptörvény alapján a parlamentnek Sulyok Tamás megbízatásának július 20-i megszüntetése után harminc napon belül kell új köztársasági elnököt választania. Az Országgyűlés ráérne akár augusztus 18-án dönteni, de a miniszterelnök korábbi ígérete szerint augusztus 20-án már az új államfő adhatja át az állami kitüntetéseket és díjakat. Ha továbbra is tartani szeretnék magukat ehhez a határidőhöz, akkor a parlamentnek jövő héten szavaznia kell. Erről itt írtunk bővebben . Magyar Péter korábban azt kérte, hogy ajánljanak neveket az államfői posztra, majd alig egy nappal ezután már be is jelentette, hogy szerinte a sakkozó Polgár Judit lenne a legalkalmasabb a feladatra. Sokan vitatták ezt az eljárást és Polgár személyét is, aki végül visszautasította a felkérést. Magyar később Romsics Ignác Széchenyi-díjas történésszel , a Vidéki prókátor néven ismertté vált ügyvéddel, Fülöp Botonddal , majd szerdán Baka Andrással, a Legfelsőbb Bíróság korábbi elnökével találkozott , de az nem derült ki, hogy ezeken a megbeszéléseken szóba került-e az esetleges jelölésük. Kerestük emiatt az érintetteket, de nem reagáltak. Kedvenceink Partnereinktől Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! "Russia's indiscriminate attacks on Kyiv and other regions cause civilian casualties by design, not by accident," Kallas said on the US social media company X. She also condemned a strike on Latvia's honorary consulate in Sloviansk, eastern Ukraine, saying it demonstrated Moscow's "utter disregard for international law." "Latvia has our full support," she said. https://www.express.co.uk/news/world/223.text: Home News World The airline has warned of long queues at 16 airports (Image: Getty) Ryanair has warned travellers to prepare for longer queues at border control after the European Union introduced new entry requirements. The bloc’s new digital Entry Exit System (EES) requires non-EU citizens entering the Schengen area – made up of 29 European countries – to register fingerprints and a photo when they arrive. The information is checked as they leave. EES, rolled out fully in April, involves people from third-party countries such as the UK having their fingerprints registered and photograph taken to enter the Schengen Area, which consists of 29 European countries, mainly in the EU. Read our Privacy Policy The introduction has led to hours-long queues at some European airports, with Ryanair blasting "the failed EES rollout" as unnecessary. Horror as teacher, 43, arrested for raping goats - video posted on social media Spain to immediately lose huge chunk of £37m of prize money after World Cup win Ryanair has warned about the impact on travellers (Image: Getty) Earlier this month, Ryanair identified popular European airports in Spain , Italy, France and Poland where passengers are suffering long EES delays. The airline warned that the sites are “not ready” to manage the high passenger volumes during the peak summer season because of “insufficient staff, kiosks and system readiness”. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT The company has warned of 16 European airports where travellers can expect "significant" queues. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Ryanair’s Chief Operations Officer, Neal McMahon, said: “Families heading away for a well-earned summer holiday should be thinking about suitcases, suncream and sangria, not standing in passport queues for hours. “The reality is that the EES system isn’t working properly and families are paying the price for a system that does not work months after launch. “Passengers should not be the testing ground for unfinished border infrastructure. “We support calls from EU Member States to urgently extend the EES flexibilities. This will give airports and border authorities the time to improve the infrastructure, fix the broken devices and hire more staff so that families can travel through Europe without disruption.” The boss of the Port of Dover has warned it will “face repeated episodes of severe congestion” throughout the summer without more flexibility in EES. Chief executive Doug Bannister predicted that queuing cars will be “spilling out of the port onto the public highway for miles” unless something changes, adding “the local impact could be dire”. The port declared a “critical incident” during the May half-term period after waiting times reached four-and-a-half hours. Shadow Home Office minister Matt Vickers lamented the “delusional attitude among EU colleagues” that “EES is working just fine”. Reiterating his call for the scheme to be halted during the peak holiday season, he added: “The Government must stand behind the interests of British travellers.” Meanwhile there are widespread reports the introduction of Etias – a new online system to pre-authorise entry to the EU – is set to be delayed until next year. From left: Utharaa Zacharias and Palaash Chaudhary of Soft-Geometry, Steffany Tran of Vy Voi, Minjae Kim, Aaron and Irisa Chan-Kawabi of Kawabi, and Dominik Tarabański (Image credit: Tracy Nguyen, Jingyu Lin) Jump to category: Soft Geometry Dominik Tarabański Vy Voi Minjae Kim Kawabi Share Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Pinterest Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Artists and designers the world over continue to choose to make the US their home. As the latest newcomers in this ‘ nation of immigrants ' join a crowd of inspiring locals with dual heritage, their varied experiences help shape creative America. To celebrate the country's role as a meeting point of creative minds, we look at the plurality of voices contributing to its enduring crucible of culture and dynamism. We speak to five studios – whose founders (all Wallpaper* US400 honorees) have roots in Poland , Vietnam, India , South Korea and China , but who have made the US their creative base – about how their heritage influences their output. Meet a new generation of American designers Soft Geometry (Image credit: Tracy Nguyen) For many creatives, geography is less a fixed point than an inheritance, carried across borders and reimagined in new contexts. This is true for Utharaa Zacharias and Palaash Chaudhary, founders of Soft-Geometry, a practice that took root in India and found a fuller expression in the US, as the two became partners in work and life. (Image credit: Tracy Nguyen) A rich cultural potpourri is the core of their practice. ‘Palaash is from Ghaziabad, near Delhi, and I am from Kochi, Kerala; it would be hard to pick two places more diametrically opposite,' says Zacharias. Growing up, they spoke different languages, ate different food and were raised in different religions, but their friendship found common ground in design. It began in college in Delhi and continued at the Savannah College of Art and Design in Georgia, where working on projects revealed a shared aesthetic. One afternoon, they scribbled in a notebook that together they made ‘soft geometries'. Text by Aditi Sharma Read more Dominik Tarabański (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) Dominik Tarabański was born in 1982 in Radymno, Poland, a small town near the Ukrainian border, and studied photography in Łódź and Warsaw. After four years moving between Polish cities, he left for New York in 2012. Heading to New York, he says, was like going to the moon; a single three-week visit decided it for him. Fashion photography paid the bills and took him between New York, Paris and London . The still lifes he made by hand, away from the crowded sets. (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) Tarabański says he is pursuing ‘this intersection of synthetic and organic', which sits ‘at the foundation of everything I do'. He contorts living matter into arrangements as deliberately impossible as a Dutch flower painting , then photographs them at the fleeting point of giving way. The finished prints are large, over 2m tall, and hold the wall like sculpture. From a rubber band and a dried stem, he makes what he calls a kind of magic: ‘Nothing becomes something.' Text by Reeme Idris Read more Wallpaper* Newsletter Receive our daily digest of inspiration, escapism and design stories from around the world direct to your inbox. Vy Voi (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) For Steffany Tran, the Vietnamese-American founder of New York -based studio Vy Voi , objects become storytellers. Their materials, form and construction reflect longstanding cultural traditions, which she interprets through her own voice. ‘I describe my practice as almost like using a metal detector and finding nuggets in history,' she says. Tran, whose parents are both refugees, grew up between San José, California , and Saigon, where she spent summers visiting her family. (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) After studying industrial design in the San Francisco Bay Area, Tran moved to New York, where she worked in traditional firms, where the fast pace and problem-solving briefs were not exactly aligned with her personal interest in the art of making. She then took up ceramics at a local community centre as a creative outlet and eventually, she decided to dedicate all her time to creating handmade objects inspired by Vietnamese craft, which she felt were missing from the contemporary design world. ‘It was almost an exercise in this idea of if you can't find it, build it yourself,' Tran says. Text by Diana Budds Read more Minjae Kim (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) Seoul -born, New York-based designer Minjae Kim discovered the US on an exchange in high school. After studying painting and architecture, and a stint of military service back home, in 2008 he travelled to Seattle to continue his studies, later moving to New York for a Master of Architecture at Columbia University. He spent three years at Studio Giancarlo Valle, then started his own practice from the basement of his old apartment during the pandemic. (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) His debut in 2021 at LA design gallery Marta catalogued Western typologies, such as a chair adapted from Freud's personal study. These were objects that differed from his understanding of the world, and he made them his by remaking them – for example, by treating fibreglass like cloth, quilting it before coating it with resin. Text by Reeme Idris Read more Kawabi (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) Lanterns are talismanic in Chinese folklore. They are beacons that guide ancestral spirits, invite prosperity, and protect against malevolent forces. For Aaron and Irisa Chan-Kawabi, founders of New York studio Kawabi, they are also symbols of belonging. (Image credit: Jingyu Lin) Whenever the designers encountered these objects in the US, typically at Chinese restaurants or souvenir shops, they were the same symmetrical red or white design. ‘How does a typology move from one culture to another?' Aaron wondered. He and Irisa saw parallels to their own experience as part of the diaspora (Irisa was born in China and grew up in Massachusetts; Aaron was born in Brooklyn to parents who emigrated from Hong Kong ) and began to contemplate what a lantern that represented their own experience might look like. https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world.text: Russia’s war on Ukraine has entered its latest phase, with each side making use of increasing numbers of long-range munitions to strike deep into the other’s territory. In the early summer of this year, there was a surge of optimism across the media when it became clear that Ukraine was stepping up its strikes at enormous ranges into Russia, and there was little that Moscow could do about it. But that optimism needs to be balanced against the new reality that with anti-missile interceptor systems exhausted, there is not much Ukraine itself can do to blunt Russian missile attacks. For now, those attacks sow misery and death by blasting residential areas with little warning: but next winter, they could once again target heating and power infrastructure and have an even more devastating effect on Ukraine’s ability to keep its people alive than last year. Russia’s campaign against Ukrainian civilian infrastructure is not new: it began almost as soon as it became clear that Russia had failed in its initial objective of swiftly overrunning the country in February 2022. But its new character today results both from massive increases in the numbers of missiles and drones available to Russia, and the way they have outstripped Ukraine’s air defences. The reluctance of allies to provide the weapons needed to take the fight to Moscow has seen the Ukrainians carry out their own campaign against their enemies’ infrastructure – but, Keir Giles writes, we know by now that Russia’s leader is happy to let his country burn.

Read more More than 280,000 people have been forced to flee their homes as devastating wildfires rage across central Spain and southwestern France. High winds have left firefighters struggling to battle flames as Spain declared a national emergency, with multiple fires merging outside Madrid. France has deployed its army, with hundreds of soldiers joining efforts to contain the flames , which have ripped through a record 98,000 hectares since January. On Saturday, authorities ordered the evacuation of large parts of Bordeaux ’s suburbs, including the areas of Le Haillan, Eysines ​and Merignac. “The fires ‌which are hitting our country have reached a level that has never ​been seen before,” French ‌prime minister Sebastien Lecornu wrote on X on Saturday. Madrid’s regional president, Isabel Diaz Ayuso, said it was the “worst fire in the history of the region” and that conditions had been made worse by a combination of high temperatures, wind, and the merging of a number of fires. open image in gallery Firefighters near Lacanau, southwestern France ( AP ) European Union countries have sent helicopters, planes and ground teams. These include 40 personnel from a Romanian forest fire team, two Portuguese and two Swedish Air Tractor planes, four helicopters – including two from Germany, one from the Czech Republic and one from Slovakia – and from Switzerland, four light helicopters and 30 ground personnel. “Europe stands alongside France and Spain in the face of the devastating wildfires ravaging them,” European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen wrote in a post on X. Residents forced to evacuate have described apocalyptic scenes as they left their homes behind. Marion Girault-Rime was awoken at around 4am on Friday by an emergency alert on her phone that instructed every citizen of the wealthy resort town of Lege-Cap Ferret to evacuate immediately. She grabbed underwear and toothbrushes and, along with her daughter Mahau and boyfriend Tony, rushed to the car. “Luckily, my husband and son were not at home,” she said. open image in gallery Marion Girault-Rime was forced to flee her home in the town of Lege-Cap Ferret ( Marion Girault-Rime/Quatre Histoires ) It was not long until they were overwhelmed by the smell of smoke as they joined hundreds of other cars fleeing the area. Ms Girault-Rime was left speechless as cinders blew across the windscreen as though it was “raining ash”, with bright red flames erupting and a towering pillar of black smoke. The scene was “frightening and spectacular ”, the 53-year-old told The Independent. Colonel Romain Moutard, the deputy director of the Landes fire and rescue service, said the fire was “apocalyptic” and described the situation as “Dante-esque” as the flames spread. The length of the final stage of the Tour de France has been shortened to allow police officers to be redeployed to battle the raging wildfires. The race’s final stage on Sunday will be reduced in length by a third, the Paris police department said, in an extraordinary measure that underscores the gravity of the fires. The UK government is advising citizens in Spain to avoid travelling through affected areas of Madrid and Avila, while those in France are being told to follow the advice of local authorities. Prospective holidaymakers are advised to check with their accommodation or travel provider before making the journey. A French foreign minister urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans. open image in gallery Firefighters from Spain’s military emergencies unit battle flames in El Tiemblo, 80km west of Madrid ( AFP/Getty ) Wildfires are also affecting parts of Scotland, with a major incident declared in the Cairngorms national park. More than 500 firefighters have been tackling the blaze, which has raged for the past 10 days and forced locals from their homes in the remote region. Residents of Nethy Bridge , a Scottish village facing evacuation, are “frustrated” that the fire has not yet been brought under control. “A lot of people are upset, angry and frustrated at the ongoing situation, because the Scottish government said a week ago [on Wednesday] that they had enough resources to deal with it, and they said on Thursday that the fire was contained,” said Sandy McCook, chair of the Nethy Bridge and Vicinity Community Council. “My argument with that is, if you said the fire was contained and you had enough resources last Wednesday and Thursday, why are we still fighting it 10 days later, and it’s still running out of control? It is still not controlled in any way, shape or form.” Mr McCook said that residents of the Cairngorms village could see large plumes of smoke from the wildfire on Friday before they were evacuated. He added: “Apocalyptic is the word for the pall of smoke that was on the go yesterday.” open image in gallery Smoke rises from the wildfire in the Cairngorms national park on Saturday ( PA ) Scotland’s first minister John Swinney has said that the Cairngorms national park wildfire is still a “very serious situation”. “Residents, businesses and people staying in the affected areas will understandably be very worried,” he added. “My thoughts are with them and I thank them for their understanding. “With the fire changing to be in the direction of Nethy Bridge yesterday afternoon, a precautionary evacuation was put in place, and a fire break was successfully established overnight to protect the village. “Police officers visited all properties in Nethy Bridge, and officers are in the village today to support residents. “The wind has changed direction overnight, which means the track of the fire has altered once again, and the threat to Nethy Bridge has reduced, for the moment at least. Ground and helicopter resources are being focused on the current path of the fire, and new fire breaks constructed.” The first minister said such situations can change “very quickly and dramatically”, reflecting the challenges faced by the Scottish Fire and Rescue Services and other responders. https://www.euronews.com/travel/2026/07/.text: Why settle for one city when you could visit four? Introducing ‘trip-maxxing’, a new travel trend which is seeing travellers swapping week-long stays in a single destination for multi-city adventures that squeeze in more sights, cultures and experiences.While doing so much might seem unrealistic – and unaffordable – it’s actually entirely possible to do it on a budget. New research from FlixBus has revealed that a number of routes across Europe offer easy connections and affordable stays.The travel company looked at destinations across the continent served by its network, identifying four-stop routes with journeys under five hours a piece.Routes were ranked based on the shortest overall travel time, and each stop was scored using a range of travel factors, from average hostel prices and ratings, to the cost of an affordable night out – that’s a low-cost meal and three beers. The research also looked at the density of attractions and nightlife within 5km of the city centre, as well as the number of UNESCO World Heritage Sites within 100km.Each city was given a score out of 10, with each route awarded a total out of 40 based on our four key ranking factors – nightlife, culture, budget and accommodation. Ten routes made the trip-maxxing list – and these are the top five. Route 1: Berlin - Prague - Vienna - BudapestThis central European route topped the list, with a score of 28.8 out of 40. Flixbus found that each city delivers across all categories, with no destination acting as a gap-filler. Berlin, the first destination, had the best score overall for nightlife and also boasts rich history and culture, and is an excellent walking city. Accommodation here is well-priced, and there’s a vast amount of things to see and do per square kilometre – something matched by very few cities in Europe.Next up is Prague, less than five hours from the German capital by bus. The capital of Czechia is home to a beautiful Gothic old town, an impressive hilltop castle, and Charles Bridge, a medieval stone arch bridge that crosses the Vltava river. It’s also a very affordable city, ideal for budget travellers. Vienna is also under five hours by bus and is an entirely different experience to Prague. Walk around the famously pretty city, famous for its slower pace of life, relaxing coffee houses, and endless culture. Don’t miss the Kunsthistorisches Museum Wien or a visit to the Vienna State Opera, and wander streets flanked by striking imperial architecture. This trip comes to a close in Budapest, under four hours from Vienna. Visits to its world-famous thermal baths and ruin bars, built inside crumbling courtyards, are a must do. The city is bisected by the Danube river, crossed by the 19th-century Chain Bridge and the architecturally impressive Fishermen’s Bastion offers sweeping views of the Hungarian capital below. Route 2: Berlin - Prague - Bratislava - BudapestThis route was awarded the highest budget score of any route in the ranking, scoring 28.1 overall. While three of the destinations are the same as the first route, it’s Bratislava which stands out as a relatively unexplored destination.Bratislava, around four hours from Prague, is often overlooked in favour of larger European cities, but Slovakia's capital has plenty to recommend it. Wander its charming cobbled Old Town, climb up to Bratislava Castle for sweeping views across the Danube, and stop off at one of the city's many independent wine bars and restaurants. It may not be the obvious choice for a standalone city break, but as part of a multi-city trip, it's well worth adding to your itinerary.Route 3: Berlin - Prague - Wroclaw - KrakówThis trip, with two of the same stops as the top two on the list, has one of the fastest total travel times in the whole ranking, at just 11.7 hours. It’s also been awarded a budget score of 8.6, which makes up for it offering three countries rather than four. After Berlin and Prague, it’s a three-hour journey to Wroclaw, Poland’s third-largest city. Spread across a network of islands linked by more than 100 bridges, Wroclaw is home to a beautiful market square that rivals Prague's, but with far fewer crowds. Wander through the university quarter, explore the historic Cathedral Island and keep an eye out for the city's famous bronze gnome statues, hidden throughout the streets.The journey ends in Kraków, around three hours further east. Poland's former royal capital is home to one of Europe's best-preserved medieval centres, with the vast Rynek Główny market square surrounded by Gothic churches, colourful townhouses and lively cafés. While the city is packed with history, it's also a great place to experience Poland's food and nightlife. Around an hour away, the Auschwitz-Birkenau Memorial and Museum is a must visit.Route 4: Amsterdam - Dortmund - Berlin - PragueScoring 27 overall, this route topped the rankings for culture and is ideal for travellers who want to begin in western Europe before making their way east.Amsterdam kicks things off with some of Europe's best museums and nightlife. Spend time exploring the Rijksmuseum, Van Gogh Museum and Anne Frank House, before wandering the UNESCO-listed canal district and the independent shops, cafés and bars of the Jordaan neighbourhood.Just over two hours away is Dortmund, one of the route's biggest surprises. Once known for coal and steel, the German city has reinvented itself as a cultural hub, with attractions including Phoenix Lake, built on the site of a former steelworks, alongside a growing food and bar scene.Finish the trip with stops in Berlin and Prague, both packed full of culture and fun nightlife. Route 5: Frankfurt - Berlin - Prague - ViennaWith an overall score of 26.9, and a nightlife score of 7.7, this route is a great option for travellers flying into one of the continent’s best-connected transport hubs before heading east through four of central Europe's most fascinating cities.Frankfurt is far more than Germany's financial capital. The Museum Embankment is home to one of the country's finest collections of museums, while the restored Römerberg Square offers a glimpse of the city's medieval past.Finish the day with a glass of traditional apple wine in the Sachsenhausen district before catching the bus east, to Berlin, then Prague and, finally, Vienna.Although this route has the longest travel time in the top five, at around 13 hours, the journeys are spread across several days, making it an easy way to experience four very different European capitals.

http://thepeninsulaqatar.com/article/25/.text: World / Europe Romania shoots down second drone in two days Published: 25 Jul 2026 - 10:25 am | Last Updated: 25 Jul 2026 - 10:27 am Representational image AFP Bucharest: Romania shot down a drone in its airspace on Saturday for the second day in a row, marking the second time since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, it said. The NATO member bordering Ukraine has seen frequent drone incursions, including drones crashing on its soil, since 2022. Its forces shot down a drone for the first time on Friday, around 114 kilometres (70 miles) from Bucharest. The military took down another drone, which "had illegally entered Romanian airspace", on Saturday at 8:34am (0534 GMT), according to defence minister Radu Miruta. It was shot down 9.6 kilometres (six miles) west of Sfantu Gheorghe in the Danube Delta near the border with Ukraine, he added. "The drone was detected by Ministry of National Defence radars entering our airspace at 8:22 and was struck a few minutes later by a Romanian F-16 fighter jet," he posted on Facebook. Drone incursions in Romania have been detected dozens of times since the start of the Ukraine war. A drone smashed into an apartment building in May, wounding two people and drawing condemnation from NATO and the European Union, which blamed Russia and warned against further incursions. https://wiky.com/2026/07/25/output-of-se.text: Sign In Search NEWS ON AIR EVENTS BLOGS PODCASTS WEATHER Output of Serbia’s biggest hydropower plant falls to a third due to low Danube levels By Thomson Reuters Jul 25, 2026 | 1:43 AM BELGRADE, July 25 (Reuters) – Serbia’s biggest hydropower plant, Djerdap 1, is producing only a third of its average daily output because the Danube river ​is at extremely low levels, as prolonged heatwaves and ‌drought affect waterways across Europe, the CEO of state power utility EPS said late on Friday. Dusan Zivkovic said that in May and June, EPS recorded the lowest production for those months since ‌the ​Djerdap 1 power plant was opened ⁠in 1970. The plant, ⁠jointly operated by Serbia and Romania, has total installed active power of 1,140 MW. “At the moment, the power plant produces about 5,000 MWh per day, which ​is a third of the average daily production,” Zivkovic told Reuters. Energy Minister Dubravka Djedovic Handanovic said on Wednesday ⁠that Serbia’s fuel imports fell ⁠to 25% of their monthly target for ​July as low Danube water levels in Hungary, Serbia and ​Romania forced barges and tankers to operate at ‌30% to 40% of their cargo capacity. The low levels of the Danube have impacted other Serbian energy facilities such as the coal-fired Kostolac power plants, where a lack ⁠of water affected cooling systems, leading to lower output, Zivkovic said. He warned of more problems ahead, but pledged a stable ⁠supply of electricity ‌to the nation of around 6.5 ⁠million. “Unfortunately, forecasts are not any better, and ​some ‌suggest that at the beginning of August ​we will ⁠have (Danube water) inflows of about 1,500 cubic meters per second, which is the biological minimum,” he said. Serbia’s hydrometeorological department forecast a minimal rise in the Danube in the coming days due to rainfall upstream. https://www.leaderlive.co.uk/news/nation.text: Do not cancel travel plans over wildfires, urges French minister By PA News Agency Share 0 Comments 3 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A French foreign minister has urged tourists not to cancel their travel plans despite unprecedented wildfires in the country’s south west. Éléonore Caroit, the minister for international partnerships, said that although France was facing an “exceptionally intense” fire season, tourists should visit as long as they remain well-informed. Massive forest fires have forced the evacuation of 200,000 people in south-western France and central Spain, including 141,000 in the Gironde and Landes departments in France. Ms Caroit told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme on Saturday: “It’s more than an incident, it really is a tragedy, nearly 50,000 hectares have been burned this year. It’s significantly worse than last year and even 2022, which was the worst year we had had. “You have entire areas that are fine, you’re seeing similar phenomena in Spain and other countries. I’m in Paris and nothing is happening, and most other regions are OK, so do please come to France and do not cancel your travel plans. “But wherever you are, please do be advised as to what might be happening.” Ms Caroit, who said the French army had been deployed to help tackle the wildfires which now number 32, also told the programme that France’s response was being bolstered by their European Union membership. A water bomber fighting wildfires In Ares, western France (Caroline Blumberg/AP) She said: “Being part of the European Union today makes every possible sense. We have activated the European Civil Protection Mechanism which is an extraordinary mechanism; solidarity is essential in the EU. “Right now, we have had the confirmation that two water bombing carriers will come from Croatia, two water tractors from Portugal, two Black Hawk helicopters from Czech Republic and Slovakia. “They’re helping us now as the situation is terrible; we’ve helped them in the past. It explains what it is to be in the EU.” Ms Caroit urged world leaders to see the fires – which have killed two firefighters, injured 42 more and are confirmed to have destroyed around 100 homes so far – as a wake-up call for climate change. A wildfire advances near San Martin de Valdeiglesias, Ávila province, Spain (Manu Fernandez/AP) She said: “(This is) something we’re seeing in many parts of the world. Remember the wildfires in California, Chile. The climate is changing, we’re having a terrible impact on it. “While leaders in the world continue to say climate change doesn’t matter, we’re seeing the concrete effects everywhere. We have to take it seriously. “(France has) invested millions but we’re seeing it’s not enough.” Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said: “My thoughts are with everyone affected by the wildfires in Europe. “I am in touch with my French and Spanish counterparts about the situation. “British nationals should follow the advice of local authorities in the area, alongside FCDO travel advice.” A British restaurant owner in Bordeaux said the city is “full of smoke and ash” and residents are wearing masks if they go outside. Lance Attwood, 58, who owns Sweeney Todd’s in Bordeaux city centre, told the Press Association: “It’s not really conducive to coming out. “The town is full of smoke and ash, so there’s a big drop in business, people are just walking around town in masks. “Our biggest concern is people’s safety and the safety of the emergency services.” Mr Attwood, who has lived in Bordeaux for 25 years, said friends who had been evacuated were focusing on recovering sentimental belongings and finding alternative living arrangements. He encouraged people to donate dry food with a long shelf-life to local charities to help those affected. Share 0 Comments Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading... https://www.planetf1.com/news/max-versta.text: Max Verstappen has weighed in on Fernando Alonso's 'rules' comment Max Verstappen believes Fernando Alonso is in a different position when it comes to walking away from Formula 1, arguing the Spaniard has already enjoyed a complete career while he still has many years ahead of him. Verstappen, at 28, still has many more years on the grid if he so wishes. Max Verstappen on Fernando Alonso’s Formula 1 future Want more PlanetF1.com coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust . Throughout this season, there’s been talk about Formula 1 losing two of its four world champions as Alonso and Verstappen weigh up their options. Neither driver is enjoying the new regulations, with the power unit’s combustion-to-battery power split forcing them to super clip and harvest battery power. While Alonso says “no talent is needed”, Verstappen complained that the new rules are “anti-racing” and dubbed it “Formula E on steroids”. Alonso told PlanetF1.com and other accredited media in Hungary that it is the rules, more than whether Aston Martin’s highly anticipated B-Spec AMR26 closes the gap to the front of the field, that will determine his future. Asked if his future on the grid was dependent on the second iteration of the AMR26, the 45-year-old explained: “Nothing, because my decision is not about the performance of this year. “This year we started on the wrong foot, and I cannot base my decision for next year on a performance that is not realistic. “I think my decision for next year is more about the rules. “Driving these cars in places like Spa or Silverstone [at the] last race is not what I’m dreaming of for my future. So we’ll see.” For Verstappen, though, the situation is a bit different. While he too has been vocal in his criticism of the regulations, at 28 years of age, he could continue for years to come. Asked about Alonso’s statement about the rules deciding his future, Verstappen said: “I fully agree with him. It is not what you want. “Of course, Fernando is 45 so it’s probably easier for him to say ‘I quit’ because he has already done, basically his career. I would love to see Fernando race until he’s 60, but I don’t think that’s realistic in Formula 1. “As a real racer, it’s tough and especially, of course, when you’re not enjoying the regulations, you’re not competitive at the moment, it’s a tough one. “Because Fernando, of course, doesn’t deserve to be P21. Fernando deserves to be in the top five, minimum. “I’m of course 28, so it’s a little bit different. I can easily stop, it’s not a problem, but I love racing. And I’m just trying to deal with what we have, even though what we have at the moment is not what I like.” While for Alonso, his choices are said to be Aston Martin or hanging up his F1 helmet, multiple sources have told PlanetF1.com that Verstappen is nearing the end of lengthy negotiations with McLaren about a potential switch. Go deeper: F1 drivers contracts F1 driver contracts: What is the contract status of every driver on the F1 2026 grid? F1 2026 driver salaries: Who are the highest-paid drivers on the grid? The Dutchman, however, reiterated in Budapest that Red Bull is his “second” family. “I am feeling good from my side. What I’m saying that there is nothing to say is because there’s nothing going on,” he said. “So for me, I’m just focused on trying to get the most out of the car. And like what I was explaining before, that’s already complicated enough to deal with. And yeah, that’s what I’m just doing. “I mean, this team is like a second family to me.” Want to be the first to know exclusive information from the F1 paddock?
