https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gy.text: By Alice Cuddy BBC News In an abandoned luxury apartment in the Syrian capital Damascus, armed men dressed in military fatigues sifted through designer clothes and documents. Scattered across the living room floor, under a sparkling crystal chandelier, were dozens of photos of the same slender man in different settings - sitting at his desk, even playing in the snow. And multiple prints of the same image, showing him smiling warmly as he shook the hand of ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad. The man was not instantly recognisable, but gold medals and gilded certificates piled nearby were inscribed with the name Hussam Luka. Known as "The Spider", Luka was one of Assad's top henchmen, accused of orchestrating atrocities and systematic torture, and sanctioned by the UK, US and European Union. Image caption, Hussam Luka's apartment was luxurious and full of miscellaneous goods As head of Syria's most powerful civilian intelligence agency, Luka was among the most feared men in the country. But much of his work was conducted from the shadows. Like others in the regime, Luka seemingly vanished overnight in December 2024 when Assad was toppled, leaving a trail of unanswered questions and demands for justice that many fear will never be realised. In his apartment, days after Assad's fall, we watched the rebels looking for clues as to where he might have gone. Image caption, One of the photos we found had been copied multiple times - showing Luka shaking hands with Assad In the corner of the living room, on a console table, was an unremarkable-looking notebook. Inside, in scribbled blue handwriting, we found dozens of names - from shopkeepers and doctors, to military officials and people with the Luka family name. Could these contacts help us learn more about The Spider and his crimes, or even help us to track him down? At one time, Luka's own phone number was hard to avoid - in the early days of the Syrian civil war, it had been spray-painted on walls around the central city of Homs. The conflict was sparked by Assad's brutal crushing of a pro-democracy uprising in 2011 - a war in which hundreds of thousands of people would go on to be killed. Luka was a local head of the Political Security Directorate, one of Assad's main intelligence agencies, and had been given the task of wresting the city from the rebels. At the time, rebel-held areas in Homs were under siege by the government, and residents were struggling to access food and medicine. Several people, including former rebel fighter Motaz al-Zaydi, told us they had resorted to eating rats. Al-Zaydi remembers Luka's name and phone number appearing on a wall in his neighbourhood, and said the message began to spread that those wanting to flee the fighting could phone the number for safe passage. Some are believed to have been granted safe transit out of the city by Luka, but others who called the number were never seen or heard from again, according to several people we spoke to, including al-Zaydi. Many told us they referred to Luka as "The Spider" because of his vast web of allies and informants, including some embedded in rebel groups. "He was everywhere," Homs residents told us. Al-Zaydi described Luka as an "evil genius" and "a fox of a man". But his most egregious action in the city, many argue, was his alleged involvement in the so-called Eid Massacre, known by some as the Children's Massacre, which the US noted when sanctioning him. It was the Muslim holiday of Eid al-Adha in September 2015, and Mohammed Towakatli's seven-year-old, Wael, was gardening in the playground he had set up in the al-Waer neighbourhood. At 17:10, just after the power ration had kicked in, Mohammed remembers the strike hitting. As Mohammed walked around the park earlier this year, now planted with rows of saplings, he recalled the names of the children killed and the games they had been playing at the time, gesturing to the places where he had found their bodies, including that of Wael. Image caption, Mohammed at the grave of his son, who was killed in a bombing in Homs "They were tiny children," he said with tears in his eyes. "The ground here was painted red with blood." Twenty-eight people were killed, including 17 children and four women, according to the Syrian Network for Human Rights. Luka, according to a Syrian activist group, and a pro-opposition newspaper at the time, was responsible for the regime's selection of targets in the area that day. His actions in Homs earned him a promotion, and by the time of the regime's collapse he ran the General Security Directorate (GSD) intelligence agency, making him one of the most powerful people in the country. The government security services could target anyone - from opposition fighters, journalists, doctors, or rights activists, to people believed to be opposed in any form to the Assad government. Those arrested were detained in Syria's political prisons, including Sednaya in Damascus - a facility so notorious it was dubbed the "human slaughterhouse". Many imprisoned there were never seen again. As head of the GSD, Luka had strategic control over Syria's detention policies, and his personnel would monitor communications to and from Sednaya. There are widespread calls across Syrian society on social media for former senior officials to be held accountable. Some also say the new Syrian government is not doing enough to bring these people to justice. Syria's Attorney General, Hassan al-Turba, told the BBC the government had launched a lawsuit against Luka, accusing him of "premeditated murder, torture, and death resulting from torture". "A warrant has been circulated domestically and we are working on circulating it internationally as well," he said, adding the administration was working to track the location and seek the extradition of Luka and other missing senior regime officials. As he continues to grieve for his son, Mohammed told the BBC he wanted Luka, alongside other senior regime officials, to be returned to Syria and executed. "They look like humans but have no humanity in them at all," he said. We had taken photos of every page of the book we discovered in Luka's apartment and, back in London, began testing every one of its 155 numbers - aware that many people close to the regime would have fled or gone to ground. Fifty-one numbers appeared to be operational. We then called these again in order of their apparent importance to Luka, starting with military commanders and relatives. Every call was unsuccessful. Anyone who answered simply hung up when we explained who we were and what we wanted - or denied knowing Luka or his family, or even being the people listed in the book. Image caption, The phone book we found in the apartment - the BBC has redacted the surnames and the first three digits of each phone number So a BBC reporter, whose own name was once on a GSD wanted list while Luka ran the agency, headed to Syria to try in person. Many of those listed in the phone book were doctors, so our reporter began booking medical appointments with some of them as a way to meet them. A doctor in Aleppo reluctantly acknowledged he had treated Luka, but then ordered our journalist to leave and returned his consultation fee. Our reporter then booked an appointment with another doctor in the phone book, this time based in Damascus. This doctor revealed he had once accompanied Luka's mother on a medical trip to Russia, but was reluctant to give us any more information, other than to vaguely direct us to a pharmacy belonging to one of Luka's daughters. Locals said she, too, had not been seen since December 2024. For months we drew a blank in our hunt for Luka. And then we had our first breakthrough. One of those listed in the book, who we tried calling again, finally answered the phone. He had been the guard for Luka's apartment block, he told us, and eventually agreed to give us the number for someone he said had been Luka's personal bodyguard - a man we are calling Mahmoud. It took weeks to secure an interview with Mahmoud. Meetings would be scheduled but he would not show up, or he would request a meeting in a private space such as a car or apartment, which our reporter judged too much of a risk. They eventually met at a hotel one night, just before midnight. Broad-shouldered and physically imposing, Mahmoud seemed to be considering every answer carefully before he spoke. He told us he was angry with Luka for leaving him behind when the regime fell. As word had spread in December 2024 that Assad's rule was on the brink of collapse - with rebels advancing on the capital - Luka had said he would stay and defend Damascus, Mahmoud told us. But by the early hours of the next morning, Luka had disappeared, taking a large sum of money with him from the office safe, Mahmoud said. Mahmoud refused to share any contact details for Luka or his family, but did give us a number for Luka's driver, who he believed had driven the former spy chief out of the capital that night. This man proved even harder to reach. When he answered the phone, his voice was nervous and unsteady. He repeatedly insisted he was just a driver, and knew nothing of Luka's activities. Multiple meetings with us were never kept, and eventually he stopped replying. We turned our attention to Luka's possible escape routes, including neighbouring Lebanon - where the Iran-backed group Hezbollah had close links with the Assad regime. One senior source in the Lebanese government told us he understood Luka had passed through Lebanon on a "good Russian passport but with a different name", before flying out to Russia. We managed to find a man, now based in Lebanon, whose name was listed in Luka's contacts book, but under a number that no longer worked. He is one of many wanted by the new Syrian government, because of his close association with the Assad regime. This man, who we cannot identify, said he had a number for Luka. We saw it, and realised it had a Russian country code. Russia was a key backer of the Assad regime, and in the days after his fall, Assad released a statement confirming that he had fled there. Many of his inner circle were believed to have followed him. Back in Luka's apartment in Damascus, we had found clues that Luka also had strong links to Moscow - awards from Russia's foreign spy service, and even a New Year's card addressed to him from a senior Russian official. Now, the Russian telephone number for him suggested we finally had proof that he was - as we had predicted - in Russia. We wanted to verify that this number really was Luka's. So a few days later, with us present, the man agreed to put the person he said was Hussam Luka on speakerphone, and ask him questions which we believed only Luka would know the answer to, based on information we had gathered during our investigation. The voice on the other end of the phone sounded confused, but answered the questions instantly and correctly. He refused, however, to speak to us directly. But our contact later agreed to call Luka again and allow us to try to interview him. The same voice answered, and we introduced ourselves, explaining that we had questions about serious allegations relating to massacres and torture committed by the former regime official. "I can't take any risk talking on the phone in the position I'm in," Luka said, his tone anxious. Asked if Russia was blocking him from talking, Luka said: "I cannot talk. I can't explain. You have to understand." When asked if he would meet us outside Russia, he said: "It's difficult." He then hung up the phone. We later obtained a second number which we were told was also for Luka - this time registered in Syria and linked to social media and messaging apps which he appeared to be still using. Over a period of a day, the BBC was able to locate him in two âsuburban areas on the outskirts of the Russian capital, Moscow. The locations seemed far removed from the luxurious lifestyle Assad is reported to be leading in exile in Russia, and to the life Luka himself once led in Syria. We knew we could not approach him in person in Russia, where Assad's henchmen are shielded from international journalists and police, so we decided to try putting our allegations to him over the phone once again. We rang the number and the same voice as before answered, the line crackly. He asked who was calling, and when told it was the BBC, he immediately hung up. We sent a message over WhatsApp, asking for his response to the many allegations against him, but he did not reply. Confirmation that Luka is in Moscow is difficult news for those in Syria seeking justice. Russia is highly unlikely to extradite officials from the regime that it long supported. The Russian government did not respond to BBC requests for comment about Luka's presence there, or whether it would ever consider an extradition request. Back in Homs, Mohammed says he will never let go of the hope that Luka, and other senior members of the Assad regime, will one day face justice. Image caption, Mohammed still hopes for justice after the death of seven-year-old Wael, pictured here "[I am] angry at all those who were with the regime and its security apparatusâ¦ They were all against us," he says. "Wael was just a seven-year-old childâ¦ All he cared about was playing and having fun." Additional reporting by Riam Dalati, Ghaith Solh and Abigail Akerman Related topics Syria Syrian civil war Homs Bashar al-Assad Russia

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cz05.text: Image source, Supplied Image caption, The body of an Indian climber who died 30 years ago wearing his green mountaineering boots has become a grim marker along the road to Everest's summit By Jehangir Ali BBC News Hindi ,Â Reporting from Skurbuchan, Ladakh Published 6 hours ago For 30 years, a dead body known as "Green Boots" has been lying in the snow, nestled under an overhanging rock, not far from Mount Everest's summit. The lime mountaineering boots worn by an Indian climber who died in 1996 have been a grim trail marker for many climbers on their way up the world's highest peak ever since. Now India is looking for a specialist high-altitude recovery team to undertake a complex and risky mission to retrieve what they say is Dorje Morup's body â arguably the most famous of the hundreds whose bodies have been left frozen on the mountain. They hope they are on the cusp of returning his remains to friends and family who never gave up hope he'd come home. "On some days, before I went to sleep, I would think that there'd be a knock on the door tonight and that when I opened, he would be there," Morup's wife told the BBC. "When he comes home, I will ask him: 'Where were you all these years?'" Disaster struck on descent Image source, Family handout Image caption, Dorje Morup was a keen mountaineer and had climbed many peaks, including Stok Kangri, the highest peak in the Ladakh mountain range The night before he left to be part of a historic Indian expedition on Everest, Morup sat with his wife at his home in Ladakh, an Indian-administered territory in another part of the Himalayas. He made her a promise: that he would come back a hero and make his country proud. "He asked me to take care of the kids and come to the airport to greet him on his return," Konchak Yangskit told the BBC at her home. A lance naik, or lance corporal, in the Indo Tibetan Border Police (ITBP), the force guarding much of India's border with China, 48-year-old Morup was no stranger to Himalayan trekking. But Yangskit says she had a strange sense of foreboding that night: "I wondered if I was ever going to see him again." Morup was one of six climbers on the ITBP expedition attempting to reach the top of Everest â which lies on the border between Nepal and the Chinese-governed territory of Tibet. Most climbers choose to ascend from the Nepalese side, but Morup's crew wanted to write their names into the history books as the first Indian expedition to do it from the treacherous Chinese side. Image caption, Morup's wife, Yangskit, says because she never saw his body, she found it difficult to believe he was dead Three out of six members of the expedition turned back due to a snowstorm, but Morup and two others - Tsewang Smanla and Tsewang Paljor â kept struggling, all the way up to the 8,849m summit. Disaster, a blizzard, struck as they descended and killed all three. Like many of the more than 300 people who have died in the Everest region since records began a century ago, their bodies remain on the mountain. Two have never been found, but the third body - that of "Green Boots" - has been lying frozen in the snow for three decades at an altitude of 8,500 metres. For years, it was assumed that "Green Boots" was another member of the expedition, Tsewang Paljor. But testimony from surviving members of the 1996 expedition and the location of the last radio contact with the climbers have now led authorities to believe the remains belong to Morup. Image source, Family handout Image caption, Morup's family is proud to show the certificate issued by the Chinese government confirming he had successfully reached the top of Everest An ITBP official, speaking anonymously because he is not authorised to speak to the media, told BBC News Hindi that Morup's clothes and climbing gear helped officials identify the body in recent years. Since then, they've been plotting how to get their comrade home so they can confirm his identity beyond doubt through DNA testing and offer his family a semblance of closure. "We never forgot him. It was only a matter of time," the ITBP official said. How difficult will it be to recover the body? Retrieving those who have died on the mountain is a dangerous, gruelling task, and, up until the past decade, very rare. Many of the bodies, like Morup's, are in what climbers call Everest's death zone â where temperatures can plunge to -40C and oxygen levels are about a third of those at sea level. "The weather and snow conditions are going to be crucial," said Tshiring Jangbu Sherpa, a prominent Nepalese mountaineer who has taken part in other recovery missions. "The north side has fewer crevasses, but it is riskier. If something bad happens from the Nepalese side, you get quickly evacuated by helicopter. But there is no such system from the Chinese side," he told BBC Hindi. Image caption, Some of photos of Morup and a few of his belongings have helped his family keep his memory alive The Chinese side of the peak â where Green Boots' body is â is steeper and doesn't have the same support structures as the southern slope, which is another complicating factor, Sherpa sources have told BBC News Nepali. "It's really tough to get that body down even in popular spring season, let alone the autumn [which has more unpredictable weather]. That's the simple reason it is still there for so many years," mountaineering guide Pemba Ongchu Sherpa said. "There would need to be 10 to 12 climbers who are capable of making summits, just to fix [support] ropes to reach that point." Green Boots will also have to be physically carried down to an altitude where it can be collected by a helicopter, or possibly yaks, and transported back to an airport â a job which also requires huge manpower. Sherpas say bodies shrouded in iced-up climbing gear often weigh several times the average man and are frequently frozen into awkward positions, making bringing them down the challenging terrain even more treacherous. The remains may also begin defrosting and decomposing once they reach lower altitudes. The start of the descent with the body would be the most difficult, Indian climber Kuntal Joisher told BBC Nepali. "It's going to be very, very risky endeavour. It's extremely steep ground with lots of rock. Logistically, this [first] 1000m is going to be a humungous challenge." "The main thing is to not put Sherpa lives at risk for a dead body." All of this makes for a hugely expensive recovery mission â experts say even the most straightforward ones cost between $40,000 and $80,000, a sum beyond the means of most families. It is more common for local teams to move people who have died out of view on the mountain: like explorer Francys Arsentiev, dubbed the Sleeping Beauty of Everest, who in 2007 was moved to a more private final resting place on Everest almost a decade after she died. But the ITBP â which is funding the recovery operation â wants Morup's body to be returned by September, and is looking for mountain rescue Sherpa groups who could do the job. Once returned to India, the body will undergo DNA testing and, if confirmed to be Morup, his remains will be given back to his family. 'My heart refused to believe he had died' For years, Morup's family back in Ladakh have struggled to come to terms with his disappearance. Now around 75, Yangskit struggles to recall even the day she was married. But the days after the tragedy remain etched in her mind. "I only knew there was a storm on the mountain. Even though we organised cremation prayers at home, my heart refused to believe he had died," she says with tears rolling down her face. "I didn't see his dead body, so it was difficult for me to believe it." Image caption, Morup's family remains cautious about what the body being returned will mean for them Image caption, Morup's eldest son, Punchok Dorjai, looks up at a framed photo of his father All that remains of Morup today are his medals and trophies, a couple of old photos from his mountain adventures â and, most importantly, a certificate from the Chinese government which states that at 17:30 on 10 May 1996, Morup reached the top of Everest. If the recovery mission is successful, Morup's son Punchok Dorjai told the BBC that the family would hold a funeral for him near the Martyrs Park in Ladakh's capital Leh. "My father gave his life for the country and he should be remembered as a martyr," Dorjai said, adding that his teammates who perished deserve the same title. The family will also proudly save a symbol of Morup's legacy at their home, to go alongside his summit certification, he said: "We are planning to keep the Green Boots." https://telex.hu/g7/penz/2026/08/08/euro.text: Menü Kereső Ha tesszük a dolgunkat, és tényleg bevezetjük az eurót, azzal sokat lehet keresni Pénz Legfontosabb Az Államadósság-kezelő Központ Zrt. bejárata – Fotó: Róka László / Nemzeti Archívum / Fókuszban Magyarország Program Elek Péter A szerző a Generali Investments CEE portfóliómenedzsere. Ez itt a Zéróosztó, a G7 elemzői szeglete, amelyben külső elemzők, szakértők cikkei olvashatók. Az írások és az azokban megfogalmazott vélemények a szerzők álláspontját tükrözik. A magyar kötvénypiac jelenleg igen kecsegtető. A Tisza-kormány hatalomra kerülésével azonnali jelentős hozamcsökkenés történt, a piac kiárazta a korábbi kormány korrupcióját, esztelen pénzszórását, az állandóan magas költségvetési hiányt, és persze még sok minden mást is. Azzal, hogy az új kormány bejelentkezett az euróra, sok gordiuszi csomót sikerült átvágnia. A magyar lakosság megtakarításainak jó része, közel 40 százaléka euróban van, másrészt sajnos a magyar lakosság az elmúlt évtizedekben egyszerűen elvesztette a bizalmát a forintban. Erre (is) nagyon jó megoldás az euró bevezetése. Sokan írtak már az (euró bevezetéséhez szükséges) ERM–II-ről, a maastrichti kritériumokról, ezeket most mellőzném. Nézzük inkább konkrétumként a magyar kötvénypiacot! Ha és amennyiben ténylegesen megtörténik az euró bevezetése hazánkban, elvileg négy év múlva, akkor a magyar, eddig forintos hozamok négy év múlva már euróban lesznek. Azok a hozamok, amelyek most forintban vannak, 2030-tól, 2031-től már euróban lesznek érvényesek. Valószínűleg az Államadósság-kezelő Központ ezért is törölte el a lakossági állampapír-kínálatból az 5 éves FIXMÁP-ot, mert nem szeretne 5,5 százalékot fizetni euróban, túl sokba kerül. Vegyünk egy nagyon egyszerű példát! Jelenleg a francia, olasz, görög 10 éves hozamok kicsit 4 százalék alatt vannak, míg a magyar 10 éves hozama 5,4 százalék. Időben természetesen nem lineárisan, hanem inkább mérföldkövekhez kötve (2027-es költségvetés, ERM–II bevezetése stb.), de a belépés dátumakor ezek a hozamok nagyjából ugyanolyan szinteken lesznek, mint a francia, görög vagy olasz. Euróban. Ha csak a 10 éves magyar kötvényeket nézzük, akkor körülbelül 150 pontnyi konvergenciafelértékelődés van ebben az eszközben. A 10 éves magyar kötvény átlagos hátralévő futamideje (duráció) 8 év, vagyis csak a magyar 10 éves kötvényben körülbelül 12 százaléknyi „upside” van. A hosszabb lejáratok esetében még több, a rövidebbekben kevesebb. A lényeg, hogy ez az egy egyszeri felértékelődés előbb-utóbb megtörténik. Ahogy már írtam, időben nem lineáris lesz a felértékelődés, biztos, hogy bizonyos mérföldkövekhez fog kötődni (2027-es költségvetés, ERM–II bevezetése, a kritériumokban való megfelelés sikeressége), de ha optimista vagyok azzal kapcsolatban, hogy ez sikerülni fog, akkor a magyar kötvényekben nagy potenciál van. Az előző gazdasági-politikai ciklus alatt sokszor voltam nagyon pesszimista a magyar kötvénypiac kapcsán. Jelenleg azonban egy dolgot nem tehetek meg: hogy alulsúlyozom a magyar kötvényeket. Nemcsak én személy szerint, hanem nemzetközi befektetőként sem. Hacsak a nemzetközi piacokon nem történik valami pánikszerű, akkor ez egy túl szép szituáció ahhoz, hogy igaz legyen. A magyar kötvények egyrészt a nemzetközi fejlett és fejlődő piacokkal fognak mozogni, másrészről konvergálni fognak az euróban denominált társaikhoz. Természetesen senki sem tudja, hogy négy év múlva a nemzetközi piacokon a hozamok hol lesznek, de az elmúlt években elég egyértelmű volt a trend: emelkedtek, az egyre magasabb államadósságokat, rossz költségvetési adatokat ugyanis egyre kevésbé tolerálja a piac. https://www.birminghammail.co.uk/news/mi.text: A Ryanair passenger said he thought he was 'going to die' as passengers prayed for their lives on 'the worst flight ever' to Birmingham Airport. Connor Horton said other travellers were "screaming and crying" and some were praying when his flight from Krakow in Poland hit turbulence on Thursday, July 23. The 25-year-old, who is a Sandwell Labour councillor covering Great Barr, Yew Tree and Tamebridge, said his journey had already been delayed by a thunderstorm before the turbulence hit. READ MORE: 'They do not represent my town' says Halesowen local after 'frightening' High Street brawl He told BirminghamLive: "People were screaming, someone was crying, the whole thing was awful. "It was only a two-hour flight and it felt like it went on. There were times when we had aggressive drops and it would shoot back up. "That's when people were getting upset and scared, I was terrified. "The sensation was awful and the whole plane was panicking. I thought 'what the f**k is going on?' and that's when I saw people praying. "It just didn't seem normal. I've never been on a flight like that. It was the worst flight of my life and I've flown across the Atlantic, the Caribbean, it was the worst one ever. "We were operated by Ryanair but it was a Polish crew and I couldn't understand their accents. We were told we would arrive early, but I'm sure we arrived ten minutes late. "Everyone clapped and sighed in relief when it landed in Birmingham. "I had never flown with Ryanair and the flight to Kraków shook me up when it landed aggressively." A Ryanair spokesperson said: “This flight from Krakow to Birmingham experienced some minor air turbulence shortly before landing at Birmingham Airport.”

The Ministry of National Defense reported that radar surveillance systems detected the drone in the border area with Ukraine at 8:22 a.m. local time. Two Romanian Air Force F-16 Fighting Falcons, operating under an air policing mission, were scrambled to intercept the target. According to the ministry, the aircraft executed standard identification and neutralization procedures, bringing the drone down in an unpopulated area. Romanian President Nicușor Dan confirmed the operation, stating that the drone was intercepted approximately 10 kilometers west of the city of Sfântu Gheorghe at around 8:30 a.m. Advertisement The defense ministry noted that the pilot responsible for Saturday’s interception was the same individual who shot down a separate drone near the city of Buzău the previous day. Ministry specialist teams have been dispatched to the crash site to conduct an investigation. The defense ministry stated that it is continuously monitoring the airspace and maintaining close contact with allied structures. Drona a fost doborâtă de un pilot român dintr-un avion F-16. — Nicușor Dan (@NicusorDanRO) July 25, 2026 First interception on Friday Saturday’s incident followed a joint operation on Friday, July 24, during which a Romanian F-16 destroyed a suspected Shahed-type drone over Buzău County. Radar systems detected the initial aerial target on Friday at 9:39 a.m. local time, roughly 20 kilometers east of Sulina on the Black Sea coast. The drone subsequently entered Romanian airspace, traveling over Sulina, Brăila, and Fetești. Two Italian Air Force Eurofighter Typhoons deployed at Mihail Kogălniceanu Air Base under NATO’s Air Policing mission were scrambled at 9:48 a.m., followed by two Romanian F-16s from the 86th Air Base at Fetești at 10:56 a.m. Chief of Defense Gen. Gheorghiță Vlad stated that the Italian aircraft engaged the drone but failed to destroy it. A Romanian F-16 then fired an air-to-air missile, destroying the target at 11:02 a.m. near Padina in Buzău County. The fragments fell into a wheat field, causing no casualties or damage. Advertisement NATO’s Allied Air Command confirmed the joint operation, emphasizing the rapid response of the allied forces. Investigations into both incidents are ongoing to determine the origin of the drones. Gen. Vlad indicated that pilots visually assessed Friday’s drone as resembling a Shahed type, which Russian forces frequently use in attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure. Romania has reported multiple instances of drones entering its airspace since the onset of the full-scale war in Ukraine. https://www.nbcnews.com/world/europe/rom.text: BUCHAREST — Romania said on ​Saturday that it had shot down a second drone breaching national airspace in as many days over a sparsely populated area near the border with Ukraine. The ⁠first drone, which Romanian prosecutors investigating the fragments said was Russian, was shot down by the NATO state on Friday, the first time it has done so after dozens of airspace ⁠breaches. President Nicusor Dan took to ​social ⁠media to say the second drone had been shot down at 8:30 a.m. (1:30 a.m. ET), 6 miles ⁠west of Sfantu Gheorghe in the Danube Delta. The defence ​ministry ⁠said the airspace breach ‌had been spotted by radar at 8:22 a.m., and two F-16 fighter jets had been scrambled. It did not specify ‌the origin of Saturday’s drone; prosecutors said ‌the drone downed on Friday had been Russian. Romania, which shares a 400-mile land border with Ukraine, said Russian drones had breached ⁠its airspace around 30 times since Moscow began attacking Ukrainian ports across the Danube River after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27920.text: Big News Network.com Trumps war on far-left terrorism goes global A landmark meeting in Washington put far-left extremism at the center of international counterterrorism efforts For years, liberal elites across the West dismissed warnings about far-left extremism as relics of the Cold War or right-wing paranoia. Today, the evidence is undeniable. A recent US-led global initiative has the ambition to finally confront this resurgence of political terrorism with the seriousness it demands. This is not a partisan crusade but a defense of civilization against those who would burn it down in the name of utopia. The West in flames Europe is bleeding from a thousand cuts inflicted by far-left networks. Railways have been repeatedly sabotaged, power grids targeted, and commercial enterprises struck, inflicting billions in cumulative losses while paralyzing supply chains and public services. Police officers have been assaulted, elected officials threatened, and communities shaken - echoing the days of the 1970s Red Brigades and Baader-Meinhof. In Germany, far-left violence surged more than 40% in a single year. The authorities logged 321 sabotage investigations in 2025 alone, which were overwhelmingly aimed at military, police, railway, and energy targets. Climate activism has fused with anti-capitalism, class warfare, feminism, and outright hostility to European industry and traditional values. What begins as protests and occupations too often escalates to sabotage harming ordinary citizens. The longest blackout in Berlin since World War II struck in early 2026, courtesy of the Vulkangruppe (Volcano Group). This far-left outfit, active since 2011 with at least 13 attacks under its belt, torched power cables near a gas-fired plant, plunging tens of thousands of households and businesses into darkness for days amid freezing temperatures. Hospitals switched to emergency power, trains halted, and daily life fractured. Their manifesto framed it as "resistance" against fossil fuels and capitalism, but the victims were everyday Germans. Italy tells a similar story of escalating chaos. During the Winter Olympics, coordinated rail sabotages forced the cancellation of roughly 40,000 train services. A premature explosion later killed two anarchists preparing yet another railway assault. Official figures show a staggering 450% rise in anti-train sabotages in 2024-2025. An attack on the TAL oil pipeline left it offline for five days. In Greece, over 80% of radical violence stems from far-left actors. These attacks are not isolated incidents but manifestations of a broader pattern of escalating political violence. In the US, violent far-left actors accounted for 63% of recorded anti-government attacks and plots in 2025. Their tactics have expanded beyond sabotage to include targeted political assassinations, including the killing of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. The threat is transnational, fluid, and growing bolder. The networks and their enablers Behind the violence lies a web of organizations blending climate hysteria with revolutionary ideology. Groups like Antifa, operating across borders, exemplify the danger. The US has designated four violent far-left entities from Germany, Italy, and Greece as Foreign Terrorist Organizations. Hungary under Viktor Orban took similar action after Antifa thugs attacked a peaceful patriotic march in Budapest, injuring participants. A 2025 European Parliament motion, backed by dozens of MEPs, called for declaring Antifa a terrorist organization and investigating its financial ties - including potential links to George Soros. Support from certain foundations - such as those associated with Soros or Germany's Rosa Luxemburg Stiftung - has sustained overlapping causes that blend radical left objectives with broader progressive efforts. Mainstream media and the liberal establishment obsessively spotlight far-right threats - often conflating them with patriotic or conservative voices - while downplaying or excusing far-left excesses. In parts of the EU, these networks have infiltrated state administrations and influential think tanks, embedding ideology into governance. This funding ecosystem sustains a global far-left apparatus that exploits open borders, lenient justice systems, and elite guilt to advance its aims. Ongoing legal proceedings, such as those in Dresden involving serious charges against Antifa members, underscore the organized nature of the threat. Trump's America steps up The Trump administration has unleashed a global campaign to crush this radical left terrorism. In mid-July, Secretary of State Marco Rubio hosted the Ministerial on the Resurgence of Political Terrorism in Washington, drawing representatives from over 65 countries, including participants from Europe, Latin America, Africa, and Asia, to address this shared challenge to governance, infrastructure security, and citizen safety. The ministerial yielded concrete outcomes that mark a new phase of coordinated international action. Delegates forged agreement on three hard-hitting pillars of action: ramped-up designations and accountability, with the US already branding four dangerous far-left groups as terrorists and reviewing more; deeper operational teamwork through intensified intelligence sharing, coordinated travel bans, and urgent defenses for railways, power grids, and other critical lifelines; and fresh US visa restrictions slamming the door on those who engage in or bankroll far-left terror. Germany stepped forward to host the next working session, while Treasury officials vowed to tear apart funding pipelines with rewards of up to millions for tips that disrupt the money flow. The approach closes critical gaps in global counterterrorism frameworks. The US is now treating far-left extremism with the same ferocity once reserved for jihadists: designating groups, imposing sanctions and visa restrictions, disrupting finances, and fostering international cooperation. Importantly, the campaign zeroes in on extremist organizations rather than any particular government or geopolitical rival. This fight against a shared ideological enemy - one hostile to traditional societies, national identities, and ordered liberty - offers common ground. Powers such as China and Russia, with their own experiences managing ideological extremism and emphasis on domestic order, might stand to benefit from - and contribute to - practical cooperation in safeguarding stability and development. The cost of selective silence The liberal establishment's selective outrage is damning. While far-right actors - frequently defenders of national sovereignty and cultural continuity - face relentless scrutiny and persecution, far-left violence is often romanticized as "protest" or explained away as a reaction to "injustice." This double standard has emboldened extremists, allowing them to infiltrate institutions and erode public safety. The US initiative may mark a turning point, both for Western countries and beyond. By placing violent far-left networks within a broader counterterrorism framework, strengthening investigations, disrupting financial support, and expanding international cooperation, it advances the principle that no movement is exempt from accountability when it embraces violence. Other governments can contribute by improving intelligence sharing, addressing transnational networks, and ensuring that public safety remains above political considerations. As violent far-left extremism becomes increasingly transnational, governments cannot afford selective approaches to political violence. Attacks on critical infrastructure and politically motivated violence threaten security, economic resilience, and public confidence across regions. A broad international coalition focused on confronting violent extremism can help reinforce a fundamental principle: political grievances cannot be pursued through terror. https://www.salon.com/2026/07/25/andrew-.text: analysis Andrew Tate’s arrest causes trouble for Trump’s youngest son The manosphere influencer has lost the president's support — but he could pose a threat to Barron By Sophia Tesfaye Senior Writer Published July 25, 2026 6:45AM (EDT) Barron Trump has defended Andrew Tate against allegations of sex trafficking (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images) Facebook X Reddit Email Save The shift was as swift as it was cold. Standing before reporters in the briefing room on Thursday, White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt was asked a direct question: Would President Donald Trump or his administration intervene to stop the extradition of Andrew and Tristan Tate to the United Kingdom on 59 charges of rape, sex trafficking, assault and extreme pornography? Her single-word response — “No” — denied the brothers, who have been championed by many MAGA media figures as examples of white male persecution, a lifeline. On Thursday, federal marshals in Miami took the Tates into custody . In addition to the charges they face in the U.K., the brothers remain embroiled in grave human-trafficking and minor-exploitation proceedings in Romania and investigations in Florida about new allegations. In the days since their arrest, their attorney Joseph McBride — who has also represented Jan. 6 defendants — has insisted the arrest is political persecution, and he has been amplifying supportive commentary online from media figures with close ties to the Trump administration. MAGA influencer and white nationalist Nick Fuentes wrote that it would be a “national humiliation” if Trump agreed to extradite the brothers to Britain over what he called “trumped up ‘Me Too’ charges.” Other far-right influencers reportedly joined in , but to no avail. For years, the brothers were treated by the MAGA ecosystem not as alleged traffickers facing serious criminal scrutiny, but as useful avatars of male grievance and anti-feminist rebellion. Trump’s refusal to intervene in the Tates’ extradition fight is a much-delayed correction. For years, the brothers were treated by the MAGA ecosystem not as alleged traffickers facing serious criminal scrutiny, but as useful avatars of male grievance and anti-feminist rebellion. That bargain is now boomeranging in the direction of a different Trump: Barron. The key to understanding how the Tate brothers rose to such political heights — and why their collapse now threatens to drag the president’s youngest son into a potentially damaging congressional spotlight — can be found in the conservative media ecosystem that laundered Andrew Tate into a right-wing icon. When mainstream platforms like YouTube, Meta and TikTok finally moved to deplatform the Tate brothers in 2022, the right-wing media apparatus stepped in to grant Tate a second — and far more dangerous — life. Tucker Carlson first gave Tate a platform on Fox News back in 2022 and later hosted a long, sympathetic interview. Elon Musk reinstated Tate’s X account, restoring his reach to over 11 million followers while repeatedly tweeting defenses that hand-waved sex trafficking allegations as political distractions. The late Charlie Kirk chimed in on behalf of Tate: “What he says is so powerful. Our society is configured towards collapsing the American man.” MAGA podcaster Candace Owens dedicated hours of airtime to declaring the Tates’ innocence while launching vicious smear campaigns against their victims. The brothers were indicted in Romania in 2023 on charges of rape and human trafficking, accused of running a criminal operation that lured women — including, prosecutors allege, a 17-year-old — into pornography and prostitution. But in February 2025, weeks after Trump’s second inauguration, Romanian authorities lifted the travel restrictions that had kept the Tates in the country, and the pair immediately boarded a private jet to Florida. At the time, the country’s foreign minister Emil Hurezeanu said that a U.S. official had expressed interest in the case . Trump, for his part, said he knew “nothing about” any pressure his administration might have applied. Related The online clip factory that’s radicalizing teen boys The reporting since then has filled in the blanks. ProPublica reported that federal authorities were told to return electronic devices they had seized from the Tates during an investigation and chided by political appointees like Paul Ingrassia — a vocal Tate defender appointed to the General Services Administration. Heidi Blake, the New Yorker reporter who has covered the Tates more exhaustively than perhaps anyone else, has traced a direct line from a Munich Security Conference conversation between U.S. special envoy Richard Grenell and Hurezeanu to Romanian prosecutors reaching out to the Tates’ lawyers within days, asking what the Americans wanted. Experts labeled the political interference highly inappropriate, but it worked. The travel ban on the brothers was lifted. Within days of Andrew Tate landing back on U.S. soil, another woman came forward accusing him of assault and strangulation — the same pattern of abuse, Blake has said, described by victim after victim in this case. This machinery surrounding was never a secret. What has been less investigated, at least until this week, is how deep the personal relationships ran — specifically, the friendship between Andrew Tate and the president’s 20-year-old son. According to reporting in the New York Times, Tate spoke with Barron Trump over a Zoom call last year with a mutual friend present, and the two discussed their shared belief that the Romanian case against Tate was an effort to silence him. That claim — the idea that a rape and trafficking prosecution amounts to censorship — is the same framing Tate’s MAGA allies have pushed for years. Barron’s older brother, Donald Trump Jr., has called Tate’s 2023 detention “absolute insanity.” Tate publicly boasted about his access to MAGA’s top circles, bragging in 2024 that he was “very close with the Trump family” and that he was looking forward to reminding Donald Trump that he was a “bulletproof bada*s.” Start your day with essential news from Salon. Sign up for our free morning newsletter , Crash Course. For Trump’s presidential campaign, the alliance delivered results. By leveraging the manosphere media network that Tate helped anchor, the campaign mobilized a wave of low-propensity young male voters in 2024. So why did the Trump White House suddenly cut the Tate brothers loose? The breakdown was not sparked by a sudden moral awakening regarding sex trafficking or rape. It was likely sparked by the cardinal sin of the MAGA media universe: political disloyalty. In February, as the administration weighed military action in the Middle East, Andrew Tate took to his livestreaming platform to launch a furious, unhinged tirade against Trump’s strike on Iran. “I do not support war with Iran for Israel,” Tate raged to his audience, accusing the administration of driving the country into disaster while ignoring domestic collapse. “If you’re at home in America right now and you feel like your country is f****d… and moral degeneracy is out of control . . . why would the U.S. going into a war with Iran benefit anybody in America at all? Give me one possible reason. NOBODY WANTS THIS WAR.” For a White House that demands absolute, unyielding fealty, Tate’s high-profile attack was an unpardonable breach. When the British government authorized 38 new criminal charges against the Tates and submitted an updated extradition request to the Justice Department, the White House’s calculation was simple. The political cost of protecting two alleged serial rapists, one of whom was actively attacking the president on foreign policy, far outweighed any remaining value they brought to the youth-culture strategy. The administration threw them to the wolves . While the administration may hope that cutting the Tates loose will close the book on this embarrassing chapter, the fallout from their tangled relationships with the first family and the wider MAGA sphere may just be beginning. Rep.Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., has formally urged House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer to open a swift investigation into the Tate brothers’ relationships within Trump’s inner circle. In a searing letter, she highlighted grave diplomatic and ethical concerns regarding whether political networks leveraged their influence to shield accused human traffickers. It doesn’t help the administration’s case that the Tate brothers were, by multiple accounts, still socializing with Trump-world figures in Washington in the days before their arrest. Ansari said she learned only this week that the brothers had traveled to D.C. for meetings, including one with Rep. Wesley Hunt, R-Texas. Our Summer sale is on! Support Salon’s bold journalism. Annual members save 58% The Arizona congresswoman wants the committee to subpoena communications between the Tates and administration officials, and she wants Barron Trump to testify under oath about whether he “influenced official actions or administration policy” about the brothers. There is no evidence that Barron engaged in criminal wrongdoing or played any role in the government’s decisions involving the Tates. But his choice to enthusiastically fraternize with a self-described misogynist facing dozens of horrific felony counts has exposed him to scrutiny. Barron Trump was not an unwitting bystander dragged into a media storm. He was an active participant in defending Andrew Tate, using his influence to validate an accused predator because it fit the edgy, anti-establishment aesthetic of the modern manosphere media. Now, as congressional scrutiny looms and the Tate brothers prepare to face trial in a U.S. federal court before being extradited to London, the president’s youngest son is left facing the stark consequences of his MAGA alliances. President Droupadi Murmu successfully wrapped up her three-country European tour, which included talks to deepen bilateral cooperation in important areas including trade and tourism. On July 20, Murmu began her journey with a state visit to Moldova—the first by an Indian head of state—during which she spoke with her Moldovan counterpart, Maia Sandu, about all aspects of bilateral relations. Additionally, the two nations decided to deepen their collaboration in a number of areas of shared interest, such as agriculture, infrastructure and logistics, healthcare and pharmaceuticals, renewable energy, and innovation. Murmu spent July 21–22 in North Macedonia following his visit to Moldova. She is the first president of India to travel to this Southeast European landlocked nation. Murmu spent July 21–22 in North Macedonia following his visit to Moldova. She is the first president of India to travel to this Southeast European landlocked nation. In addition to discussing cooperation in important areas including tourism, hospitality, and filmmaking, both nations decided to boost bilateral trade during this visit. The topic was brought up during a meeting between President Murmu and her counterpart Gordana Sijanovska-Davkova, which was followed by discussions at the delegation level. She also spoke at the first meeting of the India-North Macedonia Business Forum and the Assembly of North Macedonia. On July 23, Murmu made his first trip to Romania as an Indian head of state in more than thirty years. During her visit, among other important areas of bilateral cooperation, Romania and India decided to quadruple trade over the next three years and bolster defense collaboration. She spoke with Nicusor Dan, her Romanian counterpart, about bilateral relations. On Friday, Murmu spoke at the India-Romania Business Forum in Bucharest, the nation's capital. He also had extensive talks with Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan about bilateral relations. Additionally, the president engaged with members of the Parliamentary Friendship Group between Romania and India. In Romania, there are more than 13,500 Indians, including about 10,000 laborers. Additionally, the Bucharest University of Economic Studies here awarded Murmu an honorary doctorate. The university's highest academic honor, "Doctor Honoris Causa," is given to notable individuals who have made outstanding contributions to scholarship, public service, and international collaboration. Before heading to the airport on Saturday, Murmu had a meeting with members of the Indian community. Russia is escalating pressure on the Ukrainian supply network, launching a new wave of attacks on ports, fuel depots, energy facilities, and logistics centers throughout Ukraine. The Russian army launched earlier today, Saturday 25/7, another fierce air strike on critical military infrastructure in the ports of Mykolaiv, Odesa, and Izmail, while drone attacks took place in many other regions of Ukraine. The goal is obvious: to exhaust resources for the Ukrainian armed forces as much as possible, while fuel shortages and electricity restrictions are already being reported. And while Ukraine tries to recover from yesterday's sweeping Russian strike on a military exhibition in Kyiv, President Zelensky states that it is very likely that another powerful air strike by Russia will occur within the coming hours. Analysts already argue that the military conflict in Ukraine has entered another, much more dangerous stage, and that we are no longer talking about a special military operation but an all-out war. Black Sea ports are burning Russia's pounding of Ukraine's ports in the Black Sea continues mercilessly. Reports indicate that the Ukrainian army has already been left without fuel and electricity. On the morning of July 25, the Russian Ministry of Defense announced that the ports of Mykolaiv, Odesa, and Izmail were hit. At the port of Mykolaiv, according to the Russian announcement, a ship carrying cargo to support the Armed Forces of Ukraine ( AFU ) was destroyed. At the port of Odesa, the attacks targeted unloading and storage points for military equipment, while in Izmail, a military equipment warehouse, port unloading facilities, and fuel and lubricant storage areas were hit. Geran took action Ukrainian logistics facilities were also targeted. In the Sumy region, "Geran" type drones hit the parcel distribution center of the "Nova Poshta" company, which, according to the Russian side, was used for military logistics support. In Zaporizhzhia, "Geran-2" drones carried out a series of attacks on warehouses and a commercial center, which were also allegedly used for military purposes. The attacks caused major fires. In Kramatorsk, an ammunition warehouse was destroyed. The attack caused a fire and hours of successive explosions, with shrapnel flying in the area for at least an hour. Additionally, teams of "Geran" drones attacked targets in the Chernihiv, Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk regions, and in Donbas. Ukrainian forces left without electricity and fuel In the Sumy region, a gas station suffered damage. Four more gas stations were hit in the Poltava region, while in the Chernihiv and Kharkiv regions (in the settlements of Mena and Petropavlivka), "Geran-4 Seeker" drones destroyed two gas stations used for refueling military vehicles. At the same time, energy facilities in the Chernihiv region were hit. During the night, a 110 kV substation in Mena was struck, and during the day, a 40 kV substation in Semenivka. Severe damage is reported. Three more drones attacked a 110 kV substation in Snovsk, cutting off power to facilities used by the Ukrainian armed forces. Russian forces continue to strike the Ukrainian supply chain, affecting both the military supply and the operation of the economy. Wall Street Journal: Trump warning to Ukraine due to Chevron discontent Following attacks on tankers in the Black Sea, the administration of US President Donald Trump warned Ukraine that attacks on non-Russian ships are undesirable, reports the Wall Street Journal , citing sources. According to the newspaper, the warning came after a protest by the head of Chevron, Mike Wirth, to the White House . The cause was the recent attack by Ukrainian naval drones on four tankers near Novorossiysk, including a vessel chartered by Chevron. After the incident, loadings through the Caspian Pipeline Consortium ( CPC ) were restricted, forcing Kazakhstan to reduce oil production. Chevron holds 15% of CPC and 50% of Kazakhstan's largest oil field, Tengiz. According to the company's assessment, prolonged disruptions in the pipeline's operation may force it to reduce production at the field and jeopardize multi-billion dollar revenues from the project. "The US administration considers CPC a vital route for supplying Kazakh oil to European markets, as it represents an alternative to Russian energy resources," an American official told the newspaper. Terrific losses at the exhibition in Kyiv According to the latest information, the Ukrainian side suffered heavy losses from the Russian strike on a military equipment demonstration event near Kyiv, where drones were being presented. According to the Russian Ministry of Defense , top UAV designers and manufacturers, representatives of the leadership of the Ukrainian unmanned systems forces, as well as members of the Ukrainian security services were at the venue at the time of the attack. Ukrainian authorities confirmed that foreign delegations were present, without specifying which ones. Pole dead It was also confirmed by the Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs that among the victims was an employee of a Polish defense company. In the same attack, senior officer of the Ukrainian special forces Eduard Syrenko and Valentyna Savytska, who held a managerial position at the Center for International Cooperation and Strategic Communications of the State Protection Service of Ukraine, were also killed. Budanov called the attack a "lesson" The head of Zelenskyy's office, Kyrylo Budanov, called the attack on the military demonstration near Kyiv a "lesson." As he stated, "in conditions of full-scale war, the organizers of such events and those who approve their conduct must bear personal responsibility for the safety of people." So far it is known that the event was organized by the association of drone manufacturers "Armada." The organization claims that it was a closed practical demonstration that had not been publicly announced, although after the attack, posts promoting similar events appeared on social media. According to the statement by "Armada": "It was a practical demonstration and not an exhibition. Air target detection and interception systems, interceptor drones, counter-drone technologies, electronic warfare systems, electronic reconnaissance, radar, and other solutions were presented. Testing these systems requires an open space and the possibility of practical application." Exhibition organizer arrested According to the Office of the Prosecutor General of Ukraine, the organizer of the military exhibition held near Kyiv that was hit by a Russian missile strike, resulting in the death of 10 people, was arrested. Based on the investigation, one of the weapons manufacturers' associations organized a large-scale event without any approval from the military command, regional and local military administrations, or other competent authorities. Military personnel, representatives of state bodies, international partners, and businesses attended the event. The program, among other things, included a demonstration of air defense systems. More than 300 people were invited to the outdoor venue. At the same time, the nearest shelter, with a total area of only 34 square meters, was located about 100 meters from the venue, placing participants in conditions of increased risk from the beginning. As noted by the Office of the Prosecutor General, invitations were sent nine days before the exhibition, while the organizers informed participants of the exact location and time just one day before the start. The investigation is examining whether these actions could have contributed to Russian armed forces acquiring information to prepare a targeted attack. The main organizer of the event was arrested. He was charged under Article 367, paragraph 3, of the Criminal Code of Ukraine (official negligence causing grave consequences). In the near future, the court will decide on the detention measure to be imposed on him. Due to minor injuries sustained, the suspect is under guard in a medical facility. The name of the suspect has not been made public. Earlier it was reported that the exhibition was organized by the drone manufacturers' association "Armada," led by member of the "National Corps," Vasyl Honcharuk. Zelensky expects a new massive strike President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelensky commented on the attack, stating that this specific event should not have taken place at that location. According to him, criminal proceedings have already been initiated to investigate the incident. At the same time, he warned that a new massive Russian strike is expected over the weekend. "We know from intelligence services and from our partners that the Russians have prepared missiles for a new massive strike against Ukraine. It is possible that it will take place even today," stated Volodymyr Zelensky. The warning of the Americans US intelligence services had already warned since yesterday, Friday 24/7, that within the next 48 hours it is very likely that Russia will launch a massive air strike, possibly the largest in recent months. Reports speak of a concentration of thousands of "Geran" type unmanned aerial vehicles (drones) and a significant number of ballistic and hypersonic missiles in areas near the Ukrainian border, while there are already reports of powerful explosions in Kyiv. At the same time, the Russian army continues its advance both in Donbas and on the northern front, specifically in Kharkiv and Sumy. Raid of 4,000 drones According to Ukrainian monitoring sources citing intelligence data, US intelligence estimates that Russia may be preparing a large-scale air attack against Ukraine within the next 48 hours. According to the same sources, Russia has allegedly concentrated about 4,000 "Geran" type unmanned aerial vehicles (drones) for a possible massive attack. It is also reported that about 400 of these are jet-engine versions, which have higher speed and make interception by air defense systems more difficult. Gathering dozens of missiles In addition, the same sources claim that the concentration of missiles in potential launch areas continues. Estimates published by Ukrainian monitoring channels report: 1) In the Bryansk region: up to 21 ballistic missiles. 2) In the Kursk region: 6 ballistic missiles and 7 Zircon missiles. 3) In the Rostov region: 18 ballistic missiles. 4) In Crimea: 5 ballistic missiles and 4 Zircon missiles. It will be the largest in recent years According to Ukrainian sources, the combination of a large number of drones and missiles may be an indication of preparation for one of the largest air attacks in recent months. Recently, the Armed Forces of Ukraine ( AFU ) have carried out attacks against civilian logistics facilities in Russia. https://www.geosuper.tv/latest/58174-fur.text: Boxing Fury beat Wach ahead of Joshua showdown Fury vs Wach fight in Thailand was not televised By Web Desk July 25, 2026 Tyson Fury in action with Mariusz Wach at Max Muay Thai Stadium in Pattaya on July 24, 2026. — Reuters Former world heavyweight champion Tyson Fury forced Polish boxer Mariusz Wach to retire in a tune-up fight on Friday for his blockbuster showdown against Briton Anthony Joshua later in 2026. The bout in Thailand was not televised, but will feature in the Netflix reality show "At Home with The Furys". About 1,500 fans were there at the event at the Max Muay Thai Stadium in Pattaya. Wach had lost seven of his last 10 fights, and the 46-year-old was unable to continue at the start of the eighth round. "I went through my test tonight. Let's see if he can get through his," Fury said. Fury, who turns 38 in August, has a professional record of 36-2, suffering his only losses in two fights with Ukraine's Oleksandr Usyk in 2024. Joshua, also a former world heavyweight champion, is set to face Kristian Prenga in Saudi Arabia today. Many expected the Gypsy King to fly straight to Jeddah for the AJ fight after Joshua invited him to a face-off. Instead, Fury said he was going home. "I've got to face off with my wife. I've got to iron when I get home. I've been away for six out of the last seven months", he said. "I'm not going to Jeddah, I'm going home to my wife and kids. I'm going to regroup and hopefully we'll have a big fight signed next week." Questions still linger over where the all-British fight would be materialised, with promoter Eddie Hearn saying Joshua's contract stipulates the UK, but industry whispers suggest a venue in America. "We'll head wherever we're going to head," Fury said. "Who knows? It could be in Vegas, New York, Ireland, London. Who knows where the fight's going to be?" https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/orb.text: The Budapest Times Orbán rebrands Fidesz as freedom fighters against ‘Tisza autocracy’ Fidesz is declaring a policy of resistance rather than opposition politics, in order to build a new, broad coalition of freedom against the authoritarian system being constructed by the Tisza Party — Viktor Orbán proclaimed on Saturday in Băile Tușnad, during his lecture on the closing day of the 35th Bálványos Summer Open University and Student Camp. Speaking before an audience of several thousand gathered in front of the open-air stage, the Fidesz president assessed that the Tisza Party wants to and is beginning to build a new authoritarian system. In his view, the dismantling of democracy and the rule of law is currently under way in Hungary, in the interest of exercising exclusive power. Viktor Orbán said: “this is a criminal act,” and while it carries no consequences now, “it will matter when we restore the rule of law, and then it will matter greatly.” He indicated that through tailor-made, retroactively applicable legislation, half of the opposition had been “excluded from politics,” and that “through a tailor-made, retroactively applicable constitutional amendment, the President of the Republic was removed, the President of the Constitutional Court was removed, the Prosecutor General was dismissed, and with that, the rule of law was also abolished.” After removing Fidesz from power, the goal is to eliminate Fidesz altogether — to bar its leaders from politics and to make any political alternative impossible through illegitimate decisions, the former prime minister said. He pointed out that the roughly 3.5 million people who voted for Tisza still believe that arbitrary rule will only be used against Fidesz supporters — but they are mistaken. The essence of arbitrary rule, he said, is that power no longer recognizes its own limits, and one day Tisza voters will also wake up to find there is no one to protect them from abuses of power. According to his summary, this new power is aggressive, violent, and abuses its strength. It is not concerned with the affairs of the country but with persecuting the opposition; it is not trying to create unity but is destabilizing Hungary and disrupting social peace, the Fidesz president listed. Viktor Orbán compared the political system being built in Hungary to developments in Venezuela, which he described as a peculiar blend of communist thinking, political arbitrariness, and economic oppression. In his view, those who voted for change in the spring “I don’t think voted for an abuse of their trust.” The majority of them acted in good faith and expected fewer government mistakes and more economic results, he said. He added that after a defeat, one must always look at the world self-critically, but there is little time for that now, because “freedom is in danger in Hungary.” For this reason, the Fidesz chairman declared, the party must shift from an opposition politics built on self-criticism to a politics of resistance. Among the tasks he listed were the persistent refutation of lies spread about Fidesz, informing the public about the threats posed by the economic situation, defending the achievements of the past 16 years, protecting the victims of abuses of power, and building a coalition against autocracy. “Let us stand up for freedom, let us build the broadest possible resistance, let us create the broadest possible coalition in defense of freedom! We must protect Hungary, because we cannot be, to our shame, Europe’s banana republic!” the former prime minister stated. He added that although Fidesz is a political party, it must not concern itself with questions of power at this time — rather, its role is to serve the “national resistance.” In his view, the goal of the national resistance is the restoration of freedom, and freedom is not a matter for any party, nor is it even a question of the left or the right. “Our task is to stand by our two and a half million voters,” the Fidesz chairman declared. Viktor Orbán noted, however, that this was not enough for a majority. The hundreds of thousands still needed to form one would be brought by “the political waves generated by reality,” and together they would form “a new, broad coalition of freedom,” which would secure “a majority in favour of restoring freedom and democracy,” he said. The former prime minister touched on the fact that in April, 53 percent of Hungarians voted for Tisza and 47 percent against it, adding that this ratio would reverse sooner than people might now think. He explained this by saying that the “Tisza autocratic system” lacks the economic foundations to sustain itself. In his view, Tisza voters would soon realise that this was “not the horse they wanted.” Viktor Orbán stressed that Fidesz must now “draw the widest possible arc, with room for every freedom-loving person.” It must operate as an incubator, not strengthening itself but rather the groups of freedom-loving people, he emphasised. “Let us learn from our mistakes! Let us proudly stand by our achievements, strengthen national resistance, and support freedom-loving people! Let us stand by those who raise their voices, and let us guarantee to the people that what will be taken from them through the coming austerity measures will be given back to them by a new, calm, composed civic government! Difficult times are coming, and we will fight,” the Fidesz president concluded his speech at Tusványos. Artificial intelligence was used for the translation of parts of the original Hungarian text.
