https://travel.yahoo.com/news/articles/9.text: Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Image Credit: Baloncici / Shutterstock. Housing shortages have a way of turning quiet policy debates into loud political fights, and short-term rentals have become one of the most visible targets. From coastal Spain to the hills outside Dublin, governments are running out of patience with platforms that turn apartments into de facto hotels. What started as scattered local rules a few years ago now looks like a coordinated, continent-spanning shift toward outright restriction. Some of these countries have already pulled the trigger on partial bans. Others are still debating the details, but the direction of travel is unmistakable. Here is a country-by-country look at where the pressure is building fastest, and the reasoning driving each government's hand. 1. Spain 1. Spain (By Thomas Ledl, CC BY-SA 4.0 ) Spain has moved from warnings to enforcement with striking speed. Madrid's crackdown has already reduced tourist flats from 16,959 to 14,297, a drop of nearly sixteen percent, while regulators found that only a small fraction of listings, roughly seven percent, actually held valid licences. The national government followed up with serious financial penalties, confirming that Airbnb must face a 64 million euro fine originally imposed in December 2025 by Spain's Ministry of Social Rights, Consumer Affairs and Agenda 2030. Advertisement Advertisement Barcelona remains the most extreme case in the country, and arguably in Europe. City officials confirmed that in 2024 the council announced it would not renew the licenses for the 10,101 apartments approved for tourist use once they expire, with the cutoff set for November 2028. Spain's Constitutional Court upheld the plan in March 2025, and five neighboring municipalities have since said they will end their own tourist rentals on the same timeline. The mayor framed it plainly: the goal is to return those flats to residents in a city where rents had soared. 2. Netherlands 2. Netherlands (Image Credits: Unsplash) Amsterdam has spent years tightening the screws on holiday lets, and it is not finished yet. The city currently limits whole-home lets to 30 nights per year, but that ceiling is about to drop sharply. As of 1 April 2026, the city is set to reduce the annual cap on short-term rentals from 30 nights to just 15 per year in high-demand districts like the city centre and De Pijp, aiming to preserve its character and ensure residents aren't displaced by investors profiting from tourism. Analysts following the sector describe the change bluntly, noting that the new rules severely limit the number of nights hosts can rent out their properties, signaling the end of Airbnb-style rentals as a viable business for many hosts. The city is not alone in the Netherlands, but Amsterdam's approach has become the template other Dutch municipalities are watching closely. Given how far the cap has already fallen in just a few years, a further tightening toward something closer to zero nights for non-primary residences would not be a surprising next step. 3. Hungary 3. Hungary (Image Credits: Unsplash) Hungary crossed a line that few other European countries have dared to cross: a genuine, district-wide ban. Reporting confirms that in Budapest, the central 6th district, Terezvaros, banned short-term rentals outright as of January 1, 2026, after a local referendum and a green light from Hungary's Supreme Court. This makes it the first such ban in the country, in a district where short-term flats had grown to about 8 percent of all housing, and the city as a whole now has more Airbnbs than hotel rooms. Advertisement Advertisement What makes Hungary worth watching closely is the mechanism behind the ban. It was not simply imposed from above; it followed a public vote, which gives it a degree of democratic legitimacy that could make it easier to replicate elsewhere. Analysts covering the story note that other districts could follow, and given Budapest's citywide imbalance between tourist flats and hotel capacity, a broader municipal or even national response seems plausible within the next few years. 4. Greece 4. Greece (Image Credits: Unsplash) Athens has taken a more gradual route, but the trajectory points toward stricter limits rather than looser ones. The city imposed a freeze on new short-term rental registrations in three central municipal districts, covering tourist-heavy areas such as Plaka, Koukaki, and Exarcheia, which began in January 2025 and has been extended through 2026. Existing licensed properties can keep operating, but the door has effectively closed to newcomers in those neighborhoods. The freeze is not staying contained to the capital. Government officials have signaled the freeze may spread to Thessaloniki, Santorini, Paros, and Chania, all destinations that have struggled with the same tension between tourist demand and resident housing. If Athens extends the freeze into an outright ban, or if the government decides to formalize the policy nationally, Greece could move from cautious pilot programs to something considerably firmer. 5. Ireland 5. Ireland (Image Credits: Unsplash) Few countries illustrate the housing versus tourism standoff as starkly as Ireland. One striking comparison making the rounds shows 2,300 available rental homes on Daft.ie against upwards of 8,000 short-term lets on Airbnb, a gap that has fueled political urgency. The government's response now includes a rural planning measure that would prevent newly built one-off rural homes from being used as short-term rentals for at least 10 years after construction. Advertisement Advertisement On top of that, Dublin is preparing a national registration scheme, confirming that Ireland's new short-term rental rules, effective May 2026, require all properties rented for up to 21 nights to register with Fáilte Ireland, aimed at easing the housing crisis by potentially shifting 10,000 properties to long-term rentals. Separately, ministers agreed to restrict short-term lets in towns with populations above 20,000, giving existing operators two years to comply. None of this is a nationwide ban yet, but between rural restrictions, urban caps, and mandatory registration, Ireland is assembling most of the legal groundwork a full ban would need. 6. Portugal 6. Portugal (Image Credits: Unsplash) Portugal was an early mover in Europe's regulatory shift, and it has kept adding layers since. Its largest cities began restricting Airbnb-style rentals in 2021 by banning new licenses in designated housing pressure zones across Lisbon, Porto, and Faro. What started as a controversial experiment has since been reinforced rather than rolled back. The government followed up with structural changes rather than just zone freezes. In 2022, officials introduced mandatory registration, stricter safety rules on short-term rentals, and tax incentives for landlords to switch back to residential letting, while also increasing investment in social housing to encourage growth in affordable housing. Portugal has avoided a blanket ban so far, but the pattern of steadily narrowing where new licenses can even be issued suggests the pressure zones could eventually cover most of the country's tourist hotspots. 7. France 7. France (Image Credits: Unsplash) France has arguably passed the most sweeping national legislation of any European country. The Loi Le Meur, described as going further than any other EU member state, was adopted in November 2024 and progressively implemented throughout 2025–2026. Under the new rules, every meublé de tourisme in France must obtain a 13-digit registration number via the national Declaloc portal and display it on all listings from 20 May 2026. Advertisement Advertisement The penalties attached to noncompliance are not symbolic. Fines run as high as 10,000 euros for missing registration, 20,000 euros for false declarations, and up to 50,000 euros for more serious infractions, and platforms are legally required to pull noncompliant listings. Paris itself has already tightened the screws further, cutting the maximum number of rental days for a primary residence from 120 to 90 as of January 2025. With over 90,000 listings in the capital alone by the end of 2024, France has built one of the strictest enforcement systems in Europe, and there is little sign officials plan to loosen it. 8. Germany 8. Germany (Image Credits: Unsplash) Berlin has run one of Europe's toughest short-term rental regimes for over a decade, and courts keep backing it up. The city's Zweckentfremdungsverbot, its ban on the use of residential space for short-term rentals without special permission, was introduced in 2014 and has been upheld and strengthened over the years. That legal foundation was reaffirmed again recently, as a court ruling in September 2025 reaffirmed the city's position that residential housing must be preserved for long-term tenants. The practical effect has been significant, with the policy having successfully removed hundreds of Airbnb properties from the market in Berlin alone. Other German cities have watched Berlin's approach closely, and given how consistently German courts have sided with residential-preservation arguments, it would not be surprising to see similar permission-based bans spread to other major cities facing their own rent pressures. 9. Italy 9. Italy (Image Credits: Pexels) Italy has not banned short-term rentals outright, but the direction of its 2026 policy overhaul leaves little doubt about where things are headed. The government's draft budget would replace the reduced 21 percent tax rate for a single short-term rental property with a flat 26 percent rate applied across all short-term rental income, a move explicitly tied to concerns about overtourism and housing shortages. On top of the tax change, the country rolled out a mandatory national identification code, with more than 620,000 CIN codes issued in the first year of the national database. Advertisement Advertisement The 2026 Budget Law added another structural limit that pushes hosts toward formal business status. Under the new framework, the short-term rental tax scheme applies to a maximum of two properties per tax year, with anything from the third property onward considered a business activity requiring VAT registration. None of this amounts to a ban yet, but the combination of higher taxes, mandatory registration, and business-status thresholds is squeezing casual hosts out of the market in a way that could easily tip into stricter local bans if housing pressure keeps building. Taken together, these nine countries show a pattern rather than a coincidence. Housing scarcity, tourist overcrowding, and political frustration with platforms like Airbnb have pushed governments from mild registration rules toward genuine bans, expiring licenses, and shrinking night caps. Whether any of them reach a true nationwide ban remains uncertain, but the legal and political groundwork is already in place in most of them. For travelers and hosts alike, the safest assumption right now is that the rules will keep tightening, not loosening, at least for the next few years. How MI6 fascinates spy watchers around the world Britain’s spooks take quiet satisfaction from survey ranking Secret Intelligence Service Europe’s top espionage agency Dan Sabbagh Defence and security editor Sat 8 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google M I6 has the swagger of James Bond; its French equivalent, DGSE, the complexities of the television drama Le Bureau. The film and TV shows may be fictional, but a survey run by a French magazine that placed the British spy agency above the French as No 1 across all of Europe this week is not. L’Express , a news weekly, conducted a Eurovision-style poll of 60 current and former spies from across the continent, plus the CIA and Israel’s Mossad. Each was asked to rank their top five foreign intelligence agencies, in secret, naturally enough. MI6 was first with 251 points ahead of DGSE on 169, with other agencies trailing behind. The result did not surprise Alexandra Saviana, a deputy editor at the publication, specialising in defence and intelligence, but the margin of victory did. “It is a huge point gap,” she said, reflecting the opinions of insiders and allies, 17 of whom are or were agency chiefs in a interconnected, covert ecosystem. View image in fullscreen Desmond Llewelyn as Q and Roger Moore as James Bond in The Spy Who Loved Me (1977). Photograph: Sportsphoto/Allstar At MI6’s headquarters in Vauxhall, London, there has been no sign of a public reaction from its chief, Blaise Metreweli . But there is a quiet satisfaction at the unexpected verdict, not least because the agency values how it is perceived by both allies and adversaries. “Reputation matters a lot in the espionage game,” said a former Whitehall insider. “British spies fascinate Europe , and beyond,” L’Express explained in its cover story. Saviana added that MI6’s success in the poll was principally down to its record in recruiting and running high-level human sources over generations: a focus on human intelligence in an era dominated by technology, intercepts and satellite monitoring. “The British have the ability to play the long game, to bet on sources over 10 years, a bit like the Russians,” a former French DGSE spy told the magazine, adding “and they have a penchant for underhand tactics” without revealing what they meant. One ex-spy voiced scepticism about the survey and added that a human intelligence service such as MI6 was only as good as the high-value agents on its books. Under Richard Moore , MI6’s previous chief, there were worries that it no longer had enough. Others, including Saviana, accept that greater credit might have been given to MI6’s sister agency, the signals intelligence experts at GCHQ, but it was not in the poll. MI6’s reputation among its peers, the French publication said, was built on “long standing tradition”, including recruiting cold war assets, most notably the KGB’s Oleg Gordievsky , a double agent through late 1970s and early 80s, who helped convince Margaret Thatcher to take Mikhail Gorbachev seriously before he had to be dramatically smuggled into Finland in 1985, his cover finally blown. View image in fullscreen Ronald Reagan meeting Oleg Gordievsky, an MI6 cold war asset, in the White House, 1987. Photograph: Eraza Collection/Alamy Not every mole evaded capture. Alireza Akbari, a former Iranian deputy defence minister who had become a British citizen, was arrested on a return to Iran in 2019 and executed in 2023. Prior to his death, he confessed to being an MI6 agent. Though the confessions appeared coerced, spies from a number of countries indicated he was the person who had passed on the existence of the Fordow nuclear enrichment site in 2008. In the run-up to the 2003 Iraq war, MI6 was accused of simplistically supporting the case for war, promoting what turned out to be false sources, claiming that Iraq’s leader, Saddam Hussein, could attack UK targets within “45 minutes”, and relied on one source who described supposed chemical weapons devices that were remarkably similar to one in the Hollywood movie The Rock . It was a low point. L’Express argued that MI6 had rehabilitated itself in the run-up to the Ukraine war in February 2022, correctly warning in conjunction with the CIA that Russia was about to invade, while French and German counterparts were sceptical up until the last minute, having misjudged the situation. The chief of the German BND agency even flew into Kyiv the day before the invasion, seemingly unprepared. It reflects MI6’s close and longstanding relationship with the CIA, part of the wider Five Eyes arrangements for intelligence sharing, between the US, UK, Australia, Canada and New Zealand, that are the envy of continental Europe, even allowing for the complexities posed by Donald Trump’s chaotic presidency. “Every other country wants to say they are the sixth eye,” Saviana said. Fiction also has its advantages. Gordon Corera, a co-presenter of The Rest is Classified podcast, recalled that a former MI6 chief once told him a story of a young officer going somewhere far flung, not knowing whether the person he was trying to cultivate spoke English. “As he walked into the room the contact extended his hand and said: ‘Hello, Mr Bond.’ The former chief remarked: ‘I doubt if he would have received such a warm welcome if he’d been from the Belgian secret service.’” Explore more on these topics Espionage MI6 Europe UK security and counter-terrorism James Bond news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP View image in fullscreen The wreckage of a Nazi warship has become visible above the exceptionally low water line on the Danube near Prahovo in Serbia this week. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP Drought Nazi shipwrecks emerge from the depths as Europe’s Danube dries up Unexploded ordnance and a military motorcycle also recovered following record heat and drought conditions Oliver Holmes Sat 8 Aug 2026 06.55 EDT Last modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 08.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Record-low water levels in the Danube have exposed remnants of Europe’s Nazi past, with dozens of second world war ships emerging from the riverbed during an intense drought. In the middle of the river on the Serbian and Romanian border, a broken-up hull was visible on a sandbank that is normally underwater. Other vessels were partly submerged, some still believed to be laden with weapons. View image in fullscreen The wreckage of a second world war German warship near Prahovo, Serbia on Tuesday. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP The ships were part of Adolf Hitler’s Black Sea fleet that the German military deliberately sank towards the end of the war to slow down the Soviet advance. Historians say up to 200 German warships were scuttled in this way in September 1944. But Nazi Germany did not surrender until the following year in May 1945. Sunken WWII era ships appear as Danube levels go down amid drought The ships have been revealed during previous droughts only to disappear again as water levels rose along the second-longest river in Europe. The Serbian government has tried in the past to remove the wrecks, but most remain in place owing to the explosives they carried. View image in fullscreen The Serbian government has previously tried to remove wrecks such as the one pictured here near Prahovo. Photograph: Darko Vojinović/AP Other second world war remnants have been found in other parts of the river, including a German military motorcycle in Budapest, Hungary . In Slovakia, police recovered an unexploded British 1,543lb (700kg) bomb . Police said authorities loaded it on to a “specially modified firefighter vehicle with a sand bed, which ensured its safe transport” and took it to a 5-metre deep pit to detonate it. View image in fullscreen A second world war German military motorcycle is displayed at the defence ministry museum in Budapest, Hungary on Wednesday. Photograph: Tamas Purger/EPA In 1944, Britain’s Royal Air Force mined the river to disrupt enemy troops. The Danube, which flows through 10 countries, has become increasingly difficult to navigate as low water levels create dangerous conditions. Prolonged droughts have left major European rivers at significantly lower water levels than is typical for the time of year, creating an energy crisis as many power plants rely on their natural water supply for cooling. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Photograph: Tamas Purger/EPA Slovakia, Austria and Hungary registered record temperatures this week. Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Demis Hassabis at Google's offices in London. Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The Guardian DeepMind Google DeepMind enters a new era as co-founder Demis Hassabis shifts AI role Observers express concern that the division has lost its independence and commercial reality has taken over Dan Milmo and Aisha Down Sat 8 Aug 2026 08.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google When Sir Demis Hassabis said AI had brought the world to a “pivotal moment in human history” last month, he knew another big change was imminent. This shift was closer to home. The Nobel prize-winning head of Google DeepMind, Google’s AI unit, announced this week he was relinquishing his day-to-day duties as chief executive and becoming chair. He is also taking on the role of chief scientist at DeepMind’s parent, Alphabet. Hassabis and DeepMind have been key players in AI’s breakthrough era. The 50-year-old co-founded DeepMind and sold it to Google in 2014, which gave him the resources to oversee a number of advances. These included building the AlphaGo system that mastered the Chinese board game Go and developing AlphaFold, a programme that predicts the 3D structure of proteins. The latter resulted in Hassabis being jointly awarded the 2024 Nobel prize in chemistry. A former Google executive said the leadership overhaul showed London-based DeepMind being brought firmly into the orbit of its parent in Mountain View, California. DeepMind will now be run by Hassabis’s longstanding colleague, the US-based Koray Kavukcuoglu, who will take the non-CEO role of senior vice-president of DeepMind. “The era of DeepMind as an independent actor is over and the obvious sign of that is you have gone from a charismatic founder-leader to appointing Koray in a non-CEO leadership role. Koray is a technical character, not an inspirational figure like Demis,” said the former executive. The ex-Google employee added that it would be “galling” for Google and Hassabis that the latest iterations of Google’s flagship AI model series, Gemini, have lost ground to rival models developed by its US rivals Anthropic and OpenAI. Hassabis has said he was looking forward to focusing more on the “big picture” for AI and believed he was handing over operational management of a unit that was well placed for the competitive battles ahead. View image in fullscreen The London DeepMind office will be brought into the orbit of its parent in Mountain View, California, a former Google executive said. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Internally, DeepMind is a workplace where there have been political tensions. Employees who spoke to the Guardian said there was internal disquiet over the company’s work with the Pentagon. Earlier this year, a former Google DeepMind employee launched a legal challenge against Google, claiming they were unfairly dismissed for their views on Gaza. That employee was involved in unionisation efforts at Google DeepMind, which have taken place against a backdrop of concern that Google’s AI could assist militaries, including the Israel Defense Forces. Another Google DeepMind employee resigned from the company in mid-July, citing Google’s work with the Pentagon and the US Department of Homeland Security. One said to the Guardian that Hassabis’s departure was the “end of an era”. “Now the person we were supposed to trust to get the right outcomes for humanity has stepped away,” they said. Google DeepMind “has become just another subdivision of Google”, they added. Rosa Curling, the executive director of Foxglove, a campaign group that supported the Google DeepMind employee in their legal challenge, said: “The departure of the co-founder of a company that once prided itself on its ethical credentials is likely to cause further concern among its frontier AI staff about how their work will end up being used in the real world.” Google has said it is committed to the “private and public sector consensus” that AI should not be used for domestic mass surveillance or autonomous weaponry without “appropriate human oversight”. While Google has declined a voluntary union recognition agreement in London, it has said it valued “the constructive and direct dialogue that we have with our employees about building a positive and successful workplace”. View image in fullscreen Some Google staff have been uncomfortable about its work with the Pentagon. Photograph: Joshua Roberts/Reuters On the commercial side, a new cutting-edge model, Gemini 3.5 Pro, has yet to be released amid reports it has been delayed owing to attempts to improve its code-writing abilities – a core part of the appeal of Anthropic and OpenAI’s best products. Google’s two AI labs, London-based DeepMind and California-based Google Brain, were merged into Google DeepMind under Hassabis’s leadership three years ago. Control now appears to be moving back to the US, where Google’s co-founder Sergey Brin is reportedly playing a bigger role in AI development. Citing the departure of the leading AI researcher Yann LeCun from Meta and Geoffrey Hinton from Google as another example of “the end of an era in the AI ecosystem”, the former executive added: “This is very clearly a sign that the science-driven agenda of leadership in these labs has given way to cold, hard commercial reality that all of these companies want to make a return on the hundreds of billions of dollars they have invested in AI.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to TechScape A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Preview latest after newsletter promotion The source added, however, that Google still had the benefit of being able to combine its Gemini models with an impressive suite of products, from its all-conquering search product to its cloud platform and YouTube. Thanks to its search business it also has the money to continue investing heavily in AI, having generated net income – a US measure of profit – of $132bn (£98bn) last year. View image in fullscreen Hassabis has called for a US safety body to assess cutting-edge AI models. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters Hassabis has also taken on a more statesman-like role in recent years. The reference to a “pivotal moment” came in a blogpost in which he called for a US safety body to assess cutting-edge models, with the hope it would lead to the establishment of global standards. The need for such a body, Hassabis argued, was pressing because the tech industry was approaching the “pivotal” point of achieving AGI, the term for a theoretical state of AI where a system can perform any human cognitive task – which also means being capable of performing white collar jobs in sectors such as law, finance and health. A Google spokesperson said: “This is a move Demis has been thinking about for a while. He is very excited, and this will give him more time to focus on AI-driven scientific breakthroughs.” They disputed that the changes had anything to do with the performance of Gemini. Hassabis’s move was announced alongside the departure of Jeff Dean, a veteran Google engineer and DeepMind’s chief scientist, who is leaving along with three other top researchers to form an AI startup called Discovery Loop. According to one former Google employee, Dean’s departure could augur further personnel losses. Dean’s move also follows OpenAI’s poaching in June of Google’s Noam Shazeer, a leading figure in the field as co-author of the 2017 research paper Attention is All You Need, a crucial step in developing chatbots. “It’s hugely problematic for Google,” said Jeremy Nixon, a former AI researcher at Google and founder of Infinity Artificial Intelligence Institute, a startup. “It’s problematic because of who Jeff will hire and because the primary reason people want to work at Google is because of him and Noam Shazeer and all these other phenomenal researchers. It’s no longer true to say that if you want to work with the greatest researchers on the planet, you go to Google DeepMind.” Nixon added that Dean was an “angelic diplomat” who could “deal with these complex political organisations”. Google denies it faces a post-Dean talent crisis, pointing to attrition rates for AI talent for the first half of this year being lower than they were at this time last year. If AI is indeed facing a pivotal moment, Google has just had one. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Arron Banks said he believed the Sunday Times used hacked information, an accusation the newspaper denied. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters View image in fullscreen Arron Banks said he believed the Sunday Times used hacked information, an accusation the newspaper denied. Photograph: Toby Melville/Reuters Arron Banks Arron Banks ‘hired private detective’ to look into journalist who investigated Reform UK Asked whether he targeted reporter who investigated party finances, Brexit campaigner says: ‘When you live by the sword, you die by the sword’ Geraldine McKelvie Sat 8 Aug 2026 07.11 EDT Last modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 07.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The prominent Reform UK member and Brexit campaigner Arron Banks is said to have set private investigators on a Sunday Times journalist after he broke a series of stories about Nigel Farage . Banks is alleged to have paid for the services of investigators to examine Gabriel Pogrund, editor of the paper’s Insight investigations team. The detail emerged in the New Statesman on Friday. When approached for comment, Banks did not appear to deny it. He is said to have instructed Precision Risk and Intelligence, a firm he once owned, to examine Pogrund. The Sunday Times and the Guardian have broken a series of stories in recent months revealing how cash has poured into Reform and Farage personally from donors and wealthy benefactors. Pogrund is believed to have been targeted after a story in the Sunday Times last month revealed that Farage has received financial support from the convicted criminal George Cottrell , known as “Posh George”. In response to the New Statesman report, Banks said: “We believe the Sunday Times used hacked information and that was an area of interest. We do have an investigative arm that’s got advanced capabilities.” Asked directly whether he had paid investigators to look into Pogrund, he said: “When you live by the sword, you die by the sword.” The Sunday Times last night denied the accusation that its stories were based on illegally sourced information. The paper described the hiring of private investigators to snoop on its journalists as “reprehensible”. A spokesperson said: “If what Mr Banks claims to have done is true then it is reprehensible that his reaction to our reporting is to place a journalist under surveillance … This story was not based on hacked information. It was based on responsible and professional journalism.” The gifts the Reform UK leader Nigel Farage received in the 12 months before being elected as MP for Clacton have been subject to widespread media scrutiny in recent months. MPs are obliged to declare any political donations they received in the year before their election but Farage has repeatedly claimed that it was not until the month before the general election, in July 2024, that he decided to stand. He has claimed he was not obliged to declare any donations he received before deciding to run for election, as he was a media personality at the time. Farage admission over timing of Reform leadership talks raises fresh doubts over £5m gift Read more In April, the Guardian reported that he had accepted a £5m gift from Christopher Harborne , a billionaire donor to Reform UK. The Sunday Times has reported that Cottrell paid for security, accommodation and social media support for Farage during this time. The newspaper also said that Cottrell helped to broker a “comeback deal” for Farage to return to Reform as party leader months before he announced he would stand. Cottrell’s mother, the retired stylist Fiona Cottrell, made a series of donations to Reform UK in the weeks before the general election. Two transfers of £250,000 were made directly to the party in May 2024. She then gave £1m to Britain Means Business, a company owned by Reform UK’s deputy leader, Richard Tice. Britain Means Business gave the party two donations of £250,000 shortly afterwards. The Guardian told how they later became the subject of a suspicious activity report by the National Crime Agency. Suspicious activity reports are not crime reports but exist to identify potential incidents of money laundering. The Metropolitan police are investigating Reform UK’s finances. The Guardian revealed that both George and Fiona Cottrell have been interviewed under caution but no arrests have been made. On Saturday morning, the Guardian asked Banks if Reform UK had known about or sanctioned the surveillance on Pogrund, or if any other journalists had been targeted. “I have nothing else to add,” he said. “Other than to say I have spoken to no one at Reform on this matter, nor would I.” Reform UK was contacted for comment. Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The Guardian View image in fullscreen The former Conservative minister Ann Widdecombe was found dead at her home in Devon on 9 July. Photograph: Murdo Macleod/The Guardian UK news Widdecombe murder police reopen inquiry into alleged attempt to firebomb Farage’s home Watchdog examines handling of an incident last year that was treated as an attempted burglary Donna Ferguson and Nadeem Badshah Sat 8 Aug 2026 04.59 EDT First published on Fri 7 Aug 2026 18.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Counter-terrorism police investigating the death of Ann Widdecombe have reopened an inquiry into an incident last year, in which Nigel Farage’s home was allegedly firebombed. During the incident in April 2025, a lit incendiary device was pushed through the Reform UK leader’s letterbox, according to reports. Police did not identify any suspects during their investigation of the incident at the time, which was treated as an attempted burglary, and so the investigation was closed, pending any new lines of inquiry. Since the case was reopened, CTP London said it had identified a line of inquiry “which may have been relevant” but was “not identified and pursued by [counter-terrorism police] at the time”. The police watchdog said it was now investigating the conduct of a CTP London staff member over allegations that they “failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry”. Vicki Evans, senior national coordinator for counter-terrorism policing, said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by counter-terrorism policing south-east into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year.” CTP London made a “mandatory conduct referral” to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) on Friday. A spokesperson for the IOPC said: “We can confirm that the IOPC has decided to independently investigate the conduct of a counter-terrorism policing London staff member following a referral received earlier today. “The conduct relates to an allegation the individual failed to identify and pursue a line of inquiry relating to an attempted burglary reported in April 2025. Counter-terrorism policing London has been notified of our decision, and no further information is available at this early stage.” Widdecombe, 78, a Reform UK spokesperson and former Conservative minister, was found dead on 9 July at her home in Haytor on Dartmoor, Devon, having sustained serious injuries. Last month, a 28-year-old man was charged with the former MP’s murder. Joshua Kerry, from Rotherham in South Yorkshire, was arrested on suspicion of murder on 11 July. He was also arrested on suspicion of the commission, preparation or instigation of acts of terrorism but has not been charged with this offence. Devon and Cornwall police initially arrested a 26-year-old man from Newton Abbot in Devon, but later released him and said he was no longer part of the investigation. Widdecombe served as Conservative MP for Maidstone, Kent, for 23 years. She subsequently represented south-west England as a member of the European parliament for the Brexit party and in 2023 joined Reform UK . https://www.dw.com/en/bulgaria-unknown-d.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IUUz Rumen Radev said that Bulgarian authorities are working to determine the drone's origin [FILE: Jul 20, 2026] Image: BGNES Advertisement Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev has said that a drone entered Bulgaria 's airspace from the north and exploded near the Romanian border on Saturday morning. According to the prime minister, there were no casualties or damage to infrastructure, as the drone exploded in a sunflower field 100 meters from the border with Romania . He noted that neither of the two neighboring countries had detected the drone. Radev added that the incident occurred about 1,000 meters from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine. "We will continue to monitor the situation and strengthen surveillance. Following this incident, we will also redeploy border police anti-drone detection and countermeasure capabilities from the border with Turkey to the border with Romania," Radev said. What do we know about the drone? Speaking after an extraordinary meeting of his cabinet's security council, Radev did not specify where the drone came from or what type it was. However, he said that it was believed that the drone was carrying a significant amount of explosives given the strength of the blast and the black smoke it produced. When asked if the drone was civilian or military, Radev said that there was photographic evidence available. However, because the drone was damaged in the explosion, it was impossible to determine its type. "This is not a toy drone; it's a larger drone," he told journalists, according to the BTA news agency. However, Radev also mentioned that the drone was not detected in Bulgarian or Romanian airspace because such drones are difficult to detect due to their small size. https://www.politico.eu/article/russia-a.text: Russian airstrikes across Ukraine have killed at least 12 people and injured dozens more in multiple drone and missile attacks overnight, according to local authorities. The Ukrainian Air Force said Russia launched six missiles and 151 attack drones throughout Friday night, hitting 12 locations. Ukrainian authorities managed to down 135 drones. The attacks came as Ukraine continues to urge Western allies to provide more air defense systems and interceptor missiles. Advertisement Advertisement President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the drone attacks killed three people — a 3-year-old child and the child’s grandparents — in a village in the Kyiv region. The six ballistic missiles struck civilian infrastructure in Kyiv, killing one person, he said. “More pressure is needed. New sanctions that will prevent the production of these ballistic missiles,” Zelenskyy said on X. “And we definitely need more protection for our people,” he added, appealing to allies to provide missile interceptors to strengthen Ukraine’s defenses against Russia’s aerial assault. In the Zaporizhzhia region, in southeast Ukraine, three people were killed and four were wounded following the overnight attack, regional governor Ivan Fedorov said . A further five people were killed and nearly 50 people wounded in the regions of Kharkiv , Donetsk and Kherson , according to regional authorities. Separately, Zelenskyy visited Serbia on Saturday — his first trip to the country since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine — to meet with President Aleksandar Vučić and Prime Minister Đuro Macut. Zelenskyy said the talks had focused on rebuilding infrastructure, readying a free-trade agreement this year, and preparing for the winter to come. This article has been updated. https://www.politico.eu/article/gabriel-.text: Former prime minister and presidential candidate Gabriel Attal has filed a complaint over an alleged Russian disinformation campaign ahead of next year’s French presidential election, local news outlets reported on Saturday. Attal’s lawyers told French media that the complaint, filed on Friday, denounces “acts of foreign interference, manipulation of information, fabrication of content likely to undermine the fundamental interests of the nation and the sincerity of the upcoming presidential election.” They told BFMTV that several accounts on social network X, some of which impersonated French and international media, had disseminated fake video reports and newspaper articles attributing false statements to Attal that were “intended to discredit him as a candidate.” Advertisement Advertisement Attal, the candidate of President Emmanuel Macron’s Renaissance party, said earlier this week that he had been a victim of attempted election interference originating in Russia, and that he expected such destabilization efforts to increase ahead of the April 2027 presidential election. Viginum, the country’s agency for fighting online disinformation, confirmed it had detected the operation against Attal and said it bore the hallmarks of pro-Russian disinformation tactics. Attal is the latest French presidential candidate to have fallen victim to such disinformation campaigns. Former prime minister Edouard Philippe was reportedly targeted last week, as was center-left parliamentarian Raphaël Glucksmann .

https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/08/lann.text: Menü Kereső Rugalmas iskolakezdést, 35 perces tanórákat, kevesebb leckét javasol az alsósoknak az Oktatási Minisztérium új javaslatcsomagja Belföld Thüringer Barbara Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom 14 pontos szakmai javaslatcsomagot küldött az általános iskoláknak a közoktatásért felelős államtitkár – jelentette be Lannert Judit oktatási és gyermekügyi miniszter pénteken. „Kevesebb stressz. Több élmény. Jobb iskola. Rugalmas tanulásszervezés az alsó tagozatban” – írta Lannert hozzátéve, hogy az alsó tagozatnak a kíváncsiságról, a felfedezésről, a közös élményekről és az örömteli tanulásról kell szólnia. Szombaton felkerült a Kormany.hu oldalára a „Legyen élmény a tanulás!” című 14 pontos javaslatcsomag , amit Kókayné Lányi Marietta közoktatásért felelős államtitkár eljuttatott az iskoláknak az alsó tagozat gyermekközpontú megújítása érdekében. A javaslatok a következőket tartalmazzák: 1. Gyermekbarát iskolakezdés és napirend: A célja a tanítási nap nyugodt, biztonságos és a gyermekek életkori sajátosságaihoz igazodó kezdése, aminek a javasolt szakmai megoldása a rugalmas napkezdés lenne. „Az iskola a tanítási idő kezdete előtt alakítson ki reggeli ráhangoló idősávot beszélgetőkörrel, közös olvasással, mesehallgatással, csendes érkezéssel vagy mozgásos tevékenységgel.” 2. Rugalmas óraszervezés: rövidebb órák és komplex blokkok. Az elérni kívánt cél a figyelmi terhelés mérséklése és az elmélyült, tevékenységalapú tanulás feltételeinek megteremtése lenne. A javasolt szakmai megoldás a 35 perces tanítási órák, valamint a hosszabb, többféle tevékenységre lehetőséget biztosító, összevont tanulási blokkok alkalmazásának lehetőségének megfontolása. 3. Hosszabb mozgásos szünetek, nyugodt ebédidő és pihenőidő: A cél a tanulók fizikai és mentális regenerálódásának biztosítása lenne a tanítási nap során. A javasolt megoldás az lenne, hogy az iskola biztosítson hosszabb udvari vagy mozgásos szünetet, megfelelő időt a nyugodt étkezésre, valamint szükség szerint mese-, csendes vagy pihenőidőt. 4. Az óraszámok és tanulási tartalmak rugalmas elosztása: az elérni kívánt cél a merev napi tantárgyi rend helyett életkorhoz igazodó, változatos tanulási ritmus kialakítása lenne. A javasolt szakmai megoldások között a minisztérium többek között azt írja, hogy a helyi tanterv és az órarend tervezésekor az iskola tudatosan használja a kétévfolyamos cikluson belüli óraszám-átcsoportosítás lehetőségét. 5. Komplex, tantárgyközi élmény- és projektnapok: a cél a tanulási tartalmak összekapcsolása, a kíváncsiság, az együttműködés és a gyakorlati alkalmazás erősítése lenne. Erre azt javasolják, hogy az iskola lehetőség szerint havi rendszerességgel szervezzen a tantervi célokhoz illeszkedő komplex napokat vagy blokkokat, például mese-, víz-, erdő-, kert-, könyvtári, múzeumi, művészeti vagy helytörténeti napot. 6. Iskolán kívüli tanulási helyszínek rendszeres használata: ennek célja az lenne, hogy a tanulás személyes tapasztalathoz, a helyi környezethez és a valós élethelyzetekhez kapcsolása lenne. Ehhez a javasolt szakmai megoldás az lenne, hogy az iskola építse be éves munkatervébe a könyvtári, múzeumi, természeti, közművelődési, helytörténeti és sportlétesítményben megvalósuló foglalkozásokat, és gondoskodjon azok biztonságos, tanítási célú megszervezéséről. 7. Az alsó tagozatos házi feladat észszerű korlátozása: az elérni kívánt cél a gyermekek délutáni és családi idejének védelme, valamint az önállóan teljesíthető, valóban fejlesztő gyakorlás előtérbe helyezése lenne. A javasolt megoldás szerint a a pedagógiai program határozza meg az alsó tagozatos házi feladat mennyiségi és minőségi korlátait. Első évfolyamon és egész napos iskolában lehetőség szerint ne legyen kötelező otthoni írásbeli feladat; hétvégére és szünetre csak kivételesen adjanak kötelező feladatot. 8. A fejlesztő értékelés megerősítése: a cél az lenne, hogy az értékelés a tanuló fejlődését, önbizalmát és következő tanulási lépéseit támogassa, ne pusztán minősítsen. Azt javasolják, az iskola dolgozzon ki érthető, konkrét és személyre szabott visszajelzési gyakorlatot. Használjon fejlesztő értékelési mintákat, dolgozza ki a tanulói önértékelés módját és kezdeményezze a szöveges vagy más fejlesztő értékelési forma alkalmazását. 9. A mindennapos testnevelés élményszerű megszervezése: aminek a célja a mozgás örömének, a testi biztonságnak, az együttműködésnek és az egészséges életmód alapjainak kialakítása lenne. Bár nem törölnék a mindennapos testnevelést azt javasolják, hogy abban kapjon nagyobb szerepet a szabadtéri játék, a séta, a néptánc, a természetjárás, az ügyességi és csapatjáték, valamint más közösségi és élménymozgás. 10. A délutáni idősáv gyermekközpontú újragondolása: valószínűleg ennek fognak a legjobban örülni a gyerekek, ugyanis a kevesebb vagy egyaltalán nem létező házifeladat írása helyett ebben az időben pihenhetnének, játszhatnának. Azt javasolják, az iskola építsen be rövid, rendszeres mese-, felolvasás- vagy történethallgatási alkalmakat a tanítási nap elejére, a tanulási blokkok közé vagy a délutáni foglalkozásokba. A gyakorlat legyen minden alsó tagozatos osztály számára elérhető. 14. Bántalmazásmegelőzés és biztonságos iskolai környezet: az elérendő cél a fizikai és a digitális bántalmazás megelőzése, a társas biztonság, az elfogadás és a konfliktuskezelési kultúra fejlesztése lenne. Szervezzen rendszeres beszélgetőköröket, együttműködésre építő tanulási helyzeteketet, közös szabadidős programokat. https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/articl.text: “Miluim [IDF reserve duty] is like being on an emotional roller coaster,” was how Esther described the last few years of her husband being at war. “A rollercoaster that you forget that you're on, but you wake up right before the drop and try to breathe through it and not vomit.”Esther, 36, was born in New York but moved to Israel in 2005, aged 15, as part of an immersive high school program called Naale. Following this, she did two years of national service in the Gaza border area, and then began a degree in glass and ceramic design at Bezalel QAcademy of Arts and Design in Jerusalem. While working at Artza, the company of Itai, the brother of Jerusalem Post photojournalist Chen Schimmel, she met her husband Yonah, who is Itai's friend.Esther and Yonah began their life in Tel Aviv and were 26 weeks pregnant with their first daughter, Hallel, when war broke out on October 7.“There was a siren, and we jumped out of bed and went into the hallway. But we had no reason to think that it was a big deal, and my husband said he was going to get ready to go to the synagogue,” she said.As he was getting ready, his phone rang. The two knew immediately that it was the army, as no one else would call on Shabbat.“He said, 'I'm getting called in.' And I told him, 'Absolutely not. Do not answer your phone. If it's that important, they'll reach you after Shabbat.'”Yonah left for synagogue. While he was on his way back, there was a second siren, and Esther headed to the shelter alone.“I remember thinking that that was the moment I became a mom. Even though I hadn't given birth.”October 7 felt differentEsther told the Post that she had lived through previous wars in Israel, but October 7 felt different. “I was shaking. I didn't know what happened in the South, but I was terrified for my baby. I was reacting in a way that I'd never experienced.”When Yonah returned from synagogue, he answered a second call from his reserve unit. It was only then that Esther learned Hamas had infiltrated southern Israel.“Yonah told me that Hamas had broken into Israel, that they infiltrated the South. At that point, we had just heard that about 70 people had been killed. We heard about Nova [Supernova music festival massacre]. We didn't know yet that they [terrorists] were in the kibbutzim. I just broke down crying. I was sobbing hysterically, I couldn't breathe, I was so terrified for him.”Once she collected herself, Esther asked her husband a question that shocked him: “Do you have a will?”“I told him, if something happens, I don't care about our stuff. I need to know what happens to me. If something happens to you and they can't find your body, how long do I have to wait before I'm considered not married anymore? I do not want to be an agunah.”“He replied: 'I cannot wrap my head around that. We're not discussing this. I'm alive, I'm fine.'”Feelings of anxiety and guiltOn Saturday evening, Yonah was called up to serve with his unit: 551 [the elite paratrooper reservist unit]. Esther left to stay with her in-laws in order not to be alone.“I was just having anxiety attack after anxiety attack; it was constant. At some point, Yonah called me and said, 'I need to have a real conversation with you. I understand that it's really scary for you and that you have no control over your hormones, and it's a wild situation that you're pregnant and I'm here. But I need you to be my rock. I need to be able to talk to you about what I'm going through and where I'm going. So you need to figure out what you need to do in order to become my support system because that's what I need right now in order to survive.'”Esther said she felt guilty.“My initial reaction was that I felt selfish because he was going through something so much more scary and existential. He was going to be physically going into one of the most dangerous war zones in the world.”Fears started to run through her head: What if Yonah never got to meet their baby? What if she had to give birth in a bomb shelter, alone, without him?Around this time, Esther's aunt in the US called and suggested she come to stay with her and recuperate. While Esther immediately refused to abandon her husband, Yonah felt differently: “He said, 'Whatever you need to do, you have to do because I need you mentally stable.'”A friend helped Esther secure a seat on an evacuation flight to Poland, from where she flew to her aunt in Florida for several weeks until she felt able to return home.“We had gone through Operation Protective Edge [in 2014], so when Yonah told me he was going to Gaza, I figured he would be home in 10-14 days. I knew I had to be home when he came home for the first time.”On returning to Israel, Esther started volunteering. One day, she got a message on her phone from an unknown number. Yonah had written her a letter inside Gaza, and someone had driven it out into Israel, taken a picture, and a commander had texted it to her.“It was like 21st-century snail mail. I had to physically write a response, send it to them, and then they printed it and took it to Yonah.”A few days later, Yonah came out of Gaza and the two reunited for the first time in a month.“This was the start of nearly three years of him going in and out,” she recalled.In late December 2023, one of the men from Yonah's unit was killed, and another one was severely injured, and this led to the unit being released from reserves at the start of January.At this point, for the first time since October 7, the two were back in their apartment in Tel Aviv, which Esther said was “surreal.” After three months of seeing each other for a day here, a day there, they were suddenly living together again.An overloaded hospital and a traumatic birthAt 35 weeks pregnant, Esther began having contractions, which ultimately persisted for three weeks. At 4 a.m. one morning, when she was 38 weeks pregnant, she went into labor.When the couple arrived at Ichilov Hospital, they were met with an overloaded maternity unit, as the hospital had absorbed all the patients evacuated from the North and South.“I was told that there were women who were more urgent, and that I was not far enough along to get a bed.'”“It was pouring rain. I actively labored for 15 hours, eight of which I was standing at the front of the hospital.”Esther stopped relaying her birth story at this point because of the extreme trauma of what happened next.What followed was a six-month recovery. She couldn't be alone with her baby until Hallel was four months old because she physically could not hold her. Esther ended up having reparative surgery two months after Hallel was born.Having moved to Ra'anana after the birth, Esther thankfully had the help of her in-laws, who, to this day, have been above-and-beyond in the way they have shown up, she said. “It was the most responsible decision we've ever made. We wanted to stay in Tel Aviv, but our reality just didn't allow for it.”Because she was so incapacitated during this time, Yonah took over a large amount of what new mothers do, and as a result, Hallel became extremely bonded to her father, something that remains today.Yonah's next round of reserve duty was when Hallel was five months old.At that point, Esther was more capable but “still not 100%” and had someone coming and helping her every day. Yonah agreed to go for half of the time he was called up for, doing one and a half months instead of three.“We tried to video call Yonah, and Hallel couldn't understand the concept that she couldn't reach him through the computer. I have never seen her scream like that; she was terrified, she couldn't process why she couldn't touch him.”They did not attempt a video call again.Twenty-one months after Hallel was born, Esther gave birth to their second baby, Mia.While she was pregnant with Mia, the first Iran war broke out. Esther said that was the first time she began to see miluim in a negative light.“I was seven months pregnant running to the mamad [safe room] with a one and a half year old while Yonah was called in. Until this point, I understood miluim, but suddenly it felt pointless. I needed him more at home than the army did on the Jordanian border.”Thankfully, the second birth experience was “incredible” and not in any way comparable to the first. Yonah was home, having just finished another round of two months in the army.Motherhood in a time of war, with a husband fighting, is no walk in the park. Esther said that the two have survived it by “making a game plan” and being practical.“For me, as the mother, it's been about trying to find things that would help me through those really tough moments. You have to enter into this superhuman space; people don't see the small, tiny things that happen day to day, which actually take an exceedingly huge amount of internal resources and power.”Additionally, she said that there's a societal expectation that wives and partners of men in miluim be okay because they must be used to it. “There is an expectation that you have to be this strong home front, and that you shouldn't complain about it. There used to be more sympathy, but it's not like what it used to be.“It's not that people don't care. It's that they just want life to be normal again, which I completely understand. This has been going on for such a long time already. It's uncomfortable to think about war, and that there are families for whom life is just not normal on a regular basis.”Just because people like her don't ask for help as much anymore doesn't mean they don't need it, she said.“If you know someone who's going through it, just check in and get a cup of coffee with them. To just be there for these people is huge.”The need to not be alone, to have a distraction, is especially true for Esther in the moments right before Yonah leaves. She spoke of the process of being photographed by the Post for “HER,” which happened to be on the day of Yonah going to miluim.“You can see it in the pictures. I can't stop crying. And then there's the picture where Yonah is walking out the door, and I'm holding Hallel and my eyes are half closed. That's me gathering myself. I cry, get it out of my system, and then I'm done.”After he walked out the door, the family had a little dance party.“I guess part of our distraction, part of our survival kit, is putting on music and having a dance.”Esther said that if she had to sum up having a husband in miluim, she would compare it to being on a roller coaster.“When you're on a roller coaster, there's the climb, and then there's the crazy part, and then there's the plateau. There's the climb to the miluim, and then there's the drop of him leaving, and then the crazy twists and turns when we are figuring out how we navigate this: How do we breathe through this? And then it's over, and we can breathe. And then it happens all over again.”What helps them through the twists and turns?“We find a rhythm. I think it comes down to communication - really good communication. We get really frustrated with each other, but we try to talk about it as much as possible.”However, she said, sometimes these important conversations get cut short.“He leaves while we're working through an issue, and we have to continue it via whatever limited communication we have this time or wait until he's home again.”There's also a palpable tension in the air when he's gone, she added.“I think it's the weight of his absence and fear that he's not coming back. It's just a big rip in our equilibrium when he's gone.”During the time Yonah is away, Esther said, she has to function for the girls, but the fear is constantly hanging over her. Often, her imagination has gotten the best of her, and more than once she found herself thinking sounds in the hallway were someone from the army coming to knock on the door and tell her of her husband's death.Hallel is now old enough to understand that he leaves again and again but not why. In the beginning, it didn't seem to affect her, but as time has passed, she has become more and more clingy, throws tantrums, and gets upset. Now that Yonah is home, Hallel constantly checks in on where he is.“I've caught her walking around saying, 'Abba is home. He's just working.'”All this being said, Esther spoke glowingly about her husband. “He's just a very empathetic, kind person,” she said, adding that he is “100% committed to being her partner and the best father he can be.”“He's done the work and is very in tune with himself and knows what he is capable of giving to his family, to miluim, to his work. I love that he is connected to himself in that way.”Looking back, Esther said, she is proud of herself.“I am most proud of the fact that I had two kids in this crazy, insane time. I went back for a second. I'm really proud of myself for going through the process – I think it was the bravest thing I've ever done.”

https://www.formula1.com/en/latest/artic.text: Charles Leclerc Ferrari Lewis Hamilton Leclerc left searching for answers after Hungary Qualifying as he admits pace ‘was never at Hamilton’s level’ Charles Leclerc had no answer to the speed of Lewis Hamilton and Lando Norris during Qualifying in Hungary. Jul 25, 2026 4:57pm UTC Charles Leclerc has admitted that his pace “was never to the level” of Ferrari team mate Lewis Hamilton across Saturday’s Qualifying session for the Hungarian Grand Prix, with the Monegasque left to rue deficits in two key corners. Leclerc , who claimed pole at the Hungaroring in 2025, posted a fastest time of 1m 17.445s during the decisive Q3 phase, comparing to a 1m 17.219s from Hamilton and a 1m 17.207s from pole-sitting McLaren driver Lando Norris . Sharing his emotions after the session, Leclerc sighed: “I’m a bit disappointed. Disappointed mostly because I didn’t find a solution for Turn 1 and Turn 12 all today, really. “In FP3 already I was struggling with Turn 1 and Turn 12, and I was still losing three-tenths or something like this in Q3 in Turn 1 and Turn 12. I’m a bit disappointed with it. I’ll look into it to try and fix that for tomorrow.” Leclerc was outpaced by team mate Hamilton during Qualifying in Hungary He added: “Today there was quite a bit of a wind change, and I don’t think I did a great job anticipating it with the car set-up. I felt a little bit off from this morning, then Qualifying has been quite messy, to be honest. “We’ve been a bit unlucky in Q2 with the yellow flag in the last sector, then we were kind of trying to… We were playing catch-up. But the pace was never to the level of Lewis, so it was all about trying to maximise today. I felt I kind of did it.” Turning his attention to Sunday’s Grand Prix – which he will nonetheless start ahead of Hamilton, who was given a three-place grid penalty post-Qualifying for impeding Oscar Piastri – Leclerc pointed to the importance of nailing the long run down to Turn 1, with overtaking opportunities at a premium around the tight, twisty Budapest venue. “We were competitive all weekend,” he commented. “It’s true that today everybody seems to have done a big, big step forward that we didn’t do, but it’s still a long race tomorrow. “I do believe that our race pace is strong, but it’s true again that people have done a step forward since yesterday, so I’m pretty sure it’s going to be very close. On a track like this, the start particularly will be very key.” F1 Store - Ferrari Check out the latest Ferrari products in the F1 Store. Lewis Hamilton Ferrari Qualifying Hamilton loses P2 following Qualifying incident at the Hungarian Grand Prix Lewis Hamilton has been handed a grid penalty after initially qualifying P2 at the Hungaroring. Jul 25, 2026 4:47pm UTC Lewis Hamilton has received a three-place grid penalty for the Hungarian Grand Prix after he impeded Oscar Piastri during Qualifying, with the Briton originally claiming P2 during the session. As the top-10 drivers prepared for their final laps, Ferrari looked to be in direct competition with McLaren's Lando Norris for pole position, and it was Hamilton who provisionally took the top spot. However, Norris found the time he needed to qualify P1 for the first time this season, relegating the 41-year-old to second place before it was then revealed that Hamilton would be investigated after Qualifying. The incident unfolded as Piastri was trying to improve on his last attempt, which Hamilton was unaware of. He blocked the Australian at Turn 1, forcing him to go over track limits, abort his lap and settle for P5. Hamilton was disappointed to miss out on pole position Hamilton admitted straight after Qualifying: "I think my mind is just elsewhere right this second, because once I’d finished my lap, I don’t know if I got in the way of someone, so I’m just trying to run that through my mind, because I wasn’t aware anyone was coming." It was confirmed that he would be penalised with a grid drop, relegating him to P5 on the grid and promoting Charles Leclerc, Kimi Antonelli and Piastri by one position each. The document released after the hearing reads: "The Stewards heard from the driver of Car 44 (Lewis Hamilton), the driver of Car 81 (Oscar Piastri), team representatives and reviewed video, telemetry, team radio and in-car video evidence. "At the approach to Turn 1, Car 44 was travelling at a significantly reduced speed on the racing line while Car 81 was approaching on a push lap. "The driver of Car 44 explained that he had just completed a fast lap and did not receive the team's radio message regarding the approaching Car 81 until the latter was already in close proximity. He further stated that, due to the positioning of his car on the track, Car 81 was not visible in his mirrors. Piastri will be promoted to P4 as a result of Hamilton's penalty "Car 81, which was on a push lap, was forced to take avoiding action by running wide and being obliged to abort the lap. "Having examined the available evidence, the Stewards determined that Car 44 unnecessarily impeded Car 81 during Qualifying. "In accordance with the FIA F1 Regulations and the established penalty guidelines for this type of infringement in Qualifying, the Stewards impose a three-place grid penalty on the driver of Car 44." https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/formula1/art.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, McLaren's Lando Norris won the Hungarian Grand Prix last season By Andrew Benson F1 Correspondent at the Hungaroring Published 25 July 2026 McLaren's Lando Norris took his first grand prix pole position of the season in Hungary - but Lewis Hamilton was denied the chance to make it an all-British front row by a penalty for impeding. A three-place penalty for blocking Norris' team-mate Oscar Piastri has dropped Hamilton to fifth on the grid, and may have erased his chances of a ninth victory on a track he has almost made his own in his 20-year career. Championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who originally qualified fourth, was also given a three-place grid penalty for not slowing sufficiently under single yellow flags, following a spin for Red Bull's Max Verstappen at the final corner. The penalties mean Ferrari's Charles Leclerc will start second, Piastri third, Verstappen fourth and Hamilton fifth, with Mercedes' George Russell sixth, a place ahead of team-mate Antonelli. Hamilton had been fastest on the first runs, by just over 0.1secs from Norris, but neither the seven-time champion nor Leclerc could improve on their final attempts. Verstappen's error affected Antonelli and Russell, who were forced to slow, although in the Italian's case the stewards decided it was not by enough. Verstappen had got going again before Norris came around as the last driver on track to clinch pole in the upgraded McLaren by just 0.012 seconds. Norris cautious despite pole as it 'falls apart' for Hamilton Published 25 July Malaysia set to host F1 race in October Published 26 July Norris said: "Very happy to be back on top, especially at a track where you certainly want to be on pole. "I had confidence the whole of today. My laps in Q3 were not the best, even the one at the end, so pleasantly surprised to be on top." Hamilton was a second slower on his second run than on his first and was unhappy he had been sent out for it first. "I had a clean out-lap, and when I started my lap, already into Turn One I had a snap and I was already 0.15secs down," Hamilton said. "It just cascaded from there. "So, the last lap was the worst lap of all, and all the other laps were really good. We clearly had the car to be on pole today, and I just didn't deliver. So that's tough to swallow." On the impeding scenario, Hamilton said he had not been warned of Piastri's approach by the team: "I was told literally when he was at the apex behind me, so I had no idea he was coming. "I was the first out, so I thought everyone had finished their lap. Charles, I think, was the car that was behind me when I left the pit lane, as far as I was aware. So, yeah, crazy, because it had been clean, and obviously it wasn't intentional." Verstappen railed about the unpredictable handling of the Red Bull over the radio after his spin. His team-mate Isack Hadjar starts eighth, ahead of Racing Bulls' Arvid Lindblad and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg. Alonso 'optimistic' after progressing to Q2 Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Aston Martin team members celebrate Fernando Alonso's progress into Q2 Fernando Alonso made a major breakthrough for Aston Martin on the weekend they debuted their virtually new car by breaking out of the first session for the first time this season. Alonso will start 16th, 2.8secs off pole - but that was two seconds faster in relative pace than they had managed for some time. The veteran Spaniard, who is 45 next week, told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I feel relieved a little bit, feeling that the team understood the weaknesses of the car and this is the first step in the right direction. "We brought a few updates to this car early in the season, and it didn't work much. And we come from two years of disappointments of upgrades. So definitely there is a change in optimism in the factory and I feel optimistic." Alonso faces a decision this summer as to whether to continue his career after this season. He said that while he had no doubts managing technical partner Adrian Newey would lead the team to success in the future, he was not sure whether it would happen soon enough for him. "No-one should doubt Adrian Newey or the potential we have in Silverstone. It is a matter of time before we have the best chassis and it is a matter of time before Honda have the best engine in F1. It is a question of when." All the drivers were battling with a Hungaroring track surface that was breaking up, especially in the final two corners, where Norris said it was especially difficult to judge the grip level. Even before the incident with Verstappen, Russell was afflicted on his final run by a water leak, which was spraying water on to his rear tyres. Mercedes asked him to pull over immediately after crossing the line, and he parked at Turn One, in an attempt to avoid damaging the engine. Speaking before his penalty, Antonelli said: "I think we were just slightly out of the window with tyres, then in Q3 we did a good step and the car just felt finally a bit more alive. For sure it was a shame with the yellow flags, but it happens. P3 was on the table today but still not good enough for pole." https://www.autoweek.com/racing/formula-.text: World Champion Lando Norris finally snapped Mercedes’ unbeaten streak in qualifying this season by snatching pole position for Formula 1’s Hungarian Grand Prix.Kimi Antonelli and George Russell had fronted every Grand Prix qualifying session so far in 2026 for Mercedes, but the layout of the Hungaroring has not played to the W17’s strengths.Drivers were also struggling for consistency on a partially resurfaced track that has been slightly breaking up at some corners.A mistake on his first push lap in Q3 cost McLaren driver Norris time but he made amends on his second lap to clock a time of 1:17.207s, beating Lewis Hamilton by a mere 0.012s.It was Norris’ 17th pole of his career and his second at the Hungaroring.“It’s been a while, and I felt confident all weekend, so nice to be able to turn it into something,” Norris said.Hamilton’s second place was provisional owing to the Ferrari driver clearly impeding Oscar Piastri on the McLaren driver’s hot lap—and as expected it came with a three-place grid penalty. Hamilton will start instead P5, Piastri in third.Both Ferrari drivers rued scruffy laps, having not improved at the end, with a “disappointed” third-placed (promoted to P2) Charles Leclerc describing his session as “messy,” as the team’s wait for a first pole of the year goes on.Antonelli also was tagged with a post-qualifying penalty, with stewards having determined the Mercedes driver failed to slow sufficiently for yellow flags brought out when Red Bull’s Max Verstappen spun in Q3. Antonelli will line up seventh, gaining a spot for Hamilton’s penalty while losing three places for his own. That puts Russell in sixth, the Briton’s session slightly compromised by a minor water leak at the end which meant it was “like a water pistol being sprayed at the tires.”“The whole weekend we haven’t had the pace, we’ve looked strong in race pace, did we strike the right balance between quali and race set-up we’ll find tomorrow, but we struggled to get the tires switched on all day,” Russell said.Antonelli agreed that “we were a bit out of the window with tires, in Q3 we made a good step, the car finally felt a bit more alive,” but he rued an ill-timed yellow flag that he reckoned may have cost him one spot.Red Bull endured a troubled session, with both Verstappen and Isack Hadjar having a spin en route to sixth and eighth respectively.“The whole weekend has been tough but in qualifying especially the car is just degrading, we don’t have tire degradation, we have car degradation,” Verstappen said. “I can’t make anything [any sense] out if it, it’s very tough, the car just suddenly started oversteering a lot, every lap I did got worse and worse. Not good.”Fernando Alonso delivered hope for Aston Martin as, a week after being two seconds down on the nearest car, the Spaniard made it through to Q2.Alonso qualified in 16th place, putting the Aston Martin as the ninth-best car, faster than the struggling Williams team and new tail-enders Cadillac.FORMULA 1 AWS HUNGARIAN GRAND PRIX 2026—PROVISIONAL STARTING GRID Hungaroring—Budapest, Hungary , July 26, 2026 Pos/Driver/Team/Qualifying Time1. This photo provided by the Ukrainian Emergency Service, shows the site of Russian missile strikes in Kyiv region, Ukraine, Friday, July 24, 2026. (Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP) This photo provided by the Ukrainian Emergency Service, shows the site of Russian missile strikes in Kyiv region, Ukraine, Friday, July 24, 2026. (Ukrainian Emergency Service via AP) Ukrainian attacks on holiday camps on Saturday in the partly Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia region have killed 12 people, Moscow-installed officials said, while authorities in Ukraine’s northeastern Sumy region said a Russian drone strike killed three people there. The strikes followed a major Russian attack on Friday near Kyiv that killed at least 10 people and wounded around 100 others, part of a relentless cycle of tit-for-tat attacks that dims the potential of reaching a diplomatic end to Russia’s more than 4-year-old invasion of its neighbor . The exchange comes as Ukraine’s successful drome attacks have stalled the Russian army’s advances in an expanded campaign by Kyiv inside Russia that has been hitting high-profile targets, causing fuel shortages and piling pressure on Russian leader Vladimir Putin . Four children were among 12 people killed in the attack on the resorts in Zaporizhzhia, Yevgeny Balitsky, the Kremlin-installed regional head, said, adding that 19 others were wounded. Ukraine did not immediately comment. Sumy regional head Oleh Hryhorov said on Saturday three people were killed when a large fire broke out after a Russian drone struck a “civilian facility,” adding that the victims were drivers for private Ukrainian postal and courier service Nova Poshta. Russia’s defense ministry said it attacked a “storage and launch site” for Ukrainian drones in the Sumy region. In Zaporizhzhia, in southeastern Ukraine, a Russian drone attack late Friday hit a shopping center, causing a fire that spread over a 500-square-meter area and injuring several people, regional head Ivan Fedorov said. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned in his evening address on Friday that intelligence assessments indicated that Russia was preparing missiles for a large attack, saying there were indications that this could happen in the next 48 hours. Ukraine keeps targeting oil facilities A Ukrainian drone attack caused a fire in the grounds of the Tyumen Oil Refinery, in western Siberia, Tyumen regional Gov. Aleksandr Moor said on Saturday. Writing on X Saturday, Zelenskyy confirmed the hit on the Tyumen plant, along with a logistics facility in Yekaterinburg and a fuel and lubricants warehouse in Rostov-on-Don. Ukraine’s long-range drone technology has evolved during the war, posing a problem for Russia, whose huge land mass is hard to protect fully. Kyiv’s forces have targeted Russian oil facilities, causing fuel shortages and embarrassing President Vladimir Putin. Zelenskyy to meet Trump in Washington U.S. President Donald Trump and Zelenskyy plan to meet on Tuesday in Washington, a White House official said on Saturday, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss Trump’s schedule before it is announced. Kyiv did not immediately comment on the meeting, although Zelenskyy said in his Friday address that Kyiv was “preparing for a meeting with the President of the United States and his team.” A memorial service in Washington for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, one of Kyiv’s staunchest supporters , is slated for Tuesday. Romania shoots down second drone in 2 days Romania’s defense ministry said on Saturday its forces had “safely shot down” a drone that breached its airspace in an “unpopulated area” near the Ukrainian border. The drone was “shot down by a Romanian pilot from an F-16 aircraft,” President Nicușor Dan said in a post on Facebook. Saturday’s interception came after a drone was shot down around Padina, northeast of the Romanian capital, Bucharest, on Friday. A series of drone incursions by Russia and Ukraine have hit Romania and other NATO members since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. In June, a Ukrainian maritime drone exploded at the Black Sea port of Constanta, while three other sea drones exploded outside the port. No one was hurt. A Russian drone that was part of an attack on Ukraine in May went astray and struck an apartment building in eastern Romania, injuring two people. Copyright © 2026 The Associated Press. https://english.radio.cz/summer-film-sch.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Summer Film School honours Ester Krumbachová Facebook Twitter This year's Summer Film School in Uherské Hradiště is paying tribute to Ester Krumbachová, one of the most influential figures of the Czechoslovak New Wave. Best known as a costume designer, screenwriter and the director of The Murder of Mr. Devil, she helped shape classics such as Daisies and Diamonds of the Night. Alongside screenings of films she worked on, the festival has opened an exhibition featuring photographs by Libuše Jarcovjáková, costume designs, jewellery, amulets and personal documents. Organisers say the retrospective offers a comprehensive look at Krumbachová's lasting influence on Czech and Czechoslovak cinema.
