This massacre occurred because police deliberately delayed rescue operations, sealed off exists, and cut off food, water and other essential supplies to the miners for more than a month. So why did the ANC not take concrete actions against M&M? The answer largely lies in the instantaneous deradicalisation and bourgeoisification of the ANC. Ultra rightwing White racists assisted the ANC in this project by killing or rather wasting Chris Hani – ANC’s most grass-rooted, most radical, and most influential revolutionary anti-Apartheid leader. He was also the charismatic leader of the South African Communist Party, and the Chief of Staff of UMkhonto we Sizwe. The wasting of Hani by a far-right Polish immigrant, Janusz Walus, with a gun supplied by Clive Derby-Lewis of the ultra-right wing Conservative Party, was followed by the measured blackmail, trials, humiliation and ‘disgrace’ of Winnie Madikizela-Mandela. First, for her restless and relentless opposition and uncompromising struggle against ANC’s capitulation to the interests of White monopoly capitalism. Secondly, for her insistence that ANC must adopt concrete measures to uplift the conditions of the Black South African majority. Madikizela-Mandela’s ‘disgrace’ was followed by the expulsion, in 2012, of the radical Julius Malema – the then Youth Leader – from the ANC, supposedly for sowing seeds of division in the organisation. In reality, however, Malema was expelled for openly criticising and resisting the highly compromising positions of the ANC on national and foreign issues. …the material and cultural base for Black South Africans to enjoy democracy and economic freedom, as contained in Paragraphs 4, 5, 8 9 and 10 of the Charter, have been gravely silenced… The results are mass poverty, unemployment, family disintegration, and crimes amongst Black South Africans… Poverty amongst Black South Africans is approximately 64.2 per cent. That is, about 29.6 million Black South Africans live below the upper-bound of the poverty line in 2025/2026, while 48.8 per cent, or 10.8 million Black South Africans, live below the lower-bound and food poverty line. The deradicalisation of ANC went concurrently with its bourgeoisification. Ritualistic attention was, and is still being, paid to Paragraphs 2, 3, 6, 7, 9 and 11 of the ‘The Freedom Charter.’ These paragraphs centre on issues such as democracy, good governance, human rights and foreign policy. However, the material and cultural base for Black South Africans to enjoy democracy and economic freedom, as contained in Paragraphs 4, 5, 8 9 and 10 of the Charter, have been gravely silenced. The results are mass poverty, unemployment, family disintegration, and crimes amongst Black South Africans. Poverty amongst Black South Africans is approximately 64.2 per cent. That is, about 29.6 million Black South Africans live below the upper-bound of the poverty line in 2025/2026, while 48.8 per cent, or 10.8 million Black South Africans, live below the lower-bound and food poverty line. Of these, females comprise 48.8 to 64.2 per cent of the poor, whether on the upper-bound or lower-bound poverty lines. On the other hand, the poverty rate of White South Africans is 1.4 per cent. Black South Africans, who constitute 82 per cent of the population, or 51.6 million persons in 2025, account for 93.6 per cent of all poor people in the “Rainbow” country! Whereas, White South Africans, who constitute 4.5 per cent or approximately 4.5 million people, control over 70 per cent of the country’s land and wealth. As in the Apartheid era, 9 per cent of White South Africans still dominate and control the entire economy! The unemployment rate was 32.4 per cent for 2025, of which 38-40.2 per cent were Black South Africans. White South Africans constituted roughly 5.9 per cent of the unemployed; the “Coloured” were 21 per cent; and Indian/Asian South Africans, 6-7 per cent. The unemployment rate of Black South African women was 40.2 per cent. Yet, they still head about 42.3-43.4 per cent of the households, of the estimated 63.1 million South African population. As such, most Black South Africans are largely brought-up by their mothers and/or grandmothers, without the presence and responsibilities of the fathers. Without doubt, the poverty and unemployment rates are equally high in Nigeria. But the Nigerian economy is labour intensive, whereas that of South Africa is capital intensive. So, while Nigeria has a massive informal economy, which supplies over 90 per cent of the labour force, that of South Africa is about 21.4 per cent. Even so, South Africa’s informal economy is highly restricted, massively regulated, and offers little options for poor Black South Africans to survive. The sustainable solutions to Afrophobia and Negrophobia in South Africa lie in the implementation of Paragraphs 4,5,8,9 and 10 of ‘The Freedom Charter.’ These lay in the decolonisation and de-apartheidisation of Black South Africans… The rebuilding of the Black family. The entrenchment of Ubuntu doctrines and practices. And, the education of Black South Africans to see themselves as an organic component of the African family. The progressive underdevelopment of Black South Africans simultaneously went with the increasing decline of the ANC. The Economic Freedom Fighters (EFF), led by Malema, emerged in 2013, and uMkhonto we Sizwe (MK) Party, led by the disgraced Jacob Zuma, was registered on 7th September 2023. ANC also lost control of its seats in the National Assembly. From 279 out of 400 seats in 2004, to 264 in 2009, 249 in 2014, and 159 in 2024. ANC’s decline went concurrently with the increase in Afrophobic and xenophobic violence in 1995, 1998, 2000, late 2005 and early 2006, then 2008, 2015, 2016, 2019, 2021 to 2024, and 2026. All these indicate ANC’s desperate measures to remain politically relevant amongst Black South Africans. Hence, its tolerance and, by extension, incapacity to deal with Acrophobia and Negrophobia. African countries and peoples must, therefore, rise up against Afrophobia and Negrophobia the way they rose up against Apartheid South Africa. We can definitely count on the support of Africans in the Americas and all forces committed to emancipatory politics in this regard. But the task is primarily and largely ours as Africans. We should not count on European Union countries, or even celebrate their visa restrictions and actions against South Africans. For, as Frantz Fanon warned, we should: “Leave this Europe where they are never done talking of Man, yet murder men everywhere they find them, at the corner of every one of their own streets, in all corners of the globe.” Also, Western Europe and its North American cousins are fully aware that the Afrophobia and Negrophobia in South Africa, if not checked, confronted, combatted, and totally neutralised, will graduate to Europhobia, and the loss of their monopolies in South Africa. The ANC leaders, therefore, and not the popular masses, must be held responsible for the Afrophobia and Negrophobia. We should, accordingly, forgive the masses involved in these violent acts. Besides, Black South Africans are, in Owei Lakemfa’s words, “our brothers and sisters, so when we correct them, it should be with love. It should be like a mother chiding her child… The continent must focus on a bigger picture of Pan-African unity, integration and a New World Order built on peace, sovereignty, human rights and social justice.” The sustainable solutions to Afrophobia and Negrophobia in South Africa lie in the implementation of Paragraphs 4,5,8,9 and 10 of ‘The Freedom Charter.’ These lay in the decolonisation and de-apartheidisation of Black South Africans. The rebuilding of the Black family. The entrenchment of Ubuntu doctrines and practices. And, the education of Black South Africans to see themselves as an organic component of the African family. Until these reforms are implemented, not only will Afrophobia and Negrophobia continue to blossom, but also, the Republic of South Africa will continue to remain a “Whiteman’s country” governed by Black men and women. Ahmed Aminu-Ramatu Yusuf worked as deputy director, Cabinet Affairs Office, The Presidency, and retired as General Manager (Administration), Nigerian Meteorological Agency, (NiMet). Newsflash Newsroom , 25.07.2026, 19:35 Drone. The Romanian authorities will share with their NATO and European Union allies the results of their investigations into the two incidents involving drones that illegally entered Romanian airspace on Friday and Saturday, acting foreign minister Oana Ţoiu has announced. She also said on X that the illegal violation of national airspace is a premeditated act. Earlier, speaking to Fox News, she said that Romania’s borders and its sovereignty are non-negotiable, and that the military and NATO air policing forces will continue to monitor the land border, the Danube river and the Black Sea. On Saturday morning, a drone was shot down 10 km from Sfântu Gheorghe, in the Danube Delta by the same F-16 pilot who had destroyed another drone on Friday in Buzău county (southeast). Investigators have already determined that the first drone was a Shahed unmanned aerial vehicle, a model used by Russia in strikes on Ukraine. Acting defence minister Radu Miruţă gave assurances that the Romanian Army is doing its best with the means available to limit and eliminate the threat posed by such incidents for the population. He pointed out the need for cheaper solutions than fighter-launched missiles to shoot down drones entering Romanian airspace, but this requires further equipping the army, and the production and procurement of such systems take at least 11 months. In Brussels, European Council President António Costa congratulated the Romanian authorities on their rapid and efficient response and gave assurances that the European Union would continue to strengthen its security and deterrence capabilities. Holidays. The majority of Romanians going on holiday this summer are choosing to stay in Romania, preferring short trips and organising their travel independently rather than using travel agencies. These findings come from a survey showing that 34% of respondents are heading to the seaside, while 32% are choosing the mountains. Only one in five Romanians will travel abroad. Over 43% of those surveyed can afford a holiday of just three to four days, with rest being the primary goal for more than half of them. More than 30% of respondents state they will combine business with pleasure, and 13% intend to visit tourist attractions, while only 1% of Romanians are going on holiday for shopping. Nearly 39% of Romanians said they would not be taking a holiday at all this summer. BBC Proms. The Ministry of economy, digitalisation, entrepreneurship and tourism in Bucharest is promoting Romania as a tourist destination on a special page included in the 85,000 official brochures for 63 of the BBC Proms concerts, the oldest and one of the most prestigious classical music festivals in the world and held every summer at London’s Royal Albert Hall. On August 5, Alexandra Dariescu will become the first Romanian female pianist to perform at the BBC Proms and the first Romanian musician to be part of the festival’s line-up in the last three decades. The concert’s special brochure, running in 1,200 copies, will feature not only the promotional page for Romania as a tourist destination but also a page dedicated to Romanian cultural diplomacy in the United Kingdom. Festival. Sighișoara, in central Romania, is playing host to the 31st edition of the Medieval Art Festival, the country’s longest-running event of its kind. Activities for visitors of all ages include knightly tournaments, medieval music and theater performances, parades, interactive workshops in glassmaking, pottery, tailoring, and engraving, fire-juggling demonstrations, and dishes inspired by local cuisine. Held within the only inhabited medieval citadel in Southeast Europe, the Medieval Sighișoara Festival takes place under the High Patronage of Her Majesty Margareta, the Custodian of the Romanian Crown. https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/07/25/w.text: Trump’s heavy hand in Colombia’s right-wing victory President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella, third from right, attends with his wife, Ana Lucía Pineda, Medellín Mayor Federico Gutiérrez, left, and Rodrigo Lara, the president-elect's pick for interior minister, right, during the Independence Day parade in Bogotá, Colombia, Monday, July 20, 2026. Miguel Angel Lopez/AP Photo/Miguel Angel Lopez BOGOTÁ, Colombia — First came President Trump’s “complete and total endorsement” of Abelardo De La Espriella, the right-wing candidate in Colombia’s presidential election. Then came the support of Republican members of Congress, who asserted that De La Espriella would have US interests in mind and helped mobilize Colombians abroad, who tend to lean conservative, to vote. Then, just days before the election, US immigration authorities detained an activist critical of De La Espriella and who had urged Colombians in the United States not to vote for him. The activist, according to a memo signed by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, had been interfering with US foreign policy. De La Espriella won Colombia’s presidential vote Sunday by a razor-thin margin — helped by ballots cast outside the country — and will take office in August. Experts say that even in an era when meddling in foreign elections has become increasingly common, the recent involvement of the Trump administration and its allies in Colombia’s election has been heavy-handed. The detention of an activist who opposed a candidate endorsed by Trump was particularly striking, experts said. “The attempt to quash dissent in a coordinated manner with the Trump administration, extending from Colombia to US soil — I can’t think of anything in recent times, in the 21st century, that resembles that,” said Alexander Main, the director of international policy at the Center for Economic and Policy Research in Washington. The State Department did not respond to requests for comment about the detention of the Colombian activist. Espriella, a lawyer who had never held office, energized millions of Colombian voters, and he appeared likely to win even before Trump’s endorsement. But in Colombia, President Gustavo Petro, a leftist and political opponent of De La Espriella, seized on Trump’s endorsement as he sought to sow doubt in the result, claiming that America’s involvement amounted to “cheating” that undermined the vote. This, in turn, set those in his inner circle rushing to stop the president from flat-out rejecting the result and calling for mass protests. The day after the election, Petro flew to Panama for an event but was in such a frenzy over De La Espriella’s minuscule lead over his party’s candidate — about 250,000 votes, or less than 1 percentage point — that his top ministers convened an emergency meeting in Bogotá, Colombia, to address what Petro believed were irregularities, according to two people with direct knowledge of the events who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter. All the while, Petro kept sending messages to his millions of followers on the social platform X, and supporters streamed into the streets of the capital for a march called “Electoral Steal,” even as his party’s candidate, Iván Cepeda, counseled calm. On Wednesday, De La Espriella’s political opponent, Cepeda, conceded the election after electoral authorities completed a customary vote verification process. Since Sunday, scattered protests have broken out in Bogotá and the city of Cali, with reports of vandalism and isolated clashes with the police, but there have been no large demonstrations. The election pitted De La Espriella, a wealthy lawyer, against Cepeda, a senator, peace negotiator and stalwart of the left. De La Espriella used AI-generated images of a tiger as his campaign avatar and promised to “disembowel” political opponents, crush “narco-terrorists,” and strengthen ties to the United States. He lived in Florida for more than a decade and was recently naturalized as a US citizen. Esteban González Pons, the head of the European Union Electoral Observation Mission in Colombia, told reporters Tuesday in response to a question about Trump’s endorsement and the presence of US lawmakers in Colombia that claims of international interference were “absolutely irrelevant” to the election because “the Colombian people had voted freely.” On Election Day, two members of the U.S. Congress were in Colombia to stump for De La Espriella. Representative María Elvira Salazar, a Florida Republican, speaking in the city of Barranquilla, on Colombia’s Caribbean coast, told reporters, “We know very well that Cepeda will be Petro No. 2, so that’s why we’re with De La Espriella,” adding that a “profound closeness” with the United States was vital for Colombia’s prosperity. Senator Bernie Moreno, an Ohio Republican, who was born in Colombia and has emerged as De La Espriella’s biggest champion in Washington, also traveled to Barranquilla as an election monitor. He had raised alarms for weeks over Petro’s fraud allegations and supposed vote-buying by the left. The Republican lawmakers had spent weeks encouraging Colombians in the United States to vote, which analysts say helped tip the results in De La Espriella’s favor. In an election that saw a record-high turnout, the diaspora vote was, by most calculations, the decisive factor: De La Espriella received around 65 percent of the total overseas vote and around 80 percent in the United States. On Monday, Moreno, after meeting with De La Espriella, appeared to dangle a carrot: If Petro behaved for the next several weeks and did not interfere with the peaceful transfer of power, Moreno told a Colombian news outlet that it was “quite probable” that the US Treasury could remove him from a sanctions list. He was placed on the list last year after objecting to the Trump administration’s military strikes on boats it has said are carrying drugs. The administration has not publicly commented on the case of the progressive Colombian activist detained last week by US immigration authorities. In an interview with a prominent Colombian journalist Wednesday, the activist, Franklin Humberto Coral Garrido, better known as Beto Coral, said he had an open asylum case in the United States that gave him the legal right to remain in the country. Speaking from a detention center in Louisiana, Coral called his arrest “political persecution” and added, “My political activism focuses on Colombia, nothing related to the internal politics of the United States.” Coral was arrested by immigration authorities the same day Rubio signed a memo that said he could be deported from the United States. In the memo, a copy of which was obtained by The New York Times, Rubio noted that Coral arrived in the United States in 2015 on a tourist visa and had a pending asylum application. But “Coral Garrido has used his presence in the United States to conduct political activity in support of the Petro government” and has advocated against a candidate for president, Rubio wrote. The efforts by US officials and members of Congress to shape Colombia’s election have stirred outrage among rights groups and Democrats in Congress, who last week wrote a letter to top officials calling out what they said was “brazen interference.” It was once considered taboo for heads of state and other politicians to make public statements on foreign elections. Increasingly, though, such public intervention is becoming a regular part of global politics — on the right and the left — with Trump playing a major role in that trend. The US president has endorsed Viktor Orbán of Hungary and paid particular attention to elections in Latin America — supporting right-wing candidates in Honduras and Argentina. Presidents Javier Milei of Argentina and Daniel Noboa of Ecuador, both supporters of Trump, have also jumped in to endorse De La Espriella. Jennie Lincoln of the Carter Center, which monitors elections around the world, called this foreign involvement in the Colombian vote part of “an egregious trend of interference.” Lincoln is the head of a mission in Colombia to observe the vote, and she pointed out that the Organization of American States, a regional body, prohibits foreign interference in domestic affairs. Trump, who had repeatedly posted about De La Espriella on Truth Social, said Monday that he had spoken with him by phone to congratulate him. “He’s going to be a great president,” Trump told reporters at the White House, adding that the US relationship with Colombia would be “much better.” This article originally appeared in The New York Times .

https://theindianawaaz.com/president-mur.text: OTHER TOP STORIES President Murmu lauds Indian community’s contribution to India-Romania partnership Jul 26, 2026 Last Updated on July 26, 2026 1:21 am by INDIAN AWAAZ President Droupadi Murmu has lauded the contribution of the Indian community in Romania, describing it as a vital pillar of the growing partnership between the two countries. Addressing a reception hosted for the Indian community in Bucharest on the concluding day of her State Visit to Romania, the President said that Indians living abroad remain deeply connected to their motherland and make every Indian proud through their achievements and dedication. The President said that her interactions with Romanian President Nicușor Dan and other leaders reflected a strong commitment to taking bilateral ties to new heights. She noted that cooperation between India and Romania has expanded across a wide range of sectors, including trade, defence, renewable energy, digital technology, education, research, healthcare, science and technology, artificial intelligence, innovation, and advanced manufacturing. Referring to the India-European Union Free Trade Agreement concluded earlier this year, President Murmu said its early implementation would open new avenues for trade and investment with Romania and other European Union member states. She also highlighted the productive discussions held during the India-Romania Business Forum, where a high-level Indian business delegation explored opportunities for deeper economic engagement. The President appreciated the valuable contribution of Indian professionals, entrepreneurs, researchers, healthcare workers, and students to Romania’s development. She also thanked the Government and the people of Romania for warmly welcoming the Indian community and ensuring their safety and well-being. https://www.rbth.com/history/328985-harb.text: 8 mind-blowing facts about Harbin, the Chinese city built by Russians Go back 150 years and the area along the Songhua River was but a collection of rural settlements. Fast-forward to modern-day Harbin, and you’ll find 12 million Chinese citizens going about their lives amidst an architectural backdrop of Tsarist grandeur. The reason? Harbin is a city of perpetual re-invention and chaos. Now China’s 8 th largest urban area, current residents work on the skeleton of a village built in the early 20 th century by enterprising Russians in search of prosperity, and who tried to recreate their homeland. Today, the city is practically devoid of Russians (except a few expats), but Harbin’s history once was home to some of the Motherland’s brightest entrepreneurs, most vulnerable refugees, and its most scheming extremists. Here’s the lowdown on the city’s rich heritage. The first thing in Harbin was the train station. As the first Trans-Siberian trains made successful eastward voyages in 1896, Tsar Nicholas II’s ambitious Finance Minister, Count Sergei Witte, wasted no time in subsidizing another route: the Chinese Eastern Railway. Central to his grand plan was the newly-formed city of Harbin, which he hoped would link Baikal with Vladivostok, and then have southern routes through China. After officially acquiring town status in 1898, the area quickly became northeast China’s most buzzing metropolis, and by 1917 it was home to over 100,000 people (around 40,000 of whom were Russian). As very few had been born in the city, Harbin was an expat paradise. Count Witte was keen to make anyone looking at the Harbin skyline know who was boss. The result? St. Sophia Orthodox Cathedral (opened 1907) Volga Manor The European-style High St. in Daoli On the right: Lungmen Grand Hotel (opened in 1901) Long before the Jewish Autonomous Oblast existed, many of Russia’s Jews flocked eastwards to Harbin to escape persecution and start new lives. Since Alexander III and (to a lesser extent) Nicholas II were under the influence of their ultra-conservative childhood tutor, Konstantin Pobedonostsev, the prospect of deportations, education quotas, disenfranchisement, and even pogroms made an eastward move more tempting to Jews. By 1913, it is estimated that around 5,000 Russian Jews lived in Harbin, with this number rising to around 20,000 by 1920. Of Harbin’s Jewish legacy only two synagogues remain: one built in 1909; another in 1921; and also a large Jewish cemetery. Jewish cemetery in Harbin Although most White émigrés fled to Paris, Berlin and Prague, Harbin’s role in welcoming those persecuted by the Bolsheviks is often overlooked by historians. In a way, it makes perfect sense: starting in 1917 Harbin welcomed pro-Tsarist traders and bureaucrats. With White factions clearly taking note of this, the city’s Russian population skyrocketed from 40,000 to around 120,000 over the course of the Civil War. Although these White émigrés were mostly left stateless after 1922, their community briefly thrived in Harbin through the establishment of a Russian educational system and Russian-language media. In the 1930s, many in Harbin’s Russian community embraced fascism, mostly as an attempt to form an anti-Bolshevik Asian front with Emperor Hirohito’s Japan. The Russian Fascist Party’s most successful period was under the leadership of Konstantin Rodzaevsky, who claimed to have 20,000 members. Gladly agreeing to an alliance with Imperial Japan, Rodzaevsky’s platform called for liquidation of the Jews, re-establishing the influence of the Orthodox Church, and building a corporatist economic system along Italian lines. As a result of the RFP’s increasing power, as well as a lack of protection from the Japanese government following its annexation of Manchuria in 1931, the city’s Jewish population fell from 13,000 in 1931 to 5,000 by 1935. But things were about to become far more gruesome. The ruins of Unit 731 While officially labelled an “epidemic prevention and water supply unit,” and located just 24 km south of Harbin, Unit 731 in fact was responsible for some of the most brutal war crimes ever committed. Established in 1935 by the Japanese military, Unit 731 ran a facility for live human experimentation that even horror movies couldn’t imagine. Only in 1984 was it revealed that the Japanese subjected prisoners to live dissections, frostbite, starvation, as well as injecting them with the plague. Russians in Harbin were also targeted by the Japanese, and it's estimated that around 30 percent of the 3,000-12,000 victims of Unit 731 were Russian. Most set a 5 p.m. curfew for their children to prevent them being taken by Japanese police. Following the USSR’s sale of the Chinese Eastern Railway to Japan in 1935, as well as due to the random disappearance of people from the streets (taken by Unit 731), most Harbin Russians naturally wanted to leave. By the late 1930s the number of local Russians had fallen to around 30,000. Those who had chosen Soviet citizenship, and who had their property confiscated by the Japanese, chose to return to the USSR. Ironically, over 48,000 of them were arrested as “Japanese spies” during the Great Purge of 1936-38. When the Soviet army took the city in August 1945, many remaining residents met a similar fate: those deemed to have had any previous cooperation with the White Army, the Japanese, or the Russian Fascist Party were immediately rounded up and sent to the GULAG. Most remaining Russians in Harbin were repatriated to the Soviet Union, and in the Chinese census of 1964 just 450 Russians were counted in the city. The final two Harbin Russians died in the 1980s. A visitor of the ethnographic project "A Russian Village on Sun Island Near Harbin." Harbin’s historic Russian architecture is losing out to modern Chinese construction, but locals are fighting back. When there was talk about destroying the city’s iconic 1920s Qihong Bridge, a local movement fought to have it classified as “an immovable cultural relic.” When the Harbin Ice Festival comes to the city every year, the organizers make sure that an Ice Kremlin is built. One of the city’s historic restaurants, Lucia, has also preserved its unique Imperial Russian interior. Europe’s Bold Move Against Google Raises Bigger Questions by Sir Democracy Community This content is not subject to review by Daily Kos staff prior to publication. July 25, 2026 at 2:23 PM Recommend Story Share: Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Share on Bluesky (Opens in new window) Bluesky Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share using Native tools Share Copied to clipboard 10 Comments Add Daily Kos to Google Synopsis Synopsis (Gen Z Version) What happens when one of the world’s most powerful tech companies collides with one of the world’s toughest regulators? That’s exactly what’s unfolding in Brussels, where the European Commission has taken major action against Alphabet, the parent company of Google, led by CEO Sundar Pichai. For most of us, Google is simply part of daily life—a search engine we’ve used for years without giving it much thought. But behind every search result lies a company so influential that governments on both sides of the Atlantic are debating just how much power it should have. In this article, I’ll break down how European regulators arrived at their decision after years of investigations and oversight, and why they believe Big Tech needs stronger rules. I’ll also examine the reaction from Alphabet executives, who argue that the EU’s approach could hurt innovation, investment, and consumer choice. But this story goes far beyond Google. The dispute is quickly becoming part of a much larger clash between Europe and the United States. Since President Donald Trump returned to the White House for a second, nonconsecutive term, tensions between Washington and Brussels have grown more visible. Trade disagreements, technology regulation, and competing economic interests are increasingly pushing both sides toward confrontation rather than cooperation. And the stakes may be about to get even higher. The Trump Administration has signaled that it could impose tariffs exceeding those announced during the so-called “Liberation Day” trade measures of April 2, 2025. If that happens, European leaders could respond aggressively—potentially tearing up the trade agreement reached when Trump met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Scotland. Economists have long warned about the possibility of a full-scale transatlantic trade war. While those fears eased after the tensions surrounding Liberation Day, they may not stay buried for long. If Washington raises tariffs on European goods and Brussels retaliates with its own tariffs—what some officials call deploying the EU’s “trade bazooka”—the conflict could escalate rapidly. By the end of this article, I want readers to think about a bigger question: Is this really just a fight over Google, or is it a sign that the U.S. and Europe are entering a new era of economic rivalry? What happens next could reshape not only the future of Big Tech, but also the future of one of the world’s most important international relationships: NATO. What took Van der Leyen so long? One of the most common questions people ask is: If European regulators believed companies like Google were abusing their market power, why did it take so many years to act? The European Commission couldn’t simply decide overnight to impose a massive fine; it had to build a legally sound case capable of withstanding years of appeals from some of the world’s wealthiest and most formidable legal teams. At the same time, the Commission remained acutely aware of public scrutiny—any further delay risked testing the electorate’s patience and potentially weakening Van der Leyen’s position as EU Commission President and leader of the-right European People’s Party (E.P.P). This, in turn, could make it even more challenging for her party’s next nominee to secure support from both left- and right-leaning MEPs. Author’s Note: For context, not so very long ago, Van der Leyen had a rough time getting re-elected—some MEPs weren’t feeling her, so she had to make some unpopular moves to win them over. With the EU Parliament so divided between left and right, it makes sense that she took her time before acting on Google if she thought they broke the DMA rules. 1. Big Tech Is Complicated Unlike a traditional monopoly case involving railroads, oil companies, or banks, digital platforms operate in highly complex markets. Google isn’t just a search engine. It is part of a vast ecosystem that includes: Search Online advertising Mobile operating systems (Android) Web browsers (Chrome) Maps Cloud computing Artificial intelligence European regulators first had to determine whether Google’s dominance in one area gave it an unfair advantage in another. Proving that requires enormous amounts of data, economic analysis, and internal company documents. 2. The EU Wanted Evidence, Not Headlines European competition law requires regulators to demonstrate that a company has abused a dominant market position—not merely that it is successful. That process can involve: Investigating complaints from competitors. Gathering evidence across multiple countries. Interviewing businesses and consumers. Reviewing millions of pages of documents. Allowing the company being investigated to defend itself. Because Google’s services are used by hundreds of millions of Europeans, regulators had to move carefully to avoid unintended consequences that could affect consumers and businesses alike. 3. Big Tech Fights Back Another reason these cases take years is that companies rarely accept regulatory findings without a fight. Alphabet has some of the most sophisticated legal teams in the world. When Brussels issues a major decision, the company can challenge it in European courts, often leading to years of litigation. European officials know this in advance. As a result, they spend years building a case strong enough to survive judicial scrutiny. A weak case could be overturned, creating an embarrassing defeat for regulators and setting a precedent that weakens future enforcement. 4. The Rules Were Still Evolving For much of the 2000s and 2010s, lawmakers around the world struggled to figure out how to regulate digital platforms. When Google emerged as a dominant force, there were few laws specifically designed for: Search engines App stores Digital advertising platforms Algorithmic gatekeepers In many ways, governments were trying to regulate twenty-first-century technology using twentieth-century legal frameworks. That began to change when the EU introduced new legislation such as the Digital Markets Act (DMA) and the Digital Services Act (DSA) , which gave regulators stronger tools and clearer legal authority to oversee large technology companies. 5. Politics Also Played a Role The EU had to balance competing concerns: Protecting competition. Maintaining good relations with the United States. Encouraging innovation and investment. Avoiding accusations of targeting successful American firms. For years, some critics argued that aggressive action against U.S. tech companies could trigger diplomatic friction. Others argued that delaying enforcement allowed dominant firms to become even more powerful. As public concern about privacy, data collection, market concentration, and platform power grew, European politicians became increasingly willing to support tougher oversight. 6. Europe Wanted to Set a Global Standard Many European policymakers saw themselves as doing more than regulating Google. They viewed these cases as part of a broader effort to answer a fundamental question: Who sets the rules for the digital economy—the world’s largest technology companies or democratically elected governments? From Brussels’ perspective, the goal was to establish the principle that even the most powerful global corporations must comply with local competition rules when operating inside the European Union. The Bigger Picture The delay was not necessarily a sign of weakness or indecision. Rather, it reflected the reality that regulators were confronting an entirely new type of economic power. Building cases against digital giants required new laws, new expertise, and years of investigation. For many European officials, the eventual fines against Alphabet and other Big Tech firms are the culmination of a long campaign to prove that no company—not even one as influential as Google—is beyond regulatory oversight. For critics, however, the years of investigations demonstrate how difficult it is for governments to keep pace with technology companies that innovate and expand far faster than regulators can write rules. That debate remains unresolved, and it is likely to shape U.S.-European relations for years or decades to come. Even after Trump leaves office in January 2029, willingly or not, I sincerely doubt the EU would be as joyful that he’s gone as they were in 2021 when Biden became president. I mean that European leaders may have mixed feelings about Trump’s departure. While some might welcome the end of his more confrontational policies, others could see opportunities or leverage in maintaining continuity, or they may remain cautious due to long-standing tensions and uncertainty about future U.S. administrations. Essentially, Europe’s reaction would likely be measured rather than openly celebratory simply because transatlantic relations may be permanently destroyed if not tainted by then. How Alphabet Reacted to the Fine Not surprisingly, Alphabet executives strongly pushed back against the nearly €900 million penalty, arguing that the European Commission’s interpretation of the Digital Markets Act could force Google to scale back popular features and make its services less useful for consumers. Company leaders portrayed the ruling as an obstacle to innovation rather than a victory for competition and signaled that they were prepared to challenge the decision through the courts. Public reaction across Europe is likely to be far more mixed. Many Europeans who favor stricter oversight of Big Tech may view the fine as a necessary step toward ensuring fair competition and preventing powerful digital platforms from abusing their market position. Others, however, may question whether such aggressive regulation could have unintended consequences. Given the deep divisions in public opinion over the role of both Big Tech and EU institutions, some critics may argue that the crackdown risks making Google’s products less convenient or effective over time—particularly if European courts ultimately uphold the Commission’s decision and require lasting changes to how the company’s services operate. The Stark Divide One of the less discussed aspects of today’s transatlantic disputes is the stark difference in how the United States and Europe developed their technology sectors. Since the rise of the internet in the late twentieth century, the United States has consistently produced many of the world’s largest and most influential technology companies. Supportive investment markets, a strong venture-capital culture, world-renowned universities, and a generally business-friendly environment helped create firms such as Google, Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, Snapchat, and countless other digital platforms that would eventually reshape the global economy. Europe, by contrast, followed a different path. While the continent excelled in manufacturing, engineering, pharmaceuticals, finance, and industrial innovation, it never produced the same number of globally dominant consumer technology giants. As a result, many of the digital tools and platforms used daily by Europeans came to be controlled by American companies rather than homegrown competitors. This imbalance emerged over several presidential administrations in Washington. During the presidency of the late George H. W. Bush (1989–1993) (died during Trump’s first term), the foundations of the commercial internet were beginning to take shape. Under Bill Clinton (1993–2001) , the internet economy exploded, helping launch many of the companies that would define the digital age. During the administrations of George W. Bush (2001–2009) and Barack Obama (2009–2017) , America’s technology sector expanded into an unprecedented global force, with Silicon Valley becoming synonymous with innovation and entrepreneurship. For much of this period, European leaders did not view America’s technological dominance as a major political challenge. That began to change when Donald Trump (2017–2021) entered the White House. Although the most visible disputes between Washington and Brussels focused on trade and NATO spending, European policymakers increasingly started debating whether the continent had become too dependent on American digital infrastructure and technology companies. Relations improved during the presidency of Joe Biden (2021–2025) , as the United States and Europe worked more closely together on issues ranging from security to technology regulation. Even so, Brussels continued developing stricter rules for large digital platforms through legislation such as the Digital Markets Act and the Digital Services Act, signaling that concerns about market concentration and technological dependence had not disappeared. Since Donald Trump’s return to office for a second, nonconsecutive term in 2025 , those concerns have become more pronounced. New tariff threats, growing trade tensions, and disputes over the regulation of major American technology companies have pushed many European officials to rethink the broader transatlantic relationship. In that context, battles involving Alphabet, Meta, Apple, Amazon, and other U.S. tech giants are increasingly being viewed not simply as competition cases, but as part of a larger debate over economic sovereignty, technological independence, and Europe’s ability to chart its own course in an increasingly competitive global economy. Big Tech, Bigger Tensions: Where Do Europe and America Go From Here? The dispute over Google’s fine is about far more than competition law. At its core, it reflects a growing disagreement between Washington and Brussels over who should set the rules for the digital economy. While European policymakers argue that large technology companies must be regulated to ensure fair competition, many American officials view these actions as disproportionately targeting successful U.S. firms. If that disagreement deepens, what begins as a regulatory dispute could eventually evolve into a much broader trade conflict. One possible flashpoint would be the use of U.S. trade laws from the 1970s that grant the President authority to impose tariffs on foreign imports under certain circumstances. President Trump has previously demonstrated a willingness to use these powers aggressively, arguing that tariffs are an effective tool for protecting American economic interests and pressuring trading partners into negotiations. Should the White House conclude that European regulations unfairly discriminate against American technology companies such as Google, Apple, Meta, Amazon, or Microsoft, it could choose to respond with tariffs on a wide range of European goods. For Brussels, such a move would likely be seen as economic coercion rather than a legitimate response to technology regulation. European leaders have repeatedly insisted that the Digital Markets Act and other competition measures apply to all companies operating within the European Union, regardless of their nationality. In their view, fines imposed on Alphabet or other American firms are enforcement actions designed to uphold European law, not attacks on the United States. If Washington nevertheless proceeded with punitive tariffs, the European Union would face pressure to respond. Initially, the response could take the form of traditional retaliatory tariffs on American exports. https://okcfox.com/news/local/ou-led-stu.text: New research co-authored by an Oklahoma Museum of Natural History curator and her graduate student is offering fresh insight into how animals adapt to environmental change and why protecting genetic diversity in wildlife populations could be key to surviving what comes next. The study was led by Marcos da Cruz, a University of Oklahoma Ph.D. student in the laboratory of Dr. Hayley Lanier. Lanier, the associate curator of mammals at the Oklahoma Museum of Natural History, co-authored the research alongside an international team of collaborators from the Czech Academy of Sciences. Researchers found that much of the genetic variation animals use to adapt to new environments was inherited from distant ancestors, rather than being newly evolved in response to changing conditions. “Our study helps to show that the genes underlying climate adaptation are almost entirely dependent on retained ancestral variation, not newly evolved adaptations,” Lanier said. “The size of an animal's ancestral population helps shape the amount of genetic diversity it carries today, and that diversity provides the raw material natural selection can work with as environments change.” The team focused on the bank vole, a rodent native to Europe that thrives across a broad geographic range and lives in a variety of habitats. By sequencing the entire genome of individual animals and comparing populations from different climates, the researchers identified genetic variations associated with climate adaptation and traced where those variations came from. “It supports the idea that the past history of a population is critical for shaping future responses to climate change,” Lanier said. “The more we can do to help populations retain their genetic variation—by protecting habitats and preventing population declines—the better prepared they’ll be to adapt to future environmental challenges.” Lanier described genetically diverse populations as having something like an evolutionary “tool kit,” with a larger gene pool providing more options for future generations as conditions change. “Populations that come from large, genetically diverse ancestral populations have a much broader set of genetic variations that natural selection can draw upon,” she said. “If that diversity is lost through population declines or habitat fragmentation, species may have fewer options available as they face future environmental changes.”

https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2.text: ‘The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them.’ Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters View image in fullscreen ‘The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them.’ Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters AI (artificial intelligence) OpenAI to pause some work on AI model Astra due to security concerns Agent found to be able to find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, and to carry out cyber-attacks Eric Berger Sat 8 Aug 2026 13.00 EDT First published on Sat 8 Aug 2026 12.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google OpenAI will pause some work on an artificial intelligence model because of security concerns, the company stated Friday, following a series of incidents in which AI agents have escaped containment. The company had evaluated the agent, Astra, and found “significant advancements in agentic coding and cybersecurity”, which had moved to a “critical” threshold where it can find and exploit vulnerabilities without human intervention, or devise and execute cyber-attacks when given only a “high level desired goal”. OpenAI stated that the model was not involved in an incident in which one of its AI agents went rogue during a test, accessed the open web and hacked a startup, Hugging Face. The company discovered other instances in which autonomous agents had escaped containment, Reuters reported in July. The reports have increased concerns about advancements in AI models and humans’ ability to control them. Still, critics of the AI industry have warned that such disclosures from OpenAI and its competitors Anthropic and Meta could be designed to generate hype about the technology’s power and thus spur additional interest from investors. To prevent potential rogue behavior from AI agents, OpenAI is “implementing stricter security controls for higher-capability models and associated activities, including isolated testing environments, restricted network and tool access”, the company’s blog post stated. It will also install “enhanced model weight protections and encryption, additional monitoring and detection capabilities”. The company will pause internal activities involving Astra that do not meet these new requirements. “We’re committed to working alongside governments, safety institutes, and civil society to ensure that the frontier capabilities of models like Astra, and those that follow, are deployed responsibly and broadly for the benefit of all humanity,” the company stated. Meta also disclosed this week that one of its models hacked another company during cybersecurity testing. And the UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) announced on 4 August that agents powered by OpenAI and Anthropic had sent targeted emails to software developers in an attempt to pass a cyber challenge. “These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world,” the institute stated in a blog post. The organisation cautioned that the models’ sending of harmful software was not a case of a “model escaping its secure test environment” but rather that the group had intentionally permitted internet access to “best assess the maximum capability of models”. Still, the “behaviour was possible, sustained, and new; that alone warrants attention”, AISI said. The reports emerged while the Trump administration was finalizing a framework on how to test AI models for safety and cybersecurity risks. OpenAI and Anthropic, which have increased competition from China and other tech firms, have argued that open-source models, meaning those that allow anyone to see and modify the underlying program code, pose a security risk and pushed for additional federal regulations on them. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: The scheme reportedly involves convincing victims their bank accounts have been compromised and to protect their money they must buy gold bars. Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen The scheme reportedly involves convincing victims their bank accounts have been compromised and to protect their money they must buy gold bars. Photograph: David Gray/AFP/Getty Images New York New York authorities warn about gold bar scam targeting seniors State’s attorney general says scammers have made off with more than $100m in past two years Eric Berger Sat 8 Aug 2026 10.20 EDT Last modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 10.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Scammers in New York have been using gold bars to steal money from victims, primarily seniors, and made off with more than $100m over the past two years, the state’s attorney general announced on Friday. The scheme starts with victims receiving a fake pop-up message that states their computer or financial account has been compromised, the press release stated. The message includes a phone number to call, and when they do, the scammers convince the victims to provide remote access to their computers, which allows them to access their financial information or online bank accounts. The victims are then directed to someone posing as law enforcement who tells them that their accounts have been compromised. To protect their money, the person says, they must withdraw it and purchase gold bars or coins and then turn them over to the authorities. ‘We noticed a login from a new device’: the message from fraudsters targeting your X account Read more The scammers tell the victims not to discuss the breach with anyone and then send couriers to collect the gold. “Targeting older adults with seemingly legitimate claims that their life savings are in immediate danger is flat-out cruel,” the state attorney general, Letitia James, said. “Seniors deserve to live comfortably without fear of losing their hard-earned savings to a manipulative scam. I am urging all New Yorkers to beware of these gold bar scams and report suspicious messages related to this scam to my office.” The scam is not unique to New York. Victims in Hawaii , Maine , Washington DC and Wisconsin have reported the same thing happening to them. In one case in July, scammers targeted an 85-year-old man in DC by email and phone claiming to be US federal agents, and told him his money was at risk and to protect it by buying gold, ABC-7 News in DC reported. When the victim tried to purchase $200,000 in gold from a dealer, the seller recognized the scam and alerted law enforcement. The investigators then arrested the suspects when they arrived at the victim’s home to collect the gold. The attorney general instructed the public not to call a number provided in a pop-up, text or email and not to provide anyone they don’t know remote access to their computer. Individuals also should not provide money from a bank account at the urging of someone over the phone. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion If someone claims there is an issue with a bank account, the potential victim should contact their financial institution. Anyone concerned they may have been a victim of this scam are urged to contact law enforcement. “A scam is effective because the scammer creates a false sense of urgency, pressuring the victim into life-altering decisions on the spot and swearing them to secrecy,” the announcement stated. “The best way to combat this is to hang up and contact someone you trust and let them know your situation.” Explore more on these topics New York Scams Older people US crime news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Taras the lion Photograph: Wildlife Sanctuary View image in fullscreen Taras the lion Photograph: Wildlife Sanctuary US news Lion saved as cub from Ukraine war and brought to US battles rare fungal disease Four-year-old Taras, who now resides at a Minnesota sanctuary, was diagnosed with an often fatal infection Richard Luscombe Sat 8 Aug 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 09.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A lion that escaped the war in Ukraine after being found as a four-month-old cub inside a duffel bag at Odesa railway station is facing an even greater battle for survival in his new home in Minnesota from a rare and often fatal fungal disease. Taras, his two sisters Lesya and Stefania, and an unrelated, slightly older cub from Kyiv named Prada, were brought to the US in November 2022 by the Wildcat Sanctuary , a secluded private reserve near Sandstone, Minnesota, that arranged their rescue with the International Fund for Animal Welfare (IFAW). An American veterinarian working in Ukraine’s capital, which was under sporadic attack from Russian missiles and drones, evacuated them from Kyiv to safety in Poland, a 36-hour land journey, where they awaited import permits for the US. View image in fullscreen Caretakers take vitals during treatment of Taras the lion. Photograph: Wildlife Sanctuary Now, aged four, Taras was an energetic head of the Ukrainian pride until May, when veterinarians noticed he was sluggish and off his food. Numerous tests, including a 180-mile round trip for an expensive scan and lung biopsy at a specialist clinic in Minneapolis, diagnosed blastomycosis, a non-contagious fungal infection usually contracted from soil. The condition was blamed in the death of a white tiger called Ginger at a wildlife sanctuary in Wisconsin in June. Also known as Gilchrist’s disease, it is often fatal in humans and animals if not caught early and treated. Tammy Thies, the sanctuary’s founder and chief executive, said Taras responded well to intensive treatment, including twice daily injections of extra strength anti-fungal medication through an IV line in the early weeks, and had rejoined his pride. But he still requires oral medicine twice a day, she said, and it could still be weeks or months before sanctuary staff could be confident he was out of the woods. “He was in a fight for his life,” she said. “Usually when big cats are diagnosed with blastomycosis it’s when they’re showing respiratory distress, and by that time the disease is so advanced that even the aggressive antifungal medication can be life-threatening. There’s a very low chance of survival. “The specialist told us he had a guarded prognosis, and when I asked, ‘does he have a 30% chance?’, they all just looked at me and looked at their feet. We knew this was going to be an uphill battle, and we might not be able to save him.” Thies said Taras’s survival was his “second miracle”, after escaping the Ukraine war with his siblings. “Everybody we reached out to just told us they were sorry and not to be optimistic,” she said. “We’re just really grateful for the staff and the vet team that found this early, before he was showing breathing symptoms, because I don’t think we could have saved him.” View image in fullscreen Taras and his sister, Stefania. Photograph: Wildlife Sanctuary His reunion with his sisters was emotional. “He wanted to be with his family, so we started with one play date with a sister at a time,” she said. “We were concerned that after being away for weeks they could pick on him [but] there was so much nuzzling going on, and so much rolling around on each other, the pride welcomed him with open arms, and they’ve been inseparable ever since.” Even so, Taras still needs to be separated twice every day so his pride members do not steal his food with the medication in it. The lions’ origin is impossible to know, Thies said, but they were likely taken from their mother after birth and destined to become part of the illegal but lucrative international trade in exotic animals, at least until the start of the war thwarted the smugglers’ plans. “As borders were getting shut down and checkpoints set up, a lot of these traffickers were dumping the animals versus trying to smuggle them across the border to sell them,” she said. “It was just devastating after all he went through, after this lion had fought so hard and come out so much stronger, to then get a diagnosis of a fungal disease in his lungs, and to know he might not make it. “That was the hardest for us. He has a fight on his hands but still has a lot of life to live, and we were all going to come together and fight for him.” Explore more on these topics US news Ukraine Minnesota Animals news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.dw.com/en/thousands-attend-p.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IUvT Tens of thousands of people attended Prague's Pride march Image: Ondrej Deml/CTK/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Tens of thousands of people marched through Czech capital of Prague on Saturday as part of LGBTQ+ Pride celebrations . The festival is to last for a week. The theme of this year's event is "Times are changing." At the start of the parade, participants observed a minute of silence in memory of the victims of a van ramming near the Cristopher Street Day (CSD) parade in Berlin two weeks ago. The July 25 attack killed one person and injured around 31 others. Police said hundreds of officers were deployed to secure the parade route and added there were no major incidents Image: Ondrej Deml/CTK Photo/IMAGO The Saturday march in Prague was accompanied by enhanced security measures, including the deployment of hundreds of police officers and a de-escalation team. Participants were also told to carry banners by hand or to use plastic poles rather than wooden poles. "As every year, the aim of the festival is to raise awareness of LGBT+ issues, to show how this community lives in the Czech Republic and that it is still waiting for equal rights," the director of Prague Pride, Kamila Frohlichova, was cited by Germany's DPA news agency as saying. Marchers in Prague paid their respects to the victims of a car ramming in Berlin in late July Image: Michal Cizek/AFP What else do we know about the Pride march in Prague? According to police reports, there were no major incidents. A group of counter-demonstrators also gathered along part of the march's trajectory. The march began at Wenceslas Square in central Prague around noon (10:00 UTC/GMT) and arrived at Stvanice island in the Vltava River that passes through the city at around 2:30 p.m. local time, according to Czech media. https://www.politico.eu/article/peter-ma.text: Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar’s ruling Tisza party said on Saturday that it had nominated former Supreme Court President András Baka to become the country’s next president. Baka, who worked as a judge on the European Court of Human Rights before being elected to head the Supreme Court, was removed from his post by the Fidesz government in 2011 — a move the ECHR ruled was unlawful . “Throughout his career, Dr. András Baka has considered the principle of the separation of powers to be of paramount importance and has consistently stood up for the rule of law and judicial independence,” Tisza said in a Facebook post . Advertisement Advertisement He is “the strongest guarantee that the office of President of the Republic will regain its true dignity and its ability to unite the nation and serve as a counterbalance to the ruling majority,” it added. Parliament is set to vote on his candidacy next Tuesday. Tisza, which won a general election in the spring, enjoys a two-thirds majority in the chamber, making Baka’s election to the largely representative post a formality. The nomination comes after former President Tamás Sulyok signed a constitutional amendment that removed him from office last month, bowing to months of public pressure from Magyar. The new prime minister had called for Sulyok’s resignation following Tisza’s landslide election victory that ended Viktor Orbán’s 16-year rule. Magyar’s first choice for president, chess grandmaster Judit Polgár, declined the nomination, saying the job would be too stressful .

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgl.text: Image source, X/Reuters Image caption, The islands of Amami and Okinawa are the parts of Japan most affected by the typhoon By Jack Burgess Published 3 hours ago Typhoon Dolphin has cut power to at least 44,000 buildings and injured at least five people after hitting Japan's Okinawa island on Saturday. Flights to and from Okinawa's main airport - Naha International Airport - were cancelled as it closed on Friday as the storm arrived. The storm had maximum wind speeds of 162km/h (101mph) on Saturday and has been categorised as a "very strong" typhoon by the Japan Meteorological Agency, which warned of high waves, storm surges and lightning strikes. Dolphin is expected to make landfall on China's eastern coast late on Sunday or early on Monday. Authorities there have shut ports and schools ahead of its arrival. The main areas in Japan affected by the typhoon are the islands of Okinawa and Amami in the far south-west of the country. Five elderly people suffered non-life-threatening injuries, according to the Okinawan prefectural government. Three of them fell because of the strong winds, it said. Japan's national broadcaster NHK reports numerous accounts of trees being toppled by strong winds throughout Nago city in Okinawa, while a car was found overturned and leaking oil in a parking lot. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Satellite imagery showing Typhoon Dolphin approaching Japan's Okinawa during the week In China, Zhejiang's Ningbo Lishe International Airport said it would stop its operations from 23:30 local time on Saturday (15:30 GMT) and suspend all flights on Sunday. A coastal typhoon alert in Zhejiang has been raised to its highest level, and port and ferry services have been halted in the Chinese province. Typhoon season in the western Pacific typically occurs between May and October, when typhoons are considered more commonplace. This year is a strong El NiÃ±o year , which experts say means typhoons can grow to be more intense. In an average year of 25 cyclones reaching tropical storm strength in the region, around three usually make landfall in Japan, according to the country's meteorological agency. Some of these will be strong enough to be classified as typhoons â as was the case with Dolphin. A typhoon is the term used for storms that form in the north-west Pacific, whereas a hurricane is the term used for storms that form in the Atlantic or eastern Pacific. Beállítom The Tisza Party’s parliamentary group has nominated András Baka, the former head of the country's Supreme Court as president of Hungary, the party has announced following their Saturday meeting where the decision was made by secret ballot. Although the previous president, Tamás Sulyok’s mandate was supposed to last until March 2029, his term was ended prematurely by the 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law in mid-July. The move was part of the Tisza Party’s campaign promise to remove all “puppets appointed by Fidesz to do their bidding”. In his post announcing Baka’s nomination, Prime Minister Péter Magyar wrote: “Throughout his entire career, Dr. András Baka has regarded the principle of the separation of powers of paramount importance and has always consistently stood up for the rule of law and judicial independence. His life’s work exemplifies a commitment to the democratic rule of law and constitutional principles.” Magyar added that they are convinced that Baka’s “experience and the professional independence he has demonstrated throughout his career are of particular value during this time, as we work together to lay the foundations for Hungary’s new constitutional order.” According to the Prime Minister, during the constitutional process ahead of us, we need a president whose “professional authority, independence, and experience in public law and constitutional matters provide a solid foundation for successfully guiding our country back onto the path of the rule of law and constitutional governance, and for embodying the unity of the Hungarian nation.” —and they consider Baka worthy of the task. András Baka is a researcher specializing in human rights and minority rights issues. He became particularly well-known in 2011 when he was unlawfully removed from his position as president of the Supreme Court after criticizing the Orbán regime’s plans for reforming the judiciary. He was born in Budapest in 1952 and earned his doctorate in law from the Faculty of Law and Political Science at Budapest’s ELTE (Eötvös Lóránd University) in 1978, then worked for more than twenty years as a research fellow at the Institute of Political and Legal Sciences of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences (MTA), and later served as director general of the College of Public Administration. Between 1991 and 2008, he spent two terms serving as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights. ​​Starting in the 1980s, he was a visiting professor at several universities in the United States and has been invited on multiple occasions to lecture in France and (what was then) West Germany. During the first parliamentary term following the regime change in Hungary, between 1990-1991, Baka served as a member of Parliament for the Hungarian Democratic Forum (MDF), though he never joined the party. He also has a background in labor unions. In June 2016, the Grand Chamber at the European Court of Human Rights ruled in Baka's favor and found that he had been removed from his position as head of the Supreme Court in 2012 through ad hominem legislation due to his criticism of the Orbán government's planned judicial reforms, which threatened the independence of the courts. Subsequently, the Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers held the Hungarian state accountable for failing to implement the Strasbourg judgment in the case of Baka v. Hungary since 2016. He is likely to take office on 19 August Parliament could elect the new head of state as early as Tuesday. The vote is expected to be a mere formality, as the election of the new head of state requires the support of two-thirds of the members of Parliament, and the 141-member Tisza faction has a comfortable majority. The new president shall take office on the eighth day following the announcement of the results of Tuesday’s secret ballot, which would in this case be 19 August. In this case, the new president would be the one to present the state honors and awards customarily announced on August 20, the national holiday celebrating the founding of the Hungarian state. Pursuant to Amendment 17 of the Fundamental Law, the term of the new head of state will last until the new constitution enters into force, but no longer than five years. Previously, Péter Magyar has said that the next President of Hungary must be someone who will watch over the nation’s unity and the rule of law. According to him, the country needs someone who understands the weight of their words, is capable of calm deliberation, is willing to listen to different opinions, and is aware that all decisions they make have consequences. The former governing party, Fidesz and their coalition partner, the Christian Democratic People's party (KDNP) will not participate in electing the new head of state. They had previously indicated that they would boycott the vote because they considered Tamás Sulyok’s removal to be illegitimate. “It’s a wasted effort. Under public law, this is invalid, so holding a presidential election is pointless. The position is not vacant,” they stated . Mi Hazánk nominated energy lawyer Máté Tóth for the position, which, without the support of other parliamentary groups, can essentially be considered only a symbolic gesture, since they only have six representatives in Parliament, and the endorsement of at least one-fifth of the representatives—that is, 40 members—is required for a candidate’s name to appear on the ballot. There were ten candidates In his post on Saturday, Péter Magyar wrote that thousands of Hungarians have recommended dozens of candidates to the Tisza Party in recent weeks, including numerous distinguished experts and well-known public figures. The Tisza Party's leadership interviewed ten candidates, eventually recommending three of them to the Tisza Party's parliamentary faction on Saturday. “We are proud that, for the first time since the transition to democracy, the selection of the head of state did not involve a decision based on deals between parties or choosing from among candidates nominated by parties. Instead, the person we are recommending to lead the nation is a truly independent, nonpartisan individual with a proven track record throughout his life and profession”, the Prime Minister stated. Noting her arrival, Rashtrapati Bhavan wrote in a post on X, 'President Droupadi Murmu arrived in Delhi after completing her State visits to Moldova, North Macedonia and Romania.' https://x.com/rashtrapatibhvn/status/2081156622064537913 The President concluded her landmark visits on Saturday, securing key diplomatic breakthroughs with Moldova, North Macedonia, and Romania to significantly bolster bilateral ties across trade, defence, tourism, and core economic sectors. The diplomatic engagement marked several historic milestones, establishing Murmu as the first Indian head of state to visit both Moldova and North Macedonia. Her arrival in Romania also marked the first visit by an Indian president to the Eastern European nation in over three decades. During the final leg of her visit to Romania, which began on July 23, New Delhi and Bucharest agreed to double their trade volume over the next three years while deepening defence cooperation and allied strategic areas. President Murmu held comprehensive talks on bilateral relations with Romanian President Nicusor Dan and separately engaged with Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan. She also addressed the India-Romania Business Forum in Bucharest on Friday and interacted with members of the India-Romania Parliamentary Friendship Group. Recognising her public leadership and international outreach, the Bucharest University of Economic Studies conferred an honorary doctorate upon President Murmu. The 'Doctor Honoris Causa' represents the institution's highest academic distinction, awarded to eminent personalities for exceptional contributions to academia, public service and international cooperation. Before she departed for the airport on Saturday, President Murmu met with members of the Indian diaspora. Romania currently hosts over 13,500 Indian nationals, including approximately 10,000 workers. Earlier, during her visit to North Macedonia from July 21 to 22, President Murmu held bilateral discussions with President Gordana Sijanovska-Davkova, which were followed by delegation-level talks. Both nations resolved to double bilateral trade figures and identified joint opportunities in tourism, hospitality, and filmmaking. During her stay in Skopje, Murmu addressed the Assembly of North Macedonia and presided over the inaugural session of the India-North Macedonia Business Forum. The European visit commenced on July 20 in Moldova, where President Murmu held extensive talks with Moldovan President Maia Sandu, evaluating the entire spectrum of bilateral engagement.
