http://www.parisguardian.com/news/279209.text: 'Standing shoulder to shoulder': Macron pledges national recovery as unprecedented wildfires ravage France and Spain ANI 26 Jul 2026, 02:27 GMT+10 Paris [France], July 26 (ANI): Pledging that the nation will overcome its ongoing crisis, French President Emmanuel Macron on Saturday (local time) praised the resilience of emergency crews and citizens as 'a united people, standing shoulder to shoulder' against raging wildfires. Macron, in a post on X, confirmed full civil and military deployment, including water-bomber planes and military transport aircraft. 'In these hours when the flames are severely testing our country, France reveals what it is: a united people, standing shoulder to shoulder. Thank you to our firefighters, our military personnel, the civil security forces, our gendarmes and police officers, as well as to the farmers and entrepreneurs, who through their commitment and courage, relentlessly combat the fires,' Macron stated, noting that 'All civil and military resources are mobilized: civil security aerial resources, Canadair, Dash, water-bomber helicopters, reinforcements from across France. One first illustrates the adaptability of our armed forces: the A400M is engaged in support of operations.' The fires have heavily impacted Gironde, Landes, Occitanie, Var, Hautes-Alpes, and Haute-Corse. Acknowledging the scale of destruction, Macron noted that 'thousands of hectares have been ravaged, homes destroyed, activities disrupted, lives upended'. However, the President assured affected residents, displaced families, local mayors, and prefects of the government's unwavering commitment and said, 'We will rebuild, we will repair, and we will be there as long as it takes.' The French President further thanked Romania, Croatia, Germany, Portugal, Sweden, Switzerland, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia for dispatching critical emergency aid. 'This is Europe,' Macron declared. 'In times of trial, it brings to life the solidarity that defines it'. He also extended solidarity to neighbouring countries enduring similar conditions, adding that France's 'thoughts also go to Spain, Italy, Greece, and all the peoples who are also facing wildfires'. https://x.com/EmmanuelMacron/status/2081058742280303075 Meanwhile, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez, describing the crisis as a 'historic situation' requiring a 'historic mobilisation,' announced that nearly 100,000 hectares have burned across the national territory. With around thirty fires simultaneously active, more than 167,000 people have been evacuated to ensure their safety. The situation remains particularly critical in Gironde, where sudden weather shifts have altered the fire's dynamics. 'After a slight improvement last night and this morning, the forecasts are once again becoming unfavourable,' Nunez warned. 'The coming hours could be difficult.' Following a second interministerial crisis meeting within 24 hours, additional reinforcements have also been dispatched to Landes, Var, Corsica, and Hautes-Alpes. 'The ground resources of the firefighters have been massively redeployed to the Southwest in order to concentrate our efforts where the situation is most critical. 1,400 firefighters, 1,500 military personnel, and 1,700 internal security forces are now engaged in fighting the fires, protecting populations, and securing evacuated areas,' he wrote in a post on X. He noted that the healthcare network is actively managing the human toll, distributing 2.5 million FFP2 masks to protect against smoke, deploying 20 military ambulances, and delivering 3,500 camp beds to reception centres. The Minister added that on Monday, government officials will meet with tourism and energy leaders to plan recovery efforts. https://x.com/SebLecornu/status/2081075555202384013 The remarks come as unprecedented wildfires sweeping through western France and central Spain have forced more than 250,000 residents and tourists to flee, as raging flames destroy vast forest tracts and residential communities near Bordeaux and Madrid. According to Deutsche Welle (DW), emergency responders face blazes of historic proportions, the largest recorded in both nations in recent years, which firefighters admit are too massive to tackle head-on. Along France's Atlantic coast, approximately 44,000 people were evacuated from the Cap Ferret peninsula, with many transported to safety by boat. Near Bordeaux, the renowned wine-producing hub, entire towns were emptied 'as a precaution' as gale-force winds pushed advancing flames closer to urban areas. In total, French authorities confirm that over 197,000 people have been evacuated across the western Gironde and Landes departments. Although investigators indicate the two primary French blazes were ignited accidentally, environmental authorities emphasise that increasingly hotter and drier summer conditions have exponentially magnified the severity of such outbreaks, DW reported. The human toll across Southern Europe continues to rise. Dozens of firefighters have been injured, and three have lost their lives this week--two near Bordeaux, France, and one in Sicily, Italy, where major wildfires are also burning. On the other hand, in Spain, the Interior Ministry reported that 70,000 people have fled their homes. Spanish officials confirmed a wildfire fatality in Manises, near Valencia, where local emergency teams brought the blaze under control but noted that 'unfortunately the fire has claimed the life of one person' after the victim's body was discovered in a vehicle within a ravine, DW reported. Spain has officially declared a national emergency as two separate blazes near Madrid merged into a single massive front. Emergency management services for the Madrid region warned that the combined inferno has reached 'its peak and is currently beyond the capacity of firefighters to contain.' Meanwhile, in Guadalajara province, the largest active fire in the region has scorched roughly 32,000 hectares. Inspecting affected zones west of Madrid as local temperatures surpassed 37C (98.6F), Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez reaffirmed that the top priority remains 'to save lives.' In an official address shared on X, Prime Minister Sanchez stated, 'Our priority is safeguarding lives, defending population centres, and combating the flames. The entire State, all Administrations, are coordinating all resources for an effective response to the fires and for the reception of evacuated and confined people. Today we are in the fight and in the extinguishing, but the Government of Spain will also be in the reconstruction and recovery of the affected areas.' DW reported that in order to assist both countries, the European Commission announced the dispatch of specialised firefighting aircraft, sending three planes to France and four to Spain to support containment operations. Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief reporting from Budapest, Hungary BUDAPEST ( Worthy News ) – Hungary’s Prosecutor General Bálint Gábor Nagy resigned Wednesday unexpectedly, saying the Prosecutor’s Office must never become “an instrument of political struggle” as political turmoil deepened. Nagy, Hungary’s highest-ranking prosecutor, said sustained attacks against him had exceeded the limits of acceptable public and professional debate, threatening the independence and credibility of the Prosecutor’s Office. He said he was resigning to shield the institution from what he described as a politically motivated conflict. Prime Minister Péter Magyar, who had repeatedly urged Nagy to resign in recent months, welcomed the announcement saying Hungary had been “freed from another puppet” of former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán. “Gentlemen, who will be next?” Magyar wrote on social media platform Facebook. The resignation comes amid mounting political tensions following a series of high-profile investigations involving officials linked to Orbán’s Fidesz party. On Tuesday, investigators from Hungary’s Prosecutor’s Office raided a Fidesz data center as part of a corruption probe involving the National Cultural Fund (NKA), seizing party servers. FIDESZ RAID SPARKS OUTCRY Orbán condemned the operation as politically motivated, comparing it to the final years of Hungary’s communist Kádár era. He said the seizure had left Fidesz without internet access, digital communications, or access to internal party data. The former prime minister rejected allegations surrounding the National Cultural Fund, describing the investigation as a “staged procedure.” He argued that officials administering roughly 47 million euros (about $53 million) in government-approved cultural funding had done nothing wrong and suggested the probe was primarily intended to justify confiscating Fidesz’s servers. Orbán also claimed Hungary under the current government was “not a democracy, but arbitrary rule.” He insisted that former President Tamás Sulyok was the country’s last legitimate head of state and argued that subsequent presidential appointments would ultimately be judged by history as unlawful. Orbán also announced that János Bóka had been appointed the new parliamentary leader of Fidesz, saying he would build a strong and confident parliamentary group representing the party’s supporters. Speaking at the same news conference, Orbán voiced his full support for former Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó, who recently left Parliament to accept a senior position with Chinese electric vehicle and battery manufacturer BYD. Orbán said he remained convinced Szijjártó could continue serving Hungary’s interests outside politics. BYD APPOINTMENT UNDER SCRUTINY Separately, Hungarian media and other sources said investigators had carried out a search at the Hungarian operations of BYD after Szijjártó accepted his new position with the Chinese company. News about the raids came while Parliament’s National Security Committee also met behind closed doors to discuss potential security concerns surrounding Szijjártó’s appointment. Lawmakers questioned whether the former foreign minister, who had access to classified state information while in office, should now work for a company outside both NATO and the European Union. Participants later said the committee’s proceedings had been classified until December 31, 2051, preventing public disclosure of the discussions for the next 25 years. The developments have intensified political debate over Hungary’s national security, its relationship with China, and the government’s handling of former senior officials. POLITICAL CONFRONTATION ESCALATES Fidesz has described the raids as unprecedented since the fall of communism in 1990 and accused the government of political intimidation. The party published what it called a “Declaration of Resistance,” pledging to continue what it described as “a peaceful struggle” to restore Hungary’s democratic rule of law. The resignation of the country’s top prosecutor, the investigations involving Fidesz, and the scrutiny surrounding Szijjártó’s move to BYD highlight the increasingly bitter confrontation between Prime Minister Magyar’s government and Orbán’s Fidesz opposition. https://ianslive.in/president-murmu-retu.text: President Murmu returns to Delhi after concluding State visits to Moldova, North Macedonia, Romania IANS July 26, 2026 7:28 AM Share on | New Delhi, July 26 (IANS) President Droupadi Murmu returned to New Delhi on Sunday after successfully concluding her three-nation State visit to Moldova, North Macedonia and Romania, marking a significant diplomatic outreach aimed at strengthening India’s ties with the three European countries. Announcing her return, the official X handle of the President of India posted: “President Droupadi Murmu arrived in Delhi after completing her State visits to Moldova, North Macedonia and Romania.” During the final leg of the tour, President Murmu visited Romania, where she held wide-ranging talks with Romanian President Nicusor Dan on advancing bilateral cooperation and regional and global issues. According to the President’s Secretariat, President Murmu was warmly received by President Dan at the Cotroceni Palace in Bucharest and was accorded a ceremonial welcome and guard of honour. The two leaders held comprehensive discussions covering key aspects of the India-Romania partnership and also exchanged views on regional and global developments as well as multilateral cooperation. The visit also witnessed the signing of three Memoranda of Understanding (MoUs) to expand bilateral collaboration in the fields of science and technology, sports, and the establishment of a Chair of Indian Studies at the University of Bucharest. President Murmu’s visit was historic as it marked the first State Visit by an Indian President to Romania in nearly three decades. She was accompanied by Minister of State for Consumer Affairs, Food and Public Distribution Nimuben Jayantibhai Bambhaniya, along with Members of Parliament Dr. Dinesh Sharma and Vijay Baghel. Before arriving in Romania, President Murmu visited North Macedonia, the second stop of her three-nation tour, after concluding her engagements in Moldova. Upon her arrival in the capital, Skopje, she was welcomed by North Macedonia’s Minister of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, Timcho Mucunski. During the visit, President Murmu held discussions with President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova and Prime Minister Hristijan Mickoski, with the talks aimed at enhancing bilateral cooperation across multiple sectors and further deepening relations between the two countries. The President began her tour with a landmark visit to Moldova, becoming the first Indian President ever to visit the country. During her stay in Chisinau, she visited the Parliament of Moldova and met Speaker Igor Grosu along with members of the Parliamentary Friendship Group. According to the President’s Secretariat, President Murmu expressed confidence that the leaders of India and Moldova would continue working together to build a stronger, future-oriented and mutually beneficial partnership. https://www.gdnonline.com:443/Details/14.text: Rescuers work at the site of a Russian missile strikes in Kyiv region yesterday At least 15 people have been killed in Russian attacks on Ukraine, including 10 dead in ballistic missile strikes on an exhibition near Kyiv showcasing drone technology. Writing on social media, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said some 100 people had been injured in the daytime attack on the exhibition, attended by prominent members of the defence sector. Elsewhere, five people were killed in the eastern city of Sloviansk by Russian glide bombs. And last night, Zelensky said he had received intelligence that Russia was preparing another massive missile strike which “could happen today” or “within the next 48 hours”. Meanwhile, an overnight Ukrainian strike killed six people and wounded 26 in the Russian city of Kirov, more than 1,000km behind the front line. Ukraine also attacked warehouses of Wildberries – Russia’s biggest online retailer. After the attacks near Kyiv, there were initially fears for the safety of Defence Ministry adviser Serhiy Beskrestnov, also known as Flash, and Lyuba Shypovych, who has been involved in developing technology for the Ukrainian army. Following the incident, both took to social media to confirm they were unharmed, and Beskrestnov said he had stayed away from the event because of security concerns. Ukrainian air force spokesman Yuri Ihnat told Ukrainian TV the attack involved three ballistic missiles, only one of which was intercepted. Russia confirmed the attack. Its Defence Ministry said high-precision long-range weaponry had been used on a site where drones for use in targeting civil sites in Russia were being demonstrated. It said producers of drones, as well as representatives of Ukraine’s drone forces and security services “directly planning and carrying out strikes on Russian territory” were present. This is at least the third time since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022 that an exhibition of this kind has been hit. There has been widespread outrage that a public event of this kind was being held at all and had, apparently, been widely advertised. Zelensky said the incident was being investigated, while Ukraine’s prosecutor-general said efforts were under way to establish who decided to hold the event and what safety measures were in place. The attack came hours after the Ukrainian strikes on a factory in the city of Kirov and warehouses in north-west Russia. Zelensky said “one of the most important military facilities” in Kirov supplying “components for aircraft and missile equipment” used in strikes against Ukraine had been hit. Yesterday’s attacks on at least two Wildberries facilities in the St Petersburg area were the latest of several over the past week. The attacks on the retailer have dealt a blow to a large number of small and medium-sized businesses within Russia. After months of drone attacks on oil depots and refineries, Kyiv says it is targeting logistics hubs – such as those run by Wildberries – because they can be used to buy military equipment, in order to disrupt supplies to the Russian army. Meanwhile Zelensky is expected to travel to the US next week, and is slated to meet President Donald Trump on Tuesday, a White House official said, as Washington seeks to revive peace talks between Ukraine and Russia. Trump ally Laura Loomer, who is in Kyiv and interviewed Zelensky, quoted him as saying he intends to go to the funeral of US Senator Lindsey Graham. Meanwhile, Romanian President Nicusor Dan said a Romanian F-16 fighter jet shot down a Russian drone breaching the country’s airspace yesterday.

https://english.republika.mk/world/orban.text: The new Government of Hungary rules autocratically and wants to completely eliminate the entire opposition, said former Prime Minister Viktor Orban in his first major public address in Romania after the April elections. The Magyar regime adopted changes to the Constitution that are forcing the President to resign even though his term is not yet finished, and prosecutors are launching raids against Orban’s Fidesz party. Under the new rules, no one will be able to serve as prime minister for more than two terms in the future, and no one will be able to serve as a member of parliament for more than three terms. The new government wants to eliminate the entire opposition, Orban said. At the same time, he added that the new government lacks the capacity to govern and assessed that it will not be able to overcome the crisis this fall, which, according to him, will be caused by shortages and high prices of energy. Orban said that his party must “support groups and organizations of people who love freedom.” Fidesz currently does not function as a party, but as a service center, an incubator, a nursery, if you like, he said during his address in Romania, for a large gathering of the local Hungarian community. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: New South Wales recorded its first cases of H5 bird flu in two local birds on Saturday, including one found near Wentworth on the Murray-Darling Basin. Jack Gough, chief executive of the Invasive Species Council, said: That should be ringing alarm bells for governments because it suggests it could soon be spreading among inland bird colonies ahead of spring breeding season. Birds in the Murray-Darling basin are already in decline due to feral animals, insufficient water to critical wetlands and the loss of habitat - now they have a deadly disease to contend with. Samples from two deceased greater crested terns in NSW – the other found near Narooma on the south coast – tested positive at CSIRO’s Australian Centre for Disease Preparedness. On Saturday, a further 28 positive cases were confirmed in South Australia, bringing the state’s total to 147. An additional 13 suspected cases were also detected, including an ibis in Adelaide and a cormorant in Carpenter Rocks on the Limestone Coast.

Photograph: UK MOD Crown copyright/Royal Navy/Reuters View image in fullscreen HMS Mersey tracking the Russian Admiral Grigorovich frigate. Photograph: UK MOD Crown copyright/Royal Navy/Reuters Royal Navy Navy says it is spending 25% more time monitoring Russian vessels around UK waters Warning of increased activity as patrols spent 21 days in July shadowing Moscow’s ships in Dover Strait and North Sea Nadeem Badshah and PA Media Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.03 EDT Last modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 16.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Royal Navy has warned of increasing Russian activity around the UK’s waters after it spent 21 days in July monitoring Moscow’s ships. Naval operations to monitor Russian vessels increased by 25% last month compared with the previous year, with warships making repeated voyages through the strait of Dover and the North Sea. Offshore patrol vessels HMS Tyne, HMS Mersey and HMS Severn, alongside Wildcat helicopters from 815 Naval Air Squadron and Merlin submarine-hunting aircraft, were deployed throughout the month to shadow Russian frigates Neustrashimy and Admiral Grigorovich, which are tasked with escorting so-called “shadow fleet” tankers. Last month, the Ministry of Defence (MoD) said in its annual report that Royal Navy vessels had been “activated” 116 times in the year to March 2026, shadowing 61 Russian warships and 28 merchant vessels around the UK’s waters. This reflected a 30% increase in Russian naval activity over the previous two years and included operations to deter the spy ship Yantar, which was spotted near undersea cables off Scotland last November. Vladimir Putin has been accused of using the Kremlin’s shadow fleet of ageing vessels to evade international sanctions on its oil and fund the war in Ukraine. The increase in Russian naval activity follows the seizure of the tanker Smyrtos by Royal Marines in June, the first time British troops have directly boarded a shadow fleet vessel. The MoD said the diversion of ships from Russia to escort shadow fleet vessels meant the country was “using up valuable operational capacity to constantly guard cargo”. The UK has already imposed sanctions on more than 500 vessels, and Russia’s oil and gas revenues fell by 24% year on year in 2025. HMS Tyne was also tasked with monitoring the Neustrashimy as it carried out a live-firing exercise outside British and French waters on 20 July. Another ship, the frigate HMS Somerset, has been involved in monitoring Russian activity in the North Atlantic as part of a four-month Nato deployment searching for submarines, alongside helicopters from the Navy’s Fleet Air Arm. Somerset’s commanding officer, Cmdr Matt Millyard, said on Saturday: “This deployment demonstrates exactly what the Royal Navy exists to do: protect the UK and our allies from wherever our interests are threatened. “I am immensely proud of every single member of the ship’s company for what we have achieved over the past four months.” Explore more on these topics Royal Navy Military Russia Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Tehran, Iran. An Iranian statement said the US must never threaten the country again. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Strait of Hormuz Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz as deal still out of reach Tehran urges US to ‘correct its behaviour’ as UAE says one of its ships targeted by Iranian missile Guardian staff and agencies Sat 8 Aug 2026 17.01 EDT Last modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 20.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz, while the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile, as a deal to open the strategic waterway remained out of reach on Saturday. Iran’s politburo-like body known as the supreme national security council said the strait of Hormuz will not open until the United States “corrects its behaviour”, and its state broadcaster published a statement from the council’s secretary, Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, who is also a commander in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). The US must never threaten Iran again, the statement said, and must permanently end the war with Iran and its armed allies in the region. The US must lift the naval blockade of Iranian ports and withdraw its military from the area. It also must “completely compensate” Iran for war damage, lift sanctions and “unconditionally” release frozen assets. Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in war Read more There was no immediate comment from the US, which has wanted an acceptable deal on the strait before ending the blockade. According to the interim deal signed in June, a schedule to end sanctions and a plan for compensation would be part of the final deal, and negotiations would address frozen assets. The Iranian foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said on Saturday that they were close to reaching an agreement on navigation , “specifically the determination of a transit route”. But the waterway’s reopening is contingent on other conditions, he said, in remarks shared on social media, and blamed the situation on what he called the US violation of the interim deal. Oman, which is mediating and has made relatively few comments on the talks, said in a statement on Saturday that the discussions were continuing “in a positive and constructive atmosphere”, and condemned attacks on ships on the strait. Iran has imposed an effective blockade of the strait and wants to charge users for passage, repeatedly attacking ships it accuses of attempting to circumvent its preferred route. The US opposes any Iranian tolls in the strait, though the June deal allows Tehran to hammer out arrangements for the “future administration” of Hormuz in conjunction with fellow coastal state Oman. The 60-day period to negotiate a final deal will end in just over a week but could be extended. Iran has said it was close to reaching a separate deal with Oman to manage the strait, which runs between the two countries. Iran’s president Masoud Pezeshkian, a relative moderate, said he believed now was the best time for an agreement. “There is cohesion, strength, and unity in the country, and as far as I know, Iran is considered victorious and powerful in this war,” Iranian news agencies quoted him as saying. Continued attacks in the strait, which was free to sail through before the war, led to the collapse of an April ceasefire, and mediators have since urged both sides to return to the terms of the June memorandum. The strait, which is crucial to global supplies of oil and natural gas, had been considered an international waterway before the war. Ship transits remain low. Meanwhile, a vessel owned by Abu Dhabi’s state-owned Adnoc oil and gas company was attacked while sailing through the strait of Hormuz, Emirati authorities said earlier on Saturday. The foreign ministry said Iran fired the missile as part of attacks on commercial shipping. Adnoc said in a statement that there were no casualties following the attack early on Saturday. The company said more than a dozen of its vessels have been attacked by missiles and drones while using the strait since the US and Israel launched the war on Iran in February. One crew member has been killed and 20 others wounded, it said. Adnoc did not elaborate on the location of the attack or any damage. Later, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations centre said a vessel east of the town of Khasab, Oman had been struck by a projectile that caused a fire that was put out, and the vessel and crew were safe. It was not clear whether this was the Adnoc incident. Photograph: Scott G Winterton/The Deseret News/AP View image in fullscreen A Sikorsky Skycrane rises after refilling during efforts to fight the Widemouth 2 fire east of Fillmore, Utah, on 4 August, before it crashed on 7 August. Photograph: Scott G Winterton/The Deseret News/AP Utah Utah wildfire blocks rescuers from reaching firefighting helicopter crash site Fate of two passengers onboard helicopter that went down Friday morning remains unknown after more than 24 hours Uwa Ede-Osifo Sat 8 Aug 2026 19.43 EDT Last modified on Sat 8 Aug 2026 19.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The fate of two passengers onboard a firefighting helicopter that crashed Friday morning in Utah remains unknown after more than 24 hours, as one of the country’s largest wildfires continues to grow, preventing authorities from safely reaching the accident site. The Sikorsky S-64 helicopter, contracted by the US Forest Service, was responding on Friday to the Widemouth 2 fire, a blaze sparked in late July by lightning, when it crashed in a remote area of central Utah . Widemouth 2 has swept through more than 114,600 acres (46,400 hectares) and is 24% contained, as of Saturday. That figure marked a jump from early on Friday, where the fire’s scope was reported as reaching more than 105,000 acres, according to state data. The chopper’s crash ignited a new blaze, state authorities said at a news conference on Friday evening. The accident site is within the fire’s perimeter. “Ground resources attempted to respond immediately, but access to the scene was compromised by the emergent fire,” the US Forest Service wrote in a Saturday statement. “Without a safety zone, the Incident Management Team determined not to place lives at risk until the area is deemed safe.” Federal officials have advised the public to refrain from speculating on the nature of the crash, as search-and-rescue teams wait for fire conditions to subside to safer levels. In a Saturday daily report, however, the US National Interagency Fire Center, a coalition of state and federal agencies, said the helicopter’s “pilot and one crewmember were fatally injured”. At a Saturday morning briefing, a moment of silence was observed to honor the passengers. The US Forest Service has declined to confirm their status. “There have already been many false reports and rumors, and the victims deserve the highest level of respect and avoidance of speculation,” the agency wrote. Investigators with the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) were en route to Richfield, a city roughly 160 miles (250km) south of Salt Lake City, as of Friday. When they are able to reach the crash site, they will document the scene, before retrieving the aircraft. The western US states have faced a deadly wildfire season. In June, three firefighters died, as they battled a blaze along the Colorado-Utah border. A fourth firefighter later died from burn injuries sustained during the emergency response. "We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," Dobrindt told the newspaper Bild am Sonntag following the discovery of a drone carrying explosives at Leipzig/Halle Airport. "Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilizing Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality," Dobrindt said. He also noted that the country is stepping up research into drones to address new security threats . A new drone security research center will be established later in August at a German Aerospace Center (DLR) test airport in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt , Dobrindt said. The drones were detected at around 10 p.m. (2000 GMT) over the Bundeswehr base, a German armed forces spokesperson said. German media reported that the base hosts personnel responsible for the maintenance of US Patriot air defense systems, which play a key role in defending Ukraine against Russian aerial attacks. Drone incident at Leipzig airport The sighting in Mechernich comes just two days after the discovery of a drone carrying explosives a Ukrainian transport plane at Leipzig/Halle Airport, an incident Dobrindt called a "hybrid attack scenario." While German government officials have refrained from publicly blaming any foreign country over the Leipzig incident, some lawmakers have pointed fingers at Russia , which has been at war with Ukraine since ​its full-scale invasion of the country in 2022. https://www.dw.com/en/kosovo-pm-kurti-eg.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IV6p Opposition lawmaker Kadrijaj sparked an uproar in Kosovo's parliament after throwing an egg at caretaker PM Kurti Image: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS Advertisement Kosovo's parliament was suspended on Saturday after an opposition lawmaker threw eggs at caretaker Prime Minister Albin Kurti . "Shame on you!" Time Kadrijaj of the conservative opposition Alliance for the Future of Kosovo (AAK) party shouted in parliament before hurling eggs at Kurti. In response, Kurti said that he was "happy to pay this price" if it was the cost of dialogue. Kurti's left-wing Vetevendosje (VV) party is known for its own parliamentary disruptions, with party representatives launching tear gas in the chamber in 2018 and also on multiple occasions in 2015. Kadrijaj's AAK has seven seats in parliament, making it the fourth-largest opposition group Image: Valdrin Xhemaj/REUTERS What is the political situation in Kosovo? The incident comes after days of negotiations as Kurti attempts to gain enough opposition support to elect a new president amid Kosovo's broader political crisis. The Balkan country has held three elections in over two years. Kurti achieved his parliamentary majority with ethnic minority MPs in a December election that followed an inconclusive vote in February 2025. His VV party's share of the vote fell from 51% to 43% in a snap election in June, but it maintained a parliamentary majority alongside ethnic minority allies. However, Kurti requires a two-thirds majority in parliament to elect a president. The current negotiations seem to have ground to another stalemate, with neither side having agreed to a candidate. A constitutional deadline to elect a speaker of parliament expired on Friday. Opposition lawmakers have threatened legal action over Kurti's request for more time to negotiate. Kosovo declared independence from Serbia in 2008 after the 1998-99 war, which ended with Serbia's withdrawal following a NATO bombing campaign. Kosovo has been recognized by over half of the world's countries , including the United States and most European Union countries. Belgrade considers Kosovo to be part of Serbia. https://www.dw.com/en/ukraine-russia-pou.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IUD5 Without the necessary interceptors for its air defense, Ukraine is struggling to defend itself against relentless bombing by Russia Image: State Emergency Service of Ukraine/Handout/REUTERS Advertisement As Russia continues its relentless bombardment of Kyiv, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy is making his first visit to Serbia , a European country that has maintained friendly relations with Russia despite the latter's full-scale invasion of Ukraine . Zelenskyy arrived in Belgrade Friday evening and had dinner with his Serbian counterpart, Aleksandar Vucic . They met again for talks at the presidential palace on Saturday. Later, Zelenskyy wrote on X that he and Vucic had discussed ways to strengthen infrastructure in both countries, including ports and railways, as well as economic development, reconstruction, and job creation in Ukraine and Serbia. Representatives from both countries signed a memorandum of understanding regarding agricultural and food safety cooperation. Zelenskyy added that the leaders also discussed the challenges of the upcoming winter in Ukraine, heavily hit by ⁠Russian attacks on energy facilities, and relations with the European Union. He also thanked Vucic for a new package of humanitarian support for Ukraine. Serbia supports Ukraine's territorial integrity Vucic said that Serbia will continue to support Ukraine's independence and territorial integrity, including the territories that Russia has seized since 2014. "You have never heard a single bad word about our country, not from Volodymyr Zelenskyy nor anyone else in Ukraine, and I am extremely grateful to our Ukrainian friends for that," Vucic said. The remark appeared to address the fact that Ukraine refuses to recognize Kosovo's independence, which was declared in 2008. Belgrade considers Kosovo to be part of Serbia. Vucic said he was skeptical that either Serbia or Ukraine would quickly join the European Union. However, he added that Belgrade would support Kyiv's bid. Serbia has repeatedly refused to put sanctions on Moscow. This has angered the EU and delayed Belgrade's path to joining the bloc. Both leaders also said their countries want to improve economic cooperation and finalize a free trade agreement by the end of the year. ​ D espite its dependence on Russian energy, Serbia has supplied nonmilitary aid to Ukraine. The Kremlin has accused Serbian firms of selling munitions to Ukraine, but Vucic has denied this claim. Vucic traveled to Ukraine for a regional summit in 2025 and again this year. Despite pledging aid to Ukraine, he has refrained from signing a formal declaration of support for Ukraine in the war. Russian attacks on Kyiv continue while Kyiv strikes Russian refineries The meeting came after at least four people, including a child, were killed in overnight Russian air attacks on Ukraine's capital, Kyiv, and the surrounding region, officials said on Saturday. "Last night, Russia killed three people in Pukhivka, Kyiv region, with drone strikes," Zelenskyy wrote on X. He added that the victims were a grandfather, a grandmother and their 3-year-old grandson. Authorities said three other members of the family and a neighbor who came to their aid were hospitalized. Ukraine's air force reported downing or intercepting 135 of the 151 drones that Russia launched overnight. Meanwhile, Ukraine's General Staff announced that the military had attacked Russia's Ilsky and Syzran oil refineries overnight, resulting in fires at both locations. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9q9.text: By Tiffanie Turnbull Reporting from Dryandra, Western Australia "Eyes peeled," comes the order from the front passenger seat. Obediently, we scan the ends and tops of logs, looking between low scrub and patches of vivid wildflowers for a flash of stripes or a dart of movement. Eluding us is the numbat, a rare Australian marsupial which could be the love-child of a chipmunk and an anteater. Numbats were once populous across the bottom half of the continent, but Dryandra Woodland â in the south-western corner of Australia â is one of the few places they remain. As we slowly roll along bush tracks, researchers explain how this annual trip helps plot the species' survival. Classified as endangered until this month, numbats have been bouncing back. This team's efforts have seen them scratched off the international red list of threatened species - a rare glimmer of hope in a country facing an extinction emergency. This part of Australia is the front line of that crisis: a last stand for many species driven to the brink by feral pests, disease, urban development, habitat destruction and climate change. Winging over our car at one point is the endangered Carnaby's cockatoo. On an island just off the coast is one of the last surviving pockets of the world's rarest marsupial, the Gilbert's potoroo. Diving in the sapphire waters around it is the increasingly scarce Australian sea lion. Image source, Sharon Jones/BBC Image caption, Dryandra Woodland is one of the few places you can still find wild numbats Australia has long been celebrated as a nature haven, home to some of the world's most unique plant and animal species. More than 80% cannot be found anywhere else. But it has arguably become the extinction capital of the world, losing roughly four species every decade - and the decline is only worsening. Dedicated volunteers and under-funded conservationists have been slowing the army of increasing threats, but experts fear that without urgent action and political courage, the biodiversity Australia says it loves is headed for a bloodbath. "It's not even a case of imagining it, it's happening in front of our own eyes," Professor Euan Ritchie tells the BBC. The many threats driving extinction Image source, Sharon Jones/BBC Image caption, Dr Tony Friend first started working at Dryandra in the 80s If spotting a rare creature in the wild wasn't challenging enough, the numbat is a squirrel-sized camouflage connoisseur, explains Dr Tony Friend, the godfather of conservation in the state of Western Australia. "They just slept in today," jokes Rob McLean, president of the Numbat Taskforce, a volunteer group which makes a lot of Tony's thinly-resourced work possible. For two weeks each spring, as the young start venturing from their burrows, this team drives a daily circuit and records every numbat spotted. They log GPS coordinates, measure the distance to the road, and use a complicated equation to estimate the density of the animals in these woods and, from that, broader population health. One person sits in concentrated silence at each window, another perched in the back of the pick-up truck, ducking for the occasional limb branching from trees which rise around us. Through the trunks, we get the occasional glimpse of the razed farmland which tightly fences this pocket of protected woodland. On the side of one trail is a machine which detects and sprays feral cats and foxes with poison, another reminder of the perils numbats face. "This year's been a bit of a feast," Rob admits. For hours on end, we cruise around, seeing parrots, wallabies, a goanna and a couple of echidnas - but no numbats. Tony arrived at Dryandra back in the 80s to find a numbat population fewer than 50. Many of the culprits then were the same as those still driving extinctions across the nation today. Image source, Courtesy WA DBCA Image caption, Feral cats kill an estimated three billion animals in Australia each year Swathes of critical habitat are being cleared for development or industries like farming, mining and timber. Leaving a trail of destruction in their wake are introduced pests: fire ants, cane toads, rabbits, foxes, feral cats. Invasive weeds like lantana are choking the Australian bush, chlamydia has sent koalas to the edge of existence across much of the country, while the skin-eating chytrid fungus has caused seven frog extinctions here and counting. The changing climate is creating unliveable conditions for some species, like native flying foxes which are dropping out of trees in their thousands due to extreme temperatures. For others it is eliminating their food or their homes. Climate change is also driving natural disasters which fry and drown both plants and animals with now frightening regularity. The infamous Black Summer bushfires of 2019-20, for example, killed an estimated three billion animals. The successive years of record-breaking flooding which followed were so widespread it's impossible to estimate the impact on wildlife. Image source, Sharon Jones/BBC Image caption, The Carnaby's black cockatoo is another species barely hanging on in south-western Australia Many species once abundant across the continent are now isolated to increasingly small and disjointed patches, each impact compounding and leaving them more vulnerable to the next. There are small, yet determined, efforts to slow the momentum of decline. As a young numbat scoffs his breakfast â custard with "termite sprinkles" â at Perth Zoo, a keeper explains how this stud's upcoming release at Dryandra will help boost genetic diversity. "When you get that feedback: your babies have got babies, it's very satisfying," Vicki Power says. Breeding programmes like this have also made setting up additional populations of an array of threatened species possible. But many cannot survive in the true wild, where large-scale predator control remains an endless battle, and are instead sent to fenced nature reserves, themselves high-maintenance undertakings facing problems like in-breeding and overpopulation. Habitat protection or restoration projects have been ramping up, but they are not keeping pace with destruction, particularly in the most critical areas. Scientists are also trying to fight disease, though that's an expensive and laborious endeavour, which for most species buys only a little more time. Others are preserving genetic material in case we ever work out how to resurrect species from the dead. A hundred species lost - and counting Scientists agree that we're living though the world's sixth mass extinction event, the first caused by humans. But Australia is at the front of this trend. It leads the world in mammal extinctions, and medals when it comes to the loss of other species classes too. "Despite Australia being one of the wealthiest countries per capita in the world and having more than its fair share of world-leading scientistsâ¦ we have a truly awful record of conserving species," Ritchie says. "And things aren't getting better." The Australian government's official extinctions list sits at 67, but researchers are confident at least 100 plant and animal species have been lost forever. They suspect the true figure is far higher. The country is still discovering species which have already been wiped out. Though the rate of extinction in Australia has stayed stable, at around four per decade, the number of threatened species is still climbing quickly, and the deterioration of many is only gathering speed. This trajectory has some scary flow-on effects, experts warn. Australia's biodiversity "underpins everything", ecologist Jack Pascoe says. Think food production, tourism, construction â much of the economy. Potential scientific breakthroughs could be stymied: in medicine, agriculture and even climate change adaptation. And for First Nations Australians, the decline also threatens their culture. "We think of ourselves as custodians of all life on Earthâ¦ so there's a much more personal and social feeling of loss that comes when these things are not doing well or we lose them forever," Pascoe, a man from the Yuin Aboriginal nation, says. Decades of failures Though environment protection is a state responsibility, the federal government oversees matters of national importance. Labor took office in 2022, promising no new extinctions under its watch, and it has sought to make nature protection a defining feature of its second term. "It's well understood that nature is facing many challenges in the world today, both here in Australia, and overseasâ¦ we are losing biodiversity at an alarming rate," Environment Minister Murray Watt told the BBC in a statement. His party has significantly increased Australia's emissions reduction efforts and massively boosted renewable energy projects. There is some praise for their work on drawing critically endangered mammals back from the brink. And the passage of revamped environment laws last year was heralded as the most significant reform in a generation. The country also has an ambitious goal to halt and reverse biodiversity loss by 2030. But there's limited optimism that this will be a real turning point. The new laws are only the scaffolding of change. The substance of it is still being worked out â in the form of National Environmental Standards (NES) and a federal watchdog to enforce them. And many in the sector say the problem is not so much the regulatory tools available, but rather the political will to use them. Successive governments have failed to adequately protect the environment over the past 30 years, Australia's longest serving environment minister tells the BBC. ââThat includes his own administration. "We should have done more too," says Robert Hill, who lead the last major reforms in 1999 under John Howard's conservative coalition. Image source, Courtesy Perth Zoo Image caption, Vicki Power and Tony Friend have spent decades trying to save the numbat Many of the challenges of his era still haunt leaders today. The nation's wealth has largely been built off the back of its natural resources â often at the expense of the environment. Those riches still underpin the economy and help fund government spending on essentials like healthcare and housing. Then there's the added pressure applied by industry and the competing interests of states - whose stake in regulatory controls blurs the lines of accountability and increases bureaucratic hurdles. These battles leave even the toughest environmental advocates within governments bruised. For example, the Albanese government last year rushed through laws protecting salmon farming after lobbying by Tasmanian state officials, silencing opposition from within and ignoring advice from its own department concerning the impact of the A$1.4bn (Â£733m; $989m) industry on the survival of the Maugean Skate, an endangered ray. "The axe falls on the environmental outcome if there's the alternative of an economic one," Hill says. "Even if [the federal government] does want to act, it's still got to have the political strength to turn its aspirations into reality." Image source, Getty Images Image caption, The Albanese government passed legislation to protect salmon farming after lobbying by Tasmanian state officials There is also a belief that greater regulation alone will achieve little. Too much conservation work currently relies on philanthropists' cash and devoted volunteers, those in the sector say, and much more languishes on the to-do list due to a lack of money. The federal government directly spends about A$700m on nature protection, a fraction of the A$33bn â or 1% of GDP â conservationists say it should be. That is an eyebrow-raising figure, people like Paul Elton concede, but one they argue is reasonable. According to his research â which the government disputes â more than A$26bn is still being spent on subsidies for things like mining, intensive agriculture or fuel despite Australia signing global pledges to wind them back. "For every dollar the government is spending on positive biodiversity conservation action, there's A$26 being spent on subsidies that are causing harm to nature," he tells the BBC. "That's a pretty stark imbalance." Minister Watt didn't directly respond to questions about conservationists' demands, but said: "We remain committed to long-term environmental recovery, in partnership with state and local governments, community and environmental groups." Though public sentiment is shifting, there's scepticism the government will prioritise the environment amid competing demands and compounding crises until voters force them to do so. "The community will say to you, we should spend a lot of money on the environment. And then if you say, 'Well, what are you prepared to sacrifice to ensure that funding base?', then they're no longer interested," Hill says. In the face of so many challenges and what they see as little progress, advocates admit it's hard to hang on to hope. "We know what the problems are. We know how to address them. We know when we spend money on the environment, it pays back many times over," Ritchie, a mammal ecologist, says. "It's like being a doctor and seeing all these sick people in the community and you know how to fix them, but no one will let you do that." Image source, Sharon Jones/BBC Image caption, Volunteer 'Jacko' keeps watch from the back of the truck Small wins, like the future of the numbat, keep them fighting. There are now around 3,000 nationwide, and in Dryandra numbers have increased ten-fold. The animal has recently been taken off the international endangered species list and is now classified as near-threatened. It takes five hours, but finally synchronised cries of excitement come from the driver's seat and the back of the pick-up truck. The cause of the commotion stands frozen and alert at the end of a hollowing log. "It's not a competition," Rob says. Chuckling, he points at his rival spotter: "But I beat him by a second." The dam has broken. Over the next little while we see eight numbats, including two pairs of babies, blinking at us in the dusky light. This year's full count, Tony later tells me, is one of the best yet. "But I remind people they're not out of the woods yet," Tony says. The relief at the numbat's revival is tempered by worry this will make it harder to access the funding and support needed to cement those gains. The woylie, or brush-tailed bettong, is a cautionary tale. It recovered slightly and was taken off the threatened list only to be added again a decade later, in a worse state. "We can't walk away," Tony says, "and say 'no, they're fine,' you know?" "It's got to be accepted that continued work is needed to keep that animal on the planet." Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief KYIV/BUCHAREST/BUDAPEST ( Worthy News ) – A Russian ballistic missile strike near Ukraine’s capital Kyiv killed at least 10 people and wounded nearly 100 others Friday, Ukrainian officials said, as neighboring Romania, a member of the NATO military alliance, announced it had shot down a drone that entered its airspace. President Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed the attack, saying rescue efforts were continuing. “A rescue operation is currently underway in the Kyiv region following a Russian missile strike,” Zelensky wrote on social media platform Telegram. “We are still establishing exactly what happened and the fate of all those involved.” Be informed without depending on social media — receive Worthy News by email. Acting Kyiv Regional Governor Ruslan Oliinyk said preliminary information indicated that a Russian ballistic missile struck a private training ground where representatives of Ukraine’s defense industry had gathered for an event. Ukraine’s Council of Defense Industry confirmed that representatives of the sector were present but stressed that it had not organized the gathering. RUSSIA HITS DEFENSE GATHERING One participant, Valerii Borovyk, head of a Ukrainian drone company, said the missile struck during a defense exhibition, describing scenes of panic as people rushed for cover while emergency crews treated the wounded amid the wreckage. Ukraine’s Prosecutor General Ruslan Kravchenko said authorities had launched a criminal probe into possible negligence in organizing the event, while separately investigating the Russian missile strike as a suspected war crime. Separately, officials said a Russian airstrike killed five people and injured nine others in the eastern city of Sloviansk, damaging homes, a shop, and the grounds of Latvia’s consulate. The attacks came as Romania, which shares a 650-kilometer (400-mile) border with Ukraine, announced it had shot down a drone for the first time after it violated Romanian airspace. ROMANIA DOWNS DRONE President Nicușor Dan said a Romanian F-16 fighter pilot destroyed the drone at about 11 a.m. local time. “The area was uninhabited, so the pilot was able to shoot without any risk. Teams are now investigating the incident to establish all the details,” Dan told reporters. Romania’s Defense Ministry said two Romanian F-16s and two Italian Eurofighter Typhoon jets stationed in Romania were scrambled after radar detected the drone approaching from the direction of the Black Sea. Debris landed in a wheat field, causing no injuries or property damage. Military officials said the drone appeared to be a Russian-designed Shahed-type unmanned aircraft, though authorities stressed the investigation into its origin was continuing. REGIONAL TENSIONS GROW Romania has reported repeated drone incursions since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but Friday marked the first time its military has shot one down after an airspace violation. Romania is not alone. Other members of the NATO military alliance, including Poland, have also reported Russian drones or missiles violating or briefly entering their airspace during the war, prompting fighter jet scrambles and heightened security along the alliance’s eastern flank. The latest developments underscored growing concerns that the war could increasingly spill beyond Ukraine’s borders, even as Russia and Ukraine continue exchanging long-range missile and drone strikes with no immediate sign of a negotiated end to the armed conflict. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/people/when.text: The Budapest Times When Carlos the Jackal hid out in in Cold War Hungary Written by Alexander Stemp Following on from my article last year about the three “Hungarian Jackals” involved in the assassination attempt on President of France Charles de Gaulle in 1962, now comes the tale of another “Jackal” connection, this time Carlos the Jackal, the internationally hunted terrorist and his secret hideout in the select Budapest suburb Rózsadomb from 1979 to 1985. It still remains a mystery why Hungary allowed entry to this notorious figure sought over a series of assassinations and terrorist acts. Certainly, hosting the committed Marxist-Leninist earned the goodwill of the Communist and anti -Western world that generally supported him in defiance of mounting pressure from the West to bring him to justice, wherever he was holed up. The Hungarian authorities have not released his files and it is not known where he lived at leafy “Rose Hill”, but presumably in a nice enough villa. While it was prepared the Jackal briefly stayed at the cosmopolitan and five-star Hotel Intercontinental, today named the Marriott, a cubist structure in central Pest overlooking the River Danube. Both the hotel and the nearby monumental Inter-Continental “glass-house”, which opened in 1968, were symbols of the more progressive and prosperous Hungarian “Goulash Communism”, designed to attract the rich and famous from around the world. Everyone and everything came and went, with this newish riverside setting an obvious clandestine location for Eastern and Western diplomats, journalists, artists, prostitutes and spies during the Socialist Cold War era. Such premises were heavily bugged, having surveillance cameras, hidden microphones, discreet observers and so forth. Despite the precariousness, the hotels also served as a checkpoint where the Hungarian regime permitted various forms of contact between East and West, while still keeping tabs on one another. The Jackal remained able to carry on his illicit activities. Carlos the Jackal’s real name was Ilich Ramírez Sánchez and he was Venezuelan, born into a privileged family in 1949. Educated in Caracas, London and Moscow, he underwent guerrilla training in the Middle East, playing an active role for the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine and gaining a reputation as a fighter. He travelled around Europe and the Middle East, and led the 1975 raid on the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries headquarters in Vienna. This ended in his demanding a plane and successfully flying with hostages to Libya. Eventually he made his way to Hungary, where the authorities maintained fairly amicable relations with both East and West throughout the Cold War. Hungary was playing safe with the USSR and keeping friendly with the various anti-Western countries favourable to Carlos. While the Jackal reposed in low-profile comfort, he remained a concern and was always very closely watched by the Hungarian Secret Police. The secretive Hungarian authorities naturally kept the matter under wraps and away from the outside world. Carlos remained relatively safe on Hungarian territory and was not called upon for any services by President János Kádár. Hosts and guest basically left each another alone. But eventually his presence became an uncomfortable matter for Hungary, an irritant affecting foreign relations and the delicate balance of geopolitics. It was clear that he had overstayed his time and must go. Finally, under international pressure especially from the United States due to his continual anti-Israeli activities, he was expelled in late 1985. Hungary wanted more open relations with the West, and while it was a tricky move to expel him there was relief too. At least the country could report to the Soviets and to the rest of the world what an uncontrollable and unpredictable person he was. The “Jackal” left without issues and travelled to Syria but later was chased out. When the Cold War ended in 1989 he fled to Sudan and was finally captured by French military agents in Khartoum in 1994. Sentenced to a high-security prison in Paris, he is still serving life sentences in France today. To round off, I know nothing about how the “Carlos” part of his nickname evolved but he was dubbed “The Jackal” by The Guardian, a British newspaper, after one of its investigative correspondents reportedly found Frederick Forsyth’s 1971 novel “The Day of the Jackal” in an apartment belonging to a friend of Carlos. There is no knowing at present where this place is located but the terrorist used it to stash weapons. The book may have belonged to the original tenant or to Carlos himself, who I assume must have read it for curiosity value and inspiration, despite its chilling ending. In a 2016 interview, the Jackal described himself as a “professional revolutionary”, stating, “It’s a miracle that I’m still alive, I’ve survived so many operations”. A list of these can be found on Wikipedia. My Budapest Times story “Shadowy Hungarians had role in attempt to kill de Gaulle” can be read here . The three, Lajos Marton, Gyula Sári and László Varga, all came from working class and military backgrounds, and were staunchly anti-communist. They met during the 1956 Uprising in Hungary then went on the run from the occupying authorities and made their ways to France. The attempt by French military personnel to kill de Gaulle in the Paris suburb Petit-Clamart in August 1962 was unsuccessful. Carlos the Jackal, though, could claim many victims and one thing seems sure – there will be no memorial plaques on Rózsadomb anytime soon. https://eyemagazine.com/feature/article/.text: Eye Magazine Blog Subscribe Current issue Stockists Back issues Contact Eye Critique Newsletter Events Education Eye , the international review of graphic design, is a printed magazine about graphic design and visual culture Summer 1993 Reputations: Roman Cieslewicz ‘Posters are dying out. They need strong themes, which at present they lack. As a form of communication, they belong to another age’ Roman Cieslewicz was born in Lwow, Poland in 1930. He graduated from the Academy of Fine Arts, Cracow in 1955, moved to France in 1963 and became a French citizen in 1971. He has worked for several press and publishing houses, including Elle , Vogue and Opus , and various cultural organisations, such as the Festival d’Automne and the Pompidou Centre. A professional militant, Cieslewicz avoids the groups that are active and influential in France: the admen, the Swiss school, the ‘politicos’. Yet it was he who introduced the Polish poster to the country, unleashing all those influences which continue even now to determine French poster design, particularly in the political, social and cultural fields. Though his approach is comparable with that of the Polish school, Cieslewicz has created his own technique and language, which he applies to posters, publications, photomontages and illustration. His graphic ideas are expressed in a haunting and incisive style. His output is prolific, his approach disturbingly free, with accidental elements permitted to challenge the typographical order. Since 1975, Cieslewicz has taught at the Ecole Supérieure des Arts Graphiques in Paris. He has exhibited widely and is a member of the Alliance Graphique Internationale. He lives and works in Malakoff, in suburban Paris. Margo Rouard-Snowman: You have been a graphic designer for 40 years. Where did you train and who influenced you? Roman Cieslewicz: I don’t think anyone influenced me. But my training with George Karolak at the Academy of Fine Arts in Cracow was important – I took his classes for four years and it was everything to me. Karolak was a graphic artist of the same generation as Henryk Tomaszewski and he shared the same philosophy. He was one of the few who resisted socialist realism, and he was shunned by the establishment because he refused to modify his projects in line with its demands. Despite this, he produced superb posters for the theatre of Cracow. In his graphic composition course he taught us how to assemble the essential elements of a good poster. His method of teaching was absolutely free, but his kind of freedom was frowned on and subjected to all kinds of control. I also studied typography with Professor Gardowski, and took classes in illustration and painting. Tadeusz Kantor taught at the school and his weekly two-hour classes in scenography provided us with information and news from the west – a lifeline to the outside. In this cultural desert, with its zero information level, my only refuge was the Cracow library, where I would go to look at the magazine produced by the Blok group, a revolutionary association of poets, typographers and montagists, which provided a window to the Polish avant-garde. I would also often meet there a very committed designer, montagist and friend of John Heartfield – Mieczyslaw Berman. Berman was a Pole, living in Warsaw, and he gave me a job in his studio. He was true communist. He fled anti-semitic Poland during the war and spent five years in the Soviet army. In the Soviet Union he was influenced by the satirical montagist Zytomirski and by Alexander Rodchenko, whose work was then still unpublished. Through a combination of satire and humour in the face of serious situations, Berman managed to resist the official socialist-realist art. My studies were therefore much influenced by Karolak, Kantor, Gardowski, Berman and the Blok group. They gave me my first clear perspective on proportion, and an apprenticeship in the art of compositional imbalance – balancing elements without necessarily centring them. M R-S: In addition to your commissioned work, you also undertake personal work of your own. What is your relation to painting? RC: I’ve always liked images that have an impact on the street, but I’m a graphic artist – I’ve never pretended to be painter. I don’t like ‘image images’. What I find attractive are the icons of the street, current affairs, news items. I also like those nineteenth-century engravings with their long-winded, anecdotal texts, and torn posters, for example. The war taught us a lasting lesson: whatever the current graphic trends, it seems that serious situations give rise to an incredible number of posters. M R-S: To what extent did your family background determine your choice of career? RC: My parents were simple people whose main contribution was to give me plenty of encouragement to work. My father was a craftsman who made fireplaces, often reconstructions of old pieces he had drawn. As a child I was constantly drawing round forms. The circle was of immense importance to me, which was probably to do with the bread rolls my mother sent me to buy every morning. I still remember the wonderful signs at the baker’s. At six years old I was already taking great pleasure in the signs of the street. M R-S: How did you begin your professional career? RC: After graduating in 1955 I was taken on by a propaganda agency in Warsaw. Wag produced posters for political, social and cultural events nationwide – popular festivals, safety notices, circus announcements, theatre shows. Every national campaign required posters, but most of the time the pretext was illogical and unreasonable. Some twenty graphic designers produced around 100 posters a year, which were offset printed, in four colours, on 90 or 100 gsm paper. After Wag, in 1960-61, I worked for a magazine called You and Me , a Polish version of Elle . It had 64 pages and a print run of 10,000, and was a huge popular success. I devised its format, based on western publications. Its editor chose themes that were fresh – a break from the 1920s. There was even space for both Steinberg and Malakowski. M R-S: Given your success, what made you decide to leave Poland? RC: I wanted to leave Poland to see how my posters would stand up to the neon light of the west. I dreamed of Paris, but went first to Italy because of Eugenio Carmi, the art director of Italsider, a large iron and steel manufacturer in Genoa. I met Carmi when he came to Warsaw for an exhibition of Italian painters, and he invited me to Genoa, giving me a commission for five photomontages for the entrance hall of the manufacturing plant. The montages were each three metres by two and consisted of small elements photographed individually, then enlarged and assembled in the desired format. On a later visit to Paris I met Peter Knapp, the photographer and art director of Elle . He had seen and liked You and Me , and commissioned me to design photomontages for various columns, including the horoscope page. Soon after this, he asked me to work on the layout of the magazine. Cropping photographs and pasting up text hardly seemed creative to me, but I was dazzled by this journalistic machine: 200 people working to produce 250 pages that would end up in the bin the next day. During my time at Elle , where I later became art director, I met many people who gave me work. The publishers La Hune, Christian Bourgois (10 / 18 collections), Maimé Arnodin, Hélène Lazareff, Edmonde Charles Roux, among others – major figures in the press and publishing world at the time. M R-S: What are your favourite design techniques? RC: I use all manner of techniques: photography, painting and watercolour, but not drawing. I have a constant source of inspiration: circular forms. I’ve often used the offset screen, which I discovered at Elle , to focus on a detail of a photographic enlargement. The flexibility and round form of the screen dots make it possible to bring out each gesture of the subject. Also, because I couldn’t afford silk-screen printing equipment, I used felt pens to fill out the areas between the screens. I effectively made the screen dots by hand. A lack of equipment and the need to visualise my ideas immediately resulted in a repetitive reproduction of mechanical techniques. I find the many imperfections of the hand-made version very pleasing. My favourite colours are black and red. I don’t like blue and I adore lemon yellow, which, coupled with black, has a striking effect. For all my projects, I make sketches at a scale 1:10, that is 8 x 12cm, or 4 x 6cm for posters that are 40 x 60cm. First, I compose the format. I start with the four corners, draw one vertical, at an angle, then the outside edges. Next I position the various elements, framing more tightly and sometimes cropping as I go. I find that this classical technique of composition suits me well. My professional decisions, my responses to commissions, are dominated by impatience; the pencil expresses my ideas more quickly than any mechanical tool could. M R-S: Typography is important to your projects. What are your preferences in this area? RC: When I’m designing a poster, I think of the visual mass of the type and not of the details. Even if I’m designing 1:1 I always imagine how it would look big. I’m against the idea of reducing a poster to the size of a matchbox, because I’m convinced that each image functions in relation to the space around it, to the distance between it and the reader. My favourite type forms reflect the same idea. There are the woodcut letters you used to see on notices at the police station, and the typefaces produced by the Viennese printer Bertold, including one which, curiously enough, is called Blok. I really like that typeface: it’s bold, with magnificent proportions for short words, and it creates a good impact. I also use Milton Glaser’s Milton typeface, which is related to Cassandre’s Bifur, but modernised and stripped of all the lines which coarsened the letters. For standard book texts, I often use Rockwell. M R-S: What about the computer? RC: You can imagine anything you like and put it on computer, but it will never have the perfection of the hand-drawn image or the freedom which I value so much. I don’t like the square, aggressive teeth of the computer screen unless you deliberately incorporate this in a composed image. New images for me grow out of fortuitous accidents made by hand. Though I’ve enjoyed using Paintbox, I can’t see the computer contributing much to my work. I prefer the Polaroid because it is straightforward, ephemeral, instantaneous. It expresses a bare truth stripped of superfluous elements. M R-S: You have been in France since 1963. What do you think of French graphic design? RC: France has no strong typographic tradition – it has always refused to be influenced by the unmannered English school and has rejected the Viennese and German schools in favour of Italian aestheticism and gallantry. I say gallantry because it is the image that dominates at the expense of the sign and the type. In the 1960s, Swiss typography, in particular Helvetica, overcame the French taste for ‘tutti frutti’ and frills. After the war, and again now, American influence is strong, particularly in the press. In short, French typography has found it difficult to match the mood of the country. On the whole, it still has problems in reconciling text and image. And French graphic designers are sick because they haven’t got enough work. I also can’t stand the lack of recognition for graphic designers as a profession. M R-S: Do you think the poster is dying out? RC: I think it is. It’s no longer the means of expression it used to be, partly because of competition from television and partly because of the blandness of the subjects – household appliances and food do not inspire great design. Posters need strong themes, which at present they lack. As a form of communication, they belong to another age. M R-S: What are the links between your poster designs and your photomontages? RC: My personal work runs parallel to my commercial work and is an indispensable supplement to it. I see myself not as an artist, but as a graphic designer who makes use of all available media, whether illustration, logos, posters, journals. The visual laws vary, but the means of expression are the same. The photomontages are part of a vital ‘cleansing’ process for me. Though they are generally uncommissioned, they turn up sooner or later in my printed work. M R-S: Why are your recent illustrations, particularly in the press, much more stripped down or minimalist than some of your posters? RC: I am primarily a poster designer who has adapted his work for the press because of a lack of appropriate commissions. Poster designers who talk too much end up saying nothing. But the relationship with magazine readers is more intimate; you aren’t separated by a distance of 150 metres. The economy of means and minimalist presentation are a result of the format and the distance from the reader. And in developing my work over 40 years, I’ve become more tight-fisted. M R-S: What made you go back to doing photomontages? RC: Kamikaze’s use of black and white in 1975-76 inspired me to return to photomontages (not collages, as people sometimes call them). The montage gives a richer result than straight graphics. An image is bare if it is not supported by a word. It is a form of expression that I find appropriate to our times, perfectly adapted to contemporary mass media. M R-S: Your images have certain distinct themes. RC: The circle is an obsession which has translated into my work. There are also themes such as hands, eyes, jaws, legs, which are determined by the commissions. But beyond that I play a game to see where I can go without getting caught up in a system. Contrary to what some people think, I do not disfigure women. I am frank with them. There’s no censure involved. M R-S: What do you see as the elements of a good poster design? RC: An image, a word. And the regular to-and-fro between them. The idea is contained in the image, and it is the relationship between the image and the text which gives it force. M R-S: You are now teaching at a school of graphic arts in Paris. What recommendations would you give to students? RC: My students in the third year at the Ecole Supérieure des Arts Graphiques have to work to become graphic designers. They develop their creative skills within a framework of research and production directed towards a given theme. They create a visual message which is functional and effective with regard to the given problem, and hone their critical sensibility by proposing solutions to the problem through every stage of the process, from beginning to end. They experiment with forms, techniques, processes and materials. M R-S: What goals do you have for your own work? RC: To have more commissions for posters. To be able to comment on current affairs, on news items in the newspapers I like. To design, and to keep on designing and pursuing my attempts to ‘steer the eye’. Roman Cieslewicz died in 1996. Margo Rouard-Snowman, design writer and exhibition organiser, London / Paris First published in Eye no. 9 vol. 3, 1993 Eye is the world’s most beautiful and collectable graphic design journal, published for professional designers, students and anyone interested in critical, informed writing about graphic design and visual culture. https://tribune.com.pk/story/2620278/mil.text: Home Sindh Millers seek direct wheat imports PFMA argues open-market mechanism would ensure cheaper flour for consumers while reducing risk of corruption With Pakistan facing a wheat shortfall, the Pakistan Flour Mills Association (PFMA) has urged the federal government to allow flour mills to directly import wheat, saying the move would ensure cheaper flour for consumers, promote competition and avoid corruption risks linked to state-run imports. PFMA argued that an open-market mechanism would ensure cheaper flour for consumers while reducing the risk of corruption. Speaking to The Express Tribune , PFMA Sindh Chairman Abdul Junaid Aziz said the federal government had decided to initially import one million tonnes of wheat through the Trading Corporation of Pakistan (TCP). However, he argued that imports and distribution through the TCP, coupled with subsidies, could increase the risk of corruption. To address these concerns and promote healthy competition, he urged the government to immediately permit flour mills to import wheat directly under a deregulated, open-market mechanism. Aziz said the association had warned the government and relevant institutions two months ago that domestic wheat production was expected to fall, but the warning went unheeded. Had policymakers acted at the time, he said, Pakistan could have imported cheaper wheat from Russia and Ukraine during the ceasefire period via the Strait of Hormuz. Instead, the country would now have to rely on costlier imports from Australia, Romania and Canada. He estimated that Pakistan would need to import between three million and 3.5 million tonnes of wheat to meet domestic demand.
