https://www.jns.org/feature/how-haredi-p.text: Despite holding a fraction of Knesset seats, Shas and United Torah Judaism have become indispensable coalition partners, reshaping Israeli politics. The 25th Knesset dissolved on July 17, and while polls differ sharply over the balance between Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s bloc and its opponents, most surveys leave neither side with much room to spare. That once again places Israel’s smaller parties—particularly the Haredi parties—at the center of the coalition arithmetic that will determine who governs after the election set for Oct. 27. Therein lies one of the enduring paradoxes of Israeli politics. Shas and United Torah Judaism (UTJ) hold only about 15% of the Knesset’s 120 seats. They do not compete for the premiership, have never sought to become Israel’s largest party and campaign primarily around the interests of the communities they represent. Yet their pivotal position in coalition negotiations gives them influence far beyond their electoral strength. Their influence extends well beyond determining who becomes prime minister. Participation in successive governments has given the Haredi parties leverage over education funding, yeshivah budgets, welfare policy, national-religious institutions and the broader relationship between their communities and the state. That observation raises the central question behind the Haredi parties’ political success: How did movements representing a minority population, intent on remaining outside Israel’s broader political struggle, find themselves at the center of coalition politics? The answer lies not in electoral strength alone, but in the combination of highly organized constituencies, concentrated political priorities, Israel’s fragmented parliamentary system, effective coalition bargaining and, over time, an increasingly durable alliance with the Israeli right. 622760 (4372x2915, AR: 1.50)The Haredi rise Haredi political organization did not begin as a project to govern Israel as a whole. Its original purpose was to ensure that communities seeking to preserve a distinct religious and institutional way of life had political representatives capable of negotiating with the state. Following Israel’s establishment, Haredi parties joined the country’s early governing coalitions, using their political leverage primarily to protect independent religious education, communal autonomy and military exemptions for yeshivah students. However, their relationship with the state soon became strained. In 1952, they left the governing coalition during a dispute over military or national service for religious women and remained outside government for the next quarter-century. The major transformation came in 1977, when Menachem Begin’s Likud ended three decades of Labor dominance. Agudat Yisrael returned to government for the first time in 25 years. More significantly, genuine competition emerged between the left- and right-wing blocs, thrusting the Haredi parties into the role of kingmaker. The transformation that followed was not only political. According to Dr. Gilad Malach, a research fellow at the Israel Democracy Institute, the changes introduced under Begin also helped reshape the structure of Haredi society. “In 1977, when Begin became prime minister and formed a coalition with Agudat Yisrael, he broadened the possibility of exemption from the army and removed the numerical limits. He also substantially increased financial support for the system. From that point, studying Torah for many years and not serving at all became much more common,” he told JNS. The expansion of political influence and the growth of the Haredi institutional world developed in parallel. Greater access to state resources helped sustain a growing network of yeshivahs, kollels and communal institutions, while the expanding community increased the electoral weight of the parties representing it. The Haredi parties embraced their kingmaker role. Since the 1977 election, they have served in the coalitions of the vast majority of Israeli governments, joining administrations led by prime ministers across the political spectrum, including Yitzhak Rabin, Benjamin Netanyahu, Ehud Barak and Ehud Olmert. As political power grew, internal divisions became inevitable. The next major development came with the creation of Shas in 1984. The party emerged in response to the underrepresentation and perceived discrimination of Sephardi and Mizrahi Haredim within the predominantly Ashkenazi Haredi establishment. Led spiritually by Rabbi Ovadia Yosef and politically by figures such as Aryeh Deri, Shas developed a much broader electoral appeal than the traditional Ashkenazi Haredi parties. Its support extended beyond the strictly Haredi population to include large numbers of traditional and religious Sephardi voters. Ashkenazi Haredi politics underwent its own major split in 1988, when the Lithuanian, yeshivah-oriented Degel HaTorah broke away from the largely Hasidic Agudat Yisrael. The two parties reunited electorally in 1992 under the banner of United Torah Judaism, or UTJ. However, they continued to operate as distinct internal factions with separate rabbinic leaderships and political interests. Despite these divisions, the Haredi parties largely continued to operate as a unified political bloc, almost always sitting together in either the coalition or the opposition. Their political strength rested on collective bargaining, narrowly focused communal priorities and broad flexibility in choosing coalition partners. Right-wing bloc While the Haredi political alliance remains largely intact today, its once-independent role has diminished. The Haredi parties remain indispensable to coalition arithmetic, but they are increasingly viewed as a cornerstone of the right-wing bloc rather than as neutral kingmakers. A major shift away from political neutrality came after the 2013 election, when both Shas and UTJ were excluded from Netanyahu’s coalition. The outcome was driven by a political alliance between Yair Lapid and Naftali Bennett, whose combined strength allowed them to insist on entering the government together and effectively prevented Netanyahu from bringing the Haredi parties into the coalition. Within the Haredi political establishment, however, Lapid became the principal symbol of the new government’s approach. His Yesh Atid Party had campaigned heavily on expanding Haredi military service and reducing what it viewed as unequal privileges. The coalition subsequently advanced policies affecting conscription and Haredi education without the Haredi parties at the negotiating table. The experience reinforced a sense of political vulnerability and helped accelerate the Haredi parties’ growing alignment with Netanyahu and the right-wing bloc. In 2015, both Shas and UTJ returned to government and have remained critical members of the right-wing bloc over the past decade. Meanwhile, Haredi conscription and the relationship between religion and state have become increasingly prominent issues for centrist and left-wing parties, further strengthening the Haredi-right alliance. UTJ leader Yitzhak Goldknopf put it succinctly in a recent interview, saying, “We belong to the right-wing bloc.” The resulting alliance should not be mistaken for complete ideological convergence. UTJ has historically taken positions on diplomatic and security issues that differ from those of the nationalist right, while Shas has shown greater flexibility on some questions involving territorial concessions to the Palestinians. The modern Haredi-right bloc is therefore better understood as the product of overlapping social conservatism, decades of accumulated political trust and increasingly strong mutual dependence in coalition politics. Spending political power The political leverage accumulated by the Haredi parties is closely tied to the institutional structure of Haredi society. Educational institutions, including schools, yeshivahs and kollels, and other communal institutions depend heavily on government funding, meaning coalition agreements can directly affect the resources available to sustain the community’s social model. The central tension in Haredi political engagement, however, lies in increasing state support without accepting a proportional increase in state control. From within Haredi society, this use of political power is not necessarily understood simply as conventional interest-group politics, but rather as part of a larger religious mission. Gedalia Guttentag, deputy editor of Mishpacha magazine, described it as part of a much broader project of communal reconstruction in the aftermath of the Holocaust. “The Haredi attempt has been nothing less than the rebuilding of a Torah-based civilization. You cannot simply say that this is about supporting a small number of elite scholars. That misunderstands the project. To sustain that civilization, you need an ecosystem, large numbers of people aspiring toward Torah study,” he told JNS. “This is something that the Jewish people need; it's not something parochial; it's not something just for the Haredi community,” he added. Seen from this perspective, government support for schools, yeshivahs and kollels is not viewed solely as a material benefit. These institutions form the infrastructure through which Haredi society seeks to reproduce its religious and communal model across generations, preserving what it sees as the heart of Jewish culture. Education offers perhaps the clearest example of the balance the Haredi parties have sought to strike between state support and communal independence. Much of the Haredi school system receives substantial public funding. However, the extent of state involvement varies sharply among institutions. The two major Haredi education networks and state-Haredi schools receive full government funding and are formally required to teach the national core curriculum. Other independent schools receive reduced funding in exchange for greater autonomy, while many boys attend “exempt” institutions that receive just over half the standard level of state support and are subject to correspondingly limited core curriculum requirements. In practice, state oversight of those requirements has often been limited. The result is a system that reflects the broader Haredi political bargain: combining sufficient participation in the state to secure the resources needed to sustain communal institutions while resisting the level of state control that could fundamentally reshape them. Coalition participation is a crucial pillar of this political model. In 2023 alone, state support for yeshivahs and kollels totaled approximately 1.7 billion shekels. In a recent study, Malach found that, following the Haredi parties’ return to government, funding for yeshivahs and kollelis “increased by approximately 50%.” As a result, the number of yeshivah and kollel students rose by 7.3% during 2023, reaching roughly 167,000 at the beginning of 2024. The resulting political structure is self-reinforcing. Highly organized communities produce reliable electoral support; that support creates parliamentary leverage; and that leverage helps sustain the institutions around which communal life is organized. Conclusion Haredi political power was built not by capturing the center of Israeli politics, but by mastering the system around it. Highly organized constituencies produced disciplined representation, concentrated priorities strengthened coalition bargaining, and decades of cooperation ultimately embedded the established parties within the right-wing bloc. However, that model now faces a challenge created in part by its own success. By 2025, Israel’s Haredi population had reached approximately 1.45 million, or 14.3% of the country’s population, and is projected to reach 16% by 2030. As the community grows, its ability to fly under the political radar has diminished. The established parties therefore face a different challenge from the one they were originally created to address. Rabbi Yehoshua Pfeffer, a prominent Haredi writer and rabbi, framed it directly. “We’re not a minority anymore. We’re a big part of Israel’s Jewish majority, and therefore we have to take responsibility,” he told JNS. That shift may increasingly define the next stage of Haredi politics as Israel approaches the Oct. 27 election. The established parties remain highly effective at protecting communal autonomy and securing resources for the institutions they represent. The harder question is whether a political model developed to protect a distinct minority can adapt as that minority becomes an increasingly large and influential part of the country it once sought to keep at arm’s length.

https://www.independent.co.uk/news/world.text: Germany faces daily hybrid warfare attacks from abroad, interior minister Alexander Dobrindt was quoted as saying on Sunday, following a suspected attack attempt involving an explosive-laden drone at Leipzig/Halle Airport. Dobrindt told the newspaper Bild am Sonntag that foreign powers wanted to subdue Germany politically and socially by stirring up fear there. Dobrindt highlighted the expansion ‌of drone ​research in Germany as part ‌of the response to the ​new threats. “We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare,” Dobrindt said. “Espionage, sabotage, cyberattacks, or covert operations by foreign powers aimed at destabilising Germany or inflicting direct harm are a constant reality.” The newspaper's advance ​release ⁠of the interview did ‌not say whether he identified any countries in particular. After the drone loaded with explosives was discovered at the airport in eastern Germany on Tuesday, some German lawmakers pointed the finger at Russia, which has been at war with Ukraine since its military invasion of the country in 2022. The Russian embassy in Berlin on Friday dismissed the Leipzig event as a "fabricated provocation", saying it was another example of accusations against Russia without evidence.

https://www.laois-nationalist.ie/news/fr.text: Sun, 26 Jul, 2026 - 08:05 Fr Paddy Byrne: A family who paid the ultimate sacrifice in life Józef and Wiktoria Ulma with five of their children were a beacon of resilience, intellect, and humanity       I WAS greatly inspired recently by the story of the Ulma family, patrons of family life and the unborn child. In a world overshadowed by terror and brutality, the story of Józef and Wiktoria Ulma and their six young children shines as a beacon of humanity and moral clarity. Living in the quiet village of Markowa in southeastern Poland during the dark years of the Holocaust, the Ulmas epitomized the extraordinary courage of ordinary people. Risking everything, they sheltered eight Jewish neighbours in their modest home, defying the oppressive machinery of Nazi Germany. Their ultimate sacrifice - losing their lives and those of their children - stands as a profound testament to the power of empathy and faith in the face of unimaginable danger. Józef and Wiktoria Ulma were a beacon of resilience, intellect, and humanity. Their lives, though marked by simplicity, were extraordinary in their depth and purpose. Józef, born in 1900, was a man of immense curiosity and practical genius. He transcended his humble beginnings. His interests were vast, ranging from horticulture to photography. Wiktoria, born in 1912, was equally remarkable. Orphaned at a young age, she displayed resilience and a zest for life, attending courses at a local Folk High School and engaging in cultural activities like village theatre. Together, the Ulmas created a household filled with love, learning, and faith. Parents to six children and expecting a seventh, their lives revolved around nurturing not only their family but also their community. Before the Second World War, Markowa was a quiet, close-knit community of about 4,500 residents, including around 120 Jews. While cultural and religious differences meant that Polish and Jewish residents lived somewhat parallel lives, relations were amicable. Jewish families in Markowa primarily engaged in trade and farming, their children attending schools alongside Polish peers. Religious gatherings often took place in nearby ÅaÅcut, at a synagogue that likely welcomed the Goldman family - the very neighbours the Ulmas would later risk everything to protect. The peaceful life of the Ulmas and their neighbours shattered with the German invasion of Poland in 1939. For the Jewish community of Markowa the occupation brought swift and devastating oppression. Early restrictions, such as wearing the Star of David, escalated into forced labour, deportations, and mass executions. By 1942, ‘Operation Reinhardt’ sought to exterminate the Jewish population in the General Government area, leaving Jewish families in Markowa desperate for refuge. Markowa fell under the jurisdiction of brutal German and local collaborators. Daily life became a litany of terror: curfews, forced labour, and deportations were commonplace. The Jewish residents, targeted with relentless persecution, were subjected to confiscations, ghettos, and ultimately, extermination. The Ulmas, known for their kindness and connection to local Jewish families, did not hesitate. In December 1942, they opened their modest home to eight Jews: Saul Goldman, his four sons, two daughters, and a young child. For over a year, these individuals lived hidden within the Ulmas’ home, sharing the family’s meagre resources. Such an act of defiance carried the ultimate risk; under the German Nazi decrees, anyone aiding Jews faced immediate execution, a punishment that extended to entire households. In the early hours of March 24, 1944, German gendarmes and local collaborators arrived at the Ulma home. The brutality was swift and unrelenting. The eight Jewish individuals hiding in the house were executed immediately. Józef and Wiktoria were then dragged outside and shot. As Wiktoria fell, in the throes of childbirth, the executioners made a harrowing decision: they would kill the children too. Eight-year-old StanisÅawa, six-year-old Barbara, five-year-old WÅadysÅaw, four-year-old Franciszek, three-year-old Antoni, and 1.5-year-old Maria were all executed. In an instant, 17 lives were extinguished, including Wiktoria’s unborn child. The Ulmas were guided by an unshakable faith. Their well-worn Bible contained underlined passages from the parable of the Good Samaritan and the commandment to love one’s neighbour, reflecting the principles that shaped their actions. These were not mere ideals; they were convictions put into practice, even at the cost of their lives. Their choice to shelter Jews was an act of profound moral courage, rooted in love and a sense of shared humanity. The family’s beatification by the Catholic Church in 2023 underscores their spiritual legacy. While their recognition as Righteous Among the Nations resonates deeply within Jewish memory, their elevation to sainthood amplifies their story on a global scale, reminding Catholics and non-Catholics alike of the universal values they represent compassion, sacrifice, and unwavering moral clarity. What makes the Ulmas’ story uniquely compelling is not just the magnitude of their sacrifice but the life they led before their tragic end. Józef and Wiktoria were not wealthy, educated elites, but rather a humble couple driven by intellectual curiosity, strong faith, and a sense of communal responsibility. They cultivated their farm, raised their children, and enriched their village through Józef’s photography, ingenuity, and activism. Their decision to protect others in a time of extreme peril was not born of wealth or privilege but of an extraordinary humanity that transcended fear. The Ulma family’s story transcends national and religious boundaries. It is a testament to the enduring power of human dignity in the face of unspeakable evil. The Ulmas stand as symbols of resistance and humanity during one of history’s darkest chapters. Their legacy challenges us to reflect on our own capacity for courage and compassion. Today, as their names appear in museums, textbooks, and prayers, the Ulmas remind the world that even in the bleakest times, ordinary people can achieve extraordinary heroism. Their story is not merely one of martyrdom but a beacon of hope and a call to action for future generations. Prayer to the Ulma Family Almighty and eternal God, we thank You for the testimony of the heroic love of the spouses Józef and Wiktoria with their children, who gave their lives to save persecuted Jews. May their prayers and example support families in Christian life and help everyone to follow the true path of holiness. Lord, if it is in accordance with Your will, kindly grant me the grace … for which I am asking You through their intercession and count them among the Blessed. Through Christ our Lord. Amen. German Historian and Academic, Tarik Cyril Amar on Na-zi Imagery, and Ethnic Cleansing Apologia in Early 2000s Lviv. Eva Karene Bartlett , Jul 22, 2026, https://evakarenebartlett.substack.com/p/german-historian-and-academic-tarik?utm_source=post-email-title&publication_id=3046064&post_id=207930798&utm_campaign=email-post-title&isFreemail=true&r=1ise1&triedRedirect=true&utm_medium=email Tarik Cyril Amar [ Tarik Cyril Amar ] lived for five years in Lviv, Ukraine, from 2001 on and off. He speaks fluent Russian and Ukrainian. A historian and author, Tarik has extensive knowledge, and first hand experience, on realities of Ukraine now whitewashed in Western corporate media, in particular the long festering and growing nationalism where Ukrainians nationalists—who committed war crimes, including ethnic cleansing in World War 2—are applauded and celebrated as “national heroes”. In our conversation, he also spoke of the lead role of his country Germany in expanding and fuelling the proxy war—in which the West has used Ukraine to fight Russia, with no actual regard for the lives of Ukrainians themselves. “It is the West that is using Ukraine as cannon fodder, and has been for years.” -Long history of Lviv support of Bandera and OUN “Even then, Lviv had a reputation as being a particularly patriotic, even nationalist, city. My personal experience at the time was that that was true, and that this tendency was on the rise. You had demonstrations celebrating the OUN (Organization of Ukrainian Nationalists in WW2). You found it in policies of public commemoration. Lviv has one of the largest monuments to Stepan Bandera in Ukraine, built or inaugurated during my time there. There was already a very consistent denial of the crimes of Ukrainian nationalists in WW2, the enormous massacres that they conducted systematically against the Poles. Nazi symbols in Lviv “You had the symbolism of the Waffen-SS division that the Nazis established in 1943. Lviv was the epicentre of that operation. Their symbolism, their coat of arms, that was there in the public space. You had the black and red of the OUN, that was prominent. You had attempts at building memorials in public spaces to the “heroism” of the nationalists. From what I can see now, it must have become much more aggressive. At the same time, there has been some resistance against forced mobilization in Lviv. On one side, there is this escalation of very strong nationalism that was already there. On the other, clearly the impact of the war is that some people are beginning to resist mobilization, even there.” -Polish demand for Ukraine to renounce the honouring of Ukrainian “nationalist heroes” doesn’t represent a change of Polish support to the war. The tension is old, the core of the tension is the systematic Ukrainian nationalist ethnic cleansing of Poles—estimates from 80,000-100,000 killed. “The killing is a message to make people leave, it’s a genocidal ethnic cleansing. What the Ukrainian nationalists did then, deliberately, systematically, and what the Israelis are doing now in Gaza, its a parallel: Commit genocide and massacres to drive people out. It is one of the things that Ukrainian nationalists will not acknowledge…it’s state policy in Ukraine to lie about this. The bigger story (regarding the recent Polish demand) is how successive Polish governments have always put the geopolitics of using Ukraine against Russia first. So there are these tensions. From time to time you get a blow up, like now with Zelensky. Has it made a difference in the way that they support Ukraine in this proxy war against Russia? It doesn’t.” -Germany in the lead in support for Ukraine and the proxy war on Russia “The war in Ukraine has always had this double aspect. On one side, superficially, it’s a war between Ukraine and Russia. But on the other side, and I think this is more important, it’s a proxy war, in which the West has used Ukraine to fight Russia. The lead Western power in this proxy war against Russia used to be the United States…Under Trump, while Washington could have made a serious contribution to end the war, that’s not what they’ve done. They’ve essentially Europeanized the war, they’ve washed their hands on the money that they have to spend on it, but are still supporting Ukraine in other ways—with intelligence, black ops, CIA connections, etc—and they’re still giving Ukraine weapons, but they make the Europeans pay for them. … The final outcome is a Western proxy war against Russia with Germany in the lead. What the German government, industry and arms manufacturers have done, they’ve intensified payments to Ukraine and military industrial cooperation cutting across the two countries: Things for the Ukrainian military industrial complex are being produced in Germany, or Germany companies are producing in Ukraine. That means that the Russians probably, very likely, are telling us the truth when they’re saying that significant Ukrainian attacks on Russia now can only be carried out because of German assistance . The Russians can point to very specific things that hurt them and that could not be done by Ukraine without (German assistance). From Russia’s perspective, there is an argument for striking at the hinterland, where these weapons and these supplies are coming from or which supports them, and that’s actually us (Germany).” Absurd Western media campaigns about defeating Russia “German war mongers have been saying for years, publicly, ‘We (Germany) have to enable Ukraine so that they can take the war home to Russia.. We need to give Ukraine the capacity to strike deep into Russia.’ Ukraine is doing that now, and we clearly are heavily involved in having created that capacity, and nurturing it and supporting it. There is clearly a coordinated media and information war campaign : Wall Street Journal, The Economist, Financial Times…they and the politicians are all doing the same things. “ They’re spreading this new story that Zelensky is producing, that Ukraine now shifts its war effort from the ground—where it is not successful–to mid range and long range drone and missile strikes against Russia. The idea is that—and this would be very unusual historically, as every expert knows—that by this particular air campaign alone, Ukraine will turn the tables and defeat Russia. You find this all over the Western public space now.” The narrative now being spread resembles earlier narratives about those miracle weapons —remember, when they got the HIMARS, the German tanks, and everybody was like, ‘Once we give them this system, they’re going to turn the war around!’ If Ukraine continues like this, that exerts pressure on the Russian leadership to counter-escalate. They’ve already started. What nobody in the West wants to acknowledge is that Russia still maintains escalation dominance, they can still escalate further beyond what Ukraine can bear or do .” – Russian willingness for negotiation, Western pushing proxy war “Right now there is a dead end. What the Europeans could have done, especially if they had coordinated with the Americans, is to nudge Ukraine, which is totally dependent on the West, and tel them, ‘We understand, you don’t want to officially lose the war, but if you want to come to a negotiated settlement, you must make certain concessions.’ That hasn’t happened. The attitude has been the opposite, which is let’s just feed more weapons and money into Ukraine, Ukraine will provide the people. It i s actually the West that is using Ukraine as cannon fodder, and has been for years.” Share this: Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook July 26, 2026 - Posted by Christina Macpherson | Uncategorized No comments yet. https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/cultur.text: Merging the everyday and the elevated, Leo Ray manages to capture the simplicity of everyday motifs - painting dogs, cats, birds, and people in slightly distorted images with classical art references.A known colorist, painter, graphic artist, and small-scale sculptor, he was born in Vilnius, Lithuania, in 1950 (then part of the USSR), where he studied theoretical physics at Vilnius University and art at Vilnius Academy of Arts. After making aliyah in 1991, he lived in Tel Aviv. Shortly thereafter, the same year, he showed his paintings in a group exhibition in Tel Aviv and entered the local art scene. Since then, he has had many individual shows in Israel and abroad. For over 30 years, up to the pandemic, he taught art at Art School, Ein Vered, and BASIS School of Sculpture, Beit Yanai, where he also headed the painting program from 2006 to 2014. He paints constantly, every day, exploring infinite painting, in which one canvas is a continuation of the previous one. During the interview for the Magazine, he showed me 99 paintings, like a chain of stories. Renaissance, classical, often referenced in Ray's modern, eclectic compositionsThe Renaissance and classical art are often referenced in Ray’s modern, eclectic compositions. When he paints in colors, which is what he is known for, his colors are vibrant and defined. When he steps away from them, he paints just in black and white. His brushstrokes are very characteristic, and he seems to play with layering oil, acrylic, and gouache. Many define his art as naive and childlike; during the interview, he told me he disagrees with those opinions. But he agreed that his art can bring out the child inside of us. In my view, Ray’s paintings put a smile on viewers’ faces. That’s why I wanted to meet this artist and introduce him to The Jerusalem Post’s wide audience of readers. In the dark times we live in, Ray brings a basic way of joy into his work.We met in his modest art studio, filled with brushes and paintings, located between car repair shops and workshops, in the industrial zone of Tel Aviv. Leo Ray welcomed me with tea; he was covered with paint, taking a break from the endless painting to talk to me.When I first saw your painting three years ago, I literally smiled! A big yellow dog was smiling from the canvas back at me. Recently, at the Freshpaint Art Fair, I saw a collection of your paintings and smiled again. They make me happy. Is it your goal to make people happy?Absolutely. Life can be very difficult, and I think one of the great functions of art is to make people happy in this or other ways. I think that, for example, the art of Charlie Chaplin is no less important, great, and artistic than some, let’s say, tragedies. I think that laughter and joy are very valuable things.Thank you for doing it. And my other thought when I saw your paintings was that they’re like illustrations for children’s books. Was it right or not? No, I never illustrated children’s books, and some people say that my style is childish. I absolutely disagree.I wouldn’t say it’s childish, but I think when you paint dogs, birds, cats, and people in not-so-realistic proportions, in a dreamlike way, it awakens the child within us.Yes, of course! I think the child in us doesn’t die before we die. That’s a great sentence! Have you painted this way all your life? Well, that’s a question: if I’ve changed. Yes, I did. One of my friends said that the painting itself changed in a way; that the process of painting became more fun over the years.In your case, or in general? How come?In general. For example, if you compare a painting by [Johannes] Vermeer to a painting by Jackson Pollock, I think Pollock had more fun. Interesting, I didn’t think about it this way… and in your case?My fun is mainly discovering what appears in the painting, what is building up in a painting I am working on.So, you don’t plan the painting; it comes in the process? Sometimes I do plan the paintings and make sketches, but usually, when I start the real one, it changes everything. We’re sitting in your studio, and there are lots of brushes, from small to extremely large ones. Do you choose them, play with them, like with instruments?Of course, brushes are very important instruments, and every brush does what it does. It has individuality. My professor once said that there is no bad brush. And he is right, because [even] a used brush makes what it makes. No new brush can make the same. So, I’m using different kinds of brushes for different kinds of, let’s say, strokes.And you also use different kinds of paints. I paint in oil, acrylic, and gouache (when on paper). And I use Indian ink. I’m trying to be democratic with the painting. I don’t think the use of a kind of material describes the style of a painting. What would you say describes your style? I would say that I do things in a concise way. I like short sentences. I like short lines in poetry. And I like short jokes. So, this kind of brief message is my style. Brief messages. And why those very defined colors, like yellow and red? Because I love them.Trained in calligraphy, 'that's why I use brushes'In opposition to your colorful world, which you are known for, you also paint only in black and white. Which kind of paint do you use for this? Sometimes I’ll use acrylic, but if I work on paper, it’s Indian ink. What do you like about black and white?In the academy, I had a leading professor who was teaching calligraphy, so I’m a little bit trained in calligraphy, and so I love it a lot. That’s why I use brushes.In your paintings, there are repetitive characters.Yes. My principal male character is a nobody. So he can have any name you want to give him. I cannot say anything about the women. This is interesting. You said the man is nobody, and women have some character? They always have some character, and they are always very tempting. And they are beautiful and gracious. Do the dogs, birds, and cats in your paintings have names? No. I don’t give names to cats and dogs. They have to think about that themselves. Are there, or were there, real cats and dogs in your life? Yes. I came here with a cat.From Lithuania, from the collapsing Soviet Union? A few months before the collapse. I came from the Soviet Union formally. I had to refuse Soviet citizenship and so on… So, I came with my cat.What was his name?It was Otto, because of the perfect symmetry of the name and the perfect symmetry of the cat. Your cat, in the painting that I’m looking at, has a symmetric face - but its legs are not symmetric... It depends on the viewing angle. If it’s a little bit twisted, you don’t see the symmetry.Your paintings often have rich textures. When do you decide to apply layers of paint? For example, this painting is mostly flat, but the child’s face is covered in more layers of paint, and the cat’s eyes are more layered.It is not a rational decision. It’s a feeling that I need here to do something. Every color, every texture has its meaning. What meaning does it have to you? The meaning is mysterious. Painting is a mysterious thing. I once said that the ultimate purpose of a painter is to deepen the mystery. And I was very surprised to find out not very long ago that almost the same words were said by Francis Bacon. So, I think like everything that is in the world, like astronomy, physics, mathematics, chess, love, and painting. These are mysterious things that can be explained, only to have a purpose to spoil them. The paintings we are talking about, despite the fact that you don’t want to describe them as naive, have naive and surrealistic elements. But you also paint in a more realistic style.Yes, there was a period when I tried to combine the realistic images with my traditional style, [by this I mean] the flat, two-dimensional, bright-colored things, and see if they go together well. I have a series of the so-called Rembrandt women, where I combined paintings made from some images from Rembrandt, more or less in a realistic style, with my images.You also portrayed Rembrandt himself in your paintings.Yes, sometimes. Apart from paintings, you also sculpt. Is it very different from painting for you?It’s a different kind of thinking; it’s a different kind of three-dimensional thing you have to plan. You grew up in Lithuania when it was still part of the Soviet Union and began your artistic education as a teenager. Could you tell me a little about that?When I was 14, I asked my parents if they would allow me to attend an art school, and they did. Can you tell me something about your parents, your family? My parents were Jewish, of course. Many generations of Vilnius Jews. Both of my parents were scientists in the field of chemistry. My sisters also went into science. So there were no art traditions from home. And what do you recall from the way you were taught art in that school? At this art school for children worked [at the time] very good Vilnius artists. I met some outstanding personalities. It’s a pity that as a child, you didn’t fully understand with whom you were dealing. The way of teaching was rather traditional. Every day we had to draw cubes, and we had to draw plastic casts of ancient, let’s say, gods and philosophers. Well, it was very hard for me as a child.Why was it hard? Well, drawing with a pencil, because when you don’t understand what you are doing, the teachers put some models, some still lifes, and you had to draw them.But despite that, you continued your art education afterward.Yes, I did. It was a master’s five-year program at the Academy of Art in Vilnius. But I’m learning all my life, whenever I start a new painting. You came to Israel in 1991, with the big wave, the aliyah of Soviet Jews. From a very different reality. Was it a cultural shock for you to come here? Yes, but now it’s gone. What was your first impression of the local art scene when you came here? I don’t remember. I don’t think that I saw the art scene when I came here. I was busy with very different things. But I started painting, of course, immediately. As if I knew what was going to happen.I came here in April 1991, and in September (same year), there was a big exhibition of newly arrived painters, organized by the Association of Artists in Tel Aviv. Two galleries chose my works from the photographs.We’re talking about the pre-Google era, so was the fact that they heard about you already a success?No, they didn’t hear about me. It was advertised everywhere; you just had to send photos and your materials to the Association of Artists. And there, the commission, the jury, chose what they liked.And since then, you... Since then, I somehow entered the art scene. One gallery in Tel Aviv chose me, and I worked with that gallery for four years.When did you start teaching in Israel? I started teaching maybe in 1993. It was the private art school established by my friend and sculptor David Zundelovitch. I taught at this school, later called the BASIS School of Sculpture, Beit Yanai, until COVID. When you taught art, what was your message to the students? I didn’t have one message. I taught them mainly composition. I think that composition is the most important thing that the art student has to learn to understand the principles, and then you can do it with anything that you want. Skills come while working, in the process. Speaking of process, please tell me about your infinite painting practice? When you say infinite painting, does it mean that each painting has a story that continues on the next canvas?Absolutely, yes. When I came up with the idea that I am moving on with the painting, I’m adding canvases one to another, and it’s an infinite thing. I thought about other infinite things, and I understood that infinite things contain everything. So, I tried there to paint things that I can paint. There are abstract pieces, there are realistic pieces, and there are realistic people.For example, these wrapped paintings [Ray pointed] are my infinite painting, so-called infinite painting, which now has 99 canvases joined together. It was exhibited in Israel and in the US. Ninety-nine? That’s very impressive! Do you paint every day? Yes. I come to the studio in the morning or early afternoon. It’s the best time to paint. Best light.Are you preparing a new exhibition right now? No, I’m just working on separate works. At the end of our conversation, I have to ask how you speak Polish, my native language, so well (we spoke on the phone before the interview, and you surprised me). Polish is a completely different language from Lithuanian and even from Russian. Where did you learn it?At first, as a child, we had a Polish-speaking nanny there, a woman who helped my mother. But I really learned it when I was young and wanted to read books that weren’t published in the USSR. There was a bookstore in Vilnius that sold books in Polish and German, and I chose Polish to read them. I really like the language. [He smiled.]Dziekuje [thank you, in Polish] for talking to me.Dziekuje for visiting me at my studio!www.leorayart.com

The seven-time champion was left 'extremely frustrated' after qualifying in Hungary, with the Ferrari pit wall taking the brunt of his ire. In the first instance, Hamilton claimed to be 'shocked' that the team elected to run first for the final laps in qualifying, denying the chance to set a time when the track was at its theoretical best. But having completed his lap, Hamilton was then not informed of a charging Oscar Piastri behind, who had just begun his effort, something that ultimately resulted in the Briton being handed a three-place grid penalty for impeding the McLaren driver at Turn 1. Hamilton was pipped to pole by Norris Read Also F1 champion hails Hamilton for using 'power' in sport to progress at Ferrari Lewis Hamilton branded UFC champion a “coward” after airborne pig hunt "Sometimes you just can’t catch a break," wrote Hamilton on social media. "Another weekend when I’ve been feeling great throughout all the sessions, but then it just falls apart. To go from being so close to pole to then starting P5 is extremely frustrating. "I always do my best to keep positive — sport is always about the highs and lows, but it’s also in the margins. Every point counts and you have to seize every opportunity." https://www.euronews.com/my-europe/2026/.text: A third drone has been shot down by Romanian forces in just three days, Romanian President Nicușor Dan has announced, adding to a string of drone-related incidents in the country.In a statement on social media, Dan said a Romanian air force F-16 fighter jet had intercepted a drone over Romania's territorial waters at around 10:13 am on Sunday morning. The incident reportedly occurred in the Sulina–Chilia area of the Danube Delta, close to the border with Ukraine."I would like to congratulate the Romanian pilots and ground crews on the professionalism, courage and efficiency with which they carry out their missions," Dan wrote on X.Romanian authorities reported that an F-16 shot down another unmanned aerial vehicle on Saturday morning, roughly 10 km west of the village of Sfântu Gheorghe in eastern Romania.Two jets were scrambled to identify and intercept the target, and the drone was "safely shot down in an unpopulated area near the border," the Romanian Defence Ministry said in a statement on Saturday.A third drone was shot down by a Romanian F-16 at around 11 am on Friday.The Romanian Prosecutor General's Office has determined that the drone intercepted on Friday was of the Shahed-type used by Russian forces in its war against Ukraine, Romanian officials have said.While investigations into the drones shot down on Saturday and Sunday are still ongoing, Dan said it was "intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania’s airspace.""Such actions are unacceptable and we are treating them with the utmost seriousness, alongside our allies," he added.Romania's growing drone problemSituated on NATO's eastern flank and on the shores of the Black Sea, Romania is particularly vulnerable to security challenges arising from Russia's war against Ukraine, which began after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of the country in February 2022.Bucharest has seen a surge in drone-related incidents and incursions into Romanian airspace in recent months, prompting officials to pledge heightened security measures across the country.In May, a Russian drone carrying explosives crashed into an apartment block in Galați, sparking a fire on the roof and injuring two people.The following month, a Ukrainian sea drone also exploded in the Romanian port of Constanta. The Ukrainian military said it had veered off course as a result of Russian electronic warfare interference.European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen has labelled such incidents "a direct consequence of Russia’s war against Ukraine."

https://www.cei.int/ansa/178219.text: Europe's Tallest Statue of the Virgin Mary Soars Above the Skies of Poland (ANSA) - KONOTOPIE, 25 LUG - In a village in central Poland, a statue of the Virgin Mary soars above the fleecy July skies: while churches are emptying in this country with a long Catholic tradition, a tycoon has had Europe's tallest Marian monument erected there. Rising to a height of 55 meters, the white silhouette of concrete and steel beams stands, rigid and solemn, amid a sea of greenery and parking lots in the rural town of Konotopie, a three-hour drive northwest of Warsaw. Its dedication and blessing are scheduled for the Feast of the Assumption, August 15. For now, construction is still in full swing, under the dazed or fervent gaze of visitors. The Poles owe this gift to a multimillionaire compatriot, Roman Karkosik, who has spent some 100 million zlotys (23.1 million euros), according to local media. He himself lives nearby, in the neighboring town of Kikol, in a restored 18th-century palace across from the parish church. - Funding Devotion - For the faithful interviewed by AFP, devotion is priceless. "People come here (...) in search of faith," says Marek Gizinski, who traveled dozens of kilometers to pray. "And as with any miracle (...) you simply can't forget it—it's downright impossible to forget," he whispers, his gaze fixed on the Virgin Mary. Some local residents, however, believe that this giant statue is not the best way to represent the Catholic faith in a country already dotted with religious monuments, many of which commemorate the Polish Pope John Paul II. The country's main site of Marian devotion—a painting known as the "Black Madonna," located in the south—attracts between 3.5 and 5 million pilgrims each year. "Rather than for the Virgin, that money 'should have been invested in a hospital or an orphanage,'" laments a couple who came from the neighborhood. Entrepreneur Karkosik and his wife, among the wealthiest people in Poland, recently came to admire their creation—in a luxury car with a chauffeur. "Last Sunday, he came to visit the construction site from the back seat of his Maybach," jokes Andrzej, the site's caretaker. - A New Pilgrimage Site? - Local officials hope the project will bring economic benefits—unanticipated in this impoverished region. "I haven't heard any negative opinions (...) Everyone is generally satisfied," Renata Golebiewska, mayor of the neighboring town of Kikol, told AFP. In 2024, municipal tax revenue per capita in Kikol amounted to just 1,117 zlotys (258 euros), according to data from the Ministry of Finance—making it one of the least well-funded municipalities in the region. The statue in Konotopie is the second-tallest in the world after the "Mother of All Asia—Tower of Peace," completed in 2021 and standing 98.15 meters tall in Batangas City, Philippines, another deeply Catholic country. The Virgin Mary holds a special place in Poland's religious and national identity, where she has been venerated for centuries as the country's patroness and protector—even as the country experiences one of the fastest rates of secularization in the world. "We hope that this place will bear the fruits of a deeper return to the faith, or at least help people deepen their faith," says the parish priest, Marek Mrowczynski. Not entirely convinced, Wanda, who came with two friends, wonders above all how much the developers "are going to pocket." kw/ks/pop/jrt (ANSA). https://www.cei.int/ansa/178237.text: Latvia will build a rocket manufacturing plant (ANSA) - VILNIUS, JUL 25 - The U.S. company Native Trading has signed a memorandum of understanding with the Latvian Ministry of Defense to develop an artillery rocket production facility in Latvia. The complex, whose construction costs range from 70 to 90 million euros, will be responsible not only for building the rockets, but also for producing the solid propellants needed to power them, loading the warheads, performing final assembly, and conducting functional tests. Latvian Defense Minister Viktors Valainis emphasized that the memorandum aims to strengthen the Baltic country's defense capabilities while promoting its economic growth and innovation. (ANSA). https://www.cei.int/ansa/178229.text: The Latvian Prosecutor's Office Launches an Investigation into AirBaltic's Finances (ANSA) - VILNIUS, JUL 25 - The Latvian Prosecutor General's Office has launched an investigation to determine whether AirBaltic's financial management complies with legal requirements. According to the announcement, the investigation was launched at the request of Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs to assess the company's management and shed light on the possible causes of the airline's crisis. Another investigation into AirBaltic's financial management had already been launched at the end of 2024, but no irregularities were found. AirBaltic is facing a particularly critical situation after two consecutive years of operating at a loss and the difficulty of finding investors willing to take over the company. (ANSA). Romania shot down a drone on Sunday, according to officials, marking the third time in as many days NATO aircraft have shot down uncrewed aerial vehicles. A Romanian F-16 fighter jet intercepted the drone at 10:13 a.m. local time close to the country's border with southwestern Ukraine, said Romanian President Nicușor Dan. Bucharest has frequently reported drone incursions from Ukraine when Russia bombards Ukrainian ports close to the Danube River, which splits Romanian soil from Ukraine. Read More on World Romania shares roughly 400 miles of land border with Ukraine. ... Drones intruding into NATO airspace have not been treated as attacks on the alliance so far, meaning they have not triggered discussions over a collective response from all 32 members. But the persistent incidents have pushed the alliance's members along Europe's eastern edge to invest in anti-drone defenses. Romania's defense ministry said on Sunday the drone was shot down "safely" little over seven miles northeast of the port of Sulina, within Romania's territorial waters. Romanian authorities didn't confirm whether the drone intercepted on Sunday was Russian-made but Dan said it was "intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania's airspace, which is, at the same time, NATO airspace and European Union airspace." On Saturday, Romanian officials said a drone had been taken out in an unpopulated area close to the border with Ukraine after it was picked up by radar systems at 8:22 a.m. local time. This incident came a day after NATO said two Romanian F-16s and two Italian Eurofighter jets were scrambled under the alliance's command on Friday to intercept a drone that had approached Romania's airspace. Romanian investigators later said the drone was Russian-made. Debris from the drone and the intercept missile landed close to two towns northeast of Bucharest, the Romanian defense ministry said. No casualties or injuries were reported. The governor of Ukraine's southwestern Odesa region, which sits next to Romania, issued several air raid alerts for the areas along the border in the early hours of Sunday. Russia's defense ministry said on Sunday it had attacked the Ukrainian port of Chornomorsk, southwest of the city of Odesa, targeting fuel tanks used by the Ukrainian military. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Friends of an injured school teacher, who has been carried into the ambulance, embrace at the site of a school shooting, in Thailand's Nonthaburi province. Photograph: Wason Wanichakorn/AP View image in fullscreen Friends of an injured school teacher, who has been carried into the ambulance, embrace at the site of a school shooting, in Thailand's Nonthaburi province. Photograph: Wason Wanichakorn/AP Thailand Thailand school shooting toll rises to nine after 12-year-old dies, police say Teenage girl treated in hospital after Friday’s school shooting has died, police say Staff and agencies Sat 8 Aug 2026 22.11 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 02.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The death toll from a school shooting in Thailand rose to nine on Saturday, after police said a 12-year-old girl caught up in Friday’s incident had died. Police at the Plai Bang Police Station in Nonthaburi Province said the girl, who had been treated at hospital with critical wounds, had died, a day after a 14-year-old boy allegedly shot his grandparents and then killed more people at his school before turning the gun on ⁠himself. Thailand school shooting: eight killed including suspected attacker, police say Read more The 14-year-old wounded more than 30 people in the ⁠shooting at the Debsirin Nonthaburi school northwest of Bangkok. Fourteen people remained in hospital on Saturday evening, seven of them in critical condition. Police are questioning more witnesses as part of their investigation, including the suspect’s parents. The boy had lived with his grandparents for 12 years after his parents had separated, Atthapol Anusit, deputy commissioner of the Provincial Police Region 1, ‌told reporters on Sunday. The suspected attacker fired at least 26 bullets with a gun belonging to his grandfather, and was found with 34 additional ammunition rounds. Police on Sunday told reporters the teenager had an air ⁠gun confiscated by a teacher last year and had watched violent content online and used social media to learn how to ⁠use a firearm. “According to witness interviews, the perpetrator had begun showing interest in ​studying the use of firearms ‌for some time, about one ‌to two years,” Atthapol said. Atthapol, who said police had so far interviewed 17 witnesses, said a knife had also been found in the boy’s bag and other evidence found at the crime scenes included a firearm, spent cartridge cases, and a personal computer. On the day of the incident, the suspected shooter remained inside the school after reports of the attack emerged, Arsit Sampantharat, the permanent secretary of the interior ministry, told PPTV. A lockdown at the school was declared over in about half an hour. Images from the scene showed students running with only socks on their feet as they were evacuated from the school. Thailand’s prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, has vowed to implement new gun laws, telling reporters only government officials on duty would be allowed to carry guns. However, he did not provide any ⁠specifics, including whether the legislation would tighten gun ownership requirements. Thailand has the highest rate of civilian gun ownership in south-east Asia, and in 2017 the Switzerland-based Small Arms Survey placed the country 13th worldwide for small-gun possession. A number of mass shootings have occurred in recent years in Thailand, including incidents at schools and a large Bangkok mall, and a 2022 attack in the country’s north-east that ‌killed 37 people including 22 children. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Labor frontbencher Jenny McAllister says Labor has ‘broadly got the legislation right’ but is open to ‘sensible amendments’ on gambling reform. Photograph: Darren England/AAP View image in fullscreen Labor frontbencher Jenny McAllister says Labor has ‘broadly got the legislation right’ but is open to ‘sensible amendments’ on gambling reform. Photograph: Darren England/AAP Gambling Labor open to ‘sensible amendments’ to gambling laws after inquiry hears alcohol and cocaine offered to punters Sources say Albanese government willing to tighten rules on betting inducements but less likely to budge on TV and online advertisements Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Josh Butler Sat 8 Aug 2026 23.58 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 00.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Albanese government is prepared to tighten rules on gambling inducements, but is less likely to budge on advertising rules, as negotiations continue on wagering legislation, which so far has lacked the support needed to pass parliament. Federal Labor is open to considering amendments to its legislation from the Coalition when MPs return to Canberra this week, sources say. The government was prepared to make changes around wagering inducements – a focus of explosive parliamentary hearings last week – as part of negotiations, but was less open to tweaking proposed rules on the frequency of advertisements on TV and online. Additional restrictions on ads are a major demand of gambling harm advocates and the Senate crossbench. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Upper house hearings have aired sensational allegations that wagering companies provided illegal drugs and access to sex workers to keep problem gamblers betting. Betting giants Sportsbet and Tabcorp say there is no evidence to substantiate these claims. “If the government’s now willing to move on some things, well, good, but the devil is going to be in the detail,” the Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young, a vocal proponent of stronger action, told the ABC on Sunday. “Inducements, of course … should be gone.” The Coalition, crossbenchers and the Greens have opposed Labor’s reforms as proposed by the communications minister, Anika Wells, meaning the legislation is unlikely to pass in its current form. Sources said the government was more inclined to deal with the Coalition and would await amendments from the opposition after its party room met in the nation’s capital this week. The government frontbencher Jenny McAllister said on Sunday that Wells was in discussion with the Coalition and had been “paying attention” to evidence from the recent parliamentary hearings. McAllister said Labor thought it had “broadly got the legislation right” but was open to “sensible amendments”. “We want to see this through the parliament,” she said. Inducements can include perks like “bonus bets”, promotional odds, rebates or more VIP enticements like hospitality at events. Luke Bateman tells inquiry gambling companies gave him drugs and alcohol – video The landmark gambling reform report from late Labor MP Peta Murphy called for a total and immediate ban on inducements and their advertising. That issue has been a key focus for advocates within the Coalition, crossbench and Greens – and even among some Labor MPs who want the government to go further. Gambling companies have opposed changes to inducements. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion Hanson-Young, speaking on the Insiders program, suggested she would support the proposed “opt-out” model for online advertising being switched to “opt-in”. Critics have argued streaming platforms would be able to show more ads during breaks in play under Labor’s current plan if they implemented a “triple lock” function including an opt-out feature. Campaigners have also criticised the legislation for allowing three TV ads per hour from 6am to 8.30pm, with a ban during live sport. Wells has previously said the government believes the current proposal strikes the correct “balance” between addressing problem gambling while not unduly penalising media companies and sporting codes which rely on wagering revenue. Labor MP Jerome Laxale last week said he would welcome Labor’s draft laws “being strengthened in the Senate”. The deputy opposition leader, Jane Hume, said the shadow communications minister, Sarah Henderson, was negotiating for new controls over inducements. Tim Wilson, the shadow treasurer, told News24 on Sunday that the Coalition wanted more action to protect children. “Under the government’s proposed bill, it doesn’t limit the capacity to advertise to children, and that’s something that I’m concerned about, making sure that we’ve got the measures that are consistent, appropriate, and also reflecting the changing nature of technology,” he said. Last week’s inquiry heard evidence that gambling ads were being played on Spotify between Disney songs for children . Hanson-Young on Sunday demanded tougher regulation from the government and stated: “If you are not prepared to do what’s needed here, well, we’ll take this out of your hands and we’ll do it in the Senate ourselves.” Explore more on these topics Gambling Australian politics Labor party Coalition news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Australia World AU politics Environment Climate crisis Indigenous Australia Immigration Media Business Health Science Tech Podcasts Newsletters

Screengrab from Nine News of the Jetstar and Qatar planes at Sydney airport on Sunday morning. Photograph: 9News View image in fullscreen Screengrab from Nine News of the Jetstar and Qatar planes at Sydney airport on Sunday morning. Photograph: 9News Sydney airport ‘Not enough air traffic controllers’: safety concerns at Sydney airport after Jetstar and Qatar planes involved in near-miss Planes narrowly avoid collision on tarmac with Jetstar A320 forced to ‘brake firmly’ as Qatar Boeing 777 towed into its path Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Adeshola Ore Sat 8 Aug 2026 22.49 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 02.05 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two planes have narrowly avoided a collision on the tarmac of Australia’s busiest airport as it struggles with staff shortages. The Jetstar and Qatar Airways planes almost collided at Sydney airport at 7am on Sunday. A Jetstar spokesperson said its plane was following instructions from air traffic control when the pilots were forced to brake “firmly” when another aircraft came into “close proximity”. “We have commenced an investigation into the incident,” they said. Initial inquiries suggested the tug vehicle pulling the Qatar aircraft may not have followed instructions, a source said. The Australian Transport Safety Bureau (ATSB) said it was investigating the “near collision”. “As reported to the ATSB, a Jetstar A320 was taxiing prior to a planned flight to Gold Coast airport when its flight crew observed a Qatar Airways Boeing 777, under tow from an aircraft tug, in close proximity on a crossing taxiway,” the safety bureau said. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “Both aircraft were stopped abruptly. A cabin crew member aboard the A320 was injured, and there was damage to the connection between the 777 nose gear and the aircraft tug.” Investigators would interview flight crew, tug operators and air traffic controllers, plus other witnesses, and review any CCTV footage, the bureau said. View image in fullscreen A stock image of a Jetstar plane landing at Sydney airport. Jetstar flight JQ402 was taxiing on the tarmac when the near-miss occurred. Photograph: Jessica Hromas/The Guardian Airservices Australia said it was working to safely manage demand at the airport “following a reported safety incident between two aircraft moving on taxiways”. “We are working with airlines to reduce delays and the impact on passenger travel as much as possible,” a spokesperson said on Sunday. “Airservices is reviewing the incident and will assist with any safety investigation.” Jetstar flight JQ402 was taxiing on the tarmac when the near-miss occurred. The incident left one crew member needing medical attention at the scene, Jetstar said. No passengers were injured. The flight was cancelled and passengers re-booked on later services. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion Jetstar to charge fees to put carry-on luggage in overhead lockers Read more The incident came after delays to more than 150 flights passing through Sydney on Saturday as the airport struggled with staffing shortages. A spokesperson for the airport said Airservices Australia, which oversees air traffic control, was managing reduced air traffic movements. Flights across the network would be affected and delays were expected, the airport spokesperson said. Airservices Australia had been unable to roster enough staff for three consecutive days, the Airlines for Australia and New Zealand chief executive, Stephen Beckett, told the ABC this weekend. Beckett called on Airservices to identify the root cause of the issue and detail plans to address it. Two weeks ago, another near-miss involving two Qantas planes occurred at Sydney airport. The ATSB is investigating the 27 July incident when a Qantas flight was cleared to cross a runway in front of one of the airline’s other planes that had just landed. Both Qantas planes were cleared to proceed following instructions from air traffic control, a Qantas spokesperson said. Air traffic control detected the “conflict” and alerted both crews, the ATSB said. Speaking about Sunday’s near-miss, the NSW premier, Chris Minns, said he was “obviously concerned”. “Not just the safety risks but we want to make sure the airport is operating at full capacity,” he told reporters. “That’s hugely important for our economy. We don’t want to see people disrupted if they go to the airport and services are cancelled because there are not enough air traffic controllers.” Minns said the government was “hopeful that there’s a plan in place to recruit more people for a highly specialised but very important job”. “We’re opening a brand new [western Sydney] airport in the not too distant future, so there’ll be even more strain on that service than there is today. It’s hard to employ people, particularly for these specialised services, because we’ve got a very tight labour market, but this isn’t a nice-to-have; it’s a must-have. It’scrucial for public safety and our economy.” Sydney airport faced significant delays on Friday with some passengers forced to sit on the tarmac for more than an hour as more than 120 flights were delayed. Qatar Airways was contacted for comment on Sunday. Photograph: Alamy View image in fullscreen The Guardian has seen internal DPD records detailing the costs of more than 3,000 temporary workers but they do not include any sick pay or pension. Photograph: Alamy Couriers/delivery industry DPD temporary workers may have missed out on sick pay and pensions, internal documents show Missing payments suggest employment laws may have been breached by recruitment agencies used by courier company Simon Goodley Sun 9 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Low-paid temporary workers at one of the UK’s top courier businesses have missed out on entitlements to sick pay and pension contributions, internal documents suggest. The payments – typically included in the “charge rate” that large brands pay recruitment companies to supply them with temporary workers – are missing from internal spreadsheets calculating the cost of employing thousands of transient staff working at DPD. This absence suggests workers have either not been paid their entitlements, were discouraged from taking days off when sick, or were removed from roles before pension contributions became due, experts said. Zoë Lagadec, principal at Mulberry’s employment law solicitors, said: “This raises questions if the workers are receiving statutory sick pay – as it doesn’t make sense that nobody gets ill – or if they are being moved on before 12 weeks service in order to avoid pension contributions.” Withholding sick pay or pension contributions when they come due would be a breach of employment law by recruitment agencies and seemingly contravenes industry guidance published by the Association of Labour Providers. The trade body’s charge rate guidance adds : “Supermarkets, brands and other labour users have a clear responsibility to ensure that labour providers throughout their supply chains are paid rates that fully reflect legal employment costs and compliance obligations. “Labour users that pay unrealistically low rates are knowingly or recklessly conniving in illegality as these rates can only be achieved through worker exploitation, tax evasion or both.” DPD promotes itself as “one of Europe’s leading parcel groups” and is wholly owned by France’s La Poste. It says its team exceeds 15,000 people , operating more than 10,000 vehicles from 84 locations and delivering more than 260m parcels a year. Its customers have included John Lewis , Marks & Spencer and Amazon . The Guardian has seen internal DPD records detailing the discrete costs of more than 3,000 temporary workers hired by the courier during the past two financial years. The documents include hourly pay rates, holiday pay, employer’s national insurance contributions and a margin for the temporary recruitment agency, but do not include any sick pay or pension. Industry experts questioned whether any temporary recruitment agency, which is technically the employer of the workers, could make any profit from DPD’s charge rates if it then paid the sick pay and pension entitlements to its thousands of staff. Sick pay is now a right on the first day’s absence, although before April it only became due after three days off. Pension contributions are paid by the employer after 12 weeks in the job. The Guardian outlined to DPD the records seen and what they appear to show. The company said: “Our commercial arrangements with our agencies allow them to fulfil their statutory obligations and are benchmarked against competitors in the industry.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion A spokesperson for the courier company added: “At DPD, we take our legal, regulatory and ethical responsibilities extremely seriously. As a client, engaging third-party employment agencies, DPD pays an agreed commercial charge rate to agency suppliers for providing temporary labour. “Under UK employment law, recruitment agencies act as the primary employers of these agency workers. Consequently, statutory obligations, including the administration and payment of Statutory Sick Pay (SSP) and auto-enrolment pension contributions, sit directly with the agency suppliers, rather than DPD as the end-user client. “Our contractual agreements require all agency partners to strictly follow all applicable employment legislation, including statutory pay and pension auto-enrolment requirements. We continuously review our procurement processes and supplier relationships to ensure our agency partners uphold the highest standards of compliance and fair treatment for all workers.” The discovery of the data comes as the temporary recruitment industry looks at how the government’s new Fair Work Agency, which came into existence on 7 April, will use its powers to enforce workers’ rights. The agency brings together much of the existing enforcement system into a single body, by combining the Gangmasters and Labour Abuse Authority, the Employment Agency Standards Inspectorate, HM Revenue and Customs’ national minimum wage enforcement unit and the Office of the Director of Labour Market Enforcement. About a third of food produced worldwide is wasted each year, according UN data. Photograph: Rich Pedroncelli/AP Food waste Plastics contamination an ‘overlooked’ concern in food waste schemes, experts say Researchers find microplastics can persist in compost, leaching into agricultural soils Ushika Kidd Sun 9 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Plastic contamination should be a central concern in efforts to deal with food waste, which campaigners call one of the most overlooked problems of the climate crisis, researchers have said. This is despite the fact that, as the chef, author and activist Max La Manna puts it, food waste management is “one of the few climate problems where everyone wins”. About one-third of all food produced worldwide is wasted each year, according to UN data. In the US, 40% of food waste goes to landfill, where it creates 30m metric tonnes of CO 2 equivalent a year – more than Cuba’s total annual CO 2 emissions in 2024, which amounted to 24.4m tonnes. A new study, published in Nature Food , used life-cycle analysis modelling to compare the impacts – in terms of climate, nutrient pollution and plastic contamination – of different food-waste management scenarios. The authors, based at the University of Vermont, compared the annual climate impacts of landfilled food waste with the climate impact of alternative recycling pathways and found that diverting food waste from landfill would reduce climate impacts by between 89% and 99%. These non-landfill scenarios could also reduce nutrient pollution in water bodies – a process called eutrophication that occurs when excess nutrients result in algal blooms. But the researchers also said that microplastics can persist in compost, which could lead to 20,000 tonnes contaminating US agricultural soils each year. To date, no study has looked at the “plastic pollution footprint” of different food-waste management strategies at national scale. Kate Porterfield, the lead author, said the method was comparable to working out a “carbon footprint of a product or process”. Essentially, the researchers looked at the process of managing food waste and “tall[ied] up what the carbon emissions are across all of those life-cycle stages”, she said. Porterfield said the large proportion of wasted food still in packaging “goes bad before it even reaches the consumer”. One approach to recycling food waste is using a mechanical “depacker”; the packaging then goes to landfill, while food waste goes to “beneficial reuse, like composting or anaerobic digestion”. However, they found that even if plastic separation technologies were 99% efficient, diverting food waste from landfill could still increase microplastic pollution in soil by an order of magnitude. “Any time where you’re diverting food waste, there is a risk of microplastic pollution” because “people aren’t perfect, machines aren’t perfect, and all of our food these days is packaged in plastic”. The US state of Vermont has “one of the most ambitious” state organics-diversion mandates in the US, according to the co-author Eric Roy. The state’s Universal Recycling Law has been fully effective from 2020 and requires food waste to be diverted from landfill. This applies to all households and means food scraps are banned from bins. The authors said their findings provided an effective evaluation of the possible countrywide scale-up of such regulations and pointed to the need for “more attention to the plastics issue” from the outset of creating these policies. Phil Holtam, a co-founder and director of the food waste social enterprise Sussex Surplus, said there was “a little bit of a misconception that [plastic packaging] is unnecessary”, and that it was a “necessary tradeoff”, essential to extending the shelf life of fresh produce, particularly for smallholder farms. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential Preview latest after newsletter promotion “That’s where the tension lies because as environmentalists we want to reduce food waste but we also want to prevent needless use of plastics.” La Manna, who has worked with farmers in the UK and also witnessed food waste working in a Michelin-starred restaurant in New York, said consumer expectations of perfect-looking food were shaping what produce even made it to store shelves and adding to the waste problem. “Some of it may be misshapen, wonky, slightly cosmetically imperfect … [which is] challenging for supermarkets because they believe consumers want a perfect cucumber. “We’re allowing ‘perfect’ to become this enemy of good.” Roy underlined that in institutions such as schools, there “may be some well-intentioned rules that actually create challenges in moving away from highly packaged foods” because “food safety is always going to be a number one concern”. Porterfield said that, ultimately, to reduce plastic contamination food waste management systems needed to be “as easy as possible to make it mindless for people to separate things efficiently”. This included addressing the phenomenon of “wish recycling”, said Roy, where people put non-recyclable items in recycling in the hope they will be recycled. He advised “old-school environmentalism” to reduce litter overall: “buy in bulk”, “make every effort to separate” – and “if in doubt, put it in the landfill stream”.
