https://www.guitarplayer.com/guitarists/.text: YOUR NEXT READ: 1 Tony Iommi reveals Ozzy Osbourne’s final text to him. “It was a hell of a shock, really” 2 Bob Dylan and Jorma Kaukonen on the 1960s guitar icon who led an electric blues revolution and died alone and unknown 3 The guitar legend who launched David Bowie and John Lennon to the top of the charts, got high with Paul McCartney and talked back to Chuck Berry All the latest guitar news, interviews, lessons, reviews, deals and more, direct to your inbox! You are now subscribed Your newsletter sign-up was successful David Bowie performs on the third and final day of the Nokia Isle of Wight Festival, June 13, 2004. (Image credit: Jo Hale/Getty Images) Share Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Email Share this article Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter David Bowie worked with many guitarists throughout his long career, from Mick Ronson to Carlos Alomar, Robert Fripp , Adrian Belew and Reeves Gabrels . But there was one player he returned to several times, from the 1970s to the final years of his life: Earl Slick. What did the Brooklyn-born guitarist give him that no other player did? “I have theories about that,” Slick tells Guitar Player via Zoom, from the kitchen of his home in New York City, while smoking a morning cigarette and opening a bottle of Gatorade. “One of the things was that, when it came down to needing that rock and roll guitar player, that was always me or Mick. And Mick left us a long time ago.” (Ronson died in 1993.) As for the others? “All those guys are wonderful,” Slick says. “But none of them are rock players. So he came back to me for that. That’s when I got called in.” You may like The guitar legend who launched David Bowie and John Lennon to the top of the charts, got high with Paul McCartney and talked back to Chuck Berry Mick Jagger on his rivalry with David Bowie — and the Ziggy Stardust–era track that was Bowie’s Rolling Stones tribute “Never feel safe. Go a little bit out of your depth”: David Bowie's advice to all his musician friends Earl Slick was not a constant in David Bowie’s universe. Few were. But the guitarist — born Frank Medeloni nearly 73 years ago — was a mainstay. He arrived in 1974, following the demise of the Spiders From Mars and Ronson’s exit, to perform on Bowie’s Diamond Dogs tour. He played on the Young Americans and Station to Station albums soon after, then returned in 1983 for the Serious Moonlight Tour as a last-minute replacement for Stevie Ray Vaughan, who famously lent his electric guitar stylings to Let’s Dance , Bowie’s 1983 commercial smash. Bowie and Slick perform on the Diamond Dogs tour, Slick's first with Bowie, at the Boston Music Hall, November 15, 1974. (Image credit: Ron Pownall/Getty Images) Nearly 20 years would pass before Slick came back once again on the tour for Bowie’s 2002 album, Heathen . That led to him working on its follow-up, Reality , and performing on the subsequent A Reality Tour , a celebrated groundbreaking global stint that was the biggest and longest of Bowie’s career. Get The Pick Newsletter All the latest guitar news, interviews, lessons, reviews, deals and more, direct to your inbox! It was there that he witnessed Bowie’s heart attack on June 23, 2004 while onstage in Prague, along with his subsequent decline. “It was amazing how he went from looking great to looking pretty ill — like, overnight,” Slick says. “We were just a month shy of a year being out.” Bowie recovered, but he canceled the remaining shows and never toured again. Slick returned for his penultimate album, 2013's The Next Day , making him the only guitarist to have worked with Bowie over such an extended range of the performer's career. What to read next “I was nervous for about a minute and said, ‘Forget it’” Steve Vai on replacing Eddie Van Halen as David Lee Roth’s guitarist for ‘Eat ‘Em and Smile’ Gary Lucas on Captain Beefheart, Lou Reed, Jeff Buckley, Bruce Springsteen and Chris Cornell “Everyone goes on about the guitar, but I just love that voice.” Phil Manzanera on working with David Gilmour The music from Slick’s latter tenures with Bowie is generously chronicled on the upcoming box set David Bowie 6. I Can’t Give Everything Away (2002–2016), due out September 12. It’s the latest and, theoretically, last in a series of massive completist collections, and features Bowie's final albums, including Reality and The Next Day , as well as the A Reality Tour live album and a previously unreleased recording from the 2002 Montreux Jazz Festival in Switzerland. Also included is “Isn’t It Evening (The Revolutionary),” a track from Slick’s 2003 solo album, Zig Zag . Co-written with and featuring Bowie, it hit the Top 10 on several U.K. charts when it was re-released there last year. It all serves to underscore the vital position Slick held with Bowie during the final era of his career, making this an apt time for him to weigh in on his impactful years with the chameleon of rock. Earl Slick and Bowie perform a warm-up show for the A Reality Tour, Poughkeepsie, New York, August 19, 2003. (Image credit: KMazur/WireImage) Was there much difference being Bowie’s “rock” guitarist compared to other things you’ve done? Well, with David I did have to have a pedalboard to cover 40 years of recordings or whatever. And I hate pedals, especially overdrive pedals. But you needed certain things. You definitely needed two delay pedals just to cover “Heroes,” just to get it bouncing all over the place. But I got a lot of free rein from David. I could literally change up bits and bobs during a show, and he liked it, actually. If you look through the concert videos, you’ll see really weird arrangements of songs and stuff. ’Cause you get bored if it’s the same song every night, so sometimes you change things up, and he liked that I did that. I had a lot of freedom to just ad lib, everywhere. You’d been out of the Bowie orbit for about 15 years when he reached out to you around 2002. How did that come about? Omigod. Reeves had left and David was looking for a guitar player, so his people tracked me down through a web site. It was called Slick-something-or-other, and it had all these old demos we kept putting out. That’s how he found me. The webmaster called and said, “I just got this email. It’s a New York number and they seem to really want to get in touch with you.” He said it was from Isolar, and I said, “I know exactly who that is. It’s David.” [ Isolar was the name for pair of Bowie’s tours in 1976 and 1978. ] We got a phone call saying, ‘Sit tight for a couple of days. David needs to rest. We’re gonna take a few days off.’” — Earl Slick The A Reality Tour was Bowie’s last and, many think, one of his best. What was your experience with it? That was a fun record to play live, especially the rockers — the title track and stuff. It was the best touring band I ever played in with David. The combination of people — it was absolutely drama free, and I’ve never seen him that relaxed and happy on a tour, ever. It was also the tour that was notoriously ended by his health issues. What do you recall from that Prague date when he had his heart attack? It was a really weird gig. At first I couldn’t figure out what was going on. It was hotter than hell in the place, and I could see he was having a hard time hitting some notes. I thought he was just baked. We were all baked. I think we were doing “The Jean Genie,” and he goes to me, “Keep vamping, just jam” — this, while he’s having a heart attack. Then he started grabbing his chest and the tour managers came over and dragged him off. A few minutes later, he comes back and joins us. He lasted about a measure or two and then he walked off. They said that he had a blocked nerve, whatever that is, and that diagnosis was wrong. We did the Hurricane Festival in Germany a couple days later; I went over to talk to him, and he was feeling horrible. We did the whole show and then we got a phone call saying, “Sit tight for a couple of days. David needs to rest. We’re gonna take a few days off.” So we just hung out in Hamburg. Nobody’s saying anything to us. And then we get phone calls saying, “Guys, we’re done. You gotta go home.” We didn’t get an explanation; we all knew he was probably getting some kind of surgery, but we weren’t getting any details about it. When we did “Heroes” at the Hurricane Festival, I swear to God it’s one of the best vocal performances he ever did of it. Two hours later, probably, he was in the hospital. Was the idea of him playing live again ever broached? It was. We were working on The Next Day ; just as I finished up my work on the track “Set the World on Fire.” We were listening back in the control room and he looks at me and goes, “This would just kick ass live.” I looked at him ready to say something, and he goes, “Don’t even think about it.” [ laughs ] That was the discussion we had about going on tour again. That was the whole discussion, and he said, “Don’t think about it.” I could see it in his eyes. I’d been with him so long, I knew he was dead serious. He ain’t going nowhere. It was disappointing, because I really thought we would have at least one good tour left in us. This was the summer of 2013, so it’s possible that he might’ve been ill already, with the cancer. We’ll never know, but I think it’s a possibility. The Next Day was another kind of odd reconnection, wasn’t it? Yeah, it was typical David. He started making that record around 2011, I think, and everybody who was brought in had to sign an NDA. I’m talking to some of the guys on the phone and nobody says a word. In the meantime, this friend of mine, a surgeon, he built a car, a Cobra, and I had this blues gig I was doing near his house in Montclair, New Jersey. I go visit and he says, “Let’s go for a ride in the Cobra before we go to the gig.” I swear to God, if we hadn’t blown up the car, I might not have been on that record.” — Earl Slick We drove for a little bit, and then the car started to do weird shit, like sputtering and stalling out. So he stops the car and two seconds later a big flame comes out of the engine. We call 911 and the fire department comes, and the cops come, and there’s TV. I guess one of the reporters figured out I was in the car and the word gets out on the Internet. The next day I get a text from Bowie: “Oh God, I saw this accident. Are you okay?” I write back, “Yeah, I’m great, I’m fine. How are you?” “Good.” Then I get a few more messages over the course of the next day or two, like, “How you doin’? What have you been up to lately?” This is not a typical thing with him. So finally I’m like, “Okay, are you trying to get to a point? What is it?” And he was, “Well, we’re making this record, and I need you to come in for a week or so and work on it.” I swear to God, if we hadn’t blown up the car, I might not have been on that record. That’s just him: It’s out of sight, out of mind sometimes, and then it’s, “Wait a minute — Slicky could do this or that.” Slick performs at a concert celebrating Bowie on what would have been his 70th birthday, at London's O2 Academy Brixton, January 8, 2017. (Image credit: Brian Rasic/WireImage) Was there a standard operating procedure when you worked together? We’d sit there and brainstorm, especially on the overdub bits. Both of us always like to have some kind of melodic lick in there somewhere, some signature in the song, and we’d just knock ideas around. Like the lick on “Valentine’s Day,” the signature lick at the beginning, we sat there and bounced it around for about 10 or 15 minutes and that lick popped out and there it was. A lot of that kind of stuff was done on the fly; we never spent lots of time. As soon as we heard something that clicked, that was it. That’s the best stuff, when it just comes out from outer space or something. What is your sense of the late-period Bowie compared to your previous years with him? Well, back in the early days — this not speaking out of school, ’cause it’s pretty well known — a lot of drugs were involved, and a lot of cocaine. Between the drugs and him having management problems and all that, he was on another planet. And then as the years went on he changed, like we all do. In the 2000s a sense of humor was there that was never there in the early days. He was funnier than hell, and he was more approachable. He turned into... I wouldn’t say a different person, but the real him came out. How did you approach guitar choices for your work with Bowie? I love Telecasters . I’ve always been a Tele player. But for the Heathen tour he said, “We do need a humbucker on some of this,” so I grabbed some Les Pauls , and by the A Reality Tour I was using pretty much my Les Pauls most of the show. I don’t think I used my Teles at all on that. I did have a Strat I used for a few things, but most of it was Les Paul. It got on the charts and we had a hit single. Funny how timing works. And I’m really glad it’s on the box set, because it turned out to be his last hit.” — Earl Slick Having “Isn’t It Evening (The Revolutionary)” on the box set is a nice postscript, especially after its success last year in the U.K. That’s a weird one. I was living in Portland [ circa 2002 ], and I just started to toodle around with my guitar, and all of a sudden I started coming up with stuff and recording bits and pieces. I ended up with a lot of them, so I called up Mark Plati and said, “When you get some time maybe we can cut an instrumental record. I got some good ideas.” I didn’t realize he was in the studio when I called him. David was there, and David says, “Earl, I heard Mark say you guys were gonna do some recording. Maybe I’ll play some tambourine or something. Maybe I’ll even sing one, or we can write one.” So I sent him a half-dozen bits and he picked the one that eventually turned into “Isn’t It Evening.” We recorded it, and we released it during the A Reality Tour , which turned out to be a bad idea, because my record got buried in there. So I just sat with that track for years and thought, One of these days, I’ll release it as a single. Then Penguin Books approached me about the memoir [ Slick’s recently published Guitar: Life and Music with David Bowie, John Lennon and Rock and Roll’s Greatest Heroes]. I said, “Ah, that’s the time to do it!” So we rearranged it and it came out about two months after the book. It got on the charts and we had a hit single. Funny how timing works. And I’m really glad it’s on the box set, because it turned out to be his last hit. (Iryna Rybakova/Ukraine's 93rd Mechanized Brigade via AP) KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — Russian ballistic missiles struck the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv early on Sunday, setting off fires and wounding at least three civilians, while attacks on other parts of the country later killed at least two people, local officials said. The strikes came as Ukraine’s successful drone attacks have stalled the Russian army’s advances in an expanded campaign inside Russia that has been causing fuel shortages and piling pressure on Russian leader Vladimir Putin. In Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine, Kremlin-installed authorities said a Ukrainian drone strike had killed four civilians in the city of Horlivka. According to Ivan Prikhodko, the city’s Russian-appointed mayor, the city had been under fire since the early hours of Sunday. According to Russia’s defense ministry, Russian forces overnight struck down 133 Ukrainian drones over Russia, the Black Sea and Crimea, the peninsula that Moscow forcibly annexed from Ukraine in 2014. Russian attacks set fire to tower block near Kyiv’s center Blasts rocked Kyiv in the early hours of Sunday, with falling debris sparking a blaze in a tower block near the historic center, according to mayor Vitali Klitschko. Elsewhere in the city, falling debris set fire to buildings, cars and car parks, Klitschko added. He said three people had been wounded, with one needing hospital treatment. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned in his evening address on Friday that intelligence assessments indicated that Russia was preparing missiles for a large attack, saying there were indications that this could happen in the next 48 hours. Russia’s defense ministry claimed on Sunday that its latest attack on Kyiv had struck sites linked to drone production. Also Sunday, a drone strike on Kharkiv — Ukraine’s second-largest city in the east — killed one person and wounded at least six others, including two children, mayor Igor Terekhov reported. In the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, a Russian glide bomb killed one man and wounded at least six other people, according to mayor Ivan Fedorov. Both Kharkiv and Zaporizhzhia have been frequent targets for Russian attacks, with Zaporizhzhia — just over 20 kilometers (12.5 miles) from the front line — suffering heavy bombardment in recent months. The war sees an escalation in tit-for-tat strikes On Friday, a major Russian strike near Kyiv killed at least 10 people and wounded around 100 others, part of a cycle of tit-for-tat attacks that dims the potential of reaching a diplomatic end to Russia’s more than 4-year-old invasion of its neighbor. Meanwhile, Finnish President Alexander Stubb claimed on Sunday that “Ukraine’s position is stronger than ever since the war began”. Following a call with his Ukrainian counterpart — and appearing to allude to Kyiv’s recent drone campaign that has struck major Russian energy sites and sought to choke off military supplies — Stubb wrote on X that “continued support from (Ukraine’s) partners is critical to keep up the momentum.” Putin calls on Russia’s navy to defend ‘shadow fleet’ tankers Putin said Western attempts to seize Russia-linked oil tankers amounted to “piracy,” and called on the Russian Navy to fight them. “We must act carefully in line with international maritime law but decisively — just as we must fight piracy and pirates,” Putin said Sunday during a speech marking Russia’s annual Navy Day. Moscow is believed to be using a fleet of hundreds of ships, many of them sailing under third-country flags, to ship oil in violation of international sanctions that followed its war on Ukraine. Last month, armed British forces boarded and detained a sanctioned tanker suspected of being part of this so-called “shadow fleet.” French authorities have also intercepted some of these vessels. Russia has traditionally marked Navy Day with a major naval parade in and near the city of St. Petersburg, with Putin personally reviewing warships. This year was the second time in a row the parade had been called off entirely while in 2024, it was scaled down. A British intelligence update published earlier this month linked the cancellations to “force protection” concerns, citing a successful Ukrainian attack on Jun. 3 against a Russian warship docked near St. Petersburg. Romania shoots down another suspected Russian drone Romania intercepted a suspected Russian drone in its airspace on Sunday, Romanian President Nicușor Dan said — the third such incursion in three days above the Eastern European nation that borders Ukraine and is a member of both NATO and the European Union. Dan called the incidents “inadmissible and intolerable” in a post on X and added that authorities found one of the earlier downed drones appears to be “a Shahed type, used by the Russian Federation in the war of aggression against Ukraine.” NATO said two Romanian F-16 fighter jets scrambled from Fetești airbase, under NATO’s operational command, in the morning hours and downed the drone over the Black Sea. A series of drone incursions by Russia and Ukraine have hit Romania and other NATO members since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The Golden Leo, an international cargo vessel, sank off the coast of ⁠Ukraine’s Black Sea port of Odesa on Sunday , a week after Ukrainian ⁠officials said ⁠it ​had been struck by Russian forces. Nine ⁠crew members were killed in the ​attack while eight ‌were evacuated to safety. The ‌ship had left the ‌port of Chornomorsk with a cargo of corn when it was shelled by Russian forces on 19 July. Russia’s defence ministry ⁠said on Sunday that its forces had ⁠struck Ukrainian ⁠ports ​and shipping. Russia claimed the container terminal ‌at Chornomorsk, near ‌Odesa, handled “military cargoes”. Russia launched seven ballistic missiles and 136 drones at Ukraine overnight into Sunday, the Ukrainian air force said. In the northern Ukrainian city of Chernihiv, a Russian drone hit ⁠a supermarket, killing two people – including a nine-year-old child – and wounding 25, emergency services said. In the eastern city of Kharkiv, one person was killed and 16 others required medical attention ‌after a daytime drone attack, said the mayor, Ihor Terekhov. A glide bomb attack killed one person and wounded six in the southern city of Zaporizhzhia, said the regional governor, Ivan Fedorov. In Kyiv , a fire broke out on the seventh and eighth floors of a multi-storey apartment block in a central district after ‌a missile attack, said the mayor, Vitali Klitschko. In Sloviansk, Donetsk region, the national oil and gas company Naftogaz said two of its employees died in a Russian attack while trying to help residents affected by an earlier strike. Russia said ⁠ areas of Ukraine ​under Moscow’s control had also come under attack, with four people killed in a Ukrainian drone strike in the Russian-occupied Ukrainian city of Horlivka. Twelve ⁠people, including two children, were ⁠injured ⁠in drone ​attack on ⁠the Russian city of Belgorod, close ⁠to ​Ukraine’s ‌border, regional authorities ‌said early on Monday. https://www.ksl.com:443/article/51602267.text: Ukraine sees highest civilian casualties since 2022     KEY TAKEAWAYS Ukraine reports highest civilian casualties since April 2022 with 377 deaths. Russian attacks include ballistic missiles targeting Kyiv; 1,700 drones used recently. Ukraine's Zelensky urges more air defense systems; Russia extends diesel export ban. KIEV, Ukraine — Ukraine has seen the highest number of civilian casualties in the war with Russia this month for more than four years, according to government figures. Russian attacks this month have killed at least 377 civilians and injured 2,129, making it the deadliest month of the war since April 2022. The attacks this month have included a high number of ballistic missiles, which are difficult to intercept, and have targeted the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, on multiple occasions. Russia has used nearly 1,700 drones, more than 1,630 guided aerial bombs and more than 50 ballistic missiles in the last week, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky. "We must undercut Russia's gamble on ballistic terror," Zelensky said in a post on X Sunday. "Every interceptor missile right now is literally helping save lives if it is here, in Ukrainian systems, not in our partners' warehouses," he added. To underline Zelensky's point, authorities said a 10-year-old child and an adult were killed, and three other people were injured in a Russian drone attack on a supermarket in Chernihiv on Sunday, according to local authorities. Zelensky has frequently appealed for more Patriot and other air defense systems capable of intercepting ballistic missiles. Ukraine has continued its drone and missile campaign against Russian energy infrastructure in the last week, with several refineries targeted. The campaign has led Russia to extend its ban on diesel exports until the end of the year. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Saturday the government will consider lifting the ban on diesel exports "as the market recovers." "Many areas of Russia and occupied Ukraine continue to struggle with fuel shortages, though Russian officials are increasingly posturing that the economic situation and fuel crisis are stabilizing," the Institute for the Study of War in Washington said Saturday. Russia has retaliated by attacking fuel stations in northern Ukraine and has also stepped up its attacks on Ukrainian ports in the Black Sea and on the Danube River. For the third consecutive day, the Romanian air force Sunday shot down a Russian drone over the Black Sea. The defense ministry said that the drone was shot down above Romanian territorial waters. Romanian President Nicusor Dan said that it was "inadmissible and intolerable" for Russia to violate Romanian airspace. Read more Andy Burnham will host Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday as his first international visitor since becoming Prime Minister. The new PM said UK support for Ukraine “remains unwavering” ahead of the visit on Monday, just a week after entering Downing Street. They will visit a naval base where Mr Burnham will announce that Britain will hand over the intellectual property behind its new “Stone Cloak” electronic warfare system, enabling Ukraine to produce the technology at scale. The tablet-sized device is designed to block Russian detection of any drones it is fitted to. The Ministry of Defence has already given thousands of the jammers to Ukrainian forces to bolster their drone operations. open image in gallery A firefighter walks at the site of a petrol station hit by a Russian airstrike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Zaporizhzhia ( Reuters ) Mr Burnham said in a statement: “Britain stands with Ukraine, shoulder to shoulder, and our support remains unwavering. “Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve and we will not back down until we achieve long-lasting and just peace for Ukraine. “Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries.” What is ‘Stone Cloak’? Following its deployment in Ukraine, the technology is expected to be incorporated into the UK’s next generation of long-range strike weapons, including Project Brakestop, the Government’s initiative to develop low-cost cruise missiles. During the visit, the two leaders will meet more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the past three weeks in the UK taking part in Exercise Sea Breeze, aimed at strengthening warfighting capabilities and counter-mine measures in the Black Sea. The new Prime Minister spoke to Mr Zelensky in one of his first calls after taking office last Monday and invited the Ukrainian leader to visit “at the earliest opportunity”. Mr Burnham, who has little foreign policy experience from his previous time in government, had vowed to maintain his predecessor Sir Keir Starmer’s resolute support for Ukraine before entering No 10. Sir Keir visited Kyiv on his final full day as Labour leader. open image in gallery Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky pay their respects at a wreath laying at the Wall of Remembrance of the Fallen for Ukraine (Stefan Rousseau/PA) ( PA Wire ) On Sunday Romania shot down a suspected Russian drone after it crossed into its airspace — the third such incursion in three days in the Eastern European nation that's both a European Union and a NATO member, the country's president said. Two Romanian F-16 fighter jets scrambled from the Fete*ti airbase, under NATO's operational command, and shot down the drone over the Black Sea, the military alliance said. "A new drone was shot down this morning, at 10:13, by an F-16 aircraft of the Romanian Air Force, over the territorial waters of Romania, in the Sulina-Chilia area," Romanian President Nicusor Dan said. He added that authorities found that one of the earlier intercepted drones appears to be "a Shahed type, used by the Russian Federation in the war of aggression against Ukraine. "This is the fourth recent downing by Romania of a drone violating NATO airspace in coordination with the alliance, said Col. Martin O'Donnell, a spokesperson for NATO's Supreme Headquarters Allied Powers Europe, known as SHAPE.Before the last three interceptions, Romanian jets shot down a drone in the sky above Estonia in May, he said. Romanian pilots and planes are based in Lithuania from where they have broad strike capabilities as part of NATO's force posture. "As we continue to prove, NATO is constantly on the watch and prepared to defend itself from any threat," O'Donnell said. https://economictimes.indiatimes.com/wea.text: For years, working abroad meant securing a foreign job or investing heavily through a golden visa programme. Today, digital nomad visas offer a new route, allowing professionals to live overseas while working remotely for employers or clients elsewhere. With no multi-crore investment requirement and remote work on the rise, they are attracting Indian software professionals, consultants, founders and content creators seeking global mobility without changing careers. Industry experts say enquiries from Indians have surged over the past three years, reflecting the shift towards flexible work and the growing appeal of countries offering a better quality of life.New mobilityA digital nomad visa is a residence permit that allows an individual to legally stay in a foreign country while earning income from an employer or clients located outside that country. Unlike traditional work visas such as the H-1B in the US, it is not tied to sponsorship by a local employer.âIt provides legal clarity to work remotely, longer stays than tourist visas, access to local services and, in some countries, simplified tax treatment or pathways to residency,â says Andri Boiko, Founder and Global CEO, GARANT IN.Varun Singh, Managing Director, XIPHIAS Immigration, calls digital nomad visas âone of the biggest shifts in global mobility over the past decadeâ. He says they allow professionals to experience living abroad without changing employers while enabling host countries to attract skilled individuals who contribute to the local economy without competing for local jobs.ALSO READ | Foreign universities in India: Should you choose an Indian campus over studying abroad? Know the pros & consOne limitation is that these visas generally donât allow local employment, requiring holders to earn foreign income. Those wanting local jobs usually need a work visa. Spain is an exception, allowing up to 20% of the main applicantâs income from local clients, while spouses can work without such restrictions.Whatâs a digital nomad visaA residence permit that lets you live in another country while working remotely for an employer or clients based outside that country. It is designed for remote workers, not people seeking local employment. It allows:Work for a foreign employer/clientNo local job sponsorship neededTemporary residenceUsually cannot take local jobsRemote work or freelancingBest suited forSoftware professionalsConsultantsContent creatorsFreelancersStartup foundersNot meant forPeople seeking local employmentThose without a stable remote incomeWhy now?The primary reason for the rise in these visas is the mainstream acceptance of remote work following the Covid-19 pandemic. âRemote work moved from a niche idea to a mainstream way of working after the pandemic, and governments quickly saw the economic upside of attracting remote earners,â says Boiko. He notes that these professionals spend on housing, food, transport and leisure without competing for local jobs, making them attractive for governments. Estoniaâs launch of the first dedicated digital nomad visa in 2020 encouraged other countries to introduce similar programmes.ALSO READ | India visa and passport services disrupted in Australia after Delhi High Court scraps government tenderSingh says professionals are no longer choosing countries only for career opportunities. Lifestyle, safety, healthcare, infrastructure and international mobility have become equally important considerations. Entrepreneurs also see overseas residence as a way to expand globally and access new clients and investors. While favourable tax regimes matter, he cautions that a visa by itself does not change tax residency.Both experts say demand from India has accelerated sharply since 2023. Boiko says software and IT professionals remain the largest applicant group, followed by consultants and freelancers, while startup founders and content creators are emerging as fast-growing segments. Investors and retirees, on the other hand, usually prefer golden visas because those programmes are investment-led.Singh says his firm has seen enquiries rise significantly over the last three years. Initially dominated by software professionals and freelancers, interest has broadened to include startup founders, senior corporate executives, consultants, digital creators, architects, designers, financial consultants and online educators. âMany of these professionals are not looking to permanently relocate. Instead, they want international exposure while maintaining their existing careers and income sources,â he says.Top destinationsSpain has emerged as the top choice for many Indians. Boiko says its relatively low income threshold, favourable tax regime, Schengen access and flexible work rules make it more attractive than rivals. Portugal, Greece, Estonia, Malta and Dubai are also popular.ALSO READ | Dubai Residential Visa: You no longer need minimum 7.5 lakh Dirhams to buy a property, Dubai Land Department makes Visa rules easierSingh says the UAE remains a top choice too due to its zero personal income tax, strong infrastructure and large Indian community. Spain and Portugal offer a European lifestyle and long-term residency prospects, while Greece and Croatia provide lower living costs. Spain grants an initial entry visa valid for up to a year. Once you arrive in Spain, you can transition or renew this into a digital nomad residence authorisation that can last up to three years, while Portugal provides a four-month entry visa followed by a two-year permit. Greece issues a one-year visa, convertible to a two-year renewable permit All three can lead to permanent residency after five years, subject to eligibility. Applicants typically need stable overseas income, work contracts, health insurance, sufficient funds and a clean record; some countries require employer approval for overseas remote work. Including visa, insurance, documentation and advisory costs, expenses can range from Rs.1.5 lakh to Rs.8 lakh; for Spain, itâs Rs.9 lakh and for Portugal, Rs.8 lakh.Tax mattersThis is where it can get challenging. âMany people assume that obtaining a foreign visa automatically changes their tax residency. That is not the case,â says Singh.Under the Income Tax Act, residency status hinges mainly on how many days you spend in India physically during a financial year, with extra rules for high earners. Time spent abroad on a digital nomad visa can push someone into Non-Resident or RNOR (Resident but Not Ordinarily Resident) status â which changes whether their worldwide income stays taxable in India. The Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA) rules and Double Taxation Avoidance Agreement (DTAA) provisions apply on top of this. âTax treatment usually follows where the work is physically performed, not where the pay cheque originates,â says Boiko.For salaried employees, overseas remote work may also require employer approval, as it can raise permanent-establishment concerns for the Indian company. âSome Indian companies are cautious about signing off on this,â Boiko notes.Challenges aheadWhile immigration itself may be straightforward, settling into another country often presents practical hurdles. Both experts identify taxation, banking, insurance, housing, employer compliance and understanding local regulations as the biggest challenges. Salaried employees may also need explicit permission from their employers, who could face tax or compliance issues arising from overseas remote work.Another important consideration is the long-term objective. Some countries, including Spain and Portugal, offer pathways to permanent residency after several years of legal residence, while others treat digital nomad visas as purely temporary arrangements with no route to settlement.For professionals with stable remote income, digital nomad visas offer an accessible alternative to golden visas. Instead of committing crores towards investment-linked residency, they allow individuals to test life abroad while continuing their careers. But experts caution these visas are not simply about working from a beach. Tax planning, employer consent, compliance and long-term immigration goals require careful consideration.

https://www.nbcsandiego.com/clear-the-sh.text: Animals How a cancer patient's cats inspired a push for pets in Poland's hospice wards Under proposed new legislation in Poland, patients would have the right to be visited in hospices and palliative care wards by their pets. By Vanessa Gera | The Associated Press • Published July 1, 2026 • Updated on July 1, 2026 at 2:13 pm BOOKMARKER AP Photo/Rafal Niedzielski) Patient Ewa Lutka-Krawczyk holds the paw of Australian shepherd therapy dog Kluska at the Palliative Medicine Clinic at the Medical University of Warsaw, Poland, Monday, June 15, 2026. When Ewa Lutka-Krawczyk was diagnosed with gallbladder cancer, her first thought was for Gaja, a shelter dog she took in three years ago. She asked her doctor to assure her she would live a few more years so the deeply attached Gaja “wouldn't be left behind.” But the prognosis was grim, and last month the 70-year-old was admitted to the palliative ward of a Warsaw hospital. Left at home with Lutka-Krawczyk's husband, Gaja was barely eating. Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7. WATCH HERE “She is waiting for me,” Lutka-Krawczyk said from her bed, where she rested with a draining tube attached to her abdomen. Under proposed new legislation in Poland, patients like Lutka-Krawczyk soon would have the right to be visited in hospices and palliative care wards by their pets. Visits are already allowed in many clinics, but there is no universal right under the law. One expert reports an ‘epidemic of loneliness’ Dr. Tomasz Dzierżanowski, director of the Palliative Medicine Clinic at the Medical University of Warsaw, where Lutka-Krawczyk is being treated, has led the proposal, which was introduced to parliament by a member of Prime Minister Donald Tusk's centrist party. Dzierżanowski said the presence of a beloved pet can ease the physical and spiritual pain of terminally ill patients at a time when society is experiencing “an epidemic of loneliness.” “We make sure that no patient dies alone,” Dzierżanowski said in an interview with The Associated Press. “When someone is suffering, it is important that someone is there for them. Ideally, that should be another human being,” he said. “Sometimes, however, there is no one." Dzierżanowski said he often sees older patients isolated because they have outlived their friends, as well as young patients feeling alone in palliative care clinics because in today's world of screens and virtual friends, they have not built the kind of friendships that earlier generations often had. Fourth of July Jun 27 Five ways to protect your pets during the Fourth of July NBA Jun 18 How Knicks' OG Anunoby is helping NYC shelter cats find their forever homes Animals Jan 31 Pet sounds: Why some dog owners share music with their 4-legged friends Dzierżanowski said the catalyst for his mission was a seriously ill cancer patient named Waldemar who was not afraid for himself but for his two cats. Dzierżanowski arranged for the cats to be brought into the ward. The man's tears of happiness and the cats' emotional reaction — as well as that of other patients and hospital staff who witnessed the reunion — “made me realize that this issue finally needed to be addressed," he said. Dzierżanowski allows pets to visit patients in his clinic when conditions allow, which means that Lukta-Krawczyk can look forward to a visit from Gaja. That pleased her when she learned of it. “In reality, animals in hospitals are already there anyway,” said Katarzyna Piekarska, the lawmaker who introduced the legislation, which is now in parliament's health committee. “That’s why it needs to be regulated in the law.” Therapy dogs are also allowed Dzierżanowski also allows visits by therapy dogs. When the AP visited, Kluska, an Australian shepherd, was making the rounds with her owner, Małgorzata Brzozowska. Kluska — whose name means “dumpling” — brought some distraction to Lutka-Krawczyk, who held the dog's paw and smiled. Medical student Malgorzata Brzozowska and her therapy dog Kluska visit the bedside of patient Ewa Lutka-Krawczyk at the Palliative Medicine Clinic at the Medical University of Warsaw, Poland, June 15, 2026. (AP Photo/Vanessa Gera) Another patient, Wojciech Zelik, a 58-year-old admitted with a tumor, propped himself up to admire the dog as Brzozowska got Kluska to perform tricks. “She has such lovely fur to pet, so fluffy,” he said, reaching over and rubbing her head. Brzozowska said therapy dog visits also help relieve the stress of nurses, cooks and other staff who tend to the terminally ill patients. Several made a fuss over Kluska, crouching down to pet her in the hallway — with the cook giving her slices of ham. Brzozowska, a medical student, said the benefits are even greater when the patients are visited by their own pets. It calms them, their loved ones — and the animals, too. “The dog isn’t as stressed,” she said. "We interpret this as meaning that he simply knows what’s happening, that he knows where the owner, who was always there before, has disappeared to.” Copyright The Associated Press This article tagged under: Animals Clear the Shelters on now The Cost of Losing Trending Stories SEAWORLD NBC 7 Responds helps families affected by SeaWorld power outage recover funds NBC 7 Responds What to know about door-to-door sales tactics targeting San Diego seniors La Mesa Man arrested after La Mesa shooting sends bullet through wall and injures neighbor Imperial Beach “Keep out of water” warning signs return to Imperial Beach after just a few days San Diego Midway Rising moves forward despite continued community opposition Weather Forecast Facebook Instagram TikTok Youtube

A mom has opened up about the rare condition that means her toddler has a permanent "mask-like face" that stops him from forming expressions. Following a textbook pregnancy without any concerns, Jeannie Hochstetler of Indiana welcomed her first child on January 29, 2025. She told Newsweek that there were "no concerns" ahead of her son’s birth, and the only sign of anything unusual was that her stomach measured small. At the time, Hochstetler, 28, believed she was having a small baby, which is not uncommon. However, it quickly became evident that something was wrong following Riley’s birth. Read More on Family & Parenting ... "He did not cry when he was born and I assumed he needed a little support adjusting to the outside world," Hochstetler said. "They whisked him away and placed oxygen on him. I remember the doctor standing above him with his chin in his hand for what seemed like hours. Looking back, I realize he knew something was wrong, he just didn’t know what." Riley was transferred to the local NICU ward at a hospital 40 minutes away. Further assessment revealed that Riley has small, webbed hands, and is also missing his right pectoral muscle. Additionally, doctors were unable to open his mouth very far, so Riley was placed on CPAP and given an NG tube for feeding. Nevertheless, Riley "remained a mystery" as doctors struggled to diagnose him. He remained in the NICU for weeks as his condition was assessed. Ultimately, one of the doctors in the ward suggested that Riley could have Poland-Moebius Syndrome, a rare congenital condition that causes facial paralysis and underdeveloped chest muscles. Given the complexities of Poland-Moebius Syndrome, Riley was transferred to a larger NICU three hours away. "This was one of the hardest parts for me. I was two weeks postpartum, watching strangers load my baby into a helicopter—what a wild introduction to parenthood," Hochstetler said. ... At three weeks old, Riley was officially diagnosed with Poland-Moebius Syndrome. The 'National Institutes of Health (NIH) suggests that Moebius Syndrome occurs in an estimated one per 50,000 live births, causing the underdevelopment of facial nerves that control expressions and eye movements. People with Moebius Syndrome can experience trouble swallowing, difficulties with speech, inability to smile or frown, hearing problems and motor delays. Poland syndrome is often linked to Moebius Syndrome, leading to missing or underdeveloped chest muscles. It was a whirlwind moment when Hochstetler was told her son’s diagnosis. She had never heard of either condition, so there was a lot of uncertainty about Riley’s future. She said: "Hearing that my baby would never smile at me was one of the hardest parts. I remember feeling grief because this was not the parenthood I envisioned. I also felt sadness for my baby and all the things he had already endured and would have to endure. "We were told that each case of Moebius is different, and we would just have to wait and see how severely Riley was affected. They told us he would not be able to form facial expressions or blink, he would have difficulty feeding, and he would be delayed with milestones." There is no cure for Moebius Syndrome, so the family can only treat the symptoms and manage Riley’s condition. Riley is missing his seventh cranial nerve, which is responsible for facial movement and he has restricted eye movement. However, he has continued to adapt and conveys his emotions in a variety of other ways. Riley uses a G-tube for feeding, but Hochstetler hopes to introduce oral feedings when his swallow gets stronger. "He has also had a strabismus surgery done at 13 months old to correct his crossed eyes," she explained. "At the same time he also had a surgery performed to fix eyelashes that laid on his eyes. He’s had two MRIs done and multiple ABRs (hearing tests). Riley has mild hearing loss in his left ear." ... "He has the best laugh in the world and it’s my favorite sound," Hochstetler told Newsweek . "He also does not hesitate to use his voice when he’s not happy. I’ve also become adept at reading his body language to know what he’s feeling." "His condition is non-progressive, which means what he’s born with won’t get worse. With therapy a lot of things can improve, and they already have. He is so adaptable and clever—he figures out how to do things in his own way. He amazes me," she continued. Following Riley’s diagnosis, Hochstetler has been documenting her family’s experiences on social media (@jeanniebontrager on TikTok) to raise awareness of Moebius Syndrome. Riley has taught her so much about strength and resilience, and Hochstetler hopes to show that love can be shown in so many different ways. Hochstetler said: "He is my biggest blessing, and I am so incredibly thankful to be his mom. He has been through so much in his short life and yet he still is one of the happiest babies." Clyde Atkins U.S. Courthouse, Monday, July 27, 2026, in Miami. (AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell) (Rebecca Blackwell/AP Photo/Rebecca Blackwell) By DAVID FISCHER, Associated Press July 27, 2026 at 3:39 pm EDT MIAMI — Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will remain in jail at least two more weeks until their next hearing as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, a federal judge said Monday. U.S. Magistrate Lauren Louis set a detention hearing for Aug. 13 to determine whether the Tates should stay in jail or be released during what could be a monthslong extradition process. The brothers weren't in court Monday or required to be there and have remained in jail since making a brief court appearance two days after their July 18 arrest . The Tates have become among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. Attorneys for the brothers said Monday that they want the U.S. government to turn over documents that U.K. officials submitted to secure their arrest. “They don't have anything but the accusations,” attorney Joseph McBride said after the hearing. “It’s just their word against our word right now.” The U.K. has until mid-September to turn over all of its materials to the State Department, Assistant U.S. Attorney Alejandra López said in court. The brothers have long claimed that their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. Jackie Perczek, another one of their attorneys, said the Tates have shown they are not a flight risk by returning to Romania every month after they were accused there of luring women for sexual exploitation. “For three years they have not fled,” she said. “They've traveled the world and every month they return to Romania.” The former professional kickboxers, who have dual U.S. and U.K. citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers shouldn't expect any help from the president. McBride said shortly after the Tates were arrested that "they’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit," he said. McBride said the extradition attempt was politically motivated, though he provided no details. Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new accusers and were brought after authorities received evidence from police in Bedfordshire, in southeastern England. The allegations, which span from 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. The brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case hasn't gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. Andrew Tate, 39, became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother.” He was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman. He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women. https://www.eng.kavkaz-uzel.eu/articles/.text: Homepage / All news 06:55, 27 July 2026 Participants in the actions in three European countries opposed the expulsion of a native of Chechnya to Russia. Activists of the Chechen diaspora held pickets in the capitals of Austria, the Czech Republic, and Finland near the German embassies in support of the Chechen refugee Muslim Alhazov, who faces deportation from Germany to Russia. As reported by " Caucasian Knot ", the authorities of European countries periodically expel refugees from the North Caucasus who seek asylum to Russia. On March 23, it became known that a native of Chechnya, who sought protection in Estonia, did not receive proper legal assistance and was deported to Russia. In Helsinki (Finland), Prague (Czech Republic), and Vienna (Austria), as well as in other European cities, activists of the Vainakh diasporas held pickets in support of the Chechen refugee Muslim Alhazov, who faces deportation from Germany to Russia, human rights activist Roza Dunaeva reported last night. Participants in the actions called on the German authorities not to expel Alhazov to Russia, as his family has been subjected to persecution, abductions, and torture for years. "Muslim Alhazov's family is among those who have suffered greatly from the authorities' persecution," Dunaeva noted on her Facebook page*. Activists demanded that the German authorities comply with international human rights obligations. "Caucasian Knot" also reported that on June 24, it became known that a native of Chechnya was deported from Lithuania after the authorities of the country denied him an extension of refugee status, despite the fact that he had legally lived there for more than 20 years . REUTERS/Evelyn Hockstein President Donald Trump's foray into nuclear politics has created a "giant firestorm" that makes a nightmare scenario increasingly likely, according to one political scientist. Robert Pape, a political scientist at the University of Chicago, argued during a recent episode of "The Court of History" podcast on the Legal AF Network that Trump's demand that Saudi Arabia sign the Abraham Accords , and thereby normalize relations with Israel , is likely to backfire. Pape noted that the agreement provides no way to prevent Saudi Arabia from enriching uranium because there is no oversight or enforcement . "President Trump seems to realize this has touched off the giant firestorm," Pape said, noting that the deal increased Saudi Arabia's chances of getting a nuclear weapon from 98% to 99.999%. Once Saudi Arabia has a nuclear weapon, it's only a matter of time before other nations start knocking, Pape said. All of a sudden, nuclear weapons would proliferate across the globe . "What does it mean for [countries] besides Iran ? It means the [United Arab Emirates] knocking on the door, 'Hey, what do you mean Saudi Arabia doesn't have to abide by these gold standards? We want to slip them as well here.' And then, of course, it doesn't take much to start looking at why Ukraine is not going down this road ... And why isn't Poland talking about doing this?" Pape said the situation could result in another forever war "quagmire" that Trump is unable to pull the U.S. out of. "If you thought you couldn't have made the situation worse, there was already a fire, and we're already pouring gasoline on the fire," Pape said. Gedvila / BNS Lithuaniaâs new government is signalling a tougher approach to migration, with President Gitanas NausÄda proposing stricter rules for foreign workers and officials insisting that migration flows could pose economic and security challenges. Under NausÄdaâs proposal, foreign workers would receive temporary work permits valid for two years and would then be required to leave Lithuania for at least six months before being allowed to return. Moreover, they would not have the right to family reunification â that is, to bring their families while they work in Lithuania. The plan has drawn criticism from legal experts and business representatives, who warn that tighter restrictions could worsen labour shortages and hurt the economy. At the same time, security officials say migration routes through the region have become part of a broader security challenge linked to Russia and Belarus. Lithuania experienced a major migration crisis in 2021, when thousands of migrants crossed or attempted to cross the border from Belarus in what the European Union described as a state-sponsored pressure campaign. âLithuania was the first country targeted by this attack. We were the first to have to make decisions in this nonstandard situation,â said conservative MP AgnÄ BilotaitÄ, who served as interior minister from 2020 to 2024. Under her leadership, Lithuania responded by interning several thousand people who had entered the country, allowing authorities to push back migrants attempting to cross from Belarus, and building a fence topped with concertina wire along the border with Belarus. Concertina razor wire along the border Lithuanian-Belarusian | D. Umbrasas / LRT Latvia faces growing pressure Lithuaniaâs neighbour Latvia is now facing a similar challenge. Nearly 8,000 migrants have attempted to enter Latvia from Belarus this year, about nine times more than the number recorded in Lithuania, according to Lithuanian officials. Antanas Montvydas, deputy head of Lithuaniaâs State Border Guard Service, said Latviaâs incomplete infrastructure and gaps in border surveillance systems have contributed to increased pressure. Migrants who enter Latvia often attempt to travel onward through Lithuania toward Western Europe. Lithuanian authorities have stopped about 1,200 people arriving from Latvia over the past six months. Recently appointed Interior Minister Martynas Katelynas said Lithuania could consider temporarily restoring border checks with Latvia if migration flows become impossible to manage. Martynas Katelynas | V. Raupelis / LRT âClearly, this would be a ânuclearâ option, but if we had no other possibility to control the flows and stop migrants at the border, not on our territory, I think we would have to take it,â Katelynas said earlier this month. However, both NausÄda and Prime Minister Mindaugas SinkeviÄius oppose restoring internal border controls with Latvia, saying it would undermine the principles of the Schengen free-travel area. âNinety percent of our problem is not with Latvia. We have no special problems in relations with Latvia, so in my view creating internal borders within the Schengen area would be a defeat and a kind of capitulation to this phenomenon,â NausÄda said. Latvia has asked Lithuania for additional assistance rather than border restrictions. Lithuania recently sent a second team of 10 border officers, while Latvian officials have said they need around 100 additional personnel. Latvian Interior Minister JÄnis Dombrava said the main challenges are increased pressure at the border and a shortage of officers. Lithuanian and Latvian border guards | VSAT Economic concerns Lithuaniaâs debate over migration also reflects a growing tension between security concerns and labour market needs. NausÄdaâs chief national security adviser, Deividas Matulionis, said the number of foreigners living in Lithuania has reached about 220,000, or 7.7% of the population, placing pressure on integration systems and contributing to social tensions. But legal expert Skirmantas Bikelis criticized what he described as misleading arguments behind the proposed restrictions. He said the number of foreign residents has remained relatively stable and warned against using isolated incidents involving foreigners to justify broader restrictions. Business representatives argue that migrant workers are essential because many sectors face long-term labour shortages. âEmployers have needed migrants for 10 years already. There are jobs that Lithuanians cannot be encouraged to take even with high salaries. Migrants are a solution,â Bikelis said. He warned that limiting foreign labour could damage the economy, particularly because work quotas for migrants are often reached before the end of the year. Giedrimas Jeglinskas, a security and defence expert, former chair of the parliamentary National Security and Defence Committee, said every foreign arrival carries risk of possible recruitment by hostile intelligence services, particularly among people arriving from Russia-speaking communities or former Soviet countries. Lithuanian border officials have repeatedly reported cases of Belarusian officers escorting migrants toward the border. Lithuanian authorities have consistently described migration via Belarus as part of a âhybrid attackâ. Baltic leaders have also warned of possible new Russian provocations targeting countries that support Ukraine. President NausÄda said critical energy and transport infrastructure could be potential targets because attacks on such facilities could have a wider impact. Officials have warned that possible attacks could include sabotage, cyberattacks, information operations and other actions aimed at weakening public trust and reducing support for Ukraine. âThe goal of Russia is to influence society, trust in institutions and reduce support for Ukraine,â Jeglinskas said. https://www.lancashiretelegraph.co.uk/ne.text: Court Crime Accrington Latvian man arrested in Accrington to be extradited By Nat Goodlad Reporter Share 0 Comments The Royal Courts of Justice in London (Image: Archive) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A man arrested in Accrington on a European arrest warrant will be extradited to Latvia to face allegations he was part of an organised drugs gang. Latvian national Dzintars Jezdauckis was detained in the town on January 30, 2024, after a warrant was issued over claims he was involved in buying, storing, transporting and reselling large quantities of narcotics in 2017. He is accused of being in an organised group supplying drugs in Latvia, an offence said to carry a possible sentence of between five and 15 years in prison if he is convicted. The Royal Courts of Justice in London (Image: Archive) Jezdauckis, who has previously served an eight-year sentence in Latvia for supplying drugs, opposed his extradition on human rights grounds, telling the courts he would rather die than return to a Latvian jail. He claimed he had been beaten and stabbed by other prisoners during his earlier sentence at Daugavgriva prison and relied on a report from forensic physician Dr Juliet Cohen, which recorded multiple scars and diagnosed him with anxiety and depression. A district judge ordered his extradition in June 2024 and rejected his arguments that returning him would breach Article 3, which prohibits inhuman or degrading treatment, and Article 8, which protects private and family life. Read more Stalker who repeatedly called victim avoids immediate prison sentence Takeaway owner fined in court after breaching hygiene laws Man appears in court charged with possessing explosives Jezdauckis appealed, and the High Court asked the Latvian authorities for more detail on where he would be held and what measures were in place to tackle violence between prisoners. They said he would initially be held in the remand section of Riga Central Prison and pointed to new capacity, including single-cell accommodation at a modern facility in Liepāja, alongside increased supervision and the ability to move prisoners who are at risk. In a ruling handed down this month, Mr Justice Kimblin found there was no real risk that this particular prisoner would suffer degrading treatment if extradited and upheld the original decision to send him back. The judge also refused him permission to renew his Article 8 challenge, saying the weighty public interest in returning those accused of serious offending to face trial meant the balance came down firmly in favour of extradition. https://www.bostonglobe.com/2026/07/27/n.text: Tate brothers will remain in jail at least 2 more weeks as they fight extradition to the UK Andrew Tate, left in black, and his brother Tristan Tate, center rear, arrive at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood International Airport in Florida on Feb. 27, 2025. JAMES JACKMAN/NYT Social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate will remain in jail at least two more weeks until their next hearing as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking, a federal judge said Monday. U.S. Magistrate Lauren Louis set a detention hearing for Aug. 13 to determine whether the Tates should stay in jail or be released during what could be a monthslong extradition process. The brothers weren’t in court Monday or required to be there and have remained in jail since making a brief court appearance two days after their July 18 arrest. The Tates have become among the world’s most polarizing internet personalities with their promotion of wealth, male dominance and misogyny through their social media empire. The new allegations are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the Tates that has spanned the U.S., Britain and Romania. The brothers have repeatedly denied wrongdoing. Get Starting Point A guide through the most important stories of the morning, delivered Monday through Friday. Enter Email Sign Up Attorneys for the brothers said Monday that they want the U.S. government to turn over documents that U.K. officials submitted to secure their arrest. “They don’t have anything but the accusations,” attorney Joseph McBride said after the hearing. “It’s just their word against our word right now.” The U.K. has until mid-September to turn over all of its materials to the State Department, Assistant U.S. Attorney Alejandra López said in court. The brothers have long claimed that their violent and misogynistic statements have been taken out of context or were intended as jokes. Jackie Perczek, another one of their attorneys, said the Tates have shown they are not a flight risk by returning to Romania every month after they were accused there of luring women for sexual exploitation. “For three years they have not fled,” she said. “They’ve traveled the world and every month they return to Romania.” The former professional kickboxers, who have dual U.S. and U.K. citizenship, have millions of social media followers and are vocal supporters of President Donald Trump. The White House has said the brothers shouldn’t expect any help from the president. McBride said shortly after the Tates were arrested that “they’ve never done nothing wrong. They shouldn’t be extradited for crimes they did not commit,” he said. McBride said the extradition attempt was politically motivated, though he provided no details. Prosecutors in Britain said the new charges relate to four new accusers and were brought after authorities received evidence from police in Bedfordshire, in southeastern England. The allegations, which span from 2010 to 2017, include rape, assault, trafficking and offenses relating to “indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.” The brothers are already charged with rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other accusers in the U.K. between 2012 and 2015. The brothers moved to Romania in 2016 and were arrested there in 2022, accused of participating in schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation. They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case hasn’t gone forward because of legal and procedural problems. Andrew Tate, 39, became known a decade ago when he was a contestant on the U.K. reality television show “Big Brother.” He was booted from the show when a video appeared to show him assaulting a woman. He has amassed over 10 million followers on X but has been banned from other platforms, including YouTube, TikTok and Instagram, for violating hate speech guidelines. He has made widely condemned comments, such as saying women who are sexually assaulted should bear some responsibility for the attacks and sharing graphic descriptions of how he might attack women.

Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters View image in fullscreen A spokesperson for Zuckerberg said the ‘assist was already under way’ by the time the yacht crew reviewed the radio request. Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters Alaska Zuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boat Small cruise ship rescued skiff in south-east Alaska even though Meta billionaire’s $300m megayacht was closer Eric Berger Sun 9 Aug 2026 15.06 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 20.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Mark Zuckerberg has faced questions over why a small cruise ship in south-east Alaska rescued a stranded skiff and its crew when his 387ft superyacht had been closer. The Silicon Valley billionaire’s yacht, worth a reported $300m, is said to have “repeatedly” declined to assist when a nearby boat called for help last week. Zuckerberg, CEO of Facebook and Instagram owner Meta Platforms, was not on board at the time, a spokesperson told Forbes . When a nearby 21ft skiff ran out of fuel between Petersburg and Juneau, the Alaska Beacon reported operators of a cruise ship that was further away than Zuckerberg’s yacht came to the rescue. “I’m on a small-ship Alaska cruise with my son,” a passenger on the UnCruise Adventures ship Wilderness Legacy posted on Bluesky . “Our boat rescued a stranded vessel last night and apparently we did that after the Coast Guard radioed Mark Zuckerberg’s yacht – which was closer – and they repeatedly refused to respond. (There was near unanimous booing when the captain announced this).” But Brian Baker, a spokesperson for Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, told Forbes that the couple were not on board his yacht, named Launchpad. The yacht crew had been operating on a different radio channel, Baker told Forbes. “The assist was already under way” by the time they reviewed the broadcast, he said. Even if he was not on his ship, the report is unlikely to boost public opinion of Zuckerberg, who has faced criticism over the societal impact of his social media platforms; his new warm relationship with Donald Trump; and his lavish , insular lifestyle . “I live in Juneau and I’ve been having to look at that excessive eyesore parked up in [Auke Bay] for too long now,” a Reddit user wrote of the yacht in response to the rescue story. “Fuck Zuckerberg.” Explore more on these topics Alaska Mark Zuckerberg Meta news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.dw.com/en/alleged-irish-crim.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IWrf Kinahan was extradited to Ireland from the UAE Image: Mark Marlow/PA Images/picture alliance Advertisement Suspected international crime boss Daniel Kinahan landed in Ireland on Sunday after being extradited from the United Arab Emirates . Following his arrival in Ireland, prosecutors charged Kinahan with directing a criminal organization during a special court sitting. Kinahan, 49, was arrested in April in Dubai after Ireland issued a warrant for "alleged serious organized crime offenses." He is accused of being the leader of a cartel linked to drug smuggling and money laundering. Irish authorities deployed an enhanced security convoy to escort the supsected crime ringleader to court Image: Brian Lawless/PA Images/picture alliance What do we know about the allegations against Kinahan? The group is thought to be the most powerful criminal organization in Ireland, with Irish police estimating its wealth at more than €1 billion ($1.15 billion). The alleged crime boss had lived openly in the UAE for about a decade before his arrest. He moved there from Spain around 2016 after the murder of one of his associates and an attempt on his life. In 2022, the United States imposed sanctions on Kinahan after linking his organization to some of the world's most notorious crime networks and offered a reward of up to $5 million for information leading to his arrest. The group is linked to a brutal feud with a smaller Irish syndicate that has resulted in 18 murders. “Since February 2016, the (Kinahan Organized Crime Group) has been involved in a gang war with another group in Ireland and Spain, resulting in numerous murders, including of two innocent bystanders,” the US Treasury Department said. Kinahan is the second alleged senior member of the cartel to be extradited to Ireland from Dubai. Sean McGovern was extradited in 2024 and was ultimately sentenced to 24 years in prison after pleading guilty to directing organized crime and attempted murder. Irish media reported that a special security convoy would be deployed to escort Kinahan to the Special Criminal Court, which handles offenses related to terrorism and organized crime. UAE, Ireland hail judicial cooperation in Kinahan extradition In a joint statement, the justice minister of the UAE and Ireland called Kinahan "one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organized crime." Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan called the extradition a "landmark of judicial cooperation with Dubai," adding that it "sends a clear message that suspected perpetrators of serious and organized crime will find no safe haven from justice." Meanwhile, Foreign Minister Helen McEntee hailed the outcome as "the culmination of years of determined work" by Irish authorities under various governments.
