Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen Protesters gather to support the Joint Awami Action Committee in Kotli, Kashmir on 30 July. Photograph: Reuters Kashmir British national shot dead in Kashmir by Pakistani security forces Mohammad Akhtar, 50, from Peterborough killed during clashes between authorities and protesters Shivam Patel Mon 10 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A British national was shot dead in Pakistan-administered Kashmir during clashes between security forces and protesters, the Guardian can reveal. Another Briton has been held in a regional prison for more than two months despite his family’s efforts to secure his release through the Foreign Office. The details, which have not been previously reported, shed light on how Britons with familial ties to the region have been affected by the clashes, which have killed dozens in the Himalayan territory and posed the biggest challenge for Pakistani authorities in recent years. Mohammad Akhtar, 50, a resident of Peterborough, was killed on 9 June after his family said Pakistani security forces opened fire on a gathering where protesters were demanding economic and electoral reforms in the disputed region that is also claimed by India. View image in fullscreen Mohammad Akhtar, from Peterborough, was killed in Kashmir. Photograph: Supplied Akhtar was staying in the city of Kotli, close to the area where the clashes occurred, and his family said he was hit by a stray bullet. “He wasn’t taking part in protests but the demonstrations were happening close to his house,” said Mohammad Saad, Akhtar’s cousin. “There was firing by the forces that day and he was hit by a stray bullet. There was a bullet wound on the side of his chest,” said Saad, adding that Akhtar’s children decided not to pursue the matter with British authorities. They could not get a police complaint registered in Kashmir and feared that the family could be targeted if the case was highlighted, said Saad. The Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) said: “The UK is deeply concerned by the situation in parts of Pakistan-administered Kashmir. “FCDO ministers and the UK high commissioner in Islamabad are in touch with their counterparts, and UK travel advice was updated on 7 August and continues to advise against all but essential travel to affected areas.” It is understood that MP Hamish Falconer, during his previous role as a Foreign Office minister, raised the situation in Kashmir in talks with his counterparts during a 16-17 June visit to Islamabad. Stephen Doughty, who currently holds the role in the Foreign Office, has also been in touch with his counterparts. Pakistan’s foreign ministry and its high commission in London did not respond to the Guardian’s requests for comment. Islamabad has been accused of launching a violent crackdown on supporters of the Joint Awami Action Committee (JAAC) , a civil society group that launched protests in Kashmir months ahead of a three-phase vote in the region that began on 27 July and which have been repeatedly disrupted by the unrest. Pakistan declared the JAAC a terrorist organisation and has imposed a communications blackout in the region since 5 June. Its security forces have been accused of fatally shooting at least 30 people during demonstrations last month – charges the government has rejected. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Preview latest after newsletter promotion The JAAC said Pakistani authorities were trying to suppress dissent and have detained scores of its supporters, who it said were ordinary Kashmiris. It has described the current elections as a “sham”, being held “at gunpoint”. Pakistan accused of fatally shooting 30 unarmed protesters in Kashmir Read more Waqas Arif, 38, a British national from Nottingham, was among those detained in the Kashmiri city of Mirpur after protests on 5 June, but his family said he did not take part in the demonstrations. His sister Sumera said: “Waqas was not involved in any kind of protests. But since my other two brothers were involved and they went for the protests with everybody else, the Pakistani forces along with the Rangers came into my house and they took my brothers away. “There is no charge. He hasn’t done anything. This is my brother, but I think there are thousands of other brothers like him from everywhere who they have put in [prison] so they can minimise the protest power … they have not even been taken to court,” she said. Arif’s wife, Varisha Kampulvi, said British authorities had not been able to make direct contact with him since he was taken to the prison in Mirpur. Kampulvi has highlighted Arif’s case to British authorities. A Foreign Office email sent to her on 26 June said: “Consular staff have been able to make contact with officials at the prison where Waqas is currently being held, although we have not had direct contact with Waqas. “The authorities have confirmed that Waqas is in good health, which we were extremely pleased to hear.” Explore more on these topics Kashmir Pakistan South and central Asia Foreign policy news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Joyce Thomas, 78, is now taking the case to a higher court. Photograph: Helena Karlsson/NWT View image in fullscreen Joyce Thomas, 78, is now taking the case to a higher court. Photograph: Helena Karlsson/NWT Sweden British widow, 78, told to leave Sweden under Brexit rules after living there for 21 years Authorities say application to stay was made too late, as UK officials say Sweden takes ‘stricter approach’ than other EU countries Lisa O’Carroll Mon 10 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 00.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 78-year-old British widow who has lived in Sweden for 21 years is fighting deportation from the country after authorities told her a post-Brexit application to stay had been submitted too late. Her case is the latest of 2,500 British people ordered to leave the country after Brexit in what campaigners and the UK’s Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office (FCDO) have said is an inexplicably hardline approach taken by the Swedish authorities. It comes two years after Sweden threatened to deport a British woman with dementia in a care home shortly before she died. Joyce Thomas, a retired nurse, was given just four weeks to leave Sweden in November, three years after her husband had died, causing huge distress. After being widowed, Thomas downsized with her dog to an apartment in Hammarö, which is close to her son and grandchildren, and to her husband’s grave. She said she sometimes felt overwhelmed by the distress of what was happening. “It is unbelievable at my age to be chucked out after being in a country for so long, when you’ve done absolutely nothing wrong,” Thomas said. “I have no criminal record, no driving penalties, nothing. And I have lived here on my own financial means. I just think nobody has actually looked into this thing. I mean, if it was their family or mother, they wouldn’t like them to be in this situation.” Holding back tears, she said: “I am not young, and the idea I would have to come back and forth to visit my son and grandchildren and to visit my husband’s grave here … it is just horrible when you sit and digest it all.” View image in fullscreen Joyce Thomas and her late husband, Gwynne. Photograph: Joyce Thomas Her husband, Gwynne, died in 2023 of cancer. It was on a trip back from the UK in 2022, when they visited their second son in Brighton, that they first learned they should have made a formal application to stay in Sweden after Brexit. She said her husband had been meticulous at keeping up with news relevant to British people in Sweden and had taken responsibility for all the administration in their household. She was sure he would have made the Brexit application had he known about it. While late applications are permissible under the UK’s withdrawal agreement with the EU, Thomas’s submission was rejected in 2024 as she could not demonstrate “reasonable grounds” for applying late. A subsequent application to stay under national immigration laws was also rejected. With the help of lawyers who are working pro bono, she is now taking the case to a higher court. “When Gwynne died it was the worst thing. We were married for 55 years; he was my best friend and meant everything to me after all those years. But, you know, it [his death] was an end. This is just unbearable limbo. It is horrible. I am not young. I have already moved from a house to a flat – and to start moving again and looking for another place? I will be dead by the time I would be settled.” The former business secretary Peter Kyle, who is MP for Brighton, said the case was “deeply concerning”. View image in fullscreen Sweden also tried to deport Kathleen Poole, seen here in a dementia care home with her son Wayne and daughter-in-law Angelica. Photograph: Angelica Poole He told the Guardian: “While immigration decisions in Sweden are a matter for the Swedish authorities, I have consistently believed that the rights of UK nationals who exercised free movement rights before Brexit should be treated fairly and with compassion.” He urged Sweden to review her case. “I hope the authorities will carefully consider all the circumstances of Mrs Thomas’s case, including her long residence in Sweden, her family connections, and the humanitarian factors involved.” The FCDO has also expressed concern, not just about Thomas but about the wider hardline approach taken by Sweden to British people living in the country since before Brexit. Data shows that Sweden has the highest number of Brexit-related deportations of Britons of all EU member states. According to Eurostat data, 2,500 British nationals have been ordered to leave the country since Brexit, one-third of the entire number of removal orders issued across the 27-member bloc since Brexit in 2021. An FCDO spokesperson said: “We regularly raise concerns regarding Sweden’s protection of citizens’ rights with both the Swedish authorities and the European Commission, which is responsible for monitoring the implementation and application of citizens’ rights matters in EU member states.” Article 18 of the EU-UK withdrawal agreement allows for late applications on “reasonable grounds”. But UK government sources said they believed Sweden was “taking a considerably stricter approach” than others. The result is that “in practice individuals are not likely to have their reasonable grounds accepted”. According to the most recent European Commission annual report on implementation of the WA, almost 4,000 applicants for post-Brexit residency status in Sweden were refused, out of 14,200 made. By contrast, Bulgaria, which has a similar number of applicants at around 16,000, refused just five people, and Belgium, which had 13,000 applicants, refused 605, according to the same report. According to FCDO analysis, Sweden’s refusal rate of 27.5% is three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3% and 4%. View image in fullscreen Joyce Thomas, 78, in her garden in August, She is facing removal from Sweden over hardline Brexit policy. Photograph: Copyright: Felix Andler/TheGuardian A spokesperson for the Swedish immigration authority, Migrationsverket, said: “In exceptional circumstances, it is still possible to submit a late application. The applicant must explain in writing why they were unable to apply within the prescribed period. Simply stating that the person was unaware of the requirement to apply is not, in itself, considered a sufficient explanation.” Explore more on these topics Sweden Brexit Migration European Union Europe Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator, with returned casualties in wheelchairs after he sent them to fight Ukrainian troops in Russia’s Kursk region. Photograph: KCNA via KNS/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Kim Jong-un, the North Korean dictator, with returned casualties in wheelchairs after he sent them to fight Ukrainian troops in Russia’s Kursk region. Photograph: KCNA via KNS/AFP/Getty Images Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: North Korea sending 50,000 troops to Russia – Zelenskyy Kim Jong-un’s regime has already provided thousands of soldiers, as well as missiles and artillery; Turkey readies arms package for Ukraine. What we know on day 1,629 Warren Murray and agencies Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.18 EDT Last modified on Sun 9 Aug 2026 21.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers will be deployed in Russia , Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said, while calling on South Korea to provide support for Ukraine’s air defence. It is an increase from the estimated 30,000 announced by the Ukrainian president in July. Kyiv had found some North Korean missiles in Ukraine’s territory, he said. “It is absolutely clear that ⁠North Korea will continue to build its experience in modern warfare, receive licences from Russia, and receive all ​kinds of military tools from them.” This month, an official at Ukraine’s military intelligence told Reuters that a North Korean missile unit has begun deploying personnel and equipment to western Russia and the unit could be equipped with 120 ballistic ⁠missiles and six launchers for strikes against Ukraine. North Korea sent an estimated 14,000 soldiers to Russia’s Kursk region in 2024, helping Moscow fight an invasion by Ukrainian forces. Thousands have been wounded or killed . North Korea has supplied ​Russia with millions ‌of artillery and mortar rounds – sometimes of dangerously low quality, according to Russian milbloggers and troops – ​as well as ballistic missiles, long-range ​artillery and multiple-launch rocket systems, according to Ukrainian and independent assessments. Zelenskyy continued that Ukraine “would very much like to receive support from South Korea in ‌an area where we have a shortage”, referring to air defence systems . “We are ready to work on the drone deal and other areas as well,” he said, adding that Ukrainian diplomats “are in contact” with Seoul to push potential deals. Ukraine is very short of high-end ​air defences and Russia has ​tried to exploit this by using ​more ballistic missiles, which are very hard to shoot down without interceptors like the US-owned Patriot. Seventy Atacms short-range ballistic missiles are part of a weapons package that Ukraine is poised to buy from Turkey , according to US congressional documents (pdf) . The US would have to approve the resale of the American-origin weapons. The state department indicated to Congress it is prepared to give permission. Along with the M39 Atacms missiles, Turkey also plans to sell Kyiv 47,000 artillery rounds, 12 M270 multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS) and more than 2,000 cluster bombs, according to the notice from the US state department. Russian missiles struck a high-rise apartment block in the Saltivskyi district of Kharkiv, killing two people and injuring 13 , said regional head Oleh Syniehubov. Zelenskyy said eight people were wounded in Odesa, where strikes damaged the power grid, the port and residential buildings. He condemned an “absolutely brutal” strike targeting energy infrastructure near a shopping centre in Pavlohrad, Dnipropetrovsk region , that wounded nine people including four children. Russia said Ukrainian drones killed five people and injured two dozen others in the Belgorod region. Zelenskyy, in his evening address on Sunday, defended Ukraine’s replies to Russia’s attacks – including strikes on Russian oil refineries, air defence systems and radar stations – as “truly just responses”. “The Russian war will be increasingly felt at home, in Russia,” he said. The World Health Organization chief, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said a WHO warehouse stocking medical supplies in the Ukrainian city of Dnipro was destroyed in strikes on Friday. “I cannot say loudly enough: attacks on health care must stop. Otherwise, people are deprived of lifesaving healthcare,” Tedros posted. “Even wars have rules. One of those is that health must be protected!” Ukrainian drone strikes damaged commercial sites and a home in the Russian city of Novorossiysk, said the mayor, Andrey Kravchenko. A major fuel terminal is located at Novorossiysk that links Kazakhstan’s oilfields to markets around the world. It has previously been a target for Ukrainian strikes. Bulgaria summoned Ukraine’s ambassador after a drone entered Bulgarian airspace , the country’s public broadcaster BNT reported on Sunday. The drone exploded on Saturday close to an international gas pipeline shortly after crossing the border from Romania, the Bulgarians said. No casualties or damage were reported. Bulgaria’s defence ministry said the incident was likely accidental and involved a drone that appeared to be a Ukrainian type. Kyiv’s foreign ministry said Ukraine did not deliberately target Bulgaria and the two sides were in “close contact” about it. A “powerful explosion” believed to be from a combat drone was reported in the village of Crocmaz, in south-east Moldova near the border with Ukraine, local police said on Sunday. No one was injured by the impact, which caused a vegetation fire in the Stefan Voda district, police said, adding that “fragments of a combat drone were found at the scene” and would be examined by specialists. Police did not specify the origin of the drone. The UK defence secretary, Wes Streeting, has urged allies to boost Ukraine’s air defences ahead of a winter that Vladimir Putin will seek to use as a “weapon” against Kyiv. Writing in the Sunday Times, Streeting warned that while Putin was currently losing the war, “Ukrainians know what winter brings, and how it can change the picture”. Allies’ efforts to assist Ukraine “must include greater resources for air defence”. “My task – alongside my German counterpart Boris Pistorius, with whom I co-chair the Ukraine defence contact group – is to turn the goodwill of some 50 nations into concrete help.” Pope Leo on Sunday said innocent people were being ⁠killed and wounded in Ukraine and Russia, and called for an end to ⁠the conflict. “Tragic incidents ⁠are ​multiplying, causing an ever-growing number of civilian victims, including children,” the pontiff said before worshippers ⁠gathered for Sunday’s Angelus prayer. “I renew my heartfelt appeal for international humanitarian law to be ⁠respected and for attacks against civilian targets to cease on ​both sides.” More than ‌16,000 civilians have been killed, according to the UN, the overwhelming majority of them Ukrainian . https://www.dw.com/en/china-typhoon-dolp.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IXFo Typhoon Dolphin has hit Shanghai on Monday, causing significant disruptions Image: Go Nakamura/REUTERS Advertisement Heavy rainfall and strong winds prompted flood alerts and more than 1,000 flight cancellations across China on Monday, even as Typhoon Dolphin weakened. China's National Meteorological Centre (NMC) issued its least severe typhoon alert on Monday morning as the storm lost power after making landfall in China's Zhejiang Province on Sunday. Despite the weaker storm, the NMC warned that parts of east and central China will continue to receive heavy rainfall. Authorities issued their most severe flash flood alert for parts of eastern and southern Zhejiang on Monday, state news broadcaster CCTV reported. China's Zhejiang province has faced the worst of Typhoon Dolphin so far Image: AFP Five districts in Beijing are also under red alerts for heavy rainfall on Monday, with risks of landslides and flooding. The storm had already forced over 300,000 people in eastern China to preemptively relocate, while bringing heavy rainfall to northern Taiwan over the weekend. In Shanghai, authorities evacuated more than 30,000 people out of high-risk areas. Overall, some one million people have been told to seek shelter. Social media images showed high speed winds and overturned trucks in Zhejiang on Sunday, where the typhoon made landfall Image: Social Media/REUTERS Typhoon Dolphin disrupts transport in Shanghai Shanghai's two main passenger airports, Pudong International Airport and Hongqiao International Airport, canceled 943 flights between them for Monday, the airport authority said in a post online. That's a reduction of capacity by nearly 40%. On Sunday, the two airports had cancelled nearly 1,500 flights, or about 60% of their scheduled travel, according to state media. The typhoon has lost some of its strength but China's weather agency still expects days of heavy rainfall Image: cnsphoto/REUTERS Public transport services in the city were also impacted, with several local trains suspended. At the same time, Zhejiang province began to resume its transport facilities. Zhejiang's Ningbo International Airport will resume flights midday on Monday but warned that some of the scheduled travel may still be delayed or canceled as the storm had "not yet completely dissipated." China is dealing with Typhoon Dolphin just two weeks after Typhoon Noul struck its southern Guangdong province. Last month, Typhoon Maysak killed 11 people and injured over 300 in the central Hubei province. Extreme weather systems are a common feature in China this time of the year, with typhoons leaving significant displacement , infrastructural damage and loss of lives. Scientists warn that the intensity and frequency of such extreme weather have increased and will continue to rise amid climate change. https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-r.text: WARSAW — A bad-tempered split in Poland’s right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party is being greeted with joy by the centrist, pro-EU government of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, but it’s unclear whether it will improve his odds of retaining power in next year’s election. Tusk’s Civic Coalition is far ahead in POLITICO’s Poll of Polls — with 32 percent support, compared with PiS’s 21 percent — but that does not offer a full picture of the electoral dynamics. All of the parties on the right together could still command a majority — but only if they’re able to cobble together a coalition after next year’s vote. Three of Tusk’s four junior coalition partners may fail to clear the 5 percent threshold needed to enter parliament. Renata Mieńkowska-Norkiene, a political scientist at the University of Warsaw, called Tusk’s chances in the 2027 race “far from certain.” Advertisement Advertisement However, the departure of former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki from PiS complicates the balance of balance of power on the right. PiS, which ruled from 2015 to 2023, formally ruptured last month , when Morawiecki stormed out, taking 40 MPs with him to form the new Development Plus party, leaving PiS with 147 deputies. The split between him and party founder and leader Jarosław Kaczyński quickly became acrimonious. Morawiecki criticized his own government’s decisions on Covid-19 restrictions and its push to tighten Poland’s abortion law, which outraged many women and saw PiS take a long-term hit in public support. “Although I oppose abortion, I believed the change would lead to catastrophe — a polling collapse. Unfortunately, I was right,” Morawiecki said on the popular YouTube show Rymanowski Live this week. He is now trying to set up a more moderate center-right party focused on economic growth which is less partisan than PiS. “Today, Poland does not need to get bogged down in ideological disputes,” he said in Monday’s interview. However, he has ruled out ever working with Tusk in the future. Advertisement Advertisement Kaczyński responded by appearing to question both Morawiecki’s loyalty and his state of mind. “Mateusz Morawiecki’s latest statements show clearly that his enemy is not Tusk, but me and Law and Justice. I have the impression that the prime minister is in some peculiar state. God willing, I am wrong,” Kaczyński said in a post on X. He twisted the knife in another post on Friday , denouncing “attacks based on lies, manipulation, and insinuations,” made by “people who, until recently, pretended they wanted to be part of PiS but decided to break away.” Mateusz Morawiecki is pictured in Brussels in March 2023. | Pool photo by Olivier Matthys via AFP/Getty Images Tusk is watching the fallout with joy. “I watch what is happening with a smile,” Tusk said at a press conference last week when asked about the turmoil within the largest opposition party. Unclear political picture Although PiS and Civic Coalition have been alternating in power for more than two decades, Poland’s current political makeup is a lot more complicated. Advertisement Advertisement Two new parties are battling for votes on the far-right — the libertarian Confederation, with 14 percent support, and the antisemitic extremist Confederation of the Polish Crown, at 11 percent. The two far-right parties are fighting each other, and also taking aim at PiS. “I feel the next prime minister should not be from PiS,” Krzysztof Bosak, one of the leaders of Confederation, said in a radio interview this week. Wojciech Machulski, a party spokesperson, denounced Morawiecki as a “puppet” with a terrible governing record but also noted : “Kaczyński is no longer the leader of the right; he no longer dominates the right.” Political analysts warned that Tusk should not assume the split will benefit his coalition. The Kaczyński and Morawiecki parties could appeal to a broader range of voters by campaigning separately, while Tusk’s prospects depend heavily on the survival of the weakest members of his coalition, said Mieńkowska-Norkiene. Advertisement Advertisement “What is more, Morawiecki could attract more conservative voters from those parties,” she added. Morawiecki is already campaigning in an effort to reach beyond PiS’s traditional right-wing electorate — this week laying out a new strategy to combat Poland’s low birth rate. “A right-wing party without a clear identity-based agenda will not be a right-wing party. But a right-wing party without a development agenda and without the ability to implement change will never come to power,” he said in his party manifesto . Anna Siewierska-Chmaj, a political scientist at the University of Rzeszów, said Tusk’s governing coalition should not rely on its enemies devouring themselves and should instead use the summer break to overhaul its political messaging. Many voters are fed up with the government’s lackluster results — although part of that stems from PiS-aligned President Karol Nawrocki blocking a lot of legislation. “The old polarization strategy of ‘us versus PiS’ will no longer suffice,” she said.

https://www.politico.eu/article/roberto-.text: PISA, Italy — Giorgia Meloni doesn’t want to be beaten at her own game. With an election approaching next year and a new far-right rival emerging , the Italian prime minister — whose political origins lie in Italy’s post-fascist right — is putting aside the moderate image she has built over her four years in office and hardening her tone on migration and security. Meloni’s government was the first in the EU to attack the Spanish government over a sudden influx of migrants from Morocco into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta last week. Advertisement Advertisement While France and other countries tightened border checks, Italy went further and announced it had suspended the EU’s free-movement Schengen agreement with Madrid. Now, in Italian airports, passengers from Spain are asked to join a different line. Meloni’s office has made clear it has no intention of lifting the controls until at least Aug. 15, escalating the clash with Spain, which retaliated by imposing checks on travelers from Italy. “We will not back down one millimeter on illegal immigration,” Meloni posted on X while her allies attacked the socialist Spanish government, accusing it of failing to manage migration flows. “Defending our borders, stopping human traffickers, and ensuring effective repatriation will continue to be this government’s policy,” she added. The clash with Spain is just the latest sign that the Italian leader is doing all she can to secure her core, hard-right electorate in the face of a challenge from the right by Roberto Vannacci , a former general and member of the European Parliament. With an election expected as early as next spring, Vannacci’s far-right National Future party has been advancing in the polls, overtaking one of Meloni’s coalition partners, the far-right League party, and gaining on another, Forza Italia, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls . For Meloni, who began her political career in the youth wing of Italy’s post-fascist movement, the challenge strikes particularly close to home. Advertisement Advertisement “There is no doubt that there is concern about containing the competition from National Future,” said Marco Tarchi, a leading right-wing political scientist. “It all boils down to a sharpening of tone. The issues — security, immigration, identity — remain the same as before.” During the electoral campaign that brought her to power in 2022, Meloni promised to crack down on illegal migration by putting in place a naval blockade off Italy’s coast. Though that project never ultimately happened, Meloni’s government did open detention hubs in Albania to house migrants while their asylum applications are processed. Vannacci, who is campaigning on security and a hard line on immigration, is calling for a more radical solution : “remigration” — a yet-to-be-detailed plan to encourage migrants to return to their countries of origin. The crisis in Ceuta, during which tens of thousands of migrants crossed from Morocco into the Spanish exclave and nearly 100 died , provided Meloni with an opportunity to show that fighting irregular migration remains an absolute priority for her government. Roberto Vannacci sings the national anthem during a rally in Genoa, Italy on July 11, 2026. | Emanuela Zampa/Getty Images Meloni’s reaction was “purely the result of domestic political calculations,” said Giorgio Gori, a member of the European Parliament from the left-wing Democratic Party. The Italian prime minister is trying to secure her electorate “by showing that she is loyal to the right-wing slogan and propaganda on migration and beyond.” For Giovanni Orsina, director of the political science department at Rome’s Luiss Guido Carli University, Meloni’s priority at this stage is “that the Brothers of Italy [Meloni’s party] doesn’t start losing votes too” — in preparation for a potential alliance with Vannacci before or after next year’s election. Advertisement Advertisement “Vannacci has been growing a lot in polls, especially over the past two months,” said Lorenzo Pregliasco from the YouTrend polling firm, noting that National Future is polling at over 7 percent . “Without Vannacci, the center-right could lose the upcoming election,” he said. “These seven points matter a lot.” The Vannacci effect Nicola Procaccini, Meloni’s lieutenant and co-chair of the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) group, denies that Meloni is shifting on policy to protect herself from Vannacci. “She stands where she has always stood,” he told POLITICO. “She simply isn’t the racist, xenophobic fascist she was made out to be when she first took office. And she isn’t one now, either.” Meloni is also facing a challenge to her support for Ukraine, with both the League and Vannacci advocating a softer line on Moscow, opposing military aid to Kyiv and arguing against an increase in defense spending. Though Meloni has portrayed herself as a strong backer of Ukraine, her reliance on the League for support has meant Italy has contributed just €3 billion in four years, roughly the equivalent of €1 a month for every Italian citizen, less than the cost of an espresso. Advertisement Advertisement Italy has also declined to join NATO’s PURL (Prioritized Ukraine Requirements List), an arms-buying scheme set up last summer after U.S. President Donald Trump ended new military aid commitments to Kyiv. Ukraine is where Meloni’s real difference with Vannacci lies, argued Tarchi, who teaches at the University of Florence and is considered the key figure of a movement called the New Right . “Otherwise, the gap is artificially exaggerated in rhetoric and posturing for tactical reasons,” he said. Meloni’s allies haven’t ruled out an alliance with Vannacci but they stress that the possibility will depend on where he stands on key values such as foreign policy. If he seeks “to position Italy, alongside Russia, China, Iran, and North Korea, clearly, it is not possible to stand together,” said Procaccini. “If, instead, he chooses the West — the democracies, Western nations, Western liberal democracies — then we can certainly stand together.”

https://telex.hu/english/2026/08/10/orba.text: Menü Kereső Orbán government's state secretary for water management contradicts Orbán's previous statement English Aradi Hanga Zsófia Andrea Horváth Kávai (translation) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom “In terms of the water generated here, we are by no means a water superpower; in fact, we are one of the poorest countries. Actually, while water flows into the country at three different points, it flows out in countless places,” said Zsolt V. Németh, a Fidesz-delegated member of parliament and the previous government’s state secretary for water management, in an interview with 24.hu . His statement sharply contradicts a previous claim made by Viktor Orbán. In 2023, speaking in Parliament in defense of his government’s plan to build several battery factories—which consume large amounts of water—in Hungary, the former prime minister said that Hungary does not suffer from water shortages, so the operation of these factories would not pose a problem. "There is more water leaving Hungary than entering it. This means we have a surplus, which we are able to use. If we want to, and if necessary, we can transport that water anywhere via the country’s canal system. If needed. Hungary does not suffer from any water shortage today, and if demand increases, we will be able to meet that demand,” he said. The former Prime Minister’s remarks, along with a statement made by former Minister of Construction and Transport János Lázár last December, have returned to the spotlight during the recent heatwave. Last December, while still serving as minister, during his committee hearing in Parliament, Lázár admitted that “the government made a mistake by not building large reservoirs ten years ago,” and instead only constructed reservoirs for aiding flood control, which are not suitable for water retention. Lázár said that “it is madness to let the fresh water flow out,” adding that “there are geographical and natural phenomena which give us cause for grave concern.” In response to the heat wave of the past few weeks, the low water level of the Danube, and the resulting energy crisis, Fidesz has accused the Tisza government of acting hastily, being unprepared, and being incompetent. János Bóka, the Fidesz faction leader, for example, said that “it has been obvious for weeks” where the Danube’s water levels were headed and that “the current situation would occur,” yet the government failed to prepare for it. According to Bóka, the fact that the power grid is still functioning at all is a result of the achievements of the past 16 years, and in terms of water retention and energy security, Viktor Orbán handed over the country in better condition than he found it in 2010. 24.hu also reached out to Zsolt V. Németh, the former State Secretary for Water Management at the Ministry of Energy on the subject. When asked whether more could have been done on water conservation, V. Németh said: “There’s always more that can be done, but instead of 300 billion forints (€828 million), doing so would require a budget closer to a thousand billion forints (€2.75 billion).” According to the former state secretary, they had approximately 330–340 billion forints available for water management, of which roughly 280 billion went toward water retention and increasing the country’s water reserves. V. Németh also noted that last year, Hungary received as much rainfall “as Israel and Botswana, and barely more than Morocco,” and said that “we are one of the poorest countries” in terms of locally generated water resources. According to V. Németh, one of the major problems is that areas where water could naturally accumulate are now occupied by cities and private land. Although under the previous administration's “Water for the Land!” program, farmers were able to offer their floodable land for this purpose, “if we want to build reservoirs the same way we have been doing, and if we're going to compensate those whose land we flood, then all the money in the world wouldn't be enough to pay for it.” V. Németh listed several necessary measures which had not been implemented—or had only been implemented partially—in recent years, and welcomed the fact that under the new government, water management had become more coordinated within the Ministry for the Living Environment, led by László Gajdos. The publication also contacted former Minister of Agriculture István Nagy, who responded to their questions by simply listing the achievements of the previous government, as well as the Kék Bolygó Foundation—founded by former President of Hungary János Áder, and heavily subsidized with public funds—which listed the various conferences on climate change and the film festivals about nature conservation it had supported. János Lázár did not respond to 24.hu’s inquiry. For more quick, accurate and impartial news from and about Hungary, subscribe to the Telex English newsletter! Beállítom Újabb részletek derültek ki arról, hogyan szervezték meg Szijjártó Péter külügyminiszteri időszakában a Külügyminisztérium sajtótájékoztatóit, írja a 444 . A cikk szerint a minisztérium munkatársait rendszeresen arra utasították, hogy jelenjenek meg a rendezvényeken, és töltsék fel az 50-60 férőhelyes konferenciatermet, miközben a független sajtó képviselőit jellemzően meg sem hívták. A 444-nek több korábbi és jelenlegi külügyes beszélt arról, hogyan működött a rendszer. A Miniszteri Kabinet előre jelezte a szervezeti egységek vezetőinek, hogy egy-egy Szijjártó-féle közös sajtótájékoztatóra hány munkatársat várnak, a vezetőknek pedig azt is előre meg kellett adniuk, kik vesznek majd részt. A munkatársaknak már fél órával a kezdés előtt el kellett foglalniuk a helyüket, és a beszámolók szerint addig nem állhattak fel, amíg Szijjártó el nem hagyta a termet. Hogy ki megy, azt több helyen önkéntes alapon próbálták megoldani, de ha nem volt elég jelentkező, kijelölték a résztvevőket. Volt olyan szervezeti egység, ahol rotációban küldték a munkatársakat, így egyeseknek körülbelül kéthetente jutott egy Szijjártó-sajtótájékoztató. A résztvevőknek nem feltétlenül volt közük a sajtótájékoztató témájához. Egy külügyes szerint a munkatársakat elsősorban az alapján osztották be, hogy kinek engedte meg az aznapi munkaterhelése, hogy részt vegyen az eseményen. A szervezés ráadásul időnként túlbiztosított volt, és előfordult, hogy más épületekből munkaidőben, rossz időben is a Bem téri főépületbe küldték a munkatársakat, majd mire odaértek, közölték velük, hogy megtelt a terem, ezért visszamehetnek dolgozni. A 444 szerint minderre azért volt szükség, mert a meghívott sajtó és a külföldi vendégek kísérete önmagában nem töltötte volna meg a termet. A független szerkesztőségeket viszont nem hívták meg, nehogy Szijjártó kellemetlen kérdéseket kapjon. Egy külügyes arról is beszámolt, hogy előfordult, hogy mindössze egy újságíró vett részt a sajtótájékoztatón, az MTI-től. A forrás állítása szerint egyszer azt is látta, ahogy a külügy sajtófőosztályának egyik munkatársa lediktálta az MTI-s újságírónak, mit kérdezzen. A lap szerint Szijjártót ezeken az eseményeken az épületen belül egy-két TEK-es is kísérte. A terem feltöltésének ugyanakkor nem sok gyakorlati jelentősége volt a közvetítések szempontjából, hiszen az élő adásokban jellemzően Szijjártó és külföldi partnere látszott, nem a háttérben ülő munkatársak. A 444 szerint így a kivezényelt külügyesek leginkább azt a látszatot kelthették, hogy jelentős érdeklődés övezi a rendezvényt. A 444 előző héten arról írt, hogy három évnyi jogi eljárás, végrehajtás és büntetőfeljelentés után jutottak hozzá olyan dokumentumokhoz, amelyek alapján részletesebben megismerhető, hogyan viszonyult a Szijjártó vezette minisztérium a sajtószabadsághoz. Szijjártó egyébként két évvel ezelőtt Guatemalában (!!!) dicsekedett azzal, hogy Magyarország mennyire szerencsés helyzetben van, mert a hazafias kormány megvédi a hazafias médiát. Ez annyira igaz, hogy a Fidesz kormányzása alatt az adófizetők pénzéből kitömött NER-es médiacégek sorra húzzák le a rolót, és küldik el az alkalmazottaikat azok után, hogy a Fidesz elvesztette az áprilisi választást. Szijjártó egyébként korábban arról is beszélt, hogy a komplett nyugat-európai sajtó hazudik a magyar sajtószabadság helyzetéről. Szijjártó egyébként nemrég hagyta ott a Fideszt és a parlamenti munkáját, hogy annak a kínai BYD-nek kezdjen el dolgozni, amelynek a magyarországi terjeszkedését külügyminiszterként aktívan segítette. Add us as a preferred source on Google for news you can trust Verstappen equalled his best result of the F1 2026 season in Hungary by finishing second as McLaren driver and reigning world champion Lando Norris took victory. The Budapest race saw Verstappen claim consecutive podium finishes for the first time in 2026 having finished third at the previous race in Belgium. An untelevised team radio snippet from Sunday’s race has revealed how Verstappen called for his Red Bull stablemates to be penalised. The footage, which cannot be reproduced here due to broadcast rights restrictions, shows Verstappen behind Lawson and Lindblad as the pair battle for position into Turn 2. Despite a blue panel flashing trackside to signify that a faster car is approaching, Lindblad and Lawson continue to fight as Verstappen closes in. Verstappen is heard saying: “Oh, they should get a penalty. This is f**king ridiculous, these morons! My God!” Lindblad and Lawson went on to finish eighth and 10th respectively. https://www.christiandaily.com/news/war-.text: Volunteer offering help at the Romania-Ukraine border Photo by Michel E / Unsplash European Christian Mission International (ECMI) reports that 160 churches have been planted across Europe by displaced Ukrainians in the four years since Russia invaded their country. In a report, ECMI said that what began as a devastating displacement through war is becoming an unexpected movement of gospel witness across Europe. “Ukrainian believers, carrying deep pain and loss, are also carrying the hope of Christ wherever they go,” said the ECMI report. Jim Memory, Strategic Partnerships Director for ECMI and Co-Regional Director for Lausanne Europe, attended a recent Ukrainian Baptist Churches in Europe Conference in Poland and came away deeply encouraged by what God is doing through Ukrainian Christians across the continent. Memory disclosed how inspiring it was to hear story after story of faithfulness under pressure. “It was a privilege to listen to their stories, make connections, and briefly speak,” he said. Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, millions of Ukrainians have been forced to flee their homes, said the report. “Yet in the midst of grief, separation, and uncertainty, God’s light is shining brighter. Among Baptists alone, around 160 Ukrainian churches have been planted across Europe during the past four years.” The report added, “Increasingly, Ukrainian believers are refusing to see themselves only as refugees. “Instead, many are embracing a different calling - missionaries sent by God into the nations of Europe.” ECMI reflected on how the Kingdom of God advanced through tragedy in the book of Acts and compared that reality with the church planting being carried out by Ukrainians displaced by war. When persecution scattered the first Christians, the gospel spread wherever they went, said the report. What looked like tragedy became the very means by which the Kingdom of God advanced. “Ukrainian Christians are arriving in unfamiliar countries carrying trauma and heartbreak, yet many are also bringing courage, prayer, hospitality, evangelistic passion, and a deep dependence on God,” said the report. “New fellowships are forming. Churches are being planted. People are hearing about Jesus through those who themselves have suffered greatly. “Their witness is a powerful reminder that darkness does not have the final word. https://www.delfi.lt/en/politics/methodo.text: Delfi EN Delfi Politics 2026.07.27 15:03 Methodological chaos and burnout hinder inclusive education, audit shows Source: Elta EN Methodological chaos and burnout hinder inclusive education, audit shows PHOTO: Josvydas Elinskas | Elta Follow Delfi on Google More than half of Lithuanian general education schools still lack educational support specialists. Although the state and local authorities are increasing funding, implementing measures to attract specialists and encouraging people to choose these professions, the shortage of specialists persists the National Audit Office said in a statement. An audit carried out by the National Audit Office, "Educational Support in Schools", revealed that, as a result, the specialists currently working in this field face heavy workloads, and a significant proportion of their working time is spent on administrative tasks rather than providing direct support to children. "If we want inclusive education to be more than just a slogan on paper, we must urgently turn our attention to those who work with children on a daily basis. Educational support specialists and teaching assistants cannot perform their duties to a high standard when, on the one hand, they are trying to manage several complex cases of behavioural difficulties across different classes, while, on the other, they are forced to fill in endless, constantly changing reports. The audit results clearly show that reducing the administrative burden and filling vacant posts would not only improve the availability of services for pupils but would also fundamentally change the well-being of the specialists themselves, which is currently bordering on professional burnout. We must eliminate methodological chaos and provide schools with practical tools and competitive remuneration in order to attract the necessary skills," emphasises Auditor General Irena Segalovičienė. Heavy workloads – the biggest obstacle to helping children The audit figures clearly illustrate the systemic shortage of specialists. In 2025, 52% of general education schools were short of at least one educational support specialist, and each specialist was responsible for between 16 and 337 pupils, depending on the school. Although as many as 76% of the selected local authorities implement various measures to attract or retain specialists, there is still a critical shortage of them in the labour market. In 2025, employers across the country were seeking 1,157 educational support specialists, while the number of jobseekers was almost three times lower. A survey of educational support specialists carried out by the National Audit Office confirmed that excessive workloads are the single greatest obstacle preventing the provision of high-quality support to children. Due to a shortage of staff, existing specialists are forced to deal with a significantly excessive number of pupils, leaving critically insufficient time for direct, individual support. Heavy workloads for specialists affect not only the children who need support, but also the teachers. In a survey carried out during the audit, as many as 41% of the teachers surveyed stated that they did not receive sufficient support from educational support specialists, as the latter are either fully occupied at school or their posts are simply unfilled. Bureaucratic burden takes time away from children Educational support specialists themselves cite the administrative burden as one of the biggest obstacles to their work. According to the National Audit Office’s survey, as many as 69% of educational support specialists stated that administration, preparing for meetings and other indirect activities account for a moderate or significant proportion of their daily work. The specialists also highlighted this issue during the auditors’ visits to schools. According to them, educational support specialists spend a large part of their working day filling in assessment tables, preparing and refining individual education plans, writing minutes and reports, completing constantly changing assessment forms, and carrying out other administrative tasks. In the schools’ view, reducing the administrative burden would allow specialists to devote considerably more time to direct interaction with children, improve the availability of support, and reduce the emotional and professional strain on the staff themselves. The work of educational support specialists is also hampered by a lack of methodological guidance and clear working standards. In the absence of standardised assessment tools and clear methodologies, they are forced to work according to varying practices, adapt to changing requirements and devote additional time to documentation. This increases the administrative burden and reduces the time that could be devoted to the children’s needs. Teaching assistants also face heavy workloads Similar systemic problems also weigh heavily on teaching assistants. In the survey, they indicated that a single assistant is often assigned to support 3–4 pupils in different classes, or to look after as many as 6–8 children with special educational needs in a single class at the same time. This means that a single staff member is often faced with several particularly complex cases of behavioural or emotional difficulties at once. Teaching assistants emphasise that children need support not only during lessons, but also during breaks, in the canteen, after school or during extracurricular activities; however, their working hours are usually scheduled exclusively for lessons. For this reason, they are physically unable to be where help is most needed, meaning that some pupils and teachers are left without any support during lessons. The lack of clarity regarding their duties also causes additional stress – as many as 24% of the teaching assistants surveyed stated that they carry out additional tasks that are entirely outside their remit, such as standing in for teachers who are ill or absent, preparing assignments or marking pupils’ work. The teaching assistants themselves emphasise that clearer regulation of their duties and stronger support from teachers and the school administration would allow them to focus on their core mission – providing high-quality support to children in the educational process. To retain specialists, it is not enough simply to attract new ones: the National Audit Office offers its recommendations With a view to preventing staff burnout and ensuring that the support provided genuinely meets children’s needs, the National Audit Office has made specific recommendations to the Ministry of Education, Science and Sport (MESS) and its subordinate institutions. First, in order to create an effective educational environment and systematically address the problem of staff shortages, the Ministry is recommended to introduce open-class models. To this end, it is necessary to update the criteria under which a second teacher or a person providing educational support must be assigned to certain classes in primary and basic education. It is also necessary to ensure continuous monitoring of the provision of educational support so that policy decisions are made on the basis of real data. To achieve this, it is recommended that schools be required to record, in the Pupil Register, the actual extent of support provided by the recommended educational support specialists to each pupil. Finally, in order to eliminate methodological inconsistencies and ensure that specialists from all educational psychology services and schools across the country assess pupils’ needs in a uniform manner, it is recommended that the Lithuanian Centre for Inclusive Education develop and implement a uniform standard for the pedagogical and psychological assessment of children and ensure the procurement or development of the necessary assessment tools. Acțiune Facebook X WhatsApp Telegram VK Two high school graduates from the Romanian city of Bacău who achieved perfect scores in the 2026 national Baccalaureate examination will each receive a 3,000 lei cash award under a decision adopted by the Bacău City Council. The measure was approved during the City Council meeting on July 20 as part of a proposal to recognize outstanding academic performance in the June–July 2026 Baccalaureate session. The recipients are Anais Pesa-Moza , a graduate of Ferdinand I National College, and Delia-Andreea Nașcu , a graduate of Vasile Alecsandri National College. During the council debate, Liberal Party (PNL) councillor Ilie Birzu proposed increasing the award from the initially planned 1,000 lei to 2,000 lei for each graduate. A subsequent amendment submitted by a Green Party councillor raised the amount to 3,000 lei, a proposal that was approved by the council. Local authorities said the initiative is intended to recognize academic excellence and reward the exceptional achievements of the two graduates in one of Romania’s most important national examinations. The Baccalaureate exam is the nationwide school-leaving examination required for admission to higher education in Romania. https://www.delfi.lt/en/politics/foreign.text: Delfi EN Delfi Politics 2026.07.27 15:00 Foreign Ministry proposes opening embassy in Brazil in October Translated by Justina Vaišvilaitė-Braziulienė Source: Elta EN Foreign Ministry proposes opening embassy in Brazil in October PHOTO: Audrius Gavėnas | Elta Follow Delfi on Google The Foreign Ministry has drafted a new government resolution proposing the opening of a Lithuanian embassy in Brazil on 1 October, revising an earlier plan to establish the mission in July. The embassy would be located in Brasilia, Brazil’s capital. Lithuania currently operates a consulate general in Sao Paulo. The ministry said the revised draft was prepared in line with the new government’s programme, which calls for expanding the network of diplomatic missions in countries and regions of strategic importance to Lithuania. According to a letter sent by the Foreign Ministry to the Finance Ministry, establishing and operating the embassy would require EUR 2 million in 2027, EUR 1.78 million in 2028 and EUR 1.36 million in 2029. In March, Foreign Minister Kęstutis Budrys told the politika.lt podcast that Lithuania needed an embassy in Brazil to better serve business interests and boost exports to Mercosur countries. He said the mission would provide an opportunity to expand Lithuania’s export markets. Source Topics It is forbidden to copy the text of this publication without a written permission from ELTA. https://english.news.cn/europe/20260727/.text: Poland's Gdynia Modernist City Center inscribed on UNESCO World Heritage List WARSAW, July 27 (Xinhua) -- The Modernist Center of Gdynia, a Baltic port city in northern Poland, was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, Poland's Ministry of Culture and National Heritage said Monday. The decision was made at the ongoing 48th session of the UNESCO World Heritage Committee in Busan, South Korea. Developed mainly in the 1920s and 1930s, Gdynia's city center reflects the large-scale application of modernist urban planning and architecture as the former village was transformed into a major port after Poland regained independence. The ministry said the city's regular street grid, close integration with the port and the Baltic Sea, and its residential, public and villa architecture embody the functional and rational principles of modernism. The inscription comes as Gdynia marks the 100th anniversary of receiving city rights. The Modernist Center of Gdynia is Poland's 18th World Heritage site, bringing the country's total to 16 cultural and two natural properties. ■ News In-depth Sports Business Culture World China Regions Asia & Pacific Europe Middle East North America South America Africa Organizations Services Weather Live & Work in China Doing Business Investment Visit China Study in China More Special Reports Photos Video Corrections About Us Contact Us Media Qiushi Journal Taiwan.cn Youth.cn GMW.cn CE.cn Ecns.cn China Daily CRI.cn China.org.cn People's Daily

https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4545.text: More than half a million visitors came to Bratislava during the first five months of 2026, with overnight stays increasing by 17.6 percent year-on-year. Visitor numbers were also 2.4 percent higher than in the record-breaking year of 2019, putting the capital on track for its most successful tourism year yet, according to the Bratislava Tourist Board (BTB). The BTB attributed the growth to improved air connectivity. "Routes with high visitor potential, such as Berlin, Rome, London and Barcelona, are particularly important for us," said BTB Board Chair Nina Erneker. The sharpest increase came from Italy, where visitor numbers more than doubled year-on-year (+104 percent) following the launch of new air routes and were 73.3 percent higher than in 2019. The number of visitors from Norway also rose significantly after a direct flight from Oslo was introduced, increasing by 52.5 percent year-on-year and by 176.7 percent compared with 2019. Growth was also recorded in traditional source markets. The number of Polish visitors increased by 5.6 percent year-on-year and by 37.8 percent compared with 2019 following the launch of a new route from Warsaw. Visitors from Germany rose by 3.9 percent year-on-year and by 16.3 percent compared with 2019, supported by flights from Dortmund and Berlin. Source: TASR

President Peter Pellegrini left for China on Sunday evening. The three-day state visit is taking place at the invitation of Chinese head of state Xi Jinping. Their talks will focus on the further development of Slovak-Chinese relations, economic cooperation and current international issues. Discussions with Chinese officials will also cover support for high value-added investment and the development of cooperation in science and research, industry, transport, logistics, agriculture and tourism. Pellegrini will also visit major technology centres, including, for example, Baidu, which is one of the world's leading companies in the fields of artificial intelligence, cloud technologies and autonomous mobility. On Friday (24 July), Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian stated that Slovakia is an important partner for China in Europe, and under the leadership of Chinese President Xi Jinping and Slovak leaders, the two countries are maintaining strong relations and achieving fruitful results in various areas. It's the fifth visit to be paid by a Slovak head of state to China since the founding of independent Slovakia and the first in 16 years. It will conclude 29 July. Source: TASR

https://www.techtimes.com/articles/32165.text: Romania's Air Force on Sunday shot down a Russian Shahed-type drone over the Black Sea near the mouth of the Danube — the third consecutive day its F-16s have intercepted and destroyed an intruder in NATO airspace, and the clearest signal yet that Europe's eastern flank has moved from passive monitoring to active kinetic defense. Romanian President Nicușor Dan confirmed the 10:13 a.m. local time intercept over the Sulina–Chilia area, about 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) northeast of Sulina in Romanian territorial waters, and called the string of violations "inadmissible and intolerable." Romania's foreign ministry summoned Russia's ambassador, calling the breaches "repeated violations." Russia has offered no public comment on any of the three incidents. It has had 33 opportunities to do so: that is the number of times Russian drones have illegally entered Romanian airspace since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, according to Romania's Defense Ministry. Most of those were tracked and allowed to exit or crash. This past weekend was different — and the difference was not only political, but technological. Exchange rate as of July 27, 2026; conversions are approximate. Three Consecutive Days, Four Total Shootdowns Two Romanian F-16 fighter jets scrambled from the Fetești airbase, operating under NATO's command authority, and shot down Sunday's drone over the Black Sea. The first confirmed shootdown occurred Friday — Romania's first successful drone intercept inside its own airspace in the four years since the war began. A second intercept followed Saturday. In all, four Romanian drone shootdowns have occurred in coordination with NATO allies in recent weeks: three this weekend and one in May, when Romania-based F-16 pilots operating out of Lithuania shot down a drone over Estonian airspace. Romania's initial investigation confirmed Friday's drone as a Shahed-type one-way attack vehicle "used by the Russian Federation in its war of aggression against Ukraine," President Dan announced. Investigations into Saturday's and Sunday's drones were still ongoing. NATO SHAPE spokesperson Col. Martin O'Donnell corroborated that the Sunday aircraft "appears to be of Russian origin." The legal authority for these intercepts rests on enabling legislation that Romania's parliament passed and interim President Ilie Bolojan signed into law. The statute specifically authorizes Romania's military to "destroy, neutralize, or take control of" unmanned aircraft breaching Romanian airspace without permission — a provision that, for years, the government was reluctant to use despite repeated drone intrusions. Russia's Sub-Threshold Campaign: What 33 Violations Prove Thirty-three drone incursions do not happen by accident. Analysts tracking Russian airspace violations documented four NATO incursions in 2022, five in 2023, six in 2024, and then 18 in 2025 — a 200 percent single-year increase that a systematic review published by The Fulcrum in February 2026, corroborated against NATO press releases and Institute for the Study of War operational assessments, described as "a deliberate campaign rather than accidental spillover." That 200 percent jump was statistically and strategically significant — not a product of incidental navigation error, but a sustained probe of NATO's detection thresholds, response times, and political will to engage. The geography of the current incidents explains the mechanism. Russia has intensified drone strikes on Ukrainian port facilities along the Danube River delta — cities like Izmayil and Reni that sit in the narrow zone where Ukrainian infrastructure, Romanian territorial waters, and Black Sea shipping lanes converge. Shahed-type drones launched toward those targets must transit a corridor that clips Romanian airspace almost by design. Whether a given drone blows past the boundary through navigation error or deliberate route-selection, the strategic effect is the same: NATO airspace is tested repeatedly, at low cost, with plausible deniability. In late May, the consequences of that campaign became tangible. A Russian Geran-2 drone struck an apartment building in Galați, Romania, injuring two civilians — the first confirmed injuries from a Russian drone strike on NATO soil. A marine drone self-detonated near an oil terminal in the Black Sea port of Constanța in June. The pattern prompted Bucharest to accelerate both the legal framework enabling drone intercepts and the hardware to execute them. How Romania Is Actually Shooting Down the Drones: MEROPS and the F-16 Combination The headline actor in Friday's first shootdown was a Romanian F-16 — specifically, one of four jets (two Romanian F-16s and two Italian Eurofighter Typhoons deployed under NATO's air policing mission) that scrambled after Romanian radar detected the drone about 20 kilometers (12.4 miles) east of Sulina. One F-16 engaged the target with an air-to-air missile, downing the Shahed over unpopulated ground near the village of Padina, in Buzău County. Sunday's intercept, per Romanian defense reporting, involved F-16s from Fetești without Italian jets: a five-minute engagement from airspace entry to intercept. But the more strategically significant technology operating in Romania's airspace is MEROPS — an AI-guided interceptor drone system that Romania officially integrated into its national air defense architecture on June 24, 2026. Romania deployed it primarily along the Danube River corridor — exactly the zone that has experienced these repeated incidents. MEROPS was developed by Project Eagle, a U.S. defense technology startup founded and funded by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt after Russia's 2022 invasion. The company later rebranded as Perennial Autonomy and brought in former Pentagon innovation chief Will Roper alongside engineers from Apple, SpaceX, and Google. It recently received a $500 million ceiling contract from the U.S. Army's JIATF-401 counter-drone task force. The system's architecture is specifically engineered for the Shahed problem: A ground control station, mobile launch platform, and the AS3 Surveyor interceptor drone operate as a single integrated unit. The Surveyor is a roughly 3-foot (0.9-meter) fixed-wing drone that reaches speeds of up to 175 mph (282 km/h), faster than the Shahed-136's cruise speed of around 115 mph (185 km/h). Onboard AI combines thermal imaging, radio-frequency detection, and radar to autonomously locate and track targets, allowing MEROPS to function even in GPS- or radio-jammed environments where conventional air defense would degrade. Each Surveyor costs approximately $14,500 to $15,000 — versus a Patriot PAC-3 interceptor at $3.9 million to $5.3 million per shot, or even a single F-16 sortie that costs multiples of the drone it is shooting down. If an interception misses, the Surveyor deploys a parachute and can be recovered and reused. Crew requirement: four people — a commander, a pilot, and two technicians — deployable on the back of a pickup truck. The operational record behind those specifications is extensive. MEROPS entered classified service with Ukrainian forces in mid-2024. By the time Romania formally integrated the system, Perennial Autonomy's German production partner Twentyfour Industries reported the Surveyor had downed more than 4,000 Russian drones in Ukraine. U.S. Army Brig. Gen. Curtis King, commanding general of the 10th Army Air and Missile Defense Command, told reporters the system "conservatively" accounts for 40 percent of all Shahed-type drones destroyed by Ukrainian air defenses. That is not a secondary air defense contribution — it is the primary one. The Shahed-136: Why a 1970s-Propeller Drone Is NATO's Persistent Headache The weapon Romania is now shooting down is, in technical terms, a fairly simple machine. The Shahed-136 — which Russia manufactures domestically at its Alabuga Special Economic Zone in Tatarstan under the designation Geran-2 — is a delta-wing one-way attack drone measuring 3.5 meters (11.5 feet) long with a 2.5-meter (8.2-foot) wingspan and a total mass of about 200 kilograms (440 pounds), according to its specifications. Its rear-mounted Mado MD-550 piston engine drives a two-bladed pusher propeller to a maximum speed of about 115 mph (185 km/h) — barely faster than a car on a German autobahn. Its standard warhead weighs 50 kilograms (110 pounds); Russia has also fielded a 90-kilogram (200-pound) heavy warhead variant since 2024. That combination of slow speed, low altitude, and small radar cross-section makes the Shahed-136 genuinely difficult for traditional air defense radars designed to track fast-moving jets and missiles. Its guidance system pairs GNSS navigation with an inertial navigation backup, and Russia's upgraded Geran-2 versions have added GLONASS, 4G modems, Starlink terminals, and AI-based computer vision to improve accuracy and jam resistance. Debris analysis of downed drones has identified Western components throughout the airframe — Texas Instruments processors, Altera FPGAs, Analog Devices radio-frequency modules, and a Polish-built fuel pump — evidence of systematic sanction evasion through third-party supply chains. Russia was producing approximately 170 Geran-2 units per day at Alabuga as of early 2026. At a domestic production cost estimated between $20,000 and $50,000 per unit, the economics of mass attrition are straightforwardly favorable for the attacker: launch enough of them at Ukrainian port cities near the Romanian border, and some will breach NATO airspace without costing Russia anything it considers prohibitive. NATO Allies Rally Behind Bucharest Belgium's Foreign Minister Maxime Prévot called Sunday's incursion "a stark reminder of the ongoing threat Russia's war poses to European security" and confirmed that 300 Belgian troops are based in Romania as part of NATO's eastern flank force. Col. O'Donnell at NATO SHAPE framed the shootdown streak within the alliance's broader hardware push: "The shootdowns come as NATO, Romania, and other nations actively acquire ground-based interceptors to enhance allied and national air defense capabilities," he said, adding that "NATO is constantly on the watch and prepared to defend itself from any threat." Romania is not building this air defense layer alone. Poland deployed MEROPS alongside Romania along NATO's eastern flank. Lithuania purchased 48 MEROPS Surveyor interceptors from Perennial Autonomy on April 22, 2026, becoming the latest NATO member to field the system. In July, NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte announced the Drone Edge Initiative — a $40 billion commitment over five years for counter-drone capabilities, drone procurement, and operator training across the alliance. Romania itself signed a separate agreement with Israel's Rafael Advanced Defense Systems in June 2026 for a layered air defense package worth more than €2 billion (approximately $2.3 billion USD), adding a mobile short-to-medium-range system to fill the gap between MEROPS's close-range interception and Patriot's long-range coverage. Romanian Pilots and a Fast Calculation: What Five Minutes Tells You One detail in Sunday's intercept warrants attention. From the moment the Shahed breached Romanian airspace to the moment a Romanian F-16 shot it down, approximately five minutes elapsed. That is the operational signature of a force that is now authorized, equipped, and practiced — not a force still debating whether to act. For context: the September 2025 incursion that preceded the enabling legislation saw two Romanian F-16s track a Geran-2 for nearly an hour before it departed on its own. The contrast between that restraint and this weekend's five-minute intercepts measures exactly how much Bucharest's posture has shifted. MEROPS's April 2026 test at the Capu Midia Air Defense Training Range on Romania's Black Sea coast exposed one documented limitation: one interceptor failed to engage a maneuvering target during evaluation. The Shahed-136 does not typically maneuver aggressively — its slow delta-wing flight profile is optimized for range, not evasion — so the operational mismatch between that test failure and the drone's real-world profile is narrow. Whether MEROPS alone or the F-16s were responsible for this weekend's kills has not been confirmed by Romanian defense officials. What is confirmed: three drones are gone, three investigations are underway, Russia's ambassador has been summoned, and NATO's eastern flank has answered 33 violations with something it did not answer the first 30 with — a missile. Frequently Asked Questions How does the MEROPS counter-drone system work, and why is it better than a traditional missile? MEROPS uses an AI-guided interceptor drone — the AS3 Surveyor — to physically intercept and destroy incoming drones like the Shahed-136. Unlike a traditional surface-to-air missile (a Patriot PAC-3 costs $3.9 million to $5.3 million per shot), each Surveyor costs approximately $14,500 to $15,000. The Surveyor homes in on targets using thermal imaging, radio-frequency sensors, and radar guided by onboard AI, making it effective even when GPS or radio links are jammed. If an intercept misses, the Surveyor deploys a parachute, lands safely, and can be reused. This cost reversal — spending $15,000 to stop a $20,000–$50,000 drone rather than $5 million — is why the U.S. Army purchased 13,000 MEROPS interceptors in the early days of the 2026 Iran conflict at $15,000 each. Why does Romania keep getting Russian drones flying into its airspace, and has this been happening for a long time? Yes. Romanian defense authorities documented 33 Russian drone incursions into Romanian airspace between February 2022 and July 2026. Until Friday, Romania had never shot one down inside its own borders. The incursions happen because Russia conducts sustained drone attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure — especially port facilities along the Danube River delta — and the flight corridors to those targets brush Romanian territorial airspace. Security analysts documented an 18-incident year in 2025 alone — a 200 percent increase over 2024 — that multiple independent reviews characterized as a deliberate campaign to test NATO's response, not a series of navigation accidents. What exactly is the Shahed-136 drone Romania shot down, and how dangerous is it? The Shahed-136 — which Russia manufactures domestically as the Geran-2 — is an Iranian-designed one-way attack drone, 3.5 meters (11.5 feet) long, weighing about 200 kilograms (440 pounds), with a maximum speed of around 115 mph (185 km/h). It carries a 50-kilogram (110-pound) high-explosive warhead in its standard configuration, with a 90-kilogram (200-pound) variant fielded by Russia since 2024. Its combination of low speed, low altitude, and small radar cross-section makes it difficult for traditional radar systems. Russia uses them in mass salvos against Ukrainian energy infrastructure, port facilities, and population centers. One struck an apartment building in Galați, Romania in late May 2026, injuring two civilians. At an estimated domestic production cost of $20,000 to $50,000 per unit and a production rate of approximately 170 per day, Russia can sustain mass Shahed campaigns indefinitely at acceptable cost — which is why the drone-on-drone intercept model MEROPS represents is strategically critical for NATO's defense economics. What does Romania's decision to start shooting down drones actually mean for the rest of NATO? Romania's shift from passive monitoring to active kinetic engagement — shooting down three drones in three consecutive days — demonstrates that a NATO member can lawfully intercept intruding hostile drones, absorb Moscow's non-response, and face no immediate escalatory consequences. That precedent matters. It suggests the sub-threshold category Russia has used to probe NATO borders for four years now has a proportional military answer that does not trigger Article 5 or a direct Russia-NAT
