Photograph: Cole Burston/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Kurdish film-maker Gabar Choli pictured in London, Ontario. Photograph: Cole Burston/The Guardian Force-fed by ICE US news ‘Shoved the tube so hard it tore my nose’: Kurdish film-maker recounts ‘inhumane’ ICE force-feeding Gabar Choli tells of how, for months, he was shackled, pinned and forcibly fed – and the physical and emotional scars the ordeal has left José Olivares Mon 10 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 06.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In June 2025, a sluggish and thin Gabar Choli, with sunken temples and bones visible under his skin, braced himself for the immigration detention center guards to charge into his cell once again. Choli was in a solitary confinement medical cell inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement ( ICE ) detention facility in south Texas where immigrants arrested in Donald Trump’s anti-immigration crackdown are detained. Choli, a 40-year-old Kurdish asylum seeker with a thick beard and long dark hair, had been on hunger strike for over two months, demanding improved conditions for detained immigrants and to be released or deported. That day in June 2025, Choli’s nose was swollen, his throat hurt and he could still taste blood from previous days of treatment for which he never gave his consent, he said. The film-maker and activist for an independent Kurdistan has spoken out for the first time, talking exclusively to the Guardian last week from Canada about the ordeal in the United States that he said “broke him”. Kurdish hunger striker says ICE force-feeding ‘mentally broke me’ Read more He recounted the vile routine as the detention center guards would rush towards him and wrestle him to the concrete cell floor, shackle his wrists and ankles, and drag him to the detention center infirmary. There, the guards pinned Choli on a bed while medical staff forcibly inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach. Choli was being force-fed by ICE . “Two guards would hold my feet; two hold my hands; one hold my head – and they would shove tubes in my nose,” Choli said. “It’s not easy to be wrestled to the ground twice a day by men that are stronger than you. And you just take it. You have 60cm of tube going through you and you just feel every centimeter of it.” An investigation by the Guardian, based on dozens of pages of court records and interviews with medical and legal experts, found that Choli was quietly and intermittently force-fed by ICE for nearly eight months – from late May 2025 until he was deported in January. He was not alone – he even met a fellow hunger striker, an Afghan man the Guardian also learned about , as they were both forcibly fed in the same ICE facility. Force-feeding is an excruciating and traumatizing process that has been widely condemned by human rights organizations as torture. For Choli and others, refusing food is a last resort to protest against harsh conditions and lack of progress in their immigration cases, but sometimes brings only harsher conditions. “I understood the necessity of making a stand for what was right,” Choli said, speaking by phone with the Guardian, talking in a very matter-of-fact way about his recent experience. At various times, Choli would sarcastically chuckle, almost incredulous now when remembering the officials’ actions. “I was respectful. I just told them I am protesting for humane treatment, nothing else. But they were determined to break me,” he said. Choli suffered swollen sinuses, a damaged esophagus, stomach problems and psychological torment, according to court records and his own account. “It just broke me, mentally broke me,” Choli said gravely. After sometimes twice-daily sessions “they would take me to [a] solitary cell and I would just choke on my blood and drink the blood from inside [my throat],” he said, describing how the feeding tube would scrape him inside. Many of his court records remain sealed and he did not have a lawyer – and medical staff there did not respond to the Guardian’s reporting – so some details in Choli’s account remain uncorroborated. View image in fullscreen The fence of the Port Isabel detention center. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/Reuters The Trump administration has not officially acknowledged force-feeding anyone in immigration jails. But an investigation by the Guardian found that since January 2025, the administration used court orders in plans to subject at least 10 hunger strikers in ICE detention to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding. However, it has since emerged that the number is even higher. Sources with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE’s parent agency, later told the Guardian that between January 2025 and 4 August 2026, ICE received “a court order for involuntary treatment for 18 hunger strikers”. DHS did not respond to questions concerning Choli’s specific case, but a spokesperson said in a statement: “ICE respects an individual’s right to refuse medical treatment where appropriate. However, when an individual’s medical condition presents a serious risk of death or permanent harm, or when other compelling legal or operational interests are implicated, ICE may seek judicial authorization for appropriate medical interventions consistent with applicable law.” “Any involuntary medical treatment is undertaken only pursuant to legal authority and under the direction of qualified medical professionals,” the spokesperson added. The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas did not respond to a detailed request for comment. ‘Stark example of brutality’: Trump’s ICE used court orders in plan to force-feed at least 10 hunger strikers in detention Read more “This likely amounts to torture,” said Dr Chanelle Diaz, an assistant professor of medicine at Columbia University’s medical center, in New York. Diaz has medically evaluated other ICE force-feeding cases and advocated for hunger strikers’ release. She reviewed the limited court records available for Choli’s case, at the Guardian’s request. “I would say that it’s even difficult to capture the degree of risk that he was being put at, long-term,” she said. Choli, a deeply religious Muslim, had been living in Vancouver, where he was a film-maker and activist campaigning for an independent nation of Kurdistan , having come to Canada in 2007 from what he considers occupied territory in Iran. His life was and is complicated. He said he had previously served nine months in prison in Canada following a 2012 drug-smuggling charge and court records show the case was related to receiving just over one kilogram of opium in the mail from Turkey. Then his activism for Kurdish independence drew death threats and in 2022 he crossed the border into the US in Blaine, Washington and requested asylum. He was quickly released by the authorities and made his way to Los Angeles to try to pursue his ambitions in film while his asylum case played out, attending regular mandatory check-ins with ICE and qualifying for a work permit. Court records say a judge denied his asylum claim in 2024 but granted him protection from deportation to Iran. Then Donald Trump returned to the White House after campaigning on a promise of mass deportation and, at a 25 February 2025 check-in with ICE, Choli was arrested. He was first sent to the Desert View Annex in California, an immigration detention center that has been repeatedly criticized for substandard conditions . While in detention, Choli says he was pressured by ICE officials to sign a deportation order to be sent to Iran. He refused and after demanding better conditions and a fairer resolution to his immigration case, he began his hunger strike on 24 March, court records show. “I am not suicidal,” Choli would later write in a declaration to a federal judge. “I am using hunger strike as the only available option to protest the abuse and mistreatment.” Choli was then transferred to the privately-run Port Isabel facility in Texas for a “higher level of medical care”, an ICE court declaration says. There, Choli refused to end his strike and was placed in a solitary medical cell, which ICE describes as administrative segregation, meaning he was under frequent observation by medical staff. It features a perpetually illuminated cell, alongside other cells in that unit with suicidal or other medically vulnerable detainees. Almost 10 days later, ICE sought their first court order to force-feed Choli. He broke his strike, believing the federal court’s involvement could help his immigration case move along. “God opened a door for me,” he said he was thinking, and wrote a letter to the federal judge requesting assistance. View image in fullscreen Kurdish film-maker Gabar Choli photographed in London, Ontario. Photograph: Cole Burston/The Guardian But three weeks later, Choli said he learned the case was closed and no one had responded to his letter. Furious, he stopped accepting meals again. On 23 May 2025, ICE and the US attorney’s office for the southern district of Texas filed a second request for a court order to conduct involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding. According to ICE’s request, a social worker at the detention facility evaluated Choli and found he was “operating under his own free will”. The World Health Organization and other medical organizations “have said that it is an individual’s right to decide to go on hunger strike, as long as they are of sound mind – which he was”, Dr Parveen Parmar said about Choli after reviewing some of his records shared by the Guardian. Parmar is a doctor and expert with Physicians for Human Rights, a New York-based advocacy group. Like Diaz, she has provided expert medical testimony in other ICE force-feeding cases and also reviewed the limited court records available for Choli’s case. “Patient autonomy is one of the core tenets of medicine,” Parmar added. But as Choli’s hunger strike went on, it threatened his health and also, in the government’s opinion, posed “a serious threat to the security and good order” of the facility, ICE argued in court filings. “The public interest is served by not allowing [Choli’s] attempts to manipulate the immigration system and by maintaining prison and inmate safety and security,” the case documents say. Such filings not only contradict federal silenceor denials about hunger strikes going on intermittently in various ICE detention facilities, but they appear to speak to a desire by authorities to limit such protests from spreading . In Choli’s case, doctors working for ICE, Dr Benjamin Salinas and Dr Shauna Kincheloe, also submitted declarations to the court last May requesting the procedures take place – and continue. One day later, the federal judge, Rolando Olvera, ordered Choli to be force-fed, without hearing from Choli himself. When contacted, Salinas told the Guardian: “Thanks for reaching out, but I’m not interested.” Kincheloe did not respond to requests from the Guardian for comment. Olvera’s assistant declined to make the judge available for comment. “Immigration detention is civil, it is not necessary,” Diaz said, referring to the fact that many alleged immigration violations, such as remaining in the US without legal status, involve civil, not criminal law. She said that ICE’s court arguments “feel like a false dichotomy”, adding that detained immigrants “could be released, that is always a choice. And that should be the default, not force-feeding.” In most cases seen by the Guardian, federal judges will often approve ICE’s requests without hearing from the hunger strikers first, or their lawyers – those that have one. Choli did not have an attorney during his detention and the entire force-feeding proceedings, records show, and was not provided with one by the government. “In my view, those proceedings shouldn’t continue without the person having legal representation if they don’t have it already,” said Rebecca Sharpless, the founding director of University of Miami’s immigration clinic. Sharpless is not familiar with Choli’s case but represented an ICE hunger striker in 2021 who was ordered force-fed. “It makes a big difference when people understand that there are people who are fighting for them – both in terms of their legal case but also their right to make choices about their body.” The very first time Choli was force-fed, he had voluntarily gone with the guards to the detention center’s infirmary. But after experiencing the painful and traumatic process for the first time, he began to resist. “First I did not resist. But after I saw they were torturing me, I started protesting: ‘I’m not coming with you people,’” he said. View image in fullscreen A security guard poses for a photo next to the group holding cells at Port Isabel. Photograph: Verónica G Cárdenas/AFP via Getty Images Then the guards, employees of the private prison company Akima Global Services, “started wrestling”, he said. Many ICE detention centers are run by private US contractors. Akima and its parent company did not respond to detailed requests for comment. During the first days of Choli’s force-feeding, his nose and throat were swollen from the repeated tube insertions and removals, according to Choli and court records. He recalled an occasion in which, while being restrained, an ICE nurse “shoved the tube so hard” that “he tore my nose from the inside”. His nose bled for days, Choli wrote in a declaration to the court recounting the incident. Parma of Physicians for Human Rights said repeated force-feeding can produce such symptoms and is “just inhumane from beginning to end”. ‘What they’re doing qualifies as torture’: new details of ICE force-feeding revealed Read more The rapid administration of nutrients after Choli had been starving himself also triggered stomach problems. During one early session last June, Choli said he immediately had diarrhea. He was then taken to a cell with no toilet, he said, where he further defecated on himself. “I kept looking at my soiled body and clothing and went on crying,” Choli wrote in the declaration to the judge. “I cried for being objectified and inhumanely treated, for seeking a humane treatment.” Weeks passed and Olvera, the judge, continued to extend the force-feeding order. Choli, with swollen sinuses, presented his declaration to the court at one hearing in mid June, telling Olvera he could not afford a lawyer and requested a court-appointed attorney. Olvera denied Choli’s request, writing in his court order that attorneys are not guaranteed in civil proceedings and that, even if Choli had one, it would be of no use – he would continue to grant force-feeding orders. The twice daily process became a grim routine. Weeks turned to months. At one point, Choli recalled a guard’s rough treatment injuring his ribs, making breathing painful for weeks. At another, guards who were restraining him “pressed so hard on my shoulder, I thought my chest was going to break in half”. “I lost my breath” and he heard the doctor say, “‘Take him to the hospital, he’s dead.’ [Then] I completely went ‘out’,” Choli said in an interview. Another time he recalls that despite his warnings a medical staffer incorrectly inserted the tube and it entered his lung, causing him to choke and then cough that end of the tube up into his mouth. Choli remembers that as he was passing out, he “lost [his] senses” and vaguely remembers “reaching for [the guard’s] hand with my mouth”. DHS, ICE and Akima did not respond to this specific allegation. Choli said that at one point he made a deal with the facility staff: on Fridays, he agreed to drink the nutritional liquids if they allowed him to pray with other detainees. “That was my opportunity to socialize,” Choli said, calling those Fridays his “peace days”. I just told them I am protesting for humane treatment, nothing else,” Choli said. “But they were determined to break me.” Much of what happens in ICE detention has been hidden from public view over successive administrations. An investigation by the Guardian last week found that the second Trump administration used court orders in plans to subject at least 10 hunger strikers in ICE detention to involuntary medical procedures . However, it has since emerged that the number is even higher. DHS sources told the Guardian over the weekend that between January 2025 and 4 August, 2026 ICE obtained court orders for involuntary medical treatment for 18 hunger strikers. The Guardian has previously found that while some people are force-fed, some give in and eat at the last minute when presented with a court order. DHS sources also said that ICE “provides involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death”. In court records reviewed by the Guardian in relation to Choli’s case and other hunger strikers, “involuntary medical treatment” is used as an umbrella term that includes the option of force-feeding. According to court records related to Choli, ICE requested the court give the agency permission “to conduct routine physical examinations and routine laboratory testing, administer hydration, and if necessary, use restraints to accomplish this involuntary monitoring, treatment and administration of nutrients, fluids and medication(s), by way of intravenous measures and/or a nasogastric tube ”. ICE and the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), its parent agency, did not respond to specific questions about Choli’s case and had not responded to questions about force-feeding for the prior articles in the investigative series , but on Friday night sent a statement by email in response to the Guardian’s reporting and requests for comment. “ICE respects an individual’s right to refuse medical treatment where appropriate,” an unnamed DHS spokesperson said. “However, when an individual’s medical condition presents a serious risk of death or permanent harm, or when other compelling legal or operational interests are implicated, ICE may seek judicial authorization for appropriate medical interventions consistent with applicable law. Any involuntary medical treatment is undertaken only pursuant to legal authority and under the direction of qualified medical professionals.” “ICE is committed to ensuring the safety, security, and well-being of all individuals in its custody,” the spokesperson added. Dozens of pages of federal court records verify that Choli was subjected to force-feeding, including declarations by ICE doctors and officers. Combined with interviews with medical and legal experts and an interview by phone with Choli himself , much of the secretive process is revealed. His case could be the longest documented case of force-feeding in ICE detention to date. Choli arrived in Blaine, Washington state, in 2022. He had been living in Vancouver where he was a film-maker and activist campaigning for an independent nation of Kurdistan, having come to Canada from what he considers occupied territory in Iran. He said he requested asylum in the US due to death threats for his political activism while in Canada, and lived in Los Angeles with a work permit while his case was in process. But he was arrested during an ICE check-in on 25 February 2025 – the month after Donald Trump returned to the White House – after his asylum case failed. He began a hunger strike in detention in California and was transferred to Texas. DHS and ICE then requested an emergency court order from a federal judge to force-feed him and perform other medical procedures, such as involuntary intravenous hydration, involuntary blood draws and urine analysis tests through forced catheterization, documents from the southern district of Texas federal court seen by the Guardian show. “I am not suicidal,” Choli wrote in a letter to the federal judge overseeing his proceedings. “I am using hunger strike as the only available option to protest the abuse and mistreatment.” ‘What they’re doing qualifies as torture’: new details of ICE force-feeding revealed Read more DHS and ICE said in court records that force-feeding Choli was necessary for his health, but also that his prolonged hunger strike posed “a serious threat to the security and good order” of the detention center. They further accused Choli of attempting to “manipulate the immigration system” by striking. During his first force feeding sessions, he recalled in an interview occasions where a nurse working for ICE “shoved the tube so hard” that “he tore my nose from the inside.” After such sessions “they would take me to solitary cell and I would just choke on my blood and drink the blood from inside [my throat],” he added. Many of his court records are sealed, so the Guardian is not able to corroborate some details in Choli’s account. He did not have legal representation throughout the eight month ordeal. The federal judge presiding over his case, Rolando Olvera, denied Choli’s request for legal assistance and extended the force-feeding order several times at ICE’s request, according to records filed in the southern district of Texas federal court. Choli suffered injuries and medical complications, including swollen sinuses, damage to his esophagus and stomach problems, court records show. “ That is just not medical care, that is torture,” Dr Chanelle Diaz, an assistant professor of medicine at Columbia University’s medical center, told the Guardian. Diaz has reviewed cases of other detained immigrants subjected to force-feeding and advocated for their release. Photograph: Nikolay Doychinov/AFP/Getty Images Weather tracker Europe Analysis Weather tracker: Europe breaks more heat records as temperatures soar Magdalena Shopova for MetDesk Drought and wildfires intensify across continent, while tropical storms bring heavy rain and disruption to east Asia Europe live – latest updates Mon 10 Aug 2026 05.32 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 05.43 EDT Share High pressure has dominated central and eastern Europe in early August, breaking temperature records across the region. Austria recorded a high of 41.2C (106.2F), while Slovakia reached 42.2C. Hungary hit a peak of 41.8C, surpassing a record set in 1905, while overnight temperatures remained above 28C in some areas, marking it as a tropical night. The extreme temperatures have been driven by a heat dome beneath the high-pressure system, which traps warm air close to the surface. The prolonged heat has dried out soil and vegetation, creating conditions conducive to the spread of wildfires. Fires have burned across Italy, France, Serbia and Bulgaria, damaging forests and forcing residents to evacuate. Water levels in the Danube, which flows through much of the affected region, have fallen to an all-time low . The receding river has exposed archaeological remains and wartime wreckage , including woolly mammoth bones, second world war ships and remains associated with the Roman-era Constantine’s Bridge. Low water levels have also affected energy production, reducing the efficiency of nuclear power plants in Slovakia and Serbia and forcing Hungary to shut down a plant because there was insufficient water for cooling. Meanwhile, a buoy in the Mediterranean recorded a sea-surface temperature of 33C. If verified, it would be the highest recorded in the region. In eastern Asia, Typhoon Dolphin made landfall in China on Sunday. The national observatory had issued a red alert for the storm – the highest level – for prolonged heavy rainfall , high wind speeds and extensive damage. Dolphin has since weakened to a tropical storm. Japan is braced for Typhoon Chan-hom, just days after Dolphin swept through northern Okinawa and the Amami islands. Chan-hom is expected to make landfall near the coast of Tohoku between Tuesday and Wednesday, with up to 80mph (129km/h) gusts and an atmospheric pressure of 985 hPa. A third system, Peilou, formed on Sunday in the western Pacific. Although it is not expected to make landfall in the Philippines , it is likely to strengthen the south-west monsoon, bringing further rain across the country. Other typhoons this year have intensified the monsoon, which has killed six people and displaced more than 380,000. Photograph: PA Wire/PA View image in fullscreen A deflated ‘mega-dinghy’ on the quayside in Dover, Kent. Photograph: PA Wire/PA Immigration and asylum Record 230 people cross Channel to UK as smugglers turn to ‘mega-dinghies’ Crossing in larger vessel highlights changing tactics despite increased enforcement on French coast UK politics live – latest updates Europe live – latest updates Diane Taylor Mon 10 Aug 2026 06.55 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 07.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A dinghy carrying a record 230 people has arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel in the early hours of Monday. It is the clearest indication yet that people smugglers in northern France are adapting their business model and escalating their so-called taxi boat strategy to evade enforcement by UK and French authorities. The development is likely to be a blow to the prime minister and home secretary. Andy Burnham has vowed to be “relentless” and “bring back control”, while Shabana Mahmood has said the government is “bearing down” on small boat crossings. French authorities told the Guardian that before an incident last week, in which a mega-dinghy carrying 173 people capsized after its engine caught fire, there had been nine mega-dinghy crossings of the Channel so far this year. Although the number crossing the Channel this year has fallen by more than 40% compared with the same period last year, the increasing use of larger vessels demonstrates how quickly people smugglers have adapted to stronger enforcement by French police on beaches in northern France. 1:22 Andy Burnham promises to be relentless in tackling small boat crossings – video The UK government has struck a deal with Germany to increase seizures of traditional dinghies and engines “upstream”. Last year, 106 people were reported to have crossed the Channel in a single dinghy in August and 125 in September. The emergence of mega-dinghies coincided with the announcement in July 2025 of the UK-France “one in, one out” deal , under which a person arriving in the UK from France by small boat can be returned in exchange for another person being brought legally to the UK to claim asylum. On 12 July this year, a mega-dinghy carrying 128 people arrived in the UK, followed by another carrying 165 people on 23 July. On 4 August, a dinghy carrying 173 people capsized after the engine caught fire . All those onboard are believed to have been rescued, with 11 sustaining minor injuries and three taken to hospital in Boulogne. The use of mega-dinghies poses an even greater risk to life than smaller vessels, which have recently carried an average of between 50 and 60 passengers, according to NGOs working with asylum seekers crossing the Channel. When small-boat crossings began in 2018, only a handful of people typically travelled in each dinghy. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen Two children in foil blankets and two women walk along the beach in Gravelines, France, after failing to board a dinghy attempting to sail into the Channel in April. Photograph: Tom Nicholson/Getty Images While there have been “green days” this year, when adverse weather has made conditions too dangerous for smugglers to launch dinghies, NGOs say many continue to wait in northern France for an opportunity to cross the Channel. They include some who have been returned to France under the one-in, one-out scheme and hope to reach the UK for a second time. Hannah Marwood, the head of legal access at Care4Calais, which delivers emergency aid to refugees, said: “Deterrence doesn’t stop people seeking safety, it just pushes them towards greater danger and greater exploitation. We’ve worked with people who were returned to France only to face violence, exploitation and unsafe conditions, leaving them with no option but to risk another dangerous journey. “Politicians keep promising that another tough policy will solve this but the evidence keeps proving them wrong. If the government is serious about stopping dangerous journeys, it needs to stop recycling failed gimmicks and create safe routes to claim asylum. When people have a safe way to reach protection, they don’t have to risk their lives to find it.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “This latest incident demonstrates the reckless and dangerous tactics employed by the criminal gangs facilitating these crossings, who continue to put lives at risk by cramming ever greater numbers of people on to unseaworthy vessels. “We are making progress, with the number of small-boat crossings down this year and the lowest number recorded for the month of July since 2020. But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum Home Office Labour Shabana Mahmood Andy Burnham France Europe news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Dinghy carrying 173 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fire Sudanese woman and 16-year-old girl reportedly die trying to cross Channel Man arrested after four die trying to cross Channel in small boat Four people die in Channel small-boat sinking Deaths of 22 children in Channel due to ‘catastrophic failure’ by UK and France, NGO says Loss of life was avoidable in worst small boat disaster in Channel, inquiry finds Two people die attempting to cross Channel in dinghy One person dead after small boat sinks in Channel, French authorities say UK access to EU crime and illegal migration data reportedly denied Man confirmed dead after crossing Channel in small boat Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Brendan McDermid/Reuters Alaska Crew of Zuckerberg yacht did not hear radio call to assist boat, Meta says Small skiff ran out of fuel off Alaska and was helped by cruise ship even though Meta CEO’s vessel was closer Zuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boat Guardian staff and agency Mon 10 Aug 2026 08.42 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 08.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The crew of a yacht owned by Mark Zuckerberg did not hear a radio call for a maritime assist from a small skiff that ran out of fuel off the coast of Alaska, and by the time it did, another nearby ship had already rendered assistance, a spokesperson for the Meta CEO said. The Alaska Beacon news outlet reported that the skiff had issued a call for assistance through the US Coast Guard last week and a nearby small cruise ship, the Wilderness Legacy, towed it into nearby Farragut Bay in south-east Alaska and refueled it. Zuckerberg faces questions over why superyacht reportedly declined to help stranded boat Read more Although it was closer, Zuckerberg’s yacht, called Launchpad, had not responded to the call. The Alaska Beacon further reported that the spokesperson told them via email on Sunday that the yacht Launchpad did not initially hear the call for assistance. “Mark and his family were not on board at the time of the incident. As the Coast Guard noted, the boat was not in distress, and by the time the crew reviewed the Coast Guard contact on a different radio channel from the one they were operating on, the assist was already underway. We’re grateful all parties are safe,” the email to said. A passenger on the cruise ship had previously described on social media how the vessel he was on went to the skiff’s assistance, while claiming that the authorities had radioed Zuckerberg’s yacht and they “repeatedly refused to respond”. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Netanyahu said he was confronting a ‘wave of rumours about Israeli weakness’. Photograph: Ronen Zvulun/Reuters View image in fullscreen Netanyahu said he was confronting a ‘wave of rumours about Israeli weakness’. Photograph: Ronen Zvulun/Reuters First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: Netanyahu rejects US-backed 15-point Gaza peace plan Israeli PM is insisting on a full Hamas disarmament before the deal can be implemented. Plus, what it feels like to get locked into an opera performance that lasts nearly 24 hours Don’t already get First Thing in your inbox? Sign up here Martin Belam Mon 10 Aug 2026 06.19 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 06.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected a US-backed 15-point peace plan for Gaza in a rare public break with Donald Trump. In a statement, Israel’s prime minister said he was confronting a “wave of rumours about Israeli weakness and Israeli withdrawals on all fronts” and rebuked US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in. Trump’s Board of Peace in July proposed the 15-point plan, which mandated that Hamas disarm in exchange for providing a full Israeli military withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and an eventual transition of power to an independent Palestinian national committee. Trump had said the agreement would be implemented in stages, but Netanyahu on Sunday said he wanted a full Hamas disarmament first in order to implement the deal. What other developments have happened in the region? Iran has issued tough new demands for reopening the strait of Hormuz , while the United Arab Emirates said one of its ships was targeted by an Iranian missile over the weekend. Tehran said the strait of Hormuz would not open until the US “corrects its behaviour”. Yemen’s Tehran-aligned Houthis have claimed responsibility for an attack on a refinery in Saudi Arabia on Sunday morning. What impact is the conflict having on seafarers in Hormuz? The US-Iran war has stranded up to 20,000 seafarers , mostly Indian and Filipino crews, with none knowing when the nightmare will end. Seventeen seafarers have died since hostilities began, the majority following Iranian strikes. Top Democrats simulate election threats as Trump continues assault on voting View image in fullscreen Chuck Schumer was among those in the room as a team of legal experts offered scenarios Democrats might face in the coming months. Photograph: Elizabeth Frantz/Reuters Chuck Schumer, the US Senate minority leader, and senators including Alex Padilla, Adam Schiff, Mark Warner, Elissa Slotkin and Raphael Warnock were among those in the room as a team of legal experts offered scenarios they might face in the coming months: an assault in real-time on the integrity of November’s election results from the right wing and their Republican opponents. What sort of exercises did they take part in? Justin Vail, who leads the DC office of the non-partisan advocacy group Protect Democracy, said: “These tabletop exercises are a standard planning tool for experts and stakeholders to prepare for potential scenarios. We’re not predicting exactly what would happen. But we do want to create a realistic context that can help us identify gaps, test our assumptions, and strengthen coordination, and then ultimately develop some recommendations to increase our preparedness.” How has Trump been working to undermine confidence in US elections? Voting rights advocates pointed toward Trump’s July primetime address as indicative of the president’s intentions – rhetorical attacks on the integrity of voting machines and elections offices, potentially escalating into more direct interference. Trump threatened the broadcast licenses of networks that refused to carry that address live, and in his speech, he again implored Congress to pass the Save America Act, which would ban mail-in ballots nationwide and impose new identification requirements on voters when they register and report to polls. Abdul El-Sayed embraces Trump claim he represents ‘very different’ America View image in fullscreen Abdul El-Sayed has pledged he will fight inequality while the president is ‘making billions of dollars off of you’. Photograph: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP/Getty Images Abdul El-Sayed, the Democratic nominee for US Senate in Michigan, embraced Donald Trump’s suggestion that the two represent “VERY DIFFERENT” versions of the US, pledging to fight inequality while the president is “making billions of dollars off of you”. “Yeah, he’s right,” El-Sayed told CNN when asked about a post by the US president that depicted an image of Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, beside a photo of El-Sayed, who is Muslim, and his wife, Sarah Jukaku, wearing a hijab. What did El-Sayed say? “One in which your overlords are two people who don’t like each other, but join in the interest of making billions of dollars off of you – or two people who genuinely love each other, enjoyed some pancakes together, want to come together to build the kind of America where they can raise a family and know that that family is going to have the good things. Donald Trump’s vision is the one you’re living in right now. Can you afford your gas? Can you afford your groceries?” In other news … View image in fullscreen Will Scharf, the new White House counsel. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP Donald Trump has appointed his staff secretary, Will Scharf , as the new White House counsel. Scharf, who helped the president win approval for his $400m ballroom, will replace David Warrington on 1 September. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has announced she is going to freeze her eggs and will be sharing the process online. The progressive New York congresswoman, 36, revealed her decision to undergo fertility treatment in a series of Instagram stories Lake Mead, the largest reservoir in the United States, has plummeted to its lowest water level since it was filled some 90 years ago , the latest sign of a deepening water crisis in the American west. Mark Zuckerberg faces questions over why his superyacht reportedly declined to help a stranded boat . The Meta CEO was not onboard at the time. Some of Taylor Swift’s songs have been removed from videos posted on social media by Donald Trump’s campaign and the White House , silencing efforts to mock the pop star. Stat of the day: More than a million people evacuated in China as record rainfall dumped on Shanghai View image in fullscreen A flooded street in Shanghai, China. Photograph: Go Nakamura/Reuters A weather station in central Shanghai recorded over 12 inches of rain in 24 hours, its highest 24-hour rainfall in more than 150 years of records, as more than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall. Building power: How clean air clubs are protecting Americans from wildfire smoke View image in fullscreen A Los Angeles fire department helicopter dropping water to contain the Walnut Fire in the Wildwood Canyon, California. Photograph: David Swanson/AFP/Getty Images Mutual aid groups that started giving out PPEs during Covid are now loaning air purifiers and distributing masks to fume-addled communities. Don’t miss this: An Indigenous photographic history of America – in pictures View image in fullscreen Marie Rexford standing over a pile of muktuk – whale skin and blubber – that she is preparing for a Thanksgiving Day feast, in 2015. Photograph: Brian Adams Spanning generations and multiple Indigenous societies and nations, Sarah Gilbert has picked highlights from In Light and Shadow, a new book tracing the visual importance of Indigenous photographers. … or this: ‘This is asking a lot of the buttocks’ View image in fullscreen Wagner launched the Bayreuth festival 150 years ago with the premiere of his epic Ring Cycle. Photograph: Brandstaetter Images/Getty Images Flora Willson explains how she was swept up in his mad, miraculous marathon of a score as she enjoys – endures? – a 23-hour Richard Wagner marathon on a rock-hard seat in a heatwave at the Bayreuth festival in Germany. It sounds like … a challenge. Climate check: World’s seas have hit hottest temperature on record for July, say scientists View image in fullscreen Durdle Door in Dorset, England. Photograph: Avalon/Universal Images Group/Getty Images The world’s seas were hotter last month than in any July on record . Sea surface temperatures hit record highs for July on the Atlantic coast and western Mediterranean. Globally, the average sea surface temperature outside the cold polar regions was the highest on record for the month, beating the previous July record set in 2023. Last Thing: Perseid meteor shower set to dazzle northern hemisphere this week View image in fullscreen A previous Perseid meteor shower seen in Spruce Knob, West Virginia. Photograph: Nasa/Bill Ingalls/EPA The Perseid summer light show is back . Up to 100 meteors an hour may be visible under ideal conditions, according to Nasa. The American Meteor Society estimates 30 to 50 meteors an hour could be seen from rural regions in the US. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/10/days-.text: Floods, landslides and accidents driven by a nine-day downpour equivalent to more than a month's worth of rain in some areas have killed at least 13 people in the northern Philippines, rescuers said on Monday.The rains, exacerbated by tropical storms, have led to school and government office closures across the main island of Luzon and flooding in the streets of the capital Manila.Four of the deaths occurred in the mountain resort of Baguio, as a rain-drenched mountainside collapsed on several houses, killing four residents, city disaster official Charles Carame told the AFP news agency.Rescuers were digging through the rubble in search of at least six others who remained missing a day after the incident, he added.State weather forecaster Dan Villamil said rains in the vacation spot four hours north of the capital were already 47% higher than normal for the whole month."The rainfall recorded for August 1-9 was highest in Baguio, with an accumulated 1,413.2 millimetres," he said, adding the city's typical downpour for the month was 963.2 millimetres.Parts of Metro Manila had recorded rain equivalent to about 90% of a typical August, he added.Landslides killed six other people elsewhere on Luzon, while another drowned, one was hit by a falling tree, and one was electrocuted, according to a civil defence office tally.While heavy rain continued to fall early on Monday evening, Public Works Secretary Vince Dizon told a news conference that floodwaters were receding."Our interventions are continuing, but we really need to fix the years and decades' worth of faulty flood mitigation interventions," Dizon told reporters, referencing a scandal over bogus flood-control projects that have cost taxpayers billions of dollars.The Philippines is the first major landmass facing the Pacific cyclone belt and the archipelago is hit by an average of 20 storms and typhoons each year, putting millions of people in disaster-prone areas in a state of constant poverty.Scientists say human-driven climate change is making extreme weather more frequent, prolonged and intense.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/10/six-c.text: Days after Colombia's newly elected President Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in, and who had vowed a battle against crime as a major part of his campaign, the leader announced the killings of six members of armed groups by Colombian forces on Sunday.The far-right leader promised a fight against criminal groups that were profiting from drug trafficking as the country experiences its worst wave of violence in the past decade.In a statement, the far-right leader said the operation was intended to send a clear and forceful message to all criminals in Colombia. "There is nowhere for them to hide when the State is determined to act. I have given specific instructions to law enforcement agencies to carry out all necessary operations that were held back by the previous administration (of Gustavo Petro)," said De la Espriella.Sunday's military operations marked the new administration's first actions against illegal groups, which campaigned on a pledge to confront "narcoterrorism without truce".In a show of force, President Abelardo de la Espriella's swearing-in ceremony was held in the southwestern city of Cali, which is known for its high violence and crime rates.De la Espriella wants to build mega-prisons similar to the one in El Salvador and increase airstrikes against guerrillas and narco traffickers.The six killed by Colombian forces on Sunday include four members of a splinter faction of the former FARC guerrilla group, as well as two members of the Gulf Clan, Colombia's main drug cartel, in Antioquia department in the northwest.Meanwhile, on Saturday, De la Espriella's first day in office was marred by two separate bombings, leaving at least one police officer dead and wounding several people. FARC guerrilla members used explosives to destroy a highway tollbooth near Cali, with two security guards suffering minor injuries, according to Colombia's army.

https://www.dw.com/en/india-student-ange.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IYSh Students have been protesting in Ranchi for over two weeks Image: Somnath Sen/ANI Advertisement Thousands of protesters in Jharkhand are marching on the eastern Indian state's parliament to demand a federal inquiry into alleged irregularities in recruitment exams for government jobs, for the tests to be canceled and for a more transparent hiring process. Police used water cannons against the protesters on Monday as they tried to breach security barricades en route to Jharkhand Legislative Assembly. The confrontation marked a sharp escalation between the authorities and the protesters. The movement began on July 25, when demonstrators started camping at Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in the state capital, Ranchi. Protesters clashed with police Monday as they marched towards the state parliament Image: ANI Video Grab In scenes reminiscent of the youth-led " Cockroach " protests that swept New Delhi last month, some protesters also went on a hunger strike . Rahul Kranti, a 40-year-old government job aspirant and one of at least six protesters participating in the hunger strike, was moved to intensive care after his health deteriorated. "The future of Jharkhand's youth will not be allowed to be sold. I will remain on hunger strike, whether I am in hospital or at the protest site," Kranti told DW. He pledged to continue his protest until the government cancels Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) exams and orders a criminal inquiry by the national Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). After hours of negotiations on Sunday, the government agreed to suspend this year's disputed JPSC exam, and three members of the commission resigned. But the protesters say the concessions fall short of their demands, which include the cancelation of the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission's Combined Graduate Level (JSSC-CGL) examination, a major recruitment test for state government jobs, and a full federal probe into alleged irregularities across Jharkhand's recruitment system for public sector jobs. At least six protesters are on hunger strike in Jharkhand Image: ANI News/IMAGO What sparked the protests in Jharkhand? The initial trigger was the latest JPSC civil services examination, which advertised just 103 government posts. More than 2,000 candidates qualified for the next stage when results were announced in early July. Then, an answer sheet began circulating online, apparently showing a candidate who had passed the exam, despite completing very little of it. The image went viral, prompting allegations that the results had been manipulated. Police have arrested the candidate at the center of the controversy, along with 10 others, and the commission's chair resigned under pressure. But the protesters say those steps have not addressed the larger problem. Devendra Nath Mahto has been on hunger strike for nine days and has lost more than 10 kilograms [FILE: August 4, 2026] Image: Somnath Sen/ANI What are the protesters' demands? The Jharkhand protesters want the exam results to be scrapped and for the exam to be repeated. They are also calling for an independent inquiry, either by retired High Court judges from outside the state, or by federal authorities. The protesters argue that a state police probe cannot adequately examine allegations involving Jharkhand's own recruitment machinery. The Jharkhand Chhatra Sangh (JCS), one of the student groups involved in the protests, is also demanding greater transparency in answer sheets and test results, biometric verification, tougher safeguards against paper leaks and accountability for officials and private, third-party recruitment agencies. The JCS also wants alleged tainted examinations from recent years to be investigated and, where necessary, canceled and retaken. "The government must clean up the entire JPSC and JSSC recruitment system, investigate those responsible, blacklist tainted agencies and make future examinations transparent and fraud-proof," S Ali, national president of the JCS, told DW. Anger at civil service recruitment exams in Jharkhand has been simmering for years Image: ANI Photo Has the Jantar Mantar playbook spread to the rest of India? The Ranchi protest began days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called off its 36-day protest in Delhi over leaked medical entrance examination papers. That movement, which saw youths stage hunger strikes and camp outside the Delhi observatory, Jantar Mantar, culminated in the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan . CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has announced plans to travel to Jharkhand, while a delegation has already reached Ranchi to support the protesters. But Jharkhand's movement is more than a mere copy of the CJP. The JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch has led the protests, alongside the Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha. Student unions, including All-India Students Association (AISA) and All India Students' Federation (AISF), have also joined. Neha Bora, AISA president, visited the protesters in Ranchi. "Whether at Jantar Mantar or in Ranchi, these protests symbolize the broken trust young people feel towards the system ," Bora told DW. "They are demanding to be heard, but also asking for changes that can prevent such crises in the future." Student leader Neha Bora (wearing glasses) joined the protesters in Ranchi Image: Yousuf Sarfaraz/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance Jharkhand has its own history of popular struggles over land, identity and political rights. Political analyst Radhika Ramaseshan said the students had clearly taken cues from Delhi, but were also drawing on that local tradition. "Jharkhand has doubtless adopted the CJP playbook to flag a different set of issues that also impinge on the future of young people," Ramaseshan told DW. "The difference is that the protesters' target is the coalition government in Ranchi, which, like the union government, responded late," she added. Chief Minister Hemant Soren has said he is open to talks, while authorities have restricted protests within 750 meters (820 yards) of the assembly through August 12. "The solution to every issue lies in dialogue, not batons and guns," Soren said at Jharkhand's annual tribal festival in Ranchi on Sunday. He sought to assure students that those responsible for the alleged recruitment irregularities would face severe punishment. India's Cockroach movement — and why it matters To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Jharkhand's youth wants more from the Ranchi government The protests in Delhi showed that a student movement built around social media , hunger strikes and anger over a compromised examination can force a national government into a major concession. The protesters in Jharkhand have already secured a win, with the cancelation of this year's disputed JPSC exam and the resignation of three members of the commission. But India's youth are refusing to stop there . Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have all seen major controversies around recruitment examinations. What has been missing in those states is a sustained movement capable of turning those grievances into broader political pressure . For now, and despite the state government's concession, the students in Ranchi are refusing to call off their protest. "We are waiting to find out what happens. These fraudulent examinations have to end, but our patience is running thin too," Motilal Mahto, one of the protesters, told DW. https://www.dw.com/en/ukrainian-drone-at.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IXX3 An increase in long-range attacks has led to a jump in Russian and Ukrainian civilian casualties, according to the UN Image: DW Advertisement A Ukrainian drone attack on the city of Nizhnekamsk, located in an energy-rich Tatarstan region of central Russia , killed at least 13 people and wounded 48 more, according to a local press service statement issued Monday. Over 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) from the Russian-Ukrainian border, the region has many major oil refineries that Kyiv has targeted in recent strikes as both sides increase long-range attacks on infrastructure. The United Nations said such attacks have led to a jump in civilian casualties in Russia and Ukraine . Unspecified industrial and civilian targets had been hit in Monday's strike, Radmir Belyayev, the mayor of Nizhnekamsk, said in a statement on Telegram. Ukraine's military ⁠said ⁠it struck the Taneco oil refinery overnight, adding that a ⁠fire was recorded at the site. The Ukrainian strikes on refineries have led to some fuel shortages and reduced Russia's oil-refining capacity. Russia has also regularly fired missiles, glide bombs and drones hitting civilian areas in Ukraine and causing thousands of civilian casualties, according to the United Nations. Russia, Ukraine: Deadly drone and missile attacks escalate To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Kyiv: Air campaign aims to bring Putin to negotiating table Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the campaign aims to force Russian President Vladimir Putin into negotiations to end the more than 4-year-old full-scale invasion of Ukraine. "We do deliver entirely justified responses, and every Russian strike will be met with our response. Russia's war will be felt more and more at their own home — in Russia," Zelenskyy said late Sunday in a social media post. Ukraine's air force said Russia fired 126 drones in its overnight attack. The Russian Defense Ministry said it shot down 456 Ukrainian drones fired overnight. The ministry, however, does not include how many drones or missiles reach their targets or how many were intercepted in the Tatarstan region. Near the front line in Ukraine, a Russian artillery strike killed five people in a village in the northeastern Kharkiv region, Ukrainian officials said. "On August 10, Russian forces carried out a massive artillery strike on the residential area of the village of Bugaivka in the Chuguiv district. Various houses were destroyed as a result of the enemy attack. Five people were killed," the regional prosecutor's office said in a statement on Telegram. https://www.dw.com/en/thai-ex-lawmaker-s.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IXPx Authorities performed CPR on Thongchai Yenprasert, president of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organization, after he was shot Image: Talingchan520/Handout/REUTERS Advertisement Thai police arrested a suspected gunman — identified as former lawmaker Chalong Riewraeng — after he allegedly fired shots that killed a local politician on Monday at a government office on the outskirts of Bangkok. Authorities said the former MP confessed to the shooting. Surrounded by police, Chalong told reporters he attempted to speak with Thongchai Yenprasert about money. "I followed him to his car and hit his car's window, saying I want to talk," the suspect said. "He said he will not talk, so I pulled my gun. I did not aim to shoot, but his driver pulled a gun and pointed it at me so I fired." Thongchai, who was chairman of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organization, died of his wounds, according to Sakon Sukprom, director of Phra Nang Klao hospital. Thongchai's driver was also shot and successfully underwent surgery, Sakon added. Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said no one in Thailand other than on-duty officials was allowed to carry a gun in public. He pointed out that the last gun-carry licences were issued three years ago and were only valid for one year. He said authorities will pursue "full legal action" against Chalong, a former member of the prime minister's party. "No matter who he is, he is now a murderer," Anutin said. Police: Shooting a 'personal issue' Nonthaburi Governor Chestha Mosikarat told reporters the suspect and victim were "friends for a long time" and the incident likely stemmed from a misunderstanding. Police said the motive for the shooting was a "personal issue." "According to his confession, it was about money that the ... chairman borrowed from him for several years, and he asked for the return of the money several times," regional Police Commander Wattana Yeechin told reporters, adding that the dispute was over several million baht (1 million baht is about €26,220 or $30,300). Second recent shooting This comes just days after a 14-year-old's shooting rampage, first at his home and then at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, left nine people dead and over 20 injured. That incident was Thailand's deadliest mass shooting in nearly four years. Prime Minister Anutin had reiterated his intention to tighten gun control laws in the wake of the shooting. The Southeast Asian country's current gun laws do not include mental health screenings and allow people as young as 20 to have guns. Thailand had around 15 guns per 100 ⁠residents, the highest rate in Southeast Asia ​by a wide margin, according to a 2017 estimate by the Small Arms Survey. Singh was acquitted last week of the sexual harassment and stalking charges brought by female athletes. The former lawmaker from Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), had denied allegations that he groped wrestlers and demanded sexual favors. In its detailed judgment, the court cited "material contradictions" in the wrestlers’ accounts, inconsistencies between their allegations and documentary evidence, and the absence of contemporaneous complaints, media reports said. The court said some allegations appeared "rehearsed, well-practiced and planted." The allegations had triggered months of protests in New Delhi in 2023 , led by prominent Indian wrestlers with hundreds joining the sit-in demonstrations accusing authorities of failing to act against Singh. Delhi police charged Singh in 2023 , and a court formally brought charges against him in 2024 over allegations involving five women. The allegations surfaced in April-May 2023 when women wrestlers protested at Delhi's Jantar Mantar, accusing the former WFI of sexually harassing women wrestlers [FILE: April 18, 2024] Image: Shrikant Singh/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance https://p.dw.com/p/5IXoc Skip next section Rhiya Ahir speaks out after online abuse over protest 08/10/2026 August 10, 2026 Rhiya Ahir speaks out after online abuse over protest Shalu Yadav Ahir’s act of defiance, standing in front of a police van carrying protesters during last month’s CJP-led demonstrations, brought her widespread attention [FILE: July 22, 2026] Image: Ashish Vaishnav/AP Photo/picture alliance Mumbai-based model Rhiya Ahir, who gained attention after standing in front of a police van carrying protesters during last month's Cockroach Janta Party-led demonstrations , has spoken about facing online abuse and threats following the protest. In an interview with DW's Shalu Yadav, Ahir said the attention had come at a "heavy price" of online trolling and harassment, adding that women should be able to express their views without being targeted. She referred to comments made about women protesters, including comments that they "should be raped" and would "enjoy it," saying such remarks could influence others and should not be allowed to go unchallenged. "I read one comment saying 'we are going to rip you apart from the middle. And nobody's going to come to lay flowers on your grave,'" she said. Ahir described the attacks as "criminal." "I will not let it slide," she said. "I will not let them feel that they can sit behind their blank screens and feel so powerful by belittling other people. Her comments come amid a wider online campaign targeting women who took part in the CJP-led protests, with reports of fake and AI-manipulated images, doxxing and threats against participants. https://p.dw.com/p/5IXTQ Skip next section Right-wing commentator arrested over sexual assault remarks targeting protesters 08/10/2026 August 10, 2026 Right-wing commentator arrested over sexual assault remarks targeting protesters Right-wing accounts on social media are targeting the women at the CJP protests, reports say [FILE: July 25, 2026] Image: Sajjad Hussain/AFP An activist who considers himself a right-wing "political commentator" was arrested in the southern state of Kerala on Sunday over remarks he allegedly made about the women at the Cockroach Janta Party-led student protests last month, media reports said. The case was registered following a complaint alleging that videos on TG Mohandas' YouTube channel, Pathrika, were intended to disturb public order and create fear and unrest . According to reports, in the videos, Mohandas allegedly said the Delhi protests could lead to gang rape and claimed that women attending it "like rape" and that some "enjoy being raped." He also called for police to open fire at protesters. News channel NDTV reported that Mohandas is a former member of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). However, the RSS has denied any association with the commentator. The BJP on Monday criticized the arrest as "discriminatory" and accused the Kerala government of attempting to divert attention from other issues, reports said. Women protesters being targeted online The development comes amid an online campaign targeting women who took part in CJP-led student protests. The countrywide stir ended last month with the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. Multiple reports indicate that young women involved in the movement are facing severe online harassment . They have been targeted with fake and AI-manipulated images, as well as a barrage of online abuse, including assault threats. https://www.politico.eu/article/giorgia-.text: Right-wing Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and center-left Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen on Monday reiterated their push to combat illegal migration after thousands of unauthorized migrants surged into Spanish exclave Ceuta in late July. “We are aware that many might be wondering about our cooperation. We come from very different political backgrounds, and we certainly do not agree on everything,” Meloni posted in a “joint message” on Facebook, sharing an archival photo of herself and Frederiksen. “We do not accept uncontrolled immigration to Europe, and we have promoted a strict immigration policy, both in our Nations and in Europe,” the statement continued. Advertisement Advertisement In response to the Ceuta crisis, which reignited Europe’s long-running debate on illegal migration, Denmark and Italy had sent a joint letter to the European Commission demanding immediate action at the EU’s external borders. The letter was co-signed by 20 other European heads of state and government. Italy has since been one of the harshest critics of Spain’s left-wing government and its migration policies, with Rome announcing border controls for travelers arriving from Spain on Friday . Meloni and Frederiksen argued that the adverse effects of illegal migration — “rising crime rates, growing pressure on public services, and an erosion of citizens’ trust” — were indisputable. “For too long, ordinary people … have paid too high a price because of uncontrolled immigration,” they said. “We are both proud of Europe’s Christian cultural heritage and want to protect it. We expect those who come to our countries and choose to make Europe their home to respect our values and not seek to impose ways of life on us that we do not share,” they said.

https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-conse.text: European People’s Party leader Manfred Weber has called for the swift establishment of migrant return hubs in Africa after tens of thousands of unauthorized migrants surged into the Spanish exclave of Ceuta in late July. In an op-ed for German outlet Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung that was published Monday, conservative boss Weber wrote: “Ceuta has shown that close cooperation with neighboring countries can work. Morocco immediately took people back. No one was able to travel onward into the Schengen area” and, he added, “Europe must quickly establish return hubs in Africa.” After tens of thousands forced their way into Ceuta — which is situated in North Africa — several international leaders pointed the finger at Spain’s left-wing government and its migration policy. Madrid had previously granted legal status to half a million unauthorized migrants . Advertisement Advertisement Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni and her right-wing government are among the harshest critics, with Rome introducing border controls for travelers from Spain on Friday and sparking retaliation from Madrid. Weber echoed proposals made last week by EU Migration Commissioner Magnus Brunner, arguing that countries outside the bloc could be offered closer trade ties, economic collaboration and legal migration opportunities in exchange for accepting the installation of return hubs. “Migrants who have no right to remain must leave Europe — no ifs, ands or buts!” he wrote, adding that returns must no longer depend on the political will of individual member countries. Weber called for expanding the EU’s border and coast guard agency Frontex to 50,000 operational personnel, working alongside national forces and monitoring member countries’ compliance with the bloc’s border rules. Weber also rejected internal border controls within Europe as a long-term solution. “They may be necessary in exceptional situations. But they do not address the root cause of the problem … There can therefore be only one answer: strong, joint European protection of the external border.” In early June , the European Parliament and European Council announced new EU rules on migrant returns, including removals to countries outside the bloc in return hubs. Weber also argued that the Ceuta crisis, which left around 100 dead, was the result of unilateral national action and said that the Spanish government’s “political signals” have had “an immediate impact on migration routes.” This article has been updated. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgj.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, A refining and petrochemical plant in Nizhnekamsk (stock photo) By Laura Gozzi Published 10 August 2026, 09:50 BST Updated Just now At least 13 people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, officials have said. One child was among the victims with 75 more people injured, Russian authorities said, in one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of Moscow's full-scale war in Ukraine. Drones struck Nizhnekamsk, more than 1,100 kilometres (680m) from the Ukrainian border. Ukraine's Armed Forces confirmed Nizhnekamsk's Tanevo oil refinery had been hit, while Ukrainian defence technology manufacturer FirePoint said its FP-1 drones had been used in the attack. The strike lasted several hours overnight and into the morning, local sources say. Oil refineries in Nizhnekamsk had already been hit on 12 June. Verified images on social media show large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background. Kyiv has recently stepped up its strikes on facilities it says contribute revenue and logistics to Russia's war on Ukraine. "The facilities Ukraine targets are used to carry out attacks against Ukraine, manufacture weapons, support Russia's war effort," said Andriy Kovalenko, head of the Ukraine's Centre for Countering Disinformation. Moscow confirmed industrial facilities were targeted but added residential areas were struck, too. "Civilian individuals who were not involved in any military operations were present," Russia's Investigative Committee said. The BBC has not independently verified this information. The head of Tatarstan, Rustam Minnikhanov, confirmed the strike and shared his condolences with the families of the deceased. "This is a tremendous pain for all of us," said Nizhnekamsk mayor Radmir Belayev. A period of mourning has been declared in Tatarstan. Ukraine's Kovalenko said "every civilian death in Russia is on [President Vladimir] Putin" and that "Russians should direct their grievances at Putin and at the decisions made within their own country". "Without Putin, there would have been no aggression. Without the aggression, these people would still be alive." More than 450 Ukrainian drones were also shot down by the Russian air defences overnight, Moscow said. Kyiv has become increasingly successful at carrying out long-range strikes on Russia, often targeting warehouses or energy infrastructure, with civilian casualties mounting. Russia, meanwhile, continues to target Ukraine with regular large-scale aerial attacks on cities and residential centres. Last week, a combined drone and missile strike on Kyiv killed 21 people. And in Kharkiv, near the front line, five people were killed overnight in a Russian artillery attack. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yr.text: Image source, Twitter/@ABDELAESPRIELLA Image caption, Hernando Forero Mosquera, aka "El ruso", is accused of leading a dissident rebel faction By Vanessa BuschschlÃ¼ter Latin America online editor Published 28 minutes ago A man suspected of leading a dissident faction of a left-wing rebel group has been killed in a military operation in central Colombia, officials say. The operation forms part of a crackdown on illegal armed groups ordered by Colombia's new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, who was sworn in on Friday. He said the killing by the security forces of Hernando Forero Mosquera and five other alleged members of armed groups on the weekend sent "a clear and powerful message to all bandits that there is nowhere for them to hide". During his campaign for the presidency, de la Espriella said he would target "narco-terrorism" relentlessly, including by launching air strikes. Image source, Colombian Presidency/Handout via REUTERS Image caption, Abelardo de la Espriella was sworn in on Friday as Colombia's new president Military intelligence officers said that Forero led a group known as Frente 28, which is one of the many dissident factions to have sprung forth from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc). The Farc, Colombia's largest left-wing rebel group , signed a peace deal with the government in 2016 but some of its members did not agree to the terms of the deal and refused to lay down their arms. These dissidents groups, which are now mainly involved in cocaine trafficking and illegal mining, are among the main driving forces behind the resurgence in violence in the country . De la Espriella said he would take a radically different approach to defeating criminal groups in the country than his predecessor in office, Gustavo Petro. Petro, the first left-wing politician to be elected president of Colombia, advocated what he called a "total peace" strategy, which prioritised negotiation over confrontation. His attempts to negotiate with a number of armed groups, however, failed as members of the illegal organisations repeatedly broke ceasefires and walked away from the talks. De la Espriella's combative approach has been met with defiance by dissident rebel groups. On Saturday, just a day after the was sworn into office, two explosive devices went off. In Cauca province, a car bomb exploded at a tollbooth, injuring two security guards, and in Cesar province, a police officer was killed by explosives dropped from a drone. In a video uploaded to social media, de la Espriella praised the military for killing Forero, who was also known as "El ruso" (The Russian), and whom he described as an explosives expert. He added that three more alleged members of the dissident group had been killed in the military operation in a rural area in Meta province. The president also said that soldiers had killed two alleged members of another criminal group, the Gulf Clan, in a separate offensive in Antioquia province. De la Espriella has the backing of US President Donald Trump, who endorsed his candidacy. On Friday, the US state department said it planned to provide $1bn (Â£740m) in security assistance to de la Espriella's government. It also welcomed Colombia into the US-led group dubbed " Shield of the Americas " - an alliance of Western Hemisphere countries which have pledged to co-operate in their fight against drug trafficking gangs and transnational crime. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly8.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images By Chris Ewokor BBC Africa Published 19 minutes ago The authorities in Mali say their soldiers killed dozens of militant Islamists as they repelled an attack on a military base on Sunday. Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), a jihadist group affiliated to al-Qaeda, said it was behind the assault where its fighters took control of the base in the town of San. The army, which also suffered casualties, disputed it had ceded control - but said its soldiers had to "retreat temporarily". It comes as Mali's security situation appears to be deteriorating, more than a decade after a jihadist insurgency began taking root in the north of the country. "The enemy was eliminated and the attack was successfully repelled. Around 40 terrorists were eliminated," Lt Col El Oumrani, the commander of the 23rd regiment in the San garrison, said in a video. He urged residents to remain vigilant, insisting that his soldiers had "not gone anywhere" and the base remained under army control. "The camp of the 23rd is not empty, it is under the custody of the army." The attack started at around 05:00 local time (GMT) on Sunday and lasted for about two hours, according to witnesses quoted by the French broadcaster RFI. The attackers came on motorcycles and on foot, some disguised in army uniforms to infiltrate the base, RFI reported the witnesses as saying. One said the militants entered the camp and held it "for a long time before leaving". "I noticed that the fighting took place between 200 and 300 metres from the camp. Several terrorists were killed by soldiers, but others fled; some even hid in houses and others went into the forest," the witness said. At least 10 soldiers were killed in the fighting and the assailants briefly took over the camp, the AFP news agency quoted security and local sources. The army told national broadcaster ORTM that the militants used drones, heavy machine guns and armoured vehicles to breach the site's perimeter. Since 2012, Mali has been plagued by insurgencies and large parts of the north and east of the country remain outside government control. April saw nationwide, co-ordinated attacks by an alliance of jihadists and separatist rebels in the north - the Azawad Liberation Front - seeking to overthrow the military regime of Gen Assimi GoÃ¯ta, who seized power in a coup in 2020. During the attacks, Defence Minister Sadio Camara was killed in an apparent suicide truck bombing on his residence near the capital, Bamako. JNIM has diversified its operations and begun targeting not only northern Mali but also central and southern Mali, showing an ability to penetrate deeper into the territory despite numerous military operations. In the wake of the coup, which was in part carried out over the failure to ease the security situation, Mali rejected French military help and instead turned to Russia. https://www.politico.eu/article/romania-.text: Romania presented Russia’s ambassador to Bucharest with fragments of drones shot down in Romanian airspace over the weekend, after summoning him to a meeting as part of a strong diplomatic pushback against the incursions. Between Friday and Sunday Romania shot down three suspected Russian drones that violated its airspace. “The Romanian side highlighted that the Russian Federation bears exclusive responsibility for all these grave incidents and for the deterioration of the regional security environment,” the Romanian Ministry of Foreign Affairs said in a statement. Romania also recalled its ambassador to Russia for consultations in Bucharest. Advertisement Advertisement Romanian Foreign Minister Oana Țoiu said the aircraft were “Shahed-type drones” used by Russia. They likely crossed into Romanian airspace during Russian attacks on Ukrainian ports in the Odesa region on the Black Sea, near Romania’s southeastern border. The country’s president, Nicușor Dan, described the repeated incursions as “inadmissible and intolerable,” saying they violated Romania’s sovereignty as well as NATO and EU airspace. Incursions by Russian drones into European airspace have become common during the past year as Moscow’s bombardment of Ukraine, which borders Romania, drags on and Vladimir Putin tests the resolve of NATO countries. The ambassador was also notified that a staff member of the Russian Embassy in Bucharest will be declared persona non grata and must leave Romania within five days.

https://www.upi.com/Entertainment_News/T.text: Morgan Spector to play Robert Langdon in Netflix's Dan Brown series July 27 (UPI) -- Morgan Spector has landed the lead role in Netflix's upcoming Dan Brown series. The streaming service announced Monday that Spector, 45, will play Harvard professor and symbologist Robert Langdon in the new show. Langdon was previously portrayed by Tom Hanks in the films The DaVinci Code, Angels & Demons and Inferno , based on Brown's works. The new, untitled series takes place in the world of Brown's latest novel, The Secret of Secrets , which follows Langdon as he investigates a secret project in Prague, according to Brown's website . Netflix said the show will see Langdon race "against ancient forces -- and the clock" to rescue his girlfriend and recover "her groundbreaking manuscript, the contents of which could forever change humanity's understanding of the mind." The series hails from Brown and Lost creator Carlton Cuse , who will serve as writer and showrunner. "Morgan is a truly wonderful actor whose work is always filled with intelligence, thoughtfulness, and humanity," Cuse told Netflix's Tudum. "He's the perfect fit for Robert Langdon -- a brilliant academic whose curiosity, intelligence, and intellect are the tools of his trade." Spector is known for playing George Russell on the HBO series The Gilded Age , which began production on Season 4 in June.
