Photograph: Alain Pitton/NurPhoto/REX/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen A ‘die-in’ organised by Extinction Rebellion in Toulouse, France, with a placard that reads ‘Do our children have a future?’, 26 March 2022. Photograph: Alain Pitton/NurPhoto/REX/Shutterstock Opinion Children's fantasy books (children's and teens) How to feel optimistic in the face of crisis? Ask the kids fighting slug-like aliens Alexander Hurst The Animorphs books taught my generation about digging deep in the face of an existential threat. We need that spirit now more than ever Mon 10 Aug 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 09.15 EDT Share R ecently I found myself thinking about slug-like aliens that crawl through people’s ears and into their brains, with the ultimate purpose of global domination. It would explain a lot about what has gone so wrong with the world, wouldn’t it? And it was why I immediately flashed back to the children’s fantasy series Animorphs when Donald Trump’s health secretary and conspiracy theorist , Robert F Kennedy Jr, admitted to having had a worm in his brain . While visiting my parents in Cleveland, Ohio recently, I realised that a few books from the children’s fantasy series were still sitting on the shelves in my old bedroom. No fewer than 54 Animorphs titles were published between 1996 and 2001, and a total of 35m copies have been sold. “I may have just landed a job thanks to Animorphs,” my childhood friend Clifton texted me with excitement in the mid-2010s, when we were fresh out of college. “It was an interview for a vegan food cart and the last question they asked me was what Animorph I would morph into. I said an orangutan.” The premise sees five adolescent friends encounter a crashed alien spaceship and then face an intergalactic war against the Yeerks, genocidal slug-adjacent beings that slither into the brains of the host species. The young humans are given the ability to transform into any animals they’ve touched, along with the simple task of defending humanity. My generation were told we could grow up to do anything, that life was a continual arc of progress towards better lives, and that the old ideological battles of the past had been laid to rest. We were empowered by what we found in the pages of Animorphs: that Jake, Cassie, Rachel, Marco and Tobias had been endowed with the power of nature itself to help Earth fend off the existential threat of alien conquest. View image in fullscreen The cover of a novel in the Animorphs series. Photograph: Scholastic Publishing Despite the optimism of the 90s, Animorphs was surprisingly dark and morally nuanced for millennial children’s fiction. Foreshadowing the real-world future, the teenagers watch parents and other family members fall under the cognitive control of the Yeerks. Looking back at the series now – and the era that produced it – the Animorphs’ baddies had to be an alien species, because it would have stretched credulity that humanity might destroy the Earth by itself, of its own volition. Now, instead of the Yeerks, we have megalomaniac billionaires and fossil fuel interests that have instilled climate denialism and defeatism into our minds – aided by media they so often control – and stripped us of the ability to even conceptualise our collective agency. The concept of discrete “generations” might be dubious, but where it holds most firmly is in shared cultural references. What millennials share is the distinct feeling of being a bridge: between the analogue and the digital; between a shared informational reality and the post-truth world; between an optimistic world and a pessimistic one. (This latter point shows up even in scientific analysis of pop music: studies have concluded that pop has become sadder .) It’s the reflex towards a hopeful worldview, and the subsequent shattering of this optimism, that lie at the heart of millennial nostalgia for the less fraught times of our youth. On social media, it’s been dubbed the “ millennial optimism era ”. You don’t have to search hard to find the sources of that nostalgia: Akon and Britney Spears coming out of the speakers at my gym, Sum 41 playing at the bougie brasserie around the corner. Meanwhile one huge comeback tour collides into the next. Onscreen, too, everything seems to be getting a remake or a reboot: Toy Story, Scary Movie, Air Bud and, if things go well, Animorphs too, which had a brief, two-season run on TV just before the turn of the millennium. Ryan Coogler, who directed Sinners, is developing a new Animorphs TV series for Disney+. Across the generational line, millennials and gen Z share the same eco-anxiety: in France, it has been found to be significantly more pronounced among those aged 15-34 than among those over 50. Researchers in India found a similar pattern , just as they did in the US. Hannah Ritchie from Our World In Data writes in her personal newsletter that older generations are actually more likely to say that we’re already feeling the impacts of the climate crisis, because they can compare today’s heatwaves and snowless winters with the climate of their childhoods. But the emotional response is different, she writes : millennials and gen Z are more likely to feel fear, guilt and outrage about it. There is a cruel irony to the fatalism of the young: those who will most suffer the consequences of the climate emergency are those most resigned to that fate. Similarly, I think there is something that doesn’t show up in data yet, but is there in gen Z’s nostalgia for the “millennial optimism era”. It’s the difference between millennials believing that all of this can and should be fought, and gen Z having no nostalgic point of reference for the plausibility of fighting it at all. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion Sinners was an intensely literate movie about history, racism and trauma, forces that sap us of our vitality, and our ability to fight back. So I’m not surprised my fellow millennial Coogler might be turning to Animorphs next. In the end, I suspect that he might circle the following: the threat to all of us is not solely alien, but an alien version of ourselves. That fighting back successfully will mean remembering who we really are. That nature is our ally, and we have to remember how indelibly our future is tied to its state of wellbeing. I can’t think of a more urgent millennial-optimist metaphor to splash on to the big screen. Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/10/power.text: At least 111 people were killed and hundreds of buildings damaged after a powerful 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck Colombia, the country's President Abelardo de la Espriella said on Monday.De la Espriella said that at least 87 people had been injured and that he had declared a state of emergency.“You are not alone. The state is present and taking action,” he said.The quake trapped residents under debris, leaving more injured and forcing people to evacuate their homes as far as the capital of Bogotá.The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people in the Choco region about 250 miles west of Bogotá, the US Geological Survey and Colombia’s counterpart reported.The USGS said it struck at a depth of 107 kilometers and was also was felt in neighbouring Ecuador and Panama, though minimal damage was reported there.The quake left cities across the west of the country ravaged.A mix of residents and search teams picked through the rubble of collapsed buildings amid concerns by authorities of aftershocks.Colombia's interior minister said more than 20 municipalities across the country had been hit.Jorge Moncayo, a 64-year-old taxi driver in Cali, said he saw plumes of dust shoot up across the city from his home in hills of the city as buildings collapsed. Residents in the city and rescue workers were searching the rubble for survivors.“My entire house shook,” he said. “I've never lived through such a powerful earthquake.”Colombia's Geological Service said on Monday that it had been “the highest magnitude earthquake registered in Colombia in the last decade” and that it had been followed by two 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude aftershocks.Authorities also reported that flights were suspended in the airports of Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago y Buenaventura and Pereira.The earthquakes left many in the Andean nation unnerved after two back-to-back quakes devastated neighbouring Venezuela in late June, destroyed hundreds of buildings and killed more than 5,000 people.At the same time the quake brought down buildings in Colombia, desperate families in Venezuela continued to search the ruins for the bodies of their loved ones.In Pereira, photos and videos published by local media showed pieces of the airport ceiling falling down on travellers taking shelter and screaming, and people running through rubble in a panic.Pereira's mayor, Mauricio Salazar, told a local radio station that at least 18 people had died and that many more were trapped under “a massive quantity of collapsed buildings.”In nearby Manizales, a city nestled in the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia, one of the towers of the neo-Gothic cathedral collapsed and fell on the nave. Jorge Eduardo Rojas, the mayor of Manizales said two people had died in the city “because of the quake” and asked residents to stay outside in case of aftershocks.Authorities in the rural state of Choco, the epicentre of the quake, reported injured people and damaged buildings in the capital, but provided few details.In Cali, a city 2 million people, Mayor Alejandro Eder said that residents were trapped in at least 19 buildings that had collapsed.Small earthquakes, known as “temblores,” are common in central and western Colombia, but those above 6.0 magnitude are rare.In 1999, a 6.2 magnitude quake near the city of Armenia, killed more than 1,100 people.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/10/chess.text: Iran will not reopen the Strait of Hormuz until the United States meets its conditions as Iranians have shown "they are professional chess players," Tehran said on Monday.“It is up to the US side to stop and make amends for its illegal and destructive actions,” Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmail Baghaei said Monday, in reference to the US blockade of Iranian ports."Lights out or lights on, Iranians showed they are professional chess players," Baghaei added, in reference to US President Donald Trump likening the negotiations to a "board game".Trump on Sunday signalled he was prepared to let economic pressure mount against Iran, apparently backing away from more military strikes after Tehran issued a list of demands for opening the Strait of Hormuz.Tehran wants Washington to lift the blockade, pay compensation for months of war damage, lift economic sanctions and release Iran's frozen assets.The closure of the Strait of Hormuz — a key waterway that normally carries roughly one-fifth of the world's traded oil supplies — has become the war’s most lasting consequence.The impasse has kept energy prices as a major focus of US politics ahead of November’s midterm elections.Iran is holding separate talks with Oman over transit through the strait, including potentially a temporary shipping corridor. However, Tehran said that any actual reopening is contingent on talks with the US.Trump had earlier been quoted by news outlet Axios as saying he was "low-keying it" with Iran."We are only semi-negotiating with them. We are just watching Iran with its huge inflation and the fact they have no money," he said."It will work out. It always works out. It's like a chess game," Trump added.Iranian official Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr on Saturday laid out Tehran's demands, including an end to the "war and aggression against Iran and its allies in Lebanon, Palestine, Yemen and Iraq".He also demanded the lifting of a US counterblockade of Iranian ports, the end of sanctions, the release of frozen Iranian assets, and compensation for wartime damage, the Tasnim news agency reported.Baghaei on Monday reiterated that "as long as the US naval blockade continues ... the necessary conditions for saying that the Strait of Hormuz has become a safe waterway will not exist".Tehran had been engaged in negotiations with Washington on ending the war launched by the US and Israel in late February, but a preliminary deal fell apart, and its officials have said talks are now limited to exchanging messages through mediators.Khamenei meets Pezeshkian?Meanwhile, Tehran reported that Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian recently met with Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not appeared in public since assuming the post early in the war."Dr Masoud Pezeshkian met Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei and spoke with him at the start of his third year in the presidency," Khamenei's office said in a statement on Sunday, without indicating the date of the meeting.Pezeshkian, who took office in July 2024, had said in early May that he met with Khamenei, also without specifying the date, but the ayatollah's office did not issue any statements at the time.Pezeshkian had said on Wednesday that communication with Khamenei was "very difficult at the moment", and speculation has swirled about the ayatollah's health after he was reportedly wounded in strikes that killed his father, Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.No clear indications exist on his actual whereabouts and condition, with US officials stating earlier in the war that the younger Khamenei was severely injured and likely "disfigured" in the opening salvo of the war on 28 February, while reports from inside Iran claimed he was in hiding out of precaution amid concerns over his safety.Pezeshkian, who is a medical doctor by trade, was also reported to have been at least partly in charge of his recovery, although there was no official confirmation of those claims.Mojtaba Khamenei's office said that the ayatollah and Pezeshkian "discussed in detail the country's issues and problems", including the "current military situation and future prospects".On Sunday, Tasnim news agency cited an IRGC general as saying that images showing Khamenei among the people and during meetings would be "published in the future," without offering a timeline.It is unclear how involved Khamenei might be in the ongoing negotiations with Washington, but reports have indicated that the IRGC — an elite paramilitary force of the Islamic Republic under the direct command of the ayatollah — is likely playing an outsized role in Tehran's positions and demands.Tehran touts 'change of perception' in the regionBaghaei said on Monday that a defence pact signed last week between Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan was "a sign of a change in the perception" of countries in the region towards the US."The countries of the region have realised that security is not a commodity that can be bought from false brokers," Baghaei said. Washington is an ally of the three signatories to the pact."Countries in the region cannot rely on the claim of security provided by the US as in the past," he added.He also said Iran was not concerned that the pact could be aimed at Tehran, considering "deep religious, historical and civilisational ties" with Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan.There was "no reason to worry that this treaty will be against Iran", Baghaei said.The three nations signed the agreement on Friday against the backdrop of a five-month war between the US and Iran, which has drawn in surrounding nations and disrupted regional shipping routes.Pakistan's foreign ministry said Friday that the pact meant an attack on any member would be regarded as an attack on all, adding it was "intended to strengthen collective deterrence".

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/10/saudi.text: Bangladesh's foreign ministry said it was in "deep shock" on Monday, after reporting the deaths of 16 citizens in a sofa factory fire in Saudi Arabia the previous day.Dhaka's Expatriates' Welfare Minister Ariful Haque Chowdhury said that there was "constant communication" with local authorities through the Bangladesh Embassy in Saudi Arabia."Officials have been instructed to ensure the speedy repatriation of the bodies of the deceased expatriates and to secure all necessary government assistance and compensation for their families," he added.Around seven million Bangladeshis work overseas — the majority in the Middle East.The civil defence agency in the Saudi capital said a fire at an unlicensed facility where furniture was upholstered had been extinguished, without providing details about any casualties."Riyadh civil defence put out a fire at an unlicensed site being used for furniture upholstery," the agency said in a post on X."The necessary regulatory procedures were subsequently completed regarding the site."Like many Gulf nations, Saudi Arabia relies on a vast number of labourers from the subcontinent to help bolster its workforce, especially with jobs involving manual labour.Reports in Saudi media estimate that over three million Bangladeshi nationals reside in the kingdom.Foreign workers in Saudi Arabia do everything from management to cleaning the streets and waiting on tables, in a society where many citizens are reluctant to take jobs they consider menial.

https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-dozens-ki.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IZRh Locals and emergency personnel in Pereira, Colombia rushed to help comb the rubble of collapsed buildings Image: REUTERS Advertisement A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning. Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country. Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities. The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast. The mayor of Cali said that 'at least 20 structures' collapsed in the quake Image: Reuters TV/REUTERS What is the latest? Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency. He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency. "As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situtation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia." What's happening on the ground? The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside. "Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin." Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, later said that at least 27 people had died in the quake. Officials in Risaralda said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor. And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira. Residents in Cali tried to rush to safety in the aftermath of Monday's earthquake Image: Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Photo/picture alliance The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were four dead and 69 wounded in her district as of late morning local time. Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined. "Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list. What do we know about the quake's size and location? The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well. The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border. One of the towers at the Cathedral of Manizales was damaged by the quake Image: John Jairo Bonilla/AP Photo/picture alliance The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south. The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter. The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors . Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela. USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake. The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake. It's like a chess game," he said of the war. https://p.dw.com/p/5IZIB Skip next section Tehran: Ships will be expected to pay for transit through the narrow waterway 08/10/2026 August 10, 2026 Tehran: Ships will be expected to pay for transit through the narrow waterway Iran has said it intends to charge commercial vessels for passage through the Strait of Hormuz, according to a statement Monday from the Foreign Ministry. Iranian media cited spokesperson Esmail Baghaei as saying that Iran was working with Oman on "mechanisms for monitoring security, protecting the environment and combating crime at sea." Fees would be for maritime services provided to ships, he explained. The dispute over transit rights in the strait, through which some 20% of the world's oil passed before the war and which is a key route for gas and fertilizer, is regarded as a key reason behind the continuation of the war against Iran. What if Iran and Oman split control of the Strait of Hormuz? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Before the United States and Israel launched the conflict against Iran at the end of February, shipping through the waterway did no incur tolls nor fees for transit. The Strait of Hormuz measures only around 39 kilometers (24 miles) at its narrowest point. Since Iran and Oman each claim the maximum 12 nautical miles allowed under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) as their territorial waters, there are no international waters in the narrowest part of the roughly 21-nautical-mile-wide strait. The UN Convention on the Law of the Sea guarantees a right of transit passage and prohibits a blockade of commercial vessels. Iran, however, does not accept this legal position. https://www.dw.com/en/india-anger-over-e.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IYSh Students have been protesting in Ranchi for over two weeks Image: Somnath Sen/ANI Advertisement Thousands of protesters in Jharkhand are marching on the eastern Indian state's parliament to demand a federal inquiry into alleged irregularities in recruitment exams for government jobs, for the tests to be canceled and for a more transparent hiring process. Police used water cannons against the protesters on Monday as they tried to breach security barricades en route to Jharkhand Legislative Assembly. The confrontation marked a sharp escalation between the authorities and the protesters. The movement began on July 25, when demonstrators started camping at Jaipal Singh Munda Stadium in the state capital, Ranchi. Cockroach revolution turns on India's leader To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video In scenes reminiscent of the youth-led " Cockroach " protests that swept New Delhi last month, some protesters also went on a hunger strike . Rahul Kranti, a 40-year-old government job aspirant and one of at least six protesters participating in the hunger strike, was moved to intensive care after his health deteriorated. "The future of Jharkhand's youth will not be allowed to be sold. I will remain on hunger strike, whether I am in hospital or at the protest site," Kranti told DW. He pledged to continue his protest until the government cancels Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) exams and orders a criminal inquiry by the national Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI). After hours of negotiations on Sunday, the government agreed to suspend this year's disputed JPSC exam, and three members of the commission resigned. But the protesters say the concessions fall short of their demands, which include the cancelation of the Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission's Combined Graduate Level (JSSC-CGL) examination, a major recruitment test for state government jobs, and a full federal probe into alleged irregularities across Jharkhand's recruitment system for public sector jobs. At least six protesters are on hunger strike in Jharkhand Image: ANI News/IMAGO What sparked the protests in Jharkhand? The initial trigger was the latest JPSC civil services examination, which advertised just 103 government posts. More than 2,000 candidates qualified for the next stage when results were announced in early July. Then, an answer sheet began circulating online, apparently showing a candidate who had passed the exam, despite completing very little of it. The image went viral, prompting allegations that the results had been manipulated. Police have arrested the candidate at the center of the controversy, along with 10 others, and the commission's chair resigned under pressure. But the protesters say those steps have not addressed the larger problem. Devendra Nath Mahto has been on hunger strike for nine days and has lost more than 10 kilograms [FILE: August 4, 2026] Image: Somnath Sen/ANI What are the protesters' demands? The Jharkhand protesters want the exam results to be scrapped and for the exam to be repeated. They are also calling for an independent inquiry, either by retired High Court judges from outside the state, or by federal authorities. The protesters argue that a state police probe cannot adequately examine allegations involving Jharkhand's own recruitment machinery. The Jharkhand Chhatra Sangh (JCS), one of the student groups involved in the protests, is also demanding greater transparency in answer sheets and test results, biometric verification, tougher safeguards against paper leaks and accountability for officials and private, third-party recruitment agencies. The JCS also wants alleged tainted examinations from recent years to be investigated and, where necessary, canceled and retaken. "The government must clean up the entire JPSC and JSSC recruitment system, investigate those responsible, blacklist tainted agencies and make future examinations transparent and fraud-proof," S Ali, national president of the JCS, told DW. Anger at civil service recruitment exams in Jharkhand has been simmering for years Image: ANI Photo Has the Jantar Mantar playbook spread to the rest of India? The Ranchi protest began days after the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) called off its 36-day protest in Delhi over leaked medical entrance examination papers. That movement, which saw youths stage hunger strikes and camp outside the Delhi observatory, Jantar Mantar, culminated in the resignation of India's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan . CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke has announced plans to travel to Jharkhand, while a delegation has already reached Ranchi to support the protesters. But Jharkhand's movement is more than a mere copy of the CJP. The JPSC-JSSC Reforms Manch has led the protests, alongside the Jharkhand Loktantrik Krantikari Morcha. Student unions, including All-India Students Association (AISA) and All India Students' Federation (AISF), have also joined. Neha Bora, AISA president, visited the protesters in Ranchi. "Whether at Jantar Mantar or in Ranchi, these protests symbolize the broken trust young people feel towards the system ," Bora told DW. "They are demanding to be heard, but also asking for changes that can prevent such crises in the future." Student leader Neha Bora (wearing glasses) joined the protesters in Ranchi Image: Yousuf Sarfaraz/SOPA Images/ZUMA/picture alliance Jharkhand has its own history of popular struggles over land, identity and political rights. Political analyst Radhika Ramaseshan said the students had clearly taken cues from Delhi, but were also drawing on that local tradition. "Jharkhand has doubtless adopted the CJP playbook to flag a different set of issues that also impinge on the future of young people," Ramaseshan told DW. "The difference is that the protesters' target is the coalition government in Ranchi, which, like the union government, responded late," she added. Chief Minister Hemant Soren has said he is open to talks, while authorities have restricted protests within 750 meters (820 yards) of the assembly through August 12. "The solution to every issue lies in dialogue, not batons and guns," Soren said at Jharkhand's annual tribal festival in Ranchi on Sunday. He sought to assure students that those responsible for the alleged recruitment irregularities would face severe punishment. India's Cockroach movement — and why it matters To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Jharkhand's youth wants more from the Ranchi government The protests in Delhi showed that a student movement built around social media , hunger strikes and anger over a compromised examination can force a national government into a major concession. The protesters in Jharkhand have already secured a win, with the cancelation of this year's disputed JPSC exam and the resignation of three members of the commission. But India's youth are refusing to stop there . Bihar, Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan have all seen major controversies around recruitment examinations. What has been missing in those states is a sustained movement capable of turning those grievances into broader political pressure . For now, and despite the state government's concession, the students in Ranchi are refusing to call off their protest. "We are waiting to find out what happens. These fraudulent examinations have to end, but our patience is running thin too," Motilal Mahto, one of the protesters, told DW. https://www.politico.eu/article/europes-.text: The brutally hot summer is set to cost the EU economy €180 billion this year — that’s equivalent to roughly 1 percent of GDP, which is all the growth the bloc was expected to generate in 2026, according to new analysis. France could lose 1.4 percentage points of growth, which is enough to push its economy into a 0.6 percent contraction, while an 0.8-point hit could almost wipe out the Netherlands’ expected expansion. “The result is not simply ‘the hottest countries lose the most,'” notes the analysis by Triodos Bank . “Spain and Italy have the highest physical exposure and the most hot days in absolute terms, but decades of acclimatisation imply that the marginal effect of any single hot day is comparatively small.” Advertisement Advertisement The biggest drag is expected to come from people struggling to work in extreme heat. Triodos estimates lost labor productivity alone could shave around 0.6 percent off EU GDP, while agricultural output could fall by between 3 and 7 percent. “At first sight this might seem modest, but it is exactly the expected economic growth for the EU this year,” said the bank of the overall €180 billion blow. And the summer is not over. France and Britain are bracing for their fifth heat wave of the season this week, with temperatures nearing 40 degrees Celsius in southeastern France and 36 degrees forecast in the U.K. The bill is already mounting beyond GDP. POLITICO estimated at least 14,000 excess deaths across the six hardest-hit European countries during the record-breaking heat wave from mid-June to early July. Drought has also hammered Europe’s energy system: Low water levels in the Danube in recent weeks have forced sharp cuts at Hungary’s Paks nuclear plant and pushed Romania to blast apart a rock to divert water toward its last operating reactor. Vessels on the Rhine and Danube have had to sail only partially loaded. In Austria, meanwhile, drought has caused an estimated €1 billion in agricultural losses , according to Austrian Hail Insurance, after some regions received more than 75 percent less rain than normal since mid-June. Triodos warned against treating this summer as a freak event, saying extreme heat “might become structural” as the planet warms. But governments can soften the damage through irrigation, insulation, cooling and shifting working hours, said the bank. “Every year adaptation without mitigation is a year borrowed against a hotter baseline.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.politico.eu/article/moldova-.text: Moldovan President Maia Sandu has blamed Russia’s war in Ukraine for a recent drone crash in the southeast of her country. A drone crashed and exploded in the village of Crocmaz on Sunday, causing a fire that damaged several properties but caused no casualties. After conducting preliminary analysis on the fragments, local police said it could be a “missile-like drone.” “I strongly condemn the latest violation of our airspace,” Sandu wrote on X, adding: “This is a direct consequence of Russia’s war, and it endangers us all.” Advertisement Advertisement Sandu said that the “risk to human life in our region is real and growing. It must stop.” The affected village is close to southwestern Ukraine, particularly the Odesa region, which came under a heavy missile and drone attack by Russia on the same day. Moldovan police said that to date, no other aircraft of this type have been found on Moldovan territory and research is continuing to establish “the exact type and origin of the aircraft as well as the circumstances of the incident.” Last week, local police discovered wreckage from a Russian Geran-2-type drone near the village of Văleni in southern Moldova. After the incidents, Moldova’s foreign ministry recalled its ambassador from Russia for consultations.

https://www.politico.eu/article/hopes-fo.text: LONDON — Nigel Farage ruled out entering talks with right-wing rival Rupert Lowe Monday — unless Lowe moves to expel a controversial ally. The pathway to power for Farage’s Reform UK was already narrowing before new Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s takeover aided a polling bounce for the governing Labour Party. While still polling in the single digits, Rupert Lowe’s splinter party has been proving it can eat into a significant chunk of Reform’s vote. Lowe formed Restore Britain after being kicked out of Reform — but he has been, at least ostensibly, dangling an olive branch for Farage to grasp in recent weeks. Advertisement Advertisement On Monday the prospect of the two warring factions signing a make-up pact seemed to be at an impasse. Farage used a press conference in Westminster to publicly state a new condition for holding discussions with “that party,” as he referred to Restore. Lowe must, he said, kick out Restore’s co-founder — a move Lowe has already rejected . “I’m always happy to meet people and talk to people — within reason,” Farage said when asked by POLITICO what his conditions for entering talks with Lowe would be. Leader of Restore Britain Rupert Lowe speaks to the media in Wigan, England on June 18, 2026. | Ryan Jenkinson/Getty Images “But I do think it’s fair to say that there are one or two people in the orbit of the upper echelons of that party who, if I sat down and talked to, I think our members and our voters would be utterly shocked that I’d done it,” he added. “So we can talk to Rupert Lowe — that’s fine. But when you have co-founders, etcetera, putting out what I would call the ‘old theory’ — the old theory that we probably haven’t heard in this country since 1936 — and you have other adjacent publicly-supportive people demanding that all Jews be removed from the country, just as an example… “So the condition I would put on it is those people would have to be out of the inner circle — and I think that for me would be the only way we could sensibly proceed.” Advertisement Advertisement The co-founder Farage referred to is Charlie Downes, who was this month accused of implying that Farage had been “ bought ” by Jewish supporters. Campaigners against anti-semitism accused Downes of perpetuating the “oldest smear” against Jewish people. Farage’s attack on “publicly-supportive people demanding that all Jews be removed from the country” is meanwhile a reference to Steve Laws, a backer of Restore Britain who is an advocate of “ total remigration .” Lowe told POLITICO in June that Laws plans “no part in our decision-making process,” although Lowe said he is “very welcome” to support the party. Lowe had already indicated his opposition to booting out Downes after the Telegraph first reported Farage’s rejection of talks. “Farage and Reform have also said that Restore Britain must outright sack Charlie Downes — putting a young Christian man out of work, just as he is looking to build his life and start a family,” Lowe wrote on X . “That is simply not how I operate.” While still polling in the single digits, Rupert Lowe’s splinter party has been proving it can eat into a significant chunk of Reform’s vote. | Darren Staples/AFP via Getty Images It’s the latest twist in a convoluted saga that is commanding attention on the right of British politics. Lowe last week offered to put “ past disagreements ” with Farage aside so that the pair can work together. But he set five conditions for doing so, including the exclusion of Conservative defectors to Reform from a future Farage cabinet. Prisons push Farage’s comments came at a press conference he held to add to pressure on the new prime minister over Britain’s prisons, which have in recent years been hovering around breaking point. Advertisement Advertisement Farage said Reform UK will begin talks with El Salvador about renting prison space so a future government he leads could deport all foreign prisoners to serve their sentences abroad — an echo of Donald Trump’s controversial policy for prisoners from the U.S. Other possible countries that could forge similar deals, Farage suggested, are Kosovo, as well as Estonia or Lithuania. Reform claimed the plans would free up 10,000 spaces in U.K. prisons. However, nearly a third of foreign nationals in detention are on remand, meaning they haven’t been convicted of a crime and are awaiting trial. Pressed about the disparity, home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf told POLITICO: “That’s not the gotcha that you might think it is. “The vast majority of those people end up being convicted — so in terms of the practical plan that we’ve laid out, it makes no difference.”

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy9w.text: Image source, Reuters Image caption, Yabloko chairmain Nikolai Rybakov was at the hearing in Moscow By Laura Gozzi Â and Â Sergey Goryashko Published 32 minutes ago Russia's only liberal, anti-war party will not be able to take part in next month's parliamentary elections, a Moscow court has ruled. Yabloko was the only registered party to oppose Russia's war on Ukraine. The case against it was brought forward by Rodina, a pro-Kremlin nationalist party. Hundreds of people - mostly very young - on Monday had stood outside the Moscow courthouse where the hearing was taking place in support of Yabloko, singing songs and waving flags. Videos posted on social media showed that when news of the verdict spread among the crowd, many started chanting: "Shame! Shame!" The lawsuit by the Rodina party accused Yabloko of publicly supporting an extremist organisation by publishing material on its website in support of the "international LGBT movement", which Russia's Supreme Court designated as extremist in 2023. Rodina also said Yabloko was guilty of copyright infringement after a senior party member had quoted the lyrics of a Soviet-era song - "Let there always be sunshine" - in an interview. At the hearing, Russia's financial monitoring service also claimed that Yabloko received money through third parties from foreign countries, including Germany and the US. The Kremlin-controlled Central Electoral Commission had approved Yabloko's candidate list in late July. But by then several party members had already been barred from running, including two deputy chairmen and deputy leader Maxim Kruglov, who was sentenced in June to seven years' imprisonment for social media posts about civilian casualties in Bucha, Mariupol and other Ukrainian cities. And last week, Yabloko had suffered a cyberattack soon after launching a donations appeal for its election campaign fund. It campaigned under the slogan "For peace and freedom! For a life without fear!" and advocated for a "ceasefire, diplomacy, and peace" and "for a Russia free from fear and political repression". Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Hundreds of young Russians gathered on Monday in support of Yabloko Hundreds gathered outside the Moscow courthouse, chanting "Russia" and "Yabloko" - the Russian word for "apple" - as the eight-hour hearing dragged on. Many carried apples as a sign of support. Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, any remaining opposition to the Kremlin has been crushed. Public shows of dissent have been suppressed by wartime censorship laws and can trigger hefty fines or long prison sentences. Because protests are no longer permitted, the Yabloko hearing offered a rare chance for likeminded Russians opposing the war to gather publicly. "For Yabloko. For freedom" was scribbled in chalk on the pavement outside the courthouse. Yabloko has not won Duma seats since 2003 but has contested every election since. Once led by presidential contender Grigory Yavlinsky, it later fractured with allies - expelling the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny in 2007 and criticising him even after he was eventually imprisoned ahead of his death in 2024. Still, Yabloko remained Russia's most consistent anti-war voice, opposing Russia's war on Chechnya, the 2014 annexation of Crimea, and the invasion of Ukraine. With ruling party United Russia's ratings down to 33% amid inflation, internet blackouts and drone strikes, Yabloko's support had been surging. The Kremlin could have allowed Yabloko to contest the election and initially appeared to be leaning in that direction, potentially to use the party's marginal result in 2021 - when it won just 1.34% of the vote - to demonstrate how unpopular an anti-war stance is in Russia. But the Kremlin appears to have changed its calculations as signs of growing dissent over the war in Ukraine emerge. Without a political force that clearly represents the opposition on the ballot, fewer people may be motivated to go to the polls. A low-turnout election, particularly among those who oppose the ruling party, is exactly what the Kremlin wants. All 10 other parties taking part in the election either support the war in Ukraine or do not openly criticise it. And although United Russia's ratings appear to be in a deep dive, the Kremlin still has the resources to deliver the outcome it wants at the election. Independent election watchdogs have been deprived of much of their ability to monitor and challenge the process. https://maritime-executive.com/corporate.text: news features Podcasts magazine newsletter Jobs advertise subscribe 179 Views Upgraded Baltic Container Terminal Handles Largest Vessel to Call at Gdynia Published Jul 27, 2026 7:17 PM by The Maritime Executive [By ICTSI] Baltic Container Terminal (BCT), International Container Terminal Services, Inc.’s (ICTSI) operation at the Port of Gdynia, Poland, successfully handled the inaugural call of MSC Venice – the largest and longest vessel to call at the Port of Gdynia. The 399-meter-long vessel with a capacity of 16,652 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEU) recently docked at BCT, demonstrating the port’s capability to service the largest container ships operating in the Baltic Sea. Piotr Gorze?ski, Port of Gdynia Authority management board president and chief executive officer, highlighted the recent developments in the port and how they paved the way for the milestone: “The maiden call of MSC Venice is a historic moment and a very tangible result of the investments that have transformed the capabilities of our ports in recent years. The deepening of port waters, the reconstruction of the Helskie Quay, and the expansion of Turning Basin No. 2 have created the conditions for the safe handling of the largest container vessels entering the Baltic Sea. This is an important step for the Port of Gdynia, BCT and the entire port and logistics sector in Gdynia.” On the other hand, Patrick Chan, BCT chief executive officer, said: “The arrival of MSC Venice is a defining moment for BCT and the Port of Gdynia. It validates the significant investments made by all stakeholders to accommodate the next generation of larger container ships and reinforces our position as a deep-water gateway port to support Poland’s economic growth.” The vessel’s arrival marks the completion of recent upgrades in BCT, which include the commissioning of new quay cranes and yard equipment—investments that have significantly expanded the terminal’s operational capabilities and capacity efficiently handle the largest container vessels in the Baltic Sea. The successful call is also a result of years of cooperation with and commitment from numerous partners – the Port of Gdynia Authority, the Maritime Office in Gdynia, the Polish Navy and all stakeholders involved in the development of the port. https://www.ibtimes.com/ai-helping-cyber.text: Artificial Intelligence is giving cybersecurity teams new tools to detect threats and automate routine work. However, that very technology is allowing cybercriminals to launch more convincing attacks faster and on a larger scale at the same time.While AI models developed by companies such as Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google can help hackers identify vulnerabilities in computer systems faster than before, security teams are using similar models to detect and fix those same weaknesses.Anthropic reported last November that Chinese hackers used its AI model for what the company called a "highly sophisticated espionage campaign." According to the company, attackers used the model to gather intelligence and support vulnerability research, illustrating how AI can accelerate multiple stages of sophisticated cyber operations.The biggest shift is not that AI allows attackers to do something entirely new, but that it dramatically reduces the time and expertise required. Tasks that once demanded specialized knowledge, such as writing convincing phishing emails in multiple languages and analyzing source code for vulnerabilities, can now be completed in minutes.A recent report from AI-native threat intelligence firm Cyble recorded 69 ransomware attacks against the US banking, finance and insurance sector in the first half of 2026. These attacks were carried out by 20 separate groups, fifteen of which managed just one attack each, a fragmentation that shows a low barrier to entry and an evolving system of threats.Echoing this view, Domininkas Virbickas, product director at VPN provider NordVPN, told International Business Times that AI was not necessarily creating new attack strategies by enhancing those that already existed.Changing the rulesEurope's multilingual environment once offered digital users a degree of accidental protection. Poor translations and unnatural wording often made fraudulent messages easier to identify. Attackers now use generative AI to remove this barrier.Before the technology became widely available, criminals often had to rely on non-native speakers or poor machine translators, making phishing attempts in smaller European countries easier to identify.Today's large language models (LLMs) can produce fluent, natural-sounding text in dozens of languages, removing one of the accidental barriers that previously limited the effectiveness of cross-border scams."AI writes beautiful texts in various languages, and that raises the bar," Virbickas said.He went on to note that the most common AI-assisted scams involve fake online shops and fraudulent websites, where victims pay for products that never arrive. "AI boosts current scam methods because they require time, effort, hosting a website, contacting people, sending emails or messages," he said. "It makes the activities cheaper and faster."Beyond producing convincing emails, AI can automate document creation, data analysis, code generation, and translation, tasks that cybercriminals routinely rely on.In the past, spelling mistakes and awkward phrasing were clear warning signs. Today, distinguishing a phishing email from a legitimate one has become more difficult. The same applies to AI-generated or manipulated images, which can appear authentic at first glance.Fighting fire with fireCybersecurity companies, VPN providers, and hosting services also use the technology to detect phishing websites and identify suspicious activity. Virbickas said large language models are used as tools to review code, but are not allowed to operate without human oversight.Developers also need to understand the risks that AI introduces and design systems that detect them, said Mantas Lukauskas, AI tech lead at Hostinger, a Lithuanian web-hosting company. "We worked on a phishing detector, and one of the features that we developed was discovering whether a domain name was real or phishing," he told International Business Times.Until recently, analyzing website imagery required specialized computer-vision models such as convolutional neural networks, or CNNs, he added. "To classify imagery, you had to use a convolutional neural network, but right now you can just send screenshots to any LLM, and it will do the work."New pitfallsOne common mistake employees make is uploading sensitive information indiscriminately into AI tools. According to Lukauskas, this can create serious risks for companies."You need to keep your data secure. You also need to understand that it can be leaked by being input into the LLMs," Lukauskas explained. In 2023, Bloomberg reported that Samsung engineers leaked internal source code by uploading it to ChatGPT.Entering proprietary code or confidential documents into public AI systems may expose sensitive information if organizations do not have appropriate privacy controls in place. This is where the threat lies. "Attackers can discover weak spots," added the AI tech lead.AI-generated code creates additional risks. It may rely on outdated software libraries, reproduce insecure coding patterns, or generate code that appears functional but contains hidden vulnerabilities. Attackers may also learn to recognize weaknesses commonly produced by particular models. "If they can identify those patterns, they may be able to exploit them. That's why relying solely on AI isn't a good idea."AI itself has become a target. As organizations integrate the technology into their products and workflows, the code has to be more secure than ever. While this integration allows for sped-up procedures and internal flows, attackers also have more opportunities to conduct malicious activities.Thinking criticallyAccording to Lukauskas, thinking critically is one of the most important things at a time when AI has become so widely used for scams and malicious activities on the web."Even if an email or a logo looks good, you're not safe," he explained. Although AI models have improved, they can still produce incorrect answers. Their outputs should be treated as suggestions rather than unquestionable facts, especially when security decisions are involved.As AI continues to develop, the cybersecurity landscape evolves as well. Users can no longer rely on obvious warning signs such as poor grammar or awkward translations. Instead, they need to verify the source of emails, websites, and requests for sensitive information, even when they might appear legitimate.Building trustAs scams become more sophisticated, cybersecurity companies face a growing challenge of their own, namely, convincing users that they can be trusted. For companies such as VPN providers, demonstrating security requires more than making promises. According to Virbickas, it involves independent audits, transparency, and continuous testing.One approach used by NordVPN is commissioning no-log reports, which include the types of information the company does not collect, store, or record any user activities. "We work with the Big Four (KPMG, PwC, Deloitte or EY) and we give them access to our servers and infrastructure. In this way, they can see what is being logged or not," Virbickas explained.The company also commissions assessments of the security of its code. Such external reviews are intended to give users evidence that a company's security and privacy claims have been independently examined.

https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/ukraine-w.text: Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Updated Tue, 28 July 2026 at 3:52 am UTC 0 Voldoymyr Zelenskyy said the drone display organised by Vasyl Goncharuk, pictured arriving in court, ‘certainly should not have taken place there’.Photograph: Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP/Getty Images A Ukrainian court remanded in custody the organiser of a weapons exhibition that was struck by Russia in an attack that killed at least 11 people. Prosecutors brought a case against Vasyl Goncharuk, head of the Armada weapons industry association, accusing him of negligence leading to loss of life after the Russian ballistic missile strike on a shooting range outside Kyiv on Friday. Volodymyr Zelenskyy said it “certainly should not have been taking place there”. Russia’s defence ministry confirmed it hit the site during “a demonstration of Ukrainian and foreign-made” drones. Goncharuk appeared at the Kyiv court limping and said he sustained light injuries in the attack. Prosecutors have said the weapons association invited more than 300 people including military personnel , state representatives and business figures without official authorisation, providing only a small shelter. The event was even promoted on social media. Agence France-Presse said its reporters saw homes in ruins and victims in body bags after the attack. Previous incidents of Russian attacks on openly held Ukrainian military gatherings have also triggered outcry and resignations. A Wildberries warehouse in the Koledino district of Moscow was reportedly on fire on Tuesday morning after being hit by drones as the Russian capital came under attack . The distribution complex for the Amazon-like chain had been targeted previously. A steel factory in Chekhnov, Moscow oblast, was also hit, the Kyiv Independent reported . The Russian regional governor, ‌Andrei Vorobyov, said an apartment ⁠building in Chekhov was damaged. Drones targeted other areas including ​Podolsk, ‌Domodedovo and ​Kolomna. The Pentagon official tasked with building ⁠a domestic drone ​industry said on Monday the US was still far behind Ukraine’s production capabilities . Travis Metz, chief operating officer of the Defense Innovation Unit, told Reuters that Ukraine would produce 6m-7m small first-person-view attack drones ​this year – roughly 500,000 a month. By comparison, the ‌Pentagon’s $1.1bn programme will have ordered ‌just under 200,000 altogether by February. But the US would catch up and lead the sector, he predicted. The Pentagon is insisting military drones must be made with US parts to foster “a wholly domestic” supply chain. None of the drones from the 19 companies competing an August test event may contain banned parts like Chinese-made ​motors or battery packs. “It’s an increasingly difficult thing,” Metz said. Ukrainian companies competing in the test, called Gauntlet II, are being required to localise production in the US as a condition of future orders. All ⁠100 members of the US Senate have been invited to ⁠a meeting ⁠on ​Tuesday evening with Volodymyr Zelenskyy . Ukraine’s president will be in Washington for the funeral of the late Republican senator Lindsey Graham, who was a strong and influential supporter of Ukraine. A Senate aide ​said voting might also begin during Zelenskyy’s visit on a bill to impose sanctions on Russia that was championed by Graham. Zelenskyy is due to meet on Tuesday with Donald Trump. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022, the war in Ukraine has changed dramatically. The Guardian’s Luke Harding looks at who has the advantage in the war now and how Zelenskyy’s strategy has shifted. Andy Burnham welcomed Zelenskyy in his first meeting with another world leader since becoming the UK prime minister , writes Pippa Crerar. “It is intended to send a very clear message,” Burnham told him. “We are with Ukraine 100%, I am personally with you 100%, and I will honour every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.” Burnham said Britain was providing new jamming technology to Ukraine that would “help them to hit their targets and help save Ukrainian lives”. The system is known as Stone Cloak . Zelenskyy posted that he was “grateful” to Britain for “today’s decision to provide Ukraine with electronic warfare technologies” that would “certainly be useful on the battlefield”. Romania’s ⁠foreign ministry ⁠said it had expelled a ⁠diplomat at Russia’s embassy after repeated violations of ⁠its national airspace by ​drones. Romanian F-16 fighter jet pilots have shot down three drones in as many days. The Russian ambassador was shown drone fragments that Romanian authorities identified as a Russian “Shahed model” . Two people were hurt in May when a drone smashed into an apartment building in the Romanian city of Galati near the border with Ukraine. Ukraine ⁠struck a Russian export ⁠terminal in ⁠the Rostov ​region , as well ⁠as oil facilities in ⁠the Yaroslavl and ​Udmurtia ‌regions, Zelenskyy said on Monday. “Last night, our long-range sanctions were effective in the Rostov region. An export terminal approximately 250km (155 miles) from the frontline was hit,” he posted. “Deep strikes also targeted oil facilities in the Yaroslavl region and the Udmurt Republic , which is 1,300km from Ukraine ’s state border.” Five people were reported killed in Russia’s Rostov region bordering Ukraine. Russian ⁠forces meanwhile struck three Ukrainian ports, including ⁠fuel ⁠loading and ​storage facilities at the port ⁠of Odesa, ​the defence ‌ministry in Moscow said ‌on Monday. Related: The Ukrainian startup taking the missile fight deep into Russia Russian strikes on frontline localities in eastern Ukraine killed ⁠seven people and ⁠injured ​more than 20 on Monday, officials said. Prosecutors in the Donetsk region said three people died ⁠in two areas near the contested city ​of Kostiantynivka. A fourth person was killed near Kramatorsk, a heavily defended “fortress” city considered critical to Ukraine’s defences. Prosecutors said a total of 18 people were ‌injured throughout Donetsk region. In Ukraine’s adjacent Dnipropetrovsk region, the governor, Oleksandr Hanzha, said three people were ​killed and six wounded in more than 50 drone and artillery attacks on five districts. Two people died near the town of Nikopol and one ​person was killed near the town ​of Syneklykove. Over ​the border ​in Russia’s Belgorod region , a Ukrainian drone struck a building, killing one person and injuring two. Donald Trump’s administration has told members ⁠of Congress it will not finish spending $400m in aid to Ukraine until fiscal year 2029, even as Kyiv runs critically low on weapons. Democrats and some ​of Trump’s fellow Republicans have criticised the Pentagon for sitting on aid for Kyiv that members of both parties pushed through last year. In May, the Pentagon sent a letter to lawmakers outlining its spending ⁠plan. It covers $200m for weapons, ammunition and explosives, $99.9m for vehicles, spares and equipment and $100m for services such as transportation of defence articles to ​Ukraine. The funds still have not been put to use. https://www.dnews.gr/eidhseis/news-in-en.text: Gross disposable income in Greece fell 2.5% from the previous quarter, according to Eurostat. Yet household spending on individual consumption rose 1.2% over the same period. Greek households entered 2026 under growing financial strain, diverging sharply from broader European trends as falling incomes forced many families to dip into savings while cutting back on long-term investment. New figures from Eurostat for the first quarter of 2026 show that, while household finances across the European Union and the eurozone remained broadly stable, Greece stood out for the deterioration in its domestic picture. Disposable incomes declined, consumer spending continued to rise, and both savings and investment weakened markedly, suggesting that households are increasingly relying on accumulated financial buffers to maintain day-to-day consumption. Gross disposable income in Greece fell 2.5% from the previous quarter, according to Eurostat. Yet household spending on individual consumption rose 1.2% over the same period, indicating that families continued to spend more despite having less income available. The gap underscores the growing pressure on household budgets as higher living costs and weaker purchasing power leave consumers with fewer options than drawing down savings. Greece recorded the second-largest decline in the household saving rate among EU member states, with the indicator falling by 3.7 percentage points from the previous quarter. Only Romania posted a steeper decline, at 5.3 percentage points, while Hungary recorded the strongest improvement, with its saving rate rising by 3.4 percentage points. Household investment also deteriorated sharply. Gross fixed capital formation—primarily spending on home purchases, construction and renovations—fell 11.8%, the steepest decline among all countries covered by the Eurostat report. Greece also recorded the largest drop in the household investment rate in the EU, down 0.7 percentage points from the previous quarter. Across the European Union, household disposable income increased 0.9% in the first quarter, while consumption rose 0.6% and household investment edged down just 0.5%. In the eurozone, disposable income increased 0.7%, consumption expanded 0.8%, and investment also slipped only marginally, by 0.5%. Broader European indicators point to a far more resilient consumer sector. Real income per capita was unchanged in the eurozone after rising 0.2% in the previous quarter, while it increased 0.1% across the EU. Real consumption per capita remained flat in the eurozone and declined only 0.2% in the EU as a whole. Eurostat attributed the resilience of household incomes across Europe largely to higher employee compensation and increased social benefits. Those gains were partly offset by lower net property income, current transfers, taxes and social contributions, which limited overall income growth. Savings trends further illustrate the divergence. The household saving rate was unchanged in the eurozone and increased by 0.2 percentage points across the EU, suggesting that many European households continue to build financial buffers despite persistent economic uncertainty. Greece moved in the opposite direction. The sharp decline in savings suggests that a growing number of households are either drawing down accumulated reserves or are no longer able to set aside money, highlighting the increasing pressure on family finances even as much of Europe experiences relative stability. https://focustaiwan.tw:443/politics/2026.text: Taiwan, Lithuania resume talks on new investment action plan Taipei, July 28 (CNA) Taiwan and Lithuania have resumed negotiations on a new economic cooperation action plan after talks were temporarily suspended, Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) confirmed Monday. In a statement provided to CNA, MOFA said discussions on the initiative, which Lithuania proposed in March to strengthen bilateral economic ties, have restarted following the approval of Lithuania's new Cabinet by the country's parliament on July 14. "Taiwan remains committed to deepening bilateral economic and trade cooperation with Lithuania based on shared democratic values," the ministry said. The statement came after Lithuania's public broadcaster, LRT, reported Saturday that negotiations, which had been on hold since June, had recently resumed. According to LRT, Lithuania's Ministry of Foreign Affairs told the Baltic News Service that negotiations on the economic cooperation action plan are currently underway with the Taiwanese Representative Office in Lithuania. The talks had stalled during a period of political transition in Lithuania. On June 18, the ruling Social Democratic Party formed a new governing coalition with the Union of Democrats "For Lithuania" and the Farmers and Greens Union after the far-right Nemunas Dawn withdrew from the previous coalition earlier that month. The new coalition led to the appointment of a Cabinet headed by Social Democratic Party Chairman Mindaugas Sinkevičius. Lithuania first proposed the action plan in March, outlining priority industries and potential projects to expand economic cooperation with Taiwan. According to LRT's earlier reporting, the proposal aims to establish "sustainable economic ties" that would support the development of Lithuania's high-tech industries, with a particular focus on attracting Taiwanese investment. Specific details of the plan, however, have not been made public. In April, Eric Huang (黃鈞耀), director-general of MOFA's Department of European Affairs, said that most of the proposed initiatives build on existing Taiwan-Lithuania cooperation in areas including laser technology, medical artificial intelligence, and financial technology (fintech). https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/life.text: Every place, country, city or town has its unique landmark that visitors seek out. For example, Rome in Italy has Trevi Fountain where people toss coins and make a wish. In Prague, they touch historic statues for luck. But in Hungary's capital, Budapest, travellers line up for hours just to rub the belly of a happy-looking bronze statue of a policeman. https://www.dw.com/en/heat-wave-threaten.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5HrGE French authorities worked to keep vacationers away around Bordeaux, banning holiday camps for children and for people with disabilities Image: Emma Da Silva/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement A forecast of an incoming heat wave across France and Spain this week is threatening to hamper firefighting efforts as some of Europe's worst wildfires in decades rage on. France's weather service forecast temperatures of up to 40 degrees Celsius (100 degrees Fahrenheit) from Tuesday, while Spain's AEMET warned of a new heat wave from Wednesday till the end of the week, with highs of 42 degree Celsius in the northeast and 39 degrees Celsius in central regions. Authorities said soaring temperatures, dry winds and low humidity would push wildfire danger to "extreme" levels, even as forests turned tinder-dry by successive heat waves this year. The return of searing temperatures, from Tuesday in France and from Wednesday in Spain, threaten to complicate fire-fighting efforts [FILE: July 23, 2026] Image: Julien De Rosa/AFP Thousands of firefighters and water-dropping aircraft raced to contain the blazes before temperatures rise further. Experts linked the scale of the fires to increasingly frequent and intense heat waves driven by climate change , as hotter and drier conditions are making wildfires more destructive. Macron warns of 'hard' times In France, President Emmanuel Macron said one fire in the Landes region had been contained, but a much larger wildfire near Bordeaux continued to burn after scorching about 42,000 hectares, forcing around 220,000 people to evacuate and destroying hundreds of homes. "The weeks ahead will be hard. We must hold firm," Macron said. Overnight on Tuesday, firefighters prevented a massive wildfire along the Atlantic coast west of Bordeaux from spreading, authorities said. According to officials, 93 firefighters have been injured since the operation began. Aid from Germany arrived in the region on Monday in the form of two transport helicopters and an A400M transport aircraft carrying equipment. In Spain, wildfires west of Madrid and in other regions have forced about 60,000 people to flee. With the coming heat wave threatening to fuel further spread of the wildfires, Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska firefighters in Spain made progress after a "positive night" against wildfires to the west of Madrid. Some 150,000 hectares of land have burned in Spain and 115,000 hectares in France since the start of this year. At a campsite near Navaluenga, west of the capital, ravaged by Spain's worst wildfire on record, the site co-owner Maria Angeles Canete said her family lost everything. "We had this campsite, we had another one, and we've lost it all. We have nothing," she told the AFP news agency. Has Europe lost control of its wildfires? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video EU firefighting resources stretched thin The European Union deployed additional firefighting aircraft to France, while EU commissioner Hadja Lahbib warned that resources are under growing strain as extreme fire conditions spread across southern and central Europe. "Extreme conditions are looming for Hungary, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, in addition to France, the Iberian Peninsula... where the situation is expected to worsen, including in Portugal starting today," Lahbib said. In Italy , a wildfire in the southern Puglia region forced the evacuation of hundreds of tourists from beaches and campgrounds, authorities said. (Image: Barnbrook Systems) This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. A record-breaking year at the Farnborough International Airshow has put a spotlight on the growing importance of global defence and technology. Barnbrook Systems, headquartered in Fareham , marked its 16th consecutive appearance at the airshow by welcoming a record number of visitors from the UK and overseas. Andrew Barnett, managing director at Barnbrook Systems, said: "It was a record year at an airshow which had a very different feel about it. "There was a greater focus than ever on defence and especially upon the application of technology for the rapidly evolving nature of modern warfare. READ MORE: Market traders frustrated over being 'turfed out' during busiest months "It was also telling that many operators, primes and militaries were seeking improved efficiencies to extend the operational life and effectiveness of their platforms amid budgetary pressures despite increasing geo-political instability." The company showcased a range of technologies at its stand, including Maintenance, Repair and Overhaul (MRO) services, its BlueCube-powered sensing and monitoring technology, and the E:BAG lithium-ion battery fire suppression device developed in partnership with Flair. Mr Barnett, who is also a board member of the Farnborough Aerospace Consortium (FAC), said: "We are now following up on contacts made at the show and business opportunities around the world to support Barnbrook’s strategic growth and support the UK and allied defence infrastructure." Among the visitors to the Barnbrook stand were MPs and representatives from Germany, the US, France, India, and Czechoslovakia. The firm also hosted a reception for the South Central Regional Defence and Security Cluster (SCRDSC), which Mr Barnett chairs. More than 120 delegates attended the SCRDSC breakfast event, held at the FAC stand, to network and explore new partnership opportunities. READ MORE: Dozens of businesses join campaign to protect free-roaming animals Defence Secretary Wes Streeting confirmed at the show that the government's £298b Defence Investment Plan will go ahead, including a £15bn uplift over the next four years. Mr Barnett said: "The Defence Investment Plan is finally out, and with the new government team in place, we are now more hopeful within the defence sector. "Mr Streeting must be prepared to fight the corner of defence and secure even greater investment, which must make its way down the supply chain through prime contractors to SMEs."
