https://www.koreaherald.com/article/1082.text: Zelenskyy and Britain's new leader discuss drone projects and missile defense for Kyiv Published : July 28, 2026 - 13:27:15 Add The Korea Herald on Google Link copied! British Prime Minister Andy Burnham (left) and Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy (right) talk during their visit to Portsmouth Naval Base in Portsmouth, Hampshire, UK, Monday. (Reuters-Yonhap) LONDON (AP) — Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and new UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham met Monday at a British naval base and discussed joint drone projects and Ukraine's urgent need for ballistic missile interceptors to counter Russian attacks. Zelenskyy’s visit was the first by a foreign leader since Burnham took office a week ago, and the prime minister said it signaled the UK's “unwavering” support for Kyiv to defend itself against Russia's 4-year-old, full-scale invasion. His predecessor, Keir Starmer, was in the Ukrainian capital less than two weeks ago in his last overseas trip before leaving office, and Burnham said he planned to visit soon. Burnham is the fifth British prime minister Zelenskyy has dealt with since Russia launched the war in 2022. "You are the first leader I have welcomed in person since taking office, and that is no accident,” Burnham told Zelenskyy. “It is intended to send a very clear message: we are with Ukraine 100 percent, I am personally with you 100 percent, and I will honor every commitment this country has made to Ukraine in full.” Zelenskyy said the two countries' relationship was “stronger than ever.” The meeting, aboard the aircraft carrier HMS Queen Elizabeth docked at Portsmouth on England’s south coast, came a day before Zelenskyy was expected to visit US President Donald Trump in Washington. Burnham said they had “talked at length” about Kyiv's need for more interceptors to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles, “particularly in terms of Ukraine protecting critical national infrastructure during the winters.” “We’ve taken away some things that we will now follow up with our partners,” Burnham said after the meeting. Russia has intensified strikes on gas stations, power facilities and other infrastructure this year in a broad campaign to strain Ukraine’s logistics and energy networks. Zelenskyy said on X that the leaders also discussed “joint defense production.” Britain and Ukraine already have a deal to work together on new drones, and Zelenskyy told Sky News beforehand that he hoped to build a “big, big factory” in Britain. They also met more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent three weeks in Britain for an exercise aimed at strengthening their fighting capabilities and measures to counter mines in the Black Sea, the UK government said. Burnham announced that the UK will give Ukraine the intellectual property behind its new “Stone Cloak” electronic warfare system, which is capable of jamming Russian air defenses to stop drones from being detected. Ukraine has expanded its campaign of frequent drone attacks deep inside Russia that have targeted oil facilities, military factories and, most recently, logistical centers, bringing the war home to millions of Russians and raising pressure on President Vladimir Putin. The raids have shattered Putin’s narrative of the conflict as something that doesn’t affect the lives of ordinary people in his country. But he has remained undeterred and Russia has ramped up its aerial campaign, regularly bombarding Ukraine with missiles and drones. Russia again attacked Ukraine overnight with 147 long-range drones, according to Ukraine's air force, which said it intercepted or jammed 123 of them. In Zaporizhzhia, one person was killed and two injured in attacks on the city that damaged a residential high-rise and several private homes overnight, according to regional administration head Ivan Fedorov. A Russian strike on the town of Balakliia in the Kharkiv region killed one person and wounded eight, according to Vitalii Karabanov, head of the city military administration. In the Nikopol district of the Dnipropetrovsk region, Russian strikes damaged a kindergarten, residential buildings and infrastructure, injuring a woman and a 6-year-old boy, according to administration head Oleksandr Hanzha. In the eastern Kharkiv region, regional council member Oleksandr Skoryk said Russian forces destroyed every gas station along the highway between Kharkiv and Poltava, a distance of about 150 kilometers. The highway is a key supply route linking Kharkiv, the country’s second-largest city and a regional hub close to the Russian border, with central Ukraine. Romania’s Ministry of National Defense said a drone briefly entered its airspace before crossing the river border into Ukraine, where explosions were subsequently reported. It said two F-16 fighter jets were deployed to monitor airspace. The drone’s incursion into Romanian airspace marked the fourth such incident in as many days. The three previous drones were all shot down by the NATO member. In Moscow, Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 276 Ukrainian drones overnight. Rostov regional Gov. Yuri Slyusar said five people, including a child, were killed when a Ukrainian drone hit an apartment building in Rostov-on-Don. Ukraine’s military General Staff said Ukrainian forces struck an export terminal in Rostov-on-Don, setting it ablaze. The Ukrainian military said other strikes in the Moscow-held part of the Kherson region targeted a ground relay station used to control drones and a bridge over the Henichesk Strait that Russia uses for military logistics. Russian fuel and supply depots were also hit. In the city of Belgorod in southwestern Russia near the border with Ukraine, a Ukrainian drone attack injured 12, including two children, according to regional emergency officials. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Ukraine struck an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea, killing a sailor. In a statement on X on Sunday, Araghchi denounced the attack as a “blatant U.N. Charter violation done at Israel’s behest to drag Europe into its war.” He said he made it clear in calls with the European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas and Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov that the attack “can't go unanswered.” Zelenskyy said on X that Ukrainian long-range strikes in the Caspian Sea over the weekend achieved “very good results,” adding the targets included “vessels involved in transporting military cargo linked to Iran, as well as a warship.” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha rejected Iran’s threats of retaliation as unjustified and groundless, saying Tehran's weapons supplies to Russia have made it a direct accomplice to Moscow's aggression. “Iran has no standing to pretend to be a victim,” he posted on X, and called its references to the UN Charter “absurd.” Sybiha said Iran’s statements were an attempt to divert attention from Russia’s attacks on civilian shipping in the Black Sea, which would be a focus of an emergency UN Security Council meeting this week. good 0 sad 0 angry 0 recommended 0 More from Headlines Firefighters battle blaze at hazardous materials warehouse in Pyeongtaek Firefighters continued to battle a large fire at a hazardous materials warehouse in Pyeongtaek, Gyeonggi Province, on Tuesday, hours after it broke out shortly after midnight. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Donald Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response to Iranian negotiators making claims for the damages from the five-month war. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP View image in fullscreen Donald Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response to Iranian negotiators making claims for the damages from the five-month war. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Iran Trump demands Iran pay compensation for decades of US soldier deaths US president’s statement is latest sign that negotations to end war and reopen strait of Hormuz have stalled Andrew Roth in Washington Mon 10 Aug 2026 16.45 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 17.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump has said he will demand that Iran pay compensation for the deaths of thousands of US soldiers and Iran’s own civilians killed in recent decades in the latest sign his negotiations to end the war and reopen the strait of Hormuz have reached an impasse. The US president is trying to end conflicts in Iran , Gaza and Lebanon, and his additional demands of Iran are likely to provoke anger in Tehran at the same time as Israel has rejected Trump’s terms for a 15-point roadmap to end the war in Gaza. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response to Iranian negotiators making similar claims for damages for the five-month war that has killed thousands and devastated Iran’s military and economy. Iran issues tough demands to reopen strait of Hormuz as deal still out of reach Read more “Now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by Gen Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Additionally, compensation should be paid to the families of the hundreds of thousands of innocent protesters that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months.” The demands are likely to be a nonstarter for Iran’s leaders in the careful peace negotiations aimed at reopening the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of global oil trade flowed before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in late February. Trump and other senior negotiators have claimed many times that a deal is imminent, although none has materialised. The remarks followed a series of setbacks for Trump’s efforts to end several Middle East conflicts before the midterm elections in November, in which high oil prices and inflation will probably hurt fellow Republicans at the polls. On Sunday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he rejected the Trump-backed Board of Peace’s 15-point plan to end Israel’s war in Gaza . Netanyahu had said Hamas must fully disarm before Israel would consider pulling out of Gaza, rather than the phased withdrawal proposed by the Board of Peace. Netanyahu framed the decision as a rejection of US pressure on Israel to make peace in several wars in the Middle East. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said. Iran plots to deal Trump a blow in midterms by keeping him entangled in war Read more Trump has not replied to Netanyahu’s statement, which was a remarkably public break between the leaders of the US and its closest ally in the Middle East. But in response to a shouted question in the Oval Office on Monday, he said his relationship with Netanyahu was “very good”. Trump has sought to increase pressure on Iran. An hour after his first post demanding war reparations from Tehran, he broadened their scope to include the victims of recent wars throughout the region. “Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!” he wrote. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Ann Widdecombe’s body was found with serious injuries at her home in Devon on 9 July. Photograph: Lucy North/PA View image in fullscreen Ann Widdecombe’s body was found with serious injuries at her home in Devon on 9 July. Photograph: Lucy North/PA UK news Ann Widdecombe police investigate whether accused had role in Farage incident Police looking into whether Joshua Kerry linked to alleged attempted burglary last year at Reform leader’s then home Vikram Dodd Police and crime correspondent Mon 10 Aug 2026 14.46 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 15.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police are investigating whether Joshua Kerry, the man charged with the murder of the former Reform UK and Conservative politician Ann Widdecombe, had any role in an attempted burglary last year at the then London home of Nigel Farage. Kerry, 28, from Rotherham, was charged with the murder of Widdecombe, 78, who was killed at her Devon home in July, after an investigation by counter-terrorism police. On Friday, police said they were reinvestigating an incident in April 2025 at a London address where Farage was living at the time, which they have said was an attempted burglary. Other sources describe it as an attempted arson. Police attended the incident, which they initially recorded primarily as a burglary. The Guardian understands detectives are studying fingerprints taken from the scene, as well as video from CCTV cameras in the area and from devices such as video doorbells. They examined the scene to see if an accelerant, such as lighter fluid, was used. On Friday, Counter Terrorism Policing (CTP) said it had referred itself to the police watchdog over the initial investigation of the April 2025 incident. It said: “As part of the ongoing investigation led by Counter Terrorism Policing South East into the murder of Ann Widdecombe, officers have reopened an investigation into an incident reported to police last year. “In April 2025, the Metropolitan police received a report of an attempted burglary at an address in the Greater London area. Enquiries were carried out by the Metropolitan police, supported by Counter Terrorism Policing London. No arrests were made and the investigation was subsequently closed, pending any new lines of inquiry. “Following the reopening of the attempted burglary investigation, Counter Terrorism Policing London identified a line of enquiry which was not identified and pursued by them at the time, which may have been relevant. As a result, to ensure their support to the initial investigation is thoroughly reviewed, Counter Terrorism Policing London made a mandatory conduct referral to the Independent Office for Police Conduct today.” On Monday, Farage said at a press conference: “It’s a great, great tragedy that it took the death of Ann for the security services in Britain to finally take seriously the safety and security of Reform politicians and Reform prominent figures.” He said he now had confidence in counter-terrorism police and said they were not trying to cover anything up. The Reform leader said of CTP’s decision to refer itself to the IOPC: “The fact they’ve done that shows you they’re not trying to cover up, they’re not trying to ignore, and I have to say I have met Laurence Taylor [the head of CTP] and I did feel a great, great confidence in it.” Widdecombe’s body was found with “serious injuries” by paramedics at her home in Haytor Vale, Devon, at 11.40am on Thursday 9 July. Kerry’s first court appearance in July heard that Widdecombe died after being hit on the head with a hammer 21 times in her home. Police have said they believed the 78-year-old former minister was attacked the day before her body was found. The attack on Widdecombe has not yet been declared a terrorist incident. CTP took the lead in the investigation because of the possibility there may have been a political motive behind her killing. CTP’s investigations continue. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Donald Trump holds a signed executive order about vaccines as the health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr looks on. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP View image in fullscreen Donald Trump holds a signed executive order about vaccines as the health and human services secretary, Robert F Kennedy Jr looks on. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Donald Trump Trump signs order attempting to override CDC vaccine schedule and break up MMR shots President and RFK Jr, the health secretary, repeatedly referred to autism during signing, though studies show no link between it and vaccines Melody Schreiber and Joseph Gedeon in Washington Mon 10 Aug 2026 18.28 EDT First published on Mon 10 Aug 2026 15.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Donald Trump has signed an executive order with plans for sweeping changes to the childhood vaccination schedule that attempts to override the authority of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). It is an attempt to undergird the changes made earlier this year to CDC vaccination recommendations, which were halted by a federal judge. The CDC is the federal agency tasked with recommending vaccines, not the White House. The order would also require that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine be broken into three separate shots, once it becomes available in the US. And it would recommend that all shots be given at separate medical visits, a frequent point Trump has made despite the safety, ease and lower costs of giving vaccines together. On a press call, a White House official said the order draws on a Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) scientific assessment published in January 2026, which examined “comparisons of the U.S. to other peer-developed nations” and looked at “where there is consensus amongst our peers on recommendations for immunizations for children”. The official said the number of recommended childhood immunizations would drop “down to 11 diseases”, compared with 18 at the end of 2024. Only six of the 17 vaccines currently routinely recommended for all children in the US would continue to have full recommendations: measles, mumps, rubella ( MMR ), diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (DTaP), polio, Hib, pneumococcal disease, HPV and varicella. “Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal,” Trump said of the MMR vaccine at the signing of the order on Monday. Five other shots would be recommended only for those at high risk: monoclonal antibodies to protect against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) as well as vaccines against hepatitis A, hepatitis B and meningococcal ACWY, which is currently recommended for teens and high-risk infants. Dengue and meningococcal B vaccines are also on this list, but dengue was already recommended only for those at risk and meningococcal B was shared clinical decision-making. And six shots would be pushed to shared clinical decision-making: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and Covid-19. This is a previously obscure category that means a provider would be required to weigh the risks and benefits, despite strong evidence for the safety and efficacy of these vaccines. On the call, the White House official said vaccines moved into this category “still are a recommendation, and so we assume that that means they’ll still be covered by insurance” and remain “available to parents that want them”, adding: “The president is interested in getting parents more choice and flexibility.” The executive order would also require the MMR vaccine to be broken into three separate shots, which is not currently possible in the US as there are no separately licensed vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella and the licensing process takes years. The order also states that, “to the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits”. This would put a financial and logistical strain on families and medical providers by creating several additional visits. The US attorney general would also be tasked with challenging state laws that conflict with the executive order. The US has no vaccination mandates. Shots that are required for school attendance are set at the state and local level. Both Trump and Robert F Kennedy, the health secretary, made repeated mentions of autism throughout the order signing, emphasizing a scientifically unproven link between vaccines and the condition. Dozens of studies show no link between the two. “Today we’re proud to officially announce the United States of America’s gold standard childhood vaccination recommendations. That has to do with many subjects including autism in particular,” Trump said at the beginning of the order signing. “I’ve seen proof of it, where they have a vaccination where it looks like the size of a bottle of soda, poured into a little child’s body and bad things happen in too many cases,” Trump later said on breaking up each shot into an individual medical visit, before adding: “This is an explosion, it’s an epidemic,” in an apparent reference to autism. Kennedy claimed at one point: “Something happened in the mid-90s that changed our children, and it has to be an environmental exposure.” On the call, officials were pressed on why Kennedy has not yet delivered the finding on the cause of autism he had promised by the previous September, and why the US president continued to suggest a vaccine-autism link without new supporting evidence from HHS. An official declined to engage directly, asking to keep the discussion “germane to today’s executive order” rather than address the broader autism-research timeline. Asked about criticism from the American Academy of Pediatrics that the administration invoked autism repeatedly during the signing without offering any concrete support for families already raising children with autism, an official pointed instead to a toolkit the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Service released on applied behavior analysis services, framing it as guidance to help states serve autistic patients and curb fraud in relevant programs. Rebuking these claims and ties to autism, Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana senator, tweeted in response to the order that it “is so wrong”. “I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism. Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe. Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong,” Cassidy wrote. Executive orders are meant as guidance to federal agencies; they are not laws passed by Congress, and thus they have no legal effect on the public. The White House official estimated that 28 states “have implemented their own vaccine recommendations or diverged from the federal guidance”. The order is intended to ensure the remaining states “are aware of this information as they go into ... their legislative sessions”, they said, and weigh “what vaccine requirements they want to implement as law in their state, particularly ... school attendance and entry requirements”. “This should have no direct operational effects,” says Dorit Reiss, a vaccines expert at UC Law San Francisco. Twenty-nine states and the District of Columbia have decoupled their vaccination requirements from the CDC, and insurance continues to cover the shots. However, “Trump has influence,” Reiss said, and the order may intensify “political pressure on states” to change school requirements. https://www.dw.com/en/turkey-mps-back-hi.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IatJ Lawmakers applaud after voting on a bill offering limited amnesty for Kurdish PKK militants at the Grand National Assembly of Turkey in Ankara Image: Adem Altan/AFP Advertisement Turkey's parliament on Monday approved legislation offering a conditional pardon and legal protections to thousands of members of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) . After around 12 hours of debate, lawmakers voted 468 to 88 in favor of the 12-article bill, with six abstentions. It was backed by President Recep Tayyip Erdogan's AK Party , its nationalist MHP allies and the pro- Kurdish DEM party. What does Turkey's new PKK law provide? The law sets out procedures for the PKK's disarmament and dissolution and the reintegration of some members into civilian life. The government has stressed that it is not a general amnesty. Some prison sentences would be suspended, while investigations and trials could be postponed for five or 10 years depending on the offense. If those covered commit no terrorism-related crime during that period, cases would be dropped and sentences considered served. Turkish lawmakers debated the bill for around 12 hours before voting on the legislation Image: Mustafa Kaya/Xinhua/picture alliance Around 3,500 PKK-linked detainees could initially be released, lawmakers said. Media reports suggest exiled members and fighters in Iraq and Syria could also benefit. People convicted of intentional killings and some serving life sentences are excluded. When will the law take effect? The measures will only come into force once Turkey's National Security Council confirms that the PKK has dissolved and surrendered all weapons. Those seeking to benefit would then have six months to apply. Ministerial and parliamentary committees are also due to monitor the process. Turkish Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz hailed the vote as a 'historic step' toward ending the decades-long conflict with the PKK [FILE: March 27, 2026] Image: Ahmet Okur/Anadolu Agency/IMAGO Turkey’s Vice President Cevdet Yilmaz called the vote a "historic step", saying "the 468 'yes' votes are of the utmost importance in terms of political consensus". What happens to Abdullah Ocalan? The law does not cover imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan, 77, who has been held on Imrali island near Istanbul since 1999. Yilmaz said Ocalan's case "does not fall within the scope of this law", but added that he could remain "in a position to contribute to the peace process". Ocalan has been central to the initiative. In February 2025, he urged the PKK to disarm and dissolve and pursue Kurdish rights through democratic means. This latest image of imprisoned PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan was provided by the pro-Kurdish DEM party [FILE: February 27, 2026] Image: DEM The PKK announced its dissolution in May 2025. Two months later, militants symbolically burned weapons at a ceremony in northern Iraq and the group said it was withdrawing fighters from Turkey. What does the PKK say? The PKK has called the legislation a "beginning" but said it contains "serious shortcomings and deficiencies." It has demanded Ocalan's release and said the process can move forward only if he "lives and works freely." The group also said fighters would not return without guarantees that they could engage in politics without prosecution over their views or organizations. Pro-Kurdish DEM lawmaker Gulistan Kilic Kocyigit said: "The people of Turkey, who have paid a heavy price for many years, now have an opportunity to consolidate peace and build democracy." Why is the bill controversial? Nationalist opposition lawmakers accuse the government of making concessions to the PKK. "How can you negotiate with terrorists? You said they would be laying down their weapons unconditionally," said Turhan Comez, a lawmaker with the nationalist opposition Iyi party. Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Iyi Party leader Musavat Dervisoglu also said the law "would pave the way" for Erdogan to remain in power. Erdogan could run again if parliament calls an early election during his current term. Why does the conflict matter? The PKK launched its insurgency in 1984. More than 40,000 people have been killed, and the conflict has caused major economic damage in Kurdish-majority southeastern Turkey and fueled decades of political and social division. The PKK initially sought an independent Kurdish state but later shifted toward demands for autonomy and expanded rights. It is designated a terrorist organization by Turkey, the United States and the European Union . Previous peace efforts failed, most recently in 2015. The initiative could also have regional effects, including closer Turkish-Iraqi ties and implications for efforts to integrate areas in Syria administered by the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) with Damascus. The SDF's dominant militia, the People's Defense Units (YPG), is seen as an offshoot of the PKK, and is considered by Ankara to be a terrorist organization. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-top-court-b.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Iaqy 'Everything we do,' said Yabloko leader Nikolai Rybakov, should be dedicated to 'stopping deaths and bringing back peace' Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance Advertisement The Supreme Court of Russia on Monday ruled in favor of the nationalist pro-Kremlin Rodina (Motherland) party and barred Yabloko (Apple) — Russia's only anti-war party — from participating in September parliamentary elections. Rodina accuses Yabloko of receiving undeclared financial support from Western sources, among other things. Arguing before the court, Yabloko vehemently denied the accusations and railed against Rodina's lack of supporting evidence. The nationalist pro-Kremlin Rodina party brought the case, accusing Yabloko of receiving foreign funding, yet without providing evidence to support the claim Image: Pavel Seleznev/TASS/picture alliance On Monday, Judge Vyacheslav Kirillov said, "The claims seeking to annul the registration of the federal list of candidates for the State Duma of the ninth convocation, nominated by the Yabloko political party, were granted." The court's decision means citizens opposed to Russia's four-and-a-half-year invasion of Ukraine — or "special military operation" as it has been legally deemed under penalty of imprisonment — have no opportunity to vote for representatives willing to articulate that opposition. Yabloko leader Nikolay Rybakov told the hundred or so supporters gathered outside the court, "Excluding Yabloko from the election means refusing dialog with people who ask questions that are uncomfortable for the authorities." "We have a long road ahead and we have a big and important task — to stop deaths and bring back peace. Everything we do should be dedicated to that," Rybakov added, vowing to appeal the decision. Yabloko — the only liberal party still operating in Russia since most of President Vladimir Putin 's opponents have been jailed, exiled or murdered — has received the backing of several exiled opposition figures, including Yulia Navalnaya , the widow of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny . Yabloko was once a strong liberal force in Russia but like other opposition outfits it has been systematically sidelined by the Kremlin. The party is currently only polling around three percent — short of the five percent threshold for entry into parliament — and has not won a seat in the federal State Duma since 2003. Putin-backing United Russia has won every single election since then and that is expected to again be the case in September. Yabloko supporters ignored the threat of repression to show support for the party's anti-war stance at the Supreme Court Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance But despite barring political opposition to the war, public opinion toward the conflict has soured, more so since Ukraine has intensified its attacks on energy and logistics infrastructure inside Russia. The non-governmental Levada Center — which is on the Kremlin's "foreign agents" list — charts support at around 66%, the lowest since Russia launched its attack against neighboring Ukraine on February 24, 2022. The Kremlin has cracked down on opposition to the war with strict censorship rules and mass arrests, with many activists and journalists preferring to flee than to face potentially deadly persecution by staying in Russia . https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-earthquak.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IZRh The powerful 7.4 magnitude quake struck early on Monday morning, causing widespread damage in Manizales and other cities Image: Giovanny Galvez/AFP Advertisement A powerful earthquake shook western Colombia early on Monday morning. Around six hours after the quake struck, Colombia's president said that 111 people had been confirmed dead around the country. Rescue teams were working to free residents after buildings collapsed in Cali and other cities. The epicenter was on the eastern tip of the Choco province on Colombia's Pacific coast. What is the latest? Colombia's newly-inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella said that he had personally taken charge of the government's response to the emergency. He said that locating anyone still potentially trapped was the highest priority for rescuers and declared a national state of emergency. "As of 12:30 [local time], the toll stood at 111 dead and 87 injured, with 1,575 homes damaged, 37 completely destroyed, 61 buildings collapsed, and 18 health centers and 52 schools damaged," de la Espriella said from Bogota. Multiple deaths after major earthquake in Colombia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the EU stands "ready to provide more support" to Colombia. The bloc's satellite service, Copernicus, has already been mobilized to aid rescuers. "Tonight, Europe's heart is with the people of Colombia," she wrote on social media. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US was "closely monitoring" the situation and stood "ready to support the people of Colombia." What's happening on the ground? The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said that at least 20 buildings had collapsed, in some cases with people trapped inside. "Residents of Cali, we currently have at least 20 collapsed structures in the city with people trapped inside; we are already managing this emergency alongside all of Cali's rescue agencies," Eder said on Instagram, posting an accompanying video statement. "I have requested support — specifically rescue personnel — from the mayors of Bogota and Medellin." Authorities in the Valle del Cauca, whose capital city is Cali, said that at least 27 people had died in the quake, in numbers issued prior to the president's address. Officials in Risaralda had said that 40 people had died across the state, at least 18 of them in the capital Pereira based on earlier comments from the mayor. The governor of the Choco region where the quake's epicenter was located, Nubia Carolina Cordoba-Curi, said there were 12 dead and 84 wounded in her district as of lunch time local time. And the mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas, said in a radio interview that two people were killed in his city, in the Caldas region not far northeast of Pereira. Residents in Cali tried to rush to safety in the aftermath of Monday's earthquake Image: Santiago Saldarriaga/AP Photo/picture alliance Colombia's civil aviation authority reported damage at six relatively minor airports and said flights were suspended while it was examined. "Damage is reported at the airports of Pereira, Manizales, Quibdo, Armenia, Cartago, and Buenaventura. For safety reasons, air operations at these terminals remain suspended until structural damage to the infrastructure is assessed," it wrote online, later adding Cali's airport to this list. What do we know about the quake's size and location? The US Geological Survey (USGS) measured the quake at magnitude 7.4. Colombia's national authority at first logged a smaller figure but later revised its reading up to 7.4 as well. The epicenter was located just south of the Tatama National Nature Reserve, near Choco's eastern state border. One of the towers at the Cathedral of Manizales was damaged by the quake Image: John Jairo Bonilla/AP Photo/picture alliance The epicenter was roughly equidistant from Colombia's three main cities, Bogota to its east, Medellin to its north and Cali to its south. The closest major population center, Cartago, is home to about 140,000 people and around 30 kilometers (roughly 20 miles) from the quake's epicenter. The USGS said the quake was also quite deep, striking around 107 kilometers below the ground. It estimated that most of the western half of Colombia would feel the tremors . Tremors could also be felt in neighboring Ecuador to the south, and to the north and east in Panama and Venezuela. USGS also recorded a fairly large aftershock, at magnitude 5.0, a little under an hour after the main quake. The so-called Ring of Fire — the world's most active belt of tectonic plates and volcanoes encircling the Pacific Ocean — runs along Colombia's coastline not far from the epicenter of Monday's quake. https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-meta-.text: The EU, Meta and TikTok on Monday agreed to create a dedicated channel with fact-checkers to flag disinformation linked to a surge of migrants arriving in Spanish territory, three people told POLITICO. Thousands of migrants arrived in late July in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in Morocco and the EU’s only land border with Africa. The influx was triggered by false narratives spreading online that told migrants they would be welcomed, according to fact-checking site Maldita.es. The Commission met with representatives from TikTok and Meta on Friday and Monday to coordinate a response to disinformation online. They agreed to set up an “enhanced information exchange and cooperation mechanism for reducing the impact of disinformation on the Ceuta crisis,” said the three people with direct knowledge of the talks, who were granted anonymity to speak freely. Advertisement Advertisement That will serve as a point of contact for platforms, fact-checkers and the Commission to quickly flag content so that it can be reviewed and taken down if necessary. The effort comes amid concerns that disinformation is promoting further crossings into the territory on Aug. 15, according to Maldita.es . Maldita.es and the European Fact-Checking Standards Network attended Monday’s meeting. The Commission operates a rapid response system under its code of conduct on disinformation, often triggered around elections. The new mechanism on Ceuta would bring a closer group of stakeholders together, two of the people said. Another meeting has been set for later this week, one of those people and the third person confirmed. Meta and TikTok said they were already actively monitoring the situation in line with their policies and had set up dedicated teams to monitor and respond to content in real time. The crisis has divided EU countries and has reignited Europe’s long-running debate on illegal migration. Italy has since been one of the harshest critics of Spain’s left-wing government and its migration policies, and has implemented border controls for travelers arriving from Spain. Former EU commissioner Thierry Breton, who was a force behind the EU’s online content rules, on Monday said the bloc should launch a disinformation inquiry into the Ceuta crisis in an interview with Italian newspaper La Stampa. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cgmk.text: Figure caption, Watch: What we know about Tupac murder suspect Duane "Keffe D" Davis By Anoushka Mutanda-Dougherty Â and Â Shaimaa Khalil ,Â Los Angeles Correspondent Published 8 hours ago It's been three decades filled with mystery, conspiracies - and anger. The drive-by shooting that killed rap superstar Tupac Shakur on 7 September 1996 changed the trajectory of hip-hop and elevated the rapper from the face of the genre to a cultural icon. His killing became one of popular culture's great mysteries, with countless theories but no arrests until 2023, when Duane "Keffe D" Davis was unexpectedly charged with murdering the famous rapper. The 63-year-old former gang boss is due to stand trial in Las Vegas, where he is accused of murder with a deadly weapon with the intent to promote, further or assist a criminal gang. He's pleaded not guilty. If convicted, he faces life in prison without parole. The trial is likely to unravel the intricacies of the bitter and deadly East Coast vs West Coast rap rivalries and turf wars between the Bloods and the Crips street gangs that were immortalised in rap lyrics and news reports in the 1990s. It could also include several celebrity witnesses - including Suge Knight, the former CEO of Death Row Records, who has been thought of as the last surviving witness to Shakur's death. But the complicated case hinges almost exclusively on one key piece of evidence: a book co-authored by Davis that he has argued is partially a piece of fiction. Jury selection in the case began on Monday, with opening arguments due to start on 17 August. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tupac's murder helped elevate the rapper from the face of gangsta rap to a cultural icon To understand how the case became so mythologised, you have to go back to rivalries that grew larger than the men at its centre. In the Los Angeles gang landscape of the 1990s, there was a vicious turf war between the Bloods, often represented by the colour red, and Crips, who often wore blue. But that territorial dispute spread through the airwaves as part of a bigger national rivalry - East Coast v West Coast rap. The genre dispute was represented by two rival record companies that defined 1990s hip-hop: Knight's Death Row Records and Sean "Diddy" Combs' Bad Boy Records. "The funny thing about it is Tupac is actually an East Coast rapper," said Jeff Pearlman, author of Only God Can Judge Me: The Many Lives of Tupac Shakur. Born in New York City, Tupac moved to northern California as a teenager. He became known as a southern California rapper after signing with Death Row Records, which included acts like Snoop Dogg and Dr Dre. Santi Elijah Holley, author of An Amerikan Family: The Shakurs and the Nation They Created, says the Death Row persona never told the whole story. Tupac's mother Afeni was a Black Panther and he grew up around the black liberation movement. Holley says his music became his politics: "His activism was his art, his lyrics." He acted in a number of Hollywood movies, and released hip-hop's first double album, All Eyez on Me, which sold over 5,000,000 copies. That album, which debuted months before his death, cemented his place in the cannon of gangsta rap, a genre that celebrated the violent life of street criminals and drug dealers. After he was shot in Las Vegas on 7 September 1996, he became immortalised as a kind of martyr for the lifestyle he helped make famous. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Duane Davis, who's accused of orchestrating Tupac's murder, was the uncle of Orlando Anderson, an alleged member of the South Side Compton Crips That fatal night began when Tupac and Knight attended a boxing match between Mike Tyson and Bruce Seldon at the MGM Grand. After the match, surveillance footage captured Tupac and members of his entourage, who police have said were associated the Mob Piru Bloods street gang, attacking a man named Orlando Anderson, an alleged member of the South Side Compton Crips. About three hours after the attack, Tupac was riding in the passenger seat of Knight's BMW driving through Las Vegas when a white Cadillac pulled alongside them and opened fire. Tupac was hit four times and died six days later. For nearly three decades, the killing remained one of America's most famous unsolved murders. There is no single explanation why. Las Vegas police have long said witnesses refused to co-operate. Members of Tupac's entourage said police initially treated them like suspects and failed to follow important leads. Within weeks of the shooting, investigators had identified Anderson from the MGM footage and questioned him. He denied involvement and was never charged; he was killed in an unrelated shooting in 1998. Over the years, police say they pursued thousands of tips, but the case stalled amid disappearing witnesses, many of whom were also killed in gang-related shootings, limited physical evidence, and a street code that forbade co-operation with police. It was years later when Anderson's uncle, Davis, started talking and according to police, blew the case wide open again. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tupac and Snoop Dogg were both part of the LA record label Death Row Records, run by Suge Knight It was ultimately the death of another legendary rapper that helped unravel Tupac's shooting death. Months after Shakur was gunned down, Biggie Smalls, or the Notorious BIG, was killed in a drive-by shooting in Los Angeles. Both rappers were the stars of their respective rival record labels - Shakur with Death Row Records and Biggie with Bad Boy Records. Biggie's case has remained unsolved, with no arrests or suspects. In the mid 2000s the Los Angeles Police Department reopened the investigation and spoke with Davis, who was at a party with Biggie before the fatal shooting. While Davis said he didn't have information about Biggie's death, he did have knowledge of Tupac's case and shared that he was in the car when the rapper was shot and killed. He told police the information in exchange that he not be charged. That deal stuck until years later, when Davis went public with his knowledge. He co-authored a memoir in 2019 titled Compton Street Legend, that claimed he not only was inside the vehicle when Tupac was shot, but he was also the person who "tossed" the gun used to kill him into the backseat of the Cadillac. He never claimed to be the person who opened fire. Davis also elaborated on the shooting to the media, detailing information to reporters in interviews. Las Vegas police said his public statements had "reinvigorated" the investigation. Over the next couple of years they spent time corroborating Davis' account and then in 2023, searched his home and seized multiple computers, two tubs of photographs and a slew of Tupac-related material, including a Vibe magazine. He was arrested later that year. Prosecutors have alleged that Tupac's killing was in retaliation for the beating of Davis' nephew - Orlando Anderson - just hours before the shooting. They claim that Davis was the architect of the crime, who ordered the shooting and supplied the deadly weapon to further gang criminal conduct. Listen to Fame Under Fire: The Tupac Murder Trial Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Months after Shakur was gunned down, Biggie Smalls or the Notorious BIG, was killed in a drive-by shooting Nevada prosecutors argued that by publicly talking about what happened on the night of Tupac's death and writing a book where he claimed to have supplied the gun, Davis had broken the agreement he entered into with law enforcement. A judge later sided with the prosecutor's argument, opening the door for Davis' arrest. Davis and his defence team have argued that the book was co-authored and sections were embellished or fictionalised to make a profit, and they should not be viewed as direct admissions. In an interview last week with a local TV news station, Davis denied being in Las Vegas when Tupac was killed and distanced himself from the memoir that lists him as an author. "I did not write that book," Davis told Fox 5. "A ghost writer wrote that." He also said he might take the stand and testify at his trial. "If I have to, I will." Trial attorney Shaun Kent told the BBC: "This is what makes this case so fascinating. The two biggest pieces of evidence against Keffe D came from Keffe D. "Keffe D has the right to take the stand and say 'I made all this up. I lied to sell copies of the book. I lied to the police. I'm a liar but I did not murder Tupac.'" Davis has also publicly stated multiple times that Bad Boy Records head Sean "Diddy" Combs had offered him $1m to kill Death Row Records rivals Tupac and Knight. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Tupac is now one of the most recogniseable faces in hip hop Combs is currently serving a 50-month prison sentence after being convicted for two counts of transportation for the purposes of prostitution in New York. He has repeatedly denied allegations that he was involved in Tupac's death. Prosecutors have released a list of potential witnesses who could be called to testify, with over 200 names, including members of Tupac's family, former mayor of Las Vegas Oscar Goodman and former Los Angeles police Detective Greg Kading. Prosecutors have also named Knight, although it's unclear if the rap impresario will testify, as he's previously said he would not. "This would be huge as he has never offered law enforcement any information that would lead to the conviction of anyone," Kent said. "This trial is going to be a legal scholar's Super Bowl." https://telex.hu/after/2026/08/10/hbo-pr.text: Menü Kereső Örökbe fogadni csak a tökéletes embereknek szabad, gyereke bárkinek lehet After frissítve Fotó: HBO Bányász Dorka Az HBO-on futó Proud története Magyarországról nézve nagyon ismerős problémákat dolgoz fel. A lengyel sorozat, ami a homoszexualitás démonizálásáról, a kelet-európai melankóliáról, a gyermekvédelem vállalhatatlan helyzetének következményeiről és a konzervatív társadalom egysíkúságáról szól, könnyen lehetett volna egy tündérmesébe torkoló, alternatív valóság is, ahol minden flottul történik. Végül nem ilyen lett. Helyette egy felnövéstörténetet kaptunk Filipről (Ignacy Liss), egy meleg férfiról, aki a gyermekvédelem legrosszabb oldalát ismerte meg. Filip árvaházban nőtt fel, ez idő alatt a hedonizmus fogalmát maradéktalanul kimerítette: ivott, drogozott és minden nap mással bújt ágyba. Mindeközben a nővére, Anka (Sylwia Boron) egyedülálló anyaként próbálja gondját viselni a kislányának. Ankán nagy teher van, a gyereknevelés mellett arra is figyel, hogy Filipet jó útra terelje. A fiatal nő hirtelen és tragikus halála után Filip lesz az unokahúga gyámja, innentől pedig fehér por már csak a pelenkázáshoz szükséges hintőpor formájában lesz a táskájában. A sorozat egyik írója és rendezője, Karol Klementewicz, aki a 2000-es évek elején még a lengyel Barátok közt (Na Wspólnej) írói csapatában dolgozott, kicsit sem riadt vissza attól, hogy egy provokatív történetet mutasson be. A Proud ötlete személyes indíttatásból született: megszületett a bátyja kisfia. Klementewicz abból inspirálódott, hogy a baba érkezése után hogyan fordult fel a családja élete. Az író saját bevallása szerint ámulva nézte, ahogy az addig hebrencs bátyja hogyan alakul át felelősségteljes szülővé. Valami hasonló történik a sorozatban Filippel is, akit a nyolcadik rész végére képtelenség nem megszeretni. Nem egyik napról a másikra lett belőle jó szülő, eleinte még voltak pillanatai, amikor legszívesebben az ember csak jól megrázta volna, hogy észhez térjen, de végül mindig unokahúga, Tosia biztonságát és egészségét helyezte minden elé, sokszor még a saját párkapcsolata is megsínylette az odaadását. A szerepet nagyon szépen és érzékenyen hozó lengyel színész a Varietynek azt mondta, hogy pontosan ezért szerette meg ennyire a karakterét, mert a megtestesítője volt annak, hogy bárki képes lehet felnőni egy ekkora feladathoz, ha képes a szeretetre és empátiára, a sorozatnak pedig fontos küldetése ezt bemutatni. Klementewicz szerint a legnagyobb probléma a sorozat készítésénél az volt, hogy Lengyelországban hiányzik a párbeszéd a különböző társadalmi rétegek között. „Senki sem fogja megváltoztatni a véleményét a műsor miatt, hiszen ez egy folyamat, de talán lesz olyan, aki a főszereplőben nem csupán a szexualitását látja” – mondta a rendező, igaz, ennek némileg ellent mond, hogy a történet nagy része Filip szexualitásáról szól. A Proudban bemutatott gyermekvédelem nem nézi jó szemmel, hogy egyedülálló férfi apa szeretne lenni, arról meg hallani sem akarnak, hogy ez a férfi ráadásul meleg is. A hivatalos szervek Facebook-kommentek stílusában kommunikálnak vele, amikor pedig Filip felkeresi a képviselőjét az ötlettel, hogy adoptálni szeretné az unokahúgát, a képviselő szavai úgy érik a nézőt, mintha egy vödör jeges vízzel borítanák nyakon. „Gyereke bárkinek lehet. Örökbe fogadni csak a tökéletes embereknek szabad” – hangzik el a sorozat legerősebb mondata. Ezután nem csoda, hogy egy egész rész Filip lázálmáról szól, ahol elviszik tőle Tosiát. A rémálom minden abszurditása ellenére fele annyira sem volt ijesztő és nyomasztó, mint a valóság. Időközben megjelenik a kislány nagymamája is, aki az egyébként is szomorú helyzetre még rátesz egy lapáttal. A feszültség végül a kislány sorsát eldöntő bírósági tárgyaláson tetőzik. Az események kellős közepén véget érő sorozat nagy eséllyel folytatódik majd, ha csak az HBO nem lép meg egy Netflixtől megszokott lépést, és hagyja inkább félbe a sztorit, de ez nagy hiba lenne. A Proud rengeteg égető problémát sorakoztatott fel az elfogadás kérdésén kívül. A gyász, az addikció, a tini terhesség, a válás és a családon belüli erőszak mind megjelentek. Az pedig rengeteget dobott a sztorin, hogy ezeket a problémákat mind nyersen és életszagúan adták át a mellékszereplők. A legmaradandóbb közülük egyértelműen Filip legjobb barátja, Kiki (Maria Sobocinska) volt, aki 16 évesen lett anya és sehogyan se talál rendes párkapcsolatot, miközben lánya apja még mindig fülig szerelmes belé. Kiki karaktere különösen jól mutatta be, hogy a szülőknek sokszor legalább annyira szükségük van a gyerekükre, mint amennyire a gyerekeknek a szüleikre. A sorozat nagy tanulsága, hogy egy társaság a bajban képes igazi családdá összekovácsolódni, ráadásul ez általában épp akkor szokott megtörténni, amikor a legnagyobb baj van. A Proud fő üzenete mégsem ez, hanem az, hogy a szülővé válás nagyon nehéz folyamat. Mindegy, hogy tudatosan, véletlen vagy egy tragédia miatt válunk szülővé, ilyenkor minden segítségre szükségünk van. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Friss az Afteren

Közben a parlamenti patkó közepén Magyar Péter asztalánál kisebb csoportosulás alakult ki, majd Gyöngyösi István és több képviselő összeállt egy közös képre is. Hallerné Nagy Anikó házelnök nem szerette volna tartalmilag minősíteni a Telexnek, hogy a Mi Hazánk képviselői nem álltak fel, amikor a parlament hétfői ülésén megemlékeztek a roma holokausztról. A házszabály alapján a megemlékezéseknek van egy keretrendszere, mondta, de a hétfői ülésen történtek nem illeszkedtek ehhez. https://telex.hu/english/2026/08/10/we-c.text: Menü Kereső We asked Szijjártó’s press secretary whether ministry staffers really used to be sent to his press conferences English Aradi Hanga Zsófia Andrea Horváth Kávai (translation) Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom During Péter Szijjártó’s tenure as Hungarian minister of foreign affairs, staff members at the ministry were regularly sent to attend his press conferences—this is what several former and current employees of the foreign ministry told 444. After the article was published, we contacted Péter Szijjártó’s press secretary, Máté Paczolay to request a response to the publication’s claims. In response to our question, Paczolay explained in detail how they organized the briefings to ensure that all seats in the room were filled. According to 444, the minister’s office would routinely notify the heads of various departments in advance about how many staff members were expected to attend each of Szijjártó’s bilateral press briefings, and prior to the events, the department heads were required to send a list with the names of those would be in attendance. According to the publication, all of this was necessary because the invited press and the delegations accompanying foreign guests would not have filled the room on their own. Paczolay wrote that “the 444 article contains both truth and misinformation” and added that in order to get the full picture, it is important to note that Péter Szijjártó was the most active government official in terms of communication. “On a less busy day, there were one or two press events at the ministry of foreign affairs; on an average day, three or four; and on a busier day, five or six.” According to the former minister’s press secretary, it is natural that when three press events were held in a single day, “the interest of the media would wane” by the third one, but they made every effort to ensure that none of the guests of the MFA were offended by having to “deliver a speech representing their country to an even mildly empty room.” Therefore, “in such cases, they would invite staff members from the relevant specialized departments. Some took advantage of the opportunity, some did not; some came gladly, while others-apparently found it an added burden.” Paczolay emphasized that participation was not mandatory. “I don’t have the exact information on this, but I’m certain that the ministerial protocol office kept making phone calls until every last seat was filled, since that was their job,” he wrote to Telex. According to the press secretary, “the heads of the various departments also found it beneficial for a staff member responsible for a given region to hear the foreign minister of that country—for which they were, in effect, responsible within the ministry—speak in person, as well as to have the opportunity to meet with members of the delegation accompanying the foreign minister.” “So yes, the seats were always filled. Sometimes there were twenty journalists and thirty invited guests in a fifty-seat room, while at other times there were three journalists and forty-seven guests.” In its article, 444 also reported that most of the press was excluded from the briefings to begin with, and a foreign affairs staffer told the paper that they once witnessed a colleague from the press department of the ministry dictating to the reporter of the state news agency (MTI) the exact questions they should ask. We asked Paczolay whether they usually coordinated questions with the correspondents of MTI, to which he replied, “No.” “We issued press releases about each event involving Péter Szijjártó, and we streamed the entire press conference live on various online platforms, so it was very rare that MTI sent a reporter in person to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,” he wrote. He acknowledged that they coordinated with the journalists attending the press conferences: “We always asked them whether they were going to have any questions, or whether they would address issues unrelated to the topic of the visit—usually matters of domestic politics.” He wrote that the reasons for this were practical: on the one hand, this allowed them to structure the moderation and adjust the planned duration of the press conference accordingly; on the other hand, they would inform Szijjártó in advance to expect that domestic politics would be brought up alongside bilateral issues. “This was the basic approach in our day-to-day work, but over the course of 12 years, there were countless unique situations requiring unique solutions, as we hosted guests from every corner of the world, each with different cultural customs and needs,” he wrote. 444 also reported that Gyula Budai, the ministerial commissioner responsible for measures to protect the economy, was present at every press conference, regardless of the subject. We also inquired about the reasons for this, and Paczolay wrote that since Budai was “essentially present at all of the foreign minister’s negotiations, he was a member of the delegation, and protocol dictates that members of the delegation need to attend press conferences because these are also part of the official program.” For more quick, accurate and impartial news from and about Hungary, subscribe to the Telex English newsletter! A Veiszer Alinda által moderált beszélgetésben hamar ráterelődött szó a politika és az irodalom viszonyára. Biró azt mondta, hogy mostanában a politikusabb szövegek érdeklik, ezért legújabb műveiben azt vizsgálja, hogy a 2020-as években mi köze van a politikának az irodalomhoz. Az antológiában szereplő írásban is azt kereste, hogy egy pici irodalmi szubkultúrára hogyan telepedett rá az elmúlt tizenhat év. Balássy Fanni szerint nagyban meghatározta korosztályának irodalmi szocializációját, hogy az Orbán János Dénes szakmai vezetésével működő Kárpát-medencei Tehetséggondozó (KMTG) akkor indult, amikor érettségiztek. „Az ember bekerül ebbe a nagyon furcsa, turbulens világba, és nem teljesen tud eligazodni” – fogalmazott a pályakezdéséről, ugyanakkor azt is megjegyezte, neki nagy segítséget jelentett, hogy voltak olyan idősebb, tapasztaltabb pályatársai, akik megmutatták, melyik irányba induljon el. Szerinte a vonzónak tűnő ösztöndíjakhoz képest nehezebb pálya ugyan keresni a saját utat és kilincselni a kiadóknál, vagy éppen arra várni, amíg a folyóiratokban publikálják egy-egy szövegét, de utána tiszta marad az ember lelkiismerete. Biró Zsombor Aurél emlékeztetett arra, hogy a KTMG ellen tiltakozva jött létre a Független Mentorháló nevű kezdeményezés, ami ugyan hamar elhalt, de aminek keretében számos nagynevű alkotó ajánlotta fel, hogy egy évig mentorál egy-egy fiatal szerzőt; őt például Potozky László vette szárnyai alá. „Aztán az SZFE-t is kihúzták alólunk. Oda is pont akkor sikerült járnom, amikor kiderült, hogy ez egy liberális hüllőkeltető” – emlékezett vissza. Mint felidézte: gyakran feltette magának a kérdést, hogy egy munkát be szabad-e vállalni, és például amiatt is utasított vissza felkérést, mert úgy gondolta, hogy egy folyóirat túl sok állami pénzt kapott. „Nagyon fiatal voltam, amikor ez a rendszer úgy gázolt át a generációm nagy részén, hogy nem volt más, mint hogy rendszerellenesek legyünk” – mondta Biró, aki szerint mindez egyszerre váltott ki keserűséget és irigységet, ugyanakkor az embernek lehet tőle morális felsőbbségtudata, ha nemet mond dolgokra. „Ebből kellene most kikecmeregni” – tette hozzá az író. Balássy Fanni szkeptikus azzal kapcsolatban, hogy a meglévő ellentétek el fognak-e simulni, és hogy a szakma képes lesz-e az együttműködésre. Szerinte ugyanis annyira erősen be vannak betonozva a szekértáborok, hogy nagyon nehéz lesz őket meghaladni. A közelmúltban megalakult Irodalmi Szakszervezetet ugyanakkor fontos és meghatározó kezdeményezésnek tartja ezen a téren. Biró szintén nagy problémának tartja, hogy jobboldali és liberális alkotók nem állnak szóba egymással, és hogy a politikai nézeteltérések sportszurkolói nézeteltéréssé fajulnak. „Az üdvös valami olyasmi lenne, hogy az emberek vállalják fel, hogy mit gondolnak a politikáról, és ki lehessen mondani azt, hogy én jobboldali vagyok, vagy én baloldali vagyok – mondta. – Szerintem egy liberális lózung, hogy a politikának nincs köze a művészethez. Ez életszerűtlen és nem igaz, és elfedése a valódi problémáknak.” A műsorban Balássy Fanni arra is kitért, hogy még mindig keresi, hogyan tud hitelesen megszólalni, de összességében jó érzéssel tölti el, hogy mostanában egy kicsit kevesebbet kell szorongani. „Furcsa, hogy valaminek ennyire hirtelen lett vége, amiről egyáltalán nem gondoltuk volna, hogy ennyire az elemeire tud bomlani” – utalt a választás utáni politikai-gazdasági átrendeződésre. Biró Zsombor Aurél reméli, hogy az utálat helyett idővel sikerül analitikusabb viszonyt kialakítani az Orbán-rendszerhez. „Az a közeg, amiben én mozgok, nagyrészt elszenvedője volt az Orbán-rendszernek. Anyagi kiszolgáltatottság van, keveset keresnek, nincs idejük azzal foglalkozni, amiben tehetségesek. Ez keserűséghez és frusztrációhoz vezet, amit azokon töltenek ki, akik körülveszik őket, és ami a saját közegük valójában” – mondta az író. A műsorvezető felvetésére Biró Zsombor Aurél a generációs ellentétekről szólva úgy fogalmazott: „Az, hogy 70 éves emberek irányítják a világot, egy 27 éves számára dühítő. Ezt értelmezhetjük folyóiratok szerkesztőségére vagy színházak vezetőire is.” Balássy Fanni pedig arról beszélt, hogy az idősebb generációkban gyakran élnek olyan reflexek, hogy a fiatalok örüljenek, hogy van munkájuk, és hogy minden rendben van körülöttük, és inkább húzzák meg magukat, ne konfrontálódjanak a hatalommal, mert az mindig veszélyes. „Ami a fiataloknak meghozta az erőt, hogy ki merték nevetni a hatalmat. Fellendült a mémkultúra és a különböző TikTok-videók gyártása. Már nem láttad benne a fenyegetést, annyira nonszensz volt a helyzet, hogy ki merted röhögni. A nevetésnek van egy ilyen szupereje, hogy elszívja a hatalomtól a fenyegetés erejét” – vélekedett a Friss tinta legutóbbi adásában Balássy Fanni. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! https://nineoclock.ro/romanian-president.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount President Nicușor Dan Highlights Romanian-French Strategic Partnership on France’s National Day Bucharest, July 15, 2026 – President Nicușor Dan underscored the strength of the Romanian-French Strategic Partnership and the longstanding friendship between the two countries in a message published on his official X account after attending France’s National Day celebrations in Paris at the invitation of French President Emmanuel Macron. France’s National Day celebrations in Paris The Romanian head of state described his participation in the Bastille Day ceremonies as a special moment, noting that this year’s celebrations coincide with the centennial of the French-Romanian Friendship Treaty, an important milestone in bilateral relations. According to President Dan, the anniversary provides an opportunity to reaffirm the Strategic Partnership between Romania and France, built on close political dialogue, expanding economic cooperation and strong security ties within the Euro-Atlantic framework. A symbolic highlight of this year’s celebrations was the participation of soldiers from Romania’s 30th Guard Brigade “Mihai Viteazul” in the traditional military parade on the Champs-Élysées. Marching alongside French troops and military contingents from allied and partner countries, the Romanian Guard’s presence reflected the close defence cooperation between Bucharest and Paris and the solidarity shared by NATO allies. President Dan described the participation of the Romanian servicemen as another tangible demonstration of the friendship between the two nations and of their commitment to common security objectives. Romania and France have developed one of the closest strategic partnerships in the European Union and NATO, cooperating extensively in the fields of defence, energy, infrastructure, education and economic development. France also plays a key role in NATO’s enhanced Forward Presence in Romania, contributing to the security of NATO’s Eastern Flank. President Nicușor Dan’s full statement, as published on X: “It is with a very special pleasure that I join, on this July 14 in Paris, the ceremonies of France’s National Day, at the invitation of President Emmanuel Macron. In this centennial year of the French-Romanian Friendship Treaty, we thus reaffirm our Strategic Partnership and the privileged friendship between Romania and France, founded on deepened cooperation at the political, economic, and security levels. I am happy and proud that the soldiers of the 30th Guard Brigade “Mihai Viteazul” are participating, alongside their French comrades and those of many other allied and partner countries, in the Champs-Élysées parade. https://nineoclock.ro/japanese-ambassado.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount ASF, Japanese Ambassador Discuss Stronger Cooperation in Financial Markets By Mihai Manea , Publisher, Nine O’Clock / Social Media: LinkedIn | Facebook | Instagram Romania’s Financial Supervisory Authority (ASF) and Japan are looking to deepen cooperation in the field of non-banking financial markets, following a meeting between ASF President Alexandru Petrescu and Japan’s Ambassador to Romania, H.E. Mr. Katae Takashi. The discussions focused on financial market stability, sustainable finance, the exchange of institutional expertise and the potential for expanding cooperation in support of investment projects involving Japanese companies operating or interested in the Romanian market. In a post published on his LinkedIn page following the meeting, ASF President Alexandru Petrescu emphasized the importance of the dialogue: “I had the pleasure of meeting today, at the headquarters of the Financial Supervisory Authority, with H.E. Mr. Katae Takashi, Ambassador of Japan to Romania. During our discussion, we addressed topics regarding the balance of financial markets, sustainable financing, as well as the relevance of the exchange of good practices between authorities and institutions with responsibilities in the financial field. Japan’s experience in the development of financial markets provides valuable benchmarks, including in terms of stimulating interest in the capital market and the professional training of specialists. In this context, we discussed capitalizing on the bilateral dialogue through exchanges of experience and cooperation initiatives as applied as possible. We also analyzed the opportunity of mechanisms through which the capital market can support the financing of projects of Japanese companies present or interested in the Romanian economy. The interest shown in the Romanian market creates important premises for strengthening collaboration in areas relevant to non-banking financial markets. The meeting was an important opportunity for institutional dialogue and reconfirmed the openness to mutual support, exchange of expertise and the development of joint initiatives relevant to non-bank financial markets.” The meeting reflects Romania’s continued efforts to strengthen its financial sector through international partnerships and the exchange of best practices. Japan, one of the world’s leading financial centres, has extensive experience in capital market development, financial education and sustainable investment, areas that are increasingly relevant to Romania’s long-term economic agenda.” The talks also highlighted the role that capital markets can play in supporting Japanese investment projects in Romania. Enhanced cooperation between the ASF and Japanese financial institutions could facilitate greater investor confidence, improve access to financing and contribute to the further development of Romania’s non-banking financial sector. The meeting is another indication of the steadily expanding Romanian-Japanese partnership, which has gained momentum in recent years across economic, financial and institutional cooperation. 02.07.2026 Follow Nine O’Clock on social media via : LinkedIn, Facebook , and Instagram. https://nineoclock.ro/between-discipline.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Between Discipline and Calling: A Conversation with TAROM Boeing 737 First Officer George Ancuța, by Dr. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi Special for Nine O’Clock by Dr. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi For millions of passengers, a flight begins when the cabin doors close and the aircraft starts taxiing toward the runway. For the crew in the cockpit, however, every departure is preceded by a rigorous sequence of checks, calculations, and decisions designed to ensure the safety of the flight. On the occasion of Romanian Aviation Day , George Ancuța, a First Officer on TAROM’s Boeing 737 fleet, speaks about what passengers rarely see: the final minutes before takeoff, the challenges posed by adverse weather, the breathtaking views from cruising altitude, and the responsibility of carrying hundreds of people who place their trust in the flight crew. It is a conversation about discipline, preparation, and a profession that continues to inspire generations. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi: Many of our readers travel by air, yet few know what happens behind the cockpit door. What takes place in the cockpit during the final minutes before takeoff? George Ancu ța: The final minutes before takeoff are among the most important of the entire flight. Inside the cockpit, every member of the crew knows exactly what needs to be done, and our attention is fully focused on the final checks. We review the weather, aircraft performance data, the route, any operational restrictions, and ensure that all systems are functioning exactly as they should. There is a principle that guides every flight: prepare for the worst and hope for the best. That is why we discuss scenarios that are highly unlikely to occur. If something unexpected happens, we want to have a plan in place already and be able to respond quickly and effectively. All of these procedures are the result of rigorous training and teamwork. From the outside, it may seem like a routine stage before departure, but in the cockpit every check and every decision serves a single purpose: flight safety. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi: Flying is one of the few experiences that allows us to leave the routines of everyday life behind, if only for a few hours. Is there a particular moment during a flight that reminds you why you chose this profession? George Ancu ța: Yes. There are many special moments, but the ones that continue to impress me every single time are the sunsets seen from the cockpit. At cruising altitude, the colors of the sky are simply spectacular and unlike anything that can truly be captured in a photograph. Every sunset is different. Sometimes it feels as though you are flying through a painting. Those are moments of calm when you realize how privileged you are to see the world from a perspective that very few people ever experience. Whenever I watch one of those sunsets, I am reminded that I chose the profession I dreamed about as a child. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi: If there is a poetic side to flying, there is also another side where nature tests the experience and preparation of the crew. For passengers, turbulence may mean a few uncomfortable minutes. For pilots, it can be a moment when experience, training, and human judgment meet the forces of nature directly. What has been the most intense moment you have experienced in the cockpit? George Ancu ța: The most intense moments are always those when you have to confront nature. Thunderstorms, severe weather, or strong turbulence remind you that, no matter how advanced modern aircraft technology has become, nature must always be respected. In such situations, experience and preparation are essential. You remain calm, continuously evaluate the available information, and make the best decisions together with your colleague in the cockpit. Communication and trust between the two pilots are just as important as the aircraft itself. Paradoxically, these are also the moments that validate your training. Every hour spent in the simulator and every procedure practiced exists precisely for the moments when you need them most. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi: Romanian Aviation Day reminds us that every flight begins with a dream. What message would you like to share with young people who aspire to become airline pilots? George Ancu ța: I would tell them never to give up on their dream. I know how distant a cockpit can seem when you are standing on the ground, watching airplanes and imagining that one day you might be the one sitting up there. I was that child too. The road was not easy. There were years of study, examinations, sacrifices, and many challenges. But every step was worth it. If you have passion, discipline, and patience, the things that seem impossible today can become reality. For me, flying is much more than operating an aircraft. It means carrying the responsibility of having hundreds of people place their trust in you and your crew. It is a responsibility that I feel on every flight and, at the same time, a privilege that I will never take for granted. If a child who once watched airplanes with admiration can one day find himself in the cockpit of a Boeing 737, then I am convinced that other young people can turn their dreams into reality as well. The important thing is to believe in yourself and never give up. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi: Thank you very much, George, for your time and for this conversation. We wish you continued success, smooth flights, and clear skies. In Closing Romanian Aviation Day reminds us that behind every flight stand professionals for whom safety is not a statistic but a responsibility embraced every day. For passengers, flying is often simply a journey between two destinations. For those in the cockpit, it remains a mission built on discipline, competence, and trust. Through their professionalism and quiet dedication, Romania’s aviators continue to give meaning to a profession that inspires both respect and admiration. George Ancu ța is a First Officer flying the Boeing 737 for TAROM, Romania’s national airline. Adrian-Leonard Mociulschi is a contributor to Nine O’Clock, as well as a musician, essayist, and university lecturer at the National University of Music Bucharest (UNMB). His interdisciplinary work explores the symbolic intersections between music, emerging technologies, and cultural ethics. He is the author of five published essay volumes with Curtea Veche Publishing, a leading Romanian publishing house, and a regular contributor to Nine O’Clock and international academic journals.
