https://nineoclock.ro/eturia-exceeds-e20.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Eturia exceeds €20 million in sales in the first half of the year Tourist numbers increased by nearly 29%, while demand is diversifying towards premium holidays, complex tours and themed experiences By Mihai Manea , Publisher, Nine O’Clock / Social Media: LinkedIn | Facebook | Instagram Eturia Group closed the first six months of the year with sales exceeding €20 million, up approximately 7% compared with the same period in 2025. The results confirm Romanians’ continued interest in tailor-made travel and long-haul destinations, as well as Eturia’s development amid increasingly diverse demand for complex tours, premium holidays and themed experiences. In the first half of the year, approximately 10,500 tourists travelled with Eturia, nearly 29% more than during the same period of the previous year. The destinations recording the highest demand included the Maldives, China, Australia, the Dominican Republic and Thailand. These preferences point to a diversified market, in which relaxing stays in exotic destinations are complemented by cultural journeys, exploration tours and long-distance itineraries. “The growth recorded during the first six months confirms that Eturia is developing on solid foundations and that our model, built around specialised consultancy and destination expertise, meets the current expectations of travellers. We remain focused on strengthening our portfolio, developing the premium segment and expanding the range of products that offer clients greater flexibility, predictability and access to carefully selected experiences,” said Sorin Stoica, CEO and Founder of Eturia. Eturia exceeds €20 million in sales in the first half of the year The Maldives and Thailand remain leading exotic destinations, while China and Australia attract travellers interested in exploration The Maldives continues to be one of the preferred choices for premium holidays, relaxation and personalised services, while Thailand maintains its appeal through its varied offering of beaches, cultural experiences, gastronomy and itineraries adapted to different types of travellers. At the same time, China and Australia highlight the growing interest in destinations that require more extensive planning and offer cultural and exploration-based experiences. The Dominican Republic completes the list of preferred destinations, being chosen primarily for exotic stays and premium services. The diversity of selected destinations shows that travellers’ preferences are expanding beyond traditional relaxation holidays. An increasing number of requests are focused on holidays that include local experiences, exploration and activities adapted to each traveller’s individual style. More than 80 escorted groups operated during the first six months Escorted group travel continues to represent an important segment for Eturia. More than 80 groups were operated during the first six months of the year, indicating that this format remains relevant for travellers seeking a well-organised experience without giving up the authenticity of discovering a destination. Group products are particularly attractive due to the balance they offer between comfort, access to expertise and carefully designed itineraries. The presence of a tour escort provides travellers with an additional level of predictability and support, particularly in the case of complex tours or long-haul destinations. At the same time, this format facilitates access to complex routes, local activities and cultural experiences that may be more difficult to organise independently. Demand is evolving from choosing a destination to creating a personal experience Data from the first part of the year indicates a diversification in the way Romanians choose their holidays. Alongside established exotic stays, interest is increasing in complex tours, long-haul travel and premium or luxury products. An increasingly visible trend is the preference for holidays developed around personal interests and objectives. Wellbeing, adventure, culture and exploration are becoming important criteria in the decision-making process, while the destination itself represents only the starting point in building the itinerary. Travellers are looking for programmes adapted to their own pace and travel style, ranging from relaxing stays and active routes to cultural experiences and in-depth exploration of a region. In this context, personalisation and specialised consultancy are playing an increasingly important role in the holiday selection process. https://nineoclock.ro/address-by-the-hon.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Address by the Hon’ble President of India, Smt. Droupadi Murmu, at the India–Moldova Business Forum: “It gives me immense pleasure to attend the India–Moldova Business Forum today. I thank you all for your presence here, including representatives of leading businesses from India and Moldova, along with members of business associations and Invest Moldova. My visit to Moldova as the first State visit by an Indian President reflects India’s commitment to deepening engagement with Moldova in all spheres, including political, economic, cultural and people-to-people ties. I am accompanied by a large business delegation from India. Their presence demonstrates the growing confidence of Indian industry in Moldova’s economic potential and its commitment to building long-term partnerships. India and Moldova have enjoyed warm and friendly relations since the establishment of diplomatic relations in 1992. Our partnership is based on mutual respect, democratic values and a shared commitment to peace, development and international cooperation. As India advances towards its vision of Viksit Bharat 2047 , we seek partnerships built on trust and shared prosperity. India today is among the fastest-growing major economies, driven by entrepreneurship, digital transformation, manufacturing excellence and a young, skilled workforce. At the same time, Moldova’s reform-oriented outlook, strategic location, talented human capital and growing integration with European markets make it an important destination for Indian businesses. There is immense potential for collaboration across diverse sectors such as digital technologies, artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, fintech, digital public infrastructure, infrastructure development, renewable energy, advanced manufacturing, logistics, agriculture, food processing, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology and healthcare. I am happy that most of these sectors are represented here today. I am greatly encouraged by the growing cooperation in the energy sector. I have been told that a high-voltage transmission line connecting this city with Romania is being implemented by Indian companies, which will contribute to enhancing Moldova’s energy resilience and regional connectivity. Indian companies are interested in participating in Moldova’s renewable energy development projects, including solar energy, battery storage, smart grids, green hydrogen and other clean technologies. India also offers excellent business opportunities for Moldovan companies in trade and investment. We remain committed to fostering a transparent, predictable and investor-friendly business environment. I invite Moldovan businesses to come and explore India. I also encourage Indian businesses to look at the opportunities in Moldova. Your enterprise, vision and commitment will be instrumental in building enduring economic partnerships. I am confident that today’s interactions will lay the foundation for new partnerships and innovative collaborations, taking economic cooperation between India and Moldova to new heights. Let us work together to write a new chapter in the India–Moldova economic partnership. I wish the Business Forum every success and all participants fruitful deliberations. https://nineoclock.ro/cristian-ioja-shap.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Cristian Iojă is a Professor at the Faculty of Geography, University of Bucharest, and a researcher at the Center for Environmental Impact and Research Studies. He is Treasurer of the Society for Urban Ecology and President of South Eastern Europe Chapter. His work focuses on urban environmental systems, environmental impact assessment, and sustainable territorial planning, with a strong emphasis on participatory methods and citizen‑science approaches. He has become an active contributor to major European research projects and a committed mentor for young researchers, shaping future experts in environmental sciences. Nine O’Clock: Could you briefly describe your professional journey and the main milestones that have shaped your career in geography and environmental studies? My professional journey began in 1997, when I joined Center for Environmental Research (CCMESI), as a volunteer, working on Danube water quality monitoring and urban ecology studies in Bucharest. In 1999, I became an assistant researcher and expanded my work into urban ecology, environmental impact assessment, and biodiversity conservation. A key milestone was my appointment as Assistant Professor, which allowed me to combine research with teaching and integrate real environmental challenges into academic training. Over time, I have coordinated interdisciplinary national and European projects and contributed to consolidating CCMESI as a center for evidence‑based environmental analysis. My career today is shaped by a focus on urban environmental diagnostics, sustainability assessment, participatory approaches, and strong international collaboration. Nine O’Clock: As Professor in the Department of Geography and Environment and Researcher in the Center for Environmental Impact and Research Studies at the University of Bucharest, what are your main priorities in research, teaching, and community engagement? My work is guided by an integrated vision that brings together research excellence, innovative teaching, and active engagement with society. In research, I am committed to refining and expanding methodologies in environmental impact assessment, urban sustainability, and citizen‑involved environmental monitoring. A constant priority is to reinforce the CCCMESI’s capacity to produce findings that are both scientifically robust and directly applicable to the needs of local and national authorities. At the same time, I place strong emphasis on international collaboration, ensuring that our projects and approaches remain connected to European research dynamics and benefit from the exchange of expertise across borders. Developing close links with the Society for Urban Ecology network has been among my main professional priorities. In teaching, I strive to create learning environments that mirror the complexity of real urban and environmental challenges. I integrate challenge‑based methods, authentic case studies, and hands‑on work with environmental data, enabling students to engage directly with stakeholders and practical problem‑solving. Developing practical competencies remains a core objective. These efforts are enriched by strong participation in Erasmus mobility programmes, the CIVIS European University initiatives, and collaborations within the Society for Urban Ecology network, which broaden students’ academic horizons and expose them to diverse international perspectives. Beyond classroom teaching, I am deeply committed to strengthening advanced environmental education at the University of Bucharest. I actively support the development and continuous improvement of the master programmes Integrated Environmental Assessment (EISM) and Environmental Policy for Sustainable Development (PMDD), contributing to curricular refinement and ensuring that students benefit from exposure to applied methodologies and European research dynamics. At the same time, I place strong emphasis on mentoring PhD students and postdoctoral researchers, helping them build solid research trajectories, engage in international networks, and contribute meaningfully to the scientific community. This comprehensive approach ensures continuity between undergraduate learning, master-level specialization, and advanced research training. In community engagement, I focus on cultivating long-term, trust‑based collaborations with municipalities, NGOs, and civic groups. These partnerships ensure that our academic work contributes meaningfully to improving environmental governance, fostering climate resilience, and strengthening public participation. The CCMESI’s involvement in European initiatives further amplifies our ability to align local priorities with international best practices, creating a productive dialogue between research, policy, and community needs. Nine O’Clock: Which recent research projects or initiatives have you been involved in, and what are their anticipated impacts? (Carmine, ScienceUs, GreenInc) Currently, I am actively involved in three major European initiatives that strengthen the University of Bucharest’s and CCMESI’s contribution to climate resilience, citizen science, and inclusive urban sustainability. CARMINE , an Horizon Europe project, coordinated by National Administration of Meteorology, focuses on developing climate‑resilient development pathways in metropolitan regions through Living Labs, co‑creation with stakeholders, and advanced tools such as Digital Twins and decision‑support services, implemented across eight European case study areas. My role is centred on linking urban environmental analysis with co‑creation processes to support long‑term collaboration between universities and local authorities for climate adaptation. ( Project website ; Climate‑ADAPT profile ) ScienceUs , an Horizon Widera project, aims to upscale and connect citizen science initiatives across Europe by integrating best practices, building an EU‑wide network, and running a structured support programme to help high‑potential citizen science projects reach broader impact. My role focuses on designing the framework for the citizen science project competition (selection logic, evaluation criteria, and support pathway) and on mentoring two selected citizen science projects—AcquaSorgente and BlueGreenTops—to strengthen their scalability, transferability, and long‑term impact. ( Project website ) GREEN‑INC , a Driving Urban Transition project, investigates how cities can deliver more effective and more equitable nature‑based solutions through inclusive climate actions, using comparative research and urban living labs in partner cities (including Bucharest). My contribution focuses on environmental assessment and context‑specific applications of green infrastructure, supporting evidence‑based guidelines and tools for more just and effective NbS implementation. ( Project website ; DUT project page ) Together, these projects consolidate CCMESI’s profile in applied urban environmental research, reinforce participatory and citizen‑science approaches, and strengthen our capacity to translate research outputs into practical tools and collaborations that can be transferred across European contexts. Nine O’Clock: How do you see the role of universities, particularly the University of Bucharest, in addressing environmental challenges in Romania and the region? Universities have a critical role as both knowledge generators and neutral facilitators capable of bringing together policymakers, citizens, and the private sector. At the University of Bucharest, our responsibility is to produce rigorous scientific evidence, train the next generation of environmental professionals, and provide independent expertise for public institutions. We can act as catalysts for climate adaptation, sustainable urban planning, and environmental justice across the region by combining research, innovation, and public engagement. Nine O’Clock: What do you consider to be the most urgent environmental issues Romania is currently facing, and how can academic research contribute to solving them? Romania faces several interconnected challenges: climate‑driven hazards in cities and rural areas, uncontrolled urban expansion, declining green infrastructure, environmental quality deterioration, and insufficient integration of environmental criteria into planning. Academic research can respond by providing high‑resolution environmental assessments, modeling future risks, evaluating policy effectiveness, and creating tools that support evidence‑based decisions. Through CCMESI, we already produce studies that directly guide authorities in improving planning, environmental protection, and investments. Nine O’Clock: Could you tell us about the international collaborations or partnerships of Center for Environmental Research is involved in, and how they benefit both students and the scientific community? Our research unit participates in extensive European networks that bring together universities, research centers, municipalities, and NGOs. These partnerships make it possible to develop joint research projects, encourage staff mobility, and share methodologies in areas such as sustainability assessment, climate resilience, and digital environmental tools. Students benefit greatly from these connections, gaining exposure to European best practices, interdisciplinary research environments, and participation in cross‑border challenge‑based learning initiatives. For the scientific community, such collaborations support the production of comparative studies, shared data infrastructures, and policy‑relevant research outcomes. A central example is our active engagement in the CIVIS European University Alliance, which facilitates joint courses, blended mobility, summer schools, and collaborative research formats across several leading European universities. Through CIVIS, our students and staff have access to a large network of expertise, multilingual working environments, and thematic hubs focused on sustainability and climate adaptation. In addition, our longstanding involvement in the Society for Urban Ecology (SURE) places our team within a global community of researchers working on urban ecosystems, biodiversity, and socio‑ecological resilience. This network opens opportunities for conference participation, working groups, and shared research initiatives addressing contemporary urban environmental challenges. Furthermore, the Center maintains multiple cooperation agreements with international universities, research institutes, and environmental NGOs, which enhance mobility, joint supervision, project development, and field‑based research. These partnerships ensure a continuous exchange of knowledge and contribute to the international visibility and scientific growth of both our students and researchers. We have embedded digital technologies at the core of both teaching and research. Students work with GIS platforms, satellite imagery, advanced spatial analysis, and environmental modeling tools from their first years. In research, these technologies support environmental impact studies, land‑use change analyses, ecosystem assessments, and the creation of decision‑support systems for local authorities. This digital foundation strengthens the department’s capacity to deliver cutting‑edge and visually communicative environmental assessments. Nine O’Clock: What advice would you give to young researchers or students who wish to build a career in geography, environmental sciences, or related fields? I would encourage young researchers to remain curious, interdisciplinary, and deeply connected to real-world challenges . Building a strong foundation in technical skills—especially AI, GIS, spatial analysis, data interpretation, and digital tools —is essential, but equally important is developing the capacity to engage with society, communicate results clearly, and collaborate across sectors. Participating in research projects, internships, and citizen‑science initiatives can accelerate both learning and career development. At the same time, I advise them to embrace opportunities whenever they arise, whether through international exchanges, research collaborations, conferences, or fieldwork. Growth often comes from stepping outside familiar areas and challenging oneself. It is also important to focus on performance, striving for continuous improvement, scientific rigor, and professional integrity. Young researchers should always look upward—toward higher standards, broader perspectives, and ambitious goals—rather than comparing themselves only to their immediate context. Finally, I encourage them not to search for shortcuts. A meaningful career in environmental sciences is built through perseverance, patience, and genuine commitment. Every stage—learning, experimenting, collaborating, and reflecting—contributes to long-term development and to becoming a responsible and impactful professional. Nine O’Clock: How do you manage to balance academic responsibilities, research, and community engagement while ensuring the development and innovation of the Center for Environmental Research? Balancing these dimensions relies on a combination of strategic planning, collaborative teamwork, and a clear sense of priorities. I approach academic responsibilities, research commitments, and community engagement as interconnected rather than separate spheres. Whenever possible, I integrate research into teaching—using ongoing projects, real environmental datasets, and stakeholder interactions to enrich student learning and to strengthen the CCMESI’s visibility and relevance. I place great emphasis on building a supportive and empowering environment within the CCMESI, which allows responsibilities to be shared effectively. Delegating tasks, encouraging autonomy among colleagues, and fostering a culture of trust help maintain continuity across activities while avoiding overload. At the same time, I maintain an active role in guiding strategic directions and ensuring coherence between individual initiatives and the CCMESI’s long‑term goals. Innovation is sustained through continuous efforts: initiating new research proposals, strengthening international and national partnerships, refining curricula, and expanding our community‑facing activities. By aligning these elements—teaching, research, collaboration, and stakeholder engagement—I ensure that the CCMESI remains dynamic, forward‑looking, and capable of responding to emerging environmental challenges while supporting the professional growth of its members. Nine O’Clock: Looking ahead, what are the strategic objectives for the Center for Environmental Research over the next five years, and what legacy do you hope to leave? Over the next five years, our priorities at CCMESI focus on consolidating the Center as a leading national and regional hub for applied environmental research. We aim to expand interdisciplinary collaborations, strengthen partnerships with public authorities, advance citizen‑science approaches, and integrate climate resilience across all major research lines. A key strategic direction is to enhance our methodological capacity—particularly in biological conservation, environmental impact assessment and sustainability diagnostics—so that we can continue to serve as a trusted scientific partner for policy, planning, and environmental governance. At the same time, we are committed to building a supportive and dynamic environment for youth development. This includes empowering master students, PhD candidates, and postdoctoral researchers through mentorship, research opportunities, and exposure to international networks. https://nineoclock.ro/vodafone-foundatio.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Over 17,600 Students and 900 Teachers Become “Explorers in the World of Artificial Intelligence” Bucharest, 27 July 2026 – Vodafone Romania Foundation, the Ministry of Education and Research, and the Economic Informatics Club Association – CyberKnowledge Club have brought artificial intelligence education closer to middle school students and their teachers through the “AI Content – School of the Future for Middle School – Explorers in the World of Artificial Intelligence” project. More than 17,600 students and over 930 teachers from 295 schools, together with 100 educational ambassadors, participated in six interactive modules exploring topics such as algorithmic bias, ethical dilemmas in AI, the responsible use of artificial intelligence, the impact of technology on the environment, and the role of digital citizens. The project responds to the findings of a 2025 study conducted by Vodafone Romania Foundation, which showed that 70% of Romanian students believe artificial intelligence will play an essential role in their professional lives, while only 54% feel that school prepares them to use this technology. Only 40% consider that their teachers have relevant AI-related skills. The data also shows that 72% of students have gained knowledge about AI outside the classroom. The initiative brought AI education closer to middle school students and teachers through interactive digital resources, practical activities, and a national network of teacher ambassadors. During the 2025–2026 school year, the project reached 17,626 students, 932 teachers, and 295 schools across Romania. The number of participating students exceeded the initial target by almost three times, while the number of participating schools was 195% above the planned objective. The national expansion of the project was supported by 100 educational ambassadors who coordinated and assisted teachers in using the resources in classrooms. The educational resources are available on the “School of the Future” platform, and the six interactive modules were designed to encourage critical thinking, debate, and the practical application of technology in contexts relevant to students’ lives. The project evaluation shows its strong relevance for the educational community. Among teachers who completed the feedback questionnaire, nearly 85% said the project helped them improve their digital skills, approximately 98% considered the activities useful for students, and more than 97% appreciated the quality of the platform’s materials. In addition, almost 99% of respondents said they would continue using the resources and methods learned after the project’s completion. The programme also aims to provide more equitable access to digital education. Participating schools came from diverse areas: 39% from large urban areas, 37% from smaller urban communities, and 24% from rural areas. The fact that almost a quarter of participating schools are rural demonstrates that the project reached communities where access to such resources is more limited and where the impact can be significant. The activities were not used only for computer science or ICT classes, but also for mathematics, Romanian language and literature, foreign languages, geography, history, social education, sciences, and technology education. This demonstrates that artificial intelligence can become a relevant topic across the entire school curriculum, not only in technical subjects. The Ministry of Education and Research played an essential role in expanding the project nationwide through institutional support and by facilitating access to schools. The partnership between the public sector, civil society, and the private sector created a scalable model for digital education based on accessible resources, teacher ambassadors, and impact evaluation. The resources developed within the project will remain freely available on the “School of the Future” platform. The project estimates an indirect impact on approximately 30,000 students and teachers who will access the content after the implementation period ends. Vodafone Romania Foundation will continue, together with its partners, to support initiatives focused on developing digital skills, promoting the responsible use of artificial intelligence, and encouraging digital well-being among children and teenagers. Hur Seung-chul By Mihai Manea , Publisher, Nine O’Clock / Social Media: LinkedIn | Facebook | Instagram On Wednesday, July 22, 2026, the Minister of Foreign Affairs of Romania, Oana Țoiu, received His Excellency Hur Seung-chul, Ambassador-designate of the Republic of Korea to Romania, on the occasion of the presentation of copies of his letters of credence. During the meeting, Minister Oana Țoiu congratulated Ambassador Hur Seung-chul on his appointment and wished him every success in the fulfillment of his mandate. She highlighted the excellent momentum of the bilateral political dialogue, including the recent meeting between the Presidents of Romania and the Republic of Korea on the sidelines of the NATO Summit in Ankara in July 2026. The Minister also referred to the ongoing working visit to the Republic of Korea by the delegation led by State Secretary Clara Volintiru, whose program includes meetings aimed at strengthening bilateral relations and exploring new areas of cooperation. The Romanian Foreign Minister also reaffirmed the importance of the Joint Declaration on Strengthening the Strategic Partnership between Romania and the Republic of Korea as the cornerstone of the bilateral relationship. Minister Oana Țoiu emphasized the excellent cooperation in the fields of the defense industry and nuclear energy, while encouraging the development of joint projects in innovation and artificial intelligence, including cooperation between the two Ministries of Foreign Affairs, as well as enhanced port cooperation between Constanța and Busan. The Foreign Minister also highlighted the substantial volume of bilateral trade, which reached nearly USD 1 billion in 2025. To further strengthen this positive trend, Minister Oana Țoiu announced that, in coordination with the Ministry of Economy, Digitalization, Entrepreneurship and Tourism, the Romanian side intends to organize the Romania–Republic of Korea Joint Committee for Industrial Cooperation in the second half of 2026 in Bucharest. The South Korean official underscored the excellent state of the Strategic Partnership between Romania and the Republic of Korea, highlighting the positive development of cooperation in areas of major mutual interest and expressing his commitment to further advancing the partnership, including through the identification of new fields of collaboration. https://nineoclock.ro/kpmg-pharma-and-he.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount KPMG: Pharma and Healthcare – Why Resilience Has Become the Industry’s New Competitive Advantage Artificial intelligence, cybersecurity, regulatory pressure, employee expectations and data-driven decision-making are transforming the pharmaceutical and healthcare sectors on multiple fronts. Businesses are operating in a world where technological, regulatory and operational challenges intersect like never before, and innovation alone is no longer enough. These topics were explored during KPMG in Romania’s conference Pharma, Healthcare & Life Sciences Transformation – Business, Tax and Legal Insights , held in Bucharest on 28 July 2026. The event was moderated by Teodora Alecu, Director, Transfer Pricing and Head of Healthcare Sector services at KPMG in Romania, and Ioana-Zenaida Rizea-Popp, Partner, Audit and Co-Head of Healthcare Sector services. Edward Davies, CEE Life Sciences Lead, as well as KPMG specialists and industry leaders, also took part in the event, which examined the trends reshaping the sector, from artificial intelligence and cybersecurity to workforce transformation, predictive analytics, tax developments and compliance. The key message emerging from the conference was clear: the businesses which will thrive in the years ahead are those able to combine innovation with trust, strong governance and operational resilience. Resilience Is No Longer Optional The pharmaceutical and healthcare sectors are entering a new stage of transformation. While innovation remains a growth driver, companies are facing a growing number of challenges, from technological disruption and cyber risks to regulatory complexity and rising expectations from patients, employees and authorities. As a result, resilience is becoming a strategic differentiator rather than a defensive capability. This broader shift was reflected throughout the discussions at KPMG in Romania’s event. Edward Davies, CEE Life Sciences Lead, highlighted the strategic opportunity for Central and Eastern Europe to strengthen its role within Europe’s trusted Life Sciences networks. Clinical research, manufacturing, regulatory execution and digital capabilities are increasingly positioning the region as an important contributor to the future of the sector. According to Davies, trust, compliance and operational resilience are becoming strategic assets alongside scientific innovation. The trend is also reflected in market developments. Romania’s pharmaceuticals market continues to expand, and is now worth approximately RON 37.7 billion. At the same time, declining market volumes are increasing pressure on companies to improve efficiency, forecasting and resource allocation. Artificial Intelligence Is Moving From Experimentation to Reality Artificial intelligence emerged as one of the most significant themes of the event, reflecting the industry’s rapid transition from pilot projects to practical implementation. According to Eurostat, 20% of EU enterprises with at least 10 employees used AI technologies in 2025 [1] , compared with 13.5% in 2024 [2] , while adoption among large enterprises was 55% [3] . As AI moves from experimentation into core business processes, companies increasingly need secure and integrated environments where data, technology, controls and human oversight can work together effectively. Companies in the sector are increasingly exploring how AI can automate processes, improve productivity and support more informed decision-making. The conversation around AI focused on a clear shift taking place across industries: Companies in the sector are moving from experimentation to real-world implementation. Ileana Ionescu, Director, and Inga Țîgai, CEE Head of Tax & Legal Technology, explored how AI is already transforming business processes, including tax and compliance activities. Their message was clear: Technology alone is not enough. Long-term success depends on reliable data, strong governance and employees who are ready to work alongside new technologies. The audience also saw practical examples of AI in action, including a solution capable of extracting and processing invoice data for further registration and analysis. Another highlight was KPMG Digital Gateway, a centralized platform designed to simplify the management of tax obligations and processes, while providing access to analytics, reporting tools, industry insights and specialized expertise across the KPMG network. AI is no longer confined to back-office functions. Increasingly, it is finding its way into products and services that directly support patient care. Speaking from an industry perspective, Vadim Fântânari, Chief AI Officer at RebelDot and Co-Founder of WakeZ, discussed the growing role of AI-enabled healthcare solutions and presented WakeZ’s medical device, currently undergoing registration with the National Agency of Medicines. Developed to support people experiencing depression, the solution illustrates how artificial intelligence is beginning to reshape areas traditionally associated with clinical care and treatment support. However, innovation must go hand in hand with accountability. Dragoș Cherciu, Lawyer at KPMG Legal – Toncescu și Asociații, highlighted the need for clear governance structures and effective risk management as companies in the sector expand the use of AI in highly regulated environments. A similar trend is evident in the regulatory and transfer pricing landscape. Alexandra Ion, Associate Director, Transfer Pricing, explained that tax authorities are increasingly relying on digital tools, advanced analytics, and data-driven risk assessment methodologies, particularly in the area of transfer pricing. As a result, companies are expected to maintain robust documentation, ensure consistency across data sources, and be prepared to support their transfer pricing positions through greater transparency and timely access to information. This evolution is making compliance processes more data-driven and reinforcing the importance of preparedness in interactions with regulators. Trust and Compliance Are Becoming Strategic Assets Another major takeaway from the event was that compliance can no longer be treated as a box-ticking exercise. Across tax, legal and healthcare regulations, authorities are increasingly relying on technology, analytics and digital tools. As a result, companies in the sector are expected not only to comply with rules but also to demonstrate compliance through evidence, documentation and effective internal controls. This is particularly relevant for interactions between pharmaceutical companies and healthcare professionals, as well as transfer pricing matters. The growing digitalization of tax administration processes facilitates a more stringent approach to enforcing compliance. In a more regulated environment, trust is becoming a business asset. Organizations that can demonstrate transparency, accountability and strong governance are likely to be better positioned to withstand scrutiny and maintain stakeholder confidence. Risk, Resilience and Long-Term Performance As companies become more digital and interconnected, resilience is increasingly shaped by their ability to manage risk across multiple fronts. Cybersecurity, workforce transformation, data-driven decision-making and regulatory compliance are no longer separate priorities, but interconnected elements of long-term business performance. Gheorghe Vlad, Director, Cyber Security, emphasized that cybersecurity must be viewed as a business issue rather than a purely technical one. In the pharmaceutical and healthcare sectors, cyber incidents can disrupt manufacturing operations, affect supply chains and ultimately have an impact on patient access to treatment. As a result, cyber resilience is becoming a boardroom priority, with companies placing greater focus on business continuity and operational preparedness. People remain at the center of this transformation. Claudia Stan, Associate Director, People Services, discussed the implications of the European Pay Transparency Directive and the evolving expectations of today’s workforce. Transparency, equitable pay practices and trust are increasingly seen as essential factors in attracting, motivating and retaining talent in a competitive labor market. At the same time, organizations are turning to forecasting and predictive analytics to strengthen decision-making in an increasingly uncertain environment. Flavia Matei, Director, Strategy & Performance, highlighted how advanced analytics can help business leaders anticipate change, improve planning and make more informed strategic decisions. Laura Grădinescu, Lawyer, Managing Associate at KPMG Legal – Toncescu și Asociații, emphasized that companies must be able to demonstrate compliance through evidence, robust documentation and effective internal controls. Completing the legal perspective, Alex Slujitoru, lawyer, Partner at KPMG Legal – Toncescu și Asociații, examined current dispute trends affecting the pharmaceutical sector and highlighted the importance of identifying and addressing risks before they evolve into larger legal or operational challenges. Looking Ahead If there was one message that connected all discussions at the event, it was that the healthcare and life sciences sectors are facing a level of transformation unlike anything seen in recent years. From AI-powered innovation and cybersecurity risks to employee expectations, compliance demands and growing regulatory scrutiny, companies in the sector are being challenged to rethink how they operate, grow and create value. In this environment, success will increasingly belong to those that can manage complexity without slowing innovation, turn data into better decisions and build lasting trust with patients, employees, regulators and society at large. The future of healthcare will not be defined by technology alone. It will be defined by how effectively companies in the sector combine innovation, responsibility and resilience. https://www.romania-insider.com/healthca.text: Healthcare Update: Healthcare workers begin nationwide strike over pay reform in Romania 28 July 2026 Irina Marica Like this article? Share it with your friends! Facebook Twitter Google Pinterest Reddit Email LinkedIn Update: The Health Ministry announced on Tuesday it is closely monitoring medical activity as healthcare workers stage a nationwide strike, adding that it has asked regional public health authorities to immediately report any incidents that could affect patient care. It said it respects employees' constitutional right to strike and remains committed to dialogue with trade unions, describing social dialogue as the basis for finding "real, balanced, and sustainable solutions" for the system. The ministry also sad it had already submitted proposals for the new pay law, including raising bonuses for emergency on-call shifts from 20% to 30%, introducing a pilot performance-based pay scheme for public healthcare staff, revising hazardous working condition bonuses, adjusting salary coefficients to address existing imbalances, and introducing a transition period for the new pay system. Plus, it initiated a memorandum to unblock the hiring of more than 7,000 positions in public healthcare facilities to help address staff shortages. "The Health Ministry will continue dialogue with trade unions and all relevant partners, with responsibility and openness, to identify the best solutions for medical staff and patients," it said, adding that ensuring the continuity of healthcare services remains its top priority. Initial story: Doctors, nurses, and other healthcare workers in hundreds of Romanian hospitals began an indefinite nationwide strike on Tuesday, July 28, after talks with the authorities failed to resolve a dispute over the planned wage law reform and other labor grievances. Union leaders said only emergency services and one-third of normal medical activity would be maintained during the strike. The Sanitas Federation, Romania's largest healthcare and social assistance union, said it was proceeding with the general strike after a mediation meeting on Monday at the Presidential Administration ended without a concrete solution. “We reiterated that the healthcare system needs urgent measures so it can care for patients as they truly deserve," Sanitas said in a statement, adding that the interim government had "ignored any form of social dialogue" before discussions resumed following a court decision suspending government steps related to the draft pay law. The federation said representatives of the Presidential Administration agreed that its demands were "correct, well-founded, and necessary," but noted that the final decision on the legislation rests with Parliament. Sanitas said it would continue talks with parliamentary parties while also attending discussions at the Health Ministry on issues that can be addressed during the caretaker government's mandate. “Until a new decision is taken by the federation's statutory bodies, the strike schedule remains unchanged. Therefore, I am telling our colleagues that on July 28 the general strike in the healthcare system begins," Sanitas president Iulian Pope said after Monday's meeting. On Tuesday morning, Pope urged healthcare workers to remain united. “What we are asking from politicians is not privileges. We are asking for responsibility toward the people who work in the system and toward patients. We are asking them to understand that healthcare cannot be run against the people who keep it standing," he wrote on Facebook. The situation doesn’t affect all hospitals, however. According to Romanian public broadcaster TVR Info , employees from all 13 state hospitals in Iași County joined the strike. Meanwhile, for example, staff at the Piatra-Neamț County Emergency Hospital will not participate because they belong to a different trade union, hospital manager Alexandru Patrașcu told Agerpres . The union said the draft of the unified wage law could reduce the income of some healthcare employees while freezing others' salaries for several years, according to TVR Info. It also cited a shortage of around 30,000 staff in Romanian hospitals, alongside concerns over capped bonuses, lower payments for weekend and holiday work, a hiring freeze, and the reduction or elimination of certain allowances. The reform is one of the milestones Romania must complete under its National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR). The measure is linked to EUR 770 million in EU funding. The general strike follows a two-hour warning strike held on July 20, during which hospitals also limited activity to emergency cases and one-third of regular medical services. irina.marica@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Inquam Photos/ George Călin ) Read next 20 July 2026 Healthcare Doctors, nurses from hundreds of hospitals in Romania on strike due to new salary law Normal Healthcare Update: Healthcare workers begin nationwide strike over pay reform in Romania 28 July 2026 Irina Marica Like this article? The ministry also sad it had already submitted proposals for the new pay law, including raising bonuses for emergency on-call shifts from 20% to 30%, introducing a pilot performance-based pay scheme for public healthcare staff, revising hazardous working condition bonuses, adjusting salary coefficients to address existing imbalances, and introducing a transition period for the new pay system. Plus, it initiated a memorandum to unblock the hiring of more than 7,000 positions in public healthcare facilities to help address staff shortages. "The Health Ministry will continue dialogue with trade unions and all relevant partners, with responsibility and openness, to identify the best solutions for medical staff and patients," it said, adding that ensuring the continuity of healthcare services remains its top priority. Initial story: Doctors, nurses, and other healthcare workers in hundreds of Romanian hospitals began an indefinite nationwide strike on Tuesday, July 28, after talks with the authorities failed to resolve a dispute over the planned wage law reform and other labor grievances. Union leaders said only emergency services and one-third of normal medical activity would be maintained during the strike. The Sanitas Federation, Romania's largest healthcare and social assistance union, said it was proceeding with the general strike after a mediation meeting on Monday at the Presidential Administration ended without a concrete solution. “We reiterated that the healthcare system needs urgent measures so it can care for patients as they truly deserve," Sanitas said in a statement, adding that the interim government had "ignored any form of social dialogue" before discussions resumed following a court decision suspending government steps related to the draft pay law. The federation said representatives of the Presidential Administration agreed that its demands were "correct, well-founded, and necessary," but noted that the final decision on the legislation rests with Parliament. Sanitas said it would continue talks with parliamentary parties while also attending discussions at the Health Ministry on issues that can be addressed during the caretaker government's mandate. “Until a new decision is taken by the federation's statutory bodies, the strike schedule remains unchanged. Therefore, I am telling our colleagues that on July 28 the general strike in the healthcare system begins," Sanitas president Iulian Pope said after Monday's meeting. On Tuesday morning, Pope urged healthcare workers to remain united. “What we are asking from politicians is not privileges. We are asking for responsibility toward the people who work in the system and toward patients. We are asking them to understand that healthcare cannot be run against the people who keep it standing," he wrote on Facebook. The situation doesn’t affect all hospitals, however. According to Romanian public broadcaster TVR Info , employees from all 13 state hospitals in Iași County joined the strike. Meanwhile, for example, staff at the Piatra-Neamț County Emergency Hospital will not participate because they belong to a different trade union, hospital manager Alexandru Patrașcu told Agerpres . The union said the draft of the unified wage law could reduce the income of some healthcare employees while freezing others' salaries for several years, according to TVR Info. It also cited a shortage of around 30,000 staff in Romanian hospitals, alongside concerns over capped bonuses, lower payments for weekend and holiday work, a hiring freeze, and the reduction or elimination of certain allowances. The reform is one of the milestones Romania must complete under its National Recovery and Resilience Plan (PNRR). The measure is linked to EUR 770 million in EU funding. The general strike follows a two-hour warning strike held on July 20, during which hospitals also limited activity to emergency cases and one-third of regular medical services. irina.marica@romania-insider.com (Photo source: Inquam Photos/ George Călin ) Read next 20 July 2026 Healthcare Doctors, nurses from hundreds of hospitals in Romania on strike due to new salary law Normal Healthcare Update: Healthcare workers begin nationwide strike over pay reform in Romania 28 July 2026 Irina Marica Like this article? By order of Minister of Foreign Affairs Oana Țoiu, the Ambassador of the Russian Federation to Bucharest was summoned to the headquarters of Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday, 27 July 2026. The summons came as a firm response to the repeated violations of Romania’s airspace between 24 and 26 July 2026, during which the Romanian Armed Forces shot down three drones that had entered the country’s territory without authorization. During the meeting, the Russian diplomat was presented with fragments of a drone destroyed on Romanian territory. According to investigations conducted by the Prosecutor’s Office, the components have been officially confirmed to be of Russian origin. The Romanian side expressed its strong protest against these illegal and irresponsible actions and reiterated the clear attribution of responsibility to the Russian Federation. It was emphasized that it is absolutely inadmissible and intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romania’s airspace, which is also NATO and European Union airspace. The Romanian side stressed that the Russian Federation bears sole responsibility for these serious incidents and for the deterioration of the regional security environment. During the meeting, the Russian Ambassador was also formally handed a diplomatic note informing him that a member of the Russian diplomatic mission in Bucharest had been declared persona non grata and is required to leave Romanian territory within five days. In addition, Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs has recalled the Romanian Ambassador to the Russian Federation to Bucharest for consultations. Romania will continue to coordinate its response closely with its NATO and European Union allies and partners and remains firmly committed to taking all necessary measures to protect its national security and its citizens. Photograph: Dado Ruvić/Reuters Nvidia Nvidia links with Wall Street firms for $500bn AI financing deal Apollo, BlackRock, Goldman Sachs and KKR among those working with chipmaker to fund infrastructure Reuters Tue 11 Aug 2026 02.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nvidia ⁠has partnered with six major Wall Street financial institutions to raise ⁠more than $500bn (£370bn) capital for artificial intelligence infrastructure. The Nvidia chief executive, Jensen Huang, said on X that the company has ⁠the option to backstop up to $125bn, or 25% of the potential deals. The move highlights how surging demand ⁠for AI computing capacity is drawing institutional investors, as governments, companies and ​startups race to build out ‌datacentres. Big tech companies have signalled that spending on AI ‌would not slow down, with combined outlays set to surpass $730bn this year. However, there has been concerns over the link between high valuations of tech companies and the need for vast investments to support their ambitions . Nvidia signed memorandums of understanding with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR for the financing platforms. The deal will create financing platforms, allowing third-party investors to treat AI “compute” as an asset class. Nvidia, which is worth $5.3tn, counts Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Facebook owner Meta among its customers. “These financing platforms ​will help customers access scarce compute at scale and build the AI factories that will power every industry and country in the age of AI,” Huang said. “Compute has become a critical infrastructure asset,” Joe Bae and Scott Nuttall, the co-chief executives of KKR, said in a joint statement. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion Nvidia said the arrangements would “create dedicated pools of ⁠capital at significant scale at attractive rates” for its customers. The ​company did ​not disclose the financial terms, ​investment commitments by individual firms or a timetable for ​deploying the planned $500bn. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: The government is facing a controversial decision over whether to approve new extraction at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields. Photograph: Martin Langer/Alamy View image in fullscreen The government is facing a controversial decision over whether to approve new extraction at the Rosebank and Jackdaw fields. Photograph: Martin Langer/Alamy First Edition newsletter Oil and gas companies Tuesday briefing: To drill or not to drill – Burnham’s first big climate test In today’s newsletter: As we enter our fifth summer heatwave, Andy Burnham’s government is looking at what the UK should do with its remaining North Sea oil and gas Michael Segalov Tue 11 Aug 2026 01.46 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 01.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. What a difference a new job can make. “To have a shot at staying within 1.5C global warming, we can’t have any new oil or gasfields … It’s irresponsible and shortsighted to be funding new #fossilfuels when we need to be getting to #NetZero.” This was the 2022 message from Miatta Fahnbulleh , now the secretary of state for energy security and net zero. It’s a testament to her remarkable rise that Fahnbulleh wasn’t even an MP when she posted it four years ago. Today, she is in the cabinet, facing (or is the face of, at least) one of the most challenging, and potentially controversial questions looming for the new government: to drill or not to drill, baby? Two sites are the focus of fierce debate. Yesterday, a public consultation on whether to greenlight extraction at one of them – Jackdaw – closed. Next Monday, it’ll be the same for the other, Rosebank. Andy Burnham has been silent about the climate crisis since taking office. As we enter yet another heatwave, what his government does next will be a defining signal of intent on the issue. But what would extraction actually mean, and how many options are open to Fahnbulleh? That’s the subject of today’s First Edition, after a roundup of this morning’s headlines. Five big stories Colombia | More than 100 people have died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia, collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira. UK weather | Almost three-quarters of England is now in drought , with four more regions officially declared, and as much of Europe braces for its fifth climate crisis-driven heatwave this summer. Crime | Police are investigating whether Joshua Kerry , the man charged with the murder of the former Reform UK and Conservative politician Ann Widdecombe, had any role in an attempted burglary last year at the then London home of Nigel Farage. China | More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China by Sunday evening as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides. Ukraine | Russia has banned voting against the war in September’s elections, after the supreme court upheld a suit brought by a small pro-Kremlin nationalist party, and stripped voters of their last option on the ballot: Yabloko, the country’s only remaining anti-war party. In depth: Two fields, one very big decision View image in fullscreen Campaigners argue that oil and gas drilling will add to carbon emissions but do little to cut energy bills and improve long-term energy security. Photograph: Joao Daniel Pereira/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock While often lumped together, Rosebank and Jackdaw are two separate sites, hundreds of miles apart. Rosebank is a proposed new oilfield 80 miles off the Shetland coast, containing 300 to 500m barrels of oil. It’s the UK’s last major undeveloped oil site. There is also gas at Rosebank, equating to roughly 1% of current demand. Jackdaw is a gasfield 150 miles east of Aberdeen. If operational, it could probably produce approximately 40,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (bpd), which at peak is equivalent to 6% of the UK’s North Sea gas supply. Jackdaw could displace 2% of the UK’s imports of gas over its nine- to 12-year lifetime. Under UK law, all oil and gas under the ground or seabed is owned by the state . It’s our collective asset. The government then dishes out licences for exploration and extraction of these fossil fuels to business. Often, these have complicated structures. Shell holds the licence to extract at Jackdaw. Rosebank is majority owned by Adura, a joint venture between Shell and Equinor (mostly owned by the Norwegian state). A minority stake of Rosebank is owned by UK-based Ithaca Energy, a subsidiary of the Israeli energy conglomerate Delek Group. Delek operates in Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territories. The case for drilling – and the holes in it Unsurprisingly, the PR from fossil fuel companies on Rosebank and Jackdaw is full of optimism. It will bring down bills! Energy security! Jobs! These are all claims that have been repeatedly debunked . The UK Energy Research Centre is scathing in its assessment: “Assertions that drilling the North Sea will provide energy resilience and affordability in the face of current fuel price shocks are a delusion.” Jackdaw would create only 27 direct full-time jobs , according to its owner . Across both sites, there would be 880 jobs created during production, and 2,700 temporary construction roles. That’s no fix for structural decline. At least 70,000 jobs in the industry were lost in the decade to 2024, despite the Tories granting hundreds of licences. BP is now shutting down its North Sea operations. As our environment editor, Fiona Harvey tells me: “Whatever government does, jobs will decline. It’s unavoidable.” Because, the UK’s gas and oil is running out. Even if extraction is minimised, supplies are depleting: 90% has already been drained dry . Experts point to this as proof that new drilling won’t bolster long-term energy security. Who benefits from oil and gas? Drill or not, our household energy prices will unlikely be affected . Anything extracted wouldn’t be funnelled to UK residents at a knock-down rate: oil and gas are sold by private companies on international markets, which set the price. The scale of output from UK production is negligible in this global context. As we’ve seen, it takes one unreliable actor in charge of the world’s largest military to send global prices spiralling. Of course, there’s money to be made from tax – though these companies aren’t famed for coughing up when HMRC comes knocking. In 2024, Shell reported a negative UK tax figure of £12.5m while posting global post-tax profits of £18bn. In the same year, Equinor’s record was no better . Even if North Sea tax revenues were collected and somehow funnelled directly into energy bill subsidies, the impact would be limited. For context, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, the Conservatives spent up to £80bn across two years shielding households and businesses from energy price hikes. Even by the oil and gas industry’s own estimates , the Rosebank and Jackdaw tax take would pale in comparison. And given the scale of tax subsidies available, campaigners suggest Rosebank could actually cost taxpayers money . That means underwriting the very businesses who help to cause the climate crisis we’re experiencing. This, of course, would be exacerbated by any fossil fuels extracted by Jackdaw and Rosebank. Burning just Rosebank’s oil and gas would produce about 250m tonnes of CO2 over its lifetime. As Areeba Hamid, co-executive director of Greenpeace UK, put it to me: “Sections of the media just keep repeating myths and lies. We are expecting a fifth summer heatwave, wild fires are burning the country, oil and gas companies are posting billions in profits , while the rightwing press and fossil fuel companies are pushing for Rosebank and Jackdaw approval. It’s pure cognitive dissonance.” Over to Burnham Under the Conservatives, Rosebank and Jackdaw were approved, but a court ruled these permits unlawful after a legal challenge from Greenpeace and Uplift. New approval needed to be sought – the results of which are impending. Labour’s 2024 manifesto ruled out new licences for North Sea exploration, while stating existing ones would not be revoked. Insiders say a compromise might be struck, with only Jackdaw OK-ed. Gas is needed for home heating and electricity generation, though in what should be diminishing quantities, and its extraction is less carbon intensive than oil. “Allowing it to go ahead is far less harmful than Rosebank,” Fiona tells me. And Jackdaw is a tieback, so can be connected to existing infrastructure. “It could therefore come online quicker.” Fahnbulleh is on holiday for the next couple of weeks. In the absence of answers, the briefing wars are in full swing. Reports that oil and gas execs are “ near certain ” that Rosebank and Jackdaw will get the go-ahead should be treated with caution, given their incentive to will this into fruition. Remember how Shabana Mahmood was definitely going to be Burnham’s chancellor? For all his flip-floppery, Starmer was generally steadfast in his climate commitments while PM, even if rightwing backlash tempered his ambitions . Burnham had a strong environmental track record as Manchester mayor. But he’s an unknown entity in Downing Street. Until last month, Ed Miliband held the energy brief, driving the last government’s decarbonisation agenda. An experienced Westminster operator with decades of experience and press attacks, Miliband was resolute enough to stick with climate plans, however often he was heralded the “MOST DANGEROUS MAN IN BRITAIN”. Fahnbulleh looks like continuity. She has Miliband’s backing and before entering parliament, she held top jobs at left-leaning thinktanks, including as CEO of the New Economics Foundation (NEF), which expressed opposition to further fossil fuel extraction. But she’s a parliamentary newbie. How she’ll respond to power and significant external pressure remains uncertain. In an interview last weekend , she struck a vague but cautious note: “We’ve always been clear that oil and gas are part of the mix … We are doing the hard trade-offs to make sure that we are doing this transition in a way that still delivers affordability.” “It’s going to be tough,” Hamid says, “but Miatta has to stick to her position. Otherwise, it’s a slippery slope: the pressure won’t stop at Rosebank and Jackdaw.” We want to hear from you What comes next after the A-level results land? We’d like to hear from students, parents and teachers about the educational and working landscape facing young people once they get their results this Thursday. Photograph: Piki Films/Allstar I enjoyed this interview with the UK Palestinian comic Sami Abu Wardeh – another reason I’m still trying to plot a trip to the Edinburgh fringe this year. Michael My grandmother introduced me to Beryl Bainbridge via a dog-eared copy of the Dressmaker, which I found rivetingly adult as a 10-year-old. Our ranking of her greatest novels reminds me I’ve still, happily, got a few more to discover. Libby Simon Hattenstone’s column on prisons is characteristically compelling, and a reminder that amid all the talk of early release , some have been forgotten. Michael The Guardian’s senior economics commentator, Aditya Chakrabortty , is brilliant on Over the Top Under the Radar podcast, discussing why he doesn’t think a wealth tax is the magic bullet many progressives claim it to be. Libby Deadpan, full of warmth and generous to a fault – do make time to read one of Sam Neill’s final interviews, on the making of Taika Waititi’s Hunt for the Wilderpeople . Libby Sport View image in fullscreen Amy Hunt reacts after crossing the finish line to win the women’s 100 meters final. Photograph: Matthias Schräder/AP European championships | Britain’s Amy Hunt sprinted to women’s 100m glory in 11.00sec in Birmingham, with Ewa Swoboda claiming silver and Delphine Nkansa a bronze. Fifa | US president Donald Trump has warned Fifa would be making a “terrible mistake” if they get rid of Gianni Infantino as the head of world football’s governing body. Football | A consortium including the Amazon founder, Jeff Bezos, is close to completing a deal for a 30% stake in Liverpool after months of talks with Fenway Sports Group. The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian “Firefighters raise alarm over surge in ‘unprecedented’ summer blazes”, is the Guardian ’s front page today, while the i Paper writes “45 million people in the UK now living in drought”, the Mirror says “High & dry”, and Metro has “It never rains … but it pours”. On politics, the Times has “Burnham demands plan to keep PC’s killers in jail” and the Express writes “Kemi: Rule out new taxes to prevent more hardship”. The Mail ’s headline is “Day small boats crisis became a BIG boats crisis”, the Telegraph says “‘No limit’ to migrant mega dinghies”, and the Sun ’s take is “Not-so-small boats crisis”. Finally, the FT splashes “Wall Street big names join Nvidia to build $500bn AI financing package”. Today in Focus View image in fullscreen Saudi Arabia’s crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman, loves a video game. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images Why did Saudi Arabia just spend billions on a video games company? Last week Saudi Arabia’s wealth fund and a group of investors spent $55bn (£41bn) on Electronic Arts, the video games company behind the Sims, Madden NFL and Battlefield. But why would such a powerful government take a risk with video games? As Keith Stuart and George Osborn tell Annie Kelly, it’s part of a pattern of superpowers and authoritarian regimes seeing games as handy propaganda tools. Cartoon of the day | Martin Rowson View image in fullscreen Illustration: The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen Darren Miles, a 60-year-old slalom skateboarder who will be competing for Team GB at the World Skate Games this month. Photograph: Jonny Weeks/The Guardian At 60, Darren Miles is about to represent Great Britain at the world championships in slalom skateboarding – a sport he took up only in his late 50s. After a lifetime on a skateboard, he noticed his flexibility fading and his old tricks becoming increasingly difficult to do. Then, during lockdown, a stranger praised him for performing a simple 180 manoeuvre. It was a life-changing inflection point. Rather than give up, Miles found a new challenge in slalom, racing downhill between cones and learning to move his body in a different way. Now, after years of skating for the joy of it, he is discovering what he can still achieve – and seeing how far he can push himself.
