https://www.theguardian.com/society/ng-i.text: Evidence heard at Matilda’s inquest showed a person engulfed by stress in the final weeks of her life. Photograph: Guardian View image in fullscreen Evidence heard at Matilda’s inquest showed a person engulfed by stress in the final weeks of her life. Photograph: Guardian Carers Matilda in pieces: what one mother’s suicide reveals about the carers broken by the system Parent-carers of disabled children are exposed to chronic levels of extreme stress and often reach crisis point before help is available – then they face a ‘fight for basic support’, experts say. This is Matilda Davis’s story Josh Halliday Tue 11 Aug 2026 01.00 EDT Share Two days before she died, Matilda Davis issued a plea on Facebook. Sharing a study that found more than 40% of parent-carers had considered suicide, she called for “greater awareness, action and change” in Britain’s broken social care system. “This speaks the words I can’t,” she wrote. Matilda, known as Tilly to her family and friends, had spent years battling for support in a regime that close observers and those who rely on it often say is increasingly confusing, fragmented and difficult to navigate. Her seven-year-old son, Jude – not his real name – has significant disabilities. She was, her friends said, an “absolutely inspirational” mother, juggling care for Jude’s five-year-old sister Lilly – also a pseudonym – alongside his appointments at therapy, physio, hospital and two schools, as well as the significant financial and administrative burden. She cherished every moment with her children. “Tilly cared more than anyone I know,” said her sister Georgina Davis, 35. “It was what she lived for.” On 3 October last year, Matilda, 36, was found dead in the bathroom of their home in Stratford-upon-Avon in the West Midlands. She had killed herself a day after saying she felt “completely exhausted” by her responsibilities, and “paralysed with anxiety” about the prospect of her looming divorce from her estranged husband, who the Guardian has chosen not to name. View image in fullscreen ‘Tilly cared more than anyone I know,’ Georgina Davis said of her sister Matilda. ‘It was what she lived for.’ After Andy Burnham promised the biggest reforms to social care in a generation, experts said Matilda’s death showed how carers were being “pushed to breaking point” by a broken system. “Health and social care services in England are failing disabled children and their parents are being left to pick up the pieces,” said Dr Siobhan O’Dwyer, one of Britain’s leading experts on family carers. “In his speech, the prime minister acknowledged that without support unpaid carers can break. But what does it mean to break? For Matilda it meant death by suicide, it meant dying alone and in pain because services failed to fully appreciate the impact of the caring role and the troubled marriage, and it meant leaving behind the children she loved more than anything else in the world. “That is a break that can never be healed, but it was entirely preventable. If the government really wants to stop other carers breaking, it’s going to need more than a heartfelt speech. It’s going to need real action.” View image in fullscreen Matilda Davis had struggled with her mental health since her son became critically unwell shortly after his birth. She gave up work as an art teacher to care for him full time. Composite: Guardian ‘I won’t be here much longer’ Evidence heard at Matilda’s inquest earlier this year, including GP records and disclosures to professionals, showed a person engulfed by stress in the final weeks of her life. Last August, she told her GP she was worried about her “ability to cope emotionally with the daily demands as a parent-carer living with a home environment, which is becoming increasingly stressful, full of anxiety and worry … My absolute focus is to ensure [Jude and Lilly] are spared the turmoil of the unrest and upset in the house.” Matilda had struggled with her mental health since Jude became critically unwell shortly after his birth. But two days before she died, she was in the “slight depths of ruin”, she told a friend in a voice note. “I’m just in pieces and I’m trying to hold it together with the children, but it’s so physically taxing and emotional with what I’m dealing with [Jude] alone,” she said. “I’m just breaking really. I’m just completely broken. I haven’t really got any physical strength in me.” Matilda had given up work as an art teacher to care for Jude full time. Social workers had not carried out a family care assessment, where professionals assess what support they might need, for almost four years by the time she died. They were due to visit the following week to carry out an updated plan. View image in fullscreen Matilda Davis told her divorce lawyer her day-to-day life was packed with ‘appointments, rehabilitation, admin, emails, phone calls, transporting/commuting’. On 2 October, Matilda told her divorce solicitor the worry was “overwhelming”. “My capacity to earn is basically nothing and will be long term,” she said. Her day-to-day life was packed with “appointments, rehabilitation, admin, emails, phone calls, transporting/commuting”, she said, which would become more complex over the coming years with Jude’s schooling and health needs. With her marriage coming to an end, Matilda said she was “desperately fearful” about the future of the family home, as she had sacrificed years of earnings to care for Jude full time. “The estate agents will not accept me as a non-earning single occupant and I have absolutely no where else suitable to go,” she said the day before she died, the inquest heard. She said she felt “financially trapped” and that it was “both physically and emotionally relentless at times”. That morning, her husband called social services to say he was concerned about Matilda’s mental health. He said she had expressed suicidal thoughts that morning by saying: “I won’t be here much longer and then you will all have to look after yourselves .” Social workers are obliged to act on welfare concerns within 24 hours and visited Matilda at home at 2pm the following day, a Friday. A note of the meeting, shared at the inquest, detailed how Matilda was “visibly upset and tearful” when they arrived and “expressed significant anxiety” about the visit. The coroner, Deborah Sewell, noted that Matilda spoke of the “emotional and psychological strain arising from relationship conflict, financial pressures, and the ongoing divorce proceedings”. Matilda told the social workers she had hit her head on the door in front of the children that morning “as a manifestation of emotional frustration”. Before they left the meeting, social workers suggested her husband look after the children that weekend and that Matilda stayed with her parents. She was reluctant to leave, having already expressed concern about how Jude would manage without her. When the social workers left at 2.30pm, Matilda “appeared calm” and there was “no indication of any suicidal ideation”, the note of the meeting recorded. Minutes later, she was dead. At the inquest in March, social workers admitted they did not ask Matilda whether she had thoughts of suicide despite knowing she was in significant distress. Nor was she directed to crisis organisations. Neither social worker who visited her that day had undertaken suicide prevention training. When told it is best practice to ask someone directly whether they have plans to kill themselves if they have expressed suicidal thoughts, one said: “Well, I’ve not done the training.” Asked whether they were concerned that Matilda had said a day earlier she “won’t be here much longer”, which they were told by her husband was a suicidal thought, the social worker added: “Obviously it is concerning she said that but she wasn’t using the word ‘suicide’.” Sewell issued a rare prevention of future deaths report in April to direct Warwickshire council to make suicide prevention training mandatory for 600 members of staff. The council said: “We extend our deepest sympathies to the family and all those affected by this tragic loss. Following Matilda’s death and the subsequent coroner’s inquest, we have implemented enhanced suicide prevention training for all social workers to equip staff with skills to identify when parents and carers need additional support and to help them to access it. “In addition, all agencies involved with this case will participate in a review to look closely at all the circumstances leading up to Matilda’s death. The purpose of the review will be to make recommendations for improving services and support.” View image in fullscreen Matilda Davis with her son. In the garden of his primary school in Birmingham, two apple trees and a rose bush have been planted in her memory. ‘Love does not mitigate the overwhelming pressure’ In research published in 2024 – and shared by Matilda two days before her death – the University of Birmingham found 42% of parent-carers had thought about suicide, many times higher than the general population. Those caring for significantly disabled children are exposed to chronic levels of extreme stress that are “compounded by other factors like poverty, domestic abuse, or social isolation”, said O’Dwyer, who led the research. She said social workers often had an “excess of professional optimism” about parents’ ability to cope with the pressures of caring for children with complex needs, particularly when they saw a devoted, loving mother – and it was often women who took on primary care responsibilities – and would think she would never act on thoughts of self-harm because she loved her children so much. “But it is possible to love your children and be pushed to the point of suicide,” O’Dwyer said. “Love does not mitigate the overwhelming pressure of caring for a disabled child in a broken system.” Contact, a charity for families with disabled children, said parents often reach crisis point before help was available and had to “fight for basic support”. Anna Bird, its chief executive, said parent-carers were being “squeezed from every direction: by the cost of living crisis, reduced services; and a support system that is increasingly confusing, fragmented and difficult to navigate”. In the garden of Jude’s primary school in Birmingham, two apple trees and a rose bush have been planted in Matilda’s memory. Twenty miles away in Stratford, her friends at a family club have raised money for a bench engraved with her name and a number for the Samaritans suicide helpline. Her sister Georgina described Matilda as “the most incredibly devoted mother”, draining her savings and driving hundreds of miles a week to get Jude the support he needed. “She would tell me how she had to really fight to get what she wanted and needed for [Jude],” she said. “[Often talking about] how exhausting it is having to continually have to battle to get the provision he so needs.” Matilda’s friend Francesca Roberts, a nursery manager, said she was constantly in awe of her ability to go “far beyond what any parent should have to do simply to access proper care and support”. “She absolutely adored her children and dedicated every part of herself to them,” she said. Matilda was “one of the most caring, devoted, and selfless people I have ever known,” she added. “She was the village that everybody dreams of having around them.” Explore more on these topics Carers Social care Parents and parenting Disability Children's health Mental health Share Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Supporters of Russia's liberal, anti-war Yabloko party crowd outside the supreme court in Moscow as it delivers its ruling banning all the party’s candidates from the September parliamentary elections. Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Supporters of Russia's liberal, anti-war Yabloko party crowd outside the supreme court in Moscow as it delivers its ruling banning all the party’s candidates from the September parliamentary elections. Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty Images Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Russia bans voting against the war Every candidate of Yabloko – the last anti-war party – barred from September elections; warning over ‘Russian Starlink’ progress. What we know on day 1,630 Warren Murray with Guardian writers and agencies Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.38 EDT Last modified on Mon 10 Aug 2026 21.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia has banned voting against the war in September’s elections . The supreme court upheld a suit brought by a small pro-Kremlin nationalist party, Roblina, and stripped voters opposed to the war of their last option on the ballot: Yabloko, the country’s only remaining anti-war party . The court banned Yabloko’s entire list of federal election candidates from standing for the State Duma of Russia’s parliament. With most of Vladimir Putin’s opponents jailed, exiled or dead , Yabloko is the only liberal party still operating in Russia. Voting options other than Putin’s de facto party, the ruling United Russia, are only tolerated if they are too weak to win; give their backing to the Kremlin; or serve as “spoilers” that draw votes away from anyone who might pose a threat to the regime. About a hundred supporters, mostly young people, gathered outside the courthouse chanting “Shame! Shame!” after the ruling was delivered. Like the Duma, the supreme court routinely rubber-stamps the Kremlin’s wishes. Addressing protesters, Yabloko leader Nikolay Rybakov said the party would appeal against the decision. In an interview with Agence France-Presse on the weekend, Rybakov said about 40 party activists were facing prosecution for opposing the war. The party’s deputy leader, Maxim Kruglov, was jailed for seven years in June over social media posts, while Rybakov was fined and barred from elections for posting a photo of Alexei Navalny. Independent polls show most Russians favour peace negotiations with Kyiv . Russian ⁠missiles and ⁠aerial ​bombs killed five people and injured about 20 others in the ⁠south-eastern Ukrainian city ​of Zaporizhzhia ⁠early ‌on ‌Tuesday, said the ‌regional governor, Ivan Fedorov. At the same time, the military administration in Kyiv said warehouses in ​a central district ‌of the capital were ablaze after missile strikes. ‌One person was reported ‌injured. A Ukrainian MiG-29 fighter ⁠jet caught fire and crashed during ⁠a combat ⁠mission when a missile misfired, ​with the pilot ejecting safely. Ukraine’s air force said the ‌pilot – who had been targeting ‌Russian positions in ‌the southern region of Odesa – was taken ‌to hospital. Russia’s rollout of a Starlink alternative to counteract its banning from the US-based system is taking place faster than predicted, with 16 satellites in orbit so far , top Ukrainian intelligence official Maj Gen ‌Vadym Skibitskyi has warned. Russia’s Rassvet system remains a far cry from Starlink, which had more than 10,000 satellites as of June and has given Kyiv a major advantage in drone operations and battlefield communications. Speaking to RBC-Ukraine, Skibitskyi, head of the Ukrainian GUR, said Rassvet has “begun launching ‌it much faster than originally planned”. Russia planned to have 292 satellites by 2027 and ‌924 by 2035. “Once Russia deploys a full satellite constellation, the system will operate like Starlink. Discussions are ​already under way on how to counter it.” Analysts have noted that while Russia has been slow to produce innovations in the war, it is quick to adapt to and copy Ukraine’s actions, introducing corresponding systems that it produces and adopts rapidly. As Russia pounds Ukraine with supersonic missiles that Ukrainians have no interceptors for, Skibitskyi said Moscow had already met its annual ⁠production targets for Zircon and Oniks missiles in the first seven ​months of 2026 ​and was exceeding its 2026 ​missile production goals by 10% to 20%. At the same time, Ukraine’s emerging ​ballistic missile industry, and drone ​production facilities, had ​become a priority target for Russia’s missile campaign. Russia’s stockpile of Iskander-M ballistic missiles, the mainstay of its supersonic strikes, was estimated at about 130, with 65 new ones made in July alone. On Tuesday, there were unconfirmed reports that Russian ballistic missile launcher systems were destroyed inside Russia, not far from the border. Ukraine drone strike on oil refinery deep inside Russia kills at least 13 Read more A Ukrainian drone strike set fire to the Taneco refinery in the Russian city of Nizhnekamsk , about 750 miles (1,200km) from the Ukrainian border, Luke Harding writes . Ukraine’s general staff said it was part of a campaign to reduce the “military potential of the Russian aggressor”. Russian authorities said at least 13 people were killed. Taneco is one of Russia’s biggest and most technologically advanced oil refineries, and part of it produces rubber and petrochemical products. Overnight into Monday, Ukraine’s armed forces hit equipment depots and a repair unit in the occupied Donetsk and Luhansk parts of eastern Ukraine , while ⁠Russian-installed local authorities said the ⁠Zaporizhzhia region in south-east Ukraine was largely without ⁠electricity on Monday ⁠after ​Ukrainian attacks destroyed key power facilities. Reuters reports that Ukraine is considering shipping grain by rail through Moldova as a more ⁠secure export option than by ⁠sea as its ports are battered by Russian attacks. Sources in Ukraine and Moldova said Kyiv wants a 50% discount on freight through Moldova to the Romanian port of Constanța. A source at Moldovan Railways said Moldova wants guarantees about the volume to be transported. The Ukrainians estimate a working corridor could provide for 10% of Ukraine’s exports. Moldovan and Ukrainian ministers met in Odesa on Monday for discussions. Rescuers search rubble in Cali as Colombia’s strongest quake in decades hits Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 11/08/2026 - 8:53 GMT+2 Rescuers in Cali search rubble after Colombia’s strongest quake this century, which killed over 130 people, left hundreds injured and many missing. … More In Cali, Colombia's third‑most populous city after Bogotá and Medellín, residents and rescue workers picked their way through shattered concrete and twisted steel on Monday 10 August 2026, searching for survivors as ambulances crowded the streets around collapsed buildings. The footage shows people clearing rubble by hand and passing debris along human chains, while injured survivors are led away from the wreckage. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT A six-month-old baby and her mother were among those pulled from beneath a five-storey building, while patients were evacuated from a hospital after part of the structure collapsed. A 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck western Colombia, killing at least 132 people and injuring 570, according to an evening update from the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, with the toll expected to rise. The US Geological Survey placed the epicentre near San Jose del Palmar in Choco province, 400 kilometres west of Bogota, at a depth of 107 kilometres. Pereira alone reported 60 deaths, and 86 buildings collapsed nationwide. Newly inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella declared a national disaster, with more than 1,600 buildings damaged. With at least 188 people still missing, Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder appealed to Bogotá and Medellín for urgent assistance. The quake was Colombia's strongest in the 21st century. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/11/at-le.text: The Colombian Association of Capital Cities reports a provisional toll of at least 132 dead and 570 injured in the departments hit by Monday's 7.4-magnitude earthquake -and its subsequent aftershocks-.Cauca and Risaralda, located to the west of the so-called Coffee Axis, are the regions with the highest number of victims, according to the newspaper "El Espectador", with at least 60 and 15 deaths respectively, plus around 13 in Chocó. Other affected regions include Caldas and Quindío.undefinedThe epicentre was in San José del Palmar, in the south-east of Chocó, bordering Valle del Cauca and Risaralda and roughly equidistant from the cities of Cali and Medellín, with the former suffering the most damage to its infrastructure. Seismographs indicate that the natural disaster originated within the Nazca plate, at a depth of around 103 kilometres. This plate sinks beneath the South American plate that forms the Andes mountain range, causing friction and events of this kind.Abelardo de la Espriella, who only recently took office as president of Colombia, travelled on Monday afternoon to Quibdó, capital of the department of Chocó, and later to Cali. As part of the reinforcement of emergency efforts, the latter city will receive 60 rescue workers from Bogotá and a further 32 members of the armed forces.The far-right leader has announced that government representatives will head the unified command posts in the affected areas, with the departments ceding their powers on the matter. "I don't want anyone going off on their own", said the president, who will travel to the Coffee Axis in the coming days. "Information will come from the Office of the President of the Republic; from no other body of the Colombian state".Cali and Pereira impose a curfewThe capital of Valle del Cauca has imposed a curfew between 20:00 on Monday and 6:00 on Tuesday and ordered the militarisation of the city in response to the emergency, which has left numerous structures damaged in Cali.Mayor Alejandro Eder has justified the move as a way to allow relief agencies to focus their efforts on searching for and rescuing those people who may still be trapped under the rubble. "We are facing threats of looting, which is why I have ordered the curfew and the militarisation of Cali", Eder said, calling on citizens to report any attempted looting or incidents that threaten public safety.undefinedHis counterpart in the Colombian city of Pereira, Mauricio Salazar, also declared a curfew on Monday to prevent looting. "As of today at 18:00 we have imposed a curfew until 5:00 to protect businesses in the city. This curfew will apply in the city centre, in Comuna Universidad and in the Cuba subcentre", explained the mayor of the departmental capital of Risaralda.In Caldas, governor Henry Gutiérrez Angel has likewise opted to impose a curfew to prevent looting and protect the population.undefinedAt the onset of the earthquake, this area suffered a blackout affecting electricity and mobile phone coverage. Up to six airports in the west of the country (Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura) still have operations suspended. The tremor was felt in neighbouring countries far from the epicentre, such as Ecuador and Panama.From Mexico, President Claudia Sheinbaum has expressed her solidarity with Colombia and said her country is ready to provide whatever support is needed in the emergency. Mexican media report that the Morena leader has made available to the Colombian authorities any assistance they may require.Among those sending messages is María Corina Machado, who has conveyed her solidarity with those affected and underlined Venezuelans' experience of this type of disaster. "We know from first-hand experience how vital international solidarity is in the face of a tragedy of this magnitude", wrote the opposition leader 'de facto' in exile. This earthquake follows two consecutive quakes of magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5 off the Venezuelan coast at the end of June. Those quakes destroyed hundreds of buildings and claimed the lives of more than 5,000 people.From Spain, Pedro Sánchez has also expressed his solidarity with the country and offered whatever assistance is needed (source in Spanish). For the time being, there are no reports of Spanish nationals among the fatalities, although the tally remains preliminary.undefined

http://www.euronews.com/next/2026/08/11/.text: When Kazakhstan became one of the world's largest crypto mining hubs five years ago, the boom strained the country’s power grid, and the government’s response resulted in most miners either leaving the country or going underground.Now the Kazakh government is looking to bring it all back home by offering tax breaks and legal certainty.The Kazakh government signed a decree designed to encourage citizens to declare cryptocurrency holdings, move them onto regulated domestic platforms and integrate digital assets into the country's economy.The authorities are offering private investors a tax break on personal income from digital asset transactions for three years, provided the assets were not connected to fraud, money laundering or linked to unlicensed crypto services.The decision has opened the door to making it easier for miners to operate in the country — and for everyone to profit.Crypto boom cut shortCryptocurrency mining uses powerful computers to solve complex mathematical problems in order to verify and add transactions to a blockchain — the ledger on which a cryptocurrency's transaction history is recorded.Miners who successfully complete them are rewarded with cryptocurrency deposited directly to their personal crypto wallets, which in some cases like Bitcoin can bring in significant profits.The downside is that the process consumes a large amount of power because the computations require sustained processing.After China banned Bitcoin mining in 2021, many miners began looking for new locations with low-cost energy.At that point Kazakhstan rapidly became the second-largest Bitcoin mining location after the US. Many tried to get in on the profits, with people even putting mining equipment on their balconies.Some went so far as to masquerade the mining farms as vegetable storage facilities, greenhouses or AI data centres at abandoned Soviet-era industrial sites to conceal their massive electricity consumption.The country did not get to enjoy the crypto bloom for too long. The rapid influx of miners placed an enormous burden on the country’s ageing electricity grid.In October 2021, surging electricity demand contributed to outages at three power plants in northeastern Kazakhstan, while rolling blackouts affected several regions. At peak, cryptocurrency miners were consuming an estimated 8% of Kazakhstan's total electricity output.Authorities responded by repeatedly tightening regulations on electricity consumption and digital asset legalisation, leading to miners' departure abroad and the proliferation of illegal operations.Kazakhstan never outright banned crypto mining, keeping its options open to potentially harness its potential in the future.According to Kazakhstan's financial regulator, Astana International Financial Centre (AIFC), Kazakh citizens own approximately 1 million crypto wallets.The AIFC, modelled on Dubai's DIFC financial free zone, has functioned as Kazakhstan's sandbox for financial innovation and serves as the regulatory home for digital asset companies operating in the country.This figure is nearly four times the number of users registered on authorised local exchanges, which in March reached 256,900.Bringing crypto assets back onshoreAttracting crypto owners back to their home countries with incentives and simplified legal frameworks has turned into a global trend in recent years, experts say.The UAE, Hong Kong and Singapore have implemented similar tax measures alongside clear licensing, regulations and access to banking services, bringing in additional revenue.The decree also addresses the energy question that triggered Kazakhstan's earlier mining crisis.Under the plan, associated gas from oil fields not required for state use can be used to generate electricity for mining operations, broadening miners' options beyond the main national grid.General Manager of Binance Kazakhstan Nurkhat Kushimov believes the tax incentive is the most important measure in the decree.“This is a strong incentive for users to choose regulated jurisdictions and platforms operating within them," Kushimov told Euronews."This approach makes working in a licensed environment more attractive, fosters trust in the market and creates the conditions for its further development,” he said.Chairman of Kazakhstan’s Association of Fintech, AI and Crypto Industry Bakhytzhan Kenzhebayev believes that the tax incentive removes one of the main uncertainties for the private investor, namely the question of when and on what basis the obligation arises. But the measure in itself is not sufficient.“Users choose a platform not based on the tax rate, but on a combination of factors: how easy it is to deposit and withdraw (the local currency), the liquidity, and how clear the rules are,” Kenzhebayev told Euronews."For a licensed participant, the predictability of the rule is more valuable than the benefit itself."President of Kazakhstan’s Blockchain and Digital Mining Association Daniyar Mubarakov told Euronews that any government support is welcome, but wonders how long this measure will work.“For certain categories of entrepreneurs preferential tax regimes mean not only a reduction in taxes in the current period, but also a possible several-fold increase in taxes in the future due to increased volumes,” Mubarakov said.Vice Minister of AI and Digital Development Gizzat Baitursynov said that his department is working on a proposal for a simplified tax regime following the expiration of the exemption in three years' time.He added that the department is also working on cancelling tax audits for private investors covering the previous three years.Beyond tax incentivesExperts say that Kazakh private investors' return to domestic platforms will depend on their competitiveness.“For most users, convenience of service, liquidity, availability of instruments, speed of transactions, and the ability to seamlessly interact with the banking system remain the key factors,” Kushimov said.According to Kenzhebayev, the main risks now lie in the legal definitions and terminology used. If the exemption is defined too broadly, it could create space to abuse the system and avoid paying taxes on other assets unrelated to crypto.“This creates the risk of a reversal of the norm in a year or two, and that causes more damage to the market than an initially high but stable rate,” Kenzhebayev explained.He also warned that the same digital asset can be treated as two different things depending on whether it falls under the AIFC or Kazakhstan's national rules, which would in turn mean companies would have to comply with two separate legal structures at once."The difficulty arises at the intersection. As a result, the participant builds two parallel infrastructures for one business, which reflects on the costs," he said.Kenzhebayev said tax breaks alone would not be enough to draw users to licensed Kazakh platforms.What would make the difference, he said, is reliable access to banking, clear rules for converting crypto into the local currency, straightforward requirements for keeping client assets safe, and a regulatory environment that does not put licensed operators at a disadvantage.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/11/hundr.text: Tropical Storm Dolphin dumped heavy rain in eastern China, causing flooding in places after making landfall as a typhoon on Sunday, leading to cancellation of hundreds of flights by aviation authorities at Shanghai airports.More than 900 flights, or about 40% of those expected, were cancelled in Shanghai’s Hongqiao and Pudong airports after about 1,300 were canceled the day before, according to Shanghai Airport Group.Shanghai also suspended some of its metro lines on Monday, and China Railway Chengdu Group suspended 115 trains, state news agency Xinhua reported.Authorities warned of risks of severe flooding and landslides in some areas. State broadcaster CCTV reported that authorities in Yueqing, a city in Zhejiang province, searched for people trapped in flooded homes.According to the China Meteorological Administration, the dolphin was moving northwest at 15 to 20 kilometers per hour and was expected to continue weakening.Dolphin made landfall Sunday evening in Taizhou in Zhejiang province with winds of 151 kph, after bringing heavy rain to northern Taiwan over the weekend.The storm had forced at least 760,000 people to preemptively relocate, including over 390,000 people in Taizhou.Authorities in Shanghai and Fujian Province said they evacuated more than 210,000 and 160,000 people, respectively, from riskier areas.While authorities in Zhejiang’s capital city, Hangzhou, temporarily closed its iconic West Lake scenic spots as well as temples, parks, and museums and will reopen on Tuesday.Storm intensified monsoon in the PhilippinesDolphin has also made an impact in the Philippines, where it has intensified seasonal monsoon rains that set off flooding and landslides on the main northern island region of Luzon.A landslide buried three houses Sunday night in the northern mountain resort city of Baguio, killing 10 people whose bodies were dug out in two days of frantic search by rescuers. Three people were rescued with injuries and brought to a hospital, Baguio officials said.The deaths from the mudslide raised the death toll in nearly a week of torrential rains, floods, and a tropical storm last week in the northern Luzon region to 19, the government’s Office of Civil Defense said.More than a million people were affected by the heavy monsoon rains and floods, including about 98,000 who were displaced from homes.Elsewhere, Tropical Storm Chan-hom began its move in the direction of Japan's Pacific coast on Monday.The Japan Meteorological Agency reported that the storm had winds of 83 kph on Monday morning and was expected to get a little stronger before making landfall on Tuesday or Wednesday.

https://www.politico.eu/article/germany-.text: German commentators are calling it a modern-day “ miracle .” Hundreds of thousands of worshippers are walking away from their churches each year. The money, however, keeps rolling in. Some 660,000 people formally quit the country’s Catholic and Protestant churches in 2025, freeing them from a levy automatically charged to registered members as a percentage of their income tax bill. Despite the exodus, the two institutions collected more than €12.5 billion through the church tax for the 2025 fiscal year, up from around €12.4 billion in 2024. The apparent miracle has a decidedly earthly explanation: Rising wages and Germany’s progressive tax system mean the shrinking pool of members is paying more. “At first glance, the development may seem contradictory,” a spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany — the umbrella organization representing Germany’s regional Protestant churches — said. “The reason is that church tax is calculated based on individual income tax.” Advertisement Members of Germany’s Catholic and Protestant churches and some Jewish communities pay an additional religious tax equal to 8 or 9 percent of their income tax liability, even if they don’t attend services. In 2021, the most recent year for which comprehensive data is available, more than 29 million people paid church tax in Germany, amounting to almost half of all income taxpayers in Europe’s largest economy. The German Finance Ministry’s 2025 payroll tax tables suggests that a single employee without children earning €50,000 gross a year pays approximately €600 in church tax annually on top of income tax, depending on the federal state. Someone earning €70,000 per year pays more than €1,000. People are registered as part of their religious community at birth or at local government offices. To stop paying the church tax, they must formally leave through a process known as Kirchenaustritt , or “church exit.” The procedure varies across Germany’s federal states but typically requires appearing in person at a registry office or local court to submit a declaration. Most states also charge an administrative fee. While those who deregister can still attend services as a visitor and access some church services, they are not allowed to have a church wedding, be a godparent or be guaranteed a church burial. In 2025, some 310,000 left the Catholic Church, while around 350,000 left one of Germany’s regional Protestant churches. Church exit The reasons people give for formally leaving their religious communities range from feeling less connected to the church to simply wanting to save money. “People are leaving the Church because they feel it no longer plays a role in their lives,” said Matthias Kopp, director of communications for the German Bishops’ Conference. “Added to this are the scandals of recent years, which have called the Church’s credibility into question,” he added. “There are also people — though this is by no means the primary reason — who leave the Church because of the church tax.” “These are processes of alienation to which we must respond,” said Kopp. For Jana Keil, a 33-year-old accountant from Berlin, the decision was both financial and moral. “I no longer wanted to support the system with church tax in light of the [child sex] abuse scandals,” she said. Lukas Heinich, a 23-year-old working student, said he formally left after completing his apprenticeship because he “didn’t feel like paying the tax or supporting the church.” That church tax revenues continue to rise despite the exodus is down to the types of taxpayers choosing to remain church members. Those who are still paying church tax in Germany are “probably the higher earners,” said Zareh Asatryan, professor of empirical economics at the University of Münster. “Those that stay will naturally earn more income because of inflation plus real wage growth, and they will just generate more revenue.” A miracle with an end date? But the continued rise in church tax revenue masks significant long-term challenges — and raises questions about how long the trend can last. While those revenues are going up, they are “relatively sluggish” and “haven’t been increasing by a lot,” said Asatryan. The increase in revenue from the church tax is considerably lower than the increase in revenue from income tax. State revenue from wage and income taxes rose by 6.65 percent in 2025, said Kopp, whereas church tax revenue increased by 1.93 percent. “Long-term projections indicate that church tax revenue will decline significantly over the coming decades as church membership continues to decrease,” said the spokesperson for the Evangelical Church in Germany. Protestant churches are already preparing for their income to decrease “through long-term planning processes,” said the spokesperson. “Without this system, the church’s religious, social and charitable work would not be possible on its current scale.”

https://www.politico.eu/article/greece-e.text: ATHENS — Sparks from Greece’s aging electricity grid are responsible for a disproportionate share of the country’s most destructive wildfires, according to preliminary data from Greece’s Arson Crimes Investigation Directorate and evidence from recent fire investigations. While power infrastructure accounts for only a small share of wildfire incidents, fires sparked by the grid often break out under the most dangerous conditions — during high winds, in periods of heavy electricity demand and often in remote, fire-prone areas — making them more likely to spread rapidly and become catastrophic. According to the Arson Crimes unit, fires linked to the electricity grid account for about 75 percent of the land burned in Greece this year. Advertisement Advertisement Two deadly wildfires in late July — one in western Attica and one on the island of Crete —were also linked to the electricity grid in preliminary findings from the Greek fire brigade. The fires destroyed more than 36,000 acres and killed four people. “Six out of 10 major fires and 55 percent of the area burnt in 2025 were caused by the power grid,” said Elias Tziritis, wildfires actions coordinator at World Wildlife Fund Greece. “Statistically speaking, the majority of fires may not start from the power grid, but these are the ones that cause the most major, devastating fires.” Loose or sagging power lines, vegetation coming in contact with cables, dust buildup on transmission equipment and other such faults can all generate sparks. The risk rises during strong winds and periods of heavy electricity demand, when aging infrastructure is under greater strain. Much of Greece’s electricity grid was installed decades ago and runs above ground through fire-prone forests and increasingly depopulated rural areas. In the 1960s, the country opted for an overhead network as a cheaper way to extend electricity across the country, while the prolonged financial crisis that began in 2009 further constrained investment in the system. Critics say Greece has moved too slowly to bury distribution lines and adapt the network to increasingly severe fire conditions. “We raised the issue years ago, calling for something to be done with the power grid urgently,” said Christos Kalogeropoulos, a retired lieutenant-general with the Fire Service and former director of the Arson Crimes unit. “We have been calling for urgent underground cabling.” Advertisement Advertisement Greece’s power distribution operator HEDNO disputes suggestions that the network is a major cause of wildfires, saying only about 1 percent of wildfire incidents recorded in 2025 were attributed to the electricity grid, compared with roughly 3 percent in the U.S. The company also said its crews have been deployed to major fire fronts to support emergency services and restore electricity to affected communities. “The easy targeting of HEDNO whenever a fire breaks out serves neither the truth nor the protection of the public but creates false impressions, and, in many cases, appears to serve short-term expediencies and self-serving agendas by covering up local responsibilities,” said the company in a statement. Following the fire in Crete, authorities arrested two HEDNO network operations and maintenance managers, who were later released. In Viotia, where a late-July fire spread into western Attica, investigators suspect sparks came from equipment on a private wind farm. A local mayor, a contractor and a company owner were taken into custody last week. A wildfire burns near Asomatos, Crete on July 30, 2026. | Costas Metaxakis/AFP via Getty Images Energy Minister Stavros Papastavrou said the government plans to tighten rules governing private power projects. But experts warn that focusing on private operators risks obscuring the broader problem of an aging public grid. Moving cables underground is expensive and time-consuming, said Paleologos Paleologou, associate professor of forest protection at the Agricultural University of Athens. Paleologou said researchers need access to detailed data on the location of power lines and pylons to model where the network is most vulnerable. “If we had that information, we could tell them where their network is vulnerable and where a fire could break out,” he said. “Since the budget is limited, we should prioritize the most difficult areas.” Advertisement Advertisement The government is currently using money from the EU Recovery and Resilience Facility to fund underground cabling. It says the share of the distribution network that is underground has risen to about 14 percent, up from 9 percent in 2021. Alexandra Sdoukou, a spokesperson for the ruling New Democracy party, said burying the entire 120,000-kilometer medium-voltage network would cost about €35 billion, requiring the government to first focus on areas under the greatest risk. Greece's Energy Ministry did not reply to a request for comment. Meanwhile, opposition parties and advocacy groups accuse the government of moving too slowly, failing to maintain the grid properly and dropping some fire-prevention projects from EU recovery funding. “There is still no public acknowledgement of the problem,” said Tziritis. “The issue should be recognized and efforts to find solutions should be taken at the government level.” Such an acknowledgement could also carry legal and financial consequences. California utility Pacific Gas & Electric filed for bankruptcy after its equipment sparked catastrophic wildfires and exposed the company to billions of dollars in liabilities. Advertisement Advertisement In Greece, the number of court cases involving fires linked to the electricity grid rose from 369 to 681 in 2024, said Kalogeropoulos. One of the few cases to result in a final ruling against HEDNO is a class action lawsuit following a 2015 wildfire in Neapoli, Laconia, which destroyed homes and large areas of woodland and farmland. Around 90 victims are now pursuing compensation. “It is a real struggle for a citizen to go after an electricity grid company,” said Evgenia Lazaraki, a lawyer representing the victims. Utilities, she said, have both the technical expertise and access to evidence needed to defend themselves, putting plaintiffs at a significant disadvantage.

https://www.politico.eu/article/europe-p.text: BERLIN — Europe is scrambling for more Patriot interceptors to donate to an increasingly desperate Ukraine, which is racing to reinforce its ballistic missile defenses before Russia’s expected winter assault. Kyiv is seeking hundreds of interceptors, but new production will come too late, the war with Iran has strained U.S. supplies, and several of Ukraine’s leading European backers say they have few left that they can safely donate. “Over the last few months, Russia fires more missiles a week at us than we get from partners over months," former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov said last week . In July, Ukrainian air defense intercepted only 29 out of 195 Russian ballistic missiles, with another 40 failing to reach their targets, Ukraine's defense ministry said . Advertisement Advertisement Germany, one of Ukraine’s top military aid donors, has already transferred Patriot systems and missiles to Ukraine. But Berlin must now balance Kyiv’s increasingly urgent needs against the minimum stocks required to protect Germany and meet its NATO commitments. Other European countries are also weighing whether to hang on to their interceptors or give them to Ukraine. “We are really reaching our limits here,” Brig. Gen. Jürgen Schrödl, a senior German defense ministry official, said at a panel in Berlin shortly after last month’s NATO summit in Ankara. “We also have to ensure our own protection.” Berlin and other Northern European capitals have urged counterparts elsewhere on the continent to examine what more military equipment and financial support they could release. “I think it’s not sustainable for Europe in the long run,” Norwegian Defense Minister Tore O. Sandvik told POLITICO. “All the European countries have to step up.” That's putting pressure on countries with stocks of Patriot interceptors like Poland, Spain and Greece. The shortage primarily concerns Patriot PAC-3 and PAC-2 missiles, which are among Ukraine’s few effective defenses against fast-moving Russian ballistic weapons. Ukraine can use other, often cheaper, air-defense systems against drones and cruise missiles. The country is racing to develop its homegrown Freyja interceptor, but the anti-ballistic system still requires investment, engineering work and testing before it can fill that role. Advertisement Advertisement Until Freyja is ready, Ukraine needs an immediate answer to Russia’s ballistic missiles. “One of the priority directions is Patriot — PAC-3 or PAC-2,” Mykhailo Podolyak, adviser to the head of Ukraine’s presidential office, told POLITICO. “The first [solution] is buying, or receiving from stockpiles, PAC-3 and PAC-2 interceptors.” Stuck in Washington The Patriot dependence makes U.S. President Donald Trump essential to Kyiv: Most PAC-3 interceptors are produced in America, which means their sale and any production deals are subject to White House decisions. During Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's meeting with Trump last month, “The main topic was Patriot interceptors,” according to a senior official familiar with the talks. Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Donald Trump speak on the sidelines of a NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey on July 8, 2026. | Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images Trump raised hopes at the Ankara summit when he said Ukraine would be allowed to produce U.S.-designed Patriot interceptors under license — a step that could eventually reduce Kyiv’s dependence on scarce American deliveries. U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matthew Whitaker made clear that production would not solve the immediate shortage. “A long-term production agreement will not be concluded before this winter,” he told Fox Business, and manufacturing the first missiles would take longer still. Advertisement Advertisement But Trump has now walked that back, last week saying: "We have not agreed to that. We're talking about it. But it's a hard thing to give away, that kind of technology." Following a Reuters report that the U.S. had almost exhausted its missile stocks thanks to the war against Iran, Trump is now focusing on rebuilding U.S. supplies. Asked on Thursday about Zelenskyy’s calls for more Patriot missiles, he said: “We want missiles too.” Ukraine has also signed a deal to get PAC-2 interceptors being made in Germany, but they are unlikely to arrive before next year. Faced with a shortage of interceptors, Kyiv is now looking at a more aggressive campaign to hit Russian launchers. "The Russians must understand that a few minutes after the launch, the entire team that launches the rocket must die from our ballistic missile," Fedorov said. Europe’s unbalanced effort That puts the immediate burden on Europe, where allies are once again searching their own arsenals — and one another’s — for interceptors that could reach Ukraine before winter. Advertisement Advertisement Germany supplied three Patriot systems from its own military stocks and subsequently arranged two more through a deal under which the U.S. would replenish the Bundeswehr. The Netherlands assembled the components for another complete system, including five launchers, a radar and missiles. But with stocks now stretched thin, governments face limits of their own. Warsaw confirmed in July that it had released several PAC-3 interceptors after requests from NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and senior U.S. commanders. Polish outlet Defence24 reported that just five missiles were transferred. Mark Rutte speaks at a press conference ahead of a NATO summit in Ankara on July 6, 2026. | Chris McGrath/Getty Images Even that triggered a political backlash. Opposition lawmakers accused the government of weakening the country’s defenses at a time when Russian missiles and drones have repeatedly strayed across its border. Countries closer to Russia are now becoming less likely to give up existing Patriots because their armed forces already regarded their air defenses as insufficient for national requirements, according to a European diplomat granted anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomatic contacts. That is shifting attention toward Southern European countries, which have contributed less to Ukraine than Germany and many Northern European donors. Advertisement Advertisement Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez confirmed in 2024 that Madrid was sending missiles to Ukraine, but the government has not disclosed their type or amount. Spain's defense ministry did not respond to a question from POLITICO whether it had recently been approached for more interceptors or was considering another transfer. It instead pointed to Spain’s wider military support for Ukraine and its NATO commitments. Greece — which traditionally sees fellow NATO member Turkey as its greatest security threat — has not announced any Patriot transfers to Ukraine. Greek media reported in July that Ukraine had requested as many as 200 older PAC-2 interceptors from Athens. The Greek defense ministry did not respond to POLITICO’s request for comment. Prying open Europe’s arsenals This isn’t the first time European allies have had to cobble together Patriot missile deliveries from their own limited stocks. At a February meeting, Ukraine's Fedorov said he and Rutte worked through a list of interceptors held by European allies, asking governments for whatever they could spare. Advertisement “Dear defense minister of Poland, can you give us five?” Fedorov recalled in this week's interview. Berlin offered to top up the effort. “If you get 20 out of all the countries, I'll give you an extra five,” Fedorov quoted German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius as saying. “That’s the exercise we had to perform to get more than 20. And it is a hard mission.” Kyiv is continuing those types of talks with its allies. “Of course, Ukrainian diplomats have been working with Spain, Greece and everyone in the world who has [PACs],” said the senior official familiar with the talks. “Everything depends on the U.S., and the lack of political will to help influences everyone else.” “The American administration could have helped, but they don’t do this. And as the result it’s been hard with everyone else,” they added. For Kyiv, the arguments over allied stockpiles are unfolding against a ticking clock. With demand for PAC-3 interceptors surging in the Middle East, the Pentagon replenishing its own stock and many European countries worrying about their own ability to fend off a future Russian attack, Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said Ukraine was struggling to buy, exchange or secure any available rounds. “We are literally fighting for every missile,” Sybiha said. Veronika Melkozerova reported from Kyiv. Advertisement

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c20e.text: Figure caption, Watch: Moment powerful earthquake shakes Colombia and crumbles buildings By JosÃ© Carlos Cueto ,Â BBC News Mundo correspondent ,Â Reporting from BogotÃ¡ ,Â Vanessa BuschschlÃ¼ter ,Â Latin America online editor Â and Â Michael Sheils McNamee Published 10 August 2026 Updated 2 hours ago At least 132 people are dead and a state of emergency has been declared after Colombia was hit by one of its largest earthquakes in years. The death toll is likely to rise, with more feared trapped under collapsed buildings. The magnitude 7.4 quake struck at 07:34 (12:34 GMT) at a depth of 103km (64 miles) in ChocÃ³ province, the country's geological service said. It was felt across an enormous area, stretching for hundreds of miles across western Colombia. Many of the deaths have been concentrated in the city of Pereira, in Colombia's coffee-growing region, with surrounding cities and the Valle del Cauca region also hit hard. The epicentre of the quake was near the village of San JosÃ© del Palmar, in ChocÃ³ province, but local mayor LeÃ³n Fabio MarÃ­n Moncada said that there had miraculously been no deaths or injuries - despite the roads in and out being damaged. More than 480 people were injured in the quakes, Colombia's Association of Capital Cities wrote in a statement update on Monday. About 55km (34 miles) from the epicenter of the earthquake, the city of Pereira saw some of the worst damage. Videos verified by the BBC show at least one building collapsing in Plaza BolÃ­var, the city's main square, with scattered debris and dust across the open space where many people had gathered. Local authorities have reported at least 40 people dead in the city's metropolitan area, with 65 collapsed buildings. People are believed to be trapped in 15 of them. A curfew is in place in some parts of the city until 05:00 local time on Tuesday. Thirty-two buildings collapsed in Cali, located about 160km south of Pereira and about 200km from the epicentre. Dan Cutler, 29, is from London but has been in Colombia for about two months as part of a big trip with his partner, and is currently in Cali. Being woken by the earthquake, he told the BBC: "I've never experienced anything like it." "We sprinted outside in our pyjamas. There's no major structural damage to the hotel, but there are surface cracks in the walls, and paint and plaster have peeled off," he says. There were also reports of deaths in Manizales, QuibdÃ³, MedellÃ­n, across the ChocÃ³ and Valle del Cauca regions. Image source, EPA Image caption, Buildings were destroyed in the city of Manizales At least two people have died in Manizales. Speaking to BBC World Service, AngÃ©lica Ãvila said she had been staying in a hotel in Manizales. She said as the earthquake hit, cracks appeared in the walls. "Everyone was screaming... I saw dust coming out of the neighbouring buildings, and bricks were falling off the walls," she said. Journalist and meteorologist Luis Felipe Molina, from Manizales, was at home when the earthquake struck - about 150km from the epicentre. He explained that due to previous earthquakes, the city has "very strict seismic-resistant building regulations" - so his building was able to resist the impact. "I have 450 books and only a few were left standing on the shelves. You could hear glass breaking and people screaming," he told BBC Mundo. "It was a terrible and terrifying experience." The country's aviation authority has reported damage at several regional airports, including those in Pereira, Manizales, QuibdÃ³, Armenia, Cartago and Buenaventura. In the capital, BogotÃ¡, trees and traffic lights shook violently, with reports of cracks in buildings but so far none of any serious damage to the city's infrastructure. Tremors were felt as far away as neighbouring Venezuela, Ecuador and Panama. The quake comes less than two months after twin quakes devastated the north of Venezuela , killing more than 6,300 people. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Dozens of buildings have collapsed in the city of Cali Colombia's President Abelardo de la Espriella has declared a national disaster situation, creating special powers to react to the emergency, including to reallocate budgets. Having only taken up the role on Friday, the new president is immediately faced with a potentially legacy-defining event. Along with the dead, he confirmed that more than 1,500 homes had been damaged. As the extent of the damage has begun to emerge, world leaders have come forward to offer support. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said it was "closely monitoring" the earthquake, and stood "ready to support", while EU chief Ursula von der Leyen said the EU's Copernicus satellite was being used in the rescue operation. The President of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, sent a message of solidarity to the Colombian people and offered personnel and equipment for rescue efforts. According to the US Geological Survey, an estimated 1.5 million people felt shaking close to magnitude seven. It stated that deep earthquakes, like the one which hit on Monday, are usually less dangerous than earthquakes which break closer to the Earth's surface. But they can release energy in a way which is damaging to buildings, with fewer but potentially stronger aftershocks. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/11/kozl.text: Menü Kereső A minisztérium szerint nem biztonságos, hiába kérik ezrek, nem gyártják újra a régi trikolóros rendszámtáblát Belföld Legfontosabb Tenczer Gábor Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „A régi trikolóros rendszámtábla újragyártása biztonsági szempontból nem kivitelezhető” – válaszolta a Közlekedési és Beruházási Minisztérium sajtóosztálya kérdésünkre, hogy lehetővé teszik-e a trikolóros rendszámtábla szerelmeseinek az újragyártást, aminek a lehetősége 2022-ben szűnt meg. A minisztérium szerint az új rendszámtáblák a korábbiakhoz képest korszerűbb kialakításúak, és több biztonsági elemet tartalmaznak, amelyek a hamisítás elleni védelmet szolgálják. Ezért az újragyártott trikolóros rendszámtáblák műszaki kialakítása nem lehet azonos a korábban kiadott változatokkal, tették hozzá. Az újragyártási lehetőség érdekében Csernus Gábor ügyvéd indított online petíciót , amit már több mint 6500-an aláírtak. Ebben kérik a kormányt és az illetékes minisztériumot, hogy vizsgálja meg a 326/2011. (XII. 28.) Korm. rendelet módosításának lehetőségét annak érdekében, hogy a korábban jogszerűen kiadott, nemzeti színű sávval ellátott (közismert nevén trikolóros) rendszámtáblák sérülés, megsemmisülés vagy elvesztés esetén ismét eredeti kivitelükben legyenek utángyárthatók, ez ugyanis 2022-től nem lehetséges. Az úgynevezett trikolóros rendszámokat 1990 augusztusa és 2004. május 1-je előtt adták ki: AAB-003 – JCZ-999 tartományban. Azaz többezres nagyságrendben, a 22–36 éves autókon láthatók. Leadni, lecserélni nem kötelező ezeket a rendszámokat most sem, csak akkor lehet gond, ha teljesen tönkremegy, elvész, vagy ellopják a táblát, mert ilyen esetben már a régi formában nem lehet újragyártatni. A legelső 3 betű 3 szám rendszerű rendszámtábla, amit tulajdonosa, Csernus Gábor felajánl a Közlekedési Minisztériumnak, ha az újragyártás kérdése megoldódik – Fotó: Csernus Gábor / Facebook Csernus Gábor szerint ezek a rendszámok a városkép részei, gazdáik nagy becsben tartják őket. Sok tulajdonos emlékszik arra a napra, amikor a Merkúr-telepen átvették az autót, ez számukra eszmei értéket is képvisel, közölte. Véleménye szerint a trikolóros rendszámok nem csupán azonosításra szolgálnak, hanem egy lezárult korszak emlékeit hordozzák, valódi, kézzelfogható kortörténeti dokumentumok, amelyeknek az eszmei és történeti értéke sokat jelent a magyar autós társadalom számára. Csernus úgy véli, hogy a Közlekedési és Beruházási Minisztérium indoklása, miszerint nem lehetséges ezeknek a rendszámoknak az újragyártása, műszakilag nem értelmezhető, továbbá nem konzekvens, mert az újragyártott rendszámtáblák is tartalmazzák a beépített biztonsági elemeket. Amennyiben nem tartalmaznák, úgy annak megoldása nem annak függvénye, hogy a trikolór vagy az Európai Unió zászlaja szerepel-e rajta, a gyártási technológiát ez nem befolyásolja – szögezte le. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/10/szij.text: Menü Kereső Megkérdeztük Szijjártó sajtófőnökét, hogy tényleg külügyeseket vezényeltek-e ki a minisztérium sajtótájékoztatóira Belföld Aradi Hanga Zsófia Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Miután a 444 több korábbi és jelenlegi külügyes beszámolója alapján arról írt, rendszeresen utasították arra a Külügyminisztérium munkatársait , hogy jelenjenek meg Szijjártó Péter sajtótájékoztatóin, megkerestük Szijjártó Péter volt sajtófőnökét, Paczolay Mátét, hogy reagáljon a lap állításaira. Paczolay kérdésünkre részletesen magyarázta el, hogyan szervezték úgy a tájékoztatókat, hogy soha ne legyen üres a terem. A 444 azt írta, a Miniszteri Kabinet rendszeresen előre jelezte a szervezeti egységek vezetőinek, hogy egy-egy Szijjártó-féle bilaterális sajtótájékoztatóra hány munkatársat várnak, a vezetőknek pedig azt is előre meg kellett adniuk, kik vesznek majd részt. A lap szerint minderre azért volt szükség, mert a meghívott sajtó és a külföldi vendégek kísérete önmagában nem töltötte volna meg a termet. Paczolay úgy fogalmazott, „a 444 cikkében vannak valós és valótlan elemek”, a teljes képhez szerinte hozzátartozik, hogy Szijjártó Péter a legaktívabban kommunikáló kormánytag volt, „a Külügyminisztériumban egy »könnyebb napon« egy-kettő, egy átlagos napon három-négy, míg egy nehezebb napon öt-hat sajtóeseményt” tartottak. Az egykori miniszter sajtófőnöke szerint természetes, hogy ha egy nap három sajtóeseményt tartottak, a harmadikra már „mérséklődött a média érdeklődése”, de arra törekedtek, hogy a Külügyminisztérium egyik vendégét se sértsék meg azzal, hogy „bármennyire is üres terem előtt kelljen beszédet tartania az országát képviselve”. Ezért „ezen esetekben a protokoll meghívta az illetékes szakmai főosztályok munkatársait. Van, aki élt a lehetőséggel, van aki nem, van aki örömmel jött, és van akinek ez plusz fáradtságot jelentett a jelek szerint.” Paczolay válaszában hangsúlyozta, hogy nem volt kötelező a részvétel. „Pontos tudásom nincs erről, de abban biztos vagyok, hogy a miniszteri protokoll addig telefonált, míg a legutolsó széket is feltöltötték, hiszen ez volt a dolguk” – írta a Telexnek. A sajtófőnök szerint „a szakterületetek vezetői pedig szintén előnyösnek találták, ha egy adott térségért felelős munkatárs élőben hallja annak az országnak a külügyminiszterét, akiért elviekben házon belül felel, valamint alkalma nyílik találkozni a külügyminisztert kísérő delegációs tagokkal”. „Szóval igen, mindig fel voltak töltve a széksorok. Volt, hogy az ötven fős teremben húsz újságíró volt és harminc meghívott vendég, de volt olyan is, hogy három újságíró volt és negyvenhét vendég.” A 444 cikkében arról is írt, a sajtó nagy részét eleve kizárták a tájékoztatókról, egy külügyes pedig azt mondta a lapnak, egyszer szem- és fültanúja volt, hogy a külügy sajtófőosztályáról egy kolléga lediktálta az MTI tudósítójának, hogy mit kérdezzen. Megkérdeztük Paczolaytól, hogy egyeztettek-e kérdéseket az MTI tudósítójával, azt válaszolta: „Nem”. „Szijjártó Péter minden eseményéről sajtóközleményt írtunk, illetve a teljes sajtótájékoztatót élőben adtuk a különböző internetes felületeken, így az MTI csak a legritkább esetben küldött személyesen tudósítót a Külügyminisztériumba” – írta. Azt elismerte, hogy egyeztettek a sajtótájékoztatókra érkező újságírókkal: „Minden esetben megkérdeztük, hogy lesz-e kérdésük, illetve lesz a látogatás témájától eltérő, általában belpolitikai kérdésük”. Azt írta, ennek gyakorlati okai voltak, egyrészt a moderációt és a sajtótájékoztató tervezett hosszát is ehhez igazították, másrészt Szijjártót is előre tájékoztatták, hogy számítson rá, hogy a bilaterális témák mellett belpolitika is lesz. „Ez volt az alap a mindennapokban, de emellett 12 év alatt még számtalan egyedi eset volt, ami egyedi megoldásokat kívánt, hiszen a világ minden sarkából érkeztek hozzánk vendégek, eltérő kulturális szokásokkal és igényekkel” – írta. A 444 azt is írta, Budai Gyula gazdaságvédelmi intézkedésekért felelős miniszteri biztos témától függetlenül az összes sajtótájékoztatón részt vett. Az ő részvételének okaira is rákérdeztünk, Paczolay azt írta, mivel Budai Gyula „lényegében a külügyminiszter minden tárgyalásán részt vett, így delegációtag volt, a delegációtagok pedig protokoll szerint részt vesznek a sajtótájékoztatókon, mivel az is a hivatalos program része”. https://hungarytoday.hu/watermelon-growe.text: Watermelon Growers Hope Warmer Weather Revives Slumping Market This year’s season did not get off to a good start , and watermelon growers are expecting sales to pick up in the coming days, based on a market summary published Monday on the website of FruitVeB, the Hungarian Fruit and Vegetable Interprofessional Organization and Marketing Board. The organization attributed the unfavorable trends to the weather; the heat wave at the end of June accelerated ripening, resulting in an abundant supply by the first week of July, but demand fell as temperatures dropped. Photo: Pexels Based on the report, the two factors are closely linked: watermelon consumption is highest during heat waves and drops significantly in cooler weather. Although industry associations asked retail chains not to slash prices, by mid-month the chains were already advertising sales at prices around 150 forints per kilogram (0.41 euros per kilogram; 1 euro = 366 forints). While this is favorable for consumers, at this price level, producers do not earn enough revenue to cover their expenses. With intensive production methods, production costs reach 4–6 million forints per hectare (10,930–16,390 euros per hectare); therefore, an acceptable profit can only be expected if net producer prices average 100–120 forints per kilogram over the entire season, FruitVeB said. According to the report, by mid-July the European watermelon market had collapsed due to the weather, causing export prices to plummet; by the last third of the month, buyers were only willing to pay a net price of 40–50 forints per kilogram. Even so, part of the crop remained unsellable because producers in other countries were also trying to offload their inventories. Hungarian growers are now hoping that the warmer weather expected in the coming days will boost demand, and that import pressure will also ease, as the melon season in the Balkan countries is drawing to a close. In the first half of August, watermelons from Szabolcs-Szatmár-Bereg and Heves counties in eastern and northern Hungary will come onto the market in increasing quantities, but due to uncertainties, price trends are unpredictable. If consumption does not pick up, watermelon production in Hungary could decline next year. https://hungarytoday.hu/european-energy-.text: European Energy Giant Expands into the Domestic Solar Power Market The Greek PPC Group is continuing its growth strategy by entering the Hungarian market through the acquisition of a major renewable energy project. The investment is part of a €24 billion strategic plan aimed at transforming the company into a leading energy player in Central and Southeastern Europe. According to a company statement , PPC Group, through its wholly owned subsidiary PPC Renewables, has reached an agreement with the Greenvolt Group. The deal involves the integration of an operational photovoltaic (solar) park with a capacity of 57.5 megawatts (MW) into PPC’s generation portfolio. The solar power plant is located near Királyegyháza in Baranya County, southwestern Hungary, and has been supplying solar electricity to the grid since July 2024. With an expected operating lifetime of more than 30 years, the project represents a long-term strategic asset for the company. A key advantage of the transaction is its financial stability. The solar power plant operates under a government-backed fixed-price power purchase agreement (PPA) with 25 years remaining. This provides PPC Group with protection against volatility in international electricity markets. Beyond the solar park itself, the agreement with Greenvolt Group also includes the right to acquire a 49 MW battery energy storage system (BESS) currently under development in the same region. The combination of renewable generation and energy storage is considered essential for maintaining the stability of modern electricity grids. The expansion into Hungary is not an isolated project but a key component of PPC Group’s new strategic growth plan for 2026–2030. At the heart of this strategy is a €24 billion investment program designed to double the company’s total installed generation capacity over the coming years. The objective is to build a unified, resilient clean energy platform extending geographically from Greece across the Balkans to Central Europe. Hungary offers ideal conditions for this expansion. The country is regarded as one of Europe’s most attractive growth markets for renewable energy. The Hungarian government is pursuing a comprehensive energy transition program that aims to increase the country’s installed photovoltaic capacity to 12 gigawatts (GW) by 2030. This expansion is supported by a stable regulatory framework aligned with European Union directives, providing investors with the planning certainty needed for large-scale infrastructure projects. Entering the Hungarian market makes our strategy for the new phase of expansion in Central and Southeastern Europe tangible,” said Konstantinos Mavros, Deputy CEO of PPC Group for Renewable Energy. Photo: Pixabay “As part of our strategy through 2030, we are entering new markets such as Hungary, Poland, and Slovakia, where we aim to develop a total of 2.2 GW of renewable energy and energy storage capacity. With this new photovoltaic project, we are integrating a highly efficient asset into our portfolio, expanding our geographic footprint, and building a resilient regional platform for clean energy,” he added. PPC Group’s long-term vision involves a far-reaching transformation. By 2030, 45% of the group’s installed generation capacity is expected to be located outside its home market of Greece. To achieve this, the company is pursuing both technological and geographic diversification. Its target energy mix will encompass the full range of modern technologies, including solar, wind, hydropower, flexible natural gas power plants, and advanced energy storage systems. Solar energy reaches record levels in the national electricity system, outperforming major European peers. https://hungarytoday.hu/flydubai-restore.text: Flydubai Restores Budapest Service, with Daily Flights Planned for Winter Season Flydubai is resuming direct flights between Hungary and the United Arab Emirates. Starting July 31, the airline will once again operate flights from Dubai International Airport (DXB) to Liszt Ferenc International Airport in Budapest (BUD). Initially offering three flights per week, the service will be expanded to daily flights with the winter schedule. The Dubai-based airline is strengthening its presence in Central and Eastern Europe. By resuming direct flights to Budapest, the airline is responding to sustained high demand, which has grown steadily since it first entered the Hungarian market in 2021. During the peak season, the reactivated route serves vacationers, business travelers, and the important VFR (visiting friends and relatives) traffic in equal measure. For flydubai CEO Ghaith Al Ghaith, the return to the Hungarian capital is a clear commitment to the market. “The resumption of flights underscores our long-term investment in Hungary and reflects the strong economic and cultural ties between the two nations. Budapest remains one of our most important strategic markets in Europe,” he explained. The renewed service not only offers travelers in the region more choice but also strengthens Dubai’s role as a global hub for business and tourism. Jeyhun Efendi, Senior Vice President of Commercial Operations at flydubai, is optimistic about the upcoming season. As we approach the busy fall-winter travel season, this flight connection creates valuable new trade and tourism opportunities in both markets,” he emphasized. For passengers from Hungary, the Dubai hub opens the door to the world. Dubai. Photo: flydubai Through the codeshare partnership with Emirates, travelers can seamlessly access flydubai’s global network with a single ticket and through-check baggage. This network now includes more than 120 destinations in the Middle East, Africa, Asia, and Southeast Asia—including popular long-haul destinations such as the Maldives, Thailand, Kenya, Sri Lanka, and Oman. The route will be served by a fleet of Boeing 737 aircraft. Passengers from Hungary will also benefit from flexible stopover options in Dubai, allowing them to explore the metropolis’s attractions, shopping districts, and family-friendly experiences. Photo: flydubai Flight operations will begin on July 31 with three weekly flights (Wednesdays, Fridays, and Sundays); starting October 25, 2026, the frequency will increase to one daily flight. The flight lands in Budapest at 9:40 p.m. and departs back to Dubai at 10:40 p.m. Fares from Budapest: Round-trip flights in Business Class starting at 802,400 forints (2,231 euros), in Economy Class starting at 182,900 forints (509 euros). Fares from Dubai: Round-trip flights in Business Class starting at 15,585 UAE dirhams (3,733 euros), in Economy Class starting at 2,987 UAE dirhams (715 euros). The flights are now available for booking via the airline’s official website, the airline’s official app, and through affiliated travel agencies and sales partners. Photo: flydubai Since its launch in June 2009, flydubai has become a major player in the region’s aviation industry. With a modern, uniform fleet of 97 Boeing 737s (including 68 Boeing 737 MAX 8s and 3 MAX 9s), the airline connects destinations in 58 countries. A key feature of its strategy remains the development of underserved markets. More than 100 routes have been launched to destinations that previously had no direct connection to Dubai. Since its founding, the airline has carried over 137 million passengers. The direct flight reduces travel time to about 4.5 hours.
