https://www.washingtonexaminer.com/news/.text: Sign In Home News Politics White House Senate House Campaigns Policy 2026 Election Opinion Editorials Op-Eds In Focus Restoring America Magazine Watch Sponsored Powering Progress ASAE – Association Leadership Examining Tax Reform Fix TSCA National Parks Inside the Corn Belt Examining Transportation TWS Archive News Politics White House Senate House Campaigns Business World Investigations Justice Supreme Court Crime Entertainment Washington Secrets Policy Defense National Security Energy and Environment Education Immigration Finance and Economy Healthcare Foreign Policy Tech Infrastructure Space 2026 Election America at 250 IN FOCUS Commentary Columnists Editorials Think Tanks Beltway Confidential Op-Eds Restoring America Patriotism and Unity Faith, Freedom, and Self-Reliance Courage, Strength, and Optimism Equality, Not Elitism Community and Family Fairness and Justice Mission Watch Magazine Magazine Quarterly Briefing Archives Games Sponsored Powering Progress ASAE – Association Leadership National Parks Examining Tax Reform Fix TSCA Inside the Corn Belt Examining Transportation Newsletters Add Washington Examiner on Google For decades, the disparate right-wing parties of Europe have sought to reverse the seemingly inevitable leftward march of the continent. They have campaigned on platforms promising to liberate their national polity from the perils of globalization and the immense, tangled bureaucracy of Brussels. The past half-decade has seen these parties creep ever closer to victory. Reform UK, the British party founded by Nigel Farage and running on an anti-immigration platform, is sitting in a comfortable lead over both establishment rivals. Alternative for Germany , a party deemed so right-wing by its opponents that mainstream lawmakers refuse to work with it, is dominating voter intention surveys. National Rally, the ever-present right-wing party of France , is on a path to victory despite the highly publicized conviction of its leader for financial crimes. Recommended Stories UK naval drones had components that secretly transmitted data to China Board of Peace undeterred by Israel’s rejection of peace plan at this stage Strong 7.4 magnitude earthquake strikes Colombia and neighboring Ecuador Germany , France, and the United Kingdom are three of the most pivotal players on the continent, and all of these right-wing parties will have their chance to flip their nations in the next three years. From the outside looking in, Europe seems like a powder keg of nationalist, populist resentment preparing to explode across the continent. Advertisement A rally for supporters of France’s National Rally, and Alice Weidel speaks to supporters. (AP) The question is: If citizens across Europe do vote in a succession of right-wing parties to lead their most powerful governments, will these disparate groups be able to form a coherent movement? The Hungarian connection Hungary, formerly governed by Prime Minister Viktor Orban , successfully positioned itself as the Western world’s beacon of national conservatism. The premier spent the better part of his time in high office building out infrastructure that spoke to a traditional, Christian, and nationalist mindset. He provided lavish tax breaks for women who had multiple children, established a state secretary position dedicated to aiding persecuted Christians, suppressed the public promotion of LGBT lifestyles, and flipped the middle finger at the European Union every chance he had. Orban embraced Hungary’s role as a global hub of right-wing ideology, flying over intelligentsia from other European countries and America, giving them cushy jobs at conservative think tanks and universities. Advertisement Orban’s worldwide relevance hit a fever pitch during the second administration of President Donald Trump , whom the Hungarian statesman had stayed loyal to even after his defeat in the 2020 election. Though nationalists are concerned primarily with the integrity of their own nations, few view this as contradicting the pursuit of international alliances with like-minded partners in an equal partnership. Some, such as Balazs Orban, the former prime minister’s political director, view such alliances as essential for the survival of independent nation-states. “The European right and everybody who cares about Western civilization should say, ‘We should win all of them.’ All of them,” Balazs Orban told the Washington Examiner in an interview, when asked how many elections in Europe had to be won in order to change the tide. Advertisement Hungary has punched far above its weight in this struggle, using the stability of the 16-year Fidesz party rule to create right-wing infrastructure that stretched across national borders, even extending across the Atlantic. Balazs Orban helped spearhead this struggle, founding the Mathias Corvinus Collegium in 2020, a conservative think tank that quickly established connections throughout the Western world. That Hungarian think tank and others have partnered with other international organizations to further plant their roots. Balazs Orban sees elections in Europe more like battles in a war for the soul of Western civilization, saying right-wing parties need unity, but more than that, they need thoughtful leadership. The kind of grandiose language pitching the current political fight as an existential struggle for the West is a common strain among nearly all European right-wing parties. Advertisement “Patriotic movements in the West are united by shared values ​​that forge us into a common movement: the democratic nation-state rather than supranational decision-making bodies; national sovereignty rather than external control; the preservation of national identity and culture rather than multiculturalism and ‘woke’ leftism; and a Christian — not Muslim — character. Yet, on this shared foundation, we naturally also have distinct national interests,” Beatrix von Storch, the deputy parliamentary group leader of AfD, told the Washington Examiner . Though Viktor Orban was ousted from power by Peter Magyar’s Tisza Party in April, he retains his leadership of Fidesz and has given no sign that he is ready to give up. “The struggle for the soul of Western civilization did not end when we lost the election,” the former prime minister told the Washington Examiner . “American and Hungarian patriots stand on the same side in this fight.” Advertisement His ousting and Magyar’s extensive efforts to purge the government of his influence have jeopardized much of the right-wing infrastructure built up over the past decade. United Kingdom: The odd one out One of the defining features of the various right-wing parties of Europe is their positions on a dialectic between an inward and outward focus — on this spectrum, Hungary can easily be considered the most outward-focused, while Reform UK is the most inward-focused. In fact, the party chafes at the propensity of observers to lump it in with a continent-wide right-wing movement. A Reform UK party supporter wears rosettes outside the party office on Friday, June 21, 2024, in Clacton-on-Sea, England. (AP Photo/Kirsty Wigglesworth) “The situations are very, very different” in each European country, Lois Perry, director of Heartland UK/Europe, told the Washington Examiner in an interview. She is close with the party and familiar with its internal dynamics but not directly affiliated with it. “Reform actually would not describe themselves necessarily as a right-wing party in the traditional sense,” she added. “… They would describe themselves as a common-sense party, a normal people’s party, which is why they’re attracting so many votes from the traditional left and the traditional right.” Reform UK falls firmly into the French National Rally’s camp in its strong focus on optics and electability. This has earned it the scorn of some further right parties on the continent, many of which Perry said would dismiss Reform as “lightweights.” Perry said Reform UK doesn’t have “any particularly strong ties” to other parties or right-wing figures within Europe, saying that the only real ties are from personal friendships and other relationships. The closest relationship is with National Rally, a relationship solidified through ideological affinity and a mutual focus on optics, not to mention geographical proximity and a shared history. Reform’s predecessor, the Brexit Party, made a splash in the European Parliament before Brexit, and memories of Farage and other British figures clashing with pro-EU politicians still brings back strong feelings of nostalgia among many still in the bloc. “As a Hungarian nationalist, I understand why the British nationalists voted to leave the EU,” Balazs Orban said. “But it’s a missed opportunity for them, and I miss them inside the European Union, because it would be much better to fight together with them against the liberal centralization of Brussels.” Perry said the sentiment is common among the right-wing parties of Europe and was recently showcased during a visit to the European Parliament. “‘We miss you guys! We miss Nigel Farage. He was a character,’” she recalled lawmakers saying with a laugh. “So in terms of having charismatic backup, then yeah, I get that.” Despite the distancing from the EU, Reform is well aware that its fortunes are still influenced significantly by the results of upcoming elections on the continent. “In terms of realpolitik … when Reform is in government, when Nigel Farage is the prime minister of the United Kingdom, it would be a lot easier to deal with a government which is not pro-mass immigration,” Perry said. The AfD-RN split and problems of unity While the right-wing parties across Europe are mostly united in grand civilizational questions and their top priorities, primarily immigration, maintaining an international alliance based on national interests is never seamless. Balasz Orban said Germany and France’s right-wing parties are the most important to see succeed — a natural answer given they’re the two biggest power players on the continent. Unfortunately for the right-wing international, National Rally and Alternative for Germany get along the least of the major right-wing parties in Europe. RN distinguishes itself with its focus on optics and electability, with longtime leader Marine Le Pen devoting extensive time and resources to its “de-demonization” campaign. This campaign has been a tremendous success in the party’s eyes, helping transform it from the fringe party that was crushed 82%-18% in the 2002 French presidential election to one viewed by many as the most likely winner of next year’s election. AfD is a different story. The party has thrived with its irreverence for Germany’s sterile political scene, paying little attention to established taboos. Though much of its rhetoric would not be out of place in the United States, the hypersensitivity of a country that distinguishes itself as having definitively left behind its nationalist past has little tolerance for narratives that depart from the consensus established during the reconstruction of the country after World War II. AfD’s leadership has largely gone to significant lengths to cull any language seen as sympathetic to the Nazi period of its history, but the party’s status as a decentralized coalition makes this more difficult than other, more message-disciplined parties on the continent. In May 2024, Maximilian Krah, an AfD member of the European Parliament, flew too close to the sun when, during an interview with the Italian daily Repubblica , he remarked that he “would never say that anyone who wore an SS uniform was automatically a criminal.” The comments led to a torrent of outrage from AfD’s then-ally, RN. AfD was expelled from their shared Identity and Democracy group, and two years later, relations still have not recovered between the right-wing front-runners of Europe’s two biggest countries. RN is not the only right-wing party that has clashed with AfD over matters of history — Poland’s right-wing parties are known to be especially sensitive toward the issue. The split has been institutionalized as well — RN and Fidesz co-founded the Patriots for Europe EP group, which, on July 8, 2024, became the third-largest in Europe with 84 members of the European Parliament. RN made up the largest constituency with 30 members, and other parties with representation include Fidesz, Italian Lega, the Czech ANO, Dutch PVV, Austrian FPO, Spanish Vox, Portuguese Chega, Belgian Vlaams Belang, and Danish DF. AfD is not represented. Part of the reason the split has remained in place is due to other issues the two parties clash on, mainly what to do with the EU and the Russia-Ukraine war. RN mainly follows leader Jordan Bardella’s stratagem of “change everything without destroying anything,” keeping the EU intact while changing its structure. AfD takes a firmer Euroskeptic stance. The Russia-Ukraine war is perhaps the most emotional break between the two. AfD is more neutral on the conflict and favors detente with Russia to diversify its international partnerships. RN is firmly on the side of Ukraine, sharing the strategy of Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni of adopting the consensus view on the war to better ingratiate itself with the European establishment. The schism has grown severe enough in recent months, with RN maneuvering in a way that almost seeks to box AfD out. The party has begun ingratiating itself with the center-right parties in Europe, primarily AfD’s rival Christian Democratic Union party, openly praising it while denigrating AfD. FORMER HUNGARIAN PRIME MINISTER VISITED WHITE HOUSE AND STATE DEPARTMENT In a May interview with a center-right German outlet, Bardella said many of AfD’s positions were “incompatible with our principles,” and liberally praised CDU Chancellor Friedrich Merz, an interview that shocked AfD lawmakers, especially due to Merz’s record-low approval ratings. AfD leader Alice Weidel suggested the remarks were made with ulterior motives. The urge to ingratiate itself with the establishment to cement its legitimacy stands as perhaps the biggest barrier to a true continent-wide, right-wing alliance as envisioned by figures such as Balazs Orban. For the time being, the impulse has driven a wedge between the two most powerful right-wing parties in Europe and could lower the other’s electoral chances. https://www.advanced-television.com/2026.text: Encompass playout services for Channel 4 July 28, 2026 Encompass Digital Media has been selected by Channel 4, the UK public service broadcasters, to deliver managed linear playout services as part of a new multi-year agreement. The announcement follows a procurement and evaluation process carried out by Channel 4 ahead of the service’s launch in 2027. Under the agreement, Encompass will partner with Channel 4 to provide channel origination, content supply chain and disaster recovery services across its portfolio, including Channel 4, E4, More4, Film4, E4 Extra and 4seven. Encompass will deliver services from its London and Riga broadcast facilities using its cloud-native Altitude platform, including Altitude Playout and Altitude Flow. The deployment is designed to support Channel 4’s broadcast operations through a managed service that combines channel origination with an integrated content supply chain. Encompass’s Altitude platforms take a software-defined, remote-first architectural approach, providing Channel 4 with technical and operational flexibility to navigate the changing playout and distribution landscape. “Channel 4 conducted a rigorous procurement process, and we’re delighted to have been selected as its managed playout partner,” commented Marc Bruce, CEO of Encompass. “This agreement reflects the strength of our technology and our experience supporting leading broadcasters with highly resilient managed services. We look forward to working closely with the Channel 4 team as we prepare for service launch next year.” “We’re pleased to be entering into this new agreement with Encompass,” added Grace Boswood, Director of Technology and Distribution at Channel 4. “Their cloud-native technology and experience supporting modern broadcast environments made them the ideal choice for our future needs, and we look forward to working together.” Other posts by : Arianespace trims ambitions for rocket update Forecast: $5tn annual SpaceX revenues Human AI; Access, Influence Who else was eyeing Globalstar? https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4547.text: Slovakia’s Interior Ministry has decided that same-sex marriages concluded abroad will not be entered into the country’s official registers. The decision follows requests from couples married in Austria and is based on Slovak law, which defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman. Prime Minister Robert Fico (SMER-SD) said Slovak legislation does not allow such registrations. However, lawyer János Fiala-Butora argues that European Union law takes precedence and says Slovakia is obliged to respect EU commitments. He added that affected couples can challenge the decision before EU institutions or international courts. The issue follows a European Court of Justice ruling concerning recognition of same-sex marriages within the EU. Source: STVR

Slovak Foreign Minister Juraj Blanár (SMER-SD) says the legacy of the First World War remains a powerful reminder that lasting peace can only be achieved through diplomacy. Marking the 112th anniversary of the outbreak of the war on Tuesday, Blanár warned that the failure of diplomacy in 1914 had devastating consequences. He noted that fighting on the Carpathian Front was among the bloodiest of the conflict, with around 400,000 men mobilised from what is now Slovakia and tens of thousands never returning. Blanár also said the world is facing the highest number of armed conflicts since the end of the Second World War, making dialogue and respect for international law more important than ever. He stressed that diplomacy must always be the first choice, not the last resort. The First World War began on 28 July 1914, when Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. The conflict lasted more than four years and claimed the lives of around 10 million soldiers, while millions more were left with lasting physical or psychological injuries. The war also affected present-day Slovakia, where the Carpathian Front stretched from Bardejov to Snina in the country's east. Source: TASR

https://www.baltictimes.com/valainis_cal.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Valainis calls on government to prepare in timely manner possible support measures for high fuel prices 2026-07-28 LETA/TBT Staff RIGA - Economics Minister Viktors Valainis (Greens/Farmers) has sent a letter to the Cabinet of Ministers (MK) calling for timely preparations to be made for the possible implementation of support measures in response to fuel prices, the Ministry of Economics (EM) informed LETA. On Monday, July 27, Valainis sent a letter to the Cabinet of Ministers, informing the government that the situation in the fuel market is becoming increasingly volatile after having been relatively stable. The sharp rise in prices for crude oil and petroleum products on global markets has reignited an upward trend in fuel prices, while persistent high geopolitical uncertainty poses a risk of further price increases. In his letter, the minister calls on the government to begin preparatory work in a timely manner for the possible activation of support measures. This involves identifying existing and potential sources of funding, as well as preparing potential solutions. The ministry notes that from July 21 to July 27, the price of Brent crude oil rose by 14.5 percent, while the price of ICE Low Sulphur Gasoil rose by 17.1 percent. Valainis points out that none of the aforementioned price thresholds have been reached yet, but the rise in fuel prices this week clearly shows that the situation is becoming increasingly tense. In his view, it is necessary to take preventive action rather than wait until a crisis has already occurred. The previously adopted decision to extend the excise tax reduction on fuel is currently helping to mitigate the impact of rising prices. The minister notes that developing support measures under extraordinary circumstances requires significantly more time, while delayed action can create significant political, economic, and social pressure at a time when residents and businesses are already feeling the sharp rise in costs. The Ministry of Economics will continue to monitor fuel prices, track developments in energy markets, and, if necessary, propose specific decisions to the MK to ensure a timely and effective response to further increases in fuel prices. Following the July 21 government meeting, Valainis told LETA that the government has outlined possible scenarios for action in the event the situation were to worsen, and that the government had also discussed support measures to be implemented even under a moderate development scenario. Valainis noted that the rise in fuel prices has created additional costs in the public sector, including in the interior and health sectors. Therefore, the government will continue to monitor the situation and work to prevent any reduction in the availability of services provided to residents. Commenting on possible support mechanisms, the minister said that, if necessary, additional funding would be allocated from the state budget. As reported, a law on limiting the increase in fuel prices, which provides for short-term measures aimed at mitigating the impact of price hikes on the Latvian economy and population, came into force on April 1. The law provides for a temporary reduction in the excise duty on diesel fuel from the current EUR 467 to EUR 396 per 1,000 liters. For marked agricultural diesel, the excise duty rate is set at EUR 21 per 1,000 liters. The reduced rates are in effect from April 1 to the end of the year. The rate cut will be effective until the end of this year. Comments Related Articles Subscribe Log In Ads Please enter your username and password. Related Articles Subscribe! https://www.delfi.lt/en/politics/boostin.text: Delfi EN Delfi Politics 2026.07.28 15:14 Boosting defence industry important to me and president – PM Translated by Justina Vaišvilaitė-Braziulienė Source: Elta EN Boosting defence industry important to me and president – PM PHOTO: Dainius Labutis | Elta Follow Delfi on Google Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevičius said Tuesday that Lithuania’s defence planning beyond 2030 must focus not only on funding the armed forces but also on developing the country’s defence industry. Following a meeting with President Gitanas Nausėda, Sinkevičius said Lithuania should aim to become not only a buyer of defence equipment but also a producer. "As we look towards 2030 and beyond, we must consider how we will achieve this with our own budget resources. We must think about how to kick-start the defence industry, as this is a crucial element that is important to me personally, to the defence minister and to the president," Sinkevičius told reporters at the Presidential Palace. He said Lithuania should develop manufacturing capabilities so that domestically produced defence equipment could serve both national needs and be exported to NATO allies. "We must not be just buyers, but also manufacturers, so that what we produce is not only for our own use but can also be exported and sold to NATO countries. Launching the defence industry is very important both to the president and to me personally," Sinkevičius said. Nausėda’s chief economic adviser, Vaidas Augustinavičius, told Žinių radijas on Tuesday that the president believes Lithuania must continue strengthening its defence capabilities as geopolitical tensions are unlikely to ease in the coming years. He said political parties should seek a broad agreement on long-term defence funding after 2030. Augustinavičius added that though defence spending as a share of GDP remains an important NATO benchmark, the key factor is the actual amount of funding needed to develop the planned capabilities. https://www.delfi.lt/en/business/real-es.text: Delfi EN Delfi Business 2026.07.28 15:07 Real estate agency warned after saying flat was available to Lithuanians only Translated by Justina Vaišvilaitė-Braziulienė Source: Elta EN Real estate agency warned after saying flat was available to Lithuanians only PHOTO: ELTA Follow Delfi on Google The Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson has issued a warning to a real estate agency after its representative told a foreign national that a rental flat was intended only for Lithuanians. The complainant said he had provided information about his income and financial situation and disclosed that he was a foreigner when contacting the agency about the flat. The agent said the flat was available only to Lithuanians but would consult the owner, according to him. The man was later asked to specify his nationality. After he said he was Persian, the agent informed him that the flat had been rented to someone else. Real estate agency Patera acknowledged that the statement about renting only to Lithuanians was inappropriate, but denied that tenants had been selected based on nationality or origin. The final decision rested with the property owner, it said. The legal group head at the Office of the Equal Opportunities Ombudsperson, Audronė Daukšaitė-Timpė, said the law prohibits both refusing services on grounds of nationality or race and publicly spreading discriminatory information about service provision. Patera was issued a warning for breaching obligations under the Equal Opportunities Act. Source Topics It is forbidden to copy the text of this publication without a written permission from ELTA. https://www.baltictimes.com/two_foreigne.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Two foreigners charged with smuggling drug-laced paper to UAE, Bahrain 2026-07-28 BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - A criminal case involving two foreign nationals accused of attempting to smuggle drug-laced paper to the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain and possessing large quantities of psychotropic substances has been referred to the Vilnius Regional Court. According to the Prosecutor General's Office, W. Sh. and Sw. S. face charges of large-scale drug smuggling and illegal possession of narcotics with intent to distribute. The pre-trial investigation was launched in September 2025 after an employee at a parcel distribution terminal in Vilnius discovered a hidden compartment in a shipment and alerted police. The packages, handed over to a courier by the defendants, were intended for delivery to the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain. During a search of an apartment rented by the suspects, police officers discovered a very large quantity of various psychotropic substances, totalling 1.78 kilograms. Investigators allege that the defendants used specialised equipment to impregnate A4 paper sheets with psychotropic substances. To evade customs controls, the sheets were concealed in hidden compartments built into shipping boxes. The defendants are currently in custody. They face up to 18 years in prison for drug smuggling and up to 15 years for possession with intent to distribute. https://www.crash.net/f1/news/1101972/1/.text: George Russell, Mercedes F1 Team, 2026 Hungarian GP © XPB Images Prefer Crash.Net on Google See our stories more often Add Mercedes has shed more light on the issue that led to George Russell’s car going into anti-stall and wrecking his Formula 1 Hungarian Grand Prix. The Briton plummeted from sixth on the grid to the back of the pack as he struggled to get off the line. It later emerged that he’d gone into anti-stall, forcing him into a recovery driver that saw him eventually finish seventh. Russell is set to start seventh in Hungary Mercedes ’ Deputy team principal Bradley Lord explained in the squad’s post-race debrief that George Russell was “under 10% of throttle” at lights out as he tried to manage a rev spike. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “As the drivers wait for the start, they hold what are called their wait revs, which is holding the engine’s RPM at a specific level,” Lord said. “As George was doing that, the revs actually rose out of proportion to what he was asking for from the throttle. “The revs hit the rev limiter at the maximum RPM that the engine allows at that point, and then George tried to get it back under control to optimise and control his start. “He wasn't able to do so, and as he was lifting right off the throttle to under 10% of throttle demand, the lights went out. Read Also Mercedes cautious of "more intense" title threat ahead of F1 resumption George Russell breaks summer silence with personal announcement “And so he made a start with effectively much too little throttle through no fault of his own. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “That meant the anti-stall kicked in so he dropped to the back of the field.” It continued a wretched run to the summer break for the 28-year-old, who retired on the opening lap of the Belgian Grand Prix after contact with Ferrari’s Lewis Hamilton. Lord praised Russell’s recovery drive, and believes he could have been higher up the field had the virtual safety car for a stricken Oscar Piastri been timed better. Russell was once again struck by misfortune “From there it was an incredible recovery drive,” he added. Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT Article continues below ADVERTISEMENT “He picked the cars in front of him off one-by-one as he went through that first stint and actually was also unlucky with the timing of the virtual safety car at the end of the race. “It came out one lap after his second stop. “Had he been able to take advantage of it and get a free stop as such under the VSC, he could have finished even higher up than his eventual P7 finishing position.” Russell is now 59 points shy of Mercedes team-mate Andrea Kimi Antonelli, who leads the standings after finishing third in Hungary. NORTH ADAMS, Mass. — City leaders last week held a ceremony marking the city as a Purple Heart Community to honor local military service members wounded or killed in combat. "This designation is much more than a sign that will stand at the entrances to our city," said Kurtis Durocher, Northern Berkshire veterans service officer at City Hall on Friday. "It is a lasting commitment and a promise to this community. We'll never forget the sacrifices made by those who are wounded or killed while serving our nation. It is a public declaration of the courage and sacrifices of combat wounded. Veterans will always have a place of honor here in North Adams." As a Purple Heart Community, North Adams will place signs throughout the city acknowledging the designation. The city will also hold a ceremony every Aug. 7 on National Purple Heart Day. During the inaugural ceremony, Durocher said he was asked by the Military Order of the Purple Heart to find a keynote speaker for the event, preferably a Purple Heart recipient. But he was unable to find someone willing to speak. With the date approaching, he decided to tell his own story. "I don't like standing up and telling my own personal story ... But I realized, in my position as a VSO, I get so many ... children of veterans who will say, 'I didn't know anything about my father until after he passed because he just didn't talk about it,'" Durocher said. "... I have been that way until I've gotten into this position, and so, now, I try to tell my story as much as I can when it is brought to me." Durocher served in the Army for 20 years and retired as a master sergeant. On Friday, he recalled a time early in his career while serving in the 82nd Airborne Division deploying to Iraq during Operation Iraqi Freedom. On Sept. 12, 2003, his squad was conducting a patrol on Route Irish in Baghdad. He was serving as a gunner on an LMTV when it was struck by a 155-millimeter artillery shell. He said the explosive had been hidden behind a guardrail and detonated using nothing more than a washing machine timer. "In an instant, everything changed. The blast knocked me unconscious. When I regained consciousness, I instinctively was removing my helmet," he said. "Almost immediately my training took over. We had been taught repeatedly that attacks like this were often followed by a secondary attack or an ambush. I quickly put my helmet back on and began searching for my machine gun." https://www.baltictimes.com/by_replacing.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive By replacing commander-in-chief of armed forces, Ukrainian president has partially yielded to public pressure - expert 2026-07-28 LETA/TBT Staff RIGA - Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has partially yielded to public pressure by replacing the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, Toms Rostoks, vice rector for research at the Latvian National Defense Academy, told LETA. As previously reported, the Ukrainian president has dismissed Commander-in-Chief Oleksandr Syrsky and appointed Mykhailo Drapatyi to replace him. Explaining these changes, Rostoks stated that the Ukrainian president wanted changes in the government, which meant the collapse of the previous government. The desire for change was linked to Ukraine’s preparations for winter, when energy issues will be critical. In the expert’s view, Zelensky decided that either the defense minister or the commander of the armed forces had to be replaced. The vice rector for research at the Latvian National Defense Academy assessed that there were several reasons for this, including the Ukrainian president’s public remarks regarding former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov’s inability to either communicate or cooperate with the commander-in-chief of the armed forces, Oleksandr Syrsky. In Rostoks’ view, this creates instability and problems within the defense sector during wartime. The expert pointed out that, under such circumstances, the role of the commander of the armed forces is more significant, and consequently, the Ukrainian president decided to dismiss the defense minister and offered Fedorov another position related to the defense sector. Rostoks also noted that Syrsky was not viewed uniformly by the Ukrainian public, and the perception had emerged that he did not value human life highly enough. The former defense minister, on the other hand, positioned himself as someone who can transform Ukraine’s armed forces to meet modern requirements, which could help reduce casualties among Ukrainian soldiers. A perception had taken hold in Ukrainian society that one of these men represents the 21st century and the other represents the Soviet past, said the vice rector for research at the Latvian National Defense Academy. He acknowledged that he could understand the public’s desire to choose the person who came with a promise to transform Ukraine’s armed forces, make them more technologically advanced, and potentially reduce military casualties. In the expert’s view, this also sparked public protests. Rostoks noted that Drapatyi is a competent individual whose career has taken a significant leap forward over the past four years. Drapatyi has participated in combat operations and their planning since 2014; therefore, in the expert’s opinion, his candidacy is not controversial. Speaking about the former defense minister, the vice rector for research at Latvian National Defense Academy highlighted his character and issues related to corruption and the waste of funds. Under Fedorov’s leadership, an investigation was conducted into the use of funds in Ukraine over the past year. In Rostoks’ view, it is not surprising that the investigation revealed either wasteful spending or situations where it is unclear how the funds were used. As in many sectors in Ukraine, corruption issues in the defense sector are pressing and particularly painful for the public, especially during wartime, the expert said. According to Rostoks, it is not surprising that both the leadership of the armed forces and the defense minister are replaced during wartime, which has happened several times in Ukraine over the past year. He added that Fedorov served as defense minister for about six months, which is too short a period to expect results and the implementation of reforms. The expert emphasized that the same applies to the positions of commander of the armed forces and commander of the joint forces, where changes have also taken place previously. Rostoks noted that this spring and summer, Ukraine is in its best position in the war against Russia since 2023, which leaves no doubt that the changes could negatively impact Ukraine’s ability to respond to Russian attacks. https://www.baltictimes.com/lithuania_wa.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Lithuania warns of Mere attempts to bypass EU sanctions via rebranding 2026-07-28 BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Lithuania's Economy and Innovation Ministry has warned of possible attempts to circumvent European Union sanctions following the sudden closure of Mere retail stores, which are linked to Russia's Svetofor Group. Deputy Minister Paulius Petrauskas said on Monday that the group may be attempting to bypass restrictions by rebranding. The ministry suspects that Mere stores could be renamed Ola. The ministry has asked the Financial Crime Investigation Service to assess whether individuals sanctioned under the European Union's 21st sanctions package are connected to companies or other entities operating in Lithuania and whether there are grounds to impose restrictive measures against them. "When sanctioned Russian business interests attempt to re-enter our market under different names or through intermediaries, it is not just a business matter - it is an attempt to circumvent European Union sanctions," Minister Edvinas Griksas said. Last week, the European Union announced sanctions against an additional 168 entities and 48 individuals, including the owners of Svetofor Group, which operates the Mere retail chain. Russian businessman Sergey Shnayder, the owner of Mere, has been added to the sanctions list. Reports of Mere store closures in Lithuania emerged last week. At the time, the company said all stores had been closed due to "technical obstacles" but declined to comment on whether the closures were temporary or related to sanctions. As of Monday, the Mere website was offline and the company's Facebook account had been deleted. Svetofor Group founders and co-owners operate more than 2,200 stores in Russia and other countries under the Svetofor, Mere and MyPrice brands. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA Heathrow airport Heathrow says need for expansion ‘clear’ as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airport West London airport reports 7.86 million passengers in July, compared with 8.15 million for Istanbul Business live – latest updates PA Media Tue 11 Aug 2026 04.02 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Heathrow airport said “the case for expansion has never been clearer” after it was overtaken as Europe’s busiest airport by Istanbul. Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.86 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s four terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million. Heathrow’s passenger numbers for July fell, while London Stansted and Manchester both had record traffic for the month. Annual figures from the trade body Airports Council International show Heathrow was Europe’s busiest airport from 1996 to 2019. EasyJet agrees to £5.7bn takeover by US private equity firm Read more The UK’s biggest airport, located west of central London, lost that position in 2020 amid coronavirus travel restrictions before regaining it in 2023 and holding the title since then. Heathrow’s July passenger total was 1.5% down compared with the same month last year, while the Turkish hub recorded a 2.3% increase. The US-Israel war on Iran has affected Heathrow’s passenger traffic. Numbers on Middle East routes were down 20.2% year on year in July. Heathrow continues to operate its two runways at near full capacity, and is seeking government permission to build a third. An expansion proposal by the airport’s owners would enable it to accommodate 150 million passengers a year - up from about 85 million in 2025. The airport said: “Heathrow is operating at capacity. The case for expansion has never been clearer, as Heathrow was overtaken in July by Istanbul airport as the busiest hub in Europe. “Our plans will ensure the country gets the infrastructure it needs to stay competitive and will deliver all-important economic growth.” The comparison, however, may not fully bolster Heathrow’s case. The airport was only opened in late 2018 and built on a brand new site away from the city and residential neighbourhoods, gradually replacing the existing Ataturk airport as the main international hub. It has a vastly bigger footprint and is able to operate 24 hours a day. The Turkish boom also owes much to its location near the Gulf, which has become the crossroads of international air travel. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Preview latest after newsletter promotion The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, launched a consultation on the renamed Heathrow expansion national policy statement in June, setting out the conditions needed if the project is to be given the go-ahead. The then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, said at the time she was determined to get “spades in the ground” for the third runway in the current parliament, and for it to be built by 2035. Andy Burnham, who sacked Reeves, has previously expressed concerns over Heathrow expansion, stating the plans divert infrastructure investment “away from the north and traps it in London”. Heathrow’s chief executive, Thomas Woldbye, said summer was “off to a flying start” but “we want to go further” by “growing our route network and passenger offering”. “Expanding Heathrow will help ensure the UK remains home to Europe’s leading hub and continues to benefit from the trade, investment and tourism that increased connectivity will bring,” he said. London Stansted said it had recorded the busiest month in the airport’s history in July, welcoming 3.1m passengers, a 6.3% increase year-on-year. Manchester also had a record July, serving 3.4m passengers. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Bashar al-Assad (pictured) and his brother Maher, who was also sentenced to death, fled to Moscow in December 2024. Photograph: ATPImages/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Bashar al-Assad (pictured) and his brother Maher, who was also sentenced to death, fled to Moscow in December 2024. Photograph: ATPImages/Getty Images Syria Syrian court sentences Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia for war crimes Verdict relates to atrocities committed during the country’s 14-year civil war in which about 500,000 people died William Christou in Beirut Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.40 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.50 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A Syrian court has sentenced the country’s former president Bashar al-Assad and his brother Maher to death in absentia for crimes against humanity and war crimes during the 14-year civil war, in which about half a million people died. The two men fled to Moscow after being ousted by a lightning rebel offensive in December 2024 which toppled the dictatorial regime in just 11 days . The former president and his brother, who commanded the feared fourth division and was considered the regime’s top security official, oversaw a brutal crackdown in which government forces killed, arrested and tortured indiscriminately to crush protests that started in 2011. The court said Bashar al-Assad had been sentenced to death for crimes of “premeditated and intentional murder of more than one person and of children” as well as “torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity”. View image in fullscreen Syrians celebrate the ruling outside the palace of justice in Damascus. Photograph: Bakr Alkasem/AFP/Getty Images It said it would pursue international legal avenues to try to prosecute the two men, but Russian officials have previously declined requests to extradite its former Syrian allies. The court also sentenced Atef Najib, Assad’s cousin and the former head of political security in Daraa, to death. Najib was responsible for the torture of a group of 15 young boys who had graffitied anti-Assad slogans on a wall in 2011 – an event that kicked off mass protests in the southern Syrian province, which then spread to the rest of the country. Najib’s trial was highly publicised, with pictures of him listening to proceedings while dressed in a prison uniform and held in a cage in court. The Syrian government has presented his trial as a landmark case in its pursuit of transitional justice, something experts say is key to healing divisions in the country. View image in fullscreen Atef Najib on trial in Damascus. Photograph: Mohammed Al Rifai/EPA Syria has experienced explosions of violence in the post-Assad era. About 1,500 mostly Alawite civilians were killed in a wave of retaliatory killings in March 2025 after militants loyal to al-Assad attacked security forces. Al-Assad belonged to the Islamic Alawite sect – a minority group in Syria – and enjoyed strong support in the group’s coastal heartland during his rule. In July 2025, more than 1,700 people were killed in massacres in the Druze-majority province of Suweida when local fighting evolved into sectarian killings. Low-level violence has continued in northern Syria until the present day, particularly targeting Alawite civilians. Syrian authorities have taken steps towards transitional justice, establishing committees and arresting Assad-era officials, in an effort to end intercommunal violence. Al-Assad became president in 2000 at the age of 34, inheriting power from his father, Hafez. He had trained as an ophthalmologist in London and was not initially supposed to be president, but became the heir after his brother, Basil, died in a car accident. Though styled as a young reformer who was supposed to allow some liberalisation in Syrian politics and its economy, his legacy was largely defined by his brutal response to the country’s revolution. Under his rule, Syria’s fearsome security apparatus was given a free hand to arrest, torture and kill civilians on an industrial scale. Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPA View image in fullscreen Narendra Modi is greeted by Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem last February. Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPA This Is India World news As conflict in the Middle East intensifies, India’s relationship with Israel deepens An Amnesty International report reveals that the country is now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. Plus, Assam floods, student anger spreads and a song to put in rotation Don’t get This is India delivered to your inbox? Sign up here Niha Masih Tue 11 Aug 2026 02.55 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 04.26 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Hello, and welcome back to This Is India . For this week’s newsletter, I’m looking at India’s evolving relationship with Israel, and how it has deepened as conflict swept across the Middle East. Why is it that India has formed an even closer bond with a country that has faced mounting international isolation and backlash over a military campaign in Gaza that has left the territory in ruins and killed more than 70,000 Palestinians , – many of whom were children? Under Narendra Modi, India’s ties with Israel have taken on a different character, for a country that once championed the Palestinian cause and led the Non-Aligned Movement. To better understand it, I turned to Stanly Johny, Indian foreign policy expert and the international affairs editor at the Hindu. He told me it isn’t just a political or diplomatic shift, “it’s also at the strategic and defence level”. The evolution of India’s role was revealed in a recent Amnesty International investigation, which showed that India was now a key part of Israel’s weapons supply chain. This represents a fundamental change. For years, New Delhi had primarily been a major customer of Israeli weapons. But, through joint ventures and manufacturing partnerships, it is now a “significant contributor” to Israel’s weapons production, according to Amnesty , which offers the most extensive account so far of the scale of India’s involvement since the war in Gaza began. Indian companies, including state-owned enterprises, have delivered drone warheads, artillery shell casings, small arms parts and military vehicle components to Israeli military suppliers despite the substantial risk these could end up in weapons deployed in Gaza, it added. By examining publicly available shipment-level trade data, Amnesty said it traced hundreds of thousands of weapons components shipped from Indian factories to Israeli military suppliers between 7 October 2023 and 30 November 2025, including: 390,516 small arms parts for military grade weapons 564,970 parts of explosive ordnance 298 components of military vehicles Many western nations, including Britain, have restricted or banned arms supply to Israel over its conduct in the war, citing risks that the weapons could be used to commit or facilitate violations of international humanitarian law. (The United States accounts for the overwhelming share of major arms transfers to Israel.) An independent United Nations commission of inquiry concluded in September that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza , and earlier this year another commission found that Israel is continuing to commit genocide by deliberately targeting Palestinian children . Separately, the international criminal court has issued an arrest warrant for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, accusing him of committing war crimes. Yet, the Amnesty report hasn’t resulted in any large-scale public debate or political backlash in India, despite some scattered media coverage. Johny believes this is a result of the support for Israel by Modi’s voter base. “There is a clear ideological confluence between Hindutva and Zionism,” he said. In rightwing circles in India and elsewhere, he argues, Israel is increasingly seen as a bulwark against the expansion of Islam. View image in fullscreen Modi has long cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. Photograph: Kobi Gideon Hindu nationalists have long admired Israel, viewing it as a model of a nationalist state that can assert itself in a volatile neighbourhood. Author Pankaj Mishra chronicled this affinity in a 2017 essay , writing that his grandfather was among high-caste Hindus who saw Israel as an example of how to deal with Muslims “in the only language they understood: that of force and more force”. The war on Gaza doesn’t appear to have significantly shifted views. A Pew Research survey published in June found that more Indians view Israel favourably (32%) than unfavourably (28%). This is in contrast to the decline of support for Israel in many western countries, including the United States, since the war. Modi, for his part, has cultivated a personal rapport with Netanyahu. In 2017, he became the first Indian prime minister to visit Israel , and Modi’s visit to Israel earlier this year came just 48 hours before Israel and the United States launched their attacks on Iran. The optics of Modi hugging Netanyahu on the tarmac, coupled with New Delhi’s noticeably muted response at the outbreak of war, were a clear sign of where India’s political establishment stands. It has not gone unnoticed. In July, after the US vice-president, JD Vance, rebuked Netanyahu by calling the US Israel’s “only powerful ally” left in the world, Netanyahu shot back : “We have some other friends, like a small country called India. It has 1.4bn people, and boy, do we have tremendous support there.” The government has previously declined to give a direct answer about weapons supplies to Israel. When asked in parliament in 2024 , external affairs minister S Jaishankar said that information is not in public domain and that exports of military products are guided by “national interest”. Amnesty identified three state-owned Indian companies – Munitions India Limited, India Optel Limited and Advanced Weapons and Equipment India Limited – supplying Israel with weapons, which it said, could expose India to the hazard of “complicity in ongoing genocide in Gaza”. Foreign ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal responded that India’s exports are governed by national laws and international obligations. The pushback has largely come from human rights activists, student bodies, trade unions, India’s left-leaning parties and the Congress party . The courts have offered no recourse, either. In 2024, a group of civil servants, activists and academics petitioned the supreme court , demanding India suspend its military exports to Israel. The court dismissed the case, ruling that the matter fell within the discretion of the executive. “In India, you don’t see any anger towards the government for its relationship with Israel, despite the allegations the Israeli government is facing,” Johny said. This, he believes, is a sign that foreign policy debates in India are being stripped of moral concern. Weapons aren’t the only thing India has sent to Israel during this period. Thousands of Indian workers have also gone to Israel, in many instances to replace Palestinians barred from entering the country after 7 October 2023. Last year, the government told parliament that more than 20,000 Indian workers , in construction work and caregiving, had moved to Israel after an agreement signed in November 2023. India, meanwhile, has shored up its own arms supplies from Israel. Between 2021 and 2025, New Delhi was Israel’s largest defence customer, accounting for 29% of total arms sales, according to Stockholm International Peace Research Institute . But for Johny, India’s growing closeness to Israel is beginning to come at a cost. The war in Iran threatens India’s energy security and could have wider economic repercussions across the Gulf, home to a large Indian diaspora. “India has to continue to stay engaged with Israel, but it is important to restore balance to its approach to west Asia,” he said, adding that it needs to forcefully defend its own interests. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Some staff are worried that North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple is being downgraded. Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Some staff are worried that North Devon district hospital in Barnstaple is being downgraded. Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian Devon Doctors at remote Devon hospital get ‘crash course’ after maternity unit shut Staff at North Devon district hospital given training in difficult births in case mothers-to-be cannot get to Exeter Steven Morris Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.07 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Doctors at one of England’s remotest hospitals have been given a “crash course” in birth emergencies after its maternity unit was shut and as fears grow that the safety of women and babies may be put at risk. From Tuesday, the maternity service at North Devon district hospital (NDDH) in Barnstaple has been suspended indefinitely owing to staff shortages, leaving many pregnant women facing a journey of at least an hour and a half when they go into labour. Women have told the Guardian they may be forced to give birth without medical help at home or even in a layby as they try to get to hospital in Exeter, more than 50 miles away, on roads often choked with traffic during the summer months. Some have said they will move from the area to give birth. A doctor at the hospital has now revealed that emergency staff at the NDDH have been given training in dealing with difficult births if mothers cannot get to Exeter. The doctor, who asked not to be named, said: “I’m hoping that we won’t see such emergencies and women will birth their babies without a problem and both will be fine, but there is a potential that we will see women who can’t make it to a maternity unit who have to be diverted to the hospital. “There’s been a crash course in learning how to deal with emergencies such as shoulder dystocia or postpartum haemorrhage. It’s been an intense time and we’re all pretty shocked. We’re capable but they’ve thrown us into a potentially very serious situation. There’s a physical risk to the public. “The emergency department and its staff are familiar with dealing with emergencies without the direct help of specialities but it’s the unfamiliarity of an obstetric emergency or neonatal collapse and having no one nearby on site to assist that is confronting.” Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS foundation trust has described the suspension as temporary but cannot put a date on when maternity services at the NDDH may return. The doctor said: “This has the potential to put a lot of strain on the emergency department. It has to deal with a high volume of patients, especially over the summer when the tourists come. It also has to deal with a large elderly population.” Some staff are worried that the hospital is being downgraded. The doctor said: “It feels like they are slowly stripping away services and moving them. It’s like they’re dismantling our hospital. That’s not fair on the public or on staff. This has hit staff morale as people are questioning what this means for the future of our hospital.” View image in fullscreen Jemima Knight, left, and her sister Harriet Knight. Photograph: Jim Wileman/The Guardian Jemima Knight, who is 18 weeks pregnant, lives two hours from the nearest hospital – and her last birth took only two hours. She said: “This is my third baby. My first required a hospital transfer in an ambulance and luckily that transfer was only 20 minutes. I do not know what the outcome of that birth would have been if the transfer time had been two hours. My second baby was born in two hours. “Even if I knew this labour would be longer than two hours, anyone who has ever had a baby knows that being strapped into a car seat in August heat in the holiday traffic whilst in active labour would be a horrific, dangerous and traumatising experience akin to torture. No woman should ever have to go through that, and that is what the hospital trust are asking us to do.” She said she was considering relocating her family to Bristol, where they could stay with relatives for her birth. “The travel time proposed for us is like suggesting that it would be appropriate to close a hospital in Bristol and tell the pregnant women they have to go and give birth in London. Knight is also worried for her sister, Harriet Knight, who is 34 weeks pregnant. Jemima said: “A safe and respectful birth is a fundamental human right, and that right has been removed for hundreds, potentially thousands, of women in Devon .” A special Devon county council meeting later this month will discuss the closure. The council leader, Julian Brazil, said: “This closure is extremely concerning. It is not a decision which would be countenanced in other parts of the country and we should not accept second-rate NHS provision here.” The trust has said it is trying to recruit extra consultants and doctors but has not been able to hire enough to run a safe service. A spokesperson for Royal Devon University Healthcare NHS foundation trust said: “The safety of women, babies and families is our top priority. We carefully considered all options but the greatest risk was continuing to provide births without sufficient medical staffing.” The trust said it recognised that some women were vulnerable and had put in place a range of support, including help with transport and finances. On the “crash course”, they said: “We have worked closely with colleagues in our urgent & emergency department, maternity services and SWAST [the ambulance trust] to agree clinical pathways for managing emergency presentations.” Asked about staff morale, the spokesperson said: “We recognise the impact this has had not only on women and birthing people, but also on our colleagues. We are actively supporting our colleagues through these temporary changes alongside our focus to reopen birthing services in North Devon as quickly as possible.” The trust denied that more services may go from the hospital. It said: “This is not the case. We are committed to providing the core acute hospital services that people in North Devon rely on. Most services continue as normal, and millions of pounds are being invested in North Devon.” Explore more on these topics Devon Hospitals Women's health NHS Health England news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story ‘Babies will be born in laybys’: maternity cuts leave women with stark choices in Devon Rising numbers of younger midwives quitting NHS in England, data shows Author of England maternity care review ‘listened to wrong voices’, says adviser How has maternity and neonatal care in England failed? Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA View image in fullscreen Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were sentenced in 2020 to 13 years for manslaughter, are due to be freed in January under the existing plans. Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA UK criminal justice Burnham ‘increasingly confident’ PC Harper’s killers will not get early release Prime minister says he has asked justice secretary to push through measures to increase the number of prison places Peter Walker and Caroline Davies Tue 11 Aug 2026 07.09 EDT First published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 03.52 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham has said he is increasingly confident he can adapt the early release scheme for prisoners to exclude the killers of PC Andrew Harper and other serious offenders, saying he understood and shared the public’s concern about their potential release. Writing on Facebook , the prime minister said on Tuesday he had asked the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to rapidly push through a series of measures to increase the number of prison places, requiring fewer people to be released early to free up room. Downing Street said on Monday that there was no feasible way of exempting just a handful of prisoners from the scheme to block the release of Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for Harper’s manslaughter. The pair were due to be freed in January under plans to release about 5,000 people early under an emergency plan to create more space in the prison estate in England and Wales. Exemptions were made for those convicted of rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences, but not manslaughter, prompting pressure to block the release of Harper’s killers, including from police and his family. View image in fullscreen PC Andrew Harper. Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA No 10 had already changed stance, saying Burnham has asked Norris to “work through further options to keep a greater number of the most serious offenders in prison, including the killers of PC Harper”. In his Facebook post, Burnham said the early release scheme could be mitigated by expanding prison places in three ways: removing foreign offenders more quickly; finding a way to release lower-risk prisoners stuck in jail on indeterminate sentences; and “making greater use of the entire prison estate including using the female estate for male offenders”. He wrote: “I am increasingly confident that a more focused approach along these lines will allow us to reduce the number of people released early and, in the case of the most serious offenders like those convicted of the killing of PC Harper, prevent their early release altogether. “In advance of the justice secretary’s proposals being presented to parliament, we will seek to engage other political parties in discussions with the aim of gaining the widest possible public and political consensus on the approach being taken.” Burnham wrote that he understood “the depth of public concern about the potential early release of those involved with the killing of PC Andrew Harper – and I share it”. “I fully appreciate the anguish of Andrew’s family and, more broadly, of all those victims and their families who may see those who caused them such harm not serve their full sentence. It is incumbent on me as prime minister to do everything within my power to minimise that possibility. And I am determined to do so.” Speaking later during a visit in Derbyshire, Burnham said he would prefer to not release any prisoners early, and that he was aware of the public feeling over the issue. “It’s my job to speak up for the public on this issue,” he said. “I take that duty very seriously indeed, and I’m confident that there’s more that can be done, and will be done to address public concern.” He added that No 10 officials had been in touch with Harper’s family on Monday night, and Norris was “in regular touch as well”. Harper, 28, was fatally injured when he got caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and was dragged down a country road as the killers fled the scene of a quad-bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in 2019. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Preview latest after newsletter promotion Cole and Bowers, two of three men sentenced over the police officer’s death, are due to be released halfway through their 13-year sentences, having been convicted of manslaughter in 2020. A petition demanding an intervention has nearly 900,000 signatures. View image in fullscreen The driver Henry Long got a longer sentence and does not qualify for early release. Photograph: Thames Valley Police/PA Prison Service officials have warned Burnham that changing the terms of the prisoners’ early release scheme so that those convicted of manslaughter, such as Cole and Bowers, remain in jail would mean further early releases would be needed within 18 months. Governors told the Guardian the prime minister’s decision last week to exempt rapists and serious child sex offenders would force thousands of sentences to be recalculated in haste and could lead to the mistaken early release of some prisoners. The early release changes were part of the Sentencing Act passed earlier this year that cut the minimum amount of time many offenders would have to spend in prison. The third man jailed for the manslaughter of Harper – the vehicle driver, Henry Long – was given a longer jail term of 16 years. Because he received what is called an extended determinate sentence, he cannot be considered for this early release scheme. Harper’s mother, Debbie Adlam, told the BBC Radio 4 Today programme on Tuesday the debate over the killers’ release had been a “rollercoaster” but that she had heard directly from Downing Street “so we’ve now got a little bit of hope”. Speaking of others affected by the early release plans, she said: “We are not alone on this journey. It’s the world that we have been thrown into. You want what is right for your family member. They’ve lost their life through somebody else’s actions. You have to be their voice. “We are not asking for a special case for Andrew here. We are not stupid, we know it needs to be done the right way.” Explore more on these topics UK criminal justice Andy Burnham Prisons and probation Angela Rayner Alex Norris Labour Police news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story PM urged not to change scheme to stop PC Andrew Harper killers’ early release What could Andy Burnham do to block early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers? https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/live.text: Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog. Democratic primaries for governor in Wisconsin and US senator in Minnesota will once again see left-wing candidates face off against more traditional ones. The party’s ideological rift, that has already been seen in contests across the States this year, shifts to the upper Midwest later today. In Wisconsin, state representative Francesca Hong, a self-described democratic socialist, is front-runner for the party’s nomination for governor in a swing state where winning the governor’s mansion is central to Democrats’ hopes for 2028 and beyond. In Minnesota, Peggy Flanagan is running for the nomination for an open Senate seat against centrist Democratic representative Angie Craig. Meanwhile, seven Minnesota Republicans are vying to face off against likely Democratic gubernatorial nominee senator Amy Klobuchar in November. The primaries come a week after Abdul El-Sayed narrowly defeated Haley Stevens in Michigan’s divisive and costly US Senate

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Rescuers seaarch for survivors in the rubble of a collapsed building in Pereira, Colombia, on Monday. Photograph: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Rescuers seaarch for survivors in the rubble of a collapsed building in Pereira, Colombia, on Monday. Photograph: Jaime Saldarriaga/AFP/Getty Images First Thing newsletter US news First Thing: Colombia reels after major earthquake kills at least 130 Buildings collapse and more than 470 people hurt in 7.4-magnitude quake. Plus, in such a vast universe why is there no sign of aliens? Martin Belam Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.11 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 08.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. More than 130 people died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia , collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in main cities, including Cali and Pereira. The US and Colombian geological surveys reported that a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck at 7.34am local time on Monday, with its epicentre in the western department of Chocó. It was felt in neighbouring Venezuela, still reeling from a deadly double earthquake on 24 June. The quake killed at least 132 people and more than 570 were injured as of Monday afternoon, according to the Colombian Association of Capital Cities, which coordinates cities across the country. How has the government responded ? In a national address, Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said: “The ⁠national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is ​needed. The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble. Colombia has a president whose heart aches for his people and who will do everything in his power to help them in the most difficult moments.” Trump reportedly hid in catering container to board secret flight from Turkey amid Iran threat View image in fullscreen A catering truck is parked next to Air Force One before Donald Trump was due to leaves the Nato summit in Ankara on 8 July. Photograph: Alex Brandon/AP Donald Trump left Turkey on a secret military flight to Britain last month when the White House said he was flying aboard ⁠Air Force One, in an extraordinary ruse – prompted by an Iranian assassination threat – that involved hiding the president in an airport catering container , according to reports. The operation took place when Trump was in Ankara for a Nato summit with world leaders, the Washington Post reported. The president reportedly boarded the old Air Force One jumbo jet in view of television cameras, and was secretly shuttled minutes later to a smaller plane via an airport catering truck, typically used to load meals and other supplies preflight, a US official told the Post. A US official told the Post that a credible threat to Trump involving Iran set the “deception operation” in motion. A similar operation took place in 2000, when Bill Clinton used an unmarked executive jet to fly into Pakistan while sending his formal Air Force One as a decoy. The Guardian has contacted the White House and the US defense department for comment. Trump signs order attempting to override CDC vaccine schedule and break up MMR shots View image in fullscreen President Donald Trump holds a signed executive order about vaccines as Robert F Kennedy looks on. Photograph: Jacquelyn Martin/AP Donald Trump has signed an executive order with plans for sweeping changes to the childhood vaccination schedule that attempts to override the authority of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). The CDC is the federal agency tasked with recommending vaccines, not the White House. Both Trump and Robert F Kennedy, the health secretary, made repeated mentions of autism throughout the signing, emphasizing a scientifically unproven link between vaccines and the condition. Dozens of studies show no link between the two. What does the order seek to change? The order would require that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine be broken into three separate shots, once it becomes available in the US. It would recommend that all shots be given at separate medical visits, a frequent point Trump has made despite the safety, ease and lower costs of giving vaccines together. Bernie Sanders calls on Silicon Valley to ‘pause AI development’ in interest of humanity View image in fullscreen Bernie Sanders says AI may ‘lead to new bioweapons’. Photograph: John Oliva/Caller-Times/USA Today Network/Reuters Connect Senator Bernie Sanders has called on Meta, OpenAI and Anthropic executives to halt their development of artificial intelligence , saying the US Senate would implement regulation if the companies continued deploying AI at their current pace. Sanders said the capabilities of these AI models had reached a critical risk threshold. The Vermont senator cited recent reports that AI was used to develop new viruses , warning if this technology fell into the “wrong hands” it might “lead to new bioweapons that result in the deaths of tens of millions of people”. All three companies have disclosed their models hacked other companies’ servers, a sign that the firms have lost control, Sanders said. What has Mark Zuckerberg said about AI this week? Sanders’s call comes as the Meta CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, presented a utopian vision of AI in a 6,000-word essay amid Silicon Valley debate over government regulation. Central to Zuckerberg’s post was an argument for free-to-download, open-weight AI models – such as the kind Meta develops – and a lack of government regulation. What has a new study suggested the impact of AI might be on carbon output ? AI-driven productivity gains will enable more planet-heating pollution from fossil fuels than they avoid by boosting energy from renewables, a study has found . In other news … View image in fullscreen Todd Blanche is sworn in. Photograph: Brendan Smialowski/AFP/Getty Images Todd Blanche, Donald Trump’s former personal lawyer, has been sworn in as US attorney general after the Senate voted narrowly in favor of his confirmation. A judge has temporarily blocked Zohran Mamdani’s pied-à-terre tax , which would place a surcharge on second homes in New York City. Republicans have named Jennifer Balkcom as the candidate to replace Chuck Edwards in North Carolina’s 11th congressional district after he had stepped away from the contest owing to a sexual harassment investigation. Nevada authorities are investigating dozens of mysterious tree poisonings in Lake Tahoe since 2022 that appear linked. Jackie, the beloved bald eagle at California’s Big Bear Lake whose livestream was followed by millions of viewers, has died . She was 14. Stat of the day: Trump’s media company, which also owns Truth Social, reports $238m loss View image in fullscreen Photograph: John Minchillo/AP Trump Media & Technology on Monday reported $238m of losses in the three months through June as the company branched into new ventures, including crypto, and began selling a new Truth API service charging $60,000-$100,000 a month for early access to potentially market-moving posts by the US president. Culture Pick: Cults, heists and big cats: TV’s 25 best ever true-crime shows View image in fullscreen Nxivm leader Keith Raniere in a court sketch. Photograph: Jane Rosenberg/Reuters This list from Michael Hogan should give you more than a few ideas for something to binge next time you get that true-crime itch. Don’t miss this: ‘Shoved the tube so hard it tore my nose’: Kurdish film-maker recounts ‘inhumane’ ICE force-feeding View image in fullscreen The Kurdish film-maker Gabar Choli. Photograph: Cole Burston/The Guardian Gabar Choli, a film-maker and activist for an independent Kurdistan, has spoken out for the first time, talking exclusively to the Guardian , about his ordeal in the US. He said being force-fed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) “broke” him. Or this: How America is losing its mall ice rinks View image in fullscreen An ice rink in Portland. Photograph: Michael Hanson/the Washington Post/Getty Images The Portland rink where Tonya Harding first skated was an affordable community institution for six decades. Its closure echoes the disappearance of mall ice across the US. Talia Barrington investigates . Climate check: July was hottest month ever recorded in US as heatwaves scorched country View image in fullscreen A family cool off in a fountain in Washington DC. Photograph: Kevin Lamarque/Reuters Last month’s average temperature was 3.3F (1.8C) higher than the 20th-century average for the contiguous US as repeated, scorching heatwaves across much of the country helping shatter all previous monthly temperature records . Scientists have made clear the increased heat in the US was being amplified by the human-caused climate crisis. Last Thing: The great silence – why haven’t we found any aliens yet? View image in fullscreen The universe should be full of aliens given its size and age. Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian I have long been obsessed with space, but one thing has always puzzled me: a universe so vast, how could we possibly be alone? Adam Kirsch has this fascinating read, asking just that question. Given the size and age of the universe, it should be full of species with technology far more advanced than our own.
