Photograph: Jason Karsh, SEIU Local 1107 View image in fullscreen HCA Sunrise hospital workers protesting in Las Vegas, Nevada, on 6 August 2026. Photograph: Jason Karsh, SEIU Local 1107 US unions HCA workers push for higher pay and more staffing amid billions in profits: ‘I’m struggling’ Largest for-profit hospital system and operator in the US reported $6.8bn in profits, while employees find it difficult to make ends meet Michael Sainato Tue 11 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Union workers with HCA Healthcare, the largest for-profit hospital system and operator in the US, are holding picket protests across the country as they push for pay and staffing increases in a new contract. The hospital system has over 300,000 employees in the US and the UK, with 22,000 US workers represented by the Service Employees International Union (SEIU) who are in contract negotiations with HCA. Workers are asking for a pathway to a $25 an hour minimum wage, improved wage scales and raises that match the increased cost of living, along with benefits including paid vacation, sick time and bolstered work protections. Esther Reyes, a single mother of three children, has worked as an environmental services technician at the HCA-owned Las Palmas hospital in El Paso, Texas , for the past two years, and said she constantly struggles to make ends meet on her $16.80 an hour salary. “Sometimes I need to decide, maybe this month I pay the water bill, then another pay for gas, but most of the time I’m not able to pay for everything,” Reyes said. Ahead of contract negotiations, Reyes and her coworkers in El Paso are set to hold an informational picket outside the hospital this week, with picket protests planned at over a dozen HCA hospitals in California , Texas, Nevada, and Florida. Reyes explained prices have been going up but salarieshave remained stagnant, and it’s a constant battle figuring out how to cover basic necessities. “I’m struggling. I struggle a lot. If they gave us the raise we want, it would be a huge blessing,” Reyes added. “I work for my family. I work for my kids. If I don’t get enough for everything, how am I supposed to cover all they need?” HCA reported $6.8bn in profits in 2025, a 17.8% increase from 2024. In early 2026, the company authorized a $10bn stock buyback program. Sam Hazen, the HCA CEO, received more than $26.5m in total compensation in 2025, 420 times more than the median compensation for HCA employees at $62,955. “We also see HCA’s profit reports, and that they are having great returns, and their profit is increasing. Meanwhile, the people doing the work are not being compensated appropriately,” said Jody Domineck, a pediatric nurse with over 20 years at HCA Sunrise hospital and medical center in Las Vegas, the largest hospital in the state, and secretary-treasurer of SEIU Local 1107. “Our work is how they’re making billions. We are just asking for fair compensation.” Domineck noted that despite the increased profit, the hospitals continue to face staffing shortages that impact both workers and patients. “There’s been multiple studies that show that the more patients you have, the higher the risk is to all patients,” said Domineck, who joined her coworkers to hold a rally around their contract demands outside the hospital on 6 August. In 2025, Nevada’s Republican governor Joe Lombardo vetoed a bill that would have established safer nurse-to-patient ratios throughout the state. HCA members are now trying to get similar ratio guarantees into their next contract. “I personally have had to walk away from a parent when their child was having a procedure, and that parent was crying in the hallway alone,” Domineck said. “I had to walk away from them because I had to see my other patients, and that was one of the kind of moments that broke me, because I, with all of my being, wanted to be there and comfort that parent, but I had to walk away to continue to provide care for the other patients, and those are the decisions nurses have to make when they have more and more patients.” A spokesperson for HCA emphasized a small number of HCA Healthcare affiliated hospitals are engaged in individual negotiations with local SEIU chapters and shared a statement on the Sunrise hospital negotiations in Las Vegas, Nevada . “At Sunrise Health System, we value every member of our team and remain committed to reaching a fair agreement through good-faith negotiations,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “While we respect our employees’ right to peacefully demonstrate, portraying this as a patient safety issue is inaccurate. The outstanding issues are about compensation. We believe the best place to reach an agreement is at the bargaining table, and we look forward to continuing negotiations on August 11 and 12.” Explore more on these topics US unions US healthcare Healthcare industry Nevada Texas Florida California news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: EJ_Rodriquez/Getty Images US midterm elections 2026 Minnesota primaries could mark change of path for Democrats and Republicans From progressive and moderate to election deniers, state sees wide spectrum of candidates in test of direction for both parties Rachel Leingang Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 06.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Minnesota voters on both sides of the aisle are weighing the direction of their parties – and their chances of winning over the general electorate – in marquee statewide races on Tuesday. On the left, Peggy Flanagan, the state lieutenant governor and a progressive, faces off against Angie Craig, a US representative, for the Democratic bid for US senate in a race punctuated by the role of immigration enforcement in the state that saw two residents killed by immigration agents in a winter surge. On the right, Mike Lindell, an election denier and pillow salesman, carries Donald Trump’s endorsement in a three-way race for the Republican nomination for governor, where Republicans face an uphill battle to challenge Amy Klobuchar, the Democratic contender and a US senator, now seeking the governor’s office. Will democratic socialist Francesca Hong shake up the establishment – or help Republicans win Wisconsin? Read more After Tuesday, the general election for the open governor and US senate seats will shape up, signaling a change for top roles in the state. Governor Tim Walz, a Democrat, initially sought a third term, but dropped his bid after ongoing fraud scandals threatened to distract from the race. Tina Smith, the Democratic US senator, decided not to run again , saying she wanted to spend time with her grandkids and make way for new faces in the chamber. She has endorsed Flanagan. The state leans Democratic. It has not elected a Republican statewide since 2006, when Tim Pawlenty won a second term as governor. A Republican presidential candidate has not won the state since 1972. Still, Republicans hope to seize on fraud problems in state programs, including criminal cases against a sprawling group accused of organized theft of meals for children, services for kids with autism and housing programs. US Senate race While Republicans have a primary for US senate on Tuesday as well, Michele Tafoya, a former National Football League sideline reporter, is likely to be the GOP nominee. On the Democratic side, polls of the race have been mixed . Flanagan has attacked Craig for supporting the Laken Riley Act, a federal law that requires immigration detention for undocumented immigrants accused of local crimes, named after a woman murdered in Georgia by an undocumented immigrant. Craig has since expressed regret for her vote, writing in March that it has “become clear that supporting any bill that gives ICE [Immigration and Customs Enforcement] new authority in this administration was the wrong decision”. Flanagan told the Guardian she appreciated that Craig has said she regrets the vote, but that she thinks Craig owes Minnesotans an apology and that the vote showed “a real lack of judgment”. “I also think it shows a pretty big disconnect from Minnesotans and the communities here,” Flanagan said. “I think it demonstrates that she doesn’t have a lot of relationships with the people who are most impacted. I think that matters.” Craig has gone after Flanagan on the fraud issue, saying Flanagan has not taken accountability for any role that allowed fraud to perpetuate. “State fraud is the No 1 issue as Minnesota voters go to the polls in November,” Craig told the New York Times . “Fairly or not, the lieutenant governor has a unique vulnerability as our statewide Senate candidate because she’s been helping run the state for the last eight years.” Craig was not available for an interview with the Guardian. The 54-year-old was first elected to congress in 2018, flipping a seat from a Republican to become the first out lesbian to be elected to US Congress from the state. She represents a purple district south of the Twin Cities, which she has pointed to as a sign of electability statewide. Flanagan, 46, served in the state house of representatives before becoming lieutenant governor in 2019. She is a citizen of the White Earth Nation and began her political career as an organizer, a vocation she says would help her build power for progressives in the Senate if she wins. “My job, as soon as I get to Washington DC, is to have 99 cups of coffee with people, to build those relationships, to find opportunities for common ground with folks on the other side of the aisle,” she said. “We may find some unexpected places to work together.” Her platform now includes support for the proposed Medicare for All system of universal healthcare, an issue that she didn’t start off her campaign supporting, but embraced after talking to people across the state who had healthcare horror stories. “They want folks who aren’t going to govern by sternly worded letter,” Flanagan said. “And I think that people are ready for big, bold change.” Tafoya, a Republican who is pro-choice, is counting on winning over independent voters. She has centered her campaign on the fraud scandals. Republican delegates at the state convention endorsed Adam Schwarze, a Marine and Navy Seal. Governor’s race Lindell, the pillow salesman, is hoping to ride Trump’s endorsement to a victory over Lisa Demuth, the Minnesota House speaker, and Kendall Qualls, a businessman. Qualls won the endorsement of Republican activists at the state party convention earlier this year. Lindell has faced opposition from the state Republican party, which has questioned his eligibility to hold office in the state, saying it wanted clarity on whether Lindell has lived in Minnesota long enough to qualify. Lindell, who is from Minnesota, has also lived in Texas. He has said he moved back to Minnesota in August 2025, though only registered to vote in the state in July 2026. Lindell, who has been sued for defamation by voting machine companies and others , has not relented in his claims that the 2020 election was stolen and that Trump had actually won. He currently faces allegations of a potential campaign finance law violation over handing out free pillows at a parade. An administrative law judge in the state recently said there was “probable cause to believe that the pillows were distributed in order to induce a voter to vote in a particular way at an election”. Lindell called the complaint “complete nonsense”. He recently stepped down as CEO of MyPillow, saying he needed to focus on his campaign for governor. He also faces millions in creditor claims over unpaid bills from the company. Alex Plechash, the Minnesota Republican party chair, said Trump’s endorsement of Lindell was a “surprise” and noted that Lindell has “significant electability concerns”. Klobuchar faces several Democratic contenders in a primary, though is likely to easily win on Tuesday. Klobuchar, who ran for president in 2020, has handily won her US Senate campaigns since she was first elected in 2006. Congressional races Multiple congressional districts in Minnesota have contested Democratic primaries on Tuesday as well. In Craig’s congressional district, the second district south of Minneapolis-St. Paul, three people with experience in the statehouse are running. Matt Little, a former state senator, Kaela Berg, a state representative, and Matt Klein, a state senator, are vying for the seat. Both Little and Berg spent time during Operation Metro Surge patrolling ICE activity. Outside spending has flooded the race in recent days. While the district is seen as purple, Cook Political Report rated it as a likely Democratic seat this cycle. In southern Minnesota’s first congressional district, previously represented by Walz, Jake Johnson, a high school math teacher, is hoping he can flip a seat now held by Brad Finstad, a Republican, though he first needs to beat Alex Eaton in the Democratic primary. In the eighth congressional district in northern Minnesota’s Iron Range, Trina Swanson, a former federal worker, faces Luke Gulbranson, who has been on reality TV show Summer House. The winner will face Pete Stauber, the Republican representative for the area, in a solidly red district. Deadly earthquake in Colombia hits Manizales, damaging cathedral and homes Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 11/08/2026 - 12:09 GMT+2 Manizales, in Colombia’s western Caldas department, was among the areas hardest hit by Monday’s 7.4-magnitude earthquake, with streets littered with rubble as rescue teams searched damaged buildings for survivors. … More Footage from 10 August shows collapsed buildings and ambulances as residents make their way through areas closed off by authorities. One of the side towers of the city’s neo-Gothic Cathedral Basilica of Our Lady of the Rosary was also brought down by the force of the tremor, sending debris into the surrounding streets. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT At least two people were killed in Manizales, while dozens of homes and commercial buildings were destroyed or severely damaged. The mayor said more than a dozen commercial properties and over 20 homes had been partially or completely destroyed. Engineers were inspecting cracked facades and weakened structures to determine which buildings needed to be evacuated. The city activated an emergency command centre, opened temporary shelters and suspended classes in schools and universities. Flights at Manizales airport were halted while engineers checked the runways and terminal for damage, while the city's cable car service was also suspended pending safety inspections. A curfew was imposed to prevent looting and allow rescue and assessment work to continue. Firefighters and rescue teams remained on the ground as authorities warned that people could still be trapped beneath the rubble. The earthquake struck at 7:34 a.m. local time on Monday, with its epicentre near San José del Palmar in Chocó, around 400 kilometres west of Bogotá. The government declared a national disaster to speed up rescue operations and provide assistance to affected communities. https://www.dw.com/en/bulgaria-drone-cra.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Iccw A Ukrainian-manufactured Maya decoy aircraft came down in a field about 100 meters from a border checkpoint with Romania Image: Mihail Ivanov/AFP Advertisement When a drone entered Bulgaria 's airspace on Saturday and exploded in a sunflower field near the northeastern village of Kardam — about 100 meters (328 feet) from a border checkpoint with Romania — the immediate question was where the aircraft had come from. Following an on-site check, the Bulgarian Defense Ministry said the drone was a Ukrainian-manufactured Maya decoy aircraft used to activate and deceive enemy drone systems. And while both Bulgarian and Ukrainian officials confirmed that the first drone explosion on Bulgarian territory since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was in no way deliberate, the case quickly became politically charged. The Kardam border crossing (pictured here) is close to a Bulgarian compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine Image: Mihail Ivanov/AFP The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry summoned Ukraine's ambassador on Monday and stressed that "any unauthorized entry into Bulgarian airspace is unacceptable." Kyiv promised to cooperate fully in clarifying the circumstances of the incident. What is known about the incident? At 8:10 a.m. local time on Saturday, a blast was heard by a police patrol near the Kardam checkpoint on the border between Bulgaria and Romania. Police and military units cordoned off the area once the exact location of the fallen drone was established in a field. In his first statement on the matter, Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev said there had been neither casualties nor damage to infrastructure but claimed that the drone had been carrying a "significant amount of explosives." Officials on the ground painted a less dramatic picture, saying the explosion did not even create a crater and that only a few sunflowers had been damaged. Drone came down near gas pipeline The drone crashed about a kilometer (0.6 miles) from Bulgaria's compressor station on the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline route, which connects Turkey and Ukraine , and in close proximity to a Romanian station. Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov (left, pictured here with Prime Minister Radev) has said Bulgaria needs 'new (anti-drone) systems that need to be bought fast' Image: BGNES This initially raised questions about whether this key infrastructure could have been a potential target. Prime Minister Radev said that neither Romanian, Bulgarian nor other NATO radars had detected the drone, pointing to the country's lack of advanced equipment capable of detecting traces of such small aircraft, which usually fly very low. Wake-up call for Bulgaria Saturday's drone incident was a wake-up call for Bulgaria in terms of its defense capability. "Yes, we need new [anti-drone] systems that need to be bought fast," Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Monday in an interview with public broadcaster BNT. While Bulgaria recently reinforced its aerial defense capacity in the northeastern part of the country following an increase in the number of drone incursions in neighboring Romania , these defenses did not prevent the airspace breach. Stoyanov said Bulgaria wants to acquire up to 10 anti-drone and electronic warfare systems through the EU's SAFE mechanism and speed up radar purchases, though h e admitted this would still be insufficient to provide "comprehensive coverage" of the country. " Drone wars have been waged next to us since 2023, and no concrete measures have been adopted," he said, adding that Bulgaria does not currently have an anti-drone strategy but that his ministry will prepare one. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy last met at the NATO summit in Ankara in July Image: BGNES With NATO members scaling up their aerial defenses, Bulgaria now joins the list of countries in Europe that have registered drone incursions linked to Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Was Russia involved? As the decoy drone was partially destroyed, officials have yet to establish its exact trajectory before it crossed Romania and entered Bulgaria. According to Stoyanov, the drone's GPS system was not protected, which could have allowed its movement to be manipulated. Although he did not actually name Russia as potentially being behind the incident, he said the crash could have been caused by what is known as a spoofing campaign, an electronic attack that manipulates a drone's GPS signals. He also pointed to a possible technical failure, as the aircraft's chip was found to be defective. The Defense Ministry declined to say whether the hypothesis of Russian spoofing was being actively investigated and referred DW's questions to the Military Prosecutor's Office, which had not replied by the time of publication. Russia praises Bulgaria's 'restrained' response Former Defense Minister Todor Tagarev, however, feels that it is most likely that Russia played a role in the drone crash. "The most probable hypothesis is that electronic warfare led to the loss of control over this drone as a result of Russia's actions," Tagarev told DW, adding that Bulgarian authorities have the necessary information to rule out this possibility if it is not the case. As the investigation continues, the government has not publicly mentioned Russia and is instead seeking answers from Ukraine. Bulgaria has declined an invitation from French President Emmanuel Macron (center left) to join the Coalition of the Willing, which last met with Ukrainian representatives in Paris in July (seen here) Image: Tom Nicholson/AFP The handling of the case was even welcomed in Moscow, with Yuri Pilipson, a senior representative of the Russian Foreign Ministry, praising Radev's government for its "more restrained" and "more rational" rhetoric toward the war in Ukraine. Crash highlights Bulgaria's 'more pragmatic' foreign policy shift The Bulgarian Foreign Ministry used the incident to reiterate that security in the region can only be achieved through diplomacy after it summoned the Ukrainian ambassador. "This war will not be decided on the battlefield, but through diplomatic steps," said Defense Minister Stoyanov, echoing the prime minister's longstanding position. A former president and fighter jet pilot, Radev won an absolute majority in parliament in April with his Progressive Bulgaria party. While the country had until then steadfastly supported Ukraine, the new government brought a change in the country's foreign policy , promising a "more pragmatic" approach, including toward the war in Ukraine. Over the past three months, Bulgaria has halted state arms supplies to Ukraine , blocked the EU's efforts to include the head of the Russian Orthodox Church in its sanctions package and declined an invitation by French President Emmanuel Macron to join the Coalition of the Willing , which brings together more than 30 countries supporting Ukraine. "I think the Bulgarian foreign minister was too quick to summon the Ukrainian ambassador rather than the Russian one," Tagarev told DW. "It doesn't matter whose drone it is, but rather whose actions caused it to end up here." https://www.dw.com/en/syria-sentences-ba.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IbdF Bashar Assad was ousted in December 2024 after rebel forces seized Damascus Image: Pavel Nemecek/CTK/picture alliance Advertisement A Syrian court on Tuesday sentenced former President Bashar Assad to death in absentia. Assad was ousted in December 2024 after rebel forces swept into Damascus, ending more than five decades of rule by the Assad family. He and his family fled to Russia, where he was granted asylum, as Syria's new authorities began pursuing former officials over alleged crimes committed during the country's civil war. What did the court say about Assad? Assad was convicted of the crimes of "premeditated and intentional murder of more than one person and of children, torture, arbitrary arrest and crimes against humanity." "The contribution of the criminal Bashar Assad to the crimes was that of the person ultimately responsible for decision-making, mobilizing state institutions to commit them," the judge said. The verdict was handed down by Damascus' Fourth Criminal Court and read out live on Syrian state television. Assad, born in 1965, became president in 2000 after the death of his father, Hafez Assad. He continued his family's decadeslong rule, maintaining the dominance of the Alawite minority in Sunni-majority Syria and the country's close alliance with Iran as well as hostility toward Israel and the US. Assad tried in absentia as Syria charges ex-regime members To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The Syrian government has been demanding that Moscow extradite Assad. Assad's brother Maher and several other figures from the ousted government were also sentenced to death in absentia. They were convicted of premeditated murder and torture resulting in death. Assad's cousin sentenced in person In the same case, the court also handed the death penalty to Atef Najib, a senior security official under Assad's rule and a cousin of the former dictator. He was arrested while trying to flee the country in January 2025 and became one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial. Najib, a former Syrian army brigadier general, headed the Political Security Branch in the southern province of Daraa when the uprising against Assad's government began in 2011. He appeared in court under tight security, standing inside a cage in a prison uniform as the judge read out the sentence. The court convicted Najib of crimes including murder, the intentional killing of children under 15 and torture resulting in death, describing the acts as crimes against humanity. https://www.politico.eu/article/latvia-m.text: Latvian authorities have discovered a tunnel used by migrants to cross the border from Belarus illegally amid long-standing concerns that Minsk is weaponizing migration against the EU. On Monday, border guards detected 15 people who had come through a 10-meter-long tunnel near the border fence between Belarus and Latvia, Riga’s Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava said Tuesday. Belarusian ruler Alexander Lukashenko is a close ally of Russian President Vladimir Putin, and his regime has supported Moscow’s war of aggression against Ukraine and taken a hostile stance toward the EU. Advertisement Advertisement Tunnels have previously been found in Lithuania, according to Baltic media , but this is the first time one has been used to cross into Latvia. “This is the first case in which a tunnel has been used for illegal crossing of the state border into Latvia. No signs of violations had previously been detected in this exact location, and no detentions of persons illegally crossing the state border had occurred there,” Dombrava wrote on X . Authorities returned all 15 people to their “country of departure” and are continuing to inspect the area around the tunnel. Latvia launched an operation Tuesday to strengthen border security. Dombrava has described illegal border crossings from Belarus as a “hybrid threat.” Authorities have prevented more than 9,000 illegal attempts to cross the border from Belarus so far this year, the Latvian State Border Guard said in a press release .

https://www.politico.eu/article/vladimir.text: Russia bombarded Ukraine with North Korean missiles overnight, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. The Russian attack killed six people and injured at least 19 in Zaporizhzhia, said the city’s mayor, Rehina Kharchenko. Four apartment buildings and several non-residential buildings were damaged in the southeastern city, Kharchenko wrote on her Telegram channel . According to Zelenskyy, the city was struck with North Korean ballistic missiles, Zircons and guided aerial bombs. In a post on X , he wrote: “It was a vicious attack, calculated to inflict maximum damage specifically on civilian infrastructure.” Advertisement Advertisement Russian President Vladimir Putin and North Korean ruler Kim Jong Un have deepened ties since the Kremlin’s war on Ukraine began. In September last year during a meeting in Beijing, Kim vowed to do “everything we can to assist Russia.” Zelenskyy also reported attacks on a Kyiv hospital and businesses overnight, with at least one person injured. The capital’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, urged residents late Monday to seek shelter. Moscow also attacked substations in Kherson and Kharkiv, causing power outages, Zelenskyy said. Further attacks took place in the Donetsk, Dnipro and Mykolaiv regions. “Every step Russia takes — increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilization — all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation,” Zelenskyy wrote. Russia has stepped up its missile attacks this summer, with Zelenskyy urging Western allies to help Kyiv strengthen its air defenses and to heap sanctions pressure on companies fueling Moscow’s war. However, Europe is running out of Patriot interceptors to shoot down Russian missiles, according to the continent’s military officials . Ukraine, meanwhile, has struck back, targeting Russian infrastructure including oil refineries and buildings belonging to e-commerce giant Wildberries. Russian state media on Tuesday reported that two Wildberries warehouses in the Voronezh region, several hundred kilometers south of Moscow, caught fire following drone strikes, killing one person. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2g.text: Figure caption, Watch: President Trump secretly switches planes to avoid Iran threat By Jessica Rawnsley Published 11 August 2026, 09:57 BST Updated 2 hours ago Donald Trump secretly swapped planes as he left a Nato summit in Turkey last month, as part of an elaborate ruse in response to a possible Iranian threat, US media report. The US president boarded Air Force One in view of television cameras before being transported to a military aircraft with the help of a catering truck, the Washington Post said. Journalists and some White House staff on board did not know he had been smuggled out. Officials told the BBC's US partner CBS News that the US had detected a credible Iranian threat to fire a missile at the plane. The White House has not confirmed the secret switch. Trump had earlier said he was Iran's "number one target" during the summit in Ankara. The clandestine manoeuvre came a day after the US renewed military strikes on Iran following a breakdown of negotiations between Washington and Tehran to end the war. Trump had arrived in Turkey aboard a newer Boeing 747-8 donated by Qatar , but announced that he would leave on the old Air Force One "for old time's sake". On 8 July, footage showed him boarding the presidential jet at Ankara airport. But according to the Washington Post, he was then secretly taken to a smaller C-32A military aircraft - a modified Boeing 757 often used by the vice-president - via a catering truck which had been elevated to plane level on the opposite side to where he had boarded. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth boarded the C-32A separately using external stairs in an effort to make the flight appear normal, according to the newspaper. Journalists and some White House staff boarded Air Force One and were reportedly told to close their window shades. They were unaware the president was no longer on board. Trump then flew to the UK en route to the US, where he reboarded the old Air Force One and was seen descending from the aircraft after it landed at RAF Mildenhall. It is unclear how he moved from the C-32A back to the legacy jet. Image source, Reuters Image caption, He then boarded the Qatar-gifted jet to fly from the UK to the US The president then transferred to the new Qatari-donated Air Force One to travel back to Washington. During that flight, Trump spoke to reporters on board where he noted the threats posed by Iran but did not mention the earlier plane swap. Asked why reporters had been told to lower the window shades on the plane from Turkey, Trump said: "Because you're probably on a dangerous flight because of the sleazebags we have to deal with." He said he had a "threat all the time" on his life, and that he is "number one" on Iran's "list". "But if I go, you go, right?", he said, adding: "Perhaps someday you want to change professions." Image source, Reuters Image caption, Trump spoke about the threat to him from Iran after boarding the presidential jet given to him by Qatar White House communications director Steven Cheung did not directly confirm or deny the reports, but said the new Air Force One was a "state-of-the-art aircraft" fitted with security measures to protect the president and his staff. US intelligence had previously warned of a specific threat of an attack on Trump or his aircraft, according to earlier reporting by CBS News. The New York Times previously reported on security concerns regarding the Qatari-gifted jet , including that the Secret Service had urged Trump to switch planes on his return from the Nato summit. Several of the publication's journalists were summoned to testify under oath in response. The Justice Department subsequently told the BBC that it was investigating illegal leaks. The US has spent months retrofitting the $400m Boeing 747-8 to prepare it for the president. Older Air Force One planes have laser technology to blind incoming missiles, sources have told CBS News. It is unclear what systems the Qatari jet has. "The new Air Force One is perfectly safe for the President's travels, but will receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall which will take approximately one month to complete," White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in a statement to CBS News. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c151.text: Image source, Reuters By Dan Johnson ,Â Reporting from Kyiv Â and Â Tom McArthur Published 3 hours ago Ukraine and Russia have continued striking each other overnight, with Volodymyr Zelensky accusing Moscow of using North Korean missiles. The Ukrainian president said strikes in Zaporizhzhia - which killed at least six and injured at least 19 - involved ballistic missiles from Russia's ally. In Voronezh, in southern Russia, warehouses belonging to the online retailer, Wildberries, were hit by Ukraine. The company, known as Russia's Amazon, has been repeatedly targeted in recent weeks. The attacks come a day after at least 13 people were killed, including one child, in Ukrainian drone strikes on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, more than 1,100 km (680 miles) from the Ukrainian border. In a video address on Monday evening, Zelensky said "for the first time" Russia "cannot wage war without reinforcements from North Korea". "The more North Korean strikes there are here in Ukraine, in Europe, the more their missiles and soldiers are used, the more they correct their shortcomings and blind spots", Zelensky said, adding that this poses a danger to the rest of the world. In his address, Zelensky also hailed a successful air strike on a Russian petrochemical plant in western Siberia on Monday as a "very significant achievement" by the Ukrainian military. He promised "more Ukrainian deep strikes, which should demonstrate to Russia and the Russians that peace is necessary". It is not the first time Zelensky has accused Russia of receiving military assistance from North Korea. He warned over the weekend that as many as 50,000 North Korean soldiers were being sent to fight with Russian forces. Zaporizhzhia Regional Governor Ivan Fedorov posted photos of vehicles and buildings on fire, saying Moscow had struck the city using missiles and guided bombs. In addition to those killed, at least 19 others were injured One person was injured in strikes on Kyiv, where air raid sirens sounded twice during the night. Explosions could be heard on the outskirts of the capital, triggering fires. Fedorov said industrial facilities, infrastructure and non-residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia were hit in the Russian attack. Ukrainian officials say Russia fired 120 drones overnight and a range of different missiles, but for the first time they have not given a number of missiles fired or intercepted. It follows an Air Force statement on Monday urging the media not to write "sensationalised headlines" or "spread pessimism" about the shortage of air defence interceptors. In Kyiv, a strike damaged a hospital, but officials say staff and patients were sheltering. Meanwhile, strikes on substations in Kherson and Kharkiv resulted in power outages. Two women have been injured in a Russian drone strike on Sumy, according to Sergiy Kryvosheenko, head of the Sumy City Military Administration. The women, aged 52 and 66, were treated at the scene, he says in a post on Telegram. The strikes also damaged civilian vehicles, warehouse buildings and infrastructure facilities, he adds. Separately, there have been reports of a fire and explosions at a logistics centre of Russia's biggest online retailer, Wildberries, in the Voronezh region. Wildberries has not yet confirmed the attack, but said that its facilities in the region, which borders Ukraine, have been evacuated. In July, Ukrainian drone attacks on several retail warehouses belonging to Wildberries disrupted the operations of a large number of small and medium-sized Russian businesses. Kyiv said at the time it was targeting logistics hubs used by Russians to buy military equipment, and disrupting supplies to the Russian army. The attack on Tatarstan this week was one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of the full-scale war in Ukraine in 2022. At least 75 people were injured in the strikes, with Ukraine's Armed Forces saying it had hit the city's Tanevo oil refinery. Verified images on social media showed large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background. The Uzkbek consulate in Tatarstan said seven of those killed were citizens of Uzbekistan. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ce34.text: Image source, Reuters By Samantha Granville Â and Â Alys Davies Published 11 August 2026, 10:42 BST Updated 2 hours ago A Syrian court has sentenced ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad to death in absentia, after convicting him of committing war crimes and crimes against humanity during the country's civil war. It is the first conviction against Assad, who fled from Damascus to Moscow with his family after his regime was overthrown in December 2024, ending his family's five-decade grip on power. Assad's cousin and the former head of political security in southern Syria's Deraa province, Atef Najib, was also sentenced to death. He had been put on trial and appeared wearing a striped prison uniform inside a cage in the courtroom as the judge read out his sentence. Deraa is widely seen as the birthplace of the uprising against Assad's rule. In March 2011, the detention and alleged torture of a group of teenagers accused of writing anti-government graffiti sparked protests in the city, which were met with a violent crackdown by security forces. That response helped ignite nationwide demonstrations that escalated into civil war in which hundreds of thousands of people were killed. Syria's interim government began trying officials associated with the Assad regime, which ruled the country for more than 50 years, earlier this year. Najib is one of the highest-ranking officials to be put on trial. He was convicted of crimes including murder, "the intentional killing of children under 15" and "torture leading to death". The court also sentenced six former military and security officials in absentia to death, including Bashar al-Assad's younger brother, Maher. He ran the army's elite Fourth Division and also fled to Moscow when the regime fell. The others convicted include former defence minister Fahd al-Freij. Image source, NurPhoto via GettyImages Image caption, Atef Najib appeared in a cage in court during his sentencing on Tuesday Nouha al-Masri has spent 15 years waiting for this moment. She is not just part of the five person prosecution team, she is also a plaintiff in this case. Masri lost her brother during the March 2011 crackdown and massacre at Al-Omari Square in Deraa. "The verdict reflects the magnitude of the sacrifices we made, the sacrifices of the martyrs, the suffering and pain of the victims, the missing, and the detainees," she told the BBC. "We have been waiting for 15 years to reclaim even a small part of our rights, for all those who have spilled our blood, committed crimes, violated our rights, killed, and tortured us." For Masri, the verdict is a new chapter. "Our demand is that this not be the end of the trials... In the new Syria, there will be no impunity from this day forward." Syria trial seen as first step on long road for Assad's victims Published 29 April The phone book that led us to Assad's spy chief in hiding Published 3 days ago Calls for justice and accountability in Syria grow after Assad's fall Published 6 January 2025 It remains unclear whether Syria's new authorities will be able to secure Bashar and Maher al-Assad's extraditions from Moscow. It is not the first move against Assad by Syria's new leadership. An arrest warrant was issued against him last December on charges of murder and torture. He left for Russia as forces under Ahmed al-Sharaa - now Syria's president - swept to power in a rapid, 11-day campaign that brought down the Assad dynasty. Since then, the new government has detained numerous former officials and security personnel, though most senior figures from the old regime, including Assad himself, remain out of reach in Russia. Attempts by Syrian opposition figures to pursue Assad through courts in Western countries during the final years of his rule did not lead to any convictions. Assad came to power in 2000 after the death of his father. The second son of Hafez al-Assad, he was not destined to be Syria's ruler until his brother, Basil, died in a car crash in 1994. Part of the Alawite minority, he continued to favour their dominance in many roles in the military, security and intelligence agencies. Much of his rule was defined by the civil war. Additional reporting by Lana Antaki in Damascus. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cp30.text: Figure caption, Watch: Huge blaze after attack on petrol tank in Libya By Basillioh Rukanga Published 4 hours ago Libyan emergency services have been battling to contain a huge blaze at a major oil plant after it was targeted by unknown attackers. The Zawiya refinery, west of the capital Tripoli, was hit in a drone strike on Monday evening - the third such incident in two days. The National Oil Corporation (NOC) said a tank containing about 4.5m litres of fuel was directly hit, triggering a huge fire that caused it to collapse. It said it was considering suspending operations if the attacks continued. There were no "serious injuries" from the fire, with most patients treated for smoke inhalation, Libya's Ambulance and Emergency Service said on Tuesday. The Zawiya refinery is the largest operational facility in Libya, with an output of 120,000 barrels per day. The NOC condemned similar attacks in past days in Zawiya, including two drone strikes on a naphtha reservoir and a water desalination plant. It called on the authorities to investigate who was behind the violence. The attacks have highlighted continuing instability in Libya, which has been split in two since a civil war broke out after the ousting of former leader Muammar Gaddafi. Colonel Gaddafi seized power in 1969 and ruled autocratically for four decades until he was toppled and killed in 2011 in a rebellion assisted by Western military intervention Since his fall, rival power centres, one based in the east backed by military commander Khalifa Haftar, and one in the west in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, have been jostling for political and military dominance. https://jowhar.com/berlin-pride-attack-s.text: Home NEWS WORLD NEWS ARTICLE POLITICS SPORT Somali TV Quran karim NEWS ARTICLE WORLD NEWS POLITICS Sport QURAN Video Somali TV privacy-policy terms and conditions Home NEWS WORLD NEWS ARTICLE POLITICS SPORT Somali TV Quran karim WORLD NEWS Facebook X Telegram WhatsApp ReddIt Pinterest Digg A 65-year-old Polish woman was killed in the attack and 29 people were injured A deadly attack near Berlin’s Pride parade is now being treated as an Islamic State-inspired act after German media reported the suspect recorded a video pledging allegiance to the extremist group. The video was discovered on the mobile phone of 21-year-old Abdul Rahman Ballout and was filmed on the day of the attack, the daily Bild reported, citing unnamed security sources. According to Bild, investigators found Ballout’s phone inside the rented minivan that was driven into a crowd just hundreds of metres from the parade route before it slammed into a tree in the Tiergarten park. Near the device, Bild said, police also recovered a sheath for a machete that Ballout is believed to have used in an attempt to attack more people after getting out of the vehicle. The assault killed a 65-year-old Polish woman and left 29 others injured. Police shot Ballout dead on Sunday, saying he charged at officers with a bladed weapon. Ballout, a German citizen with Lebanese roots, was already known to the criminal justice system. Bild said he travelled to Lebanon last year in an unsuccessful bid to fight for IS. A Lebanese judicial source said Ballout was sentenced there to three months in prison for belonging to IS. After returning to Germany, he was detained and in May a juvenile court convicted him of “planning a serious act of subversive violence,” handing down a suspended sentence of one year and 10 months. Prosecutors have been approached for confirmation. https://aviationweek.com/mro/aircraft-pr.text: Share Fast 5: APOC Aviation’s New CCO Eyes Diversification Opportunities Share Lindsay Bjerregaard July 28, 2026 Apoc Aviation CCO Craig Skilton. Credit: Apoc Aviation Craig Skilton was appointed chief commercial officer at APOC Aviation on June 17. He spoke with Aviation Week about the company’s shift toward nose-to-tail support and its diversification into new aircraft platforms. In your new role, you’re shifting from overseeing APOC Aviation’s components business to focusing on the company’s broader business development and strategy. What are your key focuses for the company in the near term? I’ve essentially gone from managing the airframe division to having to learn a little bit more about engines, a little bit more about landing gears—our two other divisions at APOC. But also within that, being accountable for our marketing and business development activities as well, so it’s been quite the change. There’s been a lot to learn along the way. APOC is well known for specializing in parts supply, but in recent years, the company has introduced more end-to-end solutions. How are your capability offerings evolving to better serve the aftermarket? APOC has recently changed its branding, aiming to be the intuitive partner of choice. The idea is that across, for example, an [Airbus] A320 fleet, we can genuinely provide a solution from nose to tail. That encompasses airframe support on components exchanges. We have a pool of nacelles and we’re really ramping up full support on that, but we also do coverage on engines. That’s whole assets and components as well. And the same thing on landing gears as well—whole asset sale exchange or loan. In previous years, we might have one division focusing on one asset type. We’re trying to join that up a little bit and offer a true service to a customer, end to end. The aim is to do that across more fleets. We’ve recently been looking at our investment strategy as well, and we’re looking at how we can diversify and provide more of a service across the new-gen platforms, but also into widebodies. APOC recently introduced a focus on Airbus A320 family components stocked for exchange. Could you tell me a bit more about the strategy behind that offering? Our warehouse is in the heart of Europe. Previously, the model was to sell and sell quickly. Now we’re looking to truly understand the demand from some of the operators we’re working with, and rather than selling, we’re holding that material for exchange and loan. That includes A320 material, but it also includes A320neo material. Some of the acquisitions that we’ve done recently have a really strong crossover into the Neo family and Neo applicability. So, in theory, for some of those high-cost, high-rotation items, we should, at almost all times, have a unit on the shelf to support an exchange, and that’s really been a strong play we’ve been making with operators in and around Europe. We’ve trebled our airline customer base in the last 12 months. That’s been a dedicated push on providing that service to the end user, rather than through a third party. We’ve done both in parallel. We’ve increased the customer base and then made sure that the stock is there to support them. APOC has been quite active in acquiring airframes and engines over the last year. What does your teardown pipeline look like right now and which disassembly partners are you working with? Currently, we’ve got an A320 and A321 going through teardown. The A320 is a younger model. That’s the one with a lot of crossover into Neo. So that’s going on at Tarmac Aerosave at the moment. We’ve got an A321 cargo [teardown] going on at Magnetic MRO in Tallinn. [The] A321 is an area for us where we hold assets, especially across the landing gears, so that was a strategic one for us—landing gears and airframe. On the engine side, we’ve recently torn down two [IAE] V2500s. That material is available, and the team is focusing on those. We’ve also done a [GE Aerospace] CF34-10, which is a bit of a new play for us into the Embraer market. So we’ve got one, and in theory another engine to follow shortly after for material on the Embraer side as well. Landing gear continues to flourish and has had a really good year. That’s across the A320. We’re looking at A330 and [ Boeing ] 777 new-gen landing gears at the moment. We’re also looking at a Neo gear. Landing gear remains our most comprehensive department and is the one that really has assets in a lot of those key markets. The aim is to grow some of those out and scale what we’re doing, but also expand into new platforms, too. We’ve recently seen some interesting developments that may impact the global parts market, such as competition for the Spirit Airlines fleet post-shutdown and industry efforts to open up China’s USM market. Which recent developments in this market have caught your attention and why? Having a strong foothold in the A320 market, we’re certainly checking what’s going on, and sometimes that changes every day. We’re trying to assess what’s going on, especially around Spirit and some of those other things. I think for us, the pivot into Neo is quite a critical one, and we do have A320 operators that we still need to service. But I think being able to service the Neo market as well derisks what we’re doing with any Spirit activity. We’re looking into China as well. It wasn’t that long ago that we hired a regional sales director in China, and he’s actively exploring that market for us. [The focus] was initially on landing gears, but now it’s company-wide, so that’s been a strategic play as well that we’ve been looking into alongside the efforts that we’ve already got in the Middle East and Asia. For us, maybe it’s not the trends so much, but trying to counteract all the different trends and the things that are going on. What we’ve done successfully in Europe, we’re trying to make sure that we can do successfully in other regions now, and like I said before, a little bit of diversification on some of our concentrated assets into one family. Lindsay Bjerregaard Email: [email protected] Lindsay Bjerregaard is managing editor for Aviation Week’s MRO portfolio. Her coverage focuses on MRO technology, workforce, and product and service news for MRO Digest, Inside MRO and Aviation Week Marketplace. Vandals desecrated two statues of Our Lady and set fire to the outdoor altar of St. James Church at the Medjugorje shrine in Bosnia and Herzegovina early Tuesday, July 28, days before the shrine's annual Mladifest youth festival. The statue of Our Lady on Podbrdo, or Apparition Hill, was doused with black paint across the face, chest, and dress, with the words "Devil in a skirt" scrawled on its pedestal, local media reported . The statue of Our Lady at the nearby Blue Cross was similarly defaced, with "EVIL" written on a nearby stone slab. A banner in Polish naming the six alleged seers was left near the Podbrdo statue . Police in Citluk received the first report at 4:30 a.m. and a report of fire at the recently renovated altar behind St. James parish church at 5 a.m., a police spokeswoman said reportedly. Surveillance footage shows a man dousing the altar with flammable liquid and igniting it. Cantonal police later confirmed to local media that a suspect was arrested Tuesday afternoon. His identity has not been released. 'Prayer, fasting, and forgiveness' "We received with great sadness the news of the act of vandalism that damaged the places of prayer in our parish," the Medjugorje parish office said in a statement , calling on the faithful to respond "as Our Lady has been teaching us in Medjugorje for more than 40 years: with prayer, fasting, and forgiveness." Cleanup began immediately, the parish said, and "the shrine remains open to all pilgrims." Bishop Petar Palic of Mostar-Duvno expressed deep sorrow, urging the faithful not to let evil "infect us with its own logic," while the Interreligious Council of Bosnia and Herzegovina condemned the attack. The Vatican granted a "nihil obstat" to devotion at Medjugorje in September 2024. Mladifest opens Aug. 1 and is expected to draw 50,000 to 60,000 pilgrims. https://www.ksmu.org/news/2026-07-28/far.text: On Air Now Playing KSMU HD1 News Farmata brings intimate classical concerts, food and rural hospitality to Fair Grove KSMU | By Jimmy Rea Published July 28, 2026 at 10:55 AM CDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Listen • 35:58 Farmata A rebuilt barn, world-class musicians and farm-to-table hospitality come together at Farmata, where a new concert series offers an intimate listening experience near Fair Grove. A new concert series near Fair Grove is combining world-class classical music with farm-grown food, sustainable living and the intimacy of a house concert. Farmata was created by cellist Steuart Pincombe and his wife, Michelle, on the rural property where they have spent the past seven years developing a homestead. The couple raises hogs, goats, ducks, geese and bees, along with elderberries, fruit trees and other crops. At the center of the project is a rebuilt barn that now hosts concerts for about 20 to 25 people. “It’s basically an invitation into our lives,” Steuart Pincombe said. “Our aim is to pull people into natural beauty, both in what I do in music and what my colleagues do, and in how we try to cultivate the land.” The Pincombe's previously lived in The Hague in the Netherlands, where Steuart performed and taught music. After returning to the United States, they began looking for a place where they could afford land, grow food, raise animals and live closer to family. They eventually settled near Fair Grove, where Steuart's parents live. The concert series developed gradually as Steuart renovated the barn, initially intending to use part of it as a teaching studio. As the space took shape, the couple began imagining small concerts inspired by intimate performances they had experienced in Europe. “We really want to be investing in the place where we live,” Michelle Pincombe said. “We moved here to try to set down roots, contribute to where we are living and celebrate what is unique about rural Missouri.” Food is included with each concert and often highlights ingredients raised on the farm or produced by neighboring farms. For the upcoming performances, Michelle plans to serve homemade Sicilian-style gelato flavored with elderberry, blackberry and pear, along with locally grown watermelon. Farmata’s next concerts will feature Steuart Pincombe on cello and Oregon musician Jonny Rodgers performing on tuned wine glasses. Rodgers adjusts the water level in each glass to change its pitch. The duo’s program will combine guided improvisation, microtonal music and arrangements of works by Estonian composer Arvo Pärt, including "Spiegel im Spiegel" and "Fratres." Microtonal music uses pitches that fall between the notes commonly heard in Western music. Steuart said the duo is approaching the technique gently, creating music intended to soothe rather than unsettle listeners. Audience members will also be invited to participate in one piece using pre-tuned wine glasses while Steuart improvises around the chords they create. The performances will begin at 7 p.m. Aug. 7 and 4 p.m. Aug. 8. Both concerts will feature the same general program, although the improvisational elements will make each performance different. Tickets and additional information are available through Farmata’s website at www.farmata.org . News Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Jimmy Rea Jimmy Rea is a proud Ozarkian with deep ties to the music community. With 2 decades of creative entrepreneurship underfoot, Jimmy has toured coast to coast and around the world with acoustic acts The HillBenders and Keller Williams. Spearheading numerous musical groups, recording projects, and live music events, Rea’s work in the Springfield music scene is a passion and lifestyle. Happily married to wife Melissa and father to Archie, they enjoy life together with 2 dogs and a cat. Hundreds of public hospitals in Romania went on an all-out strike on Tuesday. Negotiations between healthcare trade unions and the relevant ministry are continuing, with no concrete outcome following the first round of talks. In the absence of guarantees that their demands will be met, the SANITAS Federation has announced that the general strike will not be called off. Trade unionists from the Federation are protesting against the draft bill – still under debate – for the new law on a unified pay scale for public sector staff, and are calling for measures to resolve the problems within the healthcare system – the staff shortage, which affects both staff performance and the quality of services provided to patients, as well as the prospect of cuts to certain allowances. The protesters are therefore calling for vacant posts to be filled, better working conditions and a pay law that reflects the responsibility and complexity of work within the healthcare system. Parliament. On Tuesday, the Budget Committee of the Chamber of Deputies in Bucharest issued a favourable report on the draft bill to approve the SAFE Loan Agreement between the European Union and Romania, worth 16,680,055,394 euros. The draft is due to be debated in the plenary session of the Chamber of Deputies, the first chamber to consider it, and will then be sent to the Senate, which is the decision-making body. According to the draft, the servicing of the public debt relating to the loan – namely the repayment of the principal, the payment of financing costs, liquidity management costs, administrative costs and other costs associated with the loan – will be covered by the Ministry of Finance, in accordance with the legislation in force. Drones. Romania considers that Russia bears responsibility for the drones shot down in its national airspace, Acting Foreign Minister Oana Ţoiu stated at a press conference on Tuesday. She added that Romania had taken a ‘clear, firm’ stance, which included summoning the Russian ambassador to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, where he was shown fragments of one of the three drones recently shot down in Romanian airspace, as well as the results of the investigation confirming that the drone was Russian. Oana Ţoiu recalled that NATO had reaffirmed its support for Bucharest, as well as the fact that Romania is a state that does not negotiate its borders and does not permit illegal entry into its airspace. We recall that at the end of last week there were three incidents involving drones that illegally entered Romania’s airspace. Agreement. The Romanian company Oves Enterprise and Edrone, one of Ukraine’s largest drone manufacturers, have signed a strategic partnership laying the foundation for the joint production of military drones in Cluj-Napoca (north-western Romania). “Europe needs its own production capabilities and Romania must build a genuine industrial role within this ecosystem rather than remaining solely a sales market,” said Oves Enterprise in a press statement issued on Tuesday. In the initial phase, three types of military drone will be manufactured in Cluj-Napoca, namely FPV, interceptor and reconnaissance. The range of products may later be expanded to include up to 27 models. Initial production capacity will be approximately 1,000 units per month, with hopes of increasing this to between 10,000 and 15,000 units monthly. Visit. On Thursday, Romanian Prime Minister Ilie Bolojan will welcome his counterpart from the Republic of Moldova (a former Soviet republic with a predominantly Romanian-speaking population), Vasile Tofan, to Bucharest. This will be Mr Tofan’s first official visit to Romania since taking office. The agenda for the talks includes ways to accelerate bilateral projects, with a focus on those in the transport and energy sectors, designed to help ensure greater interconnectivity between the two banks of the Prut River and to address current challenges. The two senior officials will also address issues relating to the security situation in the region, against the backdrop of Russia’s ongoing war of aggression against Ukraine and the security and economic consequences of this war. Prime Minister Bolojan will reiterate Romania’s firm support for the Republic of Moldova’s accession to the EU and will discuss specific aspects of assistance and diplomatic and sectoral coordination to advance this process. Firefighters. Romania has extended the mission of the firefighter contingent deployed to southwestern France by another two weeks to assist French and international teams in extinguishing devastating wildfires and forest fires. According to a government statement, the decision reflects Bucharest’s solidarity with its European partners and its commitment to contributing to emergency management within the framework of the European Union Civil Protection Mechanism. Recently, French President Emmanuel Macron posted a message on X thanking the Romanian firefighters for their assistance in battling the fires. Survey. Around 70 per cent of Romanians living abroad for at least seven months a year rule out returning to the country in the coming year, although the majority have already made investments in Romania, according to an opinion poll published on Tuesday. The socio-professional profile of Romanians living abroad indicates significant structural stability, with 44 per cent of them in employment and 23 per cent working as managers or entrepreneurs. Romanians in the UK have the most advanced economic profile, with 29 per cent of respondents holding leadership or entrepreneurial roles, 62 per cent having a university degree, and 46 per cent earning over 3,000 euros a month. Over 60 per cent of Romanian citizens in the diaspora say they have invested considerable sums in Romania, either by providing financial support to families who have remained in the country, or in property or small businesses run by relatives. The community in Germany has the highest investment rate: 71 per cent, and the highest level of direct financial support for family: 44 per cent. Anthem Day. National Anthem Day will be celebrated on Wednesday with military ceremonies taking place at all garrisons across Romania. In Bucharest, the event will take place in Tricolor Square. The programme includes a religious service, a presentation on the meaning and symbolism of the anthem’s lyrics, and a concert performed by the Ministry of Defence’s Representative Band. National Anthem Day was established by law in 1998 and is celebrated every year on 29 July. “Awaken, Romanian!” was composed by Anton Pann, and the lyrics were written by the poet Andrei Mureșanu. https://www.miragenews.com/dna-leads-to-.text: Mirage News Mirage News Mirage News Life 29 Jul 2026 7:04 am AEST Date Time Share Police are renewing their appeal for help to identify the body of a man – also known as 'Echo Point man' – found 22 years ago in the Blue Mountains, after sourcing fresh evidence via DNA technology. About 11.30am on Friday 4 June 2004, emergency services were called to Echo Point, Katoomba, after a report of a body found in bushland. Officers attached to Blue Mountains Police Area Command attended and located the body of a man. Despite extensive inquiries over the past two decades, police have been unable to identify the man; however, fresh information has now been received via advanced DNA analysis. Based on the information received, detectives have now renewed their appeal for information and have released an updated description of the man. The man is believed to be Caucasian, more than 60 years old, about 178cm tall, of medium build, with light grey hair and frontal baldness. Detectives believe the man was also suffering from significant eyesight problems at the time. When the man was found, he was wearing a blue button up shirt, a red cardigan, a cream jacket, blue corduroy pants, a black belt, and brown work boots. Based on recent DNA analysis, detectives have been advised the man's ancestry is likely Latvian. Detectives are now hoping this latest information could lead them to identify the man. Blue Mountains Police Area Command Commander, Superintendent John Nelson, said they hope this additional information could provide leads for his team. "Despite extensive inquiries over many years, this man's identity remains unknown," Superintendent Nelson said. "Since receiving this latest information, we have focused our inquiries in this area but have been unable to identify the man, and we are now appealing to anyone with information about a man missing since early 2000s, possibly with Latvian or Middle European heritage, to contact police. "Police understand this may be a difficult subject, but identifying this man is about dignity, respect, and providing answers to family who may still be searching." Anyone who may have any information is urged to contact investigators attached to Blue Mountains Police Area Command or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. Anyone with information about this incident is urged to contact Crime Stoppers: 1800 333 000 or https://nsw.crimestoppers.com.au . Information is treated in strict confidence. The public is reminded not to report information via NSW Police social media pages. /Public Release. https://www.michigandaily.com/statement/.text: Ella Flores Brosnan/DAILY “God punished man by taking away sleep and giving him knowledge.” — “On the Heights of Despair,” Emil Cioran Open, close. I was losing feeling in my fingers. In, out. My chest was perpetually tight, so I used brute force to mechanically breathe in two-second intervals, like pouring alcohol on an open wound. It’s near the end of the school day, and I’ve officially given up. I didn’t care if I had to miss class for a week if that’s what it would take: I needed to sleep. My junior year of high school had just started, and I didn’t know how I was going to survive. For three days, I barely slept, if at all. The year before, I began struggling with bouts of insomnia . While the COVID-19 pandemic raged on, it was easier to manage relentless fatigue while at home. I could even catnap at times. Now, I had to face in-person school, and this radical change made me a wreck. I was catastrophizing about every little detail, from friends to lunch to band to teachers to homework to sort-of friends to awkward encounters possibly related to dropping a pencil until it rolls too far so that you can’t smoothly pick it up but no one around will pick it up either to which seat you pick on the first day of class because everyone knows that unassigned assigned seats exist even if a teacher doesn’t enforce them. My insomnia just heightened these thoughts. However, the ultimate disaster would be not going to school at all because then everyone would forget about me. Obviously. I was positive that the entire school would witness some astonishing, life-altering event or form a lifelong bond I would miss out on. Anxiety works in interesting ways; I hated school, but I also couldn’t stand not going. Sometimes… Have you ever heard the term “dad lore” ? On a bright and sunny day, you’ll notice the birds chirping and a gentle breeze passing by, and your seemingly normal father will share an insane backstory as if he were merely discussing the weather. My dad is excellent at dropping dad lore, and he once told a gripping tale about a childhood friend. This friend’s dad, who worked for the United States embassy in Moscow, was captured and imprisoned in a Gulag — one of many labor camps that housed political prisoners from the 1920s to the 1950s in the Soviet Union. Inside, they tortured him with sleep deprivation, among other methods. Anytime he was found sleeping, a guard would kick him awake. With time, he learned to sleep flat on his stomach with one eye open, enough to fool the guards. Fast forward two decades, my dad stumbles into his friend’s house to find his father drinking at the dining room table with one eye squeezed shut and the other wide open like a hawk’s. Despite enduring one of the most traumatic sufferings possible, Alexander Dolgun was only paid $22,000 by the U.S. Embassy as compensation. He then wrote a book about his experience before his death in 1986. The less I sleep, the more I separate into two selves. Most people are familiar with Maslow’s hierarchy of needs. Put simply, without fulfilling physiological needs like air, food, shelter and rest, a person cannot think about the other needs that make up the rest of the pyramid — safety, love and belonging, esteem and self-actualization. When I don’t sleep, I can almost picture a transparent version of my soul detaching from my physical body until I am a hollow shell. Without my “true self,” that ghostlike soul controlling my body, my husk is governed by basic animalistic needs. Humans are animals, and the only thing differentiating us from that pigeon perched on a street lamp and that horse trotting across an open field is our intelligence and sense of self. I can feel myself regressing when I deprive myself of my most fundamental need — sleep — and I despise it. When I toss and turn at night, I wrestle with my thoughts, which often turn to Dolgun. And then the guilt sets in: How can I afford the luxuries of living in a comfortable situation in the Global North yet render myself incapable of basic rest? Just relax , my soul shrieks at my shell. Soothing, right? In high school, I knew this lifestyle was unsustainable. I would hyperfixate on the higher likelihood of drastic health issues caused by sleep deprivation: cancer, diabetes, heart disease, high blood pressure, fatal accidents, obesity, dementia, depression, anxiety — you’re even three times more likely to catch the common cold. If I couldn’t control my rest, I knew the path I would march towards: I am hunched over, poisoned into senselessness, carving my name on an early tombstone. Whatever basic solutions people have suggested to treat this problem, I’ve tried and even learned some things along the way. I’ve been to a sleep doctor, undergone a sleep study where professionals tracked my brain waves, done cognitive-behavioral therapy and taken sleep medication. The medication only provides a false feeling of sleepiness — a medically induced sedation — which did nothing to sway my mind into accepting the thick blanket of sleep. During the three-day ordeal in my junior year of high school, I somehow stayed awake despite taking a Tylenol PM, which is supposed to lull you into sleep. I could feel the onset of the sedative come and go, but it did nothing to ease the jitters that kept me awake. When your mind is your enemy, your battle tactics often fail. It is extremely difficult to find a permanent or foolproof solution to insomnia. After years of experimenting, I know that the way we go about fixing sleep deprivation is all wrong. We are constantly finding solutions to a symptom of the problem instead of attacking the problem itself. Insomnia is a rising global issue that’s mostly tied to privilege — or more specifically, lack thereof. Women, the elderly and people of lower socioeconomic backgrounds are more likely to suffer from insomnia, which contributes to the lack of attention on it. The National Center for Health Statistics found that in 2020, 8.4% of American adults had taken sleeping pills every day or most days within the past 30 days. Additionally, while people residing in industrialized regions — including the U.S. — experience longer and more efficient deep sleep, their circadian rhythms are substantially more disrupted than those in non-industrial societies. In an industrialized society, you will sleep around 45 minutes longer — the conditions for rest are optimized by things like air conditioning and high-quality mattresses— but experience significant circadian dysfunction, which is linked to a higher risk of inflammation, cancer, cardiovascular disease and mental health problems. I wish I could go into more detail about how I, specifically, was feeling in these moments, but truthfully, I have gaps in my memory from sheer lack of sleep. Whenever people talk about the “high school experience,” I feel mournful because I will never get those years back. I can’t even remember half of them. Even now, as a rising senior in college, there are sleep-deprived days when I walk around campus in a dazed shell, already severed into my two halves. I do everything in my power to hold myself together some days. I still feel insane jealousy for people who can fall asleep at the drop of a hat. Even worse is when people intentionally deprive themselves of sleep to cram for tests or other obligations, and then have the audacity to complain about it. The rage that consumes me is indescribable. They’re jumping around that stupid Maslow pyramid like it’s Chutes and Ladders, mistaking their needs for their wants. In 1934, Romanian philosopher Emil Cioran published “ On the Heights of Despair ,” inspired by his bouts of insomnia, depression and insanity. Cioran describes man as the “insomniac animal,” expressing that “there is not another animal in the entire creation that wants to sleep yet cannot.” He also finds offhanded, sarcastically written “blessings” of insomnia: “Insomnia kills off the multiplicity and diversity of the world, leaving you prey to your private obsessions. What strangely enchanted tunes gush forth during those sleepless nights!” That’s certainly one way to put it. I’m not sure I would agree with Cioran, as my “private obsessions” and “strangely enchanted tunes” more closely align with microsleeps , forgetfulness and hallucinations. There is some sort of mystique surrounding the archetype of the brilliant genius insomniac, similar to that of the starving artist. As if the world may never attribute their crazy habits as the source of their hidden superhuman intellect. But most people who have suffered from severe sleep problems understand the detachment of humanity that comes along with it. I’m done running around in circles trying to make sense of my nightly woes. My final thoughts might be unpopular and futile: Insomnia is pointless and downright stupid. It is a disease that has emerged as a side effect of humanity and our increased consciousness. So many questions remain. Are there truly insomniac babies, or are they just fussy? What baby — with the low intelligence and lack of consciousness that they possess — is contaminated by anxious thoughts and a restless mind? The mysteries of sleep may remain unsolved until the end of time, which may be the only thing that can provide me peace of mind.
