https://www.jns.org/news/u-s-news/ukrain.text: Yaroslav Shilkloper, who was extradited from Poland, was the first of three defendants sentenced for operating a fake brokerage scheme that targeted American investors. Yaroslav Shilkloper, a dual citizen of Ukraine and Israel, was sentenced on Tuesday to four years in prison for his role in a fake brokerage scheme that defrauded American investors of more than $3 million, according to the U.S. Department of Justice. Shilkloper, 50, was also ordered to pay a $250,000 fine and $1.43 million in restitution. Prosecutors said he and his co-conspirators lured victims with promises of high investment returns through the companies K6 Investing, Neotron Holding Ltd. and Goldex Technology, while providing access to a fraudulent online platform that appeared to display real-time investment performance. Instead of investing the funds, the conspirators laundered the money through bank accounts in Ukraine, Georgia, Hungary, Israel, the Czech Republic and other countries under their control, according to court records. Victims who attempted to withdraw their money were blocked, threatened with legal action or manipulated into sending additional funds to the scheme. "When victims attempted to withdraw their money, they were prevented from doing so, threatened with legal action, or manipulated into sending more money to the fraud ring," per court filings. Shilkloper was arrested in Poland in 2023 and extradited to the United States in September 2024. He is the first of three defendants to be sentenced in the case. Authorities previously recovered and returned nearly $2.8 million to victims as a result of forfeiture proceedings against Shilkloper and co-conspirators in the Republic of Georgia, according to the Justice Department.

https://www.elledecor.com/life-culture/t.text: Somewhere in a shoebox, a filing cabinet, or an aunt's attic, there just might be a document that could open the door to a new citizenship. It could be a grandparent's birth certificate, a great-grandmother's naturalization papers, or an old family surname traced back to Naples or Kraków. Some European countries allow citizenship by descent, or jus sanguinis, meaning nationality can pass through family lines rather than birthplaces. In many cases, that can open the door to EU citizenship rights, including the ability to live, work, and study there. Below are five countries where ancestry may make you eligible. But just a note: the rules vary widely and often depend on what documentation you have—they also may change over time.ItalyIn Italy, citizenship by descent must come through an unbroken line of descent. The applicant must trace their family line back to someone alive after March 17, 1861 (Italian unification), and no one in the chain can have naturalized elsewhere before their child’s birth.An ancestor who naturalized abroad prior to June 14, 1912 cannot pass on citizenship, and there are a few other restrictions that can apply based on the local consulate. Applications go through the Italian consulate of residence, run about 600 euros in fees, and require apostilled, translated vital records for every generation in the chain.IrelandA parent born in Ireland makes you automatically Irish. A grandparent born on the island of Ireland means you can register through the Foreign Births Register (FBR) and become a citizen. However, if the citizen was a great-grandparent, the parent of the applicant must have registered in the FBR before the applicant was born. Registering afterward, even successfully, does not extend citizenship back a generation.Great-grandchildren who missed that window can try the discretionary “Irish associations” route under Section 16 of the 1956 Citizenship Act, but the country grants this rarely, and it requires three years of Irish residency plus proof of cultural or economic ties. FBR registration costs a fee set by the Irish government and currently takes around a year, though processing times can change.PolandIn Poland, there is no fixed generational cap, but eligibility depends on proving an unbroken chain of citizenship and no disqualifying loss of citizenship. A great-great-grandchild of a post-1920 Polish citizen can qualify, as long as no one in the chain formally renounced citizenship along the way. Poland calls this process “Confirmation of Polish Citizenship” rather than an application, because the law treats the applicant as already a citizen by descent.The anchor ancestor has to have held citizenship after 1920, when the modern Polish state reformed after World War I. Someone descended from an ancestor who left partitioned Poland before 1920, when it was still split between Austria-Hungary, Prussia, and Russia, generally cannot transmit citizenship. Confirmation goes through a Polish consulate and typically takes many months or over a year.Germany Germany runs two ancestry routes. The standard jus sanguinis path, under Section 4 of the Nationality Act, requires an unbroken chain of ancestry through a German parent or grandparent who did not naturalize elsewhere before the next generation’s birth.The second path, Article 116(2) of the Basic Law, covers descendants of people stripped of German citizenship by the Nazi regime between 1933 and 1945 for political, racial, or religious reasons. It has no statute of limitations and applies retroactively, covering groups such as children of German mothers and children of unmarried German fathers who were previously excluded from citizenship transmission. Germany allows dual citizenship on both routes, and neither requires language proficiency or residency.HungaryThere is no fixed generational limit and no residency requirement for citizenship, but applicants must pass a Hungarian language interview. The simplified naturalization track requires proof that an ancestor held Hungarian citizenship, documented through birth, marriage, or church records, followed by a basic conversational assessment at a consulate.

exhibition in Bucharest, Romania, Wednesday, May 22, 2024. Associated Press File Photo BUCHAREST, Romania — Since Russia’s full invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the war has repeatedly spilled across Romania's border as drones violate the airspace of the neighboring European Union and NATO member. Now Romania is trying something new to stop the incursions: shooting down the drones. Romanian pilots shot down the first of three drones in as many days from F-16 fighter jets starting Friday as Russia intensified attacks against Ukraine near the border. After determining the drones were of Russian origin, Romania summoned Moscow’s ambassador in protest and expelled a Russian diplomat on Monday. Drones have crossed into Romanian territory multiple times from Ukraine to the north and east, including in May when a drone injured a mother and child after crashing into an apartment block in the eastern town of Galati along the Danube River. Romanian authorities largely responded by scrambling jets, collecting debris, erecting fallout shelters near the border and frequently admonishing Moscow for its war spilling into its territory. Romania and Poland also acquired the MEROPS system , which fires short counter-drones to take down incoming stray drones, following a spate of incursions along NATO’s eastern flank late last year. Drones have crossed into the territories of multiple EU countries , but have been a persistent problem for Romania's leadership in the capital Bucharest. At least 19 have entered Romania’s airspace this year, while there have been 50 cases of drones or drone fragments identified on its territory since the war started in 2022, according to Romania's Ministry of National Defense. Romanian President Nicusor Dan on Sunday congratulated the Romanian pilots for downing the drones and blamed Russia for the incursions. “It is unacceptable and intolerable for the Russian Federation to continue violating Romanian airspace,” he said. Romania shifts the approach to stray drones Despite passing legislation last year to shoot down drones in its airspace, which was strongly opposed by nationalist political parties, Romania has avoided shooting them down until now. Romanian military analyst Radu Tudor said the May drone incident in Galati may have “changed something in the Romanian authorities’ mentality” in how to approach the issue. “This was somehow a kind of psychological trigger, in order to say: ‘OK, enough is enough,’” Tudor said. “Until now, it probably was an Allied decision in NATO not to respond with firepower, because it was somehow a danger of escalation.” “I think it’s not only a change of attitude of Romania, I think it’s a change of attitude in NATO,” he added. Before the three interceptions over the past week, Romanian pilots also shot down a stray Ukrainian drone above Estonia in May. Romanian pilots and planes are based in Lithuania to provide broad strike capabilities for NATO. “They saw so many signals that Russia is trying to provoke NATO,” Tudor said. “Romania is the only NATO country who shot down four drones on the eastern flank — three on Romania and one in Estonia.” The message sent to Moscow mirrors a statement by NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte at the organization's summit in Ankara, Turkey, earlier this month: “‘Don’t play with us’.” Russian diplomat expelled In response to the drone incursions, Romania’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs summoned Russia’s ambassador in Bucharest on Monday and presented him with fragments of a drone, saying Moscow “bears exclusive responsibility for all these grave incidents.” The ministry also expelled a member of the Russian mission, who was given five days to leave the country. “The Russian side learned what they already knew: the drones downed on Romanian territory belong to them,” Foreign Minister Oana Toiu wrote in a post on X. “Drone fragments recovered by the Ministry of National Defence and the ongoing prosecutor investigation confirm their Russian origin beyond any doubt.” The Russian embassy in Romania responded in a statement posted on its Facebook page, saying Russia “has never directed and does not direct combat drones” to Romanian territory and denied the allegation as “completely unfounded.” “An unprovoked expulsion of a Russian employee will not go unanswered,” the embassy said. Tactical shift to down errant drones Cristian Popovici, the Romanian defense ministry’s head of public relations and a former air defense officer, said tactics have been developed to eliminate errant drones. “We recorded more than 100 attacks with drones near our border with Ukraine, and many of them resulted in debris or even drones that penetrated our airspace,” he told the Associated Press. “Our pilots and our air force, we developed the tactics, procedures, and now we can face and we can eliminate this threat.” The change began when Romanian pilots shot down a drone over Estonian airspace and from that point the military applied “lessons learned” and had a “100% rate success in three days with three drones,” Popovici said. Despite the new approach to stray drones, Popovici said Romania does not plan to become entangled in the war between Russia and Ukraine. “We are in a peacetime, we are not involved in this fight,” he said. “If Russia wants to escalate with NATO, it’s up to them. I’m not sure it’s a wise move now.” Romania's President Nicusor Dan arrives for the EU summit in Brussels, Thursday, June 18, 2026. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/tesco-giv.text: Taila Nichole Thompson Updated Tue, 28 July 2026 at 10:05 pm UTC 0 Tesco is giving away free groceries this week (Image: Getty) Holidaymakers returning to the UK this week may have received a free bag of groceries as part of a new giveaway from Tesco . The supermarket teamed up with easyJet holidays and London Southend Airport to hand out complimentary bags packed with everyday essentials to passengers arriving on selected flights. The giveaway comes after Tesco research found that one in four Brits say coming home to an empty fridge is one of the most frustrating parts of returning from holiday. The free bags were available in the airport's baggage reclaim hall on Tuesday, July 29, for passengers arriving on selected easyJet flights between 12pm and 5pm. Between 12pm and 5pm this week passengers can claim free bag (Image: Getty) Each bag includes a range of groceries, including tea bags, milk, bread, baked beans, cheddar cheese, strawberries, carrots, cucumber and custard creams, along with a bottle of aloe vera body lotion. Tesco's research found that a cup of tea tops the list of things holidaymakers crave when they return home, with 57% saying it's the first thing they want after a trip. Fresh milk was also high on the list, while more than a quarter said they would reach for a custard cream. The survey also found that nearly a third of people look forward to a traditional Sunday roast after returning from holiday, while 70% said they try to eat healthier once they're back home. Passengers travelling through London Southend Airport on eligible flights will be able to collect the complimentary bags from the baggage reclaim area while stocks last. As part of the campaign, Tesco and easyJet holidays are also giving away 10 £250 Tesco vouchers via Instagram, while one winner will receive an easyJet holidays getaway worth £1,500. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Nationals leader Matt Canavan and opposition leader Angus Taylor say they will support a One Nation bill to prevent Australians linked to overseas terrorist groups from returning to Australia Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP View image in fullscreen Nationals leader Matt Canavan and opposition leader Angus Taylor say they will support a One Nation bill to prevent Australians linked to overseas terrorist groups from returning to Australia Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP Australian politics Coalition to back One Nation policy barring overseas Australians with terrorist links from returning home Angus Taylor and Matt Canavan will support Pauline Hanson’s migration bill despite vowing to fight her rightwing party Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Tom McIlroy Political editor Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Coalition will back a plan by Pauline Hanson to prevent Australian citizens with links to overseas terrorist groups from returning home, significantly elevating One Nation’s policy prescriptions on matters of national security. Despite pledging to fight Hanson’s insurgent rightwing movement amid collapsing support for their own parties, the opposition leader, Angus Taylor, and Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, both signalled support for One Nation ’s bill to bar the return of foreign fighters ahead of its introduction to the Senate on Wednesday. Key members of Taylor’s frontbench, including the shadow foreign minister, Ted O’Brien, and the shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, have offered to work with Hanson on her bill. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email “We’ll work with them on that legislation, it is important we get it right,” Duniam said. “We’d love to see it go off to a Senate committee to make sure that people who know a little more than we in the Senate know, legal experts to make sure it is robust. “We want to shut the door on terrorists, we’ve been trying for years to do this.” Even with the Coalition’s support, the One Nation bill won’t be debated in the House of Representatives without Labor facilitating its progress. Such a move would be extremely unlikely, after the home affairs minister, Tony Burke, said last month that Hanson’s plan “would last about 30 seconds in the high court”. 6:27 Barnaby Joyce suggests One Nation could welcome some refugees while barring other migrants – video But the Coalition’s support is significant, not least because national security is a traditional political strength for the Liberal and National parties. Hanson’s bill would allow Australian passports to be cancelled more easily and create new penalties for anyone assisting the return of people with links to terrorist groups. It would establish a new “foreign terrorist fighter exclusion order” regime, imposed by the federal court at the request of the home affairs minister. The Albanese government used existing exclusion orders to temporarily bar one Australian woman linked to Islamic State from returning, but conceded it did not have powers to permanently block citizens from entering the country. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion Pauline Hanson echoes Trump as she lashes out about ‘fake news’ reporting on lavish London hotel Read more Burke has argued Australian citizens blocked from returning could be more dangerous overseas and outside the reach of security agencies, while also noting countries have responsibilities to other nations to deal with their own citizens. Despite promising to fight Hanson’s rise in the polls , Canavan on Tuesday said the Nationals would work with One Nation on the bill. “I’m happy to work with anyone in parliament to make our country better, in this case, safer and more secure. “We have, for a long time, sought to ensure that those people who are subscribing to and supporting violent ideologies pay a penalty in this country, potentially lose rights or are deported.” Canavan said the Coalition had wanted to make similar moves as far back as the Abbott government. “We’ve indicated, and I know Angus has indicated, to Senator Hanson that we’re happy to work with her on her bill this week.” Taylor has a separate plan to target charities and community groups working to help Australians linked to terrorist groups return home. Photograph: Simona Granati/Corbis/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People take part in a demonstration in defense of the international criminal court at Piazza Ugo La Malfa in Rome, Italy, on 16 July 2026. Photograph: Simona Granati/Corbis/Getty Images Trump administration Human rights groups sue Trump administration over ‘crippling’ ICC sanctions Lawsuit challenges executive order targeting international criminal court for investigating Israeli crimes in Palestine Alice Speri Tue 11 Aug 2026 11.10 EDT First published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 10.40 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Four prominent US human rights organizations have accused the Trump administration of using its “crippling” sanctions regime against the international criminal court (ICC) to undermine global efforts to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity. In a lawsuit filed in federal court on Tuesday, the groups – the American Friends Service Committee, the Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch and the Open Society Institute – argued that the administration’s targeting of the ICC, as well as of groups and individuals affiliated with it or assisting its work, amounts to a “blatantly illegal attack on international justice”, the groups said. The suit challenges Trump’s February 2025 executive order , which authorized sanctions on ICC officials, judges and others working to support its investigation of Israeli crimes in Palestine – one of 18 investigations into war crimes and crimes against humanity the Netherlands-based tribunal is overseeing. US groups sue Trump administration claiming ICC sanctions violate first amendment Read more The US state department and justice department did not immediately respond to requests for comment. The US government has long opposed and sought to impede the work of the court – of which it is not a party – but those attacks escalated after the ICC prosecutor issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, and former Israeli defense minister Yoav Gallant over crimes committed in Gaza. The US responded by sanctioning ICC prosecutors, judges, three leading Palestinian human rights groups and Francesca Albanese , the UN special rapporteur on the situation of human rights in Palestinian territory. Earlier this summer, the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, also escalated efforts against the ICC, announcing a campaign aimed at “ dismantling ” it by pressuring member states to leave the court. Those attacks, and Trump’s executive order, undermine access to justice for victims of major human rights violations and criminalize the work of those seeking to combat impunity by collaborating with the court – including the plaintiffs in the case – in violation of both constitutional protections for free speech and association and US obligations under international law, the lawsuit argues. “The Trump administration took the extraordinary step to not only deny Palestinians and victims of US torture equal access to justice, but to criminalize and punish them, their lawyers and advocates, and their partners,” said Katherine Gallagher, a senior attorney at the Center for Constitutional Rights who represents victims before the ICC. “All victims of international crimes – from Sudan and Ukraine to Palestine and Afghanistan – need and deserve to have an independent and strong ICC able to fulfill its mission of ending impunity, without fear or favor.” The individuals placed under US sanctions over their work for the ICC have been subjected to travel bans, have had their bank accounts closed or frozen, and access to digital services denied. Because of the dominance of US financial and technology institutions, the sanctions have trickled down and affected their ability to access services in other countries as well. But the sanctions also affected rights groups not directly targeted – including the four plaintiffs – by hindering their ability to represent victims before the court, make legal and policy submissions to it, or collaborate with the sanctioned Palestinian groups on litigation, advocacy campaigns, research and humanitarian aid efforts. “Because of the sanctions regime and the threat of severe criminal and civil penalties ... if I continued my work as a lawyer as before, I would have been or could be prosecuted or fined,” Gallagher said in a press conference held by the groups on Tuesday. “I have therefore ceased actively practicing before the ICC. [...] The government cannot dictate which clients lawyers can represent, which defendants are off limits from accountability, and what venue for justice and accountability are permissible. Shawan Jabarin, the director of the human rights group Al Haq, one of the Palestinian organizations targeted by the Trump administration over its work with the ICC, told the Guardian in an interview last year that the sanctions had left the group unable to access its bank accounts or process donations, leaving about 45 people without pay. But Jabarin also said the impact of the sanctions had extended beyond logistical matters and created a climate of fear by which longtime allies had cut communications with the group to avoid running afoul of the sanctions regime, with potential punishments of up to 20 years in prison and exorbitant fines. “Most of them – if not all – they stopped working with us or engaging with us formally and openly,” Jabarin said at the time of several US groups with which Al Haq had collaborated in the past. He had called on those partners at the time to “fight back with all means”. Tuesday’s lawsuit follows one filed last month by Democracy in the Arab World Now (Dawn), a Washington-based advocacy group focused on US foreign policy in the Middle East, and the New York-based Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide, as well as legal challenges brought by some of the sanctioned individuals themselves, including Albanese’s family and three sitting ICC judges . James Goldston, executive director of the Open Society Justice Initiative, a program of Open Society Foundations, which the Trump administration also explicitly threatened last year, called the sanctions “an assault on the rule of law, independent judges and prosecutors, and civil society in the United States and around the world”. “Independent courts can function only when judges, prosecutors and rights advocates are free to do their work without fear of political retaliation. We believe that no one is above the law,” he said in the press conference on Tuesday. “The executive order shields the perpetrators of war crimes from scrutiny while punishing those who pursue accountability. Justice must be fair and impartial, not only directed at America’s adversaries.” Explore more on these topics Trump administration International criminal court US politics Law (US) Palestine Israel Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026.text: Ministers are urgently seeking to free up spaces in overcrowded prisons across England and Wales. Photograph: Jeff Morgan/Alamy View image in fullscreen Ministers are urgently seeking to free up spaces in overcrowded prisons across England and Wales. Photograph: Jeff Morgan/Alamy Prisons and probation Burnham’s prison plans could raise risk of mistaken releases, union warns Concerns raised over proposed changes to early release scheme as probation staff vote to strike over workloads Peter Walker , Rajeev Syal and Caroline Davies Tue 11 Aug 2026 14.48 EDT First published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.24 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham’s plan to stop the early release of PC Andrew Harper’s killers and other serious offenders could increase the risk of some more dangerous prisoners being released by mistake, unions have warned. In another blow to the proposals announced by the prime minister, probation staff have voted overwhelmingly to go on strike, warning of already unrealistic workloads. How viable are plans to free up prison space in England and Wales? Read more While the vote by members of Napo was not directly connected to the early release plans, the probation officers’ union has previously criticised the proposals as rushed. The union said the 91% vote in favour of a strike would come as a blow to ministers. Burnham said earlier he recognised “the depth of public concern” about the proposed early release of Harper’s killers and announced a change to the early release scheme. The scheme is designed to free up urgently needed spaces in overcrowded prisons across England and Wales. After an uproar about the proposed release of Harper’s killers Jessie Cole and Albert Bowers, Burnham said on Tuesday morning that he had instructed the justice secretary, Alex Norris, to find more prison spaces so the pair and other serious offenders would not be freed. Writing on Facebook, Burnham said places could be provided by removing foreign offenders more quickly, finding a way to release lower-risk prisoners stuck in jail on indeterminate sentences, and “making greater use of the entire prison estate including using the female estate for male offenders”. Downing Street had said on Monday that there was no feasible way of exempting just a handful of prisoners from the scheme to block the release of Cole and Bowers, who were sentenced to 13 years for Harper’s manslaughter. Under the scheme, they were due to be freed in January. View image in fullscreen Jessie Cole (left) and Albert Bowers, two of three men sentenced over PC Andrew Harper’s death. Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA Tom Wheatley, the president of the Prison Governors’ Association, said further changes to the scheme could lead to prisoners being wrongly released. “Mistakes are more likely due to having to recalculate sentences against a very tight deadline,” he said. Wheatley said removing overseas prisoners was likely to be difficult as many would resist this and a number did not have proper documentation. He said victims would also want to be sure that anyone sent back to home countries would properly serve their sentence there. Mark Fairhurst, the national chair of the Prison Officers’ Association, said placing men in women’s prisons would require investment and retraining. “Repurposing women’s prisons to accommodate male prisoners is not something that can simply be achieved by changing the sign above the door,” he said. “There would inevitably be additional staffing, training, security and operational requirements. “The physical design and facilities of women’s prisons are not necessarily suitable for a male population, and those differences would need to be properly assessed before any decision was taken. “You cannot create safe prison places simply by finding additional buildings. You need the staff, training, infrastructure and resources to operate them safely.” The Ministry of Justice said it was disappointed by the Napo strike vote and it would continue to engage with the union. Officials in Norris’s department are understood to be working at full speed on preparing detailed and workable plans to free up spaces by September. When the early release scheme was announced, there were exemptions for prisoners convicted of rape, serious child sexual abuse and grooming offences but not manslaughter, prompting pressure to block the release of Harper’s killers, including from police and his family. Officials initially said it would be unrealistic to just block the release of Cole and Bowers and that exempting all manslaughter cases risked not creating enough prison spaces to ease the crisis. But in his Facebook post, and speaking to reporters on a later visit to Derbyshire, Burnham said he was aware of the strength of public feeling about the plans. View image in fullscreen PC Andrew Harper was killed in Berkshire in 2019. Photograph: Thames Valley police/PA “It’s my job to speak up for the public on this issue,” he said during the visit. “I take that duty very seriously indeed, and I’m confident that there’s more that can be done, and will be done to address public concern.” He said on Facebook he understood “the depth of public concern about the potential early release of those involved with the killing of PC Andrew Harper – and I share it”. He wrote: “I am increasingly confident that a more focused approach along these lines will allow us to reduce the number of people released early and, in the case of the most serious offenders like those convicted of the killing of PC Harper, prevent their early release altogether. “In advance of the justice secretary’s proposals being presented to parliament, we will seek to engage other political parties in discussions with the aim of gaining the widest possible public and political consensus on the approach being taken.” Last week, Napo warned that ministers seemingly did not “have a clue about how ill-equipped the probation service is to take on this additional work” connected to early release, such as informing victims that a perpetrator was being released. Announcing the result of the strike ballot, Ben Cockburn, the Napo national chair, said the vote was “professionals warning they cannot protect the public properly when there are not enough people to do the work”. A union statement said: “The result should come as a blow to government as it prepares to expand early release from prison and implement Sentencing Act changes, increasing the number of people managed in the community while probation is already struggling to cope.” Harper, 28, was fatally injured when he got caught in a strap attached to the back of a car and was dragged down a country road as the killers fled the scene of a quad bike theft in Sulhamstead, Berkshire, in 2019. Cole and Bowers, two of three men sentenced over the police officer’s death, are due to be released halfway through their 13-year sentences, having been convicted of manslaughter in 2020. A petition demanding an intervention has nearly 900,000 signatures. The early release changes were part of the Sentencing Act passed earlier this year that cut the minimum amount of time many offenders would have to spend in prison. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Clifford Wilby, who also filmed the MP on his mobile phone, was found guilty of using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm, or distress. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA View image in fullscreen Clifford Wilby, who also filmed the MP on his mobile phone, was found guilty of using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm, or distress. Photograph: Jonathan Brady/PA Crime ‘Abusive’ man found guilty of harassing Stella Creasy MP on tube train Clifford Wilby, 63, blocked the Walthamstow MP from leaving, filmed her and talked about her ‘failings as a member of parliament’ Nadeem Badshah Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.46 EDT First published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.28 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 63-year-old man has been found guilty of harassing the Labour MP Stella Creasy after he was “abusive and aggressive” to her on a tube train. Clifford Wilby, of east London , saw the MP for Walthamstow in July 2025 on a Victoria Line train, Westminster magistrates court heard. He blocked her from leaving the tube carriage and started talking to her about knife crime and her “failings as a member of parliament” and then filmed her on his mobile phone, the court heard. Other passengers intervened and got in between them before Creasy left the carriage. Sarah Madden, prosecuting, said the pair first met during a Zoom meeting in 2024 in Creasy’s capacity as an MP. The meeting was terminated due to Wilby’s behaviour. Creasy, giving evidence from behind a screen, said during the online meeting he “made a series of very serious allegations”, became abusive and “referred to the fact he had been diagnosed as a psychopath”. She said he started to make a complaint about a constituent and she reminded him that she could not discuss somebody else’s case. He became “abusive, aggressive” and they terminated the conversation, said Creasy. View image in fullscreen Stella Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow. Photograph: Nicola Tree Creasy said that on 15 July last year she had boarded a Victoria line train and was intending to move further down the train at the next stop, and looked up to get off the train and made eye contact with the defendant. “He said ‘are you Stella Creasy?’, at that point my memory kicked in and I made the connection because I knew his face, he then confirmed he was Clifford Wilby,” said the MP. “He stood up and blocked my ability to leave the carriage, he began talking to me about his concerns about my constituent, he was shouting although the tube train is a loud environment.” She added: “Obviously I was concerned that I was in an enclosed space with him. He was very close. “I stated very clearly this wasn’t an appropriate conversation to be having.” Creasy said at this point she was backed up against the door of the carriage and was holding her hands out as a gesture “to say stop”. She got off the train at Finsbury Park by exiting through another door further up the carriage. Tess McCarthy, defending, put to the MP that she could have got off the train as the incident continued to which Creasy replied “no”. Wilby said he had been hoping to continue the conversation about the constituent on the tube but the MP “became quite agitated” and he was “quite shocked by her reaction”, so he pressed record on his phone “for my safety”. He added: “At no point did I stand in front of her. When I first spoke to her she was actually getting off the train and she turned around to speak to me, I stood up because it was noisy.” The defendant also denied telling Creasy in 2024 he had been diagnosed as a psychopath. The deputy chief magistrate Tan Ikram found Wilby guilty of using threatening, abusive, or insulting words or behaviour to cause harassment, alarm, or distress and adjourned sentencing until 8 September for reports. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: University of Michigan students walk on campus on 3 April 2025 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Photograph: Bill Pugliano/Getty Images View image in fullscreen University of Michigan students walk on campus on 3 April 2025 in Ann Arbor, Michigan. Photograph: Bill Pugliano/Getty Images Michigan University of Michigan to switch to pass/fail grades for first-semester students School said it is pivoting away from letter-grading system to ‘curb the mental health crisis’ among college students Edward Helmore Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.12 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The University of Michigan will pivot to a pass-or-fail-style grading system, instead of letter grades, for first-semester students in an effort to “curb the mental health crisis unfolding among college-aged individuals”. The school said in a notice on Tuesday that its goal was “to help first-year students acclimate to the demands of college and allow intrinsic motivations to guide personally meaningful academic journeys” and foster “a culture of connection and collaboration – rather than competition”. Under the pilot scheme, which applies to students in the College of Literature, Science and the Arts (LSA), transcripts will show “pass or no credit”. ‘I want to be ripped to shreds’: writers flock to MFAs - but does it breed elitist literature? Read more The move comes after a mental health study across 135 US colleges and universities published last year showed lower rates of depressive and anxiety symptoms and suicidal ideation reported by students. The 2024-2025 Healthy Minds Study said symptoms of severe depression had dropped to 18% – down from 23% in 2022 – and suicidal ideation had fallen to 11%, down from 15% over the same period. Rosario Ceballo, dean of the University of Michigan, told the University Record that the decision to drop the grade system “has the potential to not only address the alarming rates of stress, depression and anxiety among our students, but to deliver on our core promise as a liberal arts and sciences college”. Timothy McKay, LSA associate dean for undergraduate education, also told the paper that the program “would provide LSA students with a smooth on-ramp as they accelerate from high school into a rigorous college education; a chance to refine their academic skills and build early momentum”. A number of universities, including the California Institute of Technology, Swarthmore College, Wellesley College and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, are also offering similar grade-covering initiatives, according to the Wall Street Journal . The changes come as universities fight to maintain standards among both students and faculty staff. In May, Harvard faculty members voted to impose a roughly 20% cap on A grades in an effort to curb decades of grade inflation that, it said, degrades the value of top-tier academic achievement at the college. The changes at Michigan come as math and science professors at the University of California in June called on regents to reinstate college-entrance exams. Students taking first-semester calculus at UC Berkeley showed “severe preparation deficits”, they said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion “Basic mathematical fluency is analogous to literacy; without it, success in university-level Stem becomes structurally unattainable for students,” they wrote in an open letter warning that academic standards were eroding. The University of California San Diego found that the percentage of students needing remedial math classes before they could take precalculus increased to 8.5% in 2025 from 0.5% in 2020. “We now observe preparation gaps so severe that instructors must reteach middle-school mathematics while simultaneously teaching the material students need for sciences, engineering, economics and other quantitatively demanding fields,” they added. Kenneth Lowande, a former University of Michigan political science professor, told the Journal he doubted that dropping the grading system for first-semester students would make later grading any more relevant. “Grades have lost their value as an indication of quality or excellence,” he said. Photograph: Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images California Famed tourist destinations evacuated as wildfire threatens California’s Big Sur Nearly 500 personnel battle Timber fire in Los Padres national forest as blaze grows to 2,000 acres Dani Anguiano and agency Tue 11 Aug 2026 12.22 EDT First published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 09.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Evacuations have been ordered for areas along California’s famous Big Sur coast as a wildfire burns in the nearby steep, rugged mountains. The Timber fire in Monterey county started on Sunday and grew to 2,000 acres by Tuesday morning, according to Cal Fire, the state’s fire agency. Nearly 500 fire personnel had been assigned to the fire in the Los Padres national forest. The evacuations have affected famed tourist destinations such as the Nepenthe restaurant, the Henry Miller Memorial Library and the Alila Ventana resort, as well as state parks during the region’s busiest season. Part of the Pacific Coast Highway was closed for non-residents, and officials urged visitors to avoid the area entirely. ‘Unprecedented, dangerous territory’: US north-west reckons with a summer of historic wildfires Read more Firefighters worked to build containment lines along the Highway 1 corridor, Cal Fire said on Monday, and have boxed in 5% of the blaze. Ground crews are working to access difficult terrain, the agency said, but the fire is moving slowly, burning primarily along the ground through grass, brush and oak woodland and has not moved into the tree tops. Officials said they are focused on protecting area homes and keeping the fire from moving across the Pacific Coast Highway. The cause of the fire, which started on Saturday evening and now threatens 259 buildings, is still under investigation. Firefighters are fighting blazes across the US west. Canada put its military on standby on Monday to help battle deadly wildfires in British Columbia, where at least one woman has died and about 20,000 people have fled their homes. Nearly half of the fires in the region are burning out of control, according to authorities. The mayor of Summerland – home to about 12,000 people, which was ordered evacuated on Saturday night along with about 8,000 people in and around nearby Peachland – warned that the affected areas remained too dangerous to enter and that it was impossible to determine the scope of the destruction. Meanwhile, a quick-moving blaze just north of Reno, Nevada, forced about 5,500 people to evacuate. Firefighters in Spokane, Washington, strengthened containment lines around three destructive blazes in that state, allowing some evacuated residents to return home. And Oregon is experiencing its worst year on record for land burned by large wildfires, with 3,671 sq miles (9,508 sq km) scorched, said Jean Nelson-Dean, spokesperson for Northwest Interagency Coordination Center. That beats the state’s previous record set in 2024. In the foothills of California’s Sierra Nevada, firefighters have contained 90% of the Gann fire, which killed one person and destroyed 48 structures. Investigators have said the blaze was sparked by a man using a chainsaw, and arrested him last week. Gilman is said to be in poor health and was reportedly being held in a psychiatric ward of a hospital.Trump added that Moscow did not ask for a prisoner swap and that Gilman was set to land at Andrews Air Force Base near Washington, D.C on Tuesday evening."I just spoke to him, and he had one request — A GREAT cheeseburger when he lands. I will take care of that!" Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social.Gilman was arrested and detained in Russia in 2022, accused of assaulting a police officer following an incident on a train in Voronezh, to the south of Moscow. He was sentenced to four and a half years in prison over the incident, but his sentence was later extended to 10 years after he was alleged to have attacked prison staff.According to US Senator Ed Markey of Massachusetts, Gilman was diagnosed with a "dissociative stupor" around 50 days ago and became "non-responsive.""He was essentially catatonic and also suffered a severe case of pneumonia," he said.In a post on X, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio thanked Russia for working with special envoy Steve Witkoff to secure Gilman's release, which he said would allow him "to receive the necessary medical treatment here in the United States."But Rubio made it clear that while Washington was grateful for the "positive step," the Trump administration would still be pushing for the "immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans.""The President will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home," he added.Gilman was one of a number of Americans detained in Russia. Others being held in the country include Stephen Hubbard, who the State Department has labelled a "wrongful detainee," and Army Staff Sergeant Gordon Black.

https://www.dw.com/en/ebola-over-2-000-d.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Iec6 A health worker waits to be sprayed with disinfectant at a treatment center in Ituri, eastern Congo Image: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement Health authorities in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) said on Tuesday that an outbreak of a particularly virulent strain of the Bundibugyo Ebola virus currently raging in the east and northeast of the country has killed more than 2,000 people since the first case was confirmed. In all, more than 4,380 infections have been recorded. The current outbreak is the 17th ever recorded in the DRC, with Sania Nishtar of the Gavi global vaccine alliance warning it could become "the largest outbreak ever." Until now, the worst outbreak recorded in the DRC was the one that took place from 2018 to 2020 when some 3,500 infections led to 2,300 deaths. The pace of death is gathering momentum this time around, with the virus spreading faster and exhibiting a higher mortality rate than the 2014-2016 West African outbreak — the worst outbreak on record, which logged 28,000 infections and more than 11,000 deaths. Congo's Ebola outbreak exceeds 4,000 cases To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The current DRC outbreak was declared on May 15, but health authorities say the first transmissions likely took place in February of earlier still. The 1,000-death mark was not reached until nine weeks in, now — in just three-weeks' time — that figure has doubled again. The case fatality rate of the current outbreak is 45.9% compared to 39.6% in the 2014-2016 West African outbreak. 'We haven't reached the peak yet,' says DRC health minister Though there are vaccines against some strains of the Ebola virus, there are currently none approved for the rare Bundibugyo strain that is spreading across the DRC faster than health authorities can trace it. Moreover, health authorities face massive logistics challenges due to the volatile security situation in the country, where bad roads and rebel violence coupled with lack of healthcare worker pay and mass strikes make it increasingly difficult to keep tabs on the illness. "We haven't reached the peak yet," said Health Minister Samuel Roger Kamba in an interview shared by the ministry on X. "Within the next three months, we expect to have already brought the spread under control and to start seeing it decline," he added. Ebola, which is transmitted through physical contact with bodily fluids, causing a hemorrhagic fever, has killed more than 15,000 people in Africa over the past half century. Authorities in the DRC have placed restrictions on public gatherings as well as closing the airport in Ituri Province, the epicenter of the outbreak. Still, fighting and disease have forced the displacement of masses of people in the DRC, Rwanda and South Sudan. On Monday, the World Health Organization's (WHO) regional director told reporters that authorities are "chasing the virus… the virus is ahead of us." WHO, DRC officials appeal to Congolese as Ebola spreads To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What's the latest on bids to treat or vaccinate this Ebola strain? Clinical trials for two antiviral treatment methods have been ongoing since early July and on Friday the WHO recommended undertaking a full-scale human trial of the Ervebo vaccine. Although Ervebo has proven effective against the Zaire strain of Ebola, its efficacy in fighting the Bundibugyo strain is unproven. WHO officials are hopeful that it can offer some protection against the DRC strain. Vaccine alliance Gavi says it has made some 500,000 doses of Ervebo in its stockpiles available for the trial. Virologists say the new Bundibugyo strain appears to have been transmitted from animals to humans and has changed from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012. Researchers from Congo, Uganda, Belgium and other countries published findings ‌in the journal Nature Medicine on Monday, suggesting the outbreak began ‌with an animal-to-human transmission event and was then spread between people. Given the severity of the outbreak, authorities are looking into the possibility that the pathogen may have mutated. Jean Kaseya, the head of the Africa CDC, last week warned that fewer and fewer new cases could be traced back to contacts of existing confirmed patients, with researchers falling well below the WHO's targets of tracking 95% of potential contacts to contain the spread. https://www.dw.com/en/ex-marine-released.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Iebz The US national and former Marine had faced various trials and charges in Russia [FILE photo: August 2, 2024] Image: Mikhail Sergeyev/TASS/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement Russia on Tuesday released Robert Gilman, a former US Marine who had spent more than four years in prison on disputed charges, according to a group advocating for him and US officials. US President Donald Trump and the State Department both said the release was on "humanitarian grounds" and that it was not part of an exchange or prisoner swap with Russia . Who is Robert Gilman? The 32-year-old former service member had been working as a teacher in Russia when he was first detained in 2022, accused of assaulting a police officer after being ejected from a train for causing a disturbance. He was later accused of other violent offenses while incarcerated and was given a longer jail sentences, ultimately reaching a total of roughly 10 years. Advocacy group Global Reach had warned of Gilman's deteriorating health condition in detention. His mother was in Russia trying to secure his release as the news developed. What did Trump and the State Department say about the release? Trump posted about the release on his Truth Social platform, also including what appeared to be a photo of a sedentary Gilman, his mother and others on a plane, holding an American flag. "After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin , Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote. "We appreciated the decision, and the fact that Russia asked for no one in return — No exchange took place." He said that Gilman and others would land at Andrews Air Force Base in Washington later on Tuesday to be welcomed back to the US. The State Department, meanwhile, issued a statement attributed to Secretary of State Marco Rubio. "We thank Russia for working with Special Envoy Steve Witkoff to release Mr. Gilman and allowing him to receive the necessary medical treatment here in the United States," Rubio said. "While we appreciate this positive step, we are still seeking the immediate return of all other unjustly detained Americans, including wrongful detainee Stephen Hubbard." The statement lauded Trump's efforts to free US-Americans from foreign detention during his second term and concluded that Trump "will not stop until all unjustly detained Americans are home." Gilman's sister credits Trump, Democrat senator with her brother's release Gilman's sister Lexie Hudson said in a statement from advocacy group Global Reach that Trump hearing about the case and taking action was the "reason that Robert is alive today." She also thanked Democrat Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey "for leading our advocacy efforts in Congress." "The Russians treated my brother so badly," Hudson said. "They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both an American and a Marine. What did they get out of this? Why did they do this to such a wonderful person?" According to Global Reach's chief strategy officer Eric Lebson, Gilman had been in a "dissociative stupor" for 47 days, attributing this to abuse he suffered in prison. He had been moved to a civilian hospital prior to his release, and would soon be medically and psychologically assessed and treated at a US military hospital, Lebson said. Gilman's mother had traveled to Russia amid the reports of her son's deteriorating health to try to see him. "It is a tragedy that it took Robert's near-death condition for his case to receive the attention that it required for his release to be negotiated," Massachusetts Senator Markey said in the statement from Global Reach. "Throughout his detention, Robert was subjected to physical torture, forced medication, and provocations by Russian authorities. There is no doubt that his treatment by Russian authorities is the reason Robert is in this precarious state today." Gilman was arrested in January 2022, a few weeks before Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine . His prosecution proceeded as relations between Putin's Russia and NATO members deteriorated markedly. https://www.dw.com/en/can-the-new-pkk-la.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IeBb Although the PKK announced its dissolution a year ago, it remains unclear whether all its fighters will lay down their arms and return to Turkey Image: Sterk tv Advertisement One year ago, the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) burned its weapons in a symbolic ceremony. The move was seen as a sign of its willingness to disband. Since then, the Kurdish side has been calling on the Turkish government to take political steps. Now, parliament has passed a bill submitted by the conservative Islamic ruling party AKP and its ultranationalist ally. Officially called the "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration," it is intended to provide the legal framework for the ongoing peace process. According to official figures, 467 out of 592 MPs voted in favor of the bill. The ruling party and its ally see this as the beginning of a new era: Under certain conditions, the bill provides for a suspension of sentences for PKK members — but only after the PKK and its affiliated groups have been confirmed to have disbanded and disarmed, so that peace, brotherhood and solidarity can prevail throughout the entire country. The pro-Kurdish DEM party also supports the bill, but it views it only as a first step that must be followed by further reforms. The pro-Kurdish DEM party also voted in favor of the PKK law. At the same time, it is calling for swift political and legal reforms Image: Adem Altan/AFP PKK law divides society and parliament Fierce opposition came from the ultranationalist opposition party IYI. Even during consultations, its delegate Ayyuce Turkes, daughter of the founder of the ultranationalist and right-wing extremist Grey Wolves, accused the government of rushing a landmark bill through parliament. She also criticized what she felt was an overly conciliatory stance toward PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan. She avoided using his name, calling him a "baby killer" instead, just as government agencies and media have done for decades. There was even a physical altercation. The debate highlights just how deep the divides are within Turkish society. While the ultranationalist IYI party rejects the process, the MHP, from which the Grey Wolves emerged, is now among its most important supporters — even though it had, previously, vehemently opposed earlier peace initiatives. Observers believe this shift in course and the progress in the peace process are also a result of the changed security situation in the region. Among other things, they mention the fall of the Assad regime in Syria , the war in Gaza and the conflict between Israel, the United States and Iran . Syria and Iran are also home to large Kurdish populations that are supported by various regional actors. According to the prevailing view, a more stable relationship with the Kurds who live within Turkey's own borders could provide Ankara with more leeway in domestic and foreign policy. The justice committee of the Turkish parliament convened to discuss the draft "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration" Image: ANKA What's in the law? The law applies to convictions for PKK membership, propaganda, financing or intentional support of the organization and its structures. For prison sentences of up to 15 years, enforcement is to be suspended for five years; for longer or life sentences, the suspension is to last ten years. Ongoing investigations are to be put on hold. According to pro-government media, up to 3,600 prisoners could benefit from this. The prerequisite is the complete disbanding of the PKK and the surrender of all its weapons and ammunition. Both of these conditions have to be verified by Turkish authorities and, subsequently, officially confirmed by the National Security Council, chaired by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan . Excluded are PKK members who were convicted prior to June 1, 2005 — the date on which the current penal code came into force — as well as those convicted of homicide and whose convictions are final. That means the regulation does not apply to PKK founder Ocalan either. In February 2025, the 77-year-old had called on the PKK to disband, declared an end to the armed struggle and spoke out in favor of a political solution. Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video PKK views law as a mere first step The PKK also calls the bill a first step; it criticizes, however, wording and content. Its key demand remained unfulfilled: As long as Ocalan cannot directly coordinate the peace process under conditions of freedom, the issue of disarmament could not be resolved either. They said penal code regulations alone did not go far enough, more comprehensive democratization reforms were needed. The message was that as long as returning fighters or exiled politicians continued to be criminalized and were unable to engage in political activities legally, hardly any of them would leave the mountains where they've been staying. PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan in February 2026. The law passed by Turkey's parliament does not provide for his release from prison Image: DEM Even legal pro-Kurdish political activity has ben restricted in Turkey for decades: parties were banned, politicians were arrested or barred from political activity. To this day, elected mayors are being removed from office, and numerous politicians and activists are in prison. Among them are two former co-chairs of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP) that mainly represented Kurds, Selahattin Demirtas and Figen Yuksekdag. Peace without democratization? Political scientist Berk Esen criticizes the law for failing to offer concrete democratic solutions to the Kurdish issue. He also noted that, parallel to the peace process involving the PKK, the government had significantly increased the pressure on the largest opposition party CHP. For about two years, the Turkish judiciary has increasingly been cracking down on leading CHP politicians. Critics view this as an attempt to weaken the government party's strongest political rival. Among the most high-profile cases is that of former mayor of Istanbul and CHP presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu . He and hundreds of other party members are in prison, on charges of fraud and corruption. The entire CHP leadership under Ozgur Ozel was removed as well. He formed a new party several weeks ago. Criticism of Erdogan's role Esen primarily criticizes Erdogan's strong influence on the peace process. Although it is to be implemented by a committee chaired by the vice president and key ministers, who are also heads of the intelligence services and the National Security Council, Esen argues that it will ultimately be Erdogan as chairman of the National Security Council who decides when and which steps in the peace process will be implemented. This assessment is also shared by Reha Ruhavioglu, director of the Kurdish Studies Center. "Erdogan will clearly set the pace," Ruhavioglu said, attributing this to the asymmetric balance of power between the Turkish state and the PKK. In addition, Erdogan had learned his lessons from the failure of the peace talks between 2013 and 2015 and would now certainly assemble more control in his own hands. At the same time, experts say, Erdogan has his sights set firmly on the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections, and would want to limit any political risks associated with the process. Ruhavioglu expects further controversy, especially if former PKK fighters return to Turkey and remain at large. The government is therefore likely to allow their return, suspended sentences and political activity only gradually, and largely in response to public reaction. This article was originally written in German. https://www.dw.com/en/hungary-s-parliame.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ie3x Andras Baka was ousted by Orban as head of the Supreme Court in 2011, but now replaces a president whose term was cut short by Orban's successor Image: Bernadett Szabo/REUTERS Advertisement Hungary 's parliament voted in Andras Baka, formerly the head of the Supreme Court, as the country's next president on Tuesday. The symbolic step is part of new Prime Minister Peter Magyar's sweeping efforts to dismantle the legacy of former premier Viktor Orban after winning April's general elections . Baka was a staunch critic of Orban who was removed from his Supreme Court role during the former PM's tenure. Now, he will replace Tamas Sulyok, a president appointed by Orban , whose term in office was shortened via constitutional amendment in order to remove him from the largely ceremonial role. What happened in Tuesday's parliamentary vote? The vote in parliament to appoint Baka was always likely to be a formality, given the massive majority that Magyar's conservative, pro-European TISZA party holds in the chamber. It went almost entirely along party lines, 140 lawmakers voted in favor and six voted against. TISZA holds 141 seats. Orban's right-wing populist Fidesz party, which has 52 lawmakers, boycotted the vote in protest — but did so knowing it would be powerless to prevent Baka's appointment. Baka took his oath of office and gave a short speech to the chamber after Tuesday's vote Image: Bernadett Szabo/REUTERS Who is Andras Baka? Baka, 73, is a jurist and politician who was briefly a member of parliament from 1990 to 1991. He spent almost 20 years as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR), before returning to Hungary in 2009 to become president of its Supreme Court. In December 2011, not long after Orban returned to power as prime minister after a stint in opposition, he was removed from his role three years before his term was set to expire and sidelined from public life in Hungary. Magyar said Baka's life served "as an example of commitment to the democratic rule of law and constitutional principles" as the central European country needs to be "guided back onto the path of the rule of law and constitutional governance." Baka, 73, spent almost 20 years at the European Court of Human Rights earlier in his career as a jurist Image: Zoltan Balogh/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Why was Baka's appointment and his predecessor's removal contentious? Baka's appointment prompted protests from Fidesz, but also some critical comments elsewhere in Hungary, with some rights watchdogs likening the removal of Tamas Sulyok to the "illiberal" practices of the Orban-era. Sulyok, appointed in 2024, was deemed an Orban ally. Magyar used his two-thirds majority in parliament — which he holds thanks to Hungary's winner-takes-all first-past-the-post electoral system, as Orban used to — to amend the constitution and bring his term to an early end. Fidesz and their nationalist KDNP allies in parliament had called this " tyrannical " and "illegitimate," while Magyar argued it was necessary to pursue the "system change" he promised amid April's landslide election victory. Magyar briefly tapped Hungarian national treasure and chess superstar Judit Polgar as a possible replacement president, but she quickly declined, saying she did not feel she had "the strength to take on the historic responsibility of uniting a divided nation," but pledging to do "everything in my power" to support a new, independent and respected president. Magyar initially floated the notion of presidential star power, until chess phenom Judit Polgar said 'thanks, but no thanks' Image: Judit Polgar Foundation What has Baka said about the process and his appointment? Baka himself had not criticized Sulyok's removal, despite the echoes of the mechanisms used to oust him in 2011. "In a country governed by the rule of law, such extraordinary measures cannot be used, but Hungary became a captured state under Orban," he told the AFP news agency last month. He said that state officials like Sulyok "were appointed not to restrain the government's power, but to ensure the political survival of the former system even after an electoral defeat." However, speaking in parliament on Tuesday, Baka seemed to strike a conciliatory tone, even for supporters of the old regime. "There is one thing we certainly cannot do: we cannot build the new Hungary on revenge," he told parliament, vowing to "encourage public and professional debate, uphold [parliament's] openness and impartiality, and consistently insist that constitution-making must never again become the exclusive project of a single political force." https://www.dw.com/en/disrupted-monsoons.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IdqT India's cities are expanding quickly, without accounting for flood protection and drainage Image: Sanchit Khanna/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance Advertisement India 's southwest monsoon usually arrives around June, bringing most of the country's annual rainfall, and begins to retreat by September. Its timing and intensity have always varied, but the broad pattern was predictable enough for farmers, cities and businesses to plan around it. Now, this natural rhythm increasingly seems like a thing of the past . More than 100 people have been killed across India since late July as heavy monsoon rains triggered floods, landslides and lightning strikes. The northeastern state of Assam has borne the brunt, with more than 120,000 people affected by flooding. Kerala, Jammu and Kashmir, Bihar and Jharkhand have also reported deaths and widespread disruption. India's capital New Delhi has also been affected by flooding Image: Sanchit Khanna/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance The problem is not necessarily that India is receiving more rain. It is the way the rain is arriving: longer dry spells are followed by short bursts of intense rainfall that can overwhelm rivers, drainage systems and hillsides. El Nino has added to this year's variability but scientists say the longer-term changes are being driven by a changing climate. Have the monsoons entered a new era? Akshay Deoras, a senior research scientist with the UK's National Centre for Atmospheric Science and the University of Reading, cautions against describing the Indian monsoon as having entered "a fundamentally different regime." "Active and break spells have always been part of the monsoon. What appears to be changing is their intensity," Deoras told DW. He pointed out a warmer atmosphere can hold more moisture, making active spells, or periods of intense rainfall, more intense. Tidal flooding in Kerala: A crisis no one saw coming To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Madhavan Nair Rajeevan, a climate scientist and former secretary in the Ministry of Earth Sciences, says the change is visible in the behaviour of the monsoon itself. Average seasonal rainfall, he said, has not shown a systematic long-term change and the monsoon remains a robust natural phenomenon. But the timing, intensity and distribution of rainfall are all noticeably different. "The characteristics of the Indian monsoon have changed fundamentally," Rajeevan told DW. "We are witnessing an increase in short-duration rainfall extremes, longer dry spells, and changes in the frequency, intensity and distribution of monsoon weather systems." He believes the rise in extreme rainfall is more than natural variability. "It represents a structural shift in the monsoon system," he said. Villages and cities both at risk India's farmers depend heavily on the timing of rainfall. Long dry spells can disrupt sowing and reduce soil moisture and intense rain can wash away fields and damage crops . India's cities are also struggling due to rapid construction, as new roads and buildings leave less land to absorb water, thus interfering with natural drainage. Moreover, after weeks of dry weather, hard, dry soil absorbs less water. When heavy rain finally arrives, more of it floods the rivers and drains instead of replenishing groundwater. India not stepping up to extreme weather hazard "The greatest risks increasingly come from short periods of very intense rainfall," Deoras told DW, warning that India's infrastructure is increasingly out of step with this changing threat. Deoras says drainage systems and flood management are still too often designed around historical seasonal rainfall averages rather than the short, high-impact events that cause the greatest disruption. He noted that forecasting has improved, but knowing that extreme rain is coming is only useful if authorities act on the warning. Closing the flood warning gap To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Warnings, he said, need to translate into "timely, impact-based decisions" such as changing school schedules, restricting travel or closing off vulnerable areas before heavy rain arrives. Ritwick Dutta, an environmental lawyer and managing trustee of the Legal Initiative for Forest and Environment, says the problem goes beyond extreme weather itself. "It is now scientifically accepted that climate change leads to erratic rainfall patterns: high rainfall over a few days followed by long dry periods during the monsoon," Dutta told DW. "These trends have been compounded by the fact that the decision-making process in India fails to consider climate change while planning construction projects." Dutta points to the western city of Pune, where a study by the state government and the Energy and Resources Institute projects a 37% increase in rainfall by 2030. Still, Dutta says this projection has not been adequately incorporated into the city's planning, including its riverfront development. "Dams, embankments and roads are all likely to suffer major damage due to climate change, and yet we proceed as though climate change is a matter to be discussed only in conferences and workshops," Dutta said. "We are, in effect, 'weaponizing the environment'," Dutta said. India-Pakistan floods and the impact of climate change To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Dutta says India's environmental clearance system does not require climate change to be systematically factored into project decisions. "The concept of 'climate proofing' does not exist here," he said. Thousands killed in last year's monsoon The Centre for Science and Environment (CSE) found that extreme weather affected India on 331 of 334 monitored days in 2025, or 99% of the period assessed. More than 4,000 people died, about 3,000 during the monsoon, while at least 30 states and union territories experienced extreme weather simultaneously for eight consecutive months. Sunita Narain, director general of the CSE, argues that adaptation therefore needs to become part of the country's development strategy. "Climate change is no longer a future threat. It is already here in the form of extreme heat, extreme rainfall and increasingly destructive weather events," Narain told DW. "The challenge is no longer proving the science, but redesigning our economy and infrastructure to survive it," she added. "Cities, roads, drainage systems and water infrastructure can no longer be designed for yesterday's climate." Every investment, she says, must be planned for a future of more intense and unpredictable weather. In her reckoning, India must stop treating each flood as an isolated disaster and start planning for a climate in which such extremes are no longer exceptional. What can be done against extreme weather? India is facing a whole new pattern of extreme weather. It can record a rainfall deficit nationally while individual regions are underwater. Farmers can go weeks without useful rain and then lose crops in a few hours. Cities can prepare for an average monsoon and still be overwhelmed by one extraordinary downpour. "The focus now needs to move beyond documenting and discussing these changes towards developing and implementing effective, sector-specific adaptation strategies," climate scientist and former Indian official Rajeevan said. That means better flood management in cities, changes in agricultural practices, stronger water-storage systems and infrastructure designed around short-duration extreme rainfall rather than historical averages. India cannot control the monsoon or El Nino and it cannot stop global warming on its own. It can decide, however, where it builds, how it builds and if its new infrastructure is designed for the climate of its future. https://www.politico.eu/article/swarming.text: Aug. 11 is quickly becoming jellyfish invasion day at the Gravelines nuclear power plant in northern France. Despite spending hundreds of thousands of euros to protect the plant from a jellyfish swarm like the one that saw reactors shuttered on Aug. 11, 2025 , French utility provider EDF on Tuesday was again forced to bring the parts of the facility offline due to the presence of “several dozen tons” of jellyfish blocking pumping systems. “On-site teams are fully mobilized to ensure the safety of the facilities and to reconnect the reactors to the national power grid,” EDF said in a statement. Advertisement Advertisement Three fishing vessels are now “constantly patrolling off the coast of the plant" to conduct "preventive fishing operations [...] 24/7,” the company added. Tuesday’s jellyfish invasion comes a the latest in a series of climate change-driven incidents that have affected French nuclear energy during a particularly infernal summer . Nuclear power plants are typically built by rivers or on coastlines so they can use nearby water sources to cool their reactors. But a record number in France this summer have been forced to temporarily shut down due to heatwaves and droughts affecting their water supply. Rising sea temperatures have made jellyfish swarms more common along the French coast in recent years, and those swarms can affect a plant’s ability to bring in seawater — which is what happened at Gravelines. Following last year’s incident at the plant along the North Sea, EDF installed cameras and deployed fishing boats to monitor the situation. While the vessels “prevented a massive influx of jellyfish” on Saturday and Sunday, they were eventually overwhelmed as the swarm grew from “about 100 kilograms” to “several dozen tons,” the French state-owned utility giant said. Opponents of nuclear energy were quick to jump on the incident. “This only highlights that nuclear power plants are ill-equipped to deal with the consequences of climate change,” the French branch of Greenpeace said in statement. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgj.text: Image source, Reuters By Brandon Drenon and Kennedy Gotham Published 11 August 2026, 16:35 BST Updated 1 hour ago President Donald Trump said a US Marine held in a Russian prison, whose health was reportedly in extremely poor condition, has been released. "After my discussions with President Vladimir Putin, Russia has agreed to release him, very much on a Humanitarian Basis," Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that no prisoner swap took place. In 2022, Gilman, who is from Massachusetts, was arrested for allegedly kicking a police officer while aboard a train. He had recently been moved from prison to a civilian hospital in Russia after going into a catatonic-like state. Trump said the 32-year-old was on a flight back to the US accompanied by his mother, doctors, and members of the administration. According to a statement from his family, Gilman is expected to later arrive at a US military hospital in Texas where he will be assessed and treated. His health was in "life-threatening condition" after he was subjected to "harsh and abusive treatment", the family said. "The Russians treated my brother so badly. They hurt him for no reason, other than that he was both and American and a Marine," his sister, Lexi Hudson, said in the statement. "I am so grateful to President Trump for saving my brother's life," she added. Massachusetts Senator Ed Markey also helped secure her brother's release, she said. In a statement, Markey said: "Approximately 50 days ago, Robert was diagnosed with a dissociative stupor - a condition where he is non-responsive and unable to interact or eat. " In Russian confinement, Gilman was subject to repeated harassment, including forced exercise training sessions that lasted up to 16 hours and the administration of psychotropic drugs, Eric Lebson, who advocated for Gilman's release as part of the group Global Reach, told CBS News, the BBC's media partner. The abuse was so severe that at one point Gilman had required a feeding tube in his nose, according to Lebson. Gilman served in the US Marines from August 2019 to August 2020. He was arrested for allegedly kicking a police officer while drunk aboard a train to Moscow in January 2022 and was initially given a sentence of three and a half years. He was later found guilty of assaulting prison guards, after he allegedly attacked a prison inspector during a cell check. His sentence was then increased to 10 years. Lebson said five other Americans remain in Russia, each contending with medical issues. Their names are Aleksandr Antonov, David Barnes, Olga Jezler, Andre Khachatoorian, and Chuck Zimmerman.
