https://telex.hu/english/2026/08/11/andr.text: Menü Kereső Hungarian Parliament elects András Baka, former head of supreme court as president English Photo: János Bődey / Telex Madzin Emília Horváth Kávai Andrea Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom András Baka was elected as President of Hungary on Tuesday afternoon. Of the 146 representatives who voted, 140 voted in favor and 6 against Baka’s appointment. There were no abstentions. The former head of the Supreme Court was nominated for the post by the Tisza Party last Saturday. Electing a new president became necessary after the term of the previous, Fidesz-appointed president, Tamás Sulyok was ended prematurely by the adoption of 17th amendment to the Fundamental Law in mid-July. The move was part of the Tisza Party’s campaign promise to remove all “puppets appointed by Fidesz to do their bidding”. In Hungary, the president’s role is largely ceremonial. The president represents the country internationally, signs and promulgates the laws that have been passed (and has the authority to return them to Parliament for reconsideration or refer them to the Constitutional Court if he or she considers them to be contrary to the Fundamental Law), and may grant pardons, among others. The newly elected head of state, András Baka is best known to the Hungarian public for being unlawfully removed from his position as head of the Supreme Court after criticizing the Orbán regime’s plans for reforming the judiciary. Throughout his legal career he specialized in human rights and minority rights and spent more than twenty years as a research fellow at the Institute of Political and Legal Sciences of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences (MTA). He was a visiting professor at several universities in the United States, France and Germany, and spent two terms serving as a judge at the European Court of Human Rights between 1991 and 2008. Fidesz representatives did not participate in the vote because the party considers Tamás Sulyok’s removal illegitimate. The party's group leader János Bóka previously stated that by removing Sulyok from office, the Tisza government had launched an attack against the office of the presidential institution. In his view, this will make things difficult for András Baka, who will become an illegitimately elected president—a sort of “glitch in the matrix.” Instead of participating in the vote, the former governing party's MPs travelled to Tata, where they laid a wreath at the memorial erected in memory of the 1956 Revolution and War of Independence. According to the law, the new president will take office on the 8th day following his or her election, that is, on August 19. Until that happens, Ágnes Forsthoffer will continue to perform the duties of the president before returning to her post as House Speaker. Photo: János Bődey / Telex An election result alone does not restore the rule of law In his first speech as president, András Baka said that he considers it a great honor to have been asked to be president at this time and added that he accepted the nomination because, in his view, we are in a period when we must seriously reconsider how the country functions. The recent change has shown that a society is capable of reclaiming its self-determination. The question now is what we will do with it in the future, because an election result alone does not restore the rule of law. “We must uncover legal violations and monitor the use of public funds, but we cannot build the new Hungary on a foundation of revenge,” he continued. Under the previous system, the government had taken the country hostage, and by the end of those 16 years, it had resorted to governing by decree, while the separation of powers and checks and balances had ceased to exist. András Baka said that he considers it to be part of the tasks of the President of the Republic to serve as a guardian against this happening again. According to Baka, among other things, Hungary now needs independent courts, free elections, an effective constitutional court, a free public sphere, accountable governance, and a democratic, functioning constitutional culture where criticism is not treason, limits on power are not obstacles, political opponents are not enemies, and compromise is not a sign of weakness. He stressed that we are all responsible to ensure that what we've seen take place a Hungary over the past 16 years never ever happens again, he said. https://bnn-news.com/latvia-plans-mandat.text: Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Baltics Social Politics Money Interviews Opinions In Focus World Leisure Advertising Home Baltics Latvia Latvia Social Latvia plans mandatory morning alcohol tests for some police officers after fatal Priekule incident LETA July 29, 2026 Facebook Twitter Photo: Edijs Pālens/LETA Latvia plans to introduce mandatory morning alcohol tests for certain police officers nationwide following the fatal incident in Priekule, where an off-duty officer allegedly beat a man to death while intoxicated, Interior Minister Jānis Dombrava has announced. Speaking on Latvian Radio on Wednesday, Dombrava said the new measure is intended to prevent similar incidents in the future. The minister explained that, following the tragedy in Priekule, the leadership of the South Kurzeme Police Station was ordered to explain what measures were in place to prevent alcohol abuse among officers. Based on those responses, Dombrava concluded that routine alcohol testing had not been standard practice. As a result, the government plans to introduce stricter requirements, including mandatory alcohol breath tests every morning for police officers who routinely carry firearms and drive official police vehicles. Dombrava said the internal service investigation launched at the South Kurzeme Police Station could ultimately result in changes to its leadership. He added that there have been no major developments in the criminal investigation itself. The suspect remains in custody, while the Internal Security Bureau (IDB) has taken over the pre-trial investigation. The minister stressed that, regardless of the fatal outcome, it is unacceptable for a police officer to be in a public place with a blood alcohol level exceeding two per mille under any circumstances. Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs also described the incident as unacceptable but said he does not believe it points to widespread systemic problems or a culture of excessive drinking within the police force. The incident occurred during a town festival in Priekule over the weekend, when a fight broke out involving several people. One man sustained serious injuries and later died in an ambulance despite efforts by emergency medical personnel to save him. On Monday, the Kurzeme District Court ordered the suspect to remain in custody pending the investigation. The Internal Security Bureau took over the criminal proceedings from the State Police in accordance with its jurisdiction. The case is being investigated under Section 125(3) of Latvia’s Criminal Law, which covers the intentional infliction of grievous bodily harm resulting in death through negligence. According to information obtained by the LETA news agency, the detained officer is Andis Silnieks, a junior police inspector whose duties included emergency response operations. The victim was a teacher at the Liepāja Music, Art and Design Secondary School and head of its Fashion Design programme. The officer had served in the State Police since September 2022 and had no prior disciplinary record. According to State Police Chief Armands Ruks, the suspect told investigators that he does not remember what happened. https://cbn.co.za/industry-news/expos-ev.text: Demand for EVs continues its growth across Europe and South Africa with Chinese brands increasing market share, new OLX data shows Every electric vehicle market tracked by OLX Group ("OLX") is still growing at double- or triple-digit rates, and Chinese automotive brands are capturing a growing share of that demand, according to new data published recently. OLX, a global online classifieds leader with nearly 60 million daily listings across seven markets, has today published The Great Acceleration: East Meets Electric, which examines consumer demand for electric vehicles across five OLX automotive marketplaces: La Centrale (France), Autovit (Romania), Standvirtual (Portugal), Otomoto (Poland), and AutoTrader (South Africa). The data shows EV adoption maturing into a structural trend rather than a short-term reaction: every market measured has now sustained double- or triple-digit year-on-year EV lead growth, even as these growth rates ease from previously seen highs. Chinese automotive brands remain central to that story, with MG and BYD now among the leading Chinese brands in four of the five markets, as manufacturers continue to expand the availability of EVs at accessible price points. Key findings Every tracked market posted double- or triple-digit year-on-year EV lead growth in June 2026: France up +206%, South Africa up +154.6%, Romania up +66.0%, Portugal up +60.0%, and Poland up +34.3%. Portugal remains Europe's most EV-mature market, with EVs accounting for 14.9% of leads, almost double the next closest market. France remains the fastest-growing EV market in the group and the one where EV prices are still climbing (+25% year-on-year). MG and BYD are now the most consistently dominant Chinese brands across the group, appearing among the leading brands in France, Romania, Portugal and Poland. Christian Gisy, CEO of OLX, said: "The story our data tells is straightforward: where EV adoption is accelerating, demand for Chinese automotive brands is accelerating with it. That is no coincidence — Chinese manufacturers are actively expanding the market, bringing electric vehicles to consumers at lower price points than ever before. This means EVs are now more accessible for more people. The transition to electric mobility is happening faster, and more broadly, because Chinese manufacturers are in it." EV demand remains strong Consumer interest in EVs remains high across all five markets, with every market recording double- or triple-digit year-on-year growth in EV leads. France leads at +206%, followed by South Africa at +154.6%, Romania at +66%, Portugal at +60%, and Poland at +34.3%. Portugal remains the most mature EV market, with electric vehicles accounting for close to one in seven leads on the platform (14.9%). The report finds that demand, which surged in the months following the outbreak of the conflict in Iran in February 2026 as fuel costs and energy security became more prominent considerations for consumers, has since settled into a steadier, sustained pattern consistent with structural adoption rather than a short-term reaction. Chinese automotive brands are helping unlock EV growth As EV demand matures, Chinese automotive brands are moving from early experimentation to a phase where a smaller number of manufacturers are converting early interest into durable market share. MG and BYD now feature among the leading Chinese brands in four of the five markets tracked. France recorded the strongest increase in consumer demand for Chinese automotive brands, rising +276% year-on-year — more than double the next-fastest market, Romania (+119%). Portugal (+74%) and Poland (+95%) also recorded strong increases as Chinese manufacturers continued to expand their presence. Chinese manufacturers continue to adapt to local market conditions. In Romania, where EV prices declined nearly 8% year-on-year, the increased availability of Chinese-made vehicles continues to expand access to more affordable electric vehicles. This differs from France, where consumer interest in Chinese automotive brands keeps growing despite a +25% increase in EV prices, reflecting sustained demand in a supply-constrained market. Chinese manufacturers adapt to local market dynamics While EV demand is strong across all five OLX markets, the report shows Chinese manufacturers continuing to adapt their vehicle offering, pricing and market positioning to reflect each market's stage of EV adoption. Portugal, Europe's most mature EV market, continues to show Chinese brands competing on technology and model choice as much as price, with Xpeng now among the leading brands alongside MG and BYD. Poland remains the group's most diversified Chinese brand market by brand count, with MG, BYD and Omoda leading. South Africa represents a different stage of market development. Chinese brands account for the highest share of demand in the group (7.31%), led by Haval, but that demand is concentrated on petrol and hybrid SUVs rather than EVs – just 0.3% of Chinese brand demand there is electric. This reflects the influence of local infrastructure, driving conditions and consumer preferences, with Chinese manufacturers adapting their approach to each market rather than pursuing a single strategy across all five. “The +154.6% increase in EV leads shows that interest in electric mobility is growing rapidly in South Africa, even from a relatively small base,” commented George Mienie, CEO of AutoTrader South Africa. “Chinese manufacturers are helping drive this shift by offering vehicles that respond well to local priorities around affordability, technology, and practicality.” Methodology All figures are drawn from leads-based consumer activity across OLX Group's five automotive marketplace platforms. La Centrale (France), Autovit (Romania), Standvirtual (Portugal), Otomoto (Poland) and AutoTrader (South Africa). "Leads" refers to meaningful user engagement: views, enquiries, and contact events. Data is as at 30 June 2026. Full methodology is available in the report.

https://www.planetf1.com/news/fernando-a.text: Fernando Alonso has responded to Aston Martin's new performance level. Fernando Alonso has warned that, despite progress at Aston Martin , there is still “a long way to go” before the team and Honda can count themselves as contenders. An extensive upgrade was brought to Aston Martin’s chassis for the Hungarian Grand Prix, and Wednesday is set to see the debut of an updated power unit from Honda, as the AMR26 takes in a filming day. Fernando Alonso: Aston Martin has ‘long way to go’ despite progress Want more PlanetF1.com coverage? Add us as a preferred source on Google to your favourites list for news you can trust . Aston Martin fell behind Cadillac to the back of the F1 pack in recent races, with the team having opted to introduce its first significant round of upgrades in Hungary rather than smaller, incremental improvements, in the hope of a larger step in performance. Alonso got through to Q2 for the first time in 2026 as a result of its early progress, with Honda’s updated engine set to debut at the Dutch Grand Prix after the summer break. While Aston Martin had hoped to hit the ground running in 2026, its improvements at the Hungaroring saw the team seemingly leapfrog Williams, Cadillac, and Haas in the race pecking order. However, there are still further hurdles from here. “We are one team. We work together. We know our weakness and we try to help each other,” Alonso told PlanetF1.com and others in Hungary. “I think Honda was trying to help some of the weaknesses of the car at the beginning of the year. Now with the chassis, we try to help Honda as much as we can, and with also the consistency on laps, on deployment. “I think a lot of help from Aston Martin as well on that regard, on that software department. “It’s a long way to go. We understand that, we are aware of that, but this hopefully is the first step, and both factories are gaining confidence and trust in what they do, so that that probably will be more important than anything else for the next few months.” More about Aston Martin and its new updates All eyes on Aston Martin and Newey as FIA reveals 16-part AMR26 upgrade Honda confirms engine upgrade debut in new Aston Martin boost With a massive 16-part upgrade having gone onto the car, the AMR26 looked distinctly different in Hungary as the Adrian Newey-led design team made significant changes. Newey said there will be more parts to come in future races, and with so much having changed on the car, Alonso hopes to make further inroads into how to make the best of the new package. “I think as expected, more or less the correlation is good and the performance gains are there, what we expected,” Alonso explained. “I think it’s obviously early days with this new car. It’s a completely new car, new concept, so more to come, maybe on setup, optimisation, and things like that. “Next races also with the engine upgrade, it will be an interesting check in Zandvoort [of] where we are and what we can fight for.” Additional reporting by Thomas Maher Want to be the first to know exclusive information from the F1 paddock? https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/migrants-.text: Jon King Updated Wed, 29 July 2026 at 7:31 am UTC 0 Lithuania's border chief accuses Belarus of allowing migrants to dig tunnels into his country (Image: Getty) Migrants are attempting to enter an EU country via tunnels allegedly built with help from an ally of Russia . The chief of Lithuania 's State Border Guard Service (VSAT), Rustamas Liubajevas, told broadcaster 15min that his staff had found scores of places where underground routes were being dug between his country and Belarus . It comes after VSAT reported discovering a tunnel leading from Belarus into southern Lithuania. He said of the attempts: "Without logistical support from the Belarusian border guards, this would not be possible." Belarus has long weaponised migration, with the country's authoritarian ruler, Alexander Lukashenko, encouraging migrants to use his country to cross into the European Union via the Belarusian border with Latvia, Lithuania and Poland. Mr Liubajevas claimed the Belarusian authorities were either turning a blind eye to or actively helping migrants to dig the tunnels. He added that migrant smuggling attempts through tunnels have increased this year. The chief said similar methods were used on the border between Belarus and Poland. While Belarus and Russia are close allies, Lukashenko has so far kept his country out of Putin's war with Ukraine. Lukashenko allowed Russia to use the country he has ruled since 1994 as a base from which to launch its full-scale invasion in February 2022. But Minsk has been reluctant to get drawn into the war unless Belarus is attacked. The Belarusian leader is reported to have told Russian envoys last weekend that there was "no need" for Belarus to be "drawn into the war". As reported by The Japan Times , he said: "We also don't want to fight Ukrainians. That's why our position is peaceful." Mr Liubajevas's allegation of Belarusian collusion in irregular migration into the EU might suggest Lukashenko wants to continue efforts to add to the migrant crisis affecting the bloc. https://christianhistoryinstitute.org/da.text: Today: Aug 12 It Happened Today Devotional Quote of the day It Happened on JULY 29 King Olaf of Norway Used Cruelty to Force Baptisms (ABOVE: St. Olaf, 15th-c wooden figure originally in Fjeld Church, Sønhordland—Thomas B. Willson, History of the Church and State in Norway, from the Tenth to the Sixteenth Century . Westminster: Archibald Constable & Co., 1903. Public domain) KING OLAF II of Norway fell in battle on this day, 29 July 1030. In his dying moments, he is said to have cried, “God help me!” As a young man, Olaf Haraldsson fought as a Viking against Estonia, visited Denmark (which then ruled Norway), and at first fought against, then later served with, the army of King Ethelred II of England against the Danes. When Ethelred was defeated and fled to Normandy, Olaf went with him. While passing through Normandy, Olaf was baptized at Rouen under the sponsorship of the Norman king Richard II. But despite this, his battles show a man consumed with political ambition, and his writings reveal a man more interested in sexual exploits than holiness. When Olaf returned to Norway in 1015, he obtained the support of some northern earls and defeated Earl Svein, the effectual ruler of the country. Olaf brought all of Norway under his control. Still a young man in his early twenties, he attempted to extend Christianity to the inner parts of the country where it was weakest, most likely for reasons of political unity. He summoned a church synod to Moster, where his people accepted a code covering the building and maintenance of churches, establishments of the rights and duties of church officials, observance of holy days, instruction on baptism, restriction on the exposure of infants (placing weak infants outside to be killed by the elements), conditions for burial, and rules for marriage. The code also abolished the sacrifice of slaves to demons, requiring that anyone wishing to offer such a sacrifice free the slave instead. But despite some of the humane provisions of this code, Olaf still used deadly force and dreadful mutilations to compel baptism of the heathen and obtain “conversions.” This outraged his subjects. When King Canute and the Danes invaded Norway, several earls deserted Olaf, who fled to Kiev. Canute established a puppet king in Norway, but the man died in 1030, and Olaf saw an opportunity to regain his throne. He returned to Norway, showing more mercy than in the past. All the same, most Norwegians sided with the Danes. When the armies met at Stiklestad, Olaf chose as his battle cry, “On, on, Christ’s men! Cross men! King’s men!” Outnumbered, he died there. His mortal wound was delivered in revenge by a man whose ship he had captured. However, although his foes were largely of the old heathen party, they granted Olaf and his men Christian burials. Although he had offered no evidence of holiness while he lived, the people of Norway credited Olaf with miracles after his death. When Canute failed to keep his promises and raised taxes, the memory of Olaf began to look better to those who had revolted against him. His friend Bishop Grimkell declared him a martyr saint. In the following century, Pope Alexander III confirmed the declaration. Rulers of Norway, faced with the need to unite the country, found in Olaf’s memory an icon of national pride. They made him the nation’s patron saint, which proved to have a strong unifying effect. What Olaf had hoped to achieve in life was achieved through his name after his death. — Dan Graves For more on Christianity among the Vilings, consult Christian History #63, A severe salvation Don't miss an issue, subscribe now . https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/ente.text: Actor Suneil Anand, fondly launched into the Hindi film world by his father Dev Anand in âAnand aur Anandâ (1984), passed away following a heart attack in London. He was 70.âWe are comforted by the outpouring of love, prayers, and support, for which we are truly grateful. We kindly request privacy as we navigate this difficult time together,â his niece, Gina Narang, said in a statement on Tuesday.Incidentally, Dev Anand also died in the same city in 2011.âSuneil didnât seem ambitious. But he was extremely sincere towards his work. He was also very respectful towards senior actors,â recalled Raj Babbar, who worked with him in the film.âMy sincere condolences to his mother,â he added. Suneil's mother, Kalpana Kartik, a film star in the 1950s, is 94.The 1980s saw a bunch of star sons being launched in style such as Kumar Gaurav, Sunny Deol and Sanjay Dutt. Suneil also made a carefully-crafted debut with much fanfare. He had learnt kung-fu in Hong Kong and displayed a felicity with dance moves as well as action scenes in âAnand aur Anandâ.The filmâs bouncy tracks, composed by R D Burman, proved to be popular. âMr Ratan Tata who headed CBS Records at the time took keen interest in its (music) launch,â Suneil told this reporter in an email interview in 2020. But the film didnât work.Suneil also played the lead in the smartly lensed âCar Thiefâ (1986), opposite Vijeta Pandit. He also starred in âMain Tere Liyeâ (1988), directed by uncle Vijay Anand. A martial arts aficionado, he directed, âMasterâ (2001), where the fights were choreographed by Hong Kong masters. None of these films succeeded at the box-office. Suneil had been working on a movie, Vagator Mixer for some years.In his autobiography, âRomancing With Lifeâ, Dev Anand provides a vivid account of how he was over the moon on hearing the news of his sonâs birth. He was shooting for âPaying Guestâ for director Subodh Mukerji and enacting a drunken scene when the news arrived from a nursing home in Zurich. âI was in such high spirits that I gave a brilliant shot, probably my best in the film,â writes the star of superhits films such as CID, Johny Mera Naam and many more.Shortly, Dev Anand and his wife Kalpana were invited to the Karlovy Vary film festival in (then) Czechoslovakia. The actor writes that an 86-year-old delegate and Suneil, then just two weeks old, were photographed together by the local press. The front page of a local newspaper carried the photo with the caption, âThe oldest and the youngest delegates.âIn one of the chapters in the autobiography, Dev emotionally talks about flying out to Washington to meet Suneil who was studying there in a university. The Evergreen star writes how they embraced with moist eyes, how Suneil showed him around the campus, offered him a guided car tour of the US capital and helped him buy sunglasses. âThese were great fatherly moments for me after the brutally harsh working schedule I had thrown myself into all these years, that kept me away from my family,â he says.With Suneil's passing another chapter from the famed film family comes to a close.Give your child the gift of confidence! The incident occurred near the village of Salcia in Romania’s Mehedinți County, close to the border with Bulgaria. There are 186 passengers and 52 crew members on board. The vessel departed Monday evening from the Romanian city of Drobeta-Turnu Severin and was heading to Vidin, Bulgaria, but became stuck on a sandbar and was unable to continue its journey. According to authorities, the water level in the Danube remains extremely low: the river’s flow is about 1,600 cubic meters per second, which significantly complicates navigation. Attempts to refloat the ship made on Monday evening and Tuesday morning were unsuccessful. Representatives of the river administration acknowledged that the chances of freeing the vessel quickly are slim. Later, Bulgaria’s border police began evacuating the passengers. As the country’s Interior Ministry reported, the cruise ship was also running low on drinking water ahead of a scheduled stop at the port of Vidin to replenish supplies. Another boat was brought in to transport the people, but it was unable to get close enough to the stranded vessel. As a result, passengers wearing life jackets were transferred on border police patrol boats. There have been no reports of injuries. "The intelligence ombudspersons consider that there are currently no newly emerged significant factual circumstances that would provide grounds for initiating an investigation," Justas Gaidys, senior adviser at the office, said in a comment to BNS. Gaudys said the decision not to investigate was based primarily on the fact that the parliamentary Committee on National Security and Defence (NSGK) had already carried out an inquiry into the alleged prison more than a decade ago on the instruction of the Seimas. He also noted that the Prosecutor General's Office is continuing a reopened pre-trial investigation and that the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has already delivered three judgments concerning the detention of individuals at alleged CIA facilities in Lithuania. "Recognising that this issue remains significant to the public, the Ombudsperson plans to initiate an inter-agency dialogue with the competent Lithuanian authorities," Gaidys said. "The aim of this dialogue will be to assess the possibilities of obtaining new information, determine whether any additional action falls within the ombudspersons' remit, and build a comprehensive understanding of the situation," he added. Debate over the alleged CIA prison resurfaced after Lithuania lost its third case before the ECHR in July. The Strasbourg court awarded 30,000 euros to Saudi Arabian national Abd Al Rahim Hussein Al-Nashiri over his unlawful detention at a secret CIA prison in Lithuania. The court also ordered the Lithuanian authorities to seek assurances from Washington that the terrorism suspect would not face the death penalty. Allegations that the CIA operated a secret detention facility in Lithuania first emerged in 2009, when US broadcaster ABC News reported that eight terrorism suspects had been held near Vilnius between 2004 and 2005. Later that year, the Seimas Committee on National Security and Defence (NSGK) concluded that it could not establish whether detainees had been transferred to Lithuania, but found that the conditions for such transfers had existed. Earlier this year, the Prosecutor General's Office confirmed that it is continuing its investigation into the alleged unlawful transportation of people across Lithuania's state border. Any further probe should be handled by an inter-agency commission, she added. "An inter-agency commission should investigate, if we were to form one. [...] We need to decide who actually has the competence to investigate and present arguments in a way that leaves no doubt in the future," TamaÅ¡unienÄ told reporters on Wednesday. https://hungarytoday.hu/danube-falls-to-.text: Danube Falls to Record Low in Budapest The Danube’s water level near Budapest is at a record low: on Tuesday morning, the water gauge read 31 centimeters, the General Directorate of Water Management (OVF)’s reported. Based on the data, the lowest water level recorded on the river was 33 centimeters. People gather at the southern tip of Margaret Island near the central pier of Margaret Bridge in Budapest on July 28, 2026, as the Danube reaches a record-low water level of 31 centimeters. Photo: MTI/Zoltán Balogh The Central Danube Valley Water Directorate posted on its Facebook page this morning that critically low water levels have developed across many of Europe’s rivers, and on some rivers, navigation and freight transport are no longer possible. They added: At 3 a.m. on Tuesday, the water gauge at Vigadó Square in Budapest read 32 centimeters, breaking the record for the lowest water level ever measured in Budapest. Until now, the record had been the 33-centimeter low measured on October 25, 2018. However, the water level continued to drop, reaching just 31 centimeters by 8 a.m. The wreck of a World War II-era ship lies exposed on the Danube floodplain near Vámosszabadi on July 28, 2026, as record-low water levels reveal parts of the riverbed normally submerged. Photo: MTI/Csaba Krizsán Reports also noted that the lowest recorded water levels were broken at several of the authority’s Danube gauges: at 8 a.m., the water level fell 2 centimeters below the previous record at Vác, 10 centimeters lower at the Kvassay Lock in Budapest, 4 centimeters lower at the Tassi Lock in Tass, and 5 centimeters lower at Dunaújváros. At Nagymaros, the water level is still 2 centimeters higher than the previous low, and at Ercsi, it is 4 centimeters higher, but these record lows are also expected to be broken. On the Ipoly River, the water level is not yet close to the lowest level recorded to date. The water level on the Zagyva is significantly influenced by the volume of water released from the reservoirs; for now, the water level is above the lowest level ever recorded everywhere, but the water reserves stored in the reservoirs are running dangerously low. Anglers fish on the Danube floodplain near Vámosszabadi on July 28, 2026, as the river reaches a record-low water level. Photo: MTI/Csaba Krizsán On July 16, they had already reported that the Mátraverebély Reservoir had run dry, and by Tuesday morning, the Tarján Creek Reservoir contained only 85,000 cubic meters of water, meaning releases from the reservoir will soon have to stop. The primary task for the Maconkai Reservoir remains ensuring drinking water for 15,000 people, thus the water supply from this reservoir will not be used for other purposes. Forecasts show little or no significant rainfall in the coming weeks; instead, another warming trend is expected, which will increase evaporation. The authorities continue to use the tools at their disposal to mitigate the harmful effects of the water shortage, but without precipitation, available water supplies are steadily declining. Meanwhile, the 58th Blue Ribbon sailing race, which begins on Thursday, is expected to take place in light winds and extreme heat, with slower race conditions anticipated. Peak temperatures of 36–38 degrees Celsius and water temperatures of 25–27 degrees are forecast for the Lake Balaton region. Fact Based on HungaroMet’s forecast, the Chief Medical Officer has issued a Level 3 heat alert for the entire country, effective from midnight on Thursday until midnight next Tuesday. Authorities warn that the prolonged heat wave poses a serious health risk, particularly to the elderly, children, pregnant women, and people with chronic illnesses. The public is urged to stay hydrated, avoid the heat during the midday hours, and refrain from lighting outdoor fires, and authorities emphasize that it is prohibited to leave children or pets in parked cars. Related article Another Heatwave Set to Scorch the Country, with Temperatures Near 40°C Only a month after breaking its all-time heat record, Hungary faces another spell of scorching weather. https://thediplomat.com/2026/07/why-did-.text: China has imposed sanctions on two Polish entities linked to the country’s defense and high-tech sectors. The move comes in response to the European Union’s 21st sanctions package against Russia. The latest EU measures targeted several companies from China and Hong Kong that are accused of supplying Moscow with technologies and components used in Russia’s war against Ukraine. One of the Polish entities placed on China’s export control list is Wrocław University of Science and Technology (WUST), one of Poland’s leading technical universities with recognized expertise in satellite technologies, and space-related research. The other is Vigo Photonics, a high-tech manufacturer supplying components for the Polish Armed Forces as well as the Military University of Technology, Poland’s premier institution for military engineering. This is not Beijing's first move of this kind. In April, China’s Ministry of Commerce added seven European entities to its export control list in response to European measures targeting Chinese companies. Responding to questions from the Polish Press Agency on July 27, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Lin Jian emphasized that the decision was “a response to the EU’s erroneous move of listing and sanctioning Chinese companies” and stressed that “the measures do not target any specific country.” Beijing’s decision to sanction WUST is particularly striking. The university participates in EU-funded projects on military drones and battlefield artificial intelligence. At the same time, it has been engaged in joint semiconductor research with Chinese universities. “Wrocław University of Science and Technology is a poli-technical school with tradition and impact for regional and domestic Polish industry,” Krzysztof Karwowski, a researcher at the SGH Warsaw School of Economics, told The Diplomat. “It is a leader primarily in advanced photonics and is the longest-established research center in this field in Poland, creates a number of engineering partnerships in Europe, and is the core of the Polish space industry: microsatellites and satellite optics for security.” As for the implications of China’s move, Karwowski said it was “difficult to assess” at this point – “we will know them in the coming weeks.” He pointed out that WUST and Shanghai Jiao Tong University sealed a “partnership in the field of design and research on semiconductors” last year. “Given China’s activity at Polish academia, WUST may re-prioritize its collaborations in Asia, of which it has a number, to universities in India, Japan, or Korea,” Karwowski predicted. The university’s inclusion on the sanctions list is puzzling, given its close scientific cooperation with Chinese institutions. The other sanctioned entity, Vigo Photonics, specializes in manufacturing infrared detectors, building on research developed in cooperation with institutions such as the Military University of Technology. The company’s products are used across the energy, medical, railway, and defense sectors. For the Polish Armed Forces, Vigo supplies infrared detectors used in unmanned aerial vehicles, precision-guided munitions, and self-guided weapons. Its components are also integrated into observation and targeting systems installed on armored vehicles and air-defense systems acquired by the Polish military. Interestingly, the company itself had anticipated the possibility of Chinese restrictions. According to Vigo's public statement: Aware of this risk, the company has for several years sourced these substrates primarily from suppliers in Japan and Europe, capable of covering its full demand. The company also maintains inventory sufficient for more than one year of production, ensuring continuity in manufacturing infrared detectors and modules. Importantly, inclusion on China’s export control list does not automatically prohibit all trade. Under Chinese regulations, entities such as Vigo Photonics and Wrocław University of Science and Technology may still receive dual-use goods from China, provided exporters obtain the appropriate government license. In practice, this means Beijing retains discretion over future deliveries rather than imposing an outright embargo. Beijing has offered no explanation for why these particular Polish entities were selected. While it is tempting to construct a broader geopolitical narrative, several recent developments are worth noting. First, WUST is located only around 20 kilometers from the site of the recently announced Polish-Taiwanese Foxconn investment. Just weeks ago, Polish and Taiwanese officials unveiled plans for Taiwan to help revive two major industrial projects in Poland: an electric vehicle factory originally expected to be developed with Chinese partners, and a semiconductor project left behind after Intel abandoned its investment near Wrocław. Second, the sanctions coincide with Poland’s growing role in Europe’s space sector. Two weeks ago, the European Space Agency announced that a new ESA Center for Civil Security and Resilience will be established in Warsaw, supporting the development of European capabilities in strategically important fields. Space technologies remain one of the fastest-growing arenas of geopolitical competition between China and Western countries, and as Karwowski noted, WUST is central to Poland’s space program. Third, Beijing may also be responding to Poland's increasingly visible political engagement with Taiwan. Earlier this month, former Polish Prime Minister Beata Szydło led a delegation of Members of the European Parliament from the European Conservatives and Reformists (ECR) group to Taiwan, where they met President Lai Ching-te and senior representatives of Taiwan's government and business community. In crafting its latest sanctions, China may have chosen Polish institutions that are important enough to send a political message, but not so important that they would seriously damage scientific or business cooperation. In this sense, the sanctions appear to be more of a political signal than an attempt to cause major economic harm.

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: People pay their respects at the Tem Rak Samakkhi Buddhist temple in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, in front of the caskets of the grandparents shot dead by their 14-year-old grandson. Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People pay their respects at the Tem Rak Samakkhi Buddhist temple in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, in front of the caskets of the grandparents shot dead by their 14-year-old grandson. Photograph: Anthony Wallace/AFP/Getty Images Thailand Thailand suspends gun licences as teen shooter and grandparents he killed are cremated Prime minister Anutin Charnvirakul calls for tighter gun controls and ‘decisive penalties’ after nine dead in school shooting Natasha May in Bangkok and agencies Wed 12 Aug 2026 01.28 EDT First published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.20 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Thailand has suspended firearms licences after the deadly Nonthaburi school shooting , as the bodies of the teenage attacker and the grandparents he killed were cremated. The prime minister, Anutin Charnvirakul, said he had ordered the interior ministry and police to stop issuing licences to possess, purchase and carry firearms, and called for “tighter controls and decisive penalties”. The measures are temporary until a new gun control law is in place, according to government operated news-channel NBT World. Anutin had vowed to implement changes on Friday when earlier that morning a 14-year-old boy shot dead the grandparents who raised him at their home in Nonthaburi, north of Bangkok, before killing six others at his school and then turning the gun on himself. At a temple in Thailand, parents mourn a 12-year-old mass shooting victim, and a father pleads for forgiveness Read more Anutin had aimed for reforms in previous roles as minister for the interior and health after gun violence in 2022 and 2023. In 2023, a shooting saw a boy of the same age kill two people at a shopping mall using a modified pistol intended to fire blanks that police said was likely ordered online. Anutin ordered a raft of gun control measures, including a short-term ban on new licences, import restrictions and the banning of people under 20 years old from shooting ranges. However, past promises of tightening gun laws have not prevented recent shootings. While Thailand’s licensing laws appear tough on paper, the reality is the country has millions of unregistered guns. The most recent data from the Switzerland-based Small Arms Survey in 2017 showed that with over 10m civilian-owned firearms, Thailand had the highest number in south-east Asia – a rate more than one gun for every seven people – and over 4m were unregistered. The government plans to establish a designated period for people to surrender illegal firearms or inherited weapons that cannot be legally transferred, during which they may be exempt from penalties, according to government operated news-channel NBT World. Commissioner General Kitrat Phanphet of the Royal Thai police has also ordered tighter oversight of government-issued police firearms. The widely criticised “welfare gun” scheme allows eligible public officials to obtain weapons at steep discounts, but the Bangkok Post reports many of these guns end up being resold. Deputy Commissioner General Thana Chuwong will be responsible for targeting illegal weapons possession and trafficking, including illegal weapons sales through social media and other online platforms. A new school safety plan has also been introduced by the ministry of education, including stricter entry screening with guards to check for weapons before anyone enters school premises, and increased mental health counselling. View image in fullscreen The wife of a teacher killed in the Debsirin Nonthaburi school shooting weeps. Photograph: Rungroj Yongrit/EPA The reforms were foreshadowed as multi-day Buddhist funerals for the victims continued to take place. The white caskets of the first victims, the shooter’s grandparents, were laid out at the Tem Rak Samakkhi Buddhist temple on Tuesday, alongside their portraits, ahead of their cremation capping a funeral lasting several days. The boy’s smaller casket was placed to the side at the same temple, surrounded by white flowers. Among the mourners was Tawee Piewphong, who paid tribute to his brother-in-law – the grandfather – as “a man of few words, but a very kind person”. Tawee expressed shock at the killings, saying he had no idea what motivated the teenager, but also offered compassion. “I want to tell him that being 14 is just a small fraction of your entire life, and every problem has a solution. Not everything is the end of the world,” the 70-year-old said. Investigators were still seeking a motive for the shooting, but police said on Sunday that the boy had watched violent videos online and once brought an air gun to school. Officials said previously that he faced academic-related stress, and a classmate said he was bullied. “Of course I feel bad for the innocent people who were killed,” said Somjai Poosod, whose grandchildren attend the school attacked. “But I feel there is an issue of mental health that we may need to address to prevent incidents like this from happening again.” The shooting has resonated across the country, with the king and Anutin leading an outpouring of grief. On Monday, the attacker’s father told the Guardian he still did not understand why his son did it, but was left to reckon with the violence his own flesh and blood had committed. “I’m experiencing so many emotions all at once. I feel guilty and heartbroken because I’ve suffered a loss too. I’ve lost my child, as well as my parents.” The shooter used his grandfather’s gun to kill his grandparents before heading to the school. There, he shot dead five teachers and staff and wounded a 12-year-old girl who died in hospital on Saturday. 1:52 Typhoon Dolphin hits east China with heavy rainfall and strong winds – video China Mass evacuations in Beijing as Typhoon Dolphin brings more torrential rain to China Forecasters warned the Chinese capital could receive more than one-third of its average annual rainfall over 24 hours Yu-chen Li in Taipei Wed 12 Aug 2026 00.43 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 00.44 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Thousands of people have been evacuated from areas at risk of flooding and landslides in Beijing, as the remnants of Typhoon Dolphin continue to bring torrential rain to northern and central China . Forecasters warned on Tuesday that the Chinese capital could receive more than 150mm of rain over the following 24 hours, with some districts forecast to exceed 200mm – more than one-third of Beijing’s average annual rainfall of 528mm. Beijing remained under an orange rainstorm warning, the second-highest level, on Wednesday, with the heaviest rainfall expected across the morning. Floods, storms and landslides: Typhoon Dolphin ravages China – in pictures Read more Authorities closed hundreds of tourist attractions and campsites on Wednesday, with more than 1,300 tourists evacuated or turned away. Meanwhile, over 5,000 elderly people were moved from care facilities and about 1,800 people living around construction projects in mountainous or riverside areas were relocated. View image in fullscreen A person rides an electric scooter on a flooded street while avoiding fallen bicycles in Xiangyang, Hubei province. Photograph: Go Nakamura/Reuters The rain also disrupted Wednesday morning’s commute. Official local media reported that 250 bus routes had been suspended and trains were running at reduced speeds on 10 metro lines. Dolphin, the strongest typhoon to hit China so far this year , has weakened after making landfall in the eastern province of Zhejiang on Sunday, but its remnants have continued to draw large amounts of tropical moisture deep inland and drench central and northern parts of the country. The neighbouring Hebei province was also on alert for mountain floods, landslides and other geological hazards. Authorities said they had dispatched 623 teams to mountainous areas and equipped more than 2,100 at-risk villages with satellite phones or satellite messaging terminals to maintain communications during emergencies, according to state media. View image in fullscreen Cars drive on a flooded street following heavy rain brought by Typhoon Dolphin in Taizhou, Zhejiang province. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images In the central province of Henan, authorities raised the warning for torrential rain to the highest-level red alert on Wednesday morning, as downpours continue to batter large swathes of the province. More heavy rain was forecast through Thursday morning, with 24-hour rainfall totals of up to 350mm expected in some areas. Classes, business operations and non-essential outdoor activities have been suspended in the affected areas of Henan. Residents were told to avoid deep flood waters and evacuate immediately if vehicles stall in water, state media reports. China, the world’s second-largest economy, is increasingly exposed to destructive ‌weather events that scientists link to climate change. This year is proving particularly tough due to the ​emergence of the El Niño weather pattern that is driving up temperatures and fuelling more frequent and intense typhoons. Rainfall records have also been broken elsewhere in central China . Wugang in Henan received 209.5mm in a day and Xiangyang in neighbouring Hubei recorded 169.1mm, both the highest single-day rainfall totals for August, according to state media. China's C919 takes off on a test flight in Shanghai in July. The passenger jet built by Comac is scheduled to make its first international flight on Wednesday. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images View image in fullscreen China's C919 takes off on a test flight in Shanghai in July. The passenger jet built by Comac is scheduled to make its first international flight on Wednesday. Photograph: VCG/Getty Images China Passenger jet billed as China’s answer to Boeing and Airbus prepares to make first international flight The Comac C919 will fly from Beijing to Ulaanbaatar in Mongolia, although experts say it could take generations for it to challenge the west’s dominance of the industry Amy Hawkins Senior China correspondent Tue 11 Aug 2026 22.02 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 22.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google China hopes to break into the world of commercial aviation with the first international flight of a Chinese-made passenger jet scheduled for Wednesday. The Comac C919 will take off from Beijing capital international airport at 3pm, landing in Ulaanbaatar, the capital of Mongolia, just over two hours later. It has been billed as China’s alternative to the Boeing-Airbus duopoly that dominates global aviation, particularly in Asia, but analysts say it could take generations before a Chinese aircraft could meaningfully challenge their global dominance. The C919 is made by the Chinese state-owned aircraft manufacturer Commercial Aircraft Corporation of China (Comac) and is similar in size to the Boeing 737. Chinese EV sales surge to new high in Europe putting tariffs under scrutiny Read more The C919 has been flying on domestic routes operated by Chinese airlines since 2023. But Wednesday’s Air China flight to Ulaanbaatar will be the first time that the narrow-body jet is used on a commercial international route. “This is essentially a public relations move,” said Scott Kennedy, a senior adviser at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies. “Ulaanbaatar was likely chosen because of how close it is to Beijing. It doesn’t change the fact that the plane was years overdue, is composed of western components, and is less efficient than its Boeing and Airbus cousins.” China has long dreamed of building its own jet. When the C919 was unveiled in 2015 , Li Jiaxiang, the head of China’s civil aviation authority, said: “A great nation must have its own large commercial aircraft.” But progress has been slow, even while China has whizzed ahead in other hi-tech fields, such as robotics and electric vehicles (EVs). That is because aviation requires the integration of many different types of advanced science and engineering, as well as parts sourced from overseas. An analysis by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies in 2020 found that more than half of the C919’s suppliers were in the US. View image in fullscreen China’s C919, its first self-developed large passenger jetliner, is unveiled in Shanghai in November 2015. Photograph: ChinaFotoPress/Getty Images “Large passenger aircraft and jet engines are extremely complex and challenging to manufacture. They require precision components, complex electro-mechanical control systems, and the ability to coordinate a vast global supply chain,” said Kyle Chan, a fellow at Brookings focused on China’s industrial policy. “There’s a reason there are basically only two major commercial aircraft makers in the world. Building large passenger jets that are safe and reliable is an order of magnitude more difficult than making EVs,” Chan said. Last year Comac reportedly delivered only 15 units of the C919 to customers, well short of its target of 75. Comac did not respond to a request for comment. Comac primarily serves Chinese domestic airlines. In 2023, the Brunei-based airline GallopAir signed a $2bn deal to purchase 30 planes from Comac, including 15 of the C919, but the airline is not operating commercially yet. The C919 has not been approved by European or American regulators. Last year the US reportedly suspended the export of some products to Comac for use in the C919 jet amid the tit-for-tat restrictions that Beijing and Washington used against each other during the US-China trade war. The two countries later agreed a trade war truce that is set to expire in November. When US president Donald Trump visited Beijing in May for a state visit , one of the few takeaways from the trip was an agreement from China to buy 200 jets from Boeing. In return, the US provided supply guarantees for aircraft engine parts and components for its own manufacturing. China sees being able to build its own commercial aircraft as a national security priority. In a recent interview with Chinese state media, Zhang Yanzhong, an academic of the Chinese Academy of Engineering and a leading aviation expert who worked on the C919, said reliance on other countries for large aircraft technology would “threaten national strategic security”. However, there was still “a long way to go before achieving commercial success”, Zhang said. Experts have pointed out that Comac’s dependence on foreign suppliers goes beyond the supply of individual components. International suppliers have also provided guidance about how to integrate complex components and software together into sky-worthy commercial aircraft. Kennedy argued it was misleading to describe the C919 as a Chinese plane because so many of its parts were imported. He said it was “very unlikely” for Comac to become a serious challenger to Boeing and Airbus, “even a generation from now”. Chan said Comac could still face “a long road to gaining trust among airlines and passengers”. Zhang called on China’s young engineers to contribute their talents to China’s aviation ambitions, saying: “Though the journey may be fraught with difficulties, a fledgling eagle can soar faster than its parent.” Explore more on these topics China Asia Pacific Air transport news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell says the abolition of group voting tickets ‘significantly decrease’ her chances of being elected. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP View image in fullscreen Animal Justice party MP Georgie Purcell says the abolition of group voting tickets ‘significantly decrease’ her chances of being elected. Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP Victorian politics Victorian microparty MPs including Georgie Purcell to face re-election struggle after group voting tickets abolished Voters will be required to number at least five parties above the line in order of preference after bill passed upper house 33 votes to four Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent Wed 12 Aug 2026 02.15 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 02.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Prominent MPs such as Georgie Purcell and other microparty members will face an uphill battle to retain their seats in Victoria’s upper house after parliament voted to abolish group voting tickets. Victoria’s legislative council was the only remaining upper house in Australia to use the GVT system, in which voters could only choose one party above the line on the ballot paper, with their preferences then allocated by the party if it was knocked out during counting. But the electoral amendment (miscellaneous matters) bill 2026 passed the upper house on Tuesday night – 33 votes to four – which will mean GVTs cannot be used in the November state election. Instead, voters will be required to number at least five parties above the line in order of preference. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The GVT system has long been criticised by experts, including election analyst Antony Green, as they allow backroom deals between parties to flourish and enable some candidates to get elected with a small number of primary votes. “This reform is about converting the electoral system into one that rewards parties that get votes over parties who, in the past, have been elected by clever preference deals,” Green told Guardian Australia on Wednesday. “In the last decade we’ve had about 20 candidates elected with under 6% of the vote – some as low as 1% – who’ve defeated candidates with many more votes because of these preference deals. “That is impossible under a system where voters control their own preferences.” The four MPs who opposed the bill were Purcell, who leads the Animal Justice party; the Legalise Cannabis MP Rachel Payne; the Libertarian MP David Limbrick; and the Shooters, Fishers and Farmers MP Jeff Bourman. Ben Raue, an electoral analyst and founder of the Tally Room, said the four MPs represented parties that had benefited from GVTs and were “going to have a lot of trouble getting someone elected with this new system”. “That’s unfortunate for them. But ultimately this about whether GVTs are a fair way to run a democracy and I don’t think it is,” he said. “Voters should have control of their preferences.” Purcell said the changes “significantly decrease” her chances of being re-elected but that “it’s not over until it’s over”. “My team and I are dedicated to running a strong campaign and doing everything we can to secure another four years in parliament,” she said. Payne and Limbrick have also committed to running again, with the latter – who was a prominent critic of the government’s Covid-19 measures – describing his party as “underdogs”. “No one had heard of us when I was elected in 2018, I was written off in 2022 and quadrupled my vote, and they are writing us off again in 2026,” he said. The trio said they supported abolishing GVTs but only if the government also scrapped the state’s eight upper-house regions and replaced them with a single statewide electorate of 40 seats. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion That would lower the electoral quota from 16.7% to 2.4% if members were elected every four years or about 4.8% for eight-year terms. However, such a change would require a referendum. A parliamentary inquiry examining GVTs last year recommended they be abolished in time for the 2026 election and proposed holding a referendum on broader structural reform in 2028 or 2030. Victoria’s voice to parliament asks government to axe bill that will scrap prisoners’ ‘open air’ rights Read more Limbrick said the government had years to make such changes. “Instead they deliberately waited until the last minute to introduce a flawed system to try and silence diverse voices in parliament,” he said. Payne said abolishing GVTs without broader reform “benefits the major parties rather than strengthening our democracy”. “This reform is self-serving and motivated by all the wrong reasons,” she said. Based on statewide polling, Green expects the Coalition could win two seats in each region under the new system. Labor could win two seats in some regions and be reduced to one in others. He said Greens could win up to six seats – one in every metropolitan region and possibly one in the regions – while One Nation could win eight or nine seats. Green stressed that would happen “with or without group voting tickets”, given the party is polling at about 20% of the primary vote. “Whatever happens, if the Liberal party form government after the election, even with a majority, they will not have a majority in the upper house,” he said. “They will have to rely on One Nation in the upper house.” Explore more on these topics Victorian politics Victoria news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Victoria’s voice to parliament asks government to axe bill that will scrap prisoners’ ‘open air’ rights Victoria had bipartisan support for a legal right to work from home.
