https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Horace Mason (George) and daughter Michelle. The court has given him 10 days to leave Sweden. Photograph: Copyright: The Mason family View image in fullscreen Horace Mason (George) and daughter Michelle. The court has given him 10 days to leave Sweden. Photograph: Copyright: The Mason family Sweden British man with dementia told to leave Sweden after losing migration case Exclusive: Horace Mason, 74, who has lived in Sweden for 25 years, faces being deported after court ruling Lisa O’Carroll Senior correspondent Wed 12 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A 74-year-old British man who has been living in Sweden for 25 years who needs round-the-clock care for dementia has been given 10 days to leave the country after he lost a post-Brexit migration court case. The deportation order comes after a Swedish court ruling in July that the government’s drive to reduce immigration trumped the needs of a man in full-time care. British widow, 78, told to leave Sweden under Brexit rules after living there for 21 years Read more “The state’s interest in regulated immigration outweighs Horace Mason’s interest in continuing to reside” in Sweden , the migrations court of appeals ruled in July. The Masons’ family trauma echoes that of Joyce Thomas, a 78-year-old widow who the Guardian revealed on Monday was also facing deportation because of late Brexit paperwork despite living in Sweden for 21 years. The son of Horace Mason (known as George) was told by the British embassy on Friday the authorities had given him until 20 August. “It made me feel sick. We’ve been trying to keep as much information from him as possibly because with the illness he is confused and worried. “But I had to tell him on Friday what had happened and there was just a thousand questions: ‘What is going to happen? Are the police going to come and take me away. Are they going to kick the door down?’ View image in fullscreen George Mason with his son Carl. Photograph: Copyright: The Mason family “I had dinner with him again today [Monday] and it was the same: ‘What is going to happen now? Where am I going to go in England? Are they going to arrest me and put me in prison. “It’s inhumane,” his son Carl said. The UK government said it was aware of the case. “We are supporting Mr Mason and his family and are in contact with the Swedish authorities about his case.” Mason’s case comes two years after another Briton, Kathleen Poole, also suffering dementia was threatened with deportation before she died in a care home. Mason moved to Sweden from Hinckley in Leicestershire to be close to his son and grandchildren around the year 2000. “He is elderly and extremely vulnerable. He has advanced vascular dementia and vascular parkinsonism, together with other serious health problems. He is immobile, requires help with virtually every aspect of daily life and is in full-time residential dementia care in Sweden. He is not capable of simply travelling to Britain and starting a new life independently,” said Carl. When his father’s mental capacity deteriorated, a court appointed a trustee who would have power of attorney over his affairs. “That is when all the problems started,” said Carl. An application for a residence permit was made in December 2021 but was rejected last November by the Swedish migration agency on the grounds “he had not submitted documents demonstrating that he met the requirements for the right of residence” and would have to leave the country. George Mason moved to Sweden from Hinckley in Leicestershire to be close to his son and grandchildren. Photograph: The Mason family An appeal against this decision was also rejected. The family then appealed to the migration court of appeals under the Aliens Act (Chapter 5, Section 6), which permits foreign nationals residence under “particularly distressing circumstances”. The family submitted new medical evidence including his “extensive need for continuous supervision and round-the-clock care” and also argued their father had rights under article 8 of the European convention on human rights. On 23 July, the court ruled that the deportation could stand. It assessed that dementia care existed in the UK, that Mason had a daughter in the UK, although the court heard private medical evidence that she was unable to look after her father as Carl does. “Upon balancing the state’s interest in regulated immigration against what has emerged regarding Horace Mason’s private life and his adaptation to Sweden, the migration court concludes, on balance, that his deportation appears proportionate in relation to article 8.” Carl, who is now running out of time to keep his father living in Sweden, said: “I just can’t see the reasoning behind why they think that deporting a vulnerable citizen is in anybody’s benefit. It’s just beyond me.” View image in fullscreen George Mason suffers from advanced vascular dementia and vascular parkinsonism. Photograph: Copyright: The Mason family Carl is trying to mount a further challenge with the European court of human rights in Strasbourg and has launched a GoFundMe page Stötta George to cover his estimated costs of 50,000 kronor (£3,900). David Milstead, of the grassroots campaign group British in Sweden, has spent years drawing attention to the plight of some British nationals in Sweden before Brexit. He says the hardline approach of the Swedish migration agency is out of kilter with the rest of the EU. Of the 14,233 applications made by the end of 2024 to remain in Sweden, 27.5% (3,918) of applications have been refused, three times higher than any other member state and considerably higher than the EU average of between 3% and 4%. Milstead said: “The Swedish authorities resemble the proud parent at a military parade insisting that everyone except their own child is out of step. “For applications made both on time and after the deadline, Sweden’s approach to the withdrawal agreement ignores key protections in that treaty and is highly restrictive compared with other countries. As a consequence, lives are still being ruined.” Explore more on these topics Sweden Brexit European Union Europe Foreign policy Migration Health news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Forest fires sweep through the outskirts of the southern Lebanon village of Kfar Shouba on 5 August after Israeli bombing, despite the ceasefire. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Forest fires sweep through the outskirts of the southern Lebanon village of Kfar Shouba on 5 August after Israeli bombing, despite the ceasefire. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images Lebanon Israel deliberately starting wildfires in southern Lebanon, firefighters say First responders, residents and environmental groups say military dropping flares to destroy forests and crops William Christou in Beirut Wed 12 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Firefighters and residents of south Lebanon have accused the Israeli military of lighting wildfires in the region, as forested areas burned down in blazes sparked by Israeli bombing. Environmental groups said the fires in recent weeks were part of a longstanding Israeli practice of targeting Lebanon’s natural environment. On Tuesday, the Israeli military dropped flares in a wooded area outside Khiam, in south Lebanon, sparking blazes. When firefighters attempted to extinguish the flames, a drone struck close by, forcing them to withdraw, the head of the civil defence in the Nabatieh region, Hussein Fakih, said. “Most of our missions are now related to fires. There are enormous areas of woodland that have burned, I don’t have the exact figures, but in the areas close to the [frontline], around 30-40% of the land has been affected by fires,” he said. The Israeli military has caused fires across south Lebanon, in particular in olive groves and agricultural land, in the nearly two-months since the 17 June ceasefire that mostly ended fighting between Hezbollah and Israel, according to videos and testimony from first responders. map showing fires The military was asked for comment on each of the wildfire incidents, but did not respond. “They started doing this right after the ceasefire, and there have been incendiary bombs every day,” said Fakih. “Small drones come out and drop incendiary materials, [white] phosphorus shells are fired at the woodlands, in addition to illumination flares that they drop during the daytime so the vegetation catches fire.” Firefighters and residents of other areas in south Lebanon describe similar blazes being started by Israeli munitions and drones in dry scrub and woodlands. On Friday, Israeli munitions created large wildfires in two heavily forested areas: in Kfarchouba, close to the border, and between Jezzine and the western Bekaa valley. The civil defence station chief in the area, Samir Hardan, said a fire was started near Kfarchouba on Friday afternoon after a drone dropped a munition in woodlands. After battling blazes overnight and extinguishing them on Saturday, a second drone started another fire on Sunday, Hardan said. Firefighters, who are required to coordinate their movements with the Lebanese army, which relays their request to a “deconfliction” group that includes the Israeli military, were given permission to fight the fires at only two spots, and not other areas where fires were raging. According to environmental groups, the fires are part of a pattern of Israeli attacks against Lebanon’s environment, which threaten the country’s woodlands and the biodiversity they support, experts said. “These are long-established woodlands, dominated by productive stone pine alongside oak. They perform critical functions. The wider area is also an important passage and resting ground for migratory birds,” said Hisham Younes, the founder of the Lebanese conservation organisation Green Southerners. View image in fullscreen Israeli tanks make their way through the village of Zawtar al-Sharqiyah in southern Lebanon on 2 August. Photograph: Ammar Ammar/AFP/Getty Images Younes called the Israeli attacks an “ecocide”, saying they were part of the military’s pattern of assaults on south Lebanon’s environment to degrade its ecosystem with munitions, fire and chemicals. Younes said: “It is not about any single fire or attack, but a pattern of destruction that progressively erodes the ability of ecosystems to function, regenerate and sustain life. When those cascading effects also undermine livelihoods and people’s ability to return to and remain on their land, environmental destruction becomes inseparable from the wider transformation of the territory itself.” Since fighting started on 8 October 2023, when Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel in solidarity with the Hamas-led attack a day earlier, Israel has repeatedly targeted Lebanon’s woodlands. The Israeli military has said in the past that Hezbollah used these forested areas as cover for its fighters and its tunnels. Ecologists and rights groups have said that fires and other forms of widespread environmental destruction would have wider effects on civilian populations. Israeli troops used trebuchets – medieval catapults – to fling flaming debris over its border wall with Lebanon in the summer of 2024, while the Lebanese army published photos of Israeli drones that carried hoses used to douse forests in flammable materials. Health and environmental experts raised the alarm in February when Israeli planes dropped herbicides linked to cancer on farms in south Lebanon. Besides the environmental and health consequences of these fires, residents of south Lebanon have mourned the loss of the green spaces in the villages where they grew up. On 1 August, displaced residents of the border village of Yaroun found their olive and fruit groves, as well as their homes, had been set ablaze by occupying Israeli troops. People living in the nearby Christian towns of Rmeich and Aïn Ebel, among the few villages near the border not emptied out by the Israeli military, sent pictures of the fires. “They had already bulldozed the whole village. Then they set fire to the trees. What remained in this particular area were the olive trees – large groves, with very old olive trees. They started there, then the fire spread along the outskirts of the village,” said Hafez Ghasham, the mayor of Yaroun. People in Yaroun had already watched in previous months as all but 20 of the 900 houses in the village were bulldozed by the Israeli military, pooling resources to buy expensive satellite imagery of the village during their displacement. “Many of these trees, most of them, in fact, were inherited from our grandparents and parents. They have enormous sentimental value. The trees were also an important source of income for the people of the village,” Ghasham said. “They are trying to make the land uninhabitable. They are erasing our entire history, our entire culture, all our memories. Maybe the idea is that after some time, it will look as though nobody had ever lived here.” Explore more on these topics Lebanon Israel Hezbollah Wildfires Middle East and north Africa news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Insp Joel Brady with his family: ‘This is a massively positive step and great news for policing fathers.’ Photograph: Joel Brady View image in fullscreen Insp Joel Brady with his family: ‘This is a massively positive step and great news for policing fathers.’ Photograph: Joel Brady Police Paid police paternity leave to double after fathers reported being ‘ostracised’ Exclusive: Pay increases to two weeks in England and Wales after Guardian revealed officers ‘mocked’ for taking time off Alexandra Topping Political correspondent Wed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Paid paternity leave for police in England and Wales is to double, after the Guardian revealed last year that officers were “mocked and ostracised ” for taking time off to spend with their babies. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, has increased the amount of paid parental and adoption leave for officers from one week to two across all forces, with fathers’ leave upped to be in line with mothers’. Before the change, only a quarter of forces offered two weeks’ full pay, with others offering one week on full pay and the second week on statutory pay. This resulted in only 40% of officers in the latter group taking the second week’s leave, compared with 88% of those in the first group. Civilian staff in the Metropolitan police were entitled to three weeks’ paternity leave at full pay. The policing minister Sarah Jones said: “Police officers work tirelessly to protect the public, so it is right that new fathers are better supported to spend time with their families. By expanding police paternity leave, we are recognising the importance of family life.” View image in fullscreen Before the change, only a quarter of forces offered new fathers two weeks’ paternity leave on full pay. Photograph: Paul Hennell/Alamy The government is now coming under increased pressure to improve paternity leave across the public sector, which campaigners argue offers poor and patchy leave for fathers. The win for police officers has galvanised a campaign for better paternity leave for military fathers, with the Conservative peer Joanna Penn tabling an amendment to the armed forces bill that would triple paternity leave to six weeks for serving personnel. The government-led tri-forces survey last year found that nearly 30% of families in the armed forces were separated for more than three months in the last year. A survey of 450 serving parents by the campaign group The Dad Shift found that more than 95% agreed the current paternity offer was not enough. “We ask so much of our military families,” said Penn. “The least we can do is give new fathers the chance to properly support their partners and bond with their babies.” Campaigners, backed by MPs on the women and equalities select committee , are pushing for a change to give fathers six weeks of paternity leave at 90% of pay. The UK’s statutory paternity leave of two weeks, paid at £184.03 a week, is one of the worst in Europe. Recent research found one in three UK fathers took no paternity leave after the birth of their child. An 18-month government review of the UK’s parental leave system is expected to report in December. Joel Brady, a police inspector who was part of the campaign, said the policy change would give thousands of fathers in the police more “precious time” with their babies. “This is a massively positive step and great news for policing fathers who want to be there for their partners and involved in their children’s lives,” he said. “I’m optimistic that the government will now listen to dads and increase the amount of leave available to all of us.” More than 20 organisations – including a new group of Labour MPs that has been lobbying ministers to improve rights for fathers – have written to Andy Burnham urging him to commit to the men and boys’ agenda, which gathered pace under Keir Starmer. In November, the government launched the first men’s health strategy for England , and Starmer assigned the then deputy prime minister, David Lammy, to lead work across the government to improve outcomes for men and boys. Writing to the new prime minister, the group said: “Taken together, these developments represent something more significant than a series of individual policies. They represent the beginning of a new consensus: one that rejects the false choice between supporting men and supporting women.” George Gabriel, a co-founder of The Dad Shift, said: “Times are changing. This is the most active generation of dads there’s ever been and momentum is clearly building across the public sector for better paternity leave. “If Andy Burnham wants to prove his is a cost of living government then, as their review of parental leave concludes later this year, we hope they’ll get alongside working families at one of the moments that matters the most.” Explore more on these topics Police Maternity & paternity rights Metropolitan police Parents and parenting Family Employee benefits Children news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed The Filter Wellness Fashion Food Recipes Love & sex Home & garden Health & fitness Family Travel Money

Jon Pountney was one of two photographers to witness the final days inside Tata’s last blast furnace. Photograph: Jon Pountney View image in fullscreen Jon Pountney was one of two photographers to witness the final days inside Tata’s last blast furnace. Photograph: Jon Pountney Wales Eerie silence and ‘still surviving’: what happened next after steel town’s last blast furnace shut down Exhibition in Port Talbot is part of project exploring how communities experience endings and transitions Bethan McKernan Wales correspondent Wed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google M argaret Heggett, 95, does not remember a time when Port Talbot was ever quiet. Born and raised in the shadow of the steelworks, with a father, brother and husband who worked there, she never imagined what the town could look or sound like without its blast furnaces. “I’m not saying it was beautiful, but there were jobs. We did know the closure was coming and we have to move with the times but it’s affected the town a lot and it’s very sad,” she said. The south Wales town, one of the most deprived in the UK, is still grappling with the closure of the blast furnaces at its Tata Steel plant, which shut down in 2024 after more than 100 years, costing nearly 3,000 jobs. The transition has been difficult, with knock-on effects for supply chain workers and local businesses. Now, two years after the last blast furnace fell silent, an exhibition is telling the story of the closure and what has happened to the town since. View image in fullscreen The steelworks seen from the mountains overlooking Port Talbot. Photograph: Jon Pountney Steeling Ourselves , created by the Rhondda-based photographer Jon Pountney, combines photography and portraits of Port Talbot with interviews with the people living there, celebrating their “strength, creativity and determination to shape the future while preserving the memories and experiences that matter”. On display at the Plaza, a community hub, the exhibit is part of After the End, a research project by Exeter, Oxford and Liverpool John Moores universities exploring how communities experience endings and transitions. The research is intended to contribute to wider arguments about the social impact of major industrial changes, and to keep local voices in the conversation about regeneration strategies. For many interviewees, the silence after the last blast furnace shut down was eerie. “I used to camp out at night and the light was better than the northern lights,” one contributor said. “When you’re making iron, there’s 1,000-degree heat that lights the sky up and the shadow changes and it’s like a show, you know, and that’s what we were brought up on. I loved that.” View image in fullscreen A woman sunbathing on a beach with the works in the distance. Photograph: Jon Pountney Pountney was one of two photographers to witness the final days inside Tata’s last blast furnace before it closed. The exhibit also captures the beats of life in Port Talbot – friends messing about near the water, camping chairs on nearby Aberavon beach, terrace streets, pushchairs, meadows and wildlife – with the huge steelworks site almost always present in the background. Heggett said: “When I was asked to take part in the project, I’d had a glass of wine, so I thought ‘why not?’. It’s been lovely to reflect on.” View image in fullscreen Margaret Heggett, 95, was photographed for the project. Photograph: Jon Pountney People in the town felt strongly that the blast furnace closure did not mean “writing off their community”, said Patricia Kingori, a professor of global health ethics at the University of Oxford and lead researcher on After the End. “The exhibition is really rooted in hearing the experiences of people who had this ‘ending’ imposed on them, and what we can learn from them … The pace of change is such that we haven’t really reconciled yet what work and labour will look like in the future,” she said. “Port Talbot is the canary in the coalmine. The conversations the town is having are going to be repeated in all places and walks of life at some point.” Tata Steel is transitioning to a greener electric arc furnace, although the project has been hit by delays and the plant is expected to employ a fraction of the workforce it once did. “You can live the dream from Port Talbot,” one interviewee in the project said. “We’ve insisted upon that and the fact that we’re still surviving … being creative and doing all these positive things, shows that it’s actually true.” Explore more on these topics Wales Steel industry Photography Exhibitions news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Following the announcement about Andy Burnham’s early prison release scheme to alleviate overcrowding in prisons, there has been outcry from the public. Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Following the announcement about Andy Burnham’s early prison release scheme to alleviate overcrowding in prisons, there has been outcry from the public. Photograph: Peter Macdiarmid/Getty Images First Edition newsletter Prisons and probation Wednesday briefing: Why the prison crisis is about much more than early release In today’s newsletter: As ministers scramble to resolve overcrowding in prisons, experts say the crisis demands a rethink of who we lock up – and what happens when they’re set free Libby Brooks Wed 12 Aug 2026 01.47 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 01.48 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. On his family holiday last week, the prime minister, Andy Burnham, was reported to be taking daily calls from Ministry of Justice officials about his government’s early release scheme. A furious public outcry has gathered pace since it emerged that the plan – brought in by his predecessor, Keir Starmer, to alleviate overcrowding in prisons across England and Wales – might include two of the killers of PC Andrew Harper and other serious sexual offenders, including grooming gang perpetrators. After several weeks of “system says no” briefings, which Harper’s mother Debbie Adlam has described as “a rollercoaster … really draining”, yesterday Burnham endeavoured to put a pin in it until September. Announcing that he had tasked the justice secretary, Alex Norris, with fast-tracking measures to free up prison space, the prime minister insisted he was “increasingly confident” that the early release scheme can be adapted to exclude the constable’s killers. He had previously intervened to exempt grooming gang members, rapists and those convicted of “serious” child sexual offences. Norris will report to parliament early next month, and Burnham is no doubt keen that this week’s nationwide listening tour is not derailed by constant questions about early release. But the scrutiny is unlikely to recede with opposition parties calling for a U-turn and probation officers yesterday voting decisively in favour of strike action over excessive workloads – a problem they expect to get worse when the scheme starts in the autumn. For today’s newsletter, I spoke to criminal justice consultant and former repeat offender Gethin Jones , and former prison governor John Podmore , about the story missing from the early release row, and what a radical solution to the ongoing prison capacity crisis might look like. First, this morning’s headlines. Five big stories UK news | Repeated debilitating heatwaves this summer are likely to have cost the UK economy more than £4bn in lost economic output by the end of July, new analysis shows. Meta | Courts in England and Wales have joined a number of restaurants, theatres and pubs in banning the controversial Meta glasses , which can record video footage while being worn. Middle East | Firefighters and residents of south Lebanon have accused the Israeli military of lighting wildfires in the region, as forested areas burned down in blazes sparked by Israeli bombing. UK politics | Reform’s deputy leader Richard Tice has been accused of using “nasty tactics” in an attempt to intimidate journalists and deflect attention from his own financial affairs after issuing a legal threat to the Guardian. US news | Democrats called on Tuesday for a congressional briefing over a stunning charade in which Donald Trump was secretly spirited to a different plane than the one the public and press believed he was travelling on. In depth: ‘We should be locking up people we’re afraid of, not people we’re mad at’ View image in fullscreen HMP Manchester, known as Strangeways, struggled with overcrowding, riots and brutal conditions in the 1990s. Photograph: Phil Noble/PA Gethin Jones recalls watching a documentary about HMP Strangeways, the crumbling Victorian prison in Manchester that became synonymous with over-crowding and brutal conditions. The Strangeways riot of 1990 was a watershed moment in British penal history, leading to long-awaited public scrutiny and reform. While the echoes of those days are all too apparent, what he recalls most clearly was the then-governor describing prison as “society’s dustbin”. At that point, Jones was already set in his own 20-year cycle of drug misuse and offending: after a childhood in care, he received his first custodial sentence at the age of 14, and was introduced to heroin and crack cocaine in prison. He’s now a passionate advocate for the type of “human to human” intervention that eventually unlocked his own offending cycle – working with men in secure environments. “Politicians keep saying we lock people up to keep communities safe,” he says. “But the reality is that when you lock somebody up, if you do nothing with them while they’re in prison, and nothing to support them when they get out, they’re even more disadvantaged and more likely to reoffend, which is now making our communities unsafe.” The current row over early release is focused on a small percentage of offenders, he argues, while most of those in prison are low risk, high need. “They are people with poor mental health, substance misuse, no opportunities: all of these areas that our society doesn’t know how to manage, then they fall into the justice system and then they go into the dustbin, which is prison.” Why are our prisons at capacity? According to the most recent Ministry of Justice data , there are 86,536 men and women in prison custody in England and Wales, one of the highest per capita prison populations in western Europe. It’s a population that has doubled in recent decades – from about 44,000 in 1993 – for a number of interlocking reasons. The hefty courts backlog and wider system gridlock brought about by the pandemic has seen the remand population balloon to more than 15,000, almost 18% of the total in custody. Recalls – the term for people returned to prison after breaching the conditions of their release – have likewise increased by a staggering amount. There were 51,419 licence recalls in England and Wales in year ending March 2026, compared with 40,259 the previous year. Many experts see this as a direct consequence of previous early release schemes: without proper planning, the policy creates a revolving door. Others blame the risk aversion of an over-burdened probation service. Jones is working with a young man who is about to be released from prison for the second time, having been recalled a mere six days after a drug relapse meant he failed to report to his probation hostel in time. “He’s just about to get out now, and there’s still not the support in place. It will be an absolute miracle if he doesn’t get recalled again.” Added to this mix is the fact that judges are imposing ever-longer prison sentences – from an average of 16 months for an indictable offence to 1993 to 22.2 months in 2024. When he was asked to review sentencing by Keir Starmer, former Conservative justice secretary David Gauke attributed it to a “bidding war” between political parties since the 1990s over which can show themselves tougher on crime. And overseeing all of this is another revolving door: that of the entrance to the Ministry of Justice. In the past 10 years, there have been 10 justice secretaries and 13 prison ministers. What is the cost of early release? Regardless of sentence inflation, and unhappily for politicians, the public believe prisons are failing to punish prisoners for their offences and not preparing them adequately for a life beyond crime. What is unclear is how aware they are of the administrative sleight of hand whereby successive governments have driven up sentence lengths through legislation, then sought to undo the effect through early release schemes. Richard Garside, director of the Centre for Crime and Justice Studies, has written powerfully about the impact on individual victims: “What should not survive indefinitely is the current arrangement, in which parliament promises punishment that cannot be delivered, and the gap is closed administratively, out of sight, until a letter lands on a victim’s doormat.” In a Facebook post on Tuesday, the prime minister acknowledged “the anguish of [PC Andrew Harper’s] family and, more broadly, of all those victims and their families who may see those who caused them such harm not serve their full sentence”. But the operational impact is significant . Prison Service leaders are described as “terrified of another exemption” to early release as they cope with severe over-crowding, and must now navigate the haphazard system of sentence discounts and days added in order to determine who is eligible. Previous schemes resulted in some prisoners being released in error , while probation managers found their caseloads distended overnight. What could Andy Burnham do differently? In the same Facebook post, Burnham said these exemptions could be mitigated by expanding prison places in three ways: removing foreign offenders more quickly; tackling “the long-running injustice of IPP sentences” , which have kept many minor offenders locked up for decades; and re-purposing some women’s prisons for male offenders. Our home affairs editor Rajeev Syal assesses their viability here . John Podmore, former governor of Belmarsh, Brixton and Swaleside prisons, has argued consistently that prisons not only fail to rehabilitate, but in too many cases actively institutionalise despair. The longer-term solution to the present crisis is not, he tells me, to build more prison places – despite Burnham’s colleagues pushing this line yesterday. Podmore has always made a clear distinction between those who threaten the public – probably fewer than 30,000 of the current population, by his informed estimate – and the rest: “We should be locking up people we’re afraid of, not people who we’re mad at.” The government is pressing ahead with its aim to build 14,000 more prison places by 2031, mainly secure category B and C facilities – but a good proportion of the prisoner population is within 12 months of release. “We don’t need those levels of security,” Podmore says. “We need more open prisons in urban areas, more approved premises, more bail hostels.” Female prisoners – the vast majority of whom are nonviolent offenders – are in particular need of more creative facilities like Hope Street in Southampton, which offers a community alternative to prison for women so their children can remain with them. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters Preview latest after newsletter promotion For Podmore, Burnham’s devolution agenda offers a gateway to radical prison reform: a centrally run federal estate for those who require long-term high security; and oversight of prisons for lesser offenders – who have been thoroughly risk assessed – passed to local mayors. After all, as Gethin Jones has already explained, lack of resettlement support is one of the biggest hurdles facing newly released prisoners. Aren’t local authorities better placed to bring them into existing housing, education and mental health networks? Might a truly local prison have a board of governors, like a school, making its management answerable to that community? When Podmore took over HMP Brixton in 2003, it was languishing at the bottom of performance league tables, with angry headlines demanding its closure. He opened the doors, inviting in local community charities and religious groups. “And the response was, ‘What can we do?’ That’s where you change the public perception.” What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen The first real food-influencer … Anthony Bourdain in Sydney, 2005. Photograph: Fairfax Media/Getty Images I spent half my holiday sharing a cottage with a wasp nest, and was glad to read in the latest instalment of Invertebrate of the Year that my policy of non-engagement was the correct one, definitively settling an argument with my other half. Libby Josh Halliday’s piece about Matilda Davis , a mother who took her own life after she was “pushed to breaking point” by a care system that fails the parents of so many disabled children, was a moving profile of a remarkable woman. Hettie The forecast cloud cover over Glasgow suggests that solar eclipse viewing won’t be that fruitful, but I was still happy to watch our snappy public service video about how to watch it safely. Libby Anthony Bourdain was the world’s first real food influencer who taught us all to avoid brunch like the plague. Zoe Williams spoke to chefs about whether they still admire his hedonistic vibe. Hettie ICYMI, you must make time to read this brilliant and disturbing essay from Katherine Rundell about how AI stands between children and their potential for thinking. I finished it feeling angry – but also, hopeful. Hettie Sport View image in fullscreen Romell Glave and Jeremiah Azu celebrate winning gold and silver. Photograph: Mike Egerton/PA European Athletics Championships | Britain’s Romell Glave won a stunning gold in the men’s 100m at the European championships, with his teammate Jeremiah Azu picking up silver. Football | England defender Djed Spence nears Tottenham Hotspurs exit , with the club allowing him to join Inter in a move expected to cost around £25.6m. Fifa | Gianni Infantino’s opponents are working together to produce a new framework for running world football to replace what they regard as a system of patronage that Fifa has adopted since he replaced Sepp Blatter as president 10 years ago. The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian “Burnham plan to keep PC’s killers in jail could backfire, warn unions”, is the Guardian ’s front page today. The Telegraph says “Police unite to fight early release”, the Express has “Andy U-turns on early release plan”, and the Times writes “Extra safeguards needed for early release, say police”. The FT has “European car industry wary as China tightens grip on component suppliers”, the i Paper has “Summer 2026 will be UK’s hottest since records began”, and the Mail writes “Burnham” Middle-class areas must take more migrants”. Lastly, Metro leads on “The Black Wednesday shopping scramble!”. Today in Focus View image in fullscreen Farage says he’s protesting against the scrutiny into his financial affairs – and that the people of Clacton should decide whether he’s still fit to serve. Photograph: Dan Kitwood/Getty Images Could Clacton bin off Nigel Farage? Nigel Farage has taken a high risk gamble by resigning and forcing a byelection in his constituency. Nosheen Iqbal heads to Clacton to find out how voters feel. Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings View image in fullscreen Illustration: Nicola Jennings/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen Umit, a wild-caught female tiger, is released into Kazakhstan’s wilderness as part of a repopulation programme. Photograph: Amur Tiger Centre/TASS/Zuma Press/eyevine Caspian tigers were last sighted in Kazakhstan more than 70 years ago. Earlier this month, a female Amur tiger, a breed whose DNA is virtually identical to Caspians, was released into a nature reserve in Kazakhstan as part of a pioneering repopulation programme. “ Umit ,” which translates to “hope” in Kazakh, was transported to the reserve from the far east of Russia, and soon, she will be joined by more big cats. “There is a lot of work ahead on monitoring tigers and forming a stable population, but today the first and very important step has been taken,” said Kazakhstan’s environment minister. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Spanish police check documents of travellers from Italy at Madrid Barajas airport, 8 August 2026, after a dispute between the two countries. Photograph: Spanish Police/Reuters View image in fullscreen Spanish police check documents of travellers from Italy at Madrid Barajas airport, 8 August 2026, after a dispute between the two countries. Photograph: Spanish Police/Reuters Opinion Spain Ceuta showed just how easy it is to divide Europe Paul Taylor The migrant influx prompted recriminations and a tit-for-tat dispute between Italy and Spain. Putin, Erdoğan and others will have taken note Wed 12 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 03.13 EDT Share W ithin hours of the first pictures of tens of thousands of migrants swimming the short distance from Morocco to the Spanish north African enclave of Ceuta hitting social media on 30 July, 22 European Union leaders , the Trump administration and Israel had piled on to criticise Madrid. The outbreak of hysteria and recrimination was a case study in 21st-century politics, driven by real-time images in a media echo chamber where populists set the agenda on migration, propagating fear, prejudice and demagogic proposals. Above all, the kneejerk reactions undermined trust between European allies and dealt a setback to EU efforts to jointly manage migration, counter people-smuggling and resist the weaponisation of migrants by non-EU countries. That Donald Trump and JD Vance should seize the opportunity to accuse socialist Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez of inviting the mass influx by allowing more than 1 million irregular migrants already working in Spain to apply for legal status is hardly surprising, given the US administration’s own relentless drive to detain and expel illegal immigrants. On the other hand, European leaders who signed a letter to the European Commision, criticising Spain and demanding an emergency meeting of interior ministers, should ask themselves how their behaviour helps the EU implement a coherent response to migratory pressures. Many are open to charges of hypocrisy, since Germany and Italy have, between them, regularised hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrant workers at the request of employers who need their labour as the home workforce dwindles. There was also a monstrous foreign policy double standard in the initial EU response. When Poland and Lithuania faced a sudden influx of irregular migrants from Belarus in 2021, the EU rallied behind its eastern members and imposed sanctions on Minsk’s authoritarian regime, which stood accused of weaponising displaced people from the Middle East. The previous year, the EU sent its Frontex border agency to help Greece repel a surge of migrants from Turkey at the countries’ shared border in Thrace, which had apparently been encouraged by Ankara to put pressure on the EU. View image in fullscreen Crowds gather near Fnideq on the Morocco-Spain border, 31 July 2026. Photograph: Abdel Majid Bziouat/AFP/Getty Images Yet this time, EU governments quickly fell into a divisive blame game, terrified by images that recalled the loss of control over borders in south-eastern Europe in 2015, when more than 1 million mostly Syrian refugees entered the bloc. Amid the internal finger-pointing, neither the EU leaders nor the European Commission dared question the role of Morocco , whose border guards apparently stood aside as more than 72,000 Moroccans, mostly young men, risked their lives swimming to Ceuta after seeing viral social media claims that “Spain is open”. The incident occurred on Morocco’s annual Throne Day when King Mohammed VI, who does not recognise Spanish sovereignty over the territories of Ceuta and Melilla, just happened to be visiting the nearby northern city of Tétouan, once part of the Spanish protectorate. Some commentators have called the stampede to Ceuta a “ Blue March ”, in reference to the mass Green March that the king’s father, Hassan II, launched in 1975 in an attempt to claim the vast territory of Western Sahara, then a Spanish colony. “In Morocco, nothing happens by chance,” says Anna Terrón Cusí, a senior fellow at the Migration Policy Institute and a former Spanish secretary of state for immigration. Even if the stampede to Ceuta started spontaneously with social media posts, she believes “this was a multi-actor, multi-factor event. It was more a geopolitical than a migration crisis.” Intra-European party politics played a big role. It was not surprising that the Italian prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, should lead the assault on Sánchez. She heads up the hard-right Brothers of Italy movement and faces a domestic challenge in elections next year from a new, even further-right party, led by a retired general . Some Spanish and UK anti-immigration politicians rushed to Ceuta to take selfies, one from Reform UK doing a standup interview on the beach to cash in on the purported alien “invasion”. It was more bizarre that Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen, who heads a centre-left government, should co-initiate with Meloni the letter to Commission president Ursula von der Leyen, and say that the EU should consider suspending Spain from the Schengen area of open-border travel. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment Preview latest after newsletter promotion A facade of European solidarity was restored after EU interior ministers held a hastily arranged videoconference. By that time, almost all the migrants had left Ceuta and returned to Morocco after realising that they had no chance of reaching Europe. The “ invasion ” had deflated. In fact, irregular migrant arrivals in Spain fell sharply last year, while across the EU they’re down for the second successive year, and far below the 2015 crisis peak. But the damage was done. Italy and Spain are now engaging in tit-for-tat passport and nationality controls on each other’s travellers, and Russian president Vladimir Putin, Turkish president Recep Tayyip Erdoğan and King Mohammed himself will have noted how easily Europe panics and turns on its own members at the first sight of migrants on its beaches. Whether out of misinformation or malice, some EU ministers distorted the nature of the Spanish amnesty for undocumented migrants, labelling it a “pull factor” for mass migration. Italy’s foreign minister, Antonio Tajani, claimed they were being granted Spanish and therefore European citizenship, rather than simply being given a chance to apply for temporary work visas. Europe faces what in game theory is called the “ prisoners’ dilemma ”, and in social sciences a “ collective action problem ” . EU countries have a shared interest in preserving the Schengen zone of free movement, with open internal borders vital to the smooth operation of the economy, well-managed external borders to deter irregular migrants and combat people smugglers, and legal migration routes to permit an inflow of workers needed by businesses as the European population ages and shrinks. Yet they keep undermining cooperation due to a seemingly irresistible short-term political interest in anti-migration grandstanding. Paul Taylor is a senior visiting fellow at the European Policy Centre Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2026.text: Bucket cred … the mannequin welcoming visitors to step into Ljubljana’s new museum of Balkan humour. Photograph: Veronika Snoj View image in fullscreen Bucket cred … the mannequin welcoming visitors to step into Ljubljana’s new museum of Balkan humour. Photograph: Veronika Snoj Museums ‘If we exhibited all the Balkan jokes, we wouldn’t have opened’: a trip to Slovenia’s Bullshit Museum In the heart of old Ljubljana, a mannequin with a bucket on its head welcomes visitors to a new and ambitious project – a museum focusing on the varied and sometimes antagonistic humour of the former Yugoslavia Veronika Snoj Wed 12 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google O n the main promenade along the river that runs through Ljubljana, Slovenia’s capital, tourists stop to photograph a mannequin with a bucket on its head. Dressed in a pistachio jacket and red leggings, the figure sits at a table in front of one of the houses in the historic Old Town, staring at a spilled cup of Turkish coffee, popular with Slovenes and with the other Balkan and central European citizens with whom they shared a country, until it collapsed in the early 1990s. A large sign in the background reads: “Bullshit Museum: The world is off the rails, and so are we. Yebiga !” Yebiga , which can be loosely translated as “fuck it”, or “screw it”, is the red thread running through the museum that was launched in May and consists of five small rooms filled with mannequins wearing odd accessories, AI-generated images of laughing characters and scenes accompanying some of the jokes, framed or displayed on cardboard screens. The word encompasses the heart of Balkan humour, says the museum’s founder, Borut Kokelj, who wears a T-shirt emblazoned with the words: “What part of yebiga don’t you understand?” View image in fullscreen The Bullshit Museum is spotted with mannequins wearing various odd accessories. Photograph: Veronika Snoj “Even when there’s no money, when there are no jobs, when nothing is settled, everything can be solved with humour,” he says. “And for that to work, humour must have no filter”. Although it presents itself as the home of “Balkan” humour, the museum is primarily centred on the joke culture of the former Yugoslavia, the socialist federation that included the Balkan Peninsula countries that are now Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Bosnia and Herzegovina, and Kosovo. Formed out of the wreckage of the first world war, Yugoslavia was a political project to unite southern Slav and some non-Slavic minorities under a common identity and language, then officially known as Serbo-Croatian. But the genocidal wars that accompanied Yugoslavia’s disintegration in the early 1990s demonstrated that the idea of a single Yugoslav nation lacked deep foundations. The region’s different nations have since continued to define themselves through distinct religious identities, including Catholicism, Orthodoxy and Islam, but also separate dialects and languages. View image in fullscreen 1. Good morning! 2. What is he saying? 3. He said Good morning, but in Cyrillic … a cartoon at the Bullshit Museum. Photograph: Veronika Snoj “Balkan” humour, the museum suggests, may have been the glue that held Yugoslavia’s cultural bric-a-brac in place, and it is fitting that some of the jokes on display play directly on the issue of language. “A fool is a fool in both the Cyrillic and the Latin alphabets,” reads a large poster at the entrance, using both scripts: Cyrillic, being associated with Serbs and Orthodox Christianity, and the Latin alphabet being used by other, mostly non-Orthodox nations of the dissolved state. The armed conflicts that have shaped the region are also reflected in the exhibition, albeit indirectly. There is wordplay on the title of the controversial 1996 Serbian drama Lepa Sela Lepo Gore (literally “pretty villages burn nicely”), about a group of surrounded Serbian soldiers during the Bosnian war, here adapted into the absurdist line Lepa jela lepo goje (“Fine food fattens you up well”). View image in fullscreen Displays and inverted mannequin at the museum. Photograph: Veronika Snoj The role and power of women in society also seems to be a unifying factor. “Starleta is the first Balkan mythical being with the body of a woman and the head of a turkey”, reads an “encyclopedic” definition of a “starleta” – a woman who seeks fame and wealth through no other achievements than her (plastic surgery-assisted) beauty. “She wanted to marry a prince, but a horse had more money,” reads another, playing on the word konj (horse), which is used in many former Yugoslav nations to describe a “man”. Kokelj, who has collected about 25,000 jokes from the region over the years, said he resisted freighting the exhibition with politically loaded humour. “If we were to exhibit all the truly ‘Balkan’ jokes, we likely wouldn’t have opened,” he admits, referring to jokes that directly address religion, ethnicity, or national symbols. The selection also avoids jokes that mock a specific group or feature characters identified with a particular ethnic group. There are no jokes here mocking the supposed “laziness” of Montenegrins (such as this from the humour section of a local magazine: “What does a Montenegrin say before going to bed? ‘Rise, earth, so that I may lie down,’”). I find only one AI-generated “ethnic” meta-joke: it plays on the stereotype of Slovenes as a nation eager to present itself as the most “elegant” and “European”, thereby distancing itself from the rest of the region: a Slovenian man tells a joke “the Slovenian way”, using innocent euphemistic curses such as “three hundred hairy bears”, while his “Balkan” counterpart has no restraint when it comes to colourful insults. Overall, most of the jokes address everyday issues and the absurdities of life. “Life is neither nail polish nor acetone,” reads one. “We had it better, and we still complained. Now that things are getting worse, we’re complaining again,” says another. Others focus on romantic relationships: “Love is when you look like a sack of potatoes, but she sees you as fries.” Another recurring theme is the ability to laugh at oneself: “Amateurs make mistakes, but we, the experienced ones, create catastrophes.” There seems to be one element that holds the exhibition together to this day, though: rakija, the celebrated Balkan fruit brandy. It is served to visitors as they enter the museum and is described in one of the exhibits as “the first aid of every Balkan household”. It is also central to the definition of the infamous yebiga , which one exhibit describes as follows: “The Balkan way of saying: what are you going to do? Maximum feeling, minimum energy. It usually goes with rakija, a cigar and a song that hurts more than it should.” Explore more on these topics Museums Comedy Exhibitions Slovenia Slovenia holidays Europe features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Aftermath of the Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPA View image in fullscreen Aftermath of the Russian attack on Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPA Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: North Korean missiles hit Zaporizhzhia in deadly attack Zelenskyy warns Putin will use Russian election, in which opposition to the war is banned, as pretext for major call-up of troops. What we know on day 1,631 Warren Murray and agencies Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.22 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 21.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russian forces used ballistic missiles supplied by North Korea , Ukraine’s president said, in an attack on the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia where the Metinvest steel company said seven civilian workers at its plant were killed and 21 injured. Three more civilians, including a 15-year-old boy, were killed by Russian drones and artillery in the central Dnipropetrovsk region, authorities said. Russia used missiles, drones and glide bombs to attack Ukrainian cities on Tuesday, said Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the president. One strike hit the grounds of a children’s hospital, leaving two craters but not hurting anyone, the State Emergency Service said. Ukraine’s military general staff said its forces struck an oil refinery in the city of Orsk in Russia’s Orenburg region near the border with Kazakhstan, about 1,500km (930 miles) from Ukraine, causing a fire. The refinery can process about 44m barrels of crude oil a year to produce gasoline, diesel, aviation fuel and other products. The Russian online retailer Wildberries said its logistical facilities in the Voronezh region of Russia near the Ukrainian border came under attack and caught fire . Romania’s defence ministry said its navy destroyed two suspected Russian drones drifting in the Black Sea about 90 nautical miles (166km) from the port of Constanta. The Gerbera-type drones – a cut-price Russian version of the Shahed – were blown up by divers and some pieces were recovered, the ministry said, adding that Ukraine said the drones were not theirs. Russia is aiming to exploit Kyiv’s critical shortage of Patriot air defence interceptors that can stop ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said, adding that Moscow is preparing to recruit more troops for a new push on the frontline. “Every step Russia takes – increasing ballistic missile production, bringing in North Korean equipment, preparing for mobilisation – all of this shows that Moscow is preparing not for peace, but for escalation,” Zelenskyy posted. He was warned in recent days that North Korea is preparing to send up to 50,000 more troops to Russia. Zelenskyy said Ukrainian intelligence suggested Russia would use its “pseudo-election” in September as a pretext to declare a new mobilisation . Mobilisation involves the use of reservists and conscripts, which in 2022 led to protests in Russia such as recruiting offices being set on fire. “They are preparing for mobilisation in the autumn, ​immediately after the imitation of parliamentary elections,” Zelenskyy said as part of a plan to “ create the appearance that Russians supposedly support the war ”. Russia’s supreme ​court on Monday barred the Yabloko party , the only officially registered party that opposes Moscow’s ​war in Ukraine, from competing ‌in the election. Zelenskyy continued: “Then, following the so-called election, he plans an additional rapid mobilisation of several hundred thousand Russians by the end of the year, plus another similar number next year.” Zelenskyy said Ukraine had ⁠ handed proposals to US ⁠negotiators for a plan ​to end the war with Moscow. Zelenskyy offered no details on the proposals. US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were last in Moscow in January and have not yet visited Kyiv . The Institute for the Study of War, a US thinktank, has said in an analysis that the Kremlin will not seriously negotiate as long as Putin believes he might still reach his full objectives. “Ukraine’s Patriot shortages offer Russia an opportunity to cause very serious damage to Ukraine over the coming winter and will therefore contribute to delaying meaningful negotiations and protracting the war.” The UN estimates that more than 16,000 civilians detained by Russia during the war are still being “deprived of their liberty” , with many held incommunicado and on grounds that don’t comply with international law. “Widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment” of both Ukrainian civilian detainees and prisoners of war by Russia are continuing, including sexual violence, said Claudia Fuentes Julio, the UN assistant secretary general for human rights. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/12/more-.text: Over 16,000 civilians captured by Russia during its conflict in Ukraine are still "deprived of their liberty," with many being held incommunicado and for reasons that violate international law, an informal UN security council meeting has been told.According to Claudia Fuentes Julio, the UN assistant secretary-general for human rights. “Widespread and systematic torture and ill-treatment” of both Ukrainian civilian detainees and prisoners of war by Russia are continuing, including sexual violence.Julio gave the estimates at the informal meeting of the Security Council called by Latvia and the United Kingdom on Monday to spotlight the plight of civilians and soldiers taken during the war that Russia launched with a full-scale invasion of its neighbor in February 2022.The council, which counts Russia as a permanent member, heard the accounts as both Russia and Ukraine have escalated attacks in the four-year conflict.According to Julio, since the invasion, 910 Ukrainian prisoners of war and 403 civilian detainees have been interviewed by UN human rights personnel following their release.And more than 95% of the Ukrainian prisoners of war and 85% of the civilian detainees reported being tortured or ill-treated, often repeatedly, the U.N. official said.They also reported sexual attacks and inhumane conditions, including food deprivation and inadequate medical services.The Geneva-based human rights office “has documented the execution of 129 Ukrainian prisoners of war at the beginning of their captivity and the deaths of 48 Ukrainian prisoners of war in custody, resulting from torture, denial of medical care, or other inhumane conditions of detention,” Julio said.The UN has not been permitted to visit Russian detention facilities, and its estimate of the number of people detained does not include a breakdown of adults and children.Some former detainees shared their ordeal with the UNThe Security Council also heard emotionally wrenching accounts from some former detainees who shared their ordeal.Crimean Tatar human rights activist Leniie Umerova, who called herself a “political prisoner” of the Russians for almost two years, and Khuan Leyva Garsiya, a Ukrainian soldier who was among the hundreds that held out for months at the Azovstal steel plant in the besieged city of Mariupol before turning themselves over to the Russians in May 2022 shared their stories.Garsiya, who was born in Mariupol to a Ukrainian mother and Cuban father, spent 1,183 days as a POW. He said he weighed 55 kilograms (120 pounds) when he was freed, pulling out a picture of his emaciated body to show the council.Garsiya said he was tortured, beaten harder, and humiliated more than other prisoners because the Russians suspected that he was a foreign mercenary due to his Cuban ancestry or an American spy because he went to college in the United States.“Russians were outraged that someone with a connection to Cuba, whom they consider an ally, would fight against their occupation army,” said Garsiya, who is still in the Ukrainian military.UN also said Russian detainees reported abusesUN human rights experts also interviewed 816 Russians and 57 third-country national prisoners of war from over 45 countries who were members of the Russian armed forces in Ukraine, said Julio, the assistant secretary-general.About half reported torture or ill-treatment, primarily during the initial stages of captivity and interrogation by Ukrainians, she said.But UN monitors reported that once they arrived in Ukrainian detention facilities, “the conditions generally comply with international humanitarian law and have improved since 2022.”Responding to the claims, Russia’s deputy UN Ambassador Maria Zabolotskaya told the council the Russian armed forces are complying with international humanitarian law, which includes the treatment of prisoners. She claimed Russian prisoners in Ukraine faced “torture and degradation and moral and physical abuse.”She called the Security Council meeting part of “a disinformation campaign against Russia,” funded by NATO countries involved in the Ukraine conflict. The aim, she said, “is to derail efforts towards a peace settlement and to justify strikes on the territory of Russia and against civilians.”For Ukraine's part, Volodymyr Pavlichenko, Kyiv's deputy UN ambassador, expressed his displeasure that Russia was not prepared to talk about the return of POWs, "including their POWs," and all civilian detainees, including kidnaped children.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/11/belar.text: Aliaksandr Milinkevich, the physicist-turned-politician who united Belarus’s opposition forces to challenge Aliaksandr Lukashenka in the 2006 presidential election, has died at the age of 79.His death was announced on Tuesday.Milinkevich underwent a complicated operation to remove a blood clot from his carotid artery last year. He spent a prolonged period in critical condition and later underwent extensive rehabilitation.From academia to politicsMilinkevich was born in 1947, in Grodno, Belarus. After graduating from the faculty of physics and mathematics at the Grodno Pedagogical Institute, he worked as a teacher at a local school. He later earned a PhD and became an associate professor at the same institution.He went on to author dozens of academic works on quantum electronics and laser technology, as well as on Belarusian culture, art, education and more.Around the time of the Soviet Union's collapse, he moved into the public sector, and from 1990 to 1996, he served as deputy chair of the Grodno city executive committee.In 2001, he headed the campaign headquarters of Belarusian presidential candidate Semyon Domash, and five years later he ran for the presidency himself.A pro-European challengerIn 2005, Milinkevich was chosen as the candidate of the opposition democratic forces, which stood as a united front against the Lukashenka regime. A pro-European vision for Belarus became a defining feature of his campaign.The election campaign was marked by intense pressure on the opposition, including threats of criminal prosecution, disinformation campaigns in pro-government media, and arrests of opposition activists at rallies.In the end, according to the official figures, Lukashenka took 83% of the vote, with Milinkevich receiving 6%. Both in the United States and in Europe, doubts remained over the reliability of the results and the legitimacy of Lukashenka's third term in office.That same year, Milinkevich received the European Parliament’s Sakharov Prize for Freedom of Thought.After the unprecedentedly harsh suppression of protests in Belarus in 2020, he left the country and lived in exile with his family.He became an adviser to opposition leader in exile Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya and the founder of the "Free Belarusian University," with its headquarters in Warsaw.'Return to the European family'Immediately after the election, Milinkevich founded the civic movement "For Freedom," which he continued to lead for another decade.The movement championed European values and advocated for the development of civil society in Belarus, free and fair elections, democratic rights and European standards of living."By our mentality, traditions, history, culture and language, we are Europeans. For me, it has never been a matter of choosing which way we should go, east or west. For me it has been about returning to the European family from which we were forcibly taken into an empire," he said in one interview.For Milinkevich, the issue was ultimately existential - "about whether Belarusians will continue to exist in our own country. The master of the Kremlin does not recognise as a nation not only Ukrainians, but us as well," he said.'A man of exceptional dignity'Tsikhanouskaya has expressed her condolences to Milinkevich's family."A man of exceptional dignity, a kind soul and a brilliant mind, he was a true point of reference for many of us. For me, Aliaksandr was a source of support and wisdom, whose advice I always valued deeply," she wrote in a post on X."His devotion to Belarus, our language and culture, and his ability to unite and support people in the most difficult moments will remain with us," she added.President of the European Parliament Roberta Metsola also responded to the news on social media, writing: "Aliaksandr Milinkevich dedicated his life to the fight for democracy in Belarus.""His courage and legacy will stay with us. Europe continues to stand with the people of Belarus," Metsola said.In a 2006 interview, Milinkevich told Euronews: “The humiliation people feel when living in fear, the violation of their dignity — this, I believe, is the root cause of all Belarus’s problems."For years, he watched as Lukashenka’s regime crushed even the smallest expressions of dissent, stamping out any signs of resistance in Belarusian society. Yet he never lost his optimism. In fact, he said his faith in change had grown stronger after the events of 2020."We have experience, we had the fantastic year 2020, when everyone contributed to the Belarusian spirit and the desire to defend their 'self', truth, freedom. After 2020, I am an absolute optimist, because a completely different nation was born. People overcame their fear," he said.

Another Pakistani national had sustained injuries. "Pakistan strongly condemns the Houthi attack on a non-combatant commercial vessel. Such attacks endanger innocent lives, constitute a violation of international law, and pose a serious threat to freedom of navigation, maritime security, and the safety of commercial shipping in the Red Sea," the minister said in a post on X. Pakistan's foreign Ministry was in contact with Saudi Arabia and Yemen to ascertain further details of the incident, Dar said. Meanwhile, the Pakistani Embassy in Riyadh was coordinating the retrieval and repatriation of the mortal remains of their deceased nationals. Vessels under attack amid Middle East conflict On Tuesday, the US and Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis reported separate attacks on shipping as peace negotiations between Washington and Tehran seemingly stagnated once again. At the southern end of the Red Sea, a suspected Houthi attack on a small cargo vessel killed four crew members, Yemen's transport ministry had said. It was not immediately clear is this was the same vessel Dar was referring to. Commercial shipping and seafarers passing through the Middle East have increasingly come under attack by both the US and Iran since the conflict began earlier this year. https://www.dw.com/en/north-korea-tests-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5If0u This is North Korea's second ballistic missile test in less than a week Image: Ahn Young-joon/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement North Korea test-fired a ballistic missile off its east coast towards Japan early on Wednesday, its neighbors said, just days before US-South Korea Joint Military drills which Pyongyang views as invasion rehearsals. This is the second such test in less than a week. "Our military detected at around 6:00 am (2100 GMT on Tuesday) a ballistic missile launched by North Korea from the Wonsan area towards the East Sea," Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a message to reporters. Japan's Defence Minister Shinjiro Koizumi called the launch a "threat to peace and security in our region," adding that Tokyo had lodged a strong protest with North Korea through diplomatic channels in Beijing. "It's a serious problem that affects the safety of the Japanese people," he said at a press conference. Here's what we know about North Korea's test-launch from Japan: North Korea launched at least one ballistic missile on Wednesday morning Details were under close joint analysis between Japan, the US and South Korea Missile estimated to have fallen outside Japan's exclusive economic zone in the Sea of Japan Japan's prime minister issued instructions to maintain a complete state of readiness No reports of damage have been confirmed North's message ahead of joint military drills The suspected ballistic missile launch came just two days after South Korea and the US announced that they will kick off their annual joint military drills on August 17. The upcoming drills are a regular summer feature, designed to coordinate their defense against the nuclear-armed Pyongyang . North Korea has condemned these drills on several occasions before, often staging missile tests before and after the exercises. "North Korea has never simply let a South Korea-US joint military exercise pass without a response," said Lim Eul-chul, a North Korea expert at Kyungnam University. "This is a message that Pyongyang is closely watching the upcoming drills and could stage a provocation if it deems one necessary," he said. After last year's drills began , North Korean leader Kim Jong Un claimed the exercise had grown more provocative than before and showed Seoul and Washington's "will to ignite a war." He said it had prompted North Korea to respond with “proactive and overwhelming” countermeasures. On August 6, the US, South Korea and Japan detected the launch of a short-range ballistic missile from the North in what was its first ballistic weapons testing activity since late June. Pyongyang, which ususally releases details of tests a day later, did not initially confirm the launch. Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.dw.com/en/can-turkey-s-new-p.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IeBb Although the PKK announced its dissolution a year ago, it remains unclear whether all its fighters will lay down their arms Image: Sterk tv Advertisement One year ago, the outlawed Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) burned its weapons in a symbolic ceremony. The move was seen as a sign of its willingness to disband. Since then, the Kurdish side has been calling on the Turkish government to take political steps. Now, parliament has passed a bill submitted by the conservative Islamic ruling party AKP and its ultranationalist ally. Officially called the "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration," it is intended to provide the legal framework for the ongoing peace process. According to official figures, 467 out of 592 MPs voted in favor of the bill. The ruling party and its ally see this as the beginning of a new era: Under certain conditions, the bill provides for a suspension of sentences for PKK members — but only after the PKK and its affiliated groups have been confirmed to have disbanded and disarmed, so that peace, brotherhood and solidarity can prevail throughout the entire country. The pro-Kurdish DEM party also supports the bill, but it views it only as a first step that must be followed by further reforms. The pro-Kurdish DEM party also voted in favor of the PKK law. At the same time, it is calling for swift political and legal reforms Image: Adem Altan/AFP PKK law divides society and parliament Fierce opposition came from the ultranationalist opposition party IYI. Even during consultations, its delegate Ayyuce Turkes, daughter of the founder of the ultranationalist and right-wing extremist Grey Wolves, accused the government of rushing a landmark bill through parliament. She also criticized what she felt was an overly conciliatory stance toward PKK founder Abdullah Ocalan. She avoided using his name, calling him a "baby killer" instead, just as government agencies and media have done for decades. There was even a physical altercation. The debate highlights just how deep the divides are within Turkish society. While the ultranationalist IYI party rejects the process, the MHP, from which the Grey Wolves emerged, is now among its most important supporters — even though it had, previously, vehemently opposed earlier peace initiatives. Observers believe this shift in course and the progress in the peace process are also a result of the changed security situation in the region. Among other things, they mention the fall of the Assad regime in Syria , the war in Gaza and the conflict between Israel, the United States and Iran . Syria and Iran are also home to large Kurdish populations that are supported by various regional actors. According to the prevailing view, a more stable relationship with the Kurds who live within Turkey's own borders could provide Ankara with more leeway in domestic and foreign policy. The justice committee of the Turkish parliament convened to discuss the draft "Law on Strengthening National Solidarity and Social Integration" Image: ANKA What's in the law? The law applies to convictions for PKK membership, propaganda, financing or intentional support of the organization and its structures. For prison sentences of up to 15 years, enforcement is to be suspended for five years; for longer or life sentences, the suspension is to last ten years. Ongoing investigations are to be put on hold. According to pro-government media, up to 3,600 prisoners could benefit from this. The prerequisite is the complete disbanding of the PKK and the surrender of all its weapons and ammunition. Both of these conditions have to be verified by Turkish authorities and, subsequently, officially confirmed by the National Security Council, chaired by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan . Excluded are PKK members who were convicted prior to June 1, 2005 — the date on which the current penal code came into force — as well as those convicted of homicide and whose convictions are final. That means the regulation does not apply to PKK founder Ocalan either. In February 2025, the 77-year-old had called on the PKK to disband, declared an end to the armed struggle and spoke out in favor of a political solution. Turkey: An end to the Kurdish conflict? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video PKK views law as a mere first step The PKK also calls the bill a first step; it criticizes, however, wording and content. Its key demand remained unfulfilled: As long as Ocalan cannot directly coordinate the peace process under conditions of freedom, the issue of disarmament could not be resolved either. They said penal code regulations alone did not go far enough, more comprehensive democratization reforms were needed. The message was that as long as returning fighters or exiled politicians continued to be criminalized and were unable to engage in political activities legally, hardly any of them would leave the mountains where they've been staying. PKK leader Abdullah Ocalan in February 2026. The law passed by Turkey's parliament does not provide for his release from prison Image: DEM Even legal pro-Kurdish political activity has ben restricted in Turkey for decades: parties were banned, politicians were arrested or barred from political activity. To this day, elected mayors are being removed from office, and numerous politicians and activists are in prison. Among them are two former co-chairs of the Peoples' Democratic Party (HDP) that mainly represented Kurds, Selahattin Demirtas and Figen Yuksekdag. Peace without democratization? Political scientist Berk Esen criticizes the law for failing to offer concrete democratic solutions to the Kurdish issue. He also noted that, parallel to the peace process involving the PKK, the government had significantly increased the pressure on the largest opposition party CHP. For about two years, the Turkish judiciary has increasingly been cracking down on leading CHP politicians. Critics view this as an attempt to weaken the government party's strongest political rival. Among the most high-profile cases is that of former mayor of Istanbul and CHP presidential candidate Ekrem Imamoglu . He and hundreds of other party members are in prison, on charges of fraud and corruption. The entire CHP leadership under Ozgur Ozel was removed as well. He formed a new party several weeks ago. Criticism of Erdogan's role Esen primarily criticizes Erdogan's strong influence on the peace process. Although it is to be implemented by a committee chaired by the vice president and key ministers, who are also heads of the intelligence services and the National Security Council, Esen argues that it will ultimately be Erdogan as chairman of the National Security Council who decides when and which steps in the peace process will be implemented. This assessment is also shared by Reha Ruhavioglu, director of the Kurdish Studies Center. "Erdogan will clearly set the pace," Ruhavioglu said, attributing this to the asymmetric balance of power between the Turkish state and the PKK. In addition, Erdogan had learned his lessons from the failure of the peace talks between 2013 and 2015 and would now certainly assemble more control in his own hands. At the same time, experts say, Erdogan has his sights set firmly on the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections, and would want to limit any political risks associated with the process. Ruhavioglu expects further controversy, especially if former PKK fighters return to Turkey and remain at large. The government is therefore likely to allow their return, suspended sentences and political activity only gradually, and largely in response to public reaction. This article was originally written in German.
