Automotive, machinery, consumer goods, electrical equipment and business services are driving the UK–Romania economic relationship, with bilateral trade reaching £10.3 billion in the four quarters to the end of Q4 2025, up 4.9% year-on-year, according to the latest data released by the UK Department for Business and Trade. UK exports to Romania increased by 7.0% to £3.0 billion, while UK imports from Romania rose by 4.0% to £7.3 billion, positioning Romania as the UK’s 32nd-largest trading partner. UK–Romania economic relationship Trade in goods remains anchored by strong industrial and manufacturing activity. Cars were the UK’s largest goods import from Romania, reaching £1.3 billion and accounting for 30.4% of total goods imports from the country, following an 18.4% year-on-year increase. Other leading categories included beverages and tobacco, general industrial machinery and electrical goods. UK goods exports to Romania were led by beverages and tobacco, mechanical power generators and cars, highlighting the importance of established industrial supply chains and the potential for further sector-specific cooperation. Services are also becoming an increasingly important component of the bilateral relationship. UK services exports to Romania increased by 16.1%, reaching £1.5 billion and accounting for 50.5% of total UK exports to the country. Travel was the largest service category, representing 37.1% of UK services exports to Romania and 43.2% of UK services imports from Romania, followed by other business services and transportation. The significant contribution of business services reflects the growing sophistication of bilateral trade and creates further opportunities in professional services, technology, research and development, management consulting and digitalisation. Commenting on the latest data, Robert Uzună, Chairman of BRCC, stated : “The latest figures mark another increase in UK–Romania bilateral trade, confirming the positive momentum of the economic relationship. Particularly encouraging is the strength of key sectors such as automotive, machinery and electrical equipment, together with the increasing relevance of business services. These results provide a solid foundation for further development and point to new opportunities for investment, innovation and sector-specific partnerships. At BRCC, we will continue to connect companies, institutions and industry leaders, helping transform this momentum into concrete projects and sustainable long-term growth.” Robert Uzună, Chairman of the BRCC. As a central facilitator of this relationship, the British Romanian Chamber of Commerce (BRCC) continues to play a key role in building and sustaining a strong bilateral business ecosystem. Through its network of members, strategic partnerships and ongoing dialogue with public authorities in both countries, BRCC supports companies in identifying sector-specific opportunities, fostering relevant connections and developing new avenues for growth. Key fields of cooperation and further potential Beyond trade, investment flows highlight both progress and untapped potential. The stock of UK foreign direct investment in Romania stood at £752 million at the end of 2024, decreasing by 19.9% compared with the previous year and signalling an opportunity to strengthen investment pipelines and long-term capital engagement. In contrast, Romanian foreign direct investment in the UK increased by 22.2%, reaching £303 million, reflecting increased confidence and the continued international expansion of Romanian businesses. Romania’s broader economic trajectory reinforces its growing importance in the European landscape. Its GDP is projected to reach $480.8 billion in 2026, positioning the country as the world’s 39th-largest economy. Exporting activity was estimated to support approximately 2.6 million jobs in Romania in 2022, including around 103,600 jobs supported by exports to the UK. The UK’s overall market share in Romania stood at 2.2% in 2024, indicating further room for expansion, particularly in automotive, advanced manufacturing, industrial machinery, electrical equipment, business services and technology. The combination of established industrial supply chains and a growing services component provides a strong foundation for a deeper and more integrated economic relationship between Romania and the United Kingdom. About British Romanian Chamber of Commerce The British Romanian Chamber of Commerce is the premier business-led organisation promoting bilateral trade and investment between the United Kingdom and Romania. Our mission is to facilitate and increase trade between those two countries through business-to-business dialogue. The British Romanian Chamber of Commerce plays an influential role in creating and sustaining an environment in which free-trade and investment flourishes. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Ángel Aguirre speaking at a news conference in 2014. He is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice. Photograph: Jorge Lopez/Reuters View image in fullscreen Ángel Aguirre speaking at a news conference in 2014. He is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice. Photograph: Jorge Lopez/Reuters Mexico Former Mexican governor charged in case of 43 students who vanished in 2014 Ángel Aguirre indicted in case that rocked Mexico and became symbol of its brutal cartel violence Oscar Lopez Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.46 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The former governor of Guerrero state in Mexico has been formally charged over his alleged involvement in the disappearance of 43 students in 2014, a case that has become a symbol of the country’s brutal cartel violence and government impunity. Ángel Aguirre, who was arrested last week , is accused of forced disappearance and obstruction of justice for ordering the destruction of surveillance tapes that may have shed light on what happened to the students from the Ayotzinapa teacher training college on the night of 26 September 2014. On Wednesday, a judge ruled Mexico’s attorney general had presented enough evidence to formally charge Aguirre with forced disappearance and ordered that he remain in a maximum security prison awaiting trial. A lawyer for Aguirre denied his client’s wrongdoing. Guillermo Baradas told reporters: “We presented evidence demonstrating a high-level meeting attended by Mr Ángel Aguirre at the time the videos were allegedly handed over to him.” Aguirre’s indictment is the biggest breakthrough in the Ayotzinapa case since the 2022 arrest of Jesús Murillo Karam, who served as Mexico’s attorney general at the time of the students’ abduction. The brutality of the case rocked Mexico and continues to haunt the country more than a decade on. With the remains of only three students identified, it is not known what happened to the 40 others. On the night that they were abducted, the students from the Raúl Isidros Burgos teacher training college in the village of Ayotzinapa had commandeered several buses in the city of Iguala to get to a protest in Mexico City. But before they could leave Iguala, in Guerrero state, the students were attacked by a local criminal gang working with municipal police. A years-long international investigation determined that federal forces, both police and military, were also involved either by participating directly or failing to intervene as the students were taken away and presumably killed. The government at the time orchestrated an elaborate coverup, attempting to place blame for the attack solely on the criminal gang and local police. Suspects were tortured into giving false confessions and crime scene evidence was manipulated. Meltión Ortega, a spokesperson for the 43 students, said: “We want no more deception; we want to be told the truth and for those responsible to be punished. The victims from Guerrero deserve to have the actual perpetrators and the masterminds punished, rather than just seeing a charade, as has happened in serious cases of human rights violations.” Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum, has vowed to get to the bottom of what happened to the students and formed an investigative unit to dig into the case last year. “I’m going to put all my effort, all my energy, all my willpower [towards obtaining truth and justice],” she told reporters at a news conference last week. The suit followed allegations by Mandalena Lewis (pictured), a former flight attendant, that a pilot had sexually assaulted her and a colleague but that WestJet kept the pilot flying, thereby putting other employees at risk. Photograph: Olivia Bowden View image in fullscreen The suit followed allegations by Mandalena Lewis (pictured), a former flight attendant, that a pilot had sexually assaulted her and a colleague but that WestJet kept the pilot flying, thereby putting other employees at risk. Photograph: Olivia Bowden Canada Canadian airline WestJet agrees to settle flight attendants’ sexual harassment class action Female staff alleged company failed to maintain safe workplace, after allegations of sexual assault against pilot Olivia Bowden in Toronto Wed 12 Aug 2026 10.40 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 12.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Canadian airline WestJet has agreed to pay C$4.5m (£2.4m) to settle a decade-long sexual harassment class action lawsuit levelled by its female flight attendants, who alleged the company failed to maintain a safe workplace. The suit followed allegations by Mandalena Lewis, a former flight attendant, that a pilot had sexually assaulted her and a colleague, but that WestJet kept the pilot flying, thereby putting other employees at risk. A British Columbia judge on Monday approved the terms of the settlement, which were finalised on 22 June after months of negotiation. The payment will be distributed among the 3,452 flight attendants in the class action after expenses are removed, including legal fees. WestJet agreed to hire a third-party to conduct a workplace inquiry that will examine the prevalence of harassment, the extent of underreporting and how reporting systems can be made more effective. The suit had called on WestJet to implement mandatory anti-harassment training for pilots, along with an admission of wrongdoing and an admission of a breach of employee contract. None were included in the settlement. Lewis filed the initial class action against the airline in April 2016. She said she was dismayed by the results, especially given that two years ago WestJet paid out $12.5m in a baggage fee class action, nearly three times the amount agreed to in the sexual harassment suit. “I’m glad it’s over … but I’m just exhausted. I’m shaking my head,” she said, adding that she was advised the amount was the most that could be achieved given that legal expenses were piling up. Under BC law, the suit included all female flight attendants who worked for the company between 4 April 2014 and 28 February 2021, because Lewis’s suit alleged that all of them had their contracts violated by WestJet during that period because its employee policy promised that the workplace would be free from harassment. The suit claimed WestJet broke its policy by not taking enough steps to address reports of assault or to prevent harassment in the first place. Lewis said she was sexually assaulted by a WestJet pilot while on a layover in Hawaii in 2010 when she was 25 years old. In court documents, she said the same pilot had also assaulted another flight attendant in 2008. Though she reported the assault to WestJet, the pilot remained at the company and Lewis was eventually fired in 2016 for “gross insubordination”, according to court documents submitted by WestJet that year, which she and her legal team allege was retaliation for trying to hold the airline accountable internally. She said she abandoned an individual civil claim and instead created the class action after learning other flight attendants had also experienced harassment. Lewis said she reported the assault to police in Maui but alleges WestJet rerouted the pilot so he would not face questioning in Hawaii. She said fellow members of the class action suit were also disappointed with the result. Eight of them had already asked the province’s supreme court not to approve the settlement in February when some of the details first emerged, citing a low payout and a lack of accountability by WestJet. “We didn’t get justice here,” said Lewis. The case garnered national attention for exposing pilot behaviour toward female flight attendants and the vulnerability of the scores of young women who have historically been the target demographic for the job. A 2018 survey of more than 3,500 flight attendants by the US Association of Flight Attendants found that 68% had experienced sexual harassment in their careers while only 7% had reported an incident to their employer. WestJet did not respond to questions about Lewis’s claims of assault, and the allegations that it failed to keep the workplace free of harassment and does not properly investigate alleged sexual assaults. In a statement, the company said it was “pleased to have reached a mutually agreed upon settlement”. It said: “We are committed to strengthening our operations and training, focused on the safety and wellbeing of all WestJetters and we are focused on advancing a culture of empowerment.” Explore more on these topics Canada Sexual harassment Air transport Airline industry Americas news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: A near-miss incident at Sydney airport has shone a spotlight on staff shortages for air traffic controllers. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP View image in fullscreen A near-miss incident at Sydney airport has shone a spotlight on staff shortages for air traffic controllers. Photograph: Bianca de Marchi/AAP Transport Analysis What’s behind Sydney airport’s heavy delays and near-miss incident? Catie McLeod and Jonathan Barrett Air traffic controllers are short-staffed and exhausted – and new recruits face a difficult aptitude test and must train in Melbourne Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 11.01 EDT Share Travellers flying in and out of Sydney airport had already been dealing with heavy delays even before a Jetstar plane narrowly avoided colliding with a Qatar Airways plane on the tarmac early on Sunday. The day before, more than 150 flights passing through Sydney were delayed as the airport grappled with a lack of air traffic controllers, highlighting how just how delicate the rostering situation is. Two workers temporarily stood down after near-collision at Sydney airport Read more While Sunday’s incident is under investigation – an air traffic controller and a tug driver were temporarily stood down for mandatory drug and alcohol testing – the issue has shone a spotlight on the severe staffing shortages of those in charge of managing air traffic, and takeoffs and landings. ‘Doing the work of two people’ While air traffic controllers are entitled to unlimited sick leave under their terms of employment, Scott Nugent, the president of the air traffic controllers’ union Civil Air, says the issue “is that we do not have enough controllers just to fill the base roster before we have any sick leave at all”. “In practice, the only way you fill the roster is with overtime, and it relies on overtime just to do business as usual,” says Nugent. The experienced air traffic controller says workers are getting to the point where they’ve done so much overtime that they’re exhausted. Some staff are working 10 days on and then having one day off. “The reason you’ve seen these delays in the last week is because we increased the spacing between aircraft to maintain safety when we have less people,” he says. “If you’re doing the work of two people, you can only take half as many planes.” Much of the problem is tied to a pandemic-era program that incentivised a significant number of experienced staff to leave Airservices Australia, the commonwealth-owned organisation responsible for the management of the country’s skies, in 2021. With most planes grounded due to pandemic restrictions, 140 employees aged 56 or older accepted a redundancy. Soon after, the organisation embarked on a large recruitment drive but hirings have failed to keep up with demand. Gaps in rosters Despite the starting salary for a qualified air traffic controller post-training being $116,990 a year – an experienced supervisor can earn a base salary of almost $300,000 – Airservices has struggled with recruitment ever since the pandemic. In February 2024, two air traffic controllers who didn’t show up for work at Sydney airport caused cascading flight delays and cancellations across the country. Airservices narrowly avoided a similar incident in September last year. At the same time it has been trying to plug roster gaps, Airservices has been preparing for a once-in-a-generation transformation to a new flight-tracking computer system, as well as managing past allegations of workplace bullying. View image in fullscreen A plane prepares to land at Sydney airport, the busiest airport in Australia. Photograph: Izhar Khan/Reuters A review into workplace culture, conducted by the former sex discrimination commissioner Elizabeth Broderick’s firm, found 27% of staff in 2023 had experienced bullying in the past 12 months, up from 23% in 2020. From July 2022 to 2026, Airservices says it endorsed 245 controllers, most of whom qualified in 2025-2026. Over the same four-year period, 86 controllers left the organisation. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Airservices says it now has a record number of controllers across Australia. There were 985 controllers in December 2020 and 1,073 as of July this year, according to the organisation. However, the organisation says the demands on its workforce have also grown significantly, citing the new Western Sydney airport and its recent takeover of the airspace at Ballina in northern New South Wales . There still aren’t enough controllers at Sydney , Australia’s busiest airport. Tough tests and training demands A newly qualified controller can’t just fill the gap left by a retiring veteran. After 18 months of training, a newly qualified controller may be able to work in one position at a Sydney tower, such as helping organise the taxiways around the domestic airport. That person wouldn’t be qualified, for example, to work on the taxiways around the international airport, or runways, which require additional training, making newer employees less able to fill urgent vacancies. Airservices acknowledges there’s a problem. It says training experienced controllers for Sydney airport is its “top priority” but it can’t say when it will have recruited a sufficient number. Nurses sleeping in campgrounds, shops shutting and two-hour school buses: what the closure of Victoria Pass means for the Blue Mountains Read more It takes about two years to train a controller, and that’s only if someone can get past the initial screening, which includes a difficult online aptitude test as one of the first hurdles. “Only a very, very small number of people get through the application process,” says Nugent. “We’re usually talking about 2,000 people who might apply, and you hire 15 of them.” Additionally, applicants must move to Melbourne for the mandatory training. Only offering training at one location is seen as an impediment, because some applicants don’t want to relocate given there’s a risk they don’t pass. Airservices says it is considering different training locations, and says it has a new simulator in Sydney. Photograph: Ian West/PA View image in fullscreen Kyaw Zwar Minn outside at his north London residence in 2021. Photograph: Ian West/PA UK news Ex-Myanmar ambassador to UK on trial for trespassing in diplomatic residence Kyaw Zwar Minn was ousted for declaring loyalty to Aung San Suu Kyi after 2021 coup but refused to leave his home Geneva Abdul Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.01 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Myanmar’s ousted ambassador to the UK has gone on trial on trespassing charges for refusing to leave a diplomatic residence after being unceremoniously locked out of the embassy in 2021. Shortly after Myanmar’s military seized power in 2021, triggering mass protests that spiralled into a civil war, Kyaw Zwar Minn was locked out of the embassy for declaring his loyalty to the deposed civilian leader Aung San Suu Kyi. On Wednesday he appeared in a London court charged with trespassing at a diplomatic residence between May 2021 and November 2024. Kyaw Zwar Minn, who still lives at the ambassador’s residence in north-west London, has pleaded not guilty. The former ambassador argues that the current president, Min Aung Hlaing, the general who plunged Myanmar into conflict and economic chaos, is illegitimate and had no power to ask him to leave the property. Min Aung Hlaing’s pro-military party won a landslide victory in elections earlier this year that have been widely condemned as a sham. Min Aung Hlaing is wanted by the international criminal court for crimes against humanity against the Muslim Rohingya minority . Kyaw Zwar Minn’s lawyer, David Perry, told the court: “The military authorities could not lawfully terminate his licence at the address. Nor could they legitimately use the property.” View image in fullscreen Kyaw Zwar Minnu Kyi pictured in 2021. Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The Guardian Prosecutors said Myanmar’s authorities instructed the former ambassador to “hand over state-owned properties” in April 2021, and that the Foreign Office also told him to leave the residence, but he did not comply. They argue that his view of the Myanmar government – which is not formally recognised by most democratic countries, including Britain – does not provide a defence. “Having been granted permission to reside at Myanmar House as the ambassador, his refusal to vacate the diplomatic premises after he was removed from that position means that he is guilty of the offence of diplomatic trespass,” the prosecutor Louise Oakley told the court. Kyaw Zwar Minn previously told the Guardian he spent a night in his car outside the embassy in April 2021 after his then deputy, Chit Win, and a military attache, Soe Aung, locked him out of the building on the regime’s orders. He said at the time that he no longer felt safe at the north London residence and had contacted the police after former staff delivered a letter ordering him to move. Friends and relatives in Myanmar had been forced into hiding fearing reprisals as a result of his stance, he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The 68-year-old became a diplomat under Aung San Suu Kyi after a long career in the army and has called the “Rohingya issue” very important. Before his removal as ambassador, he had been told by a source in Myanmar’s foreign ministry that his staff were spying on him. He anticipated in 2021 that the crisis would lead to civil war. “You can see the military government is not going to step back,” he said. “More people will die and the economy is going to collapse. Then anything can happen in our country.” The court case comes as the war enters its sixth year. More than 100,000 people have been killed and more than 5 million displaced, according to the Council on Foreign Relations. Aung San Suu Kyi, now 81, has been detained on a range charges since the military took power. She was previously held under house arrest for 15 years under a past junta, and was awarded the Nobel peace prize in 1991. After her election as state counsellor in 2015, she became a pariah for leading a regime that excused a genocide, jailed journalists and locked up critics. https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: The funeral procession at Buckfast Abbey in Buckfastleigh. Before the service, police officers and sniffer dogs searched the grounds. Photograph: Mike Davies on behalf of Buckfast Abbey/PA View image in fullscreen The funeral procession at Buckfast Abbey in Buckfastleigh. Before the service, police officers and sniffer dogs searched the grounds. Photograph: Mike Davies on behalf of Buckfast Abbey/PA Ann Widdecombe Politicians among mourners at funeral service for Ann Widdecombe Family, friends and colleagues attend service at Buckfast Abbey, which former MP described as her ‘safe haven’ Rachel Hall Wed 12 Aug 2026 13.21 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 14.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google About 100 family, friends and colleagues of Ann Widdecombe have attended a funeral service for the former Conservative minister, who was killed in her home in Devon last month. Politicians and broadcasters were among the mourners at Buckfast Abbey in Buckfastleigh, a Catholic abbey in Devon where Widdecombe regularly worshipped and which she described as her “safe haven”. A 90-minute requiem mass – where prayers are offered for the soul of the dead – was held for the former MP and Reform UK spokesperson. Before the service, police officers and sniffer dogs could be seen searching the grounds. Widdecombe died on 8 July, aged 78, after she was hit over the head with a hammer 21 times at her home in Haytor. Joshua Kerry, 28, of Rotherham, South Yorkshire, was charged with her murder on 20 July. It is understood that Reform leader, Nigel Farage, did not attend the funeral because he did not wish to be a distraction. He is expected to attend a public memorial planned for later this year. View image in fullscreen Buckfast Abbey paid tribute to Ann Widdecombe, recalling her ‘sharp intellect’ and dedication to public service. Photograph: Mike Davies on behalf of Buckfast Abbey/PA Those slated to attend included the shadow chancellor, Mel Stride, the former Conservative justice minister Crispin Blunt and the broadcaster Iain Dale. The private mass featured a homily from the Rt Rev David Charlesworth, the abbot of Buckfast. He said: “In the midst of the shock, clamour and sometimes unwarranted comment surrounding her death, our response is to pray for the repose of her soul, to give thanks for her fortitude, and offer Holy Mass in this abbey church, which Ann called her safe haven.” An earlier statement from the abbey said: “Ann was a woman of profound faith, a faith which found expression in the public forum of politics. Ann was unafraid to express her unwavering convictions, formed through her Roman Catholic faith. She had a sharp intellect and was a dedicated public servant.” View image in fullscreen Mourners arriving for the funeral. Photograph: Matt Keeble/PA The order of service showed tributes would be paid by the Rev Roger Widdecombe, Widdecombe’s nephew, and Christian Sweeting, a close friend. Donations made in her memory will be divided between the Leprosy Mission and Abound, supporting the projects of the Christian Endeavour Hostel in India. Widdecombe was first elected as a Conservative MP for Maidstone in 1987 and became a prisons minister in the 1990s. She later became a member of the European parliament for the Brexit party. At the time of her death she was a spokesperson on immigration and justice for Reform UK. She had also appeared on Strictly Come Dancing and Celebrity Big Brother. https://www.theguardian.com/education/20.text: Jason Arday was appointed as professor of sociology of education in 2022. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Jason Arday was appointed as professor of sociology of education in 2022. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian University of Cambridge Cambridge agrees to hold independent inquiry into Jason Arday appointment Vice-chancellor Deborah Prentice says she recognises the ‘difficult case’ has damaged the university Richard Adams Education editor Wed 12 Aug 2026 12.28 EDT First published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 08.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Cambridge University’s leadership has bowed to internal pressure for an independent investigation into its appointment of Jason Arday as a professor, with its vice-chancellor admitting the affair has damaged the institution. Prof Deborah Prentice said she recognised the “anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case” but described it as an aberration that should not be used to cast aspersions on the abilities of its staff of colour. Senior Cambridge academics had called for the university to hold a fully independent inquiry into the circumstances around Arday’s appointment as professor of sociology of education, after the details of his career and life story were exposed to intense scrutiny. Dons call for Cambridge leaders to take blame for Jason Arday appointment Read more The university initially defended him as the “victim of a vile campaign to undermine his credibility” but he resigned last week after a series of his claims were called into doubt. In a letter to staff, Prentice said: “I know there is anger and anxiety around this damaging and difficult case … We will now investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the faculty of education back in 2022 and his time here in Cambridge since his appointment nearly four years ago. “That investigation, as you say, should be thorough and transparent, and will be carried out independently by senior academics from within and beyond Cambridge.” The university did not supply any details of the investigation’s membership or its terms of reference. Prentice said the investigation’s findings would be used to review Cambridge’s appointment process for senior roles, and that its education faculty bore some responsibility for Arday’s selection. She also highlighted that Arday had held positions at Durham and Glasgow universities before applying to Cambridge for a professorial chair. The rise and fall of Jason Arday: a full rundown of the questions being asked Read more “As you are fully aware, appointments to senior academic roles, as in the case of the faculty of education and Jason Arday, are currently led at department level,” she said. “I note that Durham and Glasgow universities have announced that they are also investigating the circumstances surrounding the appointment of Jason Arday to academic posts there.” However, academics at Cambridge said Prentice’s description of the appointment process was “nonsensical”, and Arday’s appointment had been made by a separate board of electors chaired by a representative of the university’s leadership. While Glasgow has announced its own investigation into Arday’s selection, Durham University declined to endorse Prentice’s comments. A spokesperson for Durham said: “Since the recent emergence of questions relating to the circumstances surrounding Jason Arday’s appointment to a chair at Cambridge University, we have looked into his appointment to a junior academic role at Durham in 2019. He was appointed following a standard, competitive recruitment process in which he met published criteria for the role. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion “He left Durham over four years ago and no longer has any formal association with us. Allegations about plagiarism in his PhD did not surface until after he had left Durham.” Prentice also recognised the effect of the controversy on other black and minority ethnic academics at Cambridge, after some had described the atmosphere as toxic. She said: “In light of the focus on this troubling case and the widespread commentary around it, I want to be very clear that we do not need the outcomes of an investigation to clearly and loudly affirm that our staff of colour are highly valued, for their scholarship, their achievements and the contributions they make to the institution and the wider academic community. “This particular case is an aberration and should not be used to cast aspersions on their work or the legitimacy of their roles at Cambridge. “The desire for quick answers and rapid responses is understandable, but we need to allow these reviews to complete their work effectively so we can learn from any mistakes and, where needed, improve our processes.” Prentice joined Cambridge from Princeton University in 2023, several months after Arday’s appointment. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/12/libya.text: The head of military intelligence for the Libyan National Army (LNA) led by Field Marshal Khalifa Haftar has been killed in a car bombing in Benghazi, authorities confirmed on Tuesday.Fawzi al-Mansouri was assassinated on Monday when an explosive stuck to his car detonated as he was leaving a local mosque at night, the statement said.Al-Mansouri was a senior figure within the LNA's intelligence apparatus and had close ties to the Haftar family.He played a key role in the LNA's campaign against jihadist groups, including the so-called Islamic State group (IS), between 2014 and 2017 in eastern Libya.Al-Mansouri, whom the LNA described as a "heroic martyr," was also a leading figure during Haftar's 2019 offensive to seize the capital Tripoli in an operation backed by Russia and Egypt.Haftar's offensive was eventually beaten back by forces loyal to the Tripoli government, which was in turn supported by Turkey.Khaled Haftar, the son of Khalifa and LNA's chief of the general staff, said in a statement that an investigation was opened, adding that "indicators point to a despicable terrorist tactic"."Terrorism is a project targeting the entire region, not just Libya," the statement added.The bombing was a setback to efforts by the Haftars to paint a picture of stability in the areas they control."An attack of this sophistication in an LNA stronghold is also a major blow to the group's security credentials," analyst with UK-based Verisk Maplecroft Hamish Kinnear said."The intelligence required to target such a high-profile figure successfully is indicative of significant capabilities on the part of the responsible actor," Kinnear added.Authorities have yet to identify the perpetrators.Tripoli government condemns 'terrorist attack'Libya has been split between rival administrations since NATO's intervention helped topple Muammar Gaddafi in 2011.Two governments are currently vying for power: the UN-recognised administration in Tripoli, led by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, and a rival administration in Benghazi backed by the elder Haftar, who is considered the de facto ruler.Dbeibah has governed since 2021 following a UN-brokered political agreement but without a fresh electoral mandate, as a planned December 2021 election was cancelled amid disputes over candidate eligibility and the legal basis for the vote.His government has faced sustained domestic opposition, including protests in Tripoli earlier this year over electricity cuts.A former Gaddafi general and close ally who defected and lived in the US for nearly two decades before returning to Libya after 2011, Haftar built the LNA into the main force in the east and south.The Tripoli-based government issued a statement denouncing a "terrorist attack" against al-Mansouri, saying it condemned the killing "regardless of one party's positions or alliances".Khaled's office later said in a statement that authorities arrested a "terrorist cell in Benghazi that was preparing to carry out acts of sabotage" but did not say whether it was linked with al-Mansouri's killing.Authorities in Benghazi held al-Mansouri's funeral on Tuesday afternoon, publishing photos that showed armed men in military fatigues with the attendance of senior LNA officials at the ceremony, including Khaled and Saddam Haftar.In a statement, the LNA said it would "not cease fighting terrorism and will continue our struggle for the stability and security of Libya, as well as for the unification of its institutions".US wants Saddam to take over Libya?Libya holds Africa's largest proven oil reserves, which have fuelled both sides of the political divide.Yet efforts remain under way to unify the country's executive powers under a Washington-mediated plan that the LNA has publicly backed.Under the leaked terms of the plan, Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah would remain in charge of the Tripoli-based government while Lieutenant General Saddam Haftar — also Khalifa's son — would be elevated to a senior national executive role, possibly heading a unified presidential structure.Saddam Haftar was appointed deputy commander-in-chief of the LNA in August 2025 as part of a restructuring that effectively distributed operational command among Khalifa's main heirs."None of this bodes well for a US plan to re-unify Libya," Kinnear said, adding that under the roadmap, neither side "is likely to be satisfied with their respective positions for long"."A new, destabilising power struggle could soon emerge."Libya expert Jalel Harchaoui said the killing would "disrupt, or at the very least delay" the US-brokered deal."The agreement rests on two premises: that security reigns supreme in Benghazi, and that for senior officers, loyalty to Saddam (Haftar's son and heir apparent) guarantees protection in the Benghazi stronghold," Harchaoui explained.But "a bomb that kills the head of military intelligence as he leaves a mosque undermines these premises," he said.Meanwhile, reunification would "require some gestures of openness toward reform and change within the army", Harchaoui concluded.

https://www.dw.com/en/eurovision-bars-co.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IiJH This year’s Eurovision Song Contest was won by Bulgaria’s entrant Dara, who won with her song "Bangaranga," meaning the 2027 contest will take place in the country for the first time Image: Georg Hochmuth/APA/AFP Advertisement Eurovision Song Contest organizers announced rule changes that would prevent countries involved in an armed conflict from hosting the event. Israel and Ukraine are among the countries the rule could affect, with both having enjoyed recent success in the competition. What did the Eurovision organizers say? Eurovision is typically staged by the broadcaster from the country that won the previous edition as part of a co-production involving members of the European Broadcasting Union (EBU). Under the new rules, "the winning broadcaster will automatically be ineligible to host the Contest if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region," the EBU said. Canada to join 2027 Eurovision Song Contest To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The EBU may commission an independent security assessment if necessary. If the winning broadcaster is deemed unable to stage the contest, another broadcaster will be selected. Why is the Eurovision changing the rules? The EBU did not name any particular country as the reason, but Israel finished second at Eurovision in both 2025 and 2026. Five countries — Spain, Ireland, the Netherlands, Slovenia and Iceland — boycotted the 2026 contest in Vienna, saying they could not participate alongside Israel because of the war in Gaza . Israel is currently involved in the war in Iran. The new rule formalizes a challenge Eurovision has faced before. Ukraine hosted the contest in 2017 despite fighting in the east of the country, but after winning Eurovision in 2022 it was unable to stage the following year's event because of Russia's full-scale invasion. Liverpool instead hosted Eurovision 2023 in the United Kingdom on Ukraine's behalf. Russia has been excluded from Eurovision since 2022, when the EBU banned it following its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. What else is changing about the Eurovision? Under the new rules, the EBU is raising the minimum age for performers from 16 to 18 to reduce pressure on young artists. Lead vocals must also be performed live and cannot be supported by pre-recorded voices. Russia launches Eurovision rival music contest after ban To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The EBU said the clarification was intended to protect the integrity of performances and ensure audiences hear the lead singer live. Eurovision director Martin Green said the contest's rules were reviewed each year to keep the competition fair and transparent. Next year's contest will be held in Bulgaria following Bulgarian pop singer Dara's victory in Eurovision 2026 in Vienna with "Bangaranga." https://www.dw.com/en/russia-why-is-the-.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IiKB Yabloko Party Chairman Nikolai Rybakov attending a hearing at the Russian Supreme Court to disqualify Yabloko from the 2026 State Duma election Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance Advertisement On Monday Russia's supreme court upheld a lawsuit against the anti-war opposition party Yabloko. Its candidates will now be barred from taking part in the parliamentary elections on September 18 to 20. The case against Yabloko was brought by the pro-Kremlin party Rodina, which accused it of infringing copyright with its election campaign materials. Rodina also made the claim that Yabloko had engaged in extremist activities and had received illegal financing from abroad. The verdict was pronounced by presiding judge Vyacheslav Kirillov. This was the same judge who, in April, banned the Russian human rights organization Memorial and designated it an extremist organization. Kirillov also previously dismissed legal complaints against the Russian prison service filed by the prominent opposition politician Alexei Navalny . Navalny spent many years in Russian prisons prior to his death in jail in 2024. At least 500 people gathered in front of the Supreme Court to show their support for Yabloko. They distributed apples and sang songs. The name Yabloko – "apple" in English – derives from the initials of the party's three founders, Grigory Yavlinsky, Yury Boldyrev and Vladimir Lukin (YaBL). The apple is now well-known as a symbol of the party. At the end of the nine-hour court session, security services threatened the people gathered outside the courthouse with arrest, also warning young men that they could be taken to an army enlistment office. Several hundred people, most of them young, gathered outside the Supreme Court to await the outcome of the hearing Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance "You are mistaken if you believe that, with a stroke of a pen, you can write off millions of people who want peace, freedom and a normal future for their country," Nikolai Rybakov, the leader of Yabloko, wrote on Telegram that evening. He insisted that the party had not broken any Russian laws, and announced that he would appeal the judgement. The Kremlin 'got scared' Grigory Yavlinsky, one of the founders of Yabloko, said those in power were afraid of Yabloko's program, which calls for an election "for peace, freedom and a life without fear" – because, he said, "removing a party with a platform like this from the election, without any real grounds, is the political system exposing itself." The lawsuit came at the same time as an appeal by Russian opposition and cultural leaders living abroad for people to support Yabloko. They include the politician Yulia Navalnaya , Alexei Navalny's widow, as well as Lyubov Sobol, Ilya Yashin and Andrei Pivovarov. The writer Dmitry Bykov, human rights activist Oleg Orlov and other prominent people also voiced their support for Yabloko. Navalnaya, who now leads the Anti-Corruption Foundation (FBK) her husband set up in 2011, responded to the verdict. The Kremlin was originally going to let Yabloko stand in the elections, she said, but those in power "got scared" and had the party blocked. Navalnaya wrote on Telegram that the powers-that-be had observed a development they wanted to stop at any cost: People were starting to join forces. This, she wrote, was less about support for Yabloko than the possibility for millions of Russians to express how they really felt about Vladimir Putin and the war in Ukraine. Andrei Pivovarov, a political activist who lives in exile in Germany and is a coordinator of the Russian Antiwar Committee , explained to DW that the opposition had not believed supporting Yabloko would bring about swift political change or an end to the war. The aim, he said, had been to make visible the extent of anti-war sentiment in Russia. "There would have been a dozen parties on the ballot who are pro-war, and one that is pro-peace. The war wouldn't end even if Yabloko were to get representatives into the State Duma. But we would have seen that a lot of Russians oppose the war," said Pivovarov. This view, he added, would not simply disappear now Yabloko has been barred from standing. What were the Kremlin's plans for Yabloko? The political scientist Ivan Preobrazhensky speculated in an interview with DW that the banning of Yabloko could be a consequence of a power struggle between different interest groups in the Kremlin. He suggested that the security bloc allied with the federal security service, the FSB, may have wanted Yabloko to act as a counterweight to the New People party. This is regarded as a project of Sergey Kiriyenko, the first deputy chief of staff of the presidential administration. Another version of events is that Kiriyenko himself may have tried to create the impression of political rivalry, and underestimated the potential of anti-war feeling in the country. Yabloko party chairman Rybakov (right) with his lawyer, during the hearing Image: Yevgeny Messman/TASS/picture alliance Preobazhensky says the government underestimated the number of people in Russia who oppose the war and are ready to support a political force campaigning for an end to the war in Ukraine . Surveys, he says, indicate that there is substantial demand for such a political alternative. He also believes that the Kremlin initially intended to let Yabloko run in the election but changed its mind when it saw how much support the party was getting. Another political scientist, Mikhail Vinogradov, thinks there was a different calculation behind the move. If Yabloko had scored very few votes in the election, the Kremlin could have painted a picture of a population solidly behind the war. A poor result would also have served to disillusion those who oppose it. Barring Yabloko makes independent election monitoring more difficult. The party is now no longer allowed to send representatives to monitor polling stations. Roman Udot, a Russian specialist in electoral observation, explains that Yabloko has also enabled access for independent observers in the past. Does the Kremlin have the situation under control? The State Duma elections are taking place at a time of growing uncertainty in Russian society, says Margarita Zavadskaya from the Finnish Institute of International Affairs. She points to data from the Russian Public Opinion Foundation (FOM), which regularly records the population's prevailing view of the situation in the country: optimism or alarm? At the end of July, 57% of those surveyed said that they were worried. This is the highest level since mobilization in the autumn of 2022. FOM surveys should be taken with a grain of salt, but Zavadskaya says an increase like this in high summer indicates that "something is not going according to plan." She gives the increase in drone attacks, deaths, fires in warehouses and rumors of a fresh mobilization as the reasons, and comments that the summer of 2026 has been the most unsettling for the people in Russia since the beginning of the full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine. She also believes the number of people who support the war is going down rather than up. The Russian leadership therefore has good reason to be nervous. "For the Kremlin, the ideal scenario would be a boring election with low turnout and no noteworthy events," says Zavadskaya. "Right now, though, this seems unlikely, as the situation in the run-up to the election does not appear normal, nor does it give the impression that the government has the situation under control." https://www.dw.com/en/germany-more-power.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ii9Z Germany is set to give its intelligence agencies new powers Image: imago/bonn-sequenz Advertisement The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (Bundesverfassungsschutz, BfV) and the Federal Intelligence Service (Bundesnachrichtendienst, BND) are secret services. Both operate covertly — the former domestically, the latter abroad. They have long complained that they have fewer powers than their counterparts in other countries. To better defend Germany against internal and external threats, the cabinet approved a draft bill on Wednesday . Parliamentary approval is still pending; the MPs' summer recess ends in early September. However, it is considered a mere formality that the Bundestag, the lower house of parliament, with the government majority of conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) and Christian Social Union (CSU) and center-left Social Democrats (SPD), will give it the green light. Germany's largest intelligence reform since World War II A new era for the German intelligence services is then expected to begin in early 2027. Their scope of operations would extend far beyond their current powers. It would then be possible, for example, to counter a cyberattack by neutralizing enemy IT systems. What is cyber warfare? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Should a state of tension or military defense arise, the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) could carry out acts of sabotage abroad. In addition, the BND, like the Office for the Protection of the Constitution, would be given the ability to manipulate or delete data. Proponents and opponents alike agree that this reform would be the largest in German history since the end of World War II in 1945. Intelligence services and police: Will they remain separate? After World War II, as a lesson learned from the atrocities committed by the Secret State Police (Gestapo) during the Nazi era, separate areas of responsibility were established in West Germany . Since then, intelligence services have been primarily responsible for gathering information, while the police handle threat prevention and law enforcement. This so-called principle of separation is now in jeopardy. Germany's Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt (CSU) speaks of "real intelligence agencies" and hopes that the planned reform will result in a more stable security architecture. "Sabotage, espionage, cyberattacks and covert operations by foreign powers require new responses," Dobrindt said. The agencies would be granted operational capabilities and active powers to effectively combat modern state terrorism and extremist violence. AI and drones: Possibilities and Risks To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Is the draft bill unconstitutional? The BND and the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution are also set to be granted new powers in their traditional core mission of collecting and analyzing information. These include the analysis of large volumes of data using artificial intelligence (AI) and the cross-referencing of biometric data with the internet. Data retention periods are also set to be extended. The Society for Civil Rights (GFF) considers large parts of the federal government's draft bill — which spans more than 700 pages — to be unconstitutional. With regard to the domestic intelligence service, the far-reaching access to private and public video surveillance in real time is seen as particularly problematic, GFF expert Kai Dittmann replied in response to a written inquiry from DW. The donation-funded nonprofit GFF believes the same applies to biometric matching against publicly available images on the internet and the training of AI using data collected by intelligence agencies. "There are no sufficient and clearly defined limits for such far-reaching intrusions, which above all affect countless innocent people," Dittmann criticizes. The GFF argues the planned additional powers for the BND would violate constitutional rights: The foreign intelligence service would no longer be limited to gathering intelligence, but would also be tasked with warding off threats, operating domestically and carrying out active cyber operations. "This blurs the constitutional boundaries between intelligence services, the police and the military," Dittmann says. Germany's spy chief believes US cooperation will continue To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Will there still be parliamentary control? The GFF also has serious concerns regarding the proposed reform of intelligence agency oversight, which is to be consolidated under the Independent Oversight Council. At the same time, there are plans to largely strip the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI) of its authority to oversee intelligence activities. Dittmann's conclusion: "The agencies are gaining significantly more power, while oversight is likely to be weakened." Clara Bünger, the domestic policy expert for the opposition socialist Left Party in the Bundestag, echoes this sentiment: "Because the intelligence agencies will no longer be required to inform those affected in many cases, effective legal protection is no longer guaranteed." Bünger announced that the Left Party will oppose what they see as authoritarian restructuring of the state. "There must never again be a secret police in Germany," she said. The Association of the Internet Industry (eco) has also expressed concerns: In light of the changing security landscape, intelligence agencies need modern technical capabilities, emphasizes board member Klaus Landefeld. "But the line is crossed when the state develops an interest in keeping security gaps open so it can continue to have access. Vulnerabilities must be closed and must not become a tool for intelligence agency access," Landefeld added. Meanwhile, Marc Henrichmann, chairman of the Parliamentary Oversight Committee for the Intelligence Services, has no such concerns. "I believe it's time to trust our own government, including our own security agencies," the Christian Democrat said in a Table Media podcast. Germany has the best-regulated intelligence services in the world, he said, and that should remain the case. This article has been translated from German. https://www.dw.com/en/italy-etna-eruptio.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IhLR Etna is Europe's most active volcano and has disrupted flights into Sicily several times in recent years Image: Etna Walk/AFP Advertisement Sicily's Catania airport on Wednesday suspended flights until at least 4 p.m. local time (1400 GMT/UTC) on Thursday, responding to fresh ash emissions from Mount Etna . The volcanic ash can pose a danger to aircraft and so has forced regulators to restrict access to the airspace around eastern Sicily, disrupting the peak summer holiday season. Where were flights affected? "Passengers are advised to check the status of their flights with their airlines," airport operator SAC said. "Further updates will follow in the coming hours." Catania airport flights have faced disruptions since late last week, becoming more intense as the eruption continues Image: Darrin Zammit Lupi/REUTERS Travel disruptions have impacted eastern Sicily in particular since last Friday, when renewed rumblings from Europe's most active volcano and shifting winds started carrying ash over the region. The airspace was fully closed only in recent days as the eruption continued. The prolonged restrictions at Catania — on Sicily's eastern coast just south of Mount Etna — have placed extra strain on Sicily's other airports during one of the busiest seasons for vacationers. Palermo Mayor Roberto Lagalla said that his city's airport had taken in around 190 flights originally scheduled to land on the eastern side of the island in recent days. For milennia, the port of Catania has sat in the foothills of Mount Etna, sometimes facing severe disruption or even damage from its eruptions Image: Giuseppe Di Stefano/Etna Walk/REUTERS Italy 's ANSA news agency also reported on Wednesday that flights were resuming at Comiso airport, a smaller hub south of Catania, after it had suspended traffic late on Tuesday. Some of the volcanic ash was also drifting south across the Mediterranean towards Malta, which had reported significant delays and some cancellations. On Wednesday, Malta International Airport continued to warn passengers of possible disruptions but said that conditions were improving. What is Mount Etna? Mount Etna is a roughly 3,400 meter (roughly 11,100 feet) stratovolcano on Sicily's eastern coast. Its precise height is ever changing, particularly amid periods of high activity when it can shed a few meters. The city of Catania is located not far to the south. Volcanic activity can lead to particularly fertile soils and other benefits that explain why cities like Catania were built so close to mountains like Etna Image: Etna Walk/AFP It is one of the tallest active volcanoes in Europe and Italy's highest peak south of the Alps. It's in an almost constant state of low-level activity and erupts in a more pronounced manner fairly frequently. It has caused disruptions at Catania airport several times in recent years . A UNESCO World Heritage Site, the first volcanic activity took place at Etna about half a million years ago. Both Roman and Greek mythology asserted that the god of blacksmithing — either Vulcan or Hephaestus — had his forge beneath Mount Etna. Roman poet Virgil wrote about an eruption at Etna in his epic poem the Aeneid, in what's thought to be a first-hand account Image: Etna Walk/AFP Edited by: Louis Oelofse If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google , so you'll always see our verified news first. https://www.politico.eu/article/eurovisi.text: Eurovision has changed its rules to block countries involved in armed conflict or any other “sensitive geopolitical situation” from hosting the annual song contest. The change comes as the last two years of the contest have been overshadowed by controversy surrounding Israel’s participation. Five countries staged an unprecedented boycott of the 2026 contest rather than compete alongside Israel. They pointed to the country’s war in Gaza — sparked by the October 2023 attack on Israel by Hamas militants — and the resulting humanitarian crisis it triggered. Advertisement Advertisement Despite this, Israel has come close to winning the 2025 and 2026 editions of the competition, garnering a strong public vote. Israel’s pubic broadcaster KAN has denied claims that results were unfairly influenced by mass voting campaigns. Eurovision is organized by the European Broadcasting Union, an alliance of 113 public service media organizations across 56 countries. Typically, the national broadcaster that wins the competition hosts the following edition in their home country. There have been some exceptions. When Ukraine won the 2022 contest, the organizers said the country could not host the following year’s contest due to Russia’s ongoing invasion raising safety concerns. The new rules would make a winning broadcaster automatically ineligible to host “if an armed conflict, a sensitive geopolitical situation, or any other situation materially affects the security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region.” The organizers could still commission an independent security assessment to determine whether a winner can safely host the contest. If a winner is deemed unable to host, the broadcasting union has the power to choose an alternative. Organizers said the rule change follows “feedback from participating broadcasters” after the 2026 contest in Vienna. They will apply from next year, when the contest takes place in Bulgaria. “These changes are about giving everyone involved greater clarity, protecting artists and ensuring the Contest continues to provide a safe and welcoming environment, while preserving the spirit and integrity that make the Eurovision Song Contest so special,” said Eurovision director Martin Green. https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-s.text: Polish Foreign Minister Radosław Sikorski on Wednesday threatened to reconsider Warsaw’s $50 million-a-year spending on Elon Musk’s Starlink network, joining a growing government backlash over new roaming restrictions set to hit Polish customers later this month. “Hey, @elonmusk, big man, stop discriminating Polish users of Starlink or we might re-think paying you $50 million p.a. for your services,” wrote Sikorski on X. The foreign minister's anger follows Starlink’s decision to exclude Poland from a shared European roaming zone that covers more than 30 countries, including Germany, Czechia, Slovakia and Lithuania. Customers within the zone can take their terminals across borders without triggering international-use restrictions. But Polish users will now face extra requirements when traveling. Advertisement Advertisement “Note: Poland is not included in the Europe region above. Accounts registered in Poland are treated as Poland-only for home-country use,” reads Starlink’s current guidance . Polish Digital Affairs Minister Krzysztof Gawkowski also went after Musk, accusing Starlink's parent company SpaceX of treating Poles as second-class customers and demanding it spell out the regulatory basis for the change. “Poland is not a second-tier market. Polish customers are not second-tier customers,” Gawkowski wrote on X. If SpaceX blames “local regulatory requirements,” Warsaw expects it to point to the specific rules rather than offer “general explanations,” he added. The new rules have applied to new customers signing up for Starlink since July 14, 2026 and will extend to existing Polish users on Aug. 17. This isn't the first time Sikorski and Musk have fought over Starlink. Last year, Musk told the Polish minister to “be quiet, small man,” after Sikorski warned that Warsaw could seek alternative providers for the satellite service it's financing for Ukraine. SpaceX did not immediately respond to POLITICO's request for comment. Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4g3.text: Figure caption, Watch: Was Donald Trump smuggled out of Air Force One in a catering truck? By Brandon Drenon Â and Â Bernd Debusmann Jr ,Â White House reporter Published 12 August 2026, 15:32 BST Updated 2 hours ago Two members of US President Donald Trump's cabinet were on a decoy plane that Trump secretly exited before boarding a different flight in Turkey last month, CBS News reports. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent remained aboard what was believed to be Air Force One and didn't join a flight that was provided to Trump over security concerns involving Iran. After Trump entered Air Force One on 8 July with both officials and members of the press, he hid on a catering truck to be clandestinely transported to a military plane. The label "Air Force One" applies to any plane the president is on, but in this case the original craft kept the call signal, becoming a decoy. Image source, Associated Press According to CBS - the BBC's US partner - Rubio and Bessent remained on board the first aircraft to maintain the line of succession in case something happened to Trump. In the event that the president dies or is incapacitated, Vice-President JD Vance would take power, followed by the Speaker of the House of Representatives and the President Pro Tempore of the Senate. The Secretary of State comes next in line, followed by the treasury secretary. Others who stayed on the initial aircraft designated as Air Force One included White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Steven Cheung, the White House's communications director. The second aircraft that flew President Trump out of Ankara also included Pete Hegseth, the defence secretary, according to US media reports. The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. Speaking to reporters on Monday night, Trump said the decision to undertake the deception was made by the US military and the Secret Service, who "wanted me to go in a different flight". The nature of the security threat remains unclear, with Trump providing no specifics, saying only that he gets "a lot of threats". "Any consequential president has a lot of threats," he added. Figure caption, Watch: What is it like to travel on Air Force One with Trump? It is also unclear what the cabinet secretaries and other officials, along with the Air Force members working on the plane, knew of the operation. Members of the press have said they were not aware that they were on a decoy flight. Various ruses, often referred to as "shell games" by Secret Service personnel, are common. Identical versions of the president's heavily armoured limousine, for example, often switch positions in motorcades, as do helicopters transporting the president in the air. More elaborate operations often take place during high-risk trips abroad, and in those cases reporters on Air Force One are typically briefed and asked not to report the movements in real-time. In March 2000, for example, then-President Bill Clinton flew to the Pakistani capital of Islamabad on an unmarked executive jet that landed after a decoy jet with the livery of Air Force One. Ahead of the trip, the White House informed USA Today reporter Susan Page - then the head of the White House Correspondent's Association - of the security arrangements. "They told me about the extraordinary security procedures being taken because of the dangers flying there, including the use of the decoy plane," Page revealed for the first time this week. "Of course, the dangers threatened the journalists covering the trip as well as President Clinton," she said in an interview with the Washington Post. It is also not currently clear what, if any, danger the occupants of the plane carrying Rubio, Bessent, other staff and the White House press pool were in during the Ankara trip. The White House Correspondent's Association has not publicly commented on the incident. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y4.text: Image source, Volodymyr Zelensky/Telegram Image caption, The Russian agriculture ministry announced it was working to redirect cargo flows to alternative ports following a barrage of Ukrainian drones By Laura Gozzi Published 12 August 2026, 18:20 BST Updated 1 hour ago A "massive" Ukrainian drone and missile strike on Russia's port of Novorossiysk has damaged two major grain export terminals and hit the last big Russian naval base on the Black Sea, reports say. Three people, including an eight-year-old child, were killed and another 24 injured in the overnight attack, local officials said. Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky said Kyiv had launched rockets, jet and naval drones in a "unique operation" to strike the Russian base, although he did not mention grain terminals being hit. Ukraine's military later said four Russian warships, including two frigates, were hit. Russia's military has not commented publicly commented on the issue. "The occupying fleet and all the infrastructure that supports it will not be safe as long as Russian aggression continues," Zelensky said in a post on social media. Most of Russia's Black Sea fleet is docked in Novorossiysk - one of the largest ports in Russia - after it was forced to vacate its former home base of Sevastopol, in the Russia-occupied Crimean peninsula, which was too exposed to Ukrainian attacks. A major grain trading company confirmed to Russia's TASS news agency that its terminal had been hit, while another told Reuters and Russian outlet RBK the same. The Russian agriculture ministry announced on Wednesday that it was working to redirect cargo flows to ports in the Baltic and Caspian Seas as well as land routes. It did not make any reference to Ukraine's attacks but said it was "taking into account current logistical constraints". Repeated explosions reportedly rang out over Novorossiysk throughout the night as air defences shot down aerial objects. An emergency situation was declared in the city on Wednesday, after the barrage of drones struck areas around the port and damaged pipelines, suspending water supply for the city. Elsewhere in the region a man was killed by drone debris, regional Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said. Several locations in the surrounding Krasnodar region were also struck by "several hundred drones" overnight, Kondratyev added, with dozens of buildings damaged, including homes. For its part, Moscow launched aerial overnight strikes which killed at least 11 civilians in Ukraine between Tuesday and Wednesday. The majority were killed when Russia hit the southern city of Zaporizhzhia with ballistic missiles and glide bombs. Russian President Vladimir Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. After a period of relative calm in the Black Sea, over the course of this summer Kyiv and Moscow resumed striking one another's ports and shipping. The last remaining sea route out of Ukraine has been badly affected by several deadly Russian strikes on cargo ships and the port of Odesa, through which Moscow seeks to put off foreign companies from trading with Ukraine. In July, the Ukrainian Agribusiness Club (UCAB) reported a 23% decrease in exports. Meanwhile, Ukraine has grown increasingly adept at carrying out long-range strikes on Russian territory. Its recent attacks on vessels in the eastern Black Sea have disrupted Russia's grain shipments, too. Russia is the world's largest wheat exporter - but according to a Moscow-based analytics company, exports for August could fall by more than half compared to the same month over the last five years due to the disruption in the Black and Azov seas. On Wednesday, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova accused Ukraine of carrying out strikes on Russian grain and agricultural infrastructure, resulting in a hike in global food prices and growing grain shortages. But Zakharova also said that for its part Russia would continue striking "facilities that [Ukraine's armed forces] use on the Black Sea to destabilise the navigation situation" until "the full elimination of threats to security projected to the Sea of Azov and the Black Sea". Concerns over how the war in Ukraine would affect global food supplies have been persistent since the start of Russia's invasion in 2022. Together, Russia and Ukraine account for a significant share of global grain trade, particularly for buyers in North Africa, the Middle East and parts of Asia. The 2022 Black Sea Grain Initiative, under which Russia agreed to lift its blockade on Ukraine's agricultural exports, did not last after Moscow resumed attacks on vessels using the maritime corridors to Odesa the following year. Ezt illusztrálandó, az asztal közepére odaraktak egy tabletet, kijelzőjén a „Győzelmi terv 2026” felirattal, alatta egy tátott szájú, nemzeti színű oroszlánnal. Kaminski egészen a 2026-os kampányig igyekezett a háttérben maradni, leginkább csak a sajtómunkatársak és a közéletet szorosan figyelők tudták, kicsoda ő. Pedig valójában már húsz éve dolgozik a Fidesznek, és jelentős szerepe volt abban, ahogy a párt kommunikációja az évek során egyre inkább elbulvárosodott. Ugyan megjelenése után Magyar Péter jelentősen erősebb volt a neten, volt idő, amikor még Orbán uralta az online teret. Ez 2010 környékén még újításnak számított, és Orbán az elsők között volt, aki élt a közösségi média adta lehetőségekkel, egy időben még a Tumblrre is posztolt. Akkoriban vette át Orbán Viktor közösségi médiás jelenlétének menedzselését Kaminski Fanny, akinek karrierjéről részletesebben is olvashat a választás előtt készített portrénkban . A Tisza Párt megerősödésére a kormánypártban sokáig technológiai kérdésként tekintettek, és jórészt annak tudták be, hogy Magyar Péterék jobban jelen vannak a digitális térben. Erről Orbán Viktor többször is beszélt , a korábbi miniszterelnök interakciókban és nézettségben rendre alulmaradt Magyarral szemben: a kampány hajrájában háromszor annyit posztolt, de így sem tudta utolérni . Ezt a hátrányt pedig a fideszes körökben is érzékelték. Mint a 444 márciusban megírta , a kampányt irányító Orbán Viktor egyre inkább Kaminskire támaszkodott a névleges kampányfőnök, Orbán Balázs helyett. Ahogy a kampány egyre inkább felpörgött, Kaminski Fanny több olyan videóban is felbukkant, amelyet Orbán Viktor kommunikációs csapata készített. Amikor a miniszterelnök kora reggel elindult otthonról, vagy megérkezett a Karmelitába, gyakran Kaminski várta egy-egy spontánnak beállított kérdéssel, de gyakorta interjúvolta meg Orbánt munka vagy utazás közben is. Így lehetett közelebb hozni az emberekhez Orbán Viktort, a spontaneitás látszatát kelteni, a miniszterelnök „emberi oldalát” bemutatni, belesni a „kulisszák” mögé, mindezt természetesen kontrollált, propagandisztikus keretek között. A rövid videók arra is lehetőséget adtak, hogy ha szükségét látták, a kampányba váratlanul berobbanó mikrosztorikra is reagáltathassák a Fidesz vezérét, miközben a fáradhatatlan vezér imidzsét is erősítik. Annak ellenére, hogy Kaminski Fanny 2010 óta Orbán Viktor stabil munkatársa, nem volt a kormányzati kommunikációs csapat alkalmazottja. Vállalkozóként azonban megtalálta a számításait: egyedüli tulajdonosa a Triton Communications Kft.-nek, amivel 2022-ben leszerződött a Miniszterelnöki Kabinetiroda. A cég bevétele 2021-ben még csak 20 millió forint volt, 2022-től viszont ugrásszerűen megnőtt: 2022-ben 260,7 millió; 2023-ban 800,8 millió; 2024-ben 942,3 millió; 2025-ben pedig már 1,087 milliárd forintos bevételt ért el . A cégnek öt alkalmazottja volt, a személyi jellegű ráfordítás tavaly 158 millió forintot tett ki. Kaminski 2025-ben 50 millió feletti osztalékot vett ki a cégből, az idei beszámolóban már csak 30 millió forint kifizetéséről döntött. Miután a kabinetiroda megkötötte a keretszerződést Kaminski cégével, négyszer meghosszabbították az évek során, és minden alkalommal emelték a megbízási díjat. A legutóbbi módosítás után, tavaly szeptembertől már a kezdeti összegnél havi 23 millióval többet, 86 millió 487 ezer forintot fizettek a Tritonnak, miközben a díjemelés ellenére a tartalmi követelmények nem változtak. A teljesítésigazolások alapján a videók átlagosan 15 másodpercesek voltak, de akadt olyan hónap, amikor mindössze 21 percnyi mozgókép és 411 fotó készült több mint 63 millió forintért. Fontos részlet, hogy a szerződést kivették a közbeszerzési eljárás hatálya alól arra való hivatkozással, hogy a miniszterelnök védett személy. Kaminski Fanny kedden arról írt a Facebookon, hogy a kormány az üggyel kapcsolatban több olyan sugalmazást tett , amelyek félrevezető képet festenek a munkájukról, ezért szeretne néhány tényt világossá tenni. Szerinte a Triton szerződésben vállalt feladata nem csak fényképek és videók készítéséből állt, a cég fejlesztette és üzemeltette a miniszterelnök honlapját, grafikai és egyéb kommunikációs szolgáltatásokat is biztosított. Kaminski szerint a szerződés teljesítésének feltétele volt a napi 24 órás rendelkezésre állás, ami nem alkalmi munkavégzést, hanem folyamatos készenlétet és szükség esetén azonnali reagálást jelentett. Azt Kaminski megerősítette, hogy a szerződés összege a négy év során emelkedett, de szerinte a kormány ehhez nem tette hozzá, ez az inflációt követte. Félrevezetőnek tartja kiemelni azt is, hogy a Triton Communications közvetlenül öt főt foglalkoztatott, mivel összesen több mint 30 ember munkájáról van szó. Elfogadja, hogy az új kormány felülvizsgálja az Orbán-kormány szerződéseit, de azt nem, hogy „ennek során egy tisztességesen működő magyar vállalkozást kiragadott számokkal, elhallgatott tényekkel és félrevezető sugalmazásokkal próbáljanak gyanúba keverni”. Tízszeres szorzóval dolgoztak? Az összeg, amit Kaminski kapott Orbán közösségi médiás jelenlétének menedzseléséért, elsőre hatalmasnak tűnhet. Ahogy egy sajtót és reklámpiacot ismerő nyilatkozónk fogalmazott, nagyobb újságok működnek akkora összegből, mint amekkorát Kaminski Fanni ötfős cége kapott a kormánytól. Arról, hogy mennyire tükrözheti a piaci realitásokat a Tritonnak havonta kifizetett összeg, több iparági szakértőt is megkérdeztünk. „Egy ilyen személy social media jelenlétét kézben tartani, csapattal, adott esetben a hét 7 napján 24 órában valóban sok feladatot jelenthet. Ezt viszont egy kisebb csapat kampányidőszakon kívül ennek töredékéért meg tudja csinálni” – írta Forgács Mariann, a social media fókuszú BeSocial ügynökség alapítója és ügyvezetője. Szerinte szakmailag semmi nem indokolja, hogy 24 órás jelenléttel vegyen részt az üzemeltetésben minden egyes munkatárs, és az elképzelhetőbb, hogy minden alkalommal 2-3 kolléga dolgozik egyidejűleg, megfelelő váltásban. A közösségi média posztok alatti moderáció az, ami nagyobb feladatot jelenthet, de szerinte ezt is lehet költséghatékony módon, egy lényegesen kisebb csapattal kezelni. „Azt gondolom, hogy egy ilyen jellegű feladatot ennek a tizedéért, de talán még olcsóbban is kényelmesen, üzletileg pozitívan el lehet látni. Persze nem ismerjük a szerződés részleteit, de nehezen tartom elképzelhetőnek, hogy szakmailag bármi indokolná ezt a minimum tízszeres szorzót.” Egy másik, névtelenséget kérő iparági forrás arról írt, hogy a legnagyobb magyar ügyfelek egy nagy ügynökségnél körülbelül 20-30 millió forintot hagynak ott havonta, úgy, hogy az egy full service szolgáltatás a social mellett esetleges kampányokkal, TV-ben futó reklámfilmekkel, aktivációkkal és egyéb feladatokkal. „Szerintem nincs olyan magyar kereskedelmi márka, ami évi 1 milliárd forintot hagy ott kreatív ügynökségnél, ami ugye jóval több és nagyobb szolgáltatás” – írta forrásunk. Fontos még, hogy ugyan egy TikTok-, és Facebook-oldal üzemeltetése önmagában pár százezer forint lehet, a politikai kommunikáció jóval speciálisabb egy céges tartalomgyártói munkánál, így szerinte egy ügynökségnek is kevésbé lehet viszonyítási alapja ehhez. A politikai kommunikáció egy bizalmi pozíciót is igényel, hiszen a közösségi médiás munkatárs gyakran egy autóban, egy repülőn utazik a miniszterelnökkel, akinek közeli munkatársa lesz. A kizárólagossággal is kalkulálni kell szerinte, mert míg egy ügynökség több hasonló céggel is leszerződhet, a politikai kommunikációt végző cég utána már nem dolgozhat a másik oldalnak. Ráadásul a jövőre nézve is rizikót jelenthet, és egyes piaci szereplők elzárkózásához vezethet az ilyen jellegű politikai elköteleződés. A politikai kommunikációs munkák nagyobb rugalmasságot is igényelnek, mindez együtt pedig ahhoz vezethet, hogy kicsit több pénzt kérhet el a kommunikációs vállalat, mintha egy céges ügyféllel dolgozna.
