A szakértő szerint ha ezt vesszük alapul, és úgy számolunk, hogy ebből az összegből semmit nem költöttek a hirdetésekre, teljesen indokolatlannak tűnik az árazás. Kaminski Fanny a feljelentésre reagálva arról írt, hogy ugyan cége csak öt főt foglalkoztatott, a munkát valójában több mint harmincan végezték, így jóval több emberre kell leosztani a havonta kifizetett összeget. Elsőre egészen meglepő lehet, hogy ennyi emberre lenne szükség a miniszterelnök közösségi médiás kommunikációjában, ezért a szakértőknél arról is érdeklődtünk, a piaci tapasztalataik alapján mennyire tűnik reálisnak ez a szám. Itt ugyanabba a probléma ütköztünk, mint az előzőekben: nem ismerjük a szerződés részleteit. Egyik forrásunk szerint azonban ha azt vesszük alapul, hogy a rendelkezésre állás miatt több csapatra is szükség volt, akik rotációban dolgoztak, és nem voltak állandó munkavállalói a cégnek, a harminc fő nem elképzelhetetlen. Ők így persze nem is voltak folyamatosan fizetve, csak amikor bedolgoztak a Tritonnak, tehát nem arról van szó, hogy harminc ember egész havi munkáját állták volna ebből a kormány által fizetett összegből. Egy jó fotós akár 200 ezer forintot is elkérhet egy napért, ha pedig a miniszterelnök vágóképeket is szeretne tenni a videókba, egyszerre több stáb munkájára is szükség lehet. Az erőműnél idén nyáron fellépett energiakrízis hátteréről, az ide vezető mulasztásokról itt írtunk részletesen. A kiemelt beruházásoknál a közbeszerzési eljárások egyszerűsített formában, indokolás nélkül folytathatók le, a szükséges közigazgatási eljárások ügyintézési határideje általában 15 nap, szakhatósági eljárásoké 8 nap, a kapcsolódó közterület-használat díjmentes, külön engedély nélkül 6 hónapig lehetséges. A paksi mederberuházásoknál a rendelet szerint a környezetvédelmi működési engedélyt 2026. szeptember 30-ig kell kérelmezni. A vízjogi létesítési engedély megszerzése alól a beruházás mentesül, de 2026. október 15-ig fennmaradási engedélyt kell kérni, vízgazdálkodási bírság nem szabható ki. A természetvédelmi engedélyezési eljárásokat 2026. október 15-ig kell megindítani, a fakivágási engedélykérelmet szintén ugyaneddig kell benyújtani, természetvédelmi bírság nem szabható ki. Deportations, detentions rise in upstate NY in 2025, data says WAMC Northeast Public Radio | By Sajina Shrestha , Maryam Ahmad Published July 29, 2026 at 4:51 PM EDT Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Bluesky Listen • 7:59 U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement / Wikimedia Commons FILE - An image of a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer taken on June 11, 2019. Since the beginning of the second Trump administration, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has been ramping up its operations throughout the country. In New York, it has led to conflict between the state and federal governments, with Gov. Kathy Hochul banning formal cooperative agreements between local law enforcement and ICE. The ban would restrict county jails from detaining individuals who are arrested for civil immigration violations. WAMC analyzed data from t he Deportation Data Project regarding detentions and deportations in New York State to understand better the expansion of ICE activity across upstate New York. The analysis is of people arrested in New York State and first detained in a New York facility — outside of New York City and Long Island. Here are three takeaways from the investigation. Press play above to listen to WAMC's Sajina Shrestha and Maryam Ahmad dig into their reporting. 1. Detention and deportation are up in the region, with more people with immigration violations getting detained and deported. Upstate New York saw a 2.6-fold increase in deportation for people who were first detained outside of New York City and Long Island. In 2024, 344 people were deported. In 2025, that number rose to 904. What's more, more people were in detention in 2025. Specifically, 438 people who were detained in 2025 were still in detention when this data was logged and pulled, which was March 2026. Also, while people were spending less time in detention in 2025, they were being moved around to different facilities more frequently. Sajina Shrestha / WAMC Deportation numbers by conviction charges More people with immigration violations are being detained and deported as opposed to convicted criminals. Immigration violations include people who may have overstayed their visa or are undocumented. In 2024, 82% of those deported were convicted criminals and only 5% of those deported were immigration violators. In 2025, immigration violators made up 46.5% of those deported. In 2025, 63.5% of people who remained in detention after being arrested had an immigration violation charge. In comparison, 27.2% of those detained had a criminal conviction. 2. Although people spent less time in detention, they were shuffled around to different facilities more frequently. A transfer between facilities and processing centers is known as a stint. A stay, on the other hand, is the amount of time someone spends in detention in total, regardless of how many transfers they have had. A person can have multiple stints in a given stay. While the average number of stints was the same in 2025 as in 2024, people have been spending less time overall in detention. So, while people deported in upstate New York in 2024 had an average stay length of 108 days, people who were deported in 2025 spent an average of 65 days; people had shorter time overall in detention in 2025, but they were sent to different facilities during that time more often. The most extreme example of this was a man who was reported to Romania after three months in detention in 2025. During those three months, he was moved between nine different facilities 14 times; those included facilities in New York, Louisiana, and Arizona. 3. Men made up the largest group of people detained and deported in 2024 and 2025. The data showed that, in 2024, 96.5% of the people deported were men, whereas in 2025, men made up 92.3% of those deported. Amongst women, that number rose from 1.2% deported in 2024 to 7% deported in 2025. These numbers also include an "unknown" category in which the person's gender was not specified. https://www.philstar.com/headlines/2026/.text: Philstar.com HOME Headlines Opinion Nation World Business Sports Entertainment Lifestyle Events Other Sections The Philippine Star Pilipino Star Ngayon HOME Bansa Metro Probinsiya Opinyon Palaro Showbiz True Confessions Dr. Love Litra-talk Kutob Komiks The Freeman HOME Cebu News Opinion Metro Cebu Region Cebu Business Cebu Sports Cebu Lifestyle Cebu Entertainment Pang-Masa HOME Police Metro Punto Mo Pang Movies PM Sports Para Manalo Para Malibang Banat HOME Balita Opinyon Kalingawan Showbiz Palaro Imong Kapalaran Punsoy Interaksyon HOME Trends + Spotlights Politics + Issues Celebrities Hobbies + Interests Rumor Cop Coupons HOME Top Stores Offers By Category Latest Posts SARA ON TRIAL SONA 2026 DUTERTE AT ICC FUEL PRICE TRACKER INFLUENCE OPS EXPLAINERS FACT CHECKS ENVIRONMENT My Profile Sign Out HOME HEADLINES OPINION NATION WORLD BUSINESS SPORTS ENTERTAINMENT LIFESTYLE EVENTS COUPONS OTHER SECTIONS Headlines Lithuania eyes sharing Ukraine-tested maritime tech with PCG MANILA, Philippines — Lithuania is looking to bring maritime security technologies emerging from the war in Ukraine to the Philippine Coast Guard, Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said, part of a widening security partnership between the two countries. Budrys said he discussed the technologies with PCG officials during a July 23 visit to the service's headquarters in Manila, describing them as systems that would make the coast guard's work easier. "I had a really good exchange with the Philippine Coast Guard on some technologies that would make their work — important work for the international community — easier," Budrys told Philstar.com in an interview on July 23. "We are talking about some technologies that ... concern the protection of the sea routes," he added. The Lithuanian minister noted that Russia's war in Ukraine has become the main driver of development in the defense industry and in dual-use technologies. "We have to use everything that we see is developing so fast in Ukraine, in their efforts and brave efforts to defend themselves, and also turn those technologies — the usable ones — in the peacetime for our own good," he said. Beyond maritime hardware, Budrys said Vilnius is offering "niche" high-tech capabilities, particularly in cybersecurity. The PCG said in a statement Monday that both sides agreed to establish a technical working group to explore cooperation in cybersecurity, professional training, and marine environmental protection, among others. Lithuania denounces Chinese vessels' behavior Budrys' visit comes amid heightened tensions in the West Philippine Sea. Lithuania has been among the most outspoken European critics of both Russian aggression and Chinese coercion, particularly after facing Beijing’s trade boycotts over its ties with Taiwan. Prior to his meeting with the PCG, Budrys told Philstar.com he had been closely following the reported incidents of harassment faced by the Coast Guard in the West Philippine Sea. On the day of Budrys's visit, the PCG had reported the China Coast Guard's (CCG) use of water cannons on Philippine vessels conducting a humanitarian fuel subsidy mission near Scarborough Shoal. Two days earlier, the PCG reported that CCG personnel had physically clubbed a Navy serviceman near Ayungin Shoal. "We were following the incidents that were happening in the West Philippine Sea, with the vessels that were acting under different covers of the civilian vessels coming from China," he told Philstar.com . "Those developments were really disturbing and [something] that all of the international community has to have its position on." He called the incidents breaches of international law and of UNCLOS. Budrys also drew a parallel with the Baltic Sea, where Lithuania and its neighbors have reported repeated damage to undersea cables and power links. At least eleven cables in the Baltic region have been severed or damaged since October 2023, caused by incidents of shadow vessels dragging their anchors across the seabed, making criminal intent difficult to prove under maritime law. "Those affected countries have to share their experience and ways on how to protect ourselves within international law, even understanding that the other side is not respecting it," Budrys said, warning that compromises in one theater threaten global stability. "If we cannot apply it here, why should it be applied somewhere else — for example, in the Strait of Hormuz?" he added. Lithuania was among 14 nations that recently marked the 10th anniversary of the 2016 South China Sea arbitral award — the landmark Hague decision that invalidated China’s expansive claims — reaffirming that the ruling remains legally binding. China's foreign ministry rejected the statement, which it said "disregards the basic facts of the South China Sea." The Philippines and Lithuania last year signed a defense cooperation agreement that included a focus on cyber- and maritime security. Lithuanian Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys also said he expects more of his country's cybersecurity and counter-disinformation firms to establish a presence in the Philippines. "There will be more presence from the ones that are dealing with cyber tools, and also that are dealing with countering different propaganda narratives," Budrys told Philstar.com in an exclusive interview on July 23. Budrys noted that several of these firms utilize AI-enabled monitoring systems. Beyond commercial tools, Lithuania is also prepared to share its operational frameworks for security operations centers, cyber legislation, e-governance infrastructure and digital public services. Lithuania is in the highest-level tier, or Tier 1, in the International Telecommunication Union's latest edition of the Global Cybersecurity Index, released in 2024. Meanwhile, the Philippines is under Tier 2 ("advancing"), already a jump from its prior classification of Tier 3 in 2020. Organizing government, civil society vs hybrid threats Budrys, who said he has spent close to 25 years in the security sector, said a lesson from Lithuania's experience is to concentrate the work in a small number of institutions rather than parcel it out across agencies. "It has to be whole-of-government approach, meaning that everyone is responsible, but you cannot share it around and everyone is doing everything," he said. "Then it will be at the end too many people in the kitchen." Vilnius said he assigned core counter-hybrid tasks to defense and strategic communications agencies, while leaning heavily on civil society — which Budrys called the "highest added value" component of Lithuania's security apparatus. He highlighted Lithuania's volunteer online networks , organized as non-governmental organizations, that track and debunk pro-Kremlin narrative operations. "We were fighting trolls with 'elves,'" Budrys said. Lithuania has mapped how responsibilities are divided among Russian state institutions, state media, and state-enabled actors — including organized crime — and is willing to share that intelligence, Vilnius' top diplomat said. Budrys noted that Lithuania is similarly targeted by China. During his trip to Manila, Budrys also met with the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) and denounced China's harassment of Philippine vessels as a breach of international law. The Lithuanian minister told Philstar.com that Lithuania was looking to share maritime security technologies refined during the war in Ukraine with the PCG. (Xinhua/Huang Jingwen) BEIJING, July 29 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang on Wednesday met with Slovak President Peter Pellegrini in Beijing. Noting that China and Slovakia share a friendship that has endured and grown stronger over time, Li said China is willing to work with Slovakia to carry forward traditional friendship, consolidate strategic mutual trust, respect each other's core interests and major concerns, expand all-round mutually beneficial cooperation, and jointly promote the development and prosperity of the two countries. China is also ready to work with Slovakia to better leverage the role of mechanisms such as the inter-governmental cooperation committee, promote high-quality Belt and Road cooperation, create highlights in cooperation in emerging fields such as artificial intelligence, and achieve a higher level of mutual benefit and win-win results, Li said, adding that China encourages more capable enterprises to invest in Slovakia. He expressed the hope that Slovakia will continue to ensure an open, transparent and non-discriminatory business environment for Chinese enterprises. As two major economies, China and Europe have a strong endogenous driving force for cooperation, which is fundamentally based on mutual benefit and win-win cooperation, Li said. He called on Slovakia to actively promote a more positive and rational direction in EU policy toward China. Pellegrini said that Slovakia attaches great importance to and is committed to promoting the long-term and stable development of bilateral relations with China, adding that the Slovak side is willing to strengthen exchanges at all levels with China, expand cooperation in investment, science and technology, transportation and logistics, artificial intelligence and other fields, and enhance people-to-people and cultural exchanges in education, youth and other areas to better benefit the two peoples. Slovakia looks forward to having more Chinese enterprises to invest in the country and will create a favorable environment for Chinese enterprises, Pellegrini said, adding that Slovakia is also willing to continue to actively participate in cooperation under the Belt and Road Initiative and within the China and Central and Eastern European Countries cooperation mechanism. Pellegrini said that Slovakia is willing to play an active role in the constructive dialogue and open, practical cooperation between Europe and China, which are in the interests of both sides and the world as well. (Xinhua/Pang Xinglei) BEIJING, July 29 (Xinhua) -- Zhao Leji, chairman of the Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (NPC), met with Slovak President Peter Pellegrini in Beijing on Wednesday. China is willing to work with Slovakia to continuously enhance strategic mutual trust, and deepen high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and cooperation in economy, trade, artificial intelligence and new energy, while promoting people-to-people bonds, Zhao said. He said the NPC stands ready to carry out friendly exchanges with the Slovak National Council in fields such as legislation and supervision, which is expected to better serve the cooperation between the two countries. Pellegrini said that the two countries' adherence to mutual respect, sovereign equality and continuous dialogue has laid a foundation for the long-term and sound development of bilateral relations. Slovakia is willing to enhance exchanges with China to promote understanding, deepen mutual trust and expand cooperation in areas such as artificial intelligence, he added. (KOTA) - The U.S. Department of Justice is looking to revoke the naturalized citizenship of ten people, including a former Rapid City Catholic priest. Marcin Garbacz, 47, is a native of Poland and became a legal permanent U.S. resident in 2008 and a naturalized citizen in 2014. Garbacz was accused of stealing about $269,000 in collections from three parishes in the Rapid City Catholic Diocese and was convicted of wire fraud and money laundering in 2020. He also pleaded guilty in 2021 to shooting videos of a 17 year old boy in the shower on a church trip to Poland. In the filing, the Justice Department says Garbacz illegally procured his citizenship by lacking the good moral character needed, providing false testimony during the naturalization process and concealing material facts and willful misrepresentations. Log In Create Free Account Russian air strikes killed at least 13 people in Ukraine on Thursday, including one in Kyiv, in attacks extending as far as the western city of Lviv, forcing neighbouring Poland to scramble fighter jets to secure its airspace. The attacks come as President Volodymyr Zelensky returns from the United States, where he said President Donald Trump agreed to give Ukraine licences for Patriot missiles. Air raid alerts sounded across most regions of Ukraine, with a Reuters witness saying explosions were heard in Kyiv. A few non-residential sites caught fire, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on the Telegram messaging app. One person was killed and two more injured in the capital, emergency services said, with six more, including two children, killed in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk and Poltava. Open this photo in gallery: People in Kyiv take shelter inside a crowded metro station during the Russian strikes. Alina Smutko/Reuters In Zelensky’s hometown, the central city of Kryvyi Rih, two girls aged 5 and 12 were among six killed, with eight injured in what Oleksandr Vilkul, the city’s defence council head, said was a direct strike by a Russian Iskander-M ballistic missile. “A dark night,” Vilkul said on Telegram, adding that the missile, launched from Russia’s Voronezh region, struck the home of a large family, and warned the death toll could increase as emergency workers clear away rubble. Open this photo in gallery: Rescuers work at the site of an apartment building in Lviv hit by Thursday's strike. Roman Baluk/Reuters In Lviv, close to Poland, rescue workers were scrambling to clear rubble to reach those trapped after Russian missiles damaged two apartment buildings and injured 26, officials said. Open this photo in gallery: One woman comforts another outside of the apartment building in Lviv. Roman Baluk/Reuters Earlier, Zelensky had warned a massive Russian attack was likely, saying the safety of Ukrainians depended on the willingness of allies to provide anti-missile defences. “It is important that our partners fully understand what is happening and that the protection of people’s lives depends directly on their willingness,” Zelensky wrote on Telegram. Russia’s defence ministry said on Thursday its forces struck what it called military facilities across Ukraine, in areas from the capital Kyiv to Lviv and Dnipropetrovsk, as well as three cargo ships. Poland, a member of the European Union and NATO, scrambled fighter jets to protect its airspace amid Russian air strikes, its armed forces said on X. Polish police in the Lublin region close to Ukraine’s border said on X they received a report of a loud bang heard in Bilgoraj county and discovered a crater and scattered debris from an unidentified object in a field. Attacks continue on Russia’s top online retailer A warehouse of Russian top online retailer Wildberries caught fire in the western city of Penza after Ukraine’s drone attack, regional governor Oleg Melnichenko said on Telegram. One person was injured and about 200 people evacuated from the site, he added, just a day after the company, which has become a frequent target of Ukraine’s attacks, evacuated another facility in central Russia. Another of its facilities, in Sarapul in Russia’s Udmurtia region, also caught fire after a drone attack, the company said separately on Thursday. Analysis: Ukrainian strike on Iranian cargo ship blurs line between two wars Its losses pile on the pain for ordinary Russians, some of whom have made online sales their main source of income, as Ukraine continues hitting energy facilities and refineries, deepening the fuel crisis in the world’s largest country by area. Drone strikes have damaged nearly a dozen Wildberries warehouses recently, destroying about 10 per cent of storage capacity and inflicting losses on tens of thousands of small businesses using the platform, the company and local authorities say. Russia’s biggest bank, Sberbank, has warned it may have to boost loan-loss provisions as attacks on Wildberries hit the finances of online retailers and their suppliers. Russia downed a total of 258 drones overnight, its defence ministry said. That figure covers Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine. Reuters could not independently verify the reports. Both Russia and Ukraine deny targeting civilians in the war following Russia’s full-scale invasion of its neighbour in February, 2022. https://www.odt.co.nz/news/australia/sea.text: The gruelling search for a missing baby has been abandoned, as police confirmed the child's mother visited police the day before her body was found alongside her toddler's in a suspected double murder-suicide. The bodies of Helena Wright, 36, and her 23-month-old daughter were found in waters near Cape Northumberland on South Australia's southeast coast on Monday after police were alerted to an empty car with its engine left running. On Wednesday afternoon, police called off a three-day search of land and sea for Ms Wright's three-month-old son, who also vanished on Monday. "Based on expert advice and available information, the infant could not have survived the period of time that has elapsed, either in the water or on land," a SA Police spokesperson said. Shocking new details have emerged in the Port MacDonnell tragedy with police confirming Helena Wright sought help the day before she and her children died. Officers also carried out a welfare check. Lifeline – 13 11 14. @mjstanley7 pic.twitter.com/iE96Mbz3ac — 7NEWS Adelaide (@7NewsAdelaide) July 29, 2026 Prevailing weather conditions forced emergency vessels out of the water for much of Tuesday and limited search efforts on the shoreline and clifftops, "significantly" reducing the likelihood of finding the baby, police said. "The reality is, after three days, the chances of finding the baby alive are zero," Superintendent Trent Cox said on Wednesday. "We've been unable to … launch water assets. We've been able to get the SES aerial drone up," he said, adding that experts had advised against deploying an underwater drone in the dangerous conditions. Despite calling off the search, authorities will continue to monitor the shoreline over coming days in the hope they can retrieve the baby's body. Authorities continue to investigate exactly how the tragedy unfolded, after revealing on Wednesday they were treating the incident as a murder-suicide. Ms Wright was originally from Estonia and had been living in Compton, a small locality outside Mount Gambier about 26km north of Port MacDonnell. Police have confirmed she attended Mt Gambier Police Station the day before the tragic incident, where she spoke to police. A call from a friend led police to conduct a welfare check at her home about 9.30am on Monday, but the home was empty. Less than two hours later, at 11.15am, police were alerted to an abandoned car left with its engine left running near Cape Northumberland. The bodies of Ms Wright and her toddler daughter were recovered from the ocean on Monday. The pair was found below the cliffs and retrieved with help from local fishermen. A coronial investigation is now under way, with a report to be prepared for the coroner. Police have spoken to the woman's husband, the father of the children, and say the deaths are being treated as a suspected murder-suicide. Earlier, officers said there was no information to suggest anyone else was involved in the incident. SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said the tragedy had shocked the community to the core. ''If it involves children, that breaks your heart … particularly when we know there was a two-month-old baby missing. That's hard to get your head around," he said on Tuesday. Major Crime detectives and specialist forensic officers remain at the scene as investigations continue.

https://www.politico.eu/article/poland-p.text: Poland’s opposition is shifting further to the right ahead of an election next year and that threatens to have a major impact for the EU and Ukraine. The nationalist Law and Justice party (PiS) that ran the country from 2015 to 2023 — picking repeated battles with Brussels over rule of law and LGBTQ+ rights — split last Friday . At its heart, the feud centers on a clash between iron-fisted party leader Jarosław Kaczyński and former Prime Minister Mateusz Morawiecki. The big question is what that rupture means for the political trajectory of a country that has one of the largest militaries in NATO and has been a key strategic ally to Kyiv since the Russian invasion. Advertisement Advertisement Allies of pro-EU Prime Minister Donald Tusk read it as good news. When Kaczyński stepped to the microphone to kick out Morawiecki, two lawmakers from Tusk’s governing coalition filmed themselves watching the speech, eating popcorn . You can see why they might be happy. Before the split, POLITICO’s Poll of Polls put Tusk’s Civic Coalition at 32 percent support and PiS at 26 percent. PiS has now slumped to 22 percent. But that is hardly the whole story. The combined forces of right-wing parties are still in a strong position if they team up for the 2027 election. And Friday’s split means that PiS is more likely to veer right in its alliances, choosing ideological consolidation over an attempt to win back the center. The wing of PiS led by Morawiecki had argued the party needed to broaden its appeal and adopt a less combative approach toward Brussels. Kaczyński instead appears determined to recapture voters who have defected further right. It is far from certain, however, how successfully Poland’s far-right parties can agree on a common agenda with PiS. Among the potential beneficiaries of Friday’s split are parties that oppose Ukraine joining the European Union — and, in the case of Grzegorz Braun’s Federation of the Polish Crown movement, advocate taking Poland out of the bloc altogether. Advertisement Advertisement Poland votes in the fall of 2027. On current polling, most plausible routes to a right-wing majority would require the Konfederacja party, Braun’s party or both. “For years, a right-wing voter in Poland had no alternative. If you had right-wing views, you voted for Law and Justice, because there was nothing else,” said Anna Bryłka, a member of the European Parliament and vice-president of Konfederacja, the biggest of the hard-right parties now gaining sway. “Today that alternative exists. Law and Justice is simply losing its hegemony on the right.” The breakup came to a head over a midnight deadline to renounce the faction Morawiecki had built inside the party, or leave. About 45 lawmakers refused to sign . Kaczyński declared them outside the party, triggering PiS’s most serious rupture in two decades. Mateusz Morawiecki is pictured during a summit in the European Parliament in Brussels on Feb. 3, 2026. | Thierry Monasse/Getty Images Morawiecki, prime minister until 2023, was hardly a centrist by European standards. But within PiS, his supporters represented a more economically liberal and tactically less confrontational camp — and a rival center of power. Yet PiS is bleeding voters rightward anyway. Kaczyński selected hardline former Education Minister Przemysław Czarnek as his preferred candidate for prime minister to win back Konfederacja’s electorate. The polls slid regardless . “Why would a voter choose the copy,” Bryłka said, “when they can vote for the original?” Advertisement Advertisement The kingmakers name their price In surveys testing a separate Morawiecki list, support for PiS falls to between 16 and 22 percent , Konfederacja takes roughly 13 to 15 percent and Braun’s party about 10 percent. Morawiecki’s Rozwój Plus (Development Plus) project has backing ranging from below the 5 percent parliamentary threshold to around 7.5 percent. No party with such weak support can govern alone. Bryłka’s conditions for forming a right-wing alliance hinge on Brussels: There must be no more transfer of powers to the EU, no softening on the climate policy that her party has opposed since 2019, and a firm “no” to Ukraine’s membership of the EU. Even Braun, whom Kaczyński has called too toxic for any coalition, is not beyond the pale for her party. “We maintain good relations,” said Michał Wawer, Konfederacja’s treasurer and a member of the national parliament. “We are ready for cooperation in government in the future, if the majority works out that way.” Morawiecki’s camp has ruled that out. “Not a chance,” said Paweł Jabłoński, a former deputy foreign minister expelled with Morawiecki. Braun’s party, he added, “is destructive.” Others in PiS are less categorical. “There is no enemy on the right,” Kaczyński loyalist Jacek Sasin told reporters Friday, floating “some form of non-aggression pact.” The real enemy, he added, was Tusk’s coalition. Advertisement Advertisement Can the right unite? For all the acrimony, Morawiecki’s breakway camp is not looking across the aisle. Jabłoński said his group wants to keep cooperating with PiS, and ruled out any deal with Tusk — whose coalition, he said, remains the opponent. The one figure who could reach across the splintered right and unify it is President Karol Nawrocki, elected last year with the support of PiS and Konfederacja voters — and talk of a single right-wing list under his presidential umbrella has circulated in Warsaw for months. Kaczyński has embraced a version of the idea. Karol Nawrocki speaks during doorstep statements as part of the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey on July 8, 2026. | Altan Gocher/Hans Lucas/AFP via Getty Images “We are working to win the election, to unite as large a part of the right as possible, so that we go on one list,” he said in June — provided Konfederacja drops its hostility toward PiS. Braun, he made clear, would not be invited. “Only Karol Nawrocki can sort this out,” Bryłka said. “He could be the patron of some reconciliation between Jarosław Kaczyński and Prime Minister Morawiecki” — a reconciliation she expects to happen sooner or later anyway. “The question is whether he wants that role,” she added. “He has all the tools — and everything suggests he does.” Advertisement Advertisement Not that governing would be simple. Building a coalition of three parties is difficult enough, Bryłka said. “From four, it’s a genuinely complicated process.” Her forecast for the next parliament? “Chaos.” But even a fragmented right would not automatically save Tusk. In one poll conducted by IBRiS , the combined support of the right-wing parties did not fall after the PiS rupture. It edged up, from 47.5 percent to 47.9 percent. The voters leaving Kaczyński appear to be shopping elsewhere on the right, not crossing over to Tusk. Meanwhile, the prime minister’s own coalition is fraying: Of his governing partners, only the Left is consistently polling above the threshold required to enter parliament. Tusk’s likeliest path to survival is the right wasting its own votes. If Morawiecki runs independently and falls below the 5 percent threshold, his supporters’ ballots would win no seats. Konfederacja is candid about the risk that would pose to the entire right. “Those 4 percent of lost votes could decide what the majority looks like,” Wawer said. Tusk has been sounding less cheerful than the lawmakers with the popcorn. “I won’t cry for Law and Justice,” he told reporters Monday, “but there is certainly nothing to celebrate.” Advertisement

https://www.fox32chicago.com/news/marine.text: Family remembers victim of deadly Fox River boating crash: 'Strongest of all of us' Magdalena Jablonska was killed in a Fox River boating crash on Saturday. Her family is remembering her as a caring person, an animal lover, and someone who brought joy to those around her. The Brief Michelle Macias says her sister, Magdalena 'Madzia' Jablonska, was the heart of their family before she was killed in Saturday's Fox River boating crash. Prosecutors allege Richard Stevenson was traveling about 80 mph in a no-wake zone when his boat struck Jablonska and her fiancé's vessel before fleeing the scene. As the family prepares for funeral services, they have launched a fundraiser benefiting an animal shelter to honor Jablonska's lifelong love of helping animals. MCHENRY COUNTY, Ill. - As Richard Stevenson remains in the McHenry County Jail awaiting future court appearances, the family of Magdalena Jablonska is remembering the woman they lost instead of the tragic way she died. What we know: Stevenson is charged with aggravated DUI and reckless homicide after prosecutors say he was operating a pontoon boat at roughly 80 mph in a posted no-wake zone on the Fox River Saturday. Stevenson is accused of hitting and running over Jablonska's boat, who was inside another boat with her fiancé and their dog. Prosecutors said the boat crash was so horrific, Jablonska suffered lacerations and was decapitated in the crash. Jablonska's family says her fiancé and dog were also injured, but are expected to be ok. Magdalena Jablonska Jablonska's family told Fox Chicago they want people to know 'Madzia' for who she was before Saturday's crash. What they're saying: For Michelle Macias, Madzia was never just an older sister. "She was my role model since I was little," said Macias. The sisters were 14 years apart in age, and Macias says Madzia naturally became a second mother while she was growing up. "She was our best friend, second mom," said Macias. Born in Poland, Madzia immigrated to the United States as a teenager before graduating from high school and enlisting in the U.S. Marine Corps. After her military service, she built a career as a project accountant while spending her free time riding motorcycles with her fiancé, traveling, visiting wineries, supporting her brothers' racing events and spoiling her beloved dog, Sasha. Above all else, Macias says family came first. The last time they saw one another was one week before the crash during Macias' youngest daughter's birthday celebration. "It was my youngest's birthday and she just stopped by really quick to give her a gift and wish her a happy birthday," Macias recalled. "I gave her a hug and I said, 'Thank you, sister,' because we never called each other by our names." Neither knew it would be their final goodbye. Like many families coping with sudden tragedy, Macias says the days immediately after the crash have been difficult to process. "That Saturday, Sunday and part of Monday's kind of a blur to me," she said. Despite the grief, she says she is trying to live up to the example her sister set. "She was the strongest of all of us and I don't want to disappoint her," Macias said. "I'm staying strong for everyone." She says every member of the family is grieving differently. "Everyone is trying to stay strong. Obviously, the adults are able to hold together better. The kids in the family, it hits them differently." Rather than asking for donations to help the family, Madzia's loved ones chose to create a fundraiser benefiting animals, something they say perfectly reflects how she lived. "I think the best thing to do in her name was... for the puppies, for the animals because that was her big thing," Macias said. "She always wanted to give and help others. What better way to remember her?" The family says the fundraiser is intended to turn an unimaginable tragedy into something positive by helping animals Madzia would have wanted to protect. What's next: Family members are still making funeral arrangements while waiting for relatives traveling from Poland to arrive in the Chicago area. Meanwhile, Stevenson remains in the McHenry County Jail, after a judge denied his request for pretrial release. His next court appearance is expected August 5th. For Macias, she hopes people remember Madzia not as a victim, but as a Marine veteran, devoted sister, loving aunt and someone who dedicated her life to helping others. https://www.theguardian.com/science/ng-i.text: Prague Castle is silhouetted against a partial solar eclipse Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPA View image in fullscreen Prague Castle is silhouetted against a partial solar eclipse Photograph: Martin Divíšek/EPA Solar eclipses Cruise ships, quiet towns and an all-day festival: millions flock to eclipse viewing spots across Europe Beginning in Russia’s remote Arctic north, the eclipse traced an arc over much of western Europe – with the best views in Spain, Iceland and Greenland Ashifa Kassam in Madrid, Miranda Bryant and Chris Michael in London Wed 12 Aug 2026 15.56 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 17.10 EDT Share It was a moment of awe shared by millions across Europe: an eclipse that blocked out the sun, plunging parts of the continent into a daytime darkness in which temperatures dropped and birds suddenly went quiet. Wednesday’s eclipse began in Russia’s remote Arctic north, going on to trace an arc over much of western Europe. From the UK to northern Italy, tens of millions of people turned to the sky as the light of the setting sun was almost completely blocked out. The most sought-after experiences were in Greenland, Iceland and Spain along with a small strip of Portugal. It was in parts of these countries that totality – referring to when the moon completely covers the sun’s light – was on offer, drawing millions of local people and thousands of tourists from across the globe into the path of the eclipse. “It was one of the most beautiful things I’ve ever seen in my life,” Sara García Alonso, a reserve astronaut for the European Space Agency, told broadcaster RTVE. “It gave me goosebumps.” Standing next to her, the astronaut Pablo Álvarez Fernández nodded in agreement: “It had been described to me so many times, but it was much more beautiful than what I had expected.” In Iceland, people flocked by air, land and sea to take in the country’s first total solar eclipse in 72 years. Amid concerns that clouds would block the view, a record 31 cruise ships plied the waters off the western part of the country, hoping to secure a top view for about 53,000 passengers and crew. View image in fullscreen The sun during a partial solar eclipse and partially obscured by clouds, the International Space Station silhouetted as it transits at roughly five miles per second. Photograph: Nasa Handout/EPA View image in fullscreen People gather to observe the total solar eclipse, as clouds cover the sky, in Reykjavik Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters View image in fullscreen Passengers on board the Ambassador cruise ship Ambition watching the start of the total solar eclipse off the coast of Greenland Photograph: Owen Humphreys/PA The eclipse-themed activities included a day-long music festival hosted by the Icelandic artist Björk in Víðistaðatún park, offering a DJ-curated backdrop as people took in the eclipse. The 10-hour set list included two minutes set aside for totality, the artist said on social media, while the festival website noted that every ticket included a pair of approved solar eclipse glasses. Those watching from Iceland included the US space agency, Nasa, which followed the moon’s shadow using a high-altitude WB-57 aircraft while Nasa-funded teams launched balloons to study the atmospheric impact of the sudden darkness and cooling. View image in fullscreen A WB-57 Canberra aircraft is pictured during a media visit ahead of a Nasa-supported mission Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters View image in fullscreen Cary Klemm, sensor equipment operator, and pilot John Gustine of Nasa’s Johnson Space Centre pose in front of a WB-57 Canberra aircraft Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters View image in fullscreen A WB-57 Canberra aircraft Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters View image in fullscreen A gyroscopic sensor system aboard a WB-57 Canberra aircraft Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters In Spain, where some of the best views of the total eclipse were expected, the hours leading up to the celestial alignment were filled with frenzied debate about weather forecasts and where best to watch the phenomenon. More than 450,000 tourists had arrived in the country from as far as Canada and Australia, crisscrossing Spain by train, bus and caravan to stake out the perfect viewing spot. View image in fullscreen The sun’s corona glows as the moon completely blocks the sun during the totality phase of the total solar eclipse as seen from San Asensio, La Rioja region, Spain Photograph: Ander Gillenea/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen People wait for a solar eclipse at the beach in A Coruña, Spain Photograph: Lavandeira/EPA View image in fullscreen A beachgoer wearing special eclipse glasses looks up during the beginning phase of a solar eclipse at Puerto de Sagunto beach near Valencia, Spain Photograph: Alberto Saiz/AP View image in fullscreen The sun’s corona glows as the moon completely blocks the sun during the totality phase of the total solar eclipse as seen from Arenal beach in Llucmajor, on the Balearic island of Mallorca Photograph: Jaime Reina/AFP/Getty Images “Our car was cancelled,” one woman, who had travelled from Brazil with her sister to take in the eclipse, said on social media. After her appeals to hitch a ride to their chosen site were met with no response, they took matters into their own hands. “So we took a three-hour bus, a 20-minute taxi and two-hour hike. Arrived at the location!” About 10,000 metres above sea level, the Spanish airline Iberia livestreamed the moment when the sun, moon and Earth aligned from a special charter flight. “Some flights take us to new destinations. Others allow us to see the world from a different perspective,” the airline said as it announced the charter flight. Spanish officials estimated that as many as 6 million people were expected to flock to the path of the eclipse, which stretched about 124 miles (200km) from A Coruña in Spain’s north-west to the Mediterranean island of Mallorca. On Wednesday, just hours before the eclipse, officials reported traffic jams on the major thoroughfares out of Madrid and Barcelona. Others took their chances in the cities. In Madrid’s Parque del Oeste, hundreds gathered in hopes of catching a good view of the eclipse, cheering as they watched the moon cover the sun – plunging the park into darkness – and gasping as the outer corona left a glowing halo around the moon. Just over a minute later, when daylight returned to the park, the crowd burst into raucous cheers. It was, in the words of César González, an astronomer and science communicator at the Madrid Planetarium, “a spectacular experience”. He had left Madrid early in the morning to set himself up in a field in northern Spain to watch the eclipse. “Until one goes and experiences it, there’s no way to explain what it is to see an eclipse.” View image in fullscreen Mario Garrido, a member of the Los Taraos amateur astrophotography group, waits to shoot a total solar eclipse in Berlanga de Duero, central Spain Photograph: Bernat Armangué/AP View image in fullscreen The moon completely covers the sun during a total solar eclipse as seen from the Javalambre Astrophysical Observatory in Arcos de las Salinas, near Teruel, Spain Photograph: Christian Hartmann/Reuters View image in fullscreen Artists use self-made artefacts to observe a solar eclipse before totality near the small village of Castell de Cabres, Spain Photograph: Eva Manez/Reuters View image in fullscreen A composite image of seven separate photographs taken with a single fixed camera shows stages of a solar eclipse before, during and after totality, as seen from Arija, Spain Photograph: Borja Suárez/Reuters He was able, however, to explain the impact. “In broad daylight, all of a sudden the light dims to a point where you can see the brightest stars in the sky. When totality starts, the temperature drops several degrees. If you’re in a field and surrounded by animals, their behaviour often changes. The birds stop singing because they think it’s nightfall. And all of this lasts for a few minutes – in this case around 1 minute and 45 seconds.” In Spain, most eclipse watchers were heading to rural areas, filling often quiet villages and towns clogged with skygazing tourists. The eclipse had helped put some parts of “empty Spain” on the map; this week people linked to Nasa turn up in northern Spain’s Villalibado to set up a live broadcast for millions of people around the world, breathing new life into a municipality whose last two residents left in 1998. Throughout human history, eclipses have sparked amazement, fear and reverence. In villages and cities across Europe, the eclipse forged ad hoc communities, as people came together to witness one of nature’s great wonders. In Camberwell, south London, an impromptu crowd of all ages gathered in Brunswick Park to experiment with different methods of seeing the eclipse, which reached 92% totality. Some held up colanders, others a spatula with holes, still others makeshift pinhole cameras made of old candy boxes. Ludmila, a Ukrainian woman in her 70s, said she had worked at an observatory in Crimea for 30 years. “What a surprise to find an actual refractor,” she said, pointing to a telescope with a solar filter taped on the end brought out by a resident. “It’s like a wonderful gift.” Later, as the eclipse passed its zenith and the sun began to set for real, dozens of neighbours who had never previously spoken to each other stayed on picnic blankets to drink beer and swap photos. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Refqa Hassan watches as Israeli settlers besiege her family home for the fourth consecutive day in the town of Qusra. Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA View image in fullscreen Refqa Hassan watches as Israeli settlers besiege her family home for the fourth consecutive day in the town of Qusra. Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA West Bank Israeli militants besiege two Palestinian families in their West Bank homes Settlers and soldiers cut off water and electricity to homes, and block medical care in campaign of terror Emma Graham-Harrison in Qusra Wed 12 Aug 2026 17.29 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 18.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Israeli militants have besieged two Palestinian families in their homes since the weekend, aiming to take over their properties in the West Bank village of Qusra through a campaign of terror. A group of settlers and soldiers set up a tent outside the home of Yousef Hassan on Sunday afternoon, trapping him inside with his wife and two young daughters. The Israeli men gathered just metres away from the spot where 28-year-old Amir Moatasem Odeh was killed by a settler in March. Another attacker stabbed his father. No one has been arrested over the murder and assault. “Every night, the settlers throw stones, use obscene language and shout during the night. We are living in a state of terror,” Hassan said. His mother, brother and sister, and three neighbours have also been blockaded inside, and their power and water have been cut off. View image in fullscreen Israeli soldiers stand guard next to settlers in front of Palestinian homes that they have blockaded in the village of Qusra. Photograph: Nidal Eshtayeh/AP Settlers used the same tactics to steal another Palestinian home in neighbouring Jalud village, driving the al Tubasi family out in July after a months-long siege. They cut off water and electricity to the homes, although a solar panel allows Hassan to keep some devices charged in Qusra. They have also blocked medical care. When his younger daughter, a two-year-old, fell ill with vomiting and a high fever on Monday, settlers blocked an ambulance from reaching the house. The girls and their mother were eventually evacuated on Tuesday. They are short on food and are drinking water and juice delivered by the ambulance that came to collect his daughter. “The situation is extremely dire,” Hassan said. On Wednesday morning, the commander of Israeli forces in the region, Gen Avi Bluth, visited the families and promised to lift the siege, an Israeli military spokesperson said. Hassan confirmed the visit. “Today, the area commander came and spoke with us and assured us that he would evacuate the settlers. For the first time, I feel that there is some seriousness on the part of the army in dealing with the settlers,” Hassan said, but added that it had not yet produced tangible results. Soldiers took the tent but not bedding and other possessions and, after brief clashes with the settlers, withdrew. “The settlers are still there in front of the house, and we are still unable to leave.” View image in fullscreen Yousef Hassan said Israeli settlers throw stones, use obscene language and shout during the night. Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA An Israeli military spokesperson said commanders were “gravely concerned” about the settlers’ actions and that soldiers who supported them would face disciplinary action, but declined to give a timeline for lifting the siege. On Wednesday evening, chief of the general staff of the Israel Defense Forces, Eyal Zamir, met other senior commanders to discuss the situation in Qusra. He ordered a battalion of infantry reservists back from leave to reinforce troops in the West Bank. “The battalion, which is currently undergoing a period of refreshment and training, will be deployed to the sector in order to strengthen operational control. Furthermore, additional soldiers will remain on standby for deployment as necessary,” a military spokesperson said. The military is working with the police to bring “those responsible for the disturbances to justice”, the spokesperson added. Israeli militants target Palestinians with near total impunity in the occupied West Bank. Since 2020, Israeli civilians and soldiers have killed more than 1,100 Palestinians there, and there has been only one indictment over those deaths. Violence is deployed as part of a broader campaign of ethnic cleansing. Israel has forcibly displaced 64 Palestinian communities over the past three years, rights group B’Tselem said. Fifteen other communities have lost residents, with more than 4,800 people driven from their homes. View image in fullscreen An Israeli settler leads his sheep as settlers besiege a Palestinian home. Photograph: Alaa Badarneh/EPA “What is happening in Qusra is not an isolated incident,” said B’Tselem’s executive director, Yuli Novak. “Settler militias, backed by the Israeli military, are expanding their attacks into Palestinian villages and towns – seizing land, attacking homes and forcing families out. Israel’s ethnic cleansing of the West Bank is accelerating and expanding in plain sight.” Dozens of Israelis from the country’s security, political and cultural elite have threatened legal action against their government over its failure to tackle “Jewish terrorism” in the occupied West Bank. As the occupying power in the West Bank, Israel is responsible under international law for ensuring the safety of Palestinian civilians and meeting their basic needs. The Israeli military has declared the area a closed military zone and blocked journalists from approaching the Palestinian homes. Israeli settlers are subject to the same orders but have not been removed. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Cornwall was one of the best places in the UK to view the solar eclipse. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The Guardian Solar eclipses ‘A magical eeriness’: Cornwall comes together for communal moment during solar eclipse People came from far and wide to witness phenomenon that has thrilled humans for thousands of years Steven Morris Cornwall Wed 12 Aug 2026 15.55 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 18.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At 6pm the beach and village began to empty, and those in the know headed up the hill towards the old granite coastguard station on the headland. “This is the best spot,” said Sennen Cove resident Lisa Redfern, who had built a pinhole camera for the eclipse out of an old Ryvita Thins box. As the moon began to hide the sun and Redfern – just about – got her makeshift device to work, she felt a little emotional. “I’d describe it as a magical eeriness,” she said. “Let’s face it, we may not see another one. We have to make the most of these moments.” It was certainly a wonderful communal moment. Redfern was part of a big group of friends and family who enjoyed a picnic (including Pringles and prosecco) on the headland. Matthew Robinson came armed with a colander and spent a frustrating few minutes getting the angle right. “The colander is a bit disappointing, but there’s a lovely atmosphere here.” 0:31 Iceland in complete darkness during total solar eclipse - video Another member of the group, seven-year-old Rina, did have the proper eclipse glasses. “It’s like someone has taken a bite out of a biscuit,” she said as the eclipse began. Strangers shared picnics, drinks and eclipse glasses, which had been very tricky to source in Cornwall . The wind picked up as the eclipse took hold and the temperature, which had reached the 30s during the day, plunged. Gulls stopped circling and landed on the surface of the water. A trio of choughs – Cornwall’s national bird – hopped around on the hillside, looking a little less graceful than usual. The swallows that had been whizzing around the thatched cottages rested for a while. Mary Bendall had positioned herself on a rock near the coastguard station with a complicated setup involving a filter over a scope that she uses to watch wildlife and her iPhone. She watched the total eclipse in 1999 with her daughter, who now works in physics, having been inspired by the experience. “I have just spoken to her – she’s in Spain. It’s cloudy there so we may be having the best of it,” Bendall said. View image in fullscreen Some set out to sea to see the eclipse. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The Guardian Across Cornwall, one of the best places in the UK to view the eclipse, towns, villages and pubs staged special events as people came from far and wide to drink in a phenomenon that has thrilled – and frightened – human beings for thousands of years In the harbour port of Falmouth, they clearly didn’t think the astronomical phenomenon was enough and an air display was arranged. One of the hotels also hosted an evening of sea shanties. Elsewhere, the playlist blaring from radios and pubs was predictable – Van Morrison’s Moondance and the Whole of the Moon by the Waterboys. Members of Kernow Astronomers were posted at the National Trust’s site Carnewas at Bedruthan, near Padstow, with telescopes fitted with filters to enable visitors to observe the eclipse safely. Inland, people had gathered on hilltops, near castles, close to one of Cornwall’s many standing stones. Carolyn Kennett, a Cornish expert in archaeoastronomy, said eclipses would almost certainly have been unexpected for ancient people and would have inspired awe, wonder and, perhaps, terror. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion She said: “An eclipse is a powerful spectacle, and for people without a modern scientific explanation, such an event would likely have carried profound meaning. View image in fullscreen A technical approach to the eclipse. Photograph: Luke Gartside/The Guardian “It is possible that witnessing an eclipse influenced the beliefs, stories, rituals or even choices of those who experienced one.” The Rev Karsten Wedgewood, priest in charge of St Just in Penwith, near Sennen, planned a picnic at a prehistoric funerary cairn, and a prayer based on psalm 8, known as the psalm for stargazers – “When I consider your heavens/the work of your fingers, / the moon and the stars …” At one point, one of the woes of modern life seemed destined to intervene when a pall of smoke from a wildfire near Land’s End airport threatened to dim the spectacle. A series of wildfires has been fought in Cornwall over the past few days but it did not affect the view from Sennen, at least. Coastguards and lifeguards had advised those intending to watch from kayaks or surfboards or take an eclipse sea dip to remember that it was going to turn a little colder and, of course, visibility would be poorer. A crew from the Cape Cornwall Pilot Gig Club put out to sea from Sennen harbour but returned before the darkness fell and fired up the barbecue instead. Surf photographer Jules River did paddle out on his board. “This is a kind of pilgrimage for me – it feels very soulful and healing to be here when this is happening.” There were good views to be had in the village as well as on the headland. Mother and daughter Lisa and Janet Grenfell, 53 and 79, plonked their camp chairs on the front and took it all in. “We remember the total eclipse in 1999 but it was cloudy. This is beautiful.” Jasmine Owen and Rory Smith arguably had the best seat in the house – a table overlooking the ocean where they tucked into fish and chips. What was better? The supper or the eclipse? Owen did not hesitate: “The chips are great, the eclipse amazing.” Explore more on these topics Solar eclipses Cornwall Space news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Europe solar eclipse: millions watch rare spectacle across Spain, UK and Iceland – as it happened WhatsApp ‘drops’, price hikes and queues: scramble for solar eclipse specs Great Britain braced to pay millions for backup electricity during solar eclipse ‘It’s going to be spectacular’: Millions flock to Spain seeking best view of total solar eclipse How to safely watch the solar eclipse Europe’s total solar eclipse: the best place to see it and how to view it safely ‘You’re hit with a slam of shadow’: Nasa’s air mission to capture rare eclipse data Where in the UK will get the best view of the solar eclipse? https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: The Democratic gubernatorial nominee, David Crowley, speaks to the press on Wednesday in Middleton, Wisconsin. Photograph: Kayla Wolf/AP View image in fullscreen The Democratic gubernatorial nominee, David Crowley, speaks to the press on Wednesday in Middleton, Wisconsin. Photograph: Kayla Wolf/AP Wisconsin Analysis Wisconsin Democrats chose a middle path – will it lead to victory in November? Rachel Leingang Democratic socialist Francesca Hong fell just short as David Crowley strives for unity for the general election Wed 12 Aug 2026 20.16 EDT First published on Wed 12 Aug 2026 16.31 EDT Share Francesca Hong, a democratic socialist, was on course to win the party’s nomination for Wisconsin governor on Wednesday by a clear margin, according to the polls – presaging the latest in an extraordinary wave of leftwing victories across the country, challenging the party’s establishment. It was not to be. In a photo finish after a messy campaign, David Crowley eked out a win by a few thousand votes over Hong, raising questions over the limits of the progressive movement that has swept through Democratic contests in recent months. Crowley, the Milwaukee county executive, had exited the race in early July, only to re-enter late in the month, with the backing of the outgoing Democratic governor, Tony Evers. The two barnstormed the state, consolidating support from a more moderate chunk of undecided voters, many of whom believed Crowley would more easily win November’s general election over Tom Tiffany, the Republican. The stakes for the governor’s race are high , both locally and nationally. Tiffany voted against certifying the 2020 election, and Wisconsin is a key part of the presidential electoral map. And Democrats want a governing trifecta after years of a split government so they can enact a more expansive agenda. Trump ally loses, mixed results for progressives: takeaways from primaries in Minnesota, Wisconsin and beyond Read more Those high stakes resonated with voters in a place where statewide elections are frequently decided by decimal points. Hong was seen as more of a gamble – and it didn’t help that when some voters just started paying attention, they found headlines focused on old tweets about canceling Thanksgiving or defunding the police, putting Hong on the defensive. “So those were the first things some people learned about her , while the first thing they learned about Crowley was that Governor Evers endorsed him,” said Michael Wagner, the director of the University of Wisconsin-Madison’s journalism school , who researches political communication. “I don’t think it was a huge effect , but it didn’t need to be.” Crowley, 40, became the first Black person to hold the role of Milwaukee county executive in 2020, just a decade after conservative Scott Walker, who would go on to become governor and dismantle workers’ rights, held the same role. “Now that this primary has come to a close, allow me to reintroduce myself,” Crowley told a cheering crowd after his win on Wednesday morning. “My name is David Crowley. I am a son of Milwaukee. I’m a community organizer by heart who has just happened to find themselves in the halls of the state capitol building, at the head of Milwaukee county government for the last six years.” ‘We have to take these people seriously’ While the results of a single race should not be overread, Hong’s loss is not an outright rebuke of a growing progressive movement, but more a sign that a democratic socialist can mount a serious race – even in a midwestern swing state. In prior years, she might have finished in third or fourth place, rather than become the clear frontrunner. “If folks overlook the growing power of people like Hong supporters, they will be doing a disservice to themselves and to the work ahead,” said Joe Zepecki, the Wisconsin Democratic consultant. “And we have to take these people seriously. We have to find space for them in the pro-democracy movement and in Democratic campaigns. It is the only way to build an enduring majority.” View image in fullscreen Francesca Hong speaks during a primary election night watch party at Atwood Music Hall in Madison, Wisconsin, on Tuesday. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Hong threw her support behind Crowley on Wednesday morning. She had previously vowed to use the grassroots movement she grew statewide to help whoever won the Democratic nomination. The Democratic gubernatorial candidates had brunch together , in a show of unity. Their work now shifts to November, and defeating Tiffany, who quickly tried to tie Crowley to Hong and her “socialist agenda”. There were strong paths to victory in a general for both Hong and Crowley, Zepecki said. For Hong, it was turning out younger voters or those disaffected by the Democratic party. For Crowley, it’s more about reaching independents and moderate Republicans, while bringing in Hong’s enthusiastic primary voters. But the headwinds against Republicans are strong, and Tiffany’s lockstep alignment with the Trump administration will probably haunt him on the campaign trail. Crowley, although backed by figures in the Democratic establishment, has bristled at the suggestion that he is an establishment candidate. “He’s just somebody who’s going to win people over once you meet him in the room,” said Dan Shafer, a Wisconsin journalist who runs the local publication the Recombobulation Area . “And I think once he was actually able to get out and do that a little bit more, he found some real success with it.” Polls of the race showed Hong with a runaway lead. They failed to detect Crowley’s surge back into the race. Chaz Nuttycombe, a pollster and executive director of State Navigate, which polled on the Wisconsin race , said he talked to a number of people in the polling industry after polls in Michigan overestimated the margins for Abdul El-Sayed. He said Hong voters were more enthusiastic about responding to the polls, and such a response bias was impossible to correct. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines US Get the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion Hong, a democratic socialist, finished half a percentage point away from winning a Democratic primary in a battleground state. Time will tell whether this was the high-water mark of progressive performance in Wisconsin – or the precursor to a future victory. In neighboring Michigan, El-Sayed’s victory in last week’s Democratic primary for US Senate came eight years after his defeat in the race for state governor. “This is a minor setback for DSA,” said Robert Lasica, the communications coordinator for the Madison Area Democratic Socialists of America. “But we have a lot of good momentum coming out of this, and we have a lot of good debriefing to do going forward.” The Madison chapter has seen its numbers grow with Hong’s campaign, and her race was the biggest project it had undertaken, he said. Her razor-thin loss shows that people want “big, significant changes” to the status quo, because it isn’t working for most people, Lasica said. ‘This is going to be a tough fight’ For now, Lasica said, most of Hong’s supporters are likely to support Crowley in the general, knowing the value a Democratic trifecta in state government could bring for material improvements in people’s lives. Election prognosticators adjusted their ratings after Crowley’s victory. Sabato’s Crystal Ball moved it from a tossup race to lean Democratic. Shafer, though, cautioned that the governor’s race will probably be close, as they often are in Wisconsin. “This is going to be a tough fight for David Crowley. It would have been a tough fight for Francesca Hong,” he said. “I get the whole national environment, the generic ballot, polling, all of those different things. But Wisconsin is always going to be a close race in a fall election.” Crowley was at work on Wednesday morning to define Tiffany as a Maga extremist who did not care about the people of Wisconsin. The framing of the primary election – as between the left and center, or progressives and the establishment – missed the point, he said, as people struggle to afford childcare, run their small businesses and grapple with wages lagging the cost of living. “From the very first day that I announced this campaign, I said the real threat wasn’t any of my primary opponents,” said Crowley. “The real opponent has always been Tom Tiffany. That remains true today.” Explore more on these topics Wisconsin Democrats US politics US midterm elections 2026 analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: Courtesy of Nxt Gen Media San Francisco San Francisco-area estate sells for $70m in sign of AI-fueled wealth explosion New owner is said to be involved in AI industry, as new class of multimillionaires is entering the real estate race Sophie Sullivan Wed 12 Aug 2026 19.22 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 19.23 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A luxury Lake Como-inspired estate in the San Francisco Bay Area has sold to a buyer “in the AI world” for a record $70m, in the latest sign of a new tech wealth boom that’s pushing home prices to extraordinary heights in the region The property south of San Francisco not only becomes the most expensive sale in its affluent town of Hillsborough, doubling a previous record, but is also the most expensive sale in northern California this year, according to listing agent Jennifer Gilson of Golden Gate Sotheby’s International Realty. Gilson declined to share any details about the buyer, other than that the new owner of 3000 Ralston Avenue is a man in the AI industry. It is the latest sign of a housing boom across Silicon Valley being driven by AI wealth. Last month, an analysis found that more than 140 San Francisco homes have sold at least $1m above their asking price in the first six months of this year. View image in fullscreen The exterior of the property. Photograph: Courtesy of Nxt Gen Media The property, known as “ Villa de Verano ”, was initially listed at $88m, and sat on the market for only four months and 22 days. Besides a six-bed, 12,400 sq ft home that is complete with its own gym, theater, spa and aquarium, the 12-acre property also features a pool, a rose garden, an amphitheater, a guest property and a sporting area fitted with seven courts and a putting green. Its opulence stands out even among other palatial Hillsborough homes, which include Bing Crosby’s $25m home, Elon Musk’s $32m former home and the Levi Strauss-connected $17.8m Koshland Estate. Yet Gilson says this sale is only a “stepping stone” into a market of homes catering to the incredibly wealthy. “Even in the last year, there’s been a major increase of buyers from the AI world,” she said. “This could be just the beginning of the ultra luxury.” View image in fullscreen The property’s pool and outdoor area. Photograph: Courtesy of Nxt Gen Media Since the San Francisco-based companies OpenAI and Anthropic filed for initial public offerings earlier this summer, a new class of multimillionaires has entered the real estate race. An analysis by brokerage Compass described a “housing market increasingly segmented by income tier and proximity to AI-driven employment centers”. Gilson said she has seen an influx of wealth among buyers coming not just from AI companies, but increasingly from other, traditional industries. She described a “definite increase” in those ultra-rich buyers taking off-market, “hidden” opportunities, meaning Gilson connects buyers to sellers without homes ever being listed. In San Mateo county, where the sale took place, the median price of a single-family home increased by 8.5% between May 2025 and May 2026. San Francisco county saw a more than one-fifth increase, with median prices jumping from $1.8m to $2.2m. Law enforcement respond to a call at a home daycare in Hopkins, Minnesota. Photograph: Carly Danek/AP View image in fullscreen Law enforcement respond to a call at a home daycare in Hopkins, Minnesota. Photograph: Carly Danek/AP Minnesota Minnesota man killed his wife and child before dying by suicide, police say Police said they believed deceased man was assailant in domestic-related homicide at daycare center Lucy Campbell Wed 12 Aug 2026 18.34 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 18.37 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A man killed a woman and their child inside a small in-home daycare center they own in Minnesota before taking his own life, police said on Wednesday. Hopkins police department said in statement they responded to a report of a stabbing at the residence on the 200 block of Tyler Avenue North around 9am in the Minneapolis suburb of Hopkins. Inside, they found two adults and a child dead. Police said it was a domestic-related homicide, and “there are no outstanding suspects and no ongoing threat to the public”. Preliminarily, they believe the deceased man was the assailant, and that he took his own life after killing the woman and their child. Brent Johnson, the Hopkins police chief, said another parent called police after witnessing the attack while bringing a child to Brown Bear Childcare. “There’s no worse scenario than this, where you drop off your child somewhere you think is safe, and you get that phone call,” he told a news conference. “I think we can all relate, [those] who have children and those who don’t. This is just a tragic situation anywhere in the world, let alone here in Hopkins.” All six other children who were at the home at the time of the incident were evacuated and have been reunited with their parents, and none were harmed, he said. The identities of the victims have not been released and Johnson declined to say how they died. Authorities are still investigating the motive. Patrick Hanlon, the city’s mayor, told reporters : “There are no strangers in this community so … we are all reeling from this tragic incident.” Jacob Frey, the Minneapolis mayor, said: “I know that our hearts and our prayers are with the people of Hopkins and any families that have been impacted. I have already touched base directly with Mayor Hanlon, offered any assistance that we possibly can provide.” Police and sheriff vehicles lined the otherwise quiet street where the daycare is located. The brown, two-story house has a mural on the garage door of a tree-lined lake and a moose. Photos on the daycare’s Facebook page show children playing with toys inside and in the backyard, with colorful decorations and artwork on the walls. Records show the daycare has been licensed by the state since 2019 and has a capacity of 10 children. It was found to be in compliance during visits in 2023, 2024 and 2025. Johnson said killings were a “rarity” in Hopkins, which has a population of about 19,000, and that his officers were shaken by the scene they found inside the home. “I could see on the look on their faces that this was one of those ones that you’ll remember for your entire career, if not life,” he said.
