https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Yvette Cooper summarised Keir Starmer’s leadership as ‘bring me solutions, not problems’. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Yvette Cooper summarised Keir Starmer’s leadership as ‘bring me solutions, not problems’. Photograph: WPA/Getty Images Yvette Cooper Yvette Cooper says Labour ‘did not do government very well’ under Starmer Health secretary praises more collegiate style under Andy Burnham and says previous No 10 sidelined her from key policy launch Rowena Mason Whitehall editor Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Yvette Cooper admits Labour has “not done government very well” in the last couple of years, and accused Keir Starmer’s No 10 of sidelining her during the launch of a key immigration policy when she was home secretary. Speaking on the Political Currency podcast with the former Conservative chancellor George Osborne, Cooper highlighted some of the difficulties ministers faced with Starmer’s leadership, which she summarised as “bring me solutions, not problems”. She said she had found a more collegiate style under Andy Burnham , and argued in favour of trying to form a national consensus around social care and reintroducing Sure Start-style children’s centres for young families under his leadership. Contrasting the new prime minister with Starmer, the health secretary said there had been “a style of leading the government that maybe doesn’t necessarily work in politics” under the last administration. As an example, she was critical of how she was in effect excluded from launching the immigration white paper in May 2025 while home secretary. At the launch, which was fronted by Starmer, he spoke of introducing policies to deal with the risk that Britain could become an “island of strangers”, which Cooper later had to defend. She told Osborne: “Keir wanted the immigration white paper. Actually, we did a lot of the work on it in the Home Office, and a whole set of plans to bring legal migration back under control, a whole set of reforms around illegal migration and so on. “But then No 10 wanted Keir to announce it on his own and to front that up, and so I didn’t see what was going to be said or what the announcement was … that was the way that No 10 operated. “It was like, well, you can sit in the front row of the launch, but actually the prime minister is going to launch it.” She added: “I think Keir’s style of leadership was ‘bring me solutions, not problems’. And I’m not sure you can do that in politics … the thing you see with Andy is ‘hang on, bring me the problems. I want to talk to you about the problems. I want to engage. I want to hear about the problems, and I want us to work together in solving them.’” Cooper contrasted Starmer’s desire to be presented with a set of options with Burnham’s more discursive approach on social care, saying he was “passionate about it” and wanted to talk about the problems and how to solve them. “He wanted me to be part of the event, launching it, to be speaking at it, to be talking about it,” she said. “I think Keir’s style of leadership, which is very effective in other ways, actually, was … it just didn’t fit with that emotion that you need to drive change and involve people and include people in politics.” During the podcast, Cooper also spoke about her ambition to build a consensus around a solution to the social care crisis, saying it was about “trying to create a sense that somebody’s going to have to solve this, and you know if it’s not this government, it’s going to have to be the next government, or we’re going to end up with a never-ending, growing crisis for our NHS because we’re not doing things to solve social care”. She said she also wanted to build national agreement around the principles of Sure Start, a programme to help young families that was cut when Osborne was chancellor. Telling Osborne she was “still angry” about his decision to cut funding for Sure Start children’s centres, she said: “I actually want to build that same national consensus on how we start our kids’ lives, so that no future government of whatever party would think, you know what, it’s OK to rip up Sure Start, because actually we establish this as something that’s so important in children’s lives.” Explore more on these topics Yvette Cooper Labour Keir Starmer Andy Burnham news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK US politics World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine Football Newsletters Business Environment UK politics Science Tech Global development Obituaries

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Aslyum hotels are being closed, but where are people to go? Composite: Posed by models; Guardian Design; Tolga Akmen/EPA; Getty Images View image in fullscreen Aslyum hotels are being closed, but where are people to go? Composite: Posed by models; Guardian Design; Tolga Akmen/EPA; Getty Images First Edition newsletter Immigration and asylum Thursday briefing: What happens after an asylum hotel closes? In today’s newsletter: With more sites closed and more lives upended, a look at the rhetoric and reality of where asylum seekers should be housed Libby Brooks Thu 13 Aug 2026 01.44 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 02.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. This week, immigration minister Anna Turley announced, with minor fanfare, the government will stop using a further 13 hotels to house asylum seekers across the country. It brings the total shut this year to 44, in pursuit of Labour’s manifesto pledge, now reiterated by Andy Burnham , to cease hotel use completely by the end of this parliament. Doing so would remove what have become highly visible symbols of an increasingly toxic debate about migration. Less than 160 to go, according to the Home Office. There was a risk the announcement might be drowned out by howls of rightwing outrage after the prime minister dared suggest that middle-class areas also ought to house asylum seekers. “We cannot have a situation where it’s only the poorest communities in the country that receive all of the dispersal of refugees and asylum seekers,” Burnham said. “I do believe all parts of the country need to play their part.” (In England , asylum seekers made up 0.29% of people in the most deprived local authorities, compared with 0.05% of people in the least deprived.) But what becomes of residents, protesters and communities after these hotels are emptied? I spoke to specialist reporter Diane Taylor , who has followed shifts in immigration policy and the individuals who must live through them for decades. First, the headlines. Five big stories Solar eclipse | Wednesday’s eclipse began in Russia’s remote Arctic north , going on to trace an arc over much of western Europe. From the UK to northern Italy, tens of millions of people turned to the sky as the light of the setting sun was almost completely blocked out. UK news | Nurses are collapsing during shifts amid “inhumane and impossible” conditions caused by extreme heat, their union has warned, as Andy Burnham promised to grapple with “the bigger questions” of climate adaptation. US politics | Karoline Leavitt will step down as White House press secretary at the end of August, Donald Trump announced. Science | Astronomers claim to have discovered a new kind of cosmic object , a black hole “star”, which is the size of the entire solar system and glows with a brilliant red light. Middle East | Israeli militants have besieged two Palestinian families in their homes since the weekend, aiming to take over their properties in the West Bank village of Qusra through a campaign of terror. In depth: ‘You can’t just magic away the intense protest and counter-protest and division’ View image in fullscreen An asylum seeker’s 12-year-old daughter, who uses a wheelchair and has epilepsy and a heart condition, is sleeping on the floor. Hotels were used as an occasional, temporary housing fix for asylum seekers pre-Covid, but became the default option in place of flats at the very start of the pandemic. The home office justification was public health – but I spoke to hotel residents back in 2020 who told me about cramped living conditions, limited access to food, drink and financial support, alongside spiralling mental distress. I still remember running through Glasgow city centre in June 2020 to reach the scene of a mass stabbing , and how my stomach dropped when I realised I was heading to a hotel housing asylum seekers. Badreddin Abdalla Adam Bosh, a Sudanese man, had stabbed six people including a police officer at the Park Inn hotel before being shot dead by police. An inquiry into his death is ongoing. To be clear: politicians across parties, support agencies and the far-right all agree that these hotels need to shut, though for different reasons. For the past six years – counter to the far-right “life-of-luxury” narrative – Diane has reported on life inside these hotels: rat infestations and food so abysmal it causes nutritional deficiencies. She has also exposed the vast profit made by private accommodation providers thanks to Home Office cash, such as Clearsprings, equating to £146 a minute over five years – yes, you read that right. What happens when a hotel closes? When a hotel closes, asylum seekers are moved – often at short notice – to houses of multiple occupancy (HMOs), former military barracks or other, usually more basic, hotels. People may have been living in the same hotel for years, and the new accommodation may be several hundred miles away, forcing people to re-build their lives – language classes, legal support, friendships – from scratch. Two barracks – Wethersfield in Essex and Crowborough in East Sussex – are now full, with planning permission being sought to turn three more into accommodation for asylum seekers: RAF Linton-on-Ouse, RAF Barnham and Bicester Garrison. Residents in the Oxfordshire village of Piddington, close to Bicester, will – in an eccentric move – hold a referendum on seceding from the UK, in protest against plans to house more than a thousand male asylum seekers in the disused army barracks. The government estimates these new sites could eventually house about 3,750 people. According to the National Audit Office, barracks are not necessarily cheaper to fund than hotels, because of hefty set-up costs. The current estimated hotel cost per night is £144, compared with dispersal accommodation such as HMOs estimated at £23.25 per night. Although cheaper than hotels and barracks, there simply aren’t enough to meet demand; however Diane suggests “you also don’t get the same punishment optics with a rundown terrace in East Ham”. Some have found the transition gruelling. Huda is a 41-year-old engineering graduate who fled death threats in Tunisia with her two daughters, one of whom has serious health conditions. When their London hotel closed last month , the family were moved to another hotel that Diane describes as “extremely basic”. There are no facilities for Huda to cook for her children, and limited storage for essential medicines and equipment. When I asked Huda, via Diane, about this new accommodation, she described mashing up food with her hands so that her daughter can swallow it. Her daughter’s seizures have intensified since the move, she sleeps on the floor and Huda is painfully blunt: “My daughter is dying slowly.” Closures, protests and transformation View image in fullscreen Antiracist protesters outside the Bell in July 2025. Photograph: Sean Smith/The Guardian Where asylum seekers go, far-right protesters often follow. Crowds of several hundred continue to throng at Crowborough every Sunday, and HMOs are now a growing target. Last Sunday in Kent, men in T-shirts bearing the logo “Christ is king” chanted “don’t unpack, you’re going back” outside an accommodation block in Broadstairs, rumoured to be earmarked for asylum seekers. And last week, over several nights of unrest in the Norfolk town of Thetford, crowds attempted to storm other suspected HMOs. Fifteen people were arrested. It’s worth noting that not every hotel has become a flashpoint. “It’s a mixed picture,” says Diane. “There are four asylum hotels near me, in a fairly middle-class area of London. Local residents and asylum seekers have lived together in a very low-key way, and I’ve never seen the slightest bit of trouble. “In the media, we always write about the extreme examples, understandably, but we don’t write about the hotels with zero problems.” The government claimed yesterday that closing hotels would have a transformative effect on local communities: “These hotels can once again attract visitors, support local jobs and drive footfall to nearby cafes, shops, restaurants and attractions, helping town centres and local economies thrive”. I put this to our resident Essex specialist Tim Burrows, who meticulously reported on a year of protests outside the Bell hotel in Epping. The Bell remains boarded up behind security fencing, with no apparent plans for reopening, and the effect on the community is clear: “While the closure of the Bell hotel has been welcomed by many in Epping, you can’t just magic away the past year or more of intense protest and counter-protest and the division that has caused.” The hotel, Tim says, “will long symbolise to one side of Epping ‘invader’ asylum seekers they blame for many of the UK’s problems, and to the other the concerning rise of far-right ethno-nationalist politics.” Where should asylum seekers be housed? The recent targeting of HMOs suggests that, as Diane tells me, where asylum seekers are housed is “almost irrelevant”. “There are people who don’t want asylum seekers here. If we put them in the sewers they would protest.” After Burnham’s comments about the distribution of asylum accommodation, Diane reminds me that there has been a fairly successful push to disperse people more widely in recent years “but, as the data shows, distribution is still not entirely equal”. It’s also the case that housing is more expensive to provide in middle-class areas. The government might also try changing the conversation to one that extends beyond houses, barracks and hotels to the people inside them. “Would it not be easier,” Diane says, “to ‘rebrand’ asylum seekers away from the scrounger, rapist stereotype into people who are grateful to be here and want to contribute any way they can – by doing work for the British community while claims are being processed.” Diane has written about some of the ad hoc volunteering initiatives already happening thanks to NGOs, but argues that having government in charge of them would mean wider and more efficient rollout. Better yet, says Diane: “Pay minimum wage for keeping streets clean, planting civic flowerbeds, growing free food for the whole area by tending community allotments. Deduct part of that to pay for accommodation. It would cut the cost to the taxpayer and boost integration.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen The discourse around Jason Arday’s departure from Cambridge is rooted in its own distorted reality. Illustration: Joe Plimmer/Guardian Pictures/Alamy/Getty I spoke to Nesrine Malik about the Jason Arday story for First Edition last week . Her wider reflections in The Long Wave are as insightful as you’d expect. (And sign up here to read more from her.) Michael I felt utterly uplifted reading Natasha Walter’s considered, hopeful and very urgent challenge to feminists everywhere to reunite from the grassroots up. Libby After reading Peter Bradshaw’s review of the new Amy Goodman documentary, Steal This Story, Please! , I’ve booked a screening ticket. Michael It’s not only because we share a moniker that I’m enjoying Stephen Libby’s new fashion column . Here he writes about the sustainable joys of using your local dry cleaner to tailor vintage finds . Libby This exclusive by Sandra Laville is jaw-dropping given the temperatures, drought and fires we’re experiencing: just 20 of 6,600 Defra staff are working on climate adaptation. Terrifying. Michael Sport View image in fullscreen Paris St Germain’s Marquinhos lifts the trophy with teammates after winning. Photograph: Angelika Warmuth/Reuters Uefa Super Cup | After Khvicha Kvaratskhelia’s opener was cancelled out by the teenage striker Brian Madjo, Désiré Doué curled in a second-half winner to give PSG a 2-1 victory against Aston Villa in Salzburg. European Athletics Championship | British runner Matt Hudson-Smith stormed to a historic third gold in the European Championship 400m to delight the home supporters in Birmingham. Cricket | Joe Root has abolished the midnight curfew for his England Test side, telling his players to “be adults” after a string of late-night incidents. The front pages View image in fullscreen Photograph: The Guardian “PM vows to tackle climate as nurses warn of heat toll”, is the Guardian ’s front page today. The Telegraph has “Burnham prepared to spend more on housing asylum seekers”, the Times runs with “Firms’ fury at zero hours reform”, the Mail says “Rewilding link to record fires”, and the Express writes “Using stairs may cut risk of early death”. The FT ’s headline is “Ukraine ceases strikes on oil tankers using Russian port after Vance request”. On the eclipse, the Sun writes in its masthead font “The Moon”, the i Paper splashes “Once in a generation”, and Metro says “Here’s blot all the fuss was about”. Today in Focus View image in fullscreen Women in Afghanistan have been imprisoned in their own homes, unable to leave without male guardians; and barred from jobs and schooling. Photograph: AFP/Getty Images The 21 million women and girls the world forgot Five years after the Taliban retook power, women inside the country explain how they have been silenced , while the Afghan journalist Zahra Joya asks why the world has looked away. Cartoon of the day | Ella Baron View image in fullscreen Illustration: Ella Baron/The Guardian The Upside A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad View image in fullscreen Getting the side-eye … Ioan Marc Jones tests out his hydration system. Photograph: David Levene/The Guardian Ioan Marc Jones has always hated running – he found it painful, boring and monotonous. But, an old football injury forced him to take up the sport properly. After conventional running advice failed, he turned to more unconventional tips from seasoned runners, including taking a shot of pickle juice, wearing nipple tape and listening to Hamlet. For the first time, Jones managed to run consistently for more than a month and discovered his own “running personality”. He may not love running yet, but he is enjoying the journey and, more importantly, starting to see himself as a runner. Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday Bored at work? And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow. Photograph: Azoor Wildlife/Alamy Seascape: the state of our oceans Marine life Too smart to eat? Why octopus farms are such a slippery problem As a controversial Spanish plan for sustainable meat on an industrial scale is dropped, it has revived the ethical debate over farming these intelligent wild animals Seascape: the state of our oceans is supported by About this content Stephen Burgen Thu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 00.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google I n 2022 Nueva Pescanova, Spain’s largest fisheries business, announced it was investing €65m (£56m) in the world’s first industrial octopus farm and processing plant near the Canary Islands’ port of Las Palmas. Despite the creatures being notoriously difficult to farm, the company predicted that by 2025 it would be producing 3,000 tonnes of octopus a year on Gran Canaria. There followed years of controversy, with activists and scientists condemning the plans to farm an animal lauded for its apparent “intelligence” , which reached near-celebrity status five years ago thanks to the Oscar-winning documentary My Octopus Teacher . Then, at the end of July 2026, Nueva Pescanova shelved plans for the farm . But why – and with what implications for the future of octopus farming? A Guardian request for comment from Nueva Pescanova was met with silence but it told the Canary Islands’ port authority in a letter that it was pulling out for “business and regulatory” reasons. View image in fullscreen An octopus paralarva at 55 days – when young cephalopods move about with the water current. Photograph: Nueva Pescanova Activists who have long opposed the farm were quick to claim a victory. “Social, scientific and political pressure has borne fruit, faced with this ethical and environmental atrocity,” Spain’s animal rights party, Pacma, said in a statement. When the Guardian visited the company’s research centre in 2023, Roberto Romero Pérez, the marine biologist overseeing aquaculture at Nueva Pescanova, had said: “The truth is that we’re finding the mood to be a bit more hostile than expected.” However, Silvia Fernández Díaz, a journalist at Canarias7 who has covered the story from the start, says that far from being a mass movement, demonstrations on the island against the project rarely attracted more than a few dozen protesters. “I believe the reality is that the farm didn’t go ahead because it wasn’t viable, not because of popular protest,” she says. Sources at Las Palmas port authority confirmed that they had not been approached by anyone from Nueva Pescanova and no work had been done on building the farm. Ian Gleadall, a marine biologist at Tohoku University in Japan who has spent 50 years researching octopuses, says he has been trying for two years to get a response from Nueva Pescanova about the Canary Islands project without success. “The same thing happened here in Japan with the fisheries company Nissui,” he says. “The company said they’d cracked it and were going to be producing massive amounts of octopus but it never happened.” Gleadall says octopuses have so far been virtually impossible to farm because the larvae of the common octopus spend at least 20 days floating in the water before they settle on the sea bed, making it difficult to move on to the next phase. Even then, he says, the hatchlings are so delicate that if anything goes wrong they die. He adds that another significant problem is what to feed the octopus: “One feed is a form of fish paste. But even if they eat it, they won’t go on eating it because octopus are very finicky – they don’t like to eat the same thing day in, day out. “Even if you could solve the feed problem,” he says, “you’d probably spend more on feed than the octopus was worth on the market.” The ethical objections to octopus farming are that the creatures are solitary and antisocial, as well as the studies showing “compelling evidence” of sentience . Richard Schweid, author of Life on the Octopus Farm , says many marine biologists hold that an octopus not only has nine brains but a mind. “[This is] something that we generally associate with higher orders of mammals, like dogs, cats, primates and humans,” he says. View image in fullscreen Activists in Madrid protest against Nueva Pescanova’s plans to farm octopuses in Las Palmas. Photograph: Sopa/Getty The idea that the octopus is somehow like us – or at least like some of our pets – was fuelled by Craig Foster’s film My Octopus Teacher, in which Foster appears to form a reciprocal relationship with a female octopus. “The octopus is a prime candidate for humans to anthropomorphise because it is so smart, so responsive, and yet so different as to be essentially unreadable,” says Schweid. Whatever the reasons for the end of the Spanish enterprise, no one has yet successfully farmed octopuses, aside from a small project in Mexico that cultivated a different species from the common octopus ( Octopus vulgaris ), found in the Mediterranean and Atlantic. While octopuses may be safe from farming for now, the UN’s food agency, the Food and Agriculture Organization, estimates that about 370,000 tonnes of octopus are caught every year , much of them off Morocco and Mauritania. The principal markets are China and Japan, while Spain consumes about 40,000 tonnes a year, or almost 1kg per person. And warming waters globally means octopuses are finding their way on to plates in new territories. Over the past two years, for example, the UK witnessed the biggest octopus bloom since 1950. ‘A symbol of what humans shouldn’t be doing’: the new world of octopus farming Read more Octopus grow fast, have a short lifespan, are high in nutrients and are much in demand, so there are plenty of incentives to find a way to farm them. “The conversion rate of what an octopus eats into a high-protein, low-fat meat is much better than any land-based livestock,” says Schweid. “Octopus is potentially a more environmentally sustainable farmed meat than beef, pork or poultry, and in a world shaped by rising temperatures it could become a meat of choice.” In the meantime, the potency of the ethical argument against farming octopuses is likely to remain a strong weapon in the armoury of those who oppose it. “An octopus is a highly intelligent, naturally solitary wild animal,” says Charlotte Reid, a campaigner at Compassion in World Farming . “These are wild animals and they belong in the wild, not these underwater prisons.” Explore more on these topics Marine life Seascape: the state of our oceans Seafood Food Fishing industry Spain Farming Ethical and green living features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Environment Climate crisis Wildlife Energy Pollution Green light

https://www.theguardian.com/news/ng-inte.text: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images The long read Russia A bungled bomb plot in Poland exposed a spy – but whose spy was he? When exiled Russian opposition campaigner Igor Rogov was accused of working for the Kremlin, his friends were shocked. Could this young activist have really been an undercover agent? The summer issue of the Long Read magazine is out now. Click here to order Shaun Walker Thu 13 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share The police came for Igor Rogov because someone had mailed him a bomb-making kit. The eclectic mix of items – a chrome vacuum flask, a pair of marker pens, a power bank and a bottle of antifreeze fluid – might have seemed innocuous to an untrained eye, but Poland was on high alert in July 2024. Two months previously, a shopping mall in Warsaw had burned down in an arson attack; an Ikea in neighbouring Lithuania was also set on fire . Authorities believed it was a sabotage campaign masterminded by Russia’s intelligence services, intended to sow panic and undermine support for Ukraine. They feared it was only a matter of time before the Kremlin escalated further. A security officer at the parcel company’s warehouse was suspicious enough about the package to call in the authorities, who arrived with sniffer dogs and special equipment. X-rays of the marker pens showed they had 1980s Soviet-produced detonators concealed inside, while the flask had a false bottom containing a sachet of metallic powder. The power bank appeared to have been tampered with in some way, and a probe of the bottled liquid showed it contained a highly volatile nitroglycerine solution. With the right expertise, the items could be turned into a powerful bomb. Police ascertained that Rogov, the parcel’s addressee, was a 27-year-old Russian political activist, who in the past had campaigned for the opposition leader Alexei Navalny and other anti-Kremlin groups. He had fled Russia two years previously, fearing arrest for his activities, and been granted asylum in Poland . He won a scholarship to attend university in Sosnowiec, an industrial city in the south-west of the country. His wife, Irina Rogova, followed him to Poland and also enrolled at the university; the couple lived in a student dormitory. It was there that authorities arrested him. Rogov’s phone, when searched, contained photographs of urban scenes in the vicinity of Sosnowiec overlaid with red arrows, apparently indicating places to hide or retrieve items. One photo was of a gas pipeline on the outskirts of town, an appealing potential target for a Russian bomb attack. The chance discovery of the package, it seemed, had led authorities to a participant, perhaps even a coordinator, of Russia’s sabotage campaign against Poland, living under deep cover as a brave opponent to the Kremlin. More than a year later, in October 2025, Polish authorities revealed they were also accusing Rogov of longstanding collaboration with the FSB , Russia’s feared security service. This suggested that his whole career as an anti-Kremlin activist might have been a cover story for his FSB work. When the case came to court, however, the judge closed proceedings to the public and press on national security grounds, fuelling further speculation and rumours about what exactly Rogov had done – especially among Russia’s exiled political opposition, where infighting, suspicions and accusations are commonplace. Although Rogov’s trial was closed, I discovered thousands of pages of documents about him and his wife in the court papers of a related case. (Some of the files were previously reported on by the Polish news site Wirtualna Polska). Those files, as well as interviews in several countries with intelligence sources and with those who knew Rogov, helped piece together a tale of exile and espionage that involved blackmail, deception and a marital crisis with dramatic consequences. (In accordance with Polish law, people mentioned in court files are identified in this story by first name only, except where they have given their consent to be interviewed and named in full. Rogov and his wife are named as they have already been widely identified as protagonists in the case.) Many who knew Rogov were shocked by his arrest. They described their friend as likable, easy-going and somewhat hapless, and struggled to imagine him as a cunning superspy, or a bomb courier with a secret life blowing up European cities on behalf of Vladimir Putin. “This is a guy who once accidentally sent half-naked photos to the group chat,” said Milia Kashapova, who was Rogov’s campaign manager when he stood in city council elections back in Russia and worked with him at close quarters for several months. “It’s hard for me to believe that all that time he was playing a double game, that he didn’t once come unstuck. If he was really collaborating all along, well, then I’d have to say that Igor Rogov is a genius.” At the beginning, the only thing Polish investigators had on Rogov was the fact that someone had mailed him the suspicious package. In his first jail interrogations, Rogov maintained it was all a big misunderstanding. He denied any knowledge of the package’s contents and insisted he would never have knowingly done anything to harm his new homeland. “I’m very grateful to Poland for taking me in and I’m ready to help you in any way I can,” he told investigators. Rogov gave his version of how his name had come to be on the package. His friend Emil, also a Russian opposition activist, had told him that a contact was bringing a parcel from Ukraine and needed someone in Poland to leave it with. Emil said the package contained “presents from Ukraine” and Rogov said he would be fine to pick it up. Some days later he received a call from a woman who introduced herself as Kristina. “I’ve got a package for you from Diesel,” she told him, adding that she had just arrived in Kraków from Ukraine. Rogov had no idea who Diesel was, but assumed this was the package Emil had asked him about. He told Kristina he was away visiting friends, but gave her his address in Sosnowiec and explained how she could mail it to him using a courier service. Polish authorities soon identified Kristina as a Ukrainian model from Odesa and put out an international arrest warrant for her. She was detained in late August at Amsterdam airport, just before boarding a plane to the US. Once delivered to Polish custody, she explained her side of the parcel story. “Diesel” was her old acquaintance – the nickname was because he worked with secondhand cars. He had found out she was planning to drive to Poland and asked if she might take a package with her. “He said he needed to distribute this stuff to poor people and was helping women and families,” Kristina told investigators. “I did think it was a weird set of things, but Diesel is a pretty weird guy.” Kristina told investigators that Diesel had put the flask, power bank and other items in her Mercedes before she embarked on the long drive to Kraków. There, she had a rendezvous with a Czech businessman who had offered to pay her €3,000 if she would spend a week with him at a luxury hotel. She ate oysters and drank champagne with the Czech, though at night they retired to separate bedrooms, the case files suggest. After she bade farewell to her new Czech friend, Kristina remembered the package. She was meant to hand it off in person, but when she called the number Diesel had given her, the man on the other end – Rogov – told her to send it via parcel courier instead. She retrieved the empty shoebox from a pair of €500 Golden Goose sneakers the Czech had bought her and filled the box with Diesel’s items. Then she wrapped it in paper and took the package to a bank of automated parcel lockers as instructed by Rogov. Having addressed the package, she shoved it into a locker that was a shade too small, causing the packaging to tear. That damage meant the courier company opened the parcel when it reached their sorting facility, discovered the suspicious contents and raised the alarm. This set in train the arrests of Rogov and Kristina. Had she picked a larger locker, the package might have gone undetected and the bomb been assembled and detonated. But by whom? Rogov, or someone else? And on whose orders? In the days after she sent the package, but before she was arrested, Kristina said she received a call from Diesel’s number. “I’m going to speak. You listen and stay quiet,” said a male voice she did not recognise. He told her the person she had mailed the package to had been detained, and that if she were also detained, she should invent a story about how she had come by the package. “All the correspondence between you and Diesel has been erased; don’t mention Diesel to anyone,” said the man. The mysterious Diesel was emerging as the key to the parcel plot. Could he be a Russian agent working in Ukraine? Polish authorities had already arrested several Ukrainians recruited by Moscow to carry out arson in Poland, and it was possible that Diesel was part of a Russian sabotage ring with Rogov, using easy access to explosives in Ukraine to source the raw materials before they were assembled and detonated in Poland. Polish authorities issued an international arrest warrant for Diesel and one for Emil, who had told Rogov about the package. Whoever Diesel was working for, one thing became clear as the questioning continued: Kristina knew nothing about the parcel’s purpose or final destination. In one of her interrogations, as investigators scrolled through her phone demanding ever more details of her encounters with various men in her contacts list, she lost her cool and asked them how this could possibly be relevant to the matter at hand. “All you’ve managed to achieve through your investigations is to prove that I’m a breaker of men’s hearts,” she told them. Kristina was released in summer 2025, after a brief trial in which the prosecutor accepted that she had carried the items without realising they were dangerous and agreed to soften the charges. She was sentenced to time already served – 304 days – and fined. She did not respond to my requests for further comment. As for Rogov, it was starting to look as if he, too, could be a tangential player in the bomb plot. He insisted he knew nothing of Diesel, and that the package had his name on it only because he had agreed to help out Emil. The biggest red flag suggesting he might be lying was the set of photographs of various urban scenes in Sosnowiec, marked with arrows, found on his phone. But he had a convincing explanation for that, too. He had sometimes ordered recreational drugs via a Telegram bot, he admitted, and would receive a photo of the pickup location with an arrow marking the drop spot. The only reason some of the locations were close to pipelines or other infrastructure was because these were desolate, empty places where hiding or retrieving a package would draw less attention, he said. The investigation, which had initially seemed like it would uncover a major Kremlin terror plot against Europe, was not going to plan. There was no proven link to Russia, and the only two arrests were of a clueless Ukrainian model and a young Russian who was apparently guilty only of the occasional purchase of recreational drugs. But something else was about to come to light about Rogov. Polish investigators were to learn that he had been credibly accused of working for the FSB for years, spying on his friends and colleagues in the Russian opposition. The source of the accusations made them hard to dismiss: it was Rogov’s wife, Irina. Igor met Irina when they were teenagers. They were both studying veterinary medicine in Saransk, a drab city about 500km (310 miles) south-east of Moscow, where they lived their whole lives before emigrating. Rogov had a cheeky smile and easygoing demeanour that made him friends easily. He got into activism as a student, though to start with he was mostly drawn to local environmental issues. He was then one of thousands of young Russians who helped out with Navalny’s ill-fated attempt to stand against Putin in the 2018 presidential election, and he later became part of Open Russia, the opposition movement set up by the exiled oligarch Mikhail Khodorkovsky. Rogov won respect in opposition circles after an incident in Minsk, in neighbouring Belarus, in August 2020, when Alexander Lukashenko, a close ally of Putin, declared victory after a rigged presidential election. Protesters took to the streets and Lukashenko launched a violent crackdown . Rogov was in Minsk as part of an informal monitoring mission organised by Open Russia. On the second evening of protests, Rogov and a fellow activist, Artem Vazhenkov, got caught up in an ambush outside a shopping mall. Black-clad riot police grabbed anyone they could lay their hands on and tossed them into armoured trucks; Rogov and Vazhenkov ended up at Minsk’s notorious Okrestina jail with hundreds of others. They were kept in a courtyard, hands tied and face-down on the ground, then moved to a packed cell holding about 40 men. “There was no attempt to get any information, like in Russian prisons. They just beat you for the hell of it,” Vazhenkov told me. The riot police broke Rogov’s ribs and fingers and left his body covered in bruises. The repeated kicks to his head in custody gave him migraines that recurred for years. View image in fullscreen Anti-government protests in Minsk, Belarus, in 2020. Photograph: Tatyana Zenkovich/EPA After three days of beatings, Rogov was released and deported to Russia. At the Open Russia office back in Moscow, he alternated between laughing and crying as he recounted the ordeal, still moving gingerly from the bruises. “We sent him to a holiday guesthouse for a couple of weeks to recover,” said Andrei Pivovarov, Open Russia’s executive director at the time. A few weeks later, Igor and Irina, then 23 and 24 years old, got married in Saransk. Vazhenkov, who attended, said it was a “typical Russian wedding”, with vodka, toasts and lots of dancing. Rogov also became more active in Open Russia; the organisation felt partly responsible for the Minsk debacle and supported him to become the official head of their Saransk branch. But a few months later, Open Russia officially dissolved itself, because its designation as “undesirable” by Russian authorities meant activists could be arrested just for being linked to it. So when Rogov ran for a seat on Saransk’s city council in the summer of 2021, he stood as an independent candidate. Getting registered to stand, even in such a low-level vote, required organised and sustained campaigning. Milia Kashapova, a 26-year-old activist formerly associated with Open Russia, moved to Saransk for a few months to be his campaign manager. The campaign was low-budget – Kashapova lived in the apartment of Rogov’s grandmother – but inventive. They spent long days canvassing on the streets and made Instagram reels featuring Igor and Irina’s cats. In the evenings they sat in bars, often with Irina, and discussed strategy. The police showed up at most public events to intimidate supporters, but this was standard practice in Russian regional politics, and Rogov ploughed on. He and his team went door-to-door, promising those who agreed to hear them out that, if elected, he would bring a breath of fresh air into the corrupt city council. In a campaign post on Telegram, he posted a picture of him and Irina with one of the cats, accompanied by the slogan: “Love and fidelity are the foundations of my family.” When polling day came, Rogov won 16% of the vote in his district, finishing third behind two broadly pro-Kremlin candidates. He thanked his supporters and announced that he planned to launch several court cases to protest against procedural violations. “Think this is the end? It’s just the beginning,” he wrote on his Telegram channel. But in the following weeks, with

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: A Ukrainian howitzer fires towards Russian troops in the Zaporizhzhia region. The Oleksandrivskyi sector takes in corners of Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Donetsk oblasts where they meet. Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen A Ukrainian howitzer fires towards Russian troops in the Zaporizhzhia region. The Oleksandrivskyi sector takes in corners of Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Donetsk oblasts where they meet. Photograph: Reuters Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Ukraine Explainer Ukraine war briefing: ‘With precision, as planned’ – Kyiv outlines battlefield gains Zelenskyy announces recapture of 745 sq km in Oleksandrivskyi sector; plea from stranded Ukrainian frontline troops. What we know on day 1,632 Warren Murray and agencies Wed 12 Aug 2026 21.37 EDT Last modified on Wed 12 Aug 2026 23.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukrainian forces have ⁠recaptured 745 sq km (288 sq miles) of Russian-occupied land in a key sector this year , Volodymyr Zelenskyy ⁠has said. “This offensive operation of ours was carried out with precision – exactly as planned.” Ukraine’s president outlined gains broadly in line with assessments from the well-regarded Ukrainian open-source group DeepState. Russia’s battlefield advances have ​slowed this year across much of the front, analysts ​say, though Russian ‌forces still threaten cities in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk region . The Russian military still regularly announces the “capture” of villages, though observers say these are often shortlived flag-raising incursions involving a handful of troops. “From January to August of this year, our warriors of the airborne assault forces and other units carried out an effective offensive operation in the Oleksandrivskyi sector … Russian losses amounted to at least 9,550 people killed and more than 6,600 people wounded.” Ukraine’s “exchange fund” was also replenished, Zelenskyy said, referring to Russian prisoners of war who can be swapped for Ukrainians held by Russia. The Oleksandrivskyi sector is a 60km (37-mile) stretch of the front taking in parts of Dnipropetrovsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Donetsk oblasts where they meet . Zelenskyy said 26 ⁠settlements there had been brought back ​under Kyiv’s control. DeepState, which tracks both sides’ positions on the front, said in its ‌latest assessment that Ukrainian forces had restored control over 19 settlements along the frontline, and pushed back Russian troops in six more settlements. The US-based Institute for the Study of War said in an assessment that Russian online sources were likely using AI-enhanced video footage to support Moscow’s claims of advances. A major Ukrainian attack on Russia’s Black Sea port city of Novorossiysk hit warships at a naval base and forced two major grain terminals to halt operations ⁠on Wednesday, according to Russian and Ukrainian officials as well as grain industry sources. Zelenskyy said two frigates, a large landing ship, a corvette and other ​vessels were hit . Describing the attack as having “strategic significance”, Ukraine’s SBU security service said ⁠Kyiv’s forces hit the Novorossiysk naval base with drones and missiles. The Russian regional governor, Veniamin Kondratyev, said the attacks killed at least two people including an eight-year-old child. Novorossiysk also hosts oil export infrastructure , including for the Caspian Pipeline Consortium owned partly by US ‌oil companies Chevron and ​Exxon Mobil, and carries Kazakh ​oil exports to market. The Financial Times (paywall) reported on Wednesday that after a request from JD Vance, the US vice-president, Ukraine agreed not to target CPC infrastructure and non-Russian vessels, as long as they were not under Ukrainian sanctions or carrying Russian oil or other cargo. Ukraine needs 5% of US Patriot interceptors to get through the winter and 10% to destroy all the ballistic missiles fired by Russia , Volodymyr Zelenskyy has told CNN. Ukraine this year “had two and a half times less interceptors than we had in 2025 … Russia has two times more ballistic missiles per month than they had before. This year, I’m asking American partners to sell me 5% of missiles [that] they have in their stocks.” As of today he had “1%”, Zelenskyy said . “From 1% to 5%, I have some months and millions [of] phone calls and anything else. I do some things which I can’t even share. It doesn’t mean that it’s out of the law. But I can’t speak about it.” Ukraine’s air force said on Wednesday it would stop publishing detailed figures on Russian ballistic missile strikes . Real-time warnings would continue unchanged, and the air force would keep providing generalised figures on Russian missile launches. Russia’s Orenburg region has introduced ⁠fuel rationing after a ⁠Ukrainian ​drone strike on the Orsk refinery this week in the Urals mountain ⁠province. “Dear residents of our ​region, I ‌will be ‌frank: a difficult fuel situation is ‌developing in the region,” said Yevgeny Solntsev, the regional governor. He announced restrictions on gasoline sales, including a ban on filling up containers, limits on ‌sale volume, and sales on odd ​or even days based on licence plate numbers. Other ‌Russian regions ​were already under similar restrictions. A group of Ukrainian soldiers appealed to their military leadership for help in a video where they told of spending four months on the frontline without rotation and drinking urine during a 12-day stint when drone-dropped water supplies did not arrive. Ukraine’s 121st Brigade command confirmed the social media video’s authenticity and said the brigade “continues to take all necessary measures to properly supply the servicemen” in what it described as “extremely difficult” battlefield conditions. Platoon commander Anatoliy Saichuk accused senior officers of lying to soldiers’ families by assuring them the men were fully supplied. “Some of my servicemen were semi-conscious for several days due to lack of water and food,” he added, saying he had eventually decided to abandon the positions when circumstances allowed. The South joint forces group, which commands the area, said the platoon was fighting in a “difficult and dynamic sector of the front”, adding the video showed “an isolated fragment of a complex operational environment”. Moldova has agreed to give Ukraine a 50% discount ⁠on rail cargo ⁠shipments ​until the end of the year, according to both governments. Ukraine, a major grain exporter by sea, has sought the alternative route because of Russian attacks on its ports and shipping. Russia ⁠struck Ukraine’s Izmail ⁠port ⁠area in ​the southern Odesa ⁠region over Wednesday night, causing ⁠damage ​and ‌fire, local ‌authorities said. Izmail, close to ‌the Romanian border, ​is home to ⁠Ukraine’s largest Danube ​port, handling ​grain ​and other ​commodities. Russia’s agriculture ministry has also said it is ‌working to redirect its export flows to alternative routes because of Ukrainian attacks in the Black Sea. https://www.dw.com/en/russia-s-putin-ang.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IjBj Putin visited a fish factory on the island of Iturup, known as Etorofu in Japanese Image: Gavriil Grigorov/AFP Advertisement Russian President Vladimir Putin has visited the far-eastern Kuril Islands for the first time, state media reported on Thursday, drawing anger from Japan . Japan has long claimed ownership of four of the Kuril Islands , including the one reportedly visited by Putin, which the Soviet Union seized toward the end of World War II . Iturup/Etorofu has a harsh climate, but mineral deposits and good fishing grounds Image: Sergei Krasnoukhov/TASS/picture alliance What is the dispute over the Kuril Islands? During his trip, Putin visited a fish-processing plant on the island, known as Iturup in Russian and Etorofu in Japanese, where he was given caviar, Russian media reported. The island belongs to four that are known in Japan as the Northern Territories and that are now Russian-occupied following the Soviet Union's takeover in 1945. At that time, Moscow deported their Japanese population of about 17,000 people, with the islands now inhabited by some 20,000 Russian citizens. The unresolved dispute was one of the key reasons why Moscow and Tokyo never signed a formal World War II peace treaty. Russian-Japanese relations have since suffered another major blow following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine launched in 2022. The volcanic Kuril archipelago runs in an arc from Russia's Kamchatka peninsula down to Japan's main northern island of Hokkaido. What has Japan said about Putin's visit? In a statement on Thursday, Japan's foreign minister, Toshimitsu Motegi, expressed Tokyo's great displeasure at Putin's visit. "The Northern Territories ... are an inherent part of Japan's territory both historically and under international law, and the government of Japan strongly protests this visit," the statement said. Strategically-located Kuril Islands The islands have seldom been visited by Russian leaders, with then-President Dmitry Medvedev in 2010 becoming the first to travel to the disputed territory. Medvedev also went there in 2015 as prime minister. Putin's visit to the Kurils came after he visited the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin, where Russia's navy was conducting drills. Putin observed a military drill by Russia's Pacific fleet in the Sakhalin Region, Image: Gavriil Grigorov/Sputnik/REUTERS The islands had considerable strategic importance for the Soviet Union, which kept a large military presence there during the Cold War amid tensions with the US and Japan. Talks on the territorial issue that have been held since the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991 have so far borne no fruit . Edited by: Rob Turner Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.dw.com/en/how-north-korea-ha.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IjBh North Korean leader Kim Jong Un (left) has profited greatly from cooperation with Russia Image: KCNA/KNS/AFP Advertisement For years, satellite images of North Korea at night showed only a few small patches of light. Electricity shortages meant that even cities remained dark. In the six years since April 2020, however, the illuminated area in the center of Pyongyang has tripled in size. The information portal NK News sees the increased illumination of the urban area as evidence that the regime has prioritized the supply of electricity to new streets and houses in the center to showcase its achievements. At the last party congress in 2021, Kim Jong Un , North Korea's leader, announced that he would build 50,000 new apartments in the capital. And he did embark on the plan: in the new neighborhood of Hwasong, for example, with the construction of two 40-story apartment blocks shaped like Hwasong intercontinental ballistic missiles. Why North Korea is now Europe's problem To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The new high-rise districts are not the only sign of North Korea's improved prosperity. People who have been visiting Pyongyang for a long time report that the city now appears more modern. There are many imported cars, including electric cars from China , smartphone apps with QR codes to make payments or to call taxis, and department stores that stock Western fashion brands and cosmetics. Pyongyang has transformed into a modern city thanks to North Korea's deals with Russia and China Image: Jon Chol Jin/AP Photo/picture alliance The regime has completed construction in Pyongyang of the biggest hospital in the country and a hothouse the size of New York's Central Park. In June 2025, Kim officially opened the five-kilometer-long (3.3 miles) beach resort of Wonsan-Kalma on the east coast, with space for 20,000 guests. In June, the Wall Street Journal described North Korea as the "world's most unlikely growth story." North Korea's lucrative war deals with Russia The dictatorship is presumably able to finance this sudden upturn thanks to the substantial income from its involvement in Russia's war against Ukraine . According to a report by the South Korean Institute for National Security Strategy (INSS) in March, North Korea earns between $7.7 billion and $14.4 billion (€6.7 billion and €12.5 billion) from the sale of munitions to Moscow and the deployment of troops. Bloomberg Economics recently estimated that between 2022 and 2025, North Korea earned more than $14 billion by providing military support for Russia. North Korea expands its role in Russia's war against Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Furthermore, it brought in another $8 billion through trade with China , the provision of North Korean workers to other countries, export business and online criminality. The hacking of the ByBit platform in February 2025 was one of the world's biggest cryptocurrency heists. Suspected North Korean hackers made off with $1.5 billion worth of Ethereum, a network with its own virtual currency. In comparison: the previous year, North Korea's entire GDP was $27 billion. North Korea's involvement in Russia's war effort It is unclear whether it was Russia or North Korea who first had the idea of using the impoverished country's massive stockpiles of munitions in Russia's war against Ukraine. Kyiv estimates that in 2024 and 2025, North Korea supplied half the munitions Russia used at the front, as well as self-propelled guns, multiple rocket launchers and ballistic missiles. Ukraine says North Korea is currently planning to transfer a missile unit to Russia to fight against Ukraine, consisting of 90 soldiers, six launch pads and up to 120 missiles. Between 16,000 and 22,000 North Korean soldiers are already helping Russia to drive Ukraine out of the border province of Kursk and clear the area of mines afterward. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy , Kim now intends to station a further 30,000 to 50,000 soldiers in Russia. Kim hails troops returning from Russia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The business is a lucrative one: The INSS report says that, every month, Kim receives $2,800 per North Korean soldier, $3,000 for an officer and $6,000 to $10,000 for every soldier killed in action. As in Soviet times, the reciprocal arrangement is conducted primarily through exchange transactions. In exchange for munitions, arms and soldiers, Russia supplies North Korea with crude oil and oil products, grain and military goods from anti-aircraft systems to the technologies for building drones, missiles and submarines. North Korea's new global stage Kim's new role as Russia's supporter has given him greater political importance and military power, as demonstrated by the launch of two 5,000-ton destroyers. In all 15 of the years he has been in power, the autocratic leader has never had this much influence, or this much money. North Korea gains critical intel by aiding Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video It's an astonishing turnaround. Kim noticeably lost weight during the COVID-19 pandemic , and at the Workers' Party congress in 202,1 he shed tears as he admitted that the national economic development strategy had fallen "far short in almost all sectors." At the next party congress five years later, with seven rows of artillery pieces lined up outside the building, Kim crowed, "Everything has fundamentally changed." The partnership with Russia has allowed North Korea to shed its status as a pariah of world politics and overcome its isolation. In June 2024, the Russian President Vladimir Putin visited Kim in Pyongyang . Chinese leader Xi Jinping came in June of this year , three months after the Belarusian dictator Alexander Lukashenko . In September 2025, Kim was in attendance at the celebrations in Beijing , alongside Xi and Putin, to mark the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II . Profits not reaching North Koreans However, observers say this economic upswing is not benefiting the majority of the population. Many households already in a precarious situation and without access to foreign currency have been hit hard by rising food prices and the devaluation of the won, the national currency. In many families, the women, too, must now go out to work in order to maintain living standards. In the spring of 2024, Kim promoted a "20x10" development program for regions beyond the well-supplied capital Pyongyang. Presumably, he intends to finance this with the new additional revenue. The plan foresees that modern factories will be built in 20 cities or regions annually, creating 200 regional industrial projects over 10 years. But according to Andrei Lankov, a professor and North Korea expert at Kookmin University in Seoul, the majority of the 20x10 projects fail. "This is because not only do the factories have no infrastructure, they also do not take into account the mechanisms for supplying electricity, equipment, and raw materials," he said. The factories are operated according to the principles of a planned economy, which is unsuited to small and medium-sized businesses. "Unlike the economic growth that took place in North Korea in the mid-2010s, the current growth was based not on internal economic reforms, but only on international good fortune," Lankov said. https://www.politico.eu/article/gabriel-.text: PARIS — Former Prime Minister Gabriel Attal is trying to jump-start his presidential prospects by taking advantage of his rivals enjoying France’s cherished August break. Attal, a former prime minister who now leads President Emmanuel Macron’s centrist political party Renaissance, is betting that by keeping a busy schedule during the holiday and meeting with people across the country — including those at vineyards, markets and ports as well as vacationers in picturesque seaside towns — he can show voters what sets him apart from the field. “It’s a rather bourgeois assumption to think that all French people take time off or go on vacation,” said a representative for Attal’s team who, like others in this story, was granted anonymity to speak candidly about campaign dynamics. “There’s no way he’s going to suspend his campaign over the summer.” Advertisement But political reality is also forcing Attal to campaign in August for the vote in April of next year. If he wants a real shot at catching up in the polls, there’s little time to waste. Surveys have consistently shown the 37-year-old trailing Edouard Philippe, his main ideological rival for centrist and center-right votes. Given the contest goes to a two-candidate runoff if nobody wins a majority in the first round, the two men have tentatively agreed that only one of them should be on the ballot so they don’t split their shared voter base — which could cost both of them a spot in the second round. Philippe, far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen, far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon and conservative candidate Bruno Retailleau are all among the presidential hopefuls taking long summer breaks, only interrupting their time off for the occasional op-ed or statement on major events like the wildfires that ravaged southwest France. Edouard Philippe speaks at a rally in northern Paris on July 5, 2026. | Simon Wohlfahrt/AFP via Getty Images Their reasoning for slowing down during the peak holiday season is straightforward: Voters want to rest and recharge, so candidates shouldn’t harass them with politics and should instead enjoy one last bit of respite before the race enters its decisive stretch. “We shouldn’t bother the French people while they’re on vacation,” said a Retailleau adviser. Attal is betting otherwise that a summer spent campaigning can help close the gap in the polls. “A campaign is about winning over the French one by one … [Attal] wants to show that he’s more determined than the others,” added his adviser. The right track It’s unclear for now to what extent Attal’s summer work will reap dividends with voters, as most pollsters who would investigate that question have themselves set out-of-office messages. But the absence of other candidates on the campaign trail has given Attal an opportunity to dominate headlines, and he’s used it to make a play for right-wing voters. Advertisement At the start of the month, Attal, a member of parliament who represents a Paris suburb, gave an interview to the right-wing weekly Le Journal du Dimanche in which he called for lower immigration, a sweeping streamlining of France’s administrative procedures and more effective enforcement of criminal sentences. He then traveled to western France, where, in front of cameras, he confronted a group of French gens du voyage — a legal classification for traditionally itinerant communities, including Roma and Manouche, and long a target of the French right — who had occupied land without authorization. The encounter can be seen below in a report from CNEWS, in French. French municipalities are required to provide designated stopping sites for traveling communities, but those obligations are not always met — or the sites provided are insufficient — sometimes resulting in unauthorized occupations of public or private land. For both Attal and Philippe, making inroads on the right will be crucial. Macron’s 2022 reelection was buoyed by older, more affluent voters who had traditionally backed conservatives. But Philippe begins that contest with a built-in advantage. Advertisement He is a former member of the conservative party Les Républicains and has always identified as a man of the right. Attal, who started his political career in the youth wing of the center-left Socialists, has resisted the label. One conservative minister in the current French government, who has not endorsed a candidate for 2027, readily described Philippe as belonging to his political camp. Attal, the minister said, has a “very flexible” ideological spine. Sarah Paillou and Anthony Lattier contributed to this report.

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c74g.text: Figure caption, Nobel Peace Prize winner Dmitry Muratov warns of the possibility of nuclear escalation under Putin By Steve Rosenberg BBC Russia Editor ,Â Reporting from Moscow Published 2 hours ago At the Moscow offices of newspaper Novaya Gazeta, the corridors are silent. There is an overwhelming sense of emptiness. "There is no newspaper anymore," former chief editor Dmitry Muratov tells me in an exclusive interview, published on the BBC News YouTube channel , external . Mr Muratov co-founded Novaya Gazeta more than 30 years ago. It became the flagship for hard-hitting independent journalism in Russia, shining a light on human rights abuses and high-level corruption. In 2021 Mr Muratov was joint winner of the Nobel Peace Prize for his efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression." The Nobel Committee noted that "six of [Novaya Gazeta's] journalists have been killed, including Anna Politkovskaya who wrote revealing articles on the war in Chechnya." It was recognition for courageous reporting. But it didn't protect the paper. Image source, EPA Image caption, Muratov auctioned off his Nobel Prize medal to support UNICEF's humanitarian efforts to support Ukrainian refguees "Putin issued a decree and the newspaper's printing presses were nationalised," Mr Muratov explains. "Its registration was revoked." Novaya Gazeta does retain a presence online. But only just: the authorities have blocked access to its website. It can only be accessed from abroad, or with the help of VPNs â virtual private networks used to circumvent restrictions. The newspaper's difficulties reflect the broader crackdown on free speech in Russia which has accelerated since the Kremlin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. "Most opinion leaders have been declared 'foreign agents', 'extremists' or 'terrorists'. Several hundred," says Dmitry Muratov. "Figures vary, but at a conservative estimate, since the start of Russia's 'special military operation' [in Ukraine] at least 1,500 people are now in prison having spoken out against current state policy. That's three times more than during the savage days of the KGB in the USSR." In his 1975 Nobel Peace Prize lecture dissident Andrei Sakharov listed the names of more than 120 political prisoners he was aware of in the Soviet Union. A decade later Amnesty International estimated more than 600 prisoners of conscience in the USSR. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Journalists Antonina Favorskaya, Konstantin Gabov, Sergey Karelin and Artyom Kriger were jailed on extremism charges for five and half years What the Kremlin had assumed in 2022 would be a short, successful "military operation" has become the bloodiest conflict in Europe since the Second World War. Yet a confident President Putin continues to predict victory for Russia. "There will never be 'victory'," counters Dmitry Muratov. "Because what has been going on for nearly five years â no matter how it ends â can no longer be considered a victory. "It cannot be a victory when two Slavic nations have ripped a million people to shreds. Or more than a million." "It seems to me that the situation with Ukraine now is this: you can destroy it, but you cannot conquer it. What do I mean by destroy? Continued escalation all the way to the use of a nuclear weapon." Does he really believe the Kremlin leader would use nuclear weapons in this war? "All those political experts who say 'Putin thinks this' or 'Putin is scared of that'â¦they're all charlatans," claims Dmitry Muratov. "It's in the same league as astrology. Nobody knows what's going on in Vladimir Putin's head. And I don't know. "I see things only as a journalist. I study big data. And since the beginning of the year the need to use nuclear weapons has been mentioned more than 500 times. When wackos say this, I pay no attention. But I've heard it discussed on state TV. And at the St Petersburg International Economic Forum, a state-run event, one of the speakers talked up the use of nuclear weapons as something favourable, something good." When he announced the mass invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, President Putin spoke of "ensuring the security of Russia." "Tell me, has security increased?" Dmitry Muratov asks. "With Ukrainian drones now attacking warehouses of [Russia's largest online retailer] Wildberries; with the petrol crisis, the disruption to mobile internet, the political prisoners? Has security increased, or not?" Despite opinion polls registering a fall in Vladimir Putin's domestic approval ratings, Russia's president â Mr Muratov believes - retains a tight grip on power. "Sorry, I don't believe all this talk about a split among members of the elite, about secret conspiracies. The country is run by Vladimir Putin. They're frightened of him. "And this fear is reinforced in every way by his main support base: the Federal Security Service (FSB)." As critical as he is of his own government, he has few illusions about the West. "[Putin] knows very well the true value of European leaders. On the one hand they talk to him about human rights. He laughs out loud because, with the other hand, they sign agreements â or used to sign agreements â with Russia on trading oil, gas, diamondsâ¦all that stuff. When they talk to Putin about European values, he truly laughs out loud. He knows the true value of people who preached to him those values." In Russia Mr Muratov has been designated a 'foreign agent', a label often used to punish critics of the Kremlin. 'Foreign agents' have limited rights: they're banned from teaching, from taking part in elections; if they sell their flat, they can't access the assets. The label is also designed to stigmatise, to create the sense in society of an enemy within. Yet the journalist appears reluctant to focus on the pressures he's under, preferring instead to highlight the plight of compatriots in prison. "What worries me most right now is that no one in the world is interested in the political prisoners who were first to speak out against the land grab in our neighbouring country," Dmitry Muratov explains. Image caption, Nadezhda Buyanova, a 68-year-old Ukrainian-born paediatrician sentenced to five and a half years in a penal colony for allegedly criticising the war in Ukraine at work He opens a folder and takes out a stack of large photographs: portraits of prisoners. One shows four journalists - Antonina Favorskaya, Konstantin Gabov, Sergey Karelin and Artyom Kriger â convicted and jailed on extremism charges. They'd been accused of links to the anti-corruption organisation of the late opposition leader Alexei Navalny. There's a photo of Alexei Gorinov: a city councillor jailed for "knowingly spreading false information" about the Russian military after he spoke out against the war in Ukraine. "And here's a wonderful pianist, Pavel Kushnir," says Dmitry Miratov. "An outstanding performer of Rachmaninoff and Schubert." The musician was arrested after posting anti-war videos. Dmitry Muratov holds up a second video. "And this is him in his coffin." Pavel Kushnir died in a pre-trial detention centre during a hunger strike. He was 39. The stream of photos and prison stories highlights the dangers for individuals framed as opponents of those in power. It's a reminder of the risks that public criticism of the authorities and the war carry. "Does being a Nobel Prize laureate give you at least some protection to say what you want?" I ask. "This is not a question for me," replies Mr Muratov. "Whenever you have the opportunity, ask the authorities that." There is one more photo. From April. "This is the newspaper's lawyer when she was waiting to get into the building. The police were searching our office. Thirteen hours it took. And they wouldn't let the lawyers in. Our managing editor Oleg Roldugin is now under house arrest." Dmitry Muratov paints a bleak picture of life in Russia for critics of the authorities. Yet there are moments of hope. "We live in a time when you stay quiet. But so many people support what we do. On the streets of Moscow, my colleagues and I hear only words of gratitude. They are spoken in a whisper. But what people think is very important." Related topics War in Ukraine Russia Nobel Prize Vladimir Putin Press freedom More on this story Who is Nobel Peace Prize winner Dmitry Muratov? https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx7.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, Russia's President Vladimir Putin tastes caviar as he visits Iturup, known in Japan as Etorofu By Koh Ewe Published 13 August 2026, 05:46 BST Updated 1 hour ago Japan said it "strongly protests" against Vladimir Putin's visit to the Kuril islands on Thursday, the first time the Russian president had visited the disputed island chain. Russian state media reported that Putin visited Iturup - known in Japan as Etorofu - one of four islands in the Kuril chain that are claimed by Russia and Japan. Japan's foreign minister Toshimitsu Motegi said the islands were "inherently Japanese territory both historically and under international law, and the Government of Japan strongly protests this visit". The countries have been locked in a dispute over the Kurils for decades, and it is the main reason Moscow and Tokyo did not sign a peace treaty after World War Two. The Kuril islands sit between Hokkaido in northern Japan and Russia's Kamchatka Peninsula. Four of the southernmost islands are claimed by Japan, which calls them the Northern Territories. They are administered by Russia. At the end of World War Two, the Soviet Union annexed the island chain and deported around 17,000 Japanese residents. During his visit, Putin sampled fish roe and spoke to island locals, Russian state media reported. Over the years, attempts to resolve the territorial dispute have made little progress. Bilateral ties have also remained frosty, with Japan imposing sanctions against Russia for its invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Japan has protested against previous visits by Russian officials to the disputed islands, including Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and his predecessor Dmitry Medvedev. The Kuril islands are a strategic area for Russia, which has beefed up its military presence on the islands over the past decade. The island of Iturup is used as its primary military air base in the region. Last month, Chinese and Russian naval warships sailed through a strait in the Kuril islands during a joint patrol. Russia also holds regular military drills near the islands, drawing condemnation from Japan. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yw.text: Image source, EPA Image caption, David McBride pleaded guilty to leaking military secrets to the media in 2023 By Lana Lam Sydney Published 4 hours ago A whistleblower jailed for leaking military secrets about Australia's involvement in Afghanistan has been released on parole after serving 27 months. In 2024, David McBride was sentenced to five years and eight months after pleading guilty to stealing top secret defence documents and giving it to the media. His actions later led to a landmark inquiry that found evidence that Australian forces had unlawfully killed 39 Afghans during the war. On Thursday, a spokesperson for the Attorney-General Michelle Rowland said McBride's "parole was considered and granted". The ex-military lawyer, who is being treated for lung cancer, will serve the rest of his sentence in the community under supervision. Shortly after the decision, advocacy group The Information Rights Project released a statement on McBride's behalf, according to national broadcaster ABC. He thanked his family "who never gave up on me and whose fighting spirit, love and humour inspired me every day" and praised "all my amazing supporters from around both Australia and the world who sent me such inspirational messages". McBride also revealed that he had been diagnosed with treatable lung cancer and would be having surgery to remove part of his lung. His lawyer Edwina Lloyd described the decision to grant his parole as "the right one", in a statement according to the ABC. She said McBride's life has been "defined by service to Australia", both as a legal officer for the Australian Defence Forces (ADF) and having served time for his crimes. During his court case , prosecutors argued that McBride's actions had been motivated by "personal vindication", and that the way he gathered, stored and then leaked the documents endangered Australia's national security and foreign policy. But McBride's lawyers asked for leniency, saying he shared the information with "honourable" intentions and out of a sense of personal duty. In sentencing McBride, the judge said while he was of "good character", sharing military secrets was a "gross breach of trust" and he had shown "no contrition" for his actions. The material he leaked to the ABC underpinned a series of reports in 2017 called The Afghan Files which provided unprecedented insight into Australia's elite special forces in Afghanistan, including allegations of war crimes. In 2020, the Brereton Report found "credible evidence" that elite soldiers have unlawfully killed 39 people. A special watchdog - the Office of the Special Investigator - was set up to look into the actions of 19 ADF members. Of its 53 cases, 39 have been finalised and two former Special Air Service (SAS) soldiers have been charged. Ben Roberts-Smith , Australia's most decorated living soldier, is facing five counts of the war crime of murder after he was charged earlier this year, while Oliver Schulz faces one count of the same charge.
