https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/08/13/volo.text: Menü Kereső Zelenszkij: Adják el Ukrajnának az amerikai Patriot-készletek 10 százalékát, és megsemmisítjük az összes orosz ballisztikus rakétát Külföld Pál Tamás Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök arra kéri az Egyesült Államokat, hogy adják el Ukrajnának a Patriot légelhárító rakétáik legalább 5-10 százalékát, hogy felvehessék a harcot az egyre gyakrabban érkező orosz ballisztikus rakétákkal. Zelenszkij szerint az Egyesült Államok jelenlegi készletének 10 százaléka elegendő lenne az összes orosz ballisztikusrakéta-támadás megállításához, míg 5 százalék elég lenne ahhoz, hogy Ukrajna átvészelje a következő telet – mondta az ukrán elnök a CNN -nek adott interjújában. Zelenszkij arról is beszélt, hogy a napjai milliónyi telefonhívással telnek, miközben a szövetségeseivel együttműködve próbál még több rakétát szerezni, gyakran olyan háttéralkuk révén is, amelyek részleteit nem hozhatja nyilvánosságra. „Ez az, amivel minden nap foglalkozom: 1 százalékról 5 százalékra növelni a rakéták számát. Milliónyi telefonhívást intézek, próbálok valamit rakétákra cserélni. Olyan dolgokat is teszek, amelyekről még beszélni sem szabad. Ez nem azt jelenti, hogy ezek törvénytelen dolgok lennének, de nem beszélhetek róluk” – mondta az ukrán elnök. Zelenszkij megerősítette, hogy nemrég valóban telefonon beszélt J. D. Vance amerikai alelnökkel, de nem kívánta részletezni, hogy az alelnök tényleg azt kérte-e tőle, hogy Ukrajna állítsa le a fekete-tengeri orosz olajkikötők elleni támadásokat. A Financial Times információi szerint az alelnök amiatt aggódik , hogy a nyersolajat szállító tartályhajókat célba vevő ukrán csapások destabilizálják az olajpiacokat, és ártanak a térségben működő amerikai cégeknek. Az elmúlt hetekben Oroszország kihasználta, hogy Ukrajna Patriot elfogórakéta-készletei csaknem teljesen kimerültek. Az orosz csapások különösen súlyosan érintették Kijevet és környékét . Az ENSZ szerint az idei július volt a leghalálosabb hónap az ukrán civilek számára 2022 áprilisa óta. „Minden éjszaka támadások vannak, és havonta négy-öt alkalommal hatalmas támadásokat hajtanak végre… szörnyű éjszakák. Az emberek nagyon hősiesek és rendkívül ellenállóak. De elfáradtak” – mondta Zelenszkij. Az orosz csapásokról ebben a cikkben írtunk részletesen. „Idén két és félszer kevesebb elfogórakétánk van, mint 2025-ben volt, míg Oroszországnak havonta kétszer annyi ballisztikus rakétája van, mint korábban” – érzékeltette a különbséget az ukrán elnök. „Idén arra kérem amerikai partnereinket, hogy adják el nekünk a készletükben lévő légvédelmi rakétáik 5 százalékát. Ha eladnak nekünk 5 százalékot, átvészeljük a telet és életeket mentünk meg” – fejtette ki Zelenszkij, hozzátéve, hogy ennek a mennyiségnek jelenleg csak az egy százalékát kapják meg. „Ha 10 százalékot tudnak nekünk eladni, akkor megsemmisítjük az összes orosz ballisztikus rakétát” – jelentette ki Zelenszkij. A Patriot rakétákból világszerte hiány van az Egyesült Államok Irán elleni háborúja miatt. A hiány Ukrajnát sújtja a legsúlyosabban, ahol a városok szinte teljesen védtelenek az Oroszország által indított éjszakai rakétacsapásokkal szemben. Zelenszkij szerint továbbra is kérdéses, hogy Donald Trump amerikai elnök azon ígérete, miszerint engedélyeznék Ukrajnának a saját Patriot elfogórakéták gyártását, miként valósulna meg a gyakorlatban. „Nagyobb amerikai szerepvállalásra van szükségünk a béketervben. https://telex.hu/g7/vilag/2026/08/13/gaz.text: Menü Kereső Elérkeztünk oda, amikor a hőség már le tudja nullázni a gazdasági növekedést Világ Legfontosabb A Rajna rekordalacsony vízállása a németországi Bacharachnál, 2026. augusztus 10-én – Fotó: Michael Probst / AP / MTI Stubnya Bence Idén nyáron sokan érezhetik azt, hogy a klímaváltozás már nemcsak a távoli jövő fenyegetése, hanem konkrét, hétköznapi következményekkel járó jelenség. A paksi atomerőmű teljesítményének csökkentése miatt az idén a korábbi éveknél közvetlenebbül, energiaválság formájában mutatkozott meg, hogyan alakítja át a hétköznapokat a felmelegedés. A válságnak komoly gazdasági vonzatai is vannak: az MBH Bank például úgy számolt, hogy a paksi helyzet hetente 0,1 százalékkal csökkenti a bruttó nemzeti össztermék idénre várható növekedését. A bank nem változtatott ugyan 1,6 százalékos GDP-növekedési prognózisán, de jelezte: ha az áramhelyzet nem rendeződik, akár több tized százalékponttal is csökkentenie kell az idei előrejelzését. Azóta az atomerőmű újabb turbinája kezdett termelni, de az előrejelzések szerint a Duna vízszintje augusztusban ismét csökkenni fog . A kormány fenékküszöb építésével és elsüllyeszthető bárkák bevetésével igyekszik elkerülni az atomerőmű teljes leállítását, majd azt követően elérni a teljes kapacitásra kapcsolását. Ha Magyarország megússza a nyarat nagyobb GDP-veszteség nélkül, akkor még szerencsés is lehet más európai uniós tagállamokhoz képest. A holland Triodos Bank nemrég közzétett előrejelzése alapján ugyanis a szélsőséges meleg és aszály 1 százalékkal – 0 százalék közelébe – csökkentheti az ez évre várható gazdasági növekedést az Európai Unióban. A bank szerint Franciaországot érintheti a legsúlyosabban a helyzet, ahol a visszatérő hőhullámok mintegy 1,4 százalékkal csökkenthetik a GDP-t, és akár 0,6 százalékos éves gazdasági visszaeséshez is vezethetnek. Olaszország, Spanyolország és Belgium szintén jelentős veszteségekkel nézhet szembe. Az Allianz becslése szerint a júniusi, két hétig tartó hőhullám önmagában 0,3 százalékponttal vethette vissza Európa GDP-jét. Az extrém időjárási jelenségek – a hőhullámok, az aszályok, a folyók alacsony vízszintje és az erdőtüzek – sokszor ugyanazokat a térségeket együttesen sújtva fejtik ki negatív gazdasági hatásukat, ami tovább erősíti a károkat. Az alacsony vízállás miatt például jelentősen korlátozott a forgalom Európa két fontos folyami szállítási útvonalán, a Rajnán és a Dunán, miközben számos atomerőmű teljesítményét is csökkenteni kellett a hűtési nehézségek miatt. A mezőgazdasági terméskilátásokat is rontották: a későn aratott termények, például a kukorica és a napraforgó terméskiesése az előrejelzések szerint már júliusban elérte a 6-7 százalékot a Reuters által idézett adatok szerint. Az ING becslése szerint Németországban az idei rekordalacsony vízállás 0,3 százalékpontos csökkenést hozhat a növekedésben (ami megegyezik a 2018-as aszály hatásaival). Magyarországon az elmúlt években a globális felmelegedés gazdasági hatásai elsősorban a mezőgazdaság gyengébb teljesítményén keresztül jelentkeztek. Habár olyan erős hatása itthon nem volt az aszálynak, mint például Argentínában – ahol 2023-ban egyes becslések szerint 3 százalékkal vetette vissza a növekedést a termés 40 százalékos csökkenése –, 2022-ben a magyar mezőgazdaság kibocsátásának volumene 16 százalékkal csökkent az előző évhez képest. Ez két negyedévben is 1-2 százalék között húzta le a GDP-t (ami viszont nagyon alacsony bázisról 4,6 százalékot nőtt az előző évhez képest, mivel a mezőgazdaságon kívül szinte minden alág felfelé húzta). Az agrárium az aszály miatt itthon tavaly is 0,1 százalékponttal húzta vissza a növekedést, ami így csak 0,3 százalékos volt. Az elmúlt években éves szinten 0,3–0,8 százalékpont között alakult a növekedési veszteség azokban az országokban, ahol az extrém hőség és a klímaváltozáshoz kapcsolódó események korlátozták a gazdasági teljesítményt – mondta Hidi János, a Cambridge Econometrics fenntartható befektetésekért felelős vezetője. Szerinte a felmelegedés több csatornán keresztül is rontja a gazdasági teljesítményt. Az egyik legközvetlenebb hatás a mezőgazdaságban jelentkezik: az aszályok és árvizek miatt csökkenhet a terméshozam, illetve az állattenyésztésben is visszaeshet a tej- és hústermelés. A hőhullámok közvetlen fizikai károkat is okozhatnak az infrastruktúrában. Nagy melegben például meglágyulhatnak a vezetékek vagy deformálódhatnak a vasúti sínek, ami az energiaellátásban és a logisztikában vezethet fennakadásokhoz. Aszály idején a vízerőművek kevesebb energiát termelnek, de – ahogy azt most a paksi atomerőmű esetében is megtapasztalhattuk – az erőművek működését is korlátozhatja, ha nem áll rendelkezésre elegendő víz a hűtéshez. Az így kialakuló energiahiány az ipari termelést is visszafoghatja. A klímaváltozás kevésbé látványos, de a gazdasági teljesítmény szempontjából fontos hatása a munkavégzés hatékonyságának romlása. A szabadban dolgozók a nagy melegben könnyebben megbetegednek, lassabban dolgoznak, és nő a hibák, illetve a balesetek kockázata is. Mindez csökkenti a munka hatékonyságát, és ha például egy épület emiatt három helyett csak négy hónap alatt készül el, az az alacsonyabb GDP-növekedésben is megmutatkozik. A vállalatok számára emellett közvetlen többletköltségeket is jelenthet a szélsőséges időjárás. Ilyen lehet a légkondicionálás, a munkavállalók számára biztosított víz költsége, a rövidebb munkaidő és sok egyéb, a hőség miatt szükségessé váló intézkedés. Ezek a kiadások végső soron szintén csökkentik a gazdasági teljesítményt. A felmelegedés GDP-re gyakorolt hatását hosszú távon vizsgáló közgazdasági kutatások historikus adatok alapján becslik meg, hogy a hőmérséklet változása milyen mértékben vetheti vissza a gazdasági növekedést. A kutatók azt veszik alapul, hogy egyes régiók gazdasági teljesítményére hogyan hatott az extrém hőség. A probléma ugyanakkor az, hogy az elmúlt évtizedekben legfeljebb 1,5 Celsius-fokos felmelegedés mellett állnak rendelkezésre tapasztalatok, a klímamodellek pedig a jelenlegi kibocsátási trendek alapján az évszázad végéig 3 fok körüli felmelegedést jeleznek előre. Mivel ilyen extrém hőhatásokra nincs precedens, a becslések is elég pontatlanok, és emiatt sok szakmai kritika is érte őket – mondta erről Hidi János. Például a 3 fokos felmelegedéshez is nagyon tág, 10 és 80 százalék között szóródó GDP-veszteség tartozik a klímakockázatok gazdasági modellezésével foglalkozó szakirodalom szerint – tette hozzá. A közgazdasági megközelítés másik problémája Hidi szerint az, hogy a klímatudósok előrejelzései szerint a 3-4 Celsius-fokos felmelegedés jóval súlyosabb következményekkel járhat annál, mint hogy a gazdaság a közgazdászok modelljei szerint működhessen tovább. Ha 2100-ig a gazdaság a klímaváltozás nélkül évente átlagosan 3 százalékot nőne, az a század végére a mainál közel kilencszer nagyobb GDP-t eredményezne. Ez még 80 százalékos veszteség mellett is jelentős bővülést jelent. A klímatudósok szerint viszont a 3 fokos felmelegedés esetén már olyan billenőpontok is hatással vannak a környezeti folyamatokra, amelyek nehezen vagy egyáltalán nem fordíthatók vissza. „Ezek már potenciálisan katasztrofális hatások, amelyek nem csak korlátozzák a gazdasági tevékenységet, hanem az alapvető működést veszélyeztetik” – hívta fel rá a figyelmet. Emiatt is nagyon fontos, hogy az elmúlt évek komolyabb gazdasági károkkal járó hőhullámai mennyiben ösztönzik majd a vállalatokat és a kormányokat a klímakockázatok határozottabb kezelésére. Hidi János szerint az emberek és az intézmények jellemzően akkor kezdenek el igazán alkalmazkodni, amikor már közvetlenül érzik a problémát. Egy súlyos hőhullám ezért akár arra ösztönözheti a vállalatokat és a kormányzatokat, hogy komolyabban vegyék a kockázatokat. Ugyanakkor az alkalmazkodás könnyen le is lassulhat, ha az időjárási szélsőségek hatásai nem minden évben ugyanolyan jelentősek. Hidi János az olajválságok példáját hozta: amikor az üzemanyag megdrágult, az Egyesült Államokban megnőtt a takarékosabb japán autók iránti kereslet. Később azonban visszatértek a nagyobb fogyasztású autókhoz, ahogy az üzemanyag újra olcsóbb lett. A kérdés, hogy a hőhullámok mennyire válnak gyakorivá. Ha az extrém hőség évről évre megismétlődik, az már felgyorsíthatja az alkalmazkodást – mondta. Kövess minket Facebookon is! Követem! Legfontosabb Friss hírek

The surprising truth about labour Mobility 4:32 ⨯ Why do Czechs stay put? The surprising truth about labour Mobility https://english.radio.cz/why-do-czechs-stay-put-surprising-truth-about-labour-mobility-8893467#player=on Copy Share on social media Facebook X Czechs are among Europe's least mobile workers. OECD and Eurostat data show they are far less likely than many other Europeans to relocate for work, often preferring to commute instead. Regional geographer and university president Jaroslav Koutský believes geography, family ties and long-standing habits all help explain why. Freedom of movement has been one of the European Union's defining principles ever since Czechia joined the bloc in 2004. The idea was straightforward: workers could move to places where jobs were available, while employers would gain access to a larger pool of labour across the single market. Example? As then European Commissioner for Jobs and Social Rights Nicolas Schmit reminded the European Parliament, labour mobility remains central to the European project: "Labour mobility is a crucial element... It is at the heart of a well-functioning single market," Schmit said, adding that mobility is "a fundamental freedom of the European Union." The reality in Czechia, however, looks rather different. According to OECD and Eurostat data, Czechs are among Europe's least geographically mobile populations. Compared with many neighbouring countries, they are far less likely to move to another region for work. While Austrians, Germans or Swedes relocate much more readily, many Czech workers choose to remain where they live and commute instead. A small country with strong local ties Why that is remains open to debate. Jaroslav Koutský, regional geographer and president of Jan Evangelista Purkyně University in Ústí nad Labem, believes Czechia's geography is part of the explanation. "Maybe we are a small country. Everything is reachable, so we don't need to change the place of living," Koutský says. "We are very fixed on these links and friendships." In other words, relatively short travel distances make commuting easier than moving house, while family and social networks encourage people to stay close to where they grew up. Even university students stay close to home Koutský sees the same tendency among today's university students. Asked whether students still spend weekends in university towns as they once did, he says the opposite has happened. "It's even worse," he says. "They just come for a lecture. And after the lecture they leave. They go home." According to Koutský, even students who rent accommodation often prefer returning to their parents whenever possible rather than building a new social life around the university. That behaviour contrasts with countries such as the United States, Britain or France, where leaving home for university is often seen as an important step towards independence. Whether the Czech pattern is driven primarily by expensive housing, improved transport links or simply a stronger attachment to home remains difficult to quantify. What is clear, however, is that more than twenty years after joining the European Union, many Czechs still make relatively little use of one of its most fundamental freedoms: the freedom to move where the work is. Pimentel / Unsplash Lithuania's State Child Rights Protection and Adoption Service has rejected claims that it decided to remove from a family a two-month-old baby who had already died after suffering from a serious illness. âThe agency said the decision concerned all children in the family because of suspected neglect, and that the parents only received the formal decision after the baby's death because the service was informed of her death several days later. The allegations emerged after the story of a family from UkmergÄ, northeastern Lithuania, spread on social media. People pointed to the perceived absurdity of ordering the removal of a baby girl who had already died, while others accused the authorities of being too heavy-handed in removing all of the family's children or reacting too late. âAccording to the family's account, the two-month-old girl, who had been diagnosed with Patau syndrome, died in hospital in Kaunas. The family said they received the child protection service's decision two days after her death. â Speaking at a press conference on Thursday, Lina BaranauskienÄ, head of the Vilnius County Child Rights Protection Division, expressed her condolences to the family and explained why the decision had been made to remove all of the children living in the household. â She said child protection officers were alerted by medical staff after an exhausted two-month-old baby was admitted to hospital. â "Removing a child from their parents is an extreme measure that is taken only in exceptional circumstances, when parents do not cooperate, refuse assistance, no improvement takes place, and the child continues to face a real threat. In this family's case, a decision was made that it was necessary to ensure the children's safety. â "We made the decision on July 27, but only on July 28 did we learn that the baby had died on Sunday, July 26," she said. â BaranauskienÄ added that the service would seek ways to improve communication between hospitals and child protection authorities to prevent similar situations in future. â She stressed that while parents' faith, beliefs and values were their own choice, a child's right to appropriate medical treatment and to life must be protected. â "In this particular case, doctors informed us that the baby had been brought to hospital exhausted and in a critical condition. She required urgent medical attention," she said. â According to BaranauskienÄ, it was not possible to establish a dialogue with the parents, although they were still being invited to cooperate and work with the authorities to find a solution. â She said the decision to remove all the children was based not only on the condition of the baby admitted to hospital, but on the overall circumstances. â "There are additional circumstances which, as I have already mentioned, mean that the children's safety must be ensured. There are concerns about their welfare, emotional security, development and health," she said. â The family had been known to child protection authorities since 2018. The service had previously received several reports, including from medical professionals, concerning inadequate healthcare for the children. â BaranauskienÄ said the family had previously received support from the UkmergÄ Social Services Centre, but had been "difficult to cooperate with" at that time as well. â "If we are still unable to establish any contact with the family in the near future, a decision will be made to remove the children from the family," she said. â She later stressed that the service would not apply to the court to remove the children if an agreement could be reached with the parents. â BaranauskienÄ also noted that home births are legal in Lithuania and confirmed that the baby had been officially registered and had a birth certificate. â The baby's father, Mintautas, told LRT that his daughter had been born with Patau syndrome, a congenital genetic disorder that prevented her from feeding normally. â He said the parents had fed her using a pipette and sought treatment at Kaunas Clinics after noticing that she was not gaining weight. â "Children with Patau syndrome do not usually live long. Most survive only a couple of months, and very few reach adolescence. It is a genetic disorder. An inability to absorb food properly is very common with this syndrome. â "There are also other symptoms, such as a cleft palate, underdeveloped eyes and an underdeveloped atrium of the heart. Many of these were later confirmed by medical tests," he said. â According to Mintautas, the girl spent the first month of her life at home. â "It was important to us that she lived surrounded by love and had the best quality of life possible, that she experienced our touch and everything that family life could offer, for as long as she could. We are grateful that she had a month to experience that. â "The second month was completely different because we could no longer be with our baby. We could only stroke her; we were not allowed to hold her for long periods or breastfeed her in hospital. Those were very painful moments," he said. LRT English Newsletter Every Friday morning. https://www.foxnews.com/world/nato-membe.text: Poland, the closest NATO member to the Ukraine-Russia war, scrambled fighter jets and placed its air defenses on high alert early Thursday as Russia launched more than 70 missiles and roughly 280 drones across Ukraine, killing at least eight and wounding dozens from Kyiv to the western city of Lviv. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, just returning from this week's U.S. visit with President Donald Trump and the funeral of late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., said the barrage exposed a critical shortage of Western-supplied interceptors, particularly against ballistic missiles. "The protection of people’s lives depends directly on their willingness" to provide Ukraine with air-defense missiles, Zelenskyy said of Kyiv’s allies. Hours later Thursday morning, the European Union disbursed $4 billion to Ukraine to finance the procurement of more drones, missiles, air defense and fighter jets, according to the European Commission. RUSSIA LAUNCHES BALLISTIC MISSILE ATTACK ON KYIV HOURS AFTER ZELENSKYY WARNS OF MAJOR STRIKE The disbursement is part of a more than $100 billion loan approved by the EU earlier this year and follows the roughly $3.5 billion installment on June 25 and $4.5 billion on June 30. Polish forces detected an unidentified object moving west through the country’s airspace shortly before 4 a.m. An F-16 was dispatched to intercept it, but the object disappeared from radar minutes later. Authorities subsequently found a crater about 33 feet wide and scattered debris in farmland near Tarnawa-Kolonia, about 1.2 miles from the closest buildings. Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said initial evidence indicated the object was a Russian Kh-101 missile, although investigators were still working to confirm its type and origin. THE TWO MOST IMPORTANT AMERICAN WEAPONS SYSTEMS NATO IS EAGER TO HAVE "All the indications are that it was a Russian Kh-101," Tusk said, adding that Polish forces were prepared to shoot it down if it had continued flying toward a populated area. He added the U.S. is interested in joining the investigation, which has initially determined the missile was not intended for Poland territory. The fate of the Ukraine-Russian war might be decided within the next 100 days, Tusk told reporters. The threat to a NATO ally is a new frontier in the long-running war and comes after Zelenskyy pressed senators to advance Graham's sweeping sanctions package. Also, Trump and Zelenskyy discussed U.S. licenses allowing Ukraine to produce Patriot interceptors, along with other defense cooperation and efforts to revive stalled diplomacy with Moscow. Six people, including two girls ages 5 and 12, were killed when a Russian Iskander-M ballistic missile struck a private home housing a large family near Kryvyi Rih, according to local officials. Seven others were reported killed in Kyiv and elsewhere in the Dnipropetrovsk and Poltava regions as the casualty count rose during rescue operations. 'WRITTEN IN OUR DNA': POLISH PILOTS WHO REMEMBER SOVIET RULE PREPARE FOR AMERICA'S MOST LETHAL FIGHTER JET "A dark night," Oleksandr Vilkul, the head of Kryvyi Rih’s defense council, wrote on Telegram. Eight people were wounded in the strike on the home. The person killed in Kyiv was a 31-year-old man, while two others were wounded, according to Ukrainian police. Russian strikes damaged residential buildings, vehicles, storage facilities, a market and a garage complex in the capital, where air raid warnings lasted more than five hours and thousands of residents sheltered in subway stations. In Lviv, about 40 miles from the Polish border, emergency crews searched damaged apartment buildings for people trapped beneath concrete and debris. Thirty people, including children, were reported injured. More than 20 residential buildings, a school and two kindergartens were damaged, officials said. "I was terrified watching the rescuers go beneath those concrete slabs," one Lviv resident told Reuters as crews pulled a boy from a damaged building. Ukraine’s air force said its defenses intercepted 55 missiles and 265 drones. But only one of nine ballistic missiles was shot down, while 11 missiles and 17 drones struck targets at 20 locations. The U.S.-made Patriot is the only system currently in Ukraine’s arsenal capable of reliably intercepting Russian ballistic missiles, which travel at several times the speed of sound. Zelenskyy has repeatedly warned that Patriot interceptors are arriving too slowly and in insufficient numbers. During his Tuesday meeting with Trump, Zelenskyy said the leaders discussed licenses for Patriot interceptor production in Ukraine. He also met with Lockheed Martin executives and told senators that domestic production would be a long-term solution but would not address Ukraine’s immediate shortage of missiles. European countries have offered to pay for additional U.S.-made interceptors. Zelenskyy’s Washington visit coincided with Senate consideration of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, named for the longtime defense hawk and outspoken Ukraine supporter who died unexpectedly earlier this month. The Senate voted 86-12 Tuesday to clear an initial procedural hurdle and voted 84-12 Wednesday to formally proceed with the legislation. Additional votes were still required before final passage. The package would impose sanctions on Russian officials, oligarchs, financial institutions, energy projects and vessels accused of helping Moscow evade existing restrictions. It would also authorize tariffs of up to 100% on goods from the five largest purchasers of Russian oil and natural gas and the leading countries facilitating sanctions evasion. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Graham negotiated the revised package with the White House shortly before his death. The legislation also includes an extension of sanctions targeting Iran’s energy and weapons sectors, a provision sought by the Trump administration. Zelenskyy met with a bipartisan group of senators before the procedural votes and called the legislation an important signal to Russia, Europe and the Ukrainian people. He watched the Senate vote from the chamber’s gallery after attending Graham’s funeral at Washington National Cathedral. Reuters and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

https://aa.com.tr/en/world/netanyahu-fli.text: World Features Netanyahu flight through Europe raises questions over ICC obligations of Rome Statute states - International law expert says Greece, Italy, France remain bound by Rome Statute obligations despite allowing Israeli premier’s aircraft to cross their airspace Selman Aksunger and Fatma Zehra Solmaz 30 July 2026 • Update : 31 July 2026 HOLLANDA Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s aircraft crossed the airspace of Greece, Italy and France on its way to the US despite an International Criminal Court (ICC) arrest warrant, raising questions over the three Rome Statute states parties’ obligations to the court. "Granting Netanyahu transit permission on the grounds of 'diplomatic necessity' does not exempt these countries from their obligations under the Rome Statute," Abdurrahman Erol, an international law expert at Istanbul Medeniyet University, said. He said ICC precedent decisions concerning Hungary, Mongolia and Italy make clear that neither diplomatic necessity nor head-of-state immunity justifies non-compliance with the court's arrest warrants. The ICC issued arrest warrants for Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant on Nov. 21, 2024, over alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip. Since then, Netanyahu’s aircraft has repeatedly crossed the airspace of Rome Statute states parties during visits to the US. States have authority over foreign aircraft in their airspace Erol said Articles 86, 88 and 89 of the Rome Statute require states parties to fully cooperate with the ICC, including carrying out arrest and surrender requests, making compliance with ICC warrants a binding legal obligation rather than a matter of discretion. He recalled that the ICC has previously found Hungary, Mongolia and Italy in breach of their obligations for failing to execute arrest warrants and, in some cases, referred them to the Assembly of States Parties (ASP). According to Erol, the argument that Netanyahu’s aircraft merely crossed the airspace of Greece, Italy and France without landing does not remove questions over their legal responsibilities. He said states exercise sovereignty over their airspace and foreign state aircraft require authorization to enter or fly over it. "The referral processes faced by Hungary, Mongolia and Italy for failing to execute ICC arrest warrants stand as a reminder that Greece, Italy and France could face similar proceedings on the same legal grounds," he added. news_share news_share_description subscription_contact subscription LATEST NEWS All Egypt denies link to ship targeted off Yemen, condemns Red Sea attacks 2 killed, 15 injured in Houthi drone attack in eastern Yemen With half of FIFA confederations revolting, can Infantino survive? Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said in a post on X that a Kh-101 cruise missile “violated the Polish airspace and fell 50 km away from the town of Lublin,” noting that the missile was armed. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said in a post on X that he had spoken with Tusk about the “violation of Poland’s airspace by a Russian missile.” “This incident is yet another reckless act by Russia and a dangerous consequence of its war against Ukraine,” Rutte said, before reaffirming the alliance’s “unwavering” commitment to supporting Kyiv. In the early hours of July 30, Warsaw scrambled fighter jets to secure its airspace amid Moscow’s aerial bombardment of its neighbor, which killed at least eight people in neighboring Ukraine, including one in Kyiv, in attacks that stretched as far as the western city of Lviv, more than 40 miles from the Polish border. “During nighttime hours, national and allied reconnaissance systems detected intense combat activity by the Russian Federation’s long-range aviation,” the Polish Operational Command of the Armed Forces stated in a July 30 post on X. Related Stories Poland Unveils First Long-Range Drone to Boost Strike Capability UK, Poland, Netherlands, Finland Make Progress on Defense Spending Plan “To ensure the safety of Polish airspace, the combat readiness of air defense system assets was elevated, including pairs of on-duty fighters and an early warning aircraft. ... At 3:40 a.m., an unidentified object moving westward was detected in Polish airspace.” Polish Operational Command said that an on-duty F-16 was then dispatched to the area to “identify and intercept” the object, but before it could be identified, “the object disappeared from radar system indications” at 3:46 a.m. Subsequently, a helicopter was sent to the last known location of the object and located “the probable crash site of the object in an undeveloped area near the village of Tarnawa-Kolonia in the Lublin Voivodeship.” “A Ground Search and Rescue Team and the relevant services were dispatched to the scene. Operational and securing actions are ongoing at the incident site,” Polish Operational Command stated. “An unidentified object moving westward was detected in Polish airspace,” the operational command of the armed forces said on X, noting that it disappeared from radars soon after the sighting at 3:40 a.m. The crater was about 10 meters wide, Polish Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Gałecka said on X, noting that it was found just more than a mile away from some buildings. Police in the Lublin area stated in a post on X that they received reports of a “powerful explosion” in Biłgoraj county, between the villages of Tarnawa Kolonia and Biskupice. “Officers discovered a crater and scattered debris from an unidentified object in a field located about 2 km (1.2 miles) from the nearest buildings, between the villages,” the police stated, noting that they had secured the area. Following the discovery, Tusk said he had established a special coordination team to investigate the incident and later posted a photograph of himself at the crash site. “All the indications are that it was a Russian Kh-101 ballistic missile, but we want to be 100 percent certain about the type of missile and who launched it,” Tusk told an emergency meeting. “There was no direct threat because the missile landed in an uninhabited area; we were ready to shoot it down had it continued its flight.” Tusk’s view was backed up by an X post from Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha, who said that “overnight, a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crossed into Poland as part of Russia’s massive strike against Ukraine, violating NATO airspace.” “This is yet another clear demonstration that strengthening Ukraine’s air defense now is urgent and serves as a guarantee for the protection of the entire Euro-Atlantic community,” Sybiha said, noting in a later post on X that he had spoken with Polish Foreign Minister Radek Sikorski. Moscow has not yet commented on the incident in Poland, but the Russian Defense Ministry confirmed in a July 30 post on Telegram that it had “launched a massive strike using long-range air, land, and sea-based precision weapons, as well as attack drones, against military industrial facilities, telecommunications and logistics centers” across a range of cities in Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in a July 30 post on X that “Kyiv and the region, as well as our Dnipro, Lviv, Poltava, Kharkiv, Mykolaiv, Sumy, Vinnytsia, Cherkasy, and Ivano-Frankivsk regions, came under attack overnight.” “Dozens of ordinary homes, civilian businesses, and infrastructure facilities were destroyed and damaged. More than 70 missiles were used in this strike, a significant number of them ballistic. There were also over 280 attack drones,” he said, noting that Ukrainian air defenses had managed to down the majority of the drones and a “significant number of cruise missiles.” In 2022, just a few months into Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, a Ukrainian missile struck a Polish village and killed two people. The incident sparked speculation that Russia had fired the missile into Polish territory. Shortly after the missile struck Polish territory, the Polish Foreign Ministry issued a statement claiming the projectile was of Russian manufacture. Soon afterward, U.S. President Joe Biden declared that “preliminary information” appeared to indicate that Russia had not fired the missile. U.S. military officials agreed, citing “initial findings” suggesting that Ukrainian air defenses had fired the missile to intercept Russian missiles. In September 2025, Poland’s Armed Forces Operational Command stated that air traffic restrictions had been introduced along the country’s eastern border with Belarus and Ukraine, following the downing of suspected Russian drones in the NATO member’s airspace. Polish authorities said at the time that a home in the village of Wyryki-Wola had likely been hit by a Russian drone that entered Poland’s airspace on the night of Sept. 9. Polish Minister for Special Services Tomasz Siemoniak told Polish television later that month that the house was likely hit by a missile fired from a Polish F-16 fighter jet. “Everything indicates that it was a missile fired by our plane, defending Poland, defending the fatherland, defending our citizens,” Siemoniak said at the time. Reuters contributed to this report. An unidentified object crashed into a field in eastern Poland on Thursday after one of Russia’s largest overnight missile and drone attacks on Ukraine prompted Warsaw to scramble fighter jets and place air defenses on high alert. (Bryan Kott/U.S. Army) By JOHN VANDIVER STARS AND STRIPES Published July 30, 2026 · A Russian missile crashed into a field in eastern Poland early Thursday, leaving a large crater after one of Russia’s largest overnight missile and drone attacks on Ukraine prompted Warsaw to scramble fighter jets and place air defenses on high alert. U.S. Army Col. Martin O’Donnell, a spokesman for NATO’s military headquarters, said the alliance activated a wide range of air defenses in response to the intrusion. He said that investigators were still assessing what type of Russian missile was involved. Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, NATO supreme allied command and head of U.S. European Command, has been in talks with Poland’s chief of defense about the alliance’s response to the incident. Grynkewich “underlined that NATO will continue to take all necessary measures to defend NATO territory,” O’Donnell said. Two NATO fighter jets, which were Polish F-16s, a NATO Multinational Multi-Role Tanker Transport Unit Airbus A330 refueling aircraft, a Polish Saab 340 Airborne Early Warning aircraft and a Polish Mi-24 helicopter, were scrambled in response, O’Donnell said. The incident unfolded as Polish and allied surveillance systems tracked a wave of Russian long-range strikes on western Ukraine, where missiles flew close enough to the border to raise concerns they could stray into NATO airspace, Polish officials said earlier Thursday. “An extremely tough night for our air defense, observation and threat detection systems,” Polish Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said in a statement Thursday. Air defense radars tracked at least a dozen missiles over western Ukraine, with one coming within about 3 miles of the Polish border before turning back east, Poland’s operational command said. Minutes later, military radar detected an unidentified object moving westward inside Polish airspace, the statement said. An F-16 assigned to quick-reaction alert duty was dispatched to intercept the object, but it disappeared from radar before the pilot could make contact, the military said. Authorities are now investigating the site in a village near Lublin where the object landed, leaving a large crater, officials said. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said in a statement Thursday the incident involved a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile that crossed into Poland, but Polish officials had not confirmed that assessment. Local residents said the object shook the ground on impact. “We’ve lived here all our lives and have never heard anything like it. The windows were almost blown out,” one resident told the Polish news outlet Lublin 112. The episode illustrates how Russia’s increasingly frequent long-range attacks on western Ukraine are testing NATO’s eastern flank, forcing Poland to repeatedly launch aircraft and elevate air defense readiness when missiles or drones approach the alliance’s borders. Since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Poland has regularly scrambled fighters during major Russian air attacks, particularly when cruise missiles and drones target areas near Lviv and other cities in western Ukraine. Such missions are designed to protect Polish airspace and reassure allies that NATO’s eastern edge remains under constant surveillance as Russia’s air campaign intensifies. The latest incident would be one of the most serious violations of Polish airspace to happen during the war in Ukraine. In November 2022, two people were killed when a missile struck the Polish village of Przewodow near the Ukrainian border. Investigators later concluded the projectile was most likely a Ukrainian air defense missile fired in response to a Russian attack. In March 2024, a Russian cruise missile briefly crossed into Polish airspace before returning to Ukraine, prompting Warsaw to demand an explanation from Moscow. Europe NATO John Vandiver covers U.S. military activities across Europe and Africa. Based in Stuttgart, Germany, he previously worked for newspapers in New Jersey, North Carolina and Maryland. He is a graduate of the University of Delaware. https://www.theatlantic.com/books/2026/0.text: The first animal narrator to make an impression on me was an amiable mutt named Harold, who, with remarkable lucidity, recounts the peculiar events of James and Deborah Howes’s 1979 novel, Bunnicula: A Rabbit-Tale of Mystery . The book, written for and beloved by children, boasts a winning premise by any metric: A fanged rabbit’s benign vampiric qualities inspire a series of animal hijinks that endanger Bunnicula and propel Harold to acts of interspecies mercy. Interrogations into rabbit vampirism aside, Bunnicula compelled me most because its narrator is a dog—one who, despite his aptitude for writing, cannot otherwise communicate with people. This textual sleight of hand ignited my fascination with a narrator’s uncanny power to describe reality as they experience it. Its impossibility (if only dogs could write books!) is what made this literary conceit so captivating—the kind of imaginative leap that most fiction makes in one way or another, although it is not always so conspicuous or playful. Every novel requires some suspension of disbelief, but a book narrated by an animal—a surprisingly common subgenre—raises unique questions about representation. We can safely assume that a human author is more qualified to render the emotional landscape of a fellow human than they are of a dog or a horse or a mountain lion. Yet what the best of these novels lose in verisimilitude, they gain in creative vision. Anna Sewell’s 1877 novel, Black Beauty , prevails as one of the standard-bearers; it adopts the first-person perspective of the titular horse to encourage more humane treatment of his species. Virginia Woolf’s motivations were more recreational when she published Flush: A Biography in 1933. Woolf, who desired a palate cleanser after finishing her experimental novel The Waves , focused her energies on the life story of the poet Elizabeth Barrett Browning’s cocker spaniel. Richard Adam’s 1972 novel, Watership Down , imagines an anthropomorphized society of rabbits with their own species-centered cosmology, who must brave the predatory wilds to make a new home. Etna: A Novel By Yoon, Paul Buy Book Most creature-oriented stories—no matter how comedic or frolicsome—will gesture, either explicitly or subtly, at the hazards inherent to animal lives. (Flush, for instance, was briefly kidnapped and returned for a ransom.) But in recent years, writers and filmmakers have magnified the peril that their nonhuman subjects navigate, laying bare the human-made disasters that now jeopardize their lives. The Academy Award–winning 2024 film Flow dramatizes the struggles of a tenacious black cat in a flooded world where all human life has vanished; the Polish movie EO tells the story of a donkey subject to agonizing abuses and fleeting joys, and culminates in a slaughterhouse scene that indicts factory farming. Among recent animal-narrated novels, the best may be Open Throat . Henry Hoke’s savage 2023 masterpiece is narrated by a queer, ravenous mountain lion who lives in the arid underbrush beneath Los Angeles’s Hollywood sign, near an unhoused encampment that he dutifully protects. Midway through the novel, a malicious hiker sets fire to the camp, forcing the mountain lion to seek refuge in the urban sprawl he refers to as “ellay.” Etna , Paul Yoon’s third novel, is the latest addition to the modern animal-in-peril narrative: the story of a military dog named Etna who is snatched up and discarded in the course of a human war. Like Open Throat , Etna excels as a keenly wrought hypothesis about not only how its chosen creature would perceive the world and its dangers, but also how those perceptions can be adapted to fiction. Although Etna tempers the exacting moral judgments at the core of Open Throat with a plot that bends toward empathy, Yoon’s critiques of humanity are just as pointed as Hoke’s, and they emerge from a similarly textured philosophy that acknowledges the fraught business of living, whether one walks on two feet or four. Like all weary, uprooted creatures, Etna longs for home, but unlike so many of the humans who commandeer his world, he possesses far less agency when it comes to finding his way back there. And yet there are compensations. Etna may lack the privilege of human sovereignty and the benefits of advanced intelligence, but he is free of the hubristic delusions that underwrite so much human-produced wreckage. As he observes to a fellow dog, “There’s no other place but here.” Read: Netflix captures the doom and dream of Watership Down In both Open Throat and Etna , brevity is central to characterizing animal consciousness. (Neither novel reaches 200 pages.) Both Yoon and Hoke also structure their works with staccato-like page breaks—a decision that cleverly evokes spans of creaturely silence. Etna is a sociable fellow, but his conversations with other animals never indulge in pleasantries. Nonhuman discourse is laconic yet earnest—and, as his narration explains, telepathic: Their common language takes the form of “dark shapes” that materialize “in a space between our eyes, shapes we could translate.” To struggle with silence is a uniquely human condition; the animal kingdom abides in it, until there is reason to sound out. For all its compactness, Etna has the shape of an epic. The story draws explicit comparisons to Homer’s The Odyssey : Its titular character tries to return to the farm where he was born after surviving a ravaging war. (The book also features a minor Greek character named Achilles.) An animal story set in motion by the basest human impulses—though also distinguished by some of our best—the novel is tied deeply into both ancient literary tradition and tragically perennial concerns. Etna prompts readers to imagine an experience of the world unbound from human social convention, but it is no less interested in the slippery distinctions between human and nonhuman desires for belonging, intimacy, and home. Yoon drew extensively on these themes in his earlier works—most recently in the novel Run Me to Earth and the Story Prize – winning collection The Hive and the Honey —and his oeuvre depicts war’s psychological and material calamities. He understands that one of the most violent disruptions a living being can sustain is sudden estrangement from their environment. And yet, in Yoon’s hands, a character’s suffering never overwhelms their capacity for tenderness. The author always insists on the enduring humanity of his displaced subject—even when they aren’t human. Nevertheless, Etna stands out among Yoon’s work ; it is, first of all, a dog’s tale. How does Etna—who keeps close company with humans but is by definition marginalized by them—hold on to himself in the face of rank, incoherent brutalities? Perhaps he must become a storyteller. “I was born near water,” he begins, in the simple declarative assertion so common to famous literary beginnings. And then, also like his bipedal narrative forebears ( David Copperfield , for instance), he quickly proceeds toward reflective ambivalence: “I would never learn what the farm was intending to do with me. Maybe nothing at all. Maybe I was supposed to grow old there.” Like any living creature, Etna can only speculate about the other shapes that his life might have taken. But Yoon is careful, with his characteristically spare, visceral imagery, to establish Etna’s early happiness. “Every day there was sand floating in daylight and the salt on our tongues. The sea wind over grass,” the dog says, in a manner both frank and wistful. He recalls his mother, steady as a planet, “her face looming over us in the sky, the tall triangles of her ears pocketing the smell of the coast.” Yoon’s fiction focuses primarily on Asian communities in Korea and Laos, and across the diaspora. Etna is set in a small, unnamed country, which makes sense; nationalism and border politics are alien to dogs. Invading forces threaten the country when Etna is still a puppy, and the looming war marks the abrupt end of his idyllic puppyhood. One frightening day, he is whisked away from the farm and sent to combat training by a military doctor named Soojin, who can communicate with certain “special” dogs by reading their minds. She is the one to bestow him with his name: All dogs, Etna explains, “had private names” that “our mothers called us by, but we never shared those.” The name Etna, volcanic in its association, aligns with the new life being imposed upon him. “You’re now war dogs, my darling,” Soojin tells Etna, as she drives him and his canine partner, Fuji, to a drop-off location. “You’ll make new friends and you’re going to work hard and save a lot of lives.” Read: How an epic and violent family history fuels fiction Etna is distressed by this turn of events—he wants to return to the farm—but he does not resist or try to flee. The novel elides any ham-fisted meditations on the dominant species’ impositions; although Yoon is clearly fond of his narrator, he nimbly avoids the tendency of many animal tales to traffic in neat parables or didactic moralism. (As a lifelong reader of Black Beauty , I freely admit that Sewell, like so many Victorian writers, does not manage this as well.) Nonetheless, Etna and his fellow creatures understand their subordinate position in the hierarchy. He and Fuji are assigned to a unit of American soldiers sent to bolster this country’s self-defense. They undergo an education in ruthlessness and become, as Soojin predicts, skilled war dogs. “I learned to be good at it,” Etna later tells another dog. “All of it.” He is not altogether regretful of this knowledge, for his adeptness brings certain pleasures: for instance, distilling the “strong clear line that was a single smell” from a landscape’s sensory chaos, even if it leads to explosives or human remains. But in the squall of war, Etna’s talents also beget inexorable demands. He is injured six times; gradually, his body accumulates “stripes of scars like old worms” that render him unrecognizable to himself. He loses his friends, both canine and human. And although Etna’s narrative voice—vulnerable, curious, endearingly direct—inclines the reader to envision the pluckiest good boy, humanity’s violence deprives him of a gentle youth. Like any soldier, Etna learns to kill on command. The war lasts four cataclysmal years. Etna’s country prevails but is demolished in the process; its people and animals are left wrecked, hungry, and homeless. One night, Etna rests near two of the surviving soldiers in his unit, eavesdropping on their boozy conversation, during which one contemplates shooting Etna as a gesture of mercy. “None of us were right in the head after what we saw and did and what our bodies and souls endured,” the soldier reasons. The dog takes no offense at this suggestion; these are “young humans,” he explains, who “had been good to their dogs” until they were lost in battle. “Everyone wanted to go home. And to go away.” Etna, like so many dogs, is an empathetic creature, and the grace he extends to these soldiers facilitates the epiphany that propels the rest of the story: He, too, wants to return home, and so he departs on a harrowing journey. In the midst of it, Etna befriends a small, eager canine, Semeru, who knows Soojin and helps Etna reunite with her. Semeru’s introduction as the sidekick brings a touch of comedic respite; he has two interspecies exchanges, with a cat and with a donkey, that made me laugh out loud. I suspect that some readers will regard his dynamic with Etna as cliché; after all, it is difficult to render an affectionate animal relationship without a touch of bathos. But Semeru provides a crucial intimacy for Etna, whose experience of the war has been one of agonizing isolation. This is, at times, a wrenching novel, strewn with broken bodies, but its atrocities never overwhelm its faith in creaturely communion, and in grief and longing that clarify, rather than obscure, one’s desires and selfhood. “What do you know about creatures?” Etna wonders to himself, about a group of missionaries he encounters on his journey. He might well ask his readers the same thing. In real life, our dogs cannot tell us what they make of the disasters we humans have wrought, nor can their fidelity absolve us. But we can see by their perked ears and wagging tails that they are waiting to see what happens next. ​When you buy a book using a link on this page, we receive a commission. https://publishingperspectives.com/2026/.text: “We are asking the state to help protect us from the relentless pressures of the market, to which we have long been exposed as the most vulnerable link in the publishing industry,” the author organization said, in a statement. Book buyers at Poland’s Świat Książki bookstore chain (credit: Świat Książki) By Jaroslaw Adamowski, Contributor T he Polish Literary Union , the country’s leading writers’ association which counts Nobel laureate Olga Tokarczuk among its members, has launched a campaign to require local publishers to pay authors list price royalties—a minimum of 10% of a book’s cover price— instead of its selling price, as net royalties. Authors Beata Dębska and Eugeniusz Dębski participate in a Polish Literary Union campaign that informs viewers that royalties from 1,000 sold copies can buy a single laptop. (Credit: the Polish Literary Union). The association is in talks with Polish authorities to include a relevant provision in a draft bill proposed by Poland’s Ministry of Culture and National Heritage designed to protect the Polish book market. “The Polish Literary Union is launching the 10% campaign, inspired by an initiative created by French children’s authors affiliated with the La Charte association. We are calling for the introduction of a statutory minimum royalty rate for writers. This is neither a radical nor an unfounded proposal,” the organization said in a statement. “In Poland, both salaried employees and people working under civil-law service contracts are guaranteed a statutory minimum wage. Yet when our readers learn that an author in Poland earns just PLN 2.87 [or $0.76] from the sale of a single book, they usually react with disbelief.” In the association’s view, very few authors active in the Polish market receive royalties that amount to 10% of a book’s cover price. “For debut authors, in particular, such a rate remains virtually unattainable. As a result, we often receive less than PLN 5 from a book that a reader purchases for PLN 50,” according to the statement. “We believe the time for change has come. In recent years, lawmakers have increasingly extended legal protections to the most vulnerable categories of workers, recognizing that they are often unable to protect their own interests.” While rare in Poland, a 10% royalty rate is considered standard in numerous European countries, including Germany and Spain, among others, according to data collected by the Polish Literary Union. “We, authors, remain outside that protection. We want to make one point absolutely clear: we are not asking for public money. We are asking the state to help protect us from the relentless pressures of the market, to which we have long been exposed as the most vulnerable link in the publishing industry,” the organization said. “It is time for the same standards to apply in Poland. Experience has shown us that appeals and requests alone are ineffective, which is why we are convinced that without legal safeguards, our situation will not change.” Meanwhile, acclaimed writer and publisher Mariusz Szczygieł, who heads the Polish nonfiction-focused publishing house Dowody , has stated that the measure could push certain publishers out of business, particularly smaller outlets that specialize in more ambitious literary works and emerging authors. This is because numerous industry players are already struggling to stay financially afloat, according to Szczygieł. “For many years, we signed contracts with our authors that provided royalties calculated as a percentage of the cover price (a fixed price that guaranteed authors at least a minimum sense of financial security—something the Union has been fighting to preserve),” he said in a social media post . The author said that, as a writer, he understands that, at their current levels, royalties often do not permit Polish authors to make a living from their work as writers. He also believes there is a need to introduce more transparency into the dealings between authors, publishers, and distributors. At the same time, Szczygieł suggests, niche publishers such as Dowody often subsidize the publication of unprofitable releases with revenue generated by bestselling titles. “At a time when almost all publishers switched to royalties based on the selling price (a variable price that depends on who the publisher sells books to and at what discount), we remained, as far as I know, the only publisher to continue using the cover price as the basis for royalties,” Szczygieł added. “Some time ago, however, in order to stay afloat, we fell into line with everyone else and abandoned royalties based on the cover price in favor of the industry standard.” Jaroslaw Adamowski is a freelance writer based in Warsaw, Poland. He has written for the Guardian, the Independent, the Jerusalem Post, and the Prague Post. Comments Sign me up. Authors, singers and musicians are appallingly treated as regards royalties in particular. I am an author and for more than fifty years a UK based publisher. The trust that authors vest in their publishers is far too often unjustified and exploited. piersdudgeon@gmail.com Polish authors are asking for a 10% royalty. At PLN 2.87 per book, the biggest plot twist isn’t in the novel—it’s the paycheck. Leave a Comment Cancel reply SUBSCRIBE Sign up to get our FREE email edition, Monday to Friday!

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001. Photograph: LegoCamera/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001. Photograph: LegoCamera/Shutterstock Air transport South Korean airport becomes busiest in world for global traffic amid Iran war Incheon airport had 38.39m international passengers in first half of 2026, as traffic diverted from Middle East hubs Raphael Rashid in Seoul Thu 13 Aug 2026 05.45 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 06.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google South Korea’s Incheon airport has become the world’s busiest airport for international passengers, in part owing to disruption in the Middle East caused by the Iran war. The airport, South Korea’s main gateway, about 30 miles (48km) west of Seoul, handled 38.39 million international passengers in the first half of 2026, according to preliminary figures compiled by the Airports Council International (ACI), the global trade body for airports. Heathrow in the UK was second, with 37.79 million, followed by Changi airport in Singapore with 34.53 million. It is the first time Incheon has topped the international passenger rankings since opening in 2001. The airport was 10th in the world in 2002, rising to fifth in 2018 and third in 2024 and 2025. Part of the increase was attributed to disruption caused by the US-Iran conflict , which weakened the role of Middle Eastern hubs such as Dubai and diverted some transfer traffic to alternative routes through east Asia, Incheon International Airport Corporation (IIAC) was quoted as saying by the Yonhap news agency. Heathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airport Read more Incheon’s international passenger traffic was up 6.3% year on year overall, with rising numbers of foreign visitors also contributing to the increase. Foreigners accounted for 39.3% of Incheon’s passengers in the first half of the year, up from 35.2% for the whole of 2025. The proportion reached a record 44.4% in the second quarter, with IIAC attributing the increase largely to growing numbers of visitors from China and Japan, according to local media. Heathrow, in west London, recorded 40 million passengers in total in the first half of the year, including both domestic and international travellers, its busiest first half on record. Passenger traffic to Asia-Pacific rose 7.9%, while capacity to the Middle East reportedly fell 16.5% owing to the regional conflict. Earlier this week Istanbul overtook Heathrow as Europe’s busiest airport by total passenger numbers. Figures published on Tuesday showed 7.9 million passengers passed through Heathrow’s terminals in July, compared with Istanbul’s 8.15 million. Incheon has also expanded its role as an international hub. It serves 101 airlines flying to 183 cities, including 158 international passenger destinations. A four-phase expansion completed in late 2024 increased the airport’s annual capacity to 106 million passengers. Kim Beom-ho, the acting president of IIAC, said the ranking reflected “the support of the government, the public’s encouragement and the hard work of everyone stationed at the airport”. South Korea also lays claim to the world’s busiest air route . The domestic corridor between Gimpo airport and Jeju island had 14.4 million seats scheduled in 2025, according to the aviation data provider OAG, more than any other route in the world. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Mina Smallman was commenting on the case of sex offender Levy, who was left free to kill two women after police failings. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA View image in fullscreen Mina Smallman was commenting on the case of sex offender Levy, who was left free to kill two women after police failings. Photograph: Stefan Rousseau/PA Metropolitan police Met police incapable of change, says mother of murdered sisters after Simon Levy case Mina Smallman, whose daughters were killed in north London park in 2020, says force ‘decides who matters’ Helena Horton Thu 13 Aug 2026 04.31 EDT First published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 03.41 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Metropolitan police does not take all cases of violence against women seriously and instead “decides who matters”, the mother of two murdered women has said. Mina Smallman, whose daughters Bibaa Henry and Nicole Smallman were killed in a north London park in 2020, also said Britain’s biggest police force was incapable of change. Two police officers were jailed in 2021 after taking photographs of the dead bodies of her daughters and sharing the images in WhatsApp groups, referring to them as “dead birds”. Commenting on the case of the sex offender Simon Levy, 40, who was left free to kill two women after police failings, she said: “One of the women that were murdered, because she was a sex worker, she wasn’t taken seriously. They didn’t look into her murder until he murdered a mother of four, and then they joined the two cases together. “How ridiculous is that. Once again, the Met is deciding who matters. Both those women’s lives were important to their families, how dare they decide that they weren’t going to look into that case.” Levy, who this week was given a whole-life sentence for his crimes, was also convicted earlier this year of sexually assaulting 11 other women, 10 of them on trains and the underground in London between 2023 and 2025. Smallman said she had been in contact with the head of the Metropolitan police, Sir Mark Rowley, after reading about the case. She told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: “After reading this case I sent a text message to Sir Mark and said: ‘How many times are you going to stand up publicly and apologise for failures in the Met?’ “It becomes a joke. The truth is, the Metropolitan police is too big for any senior team to be able to have a hands-on understanding of the day-to-day activities of that organisation.” She said the Met was incapable of change because it was “too big”. “I believe that Sir Mark Rowley wants to change the Met and wants to do things differently, but they haven’t got a clue.” She added: “We are asking them to do too much, they haven’t got the finances, it has become riddled with inactivity, corruption, misogyny, racism, and they just can’t do it.” The crime and policing minister Sarah Jones previously described Levy as a monster and said the failings that had allowed him to remain free were “deeply concerning”. Jones signalled the government would allow the relevant institutions and police watchdog to establish what had gone wrong. “The fact that Levy was able to inflict such devastating harm after being freed by police and the courts is deeply concerning,” she said. “It raises serious questions that require urgent answers.” Rowley denied that the Met had not done enough, saying: “The inference that the Met didn’t try on this death is not true, the Met tried.” But he said he did not understand why the Prison Service released Simon Levy after he sexually assaulted one of its staff members in jail. Levy was questioned by police about the assault five months after his release, which Rowley said was “too slow”. He told the Today programme: “That’s one of the things we’ve apologised for, but of course there are two mistakes in that: you’ve got he was released on licence by the Prison Service, having sexually assaulted in prison one of its people, I don’t understand that decision either. “I’m prepared to come here and be accountable, we’ve got two officers being referred to be investigated by the independent office of police complaints, we take our accountability seriously. “The rest of the system is not doing that. The Prison Service should not have released somebody who’s indecently assaulting its staff.” Explore more on these topics Metropolitan police Violence against women and girls Police London Sex work Crime England news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Complaints filed to police watchdog over Met’s handling of Al Fayed abuse allegations Met gets extension to AI project after Sadiq Khan blocked deal Met police chief calls for law to make stolen phones ‘unusable bricks’ Met warns about hate speech at Unite the Kingdom and Palestine marches Met officers investigated over handling of Mohamed Al Fayed abuse complaints Met sets up specialist unit as antisemitic hate crimes in London hit two-year high Met investigates hundreds of officers after using Palantir AI tool Met says it will resume arresting people who show support for Palestine Action Met accused of insulting black people with shake-up of anti-racism strategy Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/13/who-i.text: One of the founding figures of Iran's IRGC Mohsen Rezaei has been appointed secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council — giving one of the country's most controversial senior figures formal authority over the institution responsible for Tehran's strategic decisions.The appointment was made in a presidential decree signed by Masoud Pezeshkian on Sunday.Hours earlier, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei had separately appointed Rezaei as his personal representative on the council.With nearly five decades at the top of the Islamic Republic's security and military apparatus, Rezaei, 71, succeeds Mohammad Bagher Zolghadr, a veteran IRGC commander who resigned after around four months in the post and was appointed as a political adviser to Khamenei.Right after his appointment was announced, Rezaei has said publicly that Iran will not open a second shipping corridor in the Strait of Hormuz, that US warships entering the strait will be targeted, and that the war must end and Iran's frozen assets must be released before Hormuz can be reopened.Who is Mohsen Rezaei?Rezaei, whose birth name was Sabzvar, was born in 1954 in Khuzestan province into a Bakhtiari tribal family.Initially a political activist against the rule of Shah Reza Pahlavi in the early 1970s, Rezaei was arrested by the shah's intelligence agency SAVAK and imprisoned in Ahvaz.He was one of the founders of the Mansouroun militant group, which helped lay the groundwork for the Mojahedin of the Islamic Revolution Organisation.After the 1979 revolution, Rezaei joined the central council of the Islamic Republic and served on a 12-member committee that drafted the IRGC's constitution.In September 1981, at the age of 27, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini appointed him commander-in-chief of the Revolutionary Guards.Rezaei held the position for 16 years — making him one of the longest-serving military commanders in the history of the Islamic Republic — before stepping down in September 1997.He then became secretary of the Expediency Discernment Council, the body that resolves disputes between parliament and the Guardian Council and sets broad state policy, for nearly 24 years.He was appointed deputy president for economy under President Ebrahim Raisi in 2021, a post he left in June 2023.Despite this record of institutional prominence, Rezaei has run for president four times and lost each time. In the 2021 election, he received 3.4 million votes — fewer than the number of ballots deemed invalid in the vote.The bombing of the Jewish centre in ArgentinaRezaei's name has been associated internationally with the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community centre in Buenos Aires, which killed 85 people and injured hundreds in the deadliest terrorist attack in Argentina's history.In 2007, Argentine prosecutors sought arrest warrants for nine people in connection with the attack, including Rezaei, then IRGC commander. Interpol issued a Red Notice against him that remains in force.Tehran and Rezaei have consistently denied any involvement in the attack, describing the allegations as politically motivated.The case has nevertheless had practical consequences: Argentina protested his appointment as deputy economic president in 2021, previously objected to his attendance at the inaugurations of Nicaraguan presidents, and asked Qatar to arrest and extradite him during a visit to Doha — a request that was not carried out.Operation Karbala-4The most controversial episode of Rezaei's military command domestically was Operation Karbala-4, a December 1986 assault during the Iraq-Iran war intended to retake parts of the Faw area that was detected and repelled by Iraqi forces, resulting in heavy Iranian casualties, including frogmen units.In 2015, the remains of 175 divers who had participated in the operation, reportedly buried with their hands tied, were discovered and identified.Rezaei's subsequent claim that continuing the operation after it had been compromised was a deliberate deception ahead of the larger Operation Karbala-5 — or the siege of Basra, the largest military offensive of the war — drew sharp criticism from former officials, journalists and social media users.Qassem Soleimani, then Quds Force commander, contradicted the account by saying Karbala-4 had been the primary operation all along.Another controversy surfaced in November 2011, when Rezaei's eldest son Ahmad, who had previously defected to the US and given media interviews criticising senior Islamic Republic officials, was found dead in a Dubai hotel room.Dubai police attributed the death to an overdose of antidepressants. Rezaei's family and the Expediency Council secretariat rejected that conclusion and described the death as suspicious. The cause of Ahmad Rezaei's death has never been conclusively established.War, succession and regime in fluxRezaei's appointment comes after one of the most turbulent periods in the Islamic Republic's history.The US and Israel launched broad strikes against Iranian military targets on 28 February, killing Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, Defence Minister Mohammad Reza Ashtiani and around 40 senior military and security commanders.Ali Larijani, who had been secretary of the Supreme National Security Council since August 2025 and was regarded by many analysts as Iran's most powerful figure on the eve of the war, was killed in a subsequent wave of Israeli strikes on Tehran.Zolghadr then succeeded Larijani in that role. Under the constitution, an interim council of President Pezeshkian, judiciary chief Gholam-Hossein Mohseni Ejei and a Guardian Council-appointed cleric managed the country's leadership functions until Mojtaba Khamenei was selected as the third ayatollah on 9 March.
