http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/13/tokyo.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin visited the far-eastern Kuril islands for the first time on Thursday, prompting a "strong" protest by Japan which also claims the territory.Russian-Japanese relations have long been dogged by tensions over the contested islands, known in Japan as the Northern Territories and seized by the Soviet Union in 1945.The Kremlin posted a video of Putin in the Kuril Islands, with Russian media saying he visited a fish-processing plant where he was given caviar. Putin travelled to the Kurils after visiting the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin, where Russia's navy was conducting drills.In Sakhalin, Putin held a meeting "on ensuring the security of Russia's eastern borders," state-run media outlet RIA Novosti said.Japan, whose ties with Russia have worsened further since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 – just as Moscow's relations with China and North Korea have warmed – objected strongly."The Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan's territory both historically and under international law, and the government of Japan strongly protests this visit," said Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi in a statement.The Soviet Union took the strategically located volcanic archipelago north of Hokkaido in the final days of World War II, and has maintained a military presence there ever since.In 2010 then-president Dmitry Medvedev became the first Russian leader to visit the disputed territory. Medvedev also went there several times subsequently as prime minister under Putin’s presidency.The four contested isles are part of the volcanic Kuril archipelago, which runs in a broad arc from Russia's Kamchatka peninsula down to Japan's main northern island Hokkaido. The Soviet Union only declared war on Japan on August 8, 1945, after the atomic bomb was dropped on Hiroshima and six days before the end of the conflict.The islands' names are similar in both countries -- Kunashir, Habomai, Shikotan and Iturup in Russian, while in Japanese they are known as Kunashiri, Habomai, Shikotan and Etorofu.Their population of about 20,000 Russian citizens live in harsh climates, but the islands have mineral deposits including gold and silver, and rich fishing grounds. After the islands were occupied in 1945, Moscow deported their Japanese population of about 17,000 people.Thereafter the islands acquired strategic importance, providing air and sea bases during the Cold War as the Soviet Union confronted the United States and its closest ally in the Pacific, Japan.On several occasions it appeared that off-and-on talks between Tokyo and Moscow were making progress and in 1956, when diplomatic relations were established, where Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev suggested two of the disputed islands might be returned under a peace treaty.Although the talks resumed after the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991, no progress has been made and they remain in Russian control.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/13/us-st.text: US airstrikes against Iranian-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen last year resulted in the deaths of over 150 civilians, according to a Pentagon assessment released on Wednesday.The Pentagon review, which was sent to Congress as part of an annual report on civilian casualties, focused on three airstrikes in April 2025 conducted in response to the Houthi attacks on commercial ships in the Red Sea, a crucial global trade route that connects the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean.The US strikes targeted hostile forces in or near Houthi-controlled capital Sana'a as well as the Ras Isa port. A total of 153 civilians were killed, and 243 were injured, according to the report.The strike on the port was the most deadly, killing 80 people and injuring 171 others. At the time, the Houthis published graphic footage of the aftermath on their al-Masirah satellite news channel, showing casualties in the port.The US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, said at the time that the “strike was not intended to harm the people of Yemen.”“US forces took action to eliminate this source of fuel for the Iran-backed Houthi terrorists and deprive them of illegal revenue that has funded Houthi efforts to terrorise the entire region for over 10 years,” CENTCOM said in its statement.The command determined that the three strikes “more likely than not” resulted in civilian harm, the review said. The information was based on US intelligence sources, imagery and open-source reporting.Concerns have continued to grow among US lawmakers and human rights groups over civilian casualties in military operations during US President Donald Trump's second term, after a US missile struck a primary school in Minab in the opening days of the Iran war, killing up to 168 people.Condolence payments to victimsThe Pentagon review also considered whether condolence payments should be made to victims or their families, but determined that they were not appropriate in the three cases. The review did not explain why.The payments are one option available to the US military when civilians are killed or injured during military operations. They are not required by law and do not constitute an admission of wrongdoing.The US has made similar payments in previous cases. After a US drone strike in Afghanistan in 2021 mistakenly killed 10 civilians, including seven children, the Pentagon said it was committed to offering condolence payments to the victims' relatives.The Houthis, which are part of Iran's loose network of proxies Tehran calls "Axis of Resistance," said the attacks on ships in the Red Sea that led to the US strikes were in support of Palestinians amid the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza.The group has since threatened to close the Bab el-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea to global shipping, while reports emerged that it is also mulling introducing a transit fee following consultations with Tehran.The Strait of Hormuz — another crucial global shipping chokepoint — has been nearly completely shut to cargo vessel traffic since the beginning of the Iran war in late February.A simultaneous closure of both straits would affect roughly one third of global oil trade.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/13/oil-s.text: Oil leaking from a tanker grounded off the coast of Oman is not only endangering a nearby island but has now also reached beaches on the Gulf Arab country’s mainland, to the north of the island, Oman’s environment authority said Wednesday.Crude oil has been leaking from the tanker Caroline Bezengi—a sanctioned tanker believed to be part of Russia’s “shadow fleet"—that was carrying nearly 1 million barrels of oil when it reported an explosion in June.No party has claimed responsibility for the incident, and the cause of the explosion has not been revealed.Oman, a sultanate on the southeastern coast of the Arabian Peninsula, has been a mediator in the ongoing war in Iran, which the United States and Israel launched on 28 February.Oil spill endangering marine protected areaEnvironmental experts said an oil spill has been spreading quickly in recent weeks from the partially submerged tanker off the shores of Qabiliyah Island, endangering a marine protected area there.According to recent satellite photos, the spill is rapidly spreading over an area of more than 600 square kilometres due to the monsoon season's strong winds and currents.The beaches of Ras Madrakah on mainland Oman, around 200 kilometres north of Qabiliyah Island, have also been contaminated, according to Oman's Environment Authority, which has been keeping an eye on the leak.The authorities also warned that the southern coasts of Masirah Island, over 300 kilometres north of the submerged tanker’s location, may also be affected in the coming hours.The 247-metre Caroline Bezengi, whose owners are thought to be situated in Shanghai, is believed to be part of Russia’s “shadow fleet” and has been sanctioned by the British government and the European Union for carrying Russian oil.It had left the Black Sea port of Novorossiysk, in Russia, in May, according to geospatial data tracking company SynMax Maritime.

Skip next section Ukraine civilian casualties hit highest level since 2022 08/13/2026 August 13, 2026 Ukraine civilian casualties hit highest level since 2022 Civilian casualties in Ukraine have climbed to their highest monthly level since the early weeks of Russia's full-scale invasion, according to the United Nations. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine said it verified at least 437 civilians killed and 2,610 injured in July, a 30% rise from June and 70% more than in July 2025. July recorded the highest overall number of civilian casualties since March 2022, while the number of people killed was the highest since May 2022. The UN said the true toll was likely higher, with some reports still being verified. Since Russia launched its full-scale invasion on February 24, 2022, the UN has verified at least 16,874 civilian deaths and 51,273 injuries in Ukraine. Long-range missiles and drones remained the biggest cause of civilian casualties in July, accounting for 38% of the total. Short-range drones operating close to the frontline accounted for another 27% of casualties. “Civilians are facing intensified risks from the increased use of missiles and drones in urban centers, glide bombs in cities closer to the frontline, and short-range drones," said head of the mission Danielle Bell. Russia launched at least 429 missiles during the month, more than twice the number fired in June, according to the UN. The deadliest attack came on July 2, when Russian forces launched 74 missiles and almost 500 long-range drones, mostly against Kyiv. At least 30 civilians were killed and 104 injured. https://www.dw.com/en/how-germany-s-dron.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IlIk One defense method: Interceptor drones chase drones and capture them with a net Image: Sina Schuldt/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement How could a drone laden with explosives fly unhindered into Leipzig/Halle airport, where it remained apparently unnoticed for several hours? After last week's incident, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt spoke of a "hybrid attack scenario" which he suspected came from "foreign powers." Suspicion has been directed at Russia, also because the drone was said to have been located near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo plane. The Federal Prosecutor's Office has taken over the investigation. The fact that the drone was loaded with explosives and able to reach the airport demonstrates a new level of threat. However, drone sightings over airports and ports, industrial sites and military properties have been increasing in Germany. In 2025, Germany's Federal Criminal Police Office (BKA) recorded more than 1,000 suspicious drone flights . Last October, drones disrupted air traffic in Munich for several hours, stranding numerous passengers. There is not sufficient drone protection at German airports, warned security expert Nico Lange. "We do not possess the sensor networks and sensor beams needed to spot all types of drones, especially low-flying, slow drones," he told DW. Leipzig drone threat prompts security concerns in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The European Association for Unmanned Aviation has also long pointed out weak points in Germany's drone defense. "That a drone could apparently reach the airport tarmac and be discovered rather by chance, shows where the core of the problem is," said chairperson Gerald Wissel in relation to the latest incident. The association suggests "the establishment of real-time monitoring of the lower airspace as well as the mandatory tracking of all airspace participants via ADS-L" — a radio communications system that makes drones in an airspace electronically visible. State police, federal police, or Bundeswehr For a long time, Germany did little to address the issue of drone defense. Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt wants to remedy this by setting up new institutions. In December, he launched the Joint Counter Drone Center (GDAZ) in Berlin. There, information from the federal police, state police, secret service and armed forces is collated around the clock. But the incident at Leipzig airport shows that even a new hub is of little use if a dangerous drone at a large airport cannot be discovered and intercepted. Drones move quickly. Responses must therefore be decided within minutes. Doing so is made more difficult by Germany's system of divided responsibilities. If a suspicious drone takes off, it is initially a matter for the state police. Germany has 16 police authorities, one for each of its 16 states. It is only when the drone moves over a large airport or railway facility that the federal police are allowed to step in. Europe's defense: Latest drone technology shown in Berlin To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Unclear responsibilities Security experts and opposition politicians in Germany's Bundestag federal parliament have called for clear regulation and consolidation of responsibilities. "The muddle over responsibilities in drone defense is a substantial danger to our domestic security," said Irene Mihalic, lawmaker with the opposition Green Party and herself a former police officer. Many, including the Greens, suggest that the federal police should take the lead when it comes to drone defense. In December 2025, the federal police set up a new special unit for drone defense. Following the incident at Leipzig airport, Interior Minister Dobrindt wants to expand this. Originally, 130 staff positions across 4 locations were planned. In the future, there will be 300 personnel across 8 locations, to "be on site quickly and flexibly when needed," according to the Interior Ministry. Who is allowed to shoot down a drone in Germany? As so often happens following dramatic incidents, there have also been calls to use the Bundeswehr , Germany's armed forces. Many suggested that the military should be deployed for drone defense efforts at airports. However, current German law maintains that the police are responsible for upholding security within the country. A defense ministry spokesperson warned that protecting its own facilities, with their "tens of thousands of kilometers of fencing" is already a challenge for the Bundeswehr. Adding 24/7 protection of civilian infrastructure "would proclaim a false sense of security that we could never achieve," he argued. In an emergency, the police are allowed to ask the army for assistance. To achieve legal clarity in this regard, Germany amended its air security law in March. For the first time, it allows the Bundeswehr to shoot down drones outside their own premises to prevent "a particularly serious disaster." From printing to presses to drones To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Airports and train stations still lack protection There is also lot of catching up to do when it comes to the technical equipment for defending against drones. "There were big announcements at airports about positioning drone defense systems. They are more like detection systems. So far, they have not intercepted a single drone and at some airports they have still not yet been put in place," Manuel Atug, a spokesperson for the independent Critical Infrastructure Working Group (Arbeitsgruppe Kritische Infrastruktur) told DW. The German Police Union (GdP) is also lamenting the lack of resources for drone defense. "Unsafe train stations, unsafe airports and a police force which has to beg for money, law changes and the latest defense technology are really disconcerting," criticized GdP federal chairman Jochen Kopelke. A spokesperson for the German Interior Ministry advised that the large airports were steadily being equipped with drone defense technology. "The federal police have already procured a considerable amount of equipment. The 8 large airports are prioritized: Frankfurt (Main), Munich, Berlin, Düsseldorf, Hamburg, Cologne/Bonn, Stuttgart and Leipzig/Halle." The plan is for all of these airports to be equipped with mobile drone defense technology by the end of this year. This article was originally written in German. https://www.dw.com/en/what-would-a-north.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ike8 North Korea's Kim Jong Un honored troops lost in the Ukraine war while opening a museum in April 2024 Image: KCNA/REUTERS Advertisement North Korea is preparing a massive troop surge to help its ally Moscow in its war on Ukraine , with up to 50,000 North Koreans to be deployed in Russia , according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy . In late July, the Ukrainian leader said Russia wanted to bring in another 30,000 North Korean troops, before adding this weekend that Pyongyang decided to have between 30,000 and 50,000 North Koreans deployed on Russian territory. He did not specify if this number included the North Korean troops already taking part in the conflict. In the comments published this weekend, Zelenskyy also warned North Korea was gaining valuable experience in modern warfare and urged South Korea to boost cooperation with Ukraine on air defense and drones. Two days later, Zelenskyy said Russia had received more North Korean ballistic missiles, which were allegedly used in an attack on Zaporizhzhia. North Korea has suffered thousands of causalities in Ukraine war Russia and North Korea signed a defense pact in the summer of 2024, with North Korea starting to send combat troops to Russia several months later . Analyst believe some 14,000 to 15,000 personnel were deployed, mainly in the Kursk region. Pyongyang later agreed to send another 6,000 sappers and military construction workers. North Korea has also supplied Russia with millions of artillery rounds and ballistic missiles, according to South Korean and Ukrainian authorities. South Korean intelligence estimates that around 6,000 North Korean soldiers have been killed or wounded. This image, published by Ukrainian officials, shows North Korean soldiers being fitted for Russian uniforms Image: Ukraine Photo/Newscom/picture alliance On Thursday, Japan's Kyodo News cited Ukrainian military intelligence as confirming the upcoming North Korean surge. Ukrainian sources say up to 50,000 North Korean troops could be deployed to Russia by the end of November; The troops would reportedly take over duties in Russia's Kursk, Bryansk and Belgorod, freeing Russian forces for the Ukrainian front. Pyongyang's surge 'seems to be becoming a reality' South Korean lawmaker Yu Yong-won told DW the military cooperation between Russia and Korea was growing ever closer. Yu is a former military journalist who visited Ukraine in 2025 and again in February this year. He said he heard claims of the North Korean surge during his most recent visit to the war-torn country. "I am concerned that this seems to be becoming a reality," he told DW. North Korea expands its role in Russia's war against Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Yu noted that 30,000 to 50,000 troops would be significantly more than the roughly 20,000 troops and support forces involved in the initial deployment. "Whether such a large-scale additional troop deployment will actually take place," Yu said, "the continued expansion of military cooperation between Pyongyang and Moscow called closer attention from the South Korean government and military." Will North Koreans watch Russians' back? Han Ki-bum, a former deputy director of South Korea's National Intelligence Service, also seemed to signal caution. "Ukraine initially spoke of 30,000 additional personnel before raising the estimate to 50,000 without releasing detailed evidence about the planned deployment," he told DW. "North Korea has sufficient military manpower to make such a deployment possible without seriously weakening its defenses," according to Han. "Even though the war is largely deadlocked, a country fighting a prolonged war will always perceive that it lacks manpower," Han said. "North Korean infantry could therefore guard Russian rear areas, allowing more Russian soldiers to be deployed to front-line combat in Ukraine." Russian officials praise North Koreans "North Korea also benefits from the arrangement; its troops are gaining experience in 21st-century warfare while testing weapons under actual battlefield conditions; deeper cooperation could increase North Korea's access to Russian expertise in missile, naval and air-defense technology," Han said. North Korea gains critical intel by aiding Russia in Ukraine To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video The security expert also estimates that, out of 6,000 North Korean causalities, some 2,000 may have been killed . "Some 1,000 to 2,000 combat troops and engineers are believed to have returned home, where veterans and families of the dead have reportedly received housing and other preferential treatment ," Han said. "North Korean troops suffered heavy initial losses but became more effective as they adapted to the battlefield," Han said. "Their aggressive fighting style may explain why Putin and other Russian officials have praised their bravery." North Korean women also moving to Russia Ahn Chan-il, head of the World Institute for North Korea Studies and a former North Korean soldier, believes that "a deployment of 50,000 is militarily feasible" and that Pyongyang would send "elite special operations troops." "North Korea's special operations forces are particularly skilled in reconnaissance, surprise attacks and ambushes, and have demonstrated their combat capabilities on the Kursk front, making them attractive to the Russian military," said Ahn, who defected in 1979. "If 30,000 troops are deployed, however, the contingent would likely include not only special operations forces but also infantry, engineers, construction workers and female medical personnel," he added. Why North Korea is now Europe's problem To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video "North Korean women have recently been observed heading to Russia, but it remains unclear whether they are being sent for reconstruction work or as medical personnel." Ukraine war used as training ground for North Korean military According to Ahn, "surviving soldiers could bring valuable combat knowledge back to North Korea. Some could become junior officers or instructors, spreading lessons learned from drone warfare, reconnaissance and other aspects of the Ukraine conflict throughout the military." "However, young soldiers are being exposed to life outside one of the world's most isolated societies. More importantly, a sharp rise in casualties could make the war harder to portray as a success," added Ahn. "A limited number of fallen soldiers can be celebrated as heroes," Ahn said. "But tens of thousands of dead and wounded could leave behind grieving families and disabled veterans, potentially turning North Korea's battlefield experience into a domestic burden." Investigators later determined that the object was not an explosive, although criminal police were continuing work at the scene. A technician had discovered the suspicious item in the track bed at the entrance to the station in the town of Treuchtlingen. Specialists X-rayed the object, which was also lifted using a robot to allow further investigations. A federal police bomb disposal team is examining the object Image: Felix Kirberg/dpa/picture alliance Road and rail closures remain in place while the investigation continues. Regional services are affected, with trains terminating early at suitable stations. Replacement buses and large-capacity taxis have been arranged. Long-distance services are being diverted via the city of Ingolstadt. Police have urged people to avoid the area and take alternative routes. https://www.dw.com/en/colombia-earthquak.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IjKD About 3,500 people have been injured and nearly 500 remain unaccounted for Image: Luisa Gonzalez/REUTERS Advertisement Rescuers worked through a third straight night with time ticking towards the 72-hour mark since a powerful earthquake hit Colombia. That's the period aid agencies consider most critical for finding survivors alive, though it can stretch longer if trapped people have access to food and water. "We're entering the final phase," Cali Mayor Alejandro Eder said, adding that survivors could still be found afterward but that the odds grow steadily worse. He said crews were still detecting signs of life beneath the rubble and urged speed: "Every minute is vital." Rescue workers ask for silence as they search for survivors at the site of collapsed buildings Image: Raul Arboleda/AFP The latest on the Colombia earthquake The death toll from the quake has climbed to 265, President Abelardo de la Espriella said Wednesday. De la Espriella said roughly 3,500 people have been injured and nearly 500 remain unaccounted for, though a crowdsourced tracking site used by families put the number of missing far higher, at more than 4,100. More than 25,800 families have been affected in total, he said. The magnitude 7.4 quake — the strongest to hit Colombia in decades — struck on Monday morning near San Jose del Palmar in the northwestern Choco region. It tore through cities across western Colombia, with Cali and Pereira among the hardest hit, along with Manizales and Quibdo. In Cali, volunteer rescuer Johana Sanchez described teams pausing every 30 minutes to listen for survivors. "So far, three people have been pulled out alive and three dead," she told AFP. Officials say 140 buildings collapsed entirely and thousands of homes were damaged or destroyed. Families grapple with human toll In Palmira, Santiago Lloreda told Reuters the quake killed his mother and his 13-month-old daughter, Salma, who was too young to have fingerprints on file and would need to be identified through DNA testing. He described his mother as the family's caretaker, saying she "gave everything up to look after the baby." A man who only gave the news agency his first name, Ricardo, traveled from Miami to recover his sister's body and said his niece was awaiting surgery for a fractured skull, jaw and leg, and a collapsed lung: "She's alive. We know she's going to get better." Colombia races against time after worst quake in a decade To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Thousands have been left homeless, with many sleeping outdoors in parks or emergency shelters set up in schools and sports arenas, either because their homes were destroyed or out of fear of aftershocks. Colombia's geological service has recorded 130 aftershocks since Monday's quake. International aid set to pour in Response efforts have been especially difficult in Choco, the quake's epicenter, a remote and impoverished region already strained by decades of conflict and displacement. Additionally, lost cell service has made it hard to assess damage in communities reachable only by river. "This earthquake compounds an already severe humanitarian situation, and there is a need for increased support for the humanitarian response," said Giovanni Rizzo, Colombia director for the Norwegian Refugee Council. And UN resident coordinator María Jose Torres said in a statement Tuesday that aid groups already working in the region on an earlier peace effort were able to pivot quickly to disaster relief. The United States has pledged more than $15 million and sent response teams. Mexico has sent military aircraft carrying nearly 20 tons of food along with security personnel, with more aid and rescue specialists on standby. El Salvador's president offered two planes carrying 100 tons of supplies, and a search-and-rescue team from Mexico said it arrived directly from Venezuela, which faced its own major earthquakes in June . Quake response provides test for new Colombian president De la Espriella, inaugurated just three days before the earthquake struck, declared an economic emergency and three days of national mourning, and pledged to establish a fund to rebuild hospitals, schools, homes and infrastructure. "This is undoubtedly a tragedy of immense proportions," he said. "Our efforts are focused on those who remain missing." He has not yet detailed what the economic emergency measures will involve. Notably, de la Espriella won office on a platform of reduced public spending and a tougher security approach. Analyst Tiziano Breda, of the conflict-monitoring group ACLED, told Reuters that de la Espriella had campaigned in part on cutting funding to the country's disaster-response agency — the same unit now leading the emergency effort. Experts have cautioned that more seismic activity is possible, if not imminent. "Let's remember that Colombia is full of active fault lines," Rodrigo Leon Loya, a seismologist at the University of the Andes, told AP. "The question isn't whether it can happen again. The question is rather when an earthquake of similar magnitude will occur at another of Colombia’s seismic sources," he warned. Edited by: Rob Turner Don't let the algorithm hide the news. https://www.politico.eu/article/vladimir.text: Authorities in Tokyo lashed out at Moscow after a visit by Russian President Vladimir Putin to the disputed island of Iturup on Thursday. The island, also known by its Japanese name Etorofu, lies northeast of Japan — around 100 kilometers from the coast of Hokkaido — in the Kuril Islands chain and is claimed by both Moscow and Tokyo. Like the other disputed islands in the chain, they are administered by Russia. Japanese Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi wrote on X on Thursday: “Today, I was informed that Russian President Putin visited Iturup Island. The Northern Territories, including Iturup Island, are inherently Japanese territory both historically and under international law, and the Government of Japan strongly protests this visit.” Advertisement Advertisement Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the visit “incompatible with Japan’s consistent position on the Northern Territories” and “absolutely unacceptable.” “Even amid the harsh state of Japan-Russia relations following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Japan has made every possible effort,” wrote Takaichi on X, “but this visit can only be said to have further hardened anti-Russia sentiment within Japan and made medium- to long-term recovery of relations more difficult. I hope that the Russian side will take the gravity of this matter very seriously.” Moscow, however, claims the island chain became part of Russian territory following Japan’s defeat in World War II. The Kremlin also operates a strategically important military base on Iturup. In 2025, Japan protested a Russian shooting drill in waters in the area, including in Japan’s territorial waters, and said that the Kremlin’s “military buildup” in the area was “unacceptable.” According to Russian state media , Putin visited a fish farm on the island. The report said that he was told that the waters of the Kuril Islands are currently filled with tuna weighing up to 300 kilograms — and he was also treated to caviar. This story has been updated. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn0n.text: Image source, Ministry of Defence Image caption, Royal Marine Commandos were involved in the operation to seize the MT Smyrtos By Joshua Nevett ,Â Political reporter Â and Â Laura Gozzi ,Â Europe reporter Published 13 August 2026, 10:52 BST Updated 1 hour ago The UK government has defended its seizure of a Russian "shadow fleet" oil tanker in the English Channel, after Russian President Vladimir Putin threatened to "respond in kind". The Smyrtos has been anchored off Weymouth after Royal Marines Commandos intercepted and boarded the vessel in a first-of-its-kind operation to disrupt the sanctioned tanker in June. The vessel's captain, Ajay Pant, has been charged with breaching Russian sanctions, accused of directly or indirectly supplying or delivering prohibited Russian oil. Overseeing Russian navy drills in the Pacific Ocean, Putin scolded Western countries for "seizing our vessels", branding such action "nothing other than piracy and banditry". Western nations allege Russia has been operating a "shadow fleet" of hundreds of vessels to evade international sanctions imposed on its oil exports. These vessels stand accused of using complex ownership structures and various tactics to obscure the origin of their cargo, masking their link to Russia. The UK Ministry of Defence says Russia has a fleet of more than 700 vessels, responsible for carrying 75% of the country's sanctioned oil. This oil is a "critical lifeline for the Kremlin" in "sustaining Russia's illegal war" in Ukraine, the MoD says. On Wednesday, Putin warned Western countries against seizing more of these tankers, saying: "If these plans are put into practice, we will have to respond in kind. "And not necessarily in the waters where raids on our ships and vessels are planned, but wherever we deem it necessary and appropriate, anywhere." Viktor Liina, commander of Russia's Pacific Fleet, accused Western countries such as Britain and France of operating their own "shadow fleets". "We have the capacity to inspect and detain vessels of unfriendly states and their shadow fleets, and interagency cooperation is in place, ready to begin addressing these challenges," Liina said. In response to Putin's comments, the UK government said Britain's armed forces and law-enforcement officers had boarded the Smyrtos "in full accordance with international law". "The UK is disrupting and deterring shadow fleet vessels and their harmful maritime activity which is fuelling Russia's war with Ukraine," a government spokesperson said. The spokesperson said unlike Russia's shadow fleet, "UK armed forces and commercial vessels operate firmly in line with international maritime law". Figure caption, Watch: MoD footage shows commandos boarding and searching the tanker The Smyrtos continues to be detained by the Department of Transport at a port near Weymouth in southern England, where is it being monitored by British authorities. The ship owner is responsible for the upkeep of the vessel, including provision of supplies for crew members on board. But 22 out of the original 25 crew members were repatriated in July. Putin's warning comes as the European Union intensifies pressure on Russia's shadow fleet. In his remarks to Russian sailors, Putin singled out the EU, accusing member states of violating international maritime law and "attempting to restrict the movement of vessels belonging to our economic operators". The BBC has asked the EU for comment. Many Western countries imposed sanctions on Russian energy following Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Moscow has been accused of dodging them by shipping oil on aged tankers often with obscure ownership or insurance. To combat this tactic, in 2024 the EU began sanctioning individual shadow fleet vessels â "Putin's dark fleet", as the European Council, the bloc's top group of national leaders, put it. More than 630 vessels are sanctioned as of mid-August 2026, meaning they are banned from EU ports. Meanwhile, several individual European countries have been seizing or detaining Russian-linked vessels or have carried out boardings or detentions when sanctions violations are suspected. Most recently, the Italian navy, in conjunction with other EU countries, boarded a tanker in the central Mediterranean suspected of not being entitled to fly the flag it claimed. Although that inspection did not result in a seizure of the vessel, others have. Since the start of the year, nine shadow fleet tankers suspected of circumventing sanctions have been seized around the EU. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cly8.text: Image source, Hannibal Hanschke/EPA/Shutterstock Image caption, The 71st Eurovision final will take place on 15 May 2027 in Burgos, Bulgaria after singer Dara's win last time out By Paul Glynn Culture reporter Published 1 hour ago Eurovision 2027 will be a seaside song contest held in the Bulgarian city of Burgas, organisers have confirmed. The competition will take place in the city, which is close to the Black Sea, from 12 to 15 May, the European Broadcasting Union (EBU) and Bulgarian National Television (BNT) announced on Thursday. It comes after Bulgarian singer Dara won this year's contest in Vienna, Austria in May - her country's first Eurovision win - with her pneumatic dance anthem Bangaranga. Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green said they were "delighted" with the next choice of destination, adding that Burgas would "bring something really special" to the competition. The contest, including rehearsals, the semi-finals and grand final, will be held at Bulgaria's newest sports and entertainment venue, Arena Burgas, which was opened in 2023. 'Truly Bulgarian' "[Burgas] is a vibrant, welcoming city on the Black Sea with a strong musical and cultural identity, and it has the ambition, infrastructure and passion needed to welcome the Eurovision family," Green said. "For the first Eurovision Song Contest ever to be held in Bulgaria, we want to create something that feels truly Bulgarian while also being unmistakably Eurovision â a celebration that brings people together through music." Bulgaria's second largest city was selected for its "strong overall proposition, combining the venue and technical potential" - including hotel capacity, transport and international travel. It may come as a surprise to some Eurovision watchers that the contest will be held there and not in the capital, Sofia. Speaking at a press conference after the most recent song contest in May, the director of BNT, Milena Miltenova, said: "I'm so proud of Dara's performance. What she did last night was amazing. And I'm so proud to say welcome to Sofia next year." Dara - the winning contestant - said something similar: "I'm so happy that you're coming to Sofia next year. I'm happy that it [Eurovision] is going to be in my home." However, the EBU said Burgas was selected following a "competitive" process involving four Bulgarian cities. Image source, BNT/City of Burgas Burgas and Sofia progressed to the final stage of the selection process following the initial bids, which also included Varna and Plovdiv. Miltenova has said she is now "confident" that Bulgaria will be a "worthy" host and the country would "showcase the very best of our culture, hospitality and professionalism". She added there would now be "an intensive period of collaboration" between all involved in order "to deliver a contest that meets the high expectations of millions of viewers around the world". Burgas mayor Dimitar Nikolov added that it was an "exceptional honour". The Eurovision Song Contest can have an impact beyond the stage, with the event providing a platform for host cities and countries to put themselves in the spotlight. According to the EBU, , external Liverpool saw a â¬66m (Â£56m) economic boost after hosting in 2023, MalmÃ¶ â¬40m in 2024 and Basel â¬58m in 2025. Rule change Earlier this week, organisers of the song contest updated their rules to state that if a country involved in an armed conflict wins the competition, it will be ineligible to host it the following year. The amendment was approved by the contest's governing body, following feedback from participating broadcasters after Eurovision 2026 in Vienna. It stated that winning countries will also be disqualified from hosting if a "sensitive geopolitical situation" affects the "security, safety or stability of their state or immediate region". The update has been interpreted as a reaction to Israel's continued presence at the contest, amid criticism of its military actions in Gaza and the Middle East. Last November, following a failed attempt to have Israel suspended, five broadcasters announced they were boycotting the competition - including Eurovision powerhouses Spain and Ireland. Despite the protests, Israel's Noam Bettan ultimately took second place with his song Michelle. It marked the second year in a row that Israel had taken the runners-up position - and some participating broadcasters have privately expressed safety concerns over the contest being staged in Jerusalem or Tel Aviv, should the country win in the future. Although Israel will undoubtedly be seen as the target of the rule change, it will also affect Ukraine, which has been engaged in a protracted war since it was invaded by Russia in 2022. Ukrainian group Kalush Orchestra went on to win Eurovision that same year, in a symbolic show of public support. Following their victory, Eurovision organisers undertook a "full assessment and feasibility study" to decide whether the 2023 contest could proceed in Kyiv. They ultimately decided the security risks were too great, and the UK stepped in to host the competition in Liverpool. Related topics Eurovision Song Contest Television More on this story Bangaranga! https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9q9.text: Image source, Vikram/Instagram Image caption, Vikram, an actor from Tamil Nadu, posted a clip of him playing with the endangered animal By Zoya Mateen ,Â BBC News, Delhi Â and Â Vijayanand Arumugam ,Â Reporter, BBC Tamil Published 5 hours ago A video posted by a Tamil film star showing him cuddling an endangered gibbon has triggered an investigation by Indian wildlife officials over how he came into contact with the animal. Vikram, an award-winning actor from the southern state of Tamil Nadu, was seen hugging and playing with a lar gibbon in a now-deleted video posted on Instagram on Monday. The state's forest department has since begun investigating how the gibbon came to be at a private home and whether rules governing its possession and transfer were followed. They have not concluded that the animal was trafficked, or that Vikram owned it or was involved in bringing it into India. Vikram has not commented on the controversy yet. His public relations officer, Yuvaraj, told BBC Tamil that the media would be informed if the actor issued a statement. Lar gibbons are small apes native to south-east Asia whose international trade is tightly controlled. Officials said the animal was being kept at the home of a relative of Vikram in Chennai, the capital of Tamil Nadu state. The state's Chief Wildlife Warden Rakesh Kumar Dogra told BBC Tamil that individuals could keep a lar gibbon if they had the permits and documentation required by law. "An investigation is under way into where the lar gibbon came from. Only then can we say whether it was brought illegally," he said. The case has made national headlines. Vikram, whose real name is Kennedy John Victor, is one of the biggest names in Tamil cinema, India's popular Tamil-language film industry. His career spans more than three decades and he is known for taking on unconventional and physically demanding roles. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Lar gibbons are listed as endangered, with their numbers threatened by habitat loss, hunting and the illegal pet trade Lar gibbons are small apes covered in blonde or dark brown fur, with a distinctive ring of white fur around their faces. They live in tropical forests in small family groups and are found across parts of south-east Asia, including Thailand, Myanmar and Malaysia. The species is listed as endangered, with its numbers threatened by habitat loss, hunting and the illegal pet trade. They are also protected under CITES, an international agreement that tightly restricts trade in endangered species. India is among the countries that has incorporated protections for CITES-listed species into its wildlife laws. People who keep such animals must register them with wildlife authorities and follow rules governing their possession and transfer. "To import exotic animals, it is necessary to submit a DGFT [Directorate General of Foreign Trade] permit and a no-objection certificate, and then a wildlife conservator's certificate," Dogra said. The controversy began on Monday when Vikram posted the video of himself playing with the lar gibbon on Instagram. The footage quickly spread online, with some media reports describing the animal as the actor's new pet. It was deleted from his account within hours. The short video has since led wildlife officials down a trail stretching more than 2,000km (1,240 miles) away to the north-eastern state of Manipur. A senior Tamil Nadu forest official, speaking to BBC Tamil on condition of anonymity, said they had found the animal was among eight lar gibbons - four males and four females - that a Manipur-based man had declared on the government's PARIVESH portal in 2020. PARIVESH is the official platform used to register exotic animals and obtain environment, forest and wildlife-related permissions in India. According to records on the portal, Malaysia was listed as the animals' country of origin. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Vikram is a hugely popular name in the Tamil film industry Records cited by the official show that on 5 June this year, one male and two female lar gibbons were transferred from Manipur to a person in Perundurai in Tamil Nadu's Erode district. The stated purpose was adoption. But investigators have not yet found documentation showing that permission from Tamil Nadu's Chief Wildlife Warden had been obtained for the animals to be brought into the state, the official said. Two months later, on 5 August, one male and one female gibbon were transferred from Perundurai to Vikram's relative in Chennai, according to the Forest Department's investigation. Investigators are now trying to establish the precise origins of the gibbons and whether the necessary documentation was in place at each stage of their journey. Wildlife activists have also raised questions about how the animals originally entered India. Manipur borders Myanmar, and India's north-east has been flagged as a route for the illegal trade in exotic wildlife, although authorities have not concluded that the gibbons in this case were trafficked. The Tamil Nadu Forest Department says it is examining their documentation, including whether rules governing the international movement and possession of CITES-listed animals were followed. India's Wildlife Crime Control Bureau (WCCB), a federal agency that investigates organised wildlife crime, has also become involved in the case. Thenmozhi, the bureau's Southern Zone Deputy Director, told BBC Tamil that it had written to wildlife officials in Chennai asking them to verify documents and take appropriate action. "The lar gibbon is classified as a protected species under this agreement. They should only be handled as protected animals," Thenmozhi said, referring to CITES. The WCCB said further action would depend on what officials found during their investigation. The case comes amid wider concern about illegal trade of exotic animals into India. In recent years, customs officials have repeatedly intercepted passengers arriving from south-east Asia with live reptiles, birds and primates concealed in their luggage. In July 2025, more than 350 exotic animals , external from Bangkok were seized at Mumbai and Pune airports over a two-month period. Gibbons have also turned up in seizures: in November, customs officials in Bengaluru found , external one among exotic animals being brought in by passengers arriving from Bangkok. Chennai itself has seen several such cases. In February this year, customs officials seized 31 exotic animals from a passenger arriving from Bangkok, including tortoises, iguanas and snakes. Article content The Brampton truck driver, accused of trying to smuggle 281 bricks of cocaine worth between $5 million and $34 million over the Blue Water Bridge last year, exchanged handshakes and a bro hug with his lawyers after hearing a Sarnia judge’s decision Thursday morning. Play Video Article content “Mr. Singh is hereby found not guilty of all charges,” Justice Mark Poland said after spending an hour explaining his verdicts. But the smile quickly turned to tears as he left the courtroom and the weight of the accusations, and how a double-digit prison sentence potentially had been on deck had the judge come back with a different decision, hit him. Singh was asked for comment after he had a chance to gather himself. “Whatever evidence they have proved their innocence. I am very happy, now,” Singh said. Defence lawyer Guruveer Sangha said he thought it was the right decision. “We believed he was innocent from Day 1 based on the evidence that the Crown had. We’re just happy the judge saw what we saw from the beginning,” he said. Advertisement 3 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content Prosecutor Stephane Marinier said the judge provided thorough and thoughtful reasons. “That said, the Crown will review those reasons to determine whether or not to launch an appeal in the next 30 days,” he said. DISCOVERY OF THE DRUGS Singh, an Indian immigrant who came to Canada in 2022 on a student visa, was driving for Divine Freightlines Inc. and picked up a trailer loaded with pallets of plastic resin at Redhawk Logistics in Columbus, Ohio, mid-afternoon on March 5, 2025. On arrival at the bridge shortly after 11 p.m., his truck was sent for a mandatory inspection as it had been flagged by border officials. Officers found several black duffel bags between the skids holding large canvas sacks of resin. All 24 skids were unloaded, a drug-sniffing dog was brought in, and cocaine was found in seven of the 24 sacks. A total of 281, one-kilogram bricks of cocaine, which weighed 333 kilograms in the packaging, were found. Singh, then 23, was charged with importing cocaine and possessing cocaine for trafficking. He was freed on $200,000 bail two weeks later. Two Brampton men who run a trucking company later were charged with conspiracy to import drugs in this case. Advertisement 4 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content A trial only for Singh, who pleaded not guilty to both charges he was facing, began earlier this year at the Sarnia courthouse. It was spread out over multiple weeks and was heard by Poland without a jury. After listening to both sides’ closing arguments, he adjourned the case to Thursday for his decision. The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) and RCMP said nearly 420 kilograms of cocaine worth $11 million was seized in trucks at the Blue Water Bridge during two drug-smuggling cases on Feb. 27 and March 6, 2025. (CBSA/RCMP) THE CROWN’S CASE Marinier argued there were three viable options for how the drugs got in the trailer: They were put there by the driver who brought the trailer to Columbus. They were put there by someone else during the roughly seven hours before Singh arrived. Singh picked them up from another driver and he drove them in his cab to Columbus and put them in the trailer when he got there. There was ample opportunity to get the cocaine from another trucker coming from California while he stayed overnight in the Hebron, Ky., Marinier argued. But, he added, he didn’t have to prove any of these theories, just that Singh knew the drugs were in his trailer. He argued the evidence showed Singh knew about them beyond a reasonable doubt. He also argued Singh moved the trailer’s axles before leaving Columbus because of the added weight of the drugs and Singh was deceitful with the border officers. Advertisement 5 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content #CBSA officers at the Blue Water Bridge port of entry stopped 419 kg of suspected cocaine from entering Canada from the United States. Two individuals have been charged by @RCMPONT . #ProtectingCanadians #BorderSecurity https://t.co/2ArTGNPDiB pic.twitter.com/qsv9hZ0rHf — Canada Border Services Agency (@CanBorder) March 19, 2025 THE DEFENCE’S RESPONSE Sangha noted the trailer was unsealed and in another unknown person’s possession for about seven hours after it was loaded in Columbus. Singh was roughly 150 kilometres away at the time. When he did arrive, he was only there for 37 minutes before leaving. His client also wasn’t nervous or evasive during the inspection, his fingerprints weren’t on the drugs, and police didn’t find any coded messages on his phone, Sangha said. He argued his client was an unwitting courier and the drugs were put there by other people who were working above him. Singh testified through a Punjabi interpreter during several days and denied knowing the drugs were in his trailer and Sangha argued the Crown didn’t prove his client had knowledge or was willfully blind. Trucks on the Blue Water Bridge near Sarnia. (File photo/The Observer) THE JUDGE’S REASONS While reading his hour-plus decision on the not guilty verdicts, Poland noted a major plank in the Crown’s case was a high valued shipment of drugs would only be entrusted to a person with knowledge of its existence, and there was a further suggestion that, as the value increases, the inference they would know about the drugs becomes proportionally stronger. Advertisement 6 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content But the judge said that was unsupported by a significant amount of other compelling evidence. He also pointed out, as the value increases, the resources of the parties directing the shipment also goes up and they could possibly have a team of unobserved handlers following the shipment. Additionally, using a blind courier could have certain advantages such as the absence of a guilty conscience at border crossings. Poland also touched on a Crown argument that Singh attempted to mislead a Blue Water Bridge border officer by showing them a photo of a similar load, but not the exact one he was carrying on March 5, 2025, as it was taken one month earlier. But he pointed out the drugs were found in the front of the trailer and if he had taken a photo similar to the one he took in February, which was from the back of the trailer, it wouldn’t have shown the drugs anyway. He also pointed to the long list of things Singh would have had to do in that 37-minute window to get all 281 bricks of cocaine hidden among the sacks of resin. Advertisement 7 Story continues below This advertisement has not loaded yet, but your article continues below. Article content Poland also rejected the Crown’s argument Singh’s moving of the trailer axles in Columbus was indicative he had knowledge. The judge said he was given no information about the load balance when the trailer left the dock and it’s entirely possible it needed to be adjusted irrespective of the cocaine. Poland also said Singh’s evidence did not have any obvious contradictions or inconsistencies and his testimony was capable at least of raising a reasonable doubt of his knowledge. There have been a slew of Blue Water Bridge truck driver drug smuggling trials heard at the Sarnia courthouse in recent years and the majority have ended with convictions, but a trucker with ties to Brampton and Quebec City was also found not guilty two years ago in a $47-million seizure. tbridge@postmedia.com Article content Share this article in your social network Share this Story : Simcoe Reformer Copy Link Email X Reddit Pinterest LinkedIn Tumblr Comments You must be logged in to join the discussion or read more comments. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cn0n.text: Image source, EPA Image caption, The level of the water of the Danube is so low that the nuclear power plant's suction nozzles cannot reach it By Laura Gozzi Â and Â Paul Kirby ,Â Europe digital editor Published 30 July 2026 Hungary's only nuclear power plant will be forced to shut down entirely for the first time due to record low water levels of the River Danube, Prime Minister PÃ©ter Magyar has said. The Soviet-era Paks power plant uses the Danube for cooling but the water level is so low that the suction nozzles cannot reach it. Magyar warned Hungary's energy supply could become "critical" from Monday due to the Paks shutdown and the ongoing heatwave, which will see temperatures hover around 37C for a week. Like much of Europe, Hungary has seen very low rainfall and high temperatures for much of the summer. The waters of the Danube have fallen to the lowest levels for 30 years in several countries, including neighbouring Serbia and Romania. Magyar asked Hungarians to limit activities that required significant energy consumption between the peak times of 17:00 and 22:00, including charging electric cars and using air conditioning equipment. A "rotational shutdown regime" was also possible if the other combined efforts were not enough to maintain the balance of the national grid, Magyar said, adding the government would compile a list of electricity and water consumers whose consumption could be limited. Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, Large areas of the riverbed have been exposed in the centre of Budapest after weeks of extreme heat and drought In Romania, one of the country's only two nuclear reactors has been shut down at the Cernavoda power plant, which provides about 20% of the country's power. The first of the two 706-megawatt reactors was shut down earlier this week because the Danube's levels were so low, and state-owned company Nuclearelectrica was trying to avoid closing down the other on Thursday. If the second reactor is shut down Romania will, like Hungary, be temporarily without any nuclear energy production. Climate change is driving up temperatures around the world - but particularly in Europe. It is the fasting warming continent, heating up twice as fast as the global average, according to the Copernicus climate service. This is causing increased summer heatwaves, greater pressure on Europe's waters and more intense wildfires. Image source, Reuters Image caption, Among the wrecks exposed by the low levels of the Danube was a World War Two German warship at Prahovo in Serbia Romania's National Institute of Hydrology says the average river flow where the Danube enters the country is 4,700 cubic metres per second (m3/s) in July, whereas on Wednesday it was down to less than a third of that, at 1,600 m3/s. The institute forecast it would continue to fall to 1,500 m3/s by Tuesday. The Danube runs 2,857km (1,775 miles) through 19 countries. The Upper Danube goes from Germany to the Slovak capital Bratislava, the middle basin runs from Bratislava to the border between Serbia and Romania and the Lower Danube extends through Romania and Bulgaria into the three main branches of the Danube Delta that flow into the Black Sea. The low waters of the river have resulted in several unexpected discoveries. The remains of a sunken Hungarian cargo ship resurfaced in Croatia, while the hulks of a German river flotilla was seen in Serbia. And a resident of the northeastern Bulgarian city of Ruse found bones on the Danube river bed, which experts determined were the remains of a mammoth. They were able to recognise a lower jaw, two tusks, and possibly a mammoth rib. Image source, Inquam Photos/Ovidiu Micsik/Reuters Image caption, River flow in Serbia on the Danube is now a third of the average for July Shipping has ground to a halt on the river in Bulgaria, and border police had to evacuate 186 river cruise passengers from the Viking Ullur ship earlier this week when it ran aground close to Vidin, a city that sits on the border with Romania. There were reports of passengers running low of food and water because the cruise ship was unable to dock in Vidin, but Viking later told the BBC that "sufficient water remained available for all guests and crew throughout the incident. At no point did the vessel run out of provisions or experience a shortage". "I have never heard of such low levels over the years. There has certainly not been a similar situation since 1990," Ivan Zhekov, head of river supervision at Bulgaria's maritime administration agency told BTA news agency. Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Boats lie on the dried-out Danube riverbed in front of the Calafat-Vidin bridge, connecting Bulgaria and Romania It is not just the Danube where river levels are low. In Serbia, the levels are also very low on the Sava and Tisa, which are both tributaries of the Danube. Serbian hydrologist Dejan VladikoviÄ said the problems were not just down to the current high temperatures but also to low rainfall during the spring. He told Serbian TV channel N1 that the Danube was down to levels not seen for 50 to 60 years, and climatologists did not expect to see any improvement until mid-September. Temperatures in Serbia are set to climb as high as 38C on Friday, and locally up to 40C, with night-time temperatures in Belgrade as high as 26C. Elsewhere in Europe, forecasters say fire-prone conditions are expected to spread towards central Europe, with Greece and Turkey among the countries worst affected. Vast areas of France and Spain have just experienced some of the most intense and widespread wildfires in living memory , leading to hundreds of thocusands of evacuations. Correction 1 August: This article originally stated that food and water had been running low for passengers on the grounded Viking Ullur and another boat was unable to get close enough with provisions. It was later amended with the company's denial of any shortage. The blitz expanded Russia’s almost daily bombardment of Ukrainian cities, including the capital of Kyiv where tens of thousands spent the night sheltering in subway stations, as Moscow apparently looked to exploit Kyiv’s critical shortage of Western-supplied anti-ballistic missile defenses. NATO said a Russian missile entered Polish airspace during the onslaught and landed in a rural area. It caused no injuries or damage but could deepen tensions between the military alliance and Moscow, as wary European countries fear the 4-year-old war could spill into their territory. 1:29 Russian missile causes crater in eastern Poland as Ukraine war spills over to NATO neighbours NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called it “yet another reckless act by Russia and a dangerous consequence of its war against Ukraine.” Story continues below advertisement Canada unequivocally condemns Russia’s abhorrent strikes on Ukraine last night that killed civilians and left many injured. Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles have battered Russia’s oil sector, causing a fuel crisis. The attack came two days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with U.S. President Donald Trump and representatives of American defense companies as he pleads for swifter and bigger deliveries of Patriot air defense systems to stop Russia’s ballistic missiles. The Iran war has drained stockpiles of the U.S.-made interceptors. Trump has promised to grant Ukraine licenses to build its own Patriots, but production could take many months. Story continues below advertisement “Given the critical shortage of air defense missiles from our partners, our warriors are accomplishing truly incredible things, demonstrating a very high level of professionalism,” Zelenskyy said on social media. “This Russian terror once again proves that protection against the Russian missile threat is the most important task when it comes to saving the lives of our people,” he said. 2:07 Ukraine strikes Russia amid political turmoil in Kyiv Russia says it targeted military sites Zelenskyy said at least 10 Ukrainian regions were attacked, with dozens of homes, businesses and infrastructure facilities destroyed or damaged. Children were among the dead — a 6-year-old girl and boys aged 11 and 17 in the area of Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy’s hometown, Hanzha added. In Kyiv, Russian forces struck the capital with ballistic missiles, killing a 31-year-old man and wounding two others, the National Police press service said. More than 56,000 people sheltered in Kyiv’s subway stations overnight, according to the Facebook post from the metro system. A cruise missile attack struck the western city of Lviv, killing one person and wounding over 30, including children aged 6, 13 and 15, said Maksym Kozytskyi, head of the Lviv regional military administration. In the Poltava region, a drone hit warehouses, killing one person, said regional military head Vitalii Diakivnych. Closer to the front line, which comes under almost daily attack, Russian forces dropped three glide bombs on an industrial zone in the southern city of Kherson, killing a 56-year-old man, local officials said. 2:11 Russia-Ukraine war: Trump says Kyiv will get license to manufacture Patriot missiles More on World More videos Vance asked Ukraine to not strike Russian energy infrastructure: reports IEA expects world oil demand to fall amid surging gas prices Ukrainian drones strike major Russian refinery 800 miles from border Bridal brands prepare for Taylor Swift-inspired wedding requests Colombia earthquake strains rescuers, as criticism grows of new government’s response Crowds gather for rare celestial event in Europe as solar eclipse reaches “totality” Perseids meteor shower to peak over skies in the Maritimes Israeli settlers besiege Palestinian homes in occupied West Bank Poland says fragments indicated a Russian cruise missile A Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crossed into Poland overnight, violating NATO airspace, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X, calling it a clear demonstration that strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses would also guarantee wider European security. Michael O’Connell, the spokesperson for the alliance’s military command in Belgium. The missile quickly disappeared from radar, the Polish Armed Forces said. A helicopter flew to its last known location, where the crew discovered a probable impact site in a farming area in Lublin province, the command said. Ukraine hits more Russian depots Meanwhile, Russia’s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 258 Ukrainian drones overnight. A depot belonging to Wildberries online retailer was set ablaze in Russia’s Penza region southeast of Moscow, in the latest strike on the company’s warehouses, Penza Gov. Oleg Melnichenko. Four people were injured and 200 workers were evacuated, he said, adding that about 100 firefighters were deployed. Wildberries also reported its warehouse in Sarapul in the Udmurtia region more than 1,000 kilometers (600 miles) from Ukraine, was struck by a Ukrainian drone and set ablaze. It said the workers had been safely evacuated. Story continues below advertisement The Russian online news outlet Astra reported that another Wildberries depot in the Perm region in the Urals was also set ablaze by a Ukrainian drone strike. Regional authorities reported a Ukrainian drone attack but didn’t give information about the damage. Thursday’s attacks on Wildberries warehouses brought to 14 the number of the retailer’s depots struck by Ukrainian drones in under two weeks. Ukraine accuses Wildberries of supplying goods that can be used by the Russian military. Ukrainian drone units destroyed four more vessels belonging to Russia’s “shadow fleet” of sanctions-busting tankers, bringing the total to 205 since the operation began July 6, Robert Brovdi, commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces, said on his Telegram channel. http://www.parisguardian.com/news/279216.text: Warsaw blames Moscow after a missile crashes in Poland France24 30 Jul 2026, 19:33 GMT+10 Polandsaid Thursday that a missile that blasted a 10-metre (33 feet) crater inside its territory was likely fired byRussiain its latest mass attack onUkraine. Read moreRussian strikes across Ukraine kill at least 8, wound more than a dozen NATOand European leaders openly blamed Russia for the 4am (0200 GMT) explosion in a field that shook residents of the village of Tarnawa Kolonia, 80 kilometres (50 miles) from the border, and the windows of their homes. The massive hole and debris were found in a field two kilometres away, police said. "From the analysis of most of the traces, the recovered fragments point to a Russian Kh-101 missile," Prime Minister Donald Tusk told a news conference near the crater. "There is no reason to think that Poland was the target," he said, but added that two "objects" had violated Polands airspace. "One of them definitely did, because we have its traces here, and the other was near the Polish border, but it was a very brief signal, so there were no consequences associated with it." Poland a member of NATO and theEuropean Unionhas experienced repeat incursions by missiles and drones during Russia's war on Ukraine since 2022. NATO activation The latest missile fell as Russia staged a massive deadly attack on the Lviv region in western Ukraine, near the border with Poland. Tusk chaired a crisis unit meeting with Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz and Interior Minister Marcin Kierwinski in Lublin, the nearest city to the village. A military prosecutor's investigation has been opened to determine the origin and nature of the explosion. NATO, Ukraine and European leaders strongly condemned Russia for breaching Poland's airspace. A NATO spokesman, Martin O'Donnell, said: "In response to a Russian missile of currently unknown type that entered Polish airspace and later crashed into Polish territory one of many missiles fired by Russia at Ukraine overnight NATO and Poland activated their air and ground defences." He added that alliance commanders were "in close contact with the Polish authorities about the violation of Poland's airspace. This intrusion "reminds us that there is nothing more urgent for our two countries than to counter our common, age-old enemy, which represents a direct threat to both our nations", Ukrainian foreign minister Andriy Sybiga wrote on X, referring to Russia's attacks. A Polish F-16 fighter jet took off after the missile was detected but lost track of it, authorities initially indicated. Tusk said Polish air defence would have shot down the missile if it had deviated from its trajectory and headed toward populated areas. In a message on X addressed to Ukrainian PresidentVolodymyr Zelenskyand Tusk, French PresidentEmmanuel Macroncondemned "in the strongest possible terms the Russian strikes that killed civilians in Ukraine, as well as the violation of Polish airspace". "Our support for Ukraine and our allies will not weaken," he wrote. "The Polish people are famously unafraid ... and our thoughts are with them," EU Commission presidentUrsula von der Leyenwrote on X as she condemned the Russian attack. "To put an end to this, we are helping Ukraine win this war in every way we can," she added. During the night, Russia launched 74 missiles and 284 drones at Ukraine, killing at least eight people. In November 2022, a Ukrainian air-defence missile fell on the Polish village of Przewodow, killing two people. And in September 2025, around 20 Russian drones that entered Polish airspace were shot down or crashed. Other European states have also been hit by Russian drones and missiles since 2022, particularlyRomaniaandMoldova. I grew up with the Star Wars prequels, and I like that, despite being a gazillionaire, he’s still rocking the same flannels he always has. The legendary filmmaker — fresh off a great cameo in the movie “Minions and Monsters” — is a big racing fan, and is often seen at Formula 1 races . He also binned a Scion during the old Toyota Pro/Celebrity Race at Long Beach in one of my favorite videos ever. So he knows racing — hell, he invented podracing — but F1 president and CEO Stefano Domenicali revealed a wild bit of advice he got from the man who somehow invented both Darth Vader and Jar-Jar Binks: no one is interested in how F1 cars are driven. I don’t think that’s true, but let’s hear him out. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE The series has faced a lot of flak for its current cars that rely more heavily on battery power and have effectively changed how drivers have to drive. Certain iconic corners are no longer taken flat out, and the need to recharge batteries has led to people calling the racing artificial. It has also led to claims that F1 should offer more info about the batteries and their state of charge for fans to follow along. “I think that the truth is exactly the other way around, because no one is interested in how you drive your car,” Domenicali said, per Motorsport . “The people are interested in whether you are overtaking or not. That’s the vast majority of people.” He noted that while some people are interested in this sort of thing, casual fans aren’t. ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW! Then he delivered one of the greatest name drops I’ve ever read. “I had an interesting discussion with George Lucas in Hungary, and he was giving me an incredible view on how the new fans are watching F1,” Domenicali said. “And I think that he gave us an incredible clearance to see how we can really simplify things because the new fans are not understanding the truth, what is behind the scenes.” I think new fans appreciate the sport more once they get a firmer grasp on the behind-the-scenes stuff, but it’s interesting Lucas made this point because it sounds to me like he’s saying what’s most important is providing an entertaining product. He knows quite a bit about that. Hell, he just opened a massive museum devoted to the medium of storytelling. CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST SPORTS NEWS And, if you think about it, every race is one big story, and it makes sense that F1 would want that at the forefront for newer fans. But, if you’re already in the door, there’s always room to nerd out on the strategies and tech and science behind the sport, just like if you’re a fan of a movie, you can geek out on the plot devices and the structure and even what pen or script software the person who wrote it used. It’s an interesting thing to think about… and even more fun because it seems to have sprung from the flannel-shirted mind of one George Lucas.
