(Photo by Gavriil Grigorov / POOL / AFP) / image distributed by the Russian state owned agency Sputnik) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Thursday that preliminary information indicates Russia used a North Korean ballistic missile in the strike on the village of Radushne that killed an entire family of 10. Zelensky provided the details in a statement on Telegram, just hours after the Russian missile strike on Radushne , in the Kryvyi Rih district of the Dnipropetrovsk region, killed two parents, along with their seven children and an 18-month old grandson. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “Of course, there will still be expert examinations, everything will be verified, but as of now, it is North Korean ballistics,” Zelensky said, adding that this is the first such use “in a long while.” According to two sources cited by Reuters, the strike marked the first suspected use of such a weapon in nearly a year. Advertisement The strike drew international reactions The strike drew condemnation worldwide, especially from allied countries. European countries also reacted to a separate incident, in which a Russian missile crossed into Polish territory , exploding in a field near Lublin during the same overnight barrage. While no casualties or damage were reported in Poland, Russia’s massive missile and drone attack on Ukraine overnight Thursday, July 30, killed at least eight people and injured more than 35, including three children. A similar drone incident occurred over Romania’s territorial waters near the Sulina-Chilia area over the weekend on July 24-26, in which Romania scrambled a F-16 fighter jet to intercept a Russian-made Shahed drone. The interception marked the third such incident over the course of three consecutive days, prompting Romania’s foreign ministry ordered a Russian embassy employee to be expelled in what it called a “firm response” to drones repeatedly breaching the NATO member’s airspace along the Ukrainian border. Other Topics of Interest Crimea Bridge Closed as Explosions Rock Occupied Peninsula Russia temporarily closed the Kerch Bridge as explosions were reported across occupied Crimea and air defenses opened fire over Sevastopol. “Most importantly, though, is not just sympathy and not just condemnation, but missiles for air defense,” Zelensky said, renewing his appeal for much needed air defense systems. Advertisement North Korea’s deepening role in Russia’s war North Korea has become one of Russia’s most critical wartime partners, supplying troops, weapons and manpower in exchange for financial and technological support . Ukraine’s Military Intelligence (HUR) estimated that North Korea supplies between 25% and 40% of Russia’s artillery shells , while the two countries are also nearing completion of their first-ever road bridge over the Tumen River to ease supply flows. The first reported use of North Korean ballistic missiles by Russia dates back to Dec. 29, 2023, when one missile landed in a field in Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region. Russia deployed the missiles again just days later, on Jan. 2, 2024, during a massive strike on Kharkiv that left two people dead and injured 62 others. “The alliance between the Moscow scumbags and the deranged regime in North Korea exists for the sake of missiles,” Zelensky said, accusing Pyongyang of “killing our Ukrainian children.” Moscow signed a defense pact with Pyongyang on June 19, 2024, with both countries officially recognizing North Korean troop deployments in April 2025. Zelensky warned Wednesday, July 29 that Russia is preparing to receive 30,000 additional North Korean troops and more ballistic missile launchers. Advertisement Patriot interceptors remain central Ukraine has repeatedly identified Patriot interceptors as one of its most urgent battlefield needs, citing critical shortages of the only weapon currently capable of intercepting Russia’s ballistic missiles. “Missiles for air defense, and above all missiles for the Patriots, but also for the NASAMS, for the IRIS-Ts, for the HAWKs, and our other systems,” remains a key priority, Zelensky said, adding that he counts “on all our partners, and above all our American partners,” for delivery. On Tuesday, Zelensky held what he called a “ productive meeting ” with US President Donald Trump in the Oval office at the White House, in which the two discussed advancing Patriot interceptor production, as well as the revival of stalled diplomacy with Russia. Trump first signaled he would grant Ukraine a license to produce the missiles during the NATO summit in Ankara, Turkey on July 7-8, however, it was floated only as an idea at the time. As of Tuesday, Zelensky confirmed that the plan had moved to concrete steps, with the US allowing Ukraine to produce the missiles domestically. Also onTuesday, Zelensky met with Lockheed Martin representatives to discuss expanding joint weapons production and technology sharing . Less than a week earlier, on July 23, Zelensky announced a possible joint cooperation with Raytheon as well, without providing a specific timeline for launching production. Advertisement On July 20, Lockheed Martin unveiled cheaper Patriot interceptors , PAC-3 ACE, designed to deter air and missile threats at less than half the cost of the PAC-3 MSE as global demand surges. Picture: YURIY DYACHYSHYN / AFP via Getty Images Thu, 30 Jul, 2026 - 15:58 Peter Beaumont and agencies       Russia has been accused of violating Polish airspace, after a missile exploded in a field in the east of the country, triggering Nato air defences, in the midst of a massive air raid that killed 13 people in neighbouring Ukraine . Polish authorities said that the explosion near the village of Tarnawa-Kolonia, close to Lublin, had created a 10-metre-wide crater. Residents of Tarnawa-Kolonia reported hearing an explosion at about 4am that shook the windows of their homes, police said. Nato’s supreme ⁠allied commander for Europe, Gen Alexus Grynkewich, said: “​Nato ​will continue ​to take all necessary ​measures ‌to defend Nato ​territory.” Speaking at the scene of the explosion, in a field about 50 miles from the Ukrainian border, the Polish prime minister, Donald Tusk, said the missile was most likely Russian. “From the analysis of most of the traces, the recovered fragments point to a Russian KH-101 missile,” he told journalists. Read More Thousands of French wildfire evacuees return home as cooler weather moves in US man hikes out of mountains to get help after he was impaled by trekking pole Time running out for survivors after quake in south-west Japan He said there was no reason to think that Poland had been the target of the missile but said the Polish military had been prepared to shoot it down if it threatened a built-up area. As the attacks on Ukraine took place, Poland – a Nato member – scrambled fighter jets to protect its airspace, its armed forces said. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said in a post on X that a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile had crossed into Poland. The Russian embassy in Warsaw did not immediately respond to an email requesting comment. People hide in a Kyiv metro station, during an air raid. Picture: Credit Dmytro Laryn / Ukrainska Pravda António Costa, the president of the EU council, said on X: “Last night, Russia launched a massive combined strike against Ukraine. During the attack, Polish airspace was also violated, underlining once again that Russia’s aggression is a threat to the security of Europe as a whole.” Ursula von der ​Leyen, the European Commission president, said the ⁠Russian missile incident ⁠in ⁠Poland was ​another “unacceptable violation” of the ⁠EU’s airspace. At least 13 people in Ukraine – including one in Kyiv – died in Thursday’s attacks, which extended as far ⁠as the western city of Lviv. A missile strike in the central city of Kryvyi Rih – Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s home town – killed at least six people, including two girls, aged five and 12, the head of the town’s military administration said. Zelenskyy had warned the country hours in advance of Moscow launching the massive attack. Oleksandr Vilkul, the ‌head of the defence council, said: “In a village on the outskirts of Kryvyi Rih, a direct strike by an Iskander-M ballistic missile, launched from Voronezh, hit a private house where a large family lived, killing girls aged five and 12 and four adults.” Eight more people were wounded, he said. Another six people, including two children, were killed in the regions of Dnipropetrovsk and Poltava. The military administration for Kyiv confirmed one death, with the mayor, Vitali Klitschko, reporting fires in several districts. Earlier, he posted: “The enemy is attacking the capital with ballistic weapons. The threat of further attack remains present. Stay in shelters!” A Ukrainian soldier, at the bomb damaged Lukianivska district of Kyiv, Ukraine, looks up at the damaged buildings. Picture: Niall Carson/PA Wire In ‌Lviv, close to Poland, rescue workers were scrambling to clear rubble to reach those trapped after Russian missiles damaged two blocks of flats and injured 26 people, officials said. Late on Wednesday, Zelenskyy had posted: “The Russians prepared a massive attack several days ago, and there is a high probability that the strike will be carried out tonight … Please, in all regions of Ukraine, pay attention to air raid alerts today and stay safe.” Zelenskyy also repeated his request to Ukraine’s allies to supply Kyiv with the missiles its air defence system lacked. “It is important that our partners fully ​understand what is happening and that the protection of people’s lives depends directly on their willingness, or lack of willingness, to provide air defence missiles.” A residential apartment building is seen damaged after a Russian strike on Kyiv, Ukraine, Thursday, July 2, 2026. (AP Photo/Efrem Lukatsky) Russia’s defence ministry, commenting on the strikes, said it had used land, sea and air-launched missiles, as well as strike drones, during the raid and claimed it had targeted military industrial facilities. Elsewhere on Thursday, the ⁠Ukrainian military struck four Russian ⁠tankers ​in the Black Sea ⁠and the Sea of ⁠Azov, Ukraine’s drone ​forces ‌commander, ‌Robert Brovdi, said. Brovdi said on the Telegram app that 205 tankers – ​130 in the Sea of Azov ⁠and 75 ​in the ​Black ​Sea –had ​been ‌hit in the ​past ​three weeks. - The Guardian Read More Iranian missile hits Chinese firm’s building in Kuwait amid renewed strikes x Every Match. https://www.theglobeandmail.com/canada/a.text: Jameson Berkow Published July 30, 2026 Open this photo in gallery: Christopher Ondaatje addresses the media at the preview of two new Royal Ontario Museum galleries on Feb. 12, 2008 in Toronto. The Sir Christopher Ondaatje South Asian Gallery is on the third level of the ROM. Ashley Hutcheson/The Globe and Mail Share Save for later Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create Free Account You can find more obituaries from The Globe and Mail here . To submit a memory about someone we have recently profiled on the Obituaries page, e-mail us at obit@globeandmail.com . “Tall and elegant” is how multiple profiles have described Christopher Ondaatje over the decades. He was long-legged and, rather than simply walk, he was known to range gracefully along corridors. But those adjectives could just as easily describe his almost-century-long life. Tall, because his was a truly towering list of life experiences. Christopher Ondaatje was a self-made millionaire, an Olympic athlete, a best-selling author, a musician, a painter, a swashbuckling explorer and a deeply devoted brother, husband and father. Elegant, because each of his passions seemed to connect seamlessly together, with none seeming to overpower another. “He was probably the most active person that I’ve ever known,” David Ondaatje, Christopher’s son and a filmmaker who lives in California, said in an interview from the family home in the Bahamas where Christopher spent his final days. He died on July 20, at the age of 93. “He was always making something. He always found time to do the things he loved. He was a painter. He was a writer. He was a musician. He was a filmmaker. He made a lot of family movies. For years every Christmas we would get a movie in the mail, a new creation that he had filmed over the summer.” Revered pianist Oliver Jones transformed the jazz scene in Montreal and beyond Born in Sri Lanka in 1933, back when the country was still a British colony called Ceylon, Christopher was part of an Ondaatje lineage stretching back nearly four centuries. According to a 2019 profile in Sri Lanka’s Sunday Observer newspaper, Christopher was a direct descendant of a Brahmin physician named Ondaatje in the court of Tanjore (present day Thanjavur, a city in the south Indian state of Tamil Nadu) who was summoned by the Dutch governor of Ceylon in 1659. He was sent to boarding school (Blundell’s) in England in the mid-forties, but in 1950 his mother sent a letter saying he would have to leave as the family could no longer afford the fees. The loss of the Ondaatje family fortune was widely attributed to the alcoholism of his father, Mervyn. Christopher’s mother, Doris Gratiaen, divorced her husband around that time and Mervyn died in an accident a short time later. “Being kicked out of my house and my family in 1947 forced me to become worldly-wise and to be able to think for myself and make decisions very early on,” Christopher told Salon Magazine in May, 2000. David said that experience also helped Christopher to prioritize family above all else. “Family was so important to him because his own family broke up when he was very young in Sri Lanka. All four kids were sent to live with different people when their parents divorced. That had a big impact on him: They were all very close when they were young. Then they lost everything.” Doris brought two of Christopher’s younger siblings, Michael (future author of The English Patient , among other bestselling novels and poetry) and Janet, over to England, where she ran a Notting Hill boarding house. Jillian, his other sister, stayed behind in Sri Lanka. As the eldest, Christopher quickly set a goal of rebuilding his family’s financial position. He got his first banking job in London at the age of 17, but quickly decided he would have better fortune abroad. Christopher arrived in Canada in 1956 with just $13 in his pocket (or about $150 in 2026 dollars). He was initially unimpressed. “I stood with the other passengers in the shelter of the open shed and gazed miserably at the bleak prospect of Montreal’s Pier 26 – my first view of Canada after eight days of the Atlantic – eight cold, drizzly, sunless days in a second-rate Cunarder,” he previously told The Times. His only friend in Canada at the time was a trumpet player in a Toronto nightclub, and Christopher’s first Canadian home was a basement laundry room. He would initially earn some money by joining his friend’s band on the guitar. Christopher eventually found a banking job in what was known as “the cage” of a Toronto stockbroking company. The term was accurate, as his tasks revolved around making records of individual trades in a room enclosed by iron bars (for security) that was more akin to a jail cell than an office. He quickly broke free of that position, however, and moved to Montreal, where he got into magazine advertising. It was there he met Valda Bulins, the daughter of Latvian refugees who had a degree in chemistry from Dalhousie University. They married in 1959 and would remain together for more than 65 years. Three years later, Christopher brought his younger brother Michael over from England. “When he was 18, I pulled him out to Canada to go to university. He immediately latched onto the literary set,” Christopher told Salon. “He’s 10 years younger than me and we didn’t really have a chance to get to know one another in earlier life.” Michael dedicated his latest book, The Distance of a Shout, published earlier this year, to his older brother. Christopher “persuaded me to join him” in Canada, he wrote , “so giving me the essential gift of a new life.” “Before leaving England, he had introduced me to the pleasures of books and music, especially jazz. And for years at parties he would bring out his guitar and sing a Hoagy Carmichael song, ‘Huggin’ and Chalkin’’, and when he got to the last verse I would join in with him.” From medical research to religious tolerance, Frances Belzberg spent a lifetime supporting causes that spoke to her Shortly after bringing Michael to Canada, Christopher got into bobsledding and was selected to represent Canada at the 1964 Winter Olympics in Austria. While his own sled finished 14th, another Canadian sled won gold. Back in Canada, Christopher published his first book, a history of the prime ministers of Canada, in 1968. It was a massive success, selling several hundred thousand copies. He translated that success into a publishing company that he launched in 1970 called Pagurian Press (Pagurian is the scientific name for hermit crab). That same year, he founded Canada’s first independent institutional equity brokerage, Loewen, Ondaatje, McCutcheon & Company. Pagurian would go public on the Toronto Stock Exchange in 1979, expanding from publishing into corporate finance and investment management. By 1988, the company was reportedly worth roughly $500-million, or nearly $1.2-billion in 2026 dollars. By the age of 55, Christopher had achieved his goal of rebuilding the Ondaatje family fortune. But he had had enough of high finance. Reading The Devil Drives , a biography of Victorian explorer Sir Richard Burton, had an influence on him as significant as getting kicked out of school decades earlier. He promptly sold off all his business interests. “I was hacking my way through the jungles of finance, and I suddenly realized his was the life I would have preferred to have led,” Christopher told Salon. “I was fed up with the world of finance and greed, and the uncertainty of the economic clouds. I was worried too that I wouldn’t have enough time to do all I wanted with my life. I didn’t want to die with ‘financier’ written on my gravestone.” After having spent the past four decades of his life collecting, adventuring (he spent years tracing the source of the Nile River) and creating art, David said there is clearly no risk of that. “The next generation of the family doesn’t really know anything about his financial life. They only know him as a fun, eccentric, wonderful person.” The sheer elegance of Christopher’s manner was never more evident than in 1999, when David went with his wife and his sister to join the family patriarch on a trip to Africa. “We all kept diaries. He showed me his diary and I couldn’t believe it: every page was neatly written, every sentence was perfectly formed. Page after page after page and nothing was crossed out. No changes, no corrections. Thoughts were coming out as fully formed sentences,” David said. The journalist John Fraser, a long-time friend, said Christopher was “generous to a fault,” citing a long list of causes, charities and institutions he supported over the course of his life. Christopher received the Order of Canada in 1993 for his philanthropy and was knighted for it in 2003. Christopher was also “restless about what the next adventure was going to be,” Mr. Fraser said. Yet no matter how busy he was, David said, Christopher was still a “very present parent.” “He was very much a part of our lives. We never got the sense that there was anything more important than his family. I’ve tried to make sure my kids feel the same way,” he said. Christopher would regularly get out his guitar and sing for the family at gatherings. The songs were usually about his family and the places they went together. He became a prolific painter towards the end of his life, David said, with every member of the immediate family receiving a portrait as a present in recent years. David said one of his parents’ favourite movies was Out of Africa . After Christopher’s passing, Valda quoted from the eulogy at the end of the film: “He brought us joy.” Report an editorial error Report a technical issue Editorial code of conduct Related stories From medical research to religious tolerance, Frances Belzberg spent a lifetime supporting causes that spoke to her Why people are obsessed with a certain Charlize Theron outfit from The Odyssey Should we have a baby? https://www.smh.com.au/traveller/reviews.text: Advertisement Given the concern surrounding the routes of Middle Eastern airlines, I am considering fares with a cancellation policy. I notice most have a fee which I believe applies each way. Does this type of cancellation policy apply even if I change my mind, no reason required? S. Vlamis, Highton, Vic If considering travel via the Middle East, it makes sense to book a refundable ticket. AP The terms and conditions regarding flight cancellations vary depending on who you’ve booked through. If it’s a booking made directly with an airline, then a refundable or flexible fare generally allows you to cancel because you’ve changed your mind. However, the amount of the refund is determined by the fare conditions. A fully refundable fare will usually be from the most expensive category, but it does what the name suggests. Most other fare categories involve a cancellation fee. If you buy your ticket from an online travel agency such as Booking.com or Trip.com, it may come with a different set of conditions from the airline’s own fare rules, and these conditions are likely to be more stringent. Booking a refundable airline fare, either fully refundable or with a relatively small cancellation fee, is a sensible option. The fee you pay for cancelling a booking is a one-off fee that applies to the entire booking, it doesn’t apply to each of the outbound and return sectors of a journey. In December, my wife and I are looking at travelling by train from Tallinn to Warsaw. Is this doable, and do you have any useful tips? We are happy to stop over along the way, so any recommendations for cities to visit would be appreciated. M. Anderson, Epping, NSW Advertisement Tallinn, capital of the Baltic state of Estonia, from the tower of St Olaf’s. iStock Sign up for the Traveller newsletter The latest travel news, tips and inspiration delivered to your inbox. Sign up now. The simplest route takes you from Tallinn to Warsaw via Riga and Vilnius. Travel time from Tallinn to Riga is six hours with no transfers on the fastest train. Riga to Vilnius is a four-hour journey and Vilnius to Warsaw takes more than six hours with one change. If it’s a case of either/or, Riga is a compact, elegant city with one of Europe’s finest collections of art nouveau architecture and a lively cafe and bar scene. A highlight is the enormous Central Market, housed in former Zeppelin hangars. A full day is enough time to take in the main sights. Vilnius is more appealing if you want to explore one of Europe’s largest surviving medieval old towns with fewer tourists, and enjoy its relaxed, bohemian vibe. You would need two to three days. The Man in Seat 61 has plenty of useful information on train travel in the Baltic States, including schedules and how to buy tickets. In February next year I’m taking a bucket-list trip to Antarctica. Any idea if expedition landings will be affected by bird flu issues? M. Cartwell, Blackburn, Vic While it’s unlikely that bird flu would cause you to miss your Antarctic landings, some specific landing sites may be changed at short notice. In response to the highly pathogenic avian influenza H5N1, the International Association of Antarctica Tour Operators, which governs virtually all expedition cruise operators, has introduced biosecurity and wildlife management protocols. Before every landing, expedition staff assess wildlife colonies for signs of avian influenza. If there’s evidence of disease or unusual mortality, that landing may be cancelled and replaced with another site or a Zodiac cruise. You can also expect enhanced biosecurity, with a high likelihood of disinfection baths for footwear after landings and a requirement to avoid sitting or kneeling on the ground and keeping well away from wildlife. Antarctic cruises are always subject to the changeable nature of the environment. Sea ice, weather and whales all have a bearing on day-to-day plans, but they do not usually negatively impact the experience. Advertisement I’d like to celebrate my 50th birthday in Italy with my husband and three children, aged 20, 18 and 15. I’ve been to Italy three times but this would be a first for my family. Can you suggest a two-week itinerary for July 2027? M. Costigan, Bentleigh, Vic Via Della Lungaretta in Trastevere, Rome. iStock Italy in July will be hot, crowded and expensive. For all those reasons I’d suggest visiting in May or after mid-September. You’ll probably fly into Rome, so spend a few days there taking in the city’s amazing sights. Balance the classic tourist spots with some neighbourhood life in Trastevere. There are plenty of fun things that the kids will enjoy, such as Vespa tours or a self-drive Fiat 500 tour. CitizenM Rome Isola Tiberina is a funky, design-forward hotel near the River Tiber, a perfect location for exploring both sides of the city, and the price is reasonable. Take the train to Bologna. It’s a sophisticated, open-air museum that feels authentic rather than overtouristed. Its large student population gives it a vibrant atmosphere as well as many low-cost dining options. Take a day trip to Modena to visit the Enzo Ferrari Museum; the one at Maranello on Modena’s outskirts is quite spectacular but more difficult to access. From there head for the Cinque Terre. Stay either at Monterosso or Vernazza and spend three days swimming in the Mediterranean off the rocks, hiking between gorgeous villages, enjoying the local seafood and gelato every afternoon. Advertisement Hire a car in La Spezia and spend three to four nights in an agriturismo in the Val d’Orcia, south of Siena. Spend your time exploring this very different side of Italy, taking in Pienza, Montepulciano, the small, family-operated wineries of the region and the farm restaurants. Drive to Orvieto, spend whatever time you have left here then take the train to Rome for your flight home. Photograph: Dieudonne Dirole/AP Ebola DRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth province Man dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest ever Rachel Savage and agencies Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.17 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.12 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to a sixth province, officials have said, a day after the head of the World Health Organization said the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest in history, which killed at least 11,000 people more than a decade ago. The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday. At the same point in the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa , the previous most deadly outbreak, 755 cases had been recorded, according to WHO data. Jean Kaseya, the director general of Africa CDC, said on Thursday that a death had been recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province. The man had travelled from Isiro, in Haut-Uele province, to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died, Kaseya said. There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current outbreak. The death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 outbreak. On Wednesday, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said the current outbreak would surpass that one based on its current pace. Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have now been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported. Uganda has reported 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case there was reported on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded. The DRC outbreak is unfolding amid strikes by some unpaid health workers, global development aid cuts, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatised communities, and misinformation claiming that Ebola is not real. Ebola virus behind massive outbreak in DRC could be mutating, officials say Read more Health workers at the Nizi treatment centre in Ituri province went on strike on Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the centre, saying they had not been paid for three months. The true scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared on 15 May but the WHO says sequencing now shows it began months earlier in February. Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside contacts being monitored, and that the disease is spreading at an alarming rate. Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa, said this week: “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us.” Nonetheless, his colleague Abdirahman Mahamud, the head of the WHO’s emergency response division, sounded a note of optimism on Wednesday, saying that if the pandemic response was implemented “at the same time across the five transmission zones, we are expecting a turnaround in three months”. Even with that, Mahamud said the peak of the outbreak would not be reached for six months under a “moderate” scenario and that the outbreak could last nine to 12 months. Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from body fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, including from dead bodies, and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal. Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola causing this outbreak began last month in Ituri. Tedros said on Wednesday two vaccines developed specifically for this strain were now being tested on people for the first time. This strain of Bundibugyo is genetically different from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, making it likely that this outbreak began when the virus jumped from an infected animal to a human, researchers said in a paper published this week in the journal Nature Medicine. They had sequenced genomes from samples from 22 people with Ebola. Last week, Kaseya said officials were worried the virus could be mutating and that the Africa CDC was planning further studies with the WHO to investigate. Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this story. Photograph: Wael Hamzeh/EPA-EFE/Shutterstock Central African Republic French ambassador to CAR investigated over claims he hosted dozens of women Disciplinary proceedings under way after security concerns raised over reported visits to official residence Agence France-Presse Thu 13 Aug 2026 10.21 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 10.35 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google France has opened disciplinary proceedings against its ambassador to Central African Republic over allegations of misconduct, after claims he brought dozens of women into his official residence, raising potential security concerns. The investigation comes as Paris seeks to rebuild relations with CAR after their sharp deterioration in recent years amid Russia’s expanding influence in the former French colony. The French weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported that the ambassador, Bruno Foucher, 65, brought about 30 women between the ages of 20 and 30 into his residence during the period of January 2024 to March 2026, with some of them staying overnight. The visits prompted officials to report a security breach. The ambassador acknowledged having had sexual relations with two young women, the weekly said. The French foreign ministry said: “At the initiative of the ministry, an administrative investigation was carried out in Bangui in 2026. Upon receipt of the findings of this mission, and at the request of the minister, the ministry initiated disciplinary proceedings against the ambassador. These proceedings are ongoing.” The ministry conducted an on-site inspection in April, which led to the opening of disciplinary proceedings. Foucher is a career diplomat who has served as ambassador to CAR since 2023. He was ambassador to Lebanon from 2017 to 2020, to Iran from 2011 to 2016, and to Chad between 2006 and 2011. According to Le Canard enchaîné, which said it obtained the inspection report, the ambassador received about 15 visits a month. He also allegedly instructed staff to allow one of the young women to stay at the residence during his absence. Russia maintains a strong foothold in CAR, primarily through the Wagner paramilitary group, which plays a key role in providing security for the country’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra. French officials have accused Russians of fostering anti-French sentiment in a number of African countries. The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, praised the “complete restoration of relations” between France and CAR when he visited Bangui in March. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/Reuters Japan ‘Absolutely unacceptable’: Japan condemns visit by Vladimir Putin to disputed Kuril Islands Japanese PM says islands seized by Soviets late in second world war are part of her country under international law Gavin Blair in Tokyo Thu 13 Aug 2026 08.56 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Japanese government has reacted angrily to Vladimir Putin’s first visit to the disputed Kuril Islands, which are claimed by both Tokyo and Moscow. Japan’s foreign minister, Toshimitsu Motegi, summoned the Russian ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev, while the prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, called Putin’s actions “absolutely unacceptable”. Known in Japan as the Northern Territories and by Russia as the Southern Kurils, the islands were seized by the then Soviet Union in the closing stages of the second world war and have been a source of contention ever since. The Soviet Union declared war on Japan in August 1945 as Tokyo was about to surrender, and the dispute has prevented the two nations from signing a formal peace treaty. View image in fullscreen Putin visits a hospital. Photograph: Gavriil Grigorov/SPUTNIK/KREMLIN POOL/EPA Takaichi told reporters in Tokyo that the islands, which are just off Hokkaido, were “both historically and under international law” a part of Japan and called the visit by the Russian leader “incompatible with Japan’s consistent position” on the territory. Japanese television showed footage of Putin on the island of Etorofu, or Iturup in Russian, visiting a hospital, meeting residents and trying caviar at a processing plant, as well as comments condemning the visit by former Japanese residents who were deported when Russia took control of the islands. About 17,000 Japanese formerly lived on the islands, which today are occupied by about 20,000 Russian citizens. As well as its strategic significance, the island chain – consisting of Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and the Habomai islet group – provides access to rich fishing grounds and valuable mineral deposits. On Wednesday, Putin travelled to the nearby Russian island of Sakhalin, where he inspected navy drills and declared that the four disputed islands were recognised as Russian in international documents. Shinzo Abe, the late Japanese prime minister, had reached an entente with Putin over the territory, with visits by Japanese citizens to family graves resuming and talk of a future peace treaty. However, Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine prompted Japan to impose sanctions on personnel and entities linked to Moscow, souring bilateral relations. The Russian president acknowledged Abe’s actions in his remarks on Wednesday and went to call the recent sanctions “unprovoked”. He said: “Japan has identified Russia as a major source of threats. I would like to point out that we are not threatening Japan. On the contrary, it has territorial claims against our country.” Though it is Putin’s first visit to the islands, Dmitry Medvedev went to Kunashiri in 2010 when he was president. Medvedev was widely seen as loyal to Putin, who was prime minister at the time. Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PA Immigration and asylum Nearly 100 children detained as adults under UK-France migration deal Figures emerge in critical letter to Home Office from organisation appointed to scrutinise detention facilities Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.13 EDT First published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Nearly 100 children have been wrongly identified and detained as adults under Shabana Mahmood’s “one in, one out” deal with France , the Guardian can disclose. Home Office staff said that of 304 age-disputed cases arising from the scheme over nine months, 94 (31%) – were ultimately found to be minors. Children are supposed to be excluded from the scheme, while government policy limits immigration detention of unaccompanied children to 24 hours. The figures have emerged in a letter sent to the Home Office minister Anna Turley from Jane Leech, the interim chair of independent monitoring boards (IMBs), which scrutinise prisons and immigration detention facilities. In the highly critical letter, Leech also said some people detained under the scheme: Had been awaiting deportation for more than six months, despite being supposed be held for up to 28 days only “in exceptional cases”. Were being readied for removal to France despite having TB or requiring hospital treatment. Faced removal after being separated from family members with whom they had travelled, which she said had a “particularly damaging impact”. French officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since spring Read more The “one in, one out” initiative, launched last August, allows the UK to send somepeople who arrive by small boat back to France while agreeing to take the same number of people from France if they are judged to have a legitimate claim. Leech said the deal was “placing highly vulnerable, newly arrived individuals, including children and survivors of abuse, in detention”. In the letter to Turley, she wrote: “Your officials have informed the IMB that 304 age disputes have taken place between 15 August 2025 and 1 May 2026, of which 94 (31%) were assessed to be children. “The IMB is therefore concerned that child safeguarding mechanisms are ineffective, and believes more should be done to ensure that those whose age is under dispute are not detained in the first place.” Leech criticised the length of time it took for officials to complete age assessments. “In two cases observed by the Heathrow Board, it took 40 days or more from arrival at the IRC [immigration removal centre] to age assessment,” she wrote. Referring to the deal as Operation Hillmore, its official name within the Home Office, Leech said she had “significant concerns” about the vulnerabilities of those detained under the scheme. She wrote: “Many of those who have recently arrived present as psychologically distressed, and Boards have observed records and heard testimonies showing that many are survivors of torture and abuse.” There was evidence of poor health screening at Manston among the Hillmore detainees, Leech wrote. “Gatwick IRC recently received one individual from Manston with tuberculosis, while a second was refused admission to Brook House because of the critical state of their health, and referred directly to hospital.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion She said people were being held for lengthy periods despite the scheme being intended to operate at pace, with one man detained for 27 weeks. Government figures covering 4 August 2025 to 30 June 2026 show that 1,087 people were returned to France under the deal. During the same period, 27,920 people arrived in the UK on small boats. Imran Hussain, the executive director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, described the figures as “disturbing” and said they were the latest example of children being wrongly treated as adults by the Home Office. “Too often refugee children are being treated as adults and put into unsafe situations, at risk of abuse and neglect, and exposed to significant safeguarding risks,” he said. “We call on the government to prioritise professional assessments led by trained social workers, which has been found to be the most accurate way to determine age and therefore avoid these risks.” A Home Office spokesperson said: “Robust age assessments are essential to maintaining the integrity of our border and ensuring migrants receive appropriate safeguarding and access to services. “We will continue to strengthen and modernise this process, including through the rollout of cutting-edge AI technology from next year to support age assessment.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum Home Office France Europe Migration Foreign policy news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Government could pay higher rents to spread asylum accommodation across UK French officers halted small boats at sea 10 times since spring More than 1,100 people convicted of illegal arrival in UK since 2022 Dinghy carrying 173 people capsizes in Channel after engine catches fire Judge orders return of alleged victim of trafficking sent to France under ‘one in one out’ scheme Is Reform UK’s plan to use the navy to stop small boat crossings feasible? Photograph: Marcin Nowak/LNP Rail transport Two seriously injured after passenger train derails near Lewes in East Sussex Additional nine passengers sustain less serious injuries and major disruption to services reported Matthew Weaver and Gwyn Topham Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.38 EDT First published on Thu 13 Aug 2026 11.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Two people have been seriously injured after a passenger train derailed between Haywards Heath and Lewes in East Sussex , prompting a rapid emergency response in the area. Images of the aftermath appeared to show passengers standing on top of the toppled carriages while others could be seen in an area of heathland alongside emergency workers. British Transport Police said: “At this time we believe that two people have sustained serious injuries and a further nine patients have sustained less serious injuries. Patients have been assessed and treated at the scene, with some transported to local hospitals.” View image in fullscreen Emergency services respond to the derailed train between Haywards Heath and Lewes. Photograph: PA Assistant chief constable Ian Drummond-Smith said: “We’ve declared a major incident and a significant emergency service response is ongoing at the scene, but all passengers on the train have now been safely evacuated from the service. “Our thoughts are of course with everyone affected, and I’d like to reassure the public that we’re supporting the Rail Accident Investigation Branch [RAIB] to establish exactly what’s happened. We’ll provide further information as soon as we are able.” The RAIB has launched an inquiry into what went wrong. An aerial photograph of the scene showed three of the train’s eight carriages on their side. Rob Bradley and his six-year-old daughter Mabel were in the last of the carriages to stay upright. Speaking to the BBC he said: “We are doing OK. We were very lucky we were on the fourth carriage. The fifth went on its side. View image in fullscreen An aerial photograph of the derailment site. Photograph: BBC News “We felt the train speeding up and started to rock. Then our carriage jumped vertically upwards and we could tell it was a derailment. The emergency brakes went on the train and everything got thrown forward. “The train skidded for quite a while before it stopped. We turned around and we saw the whole back of the train was open and smoke and dust were pouring into the carriage and we saw the fifth carriage had gone on its side.” Several rail routes were closed after the Southern service came off the tracks just before 4pm. Emergency services said people should avoid the area, and that anyone travelling by rail in the area should allow up to 60 minutes extra for their journey. A spokesperson for Network Rail and Southern Rail said: “We can confirm that the 1424 Southern passenger service from Victoria to Eastbourne has derailed in the Lewes area of East Sussex. Emergency services are on site and we will update with more information when we can. Trains through the area are suspended and passengers are advised to check online at southernrailway.com for the latest service information.” View image in fullscreen Images of the aftermath appear to show passengers standing on top of the toppled carriages. Photograph: @Defianc_e/Jeremy Veitch The transport secretary, Heidi Alexander, tweeted: “Deeply concerned of reports of a derailment involving a Southern train in Lewes, Sussex. “Grateful to emergency services who are on the scene supporting those impacted. We are working quickly with the rail industry and local partners to assist passengers.” Southern said in an update on X: “If you are travelling to Gatwick airport, please allow at least an extra 150 minutes for your journey to ensure you make your flight connections and use an alternative route. “We have requested rail replacement buses to the following stations: Haywards Heath, Lewes. We will update you here on X once confirmed, but for now, please continue to travel using your own alternative route.” In an earlier update it said the derailment had occurred between Haywards Heath and Lewes, meaning there are currently no trains between Brighton and Lewes, Haywards Heath and Lewes and Seaford/Eastbourne and Lewes. View image in fullscreen The derailed train near Lewes. Photograph: BBC News The company told passengers: “You should delay your journey in this area until later on today, or use an alternative route to travel.” James MacCleary, the MP for Lewes, said: “I am aware of very concerning reports of a train crash in the Lewes area this afternoon. I am in touch with the relevant authorities now and will provide further updates as soon as I have more information. “This is clearly a very serious and developing incident, and my thoughts are with everyone affected. In the meantime, if you are concerned about someone or need urgent assistance, please contact the emergency services.” Explore more on these topics Rail transport East Sussex Transport England Southern news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

Photograph: Victoria Jones/PA Immigration and asylum Government could pay higher rents to spread asylum accommodation across UK Greater use of private rental properties would form part of PM’s plan to spread accommodation more evenly across UK Rowena Mason Whitehall editor Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.52 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.39 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ministers are considering paying higher prices for housing asylum seekers in private rental properties as part of Andy Burnham’s plan to spread accommodation more evenly across the country. Using more private rental accommodation, known as “dispersal”, as well as former military barracks, is cheaper than expensive hotels for asylum seekers. However, officials believe it may be necessary to raise the strict caps on how much the Home Office can pay landlords in rent so that the accommodation is not concentrated heavily in the most deprived areas. The move would fit with Andy Burnham’s plea this week for more areas to “play their part” in housing those seeking asylum, instead of accommodation most often falling in areas where rents are the cheapest. A Downing Street source said the biggest priority was reducing the need for accommodation for people seeking asylum overall. Nearly 100 children detained as adults under UK-France migration deal Read more The policy of national responsibility for asylum seekers is broadly supported by refugee charities but they said local councils must take the lead and people should not be sent to places without sufficient means of supporting them. Imran Hussain, director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, said: “Ever since the policy of dispersing asylum seekers away from London and the south-east was introduced, we have been clear that supporting refugees should be a national responsibility and that people should not be sent to places without adequate housing, legal advice, support services or established refugee communities. “That’s why local authorities should take the lead on asylum accommodation, using their local knowledge. Local councils should be given the powers and resources they need to provide people seeking asylum with housing, working with their local residents and also providing value for money to the taxpayer.” He added: “Poor-quality decision-making by the Home Office is keeping a large number of people in the asylum system while they wait for the courts to overturn flawed decisions. The new government’s priority should be ensuring decisions are made quickly and are right the first time.” Karen Bradley, the Conservative chair of parliament’s home affairs watchdog, pointed to her committee’s report, which said “asylum accommodation has been heavily concentrated in areas with high levels of deprivation … that is where accommodation is cheapest and the old asylum contracts prioritised cost above ensuring a fair spread across the country”. Some critics of the proposal to raise private rental payments for asylum accommodation said it would cost more but government sources said it was cheaper than using hotels, with the closures so far since the last Conservative administration having saved £1bn. They suggested the government’s aim was to ensure no single area carried a disproportionate burden, rather than decisions being driven solely by cost. A government spokesperson said: “We are already working to fairly house asylum seekers across the entire country, working closely with local authorities and listening to local concerns to help reduce the impact on communities. “The number of hotels in use has fallen from 213 in July 2024 to fewer than 160 today. Before the general election, hotel use peaked at 400 sites, costing £9m a day. “The number of asylum seekers staying in hotels has fallen by 35% over the past year and is down 63% from the peak in 2023, while overall asylum support costs have fallen by £1bn since the general election.” Record 230 people cross Channel to UK as smugglers turn to ‘mega-dinghies’ Read more Joe Robertson, a Conservative MP on the Isle of Wight, told the Telegraph, which first reported the policy proposal, that Burnham “needs to choose locations which offer the most cost-effective accommodation in the best interest of taxpayers” and that “self-serving political choices which cost more would be wrong on every level”. The policy of more “dispersal” of asylum accommodation was pursued under the last Conservative government by Robert Jenrick as immigration minister, now a Reform UK MP and finance spokesperson. Marley Morris, a researcher on migration at the IPPR thinktank, pointed out on Thursday that Jenrick had pursued the policy to allow more equitable distribution of asylum seekers across the UK and also argued it would be cheaper. “This is because it helps to reduce use of hotels, which are far more expensive than dispersal accommodation,” Morris said. Photograph: David McNew/Getty Images US news Fossils show huge carbon emissions harm forests, not ‘green the planet’ Study of 56m-year-old leaves counters claims from Trump administration members of ‘benefits’ of fossil fuel pollution Oliver Milman Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Adding huge quantities of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere is set to cause the Earth’s forests to wither and die rather than flourish, according to a new study that counters erroneous claims that fossil fuel pollution will green the planet. An analysis of fossilized leaf cells from a period known as the Paleocene-Eocene Thermal Maximum (or PETM), which occurred about 56 million years ago, has helped reconstruct how the world’s forests responded when planet-heating gases were previously being released at a rapid rate. The current galloping pace of carbon emissions from the burning of fossil fuels is unmatched in historic and prehistoric records but the PETM, when huge amounts of carbon were released over a 130,000-year period and the world heated up by as much as 8C (14F), is the closest comparison. The authors of the new paper found this prehistoric change caused a retreat in the forests that blanketed the Paleocene-Eocene world, causing them to die off as the Earth browned rather than greened, a finding they state has “chilling implications” for today’s world. View image in fullscreen Fragments of fossilized leaves like these helped the authors recreate the forest canopies of 56m years ago. Photograph: Dr. Regan Dunn “What we see is that as the carbon dioxide ramped up, the forests became very dense but then subsequently collapsed, opening up dramatically,” said Regan Dunn, a researcher at La Brea Tar Pits and the Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, who led the study. “Around 60% of the biomass of the standing vegetation was gone, it was a huge loss. This should be a concern because the rate of carbon release has never been higher than now.” Dun added: “Forests are some of our best friends and allies but we are already seeing them die back, be cut down and consumed by wildfires. It’s happening quickly, every summer the change seems faster and faster.” Trees may store less planet-heating carbon than hoped, study suggests Read more Plants like trees require carbon to build their structures and, along with water and sunlight, provide food. Once the world started to burn coal, oil and gas in huge volumes from the industrial revolution onwards, the amount of emitted carbon dioxide surged at an unprecedented rate, with atmospheric concentrations of CO 2 rising by more than 50% in little over a century. This increase in carbon did initially help boost some plant life, a change that has been seized upon by those who question the facts of climate science. Prominent figures in Donald Trump’s administration have argued that burning fossil fuels is good for the environment. “CO 2 was never a pollutant,” Doug Burgum, the interior secretary, told Fox Business earlier this year as the federal government moved to erase its own power to address the climate crisis. “When we breathe, we emit CO 2 . Plants need CO 2 to survive and grow. They thrive with more CO 2 .” On the same TV network last year, Chris Wright, Trump’s energy secretary, said that there were “pluses” to global heating as well as negatives. “A warmer planet with more CO 2 is better for growing plants,” Wright claimed. View image in fullscreen The authors compared the cuticle structure of modern leaves (pictured above under epifluorescence microscopy) with fossil leaf cuticles to create a model for canopy cover. Scale bar is 50 microns (0.05 mm). Photograph: Dr. Regan Dunn Experts have previously rejected such claims as false, with the new research paper, published in Science, showing that the Earth’s past experience demonstrates that trees require much more than CO 2 to thrive. Extra carbon dioxide traps more heat, causing trees to struggle amid extreme temperatures and a lack of key nutrients. Hotter conditions can also trigger outbreaks of pests and disease, weakening trees further, and dry out vegetation that then explodes into huge wildfires, such as those that have engulfed much of Canada and western Europe this summer. The switch from greening forests to browning forests occurred around 2000, the new paper states, when the impacts of drought and heat stress overtook the benefits of extra CO 2 . Since then, evidence has piled up of escalating global tree mortality, including trees in the tropics dying of dehydration. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion “Once the climate becomes too warm plants aren’t able to handle it, it affects their physiology and their relationship with water,” said Dunn. “Once they can’t survive because the CO 2 and temperatures are too high, that’s when you see forests die back.” There was “quite a lot of tree mortality” now occurring in Europe, North America and the Amazon, Dunn said, requiring swift cuts to carbon emissions to ensure that the world doesn’t barrel down the same path as it did 56m years ago. “There is still time to prevent the worst outcomes and best thing we can do is keep fossil fuels in the ground,” she said. “It’s important for people to understand that once we pass thresholds it takes a long time to recover from them. The 130,000 years of the PETM change on human timescales is basically forever.” Dunn and her colleagues ascertained the extent of ancient forests by analyzing fossilized cells of leaves called leaf cuticle fragments. This enabled them to ascertain the density of the forest canopy during the PETM, allowing them to calculate the advance and retreat of forests over time. View image in fullscreen The field crew excavating a trench through PETM strata in the Hanna Basin, Wyoming. Photograph: Marieke Dechesne, USGS In that past era, forests covered a much larger extent of the world than now, with no ice at the poles and much higher seas than today. But while the PETM changes occurred over many thousands of years via carbon released by the natural forces of volcanic activity, current climate change is much faster and caused by our deliberate combustion of fossil fuels. The paper is a “genuine advance” and provides a record over tens of thousands of years that shows the knock-on impacts of thinning forests, according to Trevor Keenan, a scientist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the new research. “The headline is that warming won,” Keenan said. “Carbon dioxide rose sharply, and any benefit that gave the forests was not enough to stop canopies from opening up and staying open for tens of thousands of years.” This is worrying because the pace of change today, he added. “The ancient carbon release happened over thousands of years, ours is happening over decades,” he said. “Faster forcing gives ecosystems less room to adjust. “Second, those forests faced climate change alone. Today’s forests are dealing with the same warming while also being fragmented, logged, converted to agriculture and exposed to altered fire regimes. If forests thinned under the slower and cleaner version of this experiment, that is not a reassuring precedent.” Explore more on these topics US news Climate crisis Trees and forests Greenhouse gas emissions news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: Sarah Young/Reuters BAE Systems BAE Systems to pay $36m penalty after 104 violations of US arms export rules State department says it has reached administrative settlement with company’s US arm to resolve breaches Graeme Wearden Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.35 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 14.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The UK defence company BAE Systems is to pay a $36m (£26.7m) civil penalty after breaching US arms exports regulations more than 100 times. The US Department of State announced on Thursday that it had reached an administrative settlement with the US arm of BAE to resolve 104 violations of the Arms Export Control Act and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations. The breaches included the unauthorised exports of technical data to multiple countries, including China, and violations of directorate of defense trade controls authorisations involving various countries. BAE voluntarily disclosed all but one of the alleged violations, which helped it avoid a higher penalty. It also persuaded the state department to suspend half of the penalty, on the condition that the $18m was used to strengthen BAE’s compliance programme. BAE Systems said it remained committed to ensuring full compliance with all applicable export control laws, and had “thoroughly cooperated” with the state department’s review. “We have been working diligently to implement improvements to our BAE Systems Inc compliance programme over the last several years, and we will continue to do so. We take seriously our responsibility to protect critical information and support all our customers’ security,” the company added. The state department said the settlement highlighted “the importance of exporting defence articles pursuant only to appropriate authorisation from the department”. BAE was accused of sending technical data related to printed wiring boards for use in global positioning system (GPS) to a manufacturer in China in December 2023. According to the state department, the company “recognised its supply chain team did not fully understand the export control and compliance regulations” and that its secure file transfer networks did not highlight export control warnings before the data was sent. The company also sent data related to printed wiring boards for use with military GPS to Canada in September 2021, after a licence agreement had expired, and the technical specification of an “explosive mixture” to the UK. In another breach, technical data related to a US navy guided-missile destroyer were sent to Germany. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Business Today Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning after newsletter promotion A BAE subcontractor also “furnished defence services without authorisation” on more than 17 separate occasions in Italy and France, and also in Indonesia, according to the state department. The company also accidentally exported without authorization a control system for a military gas-turbine engine to Switzerland. https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: A theatre in Mariupol, Ukraine, destroyed by Russian bombing, 25 April 2022. Photograph: Alexander Ermochenko/Reuters View image in fullscreen A theatre in Mariupol, Ukraine, destroyed by Russian bombing, 25 April 2022. Photograph: Alexander Ermochenko/Reuters Opinion Heritage Ukrainian cathedrals, Gaza’s archives, Iranian squares – modern war is systematically erasing human history Simon Jenkins It is not enough now for war to kill, it must eradicate a people’s cherished and precious heritage too Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.04 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 12.13 EDT Share W ars may not take summer holidays, but they do sometimes see exhaustion. As drones race back and forth across Ukraine and the strait of Hormuz, a grim stalemate seems to have invaded the earth beneath. Aerial bombardment knows limited resistance and even less victory or defeat. Ukraine, Russia, Israel, Iran and their allies seem able to defy diplomacy and drop bombs on each other for ever. At which point the outside world can merely count some of the costs. Vladimir Putin’s known desire to eliminate Ukraine’s historical identity has led to its cultural devastation. Two weeks ago Unesco reported the destruction or dereliction of 545 of its historic buildings, including 156 religious sites and 43 museums. The attempted eradication of what Putin himself claims to be an intrinsic part of Russia’s own history is sickening. Russia’s bombing of Kyiv’s Pechersk Lavra complex and the Dormition cathedral , coupled with shattering the magnificent St Sophia cathedral, are comparable to Ukraine bombing the Kremlin. So, too, is the attack on a cathedral and a museum in Odesa, and the destruction of a theatre in Mariupol. These are defining monuments of Ukraine’s past. Yet their dereliction has received little publicity in the west. Meanwhile in Iran the beautiful city of Isfahan might surely have been spared Donald Trump’s egotistic bomb-fest. Not so. A Reuters survey in June found the historic Naqsh-e Jahan Square, the Jameh mosque and the governor’s palace partially destroyed. In Tehran, the Persian royal palace of Golestan has been badly damaged . Unesco reports of an attack on an 1,800-year-old fortress that embraced a prehistoric settlement reputedly 63,000 years old. The most savage consequence of the collapse of order in the Middle East is the reported damage or destruction of over 80% of the buildings in Gaza. The ancient city of Gaza itself is now largely rubble. Bombed by Israel are the medieval Great Omari mosque and the church of St Porphyrius, dating from the fifth century and one of Christianity’s most ancient sites. Gaza’s archives have been destroyed. The Omari mosque’s library and the adjacent cultural centre, whose thousands of ancient documents had survived the Crusades, have reportedly been lost . The Al Qarara museum was bombed from the air and then bulldozed to the ground. A people’s entire past has been deliberately eradicated. As for Israel’s war on Lebanon, it culminated in June in what appeared to be the gratuitous bombing of the ancient port of Tyre . This included an attack on the site of the Roman hippodrome. The 1,000-year-old fortress of Beaufort was also damaged. The past is clearly without privilege. Aerial wars are unlike ground ones. Soldiers with guns have targets. So, we are constantly told, do modern missiles, but that does not explain the US bombing of an Iranian girls’ school in February. The reality is that bombers are casual because they are near invulnerable, while their victims appear small and anonymous. Bombers do not conquer territory or secure surrender. They are manifestations of leadership machismo. In the allied invasion of Italy in 1943-45, individual British and American officers were known to take steps to protect its monuments from destruction. As a result Italy’s ancient cities survived to a degree that Germany’s did not. In the aftermath, sincere efforts were made to evolve rules of war, including respect for cultural and historic monuments. War was still seen as a contest of professionals, not of cultures. The result was The Hague Convention of 1954 and the Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in 1972 . But recent years, in which we’ve seen a collapse of global governance, have left The Hague convention a paper tiger, like that other supposed discipline, the UN’s International Court of Justice. Victory today appears to lie in destroying an enemy’s identity and morale as much as in killing its people. When the Islamic State ruined much of the Iraqi city of Mosul in 2014 , it set about eliminating all traces of its past. Trump’s threat to Iran, that “a whole civilisation will die tonight”, showed an equally primitive approach to conflict. It hardly warned his bombers to spare the mosques of Isfahan. Of international bodies, Unesco is active in keeping a record of the fate of cultural heritage worldwide, but a record is just a record. Its listing of Russia’s and Israel’s devastation of their hated foes is like watching a historic tragedy unfold in real time. We might almost prefer it to happen behind our backs. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion One thing the outside world can do is help those seeking to help themselves. Thus the World Monuments Fund’s Crisis Response Program is invaluable. It sends aid, advice and materials to war zones, almost before the bombs have stopped falling. It was present in Mosul and its Ukraine Response Fund has many projects (26 of which are completed) helping to protect and stabilise bombed buildings, one day perhaps to restore them. As the west continues to meddle in foreign wars, perhaps this is the least that some of us can do. One of humanity’s deepest obligations is to its past. That past knows no national boundaries. Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: The blast outside Sigfrido Ranucci’s home near Rome in October last year almost destroyed his car and another owned by his daughter. Photograph: Cecilia Fabiano/AP View image in fullscreen The blast outside Sigfrido Ranucci’s home near Rome in October last year almost destroyed his car and another owned by his daughter. Photograph: Cecilia Fabiano/AP Italy Italian businessman admits organising bomb attack ‘to boost friend’s security’ Valter Lavitola has confessed to masterminding bombing at home of investigative reporter Sigfrido Ranucci Angela Giuffrida in Rome Thu 13 Aug 2026 09.26 EDT Last modified on Thu 13 Aug 2026 13.16 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An Italian businessman has admitted to masterminding a bomb attack at the home of Sigfrido Ranucci, a prominent investigative journalist, claiming it was intended to boost his security protection. Valter Lavitola, who was friends with Ranucci, the host of Report, an investigative programme aired by the state broadcaster, Rai, made the confession to investigators after his arrest earlier this week in connection with the case, the businessman’s lawyer, Sergio Cola, told the Italian media . It was originally thought that the mafia had been behind the attack in October last year when a rudimentary but powerful bomb was detonated outside Ranucci’s home in a town near Rome, almost destroying his car and another owned by his daughter. Four other people allegedly commissioned by Lavitola were arrested in late June on suspicion of carrying out the attack. Cola said Lavitola had orchestrated the attack in order to boost Ranucci’s security detail amid threats to his life from the mafia. “He did it for Ranucci’s good, because he was a target of attacks,” he said. View image in fullscreen Sigfrido Ranucci. Photograph: Cecilia Fabiano/LaPresse/Shutterstock Lativola denied allegations that the motive had been to enhance Ranucci’s popularity with the aim of him entering politics, something Lativola allegedly hoped to benefit from too. The allegations were outlined in an investigative report, seen by the Guardian, which included telephone conservations including one allegedly from Lavitola telling Ranucci “you will be prime minister in two years”. There has been no suggestion from investigators that Ranucci, who previously expressed shock over Lavitola’s alleged involvement, was aware of the plot. Ranucci, whose investigations for Report focus on alleged crime and corruption, often involving government ministers, is suing unnamed commentators and politicians who accused him of staging the attack for his own benefit for defamation. His lawyer, Roberto De Vita, said that if the allegations of Lavitola’s motive were correct then Ranucci was “a victim three times over”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion “He is a victim of a serious, dangerous attack, of betrayal, of being exploited by a friend in a delirious show of madness and, last but not least – and perhaps most seriously – of a massive and persistent campaign of media and political lynching that, through conjecture and insinuations, has sought to portray the victim as the more-or-less-willing beneficiary of the attack.” The case has unfolded amid a broader debate about press freedom in Italy and journalists’ safety. Ranucci has been outspoken about the alleged interference in Rai by Giorgia Meloni’s far-right government. The broadcaster opened an internal audit into his journalistic methods after it emerged in early July that Lavitola was being interrogated in connection with the bomb attack. The deputy prime minister, Matteo Salvini, has called for him to be suspended. There have been questions over Ranucci’s relationship with Lavitola, a former journalist who owns a restaurant in Rome. They became friends in 2019 after Ranucci conducted an investigation into Lavitola, who has been embroiled in several legal proceedings in the past, including one resulting in a conviction for extorting the late former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi. Ranucci told Corriere della Sella in early July that he had “never hidden” the friendship, describing it as perhaps a case of “Stockholm syndrome”.
