https://www.eng.kavkaz-uzel.eu/articles/.text: Homepage / All news 14:09, 31 July 2026 Tightening legislation in Europe has created the risk of deportation for hundreds of Chechens. The decision to deport Muslim Alkhazov to Russia has been appealed, but he remains at risk, like hundreds of other refugees from Chechnya, due to tightening immigration laws in Europe, human rights activists said. Unfair denials of asylum to Chechens in Europe have increased due to the fact that decisions on the refugees' fate are made by security services, without regard for the risks of returning to Chechnya, diaspora representatives emphasized. As reported by the " Caucasian Knot ," in July, Chechen diaspora activists held pickets outside German embassies in the capitals of Austria, the Czech Republic, and Finland in support of Chechen refugee Muslim Alkhazov, who faces deportation from Germany to Russia. Authorities in European countries periodically deport refugees from the North Caucasus seeking asylum to Russia. Thus, on March 23, it became known that a Chechen national seeking protection in Estonia did not receive adequate legal assistance and was deported to Russia. Alkhazov's defense appealed the deportation decision Human rights activist Roza Dunaeva told a "Caucasian Knot" correspondent that the decision to deport Muslim Alkhazov has been appealed. "There is no deportation yet. We have appealed and are awaiting the decision," she said. According to her, Alkhazov's family miraculously survived torture and brutal persecution. "Both the husband and wife were tortured, and their relatives were killed in 2022. Today, we are deeply concerned about the fate of Muslim Alkhazov, especially given the lack of trust in the decisions Germany makes even in such obvious cases," she said. Europe is tightening immigration laws The deportation of Chechen native Muslim Alkhazov from Germany could become part of a broader trend of expelling Chechen refugees from European countries, Svetlana Gannushkina, chair of the Civic Assistance Committee*, told a Caucasian Knot correspondent. "I know of dozens of such cases. Over the past few years, I have written about 1,500 expert opinions, studying the situation in each specific case with the support of colleagues. For some applicants, multiple certificates had to be prepared to prevent deportation. These assessments often, but unfortunately, don't always help protect people," Gannushkina said. Deportation decisions are made by migration authorities, which, based on official information from their ministries of internal affairs, often conclude that there is supposedly no longer a danger for Chechens in Russia. The human rights activist cited the formalistic approach of European migration services to risk assessment as the main reason for deportation decisions. "Deportation decisions are made by migration authorities, which, based on official information from their ministries of internal affairs, often conclude that there is supposedly no longer a danger for Chechens in Russia." "Or they acknowledge the general risk but claim there is no personal threat to a specific applicant," she explained. Svetlana Gannushkina* also expressed serious concern about the adoption of the new EU Pact on Migration and Asylum. "I see a major danger in the recently adopted EU Pact on the return of asylum seekers. This document must be implemented into the national legislation of the participating countries now." In this regard, we should expect a new large wave of deportations,” she emphasized. 19:18 23.05.2026 Analysts have confirmed the continuation of the campaign to force people to sign contracts in Chechnya Those detained for minor offenses in Chechnya are being forced to sign contracts with the Ministry of Defense. Relatives prefer to remain silent about this in order to use connections or ransom to bring the young men home, human rights activists said. Responding to a question about the risks for Chechens being returned to Russia, the human rights activist noted that the threat to their safety not only remains, but is increasing. "Of course, the danger remains." "Today, the situation is further aggravated by the fact that Ramzan Kadyrov is actively recruiting troops for military action in Ukraine [at the expense of residents of the republic]," Gannushkina* concluded. Europe believes there are no risks for refugees in Chechnya Mayrbek Taramov, a representative of the Chechen diaspora in Europe and a member of the Council of Elders of Chechens in European Countries, is confident that Europe, by deporting and extraditing Chechens to Russia, is undermining itself, since in the event of danger, including from Russia, Chechens living in European countries will rise to their defense. "This is a centuries-old tradition, genetically ingrained in Chechens by their distant ancestors, and it is precisely these people who will go to their deaths to avoid disgrace." "Personally, even though I'm an old man, I'm ready, in case of danger, to stand up for my second homeland—beautiful Sweden, which welcomed me and my relatives during a difficult period in my life," he told a "Caucasian Knot" correspondent. In his opinion, pressure must be exerted through the mass media and the European public. “As a journalist and human rights activist with 30 years of experience, I warn the migration authorities of European countries that violate international conventions that mass rallies and marches against deportation arbitrariness will be organized in their capitals, and materials exposing migration officials will be published in the mass media of these countries,” he noted. Blogger Tumso Abdurakhmanov* also notes that unfair denials of asylum to Chechens in Europe have increased. “As for the deportations of Chechens to Russia, unfortunately, we very often encounter unfair denials of asylum in EU countries, and with the coming to power of right-wing radical parties in many European countries, this trend is only intensifying,” he told a “Caucasian Knot” correspondent. According to him, deportation decisions are not made by the migration authorities. "Increasingly, decisions on granting asylum to a genuinely persecuted Chechen are made not by the migration authorities of EU countries in accordance with the criteria of the Refugee Convention, but by the secret services of these countries according to completely different criteria that in no way take into account the threat to a person's life in the event of his return to Russia," he noted. They rely on outdated reports from their Ministry of Internal Affairs and claim that everything has returned to normal in Chechnya, or assert that a native of the republic is not in personal danger. A representative of the Chechen diaspora in Europe, Roza Magomedova , notes that there are dozens of confirmed cases of deportation of Chechens in recent times. "But the real number of those deported and at risk of deportation "It could be hundreds. We in the diaspora constantly document such stories and try to help people gather evidence before it's too late. The main reason is bureaucratic red tape and the formalism of European migration services. They rely on outdated reports from their Interior Ministry and claim that everything has returned to normal in Chechnya, or they assert that a native of the republic is not in personal danger," she told a "Caucasian Knot" correspondent. She is certain that all deportees are at risk of harm. "The threat isn't just real; it's deadly. In Chechnya, a person can expect basements, torture, and fabricated criminal cases. "And today, the risks have increased exponentially," she noted. https://hungarytoday.hu/meeting-of-liber.text: Meeting of Liberal Minds: a “Delighted” Markus Söder Embraces New Relations with Péter Magyar After an eight-year diplomatic hiatus, Bavaria and Hungary have resumed their political relations at the highest level. Bavarian Minister-President Markus Söder personally traveled to Budapest on a working visit to agree with the new Hungarian Prime Minister, Péter Magyar, on a strategic realignment and the establishment of a joint intergovernmental commission. After nearly a decade of muted relations with Viktor Orbán’s national-conservative government, the Free State of Bavaria and Hungary’s new EU-aligned government are reviving their formally close ties. At the invitation of Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar, CSU leader Markus Söder traveled to the Hungarian capital, reported Index . At a joint press conference following the negotiations, both heads of government gave a positive assessment of the talks. Markus Söder emphasized the deep, historically rooted relations between the two countries. The leader of the formerly Christian centrist party celebrated “Hungary’s return to the heart of Europe” and expressed his delight at the election victory of Péter Magyar and the TISZA Party. Both parties—the CSU and the TISZA Party—are members of the European People’s Party (EPP), from which the former Hungarian ruling party, FIDESZ, had once withdrawn. Welcome back, #Ungarn ! Die Rückkehr Ungarns in die Mitte Europas und zu unseren gemeinsamen Beziehungen freut uns sehr. Bayern und Ungarn sind traditionell Freunde und Partner – umso mehr hat die Eiszeit der vergangenen Jahre geschmerzt. Jetzt nehmen wir den Kontakt wieder auf… pic.twitter.com/gkkzr1947r — Markus Söder (@Markus_Soeder) July 30, 2026 During the term of the previous government under Viktor Orbán, Hungary and Bavaria grew apart, leading Markus Söder to skip Hungary during his visits in 2019 and to sharply criticize the Hungarian head of government at the time. The strained relationship also meant that the Bavarian Minister-President never once invited Viktor Orbán to his party’s conferences. A central topic of the discussions was Hungary’s domestic political developments. According to Markus Söder, all of Europe is watching closely to see how the country is now taking concrete steps back toward what he defines as “the rule of law.” In addition to political rapprochement, the focus was on the economy. Bavaria is Hungary’s most important economic partner, accounting for 30 percent of all German investments. To put this relationship on a new footing, a new joint government commission will be established. In addition, cooperation between Hungarian and Bavarian universities is to be expanded in order to gain a technological edge in global competition. It was an honour to welcome the Minister-President of Bavaria back to Hungary after a ten-year absence. Together with @Markus_Soeder , we had an extremely productive and forward-looking discussion on future development and investment opportunities for Bavarian companies —… pic.twitter.com/4RuC0Jwu7F — Magyar Péter (Ne féljetek) (@magyarpeterMP) July 30, 2026 The two politicians agreed that, in addition to the traditional automotive industry, sectors such as cutting-edge technology, artificial intelligence, pharmaceutical research, innovation, and the defense industry must be prioritized in the future. At the same time, both heads of government took a clear stance in the European debate on mobility. The phase-out of internal combustion engines currently under discussion in Brussels must be reconsidered; the common goal is to “save the internal combustion engine.” European budget policy, the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP), and cohesion funds were also debated. To his guests’ surprise, Péter Magyar did not hold back in his criticism of Brussels’ economic policy failures. Given the complex situation facing the European Union, “more than ever, we need voices of reason as well as moderate and well-founded arguments,” said the Hungarian Prime Minister. “We are good Europeans; we trust in Europe, which is why strengthening competitiveness is important,” added Markus Söder. However, he noted, this also requires the united support of the other member states. The Hungarian head of government subsequently posted an optimistic summary on his social media page: “ It was an honor to welcome the Minister-President of Bavaria back to Hungary after a ten-year absence,” the post reads. Péter Magyar highlighted the enormous importance of major Bavarian corporations such as BMW, Audi, Siemens, and Knorr-Bremse, which together employ 57,000 Hungarians. It is rare to hold talks with a Western European leader with whom we agree on almost everything — from economic development and EU policy to the importance of high-tech industries, artificial intelligence, and research and development ,” said the Hungarian prime minister. The partnership is designed for the long term. The next bilateral meeting is scheduled for 2027. Péter Magyar also extended an invitation to Markus Söder to attend the 70th anniversary of the Hungarian Revolution and the 1956 struggle for freedom, and in turn accepted his Bavarian counterpart’s invitation for a return visit to Munich. Traditionally strong ties between the Christian Social Union of Bavaria and FIDESZ have soured following the 2015 migrant invasion, when Viktor Orbán had tried to persuade the then leader of CSU, Horst Seehofer, to resist Angela Merkel’s open-door policies. After initial hesitation and ambiguity though the leading Bavarian party had adopted its larger coalition partner, the CDU’s migration policies, severing ties with Viktor Orbán’s government. Today both parties are on the defensive to the anti-migration and euro-skeptic Alternative for Germany (AfD), a party that is dominating polls especially in East Germany. https://hungarytoday.hu/colombian-commun.text: Colombian Community Fights to Save Its Embassy in Budapest Diplomatic relations between Colombia and Hungary are facing a critical test. Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella, who will take office on August 7, has announced far-reaching austerity and restructuring measures in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs that will also have a direct impact on Central Europe. The Colombian Embassy in Budapest is set to close after eight years of continuous presence. Civil society is now mobilizing in opposition to this move. A total of 14 countries worldwide—including three on the European continent—are affected by the cuts imposed by the South American oil power, which has a population of 50 million. According to the plans, Colombia will withdraw completely from Hungary, as well as from Romania and the Czech Republic. The newly elected president provided a broad range of justifications for this far-reaching change, which vary depending on the region. While he offered ideological grounds for the withdrawal from Latin America—emphasizing that the Colombian government does not maintain diplomatic relations with “tyrannies” such as Cuba and Nicaragua—in Europe, purely fiscal arguments take center stage. Abelardo de la Espriella justified the closure of the embassy in Budapest with the need for greater frugality in the use of public funds. “We cannot maintain such a costly structure that does not yield tangible results for the country,” the president stated on his social media page. Colombia needs a diplomatic approach that is modern and efficient and serves national interests, rather than “political favoritism and bureaucracy.” Abelardo de la Espriella. Photo: Wikipedia The measures are part of an “optimization process.” However, this does not constitute a complete break in diplomatic relations with the affected countries. The protection of Colombian citizens will be guaranteed in the future through a system of co-accreditation by other embassies in the region, the politician added. In Budapest, the news has caused considerable consternation. As Világgazdaság reports, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, led by Anita Orbán, was completely taken by surprise by the plans. The Hungarian ministry confirmed to the news portal that it had received no prior indication from Bogotá and had only learned of the move through the press. According to the news portal, the Hungarian TISZA government has no immediate plans to close its own embassy in Bogotá in retaliation. Nevertheless, bilateral relations have suffered a serious blow. Hungary established official diplomatic relations with Colombia in 1973. After the Hungarian mission was reopened in 2017 by Péter Szijjártó, then foreign minister from FIDESZ, the Colombian embassy in Budapest followed suit in 2018—an era that is now coming to an abrupt end. An exact date for the closure has not yet been officially set. Protests are now mounting against the plans. The Colombian community in Hungary and Central Europe/the Balkans announced in a statement that it has launched a citizen-led initiative, which will be officially presented on August 6. In a petition that has already been signed by more than 300 verified citizens of the region, President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella is urged to reconsider the decision. The signatories emphasize that the embassy and its attached consular section in Budapest provide indispensable services to residents, students, researchers, and families. The official consular district extends far beyond Hungary and also includes Serbia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, North Macedonia, and Montenegro. Although only about 250 Colombians are officially registered in Hungary, the mission serves an estimated 600 to 1,200 Colombian nationals throughout Central Europe and the Western Balkans. Particular emphasis is placed on the embassy’s role for academics, for example through the Stipendium Hungaricum program, one of the most important educational partnerships between the two countries. In addition to everyday, essential services such as passport renewals, notarial matters, and document legalizations, the mission played a key role in providing emergency assistance, especially during the COVID-19 pandemic. Based on the statement, closing the mission in Budapest would force citizens to travel to distant embassies in other European countries for simple administrative procedures which would result in significant financial, logistical, and administrative burdens for those affected. The initiative, which continues to gather online support and physical signature lists, calls on the Colombian government to explore alternative cost-saving measures in order to protect the partnerships in culture and education that have been built up over more than five decades. The embassy in Budapest must not be abandoned, as it serves as an indispensable strategic bridge between Colombia and Central Europe. He was received by the Head of State, Nicuşor Dan, who reaffirmed Romania’s firm and consistent support for the country’s integration into the European Union. The President also welcomed the opening of the first rounds of negotiations on Moldova’s accession to the EU. “We have reaffirmed the privileged nature of the relationship between Romania and the Republic of Moldova and our commitment to continuing the development of joint projects, particularly in the economic, energy and transport sectors. These projects contribute to strengthening the resilience and prosperity of both countries and the entire region,’ Nicușor Dan added. The two officials welcomed the recent signing of the agreement for the construction of the new bridge at Ungheni, which will form part of the future link to the A8 motorway, as well as the contract for work on Section 4 of the latter. Furthermore, Nicușor Dan emphasised the support that Bucharest was providing to Chișinău with regard to strengthening resilience and security. In this context, a key focus of the discussions was the complex security situation in the region, caused by Russia’s war of aggression against Ukraine and its consequences for neighbouring states. Prime Minister Vasile Tofan expressed his gratitude for the constant and unconditional support provided by Romania. “I must say from the outset that I am coming home, I am Romanian, and I fully intend to contribute to strengthening this strategic – but, first and foremost, fraternal – relationship between our countries,” the official from Chișinău added. He was also received by the acting Romanian Prime Minister, Ilie Bolojan, who, for his part, stated that Romania would remain Chișinău’s main supporter in the process of accession to the European Union, offering the experience it had gained as a Member State and its political and diplomatic support. During the meeting, the two officials reviewed the progress of joint projects and ways of accelerating them, with a focus on those in the transport and energy sectors, which are intended to help ensure better interconnection between the two banks of the Prut. They discussed the construction of two new 400-kilovolt interconnection lines, Suceava–Bălți and Gutinaș–Strășeni, and, in the field of infrastructure, port and rail interconnection projects. The Moldovan official stated that he did not want economic relations to be limited solely to trade and exports. “We want more Romanian investment in the Republic of Moldova, companies that produce together, shared value chains, and industrial, technological and energy projects,” Vasile Tofan emphasised. The President of the Senate, Mircea Abrudean, stated after his meeting with the Prime Minister of the Republic of Moldova that the two countries enjoy a solid and consistent partnership, particularly in key areas of development for both nations – energy, infrastructure and digitalisation. Vasile Tofan also met with the Speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, Sorin Grindeanu, with whom he discussed the harmonisation of the Republic of Moldova’s legislation with European Union regulations. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/nato-forc.text: Lauran O'Toole Updated Fri, 31 July 2026 at 1:41 pm UTC 0 Poland scrambled two on-duty F-16 fighter jets (Image: Getty) A NATO member has again been forced to scramble fighter jets to intercept a Russian aircraft over the Baltic Sea as fears over World World 3 skyrocket. A pair of F-16s intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft some 40 kilometers (24 miles) north of Koobrzeg. Polish Defense Minister Wadysaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the aircraft was flying in international airspace without a flight plan and with its transponder turned off. He added that there was no violation of their airspace and the country will continue to "monitor the situation" and "firmly respond to the actions of the Russian Federation". A pair of F-16s intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft (Image: Getty) He wrote on X: "Another Successful Interception of a Russian Aircraft over the Baltic Sea. "This morning, a pair of our on-duty F-16s, 40 kilometers north of Koobrzeg, intercepted a Russian Il-20 reconnaissance aircraft. "Once again, the aircraft was flying in international airspace without a flight plan and with its transponder turned off. There was no violation of our airspace. "The Polish Armed Forces continuously monitor the situation and firmly respond to the actions of the Russian Federation, while maintaining close cooperation with NATO allies. The security of Polish airspace remains our top priority." Poland said they will 'firrmly respond to the actions of the Russian Federation' (Image: Getty) Earlier this week, NATO once again scrambled fighter jets over Poland after a cruise missile flew into Polish airspace and fell during a large-scale Russian strike on Ukraine. Footage showed smoke rising from the Lublin region, where a crater was reported after air raid sirens had sounded. Air raid systems sounded in the eastern Polish city of Lublin, where a crater was reported, and air defense systems were put on alert. Speaking about the missile incursion, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said Poland "was ready to shoot down the missile if it continued its flight". He said that "everything indicates that it was a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile". https://www.digitalspy.com/tv/a73317116/.text: Jared Leto promised on stage to sign women’s breasts at a 30 Seconds to Mars aftershow party the first time I saw him perform in London in 2009. At the time the comment was innocuous. That’s just what rock stars say.But now it feels all the more chilling after one of the women who came forward in BBC documentary Jared Leto: Hollywood’s Dark Secret insisted that when she was 14, he instructed a security guard to take her backstage at a music festival after having made a lewd comment about her chest during an autograph-signing. The girl's mother confronted Leto, but he repeated the comment, it is alleged.The woman is one of 10 who have come forward with allegations of sexual assault, grooming and statutory rape all taking place between 2002 and 2016, when he was in his 30s and 40s. He is now 54. Leto vehemently denies all the allegations. Hours after the documentary was released, a spokesperson for Leto issued a statement on his behalf, saying: "I have never sexually assaulted anyone in my entire life. These claims are absolutely and categorically false."I met Leto in the middle of that time, six months after I’d watched him perform on stage with his band at Koko, London.At the time he was marketed as a sex symbol who couldn’t get enough female attention. Women were literally throwing their knickers at him.But now as revelations emerge, I can reveal that what he was marketed as may have fuelled his alleged predatory behaviour and that Leto was actually a man wracked by low self esteem, overwhelm and stress.Six months after that gig at Koko, London in November 2009, I flew to Sziget Festival in Budapest in August 2010 where Leto’s band was also on the bill.I was working for the Daily Star’s music column Playlist at the time and had an interview with Mika lined up. But when Mika and I were talking backstage, Leto emerged stressed and frantic following his headline slot at the festival.After performing to thousands of fans, the then-38-year-old unleashed his performance anxieties, saying: "I'm not sure how good that performance was. I don't know if I sang enough – I should have sung more and danced less."His eyes were frantic. I had never seen a pop star so worried about their image.Mika and I tried to appease him. But Leto seemed on the verge of tears reflecting on his crippling jet lag and late nights.He said: "I feel so tired all the time, it's really exhausting and never ending."Leto’s insecurities felt like such a different persona from the confident, sex symbol one the public were being sold. He wasn’t sexy. He seemed desperate to be liked and loved.With so many women speaking out against him, I now fear that these insecurities mixed with an over-the-top sex symbol status he needed to maintain seeped its way into his alleged despicable treatment of women and that perhaps – like so often does with predatory, toxic men – these women became victims as his life spiralled out of control.Jared Leto: Hollywood's Dark Secret is streaming on BBC iPlayer.If you've been affected by the issues raised in this story, you can access more information from Rape Crisis England and Wales, which works towards the elimination of all forms of sexual violence and sexual misconduct, on its website or by calling the National Rape Crisis Helpline on 0808 802 9999. Rape Crisis Scotland's helpline number is 08088 01 03 02.Readers in the US are encouraged to contact RAINN, or the National Sexual Assault Hotline on 800-656-4673.

https://www.dealstreetasia.com/stories/s.text: SoftBank, PayPay, SMFG unit to invest $620m each in Seven & i The logo of Seven & i Holdings Co. is pictured at the company headquarters in Tokyo, Japan March 6, 2025. REUTERS/Issei Kato 31 July, 2026 Japan’s Seven & i Holdings has formed a strategic partnership with SoftBank Corp, PayPay and Sumitomo Mitsui Card, which will each invest 100 billion yen ($620 million) into the 7-Eleven operator, a filing showed on Friday. The total 300 billion yen investment comes after the 7-Eleven operator has struggled to turn around its business, having batted away a takeover attempt by Canadian convenience store rival Alimentation Couche-Tard last year. While Seven & i has carved out and sold off its less profitable business lines to focus on its core convenience stores, stiff competition in Japan and lacklustre results in North America have weighed on its profits. Each of Softbank, PayPay and Sumitomo Mitsui Card, the credit card arm of Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group, will acquire a 2.27% stake in Seven & i, the filing showed. Also on Friday, Seven & i announced a 400 billion yen share buyback, worth over 9% of its outstanding shares. Deal to bolster domestic business LY Corp, a SoftBank subsidiary that runs the Line messaging app along with a host of online businesses, also signed the strategic partnership, a release from the companies said. They aim to integrate their customer information and create a loyalty points ecosystem across Seven & i’s physical stores and the other companies’ online and financial customer bases, the filing said. The deal will bolster Seven & i’s higher-margin domestic business, but prospects for its larger international operations remain uncertain. Last week Seven & i aborted a potential stake purchase in Polish convenience store operator Zabka that would have expanded its presence in Europe beyond its strongholds in Japan and the U.S. It has failed to translate its $21 billion purchase of Speedway petrol stations in the U.S. into higher profitability, which has added to longstanding pressure from shareholders for higher returns. Since Couche-Tard pulled its 2,600 yen per share buyout offer in July last year, Seven & i’s shares have stagnated. They closed at 2,109 yen on Friday. https://english.radio.cz/hundreds-police.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Hundreds of police officers and a helicopter to monitor Prague Pride march Facebook Twitter Police will step up security at all accompanying events of the Prague Pride festival, which begins in Prague on Monday. Several hundred police officers will be deployed for the Pride march, which will culminate the festival the following Saturday. They will secure the entire route from Wenceslas Square to Střelecký Island, while a police helicopter will monitor the area from the air. Traffic in the city centre will be restricted on the day of the march. According to police spokesperson Eva Kropáčová, the security measures were adopted in light of recent risk assessments, including the recent attack on a similar event in Berlin. https://english.radio.cz/outgoing-ambass.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Outgoing ambassador to Egypt Jukl to head Czech Centres, Macinka announces Facebook Twitter Outgoing Czech Ambassador to Egypt Ivan Jukl will become Director General of the Czech Centres from August, Foreign Minister Petr Macinka (Motorists) announced at a press conference on the future of the organisation today. Jukl will replace Jitka Pánek Jurková, whom Macinka dismissed with effect from today. The minister also said the Foreign Ministry does not plan to close any Czech Centres and instead sees potential to expand the network, for example through cooperation with Czech expatriate associations. The Czech Centres are the Czech Republic's public diplomacy institute, established by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. Their main mission is to promote the country's reputation abroad and strengthen cultural relations with other countries. The organisation currently operates 26 branches across four continents. https://english.radio.cz/economists-gove.text: CS DE EN ES FR РУ УК Economists: Government plan to loosen fiscal rules threatens public finances Facebook Twitter Economists: Government plan to loosen fiscal rules threatens public finances 3:36 ⨯ Economists: Government plan to loosen fiscal rules threatens public finances https://english.radio.cz/economists-government-plan-loosen-fiscal-rules-threatens-public-finances-8893587#player=on Copy Share on social media Facebook X The opposition Civic Democrats said this week that they were prepared to take a Czech government plan to loosen rules on fiscal responsibility to the Constitutional Court. For their part, the coalition say they will overturn a presidential veto of the relevant bill in the coming weeks. Meanwhile, 20 economists have called on the government to drop the whole idea. One of them, Daniel Münich, explained the reasons for this appeal. “There are a couple of reasons. One is that it is extraordinarily important issue – simply cancelling, or more or less cancelling, important rules that limit the government and future governments in using public money. “The second reason is that it’s holiday season, and the new law seems to be moving through Parliament very easily, without major attention from people.” One thing you are against is the possibility of increasing expenditure by 10 percent on the basis of a decision by the State Security Council. But in these uncertain times, wouldn’t an extraordinary security situation justify the change the government is pushing for? “The Security Council is nothing other than part of the government, so in other words this would just be cutting out Parliament. “And it can’t be that way. The government should always go to the lower house and ask for changes in the original budget, which can be done very quickly. “So this is just a way of getting rid of Parliament.” The minister of finance, Alena Schillerová, says the government have no alternative to loosening these rules, which she calls a severe constraint on the Czech economy. “Of course that’s not true. “There is a very clear, very simple alternative. And that is to increase taxation on incomes. In 2021 there was a huge decrease that was originally planned to be temporary, but it has remained there until now. “The tax cut at that time in current prices was CZK 130 billion, which is quite a lot of money, and more than the government needs now to finance all its promises and obligations.” Some people may say that if this bill is passed and if the government then acts in an irresponsible manner, voters can punish the government – they can vote the government out or not vote for those parties again. “This government will be there until 2029, but fiscal problems, the payment of debt, will show up later on. “So the only case in which this government would be held to account by the public would be if some kind of external crisis occurred that would require much higher spending, which would impose an additional burden on the public finances.” In any case, the government are planning to override the president’s veto. The opposition say they will take the matter to the Constitutional Court. How do you think this will end? “We’ve never had such a case in this country, so it’s very difficult to say. “But my feeling is that the Constitutional Court will probably – though I’m a layman in this – say that Parliament sets the rules, so if this is approved by Parliament, by a majority in both chambers, they will have no additional say on this. “But we’ll see.” Business related articles play play Row over public spending as president vetoes government’s budget rules reform play play Helena Horská: “If you don’t feel safe, you won’t do business” play play Fitch move sparks fears of painful cut in Czech credit rating play play Can the Czech Republic “invest its way out” of the Covid-19 crisis? featured 'Great-grandmother of modern architecture': Villa Tugendhat marks 25 years on UNESCO list Why drought is unlikely to shut down Czech nuclear power plants Train or tram? Photograph: Issouf Sanogo/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Soldiers on patrol in Niamey. Kevin Rideout was kidnapped in Niger’s capital and no armed group claimed responsibility for the abduction. Photograph: Issouf Sanogo/AFP/Getty Images Niger American missionary kidnapped in Niger freed after nine months Kevin Rideout, who was abducted by unknown assailants in Niamey, said to be in good health and in care of US officials Associated Press in Niamey Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.48 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google An American missionary who was kidnapped in Niger in October has been released, his organisation has said. Kevin Rideout “is in good health in the care of US officials” and would soon be reunited with his extended family, SIM International said in a statement. Rideout was kidnapped in the west African country’s capital, Niamey, on 21 October by three armed individuals and was probably driven out of town, according to a security official at the time. No armed group claimed responsibility for the abduction. Niger has long been the target of attacks by armed groups, including jihadis linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State. The US embassy in Niamey issued a security alert a day after Rideout’s abduction, warning that American citizens “remain at a heightened risk of kidnapping throughout Niger, including in the capital city”. Niger is ruled by a military junta that took power in 2023 after deposing the democratically elected president, Mohamed Bazoum. The new authorities ousted western partners, including the US, which had soldiers in Niger, and forged a new security and diplomatic alliance with Russia. In June, more than 30 people were killed when gunmen attacked the main airport in Niamey. It was the second attack this year at the airport , a strategic hub that serves as the ruling military’s command, hosting its air force base and most of its drones and aircraft. It is also the headquarters of the regional alliance that brings together troops from Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso. The violence is the latest sign of armed groups increasingly targeting cities and urban centres in Africa’s Sahel region. Photograph: Lukas Coch/AAP National disability insurance scheme Pocock and crossbenchers call Labor’s NDIS overhaul ‘too far, too fast’ in scathing Senate inquiry report Greens say Labor’s reform set to ‘rip life-changing supports away from disabled people instead of raising additional revenue through taxing gas exports’ Sarah Basford Canales and Krishani Dhanji Fri 14 Aug 2026 04.04 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 04.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Cross-benchers have slammed the Albanese government’s proposed overhaul of the NDIS as going “too far, too fast” as the changes to curb the growth of the $52bn program appear set to pass the parliament as early as next week. The Greens and independent ACT senator, David Pocock , delivered scathing assessments of the bill they warn will enable blunt and indiscriminate cuts to individual budgets supporting more than 770,000 Australians with disabilities in a final Senate inquiry report released on Friday afternoon. The NDIS has given Joe vital social skills. Funding cuts leave his mother fearing how he will ‘do life’ Read more While the Labor-chaired committee recommended the bill pass, Greens senator Jordon Steele-John said the proposals would be “devastating to the lives of disabled people and their families”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The bill forms part of the government’s plan to get the NDIS “back on track” and save $37.8bn over four years by tightening the eligibility criteria and subjecting all participants to independent functional assessments from 2028. It will also give the NDIS minister, Mark Butler, the power to reduce funding categories for individuals by up to 99%. The government has already said it will apply a 50% reduction in individual participant budgets for social, civic and community participation. Without the interventions, the government estimates the $52bn-a-year scheme will more than double in cost to $117bn a year in a decade’s time. The Greens have acknowledged some changes should be made to make the NDIS work better for participants but suggested the scheme could be funded by a gas export tax. “The choice that this Labor government is making is to rip life-changing supports away from disabled people instead of raising additional revenue through taxing gas exports shows their priorities clearly,” Steele-John wrote. “This government is choosing the profits of large corporations over the lives of disabled people.” Guardian Australia has previously reported that 241,000 NDIS participants will be shifted off the scheme by June 2031 after the introduction of the functional capacity test, to keep the number of participants at about 600,000. During that period, an additional 105,000 will be stopped from entering the scheme. Those shifted from the scheme are expected to be supported by programs run by states and territories with joint funding from the Commonwealth. Pocock said no participant should be removed from the NDIS until those new programs are “funded, operating and accessible”, vowing to continue scrutiny of the changes. “The true measure of these changes will be found in the experiences of people with disability. They must remain at the centre of what comes next,” Pocock said. Coalition senators provided additional comments raising concerns that fraud and integrity within the NDIS had not been sufficiently addressed. The government is expected to land a deal with the opposition early next week in order to pass the bill in the Senate. Disability advocacy groups have been extremely critical of the government’s amendments to the NDIS, and have warned caring responsibilities will be shifted from the scheme to families, affecting women disproportionately. Women With Disabilities Australia’s chief executive, Sophie Cusworth, said the government should deliver a comprehensive gender impact assessment of the bill. “You cannot say you are working for women while looking to pass legislation that puts women’s safety, care, health and economic security at risk,” she said on Friday. “That is not gender equality. That is neglect.” Explore more on these topics National disability insurance scheme Mark Butler David Pocock news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Almost 145,000 Australians will lose support for autism under NDIS reforms, documents reveal Morrison-era GST deal with WA a multi-billion dollar mistake that should be reversed, Productivity Commission finds Labor’s tax deal with the Greens is a crucial win – but its NDIS changes could pay the price Australian Politics Ask me anything: ‘melon-gate’, One Nation’s media ban and the PM’s ambition – Australian Politics podcast Australia has been galvanised by ‘melon-gate’. The latest housing loan data shows investment in existing Australian housing is dropping in favour of new buildings. Photograph: Jono Searle/AAP View image in fullscreen The latest housing loan data shows investment in existing Australian housing is dropping in favour of new buildings. Photograph: Jono Searle/AAP Housing Lending to property investors falls sharply in ‘tiny’ step towards fairer housing market in Australia, expert says ABS data shows an almost 9% slump in new lending to investors after three interest rate hikes this year Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Cait Kelly Fri 14 Aug 2026 04.03 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In what one economist is describing as a “tiny step” toward a fairer housing market after decades of bad policy, property investors are shying away from established homes, and putting money into new builds instead, new data shows. New lending to property investors fell sharply in the three months to June, slumping almost 9%, ABS data showed, while the number of total new home loans dropped by 5.4% in the June quarter. The major banks have all reported a slump in mortgage applications in recent months, after three RBA official rate hikes and the federal budget’s investor tax changes that together have weighed on property prices . Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The ABS’s head of finance statistics, Mish Tan, said: “lending fell across all borrower types this quarter and returned to similar levels to this time last year”. Investor loans led the decline, falling by 8.6% in the June quarter after a 4.7% drop in the previous period. The number of investor loans was 2.8% higher than a year earlier, while the value of loans to investors was down by 10.2%. The number of loans to first home buyers dropped by 2.9% over the three-month period, to be flat over the year. Saul Eslake, a leading housing economist said the interest rates increases this year would be reducing the number of first home buyers.. Australia’s falling house prices have a silver lining for mortgage holders. Here’s why Read more “I don’t think it’s a cause for concern,” he said. “Whereas I would say the big fall in lending to investors for the purchase of established homes is actually something to be welcomed and celebrated. “Because it means that prospective first home buyers are facing less competition from investors motivated by tax breaks for the housing we’ve already got.” The number of loans to investors in established properties was down 14.8%, but the number of loans to investors buying new builds was up by 4.4% to a record high, a possible effect of the government’s budget carve-out for investor lending to build new housing. Eslake said more investment in new builds actually increased rental supply, rather than pitting renters against investors for established housing. He said these stats were a “tiny step” in the right direction to make Australia’s housing market more equal. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Isn’t it amazing what a policy that actually tackles the cause of outrageous house prices can do? | Grogonomics Read more “A tiny step. But at least it is in that direction, whereas we’ve been taking tens of thousands of steps in the wrong direction for the last thirty years.” National spokesperson for Everybody’s Home, Maiy Azize, said the figures show the governments tax reforms were “beginning to rebalance the market”. “The most encouraging sign is that investors are pulling back from existing homes while investment in new housing is growing. That means less competition for first home buyers trying to buy a home,” Azize said. “It also smashes the myth that immigration is the main driver of house prices. When governments change the rules and stop boosting investors, housing costs go down. “Housing becoming more affordable is a good thing, especially for people trying to buy their first home.” Explore more on these topics Housing Interest rates Australian economy Banking news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Morrison-era GST deal with WA a multi-billion dollar mistake that should be reversed, Productivity Commission finds Is Australia’s buy now, pay later boom at an end? Photograph: ICAC View image in fullscreen Dallas McInerney has told the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption that Catholic Schools NSW funding wasn’t misused. Photograph: ICAC Independent Commission Against Corruption Teachers demand more scrutiny of Catholic school funding amid allegations of ‘sham arrangement’ with NSW Liberal group Independent Education Union ‘deeply concerned … public funding for Catholic schools may have been wrongfully spent on Liberal party matters’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Penry Buckley Fri 14 Aug 2026 03.41 EDT First published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 03.29 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The union for independent school teachers in New South Wales has demanded greater scrutiny of Catholic schools as the chief executive of their governing body told a corruption inquiry payments to a lobbying firm were not a “sham arrangement” to fund Liberal party factional work. Dallas McInerney insisted to the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday that Catholic Schools NSW funding wasn’t misused. Icac is investigating whether McInerney arranged and approved illegal donations from the governing body for 600 Catholic schools to support alleged branch stacking efforts of the Christian factional group the Reformers. The group wanted more conservative policies on issues such as abortion, euthanasia and same-sex marriage. The inquiry has heard that Catholic Schools NSW paid Beckington, a lobbying company run by Reformers Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood, $130,900 through invoices for consulting services between August 2019 and August 2021. Alleged victim of Alan Jones made broadcaster soft-boiled eggs with soldiers and ironed his underpants, court told Read more Greenwood’s company, JPG Advisory, was paid $135,000 between December 2021 and December 2023. The commission has heard that Reformers Robert Assaf and Dylan Whitelaw spent work hours on factional efforts while employed at Catholic Schools NSW. On Friday, the Independent Education Union’s NSW branch, which had previously declined to comment while the inquiry was under way, said it was “deeply concerned by … [allegations] that public funding for Catholic schools may have been wrongfully spent on Liberal party matters”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The IEU NSW/ACT branch secretary, Carol Matthews, said close scrutiny of public funding “was not applied to organisations such as Catholic Schools NSW that receive funding on behalf of Catholic diocesan schools”. “Regardless of the findings of Icac in this matter, there should be greater scrutiny of bodies such as Catholic Schools NSW, which receive public funding on behalf of non-government schools,” Matthews said in a statement. About 80% of the funding distributed by Catholic Schools NSW comes from the state and federal governments. Government funding totalled about $3.8bn in 2024. The NSW premier, Chris Minns, has ruled out an independent audit of the schools governing body while Icac’s inquiry is under way. McInerney stood aside from his role as CEO before the Icac hearings began “to allow the work of Catholic Schools NSW to continue its important mission”, he said in a statement previously. Catholic Schools NSW has previously said it “does not intend … to provide responses to questions that supersede the eight-week inquiry and legal process that is under way”. McInerney on Friday was asked about messages in February 2021 between Assaf and fellow Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet, the younger brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet, who is not accused of wrongdoing. Assaf and Jean-Claude were not directly employed by Beckington. Jean-Claude Perrottet wrote to Assaf: “Ellis and I caught up with Dallas in Bowral to discuss money, had a long convo.” The counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asked if the reason for Assaf and Jean-Claude’s interest was “because they knew that the arrangement in place was that you would pay Beckington money pursuant to a sham arrangement” – under which the money would come to them. “No,” McInerney said on Friday. He said he could not recall the Bowral meeting. McInerney rejected evidence previously given by Assaf to the inquiry that Greenwood and McInerney met this year to discuss their summons. The inquiry has previously heard that Jean-Claude Perrottet received money from Beckington. When the Catholic Schools NSW contract moved in 2021 from Beckington to JPG Advisory, Assaf and Jean-Claude allegedly each received a “kickback”, in Jean-Claude’s case, 50% of the monthly retainer, after he secured the contract with McInerney. On Friday, McInerney repeatedly described Jean-Claude Perrottet as his “conduit” to Greenwood, who ran JPG. Dylan Whitelaw, who worked at Beckington after being employed by McInerney at Catholic Schools NSW, has previously given evidence there was an arrangement under which payments from the schools’ governing body to Beckington were used to fund Reformers’ activities. McInerney repeatedly denied this. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion McInerney was asked on Friday why Whitelaw, then only 21, was involved in negotiating an increase in Beckington’s retainer in 2021, and why McInerney cited Whitelaw’s departure from the company as a reason to end the contract with Beckington. “I’m not confident they’ll have the in-house expertise to support our needs in the way DW [Dylan Whitelaw] has been,” McInerney wrote to a colleague. On Friday, McInerney, who described Whitelaw as a “junior” at Beckington who carried out an “account manager” role and was responsible for “administrative interplay”, said his language had been consistent. “Your in-house expertise as an account manager is … knowing the client, the rhythms, the relationships, how they service,” he said. The inquiry has previously heard that McInerney came to know Whitelaw through the Mittagoing Liberal branch after first meeting his parents. He employed Whitelaw at Catholic Schools NSW in 2019 after he graduated high school. On Thursday, McInerney said correspondence leading up to the Beckington contract in which he told Ellis to get an ABN and a mailbox was “traditional due diligence”. He denied he was attempting to provide “a veneer of legitimacy” to the contract. On Friday, the inquiry – and McInerney – learned that the ABN provided by Ellis in fact belonged to Ellis’s sister. After Curtin suggested it showed due diligence “wasn’t particularly effective”, McInerney said: “I will add the point [that] I thought it was, but I’m happy to be enlightened”. The inquiry heard Beckington later wrote Catholic Schools NSW’s name incorrectly on invoices. After Curtin suggested evidence of written work by Beckington was “de minimis”, apart from calendar entries for monthly meetings, McInerney insisted Beckington did consult for Catholic Schools NSW. Asked if Beckington’s input was “only ever given orally”, McInerney said that Beckington had contributed to two “forward plans for public affairs and engagement in 2019” which involved “exhaustive planning sessions”. The commission heard McInerney provided the two documents but there was no written evidence of Beckington being involved in the drafting process. McInerney was expected to appear again before Icac next week. Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A firefighter hoses down the ground as flames continue to burn in the Landes forest in Luglon, south-west France, on Friday. Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty Images France Almost 500 arrested on suspicion of starting wildfires in France this summer More than 180 minors among those detained, as firefighters tackle blazes across Europe amid record-breaking heatwave Europe heatwave – latest updates Jon Henley in Paris Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.18 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Almost 500 people have been arrested on suspicion of starting wildfires in France since the start of the summer, authorities have said, as firefighters in half a dozen European countries tackle ferocious blazes amid a record-breaking heatwave. With three out of five Europeans facing temperatures of at least 30C on Friday and about 150 million enduring 35C or more, France’s interior ministry said 474 people, including 183 minors, had been detained over wildfires in the country since 1 July. About 70% of those arrested were suspected of deliberately starting fires and the rest of doing so accidentally, it said. French media said a 15-year-old boy had been detained in connection with a fire near Bordeaux airport that killed two firefighters in July. Europe is the world’s fastest warming continent. What is to blame? Read more French authorities on Friday evacuated more than 525 people from the village of Luglon in the south-west region of Landes after a new wildfire tore through almost 1,100 hectares (2,700 acres) of tinder-dry pine forest in less than 24 hours. “The situation is unfavourable and the fire remains raging,” Gilles Clavreul, a regional official, told reporters, ​adding that 500 firefighters were tackling ‌the flames and six water-dumping aircraft ‌had been sent to assist. Roads to the village were closed. View image in fullscreen A firefighter with the French air force looks on as a wildfire burns through the Landes forest in Luglon, south-west France. Photograph: Romain Perrocheau/AFP/Getty Images Luglon is about 62 miles (100km) south-east of the popular holiday destinations of Arcachon Bay and the Lège-Cap-Ferret peninsula where two huge wildfires destroyed more than 50,000 hectares in late July, forcing the evacuation of as many as 220,000 people . Scientists say climate breakdown is causing more frequent and more extreme weather events, evaporating soils and waterways, fuelling wildfires and leading to thousands of excess deaths in France. Europe is heating at about twice the global average rate. In western Germany , more than 2,000 people fled their homes early on Friday morning to take shelter in a nearby primary school after a ⁠wildfire in the nearby Hürtgen forest spread to within a few hundred metres of the village of Gey. “This forest fire threatens to hit the local ‌community hard,” Mona Neubaur, the deputy premier of the state of North Rhine-Westphalia, posted on social media. Unexploded second world war ordnance was also hampering firefighting efforts. View image in fullscreen A police helicopter carries water to be dumped on ⁠wildfire in the Hürtgen forest in western Germany. Photograph: Roberto Pfeil/afp/AFP/Getty Images The news agency dpa reported explosions could be heard as munitions detonated in the flames, forcing firefighters to stay out of the area, not far from the Belgian border, for safety. German army tanks and helicopters were providing support. In Croatia , a wildfire driven by strong winds descended on the tourist town of Lokva Rogoznica on the Dalmatian coast overnight, engulfing houses, forcing about 1,000 people to evacuate and injuring several dozen, ⁠fire brigade and ⁠health officials ​said. Of 36 people treated by ambulance services in the city of Split, about 15.5 miles to the north, 14 were admitted to hospital and seven had life-threatening injuries, local health officials said. Emergency ​shelters opened in several nearby towns. View image in fullscreen Croatia’s prime minister described the blaze that spread to Omiš as ‘one of the worst fires in recent years’. Photograph: Jakov Prkic/CROPIX/SIPA/Shutterstock “It was a strong fire, it swept everything on ‌its way ... there has been huge material damage,” Slavko Tucaković, the regional chief fire commander, said on Friday, adding that the blaze appeared to have calmed by Friday morning. The country’s prime minister, Andrej ‌Plenković, said on a visit nearby Omiš, where the evacuees were sheltering in a sports hall, that the blaze was “one of the worst fires in recent years” but “the most important” there were no confirmed fatalities so far. A stretch of a major coastal highway ​was shut. “Everything flared ‌up in a ​second,” Goran Lović, ​the owner of a cafe near where the fire broke out, told the Jutarnji List newspaper. “It just happened all of a sudden, there was an open flame.” View image in fullscreen A painting is removed as a wildfire nears the San Juan de la Peña monastery in Aragón, north-east Spain. Photograph: UME/AFP/Getty Images In north-east Spain , an army unit removed the remains of three 11th-century Aragonese kings from the San Juan de la Peña monastery after it was threatened by a wildfire and took them to a ​museum in nearby Huesca. The fire, which began on Monday, intensified on ⁠Thursday, authorities said, driven by higher temperatures and strong winds that have enabled it burn through more ​than 9,000 hectares, forcing ​the evacuation of 16 towns and villages. A ​much larger wildfire in southern Spain also worsened on Thursday. It has so far burned 31,000 hectares in the province of Huelva and forced the evacuation of about 700 people. View image in fullscreen Local residents and tourists are evacuated from Siviri as a forest fire threatens the resort on Halkidiki peninsula, Greece. Photograph: Alexandros Avramidis/Reuters In northern Greece, a fleet of small boats evacuated about 500 holidaymakers from beaches on Thursday as a forest fire threatened Siviri and Fourka, two popular resorts on the Halkidiki peninsula, south of the city of Thessaloniki. The 2-mile-long fire front, with flames up to 30 metres (98ft) high, was brought under control later in the day, the regional civil protection chief said, though crews remained on alert for flare-ups. Two injured firefighters were taken to hospital, the fire service added. A maximum level-five alert for fires was issued for much of the Greek mainland and local officials in Halkidiki have banned access to the region’s dense pine forests. Winds of up to 62 mph are forecast for Friday. View image in fullscreen The remains of homes in Stoke-on-Trent smoulder on Friday as wildfire raced across the West Midlands Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images In the UK, wildfires raced across the West Midlands , burning several houses to the ground in “one of the most significant” incidents the region’s fire service has ever had to deal with, the regional fire chief, Simon Tuhill, said. The Albanian embassy says most of the cohort that arrived by small boat that year have since left the UK. Photograph: Florion Goga/Reuters Immigration and asylum Albanian ambassador attacks UK right wing for ‘unhinged’ fixation with 2022 migrant surge Exclusive: Uran Ferizi says arrivals fell sharply after short-lived influx, but country continues to be stigmatised Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.29 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 06.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The number of Albanians who travelled to Britain in small boats four years ago remains the focus of “unhinged” and “hysterical” criticisms from rightwing politicians and the media, according to the country’s UK ambassador. Uran Ferizi said the influx of more than 12,000 people from the Balkan state in 2022 was “real”, “exceptional” and “short-lived”, but the Albanian community in the UK was still being framed by those events by Reform UK and the Daily Telegraph. He called on Nigel Farage’s party to stop “Albanian-spotting”, and said that the UK’s visa policy at the time – which granted a lower percentage of visas to Albanians compared with other Balkan countries – may have pushed some vulnerable people toward people traffickers. Ferizi’s office has produced a 10-page report based principally on data from the Home Office and the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford. It said 12,658 Albanians crossed the Channel in 2022 – a dramatic spike, but equivalent to only about 1% of overall UK long-term immigration that year. Arrivals then fell sharply, and the embassy’s analysis suggests most of that cohort has since left the UK. View image in fullscreen Uran Ferizi presents his credentials to King Charles at Buckingham Palace in May 2024. The Albanian ambassador has accused the rightwing media of demonising the Albanian community in the UK. Photograph: Yui Mok/AFP/Getty Images Ferizi, whose first experience of Britain was as a teenage stowaway before he went on to read mathematics at the University of Oxford four years later, said some of the fixation with Albanians “sounds unhinged”. “A loud minority in British politics and media has kept the Albanian migration crisis alive long after it ended in the data,” he said. “Actual contact tends to ruin the story. I attended Reform UK’s conference last year, and by the end of a pub quiz my table had concluded that the Albanian ambassador was ‘actually alright’. Reform might do more for Britain by addressing youth unemployment and welfare than by Albanian-spotting. “Unfortunately, the framing is contagious. Conservatives, and regrettably some in government, can seem keener to compete with Reform’s headlines than interrogate the evidence.” According to Ferizi’s report, Albanian applicants for UK visas had an approval rate of just 65.5% over 2018–25, compared with about 90% across the other western Balkan countries, with more than 70,000 Albanian applications refused. Ferizi argues that this deserves greater scrutiny. “When the legal route is unusually difficult, you cannot discuss the irregular route as though the two have nothing to do with each other,” he said. The report stops short of claiming visa refusals caused the Channel surge, but raises the possibility that restricted legal access made some young Albanians more vulnerable to smugglers and traffickers. “The surge was real,” Ferizi said. “But it was exceptional, it was short-lived, and Britain is still talking about Albanians as though 2022 never ended.” Ferizi has criticised the Daily Telegraph’s coverage of Albanians for demonising the community as criminals. In an unpublished letter sent to the newspaper, he cited an article from 2024 which claimed that one in 50 Albanians in the UK were in prison, the worst rate of any nationality. “Adjusted for age, sex and other relevant factors as any comparison should be, the rate shrinks dramatically,” he said. “Left unadjusted, it gives you the headline you want.” Reform and the Telegraph have been approached for a comment. Sign up here Martin Belam Fri 14 Aug 2026 07.35 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 07.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. The extent to which federal law enforcement targeted political opponents and peaceful organizers has been laid bare in newly disclosed court documents . Internal investigative files reveal that the Department of Homeland Security launched a sweeping surveillance operation against anti-ICE protesters, major labor unions and left-leaning advocacy groups – sending undercover agents to infiltrate community meetings and issuing administrative subpoenas to seize financial records. The documents show that DHS investigators obtained financial records of unions and non-profits, as part of an inquiry into “domestic terrorist financing”. What did undercover government agents do? They infiltrated community meetings, joined private activist Signal chats and surreptitiously recorded audio at local events – including a “resistance skills training” at a public library and a sparring session at a church gym, where an agent accidentally dropped his recording device. Agents posed as activists and actively engaged participants by offering to help with “direct-action” protests. How have activists responded? Emilia González Avalos, the executive director of Unidos MN, a Minneapolis social justice non-profit group, said: “I believe that this is a clear attempt to intimidate us, to punish and politically repress disagreement and difference. And that is not the America that we have built through hundreds of years. And it’s definitely not the America that we are organizing for.” Crimea bomb kills ‘Ukrainian sub commander who defected’ View image in fullscreen A portrait of Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, in Sevastopol, where the attack took place. Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty Images A Russian military officer labelled as a Ukrainian defector ⁠was killed in a ⁠bomb ​attack on Thursday in Russian-annexed Crimea. Robert Shageyev was described on Russian Telegram channels as ‌a former Ukrainian naval officer who switched allegiance to ‌Russia during Moscow’s annexation of Crimea in 2014 when he was commanding Ukraine’s only submarine, the Zaporizhzhia. Where did the attack take place? The attack took place in Sevastopol, the biggest city in Russian-annexed Crimea. ​The regional governor, Mikhail Razvozhayev, said a woman had been arrested on suspicion of ⁠assassinating Shageyev on behalf of Ukrainian special services. What has Poland said about Russian activity there? A Russian plan to kill a Ukrainian American citizen in Warsaw was thwarted by Poland before it could be carried out, the Polish prime minister has said . Donald Tusk said it was the first time that “someone on the order of Russia” had sought to attack a US citizen on the territory of another Nato country. Massachusetts teen accused of killing mother and brother used ChatGPT View image in fullscreen Arjun Aravind listens as his lawyer Debra DeWitt speaks. Photograph: Lane Turner/The Boston Globe/AP A Massachusetts teenager accused of killing his mother and younger brother is being held without bail as authorities investigate a double-murder case that prosecutors say is connected to his use of ChatGPT . Arjun Aravind, 17, appeared for his arraignment in Concord district court on Thursday morning, where a not-guilty plea to murder and several additional charges was entered on his behalf. What did the county district attorney say? Marian Ryan said in a press conference: “The investigation has so far shown that Arjun had recently been demonstrating some concerning behavior, including using the internet and ChatGPT to make searches for theoretical ideas or fantasy stories regarding the killing of his family.” WNBA condemns ‘bad-faith’ efforts to fuel transgender player debate View image in fullscreen Golden State Valkyries’ Tiffany Hayes, front, steals the ball from Chicago Sky’s Gabriela Jacquez in the first half of a WNBA basketball game in San Francisco. Photograph: Carlos Avila Gonzalez/San Francisco Chronicle/AP The WNBA on has criticized those trying to create a narrative about transgender women playing in the league . A league spokesperson said “There are no immediate eligibility matters affecting the WNBA, and we strongly denounce the bad-faith efforts to use these topics to demean or marginalize others.” The statement came hours after an anti-hate taskforce met virtually and discussed a variety of topics, including social media vitriol and transgender athletes. There has never been a trans woman – a person assigned male at birth who transitions to align with their gender identity – on a WNBA roster.
