Ben Crump, Christine Wells-Wonsley, Elmore Wonsley, and Al Sharpton onstage at the NABJ convention in Atlanta. Photograph: Paras Griffin/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Ben Crump, Christine Wells-Wonsley, Elmore Wonsley, and Al Sharpton onstage at the NABJ convention in Atlanta. Photograph: Paras Griffin/Getty Images Georgia Nolan Wells’ parents recount ordeal of son’s death at Atlanta convention Ben Crump and Rev Al Sharpton, also present at National Association of Black Journalists, demanded ‘truth’ and ‘transparency’ in Wells’ case Adria R Walker Fri 14 Aug 2026 07.02 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google On Thursday morning, the parents of Nolan Wells, Christine Wells-Wonsley and Elmore Wonsley, along with Ben Crump, the civil rights attorney, and Rev Al Sharpton, the famed civil rights activist, spoke at the National Association of Black Journalists (NABJ) convention in Atlanta. Wells was an 18-year-old college student who was found dead on 6 July after a boating trip with friends, and his death captured national attention . Wells went missing on 4 July and a photo of the teen, who was Black, and his three friends on the trip, who were white, went viral. Social media users have speculated that Wells’s disappearance, death and the perceived lack of urgency in the county’s investigation into what happened to the teen are because of his race. During Thursday’s talk, moderated by Tiffany Cross, a journalist, Wells-Wonsley and Wonsley narrated the days during which Wells was still missing, leading up to the day their son’s body was found. They described a harrowing string of events, including a lack of urgency by law enforcement and what they called “inconsistencies” in narratives and information provided by some of Wells’ friends. Wells-Wonsley also described the numerous professional and personal attacks she has received since her son’s death. On Saturday, 3 July, the last day she saw her son alive, Wells-Wonsley said he made dinner for the family, hugged his mom and left home. The next day, she said, she and her sister realized that it was late and they hadn’t heard from Wells. She called his phone repeatedly, but he never answered. Later that night, she received a call from one of his friends asking if she had heard from Wells. Confused, Wells-Wonsley said that she thought her son was with the friends. After Wells-Wonsley mentioned that Life360, a tracking app, showed that Wells’ phone was back in the Ocean Spring area, where he lived, the friend then told her that Wells remained on the island with a girl he met that day, she said. “I said, ‘What?’ Because we know our children. Nolan isn’t one to [say]: ‘Oh, I’m going to throw caution to the wind and I’m going to stay here with this girl that I just met,’” Wells-Wonsley told a packed audience. Wells-Wonsley said she called several different agencies – the Mississippi department of marine resources, which called the Coast Guard; the Ocean Springs police department; the Jackson county sheriff’s department – which all told her that Wells’ case was outside of their jurisdiction. She said she even visited a local hospital to see if the teen was there. Eventually, the Jackson county sheriff’s department said it would take the case. After midnight, Wells’ parents met with an officer at a McDonald’s parking lot that night to provide information about Nolan. “He was just like, ‘OK, thanks.’ I was like: ‘Where is the urgency?’” Wells-Wonsley said. “As far as we know, there were no [search] boats on the water that night.” The family said the next morning, they went to the island with Wells’ high school football coach who offered his own boat and looked for Wells themselves. John Ledbetter, the Jackson county sheriff, has said that he does not suspect any foul play in Wells’ death, and that the others on the boat are cooperating with the police investigation. No suspects have been named, nor has anyone been taken into custody with regards to Wells’ disappearance and death. Three people have been arrested, however, in separate cases : an Illinois man who allegedly threatened to kill police officers; an Ohio woman who allegedly made threatening calls to the Jackson county sheriff’s office and the George county chancery office; and a California man who was indicted for allegedly making violent threats on social media to Ashlee Cole, a Jackson county chancery court judge and the stepmother of one of Wells’ friends. The three people who went boating with Wells have all retained attorneys. More than a month later, though, Wells’ family is still demanding answers. They don’t know why the teen did not return with his friends nor when or how he died. The state of Mississippi has not yet released its autopsy; the Jackson county district attorney said the autopsy would not be released until a grand jury was convened. An independent autopsy commissioned by Wells’ family said the teen’s cause of death was inconclusive. Crump, who has represented families in high-profile cases of racial violence, said that Wells’ family is focused only on getting answers. Wells’ parents “wanted the truth. They had concerns about whether they were going to get a fair and impartial investigation,” Crump said on Thursday. “From that day, it’s been the same objective ... We want truth. We want transparency.” Wells’ parents, Crump, Sharpton and Lucy McBath, a Georgia representative, called for a federal review of the investigation into Nolan’s disappearance and death. “We want to make sure that every stone is turned because his life matters,” McBath said during a later NABJ press conference. The congressional Black caucus chair, Yvette D Clarke, and other members of the caucus also sent a letter to Todd Blanche, the US attorney genera, and Kash Patel, the FBI director, urging them to launch an independent review of the case. Next Wednesday, 19 August, would have been Wells’ 19th birthday. “Fourth of July will never be the same to Christine and Elmore, and on the 19th, next Wednesday, his family ... we’re all asking for prayer for Nolan,” Crump said on Thursday. “Can we pray together in unity to say let’s get the truth of what happened to Nolan Wells? Can we do that, America? Can we at least do that? Everyone who claimed to be his friend, can we come together in unity and pray for the truth?” Explore more on these topics Georgia Atlanta Race news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: ‘In the days after the executive orders were signed, companies that kept their DEI policies actually performed better on the stock market than those that didn’t.’ Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images View image in fullscreen ‘In the days after the executive orders were signed, companies that kept their DEI policies actually performed better on the stock market than those that didn’t.’ Composite: The Guardian/Getty Images DEI policies US firms that kept DEI policies despite ‘go woke, go broke’ threats thrived Exclusive: Companies that kept policies did just as well financially, even after Trump’s executive order, as those that didn’t Gaya Gupta Fri 14 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.43 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Conservative backlash was supposed to put an end to the diversity, inclusion and equity (DEI) movement as companies were warned “go woke, go broke”. In January 2025, Donald Trump delivered a death knell, ending DEI within the federal government with executive orders and threatening to target companies that still supported it. Companies including Google, Goldman Sachs, McDonald’s and Walmart that had embraced DEI years earlier fell into line and announced an end to their policies. But new research published Friday and shared exclusively with the Guardian found that companies that resisted the pressure and kept their DEI practices, including Costco, Apple and Delta Air Lines, performed just as well as their competitors who pulled back. For the research, Jacob Grumbach, an associate professor at at the University of California at Berkeley’s Goldman School of Public Policy, analyzed how S&P 500 companies fared after Trump’s January executive order. He used what economists define as “abnormal returns” – the difference between how a stock was expected to perform versus how it actually performed – to isolate the impact of a company’s DEI decision. What he found was the firms that kept their DEI policies or voted down anti-DEI shareholder resolutions did just as well financially, even after Trump’s executive order, as firms that didn’t. In the days after the executive orders were signed, companies that kept their DEI policies actually performed better on the stock market than those that didn’t. Chart of companies’ stock performance after Trump’s anti-DEI executive order Whether or not DEI benefits a company’s bottom line can depend on its consumers. Grumbach noted companies that publicly stood firm on their DEI policies might have known they could weather a political storm. Apple, for example, may have known it could maintain its DEI efforts in a way that Tractor Supply, another prominent company that pulled back its policies, could not. The “go woke, go broke” movement found its power in 2023, when a series of conservative backlashes against companies gained momentum. Bud Light sales dropped following a conservative boycott after the beer company featured transgender influencer Dylan Mulvaney. Target became an embodiment of its name after fury erupted over its pride month merchandise. Ron DeSantis , the Florida governor, embarked on a prolonged fight with Disney after the company vocally opposed the state’s “don’t say gay” bill. “Cracker Barrel has fallen,” a conservative group wrote after the restaurant chain celebrated pride month on social media Then, also in 2023, the US supreme court ruled that race-conscious admissions policies in higher education were unconstitutional , opening the floodgates for legal challenges against DEI policies in other places, including the workplace. “That really created a lot of fear and panic in corporate America and is what led to a lot of the pullbacks around DEI,” said David Glasgow, executive director of the Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion and Belonging at New York University’s law school. “When Trump came into office for the second time, that just poured fuel on an already raging fire.” After Trump’s executive orders, companies had to weigh the risks. Many quietly scrapped the DEI promises they had made after the murder of George Floyd and the racial reckoning it inspired. Some ended up facing a reverse backlash: the Twin Cities Pride parade dropped Target, which is based in Minneapolis, as a sponsor after the company withdrew some of its DEI policies. But the reality of this pullback was likely different from what was seen in the headlines, Glasgow said. Of the many companies he spoke to, most “made adjustments to their diversity principles on account of legal and regulatory environments”. “Often what’s going on is something more in the messy middle, where they’re sticking with some things, deleting others and then reframing or rebranding some,” Glasgow said. While there was “no perfect way” to measure whether a firm was pulling back its DEI policies, Grumbach kept track of company policies by analyzing news coverage, pulling anti-DEI shareholder proposals and keeping track of the proposals’ votes, and using data from an activist group called DEI Watch, which maintains a tracker of companies. “No matter how we measure DEI in companies, we find the same answer,” he said: holding on to DEI promises ultimately had no impact on financial performance. Grumbach said the implications go beyond DEI and illustrates how organizations fare after resisting authoritarian policies. “What happens when you don’t comply with that executive branch pressure in a moment of great fear in these civil society organizations?” Grumbach said. “This shows that large US corporations really do have leeway and the ability to sort of do noncompliance to executive branch pressure and end up fine.” Explore more on these topics DEI policies Trump administration US politics news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Ukrainian firefighters at a site hit by Russian ballistic missiles, Kyiv, 5 August 2026. Photograph: Tetiana Dzhafarova/AFP/Getty Images Opinion Ukraine Patriot missiles have been a godsend for Ukraine against Putin, but they’re running out. Kyiv needs help and fast Jack Watling Europe and Nato have known for years that interceptor production can’t keep up with demand and now disaster looms, putting us all in danger Fri 14 Aug 2026 04.54 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 05.55 EDT Share “I nvincible.” That was how Vladimir Putin described Russia’s latest generation of ballistic missiles in 2018 . In 2022 he would unleash this arsenal to strike across Ukraine, hitting command centres, critical infrastructure and airfields. Then, in 2023, Ukraine received Patriot air defence systems from its international partners. The US-supplied missile interceptor would prove to be an effective shield against Russian strikes. But this year, supplies of Patriot missiles have run out and Kyiv has suffered the consequences. Intercepts have gone from more than 70% to none, so that night after night Russia strikes Ukraine’s infrastructure with impunity. This tragedy was long foretold, and there are no quick fixes. While the military narrative of the war has largely been of cheap mass-produced Ukrainian weapons overwhelming exquisite Russian military hardware, most of the serious damage from Russia’s long-range strikes has come from cruise and ballistic missiles, and Ukraine’s campaign has suffered for want of them. Countering ballistic missiles is not a simple or cheap activity . To intercept a tactical ballistic missile, such as Russia’s Iskander, a defensive system needs to be remarkably sophisticated. Its target will be descending from the high atmosphere at more than five times the speed of sound. The incoming missile will also be manoeuvring through the air, rather than following a predictable ballistic trajectory. The defensive system needs to be able to track the precise location of this incoming missile and communicate this to the intercepting missile, allowing the latter to adjust course while climbing against gravity. Building the radars, data links and interceptors for such a task involves a huge amount of research and development, and across Nato most states have been happy for Washington to invest over decades to make the Patriot up to the job. The US and licensed manufacturers in Germany and Japan are able to produce about 840 Patriot interceptors a year. About 240 of these are older, larger PAC-2 interceptors, which climb until they are close to the target and then explode – meaning they must carry the weight of a warhead to the target – and 600 are PAC-3s, which are smaller and fly directly into the target. The latter approach is more effective but requires even more precise navigation. The former can be used against other target types. Russia produces about 750 Iskander missiles a year and is looking to increase production. In addition, Russia uses air-launched Kinzhal ballistic missiles and repurposed air-defence missiles to conduct strikes, along with its arsenal of cruise missiles and drones. To have a high probability of success, it is generally recommended to fire two to three interceptors against each ballistic missile. When you also factor in that the launchers themselves can only protect a relatively small area, and Ukraine is a vast country, then it becomes clear that Kyiv would ideally have three to four times the annual global production capacity of Patriot missiles to protect itself. Countries supporting Ukraine have therefore had to give their own stockpiles to Kyiv. Even before the US decision to attack Iran, western allies were nervous about depleting their own stocks by giving Patriot missiles to Ukraine, knowing that it would take a long time for them to be resupplied. The US attack on Iran – prompting Tehran to fire ballistic missiles across the Middle East – has created an acute global shortage. Where Russia usually fires fewer than 10 ballistic missiles in a single attack, Iran has launched upwards of 170 a day during the current and last year’s war. A portion of Iran’s missiles were also advanced. In one instance, it took 17 Patriot interceptors to defeat a missile. And Iran has many more missiles in storage. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Matters of Opinion Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more after newsletter promotion Amid war in Ukraine, the fleeting moments of despair and salvation I witness are what truly tell the story | Charlotte Higgins Read more The point is that Ukraine is not going to receive enough Patriots between now and the winter to save its critical national infrastructure, irrespective of whether some countries make the political gesture of releasing a few more from their stockpiles. At this point, Kyiv must plan for a winter with severely disrupted power, and disperse and fortify life-support systems such as water, sanitation, power and heating. Kyiv is trying to convince the US to activate Starlink satellite navigation modules over Russian territory to enable its drones to hunt for the Russian missile launchers. But, as the US recently found in Iran, pulling off this kind of mission over a large area is extremely difficult. Another line of effort in Kyiv is to attack the production of Russia’s ballistic missiles. These factories are well defended. To succeed, Ukraine’s partners will need to expand the funding and industrial capacity behind Ukraine’s nascent cruise-missile industry, or reopen questions of providing weapons systems such as Germany’s Taurus (which Berlin didn’t provide to Ukraine for fear of military escalation). But the real lesson here is that Nato members have abjectly failed in defence planning. The numbers in this equation have been known since before 2022 and yet the investments to expand Patriot production (or mature alternative systems such as the Franco-Italian SAMP-T ) have not been made. Such a level of complacency is devastating for Ukraine today, but it also risks Europe being bereft of defences in the future. It remains remarkable that Europe – watching the consequences unfold on its very borders – has remained so idle. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/14/tehra.text: Hossein Taeb, the cleric who commanded the Basij during the 2009 crackdown on the Green Movement and led the Revolutionary Guards' intelligence service for 13 years, has been reappointed as head of the IRGC's militia.The decision to bring back one of the Islamic Republic's most senior internal security figures to a frontline position in the early months of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei's rule is part of a recent reshuffle among the Islamic Republic's political, military and security elites.The appointment signals that the Tehran regime's new leadership is preparing for possible unrest at home, amid the ongoing war with the US and mounting economic pressure from sanctions.Who is Hossein Taeb?Taeb joined the IRGC as a teenager and later served in the Ministry of Intelligence before returning to the Guards.He became Basij commander in July 2008, less than a year before Iran's disputed presidential election triggered the mass demonstrations of June 2009 known as the Green Movement.The Basij played a central role in the crackdown that followed. The US sanctioned Taeb in 2010 over his command responsibility for the violence, with the EU following suit in 2011.In late 2009, he was appointed the first head of the newly created IRGC Intelligence Organisation.He held that position for roughly 13 years, during which the body became one of the country's most powerful security institutions, at times competing with and frequently overshadowing the civilian Ministry of Intelligence.Under his tenure, the organisation expanded into cases involving political opponents, journalists, environmental activists and dual nationals.The most prominent operation associated with his time as IRGC intelligence chief was the capture and extradition of Ruhollah Zam, an Iranian dissident living in France who ran the popular Telegram channel Amad News.The IRGC brought Zam to Iran in 2019. He was executed in 2020.Taeb was replaced in June 2022 by Mohammad Kazemi and moved to an advisory role under the IRGC commander.His removal followed a period of significant intelligence failures, including operations attributed to Israel that exposed serious weaknesses in Iran's counter-intelligence.These included alleged penetrations of sensitive sites and the killing of nuclear scientist Mohsen Fakhrizadeh in November 2020 outside Tehran.Iranian authorities never publicly confirmed those failures as the reason for his departure.Taeb was not expelled from the security establishment, but was instead moved directly into another senior position.Taeb and Mojtaba Khamenei are reported to have longstanding ties dating back to the Iran-Iraq War, during which both were associated with the Habib battalion of the IRGC's 27th Mohammad Rasulollah Division.Networks formed at the time later became significant pathways to institutional advancement within Iran's security structure for the most loyal cadre.His return to the Basij under Mojtaba Khamenei's leadership, rather than his retirement after the 2022 setback, suggests those ties remain close.Why the Basij mattersThe Basij maintains a presence in neighbourhoods, places of worship, universities and government offices and has been used to monitor citizens and communities, mobilise regime support and suppress protests.The order appointing Taeb emphasised expanding the Basij's "popular intelligence network," improving training and integrating new technologies — language that points to Tehran's renewed interest in its domestic surveillance.Placing a veteran intelligence official in charge of the Basij could allow the force to shift from a body deployed reactively after protests erupt to one embedded in a broader system that detects and contains dissent before it spreads.The choice of Taeb — who has moved from one top position to another within the security apparatus over four decades without being permanently removed from the establishment's core — also indicates that the IRGC, an elite paramilitary corps that answers directly to the ayatollah, remains crucial to decision-making in Tehran.Former president Mahmoud Ahmadinejad publicly accused him in 2018 of fabricating cases against political opponents, in a rare public dispute over power between the presidency and the IRGC intelligence apparatus.During Hassan Rouhani's presidency, the IRGC intelligence service under Taeb openly challenged the civilian Ministry of Intelligence in several high-profile cases, in another shift in security and political power toward institutions directly linked to the ayatollah.

In quake-hit Cali, ‘hugs here’ station brings comfort amid rubble Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 14/08/2026 - 12:11 GMT+2 In quake-hit Cali, residents find comfort at a “hugs here” station, as Andres Solomon and volunteers share solidarity while rescuers clear rubble. … More As Cali recovers from the 7.4‑magnitude earthquake that struck on 10 August, 46‑year‑old local musician Andres Solomon has been offering free hugs to residents in the quake‑hit Capri neighbourhood. Sitting beneath the trees beside a cardboard sign reading “ HUGS HERE ” and “CHEER UP!” . Solomon says he wanted to offer emotional support alongside the material aid reaching the area, listening to people, embracing them and helping them release some of the pain of what he describes as a “collective trauma”. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Andres Solomon’s simple gesture has become a small but striking symbol of comfort amid the rubble and twisted metal, as residents, volunteers and community leaders gather nearby and rescue teams continue their search and recovery work. The earthquake, described as the strongest to hit Colombia this century , has killed at least 265 people and left communities dealing with loss and uncertainty. On 13 August, Solomon said people needed to face the reality of the disaster together, just as volunteers were working side by side to remove rubble. Lyda Arias, president of Colombia’s Evangelical Confederation, said the suffering was difficult to witness and called for both prayer and action. Unprecedented rainfall in Japan leaves at least four dead in Chiba prefecture Copy/paste the link below: Copy Copy/paste the article video embed link below: Copy Updated: 14/08/2026 - 10:32 GMT+2 Unprecedented rainfall battered Japan on Thursday, leaving at least four people dead and flooding parts of Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo. Authorities issued the region’s highest-level rain warning for the first time, while landslide alerts and power cuts affected thousands of residents. … More Nearly 26,000 households were left without power , while 45 homes were flooded and another 39 reported water entering below floor level. Hundreds of people spent the night in shelters or at Chiba station after rail services were suspended. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT The disruption was particularly severe around Narita Airport , where about 7,000 travellers were stranded overnight after trains were cancelled, with many sleeping on terminal floors. In rural Chiba, more than a dozen cars were abandoned on flooded roads. A man in his 60s or 70s was found dead in floodwater, while a 66-year-old woman died after becoming trapped in her submerged car, according to the Chiba disaster management office. The Japan Meteorological Agency warned that the rainfall could be unprecedented. The highest-level warning was downgraded to level four on Friday morning, although the risk of further flooding and landslides remained. By Friday morning, the Landes prefecture said more than 1,100 hectares had burned. No homes had been destroyed, but residents and a nearby campsite were evacuated as a precaution and taken to a reception centre in Sabres . Two departmental roads around Luglon were also closed to traffic. ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Around 500 firefighters were deployed alongside 40 forest‑fire vehicles , with aircraft including Canadairs, Dash water‑bombers and Air Tractors supporting the operation. Rising humidity overnight slowed the flames, but authorities warned that stronger winds could quickly worsen conditions. The fire came during a severe heatwave, with temperatures above 40 °C recorded in parts of the Landes. It followed several major fires in south‑western France this summer, including a blaze near Biscarrosse that burned about 3,700 hectares and destroyed around 200 homes and buildings. https://www.dw.com/en/can-a-massive-mado.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IpP1 People have been coming to see the statue of the Virgin Mary in Konotopie even before it is officially opened to the public on Saturday Image: Mateusz Kaczmarek/REUTERS Advertisement With its grain fields, meadows and lake, the countryside around the tiny village of Konotopie in central Poland is idyllic. Towering above all this is a monumental statue of the Virgin Mary. Home to just 120 residents and situated about 160 kilometers (99 miles) northwest of the capital, Warsaw, the previously little-known village of Konotopie has been in the headlines for weeks now as a result of the massive statue. The snow-white structure, which is visible for miles around, is over 55 meters (180 feet) tall. The statue itself is 40.6 meters high and stands on a 15-meter-high pedestal shaped like a crown that is intended to serve as a viewing platform. The figure dwarfs Rio de Janeiro's famous statue of Christ the Redeemer, which reaches a total height of 38 meters including its base. A 'pile of concrete' or a 'fantastic achievement'? The statue will be officially inaugurated on Saturday, August 15, the feast of the Assumption of Mary, a major holy day in the Catholic calendar. Although final construction work is still underway and the site remains fenced off and guarded, thousands of people — both pilgrims and sightseers — have been flocking to see it for months. Opinion about the project is divided. "It's a nightmare," one critic of the statue told the weekly magazine Newsweek, "a complete waste. Instead of investing that money in useful projects, they financed a giant pile of concrete." "This Mary is absolutely beautiful. My utmost respect. A fantastic achievement," said one devout lady visiting the site, according to the right-wing conservative weekly Sieci . Wealthy, devout benefactor The benefactor behind the statue, 75-year-old Roman Karkosik, hails from a nearby village and is one of Poland's wealthiest individuals. Nearly 40 years ago, when the shortage economy of socialism gave way to free-market capitalism after the collapse of communism in eastern Europe, Karkosik was a young graduate from technical high school. He started out as a bartender, but moved on to buying and selling scrap metal, producing soft drinks and later became the first entrepreneur in Poland to manufacture plastic bottles. The inauguration ceremony for the Marian statue coincides with a major Catholic holy day, the Feast of the Assumption of Mary, on August 15 Image: Kuba Stezycki/REUTERS Karkosik made a name for himself on the Warsaw Stock Exchange. Some journalists have compared his role in Poland to Warren Buffett's influence on Wall Street. His fortune is estimated at roughly €442 million ($511 million), and he ranks 44th on Wprost magazine's list of Poland's richest people. He lives in an 18th-century manor in the town of Kikol, just two kilometers from Konotopie. A 'gesture of gratitude' Karkosik and his wife, Grazyna, avoid both public appearances and contact with the media. The cost of the statue remains a closely guarded secret. Media reports speculate that the project may have cost as much as €23 million. The Karkosiks have described the Marian statue as a "gesture of gratitude." According to media reports, the devout businessman wanted to thank the Virgin Mary for his recovery from a serious illness. His two brothers, who were also successful businessmen, both died prematurely after illnesses. This is not the first time Karkosik has provided money for a religious structure. Back in 2011, he funded the construction of a church at a nearby pilgrimage site. Artist feared seeing the finished statue "I was afraid to come to Konotopie to see what had become of my design in reality," sculptor Adam Jakub Matejkowski told Polish media. Worried that the hands and face of the Virgin Mary might appear distorted, Matejkowski only visited the site in July. "I opened my eyes and was stunned. The Mother of God is opening her arms to embrace us," he said with satisfaction. "That was exactly my intention: for the figure to have a human character, to come toward us," he explained. The statue of Jesus Christ the King of the Universe in Swiebodzin, one of the tallest Jesus statues in the world, is also in Poland Image: Monika Skolimowska/ZB/dpa/picture alliance Matejkowski says the statue has the facial expression of his 11-year-old daughter and the delicate facial features of his wife. Region hopes for economic boost Konotopie is situated in one of Poland's economically weak regions. There are no major industrial employers here, and jobs are scarce. Local leaders hope the Marian statue will stimulate economic growth. "The monument is not only a spiritual landmark but also a strategic asset for the region. We expect it to attract more investors and tourists, which will benefit the local economy," Krzysztof Kowalewski of the authorities in the nearby town of Kikol told Polish media. Mayor Renata Golebiewska has said that revenues at local restaurants and bars have already broken local records. Not the first statue of its kind in Poland Poland is well known for its monumental Christian structures. Following Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, a massive basilica was built in the village of Lichen in central Poland, overshadowing even the cathedrals of Paris and Cologne in scale. The basilica is 138 meters (453 feet) long, 77 meters wide, and features a dome with a diameter of 35 meters. It can accommodate 20,000 worshippers. Since 2010, Poland has also been home to the world's tallest statue of Jesus. Located in Swiebodzin near the German border, the 36-meter-high statue stands on a 17-meter-high mound. Rising secularization Whether all these gigantic monuments can stop the ongoing secularization of Polish society, however, remains highly questionable. Although Poland is still one of the most Catholic countries in Europe, public trust in the Church continues to decline . For centuries, the Catholic faith was a key part of Polish identity. A huge statue of Pope John Paul II, who was born in Poland and was head of the Catholic Church from 1978 to 2005, in Czestochowa Image: Waldemar Deska/dpa/picture alliance In the 19th century, when the territory that now makes up Poland was not an independent state and was divided up among foreign powers, Catholicism played a major role in the resistance to Protestant Prussia and Orthodox Russia. After World War II, despite ideological differences, the anti-communist opposition and the Catholic Church in Poland worked together against the communist dictatorship. During this period, churches became refuges for persecuted dissidents, and several priests were murdered by the secret police. Pope John Paul II , himself Polish, also played a significant role in the struggle against the regime. Catholicism in modern-day Poland Since Poland's transition to democracy in 1989, however, the Catholic Church has experienced a crisis similar to that seen across Europe. According to a September 2025 survey conducted by the Polish polling institute IBRIS, only 35% of Poles still trust the Church, down from 58% in 2016. Distrust rose from 24% to 47% over the same period. In 2026, the annual number of priests ordained in Poland fell below 200 for the first time since 2000. Church attendance has also been steadily declining, especially among young people. Even a gigantic Madonna is unlikely to reverse that trend. This article was originally published in German. https://www.dw.com/en/nato-jets-shoot-do.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IofK The Italian Eurofighter was scrambled from a base in neighboring Lithuania Image: GIUSEPPE LAMI/ANSA/picture alliance Advertisement NATO fighter jets have shot down a drone that entered Latvian airspace, the alliance and Latvian authorities said Friday. Two Italian Eurofighters were scrambled and one destroyed the unmanned aircraft, while two Turkish F-16s were also deployed under NATO command. What happened over Latvia? Latvia's military initially issued an air alert and urged people in affected areas to remain indoors and seek shelter. Authorities said the foreign drone entered Latvian airspace over the Balvi region as a result of Russian electronic warfare activity. It was not immediately clear where the drone originated, and NATO said an investigation was underway. Latvian authorities did not identify the drone as Ukrainian. However, the reference to Russian electronic warfare raised the possibility that a Ukrainian drone targeting Russia had been forced off course by interference. How Baltic states are responding to Russia's hybrid warfare To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Ukrainian forces had attacked targets in northwestern Russia overnight, according to Latvian media. Has this happened before? Latvia and other NATO countries along the alliance's eastern flank have faced repeated incursions by drones since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. A stray drone was also shot down over Latvia in early June , while other Ukrainian drones heading toward northwestern Russia have previously entered Latvian airspace and crashed. Romanian and Spanish fighter jets were also deployed on Thursday after drones entered Romanian airspace near Ukraine. Why are Italian jets defending Latvian airspace? Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania do not operate their own fighter aircraft, so NATO allies rotate responsibility for policing their skies. The Italian Eurofighters involved in Friday's interception are based at Siauliai air base in Lithuania. https://www.dw.com/en/zambia-suspends-vo.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IpFh The commission said there had been instances where ​marked ballot papers in ballot boxes ⁠had ​been ​stolen Image: Moses Mwape/REUTERS Advertisement Zambia 's electoral commission has suspended the counting and announcement of election results nationwide with immediate effect, citing violence directed at election officials. The commission said ballot papers had also been stolen in some cases and that it would review the suspension within 24 hours. Why has Zambia suspended vote counting? The Electoral Commission of Zambia said the decision followed incidents of violence targeting polling staff. It added that ballot papers had been stolen in some locations, though it did not immediately give details on where the incidents occurred or how widespread they were. The general election is a major test for President Hakainde Hichilema, whose economic reform program has been weighed against widespread frustration over the cost of living. Around 8 million people were registered to vote in the southern African country of about 22 million people. Can Zambia trust election referee? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Voters were also choosing members of parliament and local councillors at more than 13,500 polling stations. Were there problems during voting? Long queues formed before dawn at polling stations in Lusaka, with some voters gathering around makeshift fires as they waited. Local observers reported delays and frustration at some polling stations because of poor voter guidance, confusion over voter rolls and crowd-management problems. European Union observers were monitoring the election. Hichilema came to power in 2021 after defeating longtime rival Edgar Lungu , who served as president from 2015 to 2021 and died in 2025. Lungu's political legacy still looms over the election, with Hichilema's main challenger Brian Mundubile leading an opposition alliance backed by many of the former president's supporters. https://www.dw.com/en/berlin-s-russian-h.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/4wSVN The Russian House has been a fixture on Berlin's Friedrichstrasse since 1984 Image: Schoening/picture alliance Advertisement The Russian House is centrally located on Friedrichstrasse in the heart of the German capital. As a throwback to a bygone era of friendly German-Russian relations , it is the subject of fierce disagreements and has long been a bone of contention in Berlin . The massive seven-story building covering an area of almost 30,000 square meters opened in 1984. At that time, back in the days of the East German state , its role was to celebrate friendship with the Soviet Union through concerts, film screenings and book readings. It even had its own small bookstore. But now, more than 40 years later, French authorities have linked the building to possible activities by Russian intelligence services. "In light of the measures taken against German cultural institutions and organizations , the federal government is comprehensively and continuously reviewing the legal basis of the Russian House under international treaty law,” said German Foreign Ministry spokesperson Martin Giese at a press conference in Berlin earlier this week. In response to a question from DW about the organization's future activities, Giese emphasized that there are two bilateral agreements between Germany and Russia regarding real estate matters that cannot be easily revoked. "It is, so to speak, an agreement that governs both the Russian House here in Berlin and the Goethe-Institut that we operate in Moscow," Giese said. Any action taken against one would also have direct consequences for the other. German tax money for Russian propaganda? The property on Friedrichstrasse belongs to Germany, yet the building is run by the Russian agency Rossotrudnichestvo, the Federal Agency for the Commonwealth of Independent States, Compatriots Living Abroad and International Humanitarian Cooperation. Rossotrudnichestvo, whose primary purpose is to promote the Russian language abroad, currently has dozens of similar institutions worldwide. The German Foreign Office has repeatedly stated that the employees of the institute have diplomatic status in Germany. Since 2022, following Russia's invasion of Ukraine , the agency has been on the EU sanctions list. At the time, the EU justified this by stating that the agency's goal was to consolidate "a wider public perception of the occupied Ukrainian territories as Russian." Moscow still maintains that the Russian House is a place to celebrate the friendship between the two countries: "The Russian House is Russia's cultural embassy in the heart of Berlin," according to the Russian Embassy's website. The events that take place there attract 200,000 visitors a year, according to Russian House organizers. Critics label them as propaganda. Symbols of friendship remained on display in Berlin's Russian House in October 2023, more than year after the Russian invasion of Ukraine Image: Dmyrto Katkov/DW Berlin media outlets have repeatedly reported on events at the in-house cinema where, for example, a Holocaust film was shown in which Ukrainian citizens were portrayed as Nazis . In an interview in August 2025, Robin Wagener, a member of the Bundestag for the opposition Green Party , told DW: "It is time we recognized that this is not mutual cultural exchange, but Russian war propaganda in Germany." Germany fears closure of Goethe-Institut in Moscow The Russian House is owned by the Russian Federation, but the Federal Republic of Germany pays the property tax for the building on the basis of its legal obligation under the bilateral German-Russian agreement on property issues relating to cultural institutes. Moscow and Berlin are also bound by the Intergovernmental Agreement on Cultural Cooperation, which was signed in December 1992 and entered into force in May 1993. It has a term of five years and is automatically extended for the same period unless one of the parties notifies the other at least six months before the expiration of the respective term. Both agreements — regarding the property of the Russian House and the Goethe-Institut, as well as the cultural cooperation between Russia and Germany — remain in force even in the fifth year of Russia's war against Ukraine. It is an open secret that the German government is shying away from conflict over the Russian House because it fears the Russian government could respond by closing the Goethe-Institut in Moscow. The institute was already forced to significantly scale back its operations in Russia in May 2023, when restrictions were imposed on the number of German officials in Russia. A few weeks earlier, the Goethe-Institut's bank accounts in Russia were frozen in retaliation after the Berlin Public Prosecutor's Office opened a preliminary investigation against the Russian House for violating sanctions and ordered the freeze of its accounts. Berlin detains German-Ukrainian woman for Russian espionage To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video So far, the Goethe-Institut continues to offer digital language courses in Russia. The libraries at its branches in Moscow and St. Petersburg continue to receive the latest German literature despite logistical difficulties, as representatives of the institute assured DW earlier this year. Direct Russian-German contacts have become virtually impossible According the cultural agreement, the contracting parties welcome "direct contacts between social groups and associations, including trade unions, churches, religious communities, artists' associations and political, cultural and other foundations." However, in recent years, several German foundations in Russia have been classified as "undesirable organizations." This includes the foundations run by Germany's established political parties. Anyone who cooperates with "undesirable organizations" faces criminal prosecution in Russia. This makes all direct contact provided for in the cultural agreement virtually impossible. The Ceuta government put the number of immigrants that have entered the city from Morocco in the past 24 hours at 60,000. A huge crowd of migrants poured into the Spanish territory of Ceuta overnight, after breaching the country’s border with Morocco. At least 41 died in the process. The Associated Press reported that the Ceuta government put the number of immigrants who have entered the city from Morocco in the past 24 hours at 60,000. Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain located on the northern coast of Africa. It shares its only land border with Morocco and, together with Melilla, another Spanish city, forms the European Union’s only land border with Africa. This incident occurred a day after Ceuta’s government said between 1,500 and 2,000 people entered in the last 10 days. Stay Ahead with Premium Times Follow us on Google News and never miss breaking stories, investigations, and in-depth reporting. Spain’s Prime Minister, Pedro Sanchez, has described the incident as an attack on Spain’s “territorial integrity” while vowing to ensure the safety of Ceuta residents. In a post on X, he said, “What has happened is an attack on Spain’s territorial integrity and deserves our most resounding and energetic condemnation.” He stated that his government was intensifying the presence of the “Security Forces and Corps in the city,” and that it would expedite the “repatriation files of the migrants who arrived irregularly.” “We will deploy a physical containment barrier in the sea to facilitate repatriation at the border, in compliance with the Supreme Court ruling,” he said. Authorities disclosed on Friday that some of the migrants died in the stampede while trying to breach the frontier, crossing the breakwater fence at Tarajal beach. Rachid Sbihi, who leads a local workers association representing Civil Guard officers, told the Associated Press that some of the 18 who died also drowned. Spanish broadcaster RTVE shared images of burned cars on the Moroccan side of the border after reported clashes. NBC also reported that video footage that surfaced showed several Moroccans walking around the breakwaters onto local roads. Most of them appeared to be young men, but the crowd also included families with women and small children. The deadly attempt to enter Ceuta is the latest in a series of dangerous crossings into Europe that have been recorded. Ceuta authorities described the situation as a “serious humanitarian crisis”. The mass migration also caused the regional president, Jesus Vivas, to declare an “absolute humanitarian and social emergency” on Thursday and call on Madrid to send troops to reassert control of the border. However, Spain’s Interior Ministry rejected calls to declare a national emergency, stating that such a measure does not apply to migration crises, but it promised additional resources. Meanwhile, the mass arrival by sea and land is threatening to trigger a political crisis for Pedro Sánchez, a left-wing, pro-immigration leader. European leaders have called for Spain’s temporary suspension from the bloc’s Schengen free-travel zone because of fears of a fresh migration crisis, leading to a diplomatic row between Rome and Madrid. France said it was increasing checks on its border with Spain. The Italian Prime Minister, Giorgia Meloni, threatened to demand Spain’s suspension from the 29-member Schengen zone, which stretches from Portugal to Poland. Ms Meloni warned of a threat to European security. “The images coming from Ceuta are striking and demonstrate, once again, that uncontrolled illegal migration poses a concrete threat to the security of Europe’s borders,” she said. Approximately 40% of end-buyers are looking for houses, villas and large apartments, while studios and one-bedroom apartments account for 48% of all properties viewed and saved in the North Bucharest app. Romania’s residential market continues to be driven by genuine demand, while buyer profiles and purchasing preferences continue to evolve. Based on aggregated data from the North Bucharest app and the company’s commercial activity over the past few months, North Bucharest Investments ‘ latest analysis highlights two key trends shaping today’s market: growing demand for spacious homes intended for owner-occupation and strengthening investment demand from Romanians living abroad. According to the analysis, approximately 40% of active end-buyers are currently searching for houses, villas and large apartments , typically within a budget range of €600,000 to €800,000 . This category of buyers primarily values space, comfort, construction quality and premium locations, making them less sensitive to short-term market fluctuations. At the same time, North Bucharest Investments has observed steadily increasing interest from Romanians living abroad , who continue to return to Romania’s residential market with investment objectives. Most are focusing on studios and one-bedroom apartments , recognising their strong rental potential and long-term capital appreciation. This trend is also reflected in user behaviour within the North Bucharest app, where 48% of all properties viewed and saved over the recent period are studios and one-bedroom apartments, making them the platform’s most popular property category. Continued demand is also reflected in the performance of the North Bucharest digital platform. Over the past 30 days, the application recorded a 42% increase in users , generating more than 115,000 interactions , while usage of the AI Search feature increased by approximately 35% compared to the previous month. During the same period, users generated more than 51,700 property gallery swipes , over 30,400 AI-powered searches , more than 10,500 Property Tinder interactions , nearly 8,800 Property Tinder Quiz responses , over 8,100 content views , approximately 7,200 screen navigations , more than 5,500 mortgage calculator sessions , and over 4,000 property search filters . The North Bucharest app provides access to more than 1,400 completed properties and over 100 residential developments , bringing together AI Search, a 24/7 AI-powered virtual assistant, Property Tinder, a mortgage calculator, an interactive map, smart alerts and direct access to experienced real estate consultants within a single platform. Vlad Musteață, CEO of North Bucharest Investments , said: “Our analysis of data generated through the North Bucharest app confirms that Romania’s residential market remains active and that buyer behaviour continues to evolve. We are seeing growing demand for houses, villas and spacious apartments from end-buyers, while Romanians living abroad continue to view Bucharest’s residential market as an attractive investment opportunity. We currently have approximately 190 transactions at various stages of completion, a volume comparable to the same period last year, confirming that demand for residential properties remains strong. These transactions depend on the restoration of ANCPI’s operational workflows, and once its operations return to normal, we expect the pace of transaction completions to accelerate accordingly.” The North Bucharest Investments analysis shows that Bucharest’s residential market continues to be supported by genuine demand from both end-buyers and investors. At the same time, insights generated through the North Bucharest app provide a valuable picture of evolving consumer preferences and confirm the increasingly important role of technology and artificial intelligence in the property search and home-buying process. https://nineoclock.ro/medlife-launches-t.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Bucharest, July 31, 2026 – MedLife , in partnership with the Tășuleasa Social Association , announces the launch of an observational study conducted along Via Transilvanica, built around the concept of Good Stress (eustress) —a principle that is gaining increasing recognition in lifestyle medicine and longevity research. The concept suggests that controlled exposure to physical and mental challenges can activate the body’s natural adaptive mechanisms and strengthen both physical and emotional resilience. The study aims to evaluate the impact of long-distance walking on physical and emotional health in a real-world setting of sustained physical effort. It will investigate how the body responds to a multi-day walking experience in nature by analyzing biological markers alongside changes in well-being, energy levels, perceived stress, and emotional state. The study will examine, under real-life conditions, how long-distance walking influences physical health, emotional well-being, and the body’s ability to adapt to stress. The initiative builds on the findings of a recent MedLife perception study, which revealed that only one in eight Romanians regularly goes hiking, while most people continue to associate walking primarily with physical health benefits rather than its positive effects on emotional well-being. The observational study will combine objective medical measurements with qualitative research to better understand the effects of sustained walking in nature on the human body. Relevant health biomarkers will be assessed before and after participants complete their route on Via Transilvanica , while in-depth interviews will explore the emotions, motivations, and personal transformations experienced throughout the journey. All medical tests and assessments included in the MedLife study will be provided free of charge to participants, as part of an important preventive healthcare initiative. Registration opens today at www.medlife.ro/stresul-bun-via-transilvanica . The initiative is part of MedLife’s broader commitment to generating meaningful data for preventive and lifestyle medicine and is based on the findings of a recent nationwide study examining Romanians’ perceptions of physical activity. The quantitative survey, conducted by Unlock Research in May 2026 on behalf of MedLife, highlighted a clear paradox. Although Romanians acknowledge the importance of physical activity for maintaining good health, increasingly sedentary lifestyles continue to dominate. More than half of respondents (56%) reported spending most of their working day sitting, 26% said they regularly walk longer distances, while only one in eight Romanians (12%) regularly goes hiking or completes nature trails. At the same time, the study found that walking is still perceived primarily through the lens of physical health. Its benefits for emotional well-being and psychological resilience remain largely underrecognized, despite the fact that frequent hikers report higher energy levels, greater overall well-being, and a stronger ability to cope with everyday challenges. Building on these findings, MedLife is launching an observational study that combines sociological research methods with biological assessments to complement perception-based data with real-world observations. The research will examine how both the body and emotional well-being respond to sustained walking in nature. https://www.naturalnews.com/2026-07-31-p.text: Polish and Romanian authorities stopped accepting further deliveries in 2022, citing falling demand. Both governments have said they will appeal the ruling. The enforcement action has raised questions about the financial stability of the two countries' air navigation agencies, which rely on the funds. Contract Origins and Refused Deliveries The contract was signed between the European Commission and Pfizer in 2021, and it obligated participating member states to purchase additional doses. By 2022, Poland and Romania refused scheduled deliveries as demand declined. Poland cited financial pressure from hosting refugees fleeing Ukraine. Romanian political scientist Dragos Moldoveanu said Romania ordered 120 million doses despite a population below 20 million and had one of the European Union's lowest vaccination rates. Pfizer filed suit in 2023 after the countries did not pay for doses they declined to accept. Earlier contract terms had already drawn criticism. The Bureau of Investigative Journalism reported in February 2021 that Pfizer was demanding countries put up sovereign assets as collateral for expected vaccine injury lawsuits [2] . Legal Enforcement and Appeals Because the contract is governed by Belgian law, the case is being heard in Brussels. Polish public broadcaster TVP World reported that Poland asked the Belgian court to delay enforcement while it appeals, but the request was rejected. Dutch attorney Meike Terhorst called the action "outrageous and unethical" and said it could endanger flights. Lukasz Wojdyga of the Warsaw Enterprise Institute said the creditor has a legal right to enforce the judgment but called targeting air-safety funding "disproportionate and irresponsible." Both governments have said they will protect the financial stability of the agencies and keep services running. Transparency and Contract Scrutiny The dispute has revived scrutiny of the EU vaccine procurement. Brussels Signal reported the EU-Pfizer contract was worth 35 billion euros ($40 billion), one of the largest contract awards in EU history. Governments and Pfizer have declined to release contract terms, saying the information is commercially confidential [3] . The European Court of Justice ruled in 2024 that the European Commission violated EU law when it denied The New York Times' request to review text messages between Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and Pfizer CEO Albert Bourla [4] . In 2025, a court ordered the disclosure of concealed texts related to the deal [5] . European Parliament member Gheorghe Piperea said the contract "ought never to have existed" because the EU exceeded its treaty powers. Transparency activist Frederic Baldan said von der Leyen negotiated directly with Bourla through self-destructing Signal messages, and that a Belgian Federal Police anti-corruption report found sufficient elements to establish offenses. Baldan said the European Public Prosecutor's Office moved to have the investigation annulled. The scale of the purchases also drew criticism from public health writers. Michel Chossudovsky questioned how a vaccine that normally takes years to develop was launched within months [6] . Joseph Mercola and Ronnie Cummins noted that the trials' only criterion of success was a reduction of moderate to severe symptoms, not prevention of infection [7] . Impact on Air Traffic Agencies and Next Steps TVP World reported that the frozen funds account for more than 80% of the revenue of Poland's air navigation agency, PANSA. Brussels Signal reported the agency could lose financial liquidity and the ability to maintain radar and communication systems. Romania Insider reported the frozen amount equals 0.2% of Romania's GDP, adding strain while the government tries to reduce its fiscal deficit. Piperea said the ruling arrived during a recession and a budgetary deficit and that Pfizer "leaves the public in danger" by depleting the funds of Romania's air traffic agency, ROMATSA. Wojdyga said he would not equate the freeze with an immediate safety threat because both agencies are operating. The Warsaw Enterprise Institute wrote that the case shows how a poorly designed public contract can create problems beyond the original agreement. Both countries have said they will continue appeals, and air navigation officials have said services remain operational. The episode illustrates the broad consequences of what critics describe as a secretive procurement process [3] . References Children's Health Defense. https://catholicphilly.com/2026/07/news/.text: Archdiocese of Philadelphia Get our newsletter Advertise with us Archdiocese of Philadelphia Get our newsletter Advertise with us News Local News Catholic Education Catholic Charities of Philadelphia People and Events Sports Obituaries Calendar of Events Submit your event USCCB News and Statements Vatican News Features Photo Features Video Features Commentaries Catholic Spirituality Podcasts Profile Hispanic Catholics Archbishop Pérez’s Messages Catholic Directory Support Our Work Newsletter Signup About Us St. Charles Seminary Receives $1 Million Anonymous Gift to Support Endowment Kevin Williams Retires From ‘Job Well Done’ for 46 Years Serving Seniors Archbishop Pérez Asks for Prayers Ahead of Days for Educators How the 1976 Eucharistic Congress Put Catholic Diversity on Display Handmaids of the Sacred Heart Mark 100 Years of Sharing ‘Joyful Love’ Archdiocesan High Schools, Teachers Union Ratify New Three-Year Contract 41 ‘Pierogi Pilgrims’ from Philadelphia Find God in Poland’s Holy Sites By Jay Sorgi • Posted July 31, 2026 More than 40 young Philadelphians traveled to Poland July 2-12 on a pilgrimage seeking God. They found the Lord in expected and unexpected places, with poignance from lost loved ones, in persistent symbols of faith that rebuilt a nation, and in the unabashed joy of a surprise engagement and future matrimony. Pauline Father Timothy Tarnacki, the director of the archdiocesan Office for Ministry with Young Adults (OMYA), took 41 Catholics on the pilgrimage themed “We Want God!” to a series of holy sites and other stops in Poland, a nation long-defined and even reborn through the Catholic faith that permeates within the Eastern European land. “With the pilgrimage design and Father Timothy’s guidance, we really saw how connected faith and culture, and truly everything is in Poland,” pilgrim Mairwen Minson said. “We visited religious sites and historical sites, but really all of them were religious. The faith is so built into Poland and it is a gift to see that.” Each participant received a 102-page journal filled with related Saints of the Day plus daily Mass readings accompanying the liturgies they would encounter during the pilgrimage. Father Tarnacki, a native of Poland who came to the United States as a boy, says the journey was not about himself but about God touching the lives of the assembled young adults under 40 years old who came with him. Yet it was impossible for him to not be touched by how he brought new friends from across an ocean to places that have deeply touched his own faith life. That includes Jasna Góra, the Sanctuary of Our Lady of Częstochowa that houses the original Black Madonna icon, and its attached monastery in Częstochowa that was part of his own pathway with the Pauline Fathers. “That is the heart of Polish spirituality, and I spent every summer there,” he said. “Throughout the year, we would be very often sent there to minister at the shrine. That’s such a big part of my formation and the charism of my community.” Laura Lindmeier encountered the day of a lifetime beside that Black Madonna icon. “The icon itself tells the story of the Polish people whose deep devotion has been tied to a history of deep suffering,” said Lindmeier, whose spiritual journey has often been anchored at the National Shrine of Our Lady of Czestochowa in Doylestown. “I encountered Our Lady’s tenderness in a new way,” she added. “Our group had the privilege of celebrating a private Mass in the chapel which houses the original miraculous icon.” Then after she helped lead music for the Mass with her boyfriend, Alvaro, the blessed surprise of a lifetime happened. “Álvaro got down on one knee and proposed immediately after the Mass had finished!” she said. “I was absolutely floored! Father Timothy’s homily that day spoke of the icon and the loving gaze of Our Lady over unique moments in our life. I felt this so clearly. Beneath her gaze, I said yes to my vocation with profound peace and joy, a vocation which promises to hold tenderness and suffering ever in tension, just as she does.” Father Tarnacki plans on being a celebrant for their wedding. Pilgrims traveled to the Sanctuary of the Birth of the Blessed Virgin Mary in Giertzwald, the Shrine of St. Faustina and the Tomb of Blessed Jerzy Popiełuszko in Warsaw, the location in Krakow where St. Stanislaus was martyred, the city of Wadowice where St. John Paul II was born and where a museum is dedicated to him, and the city’s Our Lady of the Calvary Shrine, and then a return to Krakow with a Mass at the Chapel of the Tomb of St. Faustina. “I had been struggling to talk to Mary because of some losses,” Minson said. “Going to Giertzwald, the Marian apparition site, was both the hardest and best day of the pilgrimage for me. I genuinely wanted to hide from my pain and Mary’s presence, but with the group there, I stayed and had such a healing conversation with Mary. It was incredible, to sob and get through my grief with Mary there guiding me through what I needed.” The pilgrimage also included time marking how totalitarianism attempted to drown the Catholic faith, from fascism in World War II to communism during the Cold War era. In both cases, the Church more than survived — it served as the response. The young adults saw both the horrors of the Nazi concentration and extermination camp at Auschwitz-Birkenau, and the hope and joy of the European Solidarity Centre in Gdansk, a city of the Catholic-inspired Solidarity resistance to the Soviet bloc rule of Poland at the time. “We remembered the story of St. Maximilian Kolbe as we visited the starvation bunker that served as the place of his martyrdom,” Lindmeier said of the saint’s willingness to give his life for another person at Auschwitz. “St. Maximilian Kolbe, in imitation of Christ, proves that sacrificial love is what gives these gifts their staying power and why they are worthy of laying down one’s life.” Colleen Flannery, who has Polish heritage, saw many examples of the resilience of the Polish people, deeply imbued within the Catholic faith. “We were on the pilgrimage over the Fourth of July holiday, and it felt so different not being home, but being abroad helped me to see freedom through a different lens,” she said. “It put into perspective how precious freedom is, and how important it is to safeguard and not take it for granted.” Andrea Maychak celebrated a birthday that led to a most Polish, and appropriate, surprise. Father Tarnacki “surprised me with the most appropriate birthday presents: a pierogi pillow paired with a third class relic of Pope John Paul II,” she said. “I joked the rest of the trip that I was a ‘pierogi pilgrim!’’’ The 41 who came from Philadelphia returned with more than pierogis. Father Tarnacki believes they came back changed. “It’s just amazing to see how the Lord works in these kinds of pilgrimages, because the pilgrimage is all about transformation,” he said. “It’s all about encountering God on the way, and I think that’s what has been happening through the Holy Spirit.” Join the CatholicPhilly.com family CatholicPhilly.com works to strengthen the connections between people, families and communities every day by delivering the news people need to know about the Catholic Church, especially in the Philadelphia region, and the world in which we live. The Bulgaria News Agency reported that the ship became stranded early Tuesday about 15 miles upstream from Vidin, where it planned to stop to take on supplies. https://www.thewrap.com/industry-news/de.text: Getting your Trinity Audio player ready… Members of the Block the Merger Coalition have sent three separate letters to U.K. Secretary for Culture, Media and Sport Lisa Nandy urging her to formally intervene in the pending $110 billion Paramount-Warner Bros. Discovery merger. Nandy previously informed Paramount and WBD that she’s “minded” to intervene in the deal while asking for them to address her concerns over whether the deal would result in a “sufficient plurality” of views in news media and address the need for “sufficient plurality of persons with control of the media enterprises, or the enterprises providing on-demand [program] services or both, serving that audience.” The filings from the Democracy Defenders Fund , Archival Producers Alliance (APA) , Documentary Film Council and International Documentary Association (IDA) ask Nandy to issue a Public Interest Intervention Notice (PIIN) and refer the merger for a more in-depth Phase 2 investigation with a “view to prohibition or obtaining strong, suitable, structural remedies.” Read Next UK Government ‘Minded to Intervene’ on Paramount-WBD Deal After Review The Block the Merger Coalition warned that the merged entity would become the third-largest linear broadcaster in the U.K. and reach 19% of the population through its on-demand services before accounting for HBO Max. They claimed that the deal would result in the “reduction in the plurality of persons controlling ODPS serving U.K. audiences,” citing CEO David Ellison’s plans to combine Paramount+ and HBO Max into a single platform. They also said that the merger would hand a single owner a significant proportion of children’s linear channels operating in the U.K. that could be consolidated into Paramount and extinguish a significant presence in the market; would put the CNN and CBS News archives under a single owner and “worsen discretionary gatekeeping of archival materials,” impacting U.K. documentarians’ ability to tell diverse stories; and would bring Channel 5 News, CBS News, CNN and CNN International under the common ownership of a single controlling family and could potentially “eliminate at least one distinct voice in the U.K. market for international and U.S. news programming.” APA represents over 700 archive producers from around the globe, while IDA represents over 3,500 documentary professionals across 75 countries. Read Next Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger Cleared by European Commission With Conditions The U.K. Competition and Markets Authority will decide on whether it will clear the merger, seek remedies or launch a Phase 2 investigation by Aug. 7. Meanwhile, the deal has been cleared by the U.S. Department of Justice , Warner Bros. shareholders and the European Commission , who implemented conditions such as an exit from United International Pictures. Other countries where the deal has received clearance or where relevant waiting periods have expired include Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, China, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Serbia, South Africa, Ukraine, Montenegro, New Zealand and North Macedonia. Foreign direct investment authorities in Spain, Germany, Slovenia, Belgium, Czechia, Italy, France and Romania have also signed off. In addition to the U.K., Paramount’s litigation with the 12 state attorneys general and the Writers Guild of America will move to an antitrust trial , with the date for a specific hearing to be announced. The media giant agreed to delay the closing of its merger until five days after the outcome of a trial or June 1, 2027, whichever is earliest. A Paramount shareholder and a group of consumers also filed separate lawsuits to block the merger, though the latter was denied a preliminary injunction after a judge ruled that they failed to show irreparable harm or that their case would have a likelihood of success. In the event the transaction does not close by Sept. 30, WBD shareholders will receive a 25 cent per share “ticking fee” for each quarter until closing , which translates to a payout of roughly $650 million per quarter, or $7 million per day. In the event that the deal does not close at all due to regulatory matters, Paramount will pay WBD a $7 billion termination fee. Read Next Paramount Agrees to Push Warner Bros. Merger as Far Back as Summer 2027

https://www.marinelink.com/news/low-wate.text: Low Water Levels in European Rivers Warn of Economic Impact Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. July 31, 2026 © Adobe Stock/Leonid Andronov Record low water levels in Europe's major rivers have curtailed the transport of goods, reduced electricity output and shrunk company earnings, stoking fears about the economic impact of searing heat and erratic rainfall. As Europe experiences the fastest warming of any continent and record-breaking heatwaves, drought has exposed the need to reconsider business practices. From the bustling port of Rotterdam to hydropower plants in Serbia, waterways have become a less reliable way to transport goods such as grains and oil, or to produce much-needed electricity when millions are seeking to cool their homes. "It's affecting not one region like we've seen in the past, but the whole European landscape," said Alessandro Armenia, a power analyst at commodities data and analytics firm Kpler. "Given the current dynamics, it means either we're going to see blackouts or we need to invest way more." HYDROPOWER AND NUCLEAR OUTPUT CUT Production of nuclear power in Hungary and hydropower in Serbia have fallen because of record low water levels along the Danube, which passes through major cities like Vienna, Budapest and Belgrade on its route from Germany to the Black Sea. The Paks nuclear power plant, which generates nearly half of Hungary's electricity, will be shut down on Monday, possibly for weeks because water levels on the river, which supplies cooling water to the facility, are expected to stay too low for it to operate safely. At Djerdap 1, Serbia's largest hydropower plant, output has fallen to 20% of capacity, the plant's production director Davor Maljokovic told Reuters, as the once broad shipping channel beside it has shrunk to expose sandbanks and gravel bars. The lack of water has also disrupted cooling systems at Serbia's Kostolac coal-fired power plants, forcing them to cut output, Serbia's state EPS power utility said. Both Serbia and Hungary say they will make up for the losses by importing electricity, a costly measure when demand on the spot market is high. Romania's state nuclear power producer Nuclearelectrica also had to shut one of its two reactors earlier this week for the same reason, with the second expected to soon follow, potentially depriving the country of a fifth of its electricity needs. France has also had to reduce nuclear power generation because of low water levels or rising river temperatures. WATER LEVELS ALSO DISRUPT TRANSPORT Energy is not the only loser. Cezar Gheorghe of Romanian grain market consultancy AGRIColumn told Reuters on Friday farmers along the Danube were having problems shipping their crops because low water levels stopped barges from using several river ports. “Only the ports which are closer to the Black Sea are still operational. Barges can’t go through the others,” Gheorghe said. “Crops buyers could offer farmers lower prices and load them in trucks, although there might also be a shortage of trucks.” Meanwhile, the volume of cargo transported to and from Rotterdam - Europe's largest sea port - to the Rhine has fallen slightly each week since the beginning of July and is around 10% lower than normal, a port spokesperson told Reuters. Chemical and oil product tankers and dry bulk carriers are particularly affected because of their normally greater draught compared to container barges, which means they sit deeper in the water and require greater water depths. DROUGHT REDUCES COMPANY EARNINGS Apart from the natural devastation of wildfires and temperatures that have caused thousands of excess deaths, companies' balance sheets have suffered from the changing climate. Austrian utility Verbund, which produced about 85% of its electricity from hydropower last year, said on Thursday that drought conditions reduced earnings by about €370 million in the first half compared with a year of normal hydrological conditions. French state-owned utility EDF said on Friday that full-year earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation for 2026 were expected to fall by 10% because of low market prices and as heatwaves reduced power output. In Italy, the Po River basin has entered a state of high water scarcity, threatening rice crops and drinking water supplies across the north. Chief Executive of regional utility A2A, Renato Mazzoncini, said he expected hydropower production this year of 3.9 TWh compared to a historical average of 4.1. "Some of our reservoirs are under pressure," he said. "We practically need to start doing a rain dance."
