https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/run.text: The Budapest Times Running on empty: the Danube is draining the lights Following a trial run on Friday evening, the Dunamenti Power Plant is expected to operate at full capacity from Saturday, while the Paks nuclear power plant is currently running at close to half of its nominal output. Due to falling water levels caused by continuing heat and drought, further production cutbacks and a temporary complete shutdown of the nuclear power plant will be necessary in the coming days. Prime Minister Péter Magyar announced on Friday that Hungary is facing an energy crisis of unprecedented difficulty and complexity. At a press conference held at Mol’s Duna Refinery in Százhalombatta, the Prime Minister outlined that the Paks nuclear power plant is operating at a reduced output of approximately 940 megawatts — compared to its nominal 2,000 megawatts — due to the Danube reaching a record low water level. Péter Magyar stated that the water level had dropped to -124 centimetres by Friday, and that at -134 centimetres the plant must be shut down for safety reasons. The head of government warned that expert forecasts indicate the water level could fall as low as -144 centimetres, and stressed that no rise is expected in the short term. He said that in the critical situation very little power plant capacity is available in Hungary, and that following the loss of output from the Paks nuclear power plant, the country would rely primarily on solar power plants, a few gas-fired power plants, and imports. The production shortfall from Paks would be offset by increasing import capacity, with imports potentially rising from 3,600–3,800 megawatts to as much as 4,500–5,000 megawatts. The country imports electricity from all of its neighbouring countries. Péter Magyar called it disinformation that Hungary could face difficulties because it exports electricity to Ukraine, and said it was also false that the utility cost reduction scheme was under threat. He noted that it cannot be entirely ruled out that residential electricity restrictions may be necessary; however, they are doing everything possible to avoid prolonged, widespread outages. He asked Foreign Minister Anita Orbán to contact Austria, Slovakia, and Germany in order to review the water retention practices of hydroelectric power plants operating on the upper section of the Danube. The Prime Minister also stated that the restart of a block at the Dunamenti Power Plant, which was shut down due to a technical fault, could begin on Friday, with the facility potentially operating at full capacity from Saturday. At Hungary’s second largest gas-fired power plant, output had to be reduced by 380 megawatts on Wednesday evening. The Prime Minister also touched on the fact that some large consumers had already responded to the request to voluntarily limit their energy consumption — for example, Mol, one of Hungary’s largest industrial consumers, committed to reducing its electricity use by 65 megawatts, approximately 40 percent, during the critical period. He added that further large consumers would also be asked to introduce voluntary restrictions, and indicated that a legislative basis would soon be in place to allow entire plants to be shut down if necessary in order to maintain the balance of the system. He also noted that electricity consumption had come in 151 megawatts below the peak load expected for the previous day, owing to the voluntary restrictions by companies and the public. The critical period remains between 17:00 and 22:00, with network load at its highest between 18:00 and 21:00. ( AP Photo: Julia Demaree Nikhinson ) abc.net.au/news/global-politics-driven-strongmen-disturbing-directions/106982606 Link copied Share Share article For much of the past decade, a lot of what has unfolded in the world has been seen through the idea of the rise of strongmen in global politics. Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin have headed the list, along with Recep Tayyip Erdoğan in Türkiye. And that's not to mention the ones who have come and gone in the meantime: Hungary's Viktor Orbán, Jair Bolsonaro in Brazil, Rodrigo Duterte in the Philippines. But so much has been transformed in the past year. In the United States and Russia, two of the strongmen may still hold unprecedented power within their countries, and seek to exert on the rest of the world, but they do so with rapidly diminishing credibility and effectiveness. Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin have headed the list of strongmen in global politics, along with Xi Jinping. ( Reuters: Kevin Lamarque/File Photo ) Trump's rambling pronouncements — someone described them this week as "fantasy announcements" — barely rate any immediate quiver in world markets, let alone diplomatic circles. For example, there was cautious early reporting in international media on Friday morning, Australian time, of his announcement on social media of a "HISTORIC agreement for the COMPLETE DISARMAMENT of Hamas and all other armed groups in Gaza". As is so often the case these days, everyone immediately wanted to know if anybody else had actually agreed to this agreement. As The New York Times reported: "There was no immediate comment from Hamas or Israel, and it was not clear whether either had signed off on the plan after years of war and a fragile ceasefire." A new conflation of important factors It's not just that some of the strongmen don't seem so strong anymore, that they often just seem to be lashing out reasonably ineffectively, or even that the "Great Powers" don't seem to be running things. It's that there is a new conflation of factors proving to be just as important, if not more so, in driving world events in increasingly disturbing directions. These include the dividend of years of greater powers' efforts at destabilising other states; the rise of states that have never quite got to be stable in the first place; and of the role of non-state actors. More recently there has been the rapidly and relentlessly expanding story of how technological change in warfare — and rapidly diminishing stockpiles of defensive weapons — are transforming geopolitical power. Will Hamas disarm? Experts say 'it's difficult to believe' Middle East analysts are sceptical Hamas will willingly lay down its weapons and that Israel will totally withdraw from Gaza. Just in this week alone, we have seen the conflicts in the Middle East and Ukraine spread inexorably: conspicuously dragging in Saudi Arabia as well as conflicts in Iraq, Syria and Yemen continuing to escalate. But Egypt has now also found itself under attack. Also, Ukraine directly attacked an Iranian vessel in the Caspian Sea, a move which linked the Iranian and Ukrainian conflicts. It also reflected Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's apparent attempts to highlight Russian support for Iran to the US president days before he went to see Trump in Washington. Then there are reports — denied by the Chinese — of a major deal to deliver Chinese arms to Iran. In Europe, NATO jets scrambled this week as a Russian missile entered Polish airspace and crashed. Ukraine has expressed alarm that North Korea is about to send another 30,000 troops to Russia to support its campaign. Yet even with all this, the impacts of the major conflicts of the time don't just involve crossfire and manpower. Trump scuttles nuclear power deal with Saudi Arabia Russia, one of the world's largest resource economies, is now importing oil from India because of the damage Ukraine has inflicted on its energy infrastructure. The European Union is struggling with a dilemma about placing sanctions on an aluminium smelter in Ireland owned by Russian interests because European nations also need the aluminium. There are reports that Ukraine has been buying Chinese drone components from an EU defence loan. The chaos that Trump's increasingly erratic interventions create was highlighted this week by the announcement of a nuclear power deal with Saudi Arabia — a 30-year legal framework that would let US companies build nuclear infrastructure and export civilian nuclear technology to Saudi Arabia while blocking foreign competitors such as China and Russia. Saudi Arabia must recognise Israel for nuclear deal, says Trump A newly brokered nuclear energy deal between the US and Saudia Arabia has drawn criticism from Israeli officials who say it tempts a nuclear arms race in the Middle East. Critics pointed out some of the alarming shortcomings of the deal. It would allow Saudi Arabia to develop a full-blown civilian nuclear industry (OK so far) but without international safeguards. Unlike stricter historical precedents like the US deal with the United Arab Emirates, reports indicate this agreement may permit Saudi enrichment on its own soil over time. As former director-general of the Australian Safeguards and Non-Proliferation Office John Carlson wrote this week: "This deal compromises both the non-proliferation standards that up to now have been applied by the United States, and the contemporary standard for International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards applied under the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT)." And, just saying, it would set up exactly the same ecosystem that the US and Israel find so threatening in Iran when it comes to nuclear power, presumably on the presumption that Saudi will always be a friendly state. Just to confuse things further, Trump then effectively scuttled the deal by saying Saudi would have to sign up to being friends with Israel under the Abraham Accords if the deal were to proceed. Which Saudi won't do. In doing so, Trump only highlighted how insane the whole situation in the Middle East really is. The irony of Israel's invasions The Arab world in general is going to remain conflicted about Israel, and possibly only become more so, as Israel escalates its brutality and ambitions in what are still technically Palestinian territories, and against Palestinian people. That is despite the Gulf states' continuing anxiety about Iran. The ambiguity of Trump's meeting with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu this week showed what a mire both countries are now in, partly because of this conflicted, ambivalent position of so many of Israel's neighbours. Israel may have felt briefly that it had emerged as the new hegemon in the region. And it continues to redefine the language of international affairs by describing invasions into other territories — now Lebanon and Syria as well as Gaza and the West Bank — as "buffer zones". Israel supporting nascent governments in the region, rather than destabilising them, at some point must become an issue. ( Reuters: Ronen Zvulun ) There is an irony in this, as analyst Gregory Gause pointed out in the latest issue of Foreign Affairs magazine. "Netanyahu believes that Israel is safer when its neighbours are weak and divided," Gause writes. "But he misses the fact that Israel's peace treaties with Egypt and Jordan, two consolidated states that can control their borders and prevent the rise of violent non-state actors in their territory, have been the enduring pillars of Israel's security for decades. "Rather than embrace the prospect of a cooperative Lebanese government willing to work against Hezbollah, Israel renewed its war in Lebanon in 2026. "In Syria, Israel captured a so-called buffer zone, encouraged Syrian Druze to resist the new government, armed Druze militias, and struck Syrian army positions — including the headquarters of the Ministry of Defence — in the name of protecting the Druze." Supporting nascent governments in the region, rather than destabilising them, at some point must become an issue. "Iran's allies, although weakened, still wield significant influence across the Arab world. In Iraq's elections in November 2025, Shiite parties aligned with Iran and the Iraqi militias it backs performed well," Gause writes. "In February, March, and April of this year, those militias lobbed missiles at US bases in the region. The new Iraqi government under Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi, like its predecessors, has filled important positions with many of Iran's local allies." Which brings us to Iran. Loading A more sophisticated assessment of Iran Two major analysts of Iran, Narges Bajoghli and Vali Nasr, both of Johns Hopkins University, have also written in the latest Foreign Affairs , offering a somewhat more sophisticated assessment of the Iranian leadership and its strategy than we get from Trump's expletive-laden assertions of imminent collapse. The new generation of Iranian leadership, the two men say, "has separated revolution from statecraft". "At home and abroad, it neither espouses revolutionary grandiosity nor advocates revolutionary activism." The new leaders, Bajoghli and Nasr write, are "establishment actors: pragmatic, hardened nationalists operating with a clear-eyed assessment of Iran's capabilities and vulnerabilities". "Unlike their predecessors, they can exercise strategic patience and act decisively. They look at Iran's weaknesses frequently and publicly — something the founding generation was too insecure to do honestly — and they treat them as problems to be solved." Trump vows to hit Iran 'hard' in expletive ridden warning In a phone interview with Fox News, the US president reportedly said the US would "beat the f****** s***" out of Iran in response to the surprise strikes. The Islamic Republic had long operated through a chaotic maze of competing power centres, which produced unending internal debate and sclerotic inertia. But they say this chaos has given way "to organisational discipline and resilience" with a structure involving defence, civilian and economic bureaucracies. As a result, Bajoghli and Nasr say, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice-President JD Vance "are wrong" in their fundamental assessment of Iran. "Tehran's defiant approach reflects neither ideological rigidity nor factional infighting," they write. "The country's leaders understand that the United States is seeking to get from talks what it could not achieve in war and that Washington is not interested in a deal but in Iran's surrender." The only problem is "Iranian leaders already claim they have won the war". "This self-confidence — rooted in the belief that the war has empowered Iran rather than weakened it — is informing their international outlook." Abroad, they say this does not mean it will abandon its regional allies, such as Hezbollah, Shiite militias in Iraq and the Houthis in Yemen. "But it will manage them with more strategic discipline and less ideological romanticism." The new Iranian leadership will not sacrifice Iran's interests at the altar of revolutionary solidarity, Bajoghli and Nasr say. "These alliances will be deployed as part of a coherent regional strategy designed to sustain Iran's strategic depth against sustained US and Israeli pressure." The most important message in that assessment, of course, is that Iran actually has a coherent regional strategy. Something that cannot necessarily be said for the great powers who might like to think they can still call the shots. Laura Tingle is the ABC's Global Affairs Editor. Photograph: Gianni Barbieux/Photo News View image in fullscreen Kobe said the gold was ‘really bricked in there – not in a safe or anything’. Photograph: Gianni Barbieux/Photo News Belgium Belgian student strikes gold worth €9m while digging a new sewer Kobe, 18, who made discovery on site of former brewery in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, at first thought trove was €1 coins Jon Henley Europe correspondent Fri 14 Aug 2026 11.52 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.30 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google For a student with a summer job working on a Belgian building site, “money down the drain” has taken on a whole new meaning: excavating the trenches for a sewage system, he stumbled across a hidden trove of gold worth an estimated €9m (£8m). “We suddenly saw something lying there,” 18-year-old Kobe told the Belgian news network VTM . “At first I thought it was €1 coins. So we started digging them up. Then we saw a gold bar. It turned out to be a bit more than we thought.” The student, who has not been further identified, was working with colleagues on the site of a former brewery on Van Langenhovestraat in Sint-Gillis-Dendermonde, about 19 miles (30km) north-west of Brussels, when they made the discovery on Tuesday. View image in fullscreen The hoard was stashed in a bag in a bricked-in cellar wall beneath the grand villa. Photograph: Facebook/Dendermonde Local Police The hoard, which includes gold coins, nuggets and numbered bullion bars, was stashed in a bag in a bricked-in cellar wall beneath the grand villa originally built for the brewery’s owner, Theophilus Van Assche, in the late 19th century. Kobe said: “It’s just not something you expect when you’re working on a regular Tuesday morning,” adding that the treasure trove appeared to have been deliberately hidden. “It was really bricked in there – not in a safe or anything.” Brewing on the site began in 1899 and ceased in 1970, and the listed property – the wrought-iron gates of which still bear the initials “VA” – is being completely renovated by the social welfare organisation CAW Oost-Vlaanderen to create new offices and housing. View image in fullscreen The trove included gold coins, nuggets and numbered bullion bars. Photograph: Facebook/Dendermonde Local Police “The Brouwershuis was a beautiful building, but it is being completely gutted,” Geert Hillaert, of CAW, told the news outlet HLN . “Ultimately, only the walls will remain. Labourers were laying drainage pipes when they stumbled across the gold.” Kobe and his colleagues called the police and notified CAW as soon as they came across the gold hoard. The treasure has since been transferred to a secure facility in Brussels pending a detailed official investigation to establish its legal ownership. Hanne Ollevier, of the East Flanders public prosecutor’s office, told HLN that authorities must first verify that the bullion was not stolen property or the proceeds of criminal activity, and was likely to spark a complex civil dispute. View image in fullscreen Belgian law requires finders to wait at least five years for potential owners to claim any treasure. Photograph: Facebook/Dendermonde Local Police The building contractors, the welfare organisation and any descendants of the once-wealthy Van Assche family could all have a claim to part of the fortune. Belgian law requires finders to wait at least five years for potential owners to claim any treasure. A former mayor of Dendermonde, Piet Buyse, told HLN that the Van Assche’s fortune had “certainly stayed in the family. It wouldn’t surprise me at all if they had decided to put at least some of it in gold, and then to hide it in a safe place.” For his part, Kobe said he and his colleagues had understood straight away that they had to hand over such a big find. “If it had been a few coins, maybe not,” he said. “But maybe we’ll get some kind of finder’s reward eventually.” Explore more on these topics Belgium Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/environment/.text: Toñi, the oldest orca in her pod, has been seen with markings on her dorsal fin that suggest pellet gun fire. Photograph: Cristina Otero Sabio/WeWhale.org and Iberian Orcas Guardians View image in fullscreen Toñi, the oldest orca in her pod, has been seen with markings on her dorsal fin that suggest pellet gun fire. Photograph: Cristina Otero Sabio/WeWhale.org and Iberian Orcas Guardians Whales Iberian orca known for ramming boats seen with suspected gunshot wounds Marine conservationist says deliberate attack would be ‘act of extreme cruelty’ against endangered population Ashifa Kassam in Madrid Fri 14 Aug 2026 11.07 EDT First published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 10.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Spanish officials have launched an investigation after the matriarch of an orca pod known for jostling and ramming boats off the Iberian Peninsula was spotted with wounds suggesting she had been shot by a pellet gun. On Friday, Spain’s environment ministry said Toñi, the oldest living member of the pod, had been seen swimming in the Strait of Gibraltar with markings on her dorsal fin that were “consistent with shots from a pellet gun”. Humpbacks return to Rio: the whales are back from the brink of extinction – but will tourism help or hinder? Read more A source from the ministry told El País that some of the projectiles remained lodged in her fin, posing a risk of infection. The ministry was in touch with officials in Portugal, the source added, as the markings were detected after the orcas had travelled from the waters off the Portuguese city of Faro. The orcas of the Iberian Peninsula burst into headlines in 2020 after sailors shared stories of rudders that had been rammed and boats that had been spun 180 degrees or tipped sideways. Since then, a small group of orcas from the pod have been blamed for damaging scores of vessels and sinking at least four boats, leaving scientists scrambling to explain the baffling behaviour. Scientists have long pushed back against the assertion that the orcas are attacking vessels, instead suggesting that the behaviour could be a form of play or a means of practising their hunting skills. In the days since Toñi’s injuries came to light, the WeWhale and Iberian Orca Guardians (IOG) association have been closely tracking the animal for any sign of weakness. “We know Toñi. We were with her a few weeks ago and these wounds were not there,” the IOG co-founder Janek Andre said. “Seeing Toñi, la abuela [the grandmother], like this is devastating,” he added. “If someone has deliberately fired a shotgun at her, this is not only an act of extreme cruelty against an individual animal. It is an attack on one of the last remaining members of a critically endangered population.” Researchers have long sought to highlight the many stressors faced by this population of orcas as they navigate life in a major shipping route. Food scarcity, injuries and pollution have left the population on a knife’s edge, reduced to between 30 and 40 individuals. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Down to Earth The planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essential after newsletter promotion In 2023, video emerged that appeared to show people launching firecrackers into the sea as orcas rammed the rudder of their vessel, hinting that the animals were now facing another threat as sailors push back against their actions. “There has been enormous public discussion about Iberian orcas and their interactions with vessels,” said Andre. “Whatever someone’s opinion about those interactions may be, shooting at these animals can never be an acceptable response. These orcas need protection, not retaliation.” Explore more on these topics Whales Spain Europe Cetaceans Marine life Wildlife news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story UK waters hit with extreme heatwave as global sea temperatures reach record levels The rise of blue-space therapy: how the sea is helping people deal with trauma, anxiety and addiction Ocean surface temperatures hit a record high for June Tiny Antarctic sea creature could be key to treating melanoma, researchers say ‘Chock full of incredible animals’: marine expedition uncovers 31 new species in two weeks Magnus the wandering walrus leaves Scotland for Norway Bioluminescent algae’s blue light harnessed to make 3D-printed shapes Plan to allow fishing around Chagos Islands alarms conservationists The influencer racing to save Thailand’s most endangered sea mammal Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: 0:47 Police release new CCTV of art heist from Italian museum – video Italy Italian police recover paintings by Cézanne, Renoir and Matisse after heist Artworks valued at total of more than $10m were stolen from Magnani Rocca Foundation near Parma in March Tiago Rogero and agencies Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.32 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Italian police have recovered three paintings by the French masters Paul Cézanne, Pierre-Auguste Renoir and Henri Matisse that were stolen earlier this year from a private museum near the northern city of Parma, authorities have said. The raid took place overnight on 22-23 March at the Magnani Rocca Foundation, about 12 miles (19km) from Parma, after a series of high-profile thefts from other European museums. Police released footage showing two masked burglars entering through a window, grabbing the three paintings from the wall and immediately leaving the building, in an operation that took less than three minutes. The recovered works are Cézanne’s Still Life with Cherries, which authorities said was valued at about $7m (£5.2m), Renoir’s Fish, valued at $3.5m, and Matisse’s Odalisque on the Terrace, valued at $23,000. A statement from the Italian Carabinieri’s art recovery squad said the paintings were found during searches ordered by prosecutors, but gave no further details. The investigation is continuing. View image in fullscreen Cézanne’s Still Life with Cherries, valued at about $7m. Photograph: Fondazione Magnani Rocca/Reuters On Thursday, civil police in São Paulo, Brazil’s largest city, said they had recovered eight Matisse illustrations that were stolen from a library on 7 December last year. The works, created for the limited-edition art book Jazz and with a combined estimated value of about $200,000, had been stolen by two thieves who, on the final day of an exhibition, overpowered a security guard and an elderly couple visiting the library before fleeing on foot. Police said they believed the theft had been ordered by Laéssio Rodrigues de Oliveira, 53, regarded as one of Brazil’s most prominent art thieves, who has been in custody since April after being arrested in connection with another case. Police found the works at a home in São Bernardo do Campo, on the outskirts of São Paulo, and said they were in good condition. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines Europe A digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week day after newsletter promotion View image in fullscreen The Matisse illustrations recovered by Brazilian police. Photograph: São Paulo police press office/AFP/Getty Images Photographs released by officers showed the illustrations laid out on a bed beside a .32 revolver that police said belonged to João Paulo Linhares de Araújo, 44, who was at the property and was arrested. Police said he had been storing the Matisse works on behalf of people accused of involvement in the theft. Three other people had previously been arrested in connection with the case. The works were returned to the library on Thursday. During the robbery, the thieves also took five engravings by the Brazilian artist Candido Portinari, which have not yet been recovered. Police said they suspected they had been sold. https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: A protest on Thursday in Larbert, about 30 miles west of Edinburgh, is said by campaigners to have been attended by more than 100 people. Photograph: Larbert residents group View image in fullscreen A protest on Thursday in Larbert, about 30 miles west of Edinburgh, is said by campaigners to have been attended by more than 100 people. Photograph: Larbert residents group Scotland Police Scotland warns ‘robust security’ needed to stop attacks on AI datacentres ‘A great deal of public opposition is likely’ to a proposed datacentre near Edinburgh, the force says Aisha Down Fri 14 Aug 2026 12.05 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Police in Scotland have issued a stark warning about the need for “robust security measures” to stop proposed AI datacentres from being attacked by protesters. There has been mounting opposition to AI infrastructure globally, including in the US where such projects have become a significant political rallying point . Police Scotland said “a great deal of public opposition is likely” to a datacentre planned in Larbert , about 30 miles west of Edinburgh, in a letter submitted as a part of a planning consultation this month. The letter encouraged the datacentre’s developer to liaise with the police to prevent “unplanned incursions for the purposes of disruption”. ‘It’s smoke and mirrors’: hope turns to fear in Scottish village chosen for AI datacentre Read more It appears to be one of the first official acknowledgments of mounting public unease about datacentre development in the UK. Police Scotland declined to comment. There are hundreds of datacentre projects in various stages of planning in Britain. Only some of these appear to be viable developments, with research groups warning of a glut of “zombie projects” waiting to connect to the grid. In Scotland there are at least 23 “hyperscale” datacentre developments in the planning process, according to the Edinburgh-based charity Action to Protect Rural Scotland (APRS). Combined, they would use more than one and a half times the power that Scotland uses at peak demand. View image in fullscreen Nearly 7,000 people have filed objections to the proposed datacentre in Larbert. Photograph: Larbert residents group Groups across Scotland have started organising opposition to planned datacentres. More than 100 people attended a protest in Larbert on Thursday, according to local campaigners. Nearly 7,000 people have filed objections to the proposed development. Similar protests are planned in the coming weeks, including one in Edinburgh in early September, when the Scottish parliament will be back in session. This summer, the Scottish National party passed a motion to freeze all new datacentres in Scotland. If that motion becomes Scottish government policy, it could pose a serious threat to the UK’s AI strategy . British officials have been pushing datacentre developers to build in Scotland. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every day Sign up to Headlines UK Get the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morning after newsletter promotion Revealed: landmark Scottish AI project has no prospect of meeting renewables promise Read more Some of the opposition to datacentres is about the physical footprint of the projects. Michael Maciocia, a Larbert resident who attended Thursday’s protest, said he and others were worried about the 200 diesel generators that Apatura, the site’s developer, planned to install as backup power for the datacentre. APRS is concerned that these could release significant quantities of nitrous oxide into the air, which could negatively affect the health of people living nearby. “Where this datacentre is planned to be built, within 50 metres of one of the buildings is a 56-bed care home for the terminally ill … Within 400 metres, there’s the 860-bed Forth Valley Royal hospital,” said Maciocia. “The amount of pollution and the noise created by these things will be horrendous in every direction.” View image in fullscreen Campaigners in Larbert are concerned about the potential health and environmental impacts of the proposed datacentre. Photograph: Larbert residents group Hazel McQueen, who also lives nearby, said: “I live extremely close to the proposed site, and since this application was submitted it has become a huge part of my life.” She says she has spent hours on top of her full-time job reading about the datacentre, attending meetings and helping to organise opposition to it. She says she is concerned for the health of her family, and of her grandson who has leukaemia. “I need to fight this for his future and the future we are leaving for him.” Scotland’s ‘green datacentres’ policy ignores emissions impact of AI, analysis shows Read more Cecilia Rikap, a professor at University College London, says there is a larger, symbolic dimension to public anger around datacentre development. “It’s the physical manifestation of AI, and there is a growing opposition to AI. People are seeing how AI is replacing the good part of their work, people are seeing how AI is undermining younger people’s capacity to think,” she said. “Ultimately, if you want to protest against generative AI or the role of big tech, you would protest at a datacentre. That’s what you can see. All the rest is much more invisible.” A spokesperson for Apatura said: “We’re committed to developing data centres in line with world-leading safety and environmental standards and in compliance with all planning regulations. We recognise that there has been opposition to the planning application and remain committed to working closely with government and local community throughout the planning process to ensure concerns are listened to and carefully considered.” Explore more on these topics Scotland Datacentres - UK Police Protest Edinburgh Planning policy Scottish politics news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Datacentre projects face fees for grid access to ease connection queue, Ofgem says Scotland could freeze datacentre projects in challenge to UK’s AI strategy Datacentres using 6% of electricity supply in UK and US, research says ‘Irresponsible’: backlash as Utah approves datacenter twice the size of Manhattan The fight against AI datacenters isn’t just about tech – it’s about democracy Google developers significantly misstate carbon emissions of proposed UK datacentres The environmental cost of datacentres is rising. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Vandals poured bubble soap and painted graffiti on the second world war memorial in Washington DC on Thursday. Photograph: Andrew Leyden/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Vandals poured bubble soap and painted graffiti on the second world war memorial in Washington DC on Thursday. Photograph: Andrew Leyden/Zuma Press Wire/Shutterstock Washington DC Woman arrested after second world war memorial in DC vandalized Suspect faces two felony charges after memorial filled with bubbles and spray-paint reading ‘Clean hands Dirty $’ Edward Helmore Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.43 EDT First published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 08.58 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A woman was arrested on Friday morning in connection with the vandalization of the National World War Two Memorial on the National Mall in Washington DC , the capital’s federal prosecutor announced. Jeanine Pirro, the US attorney for the District of Columbia, announced mid-morning that a suspect was in custody and had been charged with federal crimes. The memorial had graffiti scrawled on it and the pool polluted with soapy bubbles. “This morning, we are filing two felony charges, Depredation Against Property of the United States and Destruction of Veterans’ Memorials, in Federal District Court against Melissa L Farris, offenses that carry penalties of up to ten years in prison. She is now in custody,” Pirro posted on X , showing two images of a middle-aged woman, one of her with what appears to be a can of spray-paint at the scene. “Vandalizing our World War II Memorial is a despicable attack on a sacred monument honoring the Americans who fought and died for our freedom. Those Americans include my father and grandfather,” Pirro also said in the post. US Park Police had been investigating who graffitied the words “Clean hands dirty $” in red paint on the memorial on Washington DC ’s National Mall for the second world war and vandalized the fountain with soapy bubbles. The US interior department said: “The public should know we will find the person responsible for this disgusting act” and the non-profit Friends of the National World War II Memorial said the site should not be used for political expression. View image in fullscreen Bubble soap on the second world war memorial in Washington DC on Thursday. Photograph: Andrew Leyden/NurPhoto/Shutterstock “There are many places in our country for expression, debate and disagreement,” a statement from the organization said. “A national memorial honoring those who served and those who never returned home should never be used as a canvas for vandalism.” The Veterans of Foreign Wars military service organization said the vandalism was “an act of profound disrespect”. The memorial sits close to the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool , which has been the site of controversy in recent months. A contentious upgrade effort ordered by Donald Trump ahead of Fourth of July celebrations for the 250th anniversary of the founding of the US became mired in dispute after new surfacing separated and algae returned . Trump blamed vandals for damage to the pool lining, though prosecutions of individuals alleged to have contributed to the problems have since collapsed, including a high-profile case involving David Hearn , the US Olympian. In early June vandals etched “8647” – a numeric signal of opposition to Trump – on the National Memorial lawn. Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said: “Anyone who engages in or endorses political violence or assassination culture must be condemned in the harshest terms possible.” Leanna Townsend, a visitor to Washington DC from Florida this week, told the Washington Post upon seeing the clouds of bubbles frothing out of the pool at the second world war memorial that they seemed “a little bit juvenile and funny” but described the spray-paint as disrespectful. “I just find it to be in complete distaste, especially for the people that it’s here to honor,” she said. “Shame on the person who thought that’s appropriate. It’s not.” Sonja Weekley, visiting from Alabama, said the bubbles and spray-paint were “ridiculous and very disrespectful” – her grandparents and father-in-law had fought in the second world war, she told the outlet. “This is not political,” she said. “This is for the men and women who fought for us to be free.” In videos posted to Farris’s Facebook account, ​Farris records herself spray-painting the war memorial and asking ‌why she has not been arrested. The criminal complaint filed on Friday quotes ‌Farris as saying: “Someone has to make choices that are different and I am accountable for my actions.” In later videos posted after the incident, she appears disheveled and crying, saying she knows she upset people by her actions but was trying to get help for ‌herself. Trump has clung to claims that the reflecting pool was vandalized , despite charges being dropped . On Friday he posted to his social media platform: “First the Reflecting Pool, now this. We are on their trail! Where do these animals come from???” Reuters contributed reporting Explore more on these topics Washington DC US politics US crime Trump administration Second world war US military news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Luigi Mangione at a pre-trial hearing at Manhattan criminal court in New York on 11 August 2026. Photograph: Steven Hirsch/New York Post via AP View image in fullscreen Luigi Mangione at a pre-trial hearing at Manhattan criminal court in New York on 11 August 2026. Photograph: Steven Hirsch/New York Post via AP Brian Thompson shooting Luigi Mangione pleads guilty to causing UnitedHealthcare CEO’s death in federal case Plea comes weeks before separate case is scheduled to start in New York, and could throw proceedings into disarray Luigi Mangione trial – latest updates Victoria Bekiempis in New York Fri 14 Aug 2026 13.52 EDT First published on Fri 14 Aug 2026 06.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Luigi Mangione pleaded guilty on Friday in a federal case in relation to the killing of UnitedHealthcare executive Brian Thompson in 2024. Mangione confessed that he shot and killed Thompson outside a New York City hotel on 4 December 2024. In his federal case, he faced stalking charges, after other charges, including murder, were dropped. “I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” Mangione said towards the end of a hastily scheduled, 45-minute hearing. He added: “I knew what I was doing was illegal” but did not say that what he did was wrong or that he had any regrets. The judge, Margaret Garnett, scheduled his sentencing for 18 December. Mangione’s federal trial had been due to begin next year but will not now happen, while state charges against him were still in the balance on Friday afternoon. In the separate state case, Manhattan prosecutors have charged Mangione with murder and weapons counts and that trial is scheduled for 8 September. He had previously pleaded not guilty in both cases. Within minutes of the guilty plea to stalking charges in the federal case and his admissions in court on Friday morning, Mangione’s defense lawyer, Karen Friedman Agnifilo, said she had filed a motion to dismiss the state murder case against him. Federal prosecutor Jamie McDonald told the court the government would seek life imprisonment for the killer. Maryland-born Mangione, 28, came into court on Friday morning in beige jail scrubs with his ankles shackled, a change from recent appearances where he was in a jacket and shirt. He had been brought to the Manhattan courthouse from custody in Brooklyn. Relatives of Thompson were in court in a rare occurrence, sitting in the front row, and some of the family members began crying as Mangione told the judge what he had done. Among the relatives in court was Brian Thompson’s widow , Paulette Thompson, who was breathing heavily and grasping a loved one’s arm as Mangione described shooting her husband on a busy city sidewalk. Other family members held each other’s hands. Mangione told the court that “after years of enduring severe back pain, a broken back, [and] navigating the obstacles of the health system”, he learned that UnitedHealthcare would be holding its annual investor conference in December 2024. The location was not public but he traveled to New York City and emailed UnitedHealthcare leadership, posing as an institutional investor, to get more information, getting a response within an hour. He also researched who would be attending. Mangione then said he printed a gun with a 3-D printer and affixed it with a silencer. “I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died,” he said. “When I did so, I understood that my actions would place him in fear of death or serious bodily injury. I knew what I was doing was illegal.” There were gasps in court as the prosecution described how Brian Thompson was probably aware of what had happened to him as he turned to face his killer between the first and second bullets hitting him, as Mangione stood in the street with his gun raised. The judge said earlier that Mangione was in a fit state to plead. He was asked a series of questions. Mangione’s case has drawn extensive global attention as Thompson’s death spurred intense discussion about the US’s heavily criticized for-profit healthcare system. The attention has also been fueled by Mangione’s rise to virtual folk-hero status among some of his supporters, although there were almost none of the most vocal fans, dubbed “Mangionistas” outside the courthouse on Friday, as there had been for previous hearings. Mangione’s decision to plead guilty in the federal trial came after days of intense speculation that his case would resolve before a trial. Mere hours after a final pre-trial conference in his state case, federal prosecutors and his defense had submitted a joint letter requesting a proceeding. New York double jeopardy law could now preclude the state case from going ahead. Under New York state law, “a person may not be twice prosecuted for the same offense” and “a person may not be separately prosecuted for two offenses based upon the same act or criminal transaction”. A state appeals court decision points out , however, that these statements precede the word “unless”, with a list of exceptions. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Mangione was arrested at an Altoona, Pennsylvania, McDonald’s on 9 December 2024 after a dramatic manhunt to find Thompson’s killer. Mangione in April 2025 pleaded not guilty to federal charges that he stalked and murdered Thompson. Not long after Mangione’s arrest, Pam Bondi , then the US attorney general, announced that she would instruct prosecutors to seek the death penalty . She said that Thompson’s killing was a “premeditated, cold-blooded assassination that shocked America”. Bondi also said that her position was aligned with “Trump’s agenda to stop violent crime and Make America Safe Again”. But Judge Garnett on 30 January threw out two of the four counts in Mangione’s federal indictment including the death penalty-eligible charge of murder through use of a firearm, meaning this punishment was off the table. Garnett said that US supreme court precedents made the murder charge “incompatible” with the two stalking charges. “This case will proceed to trial on counts one and two, which charge the defendant with causing Brian Thompson’s death under two federal stalking laws,” Garnett said in her order. “The potential maximum punishment for each of those offenses is life in prison without parole. Defense attorney Friedman Agnifilo said that Mangione took full responsibility for Thompson’s death. She added, about his experience with the insurance giant UnitedHealthcare that: “Like the thousands of people who have reached out since this tragedy to share their own experiences, he believed that the system had failed him and destroyed his life.” Brian Thompson’s family issued a statement saying that the “guilty plea marks an important step toward justice for Brian and for our family. While nothing will ease the pain of losing him, we are grateful that the federal justice system has held the person responsible for this heinous act accountable.” The prosecutor, McDonald, said that there could be no celebrity in assassination and any person encouraging or excusing actions like Mangione’s was “fundamentally wrong”. “Violence is not a legitimate instrument to promote any political or social message,” he said. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: With Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache. Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty Images View image in fullscreen With Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache. Photograph: Igor Ivanko/AFP/Getty Images Russia Putin’s recruiters scramble to avoid second mass mobilisation as Ukraine losses mount Russia is losing 30,000 casualties a month, and the country’s regions are under pressure to feed the ‘meat-grinder’. Experts say it may not be enough Pjotr Sauer Fri 14 Aug 2026 09.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 14.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google In kitchens and Telegram chats across Russia, the same question is being asked with growing frequency: will Vladimir Putin order another mobilisation? Nearly five years into the war, Russia is scrambling to find enough soldiers to replenish its ranks, as voluntary recruitment slows and its forces suffer heavy losses on the battlefield in Ukraine . With Putin showing no sign of abandoning his far-reaching territorial demands, even as Russia’s summer offensive stalls, the Kremlin faces a growing manpower headache. “The problem for the Kremlin is that it is getting much harder to find people willing to fight, even for crazy money,” said Aleksei Tabalov, a human rights activist and director of an organisation that helps Russian conscripts. Putin last resorted to mobilisation in September 2022, when a series of dramatic battlefield setbacks forced the Kremlin to call up 300,000 reservists to stabilise the front. View image in fullscreen A billboard advertising ‘contract military service’ beside a highway outside Krasnodar, Russia. Photograph: AP Since then, Moscow has avoided another deeply unpopular call-up by relying largely on high paid voluntary contracts to fill the ranks with roughly 1.3 million contract soldiers Russia has recruited since. Men, particularly from Russia’s poorer regions, have been offered life-changing signing bonuses and salaries on open-ended contracts amounting to several years of local wages, alongside substantial payouts to their families if they are killed. But Russia’s heavy losses mean it must continue finding new soldiers at a high rate. Western estimates put Russian casualties at more than 30,000 killed and wounded a month, a toll that reflects the army’s attritional “meat grinder” tactics, in which troops are repeatedly sent forward in small assault groups despite heavy losses. Moscow, meanwhile, now recruits roughly 1,000 soldiers a day, according to calculations by Janis Kluge, a Russia expert at the German Institute for International and Security Affairs, which means most new recruits are used to replenish depleted units rather than expand Russia’s offensive capacity. That has once again raised the prospect of mobilisation. Top Russian officials have dismissed reports of an impending call-up, with former president Dmitry Medvedev describing them as “nonsense” and a “lying provocation” by Ukraine. Two people familiar with discussions in Moscow also said there was no indication that Putin had decided to order another mass mobilisation. A senior western official likewise said there were no signs that a decision had been taken. View image in fullscreen A firefighting helicopter drops water over a food warehouse damaged during Russian drone strikes near Kyiv, 12 August 2026. Photograph: Valentyn Ogirenko/Reuters But fears that another call-up may be on the way have nevertheless increasingly entered everyday conversations. In Telegram chats used by local sports teams, work colleagues and groups of friends, Russians swap rumours about a possible mobilisation and share advice on securing exemptions or avoiding the draft. Some speculate that a new call-up could come after September’s elections to the Duma. “It’s guesswork right now whether mobilisation will actually happen,” said Ivan Chuviliaev, a spokesperson for Get Lost, a group that helps Russian soldiers desert. But he said the renewed speculation was already being exploited to boost recruitment. “The panic around mobilisation is being used by officials to pressure men into signing contracts,” Chuviliaev said. “The message is: mobilisation is coming anyway, so you might as well sign a contract now and get a payout before you’re forced to fight.” View image in fullscreen Putin recently signed a law expanding the pool of convicted prisoners eligible to sign contracts with the army. Photograph: Russian President official/APAImages/Shutterstock For now, people familiar with the Kremlin’s thinking say the authorities appear determined to strong-arm more men into signing contracts rather than risk another mobilisation. Over the summer, lawyers and activists have documented increasingly coercive recruitment tactics in several regions, with men detained on the street by police, taken from workplaces or summoned to stations – before being brought to military recruitment offices and pressed to sign contracts. “It has turned into a hunt for people,” said Tabalov. “Under various pretexts, through deception, blackmail, violence and threats, they are forcing them to sign contracts.” Tabalov said recruiters were increasingly targeting what he described as “socially marginalised” men, including those with debts, criminal cases or other vulnerabilities that could be used to put pressure on them to enlist. In the southern Penza region, where some of the most aggressive draft methods have been reported, videos posted online have shown men being driven away in vans as relatives protested outside recruitment offices. Activists say some have been threatened with prosecution or beaten until they agreed to sign. The search has widened elsewhere too. Universities, technical colleges and vocational schools have been encouraged to recruit students into newly formed drone units, offering another source of manpower for the military. Putin recently signed a law expanding the pool of convicted prisoners eligible to sign contracts with the army, including people convicted of “serious and especially serious crimes”. Much of the responsibility for finding soldiers has been pushed down to Russia’s regions. Governors and local administrations are expected to meet recruitment targets set by Moscow, giving the Kremlin some distance from the drive while leaving regional officials responsible for finding enough men in their own territories. Around that system, a lucrative recruitment industry has emerged. Regional governments offer thousands of dollars not only to soldiers who sign contracts but also to those who find them, with “bring a friend” schemes paying residents for every person they persuade to enlist. View image in fullscreen Smoke rises from an oil refinery after a Ukrainian drone attack in Moscow, 18 June 2026. Photograph: Social Media/Reuters Private recruiters and public-sector employees scour social media for candidates, while advertisements for military contracts have become ubiquitous online. Russian regions have paid recruiters at least 7.7bn roubles ($96m) since such schemes were introduced, according to the independent Russian outlet IStories . One recruiter in central Russia, speaking to the Guardian on condition of anonymity, said his organisation was expected to find between 20 and 30 men each month, with bonuses for exceeding the target and penalties for falling short. “It was easier last year,” the recruiter said. “Now it is getting harder.” The recruiter said mobilisation was also being discussed in his office, but that there had been no orders or indications that a new draft was imminent. Another mass call-up, however, would carry significant political risks for the Kremlin. The 2022 call-up triggered one of the biggest episodes of domestic disruption since the invasion began, prompting a mass exodus of Russians and a sharp drop in Putin’s approval ratings. It would also come at a potentially sensitive moment. Recent polling suggests confidence in the course of the war is weakening, with the share of Russians who believe the campaign in Ukraine is going well falling to its lowest level since April 2022. For now, analysts say Moscow is more likely to step up recruitment efforts through higher bonuses, pressure on regional officials and increasingly coercive tactics. Whether that will be enough could ultimately determine if Putin resorts to another mobilisation, said Tabalov, the activist. The options before the Kremlin, Tabalov said, could range from another mass call-up to a more selective mobilisation, sending existing conscripts to the front or quietly calling up reservists for frontline service. “I don’t think they’ll be able to recruit enough people under the current system,” Tabalov said. “Then they’ll be faced with the question of what form mobilisation should take.” Explore more on these topics Russia Ukraine Vladimir Putin Europe news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/14/luigi.text: Luigi Mangione admitted on Friday to gunning down UnitedHealthCare chief executive Brian Thompson, as he appeared in US federal court to change his plea to guilty."On the morning of December 4, I shot Mr Thompson in Manhattan and he died," Mangione told a federal judge.Mangione also pleaded guilty to federal stalking charges, admitting matter-of-factly that he trailed the executive to an investor conference in 2024 and gunned him down in the street.Mangione, 28, said he even used a ruse to glean information about the event, contacting the health insurance company ahead of time under the guise of being an investor at a multibillion-dollar firm. Mangione is set for sentencing 18 December. When US District Judge Margaret M. Garnett asked whether he understood that he could spend the rest of his life in prison, Mangione answered neutrally: “Yes.”Mangione entered the plea at a hastily scheduled hearing in Manhattan federal court, resolving one of two cases against him in connection with Thompson’s death.Mangione's lawyers are now seeking to have his separate New York state murder case thrown out on double jeopardy grounds.“Mr. Mangione has accepted full responsibility for the death of Brian Thompson,” defence lawyer Karen Friedman said outside the court, arguing that her client shouldn't face two prosecutions over a “single tragic event.”Surveillance video of the ambush showed a masked gunman shooting Thompson, 50, from behind.Police say “delay, deny, depose” were written on the ammunition, mimicking a phrase used to describe how insurers avoid paying claims.That detail and revelations that Mangione's private writings lambasted health insurers as greedy, according to authorities, made the case a fulcrum for debate about the industry and made Mangione a celebrity for some of its critics.Mangione told the court on Friday that he pursued Thompson “after years of enduring severe pain from a broken back and navigating the obstacles of the health insurance system.”Mangione was never a UnitedHealthcare customer, according to police and the company.A University of Pennsylvania graduate from a wealthy Maryland family, he was arrested five days after the shooting, when he was spotted at a McDonald’s in Pennsylvania.Thompson led one of the United States' largest health insurers, but he wasn’t well known outside the industry.Trained as an accountant, he had worked at parent company UnitedHealth Group Inc. for 20 years and became CEO of its insurance arm, UnitedHealthcare, in 2021. He and his wife have two sons, who were in high school when their father was killed.Both the federal and state cases could lead to a life prison sentence for Mangione. A federal judge earlier this year tossed out additional charges that could have exposed him to a potential death penalty.Mangione had complained about the prospect of two trials, telling a judge in February: “It’s the same trial twice. One plus one is two. Double jeopardy by any commonsense definition.”Under New York law, a state prosecution could potentially be barred if the federal case is resolved first.The state’s double jeopardy protections kick in if a jury has been sworn in a prior prosecution, such as a federal case, or if that prosecution ends in a guilty plea. Mangione’s cases involve different charges arising from the same course of conduct.In a letter last month, state prosecutors objected to the possibility of a guilty plea in the federal case wiping out the state case.Garnett has delivered some setbacks to the defence, including ruling in January that prosecutors could use items collected from Mangione’s backpack during his arrest as evidence against him.They included a 3D-printed pistol that investigators said matched the one used to kill Thompson and a notebook in which authorities say Mangione described his intent to kill an insurance executive.In June, Mangione’s lawyers said they would pursue a psychiatric defence in the state case but reversed course a day later.The defence, involving claims that he was suffering from extreme emotional disturbance at the time of the killing, isn’t allowed in federal court.

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/14/us-ba.text: The United States has backed Japan's sovereignty over four islands controlled by Russia after Vladimir Putin became the first Russian president in 15 years to visit the disputed territory, prompting Tokyo to summon Moscow's ambassador and describe the trip as "absolutely unacceptable.""The United States remains unwavering in its support of its most important ally and in its recognition of Japanese sovereignty over the Northern Territories," the US ambassador to Tokyo George Glass said on X."At a time when the US-Japan alliance is dedicated to cultivating prosperity across the Indo-Pacific, we strongly oppose any action that undermines its peace and stability," Glass added.Russian-Japanese relations have long been dogged by the four southernmost islands in a volcanic chain off the coast of Hokkaido seized by the Soviet Union following an invasion in August 1945, in the final days of World War II.Moscow broke its formal neutrality with Japan just days before the invasion.The Japanese government maintains that the four islands and groups of islets that make up the Northern Territories — Etorofu, Kunashiri, Shikotan and Habomai — are part of its territory that the Soviets illegally occupied and Russia has continued to occupy since the breakup of the Soviet Union in 1991.The dispute has kept the two countries from signing a peace treaty that would formally end their hostilities. They terminated the state of war in 1956.Moscow has reinforced its military presence on the islands as recently as December 2021, when it deployed Bastion coastal defence missile systems on an uninhabited volcanic island in the middle of the chain.The island hosted a Japanese army base prior to the Soviet occupation. A Soviet base there was shut down amid funding shortages in the wake of the collapse of the Soviet Union.Moscow previously deployed Bal and Bastion missile systems on two of the four southernmost islands in 2016.In the following years, Moscow further beefed up its arsenal on the islands by sending top-of-the-line air defence missile systems, setting up an air base on Etorofu Island, and deploying fighter jets.The sparsely inhabited islands are strategically significant to the Kremlin as they sit at the entrance to the Sea of Okhotsk and give Russia's Pacific Fleet access to the open Pacific without passing through Japanese-controlled waters.Putin's visit was the first by a Russian president since Dmitry Medvedev in 2010.'Absolutely unacceptable'Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters "the Northern Territories are an inherent part of Japan's territory, both historically and under international law."Putin's visit "offends the sentiments of the Japanese people and is absolutely unacceptable," she added.Japan's Foreign Minister Toshimitsu Motegi said his country “strongly protests” Putin's visit to the largest of the islands, Etorofu.“The Northern Territories, including Etorofu Island, are Japan’s inherent territory both historically and from the perspective of international law,” Motegi said in a statement.He summoned Russian Ambassador Nikolay Nozdrev to the ministry in Tokyo and lodged a strong protest over the visit, requesting that he "promptly report the message back to Moscow,” the minister told reporters afterwards.Russia's embassy in Japan said the ambassador reiterated Moscow's claim that the islands are part of Russia and that Putin's trip there was not "a matter for discussion with foreign states".The Kremlin boasted about the visit by posting a video of Putin on one of the four main islands. Russian state-run media said he had visited a fish-processing plant and showed him trying local caviar.Takaichi said the visit was a further blow to the already-strained ties between the two countries over Ukraine, and that Moscow should understand the consequences.Japan imposed sanctions on Russia after Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.It also placed export controls on technology with military applications and provided financial support to Ukraine. Russia responded by designating Japan an "unfriendly state".Tokyo is now considering strengthening those sanctions as part of its countermeasures in response to Putin's trip.“We must say this visit has further hardened Japanese public sentiment toward Russia and has made it more difficult to restore bilateral relations in the medium to long term,” she said.“We hope the Russian side fully understands the seriousness of this.”

http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/14/russi.text: A Russian court has sentenced Georgy Pirogov to 23 years in a high-security penal colony for spying for Polish intelligence, with the FSB announcing the verdict the day after Poland said it had detained a Russian national suspected of planning a killing in Warsaw.The FSB said Pirogov left Russia after the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine, established contact with a representative of Polish military intelligence in Poland in April 2022, and was then tasked with collecting and passing classified information about Russian weapons used in the war.The FSB's statement did not explain when or how Pirogov returned to Russia or provide any evidence to back its claims.On Thursday, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said a Russian citizen had been detained on 7 August on suspicion of preparing an assassination in Warsaw.Tusk said Russian security services had recruited the suspect and added that the Kremlin chose the intended target because it saw him as a threat."He was inconvenient from the point of view of Putin's regime," Tusk said. The Polish premier declined to name the target, citing legal restrictions.Pirogov's trial opened in May and was held behind closed doors. The FSB said he used contacts in Russia's defence industry to obtain restricted information on the production and use of missile systems, as well as personal data of individuals with access to state secrets.The indictment also alleged he made cryptocurrency transfers to support Ukraine's armed forces, bought equipment and organised its delivery from Poland to Ukraine.The independent Russian outlet Mediazona reported that Pirogov moved to Georgia after the invasion began and worked as an industrial climber, citing relatives and human rights activists. In the summer of 2024 he travelled to Uzbekistan on a business trip and then disappeared.In July 2024 it emerged he was being held at Matrosskaya Tishina remand prison in Moscow. Independent Russian media said they did not know who detained him or under what circumstances he was brought back to Russia.Treason charges a tool of the KremlinRussia has significantly expanded its espionage and treason laws since launching the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.The maximum sentence for treason rose from 20 to 25 years after legislative changes in 2022 and 2023, and the definition of state treason was broadened to cover a wider range of contacts with foreign states and organisations.The FSB has also been given expanded powers to detain and prosecute individuals suspected of espionage without the same evidentiary threshold previously required.Treason cases in Russia numbered in the single digits annually before 2014, when Russia's initial invasion of Ukraine and annexation of Crimea prompted the first significant spike.Last year, almost 500 people, including Ukrainian citizens, were convicted in Russia on espionage and treason charges.Since Russia's full-scale invasion, Poland has become one of Ukraine's most significant military supporters, providing weapons, ammunition and training. Poland also hosts a large US military presence.Warsaw has expelled Russian diplomats and closed the Russian consulate in Kraków over espionage concerns.Poland's counter-intelligence services have reported a major increase in Russian malign interference, including sabotage and recruitment operations on Polish soil since 2022, targeting infrastructure, Ukrainian diaspora networks and individuals critical of the Kremlin.

https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-false-c.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Ii3j Abdul El-Sayed narrowly won the Michigan Democratic US Senate primary Image: Finn Gomez/Getty Images/AFP Advertisement On August 4, Abdul El-Sayed, a leading progressive candidate, won Michigan's Democratic primary for the US Senate. The 41-year-old will face Republican Mike Rogers in the November 3 midterm elections. The winner will succeed retiring Democratic Senator Gary Peters. Michigan is a battleground or so-called "swing" state , where both parties have a strong chance of winning. The large Arab American and Muslim population plays a key role. If El-Sayed wins in November, he would become the first Muslim US senator in history. Soon after his primary victory, several false claims about El-Sayed were spread online, including claims promoted by prominent political figures. Michigan is a key swing state in the upcoming midterm elections Image: Kamil Krzaczynski/AFP According to Lawrence Pintak, a journalism professor at Washington State University and author of America & Islam , El-Sayed is an ideal target for political disinformation. "He checks off all the boxes: He's a Muslim, he's a progressive, and he is vocally critical of Israel," Pintak said in a written statement to DW. DW Fact check examined claims about voting irregularities during the primaries, El-Sayed's political ideology and whether he said the US deserved the 9/11 attacks. Alleged ghost votes Claim : "Of course they cheated. Nobody actually votes for communists," a Facebook post claimed, linking to an article headlined: "Abdul El-Sayed got three times as many votes in Detroit as there are registered voters." The article states that El-Sayed "received 1.4 million votes in Detroit alone — a city with approximately 480,000 registered voters." Originally published as satire, the false claim spread as disinformation after being reposted on other pages Image: Facebook DW Fact check : False The Facebook account that shared the claim, "America's Last Line of Defense," states that "nothing on this page is real." The page has around 748,000 followers and is linked to a website run by Christopher Blair, a well-known creator of fabricated political content. The BBC once described him as the "godfather of fake news." However, this disclaimer is often lost when the content is reposted on other pages, allowing the false claim to spread without context. The invented story echoes a claim shared by US President Donald Trump days earlier about a county in Michigan: "Miracles happen in Wayne County, including more votes being cast than there are voters, by a lot." Trump did not provide any evidence to support his claim of alleged voter fraud. According to the Michigan Voter Information Center , Michigan has approximately 7.3 million active registered voters, while El-Sayed received 743,455 votes statewide in the Democratic Senate primary, not 1.4 million votes in Detroit alone. Michael Hameleers, an associate professor of political communication at the University of Amsterdam who researches misinformation and disinformation, warned about the impact of such allegations. "It is a prominent delegitimization technique to put democratic institutions and the fairness of elections in question," he said. "Especially in a context where people perceive disinformation and fraud as highly likely, it may be a fruitful strategy to cast doubt on elections." A 2023 US study found that exposure to unfounded claims of voter fraud can significantly undermine confidence in elections, particularly among Republicans and Trump supporters. Claims about political ideology Claim : US President Donald Trump has repeatedly described Abdul El-Sayed as a communist, most recently in a Truth Social post published shortly after El-Sayed's primary victory. US President Donald Trump has repeatedly claimed Abdul El-Sayed is a communist Image: @realDonaldTrump/Truth Social DW Fact check : False El-Sayed's campaign has focused on government-sponsored health insurance, taxing billionaires and reducing the influence of corporate money in politics. In the past, he has rejected claims that he is a socialist or a communist by stating he is a capitalist . "I'm not a socialist. I'm just a capitalist who understands how capitalism works," he said. El-Sayed emphasized his views on capitalism as a point of difference from self-described democratic socialist Bernie Sanders. In a recent interview with The New York Times , he responded to Trump's claims that he is a communist by saying: "The man is so clearly a joker." In a comment to DW, Lawrence Pintak also called the claims historically bizarre. He sees it as part of systematic attempts by the Republican Party "to spin 'progressive' and 'democratic socialist' to be synonyms for 'Communist.'" An analysis by Reuters found that Trump has significantly increased his use of the term in recent weeks. Pintak told DW that the loaded term works well on social media. Misattributing views on 9/11 Claim : After El-Sayed secured the Democratic nomination, his Republican opponent, Mike Rogers, posted a statement on X , calling him "someone who believes America deserved 9/11." Abdul El-Sayed will face Republican Mike Rogers during the general election in November Image: @MikeRogersForMI/X DW Fact check : False 9/11 refers to the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001, in which planes hijacked by militant ​al-Qaeda Islamists struck the World Trade Center in New York and the Pentagon near Washington, killing nearly 3,000 people. The allegation has come up repeatedly but conflates previous remarks made by El-Sayed supporter Hasan Piker with El-Sayed's own views. Piker has supported El-Sayed during his 2026 US Senate campaign, appearing with him at rallies and in livestreams. American Twitch streamer Hasan Piker has been a vocal supporter of Abdul El-Sayed's 2026 US Senate campaign Image: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo/picture alliance During a 2019 livestream, Piker said America had "deserved" 9/11, a remark that generated widespread criticism. Since then, however, he has walked back this statement . When asked by US-based fact checkers PolitiFact for evidence to support his claim, the Rogers campaign pointed to a video clip of El-Sayed refusing to disavow Piker's 2019 comments. Pintak, who researches Islamophobia, described "guilt by association" as one of the disinformation tactics used against El-Sayed. He points out that El-Sayed has become a target of disinformation at a time when the Republican Party has shifted from an anti-immigrant focus back to an anti-Muslim narrative. "Attacks on Muslim candidates, and El-Sayed himself, are nothing new," Pintak said, pointing to Islamophobic reporting during El-Sayed's 2018 campaign for Michigan governor and false claims portraying New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani as an extremist. During the 2018 midterms, Pintak led a research team that found Muslim candidates, from local school boards to Congress, were systematically targeted by "a social media narrative of manufactured outrage [that] was disproportionately Islamophobic, xenophobic, racist, and misogynistic." The researchers concluded that such attacks were often aimed at undermining candidates' legitimacy and reducing trust among voters. Where does Trump stand in the GOP ahead of the midterms?
