https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/life.text: Imagine walking into a Louis Vuitton store while on holiday, ready to look at a few bags, only to be told by the employee to stop shopping and go outside.Thatâs pretty much what happened to Indian content creator Vagmita Singh, better known as @thatindianchick_, during her solo trip to Budapest.And the reason she was told off? The weather.Vagmita shared the funny encounter in a video, explaining that she had gone to a Louis Vuitton showroom because, well, she wanted to shop. She was looking at a few bags when an employee helping her casually asked if it was her first time in Budapest."Yeah," she told him.That seemingly harmless answer apparently changed the entire conversation.According to Vagmita, the employee was genuinely shocked."First time? Then my friend, what are you doing shopping?" she recalled him saying.Apparently, Budapest had just come through a long winter and the sun was finally out. And this employee was clearly not impressed that a first-time visitor was choosing to spend the rare sunny day inside a luxury store."After such long winter, we have sun and you are shopping? Go outside. Go outside right now," Vagmita recalled him saying.Now, most people might have been a little taken aback by being told to leave a store after walking in to shop.But Vagmita took it in exactly the way it was intended - as a hilarious, slightly unexpected piece of travel advice. "Sorry, I didn't know that I would find my dad in someone else's avatar on my solo trip," she joked.And honestly, that line probably sums up the entire interaction. The funny part? She didn't exactly follow his advice completely. Vagmita revealed that she still bought the bag."Now I'm outside. Now I'm outside," she said at the end of the video, as if reassuring the employee, and perhaps her new internet audience - that she had eventually listened.The story soon started making the rounds online, with people finding the entire exchange oddly wholesome.After all, imagine being in a luxury store and having an employee basically tell you that your money would be better spent after you've actually seen the city.Some social media users joked that the man had temporarily become Vagmita's father for the day. Others loved his reaction, saying it was a refreshing reminder that travelling isn't only about shopping or ticking off tourist attractions.And then there were the solo travellers who could relate to the experience of having random encounters with strangers that somehow become the stories you remember long after the trip is over.For Vagmita, what started as a quick shopping trip turned into one of those completely unexpected holiday moments.She got the Louis Vuitton bag she wanted. She also got a lecture about enjoying the sunshine. And, perhaps most importantly, she found a story funny enough to share with thousands of people online.So yes, she went outside. But not before buying the bag.Looking for trusted parenting advice? Follow TOI Parenting Circle on Instagram for expert guidance, relatable stories, and practical tips delivered every day.

https://nineoclock.ro/fitch-ratings-affi.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Fitch Ratings Affirms Romania’s ‘BBB-’ Sovereign Rating with Negative Outlook By Mihai Manea , Publisher, Nine O’Clock / Social Media: LinkedIn | Facebook | Instagram Fitch Ratings has reaffirmed Romania’s sovereign credit rating at “BBB-” , maintaining the country in the investment-grade category. The assessment is supported by Romania’s membership in the European Union, access to capital flows and external financing, as well as the country’s GDP level and governance indicators. The agency also notes the improvement in budget execution and forecasts a 2026 budget deficit of 5.9% of GDP , below the Government’s target of 6%. “Maintaining Romania in the investment-grade category is an important achievement at a time when every political and budgetary decision is being closely monitored by markets and rating agencies. The data presented by the Ministry of Finance show that the adjustment is producing results: the cash deficit fell to 2% of GDP in the first half of the year, while Fitch projects a 2026 deficit of 5.9%, below the Government’s target. The negative outlook reminds us that political stability, the continuation of reforms, and adherence to the fiscal consolidation path remain essential criteria,” said Alexandru Nazare, Minister of Finance . Alexandru Nazare, Minister of Finance. Budget Execution Results Played a Key Role in Maintaining the Investment-Grade Rating Fitch estimates that the general government deficit will decline to 5.9% of GDP in 2026 , below the Government’s 6% target and significantly lower than the 9.3% of GDP recorded in 2024. During the first half of 2026, the cash deficit fell to RON 42 billion , representing 2% of the estimated GDP for the year, compared with RON 70 billion during the same period in 2025. Fitch highlights higher government revenues and controlled expenditure, reflecting measures adopted to contain wage and social benefit costs. The report also underlines the role of European Union funds in supporting investment and reducing Romania’s external financing needs in 2026. Resources available through the Cohesion Policy, the National Recovery and Resilience Plan (NRRP), and the European SAFE mechanism contribute to diversifying financing sources and maintaining a high level of public investment throughout the fiscal adjustment period. Political Stability and Policy Continuity Remain Essential The continued negative outlook reflects risks stemming from Romania’s still-elevated budget deficit, rising public debt, the current account imbalance, and political uncertainty. Fitch warns that prolonged political deadlock could weaken the Government’s ability to implement reforms and reduce the predictability of fiscal policy beyond 2026. “I rely on the responsibility of all political forces and state institutions to avoid political deadlock and unfunded initiatives that could jeopardize the progress achieved so far. Our priority is to safeguard Romania’s credit rating, reduce financing costs, and create the conditions for the outlook to return to stable,” said Alexandru Nazare, Minister of Finance . According to the agency, the main downside risk to Romania’s rating is the inability to continue fiscal consolidation measures and stabilize public debt, particularly in the event of prolonged political instability. Conversely, sustained progress in reducing the budget deficit and increasing confidence that public debt will stabilize could lead Fitch to revise the outlook from negative to stable . Credit ratings issued by international rating agencies are an important benchmark for investors’ perception of a country’s economy and directly influence the financing conditions available to the government, businesses, and households. Maintaining Romania’s investment-grade rating helps preserve the country’s access to international financial markets and supports confidence in its economic outlook. The evolution of public finances, institutional stability, and the continuity of economic policies will remain key factors in future rating assessments. https://nineoclock.ro/romanias-capital-m.text: ABOUT US NINE O’CLOCK STAFF 2024 COMMERCIAL OFFER – 2026 Subscribe to the Nine O’Clock 2026 CONTACT Special price offer 2026 with a 50% discount Gabriel Avră mescu: Record Growth Signals a More Mature Financial Ecosystem By Dr. Adrian Leonard Mociulschi— Special for Nine O ’ Clock For years, Romania ’ s economic potential was easier to describe than to quantify. Today, the numbers are difficult to ignore. As investors worldwide search for stability, transparency, and growth in an uncertain environment, Romania ’ s capital market is attracting attention not merely as a regional exchange, but as an increasingly credible destination for investment and long-term capital formation. According to data presented by Gabriel Avrămescu, First Vice-President of the Financial Supervisory Authority ( ASF ), and publicly reported by AGERPRES, Romania’s benchmark BET Index has reached approximately 36,000 points, more than 80% above its level a year ago. Meanwhile, the market capitalization of the Bucharest Stock Exchange (BVB) has risen to roughly RON 710 billion, an increase of 68% year-on-year. “In one year, the BET Index has broken threshold after threshold. We have reached a level of 36,000 points and recorded growth of more than 80% compared to the same period of the previous year,” Avrămescu said. These figures are notable not only because of their scale, but because of what they reveal about the evolution of Romania’s financial landscape. Strong market performance rarely emerges in isolation. It is often the product of deeper structural developments, including stronger institutions, expanding access to capital, and growing investor confidence. Central to this progress has been the Financial Supervisory Authority (ASF). While market rallies tend to capture headlines, sustainable growth depends on effective regulation, transparency, and investor protection. Predictable rules and credible oversight help create the confidence on which capital markets ultimately depend. The recent expansion of Romania’s capital market suggests that these foundations are becoming increasingly robust. The Bucharest Stock Exchange (BVB) has been equally important in shaping this trajectory. Over the past decade, it has evolved beyond its traditional role as a trading venue, increasingly positioning itself as a platform for capital formation. By connecting investors with businesses seeking funding, BVB has helped strengthen Romania’s entrepreneurial ecosystem. Initiatives such as BVB Arena reflect a broader effort to bring growth-oriented companies closer to the capital markets. Another indicator highlighted by Avrămescu is the continued expansion of Romania’s investor base. The number of investors has now surpassed 325,000, a record for the local market. More importantly, this trend points to the emergence of a stronger investment culture, increasingly oriented toward long-term wealth creation rather than short-term speculation. Yet Avrămescu regards the current achievements as a milestone rather than a destination. “We believe this is only an intermediate level, and I consider that the potential offered by the Stock Exchange and by attracting investors is much greater,” he noted. Part of that future potential may come from the planned launch of a dedicated Growth Market for small and medium-sized enterprises. According to Avrămescu, the authorization process is already at an advanced stage. “We believe that this growth market represents a bridge between entrepreneurship and the capital market,” he explained. The initiative could provide Romanian SMEs with improved access to financing while offering investors new opportunities to participate in the growth of emerging businesses. In advanced economies, capital markets serve not only as investment mechanisms but also as engines of innovation, productivity, and economic modernization. Romania appears increasingly determined to strengthen that role. The recent milestones achieved by Romania’s capital market are more than headline-grabbing statistics. They point to the gradual strengthening of the financial infrastructure needed to support future growth. For international investors, the message is becoming increasingly clear: Romania is no longer merely a market of promise. It is becoming a market of performance, where institutions, investors, and companies are translating potential into measurable results. Kyiv: At least nine people were killed and 22 civilians injured in the Ukrainian capital Kyiv after Russia launched an intense barrage of ballistic missiles and drones overnight into Saturday, authorities said. A five-story residential building in the city's Solomianskyi District was damaged by falling debris and a fire broke out. Rescue workers evacuated 35 people from the upper floors of the building, and two people died, with eight reported injured, including two children, according to Ukraine's state emergency service. In the Darnytskyi District of Kyiv, seven people were killed and another 14 injured after the attack caused fires and damage to houses, vehicles, an administrative and non-residential building, the emergency services said. Elsewhere, emergency workers extinguished a fire in a non-residential building in the capital's Shevchenkivskyi district. There was no additional information about earlier reports by the district mayor that people were trapped in another residential building. Damage to commercial and residential buildings was reported in two other city districts. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has pressed the United States and other Western partners over Ukraine's need for more Patriot anti-ballistic missile defence systems to counter missile attacks from Russia. The Ukrainian leader late Friday said he spoke to U.S. Vice President JD Vance and discussed a meeting with President Donald Trump earlier this week in Washington, which Zelenskyy described as positive and productive. The Russian air strikes on our country continue and air defence, specifically interceptors for Patriot systems against ballistic missiles, remains a top priority, Zelenskyy said Friday in a post on Telegram. At a NATO summit in Ankara in July, Trump said the U.S. would give Ukraine a license to make Patriot systems, but he appeared to move away from that commitment on Friday during a Cabinet meeting at the presidential retreat in Camp David, Maryland, saying he had not yet made a final decision on the matter. Saturday's attack on Kyiv came just two days after a large-scale Russian ballistic missile and drone attack across Ukraine killed 10 civilians and wounded more than 50 others and saw a Russian missile enter Polish airspace. From a basement shelter where she was taking cover as a second air alarm sounded for another wave, Liudmyla Nakonechna, 64, described how she was woken by loud explosions at 130 a.m. I ran into the corridor and was standing there when the bathroom door was blown off its hinges and struck me in the leg, said Nakonechna, whose health is poor after undergoing cancer treatment. I heard the sound of shattering glass. My balcony was covered in glass, and it was completely blown apart, while the windows in my bedroom were also blown out. Nakonechna had not taken cover in a shelter since Russia's full-scale invasion February 24, 2022, but the stress became too much, she said. It's getting worse by the day, Nakonechna said. Whereas before there was an attack once every two weeks, or maybe once a week, now it happens practically every day.

https://www.lrt.lt/en/news-in-english/19.text: NaujienÅ³ srautas News 1 h ago Demand for free Lithuanian language courses far exceeds places in Vilnius News 16 h ago Committee chair says threat level unchanged despite warnings of Russiaâs possible attacks News 18 h ago Ukraineâs DEMZ signs deal with Lithuania on ammunition production News 20 h ago US presses Lithuania on International Criminal Court â sources News 21 h ago Lithuanian border guard injured in migrant incident near Belarus border News 22 h ago Saudi food giant eyes investment in Lithuaniaâs shrinking dairy sector News 23 h ago Lithuanian unions criticise presidentâs proposed restrictions on migrant workers News 1 d ago LRT English Newsletter: Enduring sins News 1 d ago NATO fighter jets shoot down drone over eastern Latvia News 1 d ago Vatican expresses concern over Lithuanian priests accused of child sexual offenses News 1 d ago Lithuaniaâs justice minister revives call for public sex offender registry News 1 d ago Ukrainian defence company DEMZ to invest in ammunition plant in Lithuania News 1 d ago Lithuanian PM demands Church cooperation after priests charged with child sex offenses News 1 d ago Partial solar eclipse over Lithuania â photos News 1 d ago Lithuania exhumes remains of 81 Soviet soldiers in Vievis town centre News 2 d ago Sexual assault survivors in Lithuania face long waits for help â and lost evidence News 2026.08.01 10:00 Why the West still misunderstands Belarusâ role in Russiaâs war â opinion VB Viktar Baranau, New Eastern Europe 2026.08.01 10:00 Belarusians in Lithuania | B. GerdÅ¾iÅ«nas / LRT Western perceptions of Belarus remain clouded in uncertainty, despite its connections to the ongoing war in Ukraine. Understanding the hopes of Belarusian society will prove pivotal to properly engaging with the country when the conflict eventually comes to an end, Viktar Baranau writes for the New Eastern Europe magazine, partners of LRT English. Alaksandar Klacko recalls the first days of Russiaâs full-scale invasion without any romanticism. For him, the war began the moment he realised that missiles striking Ukrainian cities were being launched from the territory of his own country. Soon afterwards, he joined the Belarusian volunteers of the Kalinouski Regiment fighting on Ukraineâs side. He was later wounded and now lives in Lithuania. âWe understood that we were defending not only Ukraine. We were defending the future of Belarus as well,â he says. His story captures the contradiction that has shaped Belarus since February 2022. On one hand, Belarus became a crucial rear base for Russiaâs invasion: Russian troops attacked Kyiv from its territory, Belarusian infrastructure supports Russian logistics, military equipment is repaired there, and Russian soldiers receive treatment in Belarusian hospitals. On the other hand, thousands of Belarusians volunteered to help Ukrainian refugees, hundreds joined Ukrainian military units, and independent surveys consistently showed strong opposition to Belarus entering the war directly. Yet, this distinction has largely disappeared from Western analysis. Belarus is increasingly portrayed as little more than an extension of Russian foreign policy. This reflects an undeniable reality: the Lukashenko regime has become deeply integrated into Russiaâs war effort and, under international law, Belarus is complicit in the aggression against Ukraine. But this has also encouraged a broader assumption â that the interests of the regime, the Belarusian state and Belarusian society are essentially the same. That assumption obscures one of the most important political dynamics inside Belarus. While the regime has supported Russiaâs invasion, Belarusian society has largely rejected direct participation in the war. Understanding this gap is essential not only for interpreting Lukashenkoâs decisions but also for thinking about Belarusâs place in Europeâs future security architecture. Belarus being part of Russiaâs war is just one part of the story In recent weeks, the question of Belarusâs role in the war has once again come to the fore. After Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky stated that Russia was using navigation and communication systems located on Belarusian territory to strike Ukraine, he publicly demanded that Alexander Lukashenko stop their operation, threatening to destroy the facilities otherwise. Although Zelensky later reported that the equipment had been turned off, the situation itself once again returned Belarus to the headlines of international media and revived a familiar question: could Minsk become a direct participant in the war? A crowd waiting released Belarusian prisoners at the US Embassy in Vilnius last Saturday | AP Such questions have arisen regularly since February 2022. Every time Russia increases military activity or large-scale exercises are held on Belarusian territory, Western analysts again discuss the likelihood of a new offensive from the north of Ukraine. Belarus is perceived primarily as a potential Russian military springboard. This framing is quite understandable. If one judges solely by the actions of the Belarusian state, Belarus has indeed become one of the most important elements of the Russian military campaign. In January and February 2022, under the pretext of joint exercises, about 30,000 Russian servicemen were concentrated on Belarusian territory. It was from there that the advance on Kyiv began â the shortest invasion route on which the Russian command placed special bets. Russian troops used Belarusian airfields in Machulishchi, Baranovichi, and Lida, as well as radar stations and transport infrastructure. According to Ukrainian monitoring, in the first months of the war alone, at least 631 missiles were launched from Belarusian territory at Ukrainian cities. Cooperation was not limited to the first weeks of the invasion. Belarus transferred part of its equipment and ammunition from its stockpiles to Russia, provided enterprises for repairing damaged equipment, provided railway routes for supplying Russian troops, and gradually turned into an important element of the Russian military rear. According to Ukrainian intelligence, today more than five hundred Belarusian enterprises are in one way or another involved in producing goods for the Russian military-industrial complex â from electronics and optics to the repair of weapons and the production of components. Another symbol of this dependence was the deployment of Russian tactical nuclear weapons. For the first time since the collapse of the Soviet Union, Belarus has once again become a country on whose territory Russian nuclear warheads are located. Joint exercises using non-strategic nuclear weapons only cemented this role in Moscowâs strategy of nuclear blackmail. If one looks only at these facts, the conclusion seems obvious â Belarus is one of Russiaâs key allies in this war. âBelarus provides its territory, infrastructure, and resources to the Russian army. From the point of view of international law, this means complicity in aggression. There can be no two interpretations,â says the former Belarusian diplomat Pavel Slunkin. But it is precisely here, in his opinion, that Western analysis often takes a further step that is no longer so obvious. Given the Belarusian regimeâs participation in the war, the automatic conclusion is drawn that the interests of Moscow and Minsk completely coincide. âThis is the most common mistake,â says Slunkin. âYes, Russia and Belarus are in the same military space. Yes, the regimes support each other. But this does not mean that their interests fully coincide.â This conclusion has not only academic significance. Indeed, it directly affects how Europe assesses the risks of further escalation of the war. Minsk, Belarus | Pixabay If Belarus has completely lost its agency and all decisions in Minsk are made by the Kremlin, the obvious question arises: why, over three and a half years of war, has the Belarusian army never once crossed the Ukrainian border? This question is especially relevant today, when the likelihood of Belarusian territory being used again is actively discussed in the expert community. The answer is not that Lukashenko suddenly turned out to be a more independent politician than is commonly believed. According to Slunkin, the Belarusian leader acts primarily according to the logic of his own political survival. âFor Lukashenko, the current model is almost ideal. He provides Moscow with almost everything except the most expensive resource â his own army. He maintains loyalty to the Kremlin but at the same time avoids a decision that could destabilise the situation inside the country.â And the point here is not only Lukashenkoâs political calculation. Moscow itself, according to Slunkin, is not particularly interested in changing the current formula of Minskâs participation. When the question of sending Belarusian troops was being decided in 2022, the Kremlin was convinced that the operation would end quickly and on its own â there was no need to share the future victory with an ally. Since then, the calculation has changed, but the conclusion has remained the same: Russia does not need 15,000 to 20,000 unmotivated Belarusian soldiers against a Ukrainian army that has accumulated combat experience over three years of war unparalleled in Europe. A secure rear is far more valuable to Moscow: oil refineries that are not bombed, airfields and hospitals that operate without the threat of strikes, warehouses and logistics that simply function without failures. In addition, Belarusâs position remains an additional lever of pressure on the Baltic states and Poland. To exchange this quiet haven for a handful of additional bayonets that would turn Belarus itself into a legitimate military target for Ukraine would, from the Kremlinâs point of view, be simply pointless. It is here that the difference between the regime and society becomes noticeable. Lukashenko did not refuse to participate in the war. He refused only the form of participation that could threaten the stability of his own power. And in order to understand why this risk turned out to be so serious, it is necessary to look beyond the regime itself and at Belarusian society â the part of Belarus that has practically disappeared from western discussion about the war. The regime entered the war. Society did not One circumstance that western deliberations about Belarus have almost completely left out is public opinion. In authoritarian states, public opinion is often disregarded. When one person makes all the key decisions, it seems logical to focus exclusively on his motives. However, in the case of Belarus, it is precisely societal attitudes that largely explain why the countryâs participation in the war turned out to be significantly more limited than many expected in the spring of 2022. Independent sociological research consistently records the same trend: the majority of Belarusians do not support their countryâs direct involvement in the war in Ukraine. According to the latest Chatham House and Center of New Ideas surveys, only 14 percent of respondents express direct support for the Russian invasion, while overall about a third (27 percent) approve or rather approve of Russiaâs military actions. Even more telling is the attitude toward the possible sending of the Belarusian army to Ukraine: only 9 percent of Belarusians believe that their army should take part in the war. Belarussians in Lithuania | B. GerdÅ¾iÅ«nas / LRT At first glance, this looks paradoxical. Belarusian society remains one of the most pro-Russian in Europe. As of November 2025, 44 per cent of Belarusians support a geopolitical union with Russia. For a significant part of the population, it remains the main political and cultural partner. However, this sympathy almost does not convert into support for the war. The Belarusian sociologist Daria Urban explains that it is here that many external observers make a fundamental mistake: âIn the West, there is often a simplified logic: if Belarusians have a positive attitude toward Russia and choose an alliance with it, then they must automatically support the Russian war as well. But this is not the case. âThe high figure of supporters of a union with the Russian Federation is largely the result of people simply being left with no other choice. Under conditions of total isolation, Russia is perceived as the path of least resistance, as the only tangible reality, and not at all as a conscious ideological choice in favour of war.â According to Urban, Belarusiansâ attitude toward Russia and their attitude toward the war exist in completely different planes: âSociety is not sociologically monolithic; different groups of people live in non-overlapping information and value planes. And the fact that a person does not want their country to go to war does not mean automatic legitimisation of Lukashenko. Belarusians are mentally not ready to enter this conflict. We have the popular expression ânever againâ embedded at the subconscious level, so people en masse will not go to fight.â In her assessment, the truth lies somewhere in the middle. The average person adapts to the system not out of love for it, but because of the lack of an alternative: Lukashenko himself also does not want the direct participation of his army, but allows the regime to participate in the war only to the extent that it does not require the mobilisation of society. He presents this line as his own main achievement â supposedly he âpreserved peaceâ. âMost people perceive Russia as a close state, but at the same time categorically do not want Belarus to become a direct participant in hostilities. For people, these are completely different, unrelated questions.â After the mass protests of 2020, Lukashenkoâs regime found itself in a deep crisis of legitimacy. Russiaâs full-scale invasion did not automatically restore it. Rather, a new unspoken social compromise emerged: many were ready to tolerate continued authoritarian rule only as long as Belarus was not directly drawn into the war. This is precisely why Lukashenko found himself in a dual position: Moscow expects maximum support, but the decision to send the army would mean a head-on collision with the sentiments of his own society. This does not mean that public opinion determines the policy of an authoritarian regime. But it determines the price of political decisions. This is precisely why, explains Slunkin, the refusal of direct army participation should not be perceived as an example of Minskâs independent foreign policy. âThis was a decision not in the interests of Ukraine and not even in the interests of Europe. It was a decision in the interests of preserving power.â As a result, a situation has arisen that fits poorly into the scheme familiar to Western analysis. The Belarusian regime has become a full participant in the Russian war machine. Belarusian society has not. Russia's war against Ukraine | AP It is this contradiction that explains much of what has happened in the country over the past three years: from the mass unwillingness to fight to the growth in popularity of the narrative that Lukashenko supposedly âpreserved peaceâ for Belarus. But if society differs so much from the regime, why does the West continue to see Belarus as only one monolithic object? https://www.livemint.com/news/world/russ.text: Russia launched a barrage of ballistic missiles and attack drones against Ukraine’s capital overnight, killing nine people and injuring at least 30, as Ukrainian officials urged the supply of more anti-missile weapons from allies. “A horrific night for Kyiv,” Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram. “The enemy struck the capital with ballistic missiles. Residential buildings, non-residential buildings and other infrastructure were damaged or destroyed, and fires broke out in five districts of the city.” Kremlin forces deployed air- and ground-launched missiles of various types, Ukraine’s General Forces said on Telegram. In total, 358 aerial attack weapons — 35 missiles and 185 UAVs of various types - were detected. Of some 27 Iskander-type ballistic missiles, only one was intercepted, “simply because there are no interceptors for the Patriot systems,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on X. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha urged Ukraine’s allies to urgently supply additional air and missile defense systems and interceptors.“Every decision that strengthens the defense of Ukrainian skies saves human lives, while every delay leads to deaths and war crimes,” Sybiha said. “It is the battle for the skies that will define the trajectory of this war.” In Kyiv, the missiles struck 18 residential buildings, a school, and unspecified “infrastructure facilities,” Zelenskyy said. The Dnipro, Sumy, Kharkiv and Poltava regions were also targeted. A missile exploded “steps away” from Lithuania’s embassy in Kyiv, damaging the building but not causing injuries, Lithuanian President Gitanas Nauseda said on X. The Baltic nation plans to summon Russia’s representative in Vilnius after the incident, said Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys. In a statement, Russia’s defense ministry named several facilities targeted in Kyiv overnight, which it said were used to manufacture, store and transport missile weapons, drones, radar systems and electronic warfare equipment. The information can’t be independently confirmed. Separately, two vessels delivering military cargo to a Ukrainian port were also struck south of Odesa on the Black Sea, the ministry said. Russia also said its air defenses shot down 274 Ukrainian drones overnight over Russian regions and the waters of the Azov and Black seas.©2026 Bloomberg L.P.This article was generated from an automated news agency feed without modifications to text.

https://www.wirralglobe.co.uk/news/natio.text: Hungary braces for shutdown of Paks nuclear plant as Danube hits record lows By PA News Agency Share 0 Comments The Danube River due to low levels (Nicolae Dumitrache/AP This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Hungary’s only nuclear power plant will shut down for the first time in its history due to record-low water levels on the Danube River, prime minister Peter Magyar said. He added that the plant may not come back online for several weeks as the river is expected to continue receding. The Paks nuclear plant, located around 50 miles south of the capital Budapest, is operating at less than half its normal capacity, producing 965 megawatts of power rather than the usual 2,000. The plant uses water from the Danube to cool its reactors, but the exceptionally low water level has tested the ability of pumps to bring sufficient quantities into the plant. The MVM Paks Nuclear Power Plant (Daniel Kiss/AP) Speaking at a news conference at the plant on Friday, Mr Magyar said further reductions in output were imminent and that the entire plant will likely be powered down by Tuesday or Wednesday. He stressed that the shutdown can be performed safely and poses no risk to the public or environment. The Soviet-built, four-reactor plant at Paks accounts for nearly half of Hungary’s electricity production. If it is powered down, it will be the first time in its 44 years of service. Hungary and much of Central Europe has been in a prolonged period of drought in recent months, disrupting tourism, agriculture and industry and confronting residents with the realities of climate change. Water levels are not expected to rise on the Danube in the coming days or even weeks as no significant rainfall is forecast. Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar (Robert Hegedus/MTI via AP) Mr Magyar said that the Danube’s water level has only risen on three occasions in the month of August in the last 20 years, and added that the level at Paks could recede to as low as negative 144 centimetres — far below the previous record of negative 98 centimetres set in 2018. A level of negative 134 centimetres requires the full powering down of the plant, he said. A negative reading means the river has fallen below the gauge’s zero reference level, not that the river is empty. Hungary’s government has requested that companies which consume large quantities of energy voluntarily reduce their consumption to help stabilise the energy supply, particularly in peak demand hours between 5pm and 10pm. Mr Magyar said Hungarian energy conglomerate MOL had committed to reducing its electricity needs by 65 megawatt-hours, a decrease of 40% from its normal consumption. Mr Magyar announced that his party had recommended suspending parliamentary sessions planned for Monday and Tuesday in the interest of conserving energy. He also ordered that all state institutions turn off decorative lighting by Monday. Share 0 Comments Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading... https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Lily Hooper left her home in Sydney’s south-west about 8am on 12 August, after telling family she was going for a hike in the Nattai national park. Photograph: NSW Police View image in fullscreen Lily Hooper left her home in Sydney’s south-west about 8am on 12 August, after telling family she was going for a hike in the Nattai national park. Photograph: NSW Police New South Wales Fears for missing Sydney teen who hasn’t been seen since leaving for hike on Wednesday Fresh search teams to scour Nattai national park for Lily Hooper, 18, who failed to return home from a bushwalk Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Lisa Cox and AAP Fri 14 Aug 2026 21.07 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 21.18 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The search for an 18-year-old bushwalker missing in the Southern Highlands of New South Wales since Wednesday is continuing, with fresh teams arriving at the Nattai national park on Saturday morning. Lily Hooper left her home in Sydney’s south-west about 8am on 12 August, after telling family she was going for a hike in the national park, north-west of Mittagong. The experienced hiker was reported missing when she did not return that evening and could not be reached, despite having sent messages from the park earlier in the day. A search began with her car found parked on Wanganderry Road, near the start of the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail at High Range, about 11pm that night. On Saturday, NSW police said in a statement that initial inquiries indicated Hooper reached the summit of Bonnum Pic about mid-morning on Wednesday, but had made no further contact since then. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email A multi-agency search – involving local police, regional Police Rescue, NSW Ambulance, Fire and Rescue NSW, the State Emergency Service and members of Hooper’s family – has not found any further signs of the teen. Defence force personnel joined the search on Friday, with drones, an ambulance helicopter and specialist rescuers, including trail-bike riders, also involved. A NSW police spokesperson said the search continued overnight and fresh teams arrived at the park at 7am on Saturday. On Friday, Det Insp Benjamin Bowles said authorities were concerned for Hooper’s safety. But he said he remained optimistic, and that Hooper was an experienced hiker. “We have not been able to fully confirm what supplies [Hooper] had with her at the time, but we are still hopeful that we will be able to locate her safe and sound,” he said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion “We don’t have any information to suggest that this is anything other than an overdue hiker.” The NSW premier, Chris Minns, told reporters on Friday he was “praying for good news”. “Our heart goes out to that young walker’s family,” he said. “We know this must be heartbreaking and incredibly anxious.” Hooper is described as Caucasian in appearance, about 175cm tall, slim, and with long blond hair and blue eyes. She was last seen wearing a shirt and shorts, but police said it was not known what clothing or supplies she took for the hike. Police said anyone who may have seen Hooper, had information about her whereabouts or who walked the Bonnum Pic walking trail on Wednesday, should contact Moss Vale police station on 02 4869 7899 or Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Volunteers distribute hot meals at the weekly service in Charing Cross. Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Homelessness Westminster council threatens Charing Cross soup kitchen with closure Conservative authority says site is not safe for vulnerable people charity serves or general public Helena Horton Sat 15 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Westminster council is making it “impossible” for soup kitchens to operate by complaining about the “crowds of vulnerable people” who turn up to be fed, a charity has said. Steven Stuart, who founded Friends of Essex & London Homeless (FOELH) with his wife, Cheryl, a decade ago, said constant complaints from the council could force the soup kitchen to shut down. The council is also facing a licensing battle with the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, who has objected to its restrictive new draft policy that would ban new bars and pubs from opening in Soho and the West End. The council also plans to restrict “vertical drinking” – standing while having a pint – in new bars, pubs and restaurants. The homeless charity runs a weekly event in Charing Cross, where volunteers hand out hot meals. It also provides new clothes and sleeping bags to rough sleepers, and runs a food bank. But Westminster council has sent enforcement agents to the soup kitchen, warning that it cannot operate as it currently does and raising concerns about noise and litter. Phil Jones, a FOELH volunteer, said: “We’ve received notice from the council that they intend to ban us from operating our weekly soup kitchen in Charing Cross. They cite litter issues but we clear away all waste and leave the area spotless, so that’s just an excuse from them.” Stuart said: “We are facing increasing challenges with Westminster city council surrounding our weekly Charing Cross outreach. Various requirements and obstacles are making it increasingly difficult to provide the consistent support that vulnerable people have come to rely upon.” These have included a threat of a £500 parking charge for the vehicle used to transport and distribute food, and demands that the charity obtain a costly waste disposal licence. Stuart said: “We questioned whether this was proportionate or appropriate for a small, entirely volunteer-run charity carrying out a weekly homeless outreach but, nevertheless, we have now obtained the certificate to ensure we are fully compliant.” The council has also turned up on several occasions with a group of police and security officers to complain about the soup kitchen, Stuart said. “From our perspective, the scale and manner of these visits have at times felt intimidating and disproportionate given the nature of the work we are carrying out.” He has asked the council to issue permits to charities for specific days and locations, so they know what is expected of them and can carry out their volunteering without being “blind-sided” by new requirements. A Westminster city council spokesperson said the soup kitchen was not safe at present. “Soup kitchens can provide a valuable service but need to be carefully managed. Operators must treat vulnerable people with dignity and take care of the surrounding area,” they said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion “At the moment we have several kitchens operating at the same time and place, leading to large crowds of the most vulnerable people gathering in a confined area.” The spokesperson said this could lead to drug dealers turning up “looking to exploit the situation”, and that the council had received complaints from residents about “antisocial behaviour, littering and crime in Charing Cross while the soup kitchen is operating” They added: “Currently, the site is not safe for those using the service or the general public.” The Conservative council has been taking part in a crackdown on homeless people. The council’s deputy leader, Caroline Sargent, said of homeless sites in Westminster: “Local people and businesses are fed up with rough sleeping sites springing up, and so are we. This is totally unacceptable in the heart of a capital city.” Explore more on these topics Homelessness London Housing Poverty Communities Social exclusion Local government news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: Suzy Bernard, left, is part of the campaign to save the Hauts-d'Anjou pool in Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, France, which costs €100,000 a year to run View image in fullscreen Suzy Bernard, left, is part of the campaign to save the Hauts-d'Anjou pool in Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, France, which costs €100,000 a year to run France ‘In the heatwaves, it’s crucial’: the fight to save France’s rural swimming pools Ageing facilities offering daily refuge face funding threat as record temperatures parch the countryside Angelique Chrisafis in Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe and Rochefort-sur-Loire; photographs by Thomas Louapre Sat 15 Aug 2026 00.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Suzy Bernard took a breath and jumped into the deep end of her village swimming pool with a splash. “There’s a wonderful feeling of wellbeing in the water,” said the former hospital healthcare assistant, who recently learned to swim aged 75 and was now gliding along with her daughter and grandson. View image in fullscreen Suzy Bernard: ‘We’ll fight to make sure this pool survives’ The municipal swimming pool, bordered by shady oak trees in the village of Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, in western France , has been the Bernard family’s daily refuge from the sweltering heatwaves this summer. Bernard is a member of the village collective, Touche Pas à Ma Piscine (Hands Off My Pool), campaigning to defend the Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe facility and calling for more government support for rural swimming pools. “We’ll fight to make sure this pool survives and stays open,” she said. As a summer of record temperatures parched much of the French countryside, local village swimming pools, with cheap entry tickets, have often been the only shelter from the heatwaves for rural families on low incomes who cannot afford to go on holiday or who live in heat-trap homes . The pools are also crucial for teaching rural communities to swim. A total of 274 people died from drowning in France between 1 May and 15 July this year, with most deaths occurring when people jumped into rivers and waterways to cool down. Families enjoy local swimming pools in western France But France’s ageing rural swimming pools, many of which were built in 1970s, are in crisis as village mayors with shrinking budgets struggle to pay the high running costs and some pools are forced to close owing to lack of funds. In Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, a village of 3,200 people in Les Hauts-d’Anjou, a farming area of the Pays de la Loire, the new mayor, Véronique Langlais, said she was determined to keep running the village pool that opened in 1973, despite an annual cost of at least €100,000 (£85,000) to the town hall’s modest budget. Three other rural pools had closed in the surrounding countryside, making this the only pool in a radius of about 20 miles. View image in fullscreen Véronique Langlais, mayor of Hauts-d’Anjou, in the changing rooms of the Hauts-d’Anjou swimming pool “This pool is a treasure that we have to protect,” Langlais said. But any sudden need for a costly new part or major repair could force the pool’s closure owing to lack of funds. “There’s a sword of Damocles hanging over our head.” In 1969, after France’s poor swimming performance at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics , and a series of tragic drownings across the country, the government under Georges Pompidou launched a plan to build 1,000 pools in mainly rural areas to encourage swimming. Over 600 were built, but those still in use – as well as later 1980s pools – are in urgent need of costly renovation. View image in fullscreen Swimming lessons for children at the Hauts-d’Anjou outdoor swimming pool in Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe, France View image in fullscreen The outdoor swimming pool, which opened in 1973 François Gernigon, a centre-right lawmaker for the Maine-et-Loire, has petitioned the government for a funding plan. He recently surveyed rural mayors, finding more than 75% feared their village pools risked closure in the short-term. He said the heatwaves made it essential to protect pools as “the only place of leisure to relax in rural areas”. He said village pool closures “make residents feel abandoned”. View image in fullscreen Emma-Özlen Kaya: ‘We didn’t go on holiday because my parents didn’t have the budget’ Emma-Özlem Kaya, 45, is a printmaker whose Turkish father moved to Châteauneuf-sur-Sarthe in 1972 when the local tannery recruited artisan leather-workers from Istanbul. “We didn’t go on holiday because my parents didn’t have the budget,” she said. “So every day in summer, I’d grab my swimming bag and walk to the pool with my siblings and friends and we’d spend the afternoons there with our towels laid out.” She now attends water aerobics classes there and campaigns to protect the pool. View image in fullscreen The Hauts-d’Anjou outdoor swimming pool Nadine Lemonnier, a local teacher who is also part of the collective, remembered childhood summers at another local village pool: “whole days spent diving for objects and having deep teenage conversations at the edge”. For her, protecting rural pools that offered children swimming lessons was crucial because her three-year-old cousin died from drowning in a private pool. Across France, there are dozens of rural village collectives mobilising to protect local pools: campaigning, volunteering to help run them and even painting and carrying out maintenance work. View image in fullscreen Guillaume, a swimming instructor, leads an aqua aerobics class at the Louet municipal swimming pool in Rochefort-sur-Loire View image in fullscreen Chris is teaching his daughter Seren how to dive at the Louet municipal swimming pool In Rochefort-sur-Loire, a village of 2,400 people near Angers, members of the local pool support group gathered at the water’s edge. In recent years, they had decorated the village with flippers and rubber rings to convince a visiting government minister to secure funds for reopening the indoor teaching pool. They hosted a poet in residence at the pool and run theatre performances there. “It’s about making our village pool the focus of life in the community,” said Nicolas Robin, a sociologist. On 18 July 1969, at nearby Juigné-sur-Loire, 19 children drowned in the River Loire on an outing from a school holiday club – one of many tragedies that led the government to improve swimming teaching facilities. Swimming lessons remain key. There are three rivers in the area and the village is often hit by flooding in winter. View image in fullscreen The Louet River, now dry, right next to the Louet municipal swimming pool in Rochefort-sur-Loire Photograph: Thomas Louapre/The Guardian “People need to know how to swim to protect themselves in the flooding season too,” said Guillaume Lusteau, the pool’s lifeguard and swim coach. The pool sits beside the River Louet, a branch of the Loire that is usually a paddling spot. But the summer heatwaves have left the river level too low for a dip, increasing the number of swimmers at the pool. View image in fullscreen Didier Le Gall, mayor of Rochefort-sur-Loire: ‘The pool is part of our village’s identity’ The mayor, Didier Le Gall, said that in this area, with a large proportion of organic farming, health was a priority and the pool was essential, particularly for families on low incomes. “It’s important for children learning to swim, but also for the social lives of people who don’t go away on holiday,” he said. “The pool is part of our village’s identity, and in the heatwaves it has become a crucial place to cool down. The pool’s impact on mental health and physical health is considerable.” Le Gall said the town hall wanted to keep the pool open, despite the €100,000 basic running cost. “But we need help in the long-term,” he said. View image in fullscreen Louet municipal swimming pool, in Rochefort-sur-Loire View image in fullscreen Louet Municipal swimming pool, in Rochefort-sur-Loire Bruno Cheminat, 73, a former special educational needs teacher and one-time competitive swimmer, clocks up 2,000 metres every day, and has also helped with painting and maintenance work as a volunteer. “It’s beautiful to be the first in the water in the morning,” he said. Estelle, a former flight attendant who works on the pool reception, said it boosted her mood to be in the water, looking out at trees towards the church: “It’s like swimming in a picture postcard.” Explore more on these topics France Swimming Climate crisis Extreme heat Europe Europe weather features Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

Photograph: Ukrinform/Shutterstock Russia-Ukraine war at a glance Russia Explainer Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy warns Egypt of food supply threat caused by Russian strikes in Black Sea Kyiv says exports to Egypt under threat from Russian attacks; Moscow dismisses idea of Black Sea ceasefire. What we know on day 1,635 Guardian staff and agencies Fri 14 Aug 2026 21.53 EDT Last modified on Fri 14 Aug 2026 23.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned Egyptian counterpart Abdel ⁠Fattah al-Sisi of possible food supply shortages caused by Russian strikes on ⁠cargo vessels in the Black Sea . “Ukraine is one of ⁠the largest food suppliers to ​Egypt and to ‌a significant number ‌of other countries in Africa ‌and the Middle East. These supplies are now under serious threat because of Russia’s war,” Zelenskyy said on X. “We are already seeing ‌a significant reduction in supplies, and this could have very ​unpleasant consequences due to rising prices and shortages,” he said, adding that the two countries had agreed to ⁠work on solutions. Russia on Friday dismissed the idea of a ceasefire ‌with Ukraine in the Black Sea , saying it saw no grounds for “half-measures” that would ​offer a respite to the other side. In a statement, foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova accused Ukraine of “brazen acts of terrorism” against shipping, while making no ⁠mention of Russia’s own attacks. “We view these attacks (by Ukraine) as a ​deliberate policy aimed at destabilising civilian ‌shipping in the Black ‌Sea region,” Zakharova said. “At the same time, we see no signs of improvement in the situation and, consequently, no grounds for half-measures that merely grant the Kyiv regime a temporary breathing space.” Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up attacks in recent weeks against commercial ships in the ​Black Sea, driving world grain prices higher. Zakharova’s comments followed an earlier Ukraine proposal for both sides to halt their attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea in an apparent attempt to reopen a crucial grain corridor. Kyiv is said to have made the offer through a third party. Russia has intensified its online disinformation campaign in Poland , using a dispute between Warsaw and Kyiv over second world war massacres ⁠to inflame tensions between Ukraine and ⁠its key ally, Polish ​officials and researchers say. The messaging, mostly posted on social media accounts in Polish, also tries to foment anger in Poland against refugees, as opinion polls show support for the far-right growing ahead of closely contested ⁠parliamentary elections in 2027. The long-running second world war dispute between Poland and Ukraine centres on the Volhynia massacres , in which Poland says Ukrainians killed about 100,000 Poles between 1943 and 1945. The dispute intensified after ⁠Zelenskyy named an army unit after insurgents who perpetrated the massacres, prompting hard-right president Karol Nawrocki to strip his Ukrainian counterpart of a top Polish ​honour in June. Russian authorities acknowledged Friday that some regions face new petrol shortages, as Ukraine continues to attack the country’s oil refineries to blunt Russia’s capacity to pursue the war. Russia has shut down one big refinery at Orsk – about 1,300km (810 miles) from the frontline – for six months after it was attacked this week. “The situation remains tense in several regions of the country regarding fuel supplies to service stations,” the government said in a social media post. Oil companies are “taking the necessary measures to increase deliveries to the most vulnerable regions”, it said. Russian jet-powered drones have struck a home in northern Ukraine, killing a 29-year-old woman and her 9-year-old son . This attack comes after the United Nations reported that July was the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since the early weeks of Russia’s invasion. At least 437 civilians were killed and 2,610 wounded last month. Meanwhile, Ukrainian drones have targeted Russian infrastructure, including a major port north of Moscow. Romania found ⁠a second drone in national ⁠territory on ⁠Friday , ​in the south-eastern village ⁠of Plauru near the Danube border with ⁠Ukraine, the defence ​ministry said ‌on ‌Friday, after a ‌low flying drone undetected by radar systems crashed earlier. The ministry did not specify ‌the origins of the drone. ​The Nato state has seen Russian drones repeatedly breach ⁠its airspace over the ​last four ​years. Russian president Vladimir Putin told North Korean ⁠leader Kim Jong-un that Moscow and Pyongyang were cooperating across all areas to ensure ⁠regional ​security and stability, North Korean state media KCNA reported on Saturday. Putin said in a message ⁠to Kim marking the anniversary of Korea’s liberation from Japanese colonial rule that he was confident Russia and ⁠North Korea would continue “constructive joint work” on bilateral and international ​issues, KCNA said. Kim had ‌visited Pyongyang’s Liberation ‌Tower on Friday to pay tribute to Soviet soldiers who fought ‌Japan in the second world war, KCNA reported. http://www.euronews.com/2026/08/15/myste.text: At least 19 elephants have died since June in a wildlife region of southern Kenya near the Tanzanian border and Mount Kilimanjaro. The local operations head says the number has now reached 20, while authorities continue trying to establish the cause.Early tests have suggested cyanide poisoning from pesticides used on nearby farmland. But local wildlife experts say they are not convinced, as other animals feeding on the elephant carcasses have not shown signs of poisoning.According to Patrick Papatiti, head of operations for Olgulului communal lands, the elephants have reportedly suffered difficulty walking and breathing, as well as restlessness, before becoming unable to stand. "They lie down until they die. At times, you would find one struggling for a day, struggling for two or even three days until they completely die."The deaths come after Kenya experienced a severe drought in 2022, but Papatiti says current conditions do not point to a lack of food or water."Currently, we have abundant pasture around, we have water close to where these elephants go. We have protection within the ecosystem that we work."While some initial tests have suggested cyanide poisoning, Papatiti says the behaviour of scavengers around the carcasses raises questions about that explanation."We have no idea. We are still struggling with our thinking and thoughts around what is happening. We have seen hyenas eating the carcasses and they don't die. We have seen vultures feeding on the carcasses and they don't die. We have seen flies landing on the carcasses. They feast, get happy and leave. So we have no idea what this is. "The uncertainty is also raising concerns about what could happen if the cause affects other animals. "How do we know if this is going to translate into going to livestock?. Then when it gets to livestock, it is going to get to the community, local community around. So, how much are we going to lose until we fight to stop this happening?"Farmers in Kimana say they are also struggling to understand what is happening. Wildlife experts and authorities are continuing to investigate the mysterious deaths, with the cause still unresolved.

https://www.dw.com/en/indonesia-strong-e.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Irh8 The quake caused severe damage to buildings in the area Image: Selo/AFP Advertisement A powerful earthquake struck off the coast of Indonesia early on Saturday, killing at least five people, authorities said. Preliminary reports show two deaths in Sikka Regency and three in Manggarai Regency, authorities said. The epicenter of the magnitude 7.7 earthquake hit off the coast of the island of Flores at a shallow depth of 10 kilometers (6.2 miles), the US Geological Survey (USGS) said. Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive. Tsunami waves of less than 1 meter (3 feet) were recorded in several areas of the country before the warning was lifted about three hours after the quake. Where did the earthquake strike? Indonesia's Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) recorded the first quake at 4:58 am (2158 GMT) at a depth of 15 km (9 ⁠miles), followed by dozens of aftershocks. People rushed out onto the street as the quake struck Image: Arnold Welianto/AFP Video shared on social media from Maumere, the main town in Sikka Regency on Flores Island in eastern Indonesia, showed part of a building collapsing in a cloud of dust and rubble as people screamed and ran into the street. "Many buildings here were damaged ... I saw that the waiting room at the Pelni port terminal in Maumere had collapsed," Yohanna Embu, a resident of Sikka, a regency within East Nusa Tenggara province, told AP. Residents evacuated, tsunami warning lifted The initial jolt was followed by a series of aftershocks in the same area, including one of magnitude 6.1. Tourists evacuate after their hotel was severely damaged Image: REUTERS BMKG issued a tsunami warning for part of East Nusa Tenggara, West Nusa Tenggara, South Sulawesi and Southeast Sulawesi provinces, urging residents to stay away from beaches and riverbanks. The tsunami warning was later lifted. Rescue workers searching for survivors in the rubble of a destroyed building Image: BASARNAS/AP Photo/picture alliance "We have ended (the tsunami warning) but we will keep monitoring the sea level," Wijayanto, earthquake and tsunami director at BMKG, said. Before the tsunami warning was lifted, residents of Maumere on Flores Island were told to move to higher ground, according to AFP. State television also showed hundreds of people evacuating in nearby Nagekeo regency. Local TV footage showed a hospital in the district of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara Province moving patients outside. Patients and medical staff evacuated from a health center Image: Arnold Welianto/AFP Authorities assessing damage, casualties The quake caused severe damage and collapsed buildings, causing power outages in cities and villages, severely hindering rescue operations. "We are continuing to collect reports of damages and casualties, but there are communication disruptions," East Nusa Tenggara police chief Rudi Darmoko said. Local television reports showed patients at several hospitals being evacuated from buildings as a precaution. "Our students and nuns ran out in panic beneath a collapsing roof," Guidelbertus Tanga, rector of Ritapiret Seminary on Flores said. "At least one priest suffered a broken leg after jumping from the second floor of a building during the quake." There were also damages reported in some part of southern Sulawesi island. Indonesia's history of earthquakes Indonesia is located on the so-called "Ring of Fire," a region of heightened seismic activity in the Pacific basin that stretches from Southeast Asia to Japan. Here are some of the biggest earthquakes to strike the region: 1992, magnitude 7: A tsunami following a strong earthquake on the southeastern island of Flores killed about 2,500 people 2004, magnitude 9.1: A quake struck off the coast of Sumatra triggering a tsunami that killed 170,000 in Indonesia and 220,000 in several countries in the Indian Ocean 2018, magnitude 6.9: A tremor killed more than 550 people on the islands of Lombok and Sumbawa 2018, magnitude 7.5: A quake and a subsequent tsunami in Palu on Sulawesi island left more than 4,300 people dead or missing Edited by: Karl Sexton If you rely on our team for trusted reporting, please take a moment to select us as your Preferred Source on Google , so you'll always see our verified news first. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y0.text: Image source, BASARNAS Image caption, The Lorens Say Port in Maumere is among the buildings damaged by the earthquake which struck off the coast of the island of Flores By Farida Susanty ,Â BBC Indonesia, Â and Â Helen Sullivan Published 15 August 2026, 03:30 BST Updated 9 minutes ago At least fourteen people have died after a 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck Indonesia early on Saturday, the nation's disaster mitigation agency has said. BPBD said that others had been injured to varying degrees, cautioning that the figures were preliminary while search and rescue operations were ongoing. Teams are working to free anyone trapped in buildings damaged by the quake and the dozens of aftershocks that followed. A tsunami warning was issued but lifted around three hours after the initial jolt. The quake struck the island of Flores shortly before 05:00 local time on Saturday (23:00 GMT on Friday). It had a depth of 15km, Indonesia's meteorology and geophysics agency stated. Image caption, The earthquake struck around 600 miles (1,000km) away from Bali The shallower an earthquake is, the more destructive its effects on the surface tend to be. Strong aftershocks were felt in the same area, including one with a magnitude of 6.1. Video taken at the port in Maumere showed large chunks of concrete breaking off the terminal building onto passengers waiting to board an inter-island ferry. Some were thrown into the sea when the gangway to a ship collapsed. Emanuel Melkiades Laka Lena, governor of East Nusa Tenggara province, told a news conference that they were killed in their sleep by collapsing rubble. A stream of people could be seen moving inland on motorbikes after authorities issued a tsunami warning. BNPB said 2,000 people had evacuated or relocated on their own. But it will take time to assess the full extent of the destruction in the region, which is remote and mountainous. BNPB advised people to remain calm and stay away from coastal areas. "Residents should also avoid entering buildings, especially those that have already sustained cracks or structural damage," BNPB said. "A rapid assessment is currently underway to determine the number of casualties and the extent of the impact. We will provide that information after the data has been verified." Image source, Getty Images About 2,000 residents in Nagekeo were evacuated with damage reported to a number of buildings. Arnold Welianto, who lives in Talibura village, Sikka, East Nusa Tenggara, told the BBC that he was still asleep when he felt the "very strong shaking". "I was startled awake and immediately went to my child's room," he said. "Once we were outside, residents in our neighbourhood, which is located close to the shoreline, had already fled their homes and were heading toward the hills and crowding the roads, while some other residents were standing along the roadside because the sea had also receded. "The water remained low for quite some time, so everyone panicked and ran - I went around to the community health centre, and the people there had already been evacuated." Welianto said many residents were choosing to remain outdoors as ongoing aftershocks meant they were afraid to return home. Indonesia is prone to earthquakes and volcanic activity, lying along the meeting point of three major tectonic plates. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/15/laza.text: Menü Kereső Megtudtuk, hova tűnt Lázár János: nyakába vette az országot, hogy felmérje, mi maradt a Fideszből Belföld Legfontosabb Vorák Anita Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom A sok hiányzása miatt csak minimálbért kapott júliusban a parlamentben Lázár János, de a Telex megtudta, hogy ha a szavazások több mint kilencven százalékát ki is hagyta, pártügyekben nem tétlenkedett. Információnk szerint a párt megbízásából az országot járta, hogy felmérje, milyen állapotban vannak a Fidesz vidéki szervezetei az áprilisban elszenvedett választási vereség után, és mi maradt egyáltalán a pártból. A tapasztalataiból szeptemberre kell jelentést készítenie a Fidesz elnökségének, ahol ez alapján értékelik majd a párt lehetőségeit. Úgy tudjuk, hogy eddig főleg a dunántúli megyéket látogatta. Ezt az értesülésünket látszott erősíteni az is, hogy az Ugytudjuk.hu olvasója csütörtökön délután a szombathelyi Fidesz-iroda előtt fotózta le Lázárt, aki gondterhelten telefonált. Lázár János a szombathelyi Fidesz-iroda előtt 2026. augusztus 13-án – Fotó: Olvasói Fotó / Ugytudjuk.hu A lap információja szerint eligazítást tartott a Vas megyei választókerületi elnököknek, pontosabban Ágh Péternek és V. Németh Zsoltnak. Ágh Péter, aki az előző ciklusban Lázár János államtitkára volt az Építési és Közlekedési Minisztériumban, egyike azon kevés fideszes képviselőnek, aki egyéniben tudott mandátumot szerezni április 12-én. Ágh kevesebb mint 300 szavazattal győzte le a tiszás Strompová Viktóriát, akit Lázár János a kampányban leszlovákozott . Az Úgytudjuk azt írta, hogy Lázár János a jövőbeli feladatairól beszélt a két politikussal. A Telex viszont úgy értesült, ennél konkrétabb feladata is van Lázár Jánosnak. Ezért a fotó megjelenése után megkerestük őt a kérdéseinkkel, de ezekre egyelőre nem válaszolt. Havasi Bertalan, a Fidesz sajtófőnöke viszont megerősítette az értesüléseinket. „Igen, meg tudom erősíteni, Lázár János feladata – amire a pártelnök és a Fidesz elnöksége együttesen kérte fel – egy általános állapotfelmérés.” Havasi szerint Lázár a teljes, országos párt-infrastruktúra állapotát fel kell mérnie. Azt írta, ő már túl van vele egy személyes egyeztetésen, ami „nagyon részletes, professzionális és optimista hangulatú, egyórás konzultáció volt”. Havasi azt is megerősítette, hogy Lázár János határidőt is kapott. „Jelenleg a munka gőzerővel zajlik, a határidő: szeptember” – írta. Ennél többet nem árult el, azt írta, hogy amennyiben a későbbiekben szükséges lesz, majd tájékoztatják a közvéleményt, de ez alapvetően belső pártügy. Információink szerint sok helyen a városi irodákat is bezárja a Fidesz, de Lázárnak nemcsak arról kell információt gyűjtenie, hogy hol lehet ezt meglépni, hanem arról is, hogy milyen a hangulat a helyi szervezetnél, és a tagok, helyi politikusok hogyan értékelik a választási vereséget és a Fidesz jövőjét. A Telexnek küldött válaszában Havasi Bertalan is kiemelte, hogy Lázárnak nemcsak az irodákról és a helyi csoportokról kell jelentést tennie. A szombathelyi találkozó egyik résztvevője, V. Németh Zsolt is azt mondta a Népszavának , hogy Lázár nem eligazítást tartott, hanem meghallgatta őket arról, „milyen szervezeti keretekben, milyen módon és milyen megújulással látjuk el a konstruktív ellenzéki teendőinket”. V. Németh szerint rajta és Ágh Péteren kívül 10-12, a Fidesz tagságát reprezentáló ember is részt vett a találkozón. https://www.theglobeandmail.com/life/sty.text: Laura Studarus Special to The Globe and Mail Published August 1, 2026 Updated August 2, 2026 Open this photo in gallery: In Warsaw, there are plenty of opportunities to enjoy outdoor city life in August. Once summer is over, the Polish capital buttons back up. Laura Studarus/Handout/Supplied Share Save for later Please log in to bookmark this story. Log In Create Free Account It’s 5 p.m. on Aug. 1, and the entire area around Warsaw’s Rondo Dmowskiego roundabout has come to a halt. Sirens sound; hordes of motorcyclists begin revving their engines. Head bowed, locals hold up smoke sticks, creating a “fog of war” effect. This is a celebration of “W” Hour, a one-minute remembrance of the heroes of the 1944 Warsaw Uprising, a 63-day act of military resistance to Nazi occupation that ended with much of the city being destroyed. It’s also a compelling reminder that Warsaw is a city still finding ways to embrace the future while honouring its past. I’ve spent every summer in Warsaw for the past decade. While my primary motivation for the repeated visits is seeing the friends I’ve made over the years, I’ve also fallen in love with the city’s rapid evolution. And while locals leaving the city to take one last vacation before the return of autumn weather will disagree with me, August is the best time to visit Warsaw. Open this photo in gallery: A young resident holds up a smoke stick as part of Aug. 1 ‘W’ Hour ceremonies in Warsaw. Laura Studarus/Handout/Supplied The unofficial theme of the month is getting outdoors. It isn’t just the café owners dragging their tables onto the sidewalks (although spots in Savior Square could certainly give Paris a run for its money). There are simply more opportunities for outdoor socialization during the summer. Once summer is over, Warsaw buttons back up. I am not a morning person, but I will start my August weekends by dragging myself out of bed for the breakfast market Targ Śniadaniowy , a summer event which sets up shop in the Żoliborz neighbourhood on Saturdays, and the Mokotów area on Sundays. Evening owls will appreciate Nocny Market , a night market that repurposes the abandoned platforms of Warszawa Gtowna train station on the weekends. Both events showcase Warsaw’s ever-expanding bench of international food options, art and music. My favourite places: A local filmmaker’s guide to London’s parks and cycling trails A caveat on visiting Warsaw’s Old Town: The neighbourhood was fully destroyed in the Second World War. While the buildings that stand there now are beautiful, they’re a recreation of what it looked like – one that comes with overpriced restaurants. But I’ll make an exception for Jazz na Starowce , a summer-long jazz festival that’s taken residence in the colourful square for the past 32 years. Open this photo in gallery: The music of Chopin endures in live Sunday performances in Lazienki Park. Laura Studarus/Handout/Supplied But if you’re looking for more local-approved food and culture, grab bowls at Bar Pacyfik and bring them to LOT’s Summer Cinema series, an outdoor movie showing held in the shadow of the Palace of Culture on Tuesday, Thursdays, and Saturdays. Or picnic in Lazienki Park on Sundays with the accompaniment of a live Chopin piano concert series. One of Warsaw’s most famous creatives may have passed more than 170 years ago, but the long shadow of Chopin’s legacy can also be felt at Pardon, To Tu , a bar that often books local free jazz, classical and improvisational artists. The area around the Vistula River isn’t excessively built out, and that’s exactly why I like it. Along the Praga side, the banks are largely left as is, acting as an ad hoc nature preserve. (Translation: Bring bug spray.) However, on the Warsaw side, the Vistula Boulevards, a six-kilometre strip running along the river, populated by skaters, walkers and joggers, can be a particularly enjoyable place to sit in the sun during the day. This is especially true if you take up residence on one of Warsaw’s many artificial beaches. But the area comes alive at night. Floating establishments – like the aptly named BarKa – offer both drinks and evening concerts, turning the area into a shockingly well-behaved open-air bar. (Just don’t try to drink in other parts of the city – consuming alcohol in parks and streets will result in a fine.) The city has continued to pour money into this area, including opening the Ktadka walking bridge in 2024, which has become one of my favourite spots to watch the sunset. I’m a walker regardless of location, but on Sundays in the summer, Nowy Swiat and Krakowskie Przedmiescie – two streets that wind through Warsaw’s high-end shopping district and into Castle Square – go car-free. Here, the experience of strolling the streets, or just stopping for a traditional Polish doughnut (with twists such as Nutella and passion fruit) at Dobra Pączkarnia Warszawa , becomes all the more inviting. Open this photo in gallery: When riding one of the old trams on a summer weekend, buy tickets in advance or risk being fined. Laura Studarus/Handout/Supplied Public transit sightseers, the city has you as well – on the weekends during the summer, special trams from the 1940s and 1950s run along Line T . It’s delightful enough to see the candy-coloured cars rattle by, but passengers are also taken on a route that includes Filtrowa Street, the Warsaw Uprising Museum and Wola cemeteries – considered to be some of the most compelling points of interest in the city. Unlike their more modern tram car relatives, these don’t have ticket machines on board, so be sure to purchase a ticket at a nearby subway station or on a mobile app, or risk being that North American unsuccessfully trying to talk your way out of a stiff fine. (Trust me, it doesn’t work.) A ski holiday in Poland? A visit to the wild alpine fun of Zakopane August in Warsaw may start with a sombre remembrance, but the month is ultimately a celebration. The Polish capital is still in the middle of a decades-long rebuilding process, but they’ve found a balance – one that allows for both memory and progress. Just be sure to take it all in before the mercury drops. If you go Open this photo in gallery: Old Town Warsaw: A reconstruction of pre-Second World War buildings, but built on history nevertheless. Laura Studarus/Handout/Supplied Poland’s national carrier LOT is the only airline that offers regular non-stop flights between Toronto and Warsaw. If you choose to add Warsaw on to a larger European trip, be sure to book your flights into Warsaw Chopin (WAW) rather than Warsaw Modlin (WMI), to save transit times into the city. Embrace the city’s past and modernist future by staying at Hotel Warszawa , a formal Second World War target turned five-star hotel. It celebrates Warsaw’s past with a modernist design that showcases the building’s original materials and scars. The location also provides an incredible view of the Palace of Culture. Poland uses Polish ztoty . While most stores and restaurants across Warsaw accept credit cards and Apple Pay, it’s worth keeping cash handy. You’ll want funds for park ice-cream vendors and milk bars – low-cost kitchens serving traditional Polish food. Because August is a month of remembrance, the Warsaw Uprising Museum often sells out weeks in advance and requires advance reservations. Likewise, the award-winning POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews , regularly considered one of the best museums in Europe, is worth booking ahead if you have a preferred time of visit. The majority of museums in Warsaw also offer one free day every week . The writer’s hotel stay was complimentary and it did not review or approve this article.
