Photograph: Bloomberg/Getty Images Heathrow airport Heathrow passengers face disruption after flood restricts access Airport advises passengers travelling from terminals 2 and 3 to use rail and tube as pipe leak closes road Daniel Lavelle Sat 15 Aug 2026 06.36 EDT Last modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Heathrow airport has warned of disruption after flooding caused by a pipe leak restricted access to terminals 2 and 3. Water in the central terminal area means anyone trying to travel to or from either terminal is unable enter by road. Passengers are being advised to travel by rail and tube instead. Access to the terminal car parks is also impeded, leaving passengers with parked cars unable to access them. An airport spokesperson said: “Our teams are working to resolve the situation as quickly as possible. We apologise for any disruption caused. The leak has been isolated and repairs are ongoing.” The disruption comes during the school holidays, one of the airport’s busiest periods. Heathrow said 19 July had been its busiest day of the year so far with more than 267,000 passengers passing through as many schools broke up for summer. The airport was recently affected by disruption to rail services after a water leak prompted the closure of a tunnel. The airport is one of the busiest in the world, with as many as 1,300 flight movements – takeoffs and landings – every day. Heathrow announced the latest disruption on X, leading to a stream of queries and complaints from concerned travellers. “Do we have to meet and greet at T4 or 5?? When will this be resolved?,” one asked. An official response read: “We recommend heading to T5 M&G and explaining to staff that your booking has been affected by the flooding.” Another said: “I am collecting my daughter from Terminal 3 shortly; she has special needs. She has travelled via a wheelchair. Please can you advise?” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The airport replied: “You would not be able to park at Terminal 3 currently as there is no access by road; you would need to park at Terminal 4 or 5 and transfer to Terminal 3. We do have assistance teams in the terminal who would be able to advise on the best way of returning to your vehicle with a wheelchair passenger.” The consumer rights group Which? urged passengers to check airline policies on booked flights, and advised against unnecessary travel. The editor of Which? Travel, Rory Boland, said: “Passengers heading to Heathrow today will understandably be worried, so it’s important to follow the airport’s advice and avoid travelling by road to Terminals 2 and 3, instead allowing extra time and using public transport where possible. “If you’re worried you may miss your flight because of the disruption, contact your airline as soon as possible. Airlines have different policies on missed flights, so it’s worth finding out if you are entitled to a free rebooking or refund if your flight has operated. “If you’ve paid for airport parking but can no longer use it because of the road closures, contact the parking provider as soon as possible to see if you can amend your booking or get a refund. You should also check your travel insurance to see whether you’re covered for any costs you incur because of the disruption, such as a missed flight or additional travel expenses.” Explore more on these topics Heathrow airport Air transport Transport Flooding news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Heathrow says need for expansion clear as it loses title of Europe’s busiest airport Heathrow expects fall in passengers and profits this year because of Iran war Heathrow third runway GDP yield may be 90% less than previous estimates Heathrow third runway likely to harm health of millions nearby, official report warns Heathrow could be forced to allow other firms to build third runway to cut costs Heathrow passenger numbers dip as demand for international travel ebbs amid Iran war fallout Heathrow in talks with airlines to end row that could delay third runway UK aviation regulator rejects Heathrow’s plans to significantly raise landing fees Most viewed Most viewed UK UK politics Education Media Society Law Scotland Wales Northern Ireland

https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: A US sailor directs aircraft on the flight deck of the USS Abraham Lincoln during the ongoing conflict with Iran, on 31 July. Photograph: US navy/Reuters View image in fullscreen A US sailor directs aircraft on the flight deck of the USS Abraham Lincoln during the ongoing conflict with Iran, on 31 July. Photograph: US navy/Reuters US military US navy veterans and military health experts express concern over USS Abraham Lincoln sailors Prolonged deployment is coupled with reports of water shortages, plumbing issues and attempts to jump overboard Trump downplays concerns about sailors onboard USS Abraham Lincoln Anna Betts Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.00 EDT Last modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.25 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google US navy veterans and military health experts are expressing concerns about the strain on sailors aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln, which has spent nearly nine months at sea supporting US operations in the Middle East, amid reports of poor living conditions and worsening mental health among its crew. The San Diego-based aircraft carrier left port on 21 November, originally bound for the Pacific, but was redirected to the Middle East as the US-Israel war with Iran began. It has now spent more than 250 consecutive days at sea without a significant port visit, with its deployment repeatedly extended. On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the US military was preparing to replace the Lincoln with the USS George Washington, as concerns mount over the conditions aboard the Lincoln. Reports by the Navy Times and Stars and Stripes this week described shortages of supplies and water as well as plumbing problems, low morale and deteriorating mental health among the Lincoln’s roughly 5,000 sailors, and further reported that there had been multiple attempts by sailors to jump overboard. The reports prompted several Democratic lawmakers to demand answers from the Pentagon. In response to the reports, a navy official told the Guardian this week that they were aware that “extended deployments place a significant strain on our service members and their families, and we are grateful for the resilience and sacrifices they make” and said that the health and wellbeing of every Lincoln sailor was a priority. “Based on information available to the command, we have not identified an increase in reported suicidal ideation or suicide attempts aboard the ship,” they said, adding that religious, medical and mental health professionals were available as part of a “comprehensive support network” that included “onboard deployment-resilience counselors and chaplains”. The official recognized that the war had disrupted traditional supply hubs, but added that “current reports from the ship confirm continuous access to clean water, functional AC and healthy meal options”. On Thursday, Pete Hegseth claimed that the conditions aboard the Lincoln had been “completely misrepresented”. “We ​make sure that every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide ​them at every single moment,” the US defense secretary told reporters . “Some deployments are longer than others, and ⁠I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody.” Military experts said on Friday that prolonged deployments, particularly without coming ashore, can place increased strain on both the crew and the ship itself, and noted that extensions can also take a psychological toll by leaving sailors uncertain about when they will return home. Armen Kurdian, a retired US navy captain, who served aboard the Lincoln in 2005, described the carrier as a “giant floating city” with about 5,000 people aboard. “You’re feeding people 15,000 meals per day, you’ve got TV stations, communications,” he said. During his deployment, he said, he took a graduate-level business class remotely, while other sailors found different ways to occupy their downtime. “There’s always something to do,” he said, although he added that life aboard was “certainly high-ops tempo and highly stressful at times”. Sailors live in close quarters, he said, with junior enlisted personnel sleeping in open bay barracks. Kurdian recalled some plumbing problems, including broken toilets, during his deployment, and said that things becoming rusty, dirty or broken can have a “kind of depressing impact on you”. There’s never a time when you’re on the ship and everything’s working perfectly. But, is it happening a lot? “Things break on a ship,” he said. “You’re in the middle of the Gulf, you’re operating, you’ve got aircraft smacking down on decks repeatedly, hundreds of times per day, and that rattles the ship. There’s never a time when you’re on the ship and everything’s going to be working perfectly. But the question is, [is] it happening a lot?” Kurdian said that what surprised him about the Lincoln’s current deployment was not its length, but the amount of time the crew had gone without a significant port visit. “That will take a toll on people when you don’t get to stand on dry land for a while,” he said. Robert Murrett, a retired US navy vice-admiral, said that a typical aircraft-carrier deployment is closer to six months and normally includes port visits that allow sailors to rest and spend some time away from the ship. The Lincoln, Murrett said, “has had none of that since they left San Diego last November”. “They’ve been under way for that very, very long period of time, approaching nine months, and they’ve also been under combat conditions for much [of it] because of their time in the Middle East,” he said. “That’s very, very tough on a crew.” Murrett described life aboard an aircraft carrier as “tough”, calling it a “huge, compressed environment”, where there is “a lot of stress” and it can be a “very dangerous environment”. Earlier this year, the USS Gerald R Ford aircraft carrier returned home after a 326-day deployment, marking the longest US carrier deployment since the Vietnam war . That deployment had reports of a fire and complaints about food shortages. Nancy Lacore, a three-star navy rear admiral who served in the navy for 35 years, said in a statement that during her first deployment, she was “operating in that same region as the USS Abraham Lincoln”. “Just like those sailors, when we left our home port on deployment, we knew when we were supposed to come home,” said Lacore, who was ousted by Hegseth in August during his purge of senior US military officials and who is now running for Congress in South Carolina. “We had an end date, and we were counting down to it.” “Then something changed in the region and just as we thought we were heading home, our ship turned around and went back to the Gulf,” she said. “I still remember how mentally crushing it was to realize the date you’ve been holding onto is gone.” People aboard the Lincoln, she said, have “experienced that uncertainty repeatedly”. “Our Sailors are tough and resilient,” she added. “But their resilience shouldn’t be taken for granted or used as an excuse to keep asking more of them without a clear end in sight.” Our sailors are tough and resilient. But that shouldn’t be used as an excuse to ask for more without a clear end in sight Terri Tanielian, a senior behavioral scientist who has studied deployments and their impact on troops and families, said that prolonged separations are difficult, but that uncertainty over when a deployment will end can make the strain worse. “When families know what they’re planning for, or when an individual knows what they’re planning for … then that is an expectation that they can set themselves up to manage,” she said. But when those expectations change unexpectedly, she said, “like we saw, for example, in 2008, 2009 and 2010 timeframes, and with the deployments there, where we had to keep people for longer, we also saw some increases in the mental strain that the units were facing”, referring to both troops and their families. Responding to the reports about the conditions aboard the Lincoln, Tanielian said it was “heartbreaking to think about the struggles that folks are facing and to feel that they’re kind of feeling that desperate and isolated and perhaps not supported”. Support, she said, needs to extend beyond just ensuring access to psychological support: “It’s also about, are they getting enough sleep? Are they getting reset opportunities? Are they getting the opportunity to exercise? How are we helping them maintain their overall wellbeing?” Explore more on these topics US military US-Israel war on Iran Trump administration US politics US foreign policy news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed US news US politics Midterms 2026 World Climate crisis Middle East Ukraine US immigration Soccer Business Environment Tech Science Newsletters The Filter Wellness

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: The incident happened on the small Greek island of Kimolos, the birthplace of Alex McKee’s mother. Photograph: Ralf Adler/Getty Images/imageBroker RF View image in fullscreen The incident happened on the small Greek island of Kimolos, the birthplace of Alex McKee’s mother. Photograph: Ralf Adler/Getty Images/imageBroker RF Greece Safety check calls after Irish teenager electrocuted taking shower in Greece Alex McKee died when picking up showerhead in ‘outdoor and rudimentary’ bathroom on Kimolos Helena Smith in Athens Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.19 EDT Last modified on Sat 15 Aug 2026 07.21 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The death of an Irish teenager, electrocuted while taking a shower in a holiday home in Greece , has led to calls for tighter checks on appliances at tourist accommodation. Alex McKee, 17, is said to have died instantly when picking up the showerhead in a bathroom described as “outdoor and rudimentary” on Kimolos. “We are lucky there weren’t two deaths as a result of electrocution,” Agapitos Xanthis, a doctor on the island told Greek TV, recounting how the boy’s mother had described feeling a similar surge when she called him for help. “I told her to immediately turn off the mains.” McKee, from Cork, had been on the island barely three days when the tragedy occurred on 9 August. As the birthplace of his mother, Iphigenia, he and his family visited regularly, staying in the same stone house built more than 50 years ago. Greek police told the Guardian an inquiry was now focused on the building’s water heater and a possible fault in the wiring. “The house has been cordoned off and we have requested an independent expert to come and inspect the wiring,” said an officer based in Syros with oversight of the Aegean. “It is thought the fusebox may not have had a safety valve.” The teenager’s body was transported to the mainland where a postmortem conducted at a hospital in Piraeus had attributed the cause of death to electrocution. McKee, a fifth-year student in Cork, had won plaudits in Ireland for developing an innovative communication system, with two of his classmates, for people suffering from nonverbal autism. Colm Burke, the Irish Fine Gael politician for Cork North-Central paid tribute to the teenager saying: “It is extremely sad to hear that someone so young has died so tragically. He was a really talented young person with his whole life and huge career ahead of him, Earlier this year, he put a huge effort into getting to that stage in the Young Scientist and Technology Exhibition and was awarded for his efforts.” In a nation so dependent on tourism – and with visitor numbers expected to, once again, soar this year – the incident has also shone a light on electrical standards in accommodation rented out seasonally on the Greek islands. The mayor of Kimolos, Kostas Vendouris, expressed profound shock over the tragedy saying it had plunged the less than 1,000-strong island into mourning. It later emerged, however, that as a professional electrician he had signed off on the property’s electrical installation certificate in 2024 – a document that police said was also being investigated. They family signalled it would be pressing charges. “The current mayor faces huge criminal responsibility,” their lawyer Stelios Voudouris told Open TV. https://www.dw.com/en/russians-snap-up-n.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5In3o According to the UN, 90% of the buildings in Mariupol were damaged or destroyed in the 2022 siege Image: Evgeny Sosnovsky Advertisement Halyna Artemova, an English teacher, lived in Mariupol for almost 40 years, at Metallurgy Avenue 87. "It's my beloved city. When I look at the photos, it brings tears to my eyes. I know every crack in the asphalt, every tree," she told DW. Her apartment block in the city on the Sea of Azov was struck by a missile during a Russian attack in March 2022. Photographer Yevhen Sosnovsky and his wife lived in the house next door, Metallurgy Avenue 85, for 20 years. "I did everything myself, all the interior renovations, and the furniture," he said. "We invested a lot in it; we planned to spend our twilight years there, living quietly." His building also caught fire during the missile attack, and residents were driven out by Russian troops. They weren't even allowed to take food or clothing with them. Photographer Yevhen Sosnovsky documented his apartment before and after the Russian attack Image: Evgeny Sosnovsky Now there's a parking lot where Sosnovsky's apartment block used to be. Next door, where Artemova once lived, stands a new building. The Russian building contractor Su-2007, which operates in the Ukrainian regions occupied by Russia, cleared several buildings on Metallurgy Avenue that were destroyed in the war and constructed high-rise apartment blocks in their place. These form part of a residential complex now known as the Leningradsky Kvartal. "They're building on human bones, and fast, to eradicate the traces of their crimes," said Sosnovsky. DW is not allowed in to the Russian-occupied parts of Ukraine, so cannot report directly from city. However, it is possible to get an idea of what life is like in Mariupol today by talking to people who used to live there, studying satellite images, and doing research online. Newcomers benefit from cheap mortgages Many people who have moved into the new apartments on Metallurgy Avenue communicate with each other online in neighborhood forums. From these forums, it's clear that the majority bought the apartments either to live in themselves, or to rent out. In chats, they ask how they can get furniture delivered from Russia, or which kindergarten or school they should choose for their children. People are reminded that the most important thing when submitting documents is that they should be of Russian origin. Russian building contractor Su-2007 has advertised its new project in Mariupol online Image: жк-ленинградский-квартал.рф Not everyone has finished remodeling their apartments, and some people with small children take the opportunity to complain: "It's too late! Stop the goddamn renovations! Or maybe you're pro-Ukrainian and oppose Russian laws?" Economist Vyacheslav Shiryaev said apartments in the new buildings in Mariupol are being bought primarily by incomers: Russian security personnel, officials and people working in military logistics. "In addition, there are some who would just like to live by the sea but can't afford Crimea or Sochi," he said. In the Russian-occupied regions, people are offered cheap mortgages at an annual interest rate of 2% for the whole period of the mortgage — provided the borrower has Russian citizenship. The maximum they can borrow is 6 million rubles (around €63,000/$72,000), and they must be able to put down a deposit of at least 2%. Property prices have soared Dozens of apartment blocks are being built in Mariupol, and many are already occupied. Russian banks report that the port city in the occupied region tops the list for mortgage loans. Property prices have risen by a third in just one year, primarily because of the coastal location. You won't find a location like this in Russia, said Shiryaev. However, he pointed out that the apartments are of very bad quality. "Construction companies are cutting corners wherever they can, but still demanding exorbitant prices," he said. The Leningradsky Kvartal residential complex, 15 buildings of 12 to 15 floors each, is near the center of town and just 10 minutes' drive from the sea. One- and two-room apartments cost between 7.5 million and almost 10 million rubles (€104,000). Three-room apartments can be bought for upwards of 10 million rubles. Newcomers to the region are offered discounts of up to 12%. In the chats, people living in the complex say they have insured their mortgages "against war risks." If their building is destroyed, they won't have to pay back their loan. They will, however, lose their apartment. Nobody in the forum talks about the fact that there were other people living on the site of Leningradsky Kvartal just a few years ago. Dead and wounded in Mariupol According to the United Nations, 90% of the buildings in Mariupol were damaged or destroyed in the 2022 siege. Media outlets estimate that tens of thousands of people were killed. Former residents of Metallurgy Avenue told DW of neighbors who were killed or injured. Halyna Artemova lived in Mariupol for most of her life, before fleeing to Kyiv Image: Privat "A man and his son from the building next door were killed when they went out to fetch water," said Artemova. "In house number 89, a woman was buried beneath a concrete slab after a missile strike and died. A missile struck the first floor of house number 91, and a family was killed." Artemova herself was wounded by shrapnel, but managed to leave Mariupol with her elderly mother and her son. Sosnovsky was hit by a bullet. He too fled the city, with his wife and mother-in-law. Many of those who lived in buildings that were hit, but whose apartments were not destroyed, have remained in the city. However, DW was told that the occupying authorities demanded they leave their apartments nonetheless. They were promised new apartments in exchange. Ukrainian POW returns to front line after Russia torture To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video But a source told DW that none of the inhabitants of the former blocks on Metallurgy Avenue was allocated an apartment in the new Leningradsky Kvartal buildings. And those who had lost everything in the attacks could not afford a mortgage. Another source told DW that people were put in accommodation on the outskirts of town, or else in hostels. 'We were robbed of our good life' The majority of those who fled do understand why their former neighbors stayed in the city. Not everyone had the possibility of leaving Mariupol and starting again elsewhere. "The local population is being pushed out of Mariupol," said Artemova, who now lives in Kyiv with her son. Like others DW spoke with who had left the city, she said Mariupol had started to develop rapidly a few years before the Russian invasion in early 2022. People wanted to live there. "We were robbed of our ordinary life, which may have been uninteresting for some, but it was a good life. We'd go to market, knew where to buy what; we'd have a coffee, bump into a school friend with her dog and say hello," she remembered. Thousands are widely believed to have died in Russia's siege on Mariupol in 2022 Image: Evgeny Sosnovsky Neither Artemova nor Sosnovsky are considering returning to their hometown and re-registering their apartments according to the regulations of the Russian occupying authority . It's not even clear whether or not they would be allowed to enter the zone. But Ukraine is not compensating people for the loss of property there, as its authorities can't assess the situation without access to the occupied region. "They're building their shiny new houses on what used to be a graveyard. I'd like nothing better than to bomb them, but only when no one's in the buildings. It's enough to drive you to despair," said one former resident of Metallurgy Avenue. He too lived there for decades, and remembers his child's first steps, taken in an apartment that no longer exists. This is how he describes the city today: "In the center it's still OK, but if you go just a little to the left or right it smells of death." This article was originally written in Russian. https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c4gj.text: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Among those killed in the strike on Ansar included three children and two women, state media reports By Samantha Granville Published 15 August 2026, 12:24 BST Updated Just now Nine people have been killed in Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon, authorities say, in one of the deadliest days of attacks since an agreement aimed at reducing hostilities was announced in June. Lebanon's prime minister said seven people were killed in a strike on a house on the outskirts of Ansar in the Nabatieh district, which state media reported included three children and two women. Later on Saturday, another round of strikes hit the town of Deir al-Zahrani, killing two and injuring nine others, according to the Lebanese Ministry of Health. Israel's military said it had struck "Hezbollah terror infrastructure" in response to what it described as an earlier action against its soldiers. Authorities say the strike in Ansar at around 04:30 (01:30 GMT) occurred where displaced families were living. Footage on social media shows large plumes of smoke permeating through the streets of the village as sirens ring out. Lebanon's Prime Minister Nawaf Salam condemned the attacks, saying the seven civilians killed were not "military infrastructure". "Israel must halt this escalation," he said. "For the security of our people and their right to life on their land are not subject to negotiation or bargaining." The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the incident that had prompted its strike on Ansar took place in the Ali al-Taher Ridge, a strategic high ground overlooking much of south-eastern Lebanon and of the war's most fiercely contested positions. Lebanon's state-run National News Agency (NNA) also reported a series of strikes around the ridge. Near the border, several homes were reportedly destroyed in Bint Jbeil, while Israeli forces opened heavy machine gun fire towards houses, according to NNA. Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah - the armed group affiliated with Iran - launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader. Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south. Its forces continue to occupy roughly 5% of Lebanese territory. The June ceasefire framework calls for Hezbollah to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area. Lebanon's President Joseph Aoun condemned the Israeli strikes that had killed an entire family in Ansar and its "repeated violations" of the framework, which he said sent a "clear message" to the US-led negotiations. Hezbollah was not involved in the agreement and has rejected direct negotiations. The IDF says it will continue to remove threats to Israeli citizens and soldiers operating in the security zone - the 10km-deep military buffer in southern Lebanon occupied by Israel. Despite a reduction in fighting following the June agreements, Israeli strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon have continued. On Friday, Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem criticised the Lebanese authorities over the implementation of the framework, accusing them of putting pressure on the Lebanese army while Israeli attacks continued. "How can you accept this ongoing humiliation of the Lebanese army, exposing it to bombardment and Israeli pressures, instead of acting as its protectors?" he said. Lebanese and Israeli negotiators are set to meet for an eighth round of negotiations in September, but a final date has not been set. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/08/15/paks.text: Menü Kereső Megkezdték a bárkák süllyesztését Paksnál, Magyar Péter jó híreket kapott Belföld Összekapcsolt bárkák a Dunán az MVM Paksi Atomerőmű közelében 2026. augusztus 15-én – Forrás: MTI/Bodnár Boglárka Madzin Emília Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Három évtizede nem látott nehézségű, a Duna vízszintjének duzzasztásához szükséges munka folyik Paks és Dunaszentbenedek között, erről tartott sajtótájékoztatót Magyar Péter Paksnál. Jelenleg körülbelül 130 fő dolgozik a helyszínen, 50 fő a munkálatok adminisztrációját végzi, valamint több mint 100 teherautó hordja a köveket az építési helyszínre, hangzott el a sajtótájékoztatón. „Jó híreket kaptunk, mert már az erőműnél, a szivattyútelepnél is emelkedett egy centiméterrel a vízállás”, mondta Magyar. A bárkákat egyelőre körülbelül 20 centiméterrel süllyesztették. A miniszterelnök szombat reggel arról posztolt, hogy a jelenlegi előrejelzés alapján hétfő hajnalra süllyedne -132 centiméter alá a vízszint. Ha ez a forgatókönyv megvalósul, a két üzemelő turbinából az egyiket le kellene állítani. Az előrejelzések alapján akár -140 centiméter alá is süllyedhet a vízszint, ami az atomerőmű teljes lekapcsolásához vezethet. Ezt meg kell akadályozniuk, mondta Magyar, és meg is fogják akadályozni, ezért kezdték meg el a bárkák süllyesztését. A nap folyamán ötezer tonna kő fog érkezni a helyszínre, majd arról beszélt Magyar, hogy egy ilyen válság idején szerinte jogosan elvárható a teljes nemzeti összefogás. A sajtótájékoztatón a vízügyi szakemberek mellett részt vett a Kapitány István gazdasági és energetikai miniszter, Ruff Bálint Miniszterelnökséget vezető miniszter, Ruszin-Szendi Romulusz honvédelmi miniszter és a kormány nemzetbiztonsági főtanácsadója, Tóth Péter is. Kádár Pál, a Védelmi Igazgatási Hivatal főigazgatója megköszönte a védekezésre érkező, köztük a lakossági felajánlásokat is, de elsősorban kőszállításra alkalmas eszközökre van szükségük, mivel egyszerre akár 100 teherautót is igénybe vesznek a Duna két oldalán. Magyar hozzátette, hogy elsősorban cégek felajánlását várják. Több száz ember dolgozik különböző helyszíneken a siker érdekében, mondta Kádár. Arról is beszélt, hogy kéri, ne közelítsék meg a helyszínt úszók vagy kishajók a védelmi munkálatok helyszínét, mivel az balesetveszélyes lehet. Gacsályi József, az Országos Vízügyi Főigazgatóság műszaki főigazgató-helyettese arról beszélt, a fenékküszöb kialakítását három részre lehet tagolni: az egyik a jobbparti építkezés az atomerőműnél, itt közvetlenül a rézsűbe billentik a követ a parton, valamint épül egy hídfő, amin keresztül a teherautók oda tudják vinni a követ, ahova szükséges. A balparti építkezésnek az eleje könnyebb, ott szárazon zajlik a munka, a harmadik beavatkozási pont pedig a légierőé, ők végzik a betonkockák beemelését. A bárkák pozicionálása terén sok a bizonytalanság, folyamatosan figyelik. Mikor kapcsolhatják vissza a Paksi Atomerőművet? Az RTL arról kérdezett, van-e arra becslés, hogy mikor termelhet újból teljes kapacitással a Paksi Atomerőmű. Magyar Péter azt mondta, hogy a következő feladatuk az, hogy folytassák a meglévő paksi turbinák üzemeltetését, ezután lehet gondolkodni a lekapcsolt turbinák visszakapcsolásáról. But sometimes the kids fight about whose picture is better, about which picture you will like more, etc., and the act of love devolves into a yelling match fueled by pride. At which point you intervene and stop their pathetic little slap fight. And you remind your kids that both acts of love are acknowledged and cherished. Yes, you realize that one might grasp artistic ideas and talents more than the other, but that’s not the point. You’re their creator, and you want not only for both of them to know how much you love them, but you also want them to love each other as brother and sister. And so it is with us. No gift or prayer or homage to God will ever compare to the act of creation with which He blessed us. Catholic and Protestant, Orthodox and Methodist, Baptist and Presbyterian, we are all using the nanosecond of time we have to claw our way through the darkness and try to derive but a sliver of wisdom from an infinite abyss. The most we can offer up is our own scribbled messes based on our extremely limited comprehension of who God is and what He wants. So let’s stop our pathetic little slap fight. When the congregation down the road offers up a scribbled mess that doesn’t look exactly like our scribbled mess, we need to overcome our pride and concede that God will recognize their loving devotion just as much as He recognizes ours. The Trump administration says 9 million barrels a day are still getting out Middle East Iran Welcome to the mega-war: Mideast and European conflicts merge, sucking in more countries along the way—even ones claiming neutrality By Jason Ma Jason Ma Weekend Editor By Jason Ma Jason Ma Weekend Editor August 1, 2026, 1:24 PM ET A U.S. Marine with Battalion Landing Team 3/5, 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit, sights in on a M110 semi-automatic sniper system during a maritime interception operation in the U.S. Central Command area of responsibility, July 16, 2026. U.S. Marine Corps Add Fortune on Google for similar content. Add us on Google Add us on Google Wars in Iran and Ukraine are increasingly overlapping while also expanding, as the U.S. mulls whether to make another attempt at delivering a knockout blow against Tehran. Recommended Video Last weekend, Ukraine announced that it attacked an Iranian cargo ship ferrying military supplies between Iran and Russia in the Caspian Sea . Iran insisted it’s not involved in Russia’s war on Ukraine, though Kyiv has said Tehran is supplying drones to its ally. Days later, drones hit liquid natural gas tankers at a port on Egypt’s Mediterranean coast, marking the first time the country had been targeted during the Iran war and threatening the Suez Canal’s status as a safe route to get oil out of the Red Sea. Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia said it formed a military coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea as Iran-backed Houthi rebels attack ships using the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which the kingdom has relied on to export its oil and bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Riyadh said 14 countries offered support for the coalition, including Turkey, Egypt, Pakistan, Nigeria and several other Arab and African nations. Dan Alamariu, chief geopolitical strategist at Alpine Macro, pointed out in a note on Friday that Iran and its allies have struck or threatened nearly every country in the region since the war began in February. “Egypt was the largest one still untouched, and it had worked to stay that way, keeping open relations with both Washington and Tehran,” he added. “Neutrality did not exempt it.” The Mediterranean attack, which Egypt attributed to Iran, may impact European gas prices, shipping rates, and insurance costs, according to Alamariu. That’s as Iran demanded European countries hold Ukraine accountable for its attack on the ship in the Caspian Sea. “The Iran and Ukraine wars may be connecting,” he warned. “A Ukrainian strike in the Caspian Sea was followed within days by burning gas ships on the Mediterranean. It may not be coincidental, there is a tail risk of some convergence between the two conflicts.” Hamidreza Azizi, an Iran expert at the think tank SWP Berlin, also saw potential crosscurrents while laying out different interpretations of Ukraine’s strike on the Iranian ship. One is that Ukraine wants to demonstrate its value as a partner to the U.S., he explained on X last week. Another view is that Israel and the U.S. asked Ukraine to pressure Iran on their behalf amid concerns that any attacks they make on Iranian infrastructure would trigger retaliation against regional economic assets. A third interpretation is that Ukraine’s attack was in response to Houthi rebels threatening ships in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. And according to the Financial Times , Ukraine’s strike prompted speculation in Tehran that it was meant as a warning to demonstrate Iran’s Caspian coast is at risk and could be leveraged in talks with the U.S. Ukraine is already a player in the Middle East, signing a security agreement with Saudi Arabia in March to provide the kingdom with expertise Kyiv has developed in defending against Iranian-designed drones supplied to Russia. President Volodymyr Zelensky also made visits to the United Arab Emirates and Qatar to reach similar agreements U.S. Marines assigned to Battalion Landing Team 3/5, 11th Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU), conduct weapons drills on a Multi Role-Anti Armor Personnel Weapons System (MAAWS) in the hanger bay of Wasp-class amphibious assault ship USS Boxer (LHD 4), July 8, 2026. U.S. Navy Former Defense Secretary Mark Esper, who served in the first Trump administration, argued that the Iran war ought to be internationalized to include America’s allies in Asia and Europe as well as countries the border Iran, like Turkey, Armenia and Azerbaijan. “We have to globalize this conflict because it’s affecting international commerce,” he told Bloomberg TV on Thursday. “We’re taking this on too much of ourselves, or to a lesser extent with Israel. So i think it’s time to globalize it and then think about again our broader set of sanctions, blockading the entire country, squeezing them economically.” For its part, Russia is also looking to expand the map. In recent weeks, it has launching drones at Romania while a Russian missile landed in Poland, violating NATO airspace. Russian drones have also crossed into Poland previously, but the latest incident was the first known case involving a Russian missile. The Center for European Policy Analysis said on Friday that the incursions signal that Russia’s “shadow war” against NATO, which has been backing Ukraine, is moving southward . That’s after NATO allies in northern and central Europe saw so-called hybrid war attacks last year, such as the cutting of undersea cables in the Baltic Sea and drone-induced airport closures. Energy expert Daniel Yergin, S&P Global vice chairman, told CNBC on Friday that the Iran war is expanding geographically and geopolitically. “Think about all the seas—the Persian Gulf, the Red Sea, the Mediterranean, the Black Sea, the Baltic Sea, the Caspian Sea—these have all become arenas for oil war,” he said. https://www.breitbart.com/politics/2026/.text: KYIV, Ukraine (AP) – A Russian ballistic missile and drone barrage across Ukraine overnight killed at least eight civilians, including children, and injured more than 50 others, officials said Thursday, and NATO scrambled its warplanes after one of the missiles crossed the country’s western border into Poland. The blitz expanded Russia´s almost daily bombardment of Ukrainian cities, including the capital of Kyiv where tens of thousands spent the night sheltering in subway stations, as Moscow apparently looked to exploit Kyiv´s critical shortage of Western-supplied anti-ballistic missile defenses. NATO said a Russian missile entered Polish airspace during the onslaught and landed in a rural area. It caused no injuries or damage but could deepen tensions between the military alliance and Moscow, as wary European countries fear the 4-year-old war could spill into their territory. NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called it “yet another reckless act by Russia and a dangerous consequence of its war against Ukraine.” Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it was “a very serious incident,” but added: “There are absolutely no reasons to believe that Poland was the target.” Russia’s barrage struck areas of Ukraine where weapons are believed to be stored and manufactured. Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles have battered Russia’s oil sector, causing a fuel crisis. The attack came two days after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy met with U.S. President Donald Trump and representatives of American defense companies as he pleads for swifter and bigger deliveries of Patriot air defense systems to stop Russia´s ballistic missiles. The Iran war has drained stockpiles of the U.S.-made interceptors. Trump has promised to grant Ukraine licenses to build its own Patriots, but production could take many months. “Given the critical shortage of air defense missiles from our partners, our warriors are accomplishing truly incredible things, demonstrating a very high level of professionalism,” Zelenskyy said on social media. “This Russian terror once again proves that protection against the Russian missile threat is the most important task when it comes to saving the lives of our people,” he said. Zelenskyy said at least 10 Ukrainian regions were attacked, with dozens of homes, businesses and infrastructure facilities destroyed or damaged. Russia launched more than 70 missiles, a significant number of them ballistic missiles, he said, and over 280 attack drones, of which more than 260 were intercepted. The Russian Defense Ministry said it targeted Ukrainian air bases, arms factories and military telecommunications and logistics facilities, including drone factories and storage depots, as well as plants for missiles, aircraft repairs, electronics and chemicals. In the Dnipropetrovsk region, the Russian attack killed six people and wounded 10, said Oleksandr Hanzha, head of the regional military administration, in a post on Telegram. Children were among the dead – a 6-year-old girl and boys aged 11 and 17 in the area of Kryvyi Rih, Zelenskyy’s hometown, Hanzha added. The children´s parents were killed in the same attack, but two more children were pulled alive from the rubble, Zelenskyy said. “It was an ordinary home, blown (to) smithereens by a ballistic missile,” he said on X. In Kyiv, Russian forces struck the capital with ballistic missiles, killing a 31-year-old man and wounding two others, the National Police press service said. More than 56,000 people sheltered in Kyiv´s subway stations overnight, according to the Facebook post from the metro system. A cruise missile attack struck the western city of Lviv, killing one person and wounding over 30, including children aged 6, 13 and 15, said Maksym Kozytskyi, head of the Lviv regional military administration. In the Poltava region, a drone hit warehouses, killing one person, said regional military head Vitalii Diakivnych. Russian forces also dropped three powerful glide bombs on an industrial zone in the southern city of Kherson, killing a 56-year-old man, local officials said. A Russian Kh-101 cruise missile crossed into Poland overnight, violating NATO airspace, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X, calling it a clear demonstration that strengthening Ukraine´s air defenses would also guarantee wider European security. Responding to the missile alert, NATO forces in Poland scrambled two fighter jets, an attack helicopter and two other aircraft, and activated ground defenses, said Col. Michael O´Connell, the spokesperson for the alliance´s military command in Belgium. The missile quickly disappeared from radar, the Polish Armed Forces said. A helicopter flew to its last known location, where the crew discovered a probable impact site in a farming area in Lublin province, the command said. Investigators found fragments indicating that the object was a Kh-101 missile, Polish news agency PAP reported. Tusk had met with Zelenskyy in Lublin on Wednesday to discuss defense issues. NATO military commander Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich told Poland´s Defense Chief Gen. Wieslaw Kukulan the military alliance “will continue to take all necessary measures to defend NATO territory,” O´Donnell said. Meanwhile, Russia´s Defense Ministry said air defenses downed 258 Ukrainian drones overnight. A depot belonging to Wildberries online retailer was set ablaze in Russia’s Penza region southeast of Moscow, in the latest strike on the company’s warehouses, Penza Gov. Oleg Melnichenko. Four people were injured and 200 workers were evacuated, he said, adding that about 100 firefighters were deployed. Wildberries also reported its warehouse in Sarapul in the Udmurtia region more than 1,000 kilometers (600 miles) from Ukraine, was struck by a Ukrainian drone and set ablaze. It said the workers had been safely evacuated. The Russian online news outlet Astra reported that another Wildberries depot in the Perm region in the Urals was also set ablaze by a Ukrainian drone strike. Regional authorities reported a Ukrainian drone attack but didn´t give information about the damage. Thursday´s attacks on Wildberries warehouses brought to 14 the number of the retailer´s depots struck by Ukrainian drones in under two weeks. Ukraine accuses Wildberries of supplying goods that can be used by the Russian military. Ukrainian drone units destroyed four more vessels belonging to Russia´s “shadow fleet” of sanctions-busting tankers, bringing the total to 205 since the operation began July 6, Robert “Madyar” Brovdi, commander of the Unmanned Systems Forces, said on his Telegram channel. REUTERS/Cheney Orr A Fox News pundit-turned-Trump appointee has infuriated the commander in chief... again. No, it's not Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth or national security adviser Michael Waltz — this time it's U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro. "I disagree 100% with Jeanine Pirro," Trump roared on Truth Social Saturday. "I don’t know what she was thinking?" Trump's frustration with Pirro stemmed from her recent decision to drop charges against U.S. Olympic canoeist David Hearn over baseless claims that vandals sabotaged a slap-dash renovation of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. Pirro on Friday admitted in a court filing in D.C. Superior Court that damage to the pool’s sealant had been caused by “flawed installation.” Pirro said there was evidence to “significantly undermine the evidentiary basis for the indictment." Trump disagreed. "To me, it was a pure case of VANDALISM, that included the grass, which had a big 86 47 emblazoned in giant letters on it, and other elements of the surrounding area," Trump claimed. "There may have been some contractor difficulty, but the major damage was caused by VANDALS! President DJT." Trump frequently lambasts his former Fox friends. The president raged at Hegseth for mistakenly targeting Poland after Germany made Trump mad. Waltz mistakenly added The Atlantic's editor-in-chief to a Signal group chat with senior national security officials to discuss imminent strikes in Yemen. https://www.dw.com/en/how-does-eastern-e.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5I36F August 2 marks the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day, when Europe honors the memory of the victims and survivors of the Roma and Sinti genocide under Nazi Germany Image: Jacek Bednarczyk/dpa/picture alliance Advertisement It took decades before Germany recognized the Romani Holocaust — the Nazi genocide of 500,000 European Roma and Sinti during World War II . Several more decades passed before the European Holocaust Memorial Day for Sinti and Roma became an official German and European day of remembrance, celebrated each year on August 2. Based on initiatives by Polish Roma groups, the Nazi liquidation of the so-called "Gypsy Family Camp" in the Auschwitz-Birkenau Concentration and Extermination Camp on the evening of August 2-3, 1944, was first commemorated half a century later, in 1994. Germany marks the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day on August 2 Image: Joerg Carstensen/dpa/picture alliance Thousands of deported Roma and Sinti had already been killed as a result of malnutrition and disease. That evening, thousands more were forced into gas chambers, shot and beaten to death by Nazi henchmen. In 2015, the European Parliament declared this date the European Roma Holocaust Memorial Day. In Germany and other European countries, the genocide is commemorated by officials with the participation of government representatives. In some cases, representatives of European governments travel to the memorial site in Auschwitz. In most cases, however, countries hold their own memorial services — particularly in central and southeastern Europe, where Nazi extermination commonly targeted Romani peoples . These days, such memorial days also take the opportunity to raise awareness for ongoing Antiziganism and the consequences it has. Roma, Sinti persecuted in WWII still fight for recognition To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Poland: 15 years of commemoration Poland , home to an estimated 30,000 Roma, has been observing August 2 since 2011. The ceremony routinely includes a visit by parliamentary and governmental representatives to the Auschwitz Memorial. Another important day of remembrance is observed each year in the village of Szczurowa, east of Krakow, on July 3. It honors the memory of Polish Roma massacred by German troops in 1943. In 1956, Szczurowa became the first site of a European memorial for victims of the Romani Holocaust. Other small towns and villages across southeastern Poland also commemorate the killing of Polish Roma during Nazi German occupation. Czechia: A former pig farm turned memorial site In the Czech Republic , where nearly 250,000 Roma live, August 2 has been an official day of remembrance since 2015. The most important ceremony is held in Lety, south of Prague, where Roma organizations have been commemorating the genocide for decades. This is the site where German Nazis established a concentration camp in 1940, and began deporting and imprisoning Romani families from occupied Bohemia from 1942 onward. After the war, the site was used as a pig farm. It was closed in 2018, following a long controversy , and transformed into a place of remembrance. Czech President Petr Pavel and then-Prime Minister Petr Fiala both attended the opening ceremony in April 2024. Another memorial site is located in Hodonin north of Brno, at the location of a further Nazi concentration camp which imprisoned Romani people from Bohemia and Moravia. Here, one of the atrocities commemorated includes the mass deportation of Roma and Sinti to Auschwitz on August 21, 1943. The site of the former concentration camp in Lety had been used as a pig farm after World War II Image: Lubos Palata/DW Slovakia: Memorial Day established in 2005 Around half a million Roma live in Slovakia . Here, the Romani Holocaust Memorial Day has been observed on August 2 since 2005. The main ceremony is held at the Slovak National Uprising (SNU) museum in Banska Bystrica in central Slovakia. The museum honors the 1944 armed uprising against Nazi occupation. It was one of the largest anti-fascist movements in Europe during World War II. The memorial ceremony is organized by the government's Plenipotentiary for Romani Communities and non-governmental Roma initiatives. Other representatives of the state or the presidential office also take part. Hungary: Antiziganism yesterday and today Around 600,000 Roma call Hungary home. Here, since 2005, various sites have been observing the Romani Holocaust Memorial Day on August 2, following a parliamentary resolution. In Budapest alone, there are three places of remembering for the Roma murdered during the Holocaust where commemorative events are held. The reason for these and numerous other memorial sites is that Hungarian Roma were the target of deportations and killings particularly following German occupation in 1944 and under the rule of the Arrow Cross, Hungary's fascist regime. Historical remembrance in Hungary is also deeply intertwined with the racist murdering spree directed at Roma people between 2008 and 2009. In this time, four Hungarian neo-Nazis killed a total of six people and injured 55 others, some of them severely. They planned their final hate crime for the night of August 2, in the eastern village of Kisleta. After Orban, Hungary's Roma hope for change To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Romania: Deportation to Transnistria Romania , where around 2 million Roma live, Roma Holocaust Memorial Day has officially been observed since 2020. The main event is held at the Holocaust Memorial in Bucharest, which was inaugurated in 2009. Under the dictator Ion Antonescu, who was allied with Nazi Germany, Romania independently organized the mass deportation of Jews and Roma to Transnistria , where about 380,000 Jews and 11,000 Roma were murdered in camps or died from hunger and disease. In 2025, President Nicusor Dan became the first Romanian head of state to personally attend the memorial service. In 2004, Romania designated October 9 as its official Holocaust Remembrance Day. It was on that day that Jewish citizens were first deported from the Bukovina region to Transnistria. The day also explicitly honors the memory of Roma who were deported and murdered by Antonescu's regime. Bulgaria: Commemoration without day of remembrance About 700,000 Roma call Bulgaria home. Here, August 2 has yet to be declared an official day of remembrance, but it is still marked with commemorative events organized by Roma organizations. Government and state representatives also take the occasion to issue commemorative statements. Although Bulgaria was allied with Nazi Germany, it resisted German demands to deport Jews and Roma. But groups were discriminated against through a wide range of racist laws, and effectively made second-class citizens. Croatia: Focus on escape attempt Croatia has a population of about 25,000 Roma. Its parliament only declared August 2 a day of remembrance in 2014. The main commemorative ceremony is held at the site of the former concentration and extermination camp Jasenovac , where the fascist Ustashe movement imprisoned Serbs, Jews, Croats and Roma. Between 15,000 and 20,000 were murdered there. High-ranking politicians regularly take part in commemorative ceremonies. More broadly, remembrance events in Jasenovac primarily highlight April 22, when prisoners attempted to escape the extermination camp in 1945. Croatia’s shadows of the past To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video North Macedonia: Memorial Day and national holiday Around 100,000 Roma live in North Macedonia , where the Roma Holocaust Memorial Day has officially been observed on August 2 since 2017. A key remembrance ceremony is held in Skopje at the Holocaust Memorial Center for the Jews of Macedonia. In North Macedonia is also a national and religious holiday: Republic Day and St Elijah Day, respectively. because of this, public remembrance of the Roma genocide tends to receive less attention. Serbia: No official day of remembrance In Serbia , home to around 130,000 Roma, August 2 is not an official memorial day for the Roma genocide. But there are other days of remembering the genocidal policies of the Nazi and Ustase regimes which also honor the memory of the Roma killed in the genocide. This article was translated from German. https://www.taipeitimes.com/News/world/a.text: Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages Search Search All Front Page Taiwan News Business Editorial & Opinion Sports World News Features Bilingual Pages GO Home World News Warsaw, Kyiv exhume Volyn massacre victims at center of diplomatic quarrel AFP, OSTRIVKY, Ukraine Add TT as Preferred Source Beneath two now-deserted villages in western Ukraine — the site of World War II-era massacres — archeologists are uncovering the bones at the heart of a dispute that has strained relations between Warsaw and Kyiv for years. Disagreements over what happened and who is responsible for the Volyn massacres have long cast a shadow over ties between the otherwise now close neighbors. Between 1943 and 1945, about 70,000 to 100,000 civilians were killed by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) in territory occupied by Nazi Germany, according to Polish estimates of the toll. Archeologists work with human remains at the exhumation site of the World War II Volyn massacre near the destroyed village of Ostrivky, Ukraine, on Tuesday. Photo: AFP Warsaw calls it a “genocide” against the Polish minority, while Ukraine hails the UPA as freedom fighters, sees the events as a wartime “tragedy” and says that Ukrainians were killed in retaliation. Amid sunflower fields and forests, joint Polish-Ukrainian teams of archeologists have been carefully excavating the remains of victims. “We want to restore their first and last names ... to fulfill the duty that rests on us as heirs of those who were murdered here,” Polish Institute of National Remembrance (IPN) deputy president Karol Polejowski said. The remains of more than 50 people have been recovered in a series of exhumations in the area, but they have yet to be identified. A handmade wooden cross, planted near the graves, is one of the few signs that the villages ever existed. Political leaders in both countries believe the exhumations could be a first step in repairing relations, which have been strained this year by a row triggered when Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy named a military unit after the UPA. In a white tent about 10km from the Polish border, experts meticulously lay out the skeletons of recovered victims, measuring bones and carefully trying to match broken skull fragments. A small number of other artifacts — rosaries, religious medallions and shoes — have also been unearthed under the field of yellow-and-black sunflowers, one of the national symbols of Ukraine. “The remains were arranged in a highly disordered manner. Most of the bodies had been brought to the burial pit and simply dumped into it,” Ukrainian Memorial and Search Center anthropologist Olga Mineiko said. Polejowski said the victims were likely “driven to the field of death barefoot and without personal belongings.” The genetic material is collected, with the IPN appealing to Poles who believe they might have lost relatives in the massacre to provide their own to help find matches. Forensic specialists and anthropologists would also examine the bones to determine the approximate age, sex and cause of death of each of them. It is believed that between 30 to 40 percent of the 50 remains discovered so far were children, Polejowski said. The massacres have been a recurring point of contention between Warsaw and Kyiv. The UPA was a paramilitary organization tied to the Ukrainian independence movement that fought the Soviet Union’s Red Army. However, it collaborated with the Nazis when they first invaded the Soviet Union, clashed with the Polish resistance, and killed Poles, Jews and other civilians. Since Russia invaded in 2022, the UPA has been honored in Ukraine as a force that fought for independence from Moscow under the Soviet Union. Kyiv insisted Zelenskiy’s choice of name for the military unit was not directed against Warsaw, but Polish President Karol Nawrocki withdrew Poland’s highest national honor from him in response. In Poland, the issue has become even more politicized as nationalist parties seek to embolden their base ahead of parliamentary elections next year — part of a broader campaign to whip up anti-Ukrainian sentiment. Poland is home to hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian refugees — with a backlash against their presence having surged during a divisive presidential election campaign last year, won by the right-wing Nawrocki. The country is still the main hub for military and humanitarian aid deliveries to Ukraine, and Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s pro-European government has repeatedly called for a de-escalation. Warsaw has welcomed efforts by Zelenskiy to cool the tension, including the promise of opening of classified intelligence documents. Russia-Ukraine War Poland Summons Russian Ambassador Over Cruise Missile Incursion A missile, determined by Polish authorities to have been manufactured near Moscow, landed near the city of Lublin on July 30. Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk in London on May 27, 2026. Jack Taylor/Reuters Guy Birchall 8/1/2026 | Updated: 8/2/2026 0:00 X 1 Poland summoned the Russian ambassador on July 31 over the incursion of a cruise missile that crashed near the Polish city of Lublin the day before . Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said, “Today, the Polish Foreign Ministry summoned the Russian ambassador in connection with the missile that hit Polish territory yesterday,” in a post on X. The Polish Ministry of Foreign Affairs confirmed in a post on X after the meeting that Moscow’s ambassador had been served with a protest note by Robert Kupiecki, who serves as the ministry’s undersecretary of state and as national security adviser to Tusk. The summoning of the ambassador came after Poland confirmed, following an investigation on July 30, that the missile was Russian. Polish Deputy Minister of National Defense Cezary Tomczyk told Polish radio station RMF24, in an interview on July 30, that the ministry “can confirm with full responsibility that it was a Russian Kh-101 missile. ... i.e. a cruise missile capable of carrying even nuclear warheads, which exploded on impact with the ground.” He noted that the missile that struck Polish territory was part of a 70-missile-strong barrage that Moscow’s forces launched against Ukraine, 20 of which were “flying towards Poland.” Related Stories Cruise Missile Hits Poland Amid Russian Strikes on Ukraine Finland Closes Southern Airspace, Waters Over Stray Drone Risk Tomczyk said that the bulk of these missiles were “shot down by Ukraine over Ukraine,” but that the pilot tracking the missile that eventually hit the country failed to neutralize it and then “turned back 20 seconds before the border” because of the risk of being shot down by a Polish F-16. Asked if the strike was intentionally launched at Poland, Tomczyk said the government currently did not know. “In the case of the drones shot down by the Polish Army on Sept. 10 of last year, I can say with certainty that it was no accident,” he said, calling it a provocation and a test of the NATO alliance. The crater left by the impact was about 30 feet wide, Polish Interior Ministry spokesperson Karolina Gałecka said in a July 30 post on X, noting that it was found a little more than a mile away from some buildings. Polish Deputy Prime Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz shed further light on the missile’s origin in a July 31 post on X. He said that the Military Gendarmerie had confirmed that it was “manufactured in the second quarter of this year at a factory near Moscow.” “This means that Russia is using missiles produced on an ongoing basis to attack Ukraine,” he said, noting that the information confirms reports that Russian military stockpiles have been depleted. The incident provoked widespread condemnation on July 30, with NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte calling it yet another reckless act by Russia and a dangerous consequence of its war against Ukraine, before reaffirming the alliance’s “unwavering” commitment to supporting Kyiv, in a post on X. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also criticized Moscow over the incursion, calling it “another unacceptable violation of ... [European Union] airspace caused by Russia’s latest strikes on Ukraine” in a post on X. “To put an end to this, we are helping Ukraine win this war in every way we can,” she said. “And we are building a robust European security architecture on land, at sea and in the air.” U.S. Ambassador to Poland Tom Rose said that his embassy was “in constant contact” with the Polish government, U.S. Ambassador to NATO Matt Whitaker, and U.S. President Donald Trump over the incident, saying in a July 30 post on X, “Any breach of a NATO ally’s territory is a matter we take extremely seriously.” “We were lucky and grateful there were no casualties,” he said. “The United States stands firmly with Poland. We are coordinating closely with Polish authorities as the investigation proceeds and remain committed to defending Allied territory and upholding NATO’s collective security.” Despite the summoning of its ambassador by Poland, Moscow has not yet officially commented on the incident. However, the Russian Defense Ministry confirmed in a July 30 post on Telegram that it had “launched a massive strike using long-range air, land, and sea-based precision weapons, as well as attack drones, against military industrial facilities, telecommunications and logistics centers” across a range of cities in Ukraine. https://www.surinametimes.com/artikel/sp.text: Engels Spain slams 'selfish' EU response to Ceuta migrants SPAIN - Spain has condemned the "selfish, polarising and unlawful" reaction of some EU countries to the influx of about 60,000 migrants from Morocco to Ceuta. Officials say almost all those who reached the enclave on 30 July have returned, while Spain's Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said on Saturday that the death toll had risen to at least 67. It comes after Italy temporarily suspended the EU's border-free Schengen arrangement with Spain, as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called the scenes "shocking". Finland and Denmark backed Italy's move, while Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš urged a temporary suspension of Spain's Schengen membership. In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he had "serious concerns" about some European governments. He said the Spanish government had fully restored control over the border and prevented any "unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe" in less than 48 hours. While most had shown "support and solidarity", Sanchez said other European governments had chosen to attack Spain, "driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest", and pointed out that Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area. "The European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction," he stated. The Spanish leader called for an urgent meeting with EU interior ministers to "reaffirm that the security of our external borders is a shared responsibility of all Member States". Meanwhile, 22 of the EU's 27 countries also called for emergency talks in an open letter, citing "serious concerns" regarding the developments in Ceuta. Spanish officials say almost all those who reached Ceuta on July 30 have returned, while Spain’s interior minister said yesterday that the death toll from the surge in crossings had risen to at least 86. Italy temporarily suspended the EU’s border-free Schengen arrangement with Spain, as Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni called the scenes ‘shocking’. Finland and Denmark backed Italy’s move, while Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis urged a temporary suspension of Spain’s Schengen membership. EU interior ministers will meet on Tuesday by video conference to discuss the issue. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez had called for an urgent meeting to ‘reaffirm that the security of our external borders is a shared responsibility of all member states’. Twenty-two of the EU’s 27 countries also called for emergency talks in an open letter, citing ‘serious concerns’ regarding the developments in Ceuta. In a letter to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Sanchez said he had ‘serious concerns’ about some European governments. He said the Spanish government had fully restored control over the border and prevented any ‘unauthorised onward movement towards continental Europe’ in less than 48 hours. While most had shown ‘support and solidarity’, Sanchez said other European governments had chosen to attack Spain, ‘driven by prejudice, fake news, ignorance, or political interest’, and pointed out that Ceuta was not part of the Schengen area. “The European Union cannot afford this kind of selfish, polarising and unlawful reaction,” he said. Also yesterday, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he had spoken to Sanchez and the UK was ‘providing what help we can’. There were chaotic scenes on Thursday in Ceuta as border controls in the North African enclave apparently broke down. But in a news conference yesterday, Spain’s Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told reporters the situation in Ceuta had almost returned to normal. “Almost all of (the migrants) have already left Ceuta,” the minister said, adding that businesses had now reopened. “The situation has been almost entirely reversed.” He also said Spain had started to establish an inflatable maritime barrier to prevent further illegal migrant entry. But while the situation on the ground appears to be easing, political and diplomatic fallout is rippling through Madrid and other capitals. On Thursday, Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni wrote on social media that such ‘uncontrolled immigration’ was a threat to national security, before suspending the Schengen zone agreement with Spain for a month. The Schengen Area is a system of open borders spanning 29 European countries that have abolished controls at their common borders. Spain responded by summoning the Italian ambassador to Madrid, while its foreign minister said he expected ‘European solidarity and not partisan demagoguery’. Finland’s Interior Minister Mari Rantanen said she had started preparations for restoring internal border checks ‘if the need arises’. She also urged ‘all European countries’ to support Meloni’s move. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen also urged the EU to ‘consider all options, including a suspension of Schengen co-operation’. France has tightened checks on its border with Spain and said it would increase its police presence.

https://www.gazetteandherald.co.uk/news/.text: Europe’s wildfire crisis eases in west as danger shifts east to Greece By PA News Agency Share 0 Comments 2 Skip to next photo 1 / 1 Show caption 1 / 1 Share 0 Comments This article is brought to you by our exclusive subscriber partnership with our sister title USA Today, and has been written by our American colleagues. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. Europe’s wildfire emergency eased across much of western Europe on Saturday but its most dangerous front shifted to Greece, where gale-force winds drove flames through a seaside resort, forced hundreds to flee by sea and hampered firefighting aircraft. For Greece, the danger carried grim resonance: a 2018 wildfire at the seaside community of Mati, near Athens, killed 104 people, making it Europe’s deadliest wildfire this century. In south-western France, firefighters held a vast wildfire within its perimeter, with about 198,000 people now allowed home after what may have been the country’s largest peacetime evacuation. Major fires in Spain were also no longer advancing, and Portugal’s main blaze was under control. Flames burn through a forest during a wildfire near Porto Germeno (Michael Varaklas/AP) A second French fire stopped expanding overnight after racing across four square miles in six hours on Friday — “faster than a horse at full gallop”, according to the prefecture. But it remained active on Saturday and 2,500 people were still unable to return home. The gains in western Europe marked a sharp turn from the height of the crisis, when fires in France and Spain alone drove a third of a million people from homes and holiday sites, emptied towns during the summer tourism season and stretched firefighters, aircraft and emergency services across simultaneous emergencies. Europe is Earth’s fastest-warming continent, heating at more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus climate service. Rising temperatures and prolonged drought leave vegetation drier and more combustible, allowing fires to spread faster and burn more intensely. Nearly 500 firefighters battled on Saturday to protect Porto Germeno, a popular resort on the Gulf of Corinth, as flames tore through thick pine forest and smoke blocked out the sun. The fire broke out on Friday near the neighbouring coastal village of Agios Vasileios. About 300 people were evacuated by sea, and authorities issued further evacuation orders on Saturday. “A pristine forest, a paradise, was surrendered to the hands of the fire,” said Minas Tzortzanis, a 60-year-old farmer and local resident. “There are no words to explain what has happened. Destruction. Total destruction.” A firefighter works to extinguish fires in south-west France (Emma Da Silva/AP) Theodore Giannaros, a wildfire meteorologist at the National Observatory of Athens, estimated that 15 to 19 square miles had been affected. Authorities had not issued an official burned-area figure. The operation also included specialised forest-fire teams, crews temporarily deployed from France and Romania, 19 water-dropping planes and 11 helicopters. New fires erupted elsewhere in Greece. A blaze east of Nafpaktos prompted evacuation alerts for at least four villages. “The very strong to gale-force winds continue to create exceptionally difficult conditions,” climate crisis and civil protection minister Evangelos Tournas said. Extreme turbulence was preventing some aircraft from collecting water or approaching the fires closely enough to make drops, he said. The Gironde fire has burned 162 square miles of pine forest west of Bordeaux, an area four times the size of Paris. It remained contained within its perimeter on Saturday but had not been declared “fixed” — the point at which crews determine that a fire is no longer advancing. Active sectors and buried hot spots persisted. Authorities reopened more communities on Friday, but several remained largely deserted on Saturday. Much of the forested Cap Ferret peninsula stayed evacuated because a nearby hot spot could flare again. Flames burn through a forest in Greece (Michael Varaklas/AP) “Today, the fire is still not fixed. It is contained,” Lt Col Eric Pitault told reporters. Crews used tactical burns overnight. Along 149 miles of fire edge, heat could remain hidden underground and erupt again. In the Mediterranean Var region, defensive lines around the Gros Bessillon fire held overnight and no additional ground burned, Var prefect Simon Babre told French media on Saturday. The blaze had been declared fixed earlier in the week before mistral gusts revived embers on Friday and sent it racing through dry hills in temperatures approaching 42C. It remained active on Saturday, with 1,300 firefighters deployed and about 2,500 people still unable to return home. The fire’s sudden return “defies understanding”, Mr Babre said. Twenty French departments were under an orange heat warning on Saturday, mostly in the east and south-east. Eight departments faced a high forest-fire risk. For residents returning to the Gironde fire zone, the easing emergency brought a first reckoning with what had been lost. In Le Porge, one of the communities hardest hit, Matthieu Plessis returned on Saturday to the ruins of a home that had been in his family for seven generations. Just over a week earlier, smoke had turned the afternoon almost to night as flames raced along both sides of the road. Now the 40-year-old mechanic drove through blackened forest and struggled to identify what had once stood there. “There are little details here and there that I recognise, but otherwise everything is unrecognisable,” Mr Plessis said. “You don’t even know what was here anymore, or who lived where.” He had to force open the property’s gate because its key had burned. A chimney and twisted metal frames were among the few clues to where the rooms had been. The tools and machinery from his bicycle repair business were gone. “It’s not easy. I’m trying to stay strong and help other people now,” Mr Plessis said. “I don’t want to spend the next 10 years feeling sorry for myself.” Share 0 Comments Get involved with the news Send your news & photos Loading...
