https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cj4k.text: Image source, UK Ministry of Defence Image caption, Iran said two Su-24 fighter jets were used in the mission on a Qatari military base on 2 March 2026 (file photo) By Matt Spivey Published 3 hours ago Iran has called for the release of three Iranian pilots it said were captured by Qatar after two fighter jets were hit by air defences during a military operation at the start of the US-Iran war. In a letter to the head of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), Iran's Brig Gen Mohammad Bagherzadeh said the pilots - Javad Salehi, Abdul Majid Dashtian, and Imran Behroshian - had been held captive for six months. He said the body of a fourth pilot, Majid Kazemi, was returned after he was killed in the same operation on 2 March 2026 - the third day of the war. Qatar "categorically denied" Iran's claims and said it was "surprised by these misleading statements". Gen Bagherzadeh said the three pilots had been captured by Qatar after they ejected from their jets during the combat mission on a Qatari military base. In the letter to ICRC chief Mirjana Spoljaric, published by Iranian media, he accused Qatar of violating "the inalienable rights of these prisoners, contrary to all international laws and regulations". The letter also claimed the three pilots had not been allowed to meet or contact their families. Qatar's foreign affairs spokesperson Majed Mohammed Al Ansari said contact had been made with the pilots "after they violated Qatari airspace", but it did not receive a response. "The necessary measures were taken to defend our territory in accordance with international law," he added in a statement on X. Al Ansari said Qatar's search and rescue teams "carried out their duties to the fullest extent in searching for the pilots' remains". He said Qatar contacted Iran to "co-ordinate the handover of the remains of one of the pilots that were recovered", and that Tehran had yet to respond to an invitation to review details of the search and rescue operation. https://www.manchestereveningnews.co.uk/.text: Salford Quays has to be one of Greater Manchester’s most unique places to visit. Where else can you find watersports, striking modern architecture, TV studios and an island full of gnomes? Oh, and it also happens to be home to the beach - well, of sorts. More on that later. My visit to Salford Quays did get off to an interesting start thanks to a visit to the Quayside Shopping Mall. Nipping inside to use the facilities, I can see why this place is often called a ‘ghost’ shopping centre. Click here for the latest on Manchester's food & drink scene, gigs and more in our CityLife newsletter I walked past vacant shop after vacant shop, marvelling at how barren the place felt and if I’m being honest, slightly creepy too. Previously called The Lowry Outlet Mall, it was rebanded as Quayside in 2020. Some big brands still remain like the M&S Outlet and the food area is going strong. In recent years the mall has welcomed new additions like the Oxygen play centre and Kargo MKT, a popular spot for those heading to a gig at Victoria Warehouse. But the future is looking rather different for Quayside with a £16million overhaul planned. This includes the addition of a Hollywood Bowl bowling alley which has recently been given the green light, and is estimated to open in 2028. It’s set to be joined by a ‘cutting edge’ electric GoKarting track by international firm Hyperdrive Karting. But for now it still feels rather empty, so departing Quayside shopping mall with a feeling of relief, I set out to explore Salford Quays, heading in the direction of the aforementioned ‘beach’. Crossing the Plaza, I strolled past the Lowry, a striking building constructed from steel designed to look like a ship in the docks, a reminder of the area’s history and how this area has undergone a rebirth. Walking around Salford Quays today with its fancy flats and tree-lined promenades, it’s hard to imagine what this area was once like. In fact it was once the third busiest port in Britain; the Manchester Ship Canal connected the city with Liverpool, allowing ocean-bound cargo vessels to travel to and from the city, often heading to Canada. Made up of nine docks in Salford, Stretford and Manchester, the Port of Manchester operated from 1894 until their closure in 1982, after the docks rapidly declined in the 1970s, largely due to containerisation. Regeneration began when Salford City Council acquired parts of the docks in 1983, launching the Salford Quays Development Plan in 1985. Under the scheme the docks were modified to create roads, bridges and landscaped waterfronts, and watersports facilities, moorings, houses and offices soon followed. Walking beside the water today, Salford Quays couldn’t be further away from its industrial past. But its rapid regeneration does reflect the rather surreal feeling this place gives you. It’s a place that has a sort of ‘Disneyland’ feeling to it, somewhere feels manufactured rather than a place that’s slowly evolved with time. Even the names of the areas have a whiff of North America about them: Harbour City, Ontario Basin, Clippers Quay. Although this is entirely by design - many of the basins are named after places in Canada to reflect the ship routes. Yet it’s this purposeful design which also gives Salford Quays a sense of fun. Take its various footbridges; where else would you find so many colourful and quirky water crossings in Greater Manchester? A personal favourite is the Detroit Bridge, instantly recognisable thanks to its red, white and blue steel framing. On my walk to my first stop of the day, I crossed a small yet playful pale blue bridge which really wouldn’t look out of place in Disneyland. It’s here that I passed Salford Watersports Centre and Agecroft Rowing Club. It was a bit too early in the day for them to be in full swing, but the watersports centre does offer a range of activities including kayaking, open water swimming and paddle boarding - which I’ve previously tried before at this very location and can safely say is brilliant. Eventually, after passing a rather unsettling number of geese, I arrived at the ‘beach’. Well I’m using the term beach in the loosest sense of the word. It’s a sandy embankment nestled beside Clippers Quay that’s completely inaccessible to the public, although it’s very popular with water fowl. Still, it’s sparked attention on TikTok so and I suppose at the right angle - if you avoid looking at all the washed-up detritus in the sand - it’s reminiscent of a small beach and great for bird spotters. Walk a little further up and you’ll come across trendy bar Bee Orchid and the Cult & Coffee Listening Cafe coffee shop, as well as a smattering of picnic benches popular with office workers at lunch times. From here I actually crossed into another borough completely, walking over the Trafford Road Swing Bridge. Heading over towards the Wharfside Metrolink stop, it meant I had the perfect vantage point to admire the fascinating place that is Gnome Island. It’s been a feature since 2017 when the first Gnome appeared on one of the derelict concrete islands in the docks. No one knows who’s behind it but it certainly puts a smile on the face of passers-by - and passengers on board the Salford Quays River Cruise. My next stop was the Imperial War Museum North, housed in a magnificent yet unsettling building constructed of three ‘shards’. It was designed by Berlin-based architect Daniel Libeskind. Born in Poland in 1946, dozens of his relatives had been murdered in The Holocaust. Standing beside the building it does feel imposing and its presence weighs upon you. Given its huge size, I was surprised that the entrance was a small door hidden on the other side away from the water, giving you the feeling that you’re entering a much darker world. The museum is completely free to visit and is open every day from 10am to 5pm, except from December 24 to 26. It takes you through the history of warfare in the 20th and 21st centuries, spanning the First World War to 9/11, via permanent displays and changing exhibitions. The current exhibition is Spies, Lies and Deception which, as you might have guessed, looks at the world of espionage. It’s a fascinating collection of real life stories and artefacts, including match boxes used to communicate secret messages and moulds designed to disguise footprints. Entering the main exhibition space, I was startled by a huge Harrier aircraft suspended from the ceiling which takes your breath away, depending on whether you’re into aviation or concerned about how structurally sound the support is. The space is then split up into different ‘silos’ which each focus on an aspect, including technology, communication and women at war. You can explore the museum at your own pace and the displays allow you to get up close to a vast selection of artefacts. As well as the Harrier aircraft, other large items on display include a British nuclear bomb, a piece of wreckage from the September 11 attacks on New York’s World Trade Centre, and an East German Trabant. One display which particularly caught my eye was on nuclear war, it includes a rather depressing map showing the nuclear fallout range of a bomb dropped in Manchester (spoiler alert: it’s not good). Heading back out into the sunshine, it was time for a bite to eat. I crossed the bridge over to Media City, casting a fleeting glance over to the ITV Studios and the hidden set of Coronation Street, and headed to Mattina Coffee located on Blue Road. An Italian deli-turned-coffee shop, it specialises in focaccia sandwiches, lasagne, fresh coffee pastries, including generously-filled cannoli. Given that I arrived at lunchtime, the place was full of Media City employees sporting lanyards of various colours, but I still managed to grab a table. Feeling hungry, I chose a mozzarella, mortadella and pesto focaccia sandwich (£7.50), a slice of lemon and olive oil cake (£4), a pistachio amaretti biscuit (£3) and an Americano £3. They also do a £9 lunch deal where you can get a sandwich, crisps or a mini cannolo and a soft drink, an option that was popular among the Media City workers. Sitting down with my lunch, I realised that my eyes were certainly greedier than my stomach. The sandwich was massive and could easily feed two, although I imagine it would be challenging to share given how delicious it was. The focaccia was crisp on the outside with a sprinkling of salt, while the inside was soft and springy. The fillings were generous, although slightly messy and the ham did slide around a little. But the flavours were fresh and worked well together - I was just sad I couldn’t have finished it all. Moving on to the cake, it was moist and citrusy with an excellent ratio of frosting contrasting with the tangy lemon flavours. The only criticism is that the edges were a bit over-done and a tad dry. The coffee was beautiful, full-bodied and complemented the sweet cake perfectly. I saved the amaretti for later and it was the perfect small sweet treat - I can imagine it being popular with those purchasing a morning coffee or an afternoon pick-me-up. The almond biscuit came topped with a dollop of pistachio cream. Not too sweet, it had a delicate nutty flavour and slightly crumbly texture which melted in the mouth. Mattina Coffee was the ideal way to round off my visit to Salford Quays. Although as I left I did catch sight of a few diners demolishing portions of lasagna, and despite feeling stuff I couldn’t help but look longlying at them. Looks like I’ll be coming back. https://finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy.text: Oops, something went wrong U.S. markets closed Hungarian companies pivot after Orban’s allies lose political influence Simon Mugo August 2, 2026 2 min read APPB OPUSG IGNY Investing.com -- Hungarian companies associated with former Prime Minister Viktor Orban are scaling back large projects and reassessing their businesses after Péter Magyar's election victory ended Orban's 16-year rule, Reuters reported. Magyar's new government has pledged to tackle alleged favouritism in public procurement and review contracts awarded under the previous administration. Construction groups that relied heavily on state-funded infrastructure projects face the greatest risk as public tenders become more competitive. Market Epito, one of Hungary's largest construction companies, plans to shift from major developments towards a greater number of smaller housing and infrastructure projects. About one-quarter of its revenue has come from public contracts. The company is linked to Orban ally Istvan Garancsi but said its financial strength and diversified portfolio were not dependent on political cycles. Duna Aszfalt, Hungary's largest road-construction company, also said it was prepared to compete under the new system. Magyar's government has suspended an extension of a motorway in southern Hungary and asked Duna Aszfalt to repay funds received for the project before the election. Public procurement practices had faced scrutiny under Orban. A 2024 OECD survey found that Hungary had a high rate of tenders attracting only one bidder. Reforms designed to increase competition are among the European Union's conditions for releasing funding suspended over rule-of-law concerns. Parliament received broad anti-corruption legislation in June aimed at improving transparency in the use of public money. Shares of companies viewed as politically connected, including Opus Global, Appeninn, 4iG and MBH Bank, have fallen sharply as investors removed premiums associated with their previous influence. Those declines have contrasted with a broader rally in Budapest-listed stocks, supported by expectations that more transparent tenders could attract foreign investment. Analysts said some businesses built around preferential access to state contracts may not survive the transition. International companies could gain market share in construction, defence, telecommunications and media as contracts are reopened to wider competition. https://www.southcoastregister.com.au/st.text: You may often book a holiday. But how often do you holiday a book? Sometimes it happens coincidentally. I recall one visit to the Moroccan city of Tangier, exploring the narrow alleys and stairs of its medina and being reminded of Paulo Coelho's The Alchemist. It's the first stop in the journey for the main character, Santiago, who finds work in a crystal shop after all his money is stolen, earning enough to make his way to Egypt. I encountered neither jewel nor heist but, like Santiago, it was another chapter in my journey. Sometimes it's a little more planned. Travelling in Spain, through the region of La Mancha, my itinerary is focused on the inspiration Miguel de Cervantes found for Don Quixote. His house is now a museum with lots to see, but it's up on nearby hills, at a series of 12 windmills, that you can really imagine how he and his delusional knight saw them as giants with thrashing arms. The idea of literary tourism is again front of mind with the release of The Odyssey. Even though the modern movie may be the spark for some "set-jetting", it's just taking a page from centuries of travel inspired by the ancient text, with Mediterranean itineraries through Turkiye, the Greek Islands, Sicily, and more. For years, people have used books to travel to novel destinations. While Pictures from Italy by Charles Dickens encouraged 19th-century tourists to embark on their own Grand Tour, modern readers journey to Canada's Prince Edward Island because of Anne of Green Gables or the Greek island of Corfu for Gerald Durrell's famous trilogy. Dracula inspires trips to Romania for the love of fantasy, while Eat Pray Love inspires trips to Bali for the fantasy of love. Perhaps even more common - and still a form of literary tourism - is reading a book set in a destination while you are setting foot there yourself. I've done it with Burmese Days in Myanmar, The Beach in Thailand, and In Patagonia... in Patagonia. Other popular holiday reads include My Brilliant Friend in Naples, Shantaram in India, and One Hundred Years of Solitude in Colombia (my Kindle broke when I was only halfway through... but I assume it's just another 50 years of solitude). Although James Joyce's Ulysses is a notoriously difficult read, there are ways to get a taste of the epic novel on a trip to Dublin without reading even one of its 265,000 words. A good place to start is one of the city's Martello Towers, which is where I found myself one trip. These stone cylindrical towers were built along the coast in the early 1800s as a defensive system against Napoleon, and eventually Joyce spent some time staying in one of them. He used that experience as the setting for the opening of Ulysses, and now the tower is a small museum that gives you another opening into the book. Of course, if you want to explore more chapters in person, head to Dublin on June 16 - the date on which the whole novel is set - for the annual Bloomsday festival. Although literary tourism has existed for centuries, it's now entering a new chapter. Bolstered by trends like slow travel, book clubs, and even viral online BookTok posts, more people than ever are turning over a new leaf in the way they travel for literature. It's now often about more than just visiting the destination - there's also been a boom in specialised reading tours. You can do a nine-day tour in the United States that sails along the Mississippi River, following the adventures of Huckleberry Finn and Mark Twain, including his family home and the limestone caves featured in Tom Sawyer. You can take a four-day tour in the Scottish Highlands to see the medieval sites in the Outlander books, or walk for six days through mountain passes and historic temples of Japan to explore trails captured by haiku master Matsuo Basho. Or go on a 20-day expedition in northern France to see the inspirations for a range of authors like Marcel Proust, Victor Hugo, and Gustave Flaubert. From Australia, ASA Cultural Tours offers 18 days in England's East Anglia browsing through the landscapes of Arthur Ransome, the marshes of Ruth Rendell, the retreats of Beatrix Potter, and many more. Meanwhile, a small company called Better Read Tours takes it a step further with a trip to Paris for two weeks to work on your own memoir, or a week in Stratford-upon-Avon in England for a creative writing workshop. READ MORE MICHAEL TURTLE: Even beyond writer retreats, we now also have reader retreats. The Literary Man Hotel in Portugal has 100,000 books to borrow during your stay. And some tour companies are taking people away... just so they can sit there and work through a book, like a four-day sailing trip around the Spanish island of Mallorca with an itinerary that reads, "leisurely breakfast on deck, sail south with stops for swims and reading time on deck". Or, closer to home, you can have two nights near Canberra with Reading Retreats Australia where you "let the outside world melt away for a weekend that's all about you and your books". It may seem odd to travel somewhere just to read, but if the aim of a holiday is to relax and experience a new world, then you can get both of those things from a good book. The best authors stay with you, so it's also no surprise you may want to find ways to connect to them in the real world. But ultimately, whether you're out in the landscapes or just in your hotel bed, there's a good holiday to be found between the covers.

https://www.israelnationalnews.com/news/.text: Yisrael Beytenu chairman MK Avigdor Liberman this morning (Sunday) dismissed comments by Yashar party chairman Gadi Eisenkot, who said that the leaders of smaller parties in the opposition bloc should not insist on becoming prime minister. Speaking in an interview with Gideon Oko and Amichai Atali on Radio 103FM, Liberman said the discussion misses the main issue. "I think Gadi is missing the central objective here. We all need to focus on one goal-to bring down the alliance of draft evaders and the October 7 government," Liberman said. He added that Eisenkot himself has spoken about the possibility of serving as prime minister, making the issue irrelevant at this stage. According to Liberman, the debate over who should lead the government ultimately serves Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. "Both you and Gadi are falling right into Netanyahu's trap. He wants us to keep talking about who will be first and who will be second instead of dealing with the substance," he said. Related articles: Likud surges as coalition gains ground Mansour Abbas sets election goal Will United Torah Judaism split after the elections? Ben Gvir: Netanyahu planning unity government with Eisenkot Liberman added that the opposition's internal disputes only benefit Likud. When asked about his own past in the party, where he previously served as director-general, he replied: "Today's Likud has become Mahal-a Haredi-lite party. That's not a place where I intend to work." Addressing the possibility of cooperating with the Ra'am party, Liberman categorically rejected the idea. "After October 7, Ra'am cannot be part of the coalition-neither from within nor from outside. Absolutely not," he said. He argued that such cooperation would not be necessary in any case. "The real news is that we will win by a large margin, and we'll have a Hungarian-style scenario. The Zionist parties will secure an overwhelming majority, and we won't need anyone else. We'll establish a statesmanlike, Zionist government, unlike the sectoral government of the alliance of draft evaders-Goldknopf, Deri, and Netanyahu." Liberman also addressed the crisis with Iran and reports that a planned American strike had been canceled. "The Iranians are not willing to give up-not even for a moment-on their nuclear program, control of the Strait of Hormuz, or support for their regional proxies. They're simply buying time," he said. He criticized the handling of the American decisions, adding: "We've become a banana republic. It can't be that Trump announces we won't strike Iran, and everyone speaks on our behalf."

https://www.arbuturian.com/culture/books.text: Trending Old City, New Tricks: Lisbon’s Endless Temptations Bao, Bargains and Rooftops: A Tale of Three Japans Table for One, please: Dating Myself in Paris Spa of the Month: Low Wood Bay, Windermere Oxford, Collected Fashion Becomes Tea at The Kensington Town House Porto Montenegro: A Life Less Taxing Zoilo The Truth Brindisa, Battersea The Best Caddie on the West Coast A Summer Miscellany By Philip Cottam on August 2, 2026 Books Whether you’re reading poolside, on a delayed train, or hiding from the heat with the curtains drawn, Philip Cottam’s summer selection has range: espionage in Cold War Berlin, small-town America unravelling, a river fighting for its life, and one extraordinary woman’s journey through revolution and war… The Predicament by William Boyd Gabriel Drax, travel writer and part-time spy at the centre of The Predicament , first appeared on the scene in Gabriel’s Moon, first published in 2024. The Predicament sees Gabriel well and truly embedded in the secret world, caught between his two employers, MI6 and the KGB, as well as the internal politics of the CIA. To make matters even more complicated he becomes involved in an intense but somewhat on-off relationship with his MI6 handler. Gabriel certainly confronts several predicaments both personal and professional. It all makes for a heady mix that William Boyd handles deftly. The main thread of the story centres on a rogue element in the CIA and the build-up to the famous Kennedy visit to Cold War Berlin in the summer of 1963 and his subsequent assassination in Dallas later that year. Gabriel’s journey to Berlin starts with a dangerous mission to violence ridden Guatemala City. What happens sets the scene for what follows in Berlin. The Berlin section of the story is cleverly plotted around the Kennedy visit. It also sees Gabriel, part-time amateur agent, starting to acquire the street-smart skills and situational awareness he really needs to survive. With The Predicament Boyd has written a worthy successor to Gabriel’s Moon . Gabriel Drax is a more firmly established character and Boyd continues to make good use of his descriptive talents in creating the different atmospheres that surround Gabriel whether at home in London and Sussex or when in Berlin and Guatemala. Given the mention of a trip to Moscow by his Russian handler, it would seem that, having successfully navigated his way through the predicaments confronting him, Gabriel’s adventures in the world of espionage are not yet over. The Predicament is out now in paperback, published by Penguin . American Rust by Philipp Meyer With the upcoming mid-term American elections and the emergence of divisions amongst both traditional Republicans and, perhaps more significantly, amongst the MAGA base of the electoral alliance that swept Trump to power for a second term it would seem a good time to read or even re-read American Rust by Philipp Meyer. Published to acclaim in 2009 it was subsequently turned into a TV crime drama in 2021. In the novel Meyer sets out to illustrate the decline of the American middle class through the impact of an accidental murder in a fictional town set in an area of Pennsylvania known for its run-down and economically depressed steel towns. The narrative is driven by a series of relationships. The most important is that between two young friends and how they handle their differing responsibilities for the killing. There is then the old relationship between the mother of one of the young men and the Police Chief investigating the murder. The result is a series of conflicts of loyalty and integrity. All takes place in a community marked by declining prosperity and the accompanying tensions that arise when both aspirations and expectations have been damaged. Meyer makes effective use of a stream of consciousness technique as the mechanism through which he narrates his story. His characters are closely observed with their behaviours well imagined and their moral conflicts well-constructed. As for his writing style it is sparse, gritty and atmospheric. When first published American Rust drew comparisons with Faulkner and Steinbeck from some reviewers. It certainly opens the door onto how the frustration and despair of once prosperous communities at being sacrificed on the altar of globalisation led to the attraction of the MAGA movement for many. American Rust is published by Scribner UK . Is a River Alive? by Robert MacFarlane Robert Macfarlane first established himself as a master of the language of landscapes and mankind’s relationship with nature when he published Mountains of the Mind in 2003. Since then, he has gone on to publish several more looking at different aspects of those two themes, of which Is a River Alive? is the most recent. Is a River Alive? takes a journey, part elegiac and part an alarm call, to dying rivers and those trying to save them, in Ecuador, India and Quebec. Like all its predecessors the book is thoughtful and intriguing and opens doors onto nature in unexpected ways. Given the increasingly angry outcry against the pollution of our rivers and streams it is certainly timely. It also includes, appropriately close to his home in Cambridge, the story of a spring that because of lack of care frequently dries up damaging the landscape it feeds. In Ecuador MacFarlane visits a river and its tributaries in the cloud forest, a rain forest in the mountains where clouds linger amongst the trees. The river is threatened by exploitation of nearby mineral deposits. Damage to the purity of the water will also damage the virgin forest, its flora and fauna. The threat is underlined by MacFarlane’s companion, a scientist who has discovered previously unknown fungi. In India MacFarlane visits the three main rivers of Chennai which have been so damaged by chemical and other pollution. Here the fight for improvement is being driven by activists through the court system. In Quebec his river odyssey is completed with a canoe trip down the wild pure waters and rapids of one of the many rivers that flow through the province. It is an adventure that stands in stark contrast to the previous two journeys. Does MacFarlane answer the question that is his title? The answer is a resounding yes. He shows how both landscape and humanity can become impoverished if the rivers that feed them become polluted and die through a combination of thoughtlessness and greed. His style is not polemical. It is subtle, elegant and thought-provoking. Above all he brings the landscapes that enthral him to life . Is a River Alice? is published by Penguin . I, Vera by Miranda Seymour Miranda Seymour has written an unputdownable biography with I, Vera . She has certainly been helped by her protagonist and the turbulent times she lived through. Born a Lithuanian Princess in 1870 Vera Ignatievna Gedroits grew up to become the first woman in the Russian Empire to become a doctor at the Imperial Court, a battlefield surgeon and a professor of medicine. She was also a writer, both medical and literary, as well as an occasional poet. All this while living openly as a lesbian, getting arrested as a student political activist, surviving the violence of the October Revolution, although she did get wounded. She also avoided the frequent Bolshevik purges that followed the revolution until 1930 despite her connections with the Imperial family. Her eventful life ended two years later when she died of cancer while still in the company of her longtime partner the Countess Maria Nirod. For all her privileged upbringing and her close connection to the Imperial family Vera was in no doubt that her commitment as a doctor was especially for those who needed her skills most. It was not a coincidence that during her first job as a qualified doctor in a hospital attached to a factory she was known as the ‘people’s doctor’. She never worried about danger and became a military surgeon during the Russo-Japanese War, the First World War and the civil war that followed the October Revolution. As for her lesbianism she had to be discreet at first, especially when attached to the Imperial Court at Tsarskoe Selo (now usually called Pushkin). Her long relationship with the Countess Maria Nirod, which began during the time Vera was recovering from her wound in 1918, was more open. This was because of the more relaxed atmosphere towards social mores in the early years of post-Imperial Russia. Miranda Seymour has produced a real page-turner while at the same time remaining true to the historical record even when it contradicts Vera herself. She did write five autobiographies. Seymour also puts Vera’s significant achievements in context, whether her contributions to medical science or just in navigating the very different social and political environments of Imperial and Revolutionary Russia. Above all the story she tells of this remarkable and praiseworthy woman makes for a life-enhancing read. I, Vera is out now published by William Collins, available from Daunt Books . https://tiranaexaminer.com/the-full-cycl.text: The Full Cycle 31.07.26 SPAK’s chief says the law already allows his investigators to make arrests. He is right. That is not the question. Renada Bici , Legal Desk When officers of the National Bureau of Investigation arrested Adi Çobo Bazholi in Durrës earlier this month, the operation was noted less for the man in handcuffs than for who was missing from the picture. The State Police, which for three decades has carried out the significant arrests of the Republic, appeared nowhere in the accounts of this one. The Bureau planned the operation, staffed it, and closed it, and the commentary that followed read the police’s absence as the message it appeared to be, a prosecution demonstrating that it no longer needs to knock on the ministry’s door before it knocks on anyone else’s. On Thursday, in an informal meeting with journalists in Tirana, the head of the Special Prosecution, Klodian Braho, converted the demonstration into a program. SPAK, he said, intends to create a special group for operational actions, with full independence in its activity. He was careful with the frame. The law does not condition arrests on the Bureau alone, he said, and the institution does not aim to replace the State Police and cannot function without cooperating with it. But the destination was stated plainly enough. The special group is coming, and it will answer to no one outside the structure that created it. We have written before about what SPAK’s independence means and whom it runs against. In May we asked what happens when a special prosecution begins to behave as a state within the state in its dealings with foreign governments, and the question beneath that one, how anyone outside the institution verifies whom it answers to, has followed the file ever since. Thursday’s announcement belongs to the same file. An institution that investigates, intercepts, prosecutes, and seizes now proposes to add the one function it lacked, the armed execution of its own orders. Before anyone reaches for the phrase power grab, and before anyone reaches for the phrase capacity building, it is worth doing what neither camp will do, which is to read the statute. What the law says Begin where Braho begins, because on his narrow point he is correct. Law 95/2016 defines the National Bureau of Investigation as a specialized structure of the Judicial Police, investigating criminal offenses within the Special Prosecution’s jurisdiction according to the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure. That last clause does the work. The Code assigns the acts of compulsion, among them the execution of arrests and detentions, to the judicial police as such. It does not say which judicial police. An arrest warrant issued by a special prosecutor and executed by a Bureau investigator sits comfortably inside the Code’s text. Nothing in the statute reserves the physical act of arrest to the State Police, and the chief prosecutor is entitled to say so. He is entitled to say something else, too. The distrust behind the Durrës operation is not paranoia. Operations against wanted persons have failed repeatedly in circumstances that suggest advance warning, and the suspicion inside SPAK that actions are deconspired by segments of the State Police is by now an open secret of Albanian law enforcement. The institution holds security measures and convictions in absentia that no one has executed. A prosecution that cannot produce the bodies of the people it has lawfully ordered detained is failing at something elementary, and Braho did not invent the failure. He inherited it. So the narrow claim stands. If the question were whether a Bureau investigator may lay hands on a wanted man, the answer would be yes, and this piece would end here. What the law does not say The question is different, and the statute itself shows why. There is a distance, which Braho’s own formulation quietly acknowledged, between an arrest and a standing tactical unit. The first is an act the law authorizes. The second is an institution the law would have to create, with weapons, vehicles, entry equipment, use of force doctrine, selection standards, training cycles, and a command chain, maintained permanently. The Code of Criminal Procedure supplies the act. Nothing in Albanian law contemplates the institution. Read Law 95/2016 for what it built the Bureau to be. Its investigators are recruited, by the statute’s own terms, from the State Police directorates responsible for investigating organized crime, economic crime, and narcotics trafficking, and from other institutions with judicial police functions. These are detectives. The statute vets them, secures them, polygraphs them, and subjects their families to financial monitoring, all in the service of one design idea, an investigative body that cannot be bought. Nowhere does it provide for tactical operators, because the drafters never imagined the Bureau kicking doors. They imagined it building files while the State Police kicked doors. We know this is not an oversight, because the drafters showed us how they legislate when they intend to hand the Bureau an operational capability. The statute states expressly that the Bureau is the institution that executes interception orders requested by the Special Prosecution and authorized by the anti-corruption courts. Interception is precisely the kind of function the drafters refused to leave with structures they did not trust, so they said so, in text, with the capability named and assigned. When the legislature of 2016 wanted the Bureau to own an operational function, it wrote a sentence. There is no sentence for a tactical intervention group. Braho has an available answer, and it deserves to be met rather than avoided. The Bureau already contains capabilities the statute never names, an analysis function, digital forensics, financial investigation cells, and nobody argues that each required an act of parliament. The answer fails at one word, and the word is force. What separates a tactical unit from an analysis sector is the authority to apply physical coercion to persons, and in the Albanian constitutional order coercion is never an administrative detail. The Constitution declares law the basis and the boundary of the activity of the state, and permits the limitation of rights and freedoms only by law. That is why the State Police carries its weapons under a statute, why its use of force is graduated in legal text rather than in internal circulars, and why every armed formation of the Republic, army, police, Republican Guard, exists by a law that names it. An analysis sector organizes labor. A tactical unit organizes violence. The first can live in an internal order. The second cannot, and the silence of Law 95/2016 is therefore not a gap the institution may fill for itself. It is a boundary. Which gives the phrase Braho chose its proper weight. Full independence in its activity, resting on what? The Bureau’s independence is not a mood. It is a set of enumerated guarantees written into Law 95/2016, each running against a named threat, ministerial interference, political appointment, financial capture. A unit with full independence in its operational activity has no statutory referent at all. The chief prosecutor has described an institution that does not exist in Albanian law and announced that he intends to operate it. Who commands it Suppose the group is created anyway, by internal order and budget line, the way institutions grow when no one stops them. Follow the command chain the existing statute would impose on it, because this is where the legal problem becomes a constitutional one. Law 95/2016 provides that the Bureau’s director, its investigators, and its judicial police services are directed and controlled by the prosecutors of the Special Prosecution. Every function the Bureau performs runs up that chain. Place a tactical unit inside the Bureau and the sentence does not bend to accommodate it. The unit’s raids, its entries, its escalations of force would be directed and controlled by prosecutors. And here precision matters, because judicial police working under prosecutorial direction is ordinary from Rome to Bucharest, and SPAK’s defenders will say so. What is not ordinary, what no European democracy houses on purpose, is a standing armed intervention unit that a prosecution office owns, staffs, and commands as its own organ. The continent’s legal orders keep the prosecutorial brain and the tactical hand in separate institutions, on the theory that whoever decides which door to breach should not also employ the men holding the ram. Albania would be fusing them, and fusing them without a single deputy voting on the question. Now run the incident that every armed unit eventually produces. A raid goes wrong. A man is shot on a staircase in Durrës and the family says he was unarmed. Who investigates? The jurisdiction of the Special Prosecution covers, among other things, criminal offenses committed by high officials and by the structures within its own perimeter. The institution whose unit fired the shot is the institution with jurisdiction over the shooting. The State Police answers for its operations to a ministry, to a parliament that can summon the minister on a Tuesday, and to a prosecution that sits outside it. The special group would answer to the prosecutors who sent it, and then, if it erred, to the same prosecutors again. A closed loop is not accountability. It is the absence of accountability wearing its uniform. None of this is an accusation against the men and women of the Bureau, whose vetting is the most severe applied to any public servants in the country. It is an observation about design. The severity of the vetting was the substitute for external control, and it was calibrated for detectives holding files. It was never calibrated for a formation holding rifles, because the drafters never put rifles in the design. What other countries did Braho told the Law Committee that the full investigative cycle within one structure is a practice seen in homologous institutions abroad. The comparison deserves to be taken seriously, which means taken precisely. Italy’s Direzione Investigativa Antimafia is the comparison SPAK’s defenders reach for. But the DIA sits inside the Interior Ministry, staffed by seconded members of the ordinary police forces, answerable up a ministerial chain to a government that parliament can dismiss. It works for the anti-mafia prosecutors. It does not belong to them. Italy separated the prosecutorial brain from the operational hand deliberately, having learned what concentrations of both look like. Romania is the comparison SPAK’s defenders avoid. The National Anticorruption Directorate solved its own capability gap by leaning on the intelligence service through cooperation arrangements the public was never shown, prosecutors and covert operators fused into what critics called the parallel state. When the Constitutional Court dismantled the arrangement, ruling that intelligence structures could not serve as organs of criminal investigation and pulling the secret protocols into the light, the damage was not contained to the arrangements themselves. It contaminated years of convictions and handed every corrupt defendant in the country a legitimacy argument that Romanian anticorruption has still not outrun. The lesson of Bucharest is not that special prosecutions must never acquire operational reach. It is that operational reach acquired outside statute eventually destroys the institution it was meant to serve. And the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, the newest homologous institution of them all and the one Albania’s accession path actually points toward, owns no operational capability whatsoever. It investigates and prosecutes across more than twenty member states and executes nothing itself, relying entirely on national enforcement authorities. The most modern prosecution structure in Europe was built, on purpose, without the very organ SPAK now proposes to grow. The full cycle is not the European practice. It is the exception European designers keep declining to make. The honest problem and the honest answer We do not dismiss the problem Braho is solving. A prosecution that must route its most sensitive operations through a police force it has concrete reasons to distrust will keep losing fugitives. The status quo is measured in failed operations and unexecuted warrants, and every escaped defendant is a small amnesty granted by leak. The people demanding that SPAK simply trust the State Police harder are demanding that it keep paying for that trust in fugitives. But the answer to an institution that cannot be trusted is not an institution that cannot be checked. It is a rule. If the special group is to exist, and there is a serious case that some version of it should, then it must be built the way the Bureau itself was built in 2016, in public, by statute, with its limits written before its weapons are issued. That means, first, a law and not an internal order. An amendment to Law 95/2016 that names the unit, fixes its maximum strength, defines its mission in a closed list, and states what remains exclusively with the State Police, so that cooperation is a legal boundary rather than a monthly negotiation. The Kuvend created the Bureau’s interception capability in text. It can create this one the same way, or the capability should not exist. Second, a use of force regime enacted, not improvised. The State Police carries its weapons under a statutory framework that took years to refine. A prosecutorial tactical unit operating on the general judicial police provisions, with no dedicated rules of engagement, would make every operation a legal experiment conducted on live subjects. Third, an accountability mechanism that breaks the closed loop. Any use of force by the unit investigated outside SPAK’s own perimeter, by designation in the statute, so that the institution never sits as prosecutor of its own hand. And a standing reporting duty, operation by operation, to the High Prosecutorial Council and in aggregate to the Kuvend, in the annual report that is currently the only window the public has into the Bureau at all. Fourth, a sunset. Extraordinary powers granted on an extraordinary rationale should lapse when the rationale is no longer proven, and this is not an imported habit. The justice reform itself was built that way. Its vetting bodies were created as transitional instruments with expiry written into the constitutional annex, on the understanding that emergency architecture must not quietly become permanent architecture, and when their mandate ran out, extending it required a fresh vote. The distrust of the State Police is the emergency that justifies this unit. Let the statute expire in five years unless renewed, so that the parliament which grants the capability on that rationale is made to ask, at least once, whether the rationale still holds. Braho says the structure should be able to perform the entire cycle of investigative actions itself. Perhaps it should. But there are two full cycles in a state governed by law, and they are not interchangeable. One runs from surveillance to file to warrant to arrest, and it can, with care, be housed in a single institution. The other runs from proposal to debate to vote to statute to oversight, and it cannot be housed anywhere except the parliament. The chief prosecutor is asking for the first cycle. He can have it the day he submits to the second. https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/cultur.text: For many, summer is a time for travel and discovery. I encourage readers of this column to visit galleries and museums and to immerse themselves in art while traveling in Israel. Local artists have so much to offer.This month, I decided to feature multidisciplinary artists whose ongoing exhibitions in Beersheba, Bat Yam, and Tel Aviv can create an alternative reality for the viewers. Artists who build an experience and encompass the space, whether by theatrical light structures that have taken over the entire museum area, or an intimate, very moving installation, in just one tiny room. I also spoke to an artist who paints additional space on canvas, symbolically adding lines, as if it were another truth. These three artists agreed to answer my three questions:What inspires you? What do you call art? What, in your opinion, makes your artwork different from that of other artists?Anna Fromchenko, widely exhibited artist, both solo and as part of a groupAnna Fromchenko is a multidisciplinary artist, born in Bucharest, Romania, in 1952. At the age of eight, she made aliyah with her family and moved to Givatayim in central Israel, where she grew up. She now lives and works in Tel Aviv. Fromchenko studied painting at the Kalisher School of Arts in Tel Aviv (1969-1971), and then art history, film, and television at Tel Aviv University, graduating with a BA in 1976. Her work can be found in numerous private collections and the Petah Tikva Museum of Art. It has been widely exhibited in solo and group exhibitions in Israel and abroad.Her work spans painting, photography, video, and site-specific installations. She explores memory, identity, and the human condition, transforming complex social issues into multi-layered visual experiences. The artist shows contemporary social and political realities through visual narratives. Fromchenko seems to remove objects from their original context and imbue them with new, poetic meaning, just as in the case of her latest exhibition, The Wishing Well, on display at the Negev Museum of Art in Beersheba. The Wishing Well, a site-specific work, combines video, sound, and sculpture. When we met at the museum, Fromchenko told me that this work, despite being rooted in biblical traditions and being physically in Beersheba, is not connected to the biblical well of Abraham [there].The video is placed on the museum's floor among stones on which visitors can sit, in a small, dark room, behind a black curtain, where the lights change, and the sound of water creates the impression of an authentic well, but it is an illusion. The sound of water rising and falling, in rhythm with breathing, is almost meditative. In addition to the sound of water, there is also recited, whispered poetry with the repeated line: “You cannot see the water / through the water.” Fromchenko created a very moving and intimate space. Inspiration: My inspiration emerges from a dialogue with reality. It begins with a phenomenon or a figure that compels me to respond, transforming it through artistic action into a dialogue with the viewer.My artistic practice is about conveying an experience that triggers a chain of responses around conceptual themes, generating an ongoing conversation with the audience. I also draw inspiration from literature and poetry.Meaning of art: For me, art is the sublimation of reality, both for the artist and for the viewer. It is a language beyond language – a means of connecting people.The dialogue that unfolds between the viewer and the artwork creates the metaphysical dimension of the piece. The richer and more meaningful that dialogue becomes, the more powerful the work's metaphysical presence.Fromchenko's art: Because my practice is conceptual, the subject changes from one project to another, and with it the technique and artistic medium. This is how my multidisciplinary approach finds expression through painting, sculpture, photography, video, and writing.For example, in a project titled Iran, Iran, I first painted the ejection seat of a fighter jet as a metaphor for our condition of risk and rescue within the geopolitical space we inhabit. I later transformed it into a monumental sculpture, as well as a smaller sculpture produced from a 3D-printed model, among other iterations. In another project, I photographed the interiors of abandoned beehives and transformed the images into immersive video installations, inviting viewers to experience the sensation of entering a gigantic beehive. In my current work, The Wishing Well, which emerged from an inner dialogue about how to lift myself out of a dark pit on my own, I constructed the rim of a real well and created a video of water slowly rising and falling within it, accompanied by the sound of prayers, supplications, and singing.As a deep and hidden space, the well can become a pit of falling, entrapment, and death, while simultaneously representing an inner realm of memory, the subconscious, and hidden layers of the psyche. This duality lies at the heart of the work. Across many cultures, the idea of the “wishing well” recurs as a metaphysical gateway of hope, faith, and enchantment – a place where people cast their longings and prayers beyond the visible and the present.www.anna-fromchenko.com/Omer Sheizaf, internationally recognized lighting design expertBorn in 1982 in Ramat Gan and today based in Tel Aviv-Jaffa, Omer Sheizaf holds a BA in Literature and Philosophy from Tel Aviv University (2012) and an MFA from Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design (2018). He is a multidisciplinary artist with expertise in lighting design, which has earned him international recognition.He has designed for the LA Dance Project, Batsheva Dance Company, and others. Among his numerous awards, he won the 2009 Israel Fringe Award for Best Lighting. Sheizaf teaches at the School of Visual Theater in Jerusalem. His artwork has been exhibited in various museums and galleries, including the Tel Aviv Museum of Art, Holon Digital Art Center, Muza, and more. Through sculpture, installation, and audiovisual performance, Sheizaf explores the relationship between the performative and the environmental areas.In the exhibition Redden, which opened this month at the Bat Yam Museum of Art, the installation designed specifically for the museum, Sheizaf created large-scale lighting on the circular ceiling and in theatrical spaces upstairs, including a disassembled motorcycle and urban-themed dioramas. In my eyes, the artist transforms the exhibition space into a stage where light, sound, and sculpture play equal roles, and visitors become additional actors in the performance, each in their own unique way. In this show, Sheizaf creates an alternative reality that also alludes to the play on words in the exhibition's Hebrew name, Maadim, which can be translated into English as “becoming red” and “Mars.” During our conversation, Shaizaf explained that he isn't interested in planets or observing the sky as much as he is in the possibility of an alternative place for refugees, for humanity. Entering Redden, we get a taste of it, for sure.Inspiration: I find my inspiration in observing different elements of the urban landscape. This is what I did most of my childhood, and in many ways, not much has changed since then. I grew up among the grey streets of Ramat Gan, wandering around in search of something interesting or imagining distant worlds.Sometimes I would discover an old sculpture abandoned in a pile of trash, a strange light coming through a window, or a neglected electronics shop selling records. These were my moments of excitement.Meaning of art: Art is the ability of something to become new, to become different, to open a new path that does not follow a predetermined plan. It is essentially a liberal force, one that liberates us from old structures and fixed perspectives. Art clears the mind when it becomes trapped within patterns that have remained unchanged for too long.It is the opposite of cliché and the opposite of conservatism. It is closer to madness than to culture, and the origin of them both. The artwork is not only the object, but the entire situation around it: the atmosphere, the movement, the sound, the light, and the experience that unfolds in front of the viewer.Sheizaf's art: I work with light, sound, and effects that come from the world of theater. I believe that the connection between theatre, sculpture, and installation is a central element in my work. My installations contain dramaturgy and a sense of time; they unfold through sequences and transformations.I came to visual art through theater. I grew up on stage and around it. I learned how to tie ropes and fabrics, climb high wooden structures, and release hidden mechanisms at the precise moment required in a performance. I bring this knowledge into my sculptural practice. My material is the effect itself, and it is built from my personal history, from the things that have fascinated me throughout my life, and from the place I come from.I am deeply interested in theatrical effects and old forms of magic. The aesthetics of my work are often drawn from worlds of illusion and ancient mysticism, a kind of secular mysticism that exists within the theatrical realm.I [also] come from an alternative culture, and I believe that the worlds and characters that emerge in my work are, in many ways, rooted in those places. The worlds of darkness, otherness, and queerness connected to a distorted, imperfect, and unconventional sound.www.instagram.com/omer.sheizaf/Tali Navon, painter, video and installation artistTali Navon, a painter, video and installation artist, was born in Givatayim in 1964 and lives and works in Tel Aviv. She studied textile art at the Shenkar College of Engineering and Design (1991), fine art at the Kalisher School of Art (1995), and film at Tel Aviv University (2000).Her work has been presented in solo and group exhibitions abroad and in Israel, including at the Israel Museum, Petah Tikva Museum, Ashdod Museum, Haifa Museum, Beit Reuven Museum, Mana Katz Museum, and the Wilfrid Israel Museum of Asian Art and Studies in Hazorei.Her video works have been presented at the Jerusalem Film Festival, Middlebury College in Vermont, the Total Museum of Contemporary Art in Seoul, and other art venues worldwide.She has gained recognition for her interdisciplinary exploration of local and global cultural phenomena and historical narratives. Navon explores themes of contemporary culture, urban planning, identity, motherhood, and the fragility and innocence of childhood. She incorporates elements of drawing into her minimalist paintings, which are often indistinguishable from drawings. In her latest exhibition, Study Room, recently opened at the Rothschild Art Gallery in Tel Aviv, the artist explores workspaces as places of creation.The works are created in a conservative color palette, but unconventionally, as Navon explained, painting on a lying-flat canvas (not standing or hung) allows her to add more water to the oil paints, dilute the paint, penetrate it, and give it a watercolor effect. What caught my attention were objects – just their contours, painted in white lines, as added on top of the painting. She told me they are, in a sense, metaphysical; the artist explores the future of the book when we can no longer touch it.In Study Room, Navon also shows a series called Readers, 10 small oil works on glass. Again, the technique the artist uses, in effect, reminds one of watercolors. “The choice of technique is a matter of feeling,” noted Navon.The exhibition traces the act of painting and writing to propose a parallel between them. The artist, who also placed her chair and table in the gallery, invites viewers into her very intimate creative world.Inspiration: I love observing and looking at my environment. I love humanity and wonder about the human condition. What inspires people to act within an existing reality? I also love to examine the past and place it in the present: what has changed and what will always remain the same.A lot of my work is based on archival items, diaries, and archival films. I treat the archives not as a static graveyard of facts, but as a living archive, like the regional history of [for example] Petah Tikva, the literary and cultural weight of Beit Bialik, or the deeply personal, humanitarian legacy found in Wilfrid Israel's diaries at the Wilfrid Museum [solo exhibition there in 2025]. Meaning of art: I call art [what] works that make you think. That point to a topic, that raise questions, that wonder and investigate. If I reflect on the art world, I find a lot of apocalyptic art. I think it's more challenging to create art that offers solutions for existing situations, that marks a future that can exist. Art that dares to build a tangible, alternative future. That requires an entirely different level of rigorous intellectual and creative heavy lifting.Navon's art: I create within my own world. The loyalty to myself is very important to me. I am aware that the urge to create is inherent in me, and I cannot ever tell myself to stop. I am very true to myself, and the art I make is me; my art is part of my identity. It is a private sanctuary. I am actually the sole architect of that world, and I keep it entirely mine.By injecting my own impressions, interpretations, and contemporary artifacts into the mix, I create a dialogue [with archives]. I am giving a voice to the silent spaces between the official records. My new archive becomes a subjective, deeply human response to an objective history.www.instagram.com/tali.navon/

https://www.carlow-nationalist.ie/opinio.text: Sun, 02 Aug, 2026 - 09:53 Fr Paddy Byrne: The enduring courage and compassion of the Ulma family Stock image of two people holding hands in compassion       Fr Paddy Byrne The Ulma family showed extraordinary compassion and bravery in the direst situations I WAS greatly inspired recently by the story of the Ulma family, patrons of family life and the unborn child. In a world overshadowed by terror and brutality, the story of Józef and Wiktoria Ulma and their six young children shines as a beacon of humanity and moral clarity. Living in the quiet village of Markowa in southeastern Poland during the dark years of the Holocaust, the Ulmas epitomised the extraordinary courage of ordinary people. Risking everything, they sheltered eight Jewish neighbours in their modest home, defying the oppressive machinery of Nazi Germany. Their ultimate sacrifice - losing their lives and those of their children - stands as a profound testament to the power of empathy and faith in the face of unimaginable danger. Józef and Wiktoria Ulma were beacons of resilience, intellect and humanity. Their lives, though marked by simplicity, were extraordinary in their depth and purpose. Józef, born in 1900, was a man of immense curiosity and practical genius. He transcended his humble beginnings. His interests were vast, ranging from horticulture to photography. Wiktoria, born in 1912, was equally remarkable. Orphaned at a young age, she displayed resilience and a zest for life, attending courses at a local folk high school and engaging in cultural activities like village theatre. Together, the Ulmas created a household filled with love, learning and faith. Parents to six children and expecting a seventh, their lives revolved around nurturing not only their family but also their community. Before the second World War, Markowa was a quiet, close-knit community of about 4,500 residents, including around 120 Jews. While cultural and religious differences meant that Polish and Jewish residents lived somewhat parallel lives, relations were amicable. Jewish families in Markowa primarily engaged in trade and farming, their children attending schools alongside Polish peers. Religious gatherings often took place in nearby ÅaÅcut, at a synagogue that likely welcomed the Goldman family - the very neighbours the Ulmas would later risk everything to protect. The peaceful life of the Ulmas and their neighbours was shattered with the German invasion of Poland in 1939. For the Jewish community of Markowa, the occupation brought swift and devastating oppression. Early restrictions, such as wearing the Star of David, escalated into forced labour, deportations and mass executions. By 1942, Operation Reinhardt sought to exterminate the Jewish population in the general government area, leaving Jewish families in Markowa desperate for refuge. Markowa fell under the jurisdiction of brutal German and local collaborators. Daily life became a litany of terror: curfews, forced labour and deportations were commonplace. The Jewish residents, targeted with relentless persecution, were subjected to confiscations, ghettoisation and ultimately, extermination. The Ulmas, known for their kindness and connection to local Jewish families, did not hesitate. In December 1942, they opened their modest home to eight Jews: Saul Goldman, his four sons, two daughters and a young child. For over a year, these individuals lived hidden within the Ulmas’ home, sharing the family’s meagre resources. Such an act of defiance carried the ultimate risk; under the German Nazi decrees, anyone aiding Jews faced immediate execution, a punishment that extended to entire households. In the early hours of 24 March 1944, German gendarmes and local collaborators arrived at the Ulma home. The brutality was swift and unrelenting. The eight Jewish individuals hiding in the house were executed immediately. Józef and Wiktoria were then dragged outside and shot. As Wiktoria fell, in the throes of childbirth, the executioners made a harrowing decision: they would kill the children too. The Ulmas were guided by an unshakable faith. Their well-worn bible contained underlined passages from the parable of the Good Samaritan and the commandment to love one’s neighbour, reflecting the principles that shaped their actions. Their choice to shelter Jews was an act of profound moral courage, rooted in love and a sense of shared humanity. The family’s beatification by the Catholic Church in 2023 underscores their spiritual legacy. While their recognition as Righteous Among the Nations resonates deeply within Jewish memory, their elevation to sainthood amplifies their story on a global scale, reminding Catholics and non-Catholics alike of the universal values they represent compassion, sacrifice and unwavering moral clarity. The Ulma family’s story transcends national and religious boundaries. It is a testament to the enduring power of human dignity in the face of unspeakable evil. The Ulmas stand as symbols of resistance and humanity during one of history’s darkest chapters. Their legacy challenges us to reflect on our own capacity for courage and compassion. Today, as their names appear in museums, textbooks and prayers, the Ulmas remind the world that even in the bleakest times, ordinary people can achieve extraordinary heroism. Their story is not merely one of martyrdom but a beacon of hope. too. https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/a.text: A collapsed house in Nagekeo in Indonesia’s East Nusa Tenggara province after the 7.7 magnitude earthquake. Photograph: Ignasius Kunda/EPA View image in fullscreen A collapsed house in Nagekeo in Indonesia’s East Nusa Tenggara province after the 7.7 magnitude earthquake. Photograph: Ignasius Kunda/EPA Indonesia Rescue teams search for survivors in Indonesia after powerful earthquake Searchers dig through collapsed buildings and debris after 7.7 magnitude quake killed at least 47 people Associated Press Sat 15 Aug 2026 23.57 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Rescue crews dug through collapsed buildings and landslide debris in eastern Indonesia on Sunday as they searched for bodies and possible survivors a day after a powerful earthquake killed at least 47 people, injured more than 100 and displaced thousands. At least 24 people died in Manggarai regency and 17 in neighbouring East Manggarai, with additional fatalities reported in Sikka, Ngada and Ende regencies, the national disaster management agency said. Rescuers were still searching for people feared buried beneath landslides triggered by the quake across six regencies on Flores, a predominantly Catholic island in Muslim-majority Indonesia . Powerful earthquake kills dozens in eastern Indonesia Read more The magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck 68km (42 miles) north-northwest of Ende in East Nusa Tenggara province, the USGS said. The quake, at a depth of about 10km (6 miles) off the coast of Flores, rattled much of the island and sent residents fleeing in panic. Tremors were also felt in neighbouring West Nusa Tenggara and parts of southern Sulawesi. View image in fullscreen A crack in the road in East Nusa Tenggara after the quake. Photograph: Ignasius Kunda/EPA The disaster agency said the quake destroyed more than 900 homes and damaged nearly 450 more, forcing about 5,000 people into temporary shelters. Thousands more spent the night outdoors, fearing strong aftershocks. At least 167 public facilities, including schools, health centres and churches, were also damaged. Relief workers have begun distributing rice, ready-to-eat meals, drinking water, blankets and medicine, while emergency shelters were being set up for displaced residents. Authorities said restoring electricity and communications as well as delivering aid to remote villages isolated by landslides remained among the biggest challenges. View image in fullscreen Earthquake victims are treated in a temporary medical tent amid fears of aftershocks in Ruteng. Photograph: Juni Kriswanto/AFP/Getty Images The quake also struck Labuan Bajo, the gateway to Komodo national park, one of Indonesia’s best-known tourist destinations. Landslides blocked sections of the Trans-Flores Highway, a roughly 700km (435 mile) road linking communities across the mountainous island. Many residents continued to sleep outside rather than risk returning to damaged homes. “The shaking was terrifying, so intense that my house nearly collapsed,” said Anastasia Imad, a farmer in Labuan Bajo, speaking from a makeshift green tent beside her damaged home. “We feared the aftershocks would bring it down on us while we slept.” View image in fullscreen People in the coastal village of Nangahale in Sikka regency spent the night in a field. Photograph: Arnold Welianto/AFP/Getty Images Teams resumed searches on Sunday in areas that had remained inaccessible since the quake, particularly in Manggarai, East Manggarai and Nagekeo regencies. “We have cleared most landslides and reopened roads to previously isolated villages, although communication disruptions and power outages continue to hamper search efforts,” said Fathur Rahman, head of the search and rescue office in Maumere, the capital of Sikka regency. He said rescuers were focusing on searching the rubble of collapsed homes and other buildings for possible victims. Indonesia, an archipelago of more than 17,000 islands, is prone to earthquakes and volcanic eruptions because of its location on the Pacific “ring of fire”, a horseshoe-shaped arc of seismic faults and volcanoes. Flores has experienced some of the country’s deadliest disasters. A powerful earthquake and tsunami in 1992 killed about 2,500 people on the island. In 2018, a magnitude 7.5 earthquake triggered a tsunami on Sulawesi that killed more than 4,400 people. In 2004, a magnitude 9.1 quake off Sumatra unleashed a tsunami that killed about 230,000 people in a dozen countries. https://www.theguardian.com/money/2026/a.text: Common AI tools can accurately detect where a photo was taken more than 90% of the time. Photograph: Sean Pavone/Alamy View image in fullscreen Common AI tools can accurately detect where a photo was taken more than 90% of the time. Photograph: Sean Pavone/Alamy Scam watch Scams ‘We detected unusual activity’: the scam that uses AI to exploit your holiday photos Fraudsters use pictures posted on Instagram or Facebook to create emails seeking bank account details Shane Hickey Sun 16 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 02.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Y ou are on a short break in Porto and post some pictures of your family on Instagram or Facebook. With a small section of the Douro river in the background, you think it could have been taken anywhere. A few days later, you get a text saying that your card was compromised. “We detected unusual activity while you were travelling in Porto – please verify immediately,” says the message. You click on the link to confirm your bank details. Since you have not put any details of your trip on any of your social networks – bar the indistinct pictures – you don’t suspect there is anything suspicious about the messages. But the text was a fraud designed to extract your financial details. The criminals behind it figured out where you had been on holidays – lending credibility to their text – by using AI to analyse the image for the most sparse signs of where it was taken. View image in fullscreen Image showing how AI identifies the location where holiday pictures were taken. Photograph: McAfee Labs New research has shown that by picking up on details in the picture – such as the background, the architecture, the signage or the light – the AI agent can pinpoint where it was taken. For criminals, this information gives attempts to defraud by text message or email an added legitimacy. McAfee, the producer of anti-virus software, used two freely available AI models to test more than 21,000 travel images. One of the models identified 91% of images accurately while the other got 87%. Staff were then asked to replicate the experiment with their own pictures and became uncomfortable with how easy their travels were pinpointed. The company says that it shows that computers don’t need photos to be tagged or attached metadata to identify where they are taken. “What AI does is give context … so that makes the scam [and] makes the threats credible,” says Vonny Gamot, the head of EMEA at McAfee. What it looks like Pictures are more likely to be identified by AI if they have recognisable landmarks, skylines, signage and street markings. Food stalls and storefronts can also pinpoint quickly where the picture was taken. If the picture is taken on a beach or a hotel room, the accuracy of the AI is lowered. But McAfee reports that it is likely that the system can identify which country they were taken in – which is all the scammers need. View image in fullscreen Image showing how AI identifies the location where holiday pictures were taken. Photograph: McAfee Labs When a staff member tested ChatGPT to identify a picture of a river with some trees in the foreground, it correctly pinpointed it as Hastings-on-Hudson, an area in New York state. Another picture of a group of flowers was identified as the Keukenhof gardens in the Netherlands. The AI agent correctly deduced that the layout of the tulips, along with smaller blue flowers planted between them, meant that it was the famous gardens in the picture. Criminals can use the information to make their approaches more convincing. They might say that your card was flagged for unusual activity while you were somewhere. Or that they are calling you after your stay in a particular hotel. Or that they want to confirm your identity because there has been an attempt to log in to your account from that country. What to do If you want to post pictures, delay until after you get home and change your settings so that only the people you know can see them. As with all scams, be wary about any urgency in the messages you are sent, such as being told that you need to act immediately. Fraudsters use this as a tactic in the hope that people react without thinking something through fully. Don’t click on links that are provided in texts or emails; instead contact the company or bank through the details on their website or on the back of your bank card.
