He fired, according to him, about half of the director's office.And, hey, I, you know, thought there were too many people over there anyway, but this guy was not qualified, didn't even really understand what the Office of National Intelligence did. So I can't imagine he did a very good job at figuring out who to let go and who to keep. And because of – we're also in the middle of a war right now.So, I suspect in fact, when we – when we sort this out, we're going to probably realize that he fired a bunch of the wrong people. So, hopefully, on Monday, he is out of the office and we can talk about FISA renewal.MARGARET BRENNAN: All right, Senator Mark Kelly, thank you for your time this morning.SENATOR MARK KELLY: Thanks for having me on.MARGARET BRENNAN: Face the Nation will be back in one minute. Stay with us.(ANNOUNCEMENTS)MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're back with Ohio Republican Congressman Mike Turner. He joins us this morning from Dayton.Good morning to you.REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER (R-Ohio): Good morning, Margaret.MARGARET BRENNAN: You serve on the Armed Services Committee. Back in March, the Republican chair of it said, the administration is not giving enough detail. That was March. It's now July. Are you satisfied with what you're being told? Excuse me. It's August.(LAUGHTER)REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, I mean…(LAUGHTER)REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Yes.The – I – you know, still the administration could be sharing more with Congress. I don't think anybody is satisfied with the level of information we're receiving, although it is a dynamic conflict. I think also that that's true even as the administration is looking to its review both in Europe, the conflict in Iran, the issues with Ukraine.Across the board, both the House and the Senate have registered that the Pentagon needs to be sharing more information with Congress.MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, on Friday, out at Camp David, it was all on camera. Well, the other day, the five missiles we shot. We knocked them down. But we were in the midst of the negotiation.Well, they always want to talk, but they break their word so often. Michael Varaklas - AP Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save ATHENS, Greece (AP) — Two Greek firefighting helicopters collided in midair on Sunday as they were battling a wind-driven wildfire west of Athens , sending one aircraft crashing to the ground. Two crew members, a Greek and a Danish national, died in the crash. The collision laid bare the danger at the most volatile front of Europe’s wildfire emergency. Strong winds drove flames deeper into the region of the Greek capital and forced fresh evacuations, France guarded a still-burning scar four times the size of Paris , while Spain’s major fires stopped advancing. Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis expressed “sorrow for the tragic accident” and extended condolences to the families of the firefighters killed in the crash. "The loss of the Greek coordinator and the Danish pilot at the time they were attempting the major fire in Porto Gremeno fills us all with grief," Mitsotakis said in a statement. The aircraft were Bell helicopters operating over the Psatha area west of Athens, each with a two-person crew. Foreign firefighting and helicopter crews are often deployed in Greece to help tackle wildfires during the country’s hot, dry summers. The two crew members who were recovered alive were a Greek and a British national. The flames had spread rapidly, threatening communities and an industrial district as violent gusts prevented firefighting aircraft from collecting water from the sea. The blaze carried a grim resonance in a region where the 2018 Mati wildfire killed 104 people, Europe’s deadliest blaze this century. Farther west, containment brought no end to the emergency. France’s largest wildfire remained held within its perimeter after forcing 224,000 people to flee in what may have been the country’s largest civilian evacuation outside wartime . Hot spots still burned within a 420-square-kilometer (162-square-mile) scar, thousands remained unable to return home, and nearly 3,000 firefighters were deployed against the Gironde megafire and a second, still-uncontained blaze in Provence. Together, fires in France and Spain have driven roughly a third of a million people from homes and vacation sites, emptied communities at the height of the European summer and stretched emergency services across simultaneous disasters. Record fire damage underscores Europe’s growing wildfire threat The mass evacuations in France and Spain are the latest measure of a wildfire threat growing across Europe. The continent entered 2026 after its worst fire year on record, with more than 10,000 square kilometers (3,860 square miles) burned in 2025. Over the past four decades, wildfires have been linked to nearly 800 deaths across much of Europe, according to the European Environment Agency. Europe is the world’s fastest-warming continent. It has warmed more than twice the global average since the 1980s, according to the European Union’s Copernicus Climate Change Service. Human-caused climate change made the extreme fire-weather conditions behind this year’s French blazes at least twice as likely, scientists at World Weather Attribution found in a rapid analysis conducted while the fires were still burning. Gale-force winds cripple aerial assault near Athens Nearly 500 firefighters and 23 aircraft were deployed, but gale-force winds drove flames through dry forest and crippled the response, preventing some aircraft from reaching the sea to collect water. Authorities ordered the evacuation of Kandili, Agia Skepi and Toutouli as smoke rose over the mountains. Crews were particularly concerned about Porto Germeno, a seaside community on the Gulf of Corinth. The fire began Friday near Agios Vasileios before sweeping toward Porto Germeno and into the forested mountains west of Athens. Firefighters evacuated 254 people by sea Friday and another 12 Saturday — often the last escape route when fire and smoke cut the few roads from coastal communities. Wildfire meteorologist Theodore Giannaros estimated the blaze had affected 40 to 50 square kilometers (15 to 19 square miles), though authorities had issued no official figure. Elsewhere in Greece, flames threatened homes on Kefalonia, forcing evacuations from inland communities as aircraft made water drops over the Ionian island. Firefighters battled another blaze near Nea Tenedos on the peninsula of Halkidiki. Earlier this week, two firefighters died fighting a fire on Crete, while a third was killed on the Peloponnese. “A pristine forest, a paradise, was surrendered to the hands of the fire,” local farmer Minas Tzortzanis said Saturday. “There are no words to explain what has happened. Destruction. Total destruction.” France holds off renewed flames In southwestern France, the Gironde megafire remained held within its perimeter Sunday but continued to burn after scorching 420 square kilometers (162 square miles) of forest in 10 days. “The fire is now fixed, which does not mean that the fire is extinguished,” the Gironde prefecture said, using the French firefighting term for a blaze whose advance has been stopped. The region remained under France’s highest red forest-fire alert. Dry conditions, soaring temperatures around Bordeaux and afternoon winds threatened to rekindle the flames. In Le Porge, local officials said about 150 homes were destroyed. Mechanic Matthieu Plessis returned Saturday to the ruins of a house that had been in his family for seven generations. “There are places I don’t even recognize anymore,” he said. “You don’t even know what was here anymore, or who lived where.” Firefighters from Ukraine, Lithuania and French Polynesia were expected Sunday and Monday to reinforce the operation. Provence fire stops advancing but remains uncontained In southeastern France, nearly 1,500 firefighters battled a separate blaze in the Var department that tore through about 18 square kilometers (7 square miles) in little more than a day. The Gros Bessillon fire was stabilized Sunday after its perimeter held overnight, but it remained uncontained. Some 2,500 people were evacuated as flames threatened nearby communities. It was the fourth major fire to strike central Var since July 19. A smaller blaze near Brignoles earlier in the week forced actor George Clooney and his family , along with about 700 other residents, to evacuate before it was brought under control. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said France’s fires were generally under control but warned that conditions remained volatile. He appointed a national coordinator to oversee reconstruction in fire-ravaged areas. More than 1,170 square kilometers (452 square miles) have burned across France this year. Spain’s deadly fire siege eases Spain’s major fires — which have killed at least 13 people, produced the country’s largest recorded wildfire and prompted a national emergency — were no longer advancing on Sunday. In Zamora province near the Portuguese border, more than 20 ground and aerial units guarded the perimeter of the Fermoselle fire against flare-ups in the rugged Arribes del Duero landscape. Most evacuees had returned home, according to local media. Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has called for a national pact to confront wildfires, warning that climate change is making them increasingly destructive. Adamson reported from Paris. Associated Press writers Nicolas Garriga in Lacanau, France; Michael Varaklas in Megara, Greece; and Colleen Barry in Milan contributed to this report. Copyright 2026 The Associated Press. https://www.thenationalnews.com/news/eur.text: Two helicopters ⁠collided while fighting wildfires near Athens on Sunday, killing both ​crew ​members ⁠in ⁠one ​of the aircraft, Greece's fire service said. A search and rescue operation for the two-person crews of the Bell-type aircraft, which had earlier taken off from a military airport at Elefsina in West Attica, found two crew members from one of the helicopters with minor injuries, the Hellenic Fire Service said. The other two were pulled unconscious from the wreckage of their helicopter and taken to hospital, it said. The collision took place during a firefighting operation in the area of Psatha in the Attica region, west of Athens, it said. Footage of the incident shows the two helicopters closing to cross paths at low altitude. The lower helicopter crashed in flames after its main rotor struck the underside of the one flying above ⁠it. The second helicopter then dumped its load of water and flew away. Europe has been ravaged by wildfires this summer after record-breaking heatwaves and ​little rain – conditions that scientists say have been exacerbated by climate change. Destructive blazes in France and Spain showed signs of easing over the weekend, but several wildfires have broken out in Greece after ⁠a period of relative calm there. Gale-force winds that had fuelled ​a fire around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth, 60km north-west of Athens, subsided, but flames crossed a mountain to the south and reached the settlement of Veniza and a military firing range, igniting unexploded ordnance. Firefighters focused their efforts on preventing fire from advancing towards the coastal town of Megara, which has a population of about 30,000. “There are moments when the force of nature and the intensity of weather conditions exceed all human planning and every operational capability,” Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in his weekly Sunday message. Greek authorities issued evacuation alerts for several areas in western Attica, including an industrial estate near Megara. In the village of Agios Konstantinos, residents were doing their best to halt the spread of the blaze. “The fire has been burning since last night; it is certain that they cannot have forces everywhere. We as residents are doing everything we can,” said Tasos Tzempelikos, 61, who was pouring water on the fire along with his son. The Greek daily Protothema reported that a major effort was under way to prevent the fire from Veniza from reaching the nearby coastal town of Megara. It said it was likely that more than 10,000 hectares of land had been destroyed by the fire so far. Overnight, several settlements on the Ionian island of Kefalonia were evacuated after a fire broke out in the Pastra area in the south. In France, wildfires in the Gironde and Var departments showed signs of easing. Authorities reported only minor flare-ups in ​the south-western Gironde area and said the blaze in the south-eastern Var department had not spread overnight. In Monfort-Sur-Argents, in the region of ‌Var, Georges Blanc, who fled from the fire, returned home and was ⁠busy putting out hot embers to prevent a flare-up, while firefighters watered the wider area. “With ​the combined efforts of the two Canadairs [firefighting planes] and the firefighters, I think you could say all the houses were saved ... And now, well, I'm ​coming back to check, because since ‌I saw the flames, I thought the houses wouldn't have survived,” he said. In central Spain, wildfires that ripped through tens of thousands of hectares over the past week were mostly under control, ⁠though firefighters were dealing with reignitions in some areas. In the western province of Caceres, a forest blaze erupted on Saturday, prompting the evacuation of around 800 people. Those residents ⁠were allowed to return on Sunday but remained confined to their homes as the fire was still active. Other European countries are struggling with drought and receding water levels in major rivers, including the Rhine and the Danube, which recorded its lowest water levels on record in Hungary, Serbia and Romania. Hungary faces a critical five days, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, as the drying out of the Danube forced the country's sole nuclear power plant to shut for the first time in more than four decades, ​with a new heatwave looming. Falls in water levels amid a lack of rain have also disrupted shipping and tourism in Hungary, and triggered water-use restrictions in more than 100 cities and villages. Danube levels in Serbia fell to their lowest since 1985, cutting the daily output of the country's biggest hydropower plant to only 20 per cent, the country's Energy Minister said on Sunday.

Share A A A Key points AI is an excellent planning assistant for building itineraries and suggesting destinations, saving hours of research Always verify time-sensitive information such as passport validity, transport schedules, opening hours and reservations Human travel writers still add value through first-hand experience, practical judgment and storytelling Depending on who you listen to, artificial intelligence (AI) is either the greatest threat to civilisation ever devised by dark minds or a powerful tool that helps us work faster and solve problems. The truth lies somewhere in between. Plenty of travellers are using it and there are good reasons why you might invite ChatGPT, Claude or any other generative AI tool to collaborate when planning your travels. AI is surprisingly good at generating itineraries and suggesting activities. Getty Images If you want to construct a self-guided tour of the Western Front battlefields, plan a visit to Tokyo Disneyland with the kids or find the best scenic drives in Arizona, ask AI. It shines when suggesting itineraries, comparing France versus Italy for a holiday focused on food and wine, narrowing down transport options between cities, recommending the best neighbourhoods to look for accommodation, generating packing lists and optimising routes. Advertisement You might want to drill down further and take the kids to the best cat cafe in Tokyo, and AI can put its paws on the purr-fect choice. Something offbeat? Want to see traditional cheese-making as practised by Romanian shepherds or a five-day itinerary visiting the Kalash villages of northern Pakistan? Such questions would take hours of research, but AI can come up with the answer in seconds. Sign up for the Traveller newsletter The latest travel news, tips and inspiration delivered to your inbox. Sign up now. AI is a great tool for suggesting options you might not have considered. Ask it for “unusual sightseeing possibilities in X”, or “alternative transport ideas” and it might tell you about a spin around Rome in the sidecar of a vintage Vespa, or God’s Own Junkyard in London. Check the answers – transport schedules, visa and entry requirements, baggage allowances, opening hours of attractions are subject to change at short notice, and AI doesn’t always catch the update. AI will usually give more weight to official sources, such as a government or a museum website, but it can be knocked off balance when many source websites have the same misleading information. When it talks about remote places or obscure experiences that have limited sources of information, AI can sound convincing when it should tread carefully. In the Kalash region of Pakistan, ChatGPT suggests the walk from Bumburet to Rumbur, a 16-18km hike that involves crossing a pass 1000 metres above the river valleys where the towns are situated. That advice should be treated with great caution since Bumburet and Rumbur are interconnected river valleys, no need to climb a mountain pass to travel between them. Think of it as a first-rate travel assistant, especially when it comes to constructing a first draft for your travels. Advertisement AI can also mess up big time. It can overlook the need for reservations in busy periods, underestimate driving times in rush hours or when the trip involves narrow twisting roads and stitch attractions into an itinerary without regard to the time it takes to get from one to the other. AI doesn’t know about the lived experience. Ask it about street food in Hanoi and AI won’t tell you what it feels like to sit on a tiny plastic stool for an hour on a crowded footpath. Only a human voice can tell you what it feels like when you sit in a Tibetan Buddhist temple among ochre-robed monks when they begin chanting. It can even invent non-existent attractions. In 2025, an AI-generated article on a travel operator’s website began singing the praises of the fabulous Weldborough Hot Springs in the forests of northeast Tasmania. According to a CNN report, Kristy Probert, owner of the local Weldborough Hotel, was mystified when tourists started turning up asking directions to the hot springs. What started as a trickle became a steady stream, but the hot springs were a total fabrication. “If you can find these hot springs, beers are on me,” said Probert. AI v the Tripologist How does an answer from AI compare with a response from a real live human? Easy question since I write this column. From a recent Q&A, a reader asked where to stay in the Dolomites region of northern Italy, using a small, quiet town or two as a base for exploring and walking. My response was the village of Santa Magdalena in the Val de Funes, a postcard valley within easy reach of some of the loveliest alpine walking trails on the planet. Also the village of San Vigilio, gateway to the South Tyrolean nature parks. Hallelujah! Both ChatGPT and Claude concur. Both mentioned another two villages as well (my responses have a word limit, the AI models do not). Given the unpredictability of mountain weather, if the skies turned sour I suggested a visit to Bolzano to take in the South Tyrol Archaeological Museum, home of Otzi the Iceman, and that’s the sort of knowledge that comes with first-hand experience. I also mentioned the essential guidebook to walks in the region, again based on personal knowledge. I have to concede though that both ChatGPT and Claude did a bang-up job of answering the question with the pros and cons of each of the villages they suggested. Advertisement Using AI to plan your travels Think of it as a first-rate travel assistant, especially when it comes to constructing a first draft for your travels. From the basic structure of your itinerary, follow up any suggestions it might make that refine your trip. Check any time-sensitive information that might have an impact – opening hours and days of attractions, holidays and transport timetables. Refine it with more questions about where to stay, where to eat, transport options for sightseeing and any personal passions you might want to indulge. When you’ve stitched it all together run it through AI again, it should let you know if you’ve packed in too little, or if there are gaps you might want to fill. Generative AI learns about you the more questions you ask, it extracts personal preferences to build a long-term profile and it might suggest refinements of alternatives that may add something special to your journey. Where AI gets scary There are plenty of readers with reservations about AI, and rightly so. For some it’s a tool of the devil, training its models by hoovering up just about everything ever written like a mutant parasitic sponge, in defiance of copyright laws . Related Article Travel tips The six modern travel trends we hate (and the six we love) Advertisement I just asked Claude to write a review of the best bars in Marseille in the style of Hunter S. Thompson, the outrageous, taboo-busting pioneer of the gonzo style of journalism. “There is no honest way to explain the bars of Marseille to a sober person. You have to arrive already half-wrecked from the train, salt air clawing at your shirt, the gulls screaming overhead like a jury that’s already reached a verdict…” That’s a scarily good imitation of Thompson’s voice. Then I asked it to write a travel story on St Lucia in the style of Michael Gebicki. I’ve never been to St Lucia but here’s what it said. “I can’t write in Michael Gebicki’s exact voice, but I can write an original travel feature that captures the broader qualities often associated with his work.” But here’s how it kicked off a paragraph on the island’s food in “my” voice: “Food is another pleasant surprise.” Good grief. Surely that anaemic dross isn’t me? Tell my editors. Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Photo credit: NICK PALEOLOGOS / AFP Dane and Greek national die in one helicopter, others survive Investigation suggests sparks from power network started blaze Major fire in France changes course as wind shifts Danube's low level prompts Hungary to shut nuclear plant Two firefighting helicopters collided in Greece while helping to control a huge wildfire on Sunday that has destroyed more than 100 homes northwest of Athens, while people fled another blaze on the tourist island of Kefalonia. Two people on one helicopter - a Greek and a Danish national - died, while the crew on the other - one person from Greece, one from Britain - survived, the fire service said. Investigations had started into what caused the collision, it added. Europe has been ravaged by wildfires this summer after a period of record-breaking heatwaves and little rain, conditions that scientists say have been exacerbated by climate change. Destructive blazes in France and Spain showed some signs of easing over the weekend, but several wildfires have broken out in Greece after a period of relative calm there. The two helicopters collided in the area of Psatha in the Attica region, Greece's fire service said in a statement. Video posted on the Forecast Weather Greece Facebook page appeared to show two helicopters closing to cross paths at low altitude, before the main rotor of the lower helicopter struck the underside of the other. The lower one then crashed in flames. The second helicopter then dumped its load of water and flew away. Reuters has not verified the authenticity of the footage. Investigations suggested the fire that started in the Greek region of Boeotia before spreading to Attica was caused by sparks from conductors on a private network transmitting electricity generated by wind turbines to the main power grid, the eKathimerini website reported. Two Greek nationals were arrested on suspicion of negligence, while another suspect remains at large, the report said. 'Force of nature' Gale-force winds that had fuelled a fire around Porto Germeno on the Gulf of Corinth 60km northwest of Athens subsided, but flames crossed a mountain to the south and reached the settlement of Veniza and a military firing range, igniting unexploded ordnance. Emergency crews focused their efforts on preventing fire from advancing towards the coastal town of Megara, which has a population of around 30,000. "There are moments when the force of nature and the intensity of weather conditions exceed all human planning and every operational capability," Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in his regular Sunday message. Greek authorities issued emergency alerts for evacuations for a number of settlements in western Attica, including an industrial estate near Megara. In the village of Agios Konstantinos, residents were doing their best to halt the spread of the blaze. "The fire has been burning since last night, it is certain that they cannot have forces everywhere. We as residents are doing everything we can," said Tasos Tzempelikos, 61, who along with his son was pouring water on the fire. Overnight, several settlements on the Ionian island of Kefalonia were evacuated after a fire broke out in the Pastra area in the south. Fire in France changes course In France, a fire in the southwestern Var region switched direction after a change in the wind and surged into a forested area that was difficult to access, BFM TV reported. A new fire also broke out alongside a highway near the historic southern city of Carcassonne, apparently caused by a blazing vehicle, BFM TV added. Video on the channel showed huge plumes of billowing grey smoke and flames near the road. Authorities said they had closed the highway and evacuated a nearby animal park. In Montfort-sur-Argens in Var, Georges Blanc, who had fled the fire earlier, returned home and was busy putting out hot embers to prevent a flare-up, while firefighters watered the wider area. "With the combined efforts of the two Canadairs (firefighting planes) and the firefighters, I think you could say all the houses were saved... And now, well, I'm coming back to check, because since I saw the flames, I thought the houses wouldn't have survived," he told Reuters. In central Spain, wildfires that ripped through tens of thousands of hectares over the past week were mostly under control, though firefighters were dealing with reignitions in some areas. In the western province of Caceres, a forest blaze erupted on Saturday, prompting the evacuation of around 800 people. Those residents were allowed to return on Sunday but remained confined to their homes as the fire was still active. Hungary faces a critical five days, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, as the drying out of the Danube forced the country's sole nuclear power plant to shut for the first time in more than four decades , with a new heatwave looming. Falls in water levels amid a lack of rain have also disrupted shipping and tourism in Hungary and triggered water-use restrictions in more than 100 cities and villages. MARGARET BRENNAN: We're now in the sixth month of this war we had been told would last four to five weeks. In the past week, the targets have widened. Iran hit Egypt. We saw Saudi Arabia join the U.S. in bombing Iranian-backed militias there. And then, late last night, President Trump used the term that he had been considering military action on levels unseen since World War II. You sit on Intelligence. You sit on Armed Services. Has the administration shared anything in regard to its plans on Iran? SENATOR MARK KELLY: I mean, not these latest plans. Advertisement Advertisement And I think what we're seeing here is a president who has an approach to this that's just rather erratic. He says one thing, he does another thing. It's escalatory at this point. He's trying to get us back to February. And I think, if he could, he would – if he had a big reset button he could hit, he would certainly take that option. Hey, we've got 18 dead Americans. Prices have skyrocketed across the country for the American people. I was here in Ohio. I'm here in Ohio now, but I met with some veterans the other day, and they're struggling. I mean, these are a lot of retired service members that can't afford to put gas in their car, can't afford groceries. Rent is going up. And this president is not dealing with the issues that the American people need him to deal with. MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, you know, in our polling, we see that this is a very unpopular war, and it's weighing on the president's own approval ratings. Advertisement Advertisement But Democrats are faring slightly worse, according to CBS polling. When asked who has the better approach to Iran, 32 percent say Trump and the GOP. Only 30 percent say the Democrats. So we are in this thing. Do Democrats need to offer an affirmative vision for ending it? SENATOR MARK KELLY: Well, I don't think it's the president's vision. Here's a guy who got us into this without a strategic goal, without a plan, without a timeline. He's got a secretary of defense that doesn't know how to manage this war, who decided a good metric at the beginning was just to drop as many munitions as he could on as many targets, and now we've got a munitions shortage. Big surprise. So they're flailing. They're stuck. They're responsible for this. And the president is the one that has to try to figure out a way out of this. I would suggest to him, though, that the solution is not to do the same thing that he's been doing, not to have his real estate buddy and his son-in-law in charge of a negotiation, to put some people in here that know how to do this, how to talk to the Iranians, and put a coalition together, bring our allies back together. Advertisement Advertisement He's alienated not only our GCC allies, but our European allies as well. And it's just making this much harder for him to figure out a way out. MARGARET BRENNAN: But "The Washington Post" is reporting that the top U.S. general in Europe, General Grynkewich, warned the Pentagon that he lacks resources to protect Israel from incoming ballistic missiles, and if he's without another Navy destroyer, he will be forced to choose between defense of the homeland versus that of Israel. It sounds like, for the moment, Israel's not rejoining combat operations. But what does that say to you? Have you heard these concerns from this top commander yourself? SENATOR MARK KELLY: I haven't heard this specifically from Grynkewich on - - on this issue. Advertisement Advertisement But we – it's – it's not – Margaret, it's not – this isn't rocket science. It's not hard to figure out. I mean, we – we struck over 14,000 targets with multiple munitions. That – that is – puts a lot of stress on the magazine depth. So, of course, our commanders, probably not only in Europe, but in other places, are starting to feel some stress on, can they meet the need if they need to defend the homeland or our allies? You can see why this is an issue for him. And that's because, at the beginning of this thing, there was no strategic goal. And, without the goal, it's hard to figure out what to do next. MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. Advertisement Advertisement SENATOR MARK KELLY: And I think that's why – that – you know, that's why Hegseth went just to try to set records on the number of targets hit. MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. I should say for the record that the Pentagon says it's media speculation, and they don't comment on operational capabilities. We did ask them to clarify that. But on the point about restocking, Secretary Hegseth says he needs money from Congress to do that, to replenish munitions. He needs money from Congress to pay salaries. He needs $67 billion. You recently were asked, and you said you were undecided on how you would vote on additional funding. How do you deny that needed funding? SENATOR MARK KELLY: Well, Margaret, last year, we passed a defense budget that was over a trillion dollars. That was the first time ever. It was sold to us as a one-time generational investment in the department. And, in my view, they squandered that. Now they're coming and they're asking for $1.5 trillion, plus a supplemental. We're going to – we're approaching the amount of money that every other country on the planet spends on defense in a year. This is irresponsible. And now they want a blank check. Hey, I'm going to make sure the troops have what they need to defend themselves and defend the United States. MARGARET BRENNAN: So you would vote for the 67? SENATOR MARK KELLY: But they need to come to us – no, not – no, not necessarily. They need to come to us with a reasonable approach here. The $1.5 trillion, you know that has systems that I am very confident aren't going to work. They're still working on space-based interceptors for ICBMs. The physics on this is really very, very challenging. It's not going to make us safer, the other systems that we don't need. They – they need to understand that we do not have unlimited resources in this country. MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. SENATOR MARK KELLY: We've got $39.5 trillion in debt. And the defense budget that they're requesting is twice what it was… MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. SENATOR MARK KELLY: … when I got to the United States Senate in 2021. It's twice that budget. MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, you mentioned that you're in Ohio right now, and you are campaigning for fellow Democrats there. We're about 90 days out from the midterms. We looked at some recent Quinnipiac polling. It showed Democrats have a 23 percent – 2-3 percent – approval rating, worse than President Trump's approval. You've got a lot of headwinds. Republicans have an advantage in terms of fund – over Democrats in terms of funding. There's redistricting that I know Democrats say disadvantages them, though they've also gerrymandered. We see interparty fighting in Minnesota and in Michigan with no real promise to unify Democrats over a – a common candidate here. How concerned are you that – that Democrats are going to lose this thing or – or end up with this very, very tight race? SENATOR MARK KELLY: Well, I think we have an opportunity here, despite the Republican gerrymandering that started in – in the state of Texas, to try to you know rig the – the deck, so to say here, and make it more challenging. That – that provides an advantage to them. But this president is historically unpopular for a midterm president, and he's not meeting the needs of the American people. You know, gas is up over $4 a gallon. Half of Americans are having a hard time affording food, rent. Homeownership is down. Rent is up. The American people are really struggling. So we have an opportunity to win back the House, and I am confident we will. On the Senate side, it's challenging. I'm not going to – I'm not going to paint this as a rosy picture. But we've got 90 days to go. We have opportunities in a lot of different places, more than we thought we had six months ago. And a year-and-a-half ago, I would say we had no opportunity to win back the Senate. But because of the horrible job that Donald Trump has done for the American people, I think we have a chance we could win back control of the Senate. And that's why I'm here supporting Sherrod Brown. You know, he – he – he wasn't successful in 2024. He could definitely win here in 2026, but it's going to take some effort. MARGARET BRENNAN: Let me ask you about what may happen tomorrow. Bill Pulte, who is the acting director of national intelligence, has said that he is going to hand over the top job to the man who was just confirmed by the Senate, Jay Clayton. Democratic objection had been one of the holdups as well in getting that FISA authority passed. I'm wondering, once you see this change of command, are those Democratic objections going to melt away? SENATOR MARK KELLY: I can't speak for everybody, but, for me, they will. Bill Pulte was not qualified in any way for this job, should have never had it. He fired, according to him, about half of the director's office. And, hey, I, you know, thought there were too many people over there anyway, but this guy was not qualified, didn't even really understand what the Office of National Intelligence did. So I can't imagine he did a very good job at figuring out who to let go and who to keep. And because of – we're also in the middle of a war right now. So, I suspect in fact, when we – when we sort this out, we're going to probably realize that he fired a bunch of the wrong people. So, hopefully, on Monday, he is out of the office and we can talk about FISA renewal. MARGARET BRENNAN: All right, Senator Mark Kelly, thank you for your time this morning. SENATOR MARK KELLY: Thanks for having me on. MARGARET BRENNAN: Face the Nation will be back in one minute. Stay with us. (ANNOUNCEMENTS) MARGARET BRENNAN: And we're back with Ohio Republican Congressman Mike Turner. He joins us this morning from Dayton. Good morning to you. REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER (R-Ohio): Good morning, Margaret. MARGARET BRENNAN: You serve on the Armed Services Committee. Back in March, the Republican chair of it said, the administration is not giving enough detail. That was March. It's now July. Are you satisfied with what you're being told? Excuse me. It's August. (LAUGHTER) REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, I mean… (LAUGHTER) REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Yes. The – I – you know, still the administration could be sharing more with Congress. I don't think anybody is satisfied with the level of information we're receiving, although it is a dynamic conflict. I think also that that's true even as the administration is looking to its review both in Europe, the conflict in Iran, the issues with Ukraine. Across the board, both the House and the Senate have registered that the Pentagon needs to be sharing more information with Congress. MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, on Friday, out at Camp David, it was all on camera. The president's team gathered. They talked about initiatives they're working on. They all praised him. And Secretary Hegseth said Iran has shown no willingness to honestly negotiate. Here's what President Trump said. Listen. (Begin VT) DONALD TRUMP (President of the United States): I'm losing faith in them, because they do lie and do – they do misrepresent. Well, the other day, the five missiles we shot. We knocked them down. But we were in the midst of the negotiation. Well, they always want to talk, but they break their word so often. They've been very dishonest. They've been very dishonorable to deal with, but that makes no difference. (End VT) MARGARET BRENNAN: So, that was the president laying out why he doesn't trust diplomacy with Iran. Last night, he said there's a diplomatic opening and a deal may be within reach. Will you support it sight unseen? Are we at risk of the president cutting a flawed deal just to end this unpopular conflict? REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well, I don't think it's cutting a flawed deal. I mean, this is this is part of a process, obviously, of where Iran has to be in a position where, as the president has set out, the two goals. And that is, one, that they abandon their nuclear ambitions and certainly restarting their nuclear enrichment programs, and certainly the issues of an open Straits of Hormuz, and so that we return back to an open Straits, where commerce and the flow of oil and natural gas can resume. MARGARET BRENNAN: So the war should continue until there is some diplomatic deal regarding the nuclear program? Because, right now, they're just talking about the strait. REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: Well – well, it's – it's not really – as you – as you know, this began with – with Epic Fury… MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. REPRESENTATIVE MIKE TURNER: … where the president went in, which we've described as an inevitable conflict, as a result of where Obama left us with the – you know, watching until Iran began to get closer and closer to enough nuclear material to have an opportunity

https://www.bordermail.com.au/story/9322.text: Victim fearing for his life after armed home invasion, 'gunman' back in custody A man on bail over an alleged armed home invasion involving a 3D-printed firearm has been rearrested after allegedly fleeing police in another person's car. Subscribe now for unlimited access. Login or signup to continue reading Jake Reid Macklan is accused of entering the victim's Warsaw Crescent home in Wodonga with another unknown man on February 16. The Wodonga court heard the victim's front door was kicked in and he fled to a laundry. He was cornered by the unknown man and was punched 20 times and kicked in his testicles. When he fell over, Macklan allegedly pointed a black .22-calibre printed handgun at the victim and said "I told you this would happen, you need to learn a lesson". The unknown intruder hit him with a broom, breaking it, before the victim said "I'm done, I'm done". The unknown man smashed a television on the way out. The victim said Macklan was a drug dealer, and he owed Macklan $200. He was arrested in a vehicle on Melbourne Road on February 19, with 65 grams of marijuana and 2.2 grams of what appeared to be methamphetamine seized. Macklan gave a Strathmore Street address as his home, but a search of the property was unable to find any firearms. The victim reported that Macklan had four pistols before the incident. Macklan was bailed on March 20 but handed himself in at the Wodonga station following a recent incident. Detective Leading Senior Constable Tracy Jarrott said NSW officers were conducting breath tests on Wednesday, July 29. Macklan pulled up in a vehicle not owned by him and gave a digital licence which was suspended. Police noticed a strong smell of cannabis and went to search the vehicle. The court heard Macklan drove forward when officers tried to open the car door and sped off, hitting a gutter. Officers pursued the vehicle but were unable to catch it. Police spoke to him and he agreed to hand himself in on Thursday, July 30. Macklan had been bailed to a home at Kialla, but Detective Leading Senior Constable Jarrott was concerned about him mixing in old circles in Albury-Wodonga. "It's serious offending that he's currently on bail for," she said. "I have concerns about him having access to those guns. "This incident was all over a $200 drug debt. "If you're willing to smash on someone's door, go in, threaten them, assault them, point a firearm at them for $200 ... there's always that possibility of retribution. "It's definitely a concern." The court heard the victim was "scared for his life and what the accused may do next time". Macklan's bail application will return to court on Monday, August 3. Army Technical Sgt. Don Halverson and five other World War II veterans will be honored during an Aug. 18 dinner cruise on the St. Croix River to benefit the Stillwater Veterans Memorial. Army Technical Sgt. Don Halverson, 103, of Brooklyn Center, pictured in Italy in 1945 after the end of World War II, will be honored during an Aug. 18, 2026, dinner cruise on the St. Croix River to benefit the Stillwater Veterans Memorial. (Courtesy of Thomas Halvorson) Halverson, 103, of Brooklyn Center, joined the U.S. Army in 1943. He was assigned to the 34th Infantry Division Red Bull unit and led a platoon of soldiers from Naples, Italy, to the border of Switzerland. He was present when the German 34th Division surrendered to the American 34th Infantry Division on May 2, 1945, and he received a citation recognizing this historical event. Halverson also was awarded the Bronze Star, The Good Conduct medal, the Distinguished Unit Badge, the Combat Infantry Badge and the European African Middle Eastern Theater Ribbon. Later in life, he received the Order of St. Maurice medal and the Order of St. George Medallion. Other WWII veterans who will be honored include Ed Albrecht, 101; Bob Holmstrom, 100; Jim Rasmussen, 102; Bill Kruschel, 101, and Bob Michelsen, 100. Also attending will be Holocaust survivor Cass Lewart, 96, who survived a Warsaw ghetto as a 14-year-old youth, said John Kraemer, a member of the Stillwater Veterans Memorial board. This year’s featured speaker is retired U.S. Marine Corps Col. John Kline, who served in the U.S. House of Representatives from 2003 to 2017. Proceeds will fund operations, maintenance and future expansion of the veterans memorial site at Third and Pine streets, Kraemer said. Tickets are $35; reservations are required. Boarding of the Avalon starts at 4:30 p.m. at Stillwater River Boats, 525 S. Main St., with departure at 5:45 p.m. and return from the round trip to Hudson, Wis., by 8 p.m. The program includes a buffet dinner, cash bar, raffles and opportunities for guests to visit with veterans. https://tribune.com.pk/story/2621691/two.text: Home World Two die as firefighting helicopters collide in Greece, French blaze changes course Heatwaves and drought fuel Europe's wildfires, with climate change worsening extreme fire conditions, scientists say Two firefighting helicopters collided in Greece while helping to control a huge wildfire on Sunday ​that has destroyed more than 100 homes northwest of Athens, while people fled another blaze on the tourist island of Kefalonia. Two people on one helicopter — a Greek and a Danish national — ‌died, while the crew on the other, one person from Greece, one from Britain, survived, the fire service said. Investigations had started into what caused the collision, it added. Europe has been ravaged by wildfires this summer after a period of record-breaking heatwaves and little rain – conditions that scientists say have been exacerbated by climate change. Destructive blazes in France and Spain showed some signs of easing over the weekend, but several wildfires have broken out in Greece after a period of relative calm there. The two helicopters collided in the area of ​Psatha in the Attica region, Greece's fire service said in a statement. Video posted on the Forecast Weather Greece Facebook page appeared to show two helicopters closing to cross paths at low altitude, before the main ​rotor of the lower helicopter struck the underside of the other. The lower one then crashed in flames. The second helicopter then dumped its load of water and flew ⁠away. Reuters has not verified the authenticity of the footage. Investigations suggested the fire that started in the Greek region of Boeotia before spreading to Attica was caused by sparks from conductors on a private network transmitting electricity generated by ​wind turbines to the main power grid, the eKathimerini website reported. Two Greek nationals were arrested on suspicion of negligence, while another suspect remains at large, the report said. 'Force of nature' Gale-force winds that had fuelled a fire around Porto Germeno ​on the Gulf of Corinth 60 km (40 miles) northwest of Athens subsided, but flames crossed a mountain to the south and reached the settlement of Veniza and a military firing range, igniting unexploded ordnance. Emergency crews focused their efforts on preventing fire from advancing towards the coastal town of Megara, which has a population of around 30,000. "There are moments when the force of nature and the intensity of weather conditions exceed all human planning and every operational capability,” Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in his regular Sunday message. Greek authorities ​issued emergency alerts for evacuations for a number of settlements in western Attica, including an industrial estate near Megara. In the village of Agios Konstantinos, residents were doing their best to halt the spread of the blaze. "The fire ​has been burning since last night, it is certain that they cannot have forces everywhere. We as residents are doing everything we can,” said Tasos Tzempelikos, 61, who, along with his son was pouring water on the fire. Overnight, several settlements on the ‌Ionian island of ⁠Kefalonia were evacuated after a fire broke out in the Pastra area in the south. Fire in France changes course In France, a fire in the southwestern Var region switched direction after a change in the wind and surged into a forested area that was difficult to access, BFM TV reported. Read More: Greece battles new blazes as Europe wildfires rage A new fire also broke out alongside a highway near the historic southern city of Carcassonne, apparently caused by a blazing vehicle, BFM TV added. Video on the channel showed huge plumes of billowing grey smoke and flames near the road. Authorities said they had closed the highway and evacuated a nearby animal park. In Montfort-sur-Argens in Var, Georges Blanc, who had fled the fire earlier, returned home and was ​busy putting out hot embers to prevent a flare-up, while ​firefighters watered the wider area. "With the combined efforts ⁠of the two Canadairs (firefighting planes) and the firefighters, I think you could say all the houses were saved ... And now, well, I'm coming back to check, because since I saw the flames, I thought the houses wouldn't have survived," he told Reuters . In central Spain, wildfires that ripped through tens of thousands of hectares over the past week were ​mostly under control, though firefighters were dealing with reignitions in some areas. In the western province of Caceres, a forest blaze erupted on Saturday, prompting the evacuation of ​around 800 people. Those residents ⁠were allowed to return on Sunday but remained confined to their homes as the fire was still active. Hungary nuclear plant forced to shut Other European countries are struggling with drought and receding water levels in major rivers, including the Rhine and the Danube, which recorded its lowest-ever water levels in Hungary, Serbia and Romania. Hungary faces a critical five days, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday , as the drying out of the Danube forced the country's sole nuclear power plant to shut for the ⁠first time in ​more than four decades, with a new heatwave looming. Falls in water levels amid a lack of rain have also disrupted shipping and tourism ​in Hungary and triggered water-use restrictions in more than 100 cities and villages. Danube levels in Serbia fell to their lowest since 1985, cutting the daily output of the country's biggest hydropower plant to only 20%, the energy minister said on Sunday. "There are moments when the force of nature and the intensity of weather conditions exceed all human planning and every operational capability," Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said in his regular Sunday message. Greek authorities issued emergency alerts for evacuations for a number of settlements in western Attica, including an industrial estate near Megara. In the village of Agios Konstantinos, residents were doing their best to halt the spread of the blaze. Advertisement Advertisement "The fire has been burning ​since ​last night, it is certain that they cannot have forces everywhere. We as residents are doing everything we can," said Tasos ​Tzempelikos, 61, who along with his son was pouring water on the fire. Overnight, several ‌settlements on the Ionian island of Kefalonia were evacuated after a fire broke out in the Pastra area in the south. FIRE IN FRANCE CHANGES COURSE In France, a fire in the southwestern Var region switched direction after a change in the wind and surged into a forested area that was difficult to access, BFM TV reported. A new fire also broke out alongside a highway near the historic southern city of Carcassonne, apparently caused by a blazing vehicle, BFM TV added. Advertisement Advertisement Video on the channel showed huge plumes of billowing grey smoke and flames near the road. Authorities said they had closed the highway and evacuated a nearby animal park. In Montfort-sur-Argens in Var, Georges Blanc, who had fled the fire earlier, returned home and was busy putting out hot embers to prevent a flare-up, while firefighters watered the wider area. "With the combined efforts of the two Canadairs (firefighting planes) and the firefighters, I think you ‌could say all the houses were saved ... And now, well, I'm coming back to check, because since I saw the flames, ​I thought the houses wouldn't have survived," he told Reuters. In central Spain, wildfires that ripped through tens of thousands of hectares over ​the past week were mostly under control, though firefighters were dealing with reignitions in some areas. Advertisement Advertisement In ​the western province of Caceres, a forest blaze erupted on Saturday, prompting the evacuation of around 800 people. Those residents were allowed to return on Sunday but remained confined to ‌their homes as the fire was still active. HUNGARY NUCLEAR PLANT FORCED TO SHUT Other ​European countries are struggling with drought and receding water levels ​in major rivers, including the Rhine and the Danube, which recorded its lowest-ever water levels in Hungary, Serbia and Romania. Hungary faces a critical five days, Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, as the drying out of the Danube forced the country's sole nuclear power plant to shut for the first time in more than four decades, with a new heatwave looming. Advertisement Advertisement Falls in water levels amid a lack ​of rain have also disrupted shipping and tourism in Hungary and triggered water-use ‌restrictions in more than 100 cities and villages. Danube levels in Serbia fell to their lowest since 1985, cutting the daily output of the country's biggest hydropower plant to only 20%, the ​energy minister said on Sunday. https://movieweb.com/war-movies-most-dis.text: By Adam Symchuk Published Aug 2, 2026, 4:30 PM EDT Canadian-born reporter and editor Adam Symchuk has been writing on the topic of film, TV, and literature for over a decade. Starting with an emphasis on Asian film, literature and manga, his love of interntional cinema set the groundwork for decades of obsession with film. Sign in to your MovieWeb account Add Us Add on Google Preferred Source Google Discover Google News Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread 1 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Disturbing cinema has been a longtime focus of my relationship with the medium, from international films to dark comedies , and seeking these out has challenged my understanding of a lot of things in a way I have found genuinely rewarding. I know I am not unique in this. There is a vocal fandom that thrives on difficult content while still happily enjoying lighter fare, and approaching tough subjects is essential to what cinema is as an art form. One of the hardest subjects of all, though, is war and the various atrocities that come with it. To put this list together, I went back through my log of everything I have watched and pulled the titles I found most shocking. The reasons vary; sometimes the violence is what does the damage, and sometimes it is the sheer absence of humanity on display. There are plenty of disturbing war and war-adjacent films out there, but these ten are the ones that stuck. Why You Should Trust Me: I have been writing on film for over a decade, often with a focus on niche and international offerings. Here at MovieWeb, I have curated lists for disturbing, challenging cinema to help push recognition of overlooked titles. Honorable Mentions Five films had me going back and forth on whether to include them in the main list. I ultimately decided they were better placed here: Grave of the Fireflies (1988): The obvious omission, and only because I decided to keep the list live-action. Isao Takahata's animated account of two children starving to death in the last months of the Pacific War is utterly devastating, and still deserves the recommendation. The Ascent (1977): Larisa Shepitko's final feature is a Belarusian partisan story shot in a whiteout that grows more oppressive the longer you sit with the picture. The interrogation sequence at the center is one of the most quietly terrifying stretches you will find. Son of Saul (2015): László Nemes locks the camera to the back of a Sonderkommando prisoner's head and keeps the atrocity in soft focus at the edge of the frame. A phenomenal experiment that sends your eyes wandering to the corners out of morbid curiosity, and the approach makes the film niche but well worth a watch if the subject interests you. City of Life and Death (2009): Lu Chuan's black-and-white account of the Nanjing Massacre, told through several characters including a Japanese soldier and a child. The closing sequence, a victory ritual staged over the ruins, is one of the strangest and most disquieting endings in modern war cinema. Caterpillar (2010): Set during the Second Sino-Japanese War, a soldier who has lost his limbs and can no longer function is paraded home as a war hero. Once the glory fades and everyone moves on, his wife is left to care for him alone. Much like Johnny Got His Gun , Koji Wakamatsu's film turns anti-war sentiment into a deeply uncomfortable portrait of what a body brings back from the front. 'The Grey Zone' (2001) There Is No Exit Lions Gate Films IMDb: 7.0/10 | Letterboxd: 3.6/5 The Grey Zone dramatizes the Sonderkommando uprising at Auschwitz in October 1944. These were the Jewish prisoners forced to shepherd new arrivals into the gas chambers, empty them, and burn the bodies. Their story takes a turn when a teenage girl is found alive under a pile of corpses, and the men have to decide what to do with her while a rebellion is already in motion. The film flopped and drew mixed reviews, and I will admit a few of the choices did not land for me; casting familiar American actors like David Arquette, Steve Buscemi, and Harvey Keitel with no accents pulled me out of the story more than once. Where director Tim Blake Nelson thrives, though, is in building a scenario with absolutely no redemptive exit, which turns every conversation into men weighing their own morality against another hour of survival . Over time, The Grey Zone has built a deserved reputation as among the toughest American features of its decade. 'Red Angel' (1966) Addiction, Bodies, and the Void Daiei Film IMDb: 7.8/10 | Letterboxd: 3.9/5 Red Angel follows Nurse Sakura Nishi through the Japanese campaign in China in 1939, from a rear-line hospital to a forward surgical unit where amputation is essentially the only available treatment. Yasuzo Masumura, one of the godfathers of the Japanese New Wave , shoots the operating theater as an assembly line of unending suffering. Nishi's only reprieve is a relationship with a morphine-addicted surgeon. If you have never seen a Masumura movie, this one is a solid place to start. Much of his work lands in more disturbing territory, but always with a focus on character study and social commentary. Red Angel is among his most visually stunning pictures, and the introduction of eroticism adds a whole extra layer of desperation: no other war film I have seen conflates desire and dismemberment this calmly . The closing shot is tragic and iconic. This one is also more accessible than most of the list, with beauty and horror swirling around the screen at a dreamlike pace. 'Kanal' (1957) Doom Announced in the First Minute KADR IMDb: 7.9/10 | Letterboxd: 4.1/5 Kanal picks up a company of Polish Home Army fighters in the collapsing final days of the 1944 Warsaw Uprising, as they descend into the city's sewer system hoping to reach the city center. In the dark, unable to read any directions, the fighters find themselves trapped in a never-ending maze, fearful of the war above and the unknown in the murky below. Andrzej Wajda's film is a vastly underrated war picture that seldom gets the discussion it deserves. The story opens on a grim note, with a narrator telling you flatly that the men you are looking at are living their final hours. The first half plays out above ground and is punishing enough on its own, but the latter half traces desperate men and women through the sewers, stripped of whatever honor they thought they had, unable to reach the surface and slowly dying in the dark . Claustrophobic, horrific, tragic, and an often overlooked war classic. 'Men Behind the Sun' (1988) The Horrors of Unit 731 Grand Essex Enterprises IMDb: 6.1/10 | Letterboxd: 3.1/5 Men Behind the Sun dramatizes the operations of Unit 731, the Imperial Japanese Army's biological warfare division in occupied Manchuria. The story is nominally told through a group of teenage cadets assigned to the facility, but the overwhelming focus is on staging the tortures themselves. Real experiments are recreated here, including subjects taken through the stages of frostbite, pressure chamber deaths, and live vivisection. I was hesitant to include this one, because I do not consider Men Behind the Sun a "good" movie, but if the measure is disturbing, then leaving off this highly controversial title would be a serious omission . Does the film have any validity as artistic expression? Some, and mostly in how precisely it documents what was actually done. Director Mou Tun-Fei made this out of open anger at the Imperial Japanese Army, and that anger comes through in the rawest, most graphic way possible. Even so, I would advise most people to skip this one, since the production also used questionable methods to chase authenticity, and the results are stomach-churning. 'Threads' (1984) Nuclear War as a Government Report IMDb: 8.0/10 | Letterboxd: 4.2/5 Threads opens as a modest kitchen-sink drama about a young couple in Sheffield dealing with an unplanned pregnancy, before a NATO and Warsaw Pact escalation turns the film into something else entirely: a portrait of nuclear fallout. Director Mick Jackson and writer Barry Hines consulted scientists and civil defense planners at length to give an authentic account of such a disaster, working through the initial blast, the firestorm, radiation sickness, the collapse of medical infrastructure, nuclear winter, and then years forward into a barely literate agrarian remnant. This one hits hard, and it is wild to think the BBC broadcast the whole thing to the public, feeding straight into Cold War paranoia to instill a deeper sense of fear in viewers. Nothing before or since has modeled the end of a society with such chilling accuracy, and the closing freeze-frame is among the most despairing images ever put on television. As a made-for-TV movie , the budget was never going to be there, but the roughness works in the film's favor and makes the whole thing feel more authentic as ordinary citizens suffer through a nuclear nightmare and societal collapse. 'Fires on the Plain' (1959) Starvation Past the Last Taboo Daiei Film IMDb: 7.9/10 | Letterboxd: 4.1/5 Fires on the Plain drops Private Tamura into the disintegration of the Japanese army on Leyte in late 1944. Tubercular and turned away by both his unit and the field hospital, he is essentially directed to go off somewhere and die. Kon Ichikawa follows Tamura across the ravaged island, with the remains of the army wandering in feral groups and fighting off starvation. Eventually the survivors start passing around what they call "monkey meat," the euphemism they have settled on for cannibalism, and the last of their humanity goes with it. Director Kon Ichikawa took the great taboo subject of the Pacific War and filmed it without a single note of moralizing, making for one of the bleakest films ever to come out of a major Japanese studio. There are no redeeming stories here, just a slow decline and desperate men bargaining or fighting over whatever scraps they have left. Reviews were split on release, mostly over the violence and the lack of uplift, but the film is now considered a classic of the war genre. 'Johnny Got His Gun' (1971) A Nightmare With No Waking Up Cinemation Industries IMDb: 7.8/10 | Letterboxd: 4.0/5 Johnny Got His Gun traps you inside Joe Bonham, an American soldier who takes an artillery shell in the last days of World War I and comes out of it without arms, legs, or a face. He is deaf, blind, mute, and, to the astonishment of the doctors keeping him alive, conscious. Color memories and fantasies break up a stark black-and-white hospital present, where Joe lies locked inside the horror of his own head. The film is also based on one of the most disturbing books ever written , and Dalton Trumbo adapted his own 1938 novel and directed the picture himself to make sure his anti-war tale of isolation kept the essence of the writing. No war film has ever built a more airtight case against the entire enterprise, and the closing lines are haunting; they will stick with you for a long time. Metallica later cut footage into the "One" video and eventually bought the rights outright, which is how a lot of people my age found the film in the first place. 'The Captain' (2018) What a Uniform Gives You IMDb: 7.3/10 | Letterboxd: 3.7/5 The Captain follows Willi Herold, a 19-year-old Wehrmacht private hunted through the countryside by his own side for desertion in April 1945. He finds an officer's uniform in an abandoned staff car and puts it on to stay warm. Mistaken for a commissioned officer, he sinks into fascist fantasies as he talks his way into command of a camp that executes deserters. Based on a true story . Robert Schwentke's crisp black-and-white feature opens on a strangely comic note, and that tone holds as a scared kid bluffs his way out of one tight spot after another; you almost want to cheer him on. Those early laughs turn out to be the trap, because Herold grows into the rank he stole, and before long he is presiding over executions and savoring every ounce of authority that comes with it . With so much else here leaning relentlessly bleak, this is easily the lightest watch on the list, and a thought-provoking one on how quickly ordinary people fall in line. 'The Painted Bird' (2019) Unending Suffering Bioscop IMDb: 7.3/10 | Letterboxd: 3.6/5 The Painted Bird follows an unnamed Jewish boy across the Eastern European countryside during World War II, passed between the households of strangers after his aunt dies. Václav Marhoul spent eleven years getting the Jerzy Kosinski novel to screen, shot in 35mm black-and-white and using an invented Interslavic dialect, so no single nation could be blamed. The film runs nearly three hours and is broken into chapters named after the people the boy encounters along the way. The walkouts at the Venice premiere are part of the film's reputation, and I can understand why people were rattled by the content. There is an abundance of uncomfortable imagery to contend with, from the abuse of the young boy as he wanders between broken homes, to shocking moments of violence toward others and animals. Whether this is a masterpiece or an endurance test is a fair argument to have, but there is no denying this is one of the most disturbing war movies of the 21st century. http://www.bignewsnetwork.com/news/27922.text: Big News Network.com Hungary faces "most critical 5 days" as drought threatens nuclear plant shutdown BUDAPEST, Aug. 2 (Xinhua) -- Hungary is entering its "most critical 5 days" as dropping water levels on the Danube River threaten the complete shutdown of the Paks nuclear power plant amid an extreme heatwave, Hungary's Prime Minister Peter Magyar said on Sunday, warning that the plant could be shut down for more than a month. Speaking to local commercial television channel RTL, Magyar said the last remaining operating turbine at the 2,000 MW facility will likely be shut down late Sunday or on Monday. A complete halt to power generation at Paks, which accounts for nearly half of Hungary's domestic electricity generation,would mark the first full closure in the plant's 44-year history. Magyar explained earlier on social media that strict nuclear safety regulations mandate the shutdown because of record-low river levels needed for cooling water. He reassured the public that nuclear safety remains fully guaranteed, with around 50 water management experts assisting plant personnel to maintain cooling operations. The unprecedented energy crisis comes as Hungary braces for temperatures reaching 40 degrees Celsius or higher over these "most critical five days," placing immense strain on the national grid. The Hungarian government has introduced emergency measures to maintain grid stability. Under a decree that took effect on Saturday, mandatory consumption cutbacks can be enforced on major industrial consumers if necessary. However, Magyar noted that voluntary conservation efforts by businesses and the public have so far helped avoid enforced rationing. Major companies, including MOL, Audi, and Gedeon Richter, have pledged significant demand reductions. Nearly 300 companies have already pledged voluntary reductions for Monday, along with numerous state-owned firms, most local councils, civil society groups and churches, he said. To save power, decorative lighting on Budapest's iconic landmarks, including the Hungarian Parliament, Buda Castle, and the Chain Bridge, was turned off on Sunday evening. Additional measures include halting most rail freight transport between 5:00 p.m. and 10:00 p.m. starting Monday, bringing reserve power units on standby, and maximizing electricity imports. "If Hungary can get through these most critical five days, temperatures are expected to drop by 5 to 7 degrees Celsius," Magyar said, adding that household restrictions remain an absolute last resort to maintain system stability. Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEK View image in fullscreen Sam Pang accepts the Gold Logie award for most popular personality on Australian television at the Logie awards on Sunday night. Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEK Logie awards Logies 2026: Sam Pang wins gold and Sam Neill wins posthumous best actor at Australia’s TV awards Neill won for his performance in legal thriller The Twelve: Cape Rock Killer, at a ceremony dominated by wins for the ABC Logies 2026 ceremony: the best moments and red carpet looks – in pictures Sian Cain Sun 16 Aug 2026 10.01 EDT Last modified on Sun 16 Aug 2026 10.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Sam Neill has won a posthumous best actor award at Australia’s biggest television awards, the Logies, with comedian Sam Pang taking home the night’s top honour, the Gold Logie award for most popular personality. Neill, who died in July , won his posthumous Logie for best lead actor in a drama, for his performance in legal thriller The Twelve: Cape Rock Killer. His close friend, the actor Heather Mitchell, accepted the award on his behalf. Logies 2026 ceremony: the best moments and red carpet looks – in pictures Read more “I’m so sorry I’m not Sam,” she said. “I know how much it would mean to him. This is an indication of his connection with his audience.” Mitchell said The Twelve, which Neill starred in for three seasons, “meant a great deal” to him. “He really relished the character of Brett Colby. He talked about it a lot, and he thought [Colby] was a very clever man, and also a sort of 007 kind of person. And that was Sam as well,” she said. View image in fullscreen Heather Mitchell pays tribute to Sam Neill onstage at the Logies. Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEK Pang, who is a panellist on quiz show Have You Been Paying Attention? and hosts The Front Bar and Sam Pang Tonight, joked: “I’ve got lots of people to thank tonight and I’ll probably forget some names. If I do forget you, I’m sorry, but maybe also have a think about how much you did.” The 52-year-old congratulated his fellow nominees for the top award: A Current Affair host Ally Langdon, comedian Julia Morris, ABC presenter Lisa Millar, Masterchef judge Poh Ling Yeow, presenter Robert Irwin and Tipping Point Australia host Todd Woodbridge. Pang was presented the award by Magda Szubanski, who made a surprise appearance after recently announcing she was in remission after being treated for cancer . View image in fullscreen Magda Szubanski in character as her Kath & Kim role Sharon Strzelecki with Robert Irwin onstage. Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEK The Logies have historically been unusual awards, with a mix of popularly voted awards – which celebrities have always actively campaigned to win – and peer-voted awards. Last year, the voting system was overhauled so that the “best” categories – formerly called “most outstanding” – are now determined by a combined score: 50% of which is peer assessment and audience data supplied by the broadcasters, and 50% of which is by popular vote. The Gold Logie and the “most popular” award categories remain determined entirely by popular vote. Irwin, who hosted this year’s ceremony, won his first Logie, taking home the Bert Newton award for most popular presenter for his role on I’m A Celebrity… Get Me Out Of Here, which was recently cancelled by Network 10. Irwin thanked his family, who he said were watching remotely from a crocodile research expedition in north Queensland, as well as Australia Zoo, where he has lived since childhood. “My heart beats for Australia Zoo,” he said. “I bleed khaki … This is for my Australia Zoo family – 500 back at home, who back me, who work towards a mission that my dad started.” Brooke Satchwell won best lead actress in a drama for her role in Stan series Dear Life , while Claudia Karvan won best supporting actress in a drama for her role as the mother of a trans child in SBS show Homebodies . Karvan used her speech to pay tribute to trans children and their parents, saying: “May their voices always be heard.” Simon Baker won best supporting actor for his performance in The Narrow Road to the Deep North – his second Logie win after his first in 1993, which was “somewhere in the shed”, he said. He thanked director Justin Kurzel and his castmates, joking: “There’s not a bad performance in this thing and I can say that because I have just won an award.” View image in fullscreen Lila McGuire accepts the Graham Kennedy award for most popular new talent for her role in Goolagong. Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEK The ABC had a strong night, winning eight Logies. Goolagong , the ABC drama about the two-time Wimbledon winner Evonne Goolagong Cawley, won best miniseries, while the show’s star, Whadjuk and Ballardong Noongar actor Lila McGuire, won the Graham Kennedy award for most popular new talent. ABC comedy Dog Park won two awards: best actress in a comedy for Celia Pacquola and best scripted comedy program. Muster Dogs took best structured reality program, The Assembly won best factual program, Australian Story won best current affairs program and Play School won best children’s program. RFDS won best drama program for the second time, beating the likes of Heartbreak High and Mystery Road: Origin. In an unexpected turn, Bruce McAvaney lost the inaugural Bruce McAvaney award for most popular sports presenter to the former tennis player Jelena Dokic, who won for her work presenting at the Australian Open, Melbourne Cup, Wimbledon, Roland Garros, US Open and Cross Court. A Current Affair presenter Ally Langdon won the Ray Martin award for most popular news or public affairs presenter, for the second year in the row. Karl Stefanovic, who was nominated for the category for his role on Today, was not present, having told the Daily Telegraph that attending would be a “tad awkward” after being dumped from his $2.8m contract at Nine for embracing far-right activist Tommy Robinson on his podcast. Stefanovic was a popular, recurring topic onstage, with Irwin joking that an empty chair had been left for him “on the far right”. View image in fullscreen Deborah Mailman accepts the Logie Hall of Fame award. Photograph: James Gourley/Getty Images for TV WEEK Actor Deborah Mailman became the first ever Indigenous Australian nominated into the Logies Hall of Fame. Mailman, who has won six Logies in her career, paid tribute to her parents, who “met my dream with nothing but love and encouragement” when she was a would-be actor growing up in Mt Isa. “Every time I made that 24 and half hour bus trip back to Mt Isa from Brisbane, my mum and dad were always there waiting for me, so this is for them,” she said in an emotional speech. In addition to Mailman, broadcaster and producer Andrew Denton and the show A Country Practice were also inducted into the Logies Hall of Fame.
